shelves.title: Albumin in sepsis & critical illness Deposit #1 · Oct 23, 2026
shelves.question: Does giving albumin change survival — and what do the level, and its fall, tell you?
shelves.balance: Giving albumin as a fluid does not change overall survival (SAFE; ALBIOS), with a hypothesis-generating hint in severe sepsis. The level and its trajectory are strong prognostic signals — persistently low or falling is worse, rising is better — but nearly all trajectory evidence is retrospective, and this shelf grades it Low, honestly. The resuscitation trials match the measurement lesson: albumin as a drug shows no overall mortality advantage; albumin as a measurement predicts by its trajectory, not its door value.

cards.headline: SAFE: albumin vs saline in the ICU
cards.summary: 28-day deaths 726 vs 729 ; RR 0.99 (0.91–1.09) — 6,997 ICU patients in the landmark randomized trial.
cards.type: Multicenter, randomized, double-blind trial, N Engl J Med 2004
cards.people: 6,997 ICU patients (3,497 albumin, 3,500 saline)
cards.result: Deaths at 28 days: 726 vs 729 ; relative risk of death 0.99 (0.91–1.09)
cards.watchOut: General ICU mix, not a sepsis-only trial
cards.source: Finfer et al., N Engl J Med 2004; PMID 15163774
cards.search: safe albumin saline icu resuscitation randomized trial finfer new england journal 2004 fluid 28-day death relative risk pmid 15163774 sepsis

cards.headline: SAFE severe sepsis subgroup
cards.summary: Adjusted OR 0.71 (0.52–0.97) ; unadjusted RR 0.87 (0.74–1.02) — 1,218 patients with severe sepsis inside SAFE.
cards.type: Pre-defined subgroup analysis of the SAFE randomized trial, Intensive Care Med 2011
cards.people: 1,218 patients with severe sepsis (603 albumin, 615 saline)
cards.result: Adjusted odds ratio for death 0.71 (0.52–0.97) in the 919 with complete baseline data; unadjusted relative risk 0.87 (0.74–1.02)
cards.watchOut: The unadjusted result includes no effect; a subgroup of a larger trial — hypothesis-generating
cards.source: SAFE Study Investigators, Intensive Care Med 2011; PMID 20924555
cards.search: safe severe sepsis subgroup albumin saline adjusted odds ratio intensive care medicine 2011 pmid 20924555 hypothesis generating organ function

cards.headline: ALBIOS: albumin replacement in severe sepsis
cards.summary: 28-day death 31.8% vs 32.0% (RR 1.00) ; 90-day 41.1% vs 43.6% (RR 0.94) — 1,818 patients, open-label RCT.
cards.type: Multicenter, open-label randomized trial, 100 ICUs, N Engl J Med 2014
cards.people: 1,818 patients with severe sepsis
cards.watchOut: Open-label: clinicians knew who received albumin
cards.source: Caironi et al., N Engl J Med 2014; PMID 24635772
cards.search: albios albumin replacement severe sepsis caironi randomized trial open label new england journal 2014 crystalloid 90-day pmid 24635772

cards.headline: Vincent 2003: low albumin and outcome in acute illness
cards.summary: Per 10 g/L fall in albumin: mortality odds +137% , morbidity +89% , ICU stay +28% , hospital stay +71% — 90 cohorts, 291,433 patients.
cards.type: Meta-analysis of cohort studies, Ann Surg 2003
cards.people: 90 cohort studies, 291,433 patients
cards.result: Each 10 g/L fall: mortality odds +137% , morbidity +89% , ICU stay +28% , hospital stay +71% , resource use +66%
cards.watchOut: Associations from adjusted observational studies; the albumin trials were small
cards.source: Vincent et al., Ann Surg 2003; PMID 12616115
cards.search: vincent 2003 low albumin outcome acute illness meta-analysis hypoalbuminemia mortality odds morbidity annals of surgery pmid 12616115 cohorts

cards.headline: He 2026: albumin trajectories in sepsis (MIMIC-IV)
cards.summary: 28-day mortality HR 0.72 (high trajectory) and 0.77 (moderate) vs persistently low — 1,714 sepsis patients.
cards.type: Retrospective cohort, MIMIC-IV, BMC Infect Dis 2026
cards.people: 1,714 sepsis patients: persistently low 477, moderate 749, high 488
cards.result: 28-day mortality vs persistently low: HR 0.72 (0.56–0.93) high, 0.77 (0.61–0.96) moderate; 90-day: 0.74 and 0.72
cards.watchOut: Only patients alive on day 5 were included; 51.8% received albumin therapy
cards.source: He et al., BMC Infect Dis 2026; PMID 42469645
cards.search: he 2026 albumin trajectories sepsis mimic-iv retrospective persistently low hazard ratio bmc infectious diseases pmid 42469645 days 1 3 5

cards.headline: Gao 2026: trajectories after sepsis kidney injury
cards.summary: Steady 2.0 vs 3.0 g/dL: mortality HR 1.89–2.00 across 30–365 days — 1,914 patients after sepsis-associated kidney injury.
cards.type: Retrospective cohort, MIMIC-IV, group-based trajectory modeling, Front Med 2026
cards.people: 1,914 patients in five trajectory groups
cards.watchOut: Patients who died within 8 days of kidney injury were excluded
cards.source: Gao et al., Front Med 2026; PMID 42292189
cards.search: gao 2026 albumin trajectories sepsis-associated acute kidney injury mimic-iv steady mortality hazard ratio frontiers medicine pmid 42292189

cards.headline: Tie 2024: trajectories in ICU sepsis (West China)
cards.summary: 28-day mortality 60.0% in the stable-low group vs 38.3% in the rising group; adjusted HR 0.51 — 1,950 patients.
cards.type: Retrospective cohort, group-based trajectory modeling, Front Nutr 2024
cards.people: 1,950 ICU sepsis patients, West China Hospital, 2015–2022; four trajectories
cards.result: 28-day mortality: stable low 60.0% , rising 38.3% , stable mid 45.4% , stable high 41.8% ; adjusted HR vs stable low: rising 0.51 (0.37–0.69)
cards.watchOut: Single-center retrospective study; missing data filled by multiple imputation
cards.source: Tie et al., Front Nutr 2024; PMID 39101009
cards.search: tie 2024 albumin trajectories icu sepsis west china hospital stable low rising mortality frontiers nutrition pmid 39101009

cards.headline: Kendall 2019: albumin trend and death in sepsis
cards.summary: Survival probability fell 70.6% with a strong negative albumin trend — retrospective; sample size not in the abstract.
cards.type: Retrospective correlational study of medical records, Biol Res Nurs 2019
cards.people: ICU patients with a primary sepsis diagnosis, one Midwestern regional medical center (n not in abstract)
cards.result: Survival probability fell 70.6% with a strong negative trend; 63.4% when admission albumin ≤2.45 g/dL; 76.4% when the lowest albumin ≤1.45 g/dL
cards.watchOut: Retrospective single-center record review; sample size not stated
cards.source: Kendall et al., Biol Res Nurs 2019; PMID 30722677
cards.search: kendall 2019 albumin trend death sepsis retrospective survival probability negative trend biological research nursing pmid 30722677

cards.headline: McCluskey 1996: serial albumin vs APACHE II
cards.summary: Albumin measured after 24 hours classified outcome as accurately as admission APACHE II — 348 ICU patients.
cards.people: 348 consecutive adult ICU patients over one year
cards.result: Admission albumin was lower in non-survivors and fell faster (P<0.001); albumin after 24 hours classified outcome as accurately as admission APACHE II; combining the two did not improve accuracy
cards.watchOut: Retrospective, single ICU, albumin followed for only 72 hours
cards.source: McCluskey et al., Anaesthesia 1996; PMID 8795312
cards.search: mccluskey 1996 serial albumin apache ii icu outcome 72 hours retrospective anaesthesia pmid 8795312

cards.headline: Yap 2002: albumin in a general ICU
cards.summary: Albumin fell in both groups, separated survivors poorly, and added no gain over APACHE II — 1,003 ICU patients.
cards.people: 1,003 ICU patients over 18 months
cards.result: Albumin fell after admission in both survivors and non-survivors; non-survivors had lower albumin, but it separated the groups poorly (low sensitivity and specificity); no gain over APACHE II
cards.watchOut: Retrospective single-ICU study; albumin followed for 72 hours only
cards.source: Yap et al., Anaesth Intensive Care 2002; PMID 12002929
cards.search: yap 2002 albumin mortality general icu retrospective survivors discrimination apache ii anaesthesia intensive care pmid 12002929

cards.headline: Ghimire 2023: serial albumin days 1, 3, 5
cards.summary: Day 5 albumin 3.31 vs 2.92 g/dL , survivors vs non-survivors ( P=.003 ) — 78 ICU patients, prospective.
cards.type: Prospective observational study, one tertiary hospital, Medicine 2023
cards.people: 78 ICU patients (59 survivors, 19 non-survivors)
cards.result: Albumin, survivors vs non-survivors: day 1 3.42 vs 3.30 (P=.234); day 3 3.31 vs 3.02 (P=.001); day 5 3.31 vs 2.92 g/dL (P=.003)
cards.watchOut: Small single-center study with only 19 deaths
cards.source: Ghimire et al., Medicine 2023; PMID 37960756
cards.search: ghimire 2023 serial albumin days 1 3 5 icu prospective survivors non-survivors medicine baltimore pmid 37960756

cards.headline: John 2025: serial lactate and albumin in sepsis
cards.summary: Day 5 albumin 3.43 vs 3.05 g/dL , recovered vs died ( P=0.01 ) — 95 ICU sepsis patients, prospective.
cards.type: Prospective cohort, one medical ICU (India), J Clin Diagn Res 2025
cards.people: 95 ICU sepsis patients: 75 recovered, 20 died
cards.result: Albumin, recovered vs died: day 1 2.82 vs 2.87 (P=0.72); day 3 3.05 vs 2.96 (P=0.51); day 5 3.43 vs 3.05 g/dL (P=0.01)
cards.watchOut: Single center with 20 deaths
cards.source: John et al., J Clin Diagn Res 2025;19(6):OC01-OC05
cards.search: john 2025 serial lactate albumin sepsis prospective days 1 3 5 recovered died journal clinical diagnostic research india

cards.headline: Saravanakumar 2020: serial albumin in ventilated sepsis
cards.summary: Day 5 albumin 2.72 vs 2.32 g/dL , survivors vs non-survivors, all P<0.001 — 70 ventilated sepsis patients.
cards.type: Observational study, one medical college hospital (India), J Med Sci Clin Res 2020
cards.people: 70 sepsis patients on mechanical ventilation: 43 survivors, 27 non-survivors
cards.result: Albumin, survivors vs non-survivors: day 1 3.72 vs 3.11 ; day 3 3.17 vs 2.65 ; day 5 2.72 vs 2.32 g/dL ; all P<0.001. Both groups fell
cards.watchOut: Patients who died within 5 days were excluded, so non-survivors are late deaths
cards.source: Saravanakumar et al., J Med Sci Clin Res 2020;8(11):526-531

cards.headline: Pandey 2016: serial albumin after head injury
cards.summary: Day 10 albumin 3.44 vs 2.63 g/dL , survivors vs non-survivors — 200 traumatic brain injury patients.
cards.type: Prospective case-control study, Asian J Med Sci 2016
cards.people: 200 traumatic brain injury patients (177 survivors, 23 non-survivors) and 50 healthy controls
cards.result: Albumin, survivors vs non-survivors: day 1 3.81 vs 3.35 ; day 5 3.49 vs 2.74 ; day 10 3.44 vs 2.63 g/dL
cards.watchOut: A head-injury population, not sepsis, with only 23 deaths
cards.source: Pandey et al., Asian J Med Sci 2016;7(4):31-38

cards.headline: Kokkoris 2024: lab trends in critical COVID-19
cards.summary: Admission albumin 3.3 vs 3.0 g/dL , survivors vs non-survivors ( P=0.001 ), declining in parallel — 733 ICU patients.
cards.type: Cohort study of routine laboratory values, Biomed Rep 2024
cards.people: 733 ICU patients with COVID-19 (380 survivors, 353 non-survivors)
cards.result: Admission albumin 3.3 vs 3.0 g/dL (P=0.001); both groups declined in parallel; albumin lower in non-survivors overall (P=0.001)
cards.watchOut: A COVID-19 cohort, not general sepsis; between-group differences are small
cards.source: Kokkoris et al., Biomed Rep 2024; PMID 38124763
cards.search: kokkoris 2024 laboratory trends critical covid-19 albumin admission decline cohort biomedical reports pmid 38124763

cards.headline: Rhee 2022: albumin change on kidney replacement therapy
cards.summary: Increasing vs persistently low HR 0.481 ; decreasing vs persistently high HR 1.911 — 793 patients on CRRT.
cards.type: Single-center retrospective cohort, J Intensive Care 2022
cards.people: 793 patients with acute kidney injury on CRRT ≥72 hours
cards.result: In-hospital mortality: increasing vs persistently low HR 0.481 (0.340–0.680) ; decreasing vs persistently high HR 1.911 (1.394–2.620)
cards.watchOut: Albumin grouped by only two timepoints (CRRT start and end) at a 3.0 g/dL cutoff
cards.source: Rhee et al., J Intensive Care 2022; PMID 35672868

cards.headline: Turcato 2026: fluids, norepinephrine and the albumin fall
cards.summary: Each 1% rise in fluid balance → albumin −0.029 g/dL ; early norepinephrine flattened the fall ( −0.043 → −0.008 ); albumin mediated 18.6% of the fluid–mortality link — 389 patients.
cards.type: Prospective longitudinal cohort, intermediate care unit, J Clin Med 2026
cards.people: 389 patients with community-acquired sepsis
cards.result: Each 1% rise in cumulative fluid balance → albumin −0.029 g/dL (P<0.001); albumin slope −0.043 before norepinephrine, −0.008 after; albumin mediated 18.6% of the fluid-to-mortality association
cards.watchOut: The norepinephrine finding is an association; the authors say randomized evidence is needed
cards.source: Turcato et al., J Clin Med 2026; PMID 42122937
cards.search: turcato 2026 fluids norepinephrine albumin fall sepsis fluid balance prospective mediated mortality journal clinical medicine pmid 42122937

cards.headline: Turcato 2026: albumin leak and recovery indices
cards.summary: Leak index +0.34%/h on day 1 → −0.07%/h by day 5; the two indices inversely correlated ( ρ=−0.54 ) — same 389 patients.
cards.type: Prospective longitudinal cohort (same 389-patient population as Card 17), J Clin Med 2026
cards.people: 389 sepsis patients; 1,897 observations over up to five reassessments
cards.result: Leak index peaked day 1 at +0.34%/h , −0.07%/h by day 5; indices inversely correlated ( ρ=−0.54 , P<0.001); “dissociation” state rose 2.3% → 22.6% by day 5
cards.watchOut: The indices are derived from routine laboratory values, not measured directly
cards.source: Turcato et al., J Clin Med 2026; PMID 41899349
cards.search: turcato 2026 albumin leak index recovery indices sepsis prospective dissociation journal clinical medicine pmid 41899349

cards.headline: Lou 2026: biomarker trajectories in burn sepsis
cards.summary: 21-day mortality 17.92% ; albumin AUC 0.729 at day 7; only the Burn Index stayed independently associated — 943 patients.
cards.people: 943 adult burn patients with sepsis
cards.result: 21-day mortality 17.92% ; trajectories differed for 11 biomarkers; albumin AUC 0.729 at day 7; only Burn Index independently associated (HR 1.066)
cards.watchOut: Shares most authors with Card 20, so the two cohorts probably overlap

cards.headline: Xu 2026: biomarker phenotypes in burn sepsis
cards.summary: High-risk phenotype mortality 15.7% vs 8.8% ; albumin C-index 0.604 — 712 burn sepsis patients.
cards.type: Retrospective single-center cohort with growth mixture modeling, burn ICU, Front Cell Infect Microbiol 2026
cards.people: 712 adult burn patients with sepsis
cards.result: High-risk phenotype (n=267) mortality 15.7% vs low-risk (n=445) 8.8% (P=0.005); baseline albumin C-index 0.604 ; no biomarker stayed independent in multivariable analysis
cards.watchOut: Source inconsistency: the paper prints 17.9% mortality with 81 deaths in 712 patients (11.4%); shares most authors with Card 19, so cohorts probably overlap

cards.headline: Baig 2022: early albumin in COVID-19 pneumonia
cards.summary: Day 4 albumin 3.83 vs 2.96 g/dL , discharged vs died — 76 COVID-19 pneumonia ICU patients.
cards.type: Retrospective cohort, two hospitals in Lahore, Pak J Med Sci 2022
cards.people: 76 COVID-19 pneumonia ICU patients who stayed at least 4 days; 38 died
cards.result: Day 4 albumin 3.83 vs 2.96 g/dL , discharged vs died; strong negative correlation between albumin fall and deaths reported
cards.watchOut: Only patients who stayed 4 or more days were included, so early deaths are missing
cards.source: Baig et al., Pak J Med Sci 2022; PMID 35480533

cards.headline: Takegawa 2019: nutrition markers in prolonged sepsis
cards.summary: Falls in albumin, protein, cholesterol and cholinesterase each associated with death ( P<.05 ); no effect sizes in the abstract — 136 patients.
cards.type: Retrospective observational study, time-dependent Cox regression, J Crit Care 2019
cards.people: 136 septic ICU patients with stays longer than 7 days
cards.result: Falls in albumin, total protein, total cholesterol and cholinesterase each associated with risk of death ( P<.05 ); the abstract gives no hazard ratios
cards.watchOut: Only patients who stayed more than 7 days were included, so early deaths are excluded by design
cards.source: Takegawa et al., J Crit Care 2019; PMID 30825787
cards.search: takegawa 2019 nutrition nutritional markers prolonged sepsis albumin protein cholesterol cholinesterase retrospective journal critical care pmid 30825787

cards.headline: In septic shock, albumin escaped from the blood vessels more than three times as fast.
cards.summary: Transcapillary escape rate ~5%/h normally — over 10× the rates of synthesis and catabolism; up >300% in septic shock, +100% after cardiac surgery, 2× normal in cachectic cancer.
cards.type: Physiological study measuring the transcapillary escape rate of albumin
cards.people: Patients with septic shock or undergoing cardiac surgery, cachectic cancer patients, and healthy individuals; the published abstract does not give group sizes
cards.result: The transcapillary escape rate of albumin was normally about 5% per hour — more than 10 times the rates of synthesis and catabolism. It rose by more than 300% in patients with septic shock, increased by an average of 100% within 7 hours of cardiac surgery, and was twice that of healthy individuals in cachectic cancer patients
cards.watchOut: A 1985 physiological study; the abstract does not report group sizes. It establishes a mechanism for falling albumin, not evidence that giving albumin improves outcomes
cards.source: Fleck A, Raines G, Hawker F, Trotter J, Wallace PI, Ledingham IM, Calman KC. Increased vascular permeability: a major cause of hypoalbuminaemia in disease and injury. Lancet 1985;1(8432):781–784. DOI 10.1016/S0140-6736(85)91447-3. PMID 2858667
cards.search: fleck 1985 albumin transcapillary escape rate vascular permeability hypoalbuminaemia lancet septic shock cardiac surgery cachectic cancer synthesis catabolism pmid 2858667

shelves.title: Low phosphate, breathing muscles and weaning Deposit #4 · Oct 23, 2026
shelves.question: What does low phosphate do to breathing muscles, ventilator weaning, and survival?
shelves.balance: Low phosphate travels with weak breathing muscles and harder ventilator weaning — the 1988 classic showed strength returning as phosphate was repleted, but nothing here is randomized, and the weaning data rest on handfuls of events.

cards.headline: Hypophosphatemia and respiratory muscle weakness
cards.summary: Weakness in 16/23 low-phosphate patients vs 0/11 controls (p<0.001); inspiratory pressure −37 → −49 cm H₂O after repletion (p<0.003).
cards.type: Prospective observational study with repletion measurements, Am J Med 1988
cards.people: 23 low-phosphate inpatients vs 11 controls
cards.result: Respiratory muscle weakness in 16/23 vs 0/11 (p<0.001); inspiratory pressure −37 → −49 cm H₂O after repletion (p<0.003)
cards.watchOut: Small and observational — strength was measured as phosphate was repleted, not in a randomized comparison
cards.source: Gravelyn et al., Am J Med 1988
cards.search: gravelyn 1988 hypophosphatemia phosphate respiratory muscle weakness inspiratory pressure repletion american journal medicine low phosphate inpatients

cards.headline: Phosphate and ventilator weaning in a respiratory ICU
cards.summary: Weaning failure 8/35 with day-2 phosphate ≤2.5 mg/dL vs 0/19 above (p=0.040); day-2 phosphate 1.69 vs 2.23 mg/dL — 54 ventilated adults, Egypt.
cards.type: Prospective cohort, Egypt J Chest Dis Tuberc 2026
cards.people: 54 ventilated adults (Egypt)
cards.result: Weaning failure 8/35 with day-2 phosphate ≤2.5 mg/dL vs 0/19 above (p=0.040); day-2 phosphate 1.69 vs 2.23 mg/dL
cards.watchOut: Only 8 weaning failures in total — the comparison rests on a handful of events
cards.source: Youseif et al., Egypt J Chest Dis Tuberc 2026
cards.search: youseif 2026 phosphate ventilator weaning respiratory icu egypt prospective cohort weaning failure day-2 egyptian journal chest diseases tuberculosis

cards.headline: Hypophosphatemia and pediatric ventilation duration
cards.summary: Ventilation 7.7 vs 4.1 days (p=0.02); PICU stay 9.7 vs 5.0 days (p=0.001) — 118 PICU children, Türkiye.
cards.people: 118 PICU children (Türkiye)
cards.result: Ventilation 7.7 vs 4.1 days (p=0.02); PICU stay 9.7 vs 5.0 days (p=0.001)
cards.watchOut: Retrospective — low phosphate may mark sicker children rather than cause the longer ventilation
cards.source: Kılıç et al., J Crit Care 2012
cards.search: kilic 2012 hypophosphatemia phosphate pediatric ventilation duration picu children retrospective cohort journal critical care turkiye turkey

shelves.title: Grip strength, mortality and weaning Deposit #6 · Oct 23, 2026
shelves.question: What does a squeeze of the hand predict — about dying, and about coming off a ventilator?
shelves.balance: In the community, weaker grip is one of the most consistent mortality signals in epidemiology — per 5 kg lower grip, death rates run about 16–20% higher in half a million UK Biobank participants, dose-responsive across 3.1 million people pooled — and an uneven grip between the hands adds a further ~12%. In the ICU the picture splits: grip tracks difficult and prolonged weaning, but the largest study found it did not predict extubation failure, and the pooled extubation difference was not significant. Grip is a strong risk marker; nothing on this shelf shows that strengthening it changes outcomes.

cards.headline: Weaker grip, higher death risk (UK Biobank)
cards.summary: Cohort, 502,293 adults — per 5 kg lower grip: all-cause death HR 1.20 (women) / 1.16 (men); cardiovascular 1.19 / 1.22 ; respiratory 1.31 / 1.24 ; prostate cancer 1.05 (NS) .
cards.people: 502,293 adults aged 40–69 (54% women); 13,322 died (2.7%) over a mean 7.1 years
cards.result: Per 5 kg lower grip, women / men: all-cause death HR 1.20 (1.17–1.23) / 1.16 (1.15–1.17) ; cardiovascular 1.19 / 1.22 ; respiratory 1.31 / 1.24 ; all cancer 1.17 / 1.10 ; prostate cancer 1.05 (0.96–1.15) , not significant. Adding grip to an office-based risk score raised the C-index by 0.013
cards.watchOut: An observational cohort, so residual confounding cannot be excluded, and the gain in prediction is small
cards.source: Celis-Morales et al., BMJ 2018; PMID 29739772
cards.search: grip strength death mortality uk biobank cohort celis-morales bmj 2018 hazard ratio per 5 kg pmid 29739772 cardiovascular respiratory

cards.headline: How grip is expressed vs death (NHANES)
cards.summary: Cohort, 9,583 US adults — per 5 kg lower mean grip: HR 1.36 (men) / 1.49 (women); lowest fifth 2.20 / 2.52 ; plain kilograms predicted best.
cards.type: Prospective cohort, NHANES 2011–2014 linked to the National Death Index, Sci Rep 2024
cards.people: 9,583 adults aged 20 or older; 805 deaths over a median 6.75 years
cards.result: Per 5 kg lower mean grip (fully adjusted): men HR 1.36 (1.26–1.48) , women 1.49 (1.30–1.69) ; lowest 20% of grip: men 2.20 , women 2.52 . The simplest measure — absolute grip in kg — predicted best, followed by grip/height²
cards.watchOut: Grip was measured once at baseline, and deaths of all causes (including accidents) were counted
cards.source: Chai et al., Sci Rep 2024
cards.search: grip strength expression death nhanes cohort chai scientific reports 2024 absolute kilograms bmi height national death index

cards.headline: Does the expression of grip change prediction? (UK Biobank)
cards.summary: Cohort, 356,721 people — associations did not meaningfully differ by kg, relative, or z-score expression of grip.
cards.people: 356,721 participants aged 37–73; 6,234 died (1.7%); mean follow-up 5.0 years for death
cards.result: Higher grip went with lower death risk and disease incidence, and the associations did not meaningfully differ whether grip was in kg, relative to height, weight, fat-free mass or BMI, or a z-score; the gain in prediction was also little affected
cards.watchOut: Follow-up was short (about 5 years), and the abstract gives no hazard ratios to compare
cards.source: Ho et al., Age Ageing 2019; PMID 31204772
cards.search: grip strength expression prediction uk biobank cohort ho age ageing 2019 z-score relative kilograms pmid 31204772

cards.headline: The dose-response curve (48 cohorts)
cards.summary: Meta-analysis, 3,135,473 people — all-cause death fell near-linearly across 26–50 kg ; cancer showed a U-shaped trend.
cards.type: Systematic review with dose-response meta-analysis of prospective cohorts, Ageing Res Rev 2022
cards.people: 48 studies, 3,135,473 healthy adults (49.6% women, ages 35–85)
cards.result: All-cause death fell in a close-to-linear way across 26–50 kg of grip; cancer death showed a trend toward a U shape , with significant risk reduction between 16 and 33 kg; cardiovascular death fell close to linearly between 24 and 40 kg
cards.watchOut: Heterogeneity was high for cancer and cardiovascular death, and the abstract gives no pooled hazard ratios
cards.source: López-Bueno et al., Ageing Res Rev 2022; PMID 36332759
cards.search: grip strength dose-response meta-analysis mortality lopez-bueno ageing research reviews 2022 cohorts pmid 36332759 cancer cardiovascular

cards.headline: Grip and healthy habits (SHARE, 16 years)
cards.summary: Cohort, 12,693 adults 50+ — higher grip, lower death in every lifestyle stratum ; combined risk reductions 43–64% .
cards.type: Prospective cohort (SHARE, 2004–2020), 16 years, Am J Prev Med 2026
cards.people: 12,693 adults aged 50 or older
cards.result: Higher grip went with lower all-cause death in every stratum — smoking HR 0.70 , alcohol 0.60 , moderate activity 0.51 , vigorous activity 0.55 , sleeping trouble 0.60 ; combining higher grip with healthy behaviors gave risk reductions of 43% to 64%
cards.watchOut: Healthy behaviors were self-reported
cards.source: Blanchet et al., Am J Prev Med 2026; PMID 41655654
cards.search: grip strength healthy habits lifestyle share cohort blanchet american journal preventive medicine 2026 smoking alcohol activity sleep pmid 41655654

cards.headline: Grip, inflammation (CRP) and death (SHARE)
cards.summary: Cohort, 20,941 adults — at high CRP, 10th-percentile grip HR 1.84 vs median; 90th percentile 0.57 ; interaction p=0.013 .
cards.type: Prospective cohort with time-varying Cox models (SHARE waves 6–9), J Cachexia Sarcopenia Muscle 2026
cards.people: 20,941 adults (mean age 68); follow-up 4.8–5.3 years
cards.result: At CRP >3 mg/L, vs median grip: 10th percentile HR 1.84 (1.59–2.14) , 90th percentile 0.57 (0.43–0.74) ; at CRP >10 and >25 the pattern held (10th percentile 1.69 and 1.92). Interaction between CRP and grip p = 0.013
cards.watchOut: Follow-up was about 5 years, and observational data cannot show that raising grip lowers death
cards.source: Tur-Boned et al., J Cachexia Sarcopenia Muscle 2026; PMID 41895225
cards.search: grip strength inflammation crp death share cohort tur-boned cachexia sarcopenia muscle 2026 interaction pmid 41895225

cards.headline: Grip and death in Korean older adults
cards.summary: Cohort, 9,229 adults — lowest vs highest grip quartile HR 2.06 ; premature death 2.34 .
cards.type: Prospective cohort (Korean Longitudinal Study of Ageing, 2006–2016), Int J Environ Res Public Health 2021
cards.people: 9,229 middle-aged and older adults
cards.result: All-cause death, lowest vs highest grip quartile: HR 2.06 (1.62–2.63) ; weakness by the Asian sarcopenia working group definition 1.56 ; premature death: lowest quartile 2.34 , weakness 1.80
cards.watchOut: An observational cohort in one country, so confounding cannot be excluded
cards.source: Kim J, Int J Environ Res Public Health 2021; PMID 35010298
cards.search: grip strength death korean older adults cohort kim international journal environmental research public health 2021 quartile premature pmid 35010298

cards.headline: The gap between the hands (SHARE, 28 countries)
cards.summary: Cohort, 107,256 adults — hand difference ≥15 kg vs 0–3 kg: all-cause HR 1.39 ; cardiovascular 1.58 .
cards.type: Prospective cohort, time-varying Cox regression (SHARE), Prog Cardiovasc Dis 2026

shelves.title: BMI and ICU extubation
shelves.question: Does a patient’s weight — especially being underweight — change the odds the breathing tube has to go back in after extubation?
shelves.balance: Both fully-checked cohorts point the same way: being underweight when the tube comes out travels with higher odds of needing it back within 72 hours — adjusted OR 1.58 in a 41,016-patient Japanese registry and 3.80 in a small Taiwan cohort — while obesity sat below the mid-range reference (0.69) in the big registry. Both studies are observational and graded Low: thin ICU patients are often ill in ways a BMI number doesn’t capture, so this reads as an association to weigh at the bedside, not a cause.

cards.headline: Lower BMI and reintubation in JIPAD
cards.summary: Reintubation within 72 hours in 2,436 patients (5.9%) — 8.4% underweight vs 4.3% with obesity; adjusted OR 1.58 for underweight, 0.69 for obesity vs BMI 22.0–24.9.
cards.people: 41,016 adults from 131 Japanese ICUs, mechanically ventilated for at least 24 hours and subsequently extubated
cards.result: Reintubation within 72 hours occurred in 2,436 patients (5.9%). Rates were 8.4% with BMI <18.5 kg/m² and 4.3% with BMI ≥30.0 kg/m². Compared with BMI 22.0–24.9 kg/m², adjusted odds ratios were 1.58 (95% CI 1.39–1.80) for underweight and 0.69 (95% CI 0.57–0.84) for obesity.
cards.watchOut: Residual confounding and exclusion of patients never liberated from ventilation limit causal interpretation and generalizability.
cards.source: Maezawa T, Sakuraya M, Goto T. Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care. 2026. PMID: 41654980.

cards.headline: Underweight and failure after planned extubation
cards.summary: Reintubation within 72 hours in 19/268 (7.1%) — underweight vs normal weight: adjusted OR 3.80 (95% CI 1.23–11.7).
cards.people: 268 adult medical/surgical ICU patients in northern Taiwan, ventilated for more than 72 hours, who passed a spontaneous breathing trial and underwent planned extubation
cards.result: Reintubation within 72 hours occurred in 19/268 (7.1%; 95% CI 4.3–10.9%). Events were 8/50 among underweight patients, 9/135 among normal-weight patients, and 2/83 among overweight patients. Underweight (BMI <18.5 kg/m²), compared with normal weight (BMI 18.5–24.9 kg/m²), had an adjusted odds ratio of 3.80 (95% CI 1.23–11.7).
cards.watchOut: Few failures in a single hospital produced a wide confidence interval and leave uncertainty about generalizability.

cards.headline: Obesity and weaning from invasive ventilation (WEAN SAFE)
cards.summary: Weaning success and ICU/hospital mortality did NOT differ across BMI groups — obesity slowed the process (later attempts, more support, longer stays) without changing the outcome.
cards.type: Secondary analysis of the international WEAN SAFE cohort
cards.people: 5,869 patients ventilated at least 2 days; 4,523 reached weaning eligibility; 4,302 with BMI data analyzed. Obesity class II–III: 431 patients (9.5% of eligible)
cards.result: Weaning success and ICU/hospital mortality did NOT differ across BMI groups; after adjustment there was no independent relationship between obesity and weaning delay, weaning success, or survival. Class II–III obesity patients had later first separation attempts, longer time to weaning success, more post-extubation noninvasive ventilation, and longer ICU stays. Higher PEEP at weaning eligibility predicted failure in normal/overweight patients but not in patients with obesity.
cards.watchOut: Observational; obesity changes the process (slower, more support) without changing the outcome — confounding by care patterns is possible.
cards.source: Bell A, et al. Annals of Intensive Care. 2025. PMID: 41116142.

cards.headline: Low CT muscle area and weaning failure
cards.summary: Low thoracic muscle area: adjusted OR 3.63 for weaning failure in younger patients, 1.68 (NS) in older — but the age interaction itself was not significant (p=0.061).
cards.people: 816 screened; composite weaning failure in 290 patients (47.8%); fully adjusted complete-case models n=539
cards.result: Low thoracic muscle area was associated with composite weaning failure in younger patients (adjusted OR 3.63, 95% CI 1.67–7.87) and, nonsignificantly, in older patients (1.68, 0.91–3.13). In younger patients, mortality was 20.6% with low muscle area vs 10.8% without.
cards.watchOut: The age interaction itself was NOT significant (p=0.061) and disappeared with height normalization — so ‘works in the young, not the old’ is a point-estimate story, not a proven difference. Exploratory, single-center.
cards.source: Jung S, et al. Journal of Clinical Medicine. 2026. PMID: 42590207.

shelves.title: ACTH response, cortisol binding, and survival in sepsis Deposit #13 · Oct 23, 2026
shelves.question: In sepsis and septic shock, do cortisol levels, the ACTH stimulation response, and cortisol’s binding protein predict who dies — and does treating a blunted response help?
shelves.balance: The ACTH test sorts septic-shock patients by risk (26/67/82%), and the shelf now anchors how common failure is — 9% of severe-sepsis patients fail the test, split between secondary adrenal insufficiency and adrenal dysfunction — and the mechanism underneath: cortisol alone raises glucose production entirely through gluconeogenesis, and growth hormone raises it by sustaining glycogenolysis. The treatment evidence is still one 43-patient pilot.

cards.headline: Pituitary–adrenal function in SIRS and bacteremia (1995)
cards.summary: Prospective cohort, 113 SIRS patients — baseline cortisol was the same with or without bacteremia ( 25.4 vs 25.1 µg/dL ), but the ACTH increment was smaller with bacteremia ( 14.7 vs 18.9 µg/dL ).
cards.type: Prospective observational cohort with a 250-µg intravenous ACTH stimulation test, Endocrine 1995
cards.people: 113 patients with systemic inflammatory response syndrome; 26% had bacteremia
cards.result: Overall mortality was 28% . Baseline cortisol and Δcortisol were significant mortality indicators in multivariable analysis. Baseline cortisol was similar with and without bacteremia ( 25.4 ± 1.9 vs 25.1 ± 2.5 µg/dL ), but Δcortisol was smaller with bacteremia ( 14.7 ± 2.2 vs 18.9 ± 1.2 µg/dL ; P<0.05)
cards.watchOut: A heterogeneous SIRS-era cohort, and the accessible published abstract does not provide adjusted effect sizes for mortality
cards.source: Tayek & Atienza, Endocrine 1995; PMID 21153181
cards.search: pituitary adrenal function sirs bacteremia tayek atienza endocrine 1995 prospective cohort acth stimulation cortisol increment pmid 21153181

cards.headline: Annane’s three-level classification in septic shock
cards.summary: Prospective two-center cohort, 189 patients — 28-day mortality 26% (good response), 67% (intermediate), 82% (high baseline, blunted response); a response over 9 µg/dL carried OR 0.21 for death.
cards.type: Prospective two-center cohort with a 250-µg corticotropin test at septic-shock onset, JAMA 2000
cards.people: 189 adults with septic shock
cards.result: 28-day mortality was 26% (15/57) with baseline cortisol ≤34 µg/dL and Δmax >9 µg/dL, 67% (66/98) in the intermediate group, and 82% (28/34) with baseline >34 and Δmax ≤9 (P<0.001). In multivariable analysis, Δmax >9 µg/dL had OR 0.21 (95% CI 0.09–0.47) for death
cards.watchOut: The thresholds and three-level model were derived and evaluated in the same cohort and require external validation
cards.source: Annane et al., JAMA 2000; PMID 10697064
cards.search: annane three level classification septic shock jama 2000 prospective cohort corticotropin baseline cortisol delta max mortality odds ratio pmid 10697064

cards.headline: ACTH response in late septic shock
cards.summary: Retrospective cohort, 82 patients tested after 24+ hours — a maximal response under 9 µg/dL independently predicted 28-day mortality ( P=0.044 ).
cards.type: Retrospective cohort of consecutive patients receiving a short corticotropin test, Shock 2003
cards.people: 82 adults with septic shock tested more than 24 hours after vasopressor initiation
cards.result: 41 patients ( 50% ) died by day 28. A maximal cortisol response <9 µg/dL occurred in 31/82 (38%) and was an independent predictor of 28-day mortality ( P=0.044 ); baseline cortisol >20 µg/dL (P=0.0002), abnormal lactate (P=0.0098), and positive blood cultures (P=0.004) were also independent predictors
cards.watchOut: Testing occurred late and selectively in vasopressor-treated patients, and the accessible abstract does not report adjusted odds ratios
cards.source: Bollaert et al., Shock 2003; PMID 12558137
cards.search: acth response late septic shock bollaert shock 2003 retrospective cohort corticotropin maximal response mortality predictor pmid 12558137

cards.headline: The increment adds nothing beyond SOFA
cards.summary: Observational cohort, 282 ACTH-tested patients — a low increment predicted death in men ( 31% vs 11% ) but not women, and cortisol measures did not improve on SOFA.
cards.people: 522 critically ill adults had random cortisol measured; 282 underwent a 250-µg ACTH stimulation test
cards.result: Overall hospital mortality was 24% . Δcortisol ≤9 µg/dL was associated with greater mortality in men ( 31% vs 11% ; P<0.01) but not women ( 30% vs 29% ; P=0.8). Cortisol measures did not add to mortality predicted by SOFA. Corticosteroid-treated and untreated patients had mortality of 27% and 22% , respectively (P=0.6)
cards.watchOut: Treatment was not randomized, and the cohort included mixed critical illnesses rather than septic shock alone
cards.source: Rady et al., Arch Surg 2005
cards.search: increment adds nothing beyond sofa rady archives surgery 2005 observational cohort acth cortisol organ failure sex men women mortality

cards.headline: The CORTICUS cohort — a modest signal
cards.summary: Retrospective multicenter cohort, 477 patients, 20 European ICUs — a Δmax ≤9 µg/dL had a likelihood ratio for death of 1.38 (1.18–1.61) .
cards.type: Retrospective multicenter cohort, Crit Care Med 2007
cards.people: 477 adults from 20 European ICUs who underwent ACTH testing on the day severe sepsis began
cards.result: A Δmax ≤9 µg/dL at any baseline cortisol concentration had a likelihood ratio for death of 1.38 (95% CI 1.18–1.61) . Nonsurvivors had higher baseline cortisol than survivors ( 29.5 ± 33.5 vs 24.3 ± 16.5 µg/dL ; P=0.03), while the authors concluded that Δcortisol, rather than baseline cortisol, was associated with clinical outcome
cards.watchOut: A retrospective analysis assembled from patients selected for ACTH testing, with substantial variability in cortisol measurements
cards.source: Lipiner-Friedman et al., Crit Care Med 2007; PMID 17334243
cards.search: corticus cohort modest signal lipiner-friedman critical care medicine 2007 retrospective multicenter acth delta max likelihood ratio death pmid 17334243

cards.headline: A negative study in unstable septic shock
cards.summary: Retrospective cohort, 69 patients — ACTH responders and nonresponders had similar outcomes; baseline cortisol AUC was 0.662 .
cards.type: Retrospective single-center cohort with 250-µg ACTH testing, Rev Bras Ter Intensiva 2012
cards.people: 69 consecutive patients with septic shock and more than 6 hours of progressive hemodynamic instability
cards.result: Day-28 ICU mortality was 55% . Baseline cortisol was lower in survivors than nonsurvivors (median 19 [IQR 11–27] vs 24 [18–34] µg/dL ; P=0.047), but ACTH responders and nonresponders had similar outcomes. Baseline cortisol had AUC 0.662 (95% CI 0.536–0.773); baseline cortisol/albumin had AUC 0.75 (95% CI 0.621–0.849)
cards.watchOut: Retrospective testing of a small, selected, severely unstable cohort limits generalizability
cards.source: Dalegrave et al., Rev Bras Ter Intensiva 2012; PMID 23917934

cards.headline: High-affinity CBG falls in those who die
cards.summary: Prospective cohort, 30 septic-shock patients — total and high-affinity corticosteroid-binding globulin were lower in nonsurvivors ( P<0.009 and P=0.021 ); cortisol itself was not associated with mortality.
cards.type: Prospective single-center observational cohort with serial sampling at 0, 8, 24, 48, and 72 hours, Clin Endocrinol (Oxf) 2019
cards.people: 30 patients with septic shock and 42 with nonseptic critical illness, contributing 195 serum samples; glucocorticoid-treated patients were excluded
cards.result: Among patients with septic shock, total CBG and high-affinity CBG were lower in nonsurvivors than survivors ( P<0.009 and P=0.021 , respectively). Total and free cortisol were not associated with mortality, and albumin fell during sepsis but was not associated with mortality
cards.watchOut: Only 30 septic-shock patients were studied, and the abstract does not provide adjusted effect estimates
cards.source: Meyer et al., Clin Endocrinol 2019; PMID 30160799
cards.search: high affinity cbg falls nonsurvivors meyer clinical endocrinology 2019 prospective cohort corticosteroid binding globulin septic shock mortality pmid 30160799

cards.headline: Methylprednisolone for blunted responders — a pilot
cards.summary: Randomized double-blind pilot, 43 patients — 28-day mortality 43% on methylprednisolone vs 73% on placebo (P<0.05); very small, high-dose regimen.
cards.type: Prospective randomized double-blind placebo-controlled pilot trial, J Intensive Care Med 2022
cards.people: 54 patients underwent 250-µg ACTH testing; 11 with peak cortisol <20 µg/dL were excluded, and 43 with Δcortisol <12.9 µg/dL were randomized to methylprednisolone (n=21) or placebo (n=22)
cards.result: Methylprednisolone 20 mg IV every 8 hours for 7 days was associated with 28-day mortality of 43 ± 11% versus 73 ± 10% with placebo (P<0.05). ICU days, vasopressor days, and ventilator days did not differ significantly
cards.watchOut: A very small pilot trial with multiple outcomes and an unusually high-dose methylprednisolone regimen
cards.source: Birudaraju, Hamal & Tayek, J Intensive Care Med 2022; PMID 34516312
cards.search: methylprednisolone blunted responders pilot birudaraju hamal tayek journal intensive care medicine 2022 randomized double blind placebo mortality pmid 34516312

cards.headline: The cortisol:corticosterone ratio (HYPRESS)
cards.summary: Exploratory RCT analysis, 180 patients — a stimulated ratio over 32.2 predicted in-hospital mortality with AUC 0.80 ; in placebo patients, 90-day mortality was 41% vs 7% .
cards.type: Exploratory analysis of the double-blind HYPRESS randomized trial, using LC-MS/MS steroid profiling before and 60 minutes after 250-µg corticotropin, Crit Care 2022
cards.people: 180 adults with severe sepsis without shock and 20 healthy volunteers; mortality prediction was evaluated in the placebo subgroup (n=90)
cards.result: Cortisol response was subnormal in 12% of septic patients, while corticosterone response was subnormal in 50% . A stimulated cortisol:corticosterone ratio >32.2 predicted in-hospital mortality with AUC 0.80 (95% CI 0.70–0.88), sensitivity 83% , and specificity 78% . In placebo patients, 90-day mortality was 41% with a ratio >32.2 versus 7% with a ratio ≤32.2
cards.watchOut: The ratio and threshold were derived post hoc in only 90 untreated participants and have not been prospectively validated
cards.source: Briegel et al., Crit Care 2022; PMID 36345013
cards.search: cortisol corticosterone ratio hypress briegel critical care 2022 exploratory randomized trial analysis steroid profiling mortality auc pmid 36345013

cards.headline: Severe CBG deficiency triples the odds of death
cards.summary: Prospective cohort, 135 septic-shock patients — ICU mortality 32.4% with CBG under 200 nmol/L vs 13.9% above; adjusted OR 3.23 (1.06–9.88) .
cards.type: Prospective observational cohort, J Clin Endocrinol Metab 2022
cards.people: 135 adults with septic shock
cards.result: ICU mortality was 32.4% with mean day-1/2 CBG <200 nmol/L versus 13.9% with CBG ≥200 nmol/L (OR 2.97 , 95% CI 1.19–7.41; P=0.02). After adjustment, CBG <200 nmol/L remained associated with ICU mortality (adjusted OR 3.23 , 95% CI 1.06–9.88). 28-day mortality was 41.2% (14/34) versus 23.8% (24/101), OR 2.25 (95% CI 0.99–5.11)
cards.watchOut: A single-center observational study, and the CBG threshold was selected from prior pilot work rather than externally validated
cards.source: Meyer et al., J Clin Endocrinol Metab 2022; PMID 35152290
cards.search: severe cbg deficiency triples odds death meyer journal clinical endocrinology metabolism 2022 prospective cohort septic shock icu mortality adjusted odds pmid 35152290

cards.headline: Cortisol trajectories — staying high is ominous
cards.summary: Retrospective cohort, 258 sepsis patients — the higher-cortisol trajectory had 28-day mortality 65.9% vs 16.1% ; adjusted HR 5.29 (2.22–12.63) .
cards.type: Retrospective single-center cohort using group-based trajectory modeling of twice-daily cortisol during the first 3 days, Crit Care 2024
cards.people: 258 ICU patients with sepsis: lower-cortisol trajectory n=217 and higher-cortisol trajectory n=41
cards.result: The higher-cortisol trajectory had 28-day mortality of 65.9% versus 16.1% and 90-day mortality of 65.9% versus 19.8% (both P<0.001). The higher trajectory independently predicted 28-day mortality (adjusted HR 5.292 , 95% CI 2.218–12.626) and 90-day mortality (adjusted HR 4.571 , 95% CI 1.980–10.551)
cards.watchOut: Steroid-treated patients and patients staying in the ICU for less than 72 hours were excluded, creating important selection and survivorship bias
cards.source: Leng et al., Crit Care 2024
cards.search: cortisol trajectories staying high ominous leng critical care 2024 retrospective cohort sepsis trajectory mortality adjusted hazard ratio

cards.headline: One CBG glycoform predicts death (2026)
cards.summary: Prospective cohort, 128 septic-shock patients — the Asn347 TS3 glycoform under 27.9 nmol/L predicted ICU mortality after APACHE adjustment (HR 2.7, 1.2–6.2 ).
cards.type: Prospective observational extension study with mass-spectrometric CBG glycoform profiling, J Endocr Soc 2026
cards.people: 128 adults with septic shock sampled on ICU day 1 and again through day 7 or the last ICU day
cards.result: Mean TS3 Asn347 CBG concentration was 29.74 nmol/L in ICU nonsurvivors versus 45.16 nmol/L in survivors (P=0.007). TS3 <27.9 nmol/L was associated with ICU mortality after APACHE adjustment (HR 2.7 , 95% CI 1.2–6.2; P=0.023) and with 28-day mortality (HR 2.2 , 95% CI 1.1–4.4; P=0.023)
cards.watchOut: An extension of a single-center cohort; requires independent replication and a clinically available assay
cards.source: Lee et al., J Endocr Soc 2026; PMID 41994485
cards.search: cbg glycoform predicts death asn347 lee journal endocrine society 2026 prospective cohort septic shock mass spectrometry icu mortality apache pmid 41994485

cards.headline: Cortisol in Indian severe sepsis — high, and not predictive
cards.summary: Prospective cohort, 60 patients — basal cortisol averaged 31.8 µg/dL ; adrenal insufficiency by three common criteria ranged 48–78% ; no cortisol measure predicted 28-day mortality.
cards.type: Prospective cohort, single center (AIIMS New Delhi, 2009–2011), 1 µg cosyntropin stimulation, J Emerg Trauma Shock 2017
cards.people: 60 patients — 30 severe sepsis, 30 septic shock
cards.result: Mean basal cortisol 31.77 ± 15.9 µg/dL ; post-stimulation 37.58 ± 17.31 µg/dL . Adrenal insufficiency by three common criteria: 48.33% (basal ≤24 µg/dL), 61.67% (Δ ≤7), 78.33% (Δ ≤9). On multivariate analysis, cortisol measures were NOT associated with 28-day mortality — the authors’ conclusion: cortisol levels could not predict mortality in this cohort
cards.watchOut: Small, single-center; basal cortisol runs higher than in Western cohorts, so imported cutoffs classify very differently (AI prevalence swings 48–78% by criterion alone)
cards.source: Suresh et al., J Emerg Trauma Shock 2017; PMID 29097858
cards.search: suresh 2017 cortisol severe sepsis india aiims new delhi adrenal insufficiency basal cosyntropin stimulation 28-day mortality journal emergency trauma shock pmid 29097858

cards.headline: Manglik 2003: ACTH test failure in severe sepsis
cards.summary: In 100 patients with severe sepsis, 9% failed the 250-µg ACTH stimulation test — and the failures split into two different diseases.
cards.type: Prospective cohort with 250-µg ACTH stimulation testing, single center (Harbor-UCLA), Crit Care Med 2003
cards.people: 100 patients with severe sepsis; 40 had bacteremia and 17% were in shock
cards.result: Passers (n=91): baseline cortisol 29.3±2.5 → 40.1±2.6 at 30 min → 46.9±2.7 µg/dL at 60 min. Failures (n=9, all cortisol <20 µg/dL): 11.3±1.8 → 14.0±1.9 → 15.7±1.8 . Of the 9 failures, 4 had secondary adrenal insufficiency (normal aldosterone response) and 5 had absent aldosterone response with non-elevated ACTH (adrenal dysfunction). Sodium 128±4 vs 138±1 mmol/L and glucose 121±20 vs 163±11 mg/dL, failures vs passers (both p<.05)
cards.watchOut: n=9 failures — the split is suggestive, not definitive; no mortality outcome in the abstract; single center (Harbor-UCLA)
cards.source: Manglik S, Flores E, Lubarsky L, Fernandez F, Chhibber VL, Tayek JA. Crit Care Med 2003;31(6):1668–75. DOI 10.1097/01.CCM.0000063447.37342.A9. PMID 12794402
cards.search: manglik 2003 acth stimulation test failure severe sepsis adrenal insufficiency adrenal dysfunction aldosterone cortisol harbor-ucla tayek critical care medicine pmid 12794402

cards.headline: Khani 2001: cortisol drives glucose production through gluconeogenesis
cards.summary: Cortisol alone drives glucose production — entirely through gluconeogenesis .
cards.type: Controlled cortisol-infusion study in healthy volunteers, glucose production measured by two independent tracer methods, Clin Sci (Lond) 2001
cards.people: 16 healthy volunteers: cortisol infusion in two method groups (n=5+5) and 6 fasting-alone controls
cards.result: Fasting glucose production (GP) 12.5±0.2 µmol·min⁻¹·kg⁻¹; gluconeogenesis was 35±2% (HS reciprocal pool) / 40±2% (TK Cori-cycle) of GP at 12 h; at 16 h fasting GP was 11.5±0.6 with gluconeogenesis 55±5%/57±5% . After 4 h of high-dose cortisol: serum cortisol 660±30 nmol/L, glucose 7.9±0.5 mmol/L (≈142±9 mg/dL), GP 14.8±0.8 (all p<.05) — and the GP rise was entirely gluconeogenesis ( 66±6%/65±5% of GP). The two independent methods agreed
cards.watchOut: n=16 total, healthy volunteers, high-dose cortisol for 4 hours — mechanism, not sepsis; the metabolic-syndrome link is the authors’ inference
cards.source: Khani S, Tayek JA. Clin Sci (Lond) 2001;101(6):739–47. DOI 10.1042/cs1010739. PMID 11724664
cards.search: khani 2001 cortisol infusion glucose production gluconeogenesis fasting healthy volunteers reciprocal pool cori cycle clinical science tayek pmid 11724664

cards.headline: Ghanaat 2005: growth hormone sustains glycogenolysis
cards.summary: Growth hormone raises glucose production not by making new glucose, but by keeping glycogenolysis from falling .
cards.type: Pituitary-pancreatic clamp study in healthy fasting volunteers, Metabolism 2005
cards.people: 12 volunteers under clamp plus 6 fasting controls
cards.result: Under clamp without GH, GP was 2.43±0.19 vs 2.07±0.11 mg/kg/min (NS). After 4 h of high-dose GH: GH 20.8±3.8 vs 2.0±0.9 ng/mL, glucose 127±28 vs 86±4 mg/dL, GP 2.21±0.21 vs 1.81±0.12 (p<.05); glycogenolysis 0.94±0.21 vs 0.53±0.07 mg/kg/min (p<.05), 43±5% vs 29±3% of GP (p<.05); gluconeogenesis unchanged ( 1.26±0.15 vs 1.29±0.12 )
cards.watchOut: Healthy fasting volunteers, 4-hour infusion — the counterregulatory-hormone mechanism card, not a sepsis card; it sits on #14 because the shelf follows the stress hormones, and GH is one of them
cards.source: Ghanaat F, Tayek JA. Metabolism 2005;54(5):604–9. DOI 10.1016/j.metabol.2004.12.003. PMID 15877290
cards.search: ghanaat 2005 growth hormone glucose production glycogenolysis gluconeogenesis pituitary pancreatic clamp fasting volunteers metabolism tayek pmid 15877290

shelves.title: Diabetes vs no diabetes — ICU mortality Deposit #16 · Oct 23, 2026 · Founding shelf
shelves.question: Does pre-existing diabetes change a critically ill patient’s chance of dying?
shelves.balance: The shelf now says something sharper: pre-existing diabetes does not raise sepsis mortality — in 16,497 Taiwanese ICU patients it was identical (22.6% vs 22.6%), and across nine studies known diabetics died at half the rate of patients with new-onset hyperglycemia (12.5% vs 26.7% in hospital) at similar glucose levels, as if prior exposure adapts the body to hyperglycemia. The metabolic parallel is real — diabetes shares cancer’s raised glucose production and leucine turnover — but the albumin card (54% higher death rate per 0.5 g/dL lower) is a different population, transplant-listed lung disease, and the shelf’s mechanism section (glucose variability) still awaits its papers.

cards.headline: Diabetes did not raise sepsis mortality in Taiwan’s ICUs
cards.summary: Nationwide retrospective cohort, 16,497 patients with severe sepsis ( 4,573 with diabetes, 11,924 without) — 90-day hospital mortality 22.61% with diabetes vs 22.59% without (RR 1.00 , 0.94–1.07); adjusted OR 0.972 (0.890–1.061).
cards.type: Nationwide population-based retrospective cohort using Taiwan National Health Insurance claims, PLoS ONE 2012
cards.people: 16,497 adults with a first ICU admission for severe sepsis (4,573 with diabetes, 11,924 without)
cards.result: 90-day hospital mortality 22.61% with diabetes vs 22.59% without (RR 1.00 , 95% CI 0.94–1.07); adjusted OR 0.972 (95% CI 0.890–1.061)
cards.watchOut: Claims data, so diagnosis and severity rest on coded records
cards.source: Chang et al., PLoS ONE 2012; PMID 23236389
cards.search: chang diabetes no diabetes icu mortality severe sepsis taiwan nationwide retrospective cohort claims plos one 2012 pmid 23236389 pre-existing type 2 kidney injury 90-day hospital mortality

cards.headline: Tayek & Tayek 2012: new-onset hyperglycemia carries the risk
cards.summary: Known diabetes does not raise sepsis mortality — new-onset hyperglycemia does, more than twofold .
cards.type: Literature review of 9 studies, World J Diabetes 2012
cards.people: 9 studies reviewed; ~17% of admissions had NOH and 24% had diabetes
cards.result: Hospital mortality: NOH 26.7%±3.4% vs known DM 12.5%±3.4% (p<.05). ICU mortality (5 studies): NOH 25.3%±3.3% vs DM 12.8%±2.6% (p<.05). NOH carried a 2.7-fold increase in hospital mortality vs hyperglycemic DM; blood glucose concentrations were similar between the groups
cards.watchOut: The percentages are unweighted study-level means (±SD across studies), not patient-level pooled estimates — the direction is consistent across all nine studies, the exact pooled size is not computed; a literature review, not a meta-analysis. First author Chandler J. Tayek (the developer’s son, then a high-school student)
cards.source: Tayek CJ, Tayek JA. World J Diabetes 2012;3(2):29–34. DOI 10.4239/wjd.v3.i2.29. PMID 22375163. PMCID PMC3284518
cards.search: tayek cj tayek ja 2012 new-onset hyperglycemia noh known diabetes sepsis mortality literature review world journal diabetes chandler pmid 22375163 pmc3284518

cards.headline: Richardson 2002: diabetes as a mild injury response
cards.summary: Type 2 diabetes looks, metabolically, like a mild injury response .
cards.type: Fasting metabolic study of glucose and leucine kinetics, Am J Physiol Endocrinol Metab 2002
cards.people: 40 people after a 10-h fast: 16 with type 2 diabetes (DM), 11 with lung cancer (CA), 13 normal volunteers (NV)
cards.result: Glucose production: DM 4.22±0.6 , CA 3.53±0.3 vs NV 2.76±0.2 mg·kg lean body wt⁻¹·min⁻¹ (p<.01). Leucine oxidation: DM 27.3±1.5 , CA 19.7±1.5 vs NV 12.5±1.1 (p<.05); leucine appearance: DM 91.9±6.6 , CA 90.7±7.0 vs NV 79.1±6.0 (p<.01). Cortisol: DM 11.4±1.0 , CA 12.1±1.0 vs NV 8.9±0.7 µg/dL (p<.05). CRP: CA 23.3±6.0 vs DM 4.2±1.4 , NV 2.1±0.5 (p<.01)
cards.watchOut: Fasting physiology in 40 people, not ICU outcomes — the “mild injury response” is a metabolic parallel, not mortality evidence; CRP separates cancer from diabetes (23.3 vs 4.2), so the shared pattern is metabolic, not inflammatory
cards.source: Richardson AP, Tayek JA. Am J Physiol Endocrinol Metab 2002;282(6):E1286–90. DOI 10.1152/ajpendo.00132.2001. PMID 12006358
cards.search: richardson 2002 type 2 diabetes mild injury response glucose production leucine oxidation leucine appearance cortisol crp lung cancer fasting american journal physiology tayek pmid 12006358

cards.headline: Zisman 2009: albumin and death in lung-transplant candidates
cards.summary: In lung-transplant candidates, each 0.5 g/dL lower albumin raised the death rate 54% .
cards.type: Cohort study of UNOS registry patients, Chest 2009
cards.people: 1,269 patients with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis listed for lung transplant (UNOS 2004–2006)
cards.result: Mortality rate rose 54% per 0.5 g/dL decrease in serum albumin (95% CI 32–79% ), p for linear trend <0.0001, before and after multivariable adjustment
cards.watchOut: No diabetes arm and no ICU — this card anchors albumin as a mortality signal in a transplant-listed population, not the DM question; it sits on #17 because the developer grouped it here, and it can move
cards.source: Zisman DA, Kawut SM, Lederer DJ, Belperio JA, Lynch JP 3rd, Schwarz MI, Tayek JA, Reuben DB, Karlamangla AS. Chest 2009;135(4):929–35. DOI 10.1378/chest.08-0754. PMID 19017875. PMCID PMC2666778

shelves.title: Low creatinine and mortality Deposit #18 · Oct 23, 2026 · Founding shelf
shelves.question: Is a LOW admission creatinine a danger signal for death — not just a high one?
shelves.balance: Low creatinine as a frailty signal gains its mechanism: in 118 hemodialysis patients the creatinine-based estimate of lean body mass matched DEXA with a mean difference of zero — but the authors present it as a hypothesis, and the shelf still has no study that measured muscle mass directly against mortality.

cards.headline: Low creatinine, high mortality — the U-curve
cards.summary: Retrospective cohort, 73,994 hospitalized adults ( 973 in-hospital deaths) — vs creatinine 0.7–0.8 mg/dL, values ≤0.4 carried adjusted OR 3.29 (2.08–5.00) for in-hospital death; ≥1.5 carried 2.56 (2.07–3.17).
cards.type: Retrospective, single-center observational cohort study, Am J Med 2017
cards.people: 73,994 hospitalized adults at a tertiary referral hospital with an admission creatinine measurement (2011–2013); 973 (1.3%) died in hospital
cards.result: Mortality followed a U-shaped association across admission creatinine categories. Compared with 0.7–0.8 mg/dL, admission creatinine ≤0.4 mg/dL was associated with adjusted odds of in-hospital death of 3.29 (95% CI 2.08–5.00); creatinine ≥1.5 mg/dL was also associated with higher mortality (adjusted OR 2.56 , 95% CI 2.07–3.17)
cards.watchOut: Retrospective, single-center study; the reported adjustment set did not include a direct measure of muscle mass
cards.source: Thongprayoon et al., Am J Med 2017; PMID 27998681
cards.search: thongprayoon low creatinine high mortality u-curve u-shaped admission hospitalized adults retrospective cohort in-hospital death frailty muscle mass american journal medicine 2017 pmid 27998681

cards.headline: Creatinine goes quiet after 90
cards.summary: Retrospective cohort, 952 ICU patients aged 90+ in Germany — admission creatinine not associated with in-hospital mortality (adjusted HR 1.07 , 0.92–1.26); modest associations at 90 days ( 1.16 ) and 1 year ( 1.20 ); in-hospital mortality 28.5% , 1-year 57.1% .
cards.type: Retrospective, single-center cohort study, BMC Geriatr 2026
cards.people: 952 ICU patients aged ≥90 years admitted to a German university medical center (2008–2019); median age 92.2 years
cards.result: Admission creatinine was not independently associated with in-hospital mortality (adjusted HR 1.07 , 95% CI 0.92–1.26). Higher admission creatinine was associated with 90-day mortality (adjusted HR 1.16 , 95% CI 1.01–1.34) and 1-year mortality (adjusted HR 1.20 , 95% CI 1.06–1.36). In-hospital mortality was 28.5% , 1-year mortality 57.1%
cards.watchOut: This highly selected nonagenarian ICU cohort may not generalize to younger or broader ICU populations; the primary continuous-creatinine result does not specifically isolate very low creatinine
cards.source: Klopp et al., BMC Geriatr 2026; DOI 10.1186/s12877-026-07793-0

cards.headline: Patel 2013: creatinine as a muscle-mass marker in dialysis
cards.summary: Serum creatinine tracks muscle mass in dialysis — as a hypothesis with a pilot behind it , not a proven number.
cards.type: Cross-sectional study against DEXA measurement, J Cachexia Sarcopenia Muscle 2013
cards.people: 118 hemodialysis patients (DEXA sub-cohort; DEXA lean body mass 49.8±9.9 kg; serum creatinine 10.8±3.0 mg/dL)
cards.result: The creatinine-based equation estimated lean body mass with a mean difference of 0.0 kg (95% CI −0.6 to 0.6) against DEXA; limits of agreement −6.7 to +6.7 kg . The authors describe the association as strong and linear, with narrow CIs (spline models). Their conclusion is explicitly a hypothesis — creatinine “can serve as a reliable muscle mass biomarker if appropriate adjustment for full or residual kidney function and dietary meat intake is undertaken”
cards.watchOut: The abstract says “correlated well” but prints no correlation coefficient; the r=0.34 in Table 2 is the correlation between the difference (estimate minus DEXA) and DEXA values — a bias check, not the creatinine–LBM correlation — so no r is printed on this card; n=118, single-center, cross-sectional

shelves.title: Elevated phosphate on admission as a danger signal
shelves.question: Should elevated phosphate on admission be a danger signal?
shelves.balance: Developer’s verdict (Oct 29, 2026): POSSIBLE. Five cohorts, about 199,000 patients, and the pattern refuses to settle. Arrive with a high phosphate and you die more often — 10.7% vs 2.2% in the emergency department, adjusted odds of 3.89 at the Mayo Clinic for levels of 4.9 mg/dL or more, 16.4% vs 6.6% in-hospital mortality across 126,088 infection admissions, 25% vs 3% at 30 days in pancreatitis — and in three of those cohorts the association survives adjustment for kidney function. But the entanglement never goes away: the ED study’s high-phosphate patients had a median eGFR of 22 against 93, and the largest ICU cohort — 27,131 patients — lost the association entirely once severity and kidney function were adjusted for. Every study here is observational; nobody was randomized. A high phosphate on admission may be a danger signal in its own right, or it may be the sound of failing kidneys and severe illness. Posted as a possible, not a fact.

cards.headline: High phosphate on arrival in the emergency department: 10.7% dead within 28 days vs 2.2% with a normal level
cards.summary: Mortality was 23/215 (10.7%) in the high group vs 37/1,695 (2.2%) normal and 17/480 (3.5%) low; adjusted estimate for high phosphate 3.29 (95% CI 1.8–6.1; P<0.001).
cards.type: Retrospective cross-sectional emergency-department cohort with multivariable Cox modeling
cards.people: 2,390 emergency-department patients (Inselspital Bern, 2010–2011) with phosphate measured on admission, of 22,239 screened: 215 high (≥1.46 mmol/L, ≈4.5 mg/dL), 1,695 normal, 480 low.
cards.result: Mortality was 23/215 (10.7%) in the high group vs 37/1,695 (2.2%) normal and 17/480 (3.5%) low. Adjusted estimate for high phosphate: 3.29 (95% CI 1.8–6.1; P<0.001); for low phosphate 1.24 (0.66–2.30), not significant. The high group’s median eGFR was 22.4 mL/min/1.73 m² vs 92.8 in the normal group.
cards.watchOut: Only about 1 in 9 ED patients had a phosphate measured at all — who gets the test is itself a severity signal. The paper labels its Cox-regression estimates as odds ratios. And the kidney gap (eGFR 22 vs 93) is the confounder this whole shelf argues about.
cards.source: Haider DG et al. Hyperphosphatemia is an independent risk factor for mortality in critically ill patients: results from a cross-sectional study. PLOS ONE 2015;10(8):e0133426. PMID 26252874 · DOI 10.1371/journal.pone.0133426

cards.headline: Mayo Clinic, 42,336 admissions: phosphate ≥4.9 mg/dL on arrival — adjusted odds of in-hospital death 3.89
cards.type: Retrospective cohort, single health system, multivariable logistic regression
cards.people: 42,336 adults admitted to Mayo Clinic, Rochester, 2009–2013, with an admission phosphate; six bands from <2.5 to ≥4.9 mg/dL; reference band 3.1–3.6 mg/dL.
cards.result: A U-shape: lowest in-hospital mortality at phosphate 3.1–4.2 mg/dL. Adjusted odds ratios vs the reference band: <2.5 → 1.60 (1.25–2.05); 4.3–4.8 → 1.60 (1.29–1.97); ≥4.9 → 3.89 (3.20–4.74). The model included eGFR and the association persisted. At ≥4.9 the odds were higher still in patients with CKD (4.11; 3.16–5.39) and cardiovascular disease (5.11; 3.33–7.95).
cards.watchOut: Retrospective and single-system, and an admission phosphate is still not drawn on everyone. The U-shape’s low arm is a different question (Shelf #5); this card is the high arm.
cards.source: Cheungpasitporn W et al. Admission serum phosphate levels predict hospital mortality. Hosp Pract 2018;46:121–127. PMID 29848117 · DOI 10.1080/21548331.2018.1483172

cards.headline: 126,088 infection admissions in Israel: high phosphate on arrival — in-hospital mortality 16.4% vs 6.6%
cards.summary: In-hospital mortality 16.4% (high) vs 6.6% (normal) vs 5.6% (low); adjusted OR for 30-day mortality with high phosphate 2.43 (2.06–2.86).
cards.type: Retrospective nationwide cohort (8 tertiary hospitals), multivariable models
cards.people: 126,088 adults admitted with infections to medical and surgical departments (outside the ICU), 2001–2020; first phosphate within a week of admission: 8,549 high (>4.5 mg/dL), 92,730 normal, 24,809 low.
cards.result: In-hospital mortality: 16.4% (high) vs 6.6% (normal) vs 5.6% (low); 30-day mortality 9.8% vs 6.9%; mortality over full follow-up 74.5% vs 57.0% vs 48.7%. Adjusted odds ratio for 30-day mortality with high phosphate: 2.43 (2.06–2.86) — 2.15 (1.95–2.37) in patients with renal failure and 2.18 (1.79–2.63) without. Adjusted odds of target-organ damage: 2.00 (1.89–2.11). Though the association held with and without renal failure, 73.4% of the high group had an eGFR under 60, vs 35.2% of the normal group.
cards.watchOut: The paper’s abstract transposes two figures — it attaches 2.43 to target-organ damage; the tables give 2.43 as the adjusted 30-day-mortality odds ratio (Table 2) and 2.00 for target-organ damage (Table 3). This card follows the tables. ‘Admission’ phosphate could be drawn up to a week into the stay. Infections only.
cards.source: Frenkel A et al. Exploring the association between serum phosphate levels and mortality in patients hospitalized with infectious diseases: a nationwide study. Front Med 2024;11:1362106. PMID 38590318 · DOI 10.3389/fmed.2024.1362106

cards.headline: Acute pancreatitis: phosphate >4.5 mg/dL on admission — 30-day mortality 25% vs 3%
cards.summary: 30-day mortality 25% (high) vs 3% (normal); severe pancreatitis 60% vs 20%; adjusted OR for 30-day mortality 5.8 (2.9–11.5).
cards.type: Retrospective single-center cohort, multivariable logistic regression
cards.people: 1,000 consecutive acute-pancreatitis admissions, Kayseri City Hospital, Türkiye, November 2023–June 2025; hyperphosphatemia >4.5 mg/dL (the abstract does not state the high group’s size).
cards.result: 30-day mortality 25% (high) vs 3% (normal); severe pancreatitis 60% vs 20%; pancreatic necrosis 50% vs 10%; ICU admission 70% vs 15%. Adjusted OR for 30-day mortality: 5.8 (2.9–11.5) — and 4.7 (2.1–10.3) in a model that also adjusted for creatinine and acute kidney injury.
cards.watchOut: Single center, retrospective, a lower-tier journal — and as of this carding the paper has no PubMed record; it is cited by its DOI. The strongest renal-adjusted estimate on the shelf rests on the shelf’s weakest source.
cards.source: Özden Y, Buyukberber NM. Admission hyperphosphatemia as a predictor of severity and mortality in acute pancreatitis: a 1000-patient cohort study. World J Gastrointest Surg 2026;18(1):114227. DOI 10.4240/wjgs.v18.i1.114227 · PMID: none (no PubMed record).

cards.headline: The counterweight — 27,131 ICU patients: after adjustment, high phosphate was NOT significantly tied to 28- or 90-day death
cards.summary: After adjustment for severity scores, comorbidities, and laboratory values, neither hyperphosphatemia nor hypophosphatemia was significantly associated with 28-day or 90-day mortality.
cards.people: 27,131 ICU patients, Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center, 2001–2012; first phosphate on ICU day 1, in six bands from <2.5 to ≥4.5 mg/dL.
cards.result: Crude mortality was higher at both extremes and rose roughly linearly with phosphate. After adjustment for severity scores, comorbidities, and laboratory values, neither hyperphosphatemia nor hypophosphatemia was significantly associated with 28-day or 90-day mortality. The authors conclude it is an open question whether phosphate monitoring is necessary in the critically ill.
cards.watchOut: The paper’s medical-ICU subgroup is described as positive, but the hazard ratios as printed (0.64 and 0.72, against the 2.5–3.0 mg/dL band) point in the opposite direction — an inconsistency inside the paper that this card does not resolve. Single-center data from 2001–2012.
