shelves.title: ICU glucose variability and mortality
shelves.question: Does glucose variability predict ICU death — and does diabetes change that relationship?
shelves.balance: Variability tracks death in patients without diabetes in the two big cohorts (Sechterberger top quartile OR 1.69; Krinsley threefold crude gap at CV >40%) and in influenza (HR 1.34 per 10 points) — but the diabetes interaction is never significant (Fluit p=0.25; Krinsley’s adjusted association absent in diabetes), and hypoglycemia predicts death in both groups (ORs 2.5/4.2; NICE-SUGAR HRs 1.41/2.10). Variability is a risk marker, sharpest without diabetes; it is not shown to be a treatment target, and diabetes does not cleanly modify it.

cards.headline: Sechterberger 2013: glucose variability and ICU mortality, by diabetes status
cards.summary: Retrospective cohort, 10,320 ICU patients — without diabetes, highest variability quartile mortality 13.4% , adjusted OR 1.69 ; severe hypoglycemia OR 2.5 without diabetes, 4.2 with diabetes.
cards.people: 10,320 patients (8,682 without diabetes, 1,638 with diabetes)
cards.result: Median absolute glucose change was 0.6 mmol/L (≈11 mg/dL)/hour (IQR 0.4–0.8) without diabetes versus 0.8 (0.6–1.0) with diabetes; glucose SD was 1.7 mmol/L (≈31 mg/dL) (1.3–2.3) versus 2.1 (1.6–2.7) , both p<0.001. In patients without diabetes, the highest variability quartile had 13.4% mortality and adjusted OR 1.69 (p=0.001) . Severe hypoglycemia: adjusted OR 2.5 (95% CI 1.8–3.4) without diabetes and 4.2 (1.8–10.1) with diabetes
cards.watchOut: Different within-group variability cut points and observational treatment patterns limit causal comparisons
cards.source: Sechterberger MK et al., Crit Care 2013, DOI 10.1186/cc12572, PMID 23510051
cards.search: sechterberger 2013 glucose variability glycaemic control icu mortality diabetes retrospective cohort critical care median absolute glucose change standard deviation hypoglycemia odds ratio pmid 23510051

cards.headline: Krinsley 2013: glucose variability and mortality in an international ICU cohort
cards.summary: Multicenter cohort, 44,964 patients in 23 ICUs across nine countries — without diabetes, crude mortality at CV >40% was more than threefold that at CV <20%; no independent CV association in diabetes.
cards.type: Retrospective analysis of prospectively collected multicenter cohort data
cards.people: 44,964 patients in 23 ICUs across nine countries (32,084 without diabetes, 12,880 with diabetes)
cards.result: Among patients without diabetes, crude mortality at CV >40% was more than threefold that at CV <20%. Increased CV was not independently associated with mortality in diabetes after adjustment. Patients with diabetes had higher CV, and hypoglycemia below 70 mg/dL was independently associated with mortality in both groups. The threefold comparison is unadjusted, not an adjusted effect estimate
cards.watchOut: Center differences, glucose sampling and residual illness-severity confounding remain important
cards.source: Krinsley JS et al., Crit Care 2013, DOI 10.1186/cc12547, PMID 23452622
cards.search: krinsley 2013 glucose variability coefficient of variation mortality diabetes international multicenter cohort critical care 23 icus nine countries hypoglycemia pmid 23452622

cards.headline: Fluit 2026: glucose variability and ICU mortality in influenza
cards.summary: Multicenter cohort, 279 adults in 23 Dutch ICUs — ICU mortality rose across CV quartiles 14.5% to 32.9% ; HR 1.34 per 10-point higher CV; diabetes interaction p=0.25.
cards.people: 279 adults in 23 Dutch ICUs (202 without known diabetes, 77 with diabetes)
cards.result: ICU mortality across increasing CV quartiles was 14.5% , 18.3% , 18.8% and 32.9% . Per 10-percentage-point higher CV, the full-cohort HR adjusted for age, APACHE and diabetes was 1.34 (95% CI 1.05–1.72) . The formal diabetes-by-CV interaction was not significant (p=0.25), despite differing subgroup significance
cards.watchOut: Small diabetes subgroup and nonsignificant interaction prevent a firm conclusion of effect modification
cards.source: Fluit RC et al., BMC Infect Dis 2026, DOI 10.1186/s12879-026-13221-w, PMID 41935315
cards.search: fluit 2026 glucose variability coefficient of variation icu mortality influenza diabetes interaction dutch icus bmc infectious diseases hazard ratio pmid 41935315

cards.headline: Finfer 2012 (NICE-SUGAR): hypoglycemia and risk of death
cards.summary: Secondary analysis, 6,026 critically ill patients — mortality 23.5% without hypoglycemia, 28.5% moderate, 35.4% severe; adjusted HRs 1.41 and 2.10 .
cards.type: Observational secondary analysis within a randomized glucose-control trial
cards.people: 6,026 critically ill patients
cards.result: Mortality was 726/3,089 (23.5%) without hypoglycemia, 774/2,714 (28.5%) with moderate hypoglycemia (41–70 mg/dL), and 79/223 (35.4%) with severe hypoglycemia (≤40 mg/dL). Adjusted mortality HRs versus none were 1.41 (95% CI 1.21–1.62) and 2.10 (1.59–2.77) . These are overall estimates, not diabetes-specific subgroup estimates
cards.watchOut: Hypoglycemia was not randomized, so its association with death can include confounding and reverse causation
cards.source: NICE-SUGAR Study Investigators, Finfer S et al., N Engl J Med 2012, DOI 10.1056/nejmoa1204942, PMID 22992074
cards.search: finfer 2012 nice-sugar hypoglycemia risk of death critically ill moderate severe glucose control trial new england journal medicine hazard ratio pmid 22992074

shelves.title: When should parenteral nutrition start in the ICU?
shelves.question: In a critically ill patient whose gut cannot meet calorie targets, how early should intravenous feeding start — within two days, or not before day 8?
shelves.balance: Withholding parenteral nutrition for a week beat starting it early — fewer infections, faster recovery, same mortality — in 4,640 adults and again in 1,440 children. The exception-shaped counterweight: when enteral feeding is truly impossible, early PN at modest targets did no harm and spared some ventilator days. ‘Late by default, early only when the gut is closed’ is what the trials support. (Panel position, 2016 SCCM/ASPEN: withhold supplemental PN until day 7–8 in patients who are not malnourished — attributed, for developer verification.)

cards.headline: Waiting a week to start parenteral nutrition beat starting it early: fewer infections, faster recovery, same survival.
cards.summary: EPaNIC — late PN (not before day 8): ICU infections 22.8% vs 26.2% ; earlier discharge alive HR 1.06; ICU, hospital, and 90-day mortality the same — 4,640 adults.
cards.people: 4,640 ICU adults; early PN within 48 h vs late PN not before day 8; both groups on an early enteral protocol with tight glucose control
cards.result: ICU infections 22.8% vs 26.2% (P = 0.008); earlier discharge alive HR 1.06; ventilation >2 days 36.3% vs 40.2%; renal-replacement therapy duration 3 days shorter (median); less cholestasis; costs €1,110 lower; ICU, hospital, and 90-day mortality the same. Hypoglycemia was slightly more frequent with late PN (3.5% vs 2%)
cards.source: Casaer MP, Mesotten D, Hermans G, et al. Early versus late parenteral nutrition in critically ill adults. N Engl J Med. 2011;365:506–517. DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa1102662. PMID 21714640.
cards.search: epanic casaer 2011 early late parenteral nutrition critically ill adults new england journal infections pmid 21714640

cards.headline: When the gut could not be used, early parenteral nutrition did no harm — and spared ventilator days.
cards.summary: Doig Early PN Trial — 60-day mortality 21.5% vs 22.8% (P = 0.60); invasive ventilation 7.26 vs 7.73 days per 10 patient-ICU days — 1,372 adults with contraindications to enteral feeding.
cards.people: 1,372 adults in Australian and New Zealand ICUs with short-term relative contraindications to early enteral nutrition; early PN within 24 h vs standard care
cards.result: 60-day mortality 21.5% vs 22.8% (P = 0.60); invasive ventilation 7.26 vs 7.73 days per 10 patient-ICU days (P = 0.01); less muscle wasting and fat loss on subjective global assessment; no difference in ICU or hospital stay
cards.source: Doig GS, Simpson F, Sweetman EA, et al.; Early PN Investigators of the ANZICS Clinical Trials Group. Early parenteral nutrition in critically ill patients with short-term relative contraindications to early enteral nutrition: a randomized controlled trial. JAMA. 2013;309(20):2130–2138. DOI 10.1001/jama.2013.5124. PMID 23689848.
cards.search: doig early parenteral nutrition jama 2013 relative contraindications enteral nutrition ventilator days mortality pmid 23689848

cards.headline: In critically ill children, withholding parenteral nutrition for a week halved new infections.
cards.summary: PEPaNIC — late PN: new infections 10.7% vs 18.5% (adjusted OR 0.48); ICU stay 6.5 vs 9.2 days; mortality similar — 1,440 critically ill children.
cards.people: 1,440 critically ill children; PN within 24 h vs not before day 8
cards.result: New infections 10.7% vs 18.5% (adjusted OR 0.48, 95% CI 0.35–0.66); ICU stay 6.5 vs 9.2 days; earlier discharge alive HR 1.23; mortality similar. Hypoglycemia was more frequent with late PN (9.1% vs 4.8%)
cards.source: Fivez T, Kerklaan D, Mesotten D, et al. Early versus Late Parenteral Nutrition in Critically Ill Children. N Engl J Med. 2016;374:1111–1122. DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa1514762. PMID 26975590.
cards.search: pepanic fivez 2016 early late parenteral nutrition critically ill children new england journal infections pmid 26975590

shelves.title: Enteral or parenteral: does the route matter?
shelves.question: For early nutrition in critical illness, does feeding through the gut beat feeding through a vein — or the reverse?
shelves.balance: At trial scale, the route did not decide survival or infections — early parenteral nutrition was neither the villain of the old literature nor inferior in CALORIES. The one place route bit back: full-dose enteral feeding into a vasopressor-dependent gut caused more bowel ischemia. Route matters less than dose and timing; in shock, the gut sets the limit. (Panel position: enteral preferred over parenteral when the gut works — attributed, for developer verification.)

cards.headline: Parenteral versus enteral feeding: 30-day mortality 33.1% vs 34.2% — the route decided nothing.
cards.summary: CALORIES — 30-day mortality 33.1% vs 34.2% (RR 0.97); treated infectious complications 0.22 vs 0.21 episodes — 2,400 adults, exclusive route feeding for 5 days.
cards.people: 2,400 adults (1,188 PN / 1,195 EN analyzed); early exclusive nutrition by the assigned route for 5 days
cards.result: 30-day mortality 33.1% vs 34.2% (RR 0.97, 95% CI 0.86–1.08); treated infectious complications 0.22 vs 0.21 episodes (P = 0.72); hypoglycemia less with PN (3.7% vs 6.2%); vomiting less with PN (8.4% vs 16.2%); 90-day mortality 37.3% vs 39.1% (not significant). Target calories were not achieved in most patients in either arm
cards.source: Harvey SE, Parrott F, Harrison DA, et al.; CALORIES Trial Investigators. Trial of the route of early nutritional support in critically ill adults. N Engl J Med. 2014;371:1673–1684. DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa1409860. PMID 25271389.
cards.search: calories harvey 2014 route early nutritional support parenteral enteral critically ill adults new england journal mortality pmid 25271389

cards.headline: In shock, full-dose enteral feeding matched parenteral feeding for survival — and caused more bowel ischemia.
cards.summary: NUTRIREA-2 — 28-day mortality 37% vs 35% (P = 0.33); bowel ischemia 2% vs <1% with enteral feeding (HR 3.84) — 2,410 ventilated adults on vasopressors.
cards.type: Randomized controlled multicenter open-label trial (NUTRIREA-2), stopped early for futility
cards.people: 2,410 ventilated adults on vasopressors for shock, 44 French ICUs; early EN vs early PN, both normocaloric (20–25 kcal/kg/day), within 24 h of intubation
cards.result: 28-day mortality 37% (EN) vs 35% (PN) (P = 0.33); ICU-acquired infection 14% vs 16% (not significant); bowel ischemia 2% vs <1% (HR 3.84, 95% CI 1.43–10.3); acute colonic pseudo-obstruction HR 3.7; more vomiting and diarrhea with EN. Stopped early for futility
cards.source: Reignier J, Boisramé-Helms J, Brisard L, et al.; NUTRIREA-2 Trial Investigators. Enteral versus parenteral early nutrition in ventilated adults with shock: a randomised, controlled, multicentre, open-label, parallel-group study (NUTRIREA-2). Lancet. 2018;391:133–143. DOI 10.1016/S0140-6736(17)32146-3. PMID 29128300.
cards.search: nutrirea-2 reignier 2018 enteral parenteral early nutrition shock vasopressors lancet bowel ischemia pmid 29128300

shelves.title: Glutamine and antioxidants in the ICU: the REDOXS reversal
shelves.question: Do high-dose glutamine and antioxidant supplements help critically ill patients with multiorgan failure?
shelves.balance: The supplement era’s flagship trial reversed the field: early high-dose glutamine in multiorgan failure did not just fail — mortality ran higher at every horizon. Antioxidants were simply null. What small positive trials had promised, one large blinded trial took away. (Panel position after REDOXS: parenteral glutamine not recommended for routine use in the critically ill — attributed, for developer verification.)

cards.headline: High-dose glutamine in multiorgan failure trended toward killing more patients at 28 days — and did kill more by 6 months.
cards.summary: REDOXS (glutamine) — 28-day mortality 32.4% vs 27.2% (adjusted OR 1.28; P = 0.05); 6-month mortality 43.7% vs 37.2% — 1,223 ventilated adults with multiorgan failure.
cards.people: 1,223 ventilated adults with multiorgan failure in 40 ICUs; glutamine started within 24 h of ICU admission
cards.result: 28-day mortality 32.4% vs 27.2% (adjusted OR 1.28, 95% CI 1.00–1.64; P = 0.05); in-hospital mortality 37.2% vs 31.0% (P = 0.02); 6-month mortality 43.7% vs 37.2% (P = 0.02). Small earlier trials and meta-analyses had pointed the other way
cards.watchOut: The record names no specific product or brand — products sold today may differ in safety and effectiveness.
cards.source: Heyland D, Muscedere J, Wischmeyer PE, et al.; Canadian Critical Care Trials Group. A randomized trial of glutamine and antioxidants in critically ill patients. N Engl J Med. 2013;368:1489–1497. DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa1212722. PMID 23594003.

cards.headline: The antioxidant cocktail did nothing.
cards.summary: REDOXS (antioxidants) — high-dose selenium, zinc, beta-carotene, vitamins E and C: no effect on 28-day mortality or other clinical outcomes — same 1,223-patient factorial trial.
cards.type: Blinded 2×2 factorial randomized trial (REDOXS) — antioxidant factor
cards.people: The same 1,223 ventilated adults with multiorgan failure in 40 ICUs; antioxidants vs none, crossed with the glutamine factor
cards.result: High-dose antioxidants (selenium, zinc, beta-carotene, vitamins E and C) versus none, in the same 2×2 factorial design: no effect on 28-day mortality or other clinical outcomes

shelves.title: Gastric residual volume: a ritual on trial
shelves.question: Should gastric residuals keep being aspirated and measured in tube-fed patients — and at what volume should feeds be held?
shelves.balance: Checking gastric residuals did not prevent pneumonia, and loosening the limit from 200 to 500 mL changed nothing except the number of alarms. The monitored ritual mostly interrupted feeding. Two trials, one message: the stomach’s leftover volume is not the safety signal it was treated as. (Panel position, 2016: do not use gastric residual volumes in routine monitoring; if measured, do not hold feeds below 500 mL — attributed, for developer verification.)

cards.headline: Skipping gastric residual checks did not cause more pneumonia — and more patients reached their calorie goal.
cards.summary: Reignier 2013 — ventilator-associated pneumonia 16.7% vs 15.8% without vs with monitoring (noninferior); reaching 100% of the calorie goal more likely without monitoring (OR 1.77) — 449 ventilated adults.
cards.people: 449 ventilated adults on early enteral nutrition; 227 no monitoring vs 222 monitored every 6 h with a 250 mL cutoff
cards.result: Ventilator-associated pneumonia 16.7% vs 15.8% (difference 0.9%; 90% CI −4.8 to 6.7) — noninferior. Vomiting was more frequent without monitoring; reaching 100% of the calorie goal was more likely without monitoring (OR 1.77, 95% CI 1.25–2.51; P = 0.008); no differences in other infections, ventilation duration, stay, or mortality
cards.source: Reignier J, Mercier E, Le Gouge A, et al. Effect of not monitoring residual gastric volume on risk of ventilator-associated pneumonia in adults receiving mechanical ventilation and early enteral feeding: a randomized controlled trial. JAMA. 2013;309(3):249–256. PMID 23321763.
cards.search: reignier 2013 gastric residual volume monitoring ventilator-associated pneumonia jama noninferiority pmid 23321763

cards.headline: Raising the residual-volume limit from 200 to 500 mL changed nothing but the alarm count.
cards.summary: REGANE — gastrointestinal complications 47.8% vs 63.6% at a 500 vs 200 mL limit (P = 0.004), driven by ‘high residual volume’ events themselves; pneumonia, stay, and mortality similar — 329 ventilated adults.
cards.people: 329 ventilated adults on enteral nutrition, 28 Spanish ICUs; GRV limit 500 mL vs 200 mL
cards.result: Gastrointestinal complications 47.8% (500 mL) vs 63.6% (200 mL) (P = 0.004), driven entirely by ‘high residual volume’ events themselves (26.8% vs 42.4%); diet volume ratio higher in week 1 only (88.2% vs 84.5%); pneumonia, ventilation days, ICU stay, and mortality all similar
cards.source: Montejo JC, Miñambres E, Bordejé L, et al. Gastric residual volume during enteral nutrition in ICU patients: the REGANE study. Intensive Care Med. 2010;36(8):1386–1393. DOI 10.1007/s00134-010-1856-y. PMID 20232036.
cards.search: regane montejo 2010 gastric residual volume 500 200 enteral nutrition intensive care medicine pmid 20232036

shelves.title: Glucose control in the ICU: how tight is too tight?
shelves.question: In critically ill patients, should insulin drive blood glucose down to 80–110 mg/dL — or is that the range where tight control turns harmful?
shelves.balance: One single-center trial made tight control (80–110 mg/dL) look lifesaving; every large multicenter test after it found no benefit or harm, and hypoglycemia every time. The 140–180 target in the guidelines is not a compromise — it is where the trial record actually lands. (Panel position, SCCM/ASPEN 2016 H5, strong recommendation on moderate evidence — attributed, for developer verification.)

cards.headline: Tight glucose control cut ICU deaths from 8.0% to 4.6% — in one surgical ICU, in one center.
cards.summary: Leuven SICU 2001 — ICU mortality 4.6% vs 8.0% (P<0.04); among patients staying >5 days, 10.6% vs 20.2% ; bloodstream infections −46%, dialysis −41% — 1,548 ventilated surgical patients.
cards.type: Prospective randomized controlled trial, single center (Leuven)
cards.people: 1,548 adults receiving mechanical ventilation in a surgical ICU; intensive insulin therapy vs conventional treatment
cards.result: ICU mortality 4.6% vs 8.0% (P<0.04); among patients who stayed >5 days, 10.6% vs 20.2% (P=0.005); in-hospital mortality −34%; bloodstream infections −46%; acute renal failure requiring dialysis or hemofiltration −41%; red-cell transfusions −50%; critical-illness polyneuropathy −44%; less prolonged ventilation and ICU stay
cards.watchOut: Single-center and unblinded, with a heavy early intravenous glucose load — a result this size was never reproduced anywhere else
cards.source: Van den Berghe G, Wouters P, Weekers F, et al. Intensive insulin therapy in critically ill patients. N Engl J Med. 2001;345:1359–1367. PMID 11794168.
cards.search: leuven van den berghe 2001 intensive insulin therapy surgical icu critically ill new england journal mortality 4.6 8.0 pmid 11794168

cards.headline: In medical patients, the same protocol did not cut deaths overall — 37.3% vs 40.0%.
cards.summary: Leuven MICU 2006 — in-hospital mortality 37.3% vs 40.0% (P=0.33); hypoglycemia 18.7% vs 3.1% — 1,200 medical-ICU patients.
cards.people: 1,200 medical-ICU patients expected to require ≥3 days of care; intensive insulin (80–110 mg/dL) vs conventional treatment
cards.result: In-hospital mortality 37.3% vs 40.0% (P=0.33) — no overall benefit. In the subgroup staying ≥3 days, mortality was 43.0% vs 52.5% (P=0.009) — a post-randomization subgroup, since length of stay is itself affected by treatment. Morbidity improved: less new kidney injury, faster weaning and earlier discharge. Hypoglycemia 18.7% vs 3.1%
cards.watchOut: The favorable subgroup is defined after randomization — it cannot carry the conclusion the surgical trial suggested
cards.source: Van den Berghe G, Wilmer A, Hermans G, et al. Intensive insulin therapy in the medical ICU. N Engl J Med. 2006;354:449–461. PMID 16452557.
cards.search: leuven van den berghe 2006 intensive insulin therapy medical icu new england journal mortality hypoglycemia subgroup pmid 16452557

cards.headline: VISEP was stopped early for safety: no mortality benefit, severe hypoglycemia 17.0% vs 4.1%.
cards.summary: VISEP 2008 — 28-day mortality 24.7% vs 26.0% , no difference; severe hypoglycemia 17.0% vs 4.1% (P<0.001); serious adverse events 10.9% vs 5.2% — 537 patients with severe sepsis.
cards.type: 2×2 factorial randomized trial (insulin intensity × fluid resuscitation), 18 German ICUs — stopped early for safety
cards.people: 537 evaluable patients with severe sepsis; intensive vs conventional insulin therapy, crossed with pentastarch vs modified Ringer’s lactate
cards.result: No difference in 28-day mortality ( 24.7% vs 26.0% ) or mean organ-failure score; severe hypoglycemia 17.0% vs 4.1% (P<0.001); serious adverse events 10.9% vs 5.2% (P=0.01)
cards.watchOut: Stopped early, so underpowered for mortality — but the hypoglycemia signal needed no more power
cards.source: Brunkhorst FM, Engel C, Bloos F, et al.; German Competence Network Sepsis (SepNet). Intensive insulin therapy and pentastarch resuscitation in severe sepsis. N Engl J Med. 2008;358:125–139. PMID 18184958.
cards.search: visep brunkhorst 2008 intensive insulin therapy pentastarch severe sepsis new england journal hypoglycemia stopped early pmid 18184958

cards.headline: NICE-SUGAR: tight control killed more patients — 90-day mortality 27.5% vs 24.9%.
cards.summary: NICE-SUGAR 2009 — 90-day mortality 27.5% vs 24.9% (OR 1.14, P=0.02); severe hypoglycemia 6.8% vs 0.5% — 6,104 critically ill patients.
cards.people: 6,104 adults expected to require ≥3 days of ICU care in 42 hospitals; intensive (81–108 mg/dL) vs conventional glucose control (insulin if >180, target 144–180)
cards.result: 90-day mortality 27.5% intensive vs 24.9% conventional (OR 1.14, 95% CI 1.02–1.28; P=0.02); severe hypoglycemia 6.8% vs 0.5% (P<0.001); no significant differences in ICU or hospital days, mechanical ventilation, or renal-replacement therapy
cards.watchOut: The winning conventional arm is the ancestor of today’s 140–180 guideline target — see the developer’s note on this shelf
cards.source: The NICE-SUGAR Study Investigators. Intensive versus conventional glucose control in critically ill patients. N Engl J Med. 2009;360:1283–1297. PMID 19318384.
cards.search: nice-sugar finfer 2009 intensive versus conventional glucose control critically ill new england journal 90-day mortality hypoglycemia pmid 19318384

shelves.title: Postpyloric or gastric feeding?
shelves.question: Should tube feeds be delivered past the pylorus, into the small bowel — or is the stomach good enough?
shelves.balance: Two independent meta-analyses say feeding past the pylorus cuts pneumonia by about a third; the largest single trial found nothing; mortality never moves either way. The honest reading: fewer pneumonias on paper, no survival gain, and a harder tube to place — which is why the guidelines aim it at high aspiration risk and gastric intolerance rather than everyone. (Panel positions: SCCM/ASPEN recommend, moderate-to-high quality; ESPEN Grade B — attributed, for developer verification.)

cards.headline: Feeding past the pylorus cut pneumonia by 30% across 19 trials — and the authors rated that evidence low.
cards.summary: Alhazzani 2013 — pneumonia RR 0.70 (0.55–0.90) ; VAP RR 0.68 ; mortality RR 1.08, not significant — 19 RCTs, 1,394 patients.
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized trials, Crit Care 2013
cards.people: 19 RCTs, 1,394 critically ill adults; small-bowel vs gastric feeding
cards.result: Pneumonia RR 0.70 (95% CI 0.55–0.90) ; ventilator-associated pneumonia RR 0.68 (0.53–0.89) ; mortality RR 1.08 (0.90–1.29) , not significant; aspiration RR 0.92 (ns); vomiting RR 0.91 (ns); no differences in ICU stay or ventilation duration
cards.watchOut: The authors rated their own pneumonia evidence low quality — in tension with the guideline’s moderate-to-high rating of the same body of trials
cards.source: Alhazzani W, Almasoud A, Jaeschke R, et al. Small bowel feeding and risk of pneumonia in adult critically ill patients: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized trials. Crit Care. 2013;17:R127. PMID 23820047.
cards.search: alhazzani 2013 small bowel feeding risk pneumonia critically ill systematic review meta-analysis critical care vap pmid 23820047

cards.headline: The largest single trial found no pneumonia difference at all — VAP in 18 vs 19 patients.
cards.summary: Davies 2012 (ENTERIC) — ventilator-associated pneumonia in 18 nasojejunal vs 19 nasogastric patients, no significant difference; energy delivered 72% vs 71% of target — 180 ventilated patients.
cards.type: Multicenter, randomized, double-blind trial (ENTERIC Study), ANZICS Clinical Trials Group
cards.people: 180 mechanically ventilated adults with mildly elevated gastric residual volumes, already on nasogastric nutrition; early nasojejunal feeding via a spontaneously migrating tube vs continued nasogastric feeding
cards.result: Ventilator-associated pneumonia, diagnosed by a blinded panel, in 18 nasojejunal vs 19 nasogastric patients — no significant difference; energy delivered 72% vs 71% of estimated requirements; minor gastrointestinal hemorrhage more frequent with nasojejunal feeding; no differences in mortality or length of stay
cards.watchOut: Enrolled patients with only mildly raised residuals — not the highest-aspiration-risk group the guidelines aim postpyloric feeding at; the trial was powered for energy delivery, not pneumonia
cards.source: Davies AR, Morrison SS, Bailey MJ, et al.; ENTERIC Study Investigators; ANZICS Clinical Trials Group. A multicenter, randomized controlled trial comparing early nasojejunal with nasogastric nutrition in critical illness. Crit Care Med. 2012;40(8):2342–2348. DOI 10.1097/CCM.0b013e318255d87e. PMID 22809907.
cards.search: davies 2012 enteric nasojejunal nasogastric feeding critically ill critical care medicine ventilator-associated pneumonia anzics pmid 22809907

cards.headline: Cochrane’s independent pool agrees: pneumonia RR 0.65, moderate-quality evidence.
cards.summary: Alkhawaja 2015 (Cochrane) — pneumonia RR 0.65 (0.51–0.84) , 9 trials / 819 participants; mortality RR 1.03, no difference — 14 trials, 1,109 participants.
cards.type: Systematic review, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2015
cards.people: 14 trials, 1,109 critically ill adults; post-pyloric vs gastric tube feeding
cards.result: Pneumonia RR 0.65 (95% CI 0.51–0.84) — 9 studies, 819 participants, moderate-quality evidence; mortality RR 1.03 (0.83–1.29) — no difference; the percentage of nutrition delivered was 7.8 points higher with post-pyloric feeding (low-quality evidence); no clear differences in ventilation duration or ICU stay
cards.watchOut: Caregivers were unblinded in most trials, and post-pyloric placement is technically difficult — the review leaves the placement method to local practice
cards.source: Alkhawaja S, Martin C, Butler RJ, Gwadry-Sridhar F. Post-pyloric versus gastric tube feeding for preventing pneumonia and improving nutritional outcomes in critically ill adults. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2015;(8):CD008875. DOI 10.1002/14651858.CD008875.pub2. PMID 26241698.
cards.search: alkhawaja 2015 cochrane post-pyloric versus gastric tube feeding preventing pneumonia critically ill adults cd008875 pmid 26241698

shelves.title: Early enteral nutrition: start within 24–48 hours?
shelves.question: Should enteral nutrition start within 24–48 hours of injury or ICU admission — or can it wait?
shelves.balance: Start the gut early and infections fall and hospital stay shortens. A survival benefit is suggested by small-trial meta-analyses but has not been confirmed at scale — the large dose trials (EDEN, TARGET) and the timing network meta-analysis are null on mortality, and in established shock the enteral route carries a small bowel-ischaemia signal.

cards.headline: Feeding within 24 hours was linked to far fewer deaths and pneumonias — in just 234 patients across 6 small trials.
cards.summary: Doig 2009 meta-analysis — mortality OR 0.34 (0.14–0.85) , deaths 8/119 vs 19/115 ; pneumonia OR 0.31 (0.12–0.78) — 6 RCTs, 234 participants.
cards.type: Meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials, Intensive Care Med 2009
cards.people: 6 RCTs, 234 participants; enteral nutrition within 24 h of injury or ICU admission vs standard care
cards.result: Mortality OR 0.34 (95% CI 0.14–0.85) — deaths 8/119 early vs 19/115 standard. Pneumonia OR 0.31 (0.12–0.78) — 12/41 vs 22/39 , from 2 trials
cards.watchOut: Trial quality was low and sample sizes small; the authors called for a large multicentre trial to confirm. Small trials; an effect this large is likely inflated — the direction, not the size, is the finding.
cards.source: Doig GS, Heighes PT, Simpson F, Sweetman EA. Early enteral nutrition, provided within 24 h of injury or intensive care unit admission, significantly reduces mortality and pneumonia in critically ill patients: a meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials. Intensive Care Med. 2009;35(12):2018–2027. DOI 10.1007/s00134-009-1664-4. PMID 19777207.
cards.search: doig 2009 early enteral nutrition within 24 hours meta-analysis randomised controlled trials intensive care medicine mortality pneumonia pmid 19777207

cards.headline: Full feeding from day 1 caused more pneumonia, not less — 49.3% vs 30.7%.
cards.summary: Ibrahim 2002 — ventilator-associated pneumonia 49.3% vs 30.7% (P=.020) with early full feeding; C. difficile diarrhea 13.3% vs 4.0% ; hospital mortality 20.0% vs 26.7%, not significant — 150 ventilated medical-ICU patients.
cards.type: Clinical trial, JPEN J Parenter Enteral Nutr 2002
cards.people: 150 mechanically ventilated medical-ICU patients; full requirements from day 1 vs 20% of requirements days 1–4, then full from day 5
cards.result: Ventilator-associated pneumonia 49.3% early vs 30.7% late (P=.020) — more pneumonia with early feeding. C. difficile diarrhea 13.3% vs 4.0% (P=.042). ICU stay 13.6 vs 9.8 days; hospital stay 22.9 vs 16.7 days. Hospital mortality 20.0% vs 26.7% — not significant
cards.watchOut: Allocation was consecutive rather than fully randomized
cards.source: Ibrahim EH, Mehringer L, Prentice D, Sherman G, Schaiff R, Fraser V, Kollef MH. Early versus late enteral feeding of mechanically ventilated patients: results of a clinical trial. JPEN J Parenter Enteral Nutr. 2002;26(3):174–181. PMID 12005458.
cards.search: ibrahim 2002 early versus late enteral feeding mechanically ventilated ventilator-associated pneumonia vap c difficile jpen pmid 12005458

cards.headline: Cochrane found no clear difference — and rated all of the evidence very-low quality.
cards.summary: Cochrane 2019 — no clear difference in deaths within 30 days or feed intolerance; pneumonia RR 0.77 (0.55–1.06) , uncertain — 7 RCTs, 345 participants.
cards.type: Systematic review, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2019
cards.people: 7 RCTs, 345 participants; early (<48 h) vs delayed enteral nutrition, with or without supplemental parenteral nutrition
cards.result: No clear difference in deaths within 30 days (evidence from 1 study, 38 participants) or in feed intolerance; pneumonia RR 0.77 (95% CI 0.55–1.06) (4 studies, 192 participants) — uncertain. The reviewers rated all evidence very low quality
cards.watchOut: The reviewers concluded there is insufficient evidence and called for large multicentre studies with rigorous methodology
cards.source: Fuentes Padilla P, Martínez G, Vernooij RWM, Urrútia G, Roqué i Figuls M, Bonfill Cosp X. Early enteral nutrition (within 48 hours) versus delayed enteral nutrition (after 48 hours) with or without supplemental parenteral nutrition in critically ill adults. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2019;(10):CD012340. DOI 10.1002/14651858.CD012340.pub2. PMID 31684690.
cards.search: cochrane 2019 fuentes padilla early enteral nutrition within 48 hours delayed critically ill adults very low quality pmid 31684690 cd012340

cards.headline: Marik & Zaloga 2001: early vs delayed enteral nutrition — fewer infections, shorter hospital stay.
cards.summary: Marik PE & Zaloga GP, Crit Care Med 2001 — meta-analysis of early vs delayed enteral nutrition: infections significantly fewer (relative risk reduction 0.45, 95% CI 0.30–0.66 ) and hospital stay significantly shorter.
cards.people: Patients in trials of early vs delayed enteral nutrition
cards.result: Infections significantly fewer (relative risk reduction 0.45, 95% CI 0.30–0.66 ) and hospital stay significantly shorter
cards.watchOut: The claim on this card is restricted to infections and hospital stay; no mortality claim is made here.
cards.source: Marik PE & Zaloga GP, Crit Care Med 2001; PMID 11801821
cards.search: marik zaloga 2001 early delayed enteral nutrition infections hospital stay meta-analysis critical care medicine pmid 11801821

cards.headline: NUTRIREA-2: in shock, early enteral vs early parenteral — no mortality difference, more bowel ischaemia with enteral.
cards.summary: NUTRIREA-2 (Reignier J et al., Lancet Respir Med 2018) — 2,410 ventilated adults with shock, early enteral vs early parenteral at matched calories: 28-day mortality 37% vs 35% (no difference), infections similar, but bowel ischaemia 2% vs <1% (HR 3.84) and vomiting 34% vs 20% with the enteral route.
cards.people: 2,410 ventilated adults with shock; early enteral vs early parenteral at matched calories
cards.result: 28-day mortality 37% vs 35% (no difference), infections similar, but bowel ischaemia 2% vs <1% (HR 3.84) and vomiting 34% vs 20% with the enteral route
cards.watchOut: The counterweight card: in established shock, the enteral route carried more bowel ischaemia and vomiting despite matched calories.
cards.source: Reignier J et al., Lancet Respir Med 2018; PMID 29128300
cards.search: nutrirea-2 reignier 2018 early enteral parenteral shock ventilated bowel ischaemia vomiting lancet respiratory medicine pmid 29128300 counterweight

shelves.title: Vitamin C in sepsis: the rise and fall
shelves.question: Does intravenous vitamin C — alone, or in the vitamin C–thiamine–hydrocortisone cocktail — improve outcomes in sepsis, as a widely adopted before-and-after study promised?
shelves.balance: A before-and-after study launched a thousand protocols (Marik 2017 — retrospective, not randomized, and not carded here). The randomized trials then answered in sequence: no primary benefit in CITRIS-ALI, whose celebrated mortality difference was one secondary endpoint among many; no benefit for the full cocktail in VICTAS; and in LOVIT, the largest and cleanest trial, a harm signal. The Surviving Sepsis Campaign now recommends against intravenous vitamin C. The shelf keeps the correction alongside the claim. (Panel position: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021 — attributed, for developer verification.)

cards.headline: CITRIS-ALI 2019: every primary endpoint was null — the famous mortality difference (29.8% vs 46.3%) was one secondary outcome among 46.
cards.summary: CITRIS-ALI 2019 — the primary outcomes were NOT met : modified SOFA scores fell by 3.0 points on vitamin C vs 3.5 on placebo at 96 hours (P=0.86), and neither C-reactive protein nor thrombomodulin differed significantly; 28-day mortality — 29.8% vs 46.3% — was a SECONDARY outcome, one of 46 prespecified, and 43 of the 46 showed no significant difference — 167 patients with sepsis and severe acute respiratory failure in 7 US medical ICUs.
cards.people: 167 patients with sepsis and ARDS present for less than 24 hours, in 7 medical intensive care units in the United States. Intravenous vitamin C 50 mg/kg every 6 hours for 96 hours (84 patients) vs placebo — 5% dextrose in water (83)
cards.result: All primary outcomes were null. The modified SOFA score decreased by 3 points in the vitamin C group and 3.5 points in the placebo group over 96 hours (P=0.86), and plasma C-reactive protein and thrombomodulin levels did not differ significantly between groups at any measured point. Of 46 prespecified secondary outcomes, 43 showed no significant difference . The three that did — 28-day mortality 29.8% (25 of 84) vs 46.3% (38 of 82) , P=.03, plus more ICU-free days to day 28 and more hospital-free days to day 60 — were not adjusted for multiple comparisons and are labeled exploratory by the authors. This card files the mortality figure exactly where the trial put it: among the secondary outcomes, not at the top
cards.watchOut: A secondary-outcome mortality “win” among 46 comparisons, in a 167-patient trial whose primary endpoints all failed, is the classic shape of a false positive — the statistical price of looking 46 times. Patients who died or were discharged early also stopped contributing SOFA measurements, which biases the primary comparison itself. The honest summary is the authors’ own: exploratory and hypothesis-generating. The hypothesis was then tested properly — Cards 2 and 3
cards.source: Fowler AA 3rd, Truwit JD, Hite RD, et al. Effect of vitamin C infusion on organ failure and biomarkers of inflammation and vascular injury in patients with sepsis and severe acute respiratory failure: the CITRIS-ALI randomized clinical trial. JAMA. 2019;322(13):1261–1270. DOI 10.1001/jama.2019.11825. PMID 31573637.

cards.headline: VICTAS 2021: the full cocktail — vitamin C, thiamine, hydrocortisone — gave 25 vs 26 ventilator- and vasopressor-free days. Null.
cards.summary: VICTAS 2021 — the primary outcome, ventilator- and vasopressor-free days in the first 30 days, was a median of 25 days on the combination vs 26 days on placebo (median difference −1 day, 95% CI −4 to 2; P=.85 — NULL ); 30-day mortality was 22% vs 24%; the trial was terminated early for administrative reasons, at 501 of a planned 2,000 patients — adults with sepsis-induced respiratory or circulatory failure at 43 US hospitals.
cards.people: 501 patients (median age 62 years; median APACHE II score 27; median SOFA score 9) with sepsis-induced respiratory or cardiovascular dysfunction, at 43 hospitals in the United States. Vitamin C 1.5 g, thiamine 100 mg, and hydrocortisone 50 mg, each given every 6 hours for up to 96 hours (252 patients), vs matched placebo (249); open-label corticosteroids were prescribed to about a third of patients in both groups at clinician discretion
cards.result: Ventilator- and vasopressor-free days were a median of 25 days (intervention) vs 26 days (placebo) — a median difference of −1 day (95% CI −4 to 2; P=.85) : no benefit, with the point estimate at zero. Thirty-day mortality was 22% in the intervention group and 24% in the placebo group — no significant difference. The trial was terminated early for administrative reasons — funding — having enrolled 501 of a planned 2,000 patients, so a modest effect cannot be excluded; but nothing in the data points toward one
cards.watchOut: Early termination for administrative — not efficacy or futility — reasons leaves the trial underpowered, and this card reads it honestly: “no demonstrated benefit, estimate at null,” not proof that no small effect exists. A third of both arms received open-label steroids, which could in principle dilute a cocktail effect — though it is also how the cocktail would be used in real ICUs. VICTAS remains the direct randomized test of the Marik recipe, administered whole, in the patients it was designed for
cards.source: Sevransky JE, Rothman RE, Hager DN, et al; VICTAS Investigators. Effect of vitamin C, thiamine, and hydrocortisone on ventilator- and vasopressor-free days in patients with sepsis: the VICTAS randomized clinical trial. JAMA. 2021;325(8):742–750. PMID 33620405.

cards.headline: LOVIT 2022: the largest trial found harm — death or persistent organ dysfunction 44.5% vs 38.5% (RR 1.21).
cards.summary: LOVIT 2022 — the primary outcome (death or persistent organ dysfunction at day 28) occurred in 44.5% of the vitamin C group vs 38.5% of controls (risk ratio 1.21 , 95% CI 1.04–1.40; P=0.01) — a harm signal in the trial’s primary endpoint ; death alone was 35.4% vs 31.6% (RR 1.17, CI crossing 1) and persistent organ dysfunction 9.1% vs 6.9%; organ-dysfunction scores, biomarkers, and six-month survival were otherwise similar — 872 adults with sepsis receiving vasopressor therapy in the ICU.
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind trial, N Engl J Med 2022
cards.people: 872 adults who had been in the ICU for no more than 24 hours, with proven or suspected infection as the main diagnosis, and who were receiving a vasopressor — randomised in ICUs in Canada, France, and New Zealand. Vitamin C 50 mg/kg every 6 hours for up to 96 hours (435 patients) vs matched placebo (437)
cards.result: The primary outcome occurred in 191 of 429 patients ( 44.5% ) in the vitamin C group and 167 of 434 ( 38.5% ) in the control group — risk ratio 1.21 (95% CI 1.04–1.40; P=0.01) : patients who received vitamin C had a higher risk of death or persistent organ dysfunction. Death at 28 days: 35.4% vs 31.6% (RR 1.17, 0.98–1.40). Persistent organ dysfunction: 9.1% vs 6.9% (RR 1.30, 0.83–2.05). Findings were otherwise similar between the groups — organ-dysfunction scores, biomarkers, six-month survival, health-related quality of life, stage 3 acute kidney injury, and hypoglycemic episodes; one severe hypoglycemic episode and one serious anaphylaxis occurred in the vitamin C group. The harm signal is the primary endpoint of the largest trial on this shelf, and it is stated at full weight
cards.watchOut: Read the size honestly: the composite reached significance while neither component did alone, so the finding is a genuine signal, not a license to quote a precise harm magnitude. Nothing in LOVIT indicts dietary vitamin C or correction of true deficiency — the claim tested, and refuted, was pharmacologic-dose intravenous vitamin C as a treatment for unselected sepsis. Subsequent harmonized analyses of vitamin C in sepsis and COVID-19 pointed the same direction, toward harm or no benefit
cards.source: Lamontagne F, Masse MH, Menard J, et al; LOVIT Investigators and the Canadian Critical Care Trials Group. Intravenous vitamin C in adults with sepsis in the intensive care unit. N Engl J Med. 2022;386(25):2387–2398. DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa2200644. PMID 35704292.

shelves.title: Supplemental parenteral nutrition: completing the calories early
shelves.question: Does completing calories and protein early with supplemental parenteral nutrition improve survival in critical illness?
shelves.balance: The two biggest nutrition trials of the last fifteen years both favor patience: delaying parenteral completion by a week sped recovery rather than slowing it, doubling the protein dose did nothing, and the feeding route itself is a tolerance question, not a survival one. More, earlier, is not better.

cards.headline: EPaNIC (Casaer 2011): starting parenteral nutrition on day 8, not within 48 hours, got patients out of the ICU sooner.
cards.summary: Starting parenteral nutrition not before day 8, rather than within 48 hours, discharged patients alive earlier from ICU and hospital (HR 1.06, 95% CI 1.00–1.13; P=0.04) — with ICU, hospital, and 90-day mortality the same. Full card on Shelf #77.
cards.source: Casaer MP et al., N Engl J Med 2011; PMID 21714640

cards.headline: EFFORT Protein (Heyland 2023): doubling the prescribed protein dose did not help patients leave hospital alive sooner.
cards.summary: A higher prescribed protein dose (≥2.2 vs ≤1.2 g/kg/day) did not help patients leave hospital alive sooner — discharge alive by 60 days 46.1% vs 50.2% (HR 0.91, 0.77–1.07). Full card on Shelf #21.

cards.headline: CALORIES (Harvey 2014): parenteral vs enteral delivery — tolerance differed, survival did not.
cards.summary: Early parenteral vs enteral delivery: 30-day mortality 33.1% vs 34.2% (RR 0.97, 0.86–1.08; P=0.57) — tolerance differed, survival did not. Full card on Shelf #78.

cards.headline: Reading the three together: no large trial finds a survival advantage to completing calories or protein early.
cards.summary: None of the large trials finds a survival advantage to completing calories or protein early; the small single-center studies that do are where enthusiasm should be discounted — the developer’s standing caution for this literature, his own work included.
cards.type: Reading of the three trials above, side by side
cards.result: None of the large trials finds a survival advantage to completing calories or protein early

shelves.title: Steroids in septic shock
shelves.question: In septic shock, do corticosteroids save lives — or only shorten the shock?
shelves.mesh: Shock, Septic · Hydrocortisone · Fludrocortisone · Anti-Inflammatory Agents · Double-Blind Method · Respiration, Artificial · Renal Replacement Therapy · Treatment Outcome · Humans
shelves.balance: Two mega-trials, one answer on speed, two answers on survival: hydrocortisone resolves shock faster in both; a mortality benefit appeared only when fludrocortisone was added in the sicker trial population.

cards.headline: ADRENAL (Venkatesh 2018): hydrocortisone resolved shock faster — and did not change 90-day mortality.
cards.summary: Ventilated septic shock, hydrocortisone 200 mg/day by infusion vs placebo — 90-day mortality 27.9% vs 28.8% (OR 0.95, 95% CI 0.82–1.10; P=0.50): no mortality difference; fewer transfusions ( 37.0% vs 41.7% ; OR 0.82).
cards.type: Randomized placebo-controlled trial (ADRENAL), N Engl J Med 2018
cards.people: Patients with septic shock receiving mechanical ventilation
cards.result: 90-day mortality 27.9% vs 28.8% (OR 0.95 , 95% CI 0.82–1.10; P=0.50) — no mortality difference. Shock resolved faster; transfusions were fewer ( 37.0% vs 41.7% ; OR 0.82 )
cards.watchOut: The survival answer is no; the speed answer is yes — faster shock resolution is not a mortality benefit

shelves.title: Balanced crystalloids vs saline: the biggest fluid argument in critical care
shelves.question: Every ICU resuscitates with one of two fluids. Thirty years of habit says saline; physiology says balanced. What do 34,000 randomized patients say?
shelves.mesh: Critical Illness · Fluid Therapy · Sodium Chloride · Saline Solution · Crystalloid Solutions · Isotonic Solutions · Intensive Care Units · Kidney Diseases · Humans
shelves.balance: One large single-center trial said balanced fluids win by a whisker on a kidney composite; the two big blinded multicentre trials found no mortality difference at all; pooling every patient suggests a small benefit — about one life per 250 treated, with roughly a 90% probability of being real — and a probable harm in traumatic brain injury, where saline remains the safer default. Balanced crystalloids are a reasonable default for most ICU patients; saline has not been convicted; and the size of the prize, if it exists, is small.

cards.headline: SMART: the trial that started the argument (2018)
cards.result: Semler MW et al., N Engl J Med 2018;378:829–839 (PMID 29485925 · NCT02444988). In five ICUs at a single academic center, 15,802 adults were assigned by unit-level cluster crossover to balanced crystalloids (lactated Ringer's or Plasma-Lyte A) or saline. The primary outcome — major adverse kidney events within 30 days (death, new dialysis, or persistent renal dysfunction) — occurred in 14.3% on balanced fluids vs 15.4% on saline (conditional odds ratio 0.90, 95% CI 0.82–0.99; P=0.04). Read the components honestly: none was significant alone — death OR 0.90 (0.80–1.01), new dialysis 0.84 (0.68–1.02), persistent renal dysfunction 0.96 (0.84–1.11) — and 30-day in-hospital mortality was 10.3% vs 11.1% (P=0.06). The strongest signal was the prespecified sepsis subgroup: mortality 25.2% vs 29.4% (OR 0.80, 0.67–0.97). A positive composite carried by its parts, in one center, with modest fluid volumes — promising, not decisive.

cards.headline: BaSICS: 11,000 patients, double-blind — and no difference (2021)
cards.result: Zampieri FG et al., JAMA 2021;326:818–834 (PMID 34375394 · NCT02875873). Across 75 ICUs in Brazil, 11,052 critically ill patients were randomized double-blind to Plasma-Lyte 148 or saline. Ninety-day mortality: 26.4% on the balanced fluid vs 27.2% on saline (HR 0.97, 95% CI 0.90–1.05) — no difference. The sepsis subgroup, where SMART had pointed, was also null (46.7% vs 49.0%; HR 0.93, 0.82–1.06), as was the need for dialysis. Where SMART tested a unit-level strategy in one hospital, BaSICS tested the fluids themselves, blinded, at national scale — and the whisker of benefit disappeared.
cards.search: basics zampieri balanced solution plasma-lyte 148 saline critically ill patients 90-day mortality double-blind dialysis jama 2021 pmid 34375394 nct02875873 r57.9 rxcui 9863 sodium chloride

cards.headline: PLUS: the second big blinded trial agrees with the first (2022)
cards.result: Finfer S et al., N Engl J Med 2022;386:815–826 (PMID 35041780 · NCT02721654). In 53 ICUs in Australia and New Zealand, 5,037 patients received Plasma-Lyte 148 or saline under double-blind conditions. Ninety-day mortality: 21.8% vs 22.0% (OR 0.99, 95% CI 0.86–1.14) — as close to identical as a trial gets. The sepsis subgroup matched too (25.8% in both arms), and renal outcomes did not differ. The trial stopped early amid pandemic recruitment and funding problems, so it cannot exclude a small effect — but its point estimate sits exactly on no difference, beside BaSICS.

cards.headline: BEST-Living: pooling everyone — a small probable benefit, and a warning for brain injury (2023)
cards.result: Zampieri FG, Hammond NE, et al., Lancet Respir Med (PMID 38043564) — an individual-patient-data meta-analysis of all six major trials, 34,685 patients. In-hospital mortality was 16.8% with balanced crystalloids vs 17.3% with saline (OR 0.962, 95% credible interval 0.909–1.019), giving a posterior probability of about 89.5% that balanced fluids reduce mortality — a best estimate of roughly one life saved per 250 patients treated, with dialysis slightly less frequent (5.6% vs 5.9%). The exception matters: in traumatic brain injury, mortality ran the other way (19.1% vs 14.7%; OR 1.424, credible interval 1.100–1.818; ~97.5% probability of harm). The pooled answer is therefore two answers: probably a small win for the general ICU patient, probably a loss for the brain-injured one.

shelves.title: Transfusion thresholds: how low can hemoglobin go?
shelves.question: How low can hemoglobin fall before transfusion helps more than it harms — and is the infarcting heart different?
shelves.mesh: Anemia · Erythrocyte Transfusion · Blood Transfusion · Hemoglobins · Myocardial Infarction · Critical Care · Intensive Care Units · Humans
shelves.balance: For a quarter-century the answer was simple: transfusing at a hemoglobin of 7 ties transfusing higher in the ICU, in septic shock, after hip fracture, and in cardiac surgery — and uses half the blood. MINT is the one trial that leans the other way: in acute myocardial infarction, every component favored the liberal strategy without reaching significance. Seven remains the rule almost everywhere; the acutely ischemic heart is the unresolved exception, and MINT is a trend demanding a second trial, not a verdict.

cards.headline: MINT: the exception that leads this shelf — in heart attack, restriction trended worse on everything (2023)
cards.result: Carson JL et al., N Engl J Med 2023;389:2446–2456 (PMID 37952133 · NCT02981407). 3,504 patients with acute myocardial infarction and anemia (hemoglobin below 10 g/dL) were randomized to a restrictive strategy (transfuse at 7 g/dL, permitted at 8) or a liberal strategy (keep hemoglobin at or above 10). The restrictive group received a mean of 0.7 units of red cells; the liberal group 2.5. The primary outcome — death or recurrent myocardial infarction at 30 days — occurred in 16.9% on the restrictive strategy vs 14.5% on the liberal (risk ratio 1.15, 95% CI 0.99–1.34; P=0.07). Every component leaned the same way: death 9.9% vs 8.3% (RR 1.19), recurrent infarction 8.5% vs 7.2% (RR 1.19), and cardiac death showed the widest gap (about 5.5% vs 3.2%) — yet none reached significance, and heart failure was not more frequent with the extra blood (5.8% vs 6.3%). The authors' own conclusion: a liberal strategy did not significantly reduce events, but potential harms of a restrictive strategy cannot be excluded. That is why this card stands first: the largest transfusion trial ever run in heart attack points, consistently and inconclusively, against the rule every other shelf of this library supports.
cards.search: mint carson myocardial ischemia transfusion restrictive liberal acute myocardial infarction anemia hemoglobin death recurrent infarction cardiac death heart failure new england journal 2023 pmid 37952133 humans blood transfusion erythrocyte transfusion hemoglobins recurrence nct02981407 d64.9 d62 3a9z 3a94 loinc 718-7

cards.headline: TRICC: the trial that made 7 the ICU default (1999)
cards.result: Hébert PC et al., N Engl J Med 1999;340:409–417 (PMID 9971864). 838 critically ill patients were randomized to a restrictive transfusion threshold (hemoglobin 7 g/dL, maintain 7–9) or a liberal one (threshold 10, maintain 10–12). Thirty-day mortality was 18.7% with restriction vs 23.3% with the liberal strategy (P=0.11) — not significant overall, but in-hospital mortality significantly favored restriction (22.2% vs 28.1%), and the restrictive group received about half as many units. TRICC overturned the inherited 10/30 rule (hemoglobin 10, hematocrit 30) that had governed transfusion for half a century, and every threshold trial since has been a footnote to it — except, perhaps, MINT.

cards.headline: TRISS: in septic shock, 7 ties 9 — with half the blood (2014)
cards.result: Holst LB et al., N Engl J Med 2014;371:1381–1391 (PMID 25270275 · NCT01485315). 998 patients with septic shock in Scandinavian ICUs were randomized to transfusion thresholds of 7 or 9 g/dL. Ninety-day mortality: 43.0% on the lower threshold vs 45.0% on the higher (relative risk 0.94, 95% CI 0.78–1.09; P=0.44). Ischemic events, use of life support, and severe adverse reactions were similar; the lower-threshold group received a median of 1 unit of blood against 4. TRISS closed the question TRICC had opened for the sickest defined population in the ICU: even in shock, the heart and organs tolerated 7.

cards.headline: Reading the threshold trials together: one rule, one open exception
cards.result: The pattern repeats wherever it is tested at scale. TRICS III (cardiac surgery, 5,243 patients) found a 7.5 g/dL threshold noninferior to a liberal strategy; FOCUS (hip-fracture surgery in patients with cardiovascular risk, 2,016 patients) found no difference in death or independent walking between thresholds of 8 and 10. The 2023 AABB guideline accordingly recommends 7 g/dL for most hospitalized patients, 7.5 in cardiac surgery, and 8 for orthopedic surgery or preexisting cardiovascular disease. Against that wall of agreement stands a single population: acute myocardial infarction, where the one large trial (MINT, Card 1) leaned toward liberal transfusion on death, reinfarction, and cardiac death alike, without proving it. The disciplined reading: keep 7 as the default everywhere it has been tested — and treat the infarcting heart as an open question awaiting a second trial, not as a settled exception.

shelves.title: MAP targets in shock: how high is high enough?
shelves.question: Once the fluids are in and the pressors are running, what number should the nurse be chasing — and what does chasing more cost?
shelves.mesh: Shock, Septic · Vasoconstrictor Agents · Blood Pressure · Hypotension · Atrial Fibrillation · Renal Replacement Therapy · Sepsis · Humans
shelves.balance: Aim at 65 and stop chasing more. Driving mean arterial pressure to 80–85 in septic shock saved no lives and bought atrial fibrillation; letting older patients run at 60–65 spent less vasopressor and killed no one extra — if anything, the adjusted analysis favored less drug. The Surviving Sepsis target of 65 is the rare guideline number attacked from both directions that held: higher does not help, lower does not hurt, and the kidney in chronic hypertension is the one voice still arguing for a little more.

cards.headline: SEPSISPAM: pushing MAP to 80–85 saved no one — and cost atrial fibrillation (2014)
cards.result: Asfar P et al., N Engl J Med 2014;370:1583–1593 (PMID 24635770 · NCT01149278). In 29 French ICUs, 776 patients with septic shock were randomized to a mean arterial pressure target of 80–85 mm Hg or 65–70 mm Hg. Mortality at 28 days: 36.6% on the high target vs 34.0% on the low (HR 1.07, 95% CI 0.84–1.38; P=0.57); at 90 days 43.8% vs 42.3% — no benefit at either horizon, with more vasopressor for longer in the high-target arm. The one clear difference was harm: new atrial fibrillation in 6.7% vs 2.8% (P=0.02). In the prespecified stratum with chronic hypertension, the high target was kinder to kidneys — less doubling of creatinine and less renal-replacement therapy — without any mortality difference, a renal signal that has never been converted into a survival one. A final honesty note: achieved pressures ran above the paper targets (the low arm averaged about 75), so the trial compares strategies more than exact numbers.

cards.headline: The 65 trial: in older patients, less pressor was at least as safe (2020)
cards.result: Lamontagne F et al., JAMA 2020;323:938–949 (PMID 32049269 · ISRCTN10580502). 2,600 patients aged 65 or older with vasodilatory hypotension were randomized to permissive hypotension (MAP target 60–65 mm Hg) or usual care; 2,463 were in the primary analysis (mean age 75). The permissive arm got meaningfully less vasopressor — median 33 vs 38 hours, and a median total norepinephrine-equivalent dose of 17.7 vs 26.4 mg. Mortality at 90 days: 41.0% vs 43.8% — an absolute difference of −2.85 percentage points (95% CI −6.75 to 1.05) that was NOT significant in the primary unadjusted analysis (P=0.15); the prespecified adjusted analysis favored permissive hypotension (OR 0.82, 95% CI 0.68–0.98), and a chronic-hypertension subgroup leaned the same way (adjusted OR 0.67) without the trial being powered for it. Serious adverse events were similar overall. Read it precisely: less drug did not hurt, may have helped, and proved nothing outright.

cards.headline: Reading the MAP trials together: the number that survived both attacks
cards.result: The Surviving Sepsis Campaign (PMID 34599691) recommends an initial MAP target of 65 mm Hg over higher targets (a weak recommendation on moderate-quality evidence) — and 65 is almost the only number in critical care to have been randomized from both sides. From above, SEPSISPAM: forcing 80–85 added vasopressor, added atrial fibrillation, and saved no one. From below, the 65 trial: allowing 60–65 in older patients subtracted vasopressor and subtracted no lives. What remains genuinely open is individualization — the chronic-hypertension kidney signal in SEPSISPAM is real physiology in search of an outcome, and neither trial enrolled the young trauma or neuro patient. For the standard septic adult, though, the evidence now brackets the guideline: the target is a floor to defend, not a summit to chase.

shelves.title: Vasopressor choice in shock
shelves.balance: What an agent should take from this shelf: start norepinephrine — dopamine lost on rhythm, vasopressin never won outright.

cards.headline: SOAP II 2010: dopamine bought nothing and cost rhythm
cards.result: De Backer D et al., N Engl J Med 2010;362(9):779–789 (PMID 20200382 · NCT00314704). SOAP II randomized 1,679 patients with shock of any cause to dopamine or norepinephrine as the first-line vasopressor (NEJM 2010). Twenty-eight-day mortality was statistically indistinguishable: 52.5% on dopamine versus 48.5% on norepinephrine (odds ratio 1.17, 95% CI 0.97–1.42, p=0.10). The separation was in harm: arrhythmic events occurred in 24.1% of the dopamine group versus 12.4% (p<0.001), and in the prespecified cardiogenic-shock subgroup (280 patients), dopamine was associated with significantly higher 28-day mortality (p=0.03), with no such signal in septic or hypovolemic shock. The trial is why dopamine quietly left the first-line role: equal survival, double the arrhythmias.
cards.search: soap ii 2010 de backer dopamine norepinephrine first-line vasopressor shock any cause randomized trial 28-day mortality arrhythmia arrhythmic events cardiogenic shock subgroup septic hypovolemic new england journal medicine pmid 20200382 nct00314704

cards.headline: VASST 2008: the subgroup that never became a verdict
cards.result: Russell JA et al., N Engl J Med 2008;358(9):877–887 (PMID 18305265 · ISRCTN94845869). VASST randomized 778 patients with septic shock already on open-label catecholamines to low-dose vasopressin (0.01–0.03 U/min) or additional norepinephrine (NEJM 2008). Twenty-eight-day mortality was 35.4% on vasopressin versus 39.3% on norepinephrine (p=0.26); 90-day mortality was 43.9% versus 49.6% (p=0.11); serious adverse events were essentially identical (10.3% vs 10.5%). In the prospectively defined stratum of less severe septic shock, 28-day mortality favored vasopressin (26.5% vs 35.7%, p=0.05) — but the test for interaction between the severity strata was not significant (p=0.10), so the trial does not establish the subgroup effect. Fifteen years on, vasopressin remains the second agent added to norepinephrine, never the agent that replaced it.

cards.headline: How to read this shelf
cards.result: Norepinephrine's first-line status was never won in a single trial — it accumulated. Dopamine tied on survival and lost on arrhythmias (SOAP II); vasopressin tied overall and kept a subgroup story its own interaction test could not confirm (VASST). The Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021 guideline makes norepinephrine a strong recommendation as the first-line vasopressor, with vasopressin as the usual second agent added as norepinephrine doses climb rather than escalating norepinephrine indefinitely (Evans L et al. Crit Care Med. 2021;49(11):e1063–e1143 — PMID 34599691). For the agent: the absence of a challenger victory across two decades of head-to-head trials is itself the evidence — default to norepinephrine, add vasopressin second, and reach for dopamine essentially never.

shelves.title: Steroids in severe community-acquired pneumonia
shelves.question: In severe community-acquired pneumonia, do corticosteroids save lives?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Anti-Bacterial Agents · Anti-Inflammatory Agents · Community-Acquired Infections · Critical Illness · Cytokines · Double-Blind Method · Drug Administration Schedule · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · Hospital Mortality · Hospitalization · Humans · Hydrocortisone · Infusions, Intravenous · Intention to Treat Analysis · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Male · Methylprednisolone · Middle Aged · Pneumonia · Prednisone · Respiration, Artificial · Respiratory Insufficiency · Shock · Switzerland · Treatment Failure · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: The benefit tracks severity and inflammation. In the most inflamed severe patients, methylprednisolone cut treatment failure (Torres); in all-comer hospitalized pneumonia, prednisone bought faster stability, not survival, at a glucose price (STEP); the one big mortality result is in ICU-severe disease (CAPE COD) — hydrocortisone, started early, stopped early for benefit, cutting 28-day mortality nearly in half; and one underpowered trial in an older VA population (ESCAPe) found nothing. Different steroids, different populations, different power — CAPE COD is the strongest single signal steroids have produced outside septic shock, and it is one trial stopped early, which inflates effects.

cards.headline: CAPE COD 2023: hydrocortisone cut 28-day death nearly in half (6.2% vs 11.9%) in severe pneumonia — stopped early for benefit.
cards.summary: Death by day 28 in 6.2% (25/400) on hydrocortisone vs 11.9% (47/395) on placebo (difference −5.6 percentage points, 95% CI −9.6 to −1.7; P=0.006). Among patients not ventilated at baseline, intubation followed in 18.0% vs 29.5% (hazard ratio 0.59); among those not on vasopressors, 15.3% vs 25.0% went on to need them.

Among patients not ventilated at baseline, intubation followed in 18.0% vs 29.5% (hazard ratio 0.59); among those not on vasopressors, 15.3% vs 25.0% went on to need them.

shelves.title: Temperature control after cardiac arrest: the cooling era, tested twice
shelves.question: After resuscitation from cardiac arrest, does cooling patients to 33°C save lives or brains — or is avoiding fever enough?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Body Temperature · Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation · Coma · Female · Fever · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Hypothermia, Induced · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Male · Middle Aged · Models, Statistical · Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest · Single-Blind Method · Treatment Failure · Treatment Outcome · Unconsciousness · Withholding Treatment
shelves.balance: Cooling became standard on two small 2002 trials. When the big trials finally came, both said the same thing: 33°C was no better than 36°C (TTM), and hypothermia was no better than simply preventing fever (TTM2). What survived is temperature control — fever prevention — not hypothermia. A worldwide practice, narrowed by its own evidence.

cards.headline: TTM 2013: cooling to 33°C vs 36°C after cardiac arrest — death 50% vs 48%, no difference (P=0.51).
cards.summary: Death occurred in 50% (235/473) at 33°C vs 48% (225/466) at 36°C (hazard ratio 1.06, 95% CI 0.89–1.28; P=0.51). At 180 days, death or poor neurologic function: 54% vs 52% (risk ratio 1.02).
cards.type: Randomized trial, 36 ICUs in Europe and Australia
cards.people: 939 unconscious adults resuscitated from out-of-hospital cardiac arrest
cards.result: Death occurred in 50% (235/473) at 33°C vs 48% (225/466) at 36°C (hazard ratio 1.06, 95% CI 0.89–1.28; P=0.51). At 180 days, death or poor neurologic function: 54% vs 52% (risk ratio 1.02).
cards.watchOut: This trial tested one hypothermia depth against near-normothermia — not cooling against no temperature management. Its real message: the target can be warmer; it didn't license abandoning temperature control.
cards.source: Nielsen N et al., N Engl J Med 2013 (PMID 24237006 · NCT01020916)

shelves.title: Oxygen targets in critical illness: neither lower nor higher won
shelves.question: In ICU patients on oxygen, does targeting a lower (conservative) oxygen level improve outcomes — or does liberal oxygen do harm the trials should catch?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Conservative Treatment · Female · Humans · Hypoxia · Intensive Care Units · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Male · Middle Aged · Oxygen · Oxygen Inhalation Therapy · Respiration, Artificial · Respiratory Distress Syndrome · Respiratory Insufficiency · Treatment Outcome · Ventilator Weaning
shelves.balance: Both directions were tested at scale and both came back null. HOT-ICU's low vs high PaO₂ targets in hypoxemic respiratory failure: identical mortality. ICU-ROX's conservative vs usual oxygen in ventilated patients: identical ventilator-free days and survival. The wide middle is safe; the trials retire the anxiety at both ends — extremes, not targets, are where the harm lives (neither trial tested extreme hyperoxia).

cards.headline: HOT-ICU 2021: lower (60 mm Hg) vs higher (90 mm Hg) oxygen targets in hypoxemic respiratory failure — 90-day death 42.9% vs 42.4%.
cards.summary: At 90 days, 42.9% (618/1441) in the lower-target group and 42.4% (613/1447) in the higher-target group had died (adjusted risk ratio 1.02, 95% CI 0.94–1.11; P=0.64). No difference in days alive without life support, and new ischemic episodes (shock, myocardial, stroke, intestinal) were similar between groups.
cards.people: 2,928 adults with acute hypoxemic respiratory failure receiving ≥10 L/min oxygen or FiO₂ ≥0.50
cards.result: At 90 days, 42.9% (618/1441) in the lower-target group and 42.4% (613/1447) in the higher-target group had died (adjusted risk ratio 1.02, 95% CI 0.94–1.11; P=0.64). No difference in days alive without life support, and new ischemic episodes (shock, myocardial, stroke, intestinal) were similar between groups.
cards.watchOut: Targets were PaO₂-based and separation between arms was partial, as in all oxygen trials — but the confidence interval excludes any large mortality benefit for either direction. 'Lower is better' failed its biggest test; so did 'higher is safer.'

shelves.title: Early mobilization: up sooner isn't better — in the ICU it's neutral, after stroke it harmed
shelves.question: Does mobilizing critically ill patients as early and as much as possible improve recovery?
shelves.mesh: Activities of Daily Living · Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Bed Rest · Chicago · Critical Care · Critical Illness · Delirium · Early Ambulation · Exercise Therapy · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Intensive Care Units · Iowa · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Logistic Models · Male · Middle Aged · Mobility Limitation · Occupational Therapy · Physical Therapy Modalities · Procedural Sedation · Proportional Hazards Models · Quality of Life · Recovery of Function · Respiration, Artificial · Severity of Illness Index · Single-Blind Method · Statistics, Nonparametric · Stroke · Stroke Rehabilitation · Time Factors · Treatment Outcome · Walking
shelves.balance: The arc runs small-and-positive → large-and-neutral → large-and-harmful, ordered almost perfectly by trial size and by how much of the original bundle was stripped away. Schweickert's early PT/OT — bundled with daily sedation interruption — doubled independent recovery at discharge in 104 patients. TEAM tested mobilization alone at 750 patients and found nothing but more adverse events. AVERT pushed earliest-and-most after stroke in 2,104 patients and made outcomes worse. What survives: wake patients, sit them up, ambulate as tolerated. What doesn't: mobilization as a dosed, forced, earlier-is-always-better intervention.

cards.headline: Schweickert 2009: early PT/OT in ventilated patients — 59% vs 35% back to independent function at discharge (OR 2.7). The small trial that launched a worldwide practice.
cards.summary: Return to independent functional status at hospital discharge occurred in 59% (29/49) with early physical and occupational therapy vs 35% (19/55) with usual care (P=0.02; odds ratio 2.7, 95% CI 1.2–6.1). Delirium was shorter (median 2.0 vs 4.0 days) and ventilator-free days more numerous (23.5 vs 21.1).
cards.people: 104 adults receiving mechanical ventilation in a medical ICU
cards.result: Return to independent functional status at hospital discharge occurred in 59% (29/49) with early physical and occupational therapy vs 35% (19/55) with usual care (P=0.02; odds ratio 2.7, 95% CI 1.2–6.1). Delirium was shorter (median 2.0 vs 4.0 days) and ventilator-free days more numerous (23.5 vs 21.1).
cards.watchOut: Two caveats the field spent a decade learning. The therapy was bundled with daily sedation interruption — the comparison is as much about waking as moving. And it was 104 patients at one center: when TEAM (Reference 2) tested mobilization alone at 15× the scale, the effect vanished.

cards.headline: TEAM 2022: early active mobilization in ventilated ICU patients — 143 vs 145 days alive and out of hospital at 180 days; more mobilization, no gain.

shelves.title: Early continuous neuromuscular blockade in severe ARDS: ACURASYS versus ROSE
shelves.question: In adults with early moderate-to-severe ARDS, does a 48-hour continuous cisatracurium infusion improve survival compared with usual care or placebo?
shelves.balance: ACURASYS found lower adjusted 90-day mortality with cisatracurium, although the crude mortality difference was not statistically significant. ROSE, a much larger trial using high PEEP and a lighter-sedation usual-care strategy, found virtually identical 90-day mortality. Taken together, these trials do not establish a consistent survival benefit from routine early continuous neuromuscular blockade in moderate-to-severe ARDS.

cards.headline: ACURASYS: crude 90-day mortality was 31.6% with cisatracurium vs 40.7% with placebo
cards.summary: Crude 90-day mortality was 31.6% in the cisatracurium group vs 40.7% in the placebo group. The adjusted hazard ratio for death at 90 days was 0.68 (95% CI, 0.48 to 0.98; P=0.04).
cards.people: 340 ICU patients with early severe ARDS; 178 assigned cisatracurium and 162 placebo
cards.result: Crude 90-day mortality was 31.6% in the cisatracurium group vs 40.7% in the placebo group. The adjusted hazard ratio for death at 90 days was 0.68 (95% CI, 0.48 to 0.98; P=0.04).
cards.watchOut: The primary survival advantage depended on covariate adjustment; the crude 90-day mortality comparison was not statistically significant (P=0.08). The trial also used a treatment context different from the later ROSE strategy.
cards.source: N Engl J Med, 2010 · PMID 20843245 · NCT00299650

shelves.title: Dexamethasone in hospitalized COVID-19: mortality benefit depends on respiratory support
shelves.question: In hospitalized patients with COVID-19, does dexamethasone reduce 28-day mortality, and does benefit differ by respiratory support at randomization?
shelves.balance: Dexamethasone lowered 28-day mortality in patients receiving invasive mechanical ventilation (29.3% vs 41.4%) and in those receiving oxygen without invasive ventilation (23.3% vs 26.2%). It did not reduce mortality in patients receiving no respiratory support (17.8% vs 14.0%). Benefit was therefore concentrated in patients needing respiratory support.

cards.headline: RECOVERY: dexamethasone reduced mortality with ventilation or oxygen, but not without respiratory support
cards.summary: 28-day mortality with dexamethasone vs usual care was 29.3% vs 41.4% among patients receiving invasive mechanical ventilation (rate ratio 0.64; 95% CI, 0.51 to 0.81), 23.3% vs 26.2% among those receiving oxygen without invasive mechanical ventilation (rate ratio 0.82; 95% CI, 0.72 to 0.94), and 17.8% vs 14.0% among those receiving no respiratory support (rate ratio 1.19; 95% CI, 0.92 to 1.55).
cards.people: 2,104 hospitalized patients assigned dexamethasone and 4,321 assigned usual care
cards.result: 28-day mortality with dexamethasone vs usual care was 29.3% vs 41.4% among patients receiving invasive mechanical ventilation (rate ratio 0.64; 95% CI, 0.51 to 0.81), 23.3% vs 26.2% among those receiving oxygen without invasive mechanical ventilation (rate ratio 0.82; 95% CI, 0.72 to 0.94), and 17.8% vs 14.0% among those receiving no respiratory support (rate ratio 1.19; 95% CI, 0.92 to 1.55).
cards.watchOut: This open-label platform trial showed substantial heterogeneity by respiratory support at randomization: the mortality benefit applied to patients receiving invasive mechanical ventilation or oxygen, not to those receiving no respiratory support.

shelves.title: When to start dialysis in acute kidney injury
shelves.question: In critically ill patients with severe acute kidney injury and no emergency indication, does starting renal-replacement therapy early save lives — or is it better to wait?
shelves.balance: Five randomized trials, 4,636 patients with severe acute kidney injury in intensive care: in the three large multicenter trials, starting dialysis early saved no lives — 60-day mortality 48.5% vs 49.7% when the delayed strategy waited for a conventional trigger (AKIKI), 90-day mortality 58% vs 54% in septic shock (IDEAL-ICU, stopped early for futility), and 43.9% vs 43.7% with an accelerated strategy (STARRT-AKI). Waiting let about half of AKIKI's delayed-strategy patients — and 38% in STARRT-AKI's standard arm — recover without ever being dialyzed. The one positive trial, ELAIN, was small, single-center, and mostly surgical; no multicenter trial reproduced it. Early was not harmless: more catheter bloodstream infections in AKIKI (10% vs 5%) and more survivors still dependent on dialysis at 90 days in STARRT-AKI (10.4% vs 6.0%). And waiting has a limit — AKIKI-2 found that postponing beyond the usual triggers bought no extra dialysis-free days and carried higher adjusted 60-day mortality (HR 1.65). The practice these trials support: absent an emergency indication, wait and watch — but do not postpone indefinitely.

cards.headline: AKIKI: starting dialysis immediately at stage 3 kidney injury saved no lives — and half the waiting group never needed it
cards.summary: 60-day mortality: 150 of 311 (48.5%) early vs 153 of 308 (49.7%) delayed (P=0.79). RRT was used in 98% of the early group vs 51% of the delayed group.
cards.type: Multicenter randomized trial (31 ICUs, France), open-label strategies
cards.people: 620 critically ill patients with KDIGO stage 3 acute kidney injury on mechanical ventilation, catecholamine infusion, or both, with no life-threatening complication of renal failure. Early strategy: RRT immediately after randomization. Delayed strategy: RRT only for severe hyperkalemia, metabolic acidosis, pulmonary edema, blood urea nitrogen above 112 mg/dL, or oliguria for more than 72 hours.
cards.result: 60-day mortality: 150 of 311 (48.5%) early vs 153 of 308 (49.7%) delayed (P=0.79). RRT was used in 98% of the early group vs 51% of the delayed group. Catheter-related bloodstream infections were more frequent with the early strategy (10% vs 5%, P=0.03), and urine output recovered earlier in the delayed group.
cards.watchOut: Open-label by necessity. The delayed strategy's win was avoidance, not superiority — and within it, patients who eventually needed RRT did worse than those who recovered without it, a comparison no trial can randomize.
cards.source: Gaudry S et al. Initiation strategies for renal-replacement therapy in the intensive care unit. N Engl J Med 2016;375:122–133. PMID 27181456. NCT01932190.

cards.headline: ELAIN — the one positive trial: early dialysis cut 90-day mortality in a single surgical ICU
cards.type: Single-center randomized trial (University Hospital Münster, Germany)
cards.people: 231 critically ill patients (mostly surgical, many after cardiac surgery; mean SOFA about 16) with KDIGO stage 2 acute kidney injury and plasma NGAL above 150 ng/mL. Early: RRT within 8 hours of stage 2. Delayed: RRT within 12 hours of reaching stage 3, or for an absolute indication. All received continuous venovenous hemodiafiltration.
cards.result: 90-day mortality 39.3% (44 of 112) early vs 54.7% (65 of 119) delayed — HR 0.66 (0.45–0.97), P=0.03. RRT was used in 100% of the early group and 91% of the delayed group. Renal recovery was more frequent and RRT/ventilation durations shorter with the early strategy.
cards.watchOut: Single center, 231 patients, almost all surgical — the smallest and least generalizable trial on this shelf, and the only positive one. Three large multicenter trials did not reproduce it; one positive against repeated multicenter nulls is not a fact.
