cards.people: 488 patients with early-stage septic shock and severe acute kidney injury at the failure stage of the RIFLE classification, without life-threatening complications. cards.headline: STARRT-AKI, 3,019 patients worldwide: accelerated dialysis did not lower 90-day death — and left more survivors on dialysis
cards.people: 3,019 critically ill patients with severe (KDIGO stage 2–3) acute kidney injury and no emergency indication. Accelerated strategy: RRT within 12 hours of meeting eligibility. Standard strategy: RRT discouraged unless conventional indications developed or AKI persisted beyond 72 hours.
cards.result: 90-day death: 643 of 1,465 (43.9%) accelerated vs 639 of 1,462 (43.7%) standard — RR 1.00 (0.93–1.09), P=0.92. RRT was used in 96.8% vs 61.8%. Among 90-day survivors, continued dialysis dependence was 10.4% vs 6.0% (RR 1.74; 1.24–2.43). Adverse events were more frequent with the accelerated strategy (23.0% vs 16.5%, P<0.001), including more hypotension and hypophosphatemia.

cards.summary: Median RRT-free days to day 28: 12 (IQR 0–25) delayed vs 10 (0–24) more-delayed (P=0.93) — no gain from waiting longer.
cards.type: Multicenter randomized trial (39 ICUs, France), open-label
cards.people: 278 critically ill patients with KDIGO stage 3 acute kidney injury who had oliguria for more than 72 hours or a blood urea nitrogen above 112 mg/dL, without an emergency indication. Delayed strategy: RRT started just after randomization. More-delayed strategy: RRT postponed until a mandatory indication (hyperkalemia, metabolic acidosis, pulmonary edema) or BUN reached 140 mg/dL.
cards.result: Median RRT-free days to day 28: 12 (IQR 0–25) delayed vs 10 (0–24) more-delayed (P=0.93) — no gain from waiting longer. Complications potentially related to AKI or RRT did not differ.
cards.watchOut: The mortality signal is an adjusted secondary analysis in a 278-patient trial — hypothesis-raising, not proof. But it is the only randomized evidence on how far waiting can safely go, and it points the wrong way.

shelves.title: Procalcitonin-guided antibiotic decisions: fewer antibiotic days (LIKELY); a mortality claim graded POSSIBLE
shelves.question: Does a procalcitonin number help clinicians start fewer antibiotics and stop them sooner — and does anyone live longer because of it?
shelves.mesh: Procalcitonin · Calcitonin · Biomarkers · Anti-Bacterial Agents · Respiratory Tract Infections · Bacterial Infections · Humans
shelves.balance: Two claims live on this shelf and they do not share a grade. The stewardship claim — procalcitonin guidance cuts roughly 2–3 antibiotic days — replicated from PRORATA’s ICU to the Cochrane individual-patient pooling, and it is LIKELY. The mortality claim rests on that pooling’s adjusted OR 0.83, inside the not-solid band, against PRORATA’s day-60 wobble in the wrong direction and ProACT’s clean null in US emergency departments; it is POSSIBLE, and the null is printed on the shelf, not in a footnote. Where baseline prescribing is already disciplined, expect the assay to add cost, not benefit. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

cards.headline: PRORATA: procalcitonin guidance freed 2.7 antibiotic days in the ICU — with a day-60 mortality wobble that never resolved
cards.summary: Antibiotic-free days by day 28: 14.3 with procalcitonin guidance vs 11.6 control (difference 2.7 days; P<0.0001). Mortality: day 28, 21.2% vs 20.4% (noninferior); day 60, 30.0% vs 26.1% — a 3.8-point gap whose confidence interval (−2.1 to 9.7) stayed inside the wide 10% margin but points the wrong way — 621 patients analyzed.
cards.type: Multicentre, prospective, open-label randomized trial (PRORATA), Lancet 2010
cards.people: 630 ICU patients aged 18 or older with suspected bacterial infection and expected stay over 3 days (311 procalcitonin, 319 control; 621 analyzed). (The abstract does not print mean age or sex mix.)
cards.result: Mortality in the procalcitonin group was noninferior at day 28 (21.2% [65/307] vs 20.4% [64/314]; absolute difference 0.8%, 90% CI −4.6 to 6.2) and day 60 (30.0% [92/307] vs 26.1% [82/314]; difference 3.8%, −2.1 to 9.7) against a 10% noninferiority margin. Patients in the procalcitonin group had significantly more days without antibiotics (14.3 vs 11.6 days; absolute difference 2.7 days, 95% CI 1.4 to 4.1; P<0.0001).
cards.watchOut: The wobble is printed, per this shelf’s rule: the day-60 point estimate favors the control arm, and only a generous 10-point margin lets it pass as ‘noninferior’. Open-label, with physicians free to override the algorithm — the trial tests offering the number, not obeying it. Funded in part by Brahms, the assay maker.

cards.headline: ProACT: in US emergency departments, procalcitonin results changed nothing — antibiotic-days 4.2 vs 4.3 (the null, printed)
cards.summary: Antibiotic-days within 30 days: 4.2 with procalcitonin guidance vs 4.3 with usual care (difference −0.05 day; 95% CI −0.6 to 0.5; P=0.87); adverse outcomes 11.7% vs 13.1% (noninferior) — 1,656 patients. The stewardship effect did not replicate where baseline prescribing was already tight.
cards.type: Multicentre randomized trial (ProACT), N Engl J Med 2018
cards.people: 1,656 patients at 14 US hospitals (826 procalcitonin, 830 usual care); 47.2% were hospitalized and 59.4% received antibiotics within 30 days. (The abstract does not print mean age or sex mix.)
cards.result: There was no significant difference between the procalcitonin group and the usual-care group in antibiotic-days (mean 4.2 and 4.3 days; difference −0.05 day; 95% CI −0.6 to 0.5; P=0.87) or in adverse outcomes within 30 days (11.7% vs 13.1%; difference −1.5 percentage points; 95% CI −4.6 to 1.7; P<0.001 for noninferiority). The authors’ conclusion: providing procalcitonin results did not result in less antibiotic use than usual care.
cards.watchOut: The null is printed beside the positive trials on purpose: ProACT’s sites already had high adherence to pneumonia quality measures, and clinicians often prescribed against the assay’s advice — a biomarker cannot steward a system that is already stewarded, or that ignores it. cards.headline: Schuetz 2017 (Cochrane individual-patient meta-analysis): procalcitonin guidance — fewer antibiotic days, and a mortality signal graded POSSIBLE
cards.summary: Across 26 trials and 6,708 participants with acute respiratory infections: mortality 8.6% with procalcitonin guidance vs 10.0% control (adjusted odds ratio 0.83 , 95% CI 0.70 to 0.99), alongside about 2.4 fewer antibiotic days and fewer antibiotic side effects.
cards.type: Cochrane systematic review and individual participant data meta-analysis (Schuetz 2017). A systematic review — no trial registry number applies.
cards.people: 6,708 participants from 26 randomized trials of adults with acute respiratory infections, across primary care, emergency department, and ICU settings. (Pooled mean age and sex mix are not printed in the abstract record.)
cards.result: There were 286 deaths among 3,336 procalcitonin-guided participants (8.6%) and 336 among 3,372 controls (10.0%): adjusted odds ratio 0.83 (95% CI 0.70 to 0.99; P=0.037). Treatment failure was not significantly lower (23.0% vs 24.9%). Antibiotic exposure fell by about 2.4 days on the pooled estimate, and antibiotic-related side effects were less frequent — the stewardship finding that every large synthesis of this literature reproduces.
cards.watchOut: The mortality odds ratio of 0.83 sits inside this library’s 0.5–2.0 not-solid band for a single estimate, it pools settings where the biggest trial (ProACT, Card 2) was null, and PRORATA’s day-60 wobble (Reference 1) points the other way — so the mortality claim is graded POSSIBLE on this shelf, while the antibiotic-days claim, consistent across trials, is LIKELY.
cards.source: Schuetz P et al. Procalcitonin to initiate or discontinue antibiotics in acute respiratory tract infections. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2017;(10):CD004832. PMID 29025194 · No registry number (systematic review).

shelves.title: Antipsychotics do NOT treat delirium: the randomized trials are null — and in palliative care they made symptoms worse
shelves.question: In established delirium, do antipsychotic drugs shorten it, soften it, or save lives — in the ICU, as prophylaxis, or at the end of life?
shelves.mesh: Antipsychotic Agents · Critical Illness · Delirium · Dopamine Antagonists · Double-Blind Method · Haloperidol
shelves.balance: The null is the shelf, printed first. MIND-USA randomized 566 ICU patients with delirium to haloperidol, ziprasidone, or placebo: days alive without delirium or coma ran 8.5 on placebo vs 7.9 on haloperidol and 8.7 on ziprasidone (P=0.26) — every endpoint null. Prophylaxis failed too: REDUCE gave haloperidol to 1,789 high-risk ICU patients and moved neither survival nor delirium incidence. AID-ICU's primary outcome was null; its secondary mortality tilt (36.3% vs 43.3%) is printed on its card as a wrinkle, not a claim — one secondary endpoint does not repeal three null trials. In palliative care, Agar's trial found delirium symptom scores significantly WORSE on risperidone and haloperidol than on placebo. The contrast card is a different drug class: dexmedetomidine freed ventilator hours in agitated delirium (DahLIA). The PADIS guideline advises against routine antipsychotic use for delirium. What remains legitimate — a severely agitated patient endangering themselves or a lifeline — is symptom rescue, not delirium treatment, and no trial here licenses calling it therapy. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

cards.headline: MIND-USA (Girard 2018): the null, printed first — delirium/coma-free days 8.5 on placebo vs 7.9 haloperidol vs 8.7 ziprasidone (P=0.26)
cards.summary: 566 ICU patients with delirium (89% hypoactive): the median number of days alive without delirium or coma was 8.5 on placebo, 7.9 on haloperidol, and 8.7 on ziprasidone (P=0.26 for the overall effect). No significant effect on 30- or 90-day survival, time to freedom from ventilation, or discharge — all endpoints null.
cards.type: Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (MIND-USA), New England Journal of Medicine 2018
cards.people: 566 patients with acute respiratory failure or shock who developed hypoactive (89%) or hyperactive (11%) delirium in the ICU, randomized to intravenous haloperidol (192), ziprasidone (190), or placebo (184); median exposure to the assigned drug was 4 days. (The abstract record does not print mean age or sex mix.)
cards.result: Neither antipsychotic significantly altered the primary end point (odds ratios for the primary outcome: haloperidol 0.88; 95% CI 0.64–1.21; ziprasidone 1.04; 0.73–1.48, relative). There were no significant between-group differences in any secondary end point, nor in the frequency of extrapyramidal symptoms.
cards.watchOut: The commonest objection — 'but my delirious patients are agitated, not hypoactive' — is answered by the mix: the trial enrolled the real ICU population, in whom hypoactive delirium dominates. Doses were titrated every 12 hours to delirium presence, up to 20 mg of haloperidol daily. The drugs were not dramatically toxic here; they were simply not effective.
cards.source: Girard TD et al. Haloperidol and ziprasidone for treatment of delirium in critical illness. N Engl J Med. 2018. PMID 30346242 · NCT01211522. DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa1808217

cards.headline: REDUCE (van den Boogaard 2018): haloperidol PROPHYLAXIS in high-risk ICU patients — null on survival and delirium alike
cards.summary: 1,789 critically ill adults at high risk of delirium: median days survived in 28 days, 28 on 2-mg haloperidol vs 28 on placebo (difference 0; HR 1.003) — and all 15 secondary outcomes, delirium incidence included, not significantly different. 28-day survival 83.3% vs 82.6%.
cards.people: 1,789 critically ill adults (mean age 66.6 years; 61.4% men) without delirium but with an expected ICU stay of at least 2 days, at 21 Dutch ICUs where nonpharmacological delirium prevention was routine: haloperidol 1 mg three times daily (350 — that dose group was stopped early for futility), haloperidol 2 mg (732), or placebo (707).
cards.result: There was no difference in the median number of days patients survived in 28 days (28 vs 28 days; hazard ratio 1.003; 95% CI 0.78–1.30). None of the 15 secondary outcomes differed significantly, including delirium incidence, delirium-free and coma-free days, duration of mechanical ventilation, and ICU and hospital length of stay.
cards.watchOut: Prophylaxis was the strongest version of the claim — stop delirium before it starts, in units already running non-drug prevention — and it still failed on every endpoint. Note the setting: because Dutch ICUs already used the multicomponent measures of Shelf #340, REDUCE tests what the drug adds on top of good care. The answer is nothing measurable.
cards.source: van den Boogaard M et al. Effect of haloperidol on survival among critically ill adults with a high risk of delirium: the REDUCE randomized clinical trial. JAMA. 2018. PMID 29466591 · NCT01785290. DOI 10.1001/jama.2018.0160

cards.headline: AID-ICU (Andersen-Ranberg 2022): primary outcome null — the mortality tilt is a secondary wrinkle, printed as one
cards.summary: 1,000 ICU patients with delirium: days alive and out of hospital at 90 days, 35.8 on haloperidol vs 32.9 on placebo (adjusted mean difference 2.9 days; 95% CI −1.2 to 7.0; P=0.22) — NOT significant. The secondary wrinkle: 90-day mortality 36.3% vs 43.3% (adjusted absolute difference −6.9 points; −13.0 to −0.6).
cards.type: Multicenter, blinded, placebo-controlled trial (AID-ICU), New England Journal of Medicine 2022
cards.people: 1,000 adults with delirium admitted to an ICU for an acute condition, randomized to intravenous haloperidol 2.5 mg three times daily plus as-needed doses up to 20 mg/day (510) or placebo (490); 987 patients in the final analyses. (The abstract record does not print mean age or sex mix.)
cards.result: The primary outcome did not differ significantly between groups (adjusted mean difference 2.9 days; P=0.22). Mortality at 90 days was 36.3% in the haloperidol group and 43.3% in the placebo group — a secondary outcome. Serious adverse reactions occurred in 11 patients on haloperidol and 9 on placebo.
cards.watchOut: Read this card the way the shelf insists: the primary outcome — the one the trial was built and powered around — was null. The mortality difference is a secondary endpoint in a single trial, and it points against the larger null trials on this shelf (MIND-USA, REDUCE). It is a hypothesis for a future trial, not a reason to prescribe.
cards.source: Andersen-Ranberg NC et al. Haloperidol for the treatment of delirium in ICU patients. N Engl J Med. 2022. PMID 36286254 · NCT03392376 · EudraCT 2017-003829-15. DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa2211868

cards.headline: Agar 2017: in palliative-care delirium, antipsychotics made symptom scores WORSE than placebo
cards.summary: 247 patients with delirium receiving palliative care: delirium symptom scores at day 3 were significantly HIGHER (worse) on risperidone (+0.48 units; 95% CI 0.09–0.86; P=0.02) and on haloperidol (+0.24; 0.06–0.42; P=0.009) than on placebo, with more extrapyramidal effects. Placebo patients also survived better than haloperidol patients (HR 1.73 for death on haloperidol).
cards.type: Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, dose-titrated trial, JAMA Internal Medicine 2017
cards.people: 247 participants (mean age 74.9 years; 34.4% women; 88.3% with cancer) with life-limiting illness and delirium at 11 Australian inpatient hospice or hospital palliative-care services: risperidone 82, haloperidol 81, placebo 84, given every 12 hours for 72 hours with age-adjusted titration; all patients also received supportive care, treatment of delirium precipitants, and access to subcutaneous midazolam for severe distress.
cards.result: On the primary outcome, both active arms had worse delirium symptom scores than placebo at study end. Extrapyramidal effects were greater on risperidone (0.73; P=0.03) and haloperidol (0.79; P=0.01) than on placebo. Overall survival was better in the placebo group than in the haloperidol group (HR 1.73; 1.20–2.50; P=0.003) but not significantly different from the risperidone group.
cards.watchOut: This is the population where antipsychotics are most reflexively given — distressing delirium at the end of life — and it is the one trial where they did not merely fail but worsened the measured symptoms. Everyone in the trial received good palliative care, including midazolam rescue; the comparison isolates the antipsychotic's own contribution, and it was negative.

cards.headline: DahLIA (Reade 2016): the contrast — dexmedetomidine, a sedative of a different class, freed ventilator hours in agitated delirium
cards.summary: 74 ventilated patients whose agitation prevented extubation: dexmedetomidine added to standard care increased ventilator-free hours at 7 days (median 144.8 vs 127.5 hours; median difference 17.0 hours; 95% CI 4.0–33.2; P=0.01), hastened extubation (median 21.9 vs 44.3 hours), and accelerated delirium resolution (23.3 vs 40.0 hours).
cards.people: 74 randomized patients (median age 57 years; 24% women) in intensive care whose agitated delirium prevented extubation; 71 included in the analysis (39 dexmedetomidine, 32 placebo).
cards.result: Dexmedetomidine increased ventilator-free hours at 7 days compared with placebo (median difference 17.0 hours; P=0.01). Among 21 prespecified secondary outcomes, none was significantly worse with dexmedetomidine, and several favoured it, including time to extubation and time to delirium resolution.
cards.watchOut: Carded as a contrast, not a contradiction: dexmedetomidine is an α2-agonist sedative, not an antipsychotic, and this was 74 patients with one specific problem — agitation blocking extubation. It shows the shelf is not 'nothing works'; it is 'antipsychotics don't.' Small and single-question; any mortality effect is untested at this size.
cards.source: Reade MC et al. Effect of dexmedetomidine added to standard care on ventilator-free time in patients with agitated delirium: the DahLIA randomized clinical trial. JAMA. 2016. PMID 26975647 · NCT01151865. DOI 10.1001/jama.2016.2707

cards.headline: PADIS 2018: the guideline lands where the trials did — against routine antipsychotics for delirium
cards.summary: The Society of Critical Care Medicine's PADIS guideline suggests NOT routinely using haloperidol or an atypical antipsychotic to treat delirium in critically ill adults (conditional recommendation) — while a short course remains an option where a patient experiences significant distress or agitation.
cards.type: Clinical practice guideline (Society of Critical Care Medicine), Critical Care Medicine 2018
cards.people: Adult critically ill patients — the guideline's population. PADIS issued 37 recommendations across pain, agitation/sedation, delirium, immobility, and sleep disruption, built from the trial literature carded on this shelf.
cards.result: For delirium, PADIS conditionally recommends against the routine use of haloperidol and atypical antipsychotics as treatment — the guideline-level summary of the null trials above — while endorsing nonpharmacological, multicomponent care (the subject of Shelf #340) and reserving short-course sedation decisions for distressed or agitated patients.
cards.watchOut: A guideline card is a map of the evidence, not evidence itself — it is shelved last, as the field's own summary. Its carve-out (significant distress or agitation) matches this shelf's balance: symptom rescue for the endangered or suffering patient is a sedation decision, not a delirium cure.
cards.source: Devlin JW et al. Clinical practice guidelines for the prevention and management of pain, agitation/sedation, delirium, immobility, and sleep disruption in adult patients in the ICU (PADIS). Crit Care Med. 2018. PMID 30113379. DOI 10.1097/CCM.0000000000003299 (Guideline — no registry number applies.)

shelves.title: Stress-ulcer prophylaxis in the ICU: fewer bleeds, no mortality benefit — three trials, one pattern
shelves.question: In critically ill patients, does stress-ulcer prophylaxis prevent gastrointestinal bleeding — and does preventing it save lives?
shelves.mesh: Pantoprazole · Proton Pump Inhibitors · Gastrointestinal Hemorrhage · Peptic Ulcer · Intensive Care Units · Stress, Physiological
shelves.balance: Three large trials draw the same two-line picture, and this shelf states both lines on every card. Bleeding: pantoprazole or a PPI strategy reduced clinically important gastrointestinal bleeding in relative terms (SUP-ICU 2.5% vs 4.2%, RR 0.58; REVISE 1.0% vs 3.5%, HR 0.30; PEPTIC, PPI vs H2-blocker, 1.3% vs 1.8%, RR 0.73). Mortality: unmoved everywhere it was measured — SUP-ICU RR 1.02, REVISE HR 0.94 (NS), PEPTIC RR 1.05 leaning the other way. The feared costs of acid suppression (pneumonia, C. difficile) did not materialize in REVISE. So prophylaxis is a bleeding decision for high-risk patients, not a survival intervention; the PEPTIC cardiac-surgery subgroup mortality signal (RR 1.27) is flagged as a subgroup on Card 2, beside the dedicated cardiac-surgery analysis that did not confirm it. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

cards.headline: SUP-ICU (Krag 2018): pantoprazole cut clinically important bleeding (2.5% vs 4.2%; RR 0.58, relative) — 90-day mortality was 31.1% vs 30.4% (RR 1.02)
cards.summary: 3,298 ICU patients at risk for gastrointestinal bleeding, intravenous pantoprazole 40 mg vs placebo: clinically important GI bleeding 2.5% vs 4.2% (RR 0.58, relative) . On the same card, the outcome the trial was powered around: death by 90 days 510 (31.1%) vs 499 (30.4%) — RR 1.02 [0.91–1.13], P=0.76 . The composite of clinically important events (bleeding, pneumonia, C. difficile infection, myocardial ischemia) was 21.9% vs 22.6% (RR 0.96, relative). Fewer bleeds; no lives saved.
cards.type: Randomized, blinded, placebo-controlled trial (SUP-ICU), N Engl J Med 2018
cards.people: 3,298 adults admitted to European ICUs for an acute (unplanned) condition and at risk for gastrointestinal bleeding; 1,645 assigned to pantoprazole and 1,653 to placebo. The record does not state a mean age or sex split.
cards.result: At 90 days, 510 patients (31.1%) in the pantoprazole group and 499 (30.4%) in the placebo group had died (relative risk 1.02 [0.91–1.13]; P=0.76). Clinically important gastrointestinal bleeding occurred in 2.5% of the pantoprazole group vs 4.2% of the placebo group. At least one clinically important event occurred in 21.9% vs 22.6% (RR 0.96 [0.83–1.11]). The number of patients with infections or serious adverse reactions and the percentage of days alive without life support were similar in the two groups.
cards.watchOut: Bleeding prevented here is mostly bleeding that would have been treated, not bleeding that would have killed: an absolute reduction of 1.7 percentage points against a 90-day mortality of about 31% that did not move at all. Prophylaxis decisions on this shelf are bleeding-risk decisions, not survival decisions.
cards.source: Krag M et al.; SUP-ICU Investigators. Pantoprazole in patients at risk for gastrointestinal bleeding in the ICU. N Engl J Med. 2018;379:2199–2208. PMID 30354950 · NCT02467621 (verified against the record's own databank). DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa1714919

cards.headline: PEPTIC (Young 2020): PPI vs H2-blocker in 26,828 ventilated patients — bleeding RR 0.73 (relative), mortality RR 1.05; the cardiac-surgery subgroup signal did not survive its own dedicated analysis
cards.summary: Cluster-crossover trial, 50 ICUs: preferential proton-pump inhibitor vs preferential H2-receptor blocker. Clinically important upper GI bleeding 1.3% vs 1.8% — RR 0.73 [0.57–0.92], relative . In-hospital mortality by 90 days 18.3% vs 17.5% — RR 1.05 [1.00–1.10], P=0.054 , stated beside the bleeding figure as this shelf requires. A cardiac-surgery subgroup mortality signal (RR 1.27) was reported from the main trial's subgroup analysis and is flagged as a subgroup ; the dedicated PEPTIC cardiac-surgery secondary analysis (823 PPI vs 805 H2-blocker patients) found no mortality difference (adjusted OR 0.97 [0.55–1.70]) and no bleeding difference.
cards.type: Cluster-randomized crossover trial (PEPTIC), JAMA 2020; cardiac-surgery secondary analysis, Eur J Cardiothorac Surg 2022. The PEPTIC record carries no ClinicalTrials.gov databank entry; its registration is ANZCTR ACTRN12616000481471, stated in the record.
cards.people: 26,828 patients analyzed (mean age 58 years [SD 17]; 9,691 [36.1%] women) requiring invasive mechanical ventilation within 24 hours of ICU admission, at 50 ICUs in 5 countries. An estimated 4.1% of patients assigned PPI actually received an H2-blocker and 20.1% assigned H2-blocker actually received a PPI — crossover that dilutes both comparisons.
cards.result: Mortality at the hospital by day 90: 2,459 of 13,415 (18.3%) in the PPI group vs 2,333 of 13,356 (17.5%) in the H2RB group (risk ratio 1.05 [1.00–1.10]; absolute difference 0.93 percentage points [−0.01 to 1.88]; P=0.054). Clinically important upper gastrointestinal bleeding: 1.3% vs 1.8% (risk ratio 0.73 [0.57–0.92]; absolute difference −0.51 points; P=0.009). C. difficile infection and lengths of stay did not differ significantly. In the cardiac-surgery secondary analysis, hospital mortality was 4.3% (PPI) vs 4.8% (H2RB), adjusted OR 0.97 [0.55–1.70], with no differences in bleeding, C. difficile, or length of stay.
cards.watchOut: Two cautions stated on the card: the mortality point estimate leans against PPIs without reaching significance, in a trial with heavy treatment crossover (one in five H2RB-assigned patients got a PPI) — read it as 'no mortality benefit, possible small harm, unresolved'; and the cardiac-surgery RR 1.27 is a subgroup figure that its own dedicated analysis did not confirm — subgroup discipline applies (see the Subgroup analysis definition).
cards.source: Young PJ et al.; PEPTIC Investigators. Effect of stress ulcer prophylaxis with proton pump inhibitors vs histamine-2 receptor blockers on in-hospital mortality among ICU patients receiving invasive mechanical ventilation: the PEPTIC randomized clinical trial. cards.headline: REVISE (Cook 2024): pantoprazole cut clinically important bleeding (1.0% vs 3.5%; HR 0.30, relative) — mortality 29.1% vs 30.9% (HR 0.94, NS), no pneumonia or C. difficile excess
cards.summary: 4,821 invasively ventilated patients in 68 ICUs, intravenous pantoprazole 40 mg vs placebo: clinically important upper GI bleeding 25 of 2,385 (1.0%) vs 84 of 2,377 (3.5%) — HR 0.30 [0.19–0.47], relative; P<0.001 . Death at 90 days 696 of 2,390 (29.1%) vs 734 of 2,379 (30.9%) — HR 0.94 [0.85–1.04], P=0.25 , on the same card. Ventilator-associated pneumonia, C. difficile infection, and all other secondary outcomes were similar — the feared infection costs of acid suppression did not appear.
cards.type: Randomized controlled trial (REVISE), N Engl J Med 2024
cards.people: 4,821 critically ill adults undergoing invasive ventilation, randomized in 68 ICUs internationally. The record does not state a mean age or sex split.
cards.result: Clinically important upper gastrointestinal bleeding occurred in 25 of 2,385 patients (1.0%) receiving pantoprazole and 84 of 2,377 (3.5%) receiving placebo (hazard ratio 0.30 [0.19–0.47]; P<0.001). At 90 days, death was reported in 696 of 2,390 patients (29.1%) in the pantoprazole group and 734 of 2,379 (30.9%) in the placebo group (hazard ratio 0.94 [0.85–1.04]; P=0.25). Patient-important bleeding was also reduced with pantoprazole; all other secondary outcomes — including ventilator-associated pneumonia and Clostridioides difficile infection — were similar in the two groups.
cards.watchOut: REVISE is the largest placebo-controlled test on this shelf and it lands where SUP-ICU landed: a large relative reduction in an uncommon outcome (an absolute reduction of 2.5 percentage points) and no mortality effect in either direction. The registry number on this card was verified against the record's own databank — NCT03374800; an NCT number carried in the build brief (NCT03381807) did not match the record and was corrected at the gate.

shelves.title: AI sepsis alerts: a mortality claim resting on 142 randomized patients [Tier C]
shelves.question: Do machine-learning sepsis alert systems make patients with sepsis less likely to die?
shelves.mesh: Cohort Studies · Hospital Mortality · Humans · Machine Learning · Prospective Studies · Sepsis
shelves.balance: Every sepsis-alert claim eventually becomes a mortality claim, so this shelf is Tier C and its proposed grade is MAYBE (weak evidence). The randomized record is a single open-label trial of 142 patients reporting a 58% relative mortality reduction — an implausibly large effect at that sample size. The two large deployments agree on direction and disagree on size: TREWS (6,877 sepsis patients; adjusted relative mortality reduction 18.7% when providers confirmed alerts within 3 hours — a comparison of provider behavior, not of the alert) and COMPOSER (6,217 patients; 1.9-point absolute reduction in a before-and-after design). Alerts plausibly speed recognition; whether they save lives is unproven at any grade this library can defend. Tier C — mortality claim: built Nov 7, 2026 and held for the developer’s personal verdict; no approval stamp is claimed for this shelf. Proposed grade: MAYBE (weak evidence).

cards.headline: The only randomized trial (Shimabukuro 2017, BMJ Open Respiratory Research): a machine-learning sepsis predictor cut length of stay — and reported a 12.4-point mortality drop in 142 patients
cards.summary: 142 ICU patients analyzed (75 control, 67 algorithm) at two medical-surgical ICUs of one academic center, over a single winter (December 2016–February 2017). Average length of stay: 10.3 days with the machine-learning alerts vs 13.0 days with the standard detector (P=0.042) . In-hospital mortality ‘decreased by 12.4 percentage points’ with the algorithm (P=0.018) — stated by the authors as a 58.0% relative reduction . No adverse events were reported.
cards.type: Randomized controlled clinical trial (factorial, open-label), BMJ Open Respiratory Research 2017. Registry ID from the record’s own databank: NCT03015454. The record carries no MeSH headings; none are printed for this card. The record’s abstract does not print a mean age or sex mix, so none is stated here.
cards.people: Adult patients admitted to two participating medical-surgical intensive care units at UCSF Medical Center; outcomes analyzed for 75 patients in the control group (standard severe sepsis detector only) and 67 in the experimental group (detector plus machine-learning algorithm alerts).
cards.result: Average length of stay decreased from 13.0 days in the control group to 10.3 days in the experimental group (P=0.042). In-hospital mortality decreased by 12.4 percentage points when using the machine learning algorithm (P=0.018), a relative reduction of 58.0%. No adverse events were reported during the trial. The authors described this as the first randomized trial of a sepsis surveillance system to show significant differences in length of stay and in-hospital mortality.
cards.watchOut: Everything about this trial says ‘promising pilot’ except its P values: 142 patients, one center, two units, three months, open-label, with group assignment automatically revealed whenever the algorithm fired. A 58% relative mortality reduction from an alert is larger than the effect of almost any sepsis therapy ever tested — effect sizes like that, in samples like this, are precisely what replication usually shrinks. It is carded in full because it is the only randomization in the field; it cannot carry a mortality claim alone, which is why this shelf is Tier C.
cards.source: Shimabukuro DW et al. Effect of a machine learning-based severe sepsis prediction algorithm on patient survival and hospital length of stay: a randomised clinical trial. BMJ Open Respir Res. 2017;4(1):e000234. PMID 29435343 · NCT03015454. DOI 10.1136/bmjresp-2017-000234

cards.headline: TREWS at five hospitals (Adams 2022, Nature Medicine): patients whose alerts a provider confirmed within 3 hours had lower adjusted mortality — an association with provider behavior, not a randomization
cards.summary: 590,736 patients monitored by the TREWS early warning system across five hospitals; the analysis focused on 6,877 patients with sepsis flagged before antibiotics began. Patients whose alert a provider confirmed within 3 hours had, after adjustment, an absolute in-hospital mortality reduction of 3.3% [1.7–5.1] — an adjusted relative reduction of 18.7% [9.4–27.0] — plus less organ failure and shorter stay, compared with patients whose alerts were not confirmed within 3 hours. The mortality advantage was larger (adjusted absolute reduction 4.5%) in patients the system also flagged as high risk.
cards.type: Prospective, multi-site cohort study, Nature Medicine 2022. No registry ID — a prospective cohort study; none on the record.
cards.people: Patients monitored by the TREWS system at five hospitals; the outcome analysis covers 6,877 patients with sepsis identified by the alert before initiation of antibiotic therapy, grouped by whether a provider confirmed the alert within 3 hours.
cards.result: Adjusting for patient presentation and severity, patients whose alert was confirmed by a provider within 3 hours of the alert had a reduced in-hospital mortality rate (adjusted absolute reduction 3.3%; 95% CI, 1.7 to 5.1; adjusted relative reduction 18.7%; 95% CI, 9.4 to 27.0), reduced organ failure, and reduced length of stay compared with patients whose alert was not confirmed within 3 hours. Improvements were larger among patients additionally flagged as high risk (mortality adjusted absolute reduction 4.5%; 95% CI, 0.8 to 8.3).
cards.watchOut: Read the comparison carefully: it is not alert vs no alert — it is fast human response vs slow human response, among the alerted. Providers confirm alerts quickly in patients who look salvageable and slowly in patients who do not, and adjustment cannot fully remove that. The relative effect (about 0.81, relative) also sits inside the range this library treats as not solid for observational evidence. TREWS shows a deployed system can run at scale and that response time tracks outcomes; it does not show the alert caused the difference.
cards.source: Adams R et al. Prospective, multi-site study of patient outcomes after implementation of the TREWS machine learning-based early warning system for sepsis. Nat Med. 2022;28(7):1455–1460. PMID 35864252. DOI 10.1038/s41591-022-01894-0

cards.headline: COMPOSER before-and-after (Boussina 2024, NPJ Digital Medicine): deployment associated with a 1.9-point absolute mortality reduction across 6,217 ED sepsis patients
cards.summary: A before-and-after quasi-experimental study in two emergency departments of one health system: 6,217 adult septic patients across 705 pre-intervention days and 145 post-intervention days. Deployment of the COMPOSER deep-learning prediction model (via a nurse-facing advisory) was associated with a 1.9% absolute reduction in in-hospital mortality [0.3–3.5] — a 17% relative decrease — plus a 5.0-point absolute increase in sepsis bundle compliance and a smaller 72-hour rise in organ-failure (SOFA) scores, in a Bayesian structural time-series causal analysis.
cards.type: Before-and-after quasi-experimental study with Bayesian structural time-series analysis, NPJ Digital Medicine 2024. The record carries no MeSH headings and no registry ID; none are printed for this card.
cards.people: 6,217 adult patients with sepsis treated in two emergency departments of UC San Diego Health between January 1, 2021 and April 30, 2023, before and after the COMPOSER model’s advisory was switched on.
cards.result: Deployment of COMPOSER was significantly associated with a 1.9% absolute reduction (17% relative decrease) in in-hospital sepsis mortality (95% CI, 0.3% to 3.5%), a 5.0% absolute increase (10% relative increase) in sepsis bundle compliance (95% CI, 2.4% to 8.0%), and a 4% reduction (95% CI, 1.1% to 7.1%) in 72-hour change in SOFA score after sepsis onset, in confounder-adjusted causal inference analysis at the 95% credibility level.
cards.watchOut: Before-and-after designs inherit everything else that changed over the same months — staffing, sepsis campaigns, case mix, the tail of a pandemic. The time-series adjustment is the right tool and the authors used it, but the relative effect (about 0.83, relative) is inside this library’s not-solid band for observational evidence, and the post-intervention window (145 days) is much shorter than the pre window (705 days).
cards.source: Boussina A et al. Impact of a deep learning sepsis prediction model on quality of care and survival. NPJ Digit Med. 2024;7(1):14. PMID 38263386. DOI 10.1038/s41746-023-00986-6

cards.headline: Reading the sepsis-alert evidence together: one very small trial with a very large effect, two large deployments with small ones — and no second randomization
cards.summary: The field’s entire randomized evidence is 142 patients (Reference 1) reporting a 58% relative mortality reduction. The large real-world deployments (Cards 2 and 3, together over 13,000 sepsis patients) report far smaller associations — relative reductions of about 17–19% — from designs that cannot exclude confounding by provider behavior and by calendar time. Alert burden, false-alarm rates, and downstream antibiotic overuse are barely measured in any of them.
cards.type: Synthesis card — no new study. This card reads Cards 1–3 together and states why this shelf is Tier C with a proposed grade of MAYBE (weak evidence).
cards.people: The populations of Cards 1–3: ICU patients at one academic center (randomized, 2016–17), sepsis patients across five hospitals (prospective cohort), and ED sepsis patients at one health system (before-and-after, 2021–23).
cards.result: The randomized and non-randomized evidence point in the same direction (earlier recognition, better bundle compliance, lower reported mortality) with incompatible magnitudes. Under this library’s rules, a mortality claim resting on one small open-label trial plus observational associations inside the 0.5–2.0 band cannot be graded above MAYBE (weak evidence), and any mortality claim is Tier C — the developer’s personal ruling — regardless of grade.
cards.watchOut: Adoption has outrun evidence here more than anywhere else on this slate: these systems are already switched on in hundreds of hospitals. That is a reason to demand the second randomized trial, not a substitute for it.
cards.source: Synthesis of Cards 1–3 on this shelf (PMID 29435343; PMID 35864252; PMID 38263386).

shelves.title: Chlorhexidine oral care in the ICU: VAP benefit vs possible mortality signal
shelves.question: In mechanically ventilated ICU patients, does routine oral care with chlorhexidine reduce ventilator-associated pneumonia without increasing mortality, and does de-adopting it change ICU mortality?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Anti-Infective Agents, Local · Antibiotic Prophylaxis · Chlorhexidine · Humans · Pneumonia, Ventilator-Associated · Respiration, Artificial · Risk
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: chlorhexidine oral care reduced lower respiratory tract infections in cardiac surgery patients (relative risk 0.56), but in double-blind studies of non-cardiac surgery patients there was no significant VAP reduction (relative risk 0.88, CI includes 1) and a non-significant mortality increase (relative risk 1.13, 95% CI 0.99 to 1.29). The CHORAL de-adoption trial found no mortality benefit from stopping chlorhexidine (ICU mortality 23.5% intervention vs 21.2% control; adjusted OR 1.13, 95% CI 0.82 to 1.54). A mortality harm is therefore POSSIBLE, not proven, and no mortality benefit has been shown. PERSONAL to developer: ICU mortality topic. Proposed grade: POSSIBLE. Tier C — built Nov 8, 2026 and held for the developer’s personal verdict; no approval stamp is claimed for this shelf.

cards.headline: Klompas meta-analysis: pneumonia benefit only in cardiac surgery; mortality signal in non-cardiac surgery
cards.summary: Klompas 2014 (16 trials, 3,630 ventilated patients): chlorhexidine cut lower respiratory infections in cardiac surgery patients (relative risk 0.56 [0.41–0.77]); in double-blind non-cardiac studies there was no significant VAP reduction (0.88) and a non-significant mortality increase (relative risk 1.13 [0.99–1.29]) . No absolute mortality rates are in the abstract, and none are claimed.
cards.type: Systematic review / meta-analysis of randomized trials
cards.people: 16 randomized trials, 3,630 patients receiving mechanical ventilation; abstract does not state mean age or sex breakdown
cards.result: Lower respiratory tract infections were fewer in cardiac surgery patients randomized to chlorhexidine (relative risk 0.56, 95% CI 0.41 to 0.77). In double-blind studies of non-cardiac surgery patients there was no significant VAP difference (relative risk 0.88, 95% CI 0.66 to 1.16). Mortality: no significant difference in cardiac surgery studies (relative risk 0.88, 95% CI 0.25 to 2.14) and a non-significantly increased mortality in non-cardiac surgery studies (relative risk 1.13, 95% CI 0.99 to 1.29). No significant differences in duration of mechanical ventilation or ICU length of stay. Absolute mortality rates are not given in the abstract, so no absolute mortality difference is claimed here.
cards.watchOut: Mortality figures are reported completely for both strata above and neither is statistically significant; the signal must not be presented as proven harm. Earlier unstratified meta-analyses conflated cardiac and non-cardiac surgery and open-label with double-blind studies.
cards.source: Klompas M et al. JAMA Intern Med. 2014;174(5):751-61. PMID 24663255. Registry ID: none in the PubMed record (meta-analysis).

cards.headline: Reappraisal review: double-blind non-cardiac data showed no VAP benefit, with a possible mortality increase
cards.summary: The 2017 reappraisal restates the bias argument — subjective VAP diagnosis, antiseptic effects on cultures, cardiac-surgery dominance — and the same possible mortality signal. A review, used for the argument, not for effect sizes.
cards.people: Mechanically ventilated ICU patients in the trials reviewed; no new participants and no mean age or sex stated
cards.result: An updated meta-analysis restricted to double-blinded studies in non-cardiac surgery patients, as described in this review, showed no impact on VAP rates, duration of mechanical ventilation, or ICU length of stay, and a possible signal that oral chlorhexidine may increase mortality rates. No numeric effect estimates are given in this article's abstract, so none are claimed here.

cards.headline: CHORAL: de-adopting chlorhexidine did not reduce ICU mortality
cards.summary: CHORAL (3,260 patients, 6 Toronto ICUs): de-adopting chlorhexidine did not reduce ICU mortality — 23.5% vs 21.2% (adjusted OR 1.13 [0.82–1.54]); oral health scores improved. Stopping it changed nothing measurable either.
cards.people: 3,260 mechanically ventilated patients in 6 Toronto ICUs; 1,560 control and 1,700 intervention periods; abstract does not state mean age or sex breakdown
cards.result: ICU mortality was 399 of 1,700 (23.5%) in the intervention (de-adoption plus oral care bundle) period and 330 of 1,560 (21.2%) in the control period (adjusted odds ratio 1.13, 95% CI 0.82 to 1.54; P=0.46) — mortality is reported for both periods and the difference was not significant. Time to infection-related ventilator-associated complications (adjusted HR 1.06, 95% CI 0.44 to 2.57; P=0.90), time to extubation and oral procedural pain were similar; oral health dysfunction scores improved (-0.96, 95% CI -1.75 to -0.17; P=0.02).
cards.watchOut: De-adoption was bundled with a new standardized oral care bundle, so the trial does not isolate chlorhexidine removal alone; the mortality point estimate favoured neither arm significantly.
cards.source: Dale CM et al. Intensive Care Med. 2021;47(11):1295-1302. PMID 34609548. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03382730, from the record's own databank field.

shelves.title: Staphylococcus aureus bacteremia: switch to pills early in low-risk patients — and do not add a second drug for MRSA
shelves.question: In Staphylococcus aureus bloodstream infection, can carefully selected low-risk patients switch from intravenous to oral antibiotics after 5–7 days — and, in MRSA bacteremia, does adding an antistaphylococcal beta-lactam to vancomycin or daptomycin improve outcomes?
shelves.mesh: Staphylococcal Infections · Staphylococcus aureus · Bacteremia · Anti-Bacterial Agents · Administration, Oral · Administration, Intravenous · Humans
shelves.balance: The two halves of this shelf point in opposite directions, and both are printed. For the switch: SABATO randomized low-risk S. aureus bloodstream infection to oral switch after 5–7 days of IV therapy or continued IV, and the oral route was noninferior on SAB-related complications (13% vs 12%) — but the trial stopped at 213 of a planned 430 patients, used a wide 10-point noninferiority margin, and screened 5,063 patients to randomize 213, so it answers the question only for the carefully selected few. For the combination: a small pilot (CAMERA) hinted that adding flucloxacillin cleared MRSA bacteremia faster, but the adequately sized CAMERA2 trial found no benefit on its composite of death, persistence, relapse, or failure (35% vs 39%), a numerically higher 90-day mortality with combination therapy (21% vs 16%, not significant), and a clear kidney price — acute kidney injury in 23% vs 6% of patients not on dialysis at baseline. Faster blood-culture clearance did not translate into better outcomes, and the kidney harm was real. Proposed stamp: POSSIBLE for the early oral switch in low-risk SAB; LIKELY that adding an antistaphylococcal beta-lactam to standard MRSA therapy brings kidney harm without outcome benefit — proposed, pending the developer's review.

cards.headline: SABATO 2024: oral switch after 5–7 days was noninferior in low-risk S. aureus bacteremia — in a trial stopped at half its planned size
cards.summary: SABATO: switching low-risk S. aureus bloodstream infection to oral therapy after 5–7 days was noninferior — SAB-related complications 13% vs 12% (difference 0.7 points [−7.8 to 9.1]) — in a trial stopped at 213 of 430 planned patients.
cards.type: International, open-label, randomized, controlled noninferiority trial (SABATO), Lancet Infect Dis 2024; outcome assessors masked
cards.people: 213 adults with low-risk S. aureus bloodstream infection randomized (108 oral switch, 105 continued IV) at 31 tertiary hospitals in Germany, France, the Netherlands, and Spain, after 5–7 days of IV therapy; mean age 63.5 years (SD 17.2); 148 (69%) male, 65 (31%) female. Of 5,063 patients with S. aureus bloodstream infection assessed, only 213 were randomized — complicated infection, non-removable devices, and severe comorbidity were excluded.
cards.result: The composite primary endpoint (relapsing S. aureus bloodstream infection, deep-seated infection, or death attributable to the infection within 90 days) occurred in 14 (13%) of the oral-switch group vs 13 (12%) of the IV group — treatment difference 0.7 percentage points (95% CI −7.8 to 9.1), inside the 10-point noninferiority margin (p=0.013 for noninferiority). Serious adverse events occurred in 36 (34%) of 107 in the oral safety population vs 27 (26%) of 103 on IV (p=0.29).
cards.watchOut: Noninferiority rests on a wide 10-point margin and a trial halted early for slow recruitment (213 of 430 planned). The screening funnel is the fence: 5,063 assessed, 213 randomized. The result travels only to patients who pass the same low-risk screen — no complicated infection, no non-removable device, no severe comorbidity.
cards.source: Kaasch AJ et al. Efficacy and safety of an early oral switch in low-risk Staphylococcus aureus bloodstream infection (SABATO): an international, open-label, parallel-group, randomised, controlled, non-inferiority trial. Lancet Infect Dis. 2024;24(5):523-534. PMID 38244557 · NCT01792804.

cards.headline: CAMERA pilot 2016: adding flucloxacillin to vancomycin cleared MRSA bacteremia faster — a process signal, not an outcome
cards.summary: CAMERA pilot: adding flucloxacillin cleared MRSA bacteremia faster ( 1.94 vs 3.00 days ) — a process signal only; no difference in mortality, metastatic infection, or kidney injury.
cards.type: Open-label, multicenter pilot randomized controlled trial (CAMERA), Clin Infect Dis 2016
cards.people: 60 adults with MRSA bacteremia randomized to vancomycin alone (n=29) or vancomycin plus intravenous flucloxacillin 2 g every 6 hours for 7 days (n=31). (The abstract does not print mean age or sex mix.)
cards.result: Mean duration of bacteremia was 1.94 days in the combination group vs 3.00 days on standard therapy; in the trial's model, mean time to resolution of bacteremia in the combination group was 65% of that in the standard group (95% CI 41% to 102%; P=.06) — a relative measure whose confidence interval crosses no effect. There was no difference in 28- or 90-day mortality, metastatic infection, nephrotoxicity, or hepatotoxicity.
cards.watchOut: Sixty patients and a microbiologic endpoint: this pilot is the hypothesis, not the answer. Its clearance signal is exactly the kind of surrogate that CAMERA2 (next card) then tested against patient outcomes — and the outcome answer was different.
cards.source: Davis JS et al. Combination of Vancomycin and beta-Lactam Therapy for Methicillin-Resistant Staphylococcus aureus Bacteremia: A Pilot Multicenter Randomized Controlled Trial. Clin Infect Dis. 2016;62(2):173-180. PMID 26349552 · ACTRN12610000940077.

cards.headline: CAMERA2 2020: adding a beta-lactam to vancomycin or daptomycin did not improve outcomes in MRSA bacteremia — and injured kidneys (AKI 23% vs 6%)
cards.summary: CAMERA2, the adequately sized trial: the composite was 35% vs 39% (no benefit), 90-day mortality ran numerically higher with combination therapy ( 21% vs 16% ), and acute kidney injury was 23% vs 6% .
cards.type: Open-label, multicenter randomized clinical trial (CAMERA2), JAMA 2020; stopped early by the data and safety monitoring board for safety
cards.people: 352 hospitalized adults with MRSA bacteremia at 27 sites in 4 countries (174 combination, 178 standard therapy); mean age 62.2 years (SD 17.7); 121 women (34.4%). Combination was standard therapy (vancomycin or daptomycin) plus 7 days of an antistaphylococcal beta-lactam (flucloxacillin, cloxacillin, or cefazolin).
cards.result: The 90-day composite primary endpoint (mortality, persistent bacteremia at day 5, microbiological relapse, or treatment failure) occurred in 59 (35%) with combination therapy vs 68 (39%) with standard therapy (absolute difference −4.2%; 95% CI −14.3% to 6.0%) — not significant. Printed beside it, 90-day all-cause mortality was 35 (21%) vs 28 (16%) (difference 4.5%; 95% CI −3.7% to 12.7%), numerically favoring standard therapy. Persistent bacteremia at day 5 was less frequent with combination (19/166 [11%] vs 35/172 [20%]; difference −8.9%), but acute kidney injury in patients not on dialysis at baseline was far more frequent: 34/145 (23%) vs 9/145 (6%) (difference 17.2%; 95% CI 9.3% to 25.2%). The trial was terminated before its 440-patient target because of safety concerns.
cards.watchOut: The one endpoint that moved — day-5 culture persistence — is a surrogate; the endpoints patients feel (death, relapse, failure) did not improve, and the kidney harm is large and precise. Early termination means the trial could have missed a modest benefit, as its authors note; it could not have missed the AKI signal.
cards.source: Tong SYC et al. Effect of Vancomycin or Daptomycin With vs Without an Antistaphylococcal beta-Lactam on Mortality, Bacteremia, Relapse, or Treatment Failure in Patients With MRSA Bacteremia: A Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA. 2020;323(6):527-537. PMID 32044943 · NCT02365493.

cards.headline: Reading SABATO, CAMERA, and CAMERA2 together
cards.summary: One small stopped-early trial supports the early oral switch in heavily screened low-risk patients; the largest combination trial contradicts routine adjunct beta-lactams — no outcome benefit, real kidney harm.
cards.people: Adults with S. aureus bloodstream infection — split by the two questions this shelf asks: low-risk patients (any S. aureus) for the oral switch, and MRSA bacteremia for the combination question.
cards.result: The fence: (1) Oral switch is supported by exactly one randomized trial, stopped early, in a heavily screened low-risk minority (213 of 5,063 assessed) — reasonable to offer such patients, not yet proven beyond them. (2) Routine adjunct beta-lactam therapy for MRSA bacteremia is contradicted by the largest trial: no composite benefit, a numerically higher mortality (21% vs 16%, not significant), and a 17-percentage-point absolute excess of acute kidney injury. The in-flight trial that could change the switch half is the Staphylococcus aureus Network Adaptive Platform (SNAP) trial's early-oral-switch domain (protocol, Clin Infect Dis 2024, PMID 37921609); no in-flight trial is re-testing routine beta-lactam combination after CAMERA2's safety stop.
cards.watchOut: Do not let the pilot's faster clearance (a relative 65% time-to-resolution whose interval crosses 1) outrank CAMERA2's patient outcomes. And do not generalize SABATO past its screen: endocarditis, deep-seated infection, and non-removable devices were exclusions, not subgroups.

shelves.title: Gram-negative bacteremia: seven days is enough for uncomplicated infection
shelves.question: In hospitalized patients with uncomplicated gram-negative bacteremia who have achieved clinical stability, is 7 days of antibiotic therapy as good as 14 days?
shelves.mesh: Bacteremia · Gram-Negative Bacterial Infections · Anti-Bacterial Agents · Duration of Therapy · Humans
shelves.balance: Two randomized trials asked this question specifically in gram-negative bacteremia and both found the short course noninferior. Yahav 2019 randomized 604 stable, afebrile inpatients: the 90-day composite of death, relapse, complications, or prolonged/readmission hospitalization occurred in 45.8% on 7 days vs 48.3% on 14 days. Von Dach 2020 randomized 504 patients three ways and found 30-day clinical failure of 6.6% on fixed 7 days vs 5.5% on 14 days, with CRP-guided stopping lower still at 2.4%. The honest limits: both trials were open-label, both used a wide 10-point noninferiority margin, von Dach's observed event rates were far below what its margin assumed, and both excluded uncontrolled foci and complicated infection. The largest supporting trial, BALANCE 2025 (3,608 patients with bloodstream infection of any source except S. aureus; 90-day mortality 14.5% on 7 days vs 16.1% on 14 days), is not re-carded here — its home is Shelf 316 — but its direction agrees. Proposed stamp LIKELY — proposed, pending the developer's review.

cards.headline: Yahav 2019: 7 days was noninferior to 14 days for uncomplicated gram-negative bacteremia
cards.summary: Yahav: 7 days was noninferior to 14 for uncomplicated gram-negative bacteremia — the 90-day composite occurred in 45.8% vs 48.3% (risk difference −2.6% [−10.5 to 5.3]).
cards.type: Randomized, multicenter, open-label noninferiority trial, Clin Infect Dis 2019
cards.people: 604 inpatients with gram-negative bacteremia (306 assigned 7 days, 298 assigned 14 days) at 3 centers in Israel and Italy, randomized once afebrile and hemodynamically stable for at least 48 hours; patients with an uncontrolled focus of infection were excluded. The source was urinary in 411 (68%); pathogens were mainly Enterobacteriaceae (543/604, 90%). (The abstract does not print mean age or sex mix.)
cards.result: The primary outcome at 90 days — a composite of all-cause mortality; relapse, suppurative, or distant complications; and readmission or extended hospitalization (>14 days) — occurred in 140/306 (45.8%) in the 7-day group vs 144/298 (48.3%) in the 14-day group (risk difference −2.6%; 95% CI −10.5% to 5.3%), meeting the 10% noninferiority margin. No significant differences were seen in other outcomes or adverse events, except a shorter time to return to baseline functional status with the short course. A 7-day difference in median duration of covering antibiotics was achieved.
cards.watchOut: The composite is dominated by readmission/prolonged hospitalization, not death — this trial does not by itself prove mortality equivalence, and its 10-point margin is generous. It applies to patients already stable and afebrile for 48 hours with a controlled source; it says nothing about the unstable patient or the undrained focus.
cards.source: Yahav D et al. Seven Versus 14 Days of Antibiotic Therapy for Uncomplicated Gram-negative Bacteremia: A Noninferiority Randomized Controlled Trial. Clin Infect Dis. 2019;69(7):1091-1098. PMID 30535100 · NCT01737320.

cards.headline: Von Dach 2020: fixed 7 days — and CRP-guided stopping — were both noninferior to 14 days in gram-negative bacteremia
cards.summary: Von Dach: 30-day clinical failure was 2.4% CRP-guided, 6.6% fixed 7-day, 5.5% fixed 14-day — both shorter strategies noninferior to 14 days.
cards.type: Multicenter, noninferiority, point-of-care randomized clinical trial, JAMA 2020
cards.people: 504 adults hospitalized with gram-negative bacteremia at 3 Swiss tertiary hospitals, randomized on day 5 (±1) of effective therapy if afebrile for 24 hours without complicated infection or severe immunosuppression; median age 79 years (IQR 68–86); 306 of 503 (61%) women. Arms: CRP-guided duration (n=170), fixed 7 days (n=169), fixed 14 days (n=165).
cards.result: Clinical failure at day 30 (recurrent bacteremia, local or distant suppurative complication, restarting gram-negative therapy for suspected relapse, or death) occurred in 4/164 (2.4%) with CRP-guided therapy, 11/166 (6.6%) with fixed 7 days, and 9/163 (5.5%) with fixed 14 days (difference for 7-day vs 14-day, +1.1%; 1-sided 97.5% CI −∞ to 6.3; P<.001 for noninferiority; difference for CRP-guided vs 14-day, −3.1%; 1-sided 97.5% CI −∞ to 1.1%). By day 90, failure was 7.0% (CRP-guided), 10.6% (7-day), and 10.5% (14-day). Median antibiotic duration in the CRP group was 7 days (IQR 6–10).
cards.watchOut: The authors themselves flag the two weaknesses: a 10% noninferiority margin set against observed failure rates of only 2–7%, and imperfect adherence in the CRP-guided arm (21% protocol violations; durations ranging 5–28 days). The fixed 7-day arm is the cleanest read — and it matches Yahav.
cards.source: von Dach E et al. Effect of C-Reactive Protein-Guided Antibiotic Treatment Duration, 7-Day Treatment, or 14-Day Treatment on 30-Day Clinical Failure Rate in Patients With Uncomplicated Gram-Negative Bacteremia: A Randomized Clinical Trial. cards.headline: Reading the gram-negative duration trials together
cards.summary: Two independent trials agree a week is enough, and the much larger BALANCE trial — home on Shelf #316, cited here, not re-carded — points the same way — LIKELY.
cards.people: Hospitalized adults with uncomplicated gram-negative bacteremia who are stable and afebrile, with source control — the population both trials enrolled.
cards.result: The fence: two independent randomized trials (604 and 504 patients) found 7 days noninferior to 14, and the much larger BALANCE trial of bloodstream infection generally (3,608 patients; 90-day mortality 14.5% on 7 days vs 16.1% on 14 days) points the same way — BALANCE is carded at its home on Shelf 316 and is not re-carded here. What could change this shelf: a trial in the excluded populations (uncontrolled foci, severe immunosuppression, non-fermenter or highly resistant pathogens), where neither Yahav nor von Dach enrolled enough patients to speak. Until then, 'uncomplicated' is doing real work in the shelf title.
cards.watchOut: Noninferiority with 10-point margins in open-label trials is LIKELY territory, not certainty: the confidence intervals do not exclude a small absolute harm from stopping at 7 days, they exclude a large one. Neither trial licenses shortening therapy for S. aureus bacteremia (Shelf 502's separate question) or for undrained infection.
cards.source: Synthesis of PMID 30535100 (Yahav 2019) and PMID 32484534 (von Dach 2020), carded on this shelf; BALANCE 2025 (PMID 39565030) is home on Shelf 316 and is cited here, not re-carded, under the one-home rule.

shelves.title: Invasive candidiasis: an echinocandin first
shelves.question: For invasive candidiasis, should an echinocandin be the first drug — ahead of fluconazole and ahead of amphotericin B?
shelves.mesh: Candidiasis · Fungemia · Candida · Echinocandins · Anidulafungin · Caspofungin · Fluconazole · Amphotericin B · Antifungal Agents · Humans
shelves.balance: Two randomized trials, against two different comparators, point the same way. Against fluconazole (Reboli 2007), anidulafungin was noninferior and numerically superior on global response at the end of IV therapy (75.6% vs 60.2%), in a population that was 89% candidemia-only and 97% non-neutropenic; all-cause mortality was 23% vs 31%, a difference that was not significant (P=0.13) and is printed here as such — no mortality claim is made. Against amphotericin B deoxycholate (Mora-Duarte 2002), caspofungin was at least as effective (modified intention-to-treat success 73.4% vs 61.7%; in evaluable patients 80.7% vs 64.9%) with significantly fewer drug-related adverse events. No trial shows an echinocandin saving more lives; the case for 'echinocandin first' is response rates at least as good as either older drug, with amphotericin's toxicity avoided. Proposed stamp LIKELY — proposed, pending the developer's review.

cards.headline: Reboli 2007: anidulafungin was noninferior — and numerically superior — to fluconazole for invasive candidiasis (response 75.6% vs 60.2%)
cards.summary: Reboli: anidulafungin beat fluconazole on global response ( 75.6% vs 60.2% ); all-cause mortality was 23% vs 31%, not significant — no lives-saved claim is made.
cards.type: Randomized, double-blind, noninferiority trial, N Engl J Med 2007
cards.people: 245 adults in the primary efficacy analysis (positive baseline culture); 89% had candidemia only, Candida albicans was isolated in 62%, fluconazole resistance in vitro was infrequent, and 97% did not have neutropenia. Patients received IV anidulafungin or IV fluconazole, with oral fluconazole permitted after 10 days of IV therapy in both groups. (The abstract does not print mean age or sex mix.)
cards.result: Global response (clinical plus microbiologic) at the end of IV therapy: 75.6% on anidulafungin vs 60.2% on fluconazole (difference 15.4 percentage points; 95% CI 3.9 to 27.0) — noninferiority met, with the interval excluding zero; excluding the largest enrolling site, success was 73.2% vs 61.1% (difference 12.1; 95% CI −1.1 to 25.3). Adverse-event frequency and types were similar. All-cause mortality was 23% in the anidulafungin group and 31% in the fluconazole group (P=0.13) — not significant, and printed here beside the response result so the response advantage is never mistaken for a survival advantage.
cards.watchOut: A mostly non-neutropenic, mostly candidemia population with little fluconazole resistance: the trial does not test the echinocandin where fluconazole would fail (resistant species) — it tests it where fluconazole should work, and the echinocandin still did at least as well. The mortality gap favors anidulafungin numerically only; do not cite it as a mortality benefit.
cards.source: Reboli AC et al. Anidulafungin versus fluconazole for invasive candidiasis. N Engl J Med. 2007;356(24):2472-82. PMID 17568028 · NCT00056368.

cards.headline: Mora-Duarte 2002: caspofungin matched amphotericin B on response — and caused significantly fewer drug-related harms
cards.summary: Mora-Duarte: caspofungin matched amphotericin B on response ( 73.4% vs 61.7% ) with significantly fewer drug-related harms .
cards.type: Double-blind randomized trial, N Engl J Med 2002. Pre-registration-era trial — no registry number exists on the record
cards.people: 239 patients enrolled with clinical infection and a positive culture for Candida from blood or another site; 224 were in the modified intention-to-treat analysis. Patients were stratified by APACHE II score and neutropenia; baseline characteristics, including the percentage with neutropenia and mean APACHE II score, were similar between groups. (The abstract does not print mean age or sex mix.)
cards.result: Successful outcomes in the modified intention-to-treat analysis: 73.4% on caspofungin vs 61.7% on amphotericin B (difference after adjustment for APACHE II and neutropenic status, 12.7 percentage points; 95.6% CI −0.7 to 26.0). In patients meeting prespecified evaluability criteria, caspofungin was superior: 80.7% vs 64.9% (difference 15.4 points; 95.6% CI 1.1 to 29.7). In the candidemia subgroup, favorable response was 71.7% vs 62.8% (difference 10.0; 95% CI −4.5 to 24.5). Drug-related adverse events were significantly fewer with caspofungin.
cards.watchOut: The comparator is amphotericin B deoxycholate — the toxic formulation modern practice has already largely abandoned — so the tolerability margin overstates the advantage over today's liposomal alternative. The efficacy read ('at least as effective') is the part that travels.
cards.source: Mora-Duarte J et al. Comparison of caspofungin and amphotericin B for invasive candidiasis. N Engl J Med. 2002;347(25):2020-9. PMID 12490683 · No registry number (pre-registration-era trial).

cards.headline: Reading the echinocandin trials together
cards.summary: Two blinded trials against the two historical first-line drugs: an echinocandin at least as effective as either, and cleaner than amphotericin — echinocandin first — LIKELY.
cards.people: Adults with invasive candidiasis, predominantly candidemia; largely non-neutropenic in Reboli, mixed (stratified by neutropenia) in Mora-Duarte.
cards.result: The fence: two blinded randomized trials against the two historical first-line drugs each found an echinocandin at least as effective on response, with a cleaner harm profile than amphotericin B and similar harms to fluconazole. No mortality benefit is claimed or shown (Reboli mortality 23% vs 31%, P=0.13). The 24-month sweep adds a consistency check, not a challenge: rezafungin, a newer echinocandin, was tested against caspofungin (ReSTORE/STRIVE pooled analyses) — the field now compares echinocandins against each other because the class's first-line position is the premise. What could change this shelf: a mortality-powered trial of echinocandin vs azole in resistant-species or neutropenic populations, where these two trials were thin.
cards.watchOut: 'Echinocandin first' is a response-and-tolerability verdict, graded LIKELY on two trials. It is not a claim about species with reduced echinocandin susceptibility, deep-seated foci needing source control, or step-down timing — none of which these trials answer.
cards.source: Synthesis of PMID 17568028 (Reboli 2007) and PMID 12490683 (Mora-Duarte 2002), both carded on this shelf.

shelves.title: Invasive aspergillosis: voriconazole beat amphotericin B on response and survival; isavuconazole matched voriconazole with fewer drug harms
shelves.question: For primary therapy of invasive aspergillosis, what replaced amphotericin B — and is the newer triazole, isavuconazole, as good as voriconazole?
shelves.mesh: Aspergillosis · Amphotericin B · Voriconazole · Antifungal Agents · Triazoles · Mycoses · Humans
shelves.balance: One unblinded trial moved the standard. Herbrecht 2002 randomized 277 patients with definite or probable invasive aspergillosis: successful outcomes at week 12 were 52.8% on voriconazole vs 31.6% on amphotericin B deoxycholate, and 12-week survival was 70.8% vs 57.9% — mortality 29.2% vs 42.1%, hazard ratio 0.59 (95% CI 0.40 to 0.88), a relative measure printed here beside the absolute rates; because this shelf carries a mortality claim it is Tier C and returns for the developer's personal verdict. Voriconazole's price was transient visual disturbances in 44.8% of patients, against fewer severe drug-related adverse events overall than amphotericin B. Fourteen years later, SECURE found isavuconazole noninferior to voriconazole on its primary endpoint of day-42 all-cause mortality (19% vs 20%) with fewer drug-related adverse events (42% vs 60%). Proposed grade: LIKELY. Tier C — built Nov 8, 2026 and held for the developer’s personal verdict; no approval stamp is claimed for this shelf.

cards.headline: Herbrecht 2002: voriconazole beat amphotericin B on response (52.8% vs 31.6%) and on 12-week survival (70.8% vs 57.9%)
cards.summary: Herbrecht: voriconazole beat amphotericin B on response ( 52.8% vs 31.6% ) and on 12-week survival ( 70.8% vs 57.9% — mortality 29.2% vs 42.1%; HR 0.59, a relative measure) — an unblinded trial carrying a Tier C survival claim.
cards.type: Randomized, unblinded trial, N Engl J Med 2002. Pre-registration-era trial — no registry number exists on the record. Tier C card: carries a mortality claim
cards.people: 277 patients with definite or probable invasive aspergillosis received at least one dose (144 voriconazole, 133 amphotericin B deoxycholate); the underlying condition in most was allogeneic hematopoietic-cell transplantation, acute leukemia, or other hematologic disease. (The abstract does not print mean age or sex mix.)
cards.result: At week 12, successful outcomes (complete or partial response) occurred in 52.8% on voriconazole vs 31.6% on amphotericin B (absolute difference 21.2 percentage points; 95% CI 10.4 to 32.9). Survival at 12 weeks was 70.8% vs 57.9% — that is, mortality 29.2% vs 42.1%, an absolute difference of about 13 percentage points; the hazard ratio was 0.59 (95% CI 0.40 to 0.88), a relative measure. Voriconazole patients had significantly fewer severe drug-related adverse events, but transient visual disturbances were common on voriconazole (44.8%).
cards.watchOut: A single, unblinded trial against amphotericin B deoxycholate, with other licensed antifungals allowed on failure or intolerance — the survival advantage is real in this trial and unreplicated against any modern comparator. That combination (mortality claim, one trial, unblinded) is why the shelf is Tier C and capped at LIKELY.
cards.source: Herbrecht R et al. Voriconazole versus amphotericin B for primary therapy of invasive aspergillosis. N Engl J Med. 2002;347(6):408-15. PMID 12167683 · No registry number (pre-registration-era trial).

cards.headline: SECURE 2016: isavuconazole was noninferior to voriconazole for invasive mould disease (day-42 mortality 19% vs 20%) — with fewer drug-related harms
cards.summary: SECURE: isavuconazole was noninferior to voriconazole (day-42 all-cause mortality 19% vs 20% ) with fewer drug-related adverse events ( 42% vs 60% ).
cards.type: Phase 3, double-blind, global multicenter randomized noninferiority trial (SECURE), Lancet 2016
cards.people: 527 adults with suspected invasive mould disease were randomized; 516 received study medication (258 per group) and form the intention-to-treat population for the primary endpoint. (The abstract does not print mean age or sex mix.)
cards.result: All-cause mortality from first dose to day 42: 19% (48 patients) on isavuconazole vs 20% (52 patients) on voriconazole (adjusted treatment difference −1.0%; 95% CI −7.8 to 5.7), inside the 10% noninferiority margin. Treatment-emergent adverse events were near-universal in both groups (96% vs 98%), but drug-related adverse events were fewer with isavuconazole (109 patients, 42%) than voriconazole (155, 60%; p<0.001), including hepatobiliary disorders (9% vs 16%; p=0.016), eye disorders (15% vs 27%; p=0.002), and skin or subcutaneous disorders (33% vs 42%; p=0.037).
cards.watchOut: SECURE enrolled suspected invasive mould disease, not proven aspergillosis alone, and noninferiority on mortality with a 10-point margin is a 'not worse by much' statement. The tolerability advantage — fewer eye, liver, and skin drug effects — is the trial's most concrete patient-level difference.
cards.source: Maertens JA et al. Isavuconazole versus voriconazole for primary treatment of invasive mould disease caused by Aspergillus and other filamentous fungi (SECURE): a phase 3, randomised-controlled, non-inferiority trial. Lancet. 2016;387(10020):760-9. PMID 26684607 · NCT00412893.

cards.headline: Reading Herbrecht and SECURE together
cards.summary: One unblinded trial put voriconazole ahead on response and survival; one blinded trial matched the newer triazole to it with fewer harms — and no second trial replicates Herbrecht’s survival result.
cards.people: Patients with invasive aspergillosis and other invasive mould disease, predominantly with hematologic malignancy or transplantation.
cards.result: The fence: the triazole era rests on one unblinded trial (Herbrecht) in which voriconazole beat the old standard on both response and survival, and one blinded trial (SECURE) in which the newer triazole matched voriconazole on mortality with fewer drug-related harms. No trial compares any triazole against a modern liposomal amphotericin strategy for primary therapy, and no second trial replicates Herbrecht's survival result — so the survival claim is carried as Tier C, stamped LIKELY, and fenced to the comparison actually made. What could change this shelf: a head-to-head trial of a triazole vs liposomal amphotericin B, or outcome data in triazole-resistant Aspergillus, where both trials predate the resistance problem.
cards.watchOut: Do not merge the two trials' mortality numbers into a single claim: Herbrecht's is a superiority result against a toxic, abandoned comparator; SECURE's is a noninferiority result against the current standard. They support the same first-line class for different reasons.
cards.source: Synthesis of PMID 12167683 (Herbrecht 2002) and PMID 26684607 (SECURE/Maertens 2016), both carded on this shelf.

shelves.title: Severe malaria: artesunate saves more lives than quinine — in Asian adults and in African children
shelves.question: For severe falciparum malaria, does intravenous artesunate reduce mortality compared with intravenous quinine?
shelves.mesh: Malaria, Falciparum · Artemisinins · Artesunate · Quinine · Antimalarials · Sesquiterpenes · Humans
shelves.balance: Two large open-label randomized trials, on two continents and in two age groups, found the same thing. In Asian adults (SEAQUAMAT, 1,461 patients), mortality was 15% on artesunate vs 22% on quinine — an absolute difference of 7 percentage points, a relative reduction of about 35%. In African children (AQUAMAT, 5,425 children), mortality was 8.5% vs 10.9% — odds ratio 0.75, a relative reduction of 22.5% — with less coma, fewer convulsions, and less hypoglycemia on artesunate; quinine's hypoglycemia harm also appeared in SEAQUAMAT (relative risk 3.2). Neither trial was blinded, and the comparator is a drug much of the world has already replaced — but the consistency across age, continent, and baseline risk is what two-trial evidence looks like. Because this shelf claims a mortality benefit, it is Tier C and returns for the developer's personal verdict. Proposed grade: LIKELY. Tier C — built Nov 8, 2026 and held for the developer’s personal verdict; no approval stamp is claimed for this shelf.

cards.headline: SEAQUAMAT 2005: in Asian adults with severe falciparum malaria, artesunate cut mortality from 22% to 15%
cards.summary: SEAQUAMAT: in Asian adults with severe falciparum malaria, artesunate cut mortality from 22% to 15% — 7 percentage points absolute ; the abstract’s ‘34.7%’ figure is the relative reduction, mislabeled ‘absolute’ in the source and corrected on the card.
cards.type: Open-label, randomized controlled trial (SEAQUAMAT), Lancet 2005. Tier C card: mortality claim. This record prints no registry number in its databank field, so none is claimed here
cards.people: 1,461 patients admitted with severe falciparum malaria in Bangladesh, India, Indonesia, and Myanmar, assigned to intravenous artesunate (n=730; 2.4 mg/kg bolus at 0, 12, and 24 hours, then daily) or intravenous quinine (n=731; loading dose then 8-hourly infusions), with oral medication substituted when possible. (The abstract does not print mean age or sex mix; the trial's interpretation addresses adults.)
cards.result: Mortality was 107/730 (15%) on artesunate vs 164/731 (22%) on quinine — an absolute difference of 7 percentage points (p=0.0002). The abstract expresses the effect as a 34.7% reduction (95% CI 18.5 to 47.6): that figure is the relative reduction, and it is labeled relative here (the abstract itself mislabels it 'absolute'; the absolute difference from its own rates is 7 points). Artesunate was well tolerated; quinine was associated with hypoglycemia (relative risk 3.2; 95% CI 1.3 to 7.8; p=0.009).
cards.watchOut: Open-label, and the 34.7% figure must never be quoted without its label: relative, not absolute. The absolute benefit — 7 fewer deaths per 100 treated — is the number for decisions, and it is large by the standards of this library.
cards.source: Dondorp A et al. Artesunate versus quinine for treatment of severe falciparum malaria: a randomised trial. Lancet. 2005;366(9487):717-25. PMID 16125588 · No registry number printed on the PubMed record.

cards.headline: AQUAMAT 2010: in African children with severe malaria, artesunate cut mortality from 10.9% to 8.5% — with less coma, fewer convulsions, less hypoglycemia
cards.summary: AQUAMAT: in African children, artesunate cut mortality from 10.9% to 8.5% (2.4 points absolute; 22.5% relative), with less coma, fewer convulsions, and less hypoglycemia.
cards.type: Open-label, randomized trial (AQUAMAT), Lancet 2010. Tier C card: mortality claim
cards.people: 5,425 children younger than 15 years with severe falciparum malaria at 11 centers in nine African countries, assigned to parenteral artesunate (n=2,712) or parenteral quinine (n=2,713); all were analyzed for the primary outcome. (The abstract does not print mean age or sex mix.)
cards.result: In-hospital mortality: 230/2,712 (8.5%) on artesunate vs 297/2,713 (10.9%) on quinine (odds ratio stratified for study site 0.75; 95% CI 0.63 to 0.90; p=0.0022) — an absolute difference of 2.4 percentage points and a relative reduction of 22.5% (95% CI 8.1 to 36.9), labeled relative as in the source. Neurological sequelae did not differ significantly, but development of coma (3.5% vs 5.1%; OR 0.69), convulsions (8.3% vs 10.1%; OR 0.80), and deterioration of coma score (6.1% vs 7.7%; OR 0.78) were all less frequent on artesunate, as was post-treatment hypoglycemia (1.8% vs 2.8%; OR 0.63). Artesunate had no serious drug-related adverse effects.
cards.watchOut: The absolute benefit is smaller than in SEAQUAMAT (2.4 vs 7 points) because baseline mortality was lower — the relative effect is the consistent part. Open-label like its predecessor; the endpoint (in-hospital death) is the least gameable outcome an open-label trial can choose.
cards.source: Dondorp AM et al. Artesunate versus quinine in the treatment of severe falciparum malaria in African children (AQUAMAT): an open-label, randomised trial. Lancet. 2010;376(9753):1647-57. PMID 21062666 · ISRCTN50258054.
