cards.headline: Reading SEAQUAMAT and AQUAMAT together
cards.summary: The slate’s strongest mortality evidence — two large trials, independent populations, the same direction — Tier C, proposed LIKELY.
cards.people: Patients with severe falciparum malaria: predominantly adults in South and Southeast Asia (SEAQUAMAT) and children in sub-Saharan Africa (AQUAMAT) — together 6,886 randomized patients.
cards.result: The fence: this is the slate's strongest mortality evidence — two large randomized trials, independent populations, same direction, with a coherent harm pattern on the quinine side (hypoglycemia in both trials). It is stamped LIKELY rather than higher because both trials are open-label and the comparison is against quinine, a standard the world has already moved past; no trial will ethically re-run it. Tier C applies because the shelf claims fewer deaths, and the shelf states its own ceiling: artesunate is the treatment of choice for severe falciparum malaria on this evidence; nothing here speaks to uncomplicated malaria, chemoprevention, or adjunctive therapies, which live on other shelves (malaria vaccines are Shelf 449).
cards.watchOut: Quote the absolute numbers with the population attached: 15% vs 22% (Asian adults), 8.5% vs 10.9% (African children). A single pooled 'artesunate cuts deaths by a third' line would borrow SEAQUAMAT's relative reduction and hide AQUAMAT's smaller absolute margin.
cards.source: Synthesis of PMID 16125588 (SEAQUAMAT/Dondorp 2005) and PMID 21062666 (AQUAMAT/Dondorp 2010), both carded on this shelf.

shelves.title: Baricitinib in hospitalized COVID-19: ACTT-2 and COV-BARRIER
shelves.question: In hospitalized patients with COVID-19, what does adding baricitinib — to remdesivir, or to standard care — actually buy?
shelves.mesh: COVID-19 · COVID-19 Drug Treatment · Azetidines · Janus Kinase Inhibitors · Antiviral Agents · Dexamethasone · SARS-CoV-2 · Humans
shelves.balance: Baricitinib shortened recovery in ACTT-2; its mortality estimate was uncertain. COV-BARRIER reported lower mortality but did not meet its primary progression endpoint. ACTT-2 tested addition to remdesivir; COV-BARRIER tested addition to standard care, commonly including corticosteroids. COV-BARRIER mortality findings were secondary/exploratory, with nominal testing for day-28 mortality; its PubMed abstract does not report recovery time. Shelved as submitted — ChatGPT pilot deposit, gate-verified and approved by the developer Nov 6, 2026 (Tier C personal ruling; deposit 2 of 10).

cards.headline: ACTT-2: baricitinib plus remdesivir shortened recovery by a day (7 vs 8 days); the mortality estimate was uncertain (HR 0.65, CI crosses 1)
cards.summary: Median time to recovery: 7 days with baricitinib plus remdesivir vs 8 days with remdesivir alone (rate ratio 1.16 , 95% CI 1.01 to 1.32); in patients on high-flow oxygen or noninvasive ventilation, 10 vs 18 days (RR 1.51). Day-28 mortality 5.1% vs 7.8% (HR 0.65 , 0.39 to 1.09 — inconclusive) — 1,033 patients.
cards.type: Double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trial (ACTT-2), N Engl J Med 2021
cards.people: 1,033 hospitalized adults with COVID-19 underwent randomization (515 baricitinib plus remdesivir, 518 remdesivir plus placebo). (The PubMed abstract record does not print mean age or sex mix; full-text values were not verified at build — flagged in the batch report.)
cards.result: Patients receiving baricitinib had a median time to recovery of 7 days (95% CI 6 to 8) vs 8 days (7 to 9) with control (rate ratio for recovery 1.16; 95% CI 1.01 to 1.32; P=0.03), and a 30% higher odds of improvement in clinical status at day 15 (odds ratio 1.3; 1.0 to 1.6). In patients receiving high-flow oxygen or noninvasive ventilation at enrollment, recovery took 10 vs 18 days (rate ratio 1.51; 1.10 to 2.08). The 28-day mortality was 5.1% in the combination group and 7.8% in the control group (hazard ratio for death 0.65; 95% CI 0.39 to 1.09). Serious adverse events were less frequent with baricitinib (16.0% vs 24.5%, as reported in the abstract).
cards.watchOut: Recovery was the primary endpoint and mortality the secondary one — the mortality confidence interval (0.39 to 1.09) is compatible with anything from a large benefit to slight harm, so this card supports ‘recovers a day sooner’, not ‘saves lives’. Both arms received remdesivir, so the trial says nothing about baricitinib without it. Funded by NIAID (ACTT platform).
cards.source: Kalil AC et al. Baricitinib plus Remdesivir for Hospitalized Adults with Covid-19. N Engl J Med. 2021;384:795-807. PMID 33306283 · NCT04401579.

cards.headline: COV-BARRIER: baricitinib’s primary endpoint was NOT met — yet day-28 mortality ran 8% vs 13% (HR 0.57, nominal, secondary)
cards.summary: Primary progression endpoint (progression to high-flow oxygen, ventilation, or death by day 28): 27.8% baricitinib vs 30.5% placebo (OR 0.85; P=0.18 — NOT met). Day-28 mortality: 8% vs 13% (HR 0.57 , 0.41 to 0.78, nominal); day-60 mortality 10% vs 15% (HR 0.62, exploratory) — 1,525 patients.
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, parallel-group, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial (COV-BARRIER), Lancet Respir Med 2021
cards.people: 1,525 hospitalized adults with COVID-19 at 101 centres in 12 countries (764 baricitinib, 761 placebo); 79.3% were receiving systemic corticosteroids at baseline (91.3% of those dexamethasone) and 18.9% remdesivir. (The PubMed abstract record does not print mean age or sex mix; full-text values were not verified at build — flagged in the batch report.)
cards.result: The composite primary endpoint was not met: 27.8% of the baricitinib group and 30.5% of the placebo group progressed to high-flow oxygen, non-invasive ventilation, invasive mechanical ventilation, or death by day 28 (odds ratio 0.85; P=0.18). All-cause mortality by day 28 — a key secondary endpoint — was 8% with baricitinib vs 13% with placebo (hazard ratio 0.57; 95% CI 0.41–0.78; nominal significance, as the primary endpoint had failed); mortality by day 60, an exploratory endpoint, was 10% vs 15% (HR 0.62; 0.47–0.83). The abstract does not report recovery time.
cards.watchOut: Read the endpoint hierarchy before the hazard ratio: when a trial misses its primary endpoint, its secondary mortality result is hypothesis-strengthening, not confirmatory — which is why this deposit shelf is stamped POSSIBLE. The contrast with ACTT-2 (Reference 1) is structural, not contradictory: different background care (steroids here, remdesivir there), different primary questions. Funded by Eli Lilly.
cards.source: Marconi VC et al. Efficacy and safety of baricitinib for the treatment of hospitalised adults with COVID-19 (COV-BARRIER): a randomised, double-blind, parallel-group, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial. Lancet Respir Med. 2021;9:1407-1418. PMID 34480861 · NCT04421027.

shelves.title: Universal decolonization and chlorhexidine bathing in the ICU — and beyond it
shelves.question: Does universal (vs targeted) decolonization with chlorhexidine bathing ± nasal mupirocin reduce ICU infections and MRSA?
shelves.mesh: Bacteremia/psychology · Baths · Carrier State/diagnosis · Chlorhexidine/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Comparative Effectiveness Research · Cross Infection/prevention & control/transmission · Disease Transmission, Infectious/prevention & control
shelves.balance: Split — LIKELY in intensive care: in REDUCE MRSA (43 hospitals, 74,256 patients), universal decolonisation cut bloodstream infection from any pathogen more than targeted decolonisation or screening and isolation (hazard ratio 0.56 versus baseline, compared with 0.78 and 0.99; one bloodstream infection prevented per 54 patients decolonised), and in the Climo crossover trial daily chlorhexidine bathing lowered hospital-acquired bloodstream infections from 6.60 to 4.78 cases per 1,000 patient-days (a 28% relative reduction). MAYBE (weak evidence) outside intensive care: the ABATE Infection trial (53 hospitals, 339,902 patients in the intervention period) found no significant reduction in MRSA or VRE clinical cultures with universal chlorhexidine bathing plus targeted mupirocin in non-critical-care units (relative hazard ratios did not differ, p=0.17). This shelf is about skin bathing and nasal decolonisation only; chlorhexidine oral care for ventilated patients is a different intervention and lives at #469 — none of its trials is re-carded here.

cards.headline: REDUCE MRSA: universal decolonisation beat targeted decolonisation and screening — bloodstream infection hazard ratio 0.56
cards.summary: REDUCE MRSA (43 hospitals, 74,256 patients): bloodstream infection hazard ratio 0.56 for universal decolonisation vs 0.78 targeted and 0.99 screening-and-isolation.
cards.people: 43 hospitals (74 ICUs and 74,256 patients during the intervention period), with all adult ICUs in a hospital assigned to the same strategy. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Modelled hazard ratios (intervention versus baseline) for MRSA clinical isolates were 0.92 for screening and isolation (crude rate 3.2 versus 3.4 isolates per 1,000 days), 0.75 for targeted decolonisation (3.2 versus 4.3 per 1,000 days), and 0.63 for universal decolonisation (2.1 versus 3.4 per 1,000 days) (P=0.01 for the test of all groups being equal). For bloodstream infection with any pathogen, hazard ratios were 0.99 (4.1 versus 4.2 per 1,000 days), 0.78 (3.7 versus 4.8), and 0.56 (3.6 versus 6.1), respectively (P<0.001). One bloodstream infection was prevented per 54 patients who underwent decolonisation. Reductions in MRSA bloodstream infection were similar in pattern but not significant. Adverse events, in 7 patients, were mild and related to chlorhexidine.
cards.watchOut: A pragmatic cluster trial comparing each strategy with its own baseline period, not a patient-level blinded comparison; effects are modelled hazard ratios, and universal decolonisation bundled chlorhexidine bathing with nasal mupirocin, so the components cannot be separated from this record.
cards.source: Huang SS et al. Targeted versus universal decolonization to prevent ICU infection. N Engl J Med. 2013 Jun 13;368(24):2255-2265. PMID: 23718152. Registry ID: NCT00980980 (ClinicalTrials.gov, from the record's databank fields).

cards.headline: Climo 2013: daily chlorhexidine bathing lowered bloodstream infections from 6.60 to 4.78 per 1,000 patient-days in ICU and transplant units
cards.summary: Climo 2013: daily chlorhexidine bathing — bloodstream infections 4.78 vs 6.60 per 1,000 patient-days; MDRO acquisition 5.10 vs 6.60.
cards.people: 7,727 patients enrolled in 9 intensive care and bone marrow transplantation units in 6 hospitals, bathed with 2% chlorhexidine-impregnated washcloths or nonantimicrobial washcloths for 6 months, then crossed to the alternate product for 6 months.
cards.result: The overall rate of multidrug-resistant organism acquisition was 5.10 cases per 1,000 patient-days with chlorhexidine bathing versus 6.60 per 1,000 patient-days with nonantimicrobial washcloths (P=0.03) — a 23% relative reduction. Hospital-acquired bloodstream infections occurred at 4.78 versus 6.60 cases per 1,000 patient-days (P=0.007) — a 28% relative reduction, beside the absolute rates as printed. No serious skin reactions were noted during either period.
cards.watchOut: Nonblinded, unit-level crossover in ICU and bone-marrow-transplant units only; bathing alone (no nasal mupirocin component is described in this record), so it supports the bathing element of the ICU strategy rather than the full REDUCE bundle.
cards.source: Climo MW et al. Effect of daily chlorhexidine bathing on hospital-acquired infection. N Engl J Med. 2013 Feb 7;368(6):533-542. PMID: 23388005. Registry ID: NCT00502476 (ClinicalTrials.gov, from the record's databank fields).

cards.headline: ABATE: universal chlorhexidine bathing did not significantly reduce MRSA or VRE cultures in non-critical-care units
cards.summary: ABATE: on non-critical-care units, universal bathing did not significantly reduce MRSA/VRE cultures (hazard ratios 0.79 vs 0.87 against baseline).
cards.people: 53 hospitals with 194 non-critical-care units; 189,081 patients in the baseline period and 339,902 in the intervention period (156,889 routine care and 183,013 decolonisation). The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: For the primary outcome of unit-attributable MRSA- or VRE-positive clinical cultures, the hazard ratio for the intervention versus baseline period was 0.79 (95% CI 0.73-0.87) in the decolonisation group versus 0.87 (95% CI 0.79-0.95) in the routine-care group; the relative hazard ratios did not differ significantly (p=0.17). There were 25 adverse events (<1%), all involving chlorhexidine, among 183,013 patients in chlorhexidine units, and none reported for mupirocin.
cards.watchOut: The null is in general medical and surgical (non-critical-care) units, where baseline infection rates and device exposure are far lower than in ICUs — it bounds the ICU result's reach rather than contradicting it, and the within-group falls in both arms show why baseline-period comparisons alone would have misled.
cards.source: Huang SS et al. shelves.title: Surgical-site infection prevention: skin antisepsis and suture choice
shelves.question: Does chlorhexidine–alcohol skin preparation prevent surgical-site infection better than povidone-iodine — and do triclosan-coated sutures add anything?
shelves.mesh: 2-Propanol/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Analysis of Variance · Anti-Infective Agents, Local/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Antisepsis/methods · Chlorhexidine/adverse effects,analogs & derivatives,therapeutic use · Cross Infection/prevention & control · Drug Combinations
shelves.balance: Split: POSSIBLE — chlorhexidine–alcohol over povidone-iodine · LIKELY — triclosan-coated sutures do not reduce infection. Darouiche 2010 (849 patients) found overall surgical-site infection of 9.5% with chlorhexidine–alcohol vs 16.1% with povidone-iodine (relative risk 0.59) after clean-contaminated surgery — a single large trial, so that half caps at POSSIBLE. PROUD (1224 patients, 24 German hospitals) found triclosan-coated PDS Plus sutures did not reduce infection after elective midline laparotomy (14.8% vs 16.1%; odds ratio 0.91, 95% CI 0.66 to 1.25) — a very large single null trial, which under the library's rule may carry LIKELY for the null.

cards.headline: Darouiche 2010: chlorhexidine–alcohol cut surgical-site infection to 9.5% vs 16.1% with povidone-iodine
cards.summary: Darouiche 2010: chlorhexidine–alcohol cut surgical-site infection to 9.5% vs 16.1% with povidone-iodine (relative risk 0.59, relative).
cards.people: 849 adults undergoing clean-contaminated surgery qualified for the intention-to-treat analysis (409 chlorhexidine–alcohol scrub, 440 povidone-iodine scrub and paint). The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: The overall rate of surgical-site infection within 30 days was significantly lower with chlorhexidine–alcohol than povidone-iodine (9.5% vs 16.1%; P=0.004; relative risk 0.59, 95% CI 0.41 to 0.85 — a relative figure, with the absolute rates beside it). Chlorhexidine–alcohol was also more protective against superficial incisional infections (4.2% vs 8.6%, P=0.008) and deep incisional infections (1% vs 3%, P=0.05) but not organ-space infections (4.4% vs 4.5%). Per-protocol results in 813 patients were similar, and adverse events were similar in the two groups.
cards.watchOut: Single trial in clean-contaminated surgery; the comparison bundles the antiseptic and the alcohol vehicle together, so the trial cannot separate chlorhexidine's effect from alcohol's. No blinding of the operating team was possible.

cards.summary: PROUD (Diener) 2014: triclosan-coated sutures did not reduce surgical-site infection ( 14.8% vs 16.1% ; odds ratio 0.91).
cards.type: Multicentre, randomised, group-sequential superiority trial (24 German hospitals); patients, surgeons and outcome assessors masked
cards.people: 1224 adults (aged 18 or older) undergoing elective midline abdominal laparotomy for any reason, assigned to triclosan-coated PDS Plus (607) or uncoated PDS II (617) sutures for fascia closure; 1185 (587 vs 598) were analysed. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Surgical-site infection (superficial or deep, CDC criteria) within 30 days occurred in 87 of 587 (14.8%) with triclosan-coated sutures vs 96 of 598 (16.1%) with uncoated sutures (odds ratio 0.91, 95% CI 0.66 to 1.25; p=0.64 — a relative figure whose interval spans no effect). cards.headline: Synthesis: change the skin prep if you like; don't expect the suture coating to save you
cards.summary: Change the skin prep if you like (POSSIBLE); don't expect the suture coating to save you (LIKELY null).
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Darouiche 2010 (849 patients, skin antisepsis) and PROUD (1224 patients, suture coating).
cards.result: The two halves of SSI prevention tested here pull opposite ways: skin antisepsis shows a large absolute difference (9.5% vs 16.1%, relative risk 0.59) in one trial — promising but single-trial, hence POSSIBLE — while the triclosan suture coating shows a tightly-estimated null (odds ratio 0.91, CI 0.66 to 1.25) in a larger masked trial, hence LIKELY for the null. Incisional negative-pressure dressings, the third device-side SSI strategy, are carded on Shelf #651 and were also null there.
cards.watchOut: Darouiche's effect size is large for a prep change and awaits a second large trial; treat the 0.59 relative risk as an upper-bound estimate until replicated.

shelves.title: Perioperative fluids and haemodynamic therapy in major surgery
shelves.question: Does a restrictive fluid strategy harm kidneys compared with liberal fluids (RELIEF) — and does cardiac-output-guided haemodynamic therapy reduce complications (OPTIMISE)?
shelves.mesh: Abdomen/surgery · Acute Kidney Injury/etiology · Blood Loss, Surgical · Digestive System Surgical Procedures/adverse effects,mortality · Fluid Therapy/adverse effects,methods · Hypotonic Solutions/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Postoperative Complications/epidemiology,prevention & control
shelves.balance: Split: LIKELY — restrictive fluids give no survival advantage and more kidney injury · POSSIBLE — cardiac-output-guided therapy. RELIEF (3000 patients) found disability-free survival at 1 year was not higher with a restrictive regimen (81.9% vs 82.3%) while acute kidney injury was significantly more common (8.6% vs 5.0%) — a large pragmatic null-plus-harm result carrying LIKELY. OPTIMISE's own trial (734 patients) missed significance on its composite of complications and 30-day mortality (36.6% vs 43.4%; relative risk 0.84, 95% CI 0.71 to 1.01; P=0.07), and only its accompanying 38-trial meta-analysis favoured the intervention — so the guided-therapy claim rests substantially on pooled small trials and caps at POSSIBLE. Mortality was a secondary outcome in both trials and no mortality benefit is claimed for either strategy; perioperative drug questions (POISE programme) live on Shelves #352/#353.

cards.headline: RELIEF (Myles) 2018: restrictive fluids gave no disability-free-survival advantage (81.9% vs 82.3%) and more acute kidney injury (8.6% vs 5.0%)
cards.summary: RELIEF (Myles) 2018: restrictive fluids gave no disability-free-survival advantage ( 81.9% vs 82.3% ) and more acute kidney injury ( 8.6% vs 5.0% ).
cards.people: 3000 patients at increased risk of complications undergoing major abdominal surgery, assigned to a restrictive (1490 analysed for fluid volumes) or liberal (1493) intravenous-fluid regimen during and up to 24 hours after surgery; median intake was 3.7 litres (IQR 2.9 to 4.9) vs 6.1 litres (5.0 to 7.4). The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Disability-free survival at 1 year was 81.9% in the restrictive group and 82.3% in the liberal group (hazard ratio for death or disability 1.05, 95% CI 0.88 to 1.24; P=0.61 — a relative figure). Acute kidney injury at 30 days was higher with restriction: 8.6% vs 5.0% (P<0.001). Septic complications or death were 21.8% vs 19.8% (P=0.19); surgical-site infection (16.5% vs 13.6%, P=0.02) and renal-replacement therapy (0.9% vs 0.3%, P=0.048) were also higher with restriction, though the between-group differences for those were not significant after adjustment for multiple testing.
cards.watchOut: The 'liberal' arm (median 6.1 litres) is moderate by historical standards — the trial compares two modern regimens, not restriction against flooding; unblinded fluid management is inherent to the question.

cards.headline: OPTIMISE (Pearse) 2014: cardiac-output-guided therapy missed significance in its own trial (P=0.07); its 38-trial meta-analysis favoured it
cards.summary: OPTIMISE (Pearse) 2014: cardiac-output-guided therapy missed significance in its own trial (P=0.07); its 38-trial meta-analysis favoured it. No mortality benefit is claimed for either strategy.
cards.type: Pragmatic, multicentre, observer-blinded randomised trial with an updated systematic review and meta-analysis (17 UK hospitals)
cards.people: 734 high-risk patients aged 50 years or older undergoing major gastrointestinal surgery, assigned to a cardiac output-guided haemodynamic therapy algorithm for intravenous fluid and dopexamine during and 6 hours after surgery (368) or usual care (366). The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: The primary composite of 30-day moderate or major complications and mortality occurred in 36.6% of the intervention group vs 43.4% of usual care (relative risk 0.84, 95% CI 0.71 to 1.01; absolute risk reduction 6.8%, −0.3% to 13.9%; P=0.07) — not significant, and the relative figure sits inside the 0.5–2.0 band that is not solid evidence on its own. No secondary outcome differed significantly; five intervention patients (1.4%) had cardiovascular serious adverse events within 24 hours vs none in usual care. The accompanying meta-analysis of 38 trials including OPTIMISE found fewer complications with the intervention (31.5% vs 41.6%; relative risk 0.77, 0.71 to 0.83) and a non-significant mortality reduction (relative risk 0.82, 0.67 to 1.01).
cards.watchOut: The trial and its meta-analysis disagree in precision: the pooled estimate leans on many small older trials, and the intervention bundles monitoring, fluids and an inotrope (dopexamine), so no single component can be credited.
cards.source: Pearse RM et al. Effect of a perioperative, cardiac output-guided hemodynamic therapy algorithm on outcomes following major gastrointestinal surgery: a randomized clinical trial and systematic review. JAMA. 2014;311(21):2181-2190. PMID: 24842135. Registry ID: ISRCTN04386758, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Synthesis: 'less fluid' is not 'better fluid' — restriction cost kidneys, and guided therapy remains unproven by its own largest trial
cards.summary: Restriction cost kidneys (LIKELY); guided therapy remains unproven by its own largest trial (POSSIBLE).
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: RELIEF (3000 patients, fluid volume) and OPTIMISE (734 patients, guided haemodynamic therapy, plus its 38-trial pooling).
cards.result: RELIEF removes the main rationale for routine restriction (no disability-free-survival gain) and adds a concrete harm (acute kidney injury 8.6% vs 5.0%). OPTIMISE leaves goal-directed therapy in equipoise: a 6.8-point absolute composite difference that its own trial could not confirm (P=0.07), supported mainly by a meta-analysis of smaller trials. The stamps split accordingly — LIKELY on the fluid-volume answer, POSSIBLE on guided therapy. shelves.title: Postoperative nausea and vomiting: combination prophylaxis and aprepitant
shelves.question: Do antiemetic combinations outperform single agents for PONV prophylaxis — and where does aprepitant fit?
shelves.mesh: Anesthesia, General · Anesthesia, Intravenous · Anesthesia, Local · Anesthetics, Intravenous · Antiemetics/therapeutic use · Dexamethasone/therapeutic use · Droperidol/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: LIKELY: In the IMPACT factorial trial (5199 high-risk patients), ondansetron, dexamethasone and droperidol each reduced postoperative nausea and vomiting by about 26% relative, propofol by 19% relative and nitrogen (avoiding nitrous oxide) by 12% relative — and all acted independently, so combined relative risks multiply while absolute benefit scales with the patient's baseline risk. Aprepitant fits as the strongest anti-vomiting component in its head-to-head trial: aprepitant plus dexamethasone halved 48-hour vomiting versus ondansetron plus dexamethasone after craniotomy (16% vs 38%), though nausea itself was unchanged. Reserve multi-drug prophylaxis for high-risk patients, as IMPACT's authors advise.

cards.headline: IMPACT (Apfel) 2004: each antiemetic cut PONV by ~26% relative, independently — so combinations multiply
cards.summary: IMPACT (Apfel) 2004: each antiemetic cut PONV by about 26% relative , independently — so combinations multiply.
cards.type: Randomised, controlled factorial trial (5199 patients at high risk for PONV)
cards.people: 5199 patients at high risk for postoperative nausea and vomiting; 4123 were randomised across 64 combinations of six interventions (ondansetron 4 mg or none; dexamethasone 4 mg or none; droperidol 1.25 mg or none; propofol or volatile anaesthetic; nitrogen or nitrous oxide; remifentanil or fentanyl), the remainder across the first four interventions; nausea and vomiting within 24 hours was evaluated blindly. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Ondansetron, dexamethasone and droperidol each reduced the risk of postoperative nausea and vomiting by about 26% (relative reductions). Propofol reduced risk by 19% and nitrogen by 12% (both relative); total intravenous anaesthesia (propofol plus nitrogen) thus matched a single antiemetic drug. All interventions acted independently of one another and of baseline risk, so combined relative risks are estimated by multiplying the single-agent relative risks; absolute risk reduction, however, was a critical function of baseline risk. The authors' rule: use the safest or least expensive agent first, single prophylaxis for moderate risk, multiple interventions reserved for high-risk patients, and prophylaxis rarely warranted at low risk.
cards.watchOut: A factorial trial estimates each factor's average effect across all combinations of the others; droperidol's regulatory status has varied by country since 2004, which is a practice caveat, not a trial finding. Untreated, about one third of patients in this high-risk population had PONV.
cards.source: Apfel CC et al. A factorial trial of six interventions for the prevention of postoperative nausea and vomiting. N Engl J Med. 2004;350(24):2441-2451. PMID: 15190136. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — the trial predates routine registration reporting in MEDLINE records.

cards.headline: Habib 2011: aprepitant + dexamethasone halved vomiting after craniotomy vs ondansetron + dexamethasone (16% vs 38% at 48 hours) — nausea unchanged
cards.summary: Habib 2011: aprepitant + dexamethasone halved vomiting after craniotomy vs ondansetron + dexamethasone ( 16% vs 38% at 48 hours) — nausea unchanged.
cards.people: 104 patients undergoing craniotomy under general anaesthesia completed the study, receiving oral aprepitant 40 mg (or placebo) 1–3 hours before induction or intravenous ondansetron 4 mg (or placebo) near the end of surgery; all received dexamethasone 10 mg after induction, with data collected by blinded personnel for 48 hours. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Cumulative vomiting at 48 hours was 16% with aprepitant vs 38% with ondansetron (P=0.0149); vomiting was also lower at 2 hours (6% vs 21%, P=0.0419) and 24 hours (14% vs 36%, P=0.0124). There was no difference in incidence of nausea (69% vs 60%), nausea scores, rescue antiemetic use (65% vs 60%), complete response (no PONV and no rescue: 22% vs 36%) or satisfaction. The authors concluded aprepitant plus dexamethasone is more effective against vomiting in this setting, with nausea outcomes unchanged.
cards.watchOut: Small (104 patients) and confined to craniotomy, a high-vomiting-risk operation where the stakes of vomiting (intracranial pressure, haemostasis) are specific; the complete-response rate numerically favoured ondansetron, a reminder that aprepitant's win is on vomiting, not on the whole PONV syndrome.

cards.headline: Synthesis: stack independent ~26% relative reductions by baseline risk; add aprepitant when vomiting specifically must be prevented
cards.summary: Stack independent relative reductions by baseline risk; add aprepitant when vomiting specifically must be prevented — LIKELY.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: IMPACT (5199 high-risk patients, factorial) and Habib 2011 (104 craniotomy patients).
cards.result: IMPACT supplies the architecture: three drug classes each worth about a 26% relative reduction, acting independently, plus anaesthetic-technique effects of similar size — so two- and three-drug prophylaxis predictably outperforms any single agent in relative terms, with absolute gains concentrated in high-risk patients. Habib supplies aprepitant's niche within that architecture: superior vomiting prevention (16% vs 38% absolute at 48 hours) layered on dexamethasone, without improving nausea. Neither trial supports routine multi-drug prophylaxis for low-risk patients.
cards.watchOut: IMPACT's percentages are relative reductions — a 26% relative cut in a patient with 10% baseline risk is worth 2.6 absolute points, which is precisely why the authors tie the number of interventions to baseline risk.

Two different questions share this shelf, each resting on a single phase 3 trial, so each is capped at POSSIBLE. Letermovir through week 14 after stem-cell transplant cut clinically significant CMV infection by week 24 (37.5% vs 60.6% on placebo; P<0.001), with all-cause mortality at week 48 of 20.9% vs 25.5% printed beside it as the record states it — a difference the abstract does not test and this shelf does not claim. Maribavir cleared refractory or resistant CMV by week 8 in 55.7% vs 23.9% on investigator-assigned therapy (adjusted difference 32.8 percentage points; P<0.001), with fewer treatment discontinuations for adverse events (13.2% vs 31.9%). Transplant immunosuppression itself is Shelf #590 and is not re-carded here.

cards.headline: Marty 2017: letermovir prophylaxis cut clinically significant CMV infection by week 24 — 37.5% vs 60.6% (all-cause mortality at week 48: 20.9% vs 25.5%)
cards.summary: Marty 2017: letermovir prophylaxis cut clinically significant CMV infection by week 24 — 37.5% vs 60.6% (all-cause mortality at week 48: 20.9% vs 25.5%, printed on the card; no mortality claim).
cards.people: 565 CMV-seropositive allogeneic hematopoietic-cell transplant recipients aged 18 or older, randomised 2:1 to letermovir (480 mg/day, or 240 mg/day with cyclosporine) or placebo through week 14 after transplantation, starting a median of 9 days after transplant; the primary analysis covered the 495 patients with undetectable CMV DNA at randomisation (325 letermovir, 170 placebo), followed through week 48. The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: By week 24, clinically significant CMV infection (CMV disease, or viraemia leading to preemptive treatment) or an imputed primary-end-point event occurred in 122 of 325 letermovir patients (37.5%) vs 103 of 170 placebo patients (60.6%) (P<0.001). All-cause mortality at week 48 was 20.9% with letermovir and 25.5% with placebo — reported in the abstract without a significance claim, and carded here as context, not as a mortality benefit. Adverse events were similar overall; vomiting was reported in 18.5% vs 13.5%, oedema in 14.5% vs 9.4%, and atrial fibrillation or flutter in 4.6% vs 1.0%; myelotoxic and nephrotoxic event rates were similar.
cards.watchOut: Patients who discontinued or had missing week-24 data were imputed as having had an event, which inflates both arms' rates; and the endpoint is infection or preemptive treatment, not CMV disease or survival, neither of which the trial was sized to move.
cards.source: Marty FM et al. Letermovir Prophylaxis for Cytomegalovirus in Hematopoietic-Cell Transplantation. N Engl J Med. 2017;377(25):2433-2444. PMID: 29211658. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02137772 (also EudraCT 2013-003831-31, stated in the record's abstract), from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: SOLSTICE 2022: maribavir cleared refractory/resistant CMV by week 8 in 55.7% vs 23.9% on investigator-assigned therapy
cards.summary: SOLSTICE 2022: maribavir cleared refractory/resistant CMV by week 8 in 55.7% vs 23.9% on investigator-assigned therapy.
cards.people: 352 hematopoietic-cell and solid-organ transplant recipients with refractory cytomegalovirus infection, with or without resistance, randomised 2:1 to maribavir 400 mg twice daily (235) or investigator-assigned therapy (117: valganciclovir/ganciclovir, foscarnet, or cidofovir) for 8 weeks, with 12 weeks of follow-up. The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: Confirmed CMV clearance at the end of week 8 (the primary end point) was achieved by 55.7% on maribavir vs 23.9% on investigator-assigned therapy (adjusted difference 32.8 percentage points, 95% CI 22.80 to 42.74; P<0.001). Clearance plus symptom control at week 8 maintained through week 16 was achieved by 18.7% vs 10.3% (adjusted difference 9.5 points, 2.02 to 16.88; P=0.01). Treatment-emergent adverse events occurred in 97.4% vs 91.4%; maribavir had less acute kidney injury than foscarnet (8.5% vs 21.3%) and less neutropenia than valganciclovir/ganciclovir (9.4% vs 33.9%), and fewer discontinuations for adverse events (13.2% vs 31.9%). One patient per group had a fatal treatment-related adverse event.
cards.watchOut: Open-label against a deliberately heterogeneous comparator basket, and the durability gap is the story: clearance-plus-control maintained to week 16 was only 18.7% even on maribavir — week-8 clearance overstates lasting control in refractory disease.
cards.source: Avery RK et al. Maribavir for Refractory Cytomegalovirus Infections With or Without Resistance Post-Transplant: Results From a Phase 3 Randomized Clinical Trial. Clin Infect Dis. 2022;75(4):690-701. PMID: 34864943. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02931539, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Synthesis: prevention works, rescue works better than the toxic old options — POSSIBLE for each, on one trial each
cards.summary: Prevention works, rescue works better than the toxic old options — POSSIBLE for each, on one trial each.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: letermovir prophylaxis (565 randomised stem-cell recipients) and SOLSTICE (352 transplant recipients with refractory/resistant CMV).
cards.result: The two drugs bookend the CMV problem. Before infection: letermovir roughly halved the share of stem-cell recipients hitting clinically significant CMV infection by week 24 (37.5% vs 60.6%). After failure: maribavir more than doubled week-8 clearance over investigator-chosen standard drugs (55.7% vs 23.9%) while causing fewer of the kidney and marrow injuries that limit those drugs. Neither claim rests on more than one trial, and neither trial shows a survival effect — so both halves stamp POSSIBLE, as a split.
cards.watchOut: Do not merge the two populations: letermovir's trial excluded patients with detectable CMV DNA at randomisation from its primary analysis, and SOLSTICE's were already refractory — prophylaxis evidence is not treatment evidence.
cards.source: Synthesis of Marty FM et al. N Engl J Med. 2017;377(25):2433-2444. PMID: 29211658; Avery RK et al. Clin Infect Dis. 2022;75(4):690-701. PMID: 34864943. Registry IDs as on the individual cards.

shelves.title: Long-acting injectable HIV treatment: cabotegravir–rilpivirine (ATLAS, FLAIR)
shelves.question: In people already suppressed on oral therapy (ATLAS) or starting treatment (FLAIR), is monthly injectable cabotegravir–rilpivirine non-inferior to staying on daily pills?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Anti-HIV Agents/administration & dosage,adverse effects,blood · Anti-Retroviral Agents/therapeutic use · CD4 Lymphocyte Count · Drug Resistance, Viral/genetics · Drug Therapy, Combination · HIV Infections/drug therapy
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Two phase 3 noninferiority trials of monthly injectable cabotegravir plus rilpivirine agree. ATLAS (616 patients already suppressed on oral therapy): HIV-1 RNA of 50 copies/mL or more at week 48 in 1.6% on injections vs 1.0% on pills (adjusted difference 0.6 percentage points, within the 6-point margin). FLAIR (566 patients after oral induction): 2.1% vs 2.5% (adjusted difference −0.4 points). Suppression below 50 copies was 92.5–93.6% on injections vs 93.3–95.5% on pills. The price is injection-site reactions (75–86% of recipients, mostly mild or moderate, median 3 days; about 1% withdrew for injection pain in ATLAS, 4 participants for injection-related reasons in FLAIR) and more grade 3-or-higher adverse events in FLAIR's injection arm (11% vs 4%). Noninferiority in two trials earns LIKELY; HIV prevention (PrEP) is Shelf #317 and is not re-carded here.

cards.headline: ATLAS 2020: monthly injections were noninferior in already-suppressed patients — RNA ≥50 copies/mL at week 48 in 1.6% vs 1.0% on oral therapy
cards.summary: ATLAS 2020: monthly injections were noninferior in already-suppressed patients — RNA ≥50 copies/mL at week 48 in 1.6% vs 1.0% on oral therapy. (The topic file had swapped the ATLAS/FLAIR PMIDs; the cards follow the records.)
cards.people: 616 patients (308 per group) who had had plasma HIV-1 RNA below 50 copies/mL for at least 6 months on standard oral antiretroviral therapy, randomised to continue oral therapy or switch to monthly intramuscular long-acting cabotegravir plus rilpivirine. The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: At week 48, HIV-1 RNA of 50 copies/mL or more was found in 5 participants (1.6%) on long-acting therapy and 3 (1.0%) on oral therapy (adjusted difference 0.6 percentage points, 95% CI −1.2 to 2.5), meeting noninferiority (margin 6 points). Suppression below 50 copies was 92.5% vs 95.5% (adjusted difference −3.0 points, −6.7 to 0.7), also noninferior (margin −10 points). Confirmed virologic failure occurred in 3 injection and 4 oral participants. Injection-site pain occurred in 231 injection recipients (75%), mild or moderate in most cases, and 1% withdrew because of it; serious adverse events were reported in no more than 5% of either group.
cards.watchOut: Open-label, in patients already stably suppressed — the easiest population in which to succeed; it does not test the injections in people struggling with adherence, the very group for whom monthly dosing is most attractive and hardest to deliver (a missed clinic visit is a missed dose).
cards.source: Swindells S et al. Long-Acting Cabotegravir and Rilpivirine for Maintenance of HIV-1 Suppression. N Engl J Med. 2020;382(12):1112-1123. PMID: 32130809. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02951052, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: FLAIR 2020: injections after oral induction were noninferior as first treatment — RNA ≥50 copies/mL at week 48 in 2.1% vs 2.5% staying on oral therapy
cards.summary: FLAIR 2020: injections after oral induction were noninferior as first treatment — RNA ≥50 copies/mL at week 48 in 2.1% vs 2.5% staying on oral therapy.
cards.type: Phase 3, randomised, open-label noninferiority trial (after a 20-week oral induction)
cards.people: 566 antiretroviral-naive adults (283 per group) who first received 20 weeks of oral dolutegravir–abacavir–lamivudine and had HIV-1 RNA below 50 copies/mL at 16 weeks, then were randomised to continue oral therapy or switch to 1 month of oral cabotegravir plus rilpivirine followed by monthly injections. The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: At week 48, HIV-1 RNA of 50 copies/mL or more was found in 6 of 283 (2.1%) on long-acting therapy and 7 of 283 (2.5%) on oral therapy (adjusted difference −0.4 percentage points, 95% CI −2.8 to 2.1), meeting noninferiority (margin 6 points). Suppression below 50 copies was 93.6% vs 93.3% (adjusted difference 0.4 points, −3.7 to 4.5). Injection-site reactions were reported by 86% of injection recipients (median duration 3 days; 99% mild or moderate); 4 participants withdrew for injection-related reasons. Grade 3 or higher adverse events occurred in 11% (injections) vs 4% (oral), and events meeting liver-related stopping criteria in 2% vs 1%. Treatment satisfaction increased after switching, and 91% preferred long-acting therapy at week 48.
cards.watchOut: Only induction responders were randomised — patients who failed or did not tolerate the oral lead-in never entered the comparison, so FLAIR shows injections can maintain a suppression already achieved, not that they achieve it from diagnosis.
cards.source: Orkin C et al. Long-Acting Cabotegravir and Rilpivirine after Oral Induction for HIV-1 Infection. N Engl J Med. 2020;382(12):1124-1135. PMID: 32130806. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02938520, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Synthesis: monthly injections keep suppressed patients suppressed — LIKELY noninferior, at the price of injection reactions
cards.summary: Monthly injections keep suppressed patients suppressed — LIKELY noninferior, at the price of injection reactions.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: ATLAS (616 patients, switch in suppression) and FLAIR (566 patients, randomised after oral induction).
cards.result: Both trials land in the same place: week-48 virologic noninferiority by both directions of the FDA snapshot (RNA ≥50: 1.6% vs 1.0% and 2.1% vs 2.5%; RNA <50: 92.5% vs 95.5% and 93.6% vs 93.3%), confirmed virologic failure in single digits per arm, and a consistent tolerability trade — near-universal injection-site reactions, rare withdrawals, and high stated patient preference (91% in FLAIR). LIKELY for maintenance of suppression in patients like those enrolled: already suppressed, or suppressed after induction, and able to attend monthly.
cards.watchOut: Neither trial's population includes the unsuppressed or the clinic-distant; adherence failure on injections risks resistance to two drug classes at once, a harm pattern the 48-week trials were not designed to quantify.
cards.source: Synthesis of Swindells S et al. N Engl J Med. 2020;382(12):1112-1123. PMID: 32130809; Orkin C et al. N Engl J Med. 2020;382(12):1124-1135. PMID: 32130806. Registry IDs as on the individual cards.

shelves.title: Two-drug HIV treatment: dolutegravir plus lamivudine (GEMINI)
shelves.question: Can initial HIV treatment drop to two drugs — dolutegravir plus lamivudine — without losing viral suppression versus a three-drug dolutegravir regimen?
shelves.mesh: Anti-HIV Agents/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Anti-Retroviral Agents/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Drug Therapy, Combination · Emtricitabine/adverse effects,therapeutic use · HIV Infections/drug therapy,virology · HIV-1/isolation & purification · Heterocyclic Compounds, 3-Ring/adverse effects,therapeutic use
shelves.balance: LIKELY: The twin GEMINI trials (1,441 antiretroviral-naive adults, identically designed, double-blind) found two-drug dolutegravir plus lamivudine noninferior to three-drug dolutegravir plus tenofovir/emtricitabine at week 48: suppression below 50 copies/mL in 91% vs 93% pooled (adjusted difference −1.7 percentage points, 95% CI −4.4 to 1.1, against a −10-point margin), with the result consistent in each trial separately (90% vs 93% in GEMINI-1; 93% vs 94% in GEMINI-2). Drug-related adverse events were numerically fewer on two drugs (18% vs 24%). Two blinded trials earn LIKELY — scoped to the enrolled population: screening viral load of 500,000 copies/mL or less, treatment-naive. ART timing in TB co-infection is Shelf #526 and is not re-carded here.

cards.headline: GEMINI-1 and GEMINI-2 2019: two-drug dolutegravir–lamivudine was noninferior at week 48 — 91% vs 93% suppressed (pooled)
cards.summary: GEMINI-1 and GEMINI-2 2019: two-drug dolutegravir–lamivudine was noninferior at week 48 — 91% vs 93% suppressed (pooled).
cards.type: Two identically designed, multicentre, double-blind, randomised, noninferiority phase 3 trials (one combined report)
cards.people: 1,441 antiretroviral-naive adults (18 years or older) with HIV-1 infection and screening HIV-1 RNA of 500,000 copies/mL or less, at 192 centres in 21 countries, randomised to once-daily dolutegravir plus lamivudine (719) or dolutegravir plus tenofovir disoproxil fumarate and emtricitabine (722). The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: At week 48, HIV-1 RNA below 50 copies/mL was achieved in GEMINI-1 by 320 of 356 (90%) on two drugs vs 332 of 358 (93%) on three (adjusted difference −2.6 percentage points, 95% CI −6.7 to 1.5), and in GEMINI-2 by 335 of 360 (93%) vs 337 of 359 (94%) (adjusted difference −0.7 points, −4.3 to 2.9) — noninferior at the −10-point margin in both (pooled: 655 of 716 [91%] vs 669 of 717 [93%]; adjusted difference −1.7 points, −4.4 to 1.1). Drug-related adverse events occurred in 126 of 716 (18%) on two drugs vs 169 of 717 (24%) on three; discontinuations for adverse events were 15 (2%) vs 16 (2%). Two deaths in the GEMINI-2 two-drug group were judged unrelated to study medication.
cards.watchOut: The entry ceiling matters: nobody with a screening viral load above 500,000 copies/mL was enrolled, and these are 48-week data — the two-drug question that takes longer to answer is resistance after virologic failure on a regimen with no third agent in reserve.
cards.source: Cahn P et al. Dolutegravir plus lamivudine versus dolutegravir plus tenofovir disoproxil fumarate and emtricitabine in antiretroviral-naive adults with HIV-1 infection (GEMINI-1 and GEMINI-2): week 48 results from two multicentre, double-blind, randomised, non-inferiority, phase 3 trials. Lancet. 2019;393(10167):143-155. PMID: 30420123. Registry IDs: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02831673 and NCT02831764, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Synthesis: two drugs do the work of three in trial-eligible starters — LIKELY
cards.summary: Two drugs do the work of three in trial-eligible starters — LIKELY.
cards.people: Synthesis of the card above: GEMINI-1 and GEMINI-2 (1,441 treatment-naive adults, week 48).
cards.result: Twin blinded trials with the same answer in both copies (adjusted differences −2.6 and −0.7 percentage points, pooled −1.7, all comfortably inside the noninferiority margin) is as clean a noninferiority result as this library holds, and the tolerability direction favoured the smaller regimen (drug-related adverse events 18% vs 24%). The claim carded is initial therapy in adults at or below the trials' viral-load ceiling; it is not a switch claim for already-treated patients and not a claim about hepatitis B co-infection, where dropping tenofovir has consequences these trials do not address.
cards.watchOut: Do not extend GEMINI to patients with unknown resistance, hepatitis B co-infection, or very high viral loads without evidence from those populations — none was in the room.
cards.source: Synthesis of Cahn P et al. Lancet. 2019;393(10167):143-155. PMID: 30420123. Registry IDs as on the card above.

shelves.title: Prone positioning in severe ARDS (PROSEVA)
shelves.question: In severe ARDS, does prolonged early proning reduce mortality versus supine care?
shelves.mesh: Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Oxygen/blood · Positive-Pressure Respiration/methods · Prone Position · Respiratory Distress Syndrome/mortality,therapy
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — proposed pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C): One large multicentre trial (PROSEVA, 466 patients with severe ARDS) found early prolonged proning roughly halved mortality — 28-day mortality 16.0% vs 32.8% (hazard ratio 0.39, a relative figure, beside the absolute rates) and 90-day mortality 23.6% vs 41.0%. The effect is large and physiologically coherent, but it rests on a single trial, and the library's single-pivotal-trial ceiling caps a benefit claim at POSSIBLE. Benefit claims are mortality claims, so this shelf is Tier C.

cards.headline: PROSEVA 2013: early prolonged proning halved mortality in severe ARDS — 28-day death 16.0% vs 32.8%
cards.summary: PROSEVA 2013: early prolonged proning halved mortality in severe ARDS — 28-day death 16.0% vs 32.8% ; 90-day death 23.6% vs 41.0%. (Tier C — mortality claim; PROPOSED.)
cards.people: 466 patients with severe ARDS (PaO2/FiO2 <150 mm Hg on FiO2 ≥0.6, PEEP ≥5 cm water, tidal volume ~6 ml/kg predicted body weight), randomised to prone-positioning sessions of at least 16 hours (237) or supine care (229). The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: 28-day mortality was 16.0% in the prone group and 32.8% in the supine group (P<0.001); the hazard ratio for death with proning was 0.39 (95% CI 0.25 to 0.63) — a relative figure, printed beside the absolute rates. Unadjusted 90-day mortality was 23.6% vs 41.0% (P<0.001; hazard ratio 0.44, 0.29 to 0.67). Complications did not differ significantly between groups, except cardiac arrests, which were more frequent in the supine group.
cards.watchOut: A single trial — earlier proning trials were neutral, and PROSEVA's centres were experienced in proning with long (≥16-hour) sessions in the most severe patients; the result should not be extrapolated to milder ARDS or occasional short proning.
cards.source: Guérin C et al. Prone positioning in severe acute respiratory distress syndrome. N Engl J Med. 2013;368(23):2159-2168. PMID: 23688302. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00527813, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Synthesis: a large mortality effect from one expert-centre trial — POSSIBLE, Tier C
cards.summary: A large mortality effect from one expert-centre trial — POSSIBLE, Tier C.
cards.people: Synthesis of the card above: PROSEVA 2013 (466 patients with severe ARDS). No other mortality-sized proning trial is carded on this shelf.
cards.result: The shelf's claim is the mortality claim itself: 28-day death 16.0% vs 32.8% and 90-day death 23.6% vs 41.0%, with relative hazard ratios of 0.39 and 0.44 beside them. One trial, however large its effect, caps the stamp at POSSIBLE, and a mortality benefit claim is Tier C — the stamp is proposed pending the developer's personal verdict.

shelves.title: ECMO for severe ARDS: EOLIA and CESAR
shelves.question: Does early venovenous ECMO (EOLIA) or referral to an ECMO centre (CESAR) improve survival in severe ARDS versus conventional management?
shelves.mesh: Cross-Over Studies · Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation/adverse effects · Hemorrhage/etiology · Hypoxia · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Respiration, Artificial/adverse effects · Respiratory Distress Syndrome/mortality,therapy
shelves.balance: Split, proposed pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C): POSSIBLE that referral to an ECMO-based centre improves survival without severe disability — CESAR's primary composite was 63% vs 47% alive without severe disability at 6 months (relative risk 0.69 for death or severe disability) — but CESAR tested referral, and only 68 of 90 allocated patients actually received ECMO. MAYBE (weak evidence) that ECMO itself lowers mortality: EOLIA, the direct test, missed its primary endpoint (60-day mortality 35% vs 46%; relative risk 0.76, 95% CI 0.55 to 1.04; P=0.09), with 28% of controls crossing over to rescue ECMO. Survival claims are Tier C.

cards.headline: EOLIA 2018: ECMO did not significantly lower 60-day mortality — 35% vs 46%, relative risk 0.76 (0.55 to 1.04)
cards.summary: EOLIA 2018: ECMO did not significantly lower 60-day mortality — 35% vs 46% , relative risk 0.76 (0.55 to 1.04). (Tier C — mortality claims; PROPOSED.)
cards.type: International, randomised, controlled trial with rescue crossover permitted
cards.people: 249 patients with very severe ARDS (PaO2/FiO2 <50 mm Hg for >3 hours, or <80 for >6 hours, or pH <7.25 with PaCO2 ≥60 mm Hg for >6 hours), randomised to immediate venovenous ECMO (124) or continued conventional treatment (125). The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: At 60 days, 44 of 124 patients (35%) in the ECMO group and 57 of 125 (46%) in the control group had died (relative risk 0.76; 95% CI 0.55 to 1.04; P=0.09) — the primary endpoint was not met. Crossover to ECMO occurred in 35 control patients (28%) a mean of 6.5 days after randomisation, and 20 of those 35 (57%) died. Bleeding events leading to transfusion were more frequent with ECMO (46% vs 28%; absolute difference 18 percentage points) and severe thrombocytopenia more frequent (27% vs 16%), while ischaemic stroke occurred in no ECMO patients vs 5% of controls.
cards.watchOut: The 28% rescue crossover dilutes any true ECMO effect toward the null, so EOLIA does not prove ECMO is useless — but as randomised, its mortality claim is a non-significant trend, and the relative risk of 0.76 sits inside the 0.5–2.0 band that is not solid evidence on its own.
cards.source: Combes A et al. Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation for Severe Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome. N Engl J Med. 2018;378(21):1965-1975. PMID: 29791822. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01470703, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: CESAR 2009: referral for consideration of ECMO improved survival without severe disability — 63% vs 47%
cards.summary: CESAR 2009: referral for consideration of ECMO improved survival without severe disability — 63% vs 47%.
cards.type: UK-based multicentre randomised controlled trial of a referral strategy; only follow-up assessors masked
cards.people: 180 adults aged 18–65 years with severe (Murray score >3.0 or pH <7.20) but potentially reversible respiratory failure, randomised to continued conventional management (90) or referral to consideration for ECMO (90); 68 of the 90 referred patients (75%) actually received ECMO.
cards.result: 63% (57/90) of patients allocated to consideration for ECMO survived to 6 months without disability, compared with 47% (41/87) allocated to conventional management (relative risk 0.69 for death or severe disability; 95% CI 0.05 to 0.97 as printed in the record; p=0.03). Referral gained 0.03 quality-adjusted life-years at 6 months, and a lifetime model put the cost per QALY at £19,252 (95% CI 7,622 to 59,200).
cards.watchOut: CESAR randomised referral to one expert centre, not ECMO itself: a quarter of the referral group never received ECMO, so the benefit may reflect centre expertise and protocolised care as much as the circuit. The confidence interval as printed in the abstract is unusually wide at its lower bound — the composite result, not a precise effect size, is the finding.

shelves.title: High-flow oxygen and non-invasive ventilation in acute hypoxemic failure (FLORALI, HENIVOT)
shelves.question: In acute hypoxemic respiratory failure, does high-flow nasal oxygen (FLORALI) or helmet NIV (HENIVOT) beat standard oxygen or face-mask NIV on intubation and mortality?
shelves.mesh: Acute Disease · Hypoxia/etiology · Intubation, Intratracheal/statistics & numerical data · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Oxygen/administration & dosage · Oxygen Inhalation Therapy/instrumentation,methods · Positive-Pressure Respiration/instrumentation
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — proposed pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C candidate, because FLORALI's mortality difference was a secondary endpoint and is a mortality claim): Neither anchor trial won its primary endpoint — FLORALI's intubation rates did not differ significantly (38% high-flow vs 47% standard vs 50% NIV), and HENIVOT's days free of respiratory support did not differ (median 20 vs 18 days; P=0.26). What favoured the newer devices was secondary: FLORALI's 90-day mortality hazard ratios (2.01 for standard oxygen vs high-flow; 2.50 for NIV vs high-flow — relative figures, absolute rates not stated in the abstract) and HENIVOT's lower intubation rate (30% vs 51%). The 2025 RENOVATE trial then showed high-flow nasal oxygen noninferior to NIV on intubation or death at 7 days in most acute-respiratory-failure groups (39% vs 38% overall; noninferiority not established in immunocompromised patients). Promising, largely secondary-endpoint and noninferiority evidence: POSSIBLE, not more.

cards.headline: FLORALI 2015: intubation rates did not differ; 90-day mortality (secondary) favoured high-flow oxygen
cards.summary: FLORALI 2015: intubation rates did not differ; 90-day mortality (a secondary endpoint) favoured high-flow oxygen. (Tier C candidate — secondary mortality claim; PROPOSED.)
cards.people: 310 patients without hypercapnia who had acute hypoxemic respiratory failure (PaO2/FiO2 ≤300 mm Hg), randomised to high-flow nasal oxygen (106), standard face-mask oxygen (94), or noninvasive positive-pressure ventilation (110). The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: The intubation rate (primary outcome) was 38% (40/106) with high-flow oxygen, 47% (44/94) with standard oxygen, and 50% (55/110) with noninvasive ventilation (P=0.18 for all comparisons) — no significant difference. Ventilator-free days at day 28 were higher with high-flow oxygen (24±8 days vs 22±10 standard and 19±12 NIV; P=0.02). The hazard ratio for death at 90 days was 2.01 (95% CI 1.01 to 3.99) with standard oxygen versus high-flow oxygen (P=0.046) and 2.50 (95% CI 1.31 to 4.78) with NIV versus high-flow oxygen (P=0.006) — relative figures from a secondary endpoint; the abstract does not state the absolute mortality rates.
cards.watchOut: The mortality finding is a secondary endpoint in an open-label trial whose primary endpoint was null — hypothesis-strengthening, not proof. NIV here was face-mask ventilation in de novo hypoxemic failure, a different setting from COPD/ward NIV shelves.

cards.headline: HENIVOT 2021: helmet NIV did not increase days free of respiratory support vs high-flow oxygen in COVID-19 — but fewer patients were intubated
cards.summary: HENIVOT 2021: helmet NIV did not increase days free of respiratory support vs high-flow oxygen in COVID-19 — but fewer patients were intubated.
cards.type: Multicentre randomised clinical trial in 4 Italian ICUs
cards.people: 109 patients with COVID-19 and moderate-to-severe hypoxemic respiratory failure (PaO2/FiO2 ≤200) completed the trial (54 helmet NIV followed by high-flow oxygen; 55 high-flow oxygen alone); median age 65 years (IQR 55–70); 21 women (19%).
cards.result: The primary outcome — days free of respiratory support within 28 days — was a median of 20 (IQR 0–25) days with helmet NIV vs 18 (0–22) with high-flow oxygen, not statistically significant (mean difference 2 days, 95% CI −2 to 6; P=0.26). Of 9 prespecified secondary outcomes, 7 showed no significant difference. Endotracheal intubation was lower with helmet NIV (30% vs 51%; difference −21%, 95% CI −38% to −3%; P=0.03), and days free of invasive ventilation at 28 days were higher (median 28 vs 25; mean difference 3 days, 0 to 7; P=0.04). In-hospital mortality was 24% vs 25% (absolute difference −1%, 95% CI −17% to 15%; P>0.99) — no mortality difference.
cards.watchOut: A small, single-disease (COVID-19) trial whose intubation benefit is a secondary outcome; it does not establish helmet NIV outside COVID-era hypoxemic failure, and it found no mortality benefit.
cards.source: Grieco DL et al. cards.headline: RENOVATE 2025: high-flow nasal oxygen was noninferior to NIV on intubation or death at 7 days in most groups — 39% vs 38% overall
cards.summary: RENOVATE 2025 (found by the currency sweep and carded): high-flow nasal oxygen was noninferior to NIV on intubation or death at 7 days in most groups — 39% vs 38% overall; noninferiority not established in immunocompromised patients.
cards.type: Noninferiority, randomised clinical trial (Bayesian hierarchical model with dynamic borrowing across patient groups) at 33 hospitals in Brazil
cards.people: 1,800 hospitalised adults (age ≥18 years) were enrolled in five acute-respiratory-failure groups — nonimmunocompromised with hypoxemia, immunocompromised with hypoxemia, COPD exacerbation with respiratory acidosis, acute cardiogenic pulmonary oedema, and hypoxemic COVID-19; 1,766 completed the study (883 high-flow nasal oxygen, 883 NIV); mean age 64 (SD 17) years; 707 (40%) were women.
cards.result: The primary outcome (endotracheal intubation or death within 7 days) occurred in 39% (344/883) with high-flow oxygen vs 38% (336/883) with NIV overall. Noninferiority (posterior probability ≥0.992 that the odds ratio was below 1.55) was met in the nonimmunocompromised hypoxemia group (32.5% vs 33.1%; OR 1.02, 95% credible interval 0.81 to 1.26; posterior probability 0.999), acute cardiogenic pulmonary oedema (10.3% vs 21.3%; OR 0.97; 0.997), hypoxemic COVID-19 (51.3% vs 47.0%; OR 1.13; 0.997) and COPD exacerbation (28.6% vs 26.2%; OR 1.05; 0.992). In the immunocompromised hypoxemia group the outcome occurred in 57.1% (16/28) vs 36.4% (8/22), enrolment was stopped for futility, and noninferiority was not established (posterior probability 0.989). A post hoc analysis without dynamic borrowing gave some qualitatively different results in the COPD and immunocompromised groups.
cards.watchOut: A noninferiority result on a 7-day composite, estimated by borrowing strength across five different syndromes — it does not show high-flow oxygen equals NIV in every group (immunocompromised patients are the explicit exception), and it is not a mortality trial: death is one component of the composite.
cards.source: RENOVATE Investigators and the BRICNet Authors. High-Flow Nasal Oxygen vs Noninvasive Ventilation in Patients With Acute Respiratory Failure: The RENOVATE Randomized Clinical Trial. cards.headline: Synthesis: primary endpoints null in both trials; the favourable signals are secondary — POSSIBLE, Tier C candidate
cards.summary: Primary endpoints null in both anchor trials; the favourable signals are secondary — POSSIBLE, Tier C proposed.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: FLORALI 2015 (310 patients, three arms), HENIVOT 2021 (109 patients with COVID-19), and RENOVATE 2025 (1,766 completing, five respiratory-failure groups).
cards.result: High-flow oxygen is a reasonable default in de novo hypoxemic failure on comfort and ventilator-free days, helmet NIV may avert intubation, and RENOVATE's noninferiority result (intubation or death at 7 days, 39% vs 38% overall) supports high-flow oxygen as an alternative to NIV in most groups — but neither FLORALI nor HENIVOT won its primary endpoint, FLORALI's mortality difference is secondary, HENIVOT showed no mortality difference (24% vs 25%), and RENOVATE's noninferiority did not hold in immunocompromised patients. The stamp is POSSIBLE, and because a mortality claim sits on the shelf it is Tier C-proposed pending the developer's personal verdict.
cards.watchOut: Do not present FLORALI's hazard ratios as a proven mortality benefit of high-flow oxygen; the trial's own primary result was null.

shelves.title: Sedation strategy in the ICU: early dexmedetomidine and no sedation (SPICE III, NONSEDA)
shelves.question: Does sedation strategy change outcomes — early dexmedetomidine as the primary sedative (SPICE III), or a plan of no sedation versus light sedation with daily interruption (NONSEDA)?
shelves.mesh: Bradycardia/chemically induced · Procedural Sedation · Critical Illness/mortality,therapy · Dexmedetomidine/adverse effects · Drug Therapy, Combination · Hypnotics and Sedatives/adverse effects · Hypotension/chemically induced
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — proposed pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C candidate, because both trials' primary endpoints are mortality): Two large trials agree that sedation strategy does not move 90-day mortality — SPICE III: death 29.1% with early dexmedetomidine vs 29.1% with usual care (adjusted risk difference 0.0 percentage points); NONSEDA: 90-day mortality 42.4% with no sedation vs 37.0% with light sedation (difference 5.4 points, 95% CI −2.2 to 12.2; P=0.65). A concordant null from two large trials can carry LIKELY for the null; the stamp is still Tier C-proposed because the claims are mortality claims. Dexmedetomidine also caused more bradycardia and hypotension, and most dexmedetomidine patients still needed supplemental sedatives.

cards.headline: SPICE III 2019: early dexmedetomidine did not lower 90-day mortality — 29.1% vs 29.1% with usual care
cards.summary: SPICE III 2019: early dexmedetomidine did not lower 90-day mortality — 29.1% vs 29.1% with usual care. (Both trials' primary endpoints are 90-day mortality — Tier C proposed.)
cards.people: 4,000 critically ill adults ventilated for less than 12 hours and expected to need ventilation beyond the next calendar day were enrolled; the modified intention-to-treat analysis included 3,904 patients (1,948 dexmedetomidine as sole/primary sedative; 1,956 usual care — propofol, midazolam or other sedatives). The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Death from any cause at 90 days (primary outcome) occurred in 566 of 1,948 patients (29.1%) in the dexmedetomidine group and 569 of 1,956 (29.1%) in the usual-care group (adjusted risk difference 0.0 percentage points; 95% CI −2.9 to 2.8). To reach the target sedation range (−2 to +1 on the Richmond Agitation and Sedation Scale), dexmedetomidine patients received supplemental propofol (64%), midazolam (3%) or both (7%) in the first 2 days. Bradycardia and hypotension were more common with dexmedetomidine.
cards.watchOut: Open-label, and the 'dexmedetomidine strategy' was in practice dexmedetomidine plus frequent supplemental propofol — the trial tests an early-dexmedetomidine-first policy, not dexmedetomidine alone.

cards.headline: NONSEDA 2020: a plan of no sedation did not differ from light sedation on 90-day mortality — 42.4% vs 37.0%
cards.summary: NONSEDA 2020: a plan of no sedation did not differ from light sedation on 90-day mortality — 42.4% vs 37.0%. (The A2B sedation trial is fenced in the synthesis.)
cards.people: 710 mechanically ventilated ICU patients were randomised to a plan of no sedation or to light sedation (Richmond Agitation and Sedation Scale −2 to −3) with daily interruption; 700 were included in the modified intention-to-treat analysis. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Mortality at 90 days (primary outcome) was 42.4% in the nonsedation group and 37.0% in the sedation group (difference 5.4 percentage points; 95% CI −2.2 to 12.2; P=0.65) — not significant, with the point estimate favouring light sedation. ICU-free and ventilator-free days did not differ significantly; days free from coma or delirium were a median of 27 vs 26. A major thromboembolic event occurred in 1 patient (0.3%) in the nonsedation group and 10 (2.8%) in the sedation group (difference −2.5 points, 95% CI −4.8 to −0.7, unadjusted for multiple comparisons). Baseline APACHE II score was 1 point higher in the nonsedation group.

cards.headline: Synthesis: sedation strategy does not decide survival — LIKELY the null, Tier C candidate
cards.summary: Sedation strategy does not decide survival — LIKELY the null, Tier C proposed.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: SPICE III 2019 (3,904 analysed) and NONSEDA 2020 (700 analysed). The earlier dexmedetomidine-versus-benzodiazepine trials (MENDS; SEDCOM) are cited as neighbouring evidence on Shelf #137 and are pointed to there, not re-carded here, under the one-home rule.
cards.result: Two large trials, two different strategy contrasts, one answer on the outcome that matters most: 90-day mortality did not differ (29.1% vs 29.1%; 42.4% vs 37.0%). Sedation choice should therefore be made on delirium, comfort, haemodynamics and workflow — not on an expectation of saving lives. The concordant large-trial null carries LIKELY for the null; the mortality framing makes the stamp Tier C-proposed pending the developer's personal verdict. Fenced, not carded: the A2B trial (2025, 1,404 patients) compared dexmedetomidine- or clonidine-based sedation with propofol-based sedation and found no significant shortening of time to successful extubation (subdistribution hazard ratio 1.09 for dexmedetomidine vs propofol, P=0.20; 1.05 for clonidine, P=0.34) — a different question (agent choice against propofol, extubation primary) from this shelf's two mortality-primary strategy trials, and consistent with their lesson that sedation strategy does not decide the big outcomes.
cards.watchOut: NONSEDA's interval leaves room for harm from a no-sedation plan in some patients; 'no difference shown' is not a mandate to abandon light sedation.

shelves.title: How much renal replacement: intensity of CRRT and dialysis in ICU acute kidney injury (ATN, RENAL)
shelves.question: In ICU acute kidney injury, does more intensive renal replacement improve survival versus standard intensity?
shelves.mesh: Acute Kidney Injury/complications,mortality,therapy · Critical Illness · Hemodiafiltration/adverse effects,methods · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Multiple Organ Failure/etiology · Renal Dialysis/adverse effects,methods · Acute Kidney Injury/mortality,therapy
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): Two large trials, testing two different ways of intensifying renal replacement, agree exactly — ATN: 60-day mortality 53.6% with intensive therapy vs 51.5% with less-intensive (odds ratio 1.09; 95% CI 0.86 to 1.40); RENAL: 90-day mortality 44.7% in each arm (odds ratio 1.00; 0.81 to 1.23). More intensity also did not improve kidney recovery or nonrenal organ failure, and it bought more hypotension during dialysis (ATN) and more hypophosphataemia (RENAL: 65% vs 54%). A concordant null from two large trials carries LIKELY for the null. Tier C: no — the claim is the absence of a benefit, as flagged in the topic file.

cards.headline: ATN 2008: intensive renal support did not decrease 60-day mortality — 53.6% vs 51.5%
cards.summary: ATN 2008: intensive renal support did not decrease 60-day mortality — 53.6% vs 51.5%.
cards.type: Randomised trial (VA/NIH Acute Renal Failure Trial Network)
cards.people: 1,124 critically ill patients with acute kidney injury and failure of at least one nonrenal organ or sepsis, randomised to intensive or less-intensive renal-replacement therapy (intermittent haemodialysis or sustained low-efficiency dialysis six times per week plus continuous venovenous haemodiafiltration at 35 ml/kg/hour, vs three times per week plus 20 ml/kg/hour, by haemodynamic stability). The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Death from any cause by day 60 was 53.6% with intensive therapy and 51.5% with less-intensive therapy (odds ratio 1.09; 95% CI 0.86 to 1.40; P=0.47). There was no significant difference in duration of renal-replacement therapy, recovery of kidney function, or nonrenal organ failure. Hypotension during intermittent dialysis occurred in more patients assigned to intensive therapy, although the frequency of dialysis sessions complicated by hypotension was similar.
cards.watchOut: The 'less-intensive' arm was still a defined, adequate dose — ATN does not show that dose never matters, only that pushing beyond standard intensity in established ICU acute kidney injury does not help.
cards.source: VA/NIH Acute Renal Failure Trial Network; Palevsky PM et al. Intensity of renal support in critically ill patients with acute kidney injury. N Engl J Med. 2008;359(1):7-20. PMID: 18492867. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00076219, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: RENAL 2009: higher-intensity continuous therapy did not reduce 90-day mortality — 44.7% in each group
cards.summary: RENAL 2009: higher-intensity continuous therapy did not reduce 90-day mortality — 44.7% in each group.
cards.people: 1,508 critically ill adults with acute kidney injury were randomised to postdilution continuous venovenous haemodiafiltration at an effluent flow of 40 ml/kg/hour (747) or 25 ml/kg/hour (761); primary-outcome data were available for 1,464 patients (97.1%). The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: At 90 days, 322 patients in the higher-intensity group and 332 in the lower-intensity group had died — mortality 44.7% in each group (odds ratio 1.00; 95% CI 0.81 to 1.23; P=0.99). Among survivors at 90 days, 6.8% (27/399) in the higher-intensity group and 4.4% (18/411) in the lower-intensity group were still receiving renal-replacement therapy (odds ratio 1.59; 0.86 to 2.92; P=0.14). Hypophosphataemia was more common with higher intensity (65% vs 54%; P<0.001).
cards.watchOut: RENAL tested continuous therapy only, at 40 vs 25 ml/kg/hour — both above the minimum doses used in some units; the null applies to intensifying an already-adequate continuous dose.

cards.headline: Synthesis: intensifying renal replacement beyond standard dose does not save lives — LIKELY the null
cards.summary: Intensifying renal replacement beyond standard dose does not save lives — LIKELY the null.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: ATN 2008 (1,124 patients, mixed modalities) and RENAL 2009 (1,508 patients, continuous therapy).
cards.result: Two large trials, near-identical null results on mortality (odds ratios 1.09 and 1.00 — both inside the 0.5–2.0 band and centred on no effect), no recovery benefit, and small real harms from intensity. shelves.title: Early versus late tracheostomy (TracMan, Terragni)
shelves.question: Does performing tracheostomy early in anticipated prolonged ventilation reduce mortality or pneumonia versus waiting?
shelves.mesh: Critical Care · Length of Stay · Patient Admission · Respiration, Artificial/methods,mortality · Survival Analysis · Tracheostomy/methods · Intensive Care Units
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: Early tracheostomy did not reduce mortality in either trial — TracMan: 30-day mortality 30.8% early vs 31.5% late (absolute difference 0.7 points in early's favour, 95% CI −5.4 to 6.7), 2-year mortality 51.0% vs 53.7% (P=0.74); Terragni: the hazard ratio for dying was 0.80 (95% CI 0.56 to 1.15), not significant. Terragni's primary endpoint also missed significance — ventilator-associated pneumonia 14% early vs 21% late (P=0.07) — although early patients left the ventilator and the ICU sooner (hazard ratios 0.70 and 0.73 for remaining connected/in the ICU). The honest summary is 'no mortality or pneumonia proof, some process gains, and clinicians predicted prolonged ventilation poorly' (in TracMan's late arm, only 44.9% ever received a tracheostomy): POSSIBLE for the modest process benefits, no benefit stamp for mortality or pneumonia. Tier C: no, as flagged in the topic file.

cards.headline: TracMan 2013: tracheostomy within 4 days did not improve 30-day mortality — 30.8% vs 31.5%
cards.summary: TracMan 2013: tracheostomy within 4 days did not improve 30-day mortality — 30.8% vs 31.5%.
cards.type: Open, multicentre randomised clinical trial (909 patients, 72 UK critical care units)
cards.people: 909 adults ventilated for less than 4 days and judged likely to need at least 7 more days of ventilation, randomised to early tracheostomy (within 4 days; 455) or late tracheostomy (after 10 days if still indicated; 454). The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Of the early group, 91.9% received a tracheostomy; of the late group, only 44.9% did. All-cause 30-day mortality was 30.8% (95% CI 26.7% to 35.2%) in the early group and 31.5% (27.3% to 35.9%) in the late group (absolute risk reduction for early vs late 0.7%; 95% CI −5.4% to 6.7%). Two-year mortality was 51.0% vs 53.7% (P=0.74). Median critical-care stay in survivors was 13.0 vs 13.1 days (P=0.74). Tracheostomy-related complications were reported in 6.3% of patients (5.5% early, 7.8% late). The authors note clinicians' ability to predict who would need extended ventilation was limited.
cards.watchOut: The late arm's low tracheostomy rate means TracMan compares an early-tracheostomy policy with a wait-and-often-never policy — a fair strategy comparison, but it cannot isolate the effect of the procedure's timing in patients who all receive one.
cards.source: Young D et al. Effect of early vs late tracheostomy placement on survival in patients receiving mechanical ventilation: the TracMan randomized trial. JAMA. 2013;309(20):2121-2129. PMID: 23695482. Registry ID: ISRCTN28588190, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Terragni 2010: early tracheotomy did not significantly reduce ventilator-associated pneumonia — 14% vs 21% (P=0.07)
cards.summary: Terragni 2010: early tracheotomy did not significantly reduce ventilator-associated pneumonia — 14% vs 21% (P=0.07).
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial in 12 Italian ICUs
cards.people: 600 adults ventilated for 24 hours without lung infection (Simplified Acute Physiology Score II 35–65, Sequential Organ Failure Assessment score ≥5) were enrolled; 419 who met the day-2 criteria were randomised to early tracheotomy (after 6–8 days; 209 randomised, 145 received it) or late tracheotomy (after 13–15 days; 210 randomised, 119 received it). cards.result: Ventilator-associated pneumonia (primary endpoint) occurred in 30 patients in the early group (14%; 95% CI 10% to 19%) and 44 in the late group (21%; 15% to 26%) (P=0.07) — not statistically significant. Over 28 days, the hazard ratio for developing pneumonia was 0.66 (95% CI 0.42 to 1.04), for remaining on the ventilator 0.70 (0.56 to 0.87), for remaining in the ICU 0.73 (0.55 to 0.97), and for dying 0.80 (0.56 to 1.15).
cards.watchOut: Only 419 of 600 enrolled patients reached randomisation and about a third of each arm never received the assigned tracheotomy; the pneumonia hazard ratio of 0.66 sits inside the 0.5–2.0 caution band and its interval crosses 1.

cards.headline: Synthesis: no mortality or pneumonia proof for early tracheostomy; process gains only — POSSIBLE
cards.summary: No mortality or pneumonia proof for early tracheostomy; process gains only — POSSIBLE. (No mortality claim is stamped, so this shelf is not Tier C.)
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: TracMan 2013 (909 patients) and Terragni 2010 (419 randomised).
cards.result: Both trials miss their headline endpoints: 30-day mortality 30.8% vs 31.5% (TracMan) and pneumonia 14% vs 21%, P=0.07 (Terragni). What early tracheostomy plausibly buys is time — fewer days connected to the ventilator and in the ICU in Terragni — at no demonstrated survival advantage, and both trials show how often 'anticipated prolonged ventilation' never materialises. Timing remains a clinical-judgement decision, not an outcome intervention: POSSIBLE for process benefits only.
cards.watchOut: Do not cite either trial as evidence that early tracheostomy saves lives or prevents pneumonia — neither showed it.
