shelves.title: Decompressive craniectomy for traumatic brain injury (RESCUEicp, DECRA)
shelves.question: For refractory intracranial hypertension after TBI, does decompressive craniectomy save lives — and at what disability cost (RESCUEicp, last-tier; DECRA, early bifrontal)?
shelves.mesh: Brain Injuries/complications,therapy · Combined Modality Therapy · Decompressive Craniectomy/adverse effects · Persons with Disabilities · Glasgow Coma Scale · Intracranial Hypertension/drug therapy,etiology,mortality,surgery · Persistent Vegetative State/epidemiology,etiology
shelves.balance: Split, proposed pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C — a mortality-versus-disability trade-off): POSSIBLE that last-tier decompressive craniectomy for refractory intracranial hypertension lowers mortality while shifting survivors toward severe disability — RESCUEicp at 6 months: death 26.9% surgical vs 48.9% medical, but vegetative state 8.5% vs 2.1% and lower severe disability 21.9% vs 14.4%, with moderate disability and good recovery similar. POSSIBLE that the early, bifrontotemporoparietal operation in diffuse injury (DECRA) worsens outcome: worse Extended Glasgow Outcome Scale scores (odds ratio 1.84 for a worse score) and more unfavourable outcomes (odds ratio 2.21), with 6-month mortality similar (19% vs 18%). Same operation, different timing, population and technique — opposite lessons; neither result should be quoted without the other. Tier C.

cards.headline: RESCUEicp 2016: last-tier craniectomy halved mortality — 26.9% vs 48.9% — but more survivors were vegetative or severely disabled
cards.summary: RESCUEicp 2016: last-tier craniectomy halved mortality — 26.9% vs 48.9% — but more survivors were vegetative or severely disabled. (Tier C — mortality-vs-disability trade-off; PROPOSED.)
cards.type: Randomised trial (2004–2014), primary outcome analysed ordinally on the Extended Glasgow Outcome Scale
cards.people: 408 patients aged 10–65 years with traumatic brain injury and refractory elevated intracranial pressure (>25 mm Hg), randomised to decompressive craniectomy (201 analysed at 6 months) or ongoing medical care (188 analysed). The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: At 6 months the outcome distributions differed (P<0.001): death 26.9% in the surgical group vs 48.9% in the medical group; vegetative state 8.5% vs 2.1%; lower severe disability (dependent on others) 21.9% vs 14.4%; upper severe disability (independent at home) 15.4% vs 8.0%; moderate disability 23.4% vs 19.7%; good recovery 4.0% vs 6.9%. At 12 months: death 30.4% vs 52.0%; vegetative state 6.2% vs 1.7%; good recovery 9.8% vs 8.4%. Surgical patients had fewer hours with intracranial pressure above 25 mm Hg after randomisation (median 5.0 vs 17.0 hours; P<0.001) but a higher rate of adverse events (16.3% vs 9.2%; P=0.03).
cards.watchOut: This is a values-laden trade-off, not a clean win: the survival gain is bought substantially in vegetative state and dependent disability, and rates of moderate disability and good recovery were similar. Which outcome a family wants cannot be read off the trial.
cards.source: Hutchinson PJ et al. Trial of Decompressive Craniectomy for Traumatic Intracranial Hypertension. N Engl J Med. 2016;375(12):1119-1130. PMID: 27602507. Registry ID: ISRCTN66202560, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: DECRA 2011: early bifrontotemporoparietal craniectomy lowered pressure but worsened functional outcome; mortality was similar — 19% vs 18%
cards.summary: DECRA 2011: early bifrontotemporoparietal craniectomy lowered pressure but worsened functional outcome; mortality was similar — 19% vs 18%.
cards.people: 155 adults with severe diffuse traumatic brain injury and intracranial hypertension refractory to first-tier therapies, randomised to bifrontotemporoparietal decompressive craniectomy or standard care. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: The craniectomy group had less time with intracranial pressure above the treatment threshold (P<0.001), fewer interventions for raised pressure (P<0.02 for all comparisons), and fewer ICU days (P<0.001) — but worse scores on the Extended Glasgow Outcome Scale (odds ratio for a worse score 1.84; 95% CI 1.05 to 3.24; P=0.03) and a greater risk of an unfavourable outcome (odds ratio 2.21; 95% CI 1.14 to 4.26; P=0.02). Rates of death at 6 months were similar (19% craniectomy vs 18% standard care).
cards.watchOut: DECRA's operation was early and bifrontal in diffuse injury — a specific technique and timing, criticised for its thresholds and population; its harm result should not be read onto RESCUEicp's last-tier, largely unilateral operation, nor vice versa.

cards.headline: Synthesis: timing and technique decide whether craniectomy trades death for disability or simply harms — split stamp, Tier C
cards.summary: Timing and technique decide whether craniectomy trades death for disability or simply harms — split POSSIBLE, Tier C.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: RESCUEicp 2016 (408 patients, last-tier) and DECRA 2011 (155 patients, early bifrontal).
cards.result: Both trials lowered intracranial pressure; their patient outcomes diverged. Last-tier surgery (RESCUEicp) moved patients from death into survival — much of it disabled survival (death 26.9% vs 48.9%; vegetative state 8.5% vs 2.1%). Early bifrontal surgery in diffuse injury (DECRA) worsened functional outcome with no mortality difference (19% vs 18%). The shelf therefore stamps the two strategies separately, and the mortality-versus-disability trade-off is Tier C — proposed pending the developer's personal verdict.
cards.watchOut: Never quote RESCUEicp's mortality figure without its disability distribution beside it.

shelves.title: Bicarbonate for severe metabolic acidemia (BICAR-ICU)
shelves.question: In ICU patients with severe metabolic acidemia, does sodium bicarbonate infusion improve survival overall — and in the pre-specified acute-kidney-injury subgroup?
shelves.mesh: Acidosis/drug therapy,mortality · Cohort Studies · Hydrogen-Ion Concentration · Infusions, Intravenous · Intensive Care Units · Renal Replacement Therapy · Sodium Bicarbonate/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: Split, proposed pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C — mortality claims): LIKELY the null on mortality. BICAR-ICU's overall primary composite was null (66% vs 71%; p=0.24), and its pre-specified acute-kidney-injury subgroup signal (day-28 survival estimate 54% vs 37%) was then tested head-on by BICARICU-2 (2025, 627 analysed patients with severe metabolic acidemia AND moderate-to-severe acute kidney injury): day-90 mortality 62.1% with bicarbonate vs 61.7% with control (absolute difference 0.4 points; P=0.91). A subgroup signal that fails its own confirmatory trial does not survive — the AKI mortality claim is retired to MAYBE (weak evidence)'s history on this shelf and the mortality stamp is LIKELY the null across both populations. POSSIBLE that bicarbonate reduces the use of kidney replacement therapy in AKI patients: in BICARICU-2, 35% vs 50% received it (absolute difference −15.5 points) — a secondary outcome, stamped accordingly.

cards.headline: BICAR-ICU 2018: bicarbonate did not improve the primary composite overall — 66% vs 71% (p=0.24); the AKI stratum's survival differed (54% vs 37%)
cards.summary: BICAR-ICU 2018: bicarbonate did not improve the primary composite overall — 66% vs 71% (p=0.24); the AKI stratum's survival differed (54% vs 37%).
cards.type: Multicentre, open-label, randomised, phase 3 trial in 26 French ICUs
cards.people: 389 adults admitted within 48 hours to the ICU with severe acidaemia (pH ≤7.20, PaCO2 ≤45 mm Hg, bicarbonate ≤20 mmol/L) and a Sequential Organ Failure Assessment score ≥4 or lactate ≥2 mmol/L, randomised to 4.2% sodium bicarbonate infusion titrated to keep arterial pH above 7.30 (195) or no bicarbonate (194). The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: The primary outcome (death from any cause by day 28 or at least one organ failure at day 7) occurred in 128 of 195 patients (66%) in the bicarbonate group and 138 of 194 (71%) in the control group (absolute difference −5.5%, 95% CI −15.2 to 4.2; p=0.24). The Kaplan–Meier estimate of day-28 survival was 55% (95% CI 49 to 63) with bicarbonate vs 46% (40 to 54) with control (p=0.09) — not significant. In the pre-specified stratum with Acute Kidney Injury Network score 2 or 3, the day-28 survival estimate was 54% (45 to 65) vs 37% (28 to 48) (p=0.0283), and the authors state bicarbonate decreased the primary composite and day-28 mortality in that a-priori stratum. Metabolic alkalosis, hypernatraemia and hypocalcaemia were more frequent with bicarbonate, with no life-threatening complications reported.
cards.watchOut: Single open-label trial; the positive result lives entirely in one (pre-specified) subgroup while the overall primary outcome is null — the classic pattern that requires confirmation before it changes practice. That confirmatory trial (BICARICU-2, carded below) has since reported, and its mortality result is null.
cards.source: Jaber S et al. Sodium bicarbonate therapy for patients with severe metabolic acidaemia in the intensive care unit (BICAR-ICU): a multicentre, open-label, randomised controlled, phase 3 trial. Lancet. 2018;392(10141):31-40. PMID: 29910040. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02476253, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: BICARICU-2 2025: in severe metabolic acidemia WITH acute kidney injury, bicarbonate did not affect day-90 mortality — 62.1% vs 61.7%
cards.summary: BICARICU-2 2025 (found by the currency sweep and carded): in severe metabolic acidemia WITH acute kidney injury, bicarbonate did not affect day-90 mortality — 62.1% vs 61.7%.
cards.type: Randomised, open-label clinical trial in 43 French ICUs
cards.people: 640 patients were randomised and 627 analysed (314 bicarbonate, 313 control), all with severe metabolic acidemia (pH ≤7.20) and moderate-to-severe acute kidney injury; median age 67 years (IQR 59–74); men were 62% of the bicarbonate group and 59% of the control group.
cards.result: The primary outcome, day-90 all-cause mortality, was 195 of 314 patients (62.1%) in the bicarbonate group and 193 of 313 (61.7%) in the control group (absolute difference 0.4 percentage points; 95% CI −7.2 to 8.0; P=0.91). There was no evidence of a group effect on day-28 or day-180 mortality. Among 18 secondary outcomes, kidney replacement therapy was used in 109 of 314 patients (35%) in the bicarbonate group and 157 of 313 (50%) in the control group (absolute difference −15.5 points; 95% CI −23.1 to −7.8); no evidence of a group effect was found on the other secondary outcomes, including adverse events.
cards.watchOut: This trial was designed to test exactly the population BICAR-ICU's subgroup flagged — and its mortality answer is null, which is why the earlier subgroup claim does not survive as a claim on this shelf. The kidney-replacement-therapy difference is one secondary outcome among 18 and is stamped POSSIBLE, not more.

cards.summary: The subgroup signal met its confirmatory trial and failed — LIKELY the null on mortality; POSSIBLE on reduced kidney-replacement-therapy use — Tier C proposed.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: BICAR-ICU 2018 (389 patients, severe metabolic acidemia overall) and BICARICU-2 2025 (627 analysed, the acute-kidney-injury population specifically).
cards.result: Bicarbonate for severe metabolic acidemia has no demonstrated mortality benefit in either population tested: BICAR-ICU's overall composite was null (66% vs 71%), and where its pre-specified AKI stratum suggested survival benefit (54% vs 37%), the purpose-built BICARICU-2 trial found day-90 mortality of 62.1% vs 61.7%. Two trials pointing at no mortality effect earn LIKELY the null. The one positive signal left standing is kidney-replacement-therapy use in BICARICU-2 (35% vs 50%), a secondary outcome stamped POSSIBLE. Tier C-proposed pending the developer's personal verdict, because mortality claims — including retired ones — are Tier C.
cards.watchOut: Do not quote BICAR-ICU's AKI-stratum survival figures without BICARICU-2 beside them; quoted alone, they describe a claim its own confirmatory trial refuted.

shelves.title: Securing the airway: video laryngoscopy, the bougie, and preoxygenation (DEVICE, BOUGIE, PREOXI, FELLOW)
shelves.question: Do video laryngoscopy (DEVICE) and routine bougie use (BOUGIE) improve first-attempt intubation success in critically ill adults — and do non-invasive-ventilation preoxygenation (PREOXI) and apneic oxygenation (FELLOW) prevent hypoxemia?
shelves.mesh: Laryngoscopy/adverse effects,methods · Critical Illness/therapy · Intubation, Intratracheal/methods · Laryngoscopes · Emergency Service, Hospital · Video Recording · Critical Illness
shelves.balance: Split: LIKELY that video laryngoscopy raises first-attempt success (DEVICE: 85.1% vs 70.8%; absolute difference 14.3 points) and that non-invasive-ventilation preoxygenation reduces hypoxemia during intubation (PREOXI: 9.1% vs 18.5%; difference −9.4 points) — two large multicentre trials with clear primary-endpoint wins on the process outcomes they tested. POSSIBLE for the two nulls: routine bougie use did not raise first-attempt success (BOUGIE: 80.4% vs 83.0%; P=0.27), and apneic oxygenation did not raise lowest oxygen saturation in its single-centre trial (FELLOW: median 92% vs 90%; P=0.16). These are first-attempt and hypoxemia outcomes, not mortality claims — Tier C: no, after evaluating the topic file's Tier C candidacy against the brief's mortality/MI/stroke/CV-benefit rule.

cards.headline: DEVICE 2023: video laryngoscopy raised first-attempt success to 85.1% vs 70.8% with direct laryngoscopy
cards.summary: DEVICE 2023: video laryngoscopy raised first-attempt success to 85.1% vs 70.8% with direct laryngoscopy.
cards.type: Multicentre, randomised trial at 17 US emergency departments and ICUs; stopped for efficacy at the single preplanned interim analysis
cards.people: 1,417 critically ill adults undergoing tracheal intubation were included in the final analysis (705 video laryngoscope; 712 direct laryngoscope); 91.5% of intubations were performed by an emergency-medicine resident or a critical-care fellow. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Successful intubation on the first attempt (primary outcome) occurred in 600 of 705 patients (85.1%) with video laryngoscopy and 504 of 712 (70.8%) with direct laryngoscopy (absolute risk difference 14.3 percentage points; 95% CI 9.9 to 18.7; P<0.001). Severe complications during intubation occurred in 151 patients (21.4%) vs 149 (20.9%) (absolute difference 0.5 points; −3.9 to 4.9). Oesophageal intubation, dental injury and aspiration were similar between groups.
cards.watchOut: Operators were mostly trainees — exactly the group with most to gain from a video view; the absolute gain may be smaller for expert direct laryngoscopists. The endpoint is first-attempt success, not mortality.
cards.source: Prekker ME et al. Video versus Direct Laryngoscopy for Tracheal Intubation of Critically Ill Adults. N Engl J Med. 2023;389(5):418-429. PMID: 37326325. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT05239195, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: FELLOW 2016: apneic oxygenation did not raise the lowest oxygen saturation during ICU intubation — median 92% vs 90%
cards.summary: FELLOW 2016: apneic oxygenation did not raise the lowest oxygen saturation during ICU intubation — median 92% vs 90%.
cards.type: Randomised, open-label, pragmatic trial in a single medical ICU
cards.people: 150 adults undergoing endotracheal intubation in a medical ICU, randomised to 15 L/min of 100% oxygen via nasal cannula during laryngoscopy (apneic oxygenation) or no supplemental oxygen during laryngoscopy (usual care). The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: The lowest arterial oxygen saturation between induction and 2 minutes after intubation (primary outcome) was a median of 92% with apneic oxygenation vs 90% with usual care (95% CI for the difference −1.6 to 7.4%; P=0.16). There was no difference in oxygen saturation below 90% (44.7% vs 47.2%; P=0.87), below 80% (15.8% vs 25.0%; P=0.22), or a fall in saturation of more than 3% (53.9% vs 55.6%; P=0.87). Duration of ventilation, ICU stay and in-hospital mortality were similar between groups.
cards.watchOut: A single-centre, 150-patient trial — its null is stamped POSSIBLE, not LIKELY, and it predates PREOXI's positive test of a different, active preoxygenation strategy; the two are not interchangeable interventions.

cards.headline: Synthesis: see better (video) and preoxygenate actively (NIV) — LIKELY; a bougie for everyone and passive apneic oxygen — no demonstrated gain
cards.summary: See better (video) and preoxygenate actively (NIV) — LIKELY; a bougie for everyone and passive apneic oxygen — no demonstrated gain. (Endpoints are procedural; no mortality claim, not Tier C.)
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: DEVICE 2023 (1,417 patients), BOUGIE 2021 (1,102), PREOXI 2024 (1,301 enrolled) and FELLOW 2016 (150).
cards.result: The airway bundle the trials support: a video laryngoscope for the first attempt (85.1% vs 70.8% success) and non-invasive ventilation to preoxygenate (hypoxemia 9.1% vs 18.5%). The two habits the trials do not support as routine: a bougie in every intubation (80.4% vs 83.0%) and passive apneic oxygen by nasal cannula (lowest saturation 92% vs 90%). All four endpoints are procedural — no mortality claim is made or stamped on this shelf. Fenced, not carded: a newer bougie trial in critically injured patients with difficult-airway characteristics (the BEST trial, found in this shelf's currency sweep) addresses the selected difficult-airway population that BOUGIE's routine-use design did not test; it does not change the routine-use null above.
cards.watchOut: DEVICE and BOUGIE are not in conflict: they test different devices. Quoting BOUGIE against the bougie as a rescue tool, or FELLOW against NIV preoxygenation, misreads both trials.

shelves.title: Ascorbic acid, corticosteroids and thiamine in septic shock (ACTS, VITAMINS)
shelves.question: In septic shock, does the combination of ascorbic acid, hydrocortisone and thiamine reduce organ injury (SOFA change) versus placebo (ACTS) — and does it beat hydrocortisone alone on time alive and free of vasopressors (VITAMINS)?
shelves.mesh: Adrenal Cortex Hormones/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Ascorbic Acid/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Cross Infection · Drug Therapy, Combination · Hyperglycemia/chemically induced · Hypernatremia/chemically induced · Multiple Organ Failure/etiology,prevention & control
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): Two randomised trials of the three-drug 'metabolic resuscitation' combination agree. ACTS (205 patients, placebo-controlled and blinded) found no significant difference in SOFA-score change over 72 hours (adjusted mean difference −0.8 points, 95% CI −1.7 to 0.2; P=.12 for interaction), in kidney failure (31.7% versus 27.3%) or in 30-day mortality (34.7% versus 29.3%; HR 1.3, 0.8 to 2.2 — relative, not significant, and numerically favouring placebo). VITAMINS (211 patients completing the primary outcome, hydrocortisone-controlled and open-label) found time alive and free of vasopressor support to day 7 of 122.1 versus 124.6 hours (median paired difference −0.6 hours, −8.3 to 7.2; P=.83), with 90-day mortality 28.6% versus 24.5% (HR 1.18, 0.69 to 2.00). TIER C RULING (stated per the brief): NOT Tier C — the shelf's claim is an organ-injury/vasopressor-duration claim, both primaries were null, and no mortality benefit is claimed; mortality was a secondary outcome in both trials and was null in both, and it is printed beside the primaries on every card. Vitamin C alone in sepsis lives on Shelf #108 and its trials are not re-carded here.

cards.headline: ACTS 2020: the vitamin C–steroid–thiamine cocktail did not reduce SOFA organ-injury scores versus placebo (P=.12); 30-day mortality 34.7% vs 29.3%
cards.summary: ACTS 2020: the vitamin C–steroid–thiamine cocktail did not reduce SOFA organ-injury scores vs placebo (P=.12); 30-day mortality (34.7% vs 29.3%) is printed beside the primary on the card.
cards.people: 205 adult patients with septic shock enrolled at 14 US centres, randomised to parenteral ascorbic acid 1,500 mg, hydrocortisone 50 mg and thiamine 100 mg every 6 hours for 4 days (103) or matching placebo (102); 200 (98%) received at least one dose and were analysed (mean age 68 years, SD 15; 90 patients, 44%, were women).
cards.result: There was no statistically significant interaction between time and treatment for SOFA score over 72 hours: mean SOFA fell from 9.1 to 4.4 (−4.7 points) on the combination versus 9.2 to 5.1 (−4.1) on placebo (adjusted mean difference −0.8, 95% CI −1.7 to 0.2; P=.12 for interaction). Kidney failure did not differ (31.7% versus 27.3%; adjusted risk difference 0.03, −0.1 to 0.2; P=.58), nor did 30-day mortality (34.7% versus 29.3%; hazard ratio 1.3, 0.8 to 2.2 — relative; P=.26). The most common serious adverse events were hyperglycaemia (12 versus 7 patients), hypernatraemia (11 versus 7) and new hospital-acquired infection (13 versus 12). The authors conclude the data do not support routine use of the combination in septic shock.
cards.watchOut: A 205-patient trial: its mortality confidence interval (HR 0.8 to 2.2) is wide, but the point estimate favours placebo and the primary organ-injury endpoint is the claim the trial was built to test — and it is null. ACTS compared the cocktail with placebo, not with hydrocortisone alone; that comparison is VITAMINS' card.
cards.source: Moskowitz A et al. Effect of Ascorbic Acid, Corticosteroids, and Thiamine on Organ Injury in Septic Shock: The ACTS Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA. 2020;324(7):642-650. PMID: 32809003. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03389555, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: VITAMINS 2020: adding vitamin C and thiamine to hydrocortisone did not speed shock resolution — 122.1 vs 124.6 vasopressor-free hours alive (P=.83)
cards.summary: VITAMINS 2020: adding vitamin C and thiamine to hydrocortisone did not speed shock resolution (122.1 vs 124.6 vasopressor-free hours alive).
cards.people: 216 patients meeting the Sepsis-3 definition of septic shock at 10 intensive care units in Australia, New Zealand and Brazil, randomised to intravenous vitamin C 1.5 g every 6 hours, hydrocortisone 50 mg every 6 hours and thiamine 200 mg every 12 hours (109) or hydrocortisone alone (107) until shock resolution or up to 10 days; 211 provided consent and completed the primary outcome measurement (mean age 61.7 years, SD 15.0; 133 men, 63%).
cards.result: Time alive and free of vasopressor administration up to day 7 was 122.1 hours (IQR 76.3–145.4) in the combination group versus 124.6 hours (82.1–147.0) on hydrocortisone alone (median of paired differences −0.6 hours, 95% CI −8.3 to 7.2; P=.83). Of 10 prespecified secondary outcomes, 9 showed no statistically significant difference; 90-day mortality was 30 of 105 (28.6%) versus 25 of 102 (24.5%) (hazard ratio 1.18, 0.69 to 2.00 — relative). No serious adverse events were reported.
cards.watchOut: Open-label (no placebo in the control arm) and powered for vasopressor duration, not mortality; it answers 'does the cocktail add anything to hydrocortisone?' — and the answer is no detectable addition, with both trials' mortality point estimates on the wrong side of 1.0.

cards.headline: Synthesis: two comparators, two null primaries — LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) for the cocktail
cards.summary: Two comparators, two null primaries — LIKELY the null. Ruled NOT Tier C at build: no mortality benefit is claimed, and mortality was secondary and null in both trials.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: ACTS (205 patients, versus placebo, blinded) and VITAMINS (211 patients analysed, versus hydrocortisone, open-label).
cards.result: The combination was tested against both plausible comparators and failed both primaries: SOFA change −0.8 points (P=.12) against placebo, and vasopressor-free time −0.6 hours (P=.83) against hydrocortisone alone. Mortality, secondary in both, was null in both (HR 1.3 and 1.18, both relative, both numerically against the cocktail). Two randomised trials with concordant nulls support LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) for the combination as trialled. Vitamin C monotherapy and its later trials (including LOVIT) stay home on Shelf #108; nothing from that shelf is re-carded here.

shelves.title: Enteral glutamine for major burn injury (RE-ENERGIZE)
shelves.question: In patients with severe burns, does enteral glutamine supplementation reduce time to discharge alive, infections, or mortality versus placebo (RE-ENERGIZE)?
shelves.mesh: Burns/drug therapy,pathology · Canada · Critical Illness/therapy · Enteral Nutrition/adverse effects,methods · Glutamine/administration & dosage,adverse effects,therapeutic use
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): A single very large double-blind trial is enough, under this library's rule for a very large null, to carry the null at LIKELY. RE-ENERGIZE (1,200 patients analysed with severe burns, mean burn size 33% of total body surface area) found a median time to discharge alive of 40 days on enteral glutamine (0.5 g/kg/day) versus 38 days on placebo (subdistribution hazard ratio for discharge alive 0.91, 95% CI 0.80 to 1.04; P=0.17 — a relative measure, with death handled as a competing risk), and 6-month mortality of 17.2% versus 16.2% (HR 1.06, 0.80 to 1.41 — relative, printed beside the discharge outcome per this library's rule for any composite-adjacent endpoint). No substantial differences in serious adverse events were observed. TIER C note: mortality was a secondary outcome and no benefit claim is made, so the shelf is not flagged Tier C; if the developer reads the discharge-alive composite as Tier C territory, it returns for his verdict — that choice is his, and it is recorded in summary.md. The general-critical-illness glutamine trial (REDOXS) is already carded elsewhere and is fenced, not re-carded, here; the general ICU-nutrition shelves (#16, #21, #110) test different questions.

cards.headline: RE-ENERGIZE 2022: enteral glutamine did not shorten time to discharge alive in 1,200 burn patients — median 40 vs 38 days (subdistribution HR 0.91)
cards.summary: RE-ENERGIZE 2022: enteral glutamine did not shorten time to discharge alive in 1,200 burn patients (median 40 vs 38 days ); death is handled as a competing risk in the primary, disclosed on the shelf face.
cards.people: 1,209 patients with deep second- or third-degree burns (affecting at least 10–20% of total body surface area, depending on age) randomised within 72 hours of admission to enteral glutamine 0.5 g/kg/day or placebo, given every 4 hours by feeding tube or 3–4 times daily by mouth until 7 days after the last skin graft, discharge from the acute care unit, or 3 months; 1,200 were analysed (596 glutamine, 604 placebo), with a mean burn size of 33% of total body surface area. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: The median time to discharge alive from hospital (the primary outcome, censored at 90 days) was 40 days (IQR 24–87) on glutamine versus 38 days (22–75) on placebo (subdistribution hazard ratio for discharge alive 0.91, 95% CI 0.80 to 1.04; P=0.17 — a relative measure accounting for death as a competing risk). Mortality at 6 months was 17.2% on glutamine versus 16.2% on placebo (hazard ratio for death 1.06, 0.80 to 1.41 — relative). No substantial between-group differences in serious adverse events were observed.
cards.watchOut: A single trial, however large: its result is a null on the primary with point estimates marginally favouring placebo on both endpoints, so the finding is 'no benefit shown', stated once, at LIKELY under the very-large-null rule — not proof of exact equivalence at every dose or burn size. The record names no specific product or brand — products sold today may differ in safety and effectiveness.

shelves.title: Restrictive versus liberal intravenous fluid in septic shock (CLASSIC, CLOVERS, ARISE FLUIDS)
shelves.question: In patients with septic shock or sepsis-induced hypotension, does a restrictive intravenous fluid strategy (with earlier vasopressors) change mortality versus standard or liberal fluid therapy?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Intravenous · Critical Care/methods · Fluid Therapy/adverse effects,methods · Intensive Care Units · Shock, Septic/mortality,therapy · Fluid Therapy/adverse effects,methods,mortality · Sepsis/complications,mortality,therapy
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, mortality primary outcome): Three large randomised trials now agree. CLASSIC (1,554 ICU patients with septic shock) found 90-day mortality of 42.3% with fluid restriction versus 42.1% with standard therapy. CLOVERS (1,563 patients with sepsis-induced hypotension) found mortality before discharge home by day 90 of 14.0% with a restrictive, vasopressor-early strategy versus 14.9% with a liberal strategy. The currency sweep added a third, concordant trial, ARISE FLUIDS (1,000 emergency-department patients, 2026), whose primary outcome — days alive and out of hospital at day 90 — was identical at a median of 76 days in both groups. Restricting fluid (within the ranges these trials achieved, roughly 1.1–2.1 litres less) does not save lives; neither, on this evidence, does giving more.

cards.headline: CLASSIC 2022: fluid restriction in septic shock did not reduce 90-day mortality (42.3% vs 42.1%)
cards.summary: CLASSIC (2022): restriction halved fluid (1,798 vs 3,811 ml) with 90-day mortality 42.3% vs 42.1% — null.
cards.people: 1,554 patients with septic shock in the ICU who had received at least 1 litre of intravenous fluid, with shock onset within 12 hours before screening, assigned to restricted (770) or standard (784) intravenous fluid; primary outcome data available for 1,545 (99.4%). The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: In the ICU the restrictive group received a median of 1,798 ml of intravenous fluid versus 3,811 ml in the standard group. At 90 days, death had occurred in 323 of 764 patients (42.3%) in the restrictive group versus 329 of 781 (42.1%) in the standard group (adjusted absolute difference 0.1 percentage points, 95% CI −4.7 to 4.9; P=0.96). Serious adverse events occurred at least once in 29.4% versus 30.8%. Days alive without life support and days alive and out of hospital were similar.
cards.watchOut: Open-label and conducted in ICUs already practising relatively conservative fluid therapy; the achieved separation (about 2 litres) is the contrast actually tested — this trial does not test extreme restriction or extreme liberal use.
cards.source: Meyhoff TS et al. Restriction of Intravenous Fluid in ICU Patients with Septic Shock. N Engl J Med. 2022 Jun 30;386(26):2459-2470. PMID: 35709019. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03668236, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: CLOVERS 2023: a restrictive, vasopressor-early strategy did not lower mortality versus a liberal fluid strategy (14.0% vs 14.9%)
cards.summary: CLOVERS (2023): restrictive/pressor-early, mortality before discharge home by day 90 14.0% vs 14.9% — null.
cards.type: Unblinded, randomised superiority trial at 60 US centres
cards.people: 1,563 patients with sepsis-induced hypotension refractory to initial treatment with 1 to 3 litres of intravenous fluid, randomised within 4 hours to a restrictive strategy prioritising vasopressors (782) or a liberal strategy prioritising fluid (781) for 24 hours. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: The restrictive group received less intravenous fluid (difference of medians −2,134 ml, 95% CI −2,318 to −1,949) with earlier, more prevalent and longer vasopressor use. Death from any cause before discharge home by day 90 occurred in 109 patients (14.0%) in the restrictive group and 116 (14.9%) in the liberal group (estimated difference −0.9 percentage points, 95% CI −4.4 to 2.6; P=0.61). Serious adverse events were similar in the two groups.
cards.watchOut: Unblinded, and the population (early sepsis-induced hypotension, 14–15% mortality) is less sick than CLASSIC's established ICU septic shock (42% mortality); the null is consistent across both severities, which strengthens it, but neither trial tested patients before any fluid was given.

cards.headline: ARISE FLUIDS 2026: restricted fluid with early vasopressors gave the same days alive and out of hospital at day 90 (median 76 vs 76 days)
cards.summary: ARISE FLUIDS (2026): days alive and out of hospital at day 90 identical ( median 76 vs 76 ).
cards.type: Randomised trial in emergency departments (Australia and New Zealand)
cards.people: 1,000 adults presenting to the emergency department with septic shock, assigned to restricted-volume fluid with early vasopressors (499) or higher-volume fluid with later vasopressors (501) for at least 6 and up to 24 hours; 963 patients (481 vs 482) in the intention-to-treat population after consent was not obtained for 37. cards.headline: Synthesis: three large trials, three nulls — fluid volume strategy within tested ranges does not move mortality in septic shock
cards.summary: Synthesis: three large trials, three nulls — fluid-volume strategy within tested ranges does not move mortality in septic shock — LIKELY the null (Tier C).
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: CLASSIC 2022 (1,554 ICU patients), CLOVERS 2023 (1,563 patients with sepsis-induced hypotension) and ARISE FLUIDS 2026 (963 analysed, emergency department).
cards.result: Mortality was 42.3% versus 42.1% (CLASSIC, 90 days), 14.0% versus 14.9% (CLOVERS, before discharge home by day 90) and days alive and out of hospital were identical (ARISE FLUIDS). The trials differ in setting and severity and agree on the answer, which is why the null carries LIKELY — proposed, because mortality claims are Tier C and await the developer's personal verdict. Fluid TYPE (balanced crystalloids versus saline) is a different question, home on Shelf #123, and fluid volume in pancreatitis is Shelf #598; neither is re-carded here.
cards.watchOut: A null for strategy is not a licence for either extreme at the bedside: all three trials operated between protocol guardrails, and individual patients with overt overload or under-resuscitation sit outside what was randomised.

shelves.title: Peripheral-perfusion-guided resuscitation in septic shock (ANDROMEDA-SHOCK and ANDROMEDA-SHOCK-2)
shelves.question: In septic shock, does a resuscitation strategy targeting capillary-refill normalisation improve outcomes versus lactate-guided or usual care?
shelves.mesh: Capillaries/physiopathology · Fluid Therapy/methods · Hemodynamics · Intensive Care Units · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Lactic Acid/blood · Organ Dysfunction Scores
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, mortality outcome): ANDROMEDA-SHOCK (424 patients) targeted capillary-refill normalisation versus lactate clearance and did NOT significantly reduce its primary outcome, 28-day mortality (34.9% vs 43.4%; hazard ratio 0.75 relative, 95% CI 0.55 to 1.02; P=0.06), although organ dysfunction at 72 hours was less (mean SOFA 5.6 vs 6.6). The larger ANDROMEDA-SHOCK-2 (1,467 patients, found in the currency sweep) won its hierarchical composite against usual care (win ratio 1.16 relative, 95% CI 1.02 to 1.33; P=0.04), driven mainly by shorter duration of vital support rather than by mortality (individual wins for death 19.1% vs 17.8%). A bedside perfusion target probably helps organise resuscitation; a mortality benefit is not established — POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: ANDROMEDA-SHOCK 2019: capillary-refill-guided resuscitation did not significantly reduce 28-day mortality (34.9% vs 43.4%; P=0.06)
cards.summary: ANDROMEDA-SHOCK (2019): capillary-refill-guided care, 28-day mortality 34.9% vs 43.4% (HR 0.75 relative; P=0.06 — not significant).
cards.type: Multicentre, randomised trial at 28 ICUs in 5 countries
cards.people: 424 patients with septic shock (mean age 63 years; 226 [53%] women), randomised to an 8-hour step-by-step resuscitation protocol targeting normalisation of capillary refill time (212) or normalisation/decrease of lactate by more than 20% per 2 hours (212); 416 (98%) completed the trial.
cards.result: By day 28, 74 patients (34.9%) in the peripheral-perfusion group and 92 (43.4%) in the lactate group had died (hazard ratio 0.75 — a relative measure — 95% CI 0.55 to 1.02; P=0.06; risk difference −8.5%, 95% CI −18.2% to 1.2%). Peripheral-perfusion targeting was associated with less organ dysfunction at 72 hours (mean SOFA score 5.6 [SD 4.3] vs 6.6 [SD 4.7]; mean difference −1.00, 95% CI −1.97 to −0.02; P=0.045). There were no significant differences in the other 6 secondary outcomes and no protocol-related serious adverse reactions were confirmed. The hazard ratio of 0.75 sits inside the 0.5–2.0 band that is not solid evidence on its own.
cards.watchOut: A single trial whose primary outcome narrowly missed significance: the point estimate favours the perfusion target, but P=0.06 with a confidence interval crossing 1.0 cannot be printed as a mortality benefit.
cards.source: Hernández G et al. cards.headline: ANDROMEDA-SHOCK-2 2025: a personalised capillary-refill protocol beat usual care on a hierarchical composite (win ratio 1.16), driven by duration of vital support, not mortality
cards.summary: ANDROMEDA-SHOCK-2 (2025): personalised capillary-refill protocol won the hierarchical composite ( win ratio 1.16 relative), driven by duration of support.
cards.type: Randomised clinical trial at 86 centres in 19 countries
cards.people: 1,501 patients within the first 4 hours of septic shock randomised between March 2022 and April 2025; 1,467 in the primary analysis (mean age 66 [17] years; 43.3% female), assigned to a personalised haemodynamic resuscitation protocol targeting capillary refill time (720 analysed) — tailoring fluids, vasopressors and inotropes using pulse pressure, diastolic pressure, fluid responsiveness and bedside echocardiography — versus usual care (747).
cards.result: For the hierarchical composite of mortality, duration of vital support and length of hospital stay at 28 days, there were 131,131 wins (48.9%) in the intervention group versus 112,787 (42.1%) in usual care (win ratio 1.16 — a relative measure — 95% CI 1.02 to 1.33; P=0.04). Individual wins for death were 19.1% versus 17.8%; for duration of vital support, 26.4% versus 21.1%; and for length of hospital stay, 3.4% versus 3.2% — so the win came mainly from shorter vital support, not from fewer deaths.
cards.watchOut: A win-ratio composite can be positive while its mortality layer is near-neutral, as here; the intervention is also a bundle (echocardiography, fluid-responsiveness testing, inotrope tailoring), so the credit cannot be assigned to capillary refill alone.

shelves.title: Angiotensin II for catecholamine-refractory vasodilatory shock (ATHOS-3)
shelves.question: In vasodilatory shock refractory to high-dose catecholamines, does angiotensin II raise blood pressure and allow catecholamine sparing versus placebo — and did the blood-pressure response translate into a survival difference?
shelves.mesh: Angiotensin II/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Blood Pressure/drug effects · Catecholamines/administration & dosage · Drug Therapy, Combination · Hypotension/drug therapy · Organ Dysfunction Scores · Shock/drug therapy,physiopathology
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: In the single pivotal trial (ATHOS-3, 321 patients treated), angiotensin II produced the blood-pressure response it was designed for — 69.9% versus 23.4% met the hour-3 mean arterial pressure endpoint (odds ratio 7.95 relative) — and improved the cardiovascular SOFA score at 48 hours. It did not significantly change 28-day mortality (46% vs 54%; hazard ratio 0.78 relative, 95% CI 0.57 to 1.07; P=0.12), and the trial was not powered to do so. Ruled NOT Tier C at build: the shelf's claim is a blood-pressure (surrogate) claim, the primary endpoint contains no mortality component, and no mortality benefit is claimed — the null mortality result is printed on the card, not sold. A single trial with a surrogate primary caps at POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: ATHOS-3 2017: angiotensin II raised blood pressure in refractory vasodilatory shock (response 69.9% vs 23.4%), without a significant survival difference (28-day mortality 46% vs 54%)
cards.summary: ATHOS-3 (2017): angiotensin II raised blood pressure in refractory vasodilatory shock (MAP response 69.9% vs 23.4% ).
cards.people: 344 patients with vasodilatory shock receiving more than 0.2 μg of norepinephrine per kilogram per minute (or the equivalent of another vasopressor) were assigned; 321 received a study intervention (163 angiotensin II, 158 placebo) and were analysed. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: The primary endpoint (a mean arterial pressure response at hour 3 — an increase of at least 10 mm Hg or to at least 75 mm Hg without increasing background vasopressors) was reached by 114 of 163 patients (69.9%) on angiotensin II versus 37 of 158 (23.4%) on placebo (odds ratio 7.95 — a relative measure — 95% CI 4.76 to 13.3; P<0.001). At 48 hours the mean improvement in cardiovascular SOFA score was greater with angiotensin II (−1.75 vs −1.28; P=0.01). Serious adverse events were reported in 60.7% versus 67.1%. Death by day 28 occurred in 75 of 163 (46%) versus 85 of 158 (54%) (hazard ratio 0.78 relative, 95% CI 0.57 to 1.07; P=0.12 — not significant).
cards.watchOut: Blood pressure is a surrogate: the one outcome patients feel — survival — was a secondary endpoint in an underpowered comparison, and its hazard ratio of 0.78 sits inside the 0.5–2.0 band that is not solid evidence on its own. Industry-funded (La Jolla Pharmaceutical Company).

shelves.title: Early norepinephrine in septic shock resuscitation (CENSER)
shelves.question: In sepsis with hypotension presenting to the emergency department, does starting norepinephrine within the first hour improve shock control by six hours versus standard care with later vasopressors?
shelves.mesh: Hemodynamics/drug effects · Hypotension/drug therapy,etiology · Norepinephrine/administration & dosage,therapeutic use · Resuscitation/methods · Shock, Septic/complications,drug therapy,therapy · Vasoconstrictor Agents/administration & dosage,therapeutic use
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: One single-centre, double-blind phase 2 trial (CENSER, 310 patients) found early low-dose norepinephrine (median 93 versus 192 minutes from emergency-department arrival) raised shock control by 6 hours from 48.4% to 76.1% (P<0.001), with less cardiogenic pulmonary oedema (14.4% vs 27.7%) and less new arrhythmia (11% vs 20%). The 28-day mortality difference (15.5% vs 21.9%; P=0.15) was secondary, not significant, and is hypothesis-generating only — no mortality claim is made, so this shelf is not Tier C. A single-centre phase 2 trial with a process primary caps at POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: CENSER 2019: early norepinephrine improved shock control by 6 hours (76.1% vs 48.4%), with no significant 28-day mortality difference (15.5% vs 21.9%)
cards.summary: CENSER (2019): norepinephrine ~100 minutes earlier improved shock control by 6 hours ( 76.1% vs 48.4% ); 28-day mortality 15.5% vs 21.9% (NS).
cards.type: Single-centre, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 2 trial (Siriraj Hospital, Bangkok)
cards.people: 310 adults with sepsis and hypotension, randomised to early norepinephrine (155) or standard treatment (155). The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Median time from emergency-room arrival to norepinephrine was 93 versus 192 minutes (P<0.001). Shock control by 6 hours (mean arterial pressure at least 65 mm Hg with urine flow at least 0.5 ml/kg/h for 2 consecutive hours, or lactate falling at least 10%) was achieved by 118 of 155 (76.1%) versus 75 of 155 (48.4%) (P<0.001). The 28-day mortality was 24 of 155 (15.5%) versus 34 of 155 (21.9%) (P=0.15 — not significant). Cardiogenic pulmonary oedema occurred in 22 of 155 (14.4%) versus 43 of 155 (27.7%) (P=0.004) and new-onset arrhythmia in 17 of 155 (11%) versus 31 of 155 (20%) (P=0.03).
cards.watchOut: Single centre, phase 2, and powered for shock control — a composite of monitor and urine-output targets — not for mortality; the authors themselves state that further studies are needed before this approach enters routine resuscitation practice.
cards.source: Permpikul C et al. Early Use of Norepinephrine in Septic Shock Resuscitation (CENSER). A Randomized Trial. Am J Respir Crit Care Med. 2019 May 1;199(9):1097-1105. PMID: 30704260. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01945983, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Synthesis: starting the pressor early controls shock sooner; whether it saves lives is untested at scale — POSSIBLE
cards.summary: Synthesis: starting the pressor early controls shock sooner; whether it saves lives is untested at scale — POSSIBLE.
cards.people: Synthesis of the card above: CENSER 2019 (310 emergency-department patients with sepsis and hypotension).
cards.result: CENSER's contribution is timing: the same drug, started about 100 minutes sooner, controlled shock by 6 hours in 76.1% versus 48.4% and was associated with fewer fluid-overload complications. Which vasopressor to use is Shelf #129's question, and fluid-versus-pressor strategy at scale is Shelf #1070's (CLASSIC, CLOVERS, ARISE FLUIDS) — neither is re-carded here.

shelves.title: Selective decontamination of the digestive tract in ventilated ICU patients (SuDDICU)
shelves.question: In critically ill patients receiving mechanical ventilation, does selective decontamination of the digestive tract reduce hospital mortality versus standard care?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Intravenous · Anti-Bacterial Agents/administration & dosage,therapeutic use · Bacteremia/etiology,mortality,prevention & control · Critical Illness/mortality,therapy · Cross Infection/etiology,mortality,prevention & control · Cross-Over Studies · Decontamination/methods
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, hospital mortality primary outcome): The SuDDICU programme is one crossover cluster trial reported twice — the Australian report (5,982 patients; in-hospital mortality 27.0% with SDD versus 29.1% with standard care; odds ratio 0.91 relative, 95% CI 0.82 to 1.02; P=0.12) and the full international report combining Australia and Canada (9,289 randomised patients; 27.9% versus 29.5%; odds ratio 0.94 relative, 95% CI 0.84 to 1.05; P=0.27). SDD did reduce new bloodstream infections and cultures of antibiotic-resistant organisms, but noninferiority for resistance ecology was not confirmed in the ecological assessment, and mortality was not significantly reduced in either report. A very large single-trial programme with a tight confidence interval around no effect carries LIKELY (the treatment made no difference); the two reports are one trial, counted once.

cards.headline: SuDDICU 2022 (Australian report): SDD did not significantly reduce in-hospital mortality in ventilated patients (27.0% vs 29.1%; P=0.12)
cards.summary: SuDDICU, Australian report (2022): SDD did not significantly reduce in-hospital mortality ( 27.0% vs 29.1% ; P=0.12).
cards.type: Cluster, crossover, randomised clinical trial (19 ICUs, Australia), with a contemporaneous ecological assessment
cards.people: 5,982 mechanically ventilated adults (mean age 58.3 years; 36.8% women) enrolled April 2018 to May 2021; the SDD group (2,791) received 6-hourly oral paste and gastric suspension containing colistin, tobramycin and nystatin for the duration of ventilation plus a 4-day intravenous antibiotic course, versus standard care (3,191). A further 8,599 patients entered the ecological assessment.
cards.result: In-hospital deaths within 90 days were 753 of 2,791 (27.0%) with SDD versus 928 of 3,191 (29.1%) with standard care (mean difference −1.7%, 95% CI −4.8% to 1.3%; odds ratio 0.91 — a relative measure — 95% CI 0.82 to 1.02; P=0.12). Six of 8 secondary outcomes showed no significant difference; new antibiotic-resistant-organism cultures were 23.1% versus 34.6% (absolute difference −11.0%), new positive blood cultures 5.6% versus 8.1%, and new Clostridioides difficile infections 0.5% versus 0.9%. In the ecological assessment, SDD was not shown noninferior for the change in new resistant-organism cultures. The authors note the confidence interval includes a clinically important benefit.
cards.watchOut: A cluster-crossover design (ICUs, not patients, were randomised) with an ecological resistance question that remained unresolved; the adjacent record PMID 36286098 is the companion meta-analysis, not the trial, and is not carded.
cards.source: SuDDICU Investigators et al. Effect of Selective Decontamination of the Digestive Tract on Hospital Mortality in Critically Ill Patients Receiving Mechanical Ventilation: A Randomized Clinical Trial. cards.headline: SuDDICU 2026 (full international report, same trial): with Australia and Canada combined, in-hospital mortality was 27.9% versus 29.5% (odds ratio 0.94; P=0.27)
cards.summary: SuDDICU, full international report (2026; same trial): 27.9% vs 29.5% (OR 0.94 relative, 95% CI 0.84–1.05).
cards.type: Cluster, crossover, randomised trial — full report of the same SuDDICU trial (26 ICUs, Australia and Canada), counted once as evidence
cards.people: 20,000 patients in 26 ICUs: 9,289 enrolled in the randomised trial and 10,711 in the observational ecological assessment. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: At 90 days, 1,175 of 4,215 patients (27.9%) in the SDD group and 1,494 of 5,065 (29.5%) in the standard-care group had died before hospital discharge (odds ratio 0.94 — a relative measure — 95% CI 0.84 to 1.05; P=0.27). In the ecological assessment, noninferiority of SDD was not confirmed for development of new antibiotic-resistant organisms. Adverse events considered related were reported in 12 patients (0.3%) with SDD and none with standard care; serious adverse events occurred in 1.1% versus 1.2%.

cards.summary: Synthesis: SDD cuts bloodstream infection and resistant-organism cultures but not mortality — LIKELY the null on survival (Tier C).
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: the SuDDICU trial programme — Australian report 2022 (5,982 randomised patients) and full international report 2026 (9,289 randomised patients, including the Australian cohort).
cards.result: Across 9,289 randomised ventilated patients, SDD's mortality estimate sits at an odds ratio of 0.94 relative (95% CI 0.84 to 1.05) — no significant survival benefit, with less bloodstream infection and fewer resistant-organism cultures but unconfirmed ecological noninferiority. shelves.title: Probiotics to prevent ventilator-associated pneumonia (PROSPECT)
shelves.question: In critically ill ventilated patients, does enteral Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG prevent ventilator-associated pneumonia versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Anti-Bacterial Agents/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Bacterial Infections/prevention & control · Diarrhea/prevention & control · Intensive Care Units · Lacticaseibacillus rhamnosus · Pneumonia, Ventilator-Associated/prevention & control · Probiotics/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): The one large, blinded, placebo-controlled trial (PROSPECT, 2,653 patients in 44 ICUs) found ventilator-associated pneumonia in 21.9% on Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG versus 21.3% on placebo (hazard ratio 1.03 relative, 95% CI 0.87 to 1.22), with none of 20 secondary outcomes — including mortality — significantly different, and a harm signal of probiotic organisms recovered from sterile sites (1.1% vs 0.1%). A single very large blinded null with a tight confidence interval carries LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) under the library's large-null rule. Earlier smaller positive trials are superseded by this test, not pooled against it here.

cards.headline: PROSPECT 2021: Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG did not prevent ventilator-associated pneumonia (21.9% vs 21.3%) and was recovered from sterile sites in 1.1% of treated patients
cards.summary: PROSPECT (2021): Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG did not prevent VAP ( 21.9% vs 21.3% ) and was recovered from sterile sites in 15 treated patients.
cards.type: Randomised, placebo-controlled trial in 44 ICUs (Canada, United States, Saudi Arabia)
cards.people: 2,653 adults predicted to require mechanical ventilation for at least 72 hours (mean age 59.8 years [SD 16.5]; 1,063 women [40.1%]; mean APACHE II score 22.0), enrolled October 2013 to March 2019, receiving enteral L rhamnosus GG 1×10^10 colony-forming units (1,321) or placebo (1,332) twice daily in the ICU for a median of 9 days; 2,650 (99.9%) completed the trial.
cards.result: Ventilator-associated pneumonia (duplicate blinded central adjudication) developed in 289 of 1,318 patients (21.9%) on probiotics versus 284 of 1,332 (21.3%) on placebo (hazard ratio 1.03 — a relative measure — 95% CI 0.87 to 1.22; P=0.73; absolute difference 0.6%, 95% CI −2.5% to 3.7%). None of the 20 prespecified secondary outcomes, including other ICU-acquired infections, diarrhoea, antimicrobial use, mortality, or length of stay, showed a significant difference. Fifteen patients (1.1%) on probiotics versus 1 (0.1%) on placebo had L rhamnosus in a sterile site or as the sole/predominant organism in a nonsterile site (odds ratio 14.02 relative, 95% CI 1.79 to 109.58; P<0.001).
cards.watchOut: One probiotic strain at one dose: the null convicts L rhamnosus GG in ventilated adults, not every organism ever labelled a probiotic — but it is the largest and most rigorous test in this population and outranks the earlier small positive trials. I-Health donated the study product and placebo, as named in the publication's full text.
cards.source: Johnstone J et al. Effect of Probiotics on Incident Ventilator-Associated Pneumonia in Critically Ill Patients: A Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA. 2021 Sep 21;326(11):1024-1033. PMID: 34546300. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02462590, from the record's databank fields.

shelves.title: Awake prone positioning in COVID-19 hypoxaemic respiratory failure (the multinational meta-trial)
shelves.question: In awake, non-intubated patients with COVID-19 acute hypoxaemic respiratory failure on high-flow oxygen, does prone positioning reduce the composite of intubation or death within 28 days?
shelves.mesh: COVID-19/therapy · Canada · France · Ireland · Mexico · Patient Positioning · Prone Position
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, the primary composite includes death): The multinational meta-trial (six harmonised open-label trials, 1,121 patients analysed) found treatment failure (intubation or death within 28 days) in 40% with awake prone positioning versus 46% with standard care (relative risk 0.86 — a relative measure — 95% CI 0.75 to 0.98), driven by intubation (hazard ratio 0.75 relative) while mortality alone was not significantly different (hazard ratio 0.87 relative, 95% CI 0.68 to 1.11). A later French/Mexican trial of 445 patients (currency sweep) pointed the same way on the same composite (posterior probability of benefit 93.8%; mean odds ratio 0.74 relative) but was analysed in a Bayesian framework without conventional significance. Open-label positioning trials with a clinician-mediated endpoint (intubation) cap at POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: Ehrmann 2021 meta-trial: awake prone positioning reduced treatment failure (40% vs 46%; relative risk 0.86) — an intubation effect, with mortality not significantly different
cards.summary: Ehrmann meta-trial (2021): awake proning reduced treatment failure ( 40% vs 46% ; RR 0.86 relative) — an intubation effect, mortality NS.
cards.type: Prospective collaborative meta-trial of six randomised, controlled, open-label trials (Canada, France, Ireland, Mexico, USA, Spain)
cards.people: 1,126 adults requiring high-flow nasal cannula for acute hypoxaemic respiratory failure due to COVID-19, assigned to awake prone positioning (567) or standard care (559) between April 2020 and January 2021; 1,121 in the intention-to-treat analysis. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Treatment failure (intubation or death within 28 days) occurred in 223 of 564 patients (40%) with awake prone positioning versus 257 of 557 (46%) with standard care (relative risk 0.86 — a relative measure — 95% CI 0.75 to 0.98). The hazard ratio for intubation was 0.75 relative (95% CI 0.62 to 0.91) and for mortality 0.87 relative (95% CI 0.68 to 1.11 — not significant). Prespecified adverse events were few and similar in both groups.
cards.watchOut: Open-label: the decision to intubate was made by clinicians who knew the allocation, which can move the composite without moving biology; the mortality layer — the Tier C layer — is null, and no mortality benefit is claimed on this shelf.

cards.headline: Harrois 2025: daily awake proning for at least 6 hours showed a 93.8% posterior probability of reducing intubation or death, without conventional statistical significance
cards.summary: Harrois (2025): daily awake proning ≥6 hours, 93.8% posterior probability of reducing intubation or death, without conventional significance.
cards.type: Randomised clinical trial at 20 hospitals in France and 1 in Mexico (Bayesian primary analysis)
cards.people: 445 non-intubated adults with COVID-19 hypoxaemic respiratory failure requiring at least 3 L/min of oxygen, on wards and in ICUs, randomised July 2020 to August 2021 to awake prone positioning for at least 6 hours a day or standard care (mean age 60 [SD 11] years; 329 males [74%]); standard-care patients had no positioning constraint and could prone spontaneously.
cards.result: With a noninformative prior, the posterior probability that awake prone positioning decreased intubation and/or death within 28 days was 93.8% (mean odds ratio 0.74 — a relative measure — 95% credible interval 0.48 to 1.09, which crosses 1.0). shelves.title: Lower tidal volumes facilitated by extracorporeal CO2 removal (REST)
shelves.question: In acute hypoxaemic respiratory failure, does veno-venous extracorporeal CO2 removal enabling ultra-low tidal-volume ventilation reduce 90-day mortality versus standard ventilation — and at what bleeding cost?
shelves.mesh: Carbon Dioxide/blood · Early Termination of Clinical Trials · Extracorporeal Circulation/adverse effects · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Respiration, Artificial/adverse effects,methods · Respiratory Distress Syndrome/therapy · Respiratory Insufficiency/mortality,therapy
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference, harm-leaning) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, 90-day mortality primary outcome): REST (412 patients of a planned 1,120, stopped early for futility and feasibility) found 90-day mortality of 41.5% with extracorporeal CO2 removal facilitating lower tidal volumes versus 39.5% with standard care (risk ratio 1.05 relative, 95% CI 0.83 to 1.33), fewer ventilator-free days (7.1 vs 9.2), and substantially more serious adverse events (31% vs 9%), including intracranial haemorrhage in 9 patients (4.5%) versus none. Early stopping and underpowering cap the null at POSSIBLE; nothing here supports routine use.

cards.type: Multicentre, randomised, allocation-concealed, open-label, pragmatic trial (51 ICUs, UK) — stopped early
cards.people: 412 adults receiving mechanical ventilation for acute hypoxaemic respiratory failure (mean age 59 years; 143 [35%] women), randomised May 2016 to December 2019 to lower tidal-volume ventilation facilitated by extracorporeal CO2 removal for at least 48 hours (202) or standard-care conventional low tidal-volume ventilation (210); 405 (98%) completed the trial, of a planned sample size of 1,120.
cards.result: Ninety-day mortality was 41.5% in the extracorporeal CO2 removal group versus 39.5% in standard care (risk ratio 1.05 — a relative measure — 95% CI 0.83 to 1.33; absolute difference 2.0%, 95% CI −7.6% to 11.5%; P=0.68). cards.watchOut: Stopped early on data-monitoring advice for futility and feasibility at 37% of planned enrolment, so the trial may have been underpowered for a modest mortality difference — but the harm gradient (31% vs 9% serious adverse events) is a result in its own right, not a power artefact.

shelves.title: Targeted polymyxin B haemoperfusion in endotoxemic septic shock (EUPHRATES)
shelves.question: In septic shock with elevated endotoxin activity, does polymyxin B haemoperfusion reduce 28-day mortality versus sham haemoperfusion?
shelves.mesh: APACHE · Anti-Bacterial Agents/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Endotoxins/blood · Hospital Mortality · Polymyxin B/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Shock, Septic/drug therapy,mortality · Survival Analysis
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, 28-day mortality primary outcome): In the single large blinded test (EUPHRATES, 450 patients with septic shock and endotoxin activity at least 0.60), polymyxin B haemoperfusion did not reduce 28-day mortality — 37.7% versus 34.5% (relative risk 1.09 relative, 95% CI 0.85 to 1.39; P=0.49) — nor mortality in the prespecified sicker subgroup with MODS above 9 (44.5% vs 43.9%). A single trial of 450 patients caps the null at POSSIBLE, however cleanly it was run.

cards.headline: EUPHRATES 2018: polymyxin B haemoperfusion did not reduce 28-day mortality in endotoxemic septic shock (37.7% vs 34.5%)
cards.summary: EUPHRATES (2018): polymyxin B haemoperfusion did not reduce 28-day mortality in endotoxemic septic shock ( 37.7% vs 34.5% ).
cards.type: Multicentre, randomised, sham-controlled trial at 55 tertiary hospitals in North America
cards.people: 450 adult critically ill patients with septic shock and an endotoxin activity assay level of 0.60 or higher (mean age 59.8 years; 177 [39.3%] women; mean APACHE II score 29.4), enrolled September 2010 to June 2016, receiving two polymyxin B haemoperfusion treatments (90–120 minutes) plus standard therapy within 24 hours (224) or sham haemoperfusion plus standard therapy (226); 449 (99.8%) completed the study.
cards.result: Mortality at 28 days was 84 of 223 (37.7%) with haemoperfusion versus 78 of 226 (34.5%) with sham (risk difference 3.2%, 95% CI −5.7% to 12.0%; relative risk 1.09 — a relative measure — 95% CI 0.85 to 1.39; P=0.49). In patients with a multiple organ dysfunction score above 9, mortality was 65 of 146 (44.5%) versus 65 of 148 (43.9%) (risk difference 0.6%; relative risk 1.01 relative, 95% CI 0.78 to 1.31; P=0.92). Overall 264 serious adverse events were reported (65.1% treatment vs 57.3% sham), most frequently worsening of sepsis and of septic shock.
cards.watchOut: The confidence interval (relative risk 0.85 to 1.39) cannot exclude a modest benefit or harm, and the trial's enrichment strategy — treating only assay-positive patients — means the null applies to that selected population, not to unselected septic shock.

shelves.title: Beta-blockade with landiolol in septic shock (STRESS-L)
shelves.question: In patients with septic shock and persistent tachycardia on norepinephrine, does the ultra-short-acting beta-blocker landiolol improve organ failure (SOFA) over the first week versus standard care?
shelves.mesh: Shock, Septic/mortality · State Medicine · Sepsis/complications · Adrenergic beta-Antagonists/therapeutic use · Norepinephrine/therapeutic use · Tachycardia · Morpholines
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (harm-leaning; the treatment made no difference) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: the trial was stopped early on a possible-harm assessment and its mortality figures run against the intervention): STRESS-L enrolled 126 of a planned 340 patients before stopping. Mean SOFA over 14 days was 8.8 on landiolol versus 8.1 on standard care (mean difference 0.75, 95% CI −0.49 to 2.0; P=0.24) — no organ-failure benefit — while mortality was numerically higher with landiolol at day 28 (37.1% vs 25.4%) and day 90 (43.5% vs 28.6%), neither significant in this small stopped trial. Ruled Tier C at build because a mortality-carrying harm signal needs the developer's personal verdict even though the primary outcome was SOFA. POSSIBLE, and the direction of travel is against use.

cards.headline: STRESS-L 2023: landiolol did not reduce organ failure in septic shock with tachycardia (mean SOFA 8.8 vs 8.1), the trial stopped early, and mortality ran numerically higher (day 90: 43.5% vs 28.6%)
cards.summary: STRESS-L (2023): landiolol did not reduce organ failure (mean SOFA 8.8 vs 8.1 ); the trial stopped early and mortality leaned higher (+11.7 points at day 28).
cards.type: Open-label, multicentre, randomised trial in 40 UK NHS intensive care units — stopped early
cards.people: 126 adults (mean age 55.6 years; 58.7% male) with tachycardia (heart rate at least 95/min) and established septic shock treated for at least 24 hours with continuous norepinephrine (at least 0.1 μg/kg/min), randomised April 2018 to December 2021 to landiolol infusion (63) or standard care (63); 126 of a planned 340 participants (37%) were enrolled before early termination.
cards.result: The mean SOFA score from randomisation through 14 days was 8.8 (SD 3.9) with landiolol versus 8.1 (SD 3.2) with standard care (mean difference 0.75, 95% CI −0.49 to 2.0; P=0.24). Mortality at day 28 was 37.1% (23 of 62) versus 25.4% (16 of 63) (absolute difference 11.7%, 95% CI −4.4% to 27.8%; P=0.16) and at day 90 was 43.5% (27 of 62) versus 28.6% (18 of 63) (absolute difference 15%, 95% CI −1.7% to 31.6%; P=0.08). There were no differences in the number of patients having at least one adverse event. The trial was stopped on data-monitoring advice because benefit was unlikely and harm was possible.
cards.watchOut: A stopped-early trial of 126 patients cannot prove harm — both mortality confidence intervals cross zero — but futility plus a consistent adverse direction is exactly the pattern that should stop adoption, and no benefit claim of any kind survives this record.

shelves.title: Once-weekly rezafungin for candidaemia and invasive candidiasis (ReSTORE)
shelves.question: Is once-weekly rezafungin non-inferior to daily caspofungin for candidaemia and invasive candidiasis?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Intravenous · Candidiasis, Invasive/drug therapy · Caspofungin/therapeutic use · Echinocandins · Candidiasis
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: One double-blind phase 3 trial (ReSTORE, 199 randomised patients) found rezafungin non-inferior to caspofungin on both regulatory primary endpoints — day-14 global cure 59% versus 61% (weighted difference −1.1%, 95% CI −14.9 to 12.7) and day-30 all-cause mortality or unknown status 24% versus 21% (difference 2.4%, 95% CI −9.7 to 14.4) — against a wide 20% non-inferiority margin. Mortality is reported beside the cure figures on the card, and no mortality benefit is claimed, so the shelf is not Tier C. A single non-inferiority trial caps at POSSIBLE; the practical gain is once-weekly dosing, not better outcomes.

cards.headline: ReSTORE 2023: once-weekly rezafungin was non-inferior to daily caspofungin (global cure 59% vs 61%; day-30 mortality 24% vs 21%)
cards.summary: ReSTORE (2023): once-weekly rezafungin non-inferior to daily caspofungin (global cure 59% vs 61% ; day-30 mortality 24% vs 21%).
cards.type: Multicentre, double-blind, double-dummy, randomised phase 3 non-inferiority trial (66 centres, 15 countries)
cards.people: 199 adults with systemic signs and mycological confirmation of candidaemia or invasive candidiasis (118 [59%] men; 81 [41%] women; mean age 61 years [SD 15.2]) randomised to intravenous rezafungin once weekly (400 mg week 1, then 200 mg weekly, two to four doses; 100) or intravenous caspofungin daily (70 mg loading, then 50 mg; 99) for no more than 4 weeks.
cards.result: Global cure at day 14 (clinical cure, radiological cure and mycological eradication) was achieved by 55 (59%) of 93 patients on rezafungin and 57 (61%) of 94 on caspofungin (weighted treatment difference −1.1%, 95% CI −14.9 to 12.7; European primary endpoint). Death or unknown survival status at day 30 occurred in 22 (24%) of 93 versus 20 (21%) of 94 (treatment difference 2.4%, 95% CI −9.7 to 14.4; US primary endpoint). Both met the prespecified 20% non-inferiority margin. Treatment-emergent adverse events occurred in 89 (91%) of 98 versus 83 (85%) of 98 patients; serious adverse events in 55 (56%) versus 52 (53%).
cards.watchOut: Non-inferiority against a 20% margin in 187 analysed patients is a permissive standard — the confidence intervals include rezafungin being meaningfully worse on both endpoints — and the day-30 endpoint counts unknown survival status together with death, as the record states.
cards.source: Thompson GR 3rd et al. shelves.title: Sulbactam–durlobactam for carbapenem-resistant Acinetobacter infections (ATTACK)
shelves.question: In serious infections caused by Acinetobacter baumannii–calcoaceticus complex, is sulbactam–durlobactam non-inferior to colistin (both with background imipenem–cilastatin) on 28-day mortality — with less kidney injury?
shelves.mesh: Colistin/adverse effects · Cilastatin, Imipenem Drug Combination · Acinetobacter baumannii · Pneumonia, Ventilator-Associated/drug therapy · Anti-Bacterial Agents/adverse effects · beta-Lactamase Inhibitors/therapeutic use · Sepsis/drug therapy
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, 28-day mortality primary outcome): In the single pathogen-specific phase 3 trial (ATTACK, 125 patients in the primary efficacy population), 28-day all-cause mortality was 19% (12 of 63) with sulbactam–durlobactam versus 32% (20 of 62) with colistin — a difference of −13.2% (95% CI −30.0 to 3.5) that met non-inferiority against a +20% margin but does not establish superiority, since the interval crosses zero. cards.headline: ATTACK 2023: sulbactam–durlobactam was non-inferior to colistin on 28-day mortality (19% vs 32%) with significantly less nephrotoxicity (13% vs 38%)
cards.summary: ATTACK (2023): sulbactam–durlobactam non-inferior to colistin on 28-day mortality ( 19% vs 32% ) with significantly less nephrotoxicity (13% vs 38%).
cards.type: Multicentre, randomised, active-controlled, phase 3, non-inferiority trial (59 sites, 16 countries)
cards.people: 181 adults with serious infections caused by carbapenem-resistant Acinetobacter baumannii–calcoaceticus complex (176 with hospital-acquired, ventilator-associated or ventilated pneumonia; 5 with bloodstream infections) randomised to sulbactam–durlobactam or colistin, both with background imipenem–cilastatin, for 7–14 days; 125 patients with laboratory-confirmed carbapenem-resistant isolates formed the primary efficacy population. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Twenty-eight-day all-cause mortality was 12 (19%) of 63 in the sulbactam–durlobactam group and 20 (32%) of 62 in the colistin group (difference −13.2%, 95% CI −30.0 to 3.5), meeting non-inferiority (upper bound below +20%). Nephrotoxicity was significantly lower with sulbactam–durlobactam (12 [13%] of 91 vs 32 [38%] of 85; p<0.001). Serious adverse events were reported in 36 (40%) of 91 versus 42 (49%) of 86 patients, and treatment-related adverse events leading to discontinuation in 10 (11%) of 91 versus 14 (16%) of 86.
cards.watchOut: Small for a mortality trial (125 in the efficacy population) and non-inferiority was declared against a generous +20% margin; the numerically lower mortality is a signal compatible with anything from a 30-point benefit to a 3.5-point harm, and both arms also received imipenem–cilastatin.
cards.source: Kaye KS et al. Efficacy and safety of sulbactam-durlobactam versus colistin for the treatment of patients with serious infections caused by Acinetobacter baumannii-calcoaceticus complex: a multicentre, randomised, active-controlled, phase 3, non-inferiority clinical trial (ATTACK). Lancet Infect Dis. 2023 Sep;23(9):1072-1084. PMID: 37182534. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03894046, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Synthesis: a less nephrotoxic colistin alternative with non-inferior mortality on one small trial — POSSIBLE, Tier C
cards.summary: Synthesis: a less nephrotoxic colistin alternative with non-inferior mortality on one small trial — POSSIBLE (Tier C).
cards.people: Synthesis of the card above: ATTACK 2023 (181 randomised; 125 in the primary efficacy population).
cards.result: For carbapenem-resistant Acinetobacter, ATTACK offers the first randomised alternative to colistin that is not worse on mortality (19% vs 32%, non-inferiority met) and is clearly kinder to kidneys (13% vs 38% nephrotoxicity). Cefiderocol for Gram-negative pneumonia and carbapenem-resistant infections is the neighbouring new-agent question on Shelf #1088 — cross-referenced, not re-carded. The stamp is proposed pending the developer's personal verdict because the primary outcome is mortality (Tier C).
cards.watchOut: Colistin was the right comparator for the resistance era the trial ran in; where sulbactam–durlobactam is unavailable or the isolate's susceptibility differs, ATTACK does not answer what to use instead.

shelves.title: Sugammadex versus neostigmine for reversal of neuromuscular blockade
shelves.question: Does sugammadex reverse rocuronium/vecuronium blockade faster and more completely than neostigmine, with fewer residual-paralysis and adverse events — across the randomised trials and in a head-to-head trial?
shelves.mesh: Androstanols/antagonists & inhibitors · Atracurium/analogs & derivatives,antagonists & inhibitors · Cholinesterase Inhibitors/administration & dosage,adverse effects,pharmacology · Neostigmine/administration & dosage,adverse effects,pharmacology · Neuromuscular Blockade · Neuromuscular Nondepolarizing Agents/antagonists & inhibitors · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic
shelves.balance: Split: LIKELY for reversal; POSSIBLE for the pulmonary-complication benefit. On reversal, a Cochrane synthesis of 41 randomised trials (4,206 participants) plus the head-to-head trials inside it shows sugammadex reversing moderate blockade about 10 minutes faster and deep blockade about 46 minutes faster than neostigmine to a train-of-four ratio above 0.9, with fewer composite adverse events (relative risk 0.60; absolute risks 16% versus 28%), less bradycardia and fewer signs of postoperative residual paralysis — that volume of concordant randomised evidence carries LIKELY. On patient-important outcomes, the 2026 SNaPP trial (3,498 patients) found postoperative pulmonary complications or death in 19.0% on sugammadex versus 21.5% on neostigmine (risk ratio 0.88, 95% CI 0.77 to 1.00, p=0.049) — a single trial, a borderline interval touching 1.00, a relative risk inside the 0.5–2.0 band the library treats as not solid on its own, and a difference driven by atelectasis, with deaths of one versus two patients: POSSIBLE, and no mortality claim is made. Serious adverse events in the older trials were too rare to separate the drugs (fewer than 1% in both groups).

cards.headline: Hristovska 2017 (Cochrane): across 41 trials, sugammadex reversed moderate blockade 10.22 minutes faster and deep blockade 45.78 minutes faster than neostigmine, with fewer adverse events (16% vs 28%)
cards.summary: Hristovska (2017, Cochrane): across 41 trials, sugammadex reversed moderate blockade 10.22 minutes faster and deep blockade 45.78 minutes faster than neostigmine.
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials (Cochrane, updated search to May 2017)
cards.people: 41 randomised trials with 4,206 adult participants (ASA I–IV) receiving non-depolarising neuromuscular blocking agents for elective inpatient or day-case surgery; 12 trials (949 participants) contributed to the primary recovery-time meta-analyses and 28 trials (2,298) to the adverse-event meta-analyses. The abstract does not state a pooled mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: For moderate rocuronium blockade, sugammadex 2 mg/kg reached a train-of-four ratio above 0.9 in 1.96 minutes versus 12.87 minutes for neostigmine 0.05 mg/kg (mean difference 10.22 minutes, 95% CI 8.48 to 11.96; 10 studies, n=835; GRADE moderate quality). For deep blockade, sugammadex 4 mg/kg took 2.9 minutes versus 48.8 minutes for neostigmine 0.07 mg/kg (mean difference 45.78 minutes, 39.41 to 52.15; two studies, n=114; GRADE low quality). Composite adverse events were fewer with sugammadex (relative risk 0.60, 0.49 to 0.74 — a relative measure; absolute risks 16% versus 28%, number needed to treat 8), as were bradycardia (RR 0.16), postoperative nausea and vomiting (RR 0.52) and signs of postoperative residual paralysis (RR 0.40). Serious adverse events did not differ (RR 0.54, 0.13 to 2.25) and occurred in fewer than 1% of patients in both groups.
cards.watchOut: The headline deep-blockade figure comes from two trials and 114 patients at low GRADE quality, and the recovery-time meta-analysis for moderate blockade is heterogeneous (I2 = 84%): the direction is consistent, the exact number of minutes is not portable to every setting.
cards.source: Hristovska AM et al. Efficacy and safety of sugammadex versus neostigmine in reversing neuromuscular blockade in adults. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2017;(8):CD012763. PMID: 28806470. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — this is a systematic review, not a single trial.

cards.headline: Khuenl-Brady 2010: in vecuronium blockade, sugammadex restored a train-of-four ratio of 0.9 in a geometric mean 2.7 minutes versus 17.9 minutes for neostigmine
cards.summary: Khuenl-Brady (2010): in vecuronium blockade, sugammadex restored a train-of-four ratio of 0.9 in a geometric mean 2.7 minutes vs 17.9 with neostigmine.
cards.type: Multicentre, randomised, controlled trial (reversal at reappearance of the second twitch)
cards.people: Patients aged 18 years or older, ASA class I–III, scheduled for elective surgery under sevoflurane/opioid anaesthesia, who received vecuronium and were randomised at the end of surgery to sugammadex 2 mg/kg or neostigmine 50 micrograms/kg plus glycopyrrolate. The abstract does not state the total sample size, mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: The geometric mean time from administration to recovery of the train-of-four ratio to 0.9 was 2.7 minutes (95% CI 2.2 to 3.3) with sugammadex versus 17.9 minutes (13.1 to 24.3) with neostigmine (p<0.0001). Recovery times to ratios of 0.8 and 0.7 were also significantly shorter with sugammadex. No serious adverse events or unexpected side effects were reported with either drug.
cards.watchOut: A pharmacodynamic endpoint in one relaxant (vecuronium) at one depth of block: it confirms the synthesis's direction in a single trial but cannot carry the adverse-event or residual-paralysis claims, which come from the pooled data.
cards.source: Khuenl-Brady KS et al. Sugammadex provides faster reversal of vecuronium-induced neuromuscular blockade compared with neostigmine: a multicenter, randomized, controlled trial. Anesth Analg. 2010;110(1):64-73. PMID: 19713265. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields.
