cards.headline: SNaPP (Leslie 2026): postoperative pulmonary complications or death occurred in 19.0% on sugammadex versus 21.5% on neostigmine (risk ratio 0.88, CI reaching 1.00), driven by atelectasis; deaths were one versus two
cards.summary: SNaPP (2026): postoperative pulmonary complications or death in 19.0% on sugammadex vs 21.5% on neostigmine (RR 0.88 relative, CI to 1.00) — atelectasis-driven.
cards.type: Pragmatic, international, multicentre, randomised, controlled phase 4 trial (patients, outcome assessors and adjudicators masked)
cards.people: 3,498 adults aged 40 years or older having abdominal or thoracic surgery under general anaesthesia lasting at least 2 hours, with an expected stay of at least one night, at 44 hospitals in Australia, New Zealand and Hong Kong, randomly assigned to sugammadex (1,745) or neostigmine (1,753) for reversal of rocuronium- or vecuronium-induced blockade, in doses chosen by the attending anaesthetist. The abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: The primary outcome (postoperative pulmonary complications or death up to discharge, or postoperative day 7 if still in hospital) occurred in 331 of 1,743 (19.0%) in the sugammadex group and 377 of 1,752 (21.5%) in the neostigmine group (risk ratio 0.88, 95% CI 0.77 to 1.00; p=0.049 — a relative measure inside the 0.5–2.0 caution band, absolute rates beside it). Death occurred in one (0.1%) sugammadex patient and two (0.1%) neostigmine patients (risk ratio 0.50, 0.05 to 5.53). Atelectasis occurred in 18.4% versus 21.1% (risk ratio 0.86, 0.76 to 0.99), pneumonia in 2.1% versus 2.2%, and pulmonary aspiration in 0.2% versus 0.4%; acute respiratory distress syndrome was not reported, and no adverse events were deemed treatment-related.
cards.watchOut: The composite's margin is atelectasis of, in the authors' own words, uncertain clinical significance; pneumonia and aspiration did not differ, and with three deaths in total the trial says nothing about mortality — it is a pulmonary-complication result with a borderline p-value, not a survival result.
cards.source: Leslie K et al. Sugammadex versus neostigmine for reversal of neuromuscular blockade and postoperative pulmonary complications (SNaPP): an international, randomised, controlled, phase 4 trial. Lancet Respir Med. 2026;14(9):761-774. PMID: 42263720. cards.headline: Synthesis: faster, more complete reversal (LIKELY) and a single-trial, atelectasis-driven pulmonary signal (POSSIBLE)
cards.summary: Synthesis: faster, more complete reversal (LIKELY) and a single-trial, atelectasis-driven pulmonary signal (POSSIBLE).
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Hristovska 2017 (Cochrane synthesis, 41 trials, 4,206 participants), Khuenl-Brady 2010 (one head-to-head vecuronium trial within that evidence base, carded as an illustrative primary trial and counted once) and SNaPP 2026 (3,498 patients, pulmonary outcomes).
cards.result: The pooled and single-trial reversal reads agree: sugammadex reaches adequate reversal roughly 6.6 times faster than neostigmine from moderate blockade and far faster from deep blockade, with fewer adverse events and fewer signs of residual paralysis, and serious harm rare and inseparable between the drugs — LIKELY. SNaPP then asks the harder question and returns a smaller, softer answer: 19.0% versus 21.5% on a pulmonary-complications-or-death composite, a risk ratio of 0.88 whose interval reaches 1.00, carried by atelectasis while pneumonia, aspiration and death (one versus two patients) did not differ — POSSIBLE. No earlier anaesthesia shelf tests reversal agents, so nothing is re-carded here.
cards.watchOut: Do not let the reversal evidence and the pulmonary evidence borrow each other's strength: the reversal claim is many-trials strong, the pulmonary claim is one borderline trial, and neither supports a mortality claim.
cards.source: Synthesis of Hristovska AM et al. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2017;(8):CD012763. PMID: 28806470; Khuenl-Brady KS et al. Anesth Analg. 2010;110(1):64-73. PMID: 19713265; Leslie K et al. Lancet Respir Med. 2026;14(9):761-774. PMID: 42263720. Registry IDs as on the individual cards.

shelves.title: Remimazolam: for general anaesthesia, and for procedural sedation in colonoscopy
shelves.question: Is the ultra-short-acting benzodiazepine remimazolam non-inferior to propofol for induction and maintenance of general anaesthesia, with less hypotension — and superior to placebo with midazolam rescue for colonoscopy sedation?
shelves.mesh: Anesthesia, General/adverse effects · Anesthetics, Intravenous/adverse effects · Benzodiazepines · Hypnotics and Sedatives · Japan · Midazolam/adverse effects · Propofol/adverse effects
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: Each setting rests on a single randomised trial, so each is capped at POSSIBLE. For general anaesthesia, one single-blind phase IIb/III trial (375 patients) met non-inferiority against propofol on its composite efficacy endpoint (100% efficacy in all arms), with decreased blood pressure in 20.0–24.0% on remimazolam versus 49.3% on propofol — but loss of consciousness and extubation were both slower. For colonoscopy, one double-blind phase III trial (461 patients) crushed its composite endpoint against placebo (91.3% vs 1.7% success), with open-label midazolam at 25.2% — a design the FDA required, in which the placebo arm is effectively a rescue-midazolam arm. Two settings, one trial each: POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: Doi 2020: remimazolam was non-inferior to propofol for general anaesthesia (100% composite efficacy in all arms), with decreased blood pressure in 20.0–24.0% versus 49.3% — but slower loss of consciousness and extubation
cards.summary: Doi (2020): remimazolam was non-inferior to propofol for general anaesthesia ( 100% composite efficacy in all arms), with less blood-pressure depression.
cards.type: Multicentre, single-blind, randomised, parallel-group phase IIb/III non-inferiority trial
cards.people: 375 surgical patients randomised to remimazolam started at 6 or 12 mg/kg/h by infusion, or intravenous propofol bolus then infusion, for induction and maintenance of general anaesthesia. The abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: Efficacy (the composite of no intraoperative awakening or recall, no need for rescue sedatives, and no body movements) was 100% in all treatment groups, and non-inferiority of remimazolam was demonstrated (95% CI −0.0487 to 0.0250). Time to loss of consciousness was longer in both remimazolam groups than with propofol (p<0.0001 at 6 mg/kg/h; p=0.0149 at 12 mg/kg/h), as was time to extubation (p≤0.0001). Adverse drug reactions occurred in 39.3% and 42.7% on remimazolam versus 61.3% on propofol; decreased blood pressure in 20.0% and 24.0% versus 49.3%; injection-site pain in 18.7% on propofol and in no remimazolam patient.
cards.watchOut: Single-blind, with a composite endpoint every arm passed at 100% — a ceiling that cannot discriminate quality of anaesthesia — and the hypotension advantage is an adverse-drug-reaction count, not a powered haemodynamic outcome.
cards.source: Doi M et al. Efficacy and safety of remimazolam versus propofol for general anesthesia: a multicenter, single-blind, randomized, parallel-group, phase IIb/III trial. J Anesth. 2020;34(4):543-553. PMID: 32417976. Registry ID: JapicCTI 121973, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Rex 2018: for colonoscopy, remimazolam met the composite sedation endpoint in 91.3% versus 1.7% on placebo and 25.2% on open-label midazolam
cards.summary: Rex (2018): for colonoscopy, remimazolam met the composite sedation endpoint in 91.3% vs 1.7% on placebo and 25.2% on open-label midazolam.
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase III trial with an open-label midazolam arm
cards.people: 461 randomised patients undergoing outpatient colonoscopy at 12 US sites, allocated remimazolam:placebo:midazolam in a 30:6:10 ratio, all given 50–75 micrograms of fentanyl first, supervised by the endoscopist without an anaesthesia specialist; patients inadequately sedated in any arm were rescued with midazolam. The abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: The primary endpoint (procedure completion, no rescue medication, and no more than five doses in any 15-minute interval) was met in 91.3% on remimazolam, 1.7% on placebo and 25.2% on midazolam (p<0.0001 for remimazolam versus placebo). Remimazolam patients received less fentanyl, recovered neuropsychiatric function faster, were ready for discharge earlier and felt back to normal sooner than both other groups. Hypotension was less frequent with remimazolam, hypoxia occurred in 1% on remimazolam or midazolam, and there were no treatment-emergent serious adverse events.
cards.watchOut: The placebo comparison is close to a formality — a sedative against saline with midazolam rescue available — and the midazolam arm was open-label and dosed by its package insert, so the 25.2% figure is not a blinded head-to-head verdict on midazolam.
cards.source: Rex DK et al. A phase III study evaluating the efficacy and safety of remimazolam (CNS 7056) compared with placebo and midazolam in patients undergoing colonoscopy. cards.headline: Synthesis: two single-trial settings with different comparators — POSSIBLE in each
cards.summary: Synthesis: two single-trial settings with different comparators — POSSIBLE in each.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Doi 2020 (general anaesthesia versus propofol, n=375) and Rex 2018 (colonoscopy sedation, n=461).
cards.result: The two trials answer different questions and neither borrows strength from the other: remimazolam is a workable propofol alternative for general anaesthesia with less blood-pressure decrease and slower transitions, and an effective endoscopist-supervised colonoscopy sedative against a placebo-with-rescue design. One trial per setting keeps both stamps at POSSIBLE. The ICU sedation shelves (#753) test a different population and are not re-carded here.
cards.watchOut: The 171 recent small RCTs in the currency sweep show a field actively testing remimazolam procedure by procedure; until a second large trial lands in either of this shelf's two settings, replication is breadth, not depth.

shelves.title: Perioperative dexamethasone: surgical-site infection safety (PADDI) and nausea efficacy (DREAMS)
shelves.question: Does a single 8 mg perioperative dose of dexamethasone increase surgical-site infection, including in patients with diabetes (PADDI, a non-inferiority safety trial) — and does dexamethasone reduce postoperative nausea and vomiting after gastrointestinal surgery (DREAMS)?
shelves.mesh: Anesthesia, General · Antiemetics/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Dexamethasone/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Glucocorticoids/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Intention to Treat Analysis · Surgical Procedures, Operative/adverse effects · Surgical Wound Infection/etiology
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Two large pragmatic randomised trials settle the two halves of the question. On safety, PADDI (8,880 randomised) showed surgical-site infection in 8.1% on dexamethasone versus 9.1% on placebo, meeting its 2.0-percentage-point non-inferiority margin (adjusted risk difference −0.9 points, 95.6% CI −2.1 to 0.3), with results in patients with diabetes similar to the primary analysis. On efficacy, DREAMS (1,350 bowel-surgery patients) showed vomiting within 24 hours in 25.5% with dexamethasone versus 33.0% on standard care, and less rescue-antiemetic use (39.3% vs 51.9%). The diabetes question is harm exclusion, and it is carried as such: PADDI excludes an infection increase beyond its margin in the whole population, with the diabetes subgroup reported as similar — the abstract gives no separate diabetes-subgroup infection rates, and none are printed here.

cards.headline: PADDI (Corcoran 2021): dexamethasone was non-inferior to placebo for surgical-site infection (8.1% vs 9.1%; margin 2.0 points), including in the diabetes subgroup
cards.summary: PADDI (2021): dexamethasone was non-inferior to placebo for surgical-site infection ( 8.1% vs 9.1% ; margin 2.0 points), including in diabetes.
cards.type: Pragmatic, international, double-blind, placebo-controlled non-inferiority trial
cards.people: 8,880 adults undergoing non-urgent, non-cardiac surgery of at least 2 hours with a skin incision longer than 5 cm and an overnight stay, randomised to 8 mg intravenous dexamethasone or placebo during anaesthesia; 8,725 were in the modified intention-to-treat population, of whom 13.2% (576 dexamethasone, 572 placebo) had diabetes mellitus. The abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: Surgical-site infection within 30 days occurred in 8.1% (354 of 4,350) on dexamethasone and 9.1% (394 of 4,328) on placebo (risk difference adjusted for diabetes status −0.9 percentage points, 95.6% CI −2.1 to 0.3; p<0.001 for non-inferiority against the 2.0-point margin). Results for superficial, deep and organ-space infections and in patients with diabetes were similar to the primary analysis. shelves.title: Anaesthetic depth and EEG guidance: the BALANCED trial and ENGAGES
shelves.question: Does targeting a lighter plane of anaesthesia (bispectral index 50 versus 35) change one-year mortality or complications after major surgery (BALANCED) — and does EEG-guided anaesthetic delivery reduce postoperative delirium in older adults (ENGAGES)?
shelves.mesh: Anesthesia, General/adverse effects,methods,mortality · Anesthetics/adverse effects,pharmacology · Arterial Pressure · Consciousness Monitors · Postoperative Complications/epidemiology · Postoperative Period · Algorithms
shelves.balance: Split: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) on both questions — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: BALANCED's primary outcome was 1-year all-cause mortality). BALANCED (6,644 patients aged 60 or older at increased risk) found 1-year mortality of 6.5% with light anaesthesia (BIS target 50) versus 7.2% with deep anaesthesia (BIS 35) — hazard ratio 0.88, 95% CI 0.73 to 1.07: a large, well-executed null that defines a broad depth range over which anaesthesia may be safely delivered. ENGAGES (1,232 patients) found delirium in 26.0% with EEG guidance versus 23.0% with usual care (p=0.22), despite the guided group receiving less volatile agent and spending less time in EEG suppression: EEG guidance changes what the anaesthetist does without changing delirium. Each null rests on one very large trial, which the library's precedent allows to carry LIKELY (the treatment made no difference). ENGAGES also recorded fewer deaths within 30 days in the guided group (4 [0.65%] versus 19 [3.07%]) among its adverse-event data; the trial was not powered for mortality, no confidence interval is given in the abstract, and this shelf makes no mortality claim from it.

cards.headline: BALANCED (Short 2019): 1-year mortality was 6.5% with light anaesthesia (BIS 50) versus 7.2% with deep anaesthesia (BIS 35) — hazard ratio 0.88, CI crossing 1

cards.type: International, randomised controlled trial (patients and assessors masked to group allocation)
cards.people: 6,644 patients aged 60 years or older, with significant comorbidity, undergoing surgery expected to last more than 2 hours with a hospital stay of at least 2 days, at 73 centres in seven countries, randomly assigned to light general anaesthesia (BIS target 50; 3,316) or deep general anaesthesia (BIS target 35; 3,328); median achieved BIS was 47.2 versus 38.8. The abstract does not state the sex mix.
cards.result: One-year all-cause mortality was 6.5% (212 patients) in the BIS 50 group versus 7.2% (238) in the BIS 35 group (hazard ratio 0.88, 95% CI 0.73 to 1.07 — a relative measure, absolute rates beside it; absolute risk reduction 0.8%, 95% CI −0.5 to 2.0). Volatile anaesthetic use was 0.26 minimum alveolar concentration (30%) lower and mean arterial pressure 3.5 mm Hg higher in the light group. Grade 3 adverse events occurred in 29% versus 27%, and grade 4 in 8% in both groups; the most common were infections, vascular disorders, cardiac disorders and neoplasms.
cards.watchOut: The confidence interval cannot exclude a modest mortality benefit from lighter anaesthesia (down to a hazard ratio of 0.73) — 'no association shown' is the claim, not 'depth is irrelevant at the extremes'; achieved BIS values overlapped between arms, so the tested contrast is a broad mid-range, not deep-versus-awake.

cards.headline: ENGAGES (Wildes 2019): EEG-guided anaesthesia did not reduce postoperative delirium (26.0% vs 23.0%, p=0.22), despite less volatile agent and less EEG suppression
cards.summary: ENGAGES (2019): EEG-guided anaesthesia did not reduce postoperative delirium ( 26.0% vs 23.0% ; p=0.22), despite less volatile agent and less EEG suppression.
cards.people: 1,232 adults aged 60 years or older undergoing major surgery under general anaesthesia at one US hospital, randomised to EEG-guided anaesthetic administration (614) or usual care (618); median age 69 years (range 60 to 95); 563 women (45.7%); 1,213 (98.5%) assessed for the primary outcome.
cards.result: Delirium during postoperative days 1–5 occurred in 157 of 604 (26.0%) in the guided group versus 140 of 609 (23.0%) in the usual-care group (difference 3.0%, 95% CI −2.0 to 8.0; p=0.22). The guided group received a lower median end-tidal volatile concentration (0.69 vs 0.80 minimum alveolar concentration) and had less median cumulative EEG suppression (7 vs 13 minutes), with no difference in time below a mean arterial pressure of 60 mm Hg. Undesirable movement was more common in the guided group (22.3% vs 15.4%); no patient reported awareness. Within 30 days, 4 patients (0.65%) in the guided group and 19 (3.07%) in the usual-care group died — an adverse-event count from a trial powered for delirium, not mortality, with no interval estimate in the abstract.
cards.watchOut: A null on its own terms, single-centre: the guidance protocol changed drug dosing and EEG suppression but not the outcome it targeted, and the 30-day death counts are exactly the kind of unprespecified, low-count contrast that must not be upgraded into a mortality claim.

cards.result: The two trials are complementary nulls: randomising the depth target itself did not move 1-year mortality (BALANCED), and randomising the information the anaesthetist sees did not move delirium (ENGAGES). Together they say the observational link between deep anaesthesia, EEG suppression and bad outcomes does not behave like a lever. This synthesis states no mortality benefit for EEG guidance: the ENGAGES death counts are reported on its card as adverse-event data only, and the shelf's Tier C flag exists because BALANCED's primary outcome was mortality.
cards.watchOut: Both trials enrolled older, higher-risk patients having major surgery; neither speaks to depth targets in the young or in minor surgery.

shelves.title: Perioperative blood-pressure strategy: individualised management (INPRESS) and the POISE-3 strategies
shelves.question: In high-risk patients having major surgery, does an individualised strategy — norepinephrine titrated to keep systolic pressure within 10% of the patient's resting value — reduce postoperative organ dysfunction versus standard threshold-based management (INPRESS), and do the POISE-3 hypotension-avoidance and hypertension-avoidance strategies differ on major vascular complications?
shelves.mesh: Abdomen/surgery · Blood Pressure Determination · Cardiovascular Diseases/prevention & control · Epinephrine/administration & dosage · Hypotension/drug therapy · Intention to Treat Analysis · Kidney Diseases/prevention & control
shelves.balance: Split: POSSIBLE for the individualised strategy; LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) for the POISE-3 comparison — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C ruling at build: INPRESS alone would not be Tier C — its primary composite is SIRS and organ dysfunction, and 30-day mortality was a secondary outcome with no significant difference and no mortality claim made. The shelf is Tier C because the carded POISE-3 report's primary outcome is a composite of vascular death, non-fatal myocardial injury, stroke and cardiac arrest). INPRESS (298 randomised) found its primary composite in 38.1% on the individualised strategy versus 51.7% on standard management (relative risk 0.73) — one small, single-country trial, hence POSSIBLE. POISE-3 (7,490 patients) found its vascular composite in 13.9% on hypotension-avoidance versus 14.0% on hypertension-avoidance (hazard ratio 0.99): a very large null between two coherent strategies, carrying LIKELY (the treatment made no difference). The two results do not contradict each other — INPRESS individualised against the patient's own resting pressure with norepinephrine; POISE-3 compared two fixed population strategies bundled with antihypertensive-medication handling.

cards.headline: INPRESS (Futier 2017): postoperative organ dysfunction composite occurred in 38.1% with individualised blood-pressure management versus 51.7% with standard management (relative risk 0.73)
cards.summary: INPRESS (2017): postoperative organ dysfunction composite in 38.1% with individualised blood-pressure management vs 51.7% with standard care.
cards.type: Multicentre, randomised, parallel-group clinical trial (9 French hospitals)
cards.people: 298 adults at increased risk of postoperative complications (preoperative acute kidney injury risk index class III or higher) undergoing major surgery of 2 hours or longer under general anaesthesia; 292 completed the trial and were analysed (mean [SD] age 70 [7] years; 44 [15.1%] women), predominantly undergoing abdominal surgery. The individualised strategy used norepinephrine to keep systolic pressure within 10% of the patient's resting value during and for 4 hours after surgery; standard management treated systolic pressure below 80 mm Hg or more than 40% below the reference value.
cards.result: The primary outcome (systemic inflammatory response syndrome plus dysfunction of at least one of the renal, respiratory, cardiovascular, coagulation or neurologic systems by day 7) occurred in 56 of 147 (38.1%) on the individualised strategy versus 75 of 145 (51.7%) on standard management (relative risk 0.73, 95% CI 0.56 to 0.94, p=0.02 — a relative measure, absolute rates beside it; absolute risk difference −14%, −25% to −2%). Organ dysfunction by day 30 occurred in 46.3% versus 63.4% (adjusted hazard ratio 0.66, 0.52 to 0.84). There were no significant differences in severe adverse events or 30-day mortality.
cards.watchOut: One trial, 298 patients, one country, and a composite led by SIRS and laboratory-defined organ dysfunction rather than hard events; the relative risk of 0.73 sits inside the 0.5–2.0 band the library treats as not solid on its own — hence POSSIBLE despite statistical significance.

cards.headline: POISE-3 blood-pressure strategies (Marcucci 2023): major vascular complications in 13.9% on hypotension-avoidance versus 14.0% on hypertension-avoidance (hazard ratio 0.99)
cards.summary: POISE-3 (2023): major vascular complications in 13.9% on hypotension-avoidance vs 14.0% on hypertension-avoidance — null.
cards.type: Partial factorial, international, randomised controlled trial (the blood-pressure half of POISE-3; outcome adjudicators masked)
cards.people: 7,490 patients having non-cardiac surgery who were at risk for vascular complications and receiving at least one long-term antihypertensive medication, at 110 hospitals in 22 countries. The hypotension-avoidance strategy targeted an intraoperative mean arterial pressure of 80 mm Hg or more and withheld renin–angiotensin–aldosterone inhibitors around surgery, giving other antihypertensives only for systolic pressure of 130 mm Hg or more; the hypertension-avoidance strategy targeted 60 mm Hg or more and continued all antihypertensive medications. The abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: The primary outcome — a composite of vascular death, non-fatal myocardial injury after non-cardiac surgery, stroke and cardiac arrest at 30 days — occurred in 520 of 3,742 (13.9%) in the hypotension-avoidance group and 524 of 3,748 (14.0%) in the hypertension-avoidance group (hazard ratio 0.99, 95% CI 0.88 to 1.12; p=0.92 — a relative measure, absolute rates beside it). Results were consistent by number of long-term antihypertensive medications and across adherence levels, although adherence to the assigned strategies was suboptimal.
cards.watchOut: The strategies bundle two levers (an intraoperative pressure target and perioperative medication handling), so the null belongs to the bundles, not to either lever alone; and the tranexamic-acid half of POISE-3 is a different question, home on the tranexamic-acid shelves (#138, #430), not carded here. The design record at PMID 35101083 is a protocol, not the trial, and is not carded.

cards.headline: Synthesis: individualise against the patient's own pressure (one small positive trial) versus fixed strategy bundles (one very large null) — split stamp, Tier C by the POISE-3 composite
cards.summary: Synthesis: individualise against the patient's own pressure (one small positive trial, POSSIBLE) versus fixed strategy bundles (one very large null, LIKELY the null) (Tier C).
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: INPRESS (n=298, organ-dysfunction composite) and POISE-3 blood-pressure strategies (n=7,490, vascular composite).
cards.result: The apparent tension dissolves on inspection: INPRESS titrated vasopressor support to each patient's resting systolic pressure and improved a soft organ-dysfunction composite; POISE-3 contrasted two fixed MAP targets bundled with medication rules and found vascular events identical. A clinician can consistently believe both — that drifting far below a patient's own pressure is harmful, and that neither fixed bundle is superior. shelves.title: Aggressive intraoperative warming versus routine thermal management (PROTECT)
shelves.question: In non-cardiac surgery, does aggressive warming to a core temperature of at least 37 °C reduce a composite of myocardial injury, cardiac arrest and death versus routine thermal management (PROTECT)?
shelves.mesh: Anesthesia, General/adverse effects · China/epidemiology · Hemorrhage/etiology · Hypothermia/etiology,prevention & control · Surgical Wound Infection
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: the primary composite includes all-cause mortality and cardiac arrest). PROTECT randomised 5,056 patients and achieved a wide temperature separation (mean final intraoperative core temperature 37.1 °C aggressively warmed versus 35.6 °C routine), yet the composite of myocardial injury, non-fatal cardiac arrest and all-cause mortality within 30 days occurred in 9.9% versus 9.6% (common-effect relative risk 1.04, 95% CI 0.87 to 1.24, p=0.69). A very large single trial with a properly achieved intervention contrast and a null this tight carries LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) under the library's large-null precedent: across the 1.5 °C range from very mild hypothermia to full normothermia, keeping core temperature at at least 35.5 °C appears sufficient. The stamp is proposed only, because the composite carries mortality.

cards.headline: PROTECT (Sessler 2022): despite a 37.1 °C versus 35.6 °C separation, the composite of myocardial injury, cardiac arrest and death occurred in 9.9% versus 9.6% (relative risk 1.04, p=0.69)
cards.summary: PROTECT (2022): despite a 37.1 °C vs 35.6 °C separation, the composite of myocardial injury, cardiac arrest and death occurred in 9.9% vs about 9.6% — null.
cards.type: Multicentre, parallel-group, superiority randomised trial (12 sites in China and one US centre)
cards.people: 5,056 patients aged 45 years or older with at least one cardiovascular risk factor, scheduled for inpatient non-cardiac surgery expected to last 2–6 hours under general anaesthesia, randomly assigned to aggressive warming (target core temperature 37 °C) or routine thermal management (target 35.5 °C); 5,013 were in the intention-to-treat population (2,507 and 2,506). Patients requiring dialysis and those with a body-mass index above 30 kg/m2 were excluded. The abstract does not state the sex mix.
cards.result: At least one primary-outcome component (myocardial injury after non-cardiac surgery, non-fatal cardiac arrest, or all-cause mortality within 30 days) occurred in 246 of 2,497 (9.9%) in the aggressively warmed group and 239 of 2,490 (9.6%) in the routine group (common-effect relative risk 1.04, 95% CI 0.87 to 1.24, p=0.69 — a relative measure, absolute rates beside it). There were 39 adverse events with aggressive warming (17 serious) and 54 with routine management (30 serious); one serious adverse event, in an aggressively warmed patient, was deemed possibly related to thermal management.
cards.watchOut: The routine arm was actively managed to 35.5 °C, not left to drift cold: PROTECT compares normothermia with very mild hypothermia, and says nothing about the harm of deeper, unmanaged hypothermia. Patients with obesity or on dialysis were excluded.
cards.source: Sessler DI et al. Aggressive intraoperative warming versus routine thermal management during non-cardiac surgery (PROTECT): a multicentre, parallel group, superiority trial. cards.headline: Synthesis: a 5,000-patient null with the temperature contrast actually delivered — LIKELY (the treatment made no difference), proposed as Tier C
cards.summary: Synthesis: a 5,000-patient null with the temperature contrast actually delivered — LIKELY the null (Tier C).

shelves.title: Preoperative intravenous iron for anaemia before major abdominal surgery (PREVENTT)
shelves.question: In patients with anaemia undergoing major open abdominal surgery, does a single preoperative dose of intravenous iron reduce blood transfusion, complications or death versus placebo (PREVENTT) — given two to six weeks before surgery, as guidelines assumed it would?
shelves.mesh: Abdomen/surgery · Administration, Intravenous · Anemia/drug therapy · Elective Surgical Procedures · Iron/administration & dosage · Preoperative Care · United Kingdom
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C ruling at build: death is a component of PREVENTT's coprimary composite of transfusion or death, so by the mortality-in-composite test the shelf goes to the developer personally). PREVENTT (487 randomised) gave a single 1,000 mg ferric carboxymaltose dose 10–42 days before surgery and found the coprimary composite of death or transfusion in 29% on iron versus 28% on placebo (risk ratio 1.03, 95% CI 0.78 to 1.37), with transfusion counts no different (105 versus 111; rate ratio 0.98). A single moderately sized trial supports POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) rather than the large-null LIKELY: the interval still admits a transfusion benefit or harm of about a fifth either way, and no confirmatory placebo-controlled trial in abdominal surgery was pinned at build. The result contradicts the guideline-era assumption, and it is a statement about this dose, this timing and this operation class — not about treating iron deficiency for its own sake.

cards.headline: PREVENTT (Richards 2020): death or transfusion occurred in 29% on preoperative intravenous iron versus 28% on placebo (risk ratio 1.03); transfusion counts 105 versus 111
cards.summary: PREVENTT (2020): death or transfusion in 29% on preoperative intravenous iron vs 28% on placebo (RR 1.03 relative); transfusion rates identical.
cards.type: Double-blind, parallel-group, placebo-controlled randomised trial (46 UK tertiary centres)
cards.people: 487 adults with anaemia (haemoglobin below 130 g/L for men and below 120 g/L for women) identified at preoperative visits before elective major open abdominal surgery, randomly assigned to a single 1,000 mg dose of intravenous ferric carboxymaltose (244) or placebo saline (243), given 10–42 days before surgery; complete primary-endpoint data were available for 474 (97%). The abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: The coprimary composite of blood transfusion or death occurred in 69 of 237 (29%) in the intravenous iron group and 67 of 237 (28%) in the placebo group (risk ratio 1.03, 95% CI 0.78 to 1.37; p=0.84 — a relative measure, absolute rates beside it). The second coprimary endpoint, number of transfusions from randomisation to 30 days postoperatively, was 105 in the iron group versus 111 on placebo (rate ratio 0.98, 0.68 to 1.43; p=0.93). There were no significant differences in any prespecified safety endpoint.
cards.watchOut: One dose, one timing window, one operation class: the trial cannot exclude benefit from earlier treatment, repeated dosing, or a population selected for proven iron deficiency rather than anaemia alone — and its interval (0.78 to 1.37) cannot exclude a clinically useful transfusion reduction either.

shelves.title: Intraoperative ketamine to prevent postoperative delirium and pain in older adults (PODCAST)
shelves.question: In older adults undergoing major surgery, does a single subanaesthetic dose of intraoperative ketamine prevent postoperative delirium, or reduce pain and opioid use (PODCAST)?
shelves.mesh: Analgesics/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Central Nervous System Agents/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Delirium/prevention & control · Drug Administration Schedule · Intraoperative Care/methods · Ketamine/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Postoperative Pain/prevention & control
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): PODCAST is a single, large, well-conducted double-blind trial (672 randomised), and it is null on everything it aimed at: delirium in 19.45% on combined ketamine versus 19.82% on placebo (absolute difference 0.36%, 95% CI −6.07 to 7.38), no pain or opioid benefit, and a dose-related increase in postoperative hallucinations (p=0.01) and nightmares (p=0.03). A single trial caps the null at POSSIBLE under the library's rule; the trial's size and blinding keep it from falling lower. The harm signal is part of the stamp's reasoning: this is not merely 'no benefit shown', it is no benefit with more negative experiences.

cards.headline: PODCAST (Avidan 2017): delirium occurred in 19.45% on ketamine versus 19.82% on placebo, with more hallucinations and nightmares at higher ketamine doses
cards.summary: PODCAST (2017): delirium in 19.45% on ketamine vs 19.82% on placebo, with more hallucinations and nightmares at higher ketamine doses.
cards.type: International, multicentre, double-blind, randomised clinical trial (single subanaesthetic bolus after induction)
cards.people: 672 adults older than 60 years undergoing major cardiac and non-cardiac surgery under general anaesthesia, randomly assigned to placebo (222), ketamine 0.5 mg/kg (227) or ketamine 1.0 mg/kg (223); delirium assessed twice daily for the first 3 postoperative days with the Confusion Assessment Method. The abstract does not state mean age beyond the over-60 eligibility, or the sex mix.
cards.result: Delirium incidence was 19.45% in the combined ketamine groups versus 19.82% on placebo (absolute difference 0.36%, 95% CI −6.07 to 7.38; p=0.92). There were more postoperative hallucinations (p=0.01) and nightmares (p=0.03) with increasing ketamine doses compared with placebo. Adverse events overall did not differ significantly across groups (36.9% placebo, 39.6% at 0.5 mg/kg, 40.8% at 1.0 mg/kg; p=0.69), whether viewed individually or collectively.
cards.watchOut: One dose at one moment (after induction, before incision) is the tested strategy: PODCAST does not test repeated dosing, postoperative infusion, or ketamine given primarily as an analgesic adjunct with delirium as a secondary hope.

shelves.title: Two antibiotics together for severe scrub typhus (INTREST)
shelves.question: In severe scrub typhus, does combining intravenous doxycycline with azithromycin beat either drug alone on death, persistent organ dysfunction and prolonged fever?
shelves.mesh: Animals · Anti-Bacterial Agents/administration & dosage,adverse effects,therapeutic use · Azithromycin/administration & dosage,adverse effects,therapeutic use · Doxycycline/administration & dosage,therapeutic use · Scrub Typhus/drug therapy · Zoonoses · Drug Therapy, Combination
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: death is a component of the primary composite). One large multicentre double-blind trial (INTREST, 794 patients in India) found the combination beat doxycycline alone (composite 33% vs 47%) and azithromycin alone (33% vs 48%), while the two monotherapies did not differ; 28-day mortality itself was similar across all three groups and is reported as such. A single trial caps the stamp at POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: INTREST 2023: doxycycline plus azithromycin beat either drug alone on the composite of death, persistent complications and fever (33% vs 47% and 48%); 28-day mortality was similar in all groups
cards.summary: INTREST (2023): doxycycline plus azithromycin beat either drug alone on the composite of death, persistent complications and fever ( 33% vs 47% vs doxycycline alone).
cards.type: Multicentre, double-blind, randomised, controlled trial (7-day intravenous courses)
cards.people: 794 patients aged 15 years or older with severe scrub typhus and at least one organ involvement, in the modified intention-to-treat analysis; median age 48 years. The abstract does not state the sex mix. Complications at enrolment were respiratory in 62%, hepatic 54%, cardiovascular 42%, renal 30% and neurologic 20%.
cards.result: The primary composite (death from any cause at day 28, persistent complications at day 7, or persistent fever at day 5) occurred in 33% with combination therapy vs 47% with doxycycline (risk difference -13.3 percentage points; 95% CI -21.6 to -5.1; P=0.002) and vs 48% with azithromycin (risk difference -14.8 points, -23.1 to -6.5; P<0.001). Azithromycin and doxycycline monotherapy did not differ (risk difference 1.5 points, -7.0 to 10.0; P=0.73). Per-protocol results were similar. Adverse events and 28-day mortality were similar in the three groups (the abstract gives no group mortality rates, so none are printed).
cards.watchOut: The composite is driven by its softer components (persistent fever and complications) — mortality, the hardest component, did not separate. One trial, one country (India), intravenous therapy in hospitalised patients: not a verdict on oral treatment of mild scrub typhus.

shelves.title: Ceftobiprole for complicated Staphylococcus aureus bacteraemia (ERADICATE), with the TARGET skin-infection trial
shelves.question: Is ceftobiprole, a cephalosporin that binds MRSA, noninferior to daptomycin for complicated Staphylococcus aureus bacteraemia, and what does its phase 3 skin-infection trial add?
shelves.mesh: Anti-Bacterial Agents/administration & dosage,adverse effects,therapeutic use · Bacteremia/drug therapy,microbiology · Cephalosporins/administration & dosage,adverse effects,therapeutic use · Daptomycin/administration & dosage,adverse effects,therapeutic use · Methicillin-Resistant Staphylococcus aureus · Staphylococcal Infections/drug therapy,microbiology · Staphylococcus aureus
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: One pivotal trial (ERADICATE, 390 randomised) found ceftobiprole noninferior to daptomycin for overall treatment success at 70 days (69.8% vs 68.7%; adjusted difference 2.0 points, CI -7.1 to 11.1, against a 15% margin), with mortality essentially identical (9.0% vs 9.1% — reported on the card face, not claimed as a benefit). Its phase 3 skin-infection trial (TARGET, carded below) likewise showed noninferiority to vancomycin plus aztreonam in a different indication. A single bacteraemia trial caps the stamp at POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: ERADICATE 2023: ceftobiprole was noninferior to daptomycin in complicated S. aureus bacteraemia — overall success 69.8% vs 68.7%; mortality 9.0% vs 9.1%
cards.summary: ERADICATE (2023): ceftobiprole was noninferior to daptomycin in complicated S. aureus bacteraemia — overall success 69.8% vs 68.7% ; mortality identical (9.0% vs 9.1%).
cards.type: Phase 3, double-blind, double-dummy, noninferiority trial (noninferiority margin 15%)
cards.people: 390 adults with complicated S. aureus bacteraemia (including right-sided endocarditis) randomised; 387 with confirmed bacteraemia received ceftobiprole 500 mg IV (189) or daptomycin 6-10 mg/kg IV plus optional aztreonam (198). The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Overall treatment success at 70 days (survival, bacteraemia clearance, symptom improvement, no new bacteraemia-related complications, no other potentially effective antibiotics) occurred in 132 of 189 patients (69.8%) on ceftobiprole and 136 of 198 (68.7%) on daptomycin (adjusted difference 2.0 percentage points; 95% CI -7.1 to 11.1), meeting noninferiority. Mortality was 9.0% vs 9.1% and microbiologic eradication 82.0% vs 77.3%. Adverse events occurred in 63.4% vs 59.1% and serious adverse events in 18.8% vs 22.7%; gastrointestinal events (mainly mild nausea) were more frequent with ceftobiprole.
cards.watchOut: A wide 15% noninferiority margin and a composite 'success' endpoint adjudicated at 70 days: noninferiority here means 'not unacceptably worse than daptomycin on this composite', in a trial not powered for mortality or for MRSA-only subgroups.
cards.source: Holland TL et al. Ceftobiprole for Treatment of Complicated Staphylococcus aureus Bacteremia. The New England journal of medicine. 2023;389(15):1390-1401. PMID: 37754204. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03138733, from the record's databank fields.

shelves.title: Stress-ulcer prophylaxis with pantoprazole (SUP-ICU)
shelves.question: In ICU patients at risk of gastrointestinal bleeding, does prophylactic pantoprazole reduce clinically important bleeding without increasing mortality or infection?
shelves.mesh: Gastrointestinal Hemorrhage/epidemiology,prevention & control · Pantoprazole/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Proton Pump Inhibitors/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Critical Illness/mortality,therapy · Peptic Ulcer/prevention & control · Humans · Aged · Female · Male
shelves.balance: Split: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — mortality · LIKELY — less clinically important bleeding — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, mortality co-reported): SUP-ICU (3,298 ICU patients at bleeding risk) found 90-day mortality identical on pantoprazole versus placebo (31.1% vs 30.4%; relative risk 1.02 relative, 95% CI 0.91 to 1.13; P=0.76) and a composite of clinically important events no different (21.9% vs 22.6%), while clinically important gastrointestinal bleeding was lower on pantoprazole (2.5% vs 4.2%). PEPTIC (26,828 ventilated patients, cluster-crossover) compared the two prophylaxis drug classes head-to-head: in-hospital mortality by day 90 was 18.3% with PPIs versus 17.5% with H2-blockers (risk ratio 1.05 relative, 1.00 to 1.10; P=0.054), with less clinically important upper GI bleeding on PPIs (1.3% vs 1.8%; risk ratio 0.73 relative, 0.57 to 0.92). Prophylaxis prevents some bleeding and saves no lives; both halves are LIKELY on trials of this size.

cards.headline: SUP-ICU 2018: pantoprazole halved clinically important GI bleeding (2.5% vs 4.2%) with identical 90-day mortality (31.1% vs 30.4%)
cards.summary: SUP-ICU 2018: pantoprazole halved clinically important GI bleeding (2.5% vs 4.2%) with identical 90-day mortality (31.1% vs 30.4%)
cards.type: European, multicentre, parallel-group, blinded randomised trial
cards.people: 3,298 adults admitted to the ICU for an acute (unplanned) condition and at risk for gastrointestinal bleeding, randomly assigned to 40 mg intravenous pantoprazole daily (1,645) or placebo (1,653); primary-outcome data were available for 3,282 (99.5%). The abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: At 90 days, 510 patients (31.1%) in the pantoprazole group and 499 (30.4%) in the placebo group had died (relative risk 1.02 relative, 95% CI 0.91 to 1.13; P=0.76). At least one clinically important event (a composite of clinically important gastrointestinal bleeding, pneumonia, Clostridium difficile infection or myocardial ischaemia) occurred in 21.9% on pantoprazole and 22.6% on placebo (relative risk 0.96 relative, 0.83 to 1.11). Clinically important gastrointestinal bleeding occurred in 2.5% of the pantoprazole group versus 4.2% of the placebo group. Infections, serious adverse reactions and days alive without life support were similar between groups.
cards.watchOut: The bleeding benefit is absolute-small (1.7 points) against a 31% background mortality the drug does not touch — the trial's own framing is that mortality and the composite of clinically important events were similar.
cards.source: Krag M et al. Pantoprazole in Patients at Risk for Gastrointestinal Bleeding in the ICU. N Engl J Med. 2018. PMID: 30354950. cards.headline: PEPTIC 2020: PPI versus H2-blocker prophylaxis — mortality marginally higher with PPIs (18.3% vs 17.5%; P=0.054), bleeding lower (1.3% vs 1.8%)
cards.summary: PEPTIC 2020: PPI versus H2-blocker prophylaxis — mortality marginally higher with PPIs (18.3% vs 17.5%; P=0.054), bleeding lower (1.3% vs 1.8%)
cards.type: Cluster-crossover randomised clinical trial (50 ICUs, five countries)
cards.people: 26,828 patients analysed (mean age 58 years [SD 17.0]; 9,691 [36.1%] women) requiring invasive mechanical ventilation within 24 hours of ICU admission at 50 ICUs in five countries; each ICU used a PPI-preferential or H2-blocker-preferential strategy for 6-month periods in randomised sequence (13,436 randomised by site to PPI-first, 13,392 to H2-blocker-first). An estimated 4.1% of PPI-strategy patients actually received H2-blockers and 20.1% of H2-blocker-strategy patients actually received PPIs.
cards.result: In-hospital mortality by day 90 was 2,459 of 13,415 (18.3%) in the PPI group versus 2,333 of 13,356 (17.5%) in the H2-blocker group (risk ratio 1.05 relative, 95% CI 1.00 to 1.10; absolute risk difference 0.93 percentage points, −0.01 to 1.88; P=0.054). Clinically important upper gastrointestinal bleeding occurred in 1.3% (PPI) versus 1.8% (H2-blocker) (risk ratio 0.73 relative, 0.57 to 0.92; absolute difference −0.51 points; P=0.009). Clostridioides difficile infection and ICU and hospital lengths of stay did not differ significantly; one adverse event (an allergic reaction) was reported.
cards.watchOut: A strategy trial, not a drug-level trial: one in five patients in the H2-blocker periods actually received a PPI, diluting any drug difference toward the null; the mortality P value of 0.054 sits on the conventional boundary and must be quoted as not significant.
cards.source: Young PJ et al. Effect of Stress Ulcer Prophylaxis With Proton Pump Inhibitors vs Histamine-2 Receptor Blockers on In-Hospital Mortality Among ICU Patients Receiving Invasive Mechanical Ventilation: The PEPTIC Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA. 2020. PMID: 31950977. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields. cards.summary: Synthesis: prophylaxis reduces bleeding, does not reduce mortality — SPLIT (both halves LIKELY, Tier C)
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: SUP-ICU 2018 (3,298 patients, pantoprazole versus placebo) and PEPTIC 2020 (26,828 patients, PPI-strategy versus H2-blocker-strategy).
cards.result: Read together: acid suppression in the ICU prevents roughly 1–2 clinically important bleeds per 100 patients treated, and no trial shows a mortality benefit — placebo-controlled mortality was 31.1% versus 30.4%, and the class comparison if anything leaned the other way (18.3% vs 17.5%, not significant). cards.watchOut: SUP-ICU enrolled patients selected for bleeding risk; PEPTIC enrolled all ventilated patients. The bleeding rates differ between the trials for population reasons, and neither supports prophylaxis as a survival intervention.

shelves.title: Permissive underfeeding versus standard enteral feeding (PermiT)
shelves.question: In critically ill adults, does permissive underfeeding (40–60% of caloric goal, full protein) improve 90-day mortality versus standard feeding (70–100%)?
shelves.mesh: Critical Illness/mortality,therapy · Caloric Restriction · Enteral Nutrition/methods · Energy Intake · Acute Lung Injury/mortality,therapy · Humans · Adult · Female · Male
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, mortality primary/co-reported): PermiT (894 critically ill adults; permissive underfeeding at 40–60% of caloric goal with full protein versus standard feeding at 70–100%) found 90-day mortality of 27.2% versus 28.9% (relative risk 0.94 relative, 95% CI 0.76 to 1.16; P=0.58), with no differences in intolerance, infections or length of stay. EDEN (1,000 patients with acute lung injury; trophic feeding for 6 days versus full feeding) found ventilator-free days of 14.9 versus 15.0 and 60-day mortality of 23.2% versus 22.2%. Two randomised trials, two feeding-restriction strategies, one answer: eating less in the first days of critical illness neither saves nor costs lives — LIKELY (the treatment made no difference).

cards.headline: PermiT 2015: permissive underfeeding did not change 90-day mortality (27.2% vs 28.9%)
cards.summary: PermiT 2015: permissive underfeeding did not change 90-day mortality (27.2% vs 28.9%)
cards.type: Randomised trial (seven centres) of caloric dose with protein held constant
cards.people: 894 critically ill adults with medical, surgical or trauma admission categories at seven centres, randomised to permissive underfeeding (40–60% of calculated caloric requirements; 445 analysed) or standard enteral feeding (70–100%; 440) for up to 14 days, with similar protein intake in both groups (57 [SD 24] versus 59 [SD 25] g/day); 96.8% were receiving mechanical ventilation. Delivered calories were 835 (SD 297) versus 1,299 (SD 467) kcal/day. The abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: Ninety-day mortality was 121 of 445 patients (27.2%) in the permissive-underfeeding group versus 127 of 440 (28.9%) in the standard-feeding group (relative risk 0.94 relative, 95% CI 0.76 to 1.16; P=0.58). No serious adverse events were reported, and there were no significant between-group differences in feeding intolerance, diarrhoea, infections acquired in the ICU, or ICU or hospital length of stay.
cards.watchOut: PermiT restricted nonprotein calories only, with protein deliberately maintained — its null must not be quoted against protein restriction, which is a different intervention (and high-dose protein is Shelf #1302's question).
cards.source: Arabi YM et al. Permissive Underfeeding or Standard Enteral Feeding in Critically Ill Adults. N Engl J Med. 2015. PMID: 25992505. Registry ID: ISRCTN ISRCTN68144998, from the record's databank fields. cards.headline: EDEN 2012: initial trophic feeding did not improve ventilator-free days or 60-day mortality in acute lung injury (23.2% vs 22.2%)
cards.summary: EDEN 2012: initial trophic feeding did not improve ventilator-free days or 60-day mortality in acute lung injury (23.2% vs 22.2%)
cards.type: Randomised, open-label, multicentre trial (ARDS Clinical Trials Network)
cards.people: 1,000 adults within 48 hours of developing acute lung injury requiring mechanical ventilation at 44 ARDS Network hospitals, randomised to trophic enteral feeding (508) or full enteral feeding (492) for the first 6 days; delivered calories were about 400 versus 1,300 kcal/day over that period. The abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: Initial trophic feeding did not increase ventilator-free days (14.9 [95% CI 13.9 to 15.8] versus 15.0 [14.1 to 15.9]; difference −0.1, −1.4 to 1.2; P=0.89) or reduce 60-day mortality (23.2% [19.6 to 26.9] versus 22.2% [18.5 to 25.8]; difference 1.0%, −4.1 to 6.3; P=0.77) compared with full feeding, and infectious complications did not differ. The full-feeding group had more vomiting, elevated gastric residual volumes and constipation, and higher glucose values and insulin administration.
cards.watchOut: EDEN's contrast lasted only 6 days, after which everyone was managed by the full-feeding protocol — it tests initial trophic feeding, not prolonged starvation; and its population was acute lung injury specifically.
cards.source: Rice TW et al. Initial trophic vs full enteral feeding in patients with acute lung injury: the EDEN randomized trial. JAMA. 2012. PMID: 22307571. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00609180 and NCT00883948, from the record's databank fields. cards.headline: Synthesis: early caloric restriction neither helps nor harms survival — LIKELY (the treatment made no difference), Tier C
cards.summary: Synthesis: early caloric restriction neither helps nor harms survival — LIKELY (the treatment made no difference), Tier C
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: PermiT 2015 (894 critically ill adults) and EDEN 2012 (1,000 patients with acute lung injury).
cards.result: Two different restriction strategies — sustained permissive underfeeding with full protein, and 6 days of trophic feeding — both landed on mortality within 2 points of standard feeding (27.2% vs 28.9% at 90 days; 23.2% vs 22.2% at 60 days). The practical content of the null is permission: clinicians need not chase full caloric targets in the first days, and patients are not harmed by the delay. Caloric restriction in refeeding syndrome (Shelf #1065) and glutamine in burns (#1049) are different questions and are not re-carded here. The stamp is proposed pending the developer's personal verdict because the primary outcome is mortality (Tier C).
cards.watchOut: Neither trial answers what happens beyond the early phase, and neither tested protein dose — the feeding question these trials close is calories in the first days, nothing wider.
cards.source: Synthesis of Arabi YM et al. N Engl J Med. 2015. PMID: 25992505; Rice TW et al. JAMA. 2012. PMID: 22307571. Registry IDs as on the individual cards.

shelves.title: Higher protein dosing in critical illness (EFFORT Protein)
shelves.question: In mechanically ventilated patients at nutritional risk, does high-dose protein (≥2.2 g/kg/day) improve time to discharge alive versus usual dose (≤1.2 g/kg/day)?
shelves.mesh: Critical Illness/therapy · Critical Care · Intensive Care Units · Respiration, Artificial · Registries · Humans · Adult
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference, harm-leaning in subgroups) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, mortality/discharge outcome): One large pragmatic trial (EFFORT Protein, 1,301 patients analysed in 85 ICUs) found high-dose protein (at least 2.2 g/kg/day) did not improve time to discharge alive — cumulative incidence of alive discharge by 60 days was 46.1% on high dose versus 50.2% on usual dose (hazard ratio 0.91 relative, 95% CI 0.77 to 1.07; P=0.27) — and 60-day mortality was numerically higher (34.6% vs 32.1%; relative risk 1.08 relative, 0.92 to 1.26). The trial reports an apparent subgroup effect in which higher protein was particularly harmful in patients with acute kidney injury and higher organ-failure scores. A single trial with a harm-leaning subgroup pattern supports POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) and no use of high-dose protein as a default.

cards.headline: EFFORT Protein 2023: high-dose protein did not speed discharge alive (46.1% vs 50.2%) and mortality leaned the wrong way (34.6% vs 32.1%)
cards.summary: EFFORT Protein 2023: high-dose protein did not speed discharge alive (46.1% vs 50.2%) and mortality leaned the wrong way (34.6% vs 32.1%)
cards.type: International, multicentre, pragmatic, registry-based, single-blinded randomised trial
cards.people: 1,329 nutritionally high-risk adults (at least 18 years) undergoing mechanical ventilation, randomised in 85 ICUs across 16 countries between January 2018 and December 2021 to high-dose protein (at least 2.2 g/kg/day; 645 analysed) or usual-dose protein (at most 1.2 g/kg/day; 656), started within 96 hours of ICU admission and continued for up to 28 days, death, or transition to oral feeding; 1,301 (97.9%) were included in the analysis. The abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: By 60 days, the cumulative incidence of alive hospital discharge was 46.1% (95% CI 42.0 to 50.1) in the high-dose group versus 50.2% (46.0 to 54.3) in the usual-dose group (hazard ratio 0.91 relative, 0.77 to 1.07; P=0.27). The 60-day mortality rate was 34.6% (222 of 642) on high-dose protein versus 32.1% (208 of 648) on usual dose (relative risk 1.08 relative, 0.92 to 1.26). There appeared to be a subgroup effect, with higher protein provision being particularly harmful in patients with acute kidney injury and higher organ-failure scores at baseline. The authors conclude that delivering higher doses of protein to mechanically ventilated critically ill patients did not improve time to discharge alive.
cards.watchOut: Prescription was randomised, delivery was pragmatic: achieved protein separation in such trials is typically narrower than prescribed, and the AKI/organ-failure harm signal is a subgroup reading — part of the record, labelled as such, not a proven harm.
cards.source: Heyland DK et al. The effect of higher protein dosing in critically ill patients with high nutritional risk (EFFORT Protein): an international, multicentre, pragmatic, registry-based randomised trial. Lancet. 2023. PMID: 36708732. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03160547, from the record's databank fields. cards.summary: Synthesis: high-dose protein does not speed recovery and may harm the sickest kidneys — POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference), Tier C
cards.people: Synthesis of the card above: EFFORT Protein 2023 (1,301 mechanically ventilated patients analysed).
cards.result: EFFORT is the largest randomised test of the protein-dose question and it answers against escalation: no discharge benefit (46.1% vs 50.2% discharged alive by day 60) and a mortality point estimate on the wrong side (34.6% vs 32.1%). The caloric-dose question is Shelf #1301's (PermiT/EDEN) and is not re-carded here; PermiT held protein constant, which is exactly why the two shelves are separate. shelves.title: Early active mobilisation during mechanical ventilation (TEAM)
shelves.question: In ICU patients on mechanical ventilation, does protocolised early active mobilisation improve days alive and out of ICU (and mortality) versus usual-care mobilisation?
shelves.mesh: Early Ambulation/adverse effects,methods · Respiration, Artificial · Critical Care/methods · Activities of Daily Living · Intensive Care Units · Humans · Adult
shelves.balance: Split: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — at TEAM scale · POSSIBLE — functional benefit in the earlier small trial — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, mortality co-reported): TEAM (750 ventilated adults; protocolised early active mobilisation with sedation minimisation versus usual care) found no difference in days alive and out of hospital at 180 days (median 143 versus 145; difference −2.0 days, 95% CI −10 to 6; P=0.62), death by day 180 in 22.5% versus 19.5% (odds ratio 1.15 relative, 0.81 to 1.65), and significantly more mobilisation-related adverse events (9.2% vs 4.1%; P=0.005). The earlier single-centre trial (Schweickert 2009, 104 patients) had found the opposite functional result — return to independent function at discharge in 59% versus 35% (odds ratio 2.7 relative, 1.2 to 6.1) — at a mobilisation intensity and sedation-interruption bundle TEAM did not reproduce. The honest record is contested: a large null with more adverse events against a small positive trial.

cards.headline: TEAM 2022: increased early mobilisation did not increase days alive and out of hospital (143 vs 145) and caused more adverse events
cards.summary: TEAM 2022: increased early mobilisation did not increase days alive and out of hospital (143 vs 145) and caused more adverse events
cards.type: Multicentre randomised trial of increased early mobilisation versus usual care
cards.people: 750 adult ICU patients undergoing invasive mechanical ventilation, randomly assigned to increased early mobilisation (sedation minimisation and daily physiotherapy) or usual care. Mean daily active mobilisation was 20.8 (SD 14.6) minutes versus 8.8 (SD 9.0) minutes; 77% of patients in both groups could stand, by a median of 3 versus 5 days. The abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: The median number of days alive and out of the hospital at 180 days was 143 (IQR 21 to 161) in the early-mobilisation group versus 145 (51 to 164) in the usual-care group (absolute difference −2.0 days, 95% CI −10 to 6; P=0.62). By day 180, death had occurred in 22.5% of the early-mobilisation group and 19.5% of the usual-care group (odds ratio 1.15 relative, 0.81 to 1.65). Among survivors, quality of life, activities of daily living, disability, cognitive and psychological function were similar. Serious adverse events were reported in 7 patients in the early-mobilisation group and 1 in usual care; adverse events potentially due to mobilisation (arrhythmias, altered blood pressure, desaturation) occurred in 34 of 371 patients (9.2%) versus 15 of 370 (4.1%) (P=0.005).
cards.watchOut: TEAM's usual-care arms mobilised substantially (77% standing by day 5), so the trial tests an increase over contemporary practice, not mobilisation versus immobility — the contrast with 2009's control conditions is the crux of the disagreement between the two cards.
cards.source: Hodgson CL et al. Early Active Mobilization during Mechanical Ventilation in the ICU. N Engl J Med. 2022. PMID: 36286256. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03133377, from the record's databank fields. cards.headline: Schweickert 2009: early physical and occupational therapy with sedation interruption returned more patients to independent function (59% vs 35%)
cards.summary: Schweickert 2009: early physical and occupational therapy with sedation interruption returned more patients to independent function (59% vs 35%)
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (two university hospitals; outcome assessors blinded)
cards.people: 104 sedated adults on mechanical ventilation for less than 72 hours at two university hospitals, expected to continue ventilation at least 24 hours and functionally independent at baseline, randomised to early exercise and mobilisation during daily sedation interruption (49) or sedation interruption with therapy as ordered by the primary team (55). The abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: Return to independent functional status at hospital discharge occurred in 29 (59%) of the intervention group versus 19 (35%) of the control group (P=0.02; odds ratio 2.7 relative, 95% CI 1.2 to 6.1). The intervention group had a shorter duration of delirium (median 2.0 days [IQR 0.0–6.0] versus 4.0 days [2.0–8.0]; P=0.02) and more ventilator-free days (23.5 versus 21.1 days; P=0.05) over 28 days. There was one serious adverse event in 498 therapy sessions (desaturation below 80%), and therapy was discontinued for instability in 19 (4%) of sessions.
cards.watchOut: A 104-patient trial from 2009 whose control group received therapy only as ordered — a much weaker comparator than TEAM's usual care — and whose intervention bundled sedation interruption with therapy, so the active ingredient cannot be isolated.
cards.source: Schweickert WD et al. Early physical and occupational therapy in mechanically ventilated, critically ill patients: a randomised controlled trial. Lancet. 2009. PMID: 19446324. shelves.title: Flexible family visitation in the ICU (ICU Visits)
shelves.question: In ICU patients, does a flexible family-visitation policy (up to 12 h/day) reduce delirium incidence versus restricted visitation?
shelves.mesh: Delirium/prevention & control · Visitors to Patients · Family/psychology · Cross-Over Studies · Intensive Care Units/organization & administration · Humans · Female · Male
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): The one large randomised test (ICU Visits, 1,685 patients in 36 Brazilian ICUs, cluster-crossover) found delirium incidence of 18.9% with flexible visitation (up to 12 hours/day, with family education; actual visits averaged 4.8 hours) versus 20.1% with restricted visitation (median 1.5 hours/day) — an adjusted difference of −1.7 percentage points (95% CI −6.1 to 2.7; P=0.44). ICU-acquired infections and staff burnout also did not differ. What did improve was the family: anxiety (adjusted difference −1.6 points) and depression (−1.2 points) scores were significantly better with flexible visitation. A large null on the patient outcome with a real family benefit carries LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) for the delirium claim. (Journal correction: the topic draft cited this trial as NEJM 2019; the verified record is Rosa et al., JAMA 2019.)

cards.headline: ICU Visits 2019: flexible family visitation did not reduce delirium (18.9% vs 20.1%) but did reduce family anxiety and depression
cards.summary: ICU Visits 2019: flexible family visitation did not reduce delirium (18.9% vs 20.1%) but did reduce family anxiety and depression
cards.type: Cluster-crossover randomised clinical trial (36 ICUs, Brazil)
cards.people: 1,685 patients (mean age 58.5 years; 47.2% women), 1,295 family members and 826 clinicians from 36 adult ICUs in Brazil with restricted visiting hours (under 4.5 hours/day), recruited April 2017 to June 2018; 19 ICUs started with flexible visitation and 17 with restricted visitation in a cluster-crossover design. Flexible visitation was up to 12 hours/day supported by family education (837 patients); restricted visitation was a median of 1.5 hours/day (848 patients); the achieved mean daily visit duration was 4.8 versus 1.4 hours.
cards.result: The incidence of delirium during the ICU stay was 18.9% with flexible visitation versus 20.1% with restricted visitation (adjusted difference −1.7%, 95% CI −6.1 to 2.7; P=0.44). Of nine prespecified secondary outcomes, six did not differ significantly, including ICU-acquired infections (3.7% vs 4.5%; adjusted difference −0.8%, −2.1 to 1.0; P=0.38) and staff burnout (22.0% vs 24.8%; adjusted difference −3.8%, −4.8 to 12.5; P=0.36). For family members, median anxiety scores (6.0 vs 7.0; adjusted difference −1.6, −2.3 to −0.9; P<0.001) and depression scores (4.0 vs 5.0; adjusted difference −1.2, −2.0 to −0.4; P=0.003) were significantly better with flexible visitation.
cards.watchOut: The intervention bundled extended hours with structured family education, and achieved visit duration (4.8 h) was far below the 12-hour ceiling — the trial tests a realistic flexible policy, not maximal presence; the delirium confidence interval (−6.1 to 2.7) excludes a large benefit but not a small one.
cards.source: Rosa RG et al. Effect of Flexible Family Visitation on Delirium Among Patients in the Intensive Care Unit: The ICU Visits Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA. 2019. PMID: 31310297. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02932358, from the record's databank fields. shelves.title: Subglottic secretion drainage to prevent ventilator-associated pneumonia
shelves.question: In intubated patients expected to be ventilated >48–72 hours, does subglottic secretion drainage reduce ventilator-associated pneumonia versus a standard endotracheal tube?
shelves.mesh: Pneumonia, Ventilator-Associated/prevention & control · Drainage/methods · Intubation, Intratracheal/instrumentation · Humans · Aged · Female · Male
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: The patient-level randomised trial of the drainage itself (Lacherade 2010, 333 patients ventilated at least 48 hours) found microbiologically confirmed VAP in 14.8% with intermittent subglottic secretion drainage versus 25.6% without (P=0.02; a 42.2% relative risk reduction, relative), with no difference in ventilation duration or hospital mortality. The newer automation trial (MICROINHALO 2026, 250 patients analysed, cluster-randomised) tested automatic cuff-pressure management plus automatic drainage against manual management of both — and MISSED its primary endpoint: day-3 tracheal colonisation was 37% versus 41.5% (difference −4%, 95% CI −16 to 8; P=0.52), although its secondary VAP rates were lower (clinical VAP 12.6% vs 24.4%, P=0.016; microbiologically confirmed 10.2% vs 19.5%, P=0.039). One positive mid-size trial of drainage plus a null-primary automation trial supports POSSIBLE — and the shelf discloses on its face that MICROINHALO's primary endpoint was colonisation, not VAP, contrary to how the topic draft framed it.

cards.headline: Lacherade 2010: intermittent subglottic drainage reduced microbiologically confirmed VAP (14.8% vs 25.6%)
cards.summary: Lacherade 2010: intermittent subglottic drainage reduced microbiologically confirmed VAP (14.8% vs 25.6%)
cards.type: Randomised controlled clinical trial (four French centres)
cards.people: 333 adults intubated with a tracheal tube allowing drainage of subglottic secretions and expected to require mechanical ventilation for at least 48 hours, at four French centres, randomly assigned to intermittent subglottic secretion drainage (169) or no drainage (164). The abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: Microbiologically confirmed ventilator-associated pneumonia occurred in 25 of 169 patients (14.8%) in the drainage group and 42 of 164 (25.6%) in the control group (P=0.02), a relative risk reduction of 42.2% (relative; 95% CI 10.4 to 63.1). The benefit appeared in both early-onset VAP (1.2% vs 6.1%; P=0.02) and late-onset VAP (18.6% vs 33.0%; P=0.01). VAP was clinically suspected at least once in 30.2% versus 36.6% (P=0.25). No significant between-group differences were observed in duration of mechanical ventilation or hospital mortality.
cards.watchOut: The effect is on VAP incidence, not on ventilation duration or mortality — both null — and the trial predates modern VAP-prevention bundles, so its absolute rates (25.6% control) are higher than contemporary practice.
cards.source: Lacherade JC et al. Intermittent subglottic secretion drainage and ventilator-associated pneumonia: a multicenter trial. Am J Respir Crit Care Med. 2010. PMID: 20522796. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00219661, from the record's databank fields. cards.headline: MICROINHALO 2026: automatic cuff-pressure plus drainage management missed its primary endpoint — day-3 tracheal colonisation 37% vs 41.5% (P=0.52) — with lower secondary VAP rates
cards.summary: MICROINHALO 2026: automatic cuff-pressure plus drainage management missed its primary endpoint — day-3 tracheal colonisation 37% vs 41.5% (P=0.52) — with lower secondary VAP rates
cards.people: 270 critically ill intubated patients randomised in 10 ICUs (cluster-randomised), of whom 250 were analysed: 127 allocated to an endotracheal tube with automatic cuff-pressure management personalised by exhaled CO2 plus automatic subglottic drainage, and 123 to a conventional tube with manual cuff-pressure management and manual drainage. The abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: The primary endpoint — bacterial tracheal colonisation (above 10^3 CFU/mL) on day 3 after intubation — occurred in 47 patients (37%) in the automatic-management group and 51 (41.5%) among controls (absolute difference −4%, 95% CI −16 to 8; P=0.52): not superior. Rates of clinically diagnosed VAP (12.6% vs 24.4%; P=0.016) and microbiologically confirmed VAP (10.2% vs 19.5%; P=0.039) were significantly lower in the automatic group, as was the percentage of cuff-pressure values outside the safety range (10.2% vs 24.4%; P<0.001), with higher daily drainage volume (25 [IQR 8–41] mL vs 10.5 [6–17] mL; P<0.001). The authors conclude further research is warranted to confirm the observed VAP effect.
cards.watchOut: Both arms used drainage-capable tubes — MICROINHALO tests automation of cuff pressure and drainage, not drainage versus none; its VAP findings are secondary endpoints in a trial whose primary endpoint was null, and cluster randomisation across only 10 ICUs limits precision. Read it as supportive of the drainage concept, not as a second proof of it.
cards.source: De Pascale G et al. Personalized automatic management of tracheal cuff pressure and subglottic secretions drainage to prevent pneumonia in critically ill intubated patients. The MICROINHALO multicenter randomized controlled trial. Intensive Care Med. 2026. PMID: 42228008. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields (the abstract names NCT05403320). cards.summary: Synthesis: drainage reduces VAP in its direct trial; automation's own primary test was null — POSSIBLE
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Lacherade 2010 (333 patients, drainage versus none) and MICROINHALO 2026 (250 patients analysed, automatic versus manual management).
cards.result: The drainage claim rests on Lacherade: microbiologically confirmed VAP 14.8% versus 25.6%, without mortality or ventilation-duration effects. shelves.title: Lung recruitment manoeuvres with titrated PEEP in ARDS (ART)
shelves.question: In moderate-to-severe ARDS, does an aggressive lung-recruitment strategy with PEEP titration reduce 28-day mortality versus a low-PEEP strategy?
shelves.mesh: Respiratory Distress Syndrome/mortality,therapy · Positive-Pressure Respiration/adverse effects,methods · Pneumothorax/etiology · Tidal Volume · Humans · Adult · Female · Male
shelves.balance: LIKELY (harm) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, mortality harm): The one large randomised test (ART, 1,010 patients with moderate-to-severe ARDS in 120 ICUs) found an aggressive lung-recruitment manoeuvre with PEEP titrated to best respiratory-system compliance INCREASED 28-day all-cause mortality: 55.3% versus 49.3% on a low-PEEP strategy (hazard ratio 1.20 relative, 95% CI 1.01 to 1.42; P=0.041). Six-month mortality was also higher (65.3% vs 59.9%; hazard ratio 1.18 relative, 1.01 to 1.38), ventilator-free days fewer (5.3 vs 6.4), and barotrauma more frequent (5.6% vs 1.6%; P=0.001), as was pneumothorax requiring drainage (3.2% vs 1.2%). A 1,010-patient trial with concordant harm across mortality, barotrauma and ventilator-free days carries LIKELY (harm): the ART strategy should not be used routinely.

cards.headline: ART 2017: recruitment manoeuvres with titrated PEEP increased 28-day mortality in ARDS (55.3% vs 49.3%) and barotrauma (5.6% vs 1.6%)
cards.summary: ART 2017: recruitment manoeuvres with titrated PEEP increased 28-day mortality in ARDS (55.3% vs 49.3%) and barotrauma (5.6% vs 1.6%)
cards.type: Multicentre randomised trial (120 ICUs, nine countries)
cards.people: 1,010 adults with moderate to severe ARDS enrolled between November 2011 and April 2017 at 120 ICUs in nine countries (mean age 50.9 years [SD 17.4]; 37.5% female), randomised to an experimental strategy of lung recruitment manoeuvre plus PEEP titration according to best respiratory-system compliance (501) or a conventional low-PEEP strategy (509); all patients received volume-assist control ventilation until weaning.
cards.result: At 28 days, 277 of 501 patients (55.3%) in the experimental group and 251 of 509 (49.3%) in the control group had died (hazard ratio 1.20 relative, 95% CI 1.01 to 1.42; P=0.041). The experimental strategy increased 6-month mortality (65.3% vs 59.9%; hazard ratio 1.18 relative, 1.01 to 1.38; P=0.04), decreased mean ventilator-free days (5.3 vs 6.4; difference −1.1, −2.1 to −0.1; P=0.03), and increased pneumothorax requiring drainage (3.2% vs 1.2%; difference 2.0%, 0.0 to 4.0; P=0.03) and barotrauma (5.6% vs 1.6%; difference 4.0%, 1.5 to 6.5; P=0.001). There were no significant differences in ICU or hospital length of stay or in ICU or in-hospital mortality endpoints.
cards.watchOut: The verdict convicts the ART protocol as a package — an aggressive recruitment manoeuvre plus compliance-titrated PEEP — not every use of PEEP or every gentler recruitment manoeuvre; but the package is what was proposed for routine use, and its harm signals align across endpoints.
cards.source: Cavalcanti AB et al. Effect of Lung Recruitment and Titrated Positive End-Expiratory Pressure (PEEP) vs Low PEEP on Mortality in Patients With Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome: A Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA. 2017. PMID: 28973363. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01374022, from the record's databank fields.
