shelves.title: Oesophageal-pressure-guided PEEP in ARDS (EPVent)
shelves.question: In moderate-to-severe ARDS, does titrating PEEP to oesophageal pressure improve the composite of death and ventilator-free days versus an empirical high-PEEP/FiO2 table?
shelves.mesh: Respiratory Distress Syndrome/mortality,physiopathology,therapy · Positive-Pressure Respiration/methods · Esophagus/physiopathology · Pressure · Humans · Adult · Female · Male
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, death within the primary composite): The phase 2 trial (EPVent-2, 200 patients with moderate-to-severe ARDS) found no difference on its ranked composite of death and ventilator-free days (probability of a more favourable outcome with oesophageal-pressure-guided PEEP 49.6%, 95% CI 41.7 to 57.5; P=0.92), with 28-day mortality of 32.4% versus 30.6% on an empirical high-PEEP/FiO2 strategy and no difference in ventilator-free days among survivors — although rescue therapy was needed less often (3.9% vs 12.2%; P=0.04). The earlier pilot (EPVent-1, 61 patients) had shown better oxygenation (PaO2/FiO2 88 mm Hg higher at 72 hours) and compliance, a physiology result the larger trial did not convert into outcome benefit. A single 200-patient phase 2 trial supports POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference).

cards.headline: EPVent-2 2019: oesophageal-pressure-guided PEEP did not improve the death/ventilator-free-day composite (P=0.92); 28-day mortality 32.4% vs 30.6%
cards.summary: EPVent-2 2019: oesophageal-pressure-guided PEEP did not improve the death/ventilator-free-day composite (P=0.92); 28-day mortality 32.4% vs 30.6%
cards.type: Phase 2 randomised clinical trial (14 hospitals, North America)
cards.people: 200 mechanically ventilated patients aged 16 years or older with moderate to severe ARDS (PaO2:FiO2 at most 200 mm Hg) enrolled between October 2012 and September 2017 at 14 North American hospitals (mean age 56 years [SD 16]; 46% female), randomised to oesophageal-pressure-guided PEEP (102) or empirical high PEEP-FiO2 (98); all received low tidal volumes.
cards.result: The primary composite endpoint (a ranked score incorporating death and days free from mechanical ventilation among survivors through day 28) was not significantly different between groups (probability of a more favourable outcome with oesophageal-pressure-guided PEEP: 49.6%, 95% CI 41.7 to 57.5; P=0.92). At 28 days, 33 of 102 patients (32.4%) in the guided group and 30 of 98 (30.6%) in the empirical group had died (risk difference 1.7%, −11.1 to 14.6; P=0.88). Days free from mechanical ventilation among survivors did not differ (median 22 [IQR 15–24] versus 21 [16.5–24] days; P=0.85). Patients on guided PEEP were significantly less likely to receive rescue therapy (4 of 102 [3.9%] versus 12 of 98 [12.2%]; risk difference −8.3%, −15.8 to −0.8; P=0.04). None of the seven other prespecified secondary clinical endpoints differed significantly; gross barotrauma occurred in 6 guided and 5 empirical patients.
cards.watchOut: A phase 2 trial of 200 patients against an already-high-PEEP control strategy: it refutes an outcome advantage for the guided approach in this comparison, and its mortality confidence interval (−11.1 to 14.6) is wide; the rescue-therapy difference is a secondary endpoint.
cards.source: Beitler JR et al. Effect of Titrating Positive End-Expiratory Pressure (PEEP) With an Esophageal Pressure-Guided Strategy vs an Empirical High PEEP-Fio2 Strategy on Death and Days Free From Mechanical Ventilation Among Patients With Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome: A Randomized Clinical Trial. shelves.title: Corticosteroids before extubation to prevent laryngeal oedema
shelves.question: In ICU patients at high risk of post-extubation laryngeal oedema, does pre-extubation methylprednisolone reduce laryngeal oedema and reintubation?
shelves.mesh: Laryngeal Edema/classification,etiology,prevention & control · Methylprednisolone/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Glucocorticoids/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Intubation, Intratracheal/adverse effects · Double-Blind Method · Humans · Aged · Female · Male
shelves.balance: LIKELY: One large double-blind multicentre trial (François 2007, 698 patients analysed of 761 randomised, all ventilated more than 36 hours before a planned extubation) found 12-hour methylprednisolone pretreatment (20 mg starting 12 hours before extubation, then every 4 hours until tube removal) cut postextubation laryngeal oedema from 22% to 3% (P<0.0001) and overall reintubation from 8% to 4% (P=0.02); reintubations caused by laryngeal oedema fell from 54% to 8% of reintubations (P=0.005). A single trial with effects this large on both the mechanism endpoint and the clinical endpoint it feeds supports LIKELY for patients like those enrolled — ventilated more than 36 hours, planned extubation. The paediatric companion question is separate and is not carded here.

cards.headline: François 2007: methylprednisolone started 12 hours before extubation cut laryngeal oedema from 22% to 3% and reintubation from 8% to 4%
cards.summary: François 2007: methylprednisolone started 12 hours before extubation cut laryngeal oedema from 22% to 3% and reintubation from 8% to 4%
cards.people: 761 adults in intensive care units who were ventilated for more than 36 hours and underwent a planned extubation, randomised to intravenous methylprednisolone 20 mg (380) or placebo (381) 12 hours before extubation and every 4 hours until tube removal; 63 patients could not be assessed (mainly self-extubation or cancelled extubation), leaving 698 analysed (355 methylprednisolone, 343 placebo). The abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: Methylprednisolone significantly reduced the incidence of postextubation laryngeal oedema (11 of 355 [3%] versus 76 of 343 [22%]; P<0.0001), the global incidence of reintubation (13 of 355 [4%] versus 26 of 343 [8%]; P=0.02), and the proportion of reintubations secondary to laryngeal oedema (1 of 13 [8%] versus 14 of 26 [54%]; P=0.005). One patient in each group died after extubation, and atelectasia occurred in one patient given methylprednisolone.
cards.watchOut: The 12-hour lead time is the intervention: this trial does not support a steroid dose given at the moment of extubation, and its population (ventilated over 36 hours, planned extubation) excludes emergency and self-extubations — 63 randomised patients could not even be assessed for exactly those reasons.

cards.summary: Synthesis: a timed steroid pretreatment prevents most postextubation laryngeal oedema — LIKELY
cards.people: Synthesis of the card above: François 2007 (698 patients analysed, ventilated more than 36 hours).

shelves.title: Post-extubation high-flow oxygen with noninvasive ventilation in high-risk patients
shelves.question: In patients at high risk of extubation failure, does alternating high-flow nasal oxygen with NIV after extubation reduce reintubation versus high-flow oxygen alone?
shelves.mesh: Airway Extubation · Noninvasive Ventilation · Oxygen Inhalation Therapy/instrumentation,methods,statistics & numerical data · Respiratory Insufficiency/etiology,prevention & control,therapy · Humans · Aged · Female · Male
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Two randomised trials support active post-extubation support in high-risk patients. Thille 2019 (641 patients at high risk of extubation failure — over 65 or with cardiac/respiratory disease) found reintubation by day 7 in 11.8% with high-flow nasal oxygen alternating with NIV versus 18.2% with high-flow oxygen alone (difference −6.4 percentage points, 95% CI −12.0 to −0.9; P=0.02), with postextubation respiratory failure also lower (21% vs 29%) and ICU mortality not significantly different (6% vs 9%). Hernández 2016 (604 high-risk patients) found high-flow oxygen non-inferior to NIV for reintubation (22.8% vs 19.1%, within the 10-point margin) with less postextubation respiratory failure (26.9% vs 39.8%). Together: in high-risk patients, high-flow oxygen is at least NIV's equal, and alternating the two beats high-flow alone — LIKELY.

cards.headline: Thille 2019: high-flow oxygen alternating with NIV cut day-7 reintubation versus high-flow alone (11.8% vs 18.2%)
cards.summary: Thille 2019: high-flow oxygen alternating with NIV cut day-7 reintubation versus high-flow alone (11.8% vs 18.2%)
cards.type: Multicentre randomised clinical trial (30 ICUs, France)
cards.people: 648 patients at high risk of extubation failure (older than 65 years or with underlying cardiac or respiratory disease) at 30 ICUs in France, randomised immediately after extubation to high-flow nasal oxygen alone (306) or high-flow oxygen alternating with NIV (342); 641 completed the trial (mean age 70 years [SD 10]; 219 women [34%]).
cards.result: The reintubation rate at day 7 was 11.8% (40 of 339) with high-flow oxygen plus NIV versus 18.2% (55 of 302) with high-flow oxygen alone (difference −6.4%, 95% CI −12.0 to −0.9; P=0.02). Postextubation respiratory failure at day 7 was lower with the combination (21% vs 29%; difference −8.7%, −15.2 to −1.8; P=0.01), as was reintubation up to ICU discharge (12% vs 20%; difference −7.4%, −13.2 to −1.8; P=0.009). ICU mortality was not significantly different (6% versus 9%; difference −2.4%, −6.7 to 1.7; P=0.25).
cards.watchOut: The high-risk definition (age over 65 or cardiorespiratory disease) covers much of a general ICU population, but the result does not extend to low-risk extubations; and the mortality difference, though favourable, was not significant — the claim is reintubation, not survival.

cards.headline: Hernández 2016: high-flow oxygen was non-inferior to NIV for reintubation in high-risk patients (22.8% vs 19.1%) and caused less postextubation respiratory failure
cards.summary: Hernández 2016: high-flow oxygen was non-inferior to NIV for reintubation in high-risk patients (22.8% vs 19.1%) and caused less postextubation respiratory failure
cards.type: Multicentre randomised clinical trial (three ICUs, Spain) — non-inferiority design, 10-point margin
cards.people: 604 critically ill patients ready for planned extubation with at least one high-risk factor for reintubation (age over 65, APACHE II above 12 on extubation day, BMI above 30, inadequate secretion management, difficult or prolonged weaning, more than one comorbidity, heart failure as the indication for ventilation, moderate-to-severe COPD, airway patency problems, or prolonged ventilation) at three ICUs in Spain, randomised to high-flow conditioned oxygen therapy (290) or NIV (314) for 24 hours after extubation (mean age 65 years [SD 16]; 388 [64%] men).
cards.result: Reintubation within 72 hours occurred in 66 patients (22.8%) in the high-flow group versus 60 (19.1%) in the NIV group (absolute difference −3.7% as printed in the record, 95% CI −9.1% to infinity), meeting the prespecified 10-percentage-point non-inferiority margin. Postextubation respiratory failure occurred in 78 patients (26.9%) on high-flow versus 125 (39.8%) on NIV (risk difference 12.9% as printed, 95% CI 6.6% to infinity; corrected in the record). Median time to reintubation did not differ significantly (26.5 versus 21.5 hours), and median postrandomisation ICU stay was shorter with high-flow (3 versus 4 days; P=0.048).
cards.watchOut: Non-inferiority against a generous 10-point margin with the point estimate actually favouring NIV for reintubation (19.1% vs 22.8%): high-flow's win in this trial is respiratory failure and practicality, not fewer reintubations — the record's own corrected figures are printed on this card.

shelves.title: Dexamethasone to prevent post-extubation airway obstruction in children
shelves.question: In mechanically ventilated children at risk of post-extubation airway obstruction, does intravenous dexamethasone before extubation reduce obstruction/stridor and reintubation?
shelves.mesh: Airway Extubation · Airway Obstruction/prevention & control · Dexamethasone · Child · Humans · Intensive Care Units, Pediatric
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence): The only placebo-controlled randomised trial in children (Varghese 2024, 70 children in one Indian PICU) found no significant difference in its primary outcome — clinically significant stridor (Westley score at least 3) occurred in 25.7% on dexamethasone versus 31.4% on placebo (P=0.79), and reintubation was 11.4% versus 17.1% (P=0.73). The second randomised trial (Parajuli 2021, 287 children) compares low-dose with high-dose dexamethasone with no placebo arm, and its PubMed record's abstract states the design and the 12% non-inferiority margin but prints no results, so it cannot be weighted. A single small null trial plus an unweightable dose comparison is weak evidence in both directions: MAYBE (weak evidence). The adult pre-extubation steroid evidence is a different population and a different shelf (#1308) and is not imported here.

cards.headline: Varghese 2024: pre-extubation dexamethasone did not significantly reduce stridor in ventilated children (25.7% vs 31.4%; P=0.79)
cards.summary: Varghese 2024: pre-extubation dexamethasone did not significantly reduce stridor in ventilated children (25.7% vs 31.4%; P=0.79)
cards.type: Double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled trial (single PICU, India)
cards.people: 70 children in a level-3 PICU at AIIMS Raipur, India (December 2019 to September 2022), intubated for at least 24 hours and no more than 14 days, randomised to dexamethasone 0.5 mg/kg/dose for four doses (at -12 h, -6 h, 0 h and +6 h around extubation; 35 children) or placebo (35 children). Children with upper-airway anomalies or recent corticosteroids were excluded. The abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: Clinically significant stridor (Westley stridor score at least 3, the primary outcome) occurred in 9 of 35 children (25.71%) on dexamethasone versus 11 of 35 (31.42%) on placebo (P=0.792 — not significant). Reintubation occurred in 4 of 35 (11.42%) versus 6 of 35 (17.14%) (P=0.734). Five children in the dexamethasone group and six in the placebo group died (P=1.00). There was no difference in PICU stay (P=0.84) or hospital stay (P=0.75).
cards.watchOut: The authors' printed conclusion says dexamethasone 'may help in the reducing the incidence of clinically significant stridor' — but their own primary-outcome comparison is P=0.792 in 70 children; that conclusion overclaims the trial's data and is not adopted on this card. With 35 children per arm the trial also cannot exclude a moderate benefit or harm.

cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Varghese 2024 (70 children, placebo-controlled) and Parajuli 2021 (287 children, dose comparison, no results in the record).
cards.result: The paediatric question is unanswered at randomised standards: the single placebo-controlled test is null on stridor (25.7% vs 31.4%) and reintubation (11.4% vs 17.1%) but far too small to close the question, and the larger trial has no untreated arm. Pre-extubation methylprednisolone in high-risk adults (Shelf #1308) showed a large effect in a different population and is not re-carded or extrapolated here.

shelves.title: Pressure-support versus T-piece spontaneous breathing trials (Subirà)
shelves.question: In patients receiving mechanical ventilation, does a pressure-support spontaneous breathing trial produce more successful extubations than a T-piece trial?
shelves.mesh: Ventilator Weaning/methods · Positive-Pressure Respiration · Respiration, Artificial · Intubation, Intratracheal · Treatment Outcome · Humans
shelves.balance: LIKELY: One large randomised trial (Subirà 2019, 1,153 patients in 18 Spanish ICUs) found that a 30-minute pressure-support spontaneous breathing trial (8 cm H2O) produced significantly more successful extubations than a 2-hour T-piece trial — 82.3% versus 74.0% (difference 8.2 percentage points, 95% CI 3.4 to 13.0; P=.001) — with no difference in reintubation (11.1% vs 11.9%). Hospital mortality was also lower with pressure support (10.4% vs 14.9%; P=.02) and 90-day mortality lower (13.2% vs 17.3%), but those are secondary outcomes of a single trial and are not the shelf's claim. A single large, well-run trial with a clear primary-endpoint result carries LIKELY for the extubation question.

cards.headline: Subirà 2019: a 30-minute pressure-support SBT beat a 2-hour T-piece SBT for successful extubation (82.3% vs 74.0%)
cards.summary: Subirà 2019: a 30-minute pressure-support SBT beat a 2-hour T-piece SBT for successful extubation (82.3% vs 74.0%)
cards.people: 1,153 adults deemed ready for weaning after at least 24 hours of mechanical ventilation, at 18 ICUs in Spain, randomised January 2016 to April 2017 to a 2-hour T-piece SBT (578) or a 30-minute SBT with 8-cm H2O pressure support (557); mean age 62.2 (SD 15.7) years; 428 (37.1%) women; 1,018 (88.3%) completed the trial.
cards.result: Successful extubation (remaining free of mechanical ventilation 72 hours after the first SBT) occurred in 473 patients (82.3%) in the pressure-support group and 428 (74.0%) in the T-piece group (difference 8.2 percentage points, 95% CI 3.4 to 13.0; P=.001). Reintubation was 11.1% versus 11.9% (difference -0.8 points, -4.8 to 3.1; P=.63). Median ICU stay was 9 versus 10 days and median hospital stay 24 versus 24 days. Hospital mortality was 10.4% versus 14.9% (difference -4.4 points, -8.3 to -0.6; P=.02) and 90-day mortality 13.2% versus 17.3% (difference -4.1 points, -8.2 to 0.01; P=.04; hazard ratio 0.74 relative, 95% CI 0.55 to 0.99).
cards.watchOut: The comparison bundles two changes at once — mode (pressure support vs T-piece) and duration (30 minutes vs 2 hours) — so the trial cannot say which component carries the benefit; and the mortality differences, though nominally significant, are secondary outcomes in one trial and should not be quoted as a proven survival effect of the SBT technique.

shelves.title: Statins in ARDS (HARP-2 and SAILS)
shelves.question: In patients with ARDS, does enteral simvastatin (HARP-2) — or rosuvastatin in sepsis-associated ARDS (SAILS) — improve ventilator-free days or mortality?
shelves.mesh: Respiratory Distress Syndrome/drug therapy · Hydroxymethylglutaryl-CoA Reductase Inhibitors/therapeutic use · Simvastatin/therapeutic use · Rosuvastatin Calcium · Double-Blind Method · Humans
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, mortality co-reported in both trials): Two large double-blind trials of two different statins agree. HARP-2 (540 patients with ARDS of any cause; enteral simvastatin 80 mg) found ventilator-free days of 12.6 versus 11.5 (P=0.21) and 28-day mortality of 22.0% versus 26.8% (P=0.23). SAILS (745 patients with sepsis-associated ARDS; enteral rosuvastatin, stopped early for futility) found 60-day in-hospital mortality of 28.5% versus 24.9% (P=0.21), identical ventilator-free days (15.1 vs 15.1), and fewer renal-failure-free and hepatic-failure-free days on rosuvastatin. Neither statin improved any clinical outcome; the stamp is proposed pending the developer's personal verdict because mortality is co-reported (Tier C).

cards.headline: HARP-2 2014: simvastatin did not improve ventilator-free days or 28-day mortality in ARDS (22.0% vs 26.8%; P=0.23)
cards.summary: HARP-2 2014: simvastatin did not improve ventilator-free days or 28-day mortality in ARDS (22.0% vs 26.8%; P=0.23)
cards.type: Multicentre, double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled trial (UK and Ireland)
cards.people: 540 patients with onset of ARDS within the previous 48 hours, in a multicentre double-blind trial, randomised 1:1 to enteral simvastatin 80 mg once daily (259) or placebo (281) for up to 28 days. The abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: There was no significant difference in ventilator-free days to day 28 (mean 12.6 [SD 9.9] with simvastatin versus 11.5 [SD 10.4] with placebo; P=0.21), in days free of nonpulmonary organ failure (19.4 [SD 11.1] versus 17.8 [SD 11.7]; P=0.11), or in 28-day mortality (22.0% versus 26.8%; P=0.23). There was no significant difference in serious adverse events related to the study drug; the authors conclude simvastatin was safe but did not improve clinical outcomes in ARDS.
cards.watchOut: The mortality point estimate favours simvastatin numerically (22.0% vs 26.8%) but is not significant and the trial was powered on ventilator-free days; phenotype-specific (hyperinflammatory) re-analyses of HARP-2 circulate in the secondary literature but are post hoc and are not carded as trial results here.
cards.source: McAuley DF et al. Simvastatin in the acute respiratory distress syndrome. N Engl J Med. 2014. PMID: 25268516. Registry ID: ISRCTN ISRCTN88244364, from the record's databank fields. cards.headline: SAILS 2014: rosuvastatin did not improve 60-day mortality in sepsis-associated ARDS (28.5% vs 24.9%) and was stopped for futility
cards.summary: SAILS 2014: rosuvastatin did not improve 60-day mortality in sepsis-associated ARDS (28.5% vs 24.9%) and was stopped for futility
cards.type: Multicentre, double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled trial (ARDS Network) — stopped early for futility
cards.people: 745 patients with sepsis-associated ARDS enrolled of an estimated 1,000 planned, in a multicentre double-blind trial, randomised to enteral rosuvastatin or placebo; the study was stopped because of futility. The abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: There was no significant difference in 60-day in-hospital mortality (28.5% with rosuvastatin versus 24.9% with placebo; P=0.21) or in ventilator-free days to day 28 (15.1 [SD 10.8] versus 15.1 [SD 11.0]; P=0.96). Rosuvastatin was associated with fewer days free of renal failure to day 14 (10.1 [SD 5.3] versus 11.0 [SD 4.7]; P=0.01) and fewer days free of hepatic failure to day 14 (10.8 [SD 5.0] versus 11.8 [SD 4.3]; P=0.003). Creatine kinase levels above 10 times the upper limit of normal were not increased.
cards.watchOut: SAILS enrolled sepsis-associated ARDS only, while HARP-2 enrolled ARDS of any cause — the concordance across the two populations is what strengthens the null; the renal and hepatic organ-failure signals in SAILS point toward harm, not benefit, in the nonpulmonary organs.

shelves.title: Inhaled nitric oxide in acute lung injury / ARDS
shelves.question: In adults with acute lung injury/ARDS, does low-dose inhaled nitric oxide improve oxygenation, ventilator-free days or mortality?
shelves.mesh: Nitric Oxide/administration & dosage,therapeutic use · Respiratory Distress Syndrome/therapy,drug therapy · Administration, Inhalation · Humans · Middle Aged
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): Inhaled nitric oxide improves oxygenation briefly and does not improve any clinical outcome. The large triple-blind trial (Taylor 2004, 385 patients with moderately severe acute lung injury not due to sepsis) found days alive and off assisted breathing of 10.7 on nitric oxide versus 10.6 on placebo (P=.97), with mortality 23% versus 20% (P=.54), despite a statistically significant PaO2 rise that resolved by 48 hours. The earlier phase II dose-ranging trial (Dellinger 1998, 177 patients with ARDS) found the same pattern: an acute oxygenation response in 60% of treated patients, and no difference in mortality or days alive off mechanical ventilation. The claim tested is oxygenation; mortality was null in both trials and no survival benefit is claimed or implied.

cards.headline: Taylor 2004: low-dose inhaled nitric oxide did not increase days alive off assisted breathing (10.7 vs 10.6 days) or reduce mortality in acute lung injury
cards.summary: Taylor 2004: low-dose inhaled nitric oxide did not increase days alive off assisted breathing (10.7 vs 10.6 days) or reduce mortality in acute lung injury
cards.type: Multicentre, randomised, placebo-controlled, triple-blind trial (46 US hospitals)
cards.people: 385 patients with moderately severe acute lung injury (PaO2/FiO2 ratio at most 250; onset within 72 hours; sepsis excluded as the cause and no significant nonpulmonary organ dysfunction), enrolled March 1996 to September 1999 in ICUs of 46 US hospitals, randomised to placebo (nitrogen gas) or inhaled nitric oxide 5 ppm until 28 days, discontinuation of assisted breathing, or death. The abstract does not state mean age; MeSH records the population as Middle Aged, male and female.
cards.result: Days alive and off assisted breathing (the primary end point) were 10.7 (SD 9.7) days with nitric oxide versus 10.6 (SD 9.8) with placebo (P=.97; difference -0.1 day, 95% CI -2.0 to 1.9). Mortality was 23% with nitric oxide versus 20% with placebo (P=.54). Days alive after a successful 2-hour unassisted ventilation trial (11.4 vs 11.9 days; P=.54) and days alive meeting extubation oxygenation criteria (16.7 vs 17.0; P=.89) were also similar. Nitric oxide produced a statistically significant increase in PaO2 that resolved by 48 hours.
cards.watchOut: The population excludes sepsis-caused lung injury and significant nonpulmonary organ dysfunction — a narrower, less sick group than all-comer ARDS; even in this favourable population the clinical outcomes were flat, which strengthens rather than weakens the null.

cards.headline: Dellinger 1998: inhaled nitric oxide raised PaO2 acutely in ARDS but did not change mortality or days alive off ventilation (phase II)
cards.summary: Dellinger 1998: inhaled nitric oxide raised PaO2 acutely in ARDS but did not change mortality or days alive off ventilation (phase II)
cards.type: Prospective, multicentre, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase II trial (30 US hospitals)
cards.people: 177 patients with ARDS (American-European Consensus Conference definition; onset within 72 hours), enrolled over 14 months in ICUs of 30 US hospitals, randomised to placebo (nitrogen gas) or inhaled nitric oxide at 1.25, 5, 20, 40 or 80 ppm. cards.result: An acute response (PaO2 increase of at least 20%) occurred in 60% of patients receiving nitric oxide and 24% of placebo patients in the first 4 hours, with no significant differences between dose groups; oxygenation index improved over the first 4 days. There were no differences between the pooled nitric oxide groups and placebo in mortality rate, days alive and off mechanical ventilation, or days alive after meeting oxygenation criteria for extubation. Four patients had methaemoglobin concentrations above 5%; mean inspired nitrogen dioxide in treated patients was 1.5 ppm.
cards.watchOut: The record itself labels the one favourable clinical finding — more patients alive and off ventilation at day 28 in the 5-ppm group (62% vs 44%) — as a post hoc analysis of one dose subgroup among five; it is fenced here, not carded as a result: post hoc dose-subgroup findings do not overturn a null pooled primary analysis.

shelves.title: Surfactant therapy for adult ARDS
shelves.question: In adults with ARDS, does exogenous (recombinant surfactant protein-C-based) surfactant improve oxygenation or mortality versus standard care?
shelves.mesh: Pulmonary Surfactants/therapeutic use · Pulmonary Surfactant-Associated Protein C/therapeutic use · Respiratory Distress Syndrome/drug therapy · Recombinant Proteins/therapeutic use · Double-Blind Method · Humans
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): Recombinant surfactant protein C-based surfactant improves early gas exchange and does not improve survival or free patients from ventilation in adult ARDS. The phase 3 programme (Spragg 2004, two multicentre double-blind trials, 448 patients) found 28-day survival of 66% overall with no significant difference between surfactant and standard care in mortality or need for mechanical ventilation (median ventilator-free days 0), despite significantly greater improvement in blood oxygenation over the first 24 hours. The earlier North American phase I/II trial (Spragg 2003) likewise found no significant treatment benefit. A treatment that works dramatically in neonatal respiratory distress does not transfer to the adult syndrome on this evidence.

cards.headline: Spragg 2004: recombinant surfactant protein C surfactant did not improve survival in adult ARDS (two phase 3 trials, 448 patients)
cards.summary: Spragg 2004: recombinant surfactant protein C surfactant did not improve survival in adult ARDS (two phase 3 trials, 448 patients)
cards.type: Two multicentre, randomised, double-blind phase 3 trials
cards.people: 448 patients with ARDS from various causes, in two multicentre, randomised, double-blind trials, comparing standard therapy alone with standard therapy plus up to four intratracheal doses of a recombinant surfactant protein C-based surfactant within 24 hours. The abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix; MeSH records the population as Middle Aged, male and female.
cards.result: The overall survival rate was 66 percent 28 days after treatment, and the median number of ventilator-free days was 0 (68 percent range, 0 to 26); there was no significant difference between the groups in mortality or in the need for mechanical ventilation. Patients receiving surfactant had a significantly greater improvement in blood oxygenation during the initial 24 hours of treatment than patients receiving standard therapy, by both univariate and multivariate analyses.
cards.watchOut: The abstract reports the two trials pooled (448 patients) without per-arm mortality counts, so no group-specific rates are printed on this card; the record's own conclusion is unambiguous that survival did not improve. The oxygenation improvement is a 24-hour surrogate and is reported beside the null outcome, not instead of it.

cards.headline: Spragg 2003: the phase I/II trial of the same surfactant found no significant treatment benefit either
cards.summary: Spragg 2003: the phase I/II trial of the same surfactant found no significant treatment benefit either
cards.people: Patients with ARDS in a North American phase I/II trial, prospectively randomised to standard therapy or standard therapy plus one of two doses of recombinant surfactant protein C-based surfactant (Venticute), given four times over 24 hours. The abstract does not state the number of patients, mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: Surfactant administration was well tolerated. No significant treatment benefit was associated with surfactant treatment. Bronchoalveolar lavage at 48 hours showed exogenous surfactant components and interleukin-6 concentrations significantly lower than in controls (consistent with an anti-inflammatory effect), but no evidence of improved surface-tension-lowering function; exogenous surfactant was no longer detectable at 120 hours.

shelves.title: Nebulised heparin for acute lung injury and inhalation injury
shelves.question: In ventilated patients with acute lung injury (including smoke-inhalation injury), does nebulised unfractionated heparin improve ventilator-free days or prevent intubation/death?
shelves.mesh: Heparin/administration & dosage,therapeutic use · Smoke Inhalation Injury/drug therapy · Administration, Inhalation · Anticoagulants/therapeutic use · Humans
shelves.balance: Split: POSSIBLE — smoke-inhalation injury · POSSIBLE — COVID-19 (meta-trial). Two different populations, two different evidence shapes, neither strong enough for more than POSSIBLE. In smoke-inhalation injury, one small trial (Hakim 2025, 88 adults) found inhaled heparin associated with more ventilator-free days at 28 days after adjustment (P=.046) and faster weaning, with 28-day mortality comparable between groups (P=.596) — the abstract reports P values without the underlying day counts. In hospitalised, non-intubated COVID-19, a prospective meta-trial of six randomised studies (478 patients) found lower odds of intubation or death with nebulised unfractionated heparin (odds ratio 0.43 relative, 95% CI 0.26 to 0.73) and lower in-hospital mortality (odds ratio 0.26 relative, 0.13 to 0.54) — relative measures whose abstract prints no absolute event rates. Neither population's result should be read onto the other.

cards.headline: Hakim 2025: early inhaled heparin was associated with more ventilator-free days after smoke-inhalation injury (88 patients; mortality comparable)
cards.summary: Hakim 2025: early inhaled heparin was associated with more ventilator-free days after smoke-inhalation injury (88 patients; mortality comparable)
cards.people: 88 adults with smoke-inhalation injury within 24 hours, randomised to nebulised heparin 5,000 IU (44) or normal saline (44) every 4 hours until successful extubation or death, up to 14 days. The abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix; MeSH records the population as Adult, Middle Aged and Aged, male and female.
cards.result: Adjusted for burn area and burn-to-randomisation time, inhaled heparin was associated with more ventilator-free days alive at 28 days (the primary outcome; P=.046) and a higher cumulative incidence of weaning from mechanical ventilation over time (P=.007). The heparin group also had more ICU-free days (P=.015), a higher PaO2/FiO2 ratio (P=.001) and fewer mechanical-ventilation days in survivors (P<.001), but the 28-day mortality rate was comparable to control (P=.596).
cards.watchOut: The record's abstract reports adjusted P values without printing the ventilator-free-day counts or mortality rates themselves, so no absolute figures are carded; a single 88-patient trial whose primary-outcome P value is .046 after adjustment is fragile evidence, and the authors themselves call for larger trials.
cards.source: Hakim SM et al. Effect of early administration of inhaled heparin on outcomes of smoke inhalation injury: A randomized controlled trial. Burns. 2025. PMID: 40319829. cards.headline: van Haren 2025 (INHALE-HEP meta-trial): nebulised heparin was associated with lower odds of intubation or death in hospitalised COVID-19 (OR 0.43 relative)
cards.summary: van Haren 2025 (INHALE-HEP meta-trial): nebulised heparin was associated with lower odds of intubation or death in hospitalised COVID-19 (OR 0.43 relative)
cards.type: Prospective collaborative meta-trial of six randomised clinical studies
cards.people: 478 adult hospitalised but not intubated patients with COVID-19, enrolled June 2020 to December 2022 in six randomised clinical studies at 10 hospitals in six countries (Argentina, Brazil, Egypt, Indonesia, Ireland and USA), randomised to inhaled nebulised unfractionated heparin plus standard care or standard care alone; dose and nebulisation method were specific to each study. No safety issues were reported, including no instances of pulmonary or systemic bleeding in the nebulised heparin group. The abstract prints no absolute event rates for either outcome, so none are carded.
cards.watchOut: A meta-trial pools six small studies with study-specific doses and nebulisation methods, in a 2020-2022 COVID-19 population unlike today's; and both headline effects are odds ratios — relative measures — with no absolute rates in the record, so the size of any absolute benefit cannot be stated from the verified record.

cards.summary: Synthesis: two populations, two modest signals, no shared verdict — POSSIBLE in each
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Hakim 2025 (88 patients, smoke-inhalation injury, ventilated) and van Haren 2025 (478 patients, hospitalised non-intubated COVID-19, six-study meta-trial).
cards.result: Nebulised heparin has a plausible mechanism (anticoagulant, anti-inflammatory, antiviral) and two positive randomised signals, but they answer different questions in different lungs: ventilator-free days after inhalation injury in one small trial, and intubation-or-death prevention in COVID-19 in a pooled meta-trial reported in relative terms only. shelves.title: Conservative versus liberal fluid management in acute lung injury (FACTT)
shelves.question: In patients with acute lung injury, does a conservative fluid strategy improve ventilator-free days and mortality versus a liberal strategy?
shelves.mesh: Fluid Therapy/methods · Respiratory Distress Syndrome/therapy,mortality · Diuretics/therapeutic use · Furosemide/therapeutic use · Treatment Outcome · Humans
shelves.balance: Split: LIKELY — more ventilator-free days · LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — 60-day mortality — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, mortality was the primary end point). FACTT (1,000 patients with acute lung injury, ARDS Network) compared protocolised conservative versus liberal fluid management for 7 days: cumulative 7-day fluid balance was -136 mL versus +6,992 mL. Death at 60 days (the primary end point) was 25.5% conservative versus 28.4% liberal (P=0.30; 95% CI for the difference -2.6 to 8.4 percentage points) — no significant mortality difference. Ventilator-free days were 14.6 versus 12.1 (P<0.001) and ICU-free days 13.4 versus 11.2 (P<0.001), with improved oxygenation index and lung injury score and no increase in shock or nonpulmonary organ failure (dialysis 10% vs 14%; P=0.06). The fluid question in sepsis resuscitation (#1070) and balanced-crystalloid choice (#123) are different shelves' questions.

cards.headline: FACTT 2006: conservative fluid management gave 2.5 more ventilator-free days (14.6 vs 12.1) with no significant 60-day mortality difference (25.5% vs 28.4%)
cards.summary: FACTT 2006: conservative fluid management gave 2.5 more ventilator-free days (14.6 vs 12.1) with no significant 60-day mortality difference (25.5% vs 28.4%)
cards.people: 1,000 patients with acute lung injury, randomised to a conservative or a liberal fluid-management strategy applied by explicit protocols for 7 days (ARDS Network). The abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix; MeSH records the population as Middle Aged, male and female.
cards.result: Death at 60 days was 25.5 percent in the conservative-strategy group and 28.4 percent in the liberal-strategy group (P=0.30; 95 percent confidence interval for the difference, -2.6 to 8.4 percent). Mean cumulative fluid balance over the first 7 days was -136 (SE 491) mL conservative versus 6,992 (SE 502) mL liberal (P<0.001). The conservative strategy improved the oxygenation index and lung injury score and increased ventilator-free days (14.6 [SE 0.5] vs 12.1 [SE 0.5]; P<0.001) and days not spent in the ICU (13.4 [SE 0.4] vs 11.2 [SE 0.4]; P<0.001) during the first 28 days, without increasing the incidence or prevalence of shock or the use of dialysis in the first 60 days (10 percent vs 14 percent; P=0.06).
cards.watchOut: The mortality confidence interval (-2.6 to 8.4 points) excludes a large harm from the conservative strategy but not a modest one, and the strategy began after initial resuscitation in established acute lung injury — FACTT is not a trial of restricting fluids during shock resuscitation, and must not be cited as one.
cards.source: Wiedemann HP et al. Comparison of two fluid-management strategies in acute lung injury. N Engl J Med. 2006. PMID: 16714767. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00281268, from the record's databank fields. shelves.title: Dalteparin versus unfractionated heparin for ICU thromboprophylaxis (PROTECT)
shelves.question: In critically ill patients, does once-daily dalteparin reduce proximal deep-vein thrombosis or pulmonary embolism versus twice-daily unfractionated heparin, without more bleeding?
shelves.mesh: Dalteparin/therapeutic use · Heparin/therapeutic use · Venous Thrombosis/prevention & control · Pulmonary Embolism/prevention & control · Anticoagulants/therapeutic use · Humans
shelves.balance: Split: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — proximal deep-vein thrombosis · LIKELY — fewer pulmonary emboli, no extra bleeding. PROTECT (3,764 critically ill patients) tested superiority of once-daily dalteparin 5,000 IU over twice-daily unfractionated heparin 5,000 IU and did not find it on the primary outcome: proximal leg DVT occurred in 5.1% versus 5.8% (hazard ratio 0.92 relative, 95% CI 0.68 to 1.23; P=0.57). Pulmonary embolism was significantly less frequent with dalteparin (1.3% vs 2.3%; hazard ratio 0.51 relative, 0.30 to 0.88; P=0.01), major bleeding was identical (hazard ratio 1.00 relative, 0.75 to 1.34) and hospital death did not differ (hazard ratio 0.92 relative, 0.80 to 1.05). The PE finding is a secondary outcome of a trial whose primary outcome was null — real, but graded accordingly.

cards.headline: PROTECT 2011: dalteparin was not superior for proximal DVT (5.1% vs 5.8%) but pulmonary embolism was less frequent (1.3% vs 2.3%), with identical major bleeding
cards.summary: PROTECT 2011: dalteparin was not superior for proximal DVT (5.1% vs 5.8%) but pulmonary embolism was less frequent (1.3% vs 2.3%), with identical major bleeding
cards.people: 3,764 critically ill patients in a multicentre trial, randomised to subcutaneous dalteparin 5,000 IU once daily (plus once-daily placebo injection) or unfractionated heparin 5,000 IU twice daily while in the ICU; the primary outcome (proximal leg DVT) was assessed in 1,873 patients per group by scheduled compression ultrasonography. The abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix; MeSH records the population as Middle Aged, male and female.
cards.result: Proximal leg deep-vein thrombosis occurred in 96 of 1,873 patients (5.1%) on dalteparin versus 109 of 1,873 (5.8%) on unfractionated heparin (hazard ratio 0.92 relative, 95% CI 0.68 to 1.23; P=0.57). Pulmonary embolism occurred in 24 patients (1.3%) versus 43 (2.3%) (hazard ratio 0.51 relative, 95% CI 0.30 to 0.88; P=0.01). Major bleeding did not differ (hazard ratio 1.00 relative, 0.75 to 1.34; P=0.98), nor did death in hospital (hazard ratio 0.92 relative, 0.80 to 1.05; P=0.21). In prespecified per-protocol analyses, heparin-induced thrombocytopenia was less frequent with dalteparin (hazard ratio 0.27 relative, 0.08 to 0.98; P=0.046).
cards.watchOut: The trial was designed and powered as a superiority test of the ultrasound-detected DVT outcome and it failed that test; the pulmonary-embolism difference, though clinically the more important event, is a secondary outcome — quote the two together, never the PE result alone.
cards.source: Cook D et al. Dalteparin versus unfractionated heparin in critically ill patients. N Engl J Med. 2011. PMID: 21417952. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00182143, from the record's databank fields. shelves.title: Earplugs and eye masks to protect sleep and prevent delirium in the ICU
shelves.question: In ICU patients, does night-time use of earplugs and eye masks improve sleep quality and reduce delirium versus usual care?
shelves.mesh: Delirium/prevention & control · Ear Protective Devices · Eye Protective Devices · Sleep · Intensive Care Units · Humans
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: Three small single-blind randomised trials (60, 84 and 114 patients, all single-centre) point the same way: night-time earplugs plus eye masks improved measured sleep quality in every trial, and delirium measures favoured the intervention — delirium development differed significantly at several time points in the 60-patient trial (Kiliç 2023), delirium screening scores were lower by the second night in the 84-patient coronary-ICU trial (Akpinar 2022), and delirium severity scores were significantly lower on postoperative days 2-4 after cardiac surgery in the 114-patient trial (Shorofi 2024). The stamp is POSSIBLE, not more: the patients cannot be blinded to wearing the devices, the delirium outcomes are scores and time-point comparisons rather than pooled incidence figures (none of the three records prints a delirium incidence rate for both arms), and every trial is small and single-centre.

cards.headline: Kiliç 2023: eye masks and earplugs for three nights improved sleep scores and reduced delirium development at several time points (60 ICU patients)
cards.summary: Kiliç 2023: eye masks and earplugs for three nights improved sleep scores and reduced delirium development at several time points (60 ICU patients)
cards.type: Randomised, controlled, single-blind intervention study (single tertiary hospital)
cards.people: 60 patients (30 intervention, 30 control) in the medical and surgical ICUs of a tertiary hospital; both groups received environmental modifications and evidence-based non-pharmacological nursing interventions, and the intervention group additionally wore eye masks and earplugs for three nights. Delirium was assessed with the Nursing Delirium Screening Scale and sleep with the Richard-Campbell Sleep Scale. The abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix; MeSH records the population as Aged.
cards.result: There was a statistically significant difference in the development of delirium between the intervention and control groups (night of the 2nd day, P=.019; day of the 3rd day, P<.001; night of the 3rd day, P at most .001). The average total sleep quality score of the intervention group was significantly higher than the control group (P at most .001 for three nights). Staying in the internal medicine ICU was associated with delirium development (odds ratio 11.84 relative, 95% CI 3.00 to 46.66; P=.017), as were age 65 or over, hearing impairment, admission from the operating room and education level. The record's abstract prints no delirium incidence rates for either arm, so none are carded.
cards.watchOut: Thirty patients per arm, assessor-blinded only (patients know whether they are wearing a mask), and delirium reported as time-point significance tests without incidence figures — the direction is consistent but the size of any effect cannot be quantified from this record.
cards.source: Kiliç G et al. Effect of using eye masks and earplugs in preventing delirium in intensive care patients: A single-blinded, randomized, controlled trial. Nurs Crit Care. 2023. PMID: 37138379. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields. cards.headline: Akpinar 2022: earplugs and eye masks raised sleep scores and lowered delirium screening scores in a coronary ICU (84 patients)
cards.summary: Akpinar 2022: earplugs and eye masks raised sleep scores and lowered delirium screening scores in a coronary ICU (84 patients)
cards.type: Randomised controlled experimental study (single coronary ICU)
cards.people: 84 patients (42 experimental, 42 control) in a coronary intensive care unit; the experimental group used earplugs and eye masks overnight and the control group received routine care. Sleep was measured with the Richards-Campbell Sleep Questionnaire (RCSQ) and delirium with the Intensive Care Delirium Screening Checklist (ICDSC). The abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: In the experimental group the mean RCSQ score rose from 40.11 (SD 16.55) at baseline to 64.09 (SD 14.07) and 72.07 (SD 11.75) at Times 1 and 2, versus 44.07 (SD 7.30), 46.97 (SD 9.22) and 47.04 (SD 11.53) in controls; the between-group differences at Times 1 and 2 were significant (P<.001). Mean ICDSC scores in the experimental group fell from 0.47 (SD 0.50) to 0.33 and 0.19, versus 0.42, 0.50 and 0.57 in controls, with the Time 2 difference significant (P=.004).
cards.watchOut: The ICDSC values are mean severity scores under 1 point in both groups — most patients had little or no delirium by this measure — so the trial shows a small score shift, not a demonstrated reduction in delirium cases; the sleep-score gain is the trial's stronger finding.

cards.headline: Shorofi 2024: after coronary bypass surgery, eye masks and earplugs lowered delirium severity scores and improved sleep domains (114 patients)
cards.summary: Shorofi 2024: after coronary bypass surgery, eye masks and earplugs lowered delirium severity scores and improved sleep domains (114 patients)
cards.type: Single-blind, randomised controlled trial (cardiac ICU, post-CABG patients)
cards.people: 114 patients undergoing coronary artery bypass grafting in a cardiac intensive care unit, consecutively enrolled and randomised to routine care plus eye masks and earplugs overnight or routine care alone. Delirium severity was measured with the Neelon and Champagne Confusion Scale and sleep quality with the Verran and Snyder-Halpern Sleep Scale. The abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: The mean delirium severity score differed significantly between the two groups on the second, third and fourth postoperative days (P<.001). The sleep quality domains (sleep disturbance, sleep effectiveness, sleep supplementation) differed significantly between groups across the three intervention days (P<.001), and a significant interaction between the sleep-disturbance subscale and delirium severity was found. The record's abstract prints no arm-specific score values or delirium incidence rates, so none are carded.
cards.watchOut: The record's abstract contains an awkward self-contradiction — it describes the delirium-severity trend in both groups as downward while parenthetically calling that '(trending towards higher delirium severity)'; the card reports the between-group result as printed and flags the wording rather than silently resolving it. Severity scores in a post-surgical population with low delirium rates are again a soft outcome.

cards.headline: Synthesis: a cheap, safe intervention with a consistent direction and soft outcomes — POSSIBLE
cards.summary: Synthesis: a cheap, safe intervention with a consistent direction and soft outcomes — POSSIBLE
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Kiliç 2023 (60 patients), Akpinar 2022 (84 patients) and Shorofi 2024 (114 patients) — 258 patients in three single-centre trials.
cards.result: Every trial found better sleep scores with earplugs and eye masks, and every delirium measure leaned the same way; none printed a two-arm delirium incidence, none exceeded 114 patients, and none could blind the wearer. That is enough for POSSIBLE and not enough for more. Multicomponent delirium-prevention programmes and flexible family visitation (#1304) are different interventions and are not re-carded here.
cards.watchOut: Consistency across three small unblindable trials in one intervention family (all in nursing journals, two in the same journal) is weaker than the same consistency across large multicentre trials; publication bias in this literature is plausible and unmeasured.

shelves.title: Neuromuscular electrical stimulation for ICU-acquired weakness
shelves.question: In mechanically ventilated critically ill patients, does neuromuscular electrical stimulation (alone or with early activity) preserve muscle mass/strength and improve functional outcomes versus usual care?
shelves.mesh: Electric Stimulation Therapy/methods · Muscle Weakness/prevention & control · Early Ambulation/methods · Critical Illness · Respiration, Artificial · Humans
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: Two small single-centre randomised trials found better strength and functional measures when neuromuscular electrical stimulation (NMES) was added to early activity. In a four-arm Egyptian trial (Othman 2024, 124 patients), day-7 MRC strength scores were highest with combined range-of-motion exercise plus NMES (50.37) and NMES alone (49.77) versus exercise alone (44.97) and conventional care (41.10), with ICU-acquired weakness in 0% of the combined group versus 100% of controls — a separation so complete it should itself invite caution. In a Brazilian trial (Campos 2022, 139 patients), adding NMES to early mobilisation produced significantly higher Functional Status Score for the ICU at first awakening and at ICU and hospital discharge, fewer days to stand, shorter hospital stay and less ICU-acquired weakness — reported qualitatively in the record's abstract without arm-specific figures. Small samples, strength and function surrogates, and one implausibly perfect result cap the stamp at POSSIBLE. Protocolised early active mobilisation itself (TEAM) is Shelf #1303 and is not re-carded here.

cards.headline: Othman 2024: combined exercise plus NMES gave the highest day-7 strength scores and no ICU-acquired weakness in the combined arm (124 patients, four arms)
cards.summary: Othman 2024: combined exercise plus NMES gave the highest day-7 strength scores and no ICU-acquired weakness in the combined arm (124 patients, four arms)
cards.type: Single-blinded randomised controlled trial, four arms (single centre, Egypt)
cards.people: 124 mechanically ventilated patients in Alexandria, Egypt, randomised to one of four groups: range-of-motion (ROM) exercises (32), NMES (30), combined ROM plus NMES (31), or conventional care (31); ICU-acquired weakness was assessed with the Medical Research Council (MRC) scale over 7 days. The abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix; MeSH records the population as Adult and Middle Aged, male and female.
cards.result: On day 7, MRC scores were 50.37 (SD 2.34) in the ROM+NMES group, 49.77 (SD 2.19) with NMES, 44.97 (SD 3.61) with ROM and 41.10 (SD 3.84) in controls (ANOVA P<.001). ICU-acquired weakness occurred in 0% of the ROM+NMES group, 13% of the NMES group, 60% of the ROM group and 100% of the control group (P<.001). Ventilation duration was shortest in the combined group (12.80 [SD 3.80] days versus 21.80 ROM, 18.73 NMES, 20.70 control), as was ICU stay (17.43 [SD 3.17] days versus 22.53, 21.10 and 21.50).
cards.watchOut: A 0%-versus-100% split in ICU-acquired weakness between adjacent arms of a 124-patient trial is an implausibly perfect result for a condition with multifactorial causes; single-blind assessment of a strength score the assessors could influence, ~30 patients per arm, and no replication at this size mean the figures are carded as printed but weighted lightly.

cards.headline: Campos 2022: adding early NMES to early mobilisation improved functional status scores and shortened hospital stay (139 patients)
cards.summary: Campos 2022: adding early NMES to early mobilisation improved functional status scores and shortened hospital stay (139 patients)
cards.people: 139 consecutive mechanically ventilated patients included within the first 48 hours of ICU admission at the Clinical Hospital of Ribeirão Preto, University of São Paulo, Brazil, randomised to early mobilisation (EM) alone or EM plus NMES (NMES 5 days a week, 60 minutes, from the first 48 hours until ICU discharge). The abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: The EM+NMES group had a significantly higher Functional Status Score for the ICU at the first day awake and at ICU and hospital discharge, took fewer days to stand up, and had a shorter hospital length of stay, a lower frequency of ICU-acquired weakness and better global muscle strength than the EM group. The record's abstract reports these comparisons qualitatively (as significant) without printing arm-specific figures, so no numbers are imported onto this card.
cards.watchOut: A single-centre trial whose abstract gives directions and significance but no effect sizes: the reader cannot tell from the verified record whether the functional gains are large or marginal, and long-term outcomes after discharge were not assessed.

cards.headline: Synthesis: strength and function scores improve; the evidence is small and one result is too perfect — POSSIBLE
cards.summary: Synthesis: strength and function scores improve; the evidence is small and one result is too perfect — POSSIBLE
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Othman 2024 (124 patients, four arms) and Campos 2022 (139 patients) — 263 patients in two single-centre trials.
cards.result: Both trials favour adding NMES to early activity for preserving strength (day-7 MRC 50.37 combined vs 41.10 control in one; higher functional status scores in the other), and neither measures survival, long-term function or quality of life as a primary result. The intervention is cheap and low-risk, which lowers the practical bar — but the evidentiary bar is what this shelf records, and it is POSSIBLE.
cards.watchOut: MRC strength scores and ICU functional scores are assessor-measured surrogates in effectively unblinded care; until a multicentre trial reports patient-centred outcomes, 'preserves muscle' should be read as 'improves measured strength scores in small trials'.

shelves.title: Posaconazole prophylaxis against invasive fungal infection in neutropenia and graft-versus-host disease
shelves.question: In patients with prolonged neutropenia from chemotherapy, or with graft-versus-host disease on immunosuppression, does posaconazole prophylaxis prevent invasive fungal infection, compared with fluconazole or itraconazole?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Antifungal Agents/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Antineoplastic Agents/adverse effects · Female · Fluconazole/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Humans · Itraconazole/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Leukemia, Myeloid, Acute/complications,drug therapy,mortality · Male · Middle Aged · Mycoses/mortality,prevention & control · Myelodysplastic Syndromes/complications,drug therapy,mortality · Neutropenia/chemically induced,drug therapy,mortality · Opportunistic Infections/prevention & control · Single-Blind Method · Treatment Outcome · Triazoles/adverse effects,therapeutic use
shelves.balance: LIKELY — two randomised trials in two high-risk populations agree on the outcome that matters most, invasive aspergillosis. In neutropenic patients (Cornely 2007, 602 patients), proven or probable invasive fungal infections occurred in 2% on posaconazole versus 8% on fluconazole or itraconazole (P<0.001), invasive aspergillosis in 1% versus 7% (P<0.001), and overall survival was significantly longer on posaconazole (P=0.04), with more treatment-related serious adverse events (6% vs 2%). In severe graft-versus-host disease (Ullmann 2007, 600 patients), posaconazole was superior for invasive aspergillosis (2.3% vs 7.0%; P=0.006) and fungal-infection deaths were fewer (1% vs 4%; P=0.046), although the primary all-fungal-infection end point was not significant (5.3% vs 9.0%; P=0.07) and overall mortality was similar — both facts are printed on the card, not smoothed over. The primary outcome in both trials is infection, not a mortality or cardiovascular event, so this shelf is not Tier C; survival figures are printed beside the infection figures wherever the records give them.

cards.headline: Cornely 2007: in neutropenia, posaconazole cut invasive fungal infections (2% vs 8%) and invasive aspergillosis (1% vs 7%), and survival was longer
cards.summary: Cornely 2007: in neutropenia, posaconazole cut invasive fungal infections (2% vs 8%) and invasive aspergillosis (1% vs 7%), and survival was longer
cards.type: Randomised, multicentre trial with evaluators blinded to assignment
cards.people: 602 patients with prolonged neutropenia from chemotherapy for acute myelogenous leukaemia or myelodysplastic syndrome; 304 received posaconazole and 298 received fluconazole (240) or itraconazole (58), with each chemotherapy cycle, for up to 12 weeks. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Proven or probable invasive fungal infections during treatment (the primary end point) occurred in 7 patients (2%) on posaconazole versus 25 (8%) on fluconazole or itraconazole (absolute reduction −6%; 95% CI −9.7 to −2.5; P<0.001), meeting superiority criteria. Invasive aspergillosis occurred in 2 (1%) versus 20 (7%) (P<0.001). Survival was significantly longer with posaconazole (P=0.04). Serious adverse events possibly or probably related to treatment were more frequent with posaconazole (19 patients [6%] vs 6 [2%]; P=0.01); the most common treatment-related events in both groups were gastrointestinal.
cards.watchOut: The comparator is a blend — most control patients received fluconazole, which has no mould activity, so part of the measured advantage is spectrum, not potency against a like-for-like rival. The survival advantage is a secondary end point; it is printed because the record prints it, beside the infection primary.
cards.source: Cornely OA et al. Posaconazole vs. fluconazole or itraconazole prophylaxis in patients with neutropenia. The New England journal of medicine. 2007. PMID: 17251531. cards.headline: Ullmann 2007: in severe GVHD, posaconazole beat fluconazole for aspergillosis (2.3% vs 7.0%) and fungal deaths (1% vs 4%), but the all-infection primary end point was not significant (P=0.07)
cards.summary: Ullmann 2007: in severe GVHD, posaconazole beat fluconazole for aspergillosis (2.3% vs 7.0%) and fungal deaths (1% vs 4%), but the all-infection primary end point was not significant (P=0.07)
cards.people: 600 patients with graft-versus-host disease receiving immunosuppressive therapy after allogeneic stem-cell transplantation; 301 received oral posaconazole and 299 oral fluconazole, with a fixed treatment period of 112 days. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: At day 112, proven or probable invasive fungal infections (the primary end point) occurred in 5.3% on posaconazole versus 9.0% on fluconazole (odds ratio 0.56 relative; 95% CI 0.30 to 1.07; P=0.07) — not significant. Posaconazole was superior for proven or probable invasive aspergillosis (2.3% vs 7.0%; odds ratio 0.31 relative; P=0.006), and during the exposure period breakthrough infections were fewer (2.4% vs 7.6%; P=0.004). Overall mortality was similar between groups, but deaths from invasive fungal infections were fewer with posaconazole (1% vs 4%; P=0.046). Treatment-related adverse events were similar (36% vs 38%).
cards.watchOut: This card is the honest counterweight on the shelf: the GVHD trial's primary end point missed. The shelf's LIKELY stamp rests on the aspergillosis result agreeing across both trials and on Cornely's primary-endpoint win — not on pretending Ullmann's primary succeeded.

shelves.title: Empiric micafungin in ICU patients at risk of invasive candidiasis (EMPIRICUS)
shelves.question: In non-neutropenic ICU patients with ICU-acquired sepsis, multiple Candida colonisation, and multiorgan failure, does empiric micafungin improve survival free of invasive fungal infection at day 28, compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Anti-Bacterial Agents · Antifungal Agents · Candidiasis · Candidiasis, Invasive · Critical Illness · Cross Infection · Disease-Free Survival · Double-Blind Method · Drug Administration Schedule · Echinocandins · Female · Humans · Lipopeptides · Male · Micafungin · Middle Aged · Multiple Organ Failure · Time Factors
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: the primary outcome is survival free of invasive fungal infection, so death is inside the primary composite). One trial (EMPIRICUS, 260 patients in 19 French ICUs): day-28 invasive-fungal-infection-free survival was 68% on micafungin versus 60.2% on placebo (hazard ratio 1.35 relative; 95% CI 0.87 to 2.08) — not significant, with a confidence interval that cannot exclude a moderate benefit in either the high-beta-D-glucan or high-SOFA subgroups either. New proven fungal infections were fewer on micafungin (3% vs 12%; P=0.008), a secondary end point: empiric treatment prevented some infections without measurably improving the survival composite it was powered on. A single trial with a wide interval earns POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference), not a closed verdict.

cards.headline: EMPIRICUS 2016: empiric micafungin did not significantly improve day-28 fungal-infection-free survival (68% vs 60.2%; HR 1.35, 95% CI 0.87 to 2.08)
cards.summary: EMPIRICUS 2016: empiric micafungin did not significantly improve day-28 fungal-infection-free survival (68% vs 60.2%; HR 1.35, 95% CI 0.87 to 2.08)
cards.people: 260 non-neutropenic, non-transplanted critically ill adults with ICU-acquired sepsis, Candida colonisation at multiple sites, multiple organ failure, and exposure to broad-spectrum antibacterial agents, in 19 French ICUs (mean age 63 years; 35% women); 131 received micafungin 100 mg daily for 14 days and 129 placebo; 251 were in the modified intention-to-treat analysis. Median SOFA score was 8 and median colonised sites 3.
cards.result: The primary end point — survival without proven invasive fungal infection at day 28 — was reached by 82 patients (68%) on micafungin versus 79 (60.2%) on placebo (hazard ratio 1.35 relative; 95% CI 0.87 to 2.08), not significant. Results were similar in patients with (1-3)-beta-D-glucan above 80 pg/mL (HR 1.41; 95% CI 0.85 to 2.33) and in those with SOFA score above 8 (HR 1.69; 95% CI 0.96 to 2.94). New proven invasive fungal infections were less frequent on micafungin (4 of 128 [3%] vs 15 of 123 [12%]; P=0.008). The authors concluded that empiric micafungin did not increase fungal-infection-free survival.
cards.watchOut: The infection reduction without a survival-composite gain is the trial's central tension: either the prevented infections were not the lethal ones, or 260 patients cannot resolve a survival effect of this size. The subgroup hazard ratios above 1.35 with intervals crossing 1 should not be read as near-proof of benefit — they are the same data sliced thinner.
cards.source: Timsit JF et al. cards.headline: Synthesis: empiric antifungal therapy prevented infections but not the survival composite — POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference)
cards.summary: Synthesis: empiric antifungal therapy prevented infections but not the survival composite — POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference)
cards.people: Synthesis of the card above: EMPIRICUS (Timsit et al., JAMA 2016), 260 patients.
cards.result: EMPIRICUS is the randomised answer to a common ICU reflex — colonisation plus sepsis plus organ failure equals treat for Candida now. shelves.title: Inhaled amikacin to prevent ventilator-associated pneumonia (AMIKINHAL)
shelves.question: In mechanically ventilated adults, does a 3-day course of inhaled amikacin (20 mg per kilogram of ideal body weight once daily) reduce the incidence of ventilator-associated pneumonia, compared with inhaled placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Humans · Amikacin · Double-Blind Method · Pneumonia, Ventilator-Associated · Respiration, Artificial · Treatment Outcome · Administration, Inhalation · Anti-Bacterial Agents · Critical Illness
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — one pivotal trial. In AMIKINHAL (847 analysed patients ventilated for at least 72 hours), a first episode of ventilator-associated pneumonia within 28 days occurred in 15% on inhaled amikacin versus 22% on placebo (difference in restricted mean survival time to VAP 1.5 days; 95% CI 0.6 to 2.5; P=0.004), and infection-related ventilator-associated complications were fewer (18% vs 26%; hazard ratio 0.66 relative). Trial-related serious adverse effects were uncommon in both groups (1.7% vs 0.9%). Note for the developer: the drafting question specified '300 mg daily' — the record's dose is 20 mg per kilogram of ideal body weight once daily for 3 days, and the shelf's question and card follow the record. The outcome is pneumonia incidence, a process outcome the developer's evidence bar ranks below hard outcomes, and there is no mortality claim: POSSIBLE, on a single trial.

cards.people: 850 critically ill adults who had undergone invasive mechanical ventilation for at least 72 hours were randomised; 847 were analysed (417 inhaled amikacin, 430 placebo). Amikacin was dosed at 20 mg per kilogram of ideal body weight once daily for 3 days — not the 300 mg stated in this shelf's drafting note; the record governs. All three nebulisations were received by 81% (amikacin) and 83% (placebo). The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.

An infection-related ventilator-associated complication occurred in 74 (18%) versus 111 (26%) (hazard ratio 0.66 relative; 95% CI 0.50 to 0.89). Trial-related serious adverse effects occurred in 7 patients (1.7%) versus 4 (0.9%).
cards.watchOut: VAP is a diagnosis with notoriously soft edges even under blinded adjudication, and a 1.5-day restricted-mean difference is a modest absolute prize; the trial shows prevention of a complication, not of death or of ventilator days saved at a stated size. shelves.title: Valganciclovir 200 versus 100 days for CMV prophylaxis in high-risk kidney transplant (IMPACT)
shelves.question: In donor-positive/recipient-negative kidney transplant recipients, does extending valganciclovir prophylaxis from 100 to 200 days reduce cytomegalovirus disease?
shelves.mesh: Antiviral Agents · Biopsy · Cytomegalovirus · Cytomegalovirus Infections · Double-Blind Method · Female · Ganciclovir · Humans · Incidence · Kidney · Kidney Transplantation · Male · Middle Aged · Risk Factors · Safety · Valganciclovir · Viremia
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — one pivotal trial. In IMPACT (326 high-risk donor-positive/recipient-negative kidney recipients), confirmed CMV disease through month 12 after transplant occurred in 16.1% with 200 days of valganciclovir versus 36.8% with 100 days (P<0.0001) — a number needed to treat of about 5 — and confirmed viraemia was also lower (37.4% vs 50.9%; P=0.015). Note for the developer: the drafting note says the disease figures are 'at 2 years' — the record reports them through month 12 post-transplant, and the card follows the record. A single trial, however clean, earns POSSIBLE. (Letermovir prophylaxis and maribavir rescue are homed on Shelf #722; this shelf is the valganciclovir-duration question only.)

cards.result: Confirmed CMV disease up to month 12 post-transplant developed in significantly fewer patients in the 200-day group than the 100-day group (16.1% vs 36.8%; P<0.0001). Confirmed CMV viraemia was also lower (37.4% vs 50.9%; P=0.015 at month 12). Biopsy-proven acute rejection did not differ significantly (11% vs 17%; P=0.114). Adverse events occurred at similar rates in the two groups and were mostly mild to moderate and not attributed to the study drug. shelves.title: Gepotidacin for uncomplicated urogenital gonorrhoea (EAGLE-1)
shelves.question: In adolescents and adults with uncomplicated urogenital gonorrhoea, is oral gepotidacin non-inferior to ceftriaxone plus azithromycin for microbiological cure?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Male · Female · Gonorrhea · Adult · Anti-Bacterial Agents · Administration, Oral · Acenaphthenes · Adolescent · Middle Aged · Young Adult · Azithromycin · Heterocyclic Compounds, 3-Ring · Ceftriaxone · Treatment Outcome · Neisseria gonorrhoeae · Injections, Intramuscular · Drug Therapy, Combination
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — one pivotal trial, a noninferiority design. In EAGLE-1 (628 randomised; 406 in the microbiological intention-to-treat population), microbiological success at test-of-cure (days 4–8) was 92.6% on gepotidacin (two 3000 mg oral doses 10–12 hours apart) versus 91.2% on intramuscular ceftriaxone plus oral azithromycin (adjusted difference −0.1%; 95% CI −5.6 to 5.5), inside the prespecified −10% noninferiority margin. No bacterial persistence was observed in either group. Gepotidacin caused more adverse events, mainly gastrointestinal, almost all mild or moderate, with no treatment-related severe or serious events in either group. The primary population was restricted to participants with ceftriaxone-susceptible isolates at baseline — so the trial shows gepotidacin matches standard therapy where standard therapy works; it does not test the ceftriaxone-resistant scenario that motivates new gonorrhoea drugs. (Gepotidacin for urinary tract infection is homed on Shelf #1083; this shelf is gonorrhoea only.)

cards.headline: EAGLE-1 2025: gepotidacin was non-inferior to ceftriaxone plus azithromycin (microbiological success 92.6% vs 91.2%; difference −0.1%)
cards.summary: EAGLE-1 2025: gepotidacin was non-inferior to ceftriaxone plus azithromycin (microbiological success 92.6% vs 91.2%; difference −0.1%)
cards.type: Phase 3, open-label, sponsor-blinded, multicentre non-inferiority trial
cards.people: 628 participants aged 12 years and older (body weight over 45 kg) with suspected uncomplicated urogenital gonorrhoea or a positive test for Neisseria gonorrhoeae, randomised 1:1 to gepotidacin or ceftriaxone plus azithromycin; 39 (6%) discontinued prematurely, mostly lost to follow-up. The primary microbiological intention-to-treat population comprised 406 participants (202 gepotidacin, 204 comparator) with confirmed ceftriaxone-susceptible N. gonorrhoeae at baseline; 92% were male and 71% were men who have sex with men.
cards.result: Microbiological success (culture-confirmed eradication of N. gonorrhoeae from the urogenital site at test-of-cure, days 4–8) was 92.6% (187 of 202; 95% CI 88.0 to 95.8) on gepotidacin versus 91.2% (186 of 204; 95% CI 86.4 to 94.7) on ceftriaxone plus azithromycin (adjusted treatment difference −0.1%; 95% CI −5.6 to 5.5), meeting the prespecified −10% noninferiority margin. No bacterial persistence was observed in either group. Gepotidacin had higher rates of adverse events and drug-related adverse events, mainly gastrointestinal and almost all mild or moderate; no treatment-related severe or serious adverse events occurred in either group.
cards.watchOut: Two structural caveats. First, the primary analysis covers 406 of 628 randomised participants — those with confirmed susceptible isolates and a test-of-cure culture — so the estimate applies to that subset. Second, enrolling only ceftriaxone-susceptible infections means the trial cannot speak to the resistant infections for which an oral alternative is most needed; extragenital (pharyngeal, rectal) efficacy is likewise outside this record.

shelves.title: Dalbavancin step-down for complicated Staphylococcus aureus bacteraemia (DOTS)
shelves.question: In patients with complicated Staphylococcus aureus bacteraemia who have cleared blood cultures, is a two-dose dalbavancin course non-inferior to standard intravenous therapy on a desirability-of-outcome ranking at day 70?
shelves.mesh: No MeSH terms in the record
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: the desirability-of-outcome ranking includes mortality as a component). One trial (DOTS, 200 randomised patients with complicated S. aureus bacteraemia who had cleared cultures after 72 hours to 10 days of initial therapy). The drafting note says dalbavancin 'met non-inferiority'; the record requires a more careful statement, and the card follows the record: the trial's PRIMARY analysis — superiority on the day-70 desirability-of-outcome ranking (clinical success, infectious complications, safety complications, mortality, quality of life) — was NOT met (probability of a more desirable outcome with dalbavancin 47.7%; 95% CI 39.8% to 55.7%, which does not exceed the 50% superiority threshold). A SECONDARY end point, clinical efficacy at day 70, was nearly identical (73 of 100 vs 72 of 100; difference 1.0%; 95% CI −11.5 to 13.5) and met a prespecified noninferiority criterion with a wide 20% margin. Serious adverse events were 40 versus 34. Patients with CNS infection, retained infected prosthetic material, left-sided endocarditis, or severe immune compromise were excluded — the result does not reach those groups. Equal point estimates for efficacy, a failed primary superiority analysis, and a generous noninferiority margin on a secondary end point: POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: DOTS 2025: dalbavancin's primary DOOR superiority analysis was not met (47.7%; 95% CI 39.8 to 55.7); secondary clinical efficacy was equal (73% vs 72%) within a wide 20% noninferiority margin
cards.summary: DOTS 2025: dalbavancin's primary DOOR superiority analysis was not met (47.7%; 95% CI 39.8 to 55.7); secondary clinical efficacy was equal (73% vs 72%) within a wide 20% noninferiority margin
cards.people: 200 hospitalised adults with complicated S. aureus bacteraemia who had achieved blood-culture clearance after at least 72 hours and no more than 10 days of initial antibacterial therapy, at 23 centres in the US and Canada (mean age 56 years; 31% women); 100 received dalbavancin 1500 mg on days 1 and 8, and 100 received 4 to 8 weeks of standard intravenous therapy (cefazolin or an antistaphylococcal penicillin if susceptible; vancomycin or daptomycin if resistant). Excluded: central nervous system infection, retained infected prosthetic material, left-sided endocarditis, and severe immune compromise. Follow-up was 70 days (180 days for osteomyelitis); 167 participants (84%) survived to day 70 with an efficacy assessment, and those without one were counted as clinical failures.
cards.result: The primary outcome — the desirability of outcome ranking (DOOR) at day 70, combining clinical success, infectious complications, safety complications, mortality, and health-related quality of life — gave a probability of a more desirable outcome with dalbavancin versus standard therapy of 47.7% (95% CI 39.8% to 55.7%), which did not achieve the prespecified superiority criterion (confidence interval above 50%). The secondary outcome of clinical efficacy at day 70 was 73 of 100 on dalbavancin versus 72 of 100 on standard therapy (difference 1.0%; 95% CI −11.5% to 13.5%), meeting the prespecified noninferiority criterion (margin 20%). Serious adverse events were reported in 40 of 100 (dalbavancin) and 34 of 100 (standard therapy); treatment-related adverse events were uncommon in both groups. The authors concluded dalbavancin was not superior by DOOR.
cards.watchOut: The drafting note's 'met non-inferiority' headline skips the failed primary analysis; both are carded, primary first, as the gate requires. A 20% noninferiority margin on the secondary end point is wide — the data exclude inferiority beyond that margin, not a clinically meaningful gap. The excluded groups (endocarditis, retained prostheses, CNS infection) are exactly where long-acting therapy would be most tempting and least tested.
