shelves.title: Fexinidazole for late-stage gambiense sleeping sickness (Mesu)
shelves.question: In patients aged 15 and older with late-stage Trypanosoma brucei gambiense infection, is oral fexinidazole non-inferior to nifurtimox–eflornithine combination therapy for treatment success at 18 months?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Adult · Democratic Republic of the Congo · Drug Administration Schedule · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Nifurtimox · Nitroimidazoles · Treatment Outcome · Trypanocidal Agents · Trypanosoma brucei gambiense · Trypanosomiasis, African
shelves.balance: PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C). Tier C deviation, disclosed: the topic file flags this shelf not Tier C, but the trial's primary success endpoint is a composite whose first component is being alive at 18 months, so it is ruled Tier C at build under the gate rule; no mortality claim is made or supported — deaths were 3% on fexinidazole versus 2% on NECT and the trial was not powered for mortality. On the record: in the single pivotal randomised non-inferiority trial (394 patients, DRC and Central African Republic), success at 18 months was 91% (239 of 264) on fexinidazole versus 98% (124 of 130) on NECT — a difference of −6.4% (97.06% CI −11.2 to −1.6), inside the prespecified 13% margin, so non-inferiority was met on the trial's own terms while the point estimate favours NECT. Treatment-related adverse events were similar (81% versus 79%). This shelf rests on one pivotal trial and is flagged as a two-trial-gate exception candidate: it should be withdrawn or re-scoped if the developer rejects the exception. PROPOSED stamp: POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: Mesu 2018: fexinidazole met non-inferiority for 18-month success (91% vs 98%) against a wide 13% margin
cards.summary: Mesu 2018: fexinidazole met non-inferiority for 18-month success (91% vs 98%) against a wide 13% margin
cards.type: Randomised, open-label, phase 2/3 non-inferiority trial (single pivotal trial)
cards.people: 394 patients aged 15 years and older with late-stage gambiense human African trypanosomiasis at treatment centres in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (9) and the Central African Republic (1), randomised 2:1 to oral fexinidazole (264; 1800 mg daily on days 1–4, then 1200 mg daily on days 5–10) or nifurtimox–eflornithine combination therapy (130). The abstract does not print a mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Success at 18 months — alive, no trypanosomes in any body fluid, no rescue medication, and cerebrospinal fluid white-cell count ≤20 cells/µL — was recorded in 239 of 264 patients (91%) on fexinidazole versus 124 of 130 (98%) on NECT: difference −6.4% (97.06% CI −11.2 to −1.6; P=0.0029), within the prespecified acceptable margin of 13%. Treatment-related adverse events occurred in 81% versus 79%. Eleven patients died (9 [3%] on fexinidazole versus 2 [2%] on NECT).
cards.watchOut: Non-inferiority against a 13% margin is a permissive standard: the confidence interval is compatible with fexinidazole being up to about 11 percentage points worse than NECT, and the point estimate favours the intravenous-containing regimen. shelves.title: Single-dose acoziborole for gambiense sleeping sickness (Betu Kumeso)
shelves.question: In adults and adolescents with gambiense human African trypanosomiasis, what treatment success does a single oral dose of acoziborole achieve at 18 months, judged against historical standard-of-care rates (no concurrent control)?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Animals · Female · Humans · Male · Antiprotozoal Agents · Drug Therapy, Combination · Eflornithine · Nifurtimox · Prospective Studies · Trypanosoma brucei gambiense · Trypanosomiasis, African
shelves.balance: In the single pivotal study — a multicentre, open-label, SINGLE-ARM phase 2/3 trial with no concurrent control group — a single 960 mg dose of acoziborole gave an 18-month treatment success rate of 95.2% (159 of 167) in late-stage gambiense disease (98.1%, 159 of 162, in the evaluable population), and all 41 early/intermediate-stage patients completed follow-up; a post-hoc comparison put this beside a historical NECT success estimate of 94%. Four deaths occurred, none judged treatment-related; drug-related adverse events occurred in 14% and were mild or moderate. A single-arm study cannot separate the drug's effect from case mix and secular change, so the record earns no more than MAYBE (weak evidence). This shelf is flagged as a two-trial-gate exception candidate — indeed a no-randomised-trial candidate, the field being ethically constrained — and should be withdrawn or re-scoped if the developer rejects the exception.

cards.headline: Betu Kumeso 2023: single-dose acoziborole, 95.2% success at 18 months in late-stage disease — single-arm, no concurrent control
cards.summary: Betu Kumeso 2023: single-dose acoziborole, 95.2% success at 18 months in late-stage disease — single-arm, no concurrent control
cards.type: Multicentre, open-label, single-arm phase 2/3 trial (no randomised comparator)
cards.people: 208 patients aged 15 years and older with confirmed gambiense HAT enrolled at ten hospitals in the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Guinea (167 late-stage; 41 early-stage or intermediate-stage); mean age 34.0 years (SD 12.4); 117 (56%) men and 91 (44%) women. cards.result: Treatment success at 18 months (modified WHO criteria, modified intention-to-treat) was 95.2% (95% CI 91.2–97.7; 159 of 167) in late-stage patients and 98.1% (95.1–99.5; 159 of 162) in the evaluable population. cards.watchOut: There is no randomised or concurrent control: the 94% NECT figure is a historical estimate assembled post hoc, and differences in staging, follow-up intensity, and case mix between this cohort and historical series are unmeasured. shelves.title: Wolbachia mosquito deployments to control dengue: the AWED trial (Yogyakarta)
shelves.question: In a dengue-endemic city, does releasing wMel Wolbachia-infected Aedes aegypti mosquitoes reduce the incidence of virologically confirmed dengue in residents versus no deployment?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aedes · Animals · Child · Child, Preschool · Communicable Disease Control · Dengue · Dengue Virus · Female · Humans · Incidence · Indonesia · Male · Middle Aged · Mosquito Vectors · Wolbachia · Young Adult
shelves.balance: In the single cluster-randomised trial (24 geographic clusters in Yogyakarta, Indonesia; 8,144 febrile patients assessed by a test-negative design), virologically confirmed dengue occurred in 2.3% of participants in intervention clusters versus 9.4% in control clusters — a protective efficacy of 77.1% (95% CI 65.3–84.9), similar across all four serotypes — and hospitalisation for dengue was reduced by a protective efficacy of 86.2% (0.4% versus 3.0%). The effect is large, precise, and measured on clinical disease rather than a surrogate. The bounds are scope, not signal: one city, one Wolbachia strain (wMel), and one trial — this shelf is adjacent to but distinct from the dengue vaccine shelves (#448, #981), which ask about immunisation, not vector deployment. PROPOSED stamp: LIKELY.

cards.headline: AWED 2021: Wolbachia deployments cut virologically confirmed dengue by 77% and dengue hospitalisation by 86%
cards.summary: AWED 2021: Wolbachia deployments cut virologically confirmed dengue by 77% and dengue hospitalisation by 86%
cards.type: Cluster-randomised controlled trial with test-negative design (single city)
cards.people: 24 geographic clusters in Yogyakarta, Indonesia, randomised 12 to releases of wMel-infected Aedes aegypti and 12 to no deployment; 8,144 patients aged 3–45 years presenting to primary-care clinics with acute undifferentiated fever were enrolled for the test-negative efficacy assessment (3,721 in intervention clusters, 4,423 in control clusters). All clusters continued usual local mosquito control. The abstract does not print a sex mix for the enrolled patients.
cards.result: Virologically confirmed dengue occurred in 67 of 2,905 participants (2.3%) in intervention clusters versus 318 of 3,401 (9.4%) in control clusters (aggregate odds ratio 0.23, 95% CI 0.15–0.35; P=0.004), giving a protective efficacy of 77.1% (95% CI 65.3–84.9), similar against the four dengue serotypes. Hospitalisation for virologically confirmed dengue occurred in 13 of 2,905 (0.4%) versus 102 of 3,401 (3.0%) — protective efficacy 86.2% (95% CI 66.2–94.3).
cards.watchOut: One city and one Wolbachia strain: durability of introgression, spread beyond release areas, and performance in different transmission settings are not answered by this trial. Efficacy was estimated in clinic-attending febrile patients by a test-negative design, not by population-wide incidence surveillance.

shelves.title: Ebola virus disease therapeutics: the PALM trial (REGN-EB3 and mAb114)
shelves.question: In patients with Ebola virus disease, do the monoclonal antibody therapies REGN-EB3 or mAb114 reduce 28-day mortality compared with ZMapp or remdesivir?
shelves.mesh: Adenosine Monophosphate · Adolescent · Adult · Alanine · Antibodies, Monoclonal · Antiviral Agents · Child · Child, Preschool · Democratic Republic of the Congo · Disease Outbreaks · Ebolavirus · Female · Hemorrhagic Fever, Ebola · Humans · Infant · Infant, Newborn · Infusions, Intravenous · Male · RNA, Viral · Ribonucleotides · Single-Blind Method · Young Adult
shelves.balance: PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C) — mortality is the primary endpoint. In the single randomised trial conducted during the 2018–20 Democratic Republic of the Congo outbreak (681 patients), 28-day mortality was 33.5% with REGN-EB3 versus 51.3% in the contemporaneous ZMapp subgroup (P=0.002) and 35.1% with mAb114 versus 49.7% with ZMapp (P=0.007); the data and safety monitoring board stopped assignment to ZMapp and remdesivir early on the strength of an interim analysis. The abstract does not print a mortality figure for the remdesivir arm, so none is carded — comparisons against remdesivir rest on the trial's interim decision, not on a printed number here. Two independent monoclonal products beating the same control in one trial is mutually reinforcing, but it remains one trial from one outbreak. PROPOSED stamp: LIKELY.

cards.headline: PALM 2019: REGN-EB3 and mAb114 each cut Ebola mortality by roughly a third versus ZMapp
cards.summary: PALM 2019: REGN-EB3 and mAb114 each cut Ebola mortality by roughly a third versus ZMapp
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (four arms; stopped in part early on interim superiority)
cards.people: 681 patients of any age with RT-PCR-confirmed Ebola virus disease in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, enrolled November 2018 to August 2019, all receiving standard care and randomised 1:1:1:1 to ZMapp (control), remdesivir, mAb114, or REGN-EB3 (the REGN-EB3 arm was added in a later protocol version, so its comparison uses the ZMapp subgroup enrolled from that time). The abstract does not print an age or sex breakdown.
cards.result: Death at 28 days occurred in 52 of 155 patients (33.5%) on REGN-EB3 versus 79 of 154 (51.3%) in the contemporaneous ZMapp subgroup (P=0.002), and in 61 of 174 (35.1%) on mAb114 versus 84 of 169 (49.7%) on ZMapp (P=0.007). The data and safety monitoring board recommended in August 2019 that patients thereafter be assigned only to mAb114 or REGN-EB3, on an interim analysis showing superiority of both over ZMapp and remdesivir. Shorter symptom duration before admission and lower baseline viral load, creatinine, and aminotransferase levels each correlated with better survival. Four serious adverse events were judged potentially related to the trial drugs.
cards.watchOut: The abstract prints no mortality figure for the remdesivir arm — the topic file's 53.1% for remdesivir does not appear in this record and is not carded. Early stopping on an interim analysis can exaggerate effect sizes, and the REGN-EB3 comparison is against the later-enrolled ZMapp subgroup rather than the full ZMapp arm; both caveats are printed on the record itself.

shelves.title: Fully oral rifampicin–clarithromycin for limited Buruli ulcer (Phillips)
shelves.question: In limited Buruli ulcer (single lesion ≤10 cm), is eight weeks of oral rifampicin plus extended-release clarithromycin non-inferior to rifampicin plus intramuscular streptomycin for lesion healing without recurrence at 52 weeks?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Adolescent · Adult · Anti-Bacterial Agents · Benin · Buruli Ulcer · Child · Clarithromycin · Delayed-Action Preparations · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · Ghana · Humans · Male · Rifampin · Streptomycin · Wound Healing · Young Adult
shelves.balance: In the single pivotal phase 3 trial (310 recruited in Ghana and Benin; 297 with PCR-confirmed disease analysed), lesions healed without recurrence in 96% (140 of 146) on the fully oral rifampicin–clarithromycin regimen versus 95% (144 of 151) on rifampicin–streptomycin — a difference of −0.5 percentage points (95% CI −5.2 to 4.2), comfortably inside the 12% non-inferiority margin — with fewer treatment-related adverse events on the oral regimen (7% versus 13%) and the one serious ototoxicity case in the streptomycin arm. Healing rates are near-identical and the interval is narrow; the limits are a single trial, an open-label design, and a population of early, limited lesions only. PROPOSED stamp: POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: Phillips 2020: fully oral therapy healed 96% versus 95% — non-inferior, with fewer adverse events
cards.summary: Phillips 2020: fully oral therapy healed 96% versus 95% — non-inferior, with fewer adverse events
cards.type: Randomised, open-label, phase 3 non-inferiority trial (single pivotal trial)
cards.people: 310 participants aged 5 years and older with a single early, limited Buruli ulcer lesion (categories I–II, ≤10 cm) at four hospitals in Ghana and one in Benin; median age 14 years (IQR 10–29); 153 (52%) female as printed. The analysis population was the 297 with PCR-confirmed disease: 151 assigned to rifampicin plus intramuscular streptomycin (RS8) and 146 to oral rifampicin plus extended-release clarithromycin (RC8), each for 8 weeks.
cards.result: Lesion healing (full epithelialisation or stable scar) without recurrence at 52 weeks occurred in 140 of 146 patients (96%; 95% CI 91–99) on RC8 versus 144 of 151 (95%; 91–98) on RS8: difference −0.5% (95% CI −5.2 to 4.2; P=0.59), demonstrating non-inferiority against the 12% margin. Treatment-related adverse events were recorded in 9 (7%) on RC8 versus 20 (13%) on RS8; one RS8 patient developed serious ototoxicity and stopped treatment at 6 weeks. No patient needed surgical resection; four patients (two per group) had skin grafts.
cards.watchOut: Recruitment stopped at 310 of a planned 332, and neither patients nor the clinicians measuring lesions were masked. The trial covers only early, limited lesions — extensive, multiple, or osteomyelitis-complicated disease is outside the evidence.

shelves.title: Melioidosis eradication therapy: TMP-SMX alone versus TMP-SMX plus doxycycline (MERTH)
shelves.question: In melioidosis after intensive-phase therapy, is trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole alone non-inferior to TMP-SMX plus doxycycline for preventing culture-confirmed relapse?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Adult · Anti-Bacterial Agents · Double-Blind Method · Doxycycline · Female · Humans · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Male · Melioidosis · Middle Aged · Recurrence · Thailand · Treatment Outcome · Trimethoprim, Sulfamethoxazole Drug Combination
shelves.balance: In the single pivotal trial (626 patients, northeast Thailand; double-blind), culture-confirmed recurrent melioidosis occurred in 5% (16 of 311) on TMP-SMX plus placebo versus 7% (21 of 315) on TMP-SMX plus doxycycline — hazard ratio 0.81 relative (95% CI 0.42–1.55) — meeting the prespecified non-inferiority criterion (margin HR 1.7; P=0.01 for non-inferiority), with fewer adverse drug reactions on monotherapy (39% versus 53%). The confidence interval is wide in relative terms, but the absolute recurrence rates are low and close, and the simpler regimen is the safer one. Single-country programme evidence. PROPOSED stamp: POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: MERTH 2014: dropping doxycycline was non-inferior (relapse 5% vs 7%) and better tolerated
cards.summary: MERTH 2014: dropping doxycycline was non-inferior (relapse 5% vs 7%) and better tolerated
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, non-inferiority trial (single pivotal trial)
cards.people: 626 patients aged 15 years and older with culture-confirmed melioidosis at five centres in northeast Thailand, all after a course of parenteral intensive-phase therapy, randomised to 20 weeks of TMP-SMX plus placebo (311) or TMP-SMX plus doxycycline (315). The abstract does not print a mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Culture-confirmed recurrent melioidosis occurred in 16 of 311 patients (5%) on TMP-SMX alone versus 21 of 315 (7%) on the combination: hazard ratio 0.81 relative (95% CI 0.42–1.55), meeting the non-inferiority criterion against the prespecified margin of HR 1.7 (P=0.01). Adverse drug reactions were less common on monotherapy: 122 (39%) versus 167 (53%).
cards.watchOut: The non-inferiority margin (HR 1.7) was generous, and the relative-effect interval (0.42–1.55) is wide; the reassurance comes from the low, close absolute rates. shelves.title: Magnesium sulphate for severe tetanus (Thwaites)
shelves.question: In adults with severe tetanus, does a magnesium sulphate infusion reduce the need for mechanical ventilation versus standard spasm control?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Anticonvulsants · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Hypnotics and Sedatives · Infusions, Intravenous · Magnesium Sulfate · Male · Midazolam · Middle Aged · Respiration, Artificial · Severity of Illness Index · Tetanus · Tracheostomy · Vietnam
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the trial answers its primary question in the negative and its secondary questions positively, and the cards do not average them. In the single pivotal trial (Vietnam; double-blind), magnesium did not reduce the requirement for mechanical ventilation (odds ratio 0.71 relative, 95% CI 0.36–1.40; P=0.324), and survival was much the same in the two groups (no figures printed). What magnesium did do was reduce the need for other drugs: less midazolam and pipecuronium to control spasms (P=0.026 and P=0.005) and substantially less verapamil for cardiovascular instability (patients on magnesium were 4.7 times less likely to require it; 95% CI 1.4–15.9). One internal inconsistency is flagged on the card, not repaired: the abstract describes a trial of 256 patients but prints arm sizes of 97 and 98 (195 in total). PROPOSED stamp: SPLIT as above.

cards.headline: Thwaites 2006: magnesium did not reduce ventilation (OR 0.71; P=0.32) but cut spasm-drug and verapamil requirements
cards.summary: Thwaites 2006: magnesium did not reduce ventilation (OR 0.71; P=0.32) but cut spasm-drug and verapamil requirements
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (single pivotal trial)
cards.people: Patients over 15 years of age with severe tetanus at the Hospital for Tropical Medicine, Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam, randomised to a 7-day intravenous magnesium sulphate infusion or placebo. The abstract describes 256 patients in the trial but prints arm sizes of 97 (magnesium) and 98 (placebo) — 195 in total; the discrepancy is in the record and is flagged in the watch-out, not reconciled here. No patients were lost to follow-up. The abstract does not print a mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Requirement for mechanical ventilation did not differ: odds ratio 0.71 relative (95% CI 0.36–1.40; P=0.324), and survival was much the same in the two groups (the abstract prints no survival figures). Magnesium patients required significantly less midazolam (medians as printed, placebo versus magnesium: 7.1 versus 1.4 mg/kg per day; P=0.026) and less pipecuronium (2.3 versus 0.0 mg/kg per day; P=0.005) for spasm control, and were 4.7 (95% CI 1.4–15.9) times less likely to require verapamil for cardiovascular instability. Adverse-event incidence did not differ.
cards.watchOut: Two record awkwardnesses are carded as printed: the 256-versus-195 patient-count inconsistency, and the midazolam/pipecuronium medians, which the abstract prints in placebo-versus-magnesium order inside a sentence framed the other way round — the direction (magnesium lower) is fixed by the text, the figures are as printed. The trial's setting — a specialist tropical diseases hospital — bounds generalisation, and the drug-sparing outcomes are secondary endpoints.

shelves.title: Single-dose liposomal amphotericin B for visceral leishmaniasis in India (Sundar)
shelves.question: In visceral leishmaniasis in Bihar, India, is a single 10 mg/kg infusion of liposomal amphotericin B non-inferior to conventional amphotericin B deoxycholate given on alternate days for 30 days?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Amphotericin B · Antiprotozoal Agents · Child · Child, Preschool · Deoxycholic Acid · Drug Combinations · Female · Humans · India · Infusions, Intravenous · Intention to Treat Analysis · Leishmaniasis, Visceral · Male · Middle Aged · Young Adult · Creatinine · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Drug Administration Schedule · Drug Therapy, Combination · Hemoglobins · Liver · Liver Function Tests · Paromomycin · Phosphorylcholine · Recurrence
shelves.balance: Two randomised trials from the same Bihar programme agree. In the anchor trial (412 patients), cure at 6 months was 95.7% after a single 10 mg/kg liposomal amphotericin B infusion versus 96.3% with 15 alternate-day deoxycholate infusions — non-inferior, with less fever/rigor (40% versus 64%) and less anaemia (2% versus 19%). In the second trial (634 patients), three short-course combinations built on the single-dose liposomal platform (with 7 days of miltefosine, with paromomycin, or miltefosine plus paromomycin) were each non-inferior to standard amphotericin B, with cure rates of 97.5–98.7% versus 93.0% and fewer adverse events. The evidence is geographically narrow — Bihar's anthroponotic transmission — and East African disease may behave differently; within its setting it is consistent and precise. PROPOSED stamp: LIKELY.

cards.headline: Sundar 2010: one infusion cured 95.7% versus 96.3% for 15 infusions — non-inferior and gentler
cards.summary: Sundar 2010: one infusion cured 95.7% versus 96.3% for 15 infusions — non-inferior and gentler
cards.people: 412 patients with visceral leishmaniasis in Bihar, India, randomised 3:1 to a single infusion of liposomal amphotericin B 10 mg/kg (304 analysed) or amphotericin B deoxycholate 1 mg/kg on alternate days for 29 days (108 analysed). The abstract does not print an age or sex breakdown.
cards.result: Apparent cure at day 30 was 100% (304 of 304) in the liposomal group versus 98% (106 of 108) in the conventional group. Cure at 6 months was 95.7% (95% CI 93.4–97.9) versus 96.3% (92.6–99.9) — not inferior. Infusion-related fever or rigors occurred in 40% versus 64%; increased anaemia or thrombocytopenia in 2% of the liposomal group, versus increased anaemia in 19% and hypokalaemia in 2% of the conventional group; nephrotoxicity or hepatotoxicity occurred in no more than 1% in either group.
cards.watchOut: Open-label, and the 3:1 allocation leaves the conventional arm small (108 patients), so the non-inferiority judgement leans on a narrow control experience. The trial was powered and situated for Bihar; relapses beyond 6 months are not captured.

shelves.title: Pyronaridine–artesunate for uncomplicated falciparum malaria (WANECAM and the phase 3 programme)
shelves.question: In patients with repeated episodes of uncomplicated falciparum malaria, is pyronaridine–artesunate as effective and safe over two years of repeated use as artemether–lumefantrine or dihydroartemisinin–piperaquine?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Amodiaquine · Antimalarials · Artemether, Lumefantrine Drug Combination · Artemisinins · Artesunate · Child · Child, Preschool · Drug Combinations · Drug Therapy, Combination · Ethanolamines · Female · Fluorenes · Humans · Longitudinal Studies · Malaria · Male · Naphthyridines · Quinolines · Young Adult · Piperazines · Adult · Africa · Asia · Drug Resistance · Intention to Treat Analysis · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Malaria, Falciparum · Mefloquine · Middle Aged · Proportional Hazards Models
shelves.balance: Two randomised programmes agree. In WANECAM (4,710 participants in Burkina Faso, Guinea, and Mali, treated and retreated over 2 years), the 2-year malaria incidence rate on pyronaridine–artesunate was non-inferior to artemether–lumefantrine and to artesunate–amodiaquine (rate ratios 1.05 and 0.97 relative), and PCR-adjusted cure exceeded 99.5% at day 28 for all regimens; unadjusted cure favoured pyronaridine–artesunate. In the earlier phase 3 trial (1,271 patients, Asia and Africa), pyronaridine–artesunate was non-inferior to mefloquine plus artesunate (per-protocol day-28 cure 99.2% versus 97.8%). The standing caveat in both records is hepatic: transient transaminase elevations were more frequent with pyronaridine–artesunate, and WANECAM excluded patients with baseline ALT above twice the upper limit of normal. Nine deaths occurred in WANECAM, none treatment-related. PROPOSED stamp: LIKELY.

cards.headline: WANECAM 2018: pyronaridine–artesunate non-inferior across two years of repeated treatment (n=4,710)
cards.summary: WANECAM 2018: pyronaridine–artesunate non-inferior across two years of repeated treatment (n=4,710)
cards.type: Randomised, open-label, longitudinal phase 3b/4 trial (repeated episodes)
cards.people: 4,710 adults and children aged 6 months and older with microscopically confirmed malaria at seven centres in Burkina Faso, Guinea, and Mali, assigned to pyronaridine–artesunate (1,342), artemether–lumefantrine (967), artesunate–amodiaquine (1,061), or dihydroartemisinin–piperaquine (1,340), and retreated with the assigned strategy for subsequent episodes over 2 years. Patients with severe malaria, ALT above twice the upper limit of normal, or QTc above 450 ms were excluded. The abstract does not print a sex mix.
cards.result: The 2-year incidence rate of all malaria episodes was non-inferior for pyronaridine–artesunate versus artemether–lumefantrine (1.77 versus 1.87 episodes; rate ratio 1.05 relative, 95% CI 0.94–1.17) and versus artesunate–amodiaquine (1.39 versus 1.35; rate ratio 0.97, 0.87–1.07), against a 20% non-inferiority margin. For uncomplicated P. falciparum malaria, PCR-adjusted adequate clinical and parasitological response exceeded 99.5% at day 28 and 98.6% at day 42 for all regimens; unadjusted response at day 28 was higher on pyronaridine–artesunate (96.9% versus 82.3% for artemether–lumefantrine and 95.6% versus 89.0% for artesunate–amodiaquine). Mostly mild transient transaminase elevations occurred more often with pyronaridine–artesunate; nine deaths occurred, none related to study treatment.
cards.watchOut: The journal is cited as the record prints it (Lancet, 2018). The rate ratios sit either side of 1 depending on the comparator because sites allocated different regimen pairs — the comparisons are within-site, not a single four-way contrast. Liver-enzyme monitoring is part of this drug's evidence base: patients with raised baseline ALT were excluded, so retreatment safety in that group is untested here.

cards.headline: Rueangweerayut 2012: pyronaridine–artesunate non-inferior to mefloquine–artesunate in the phase 3 programme (99.2% vs 97.8%)
cards.summary: Rueangweerayut 2012: pyronaridine–artesunate non-inferior to mefloquine–artesunate in the phase 3 programme (99.2% vs 97.8%)
cards.people: 1,271 patients aged 3–60 years with uncomplicated P. falciparum malaria, 81.3% in Asia and 18.7% in Africa, randomised to fixed-dose pyronaridine–artesunate or mefloquine plus artesunate, dosed by body weight once daily for 3 days. The abstract does not print a sex mix.
cards.result: PCR-corrected adequate clinical and parasitological response at day 28 (per protocol) was 99.2% (743 of 749) on pyronaridine–artesunate versus 97.8% (360 of 368) on mefloquine plus artesunate — a difference of 1.4 percentage points (95% CI 0.0 to 3.5; P=0.05), meeting non-inferiority. Day-42 intention-to-treat efficacy was 83.1% versus 83.9%. In Cambodia, parasite clearance was prolonged on both regimens and recrudescence by day 42 was higher on pyronaridine–artesunate (10.2% versus 0%; P=0.04) — an early in-vivo artemisinin-resistance signal. Aminotransferase elevations were observed on pyronaridine–artesunate; two patients on mefloquine plus artesunate had seizures.
cards.watchOut: The Cambodian substudy result cuts against the headline: where artemisinin resistance was emerging, pyronaridine–artesunate did not protect against recrudescence better than the comparator. The trial predates current resistance patterns and should not be read as evidence about the Mekong today (see Shelf #1700's territory).

In the single pivotal trial (720 patients, one UK hospital, two winter seasons), the proportion of patients who received antibiotics while hospitalised was 84% with point-of-care testing versus 83% with routine care (difference 0.6%, 95% CI −4.9 to 6.0; P=0.84), and mean antibiotic duration did not differ (7.2 versus 7.7 days; P=0.32). What improved: single-dose or brief (<48 h) courses among treated patients (17% versus 9%; P=0.0047; number needed to test 13), mean length of stay (5.7 versus 6.8 days; P=0.0443), and appropriate antiviral treatment of influenza-positive patients (91% versus 65%). cards.headline: ResPOC 2017: no reduction in overall antibiotic use (84% vs 83%), but briefer courses, shorter stay, better influenza treatment
cards.summary: ResPOC 2017: no reduction in overall antibiotic use (84% vs 83%), but briefer courses, shorter stay, better influenza treatment
cards.type: Pragmatic, open-label, randomised controlled trial (single pivotal trial)
cards.people: 720 adults (≥18 years) presenting within 24 hours to the emergency department or acute medical unit of a large UK hospital with acute respiratory illness or fever above 37.5 °C, over two winter seasons; 362 assigned to molecular point-of-care testing (FilmArray respiratory panel) and 358 to routine clinical care; analysis was by modified intention to treat (360 versus 354). The abstract does not print a mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: The primary outcome — proportion receiving antibiotics while hospitalised — was 301 of 360 (84%) in the testing group versus 294 of 354 (83%) in controls (difference 0.6%, 95% CI −4.9 to 6.0; P=0.84). Mean antibiotic duration did not differ (7.2 [SD 5.1] versus 7.7 [4.9] days; difference −0.4, −1.2 to 0.4; P=0.32). Among patients treated with antibiotics, single doses or brief courses (<48 h) were more frequent with testing (50 of 301 [17%] versus 26 of 294 [9%]; difference 7.8%, 2.5 to 13.1; P=0.0047; number needed to test 13). Mean length of stay was shorter (5.7 [6.3] versus 6.8 [7.7] days; difference −1.1, −2.2 to −0.3; P=0.0443), and appropriate antiviral treatment of influenza-positive patients was more common (52 of 57 [91%] versus 24 of 37 [65%]; P=0.0026; number needed to test 4). Adverse outcomes did not differ (21% versus 25%; P=0.29).
cards.watchOut: Anchor correction: the topic file pinned PMID 28166743, which is this trial's PROTOCOL paper (BMC Infectious Diseases 2017) — fenced, not carded; the carded record is the results report in The Lancet Respiratory Medicine. The authors themselves note the primary outcome was blunted because many patients were started on antibiotics before test results could return — the null is partly an implementation artefact, but it is the result the design produced. Single hospital, open-label, winter seasons only.

shelves.title: Direct oral penicillin challenge in low-risk penicillin allergy (PALACE)
shelves.question: In outpatients with a low-risk penicillin allergy label, is direct oral penicillin challenge non-inferior to skin testing followed by oral challenge for delabelling safely?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Humans · Female · Middle Aged · Male · Clinical Decision Rules · Penicillins · Drug Hypersensitivity · Risk Assessment · Hypersensitivity · Anti-Bacterial Agents
shelves.balance: In the single pivotal randomised trial (377 adults analysed, six specialist centres in North America and Australia, all with PEN-FAST scores below 3), a physician-verified positive immune-mediated reaction within 1 hour of challenge occurred in 0.5% (1 of 187) after direct oral challenge versus 0.5% (1 of 190) after skin testing followed by challenge — a risk difference of 0.0084 percentage points (90% CI −1.22 to 1.24), far inside the 5-percentage-point non-inferiority margin — with no serious adverse events and similar 5-day immune-mediated event counts (9 versus 10). A provenance correction is printed on the card: the topic file's anchor PMID is a secondary summary record, not the trial; the carded record is the trial itself, which the file described as merely the decision-rule paper. The result applies only to decision-rule-defined low-risk labels. PROPOSED stamp: LIKELY.

cards.headline: PALACE 2023: direct oral challenge non-inferior — reactions 0.5% versus 0.5%, no serious events
cards.summary: PALACE 2023: direct oral challenge non-inferior — reactions 0.5% versus 0.5%, no serious events
cards.type: Randomised, open-label, multicentre non-inferiority trial (single pivotal trial)
cards.people: 382 adults with a low-risk penicillin allergy label (PEN-FAST score below 3) at six specialised centres (three in North America, three in Australia), randomised to direct oral penicillin challenge (187 analysed) or skin testing followed by oral challenge (190 analysed); median age 51 years (IQR 35–65); 247 (65.5%) female. Most patients had PEN-FAST scores of 0 or 1.
cards.result: The primary outcome — physician-verified positive immune-mediated reaction within 1 hour of the oral challenge — occurred in 1 patient (0.5%) in the direct-challenge group and 1 patient (0.5%) in the skin-test group: risk difference 0.0084 percentage points (90% CI −1.22 to 1.24), with the 1-sided 95% CI below the 5-percentage-point non-inferiority margin. In the 5 days after challenge, 9 immune-mediated adverse events were recorded in the intervention group versus 10 in the control group (risk difference −0.45 pp, 95% CI −4.87 to 3.96). No serious adverse events occurred.
cards.watchOut: Anchor correction: the topic file pinned PMID 37931260, whose record is a journal summary citing this trial, not the trial report; it is fenced and the genuine report (the file's supposed 'decision-rule' PMID) is carded. 'Low-risk' here is a specific instrument — PEN-FAST below 3, applied in specialist centres; the result does not license direct challenge for unstratified or higher-risk histories, and the trial was open-label.

shelves.title: Diagnostic algorithm for suspected UTI in nursing-home residents (Loeb minimum criteria)
shelves.question: In nursing-home residents, does implementing minimum criteria for initiating antibiotics for suspected urinary tract infection reduce antimicrobial prescriptions without increasing hospitalisation or death?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Anti-Bacterial Agents · Cluster Analysis · Drug Prescriptions · Homes for the Aged · Humans · Nursing Homes · Treatment Outcome · Urinary Tract Infections
shelves.balance: In the single cluster-randomised trial (24 nursing homes in Ontario and Idaho; outcomes in 4,217 residents), a multifaceted intervention built around a diagnostic and treatment algorithm reduced antimicrobial courses for suspected urinary tract infection from 1.59 to 1.17 courses per 1,000 resident days (weighted mean difference −0.49, 95% CI −0.93 to −0.06) — about a 26% relative reduction — and cut the share of all antimicrobial courses attributable to suspected UTI from 38.6% to 28.4%. Total antimicrobial use did not differ significantly (3.52 versus 3.93 per 1,000 resident days), and there was no significant difference in hospital admissions or mortality. The benefit is specific to UTI prescribing, delivered by a bundle (algorithm plus education and outreach), in one trial. PROPOSED stamp: POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: Loeb 2005: algorithm-based intervention cut UTI antibiotic courses (1.17 vs 1.59 per 1,000 resident days) with no outcome penalty
cards.summary: Loeb 2005: algorithm-based intervention cut UTI antibiotic courses (1.17 vs 1.59 per 1,000 resident days) with no outcome penalty
cards.people: 24 nursing homes in Ontario, Canada, and Idaho, United States (12 intervention, 12 usual care); outcomes measured in 4,217 residents. The intervention homes implemented a diagnostic and treatment algorithm for urinary tract infection through small-group sessions for nurses, videotapes, written material, outreach visits, and one-to-one physician interviews.
cards.result: Antimicrobial courses for suspected urinary tract infection were 1.17 versus 1.59 courses per 1,000 resident days (weighted mean difference −0.49, 95% CI −0.93 to −0.06) — a relative reduction of about 26%. Antimicrobials for suspected UTI were 28.4% of all courses in intervention homes versus 38.6% in usual care (weighted mean difference −9.6%, −16.9 to −2.4). Total antimicrobial use did not differ significantly (3.52 versus 3.93 per 1,000 resident days; difference −0.37, −1.17 to 0.44). No significant difference was found in hospital admissions or mortality.
cards.watchOut: The intervention was a bundle; the trial cannot separate the algorithm's contribution from the education and outreach wrapped around it. The abstract prints no resident-level age or sex data, and no registry ID appears in the record's databank fields (2005 trial). 'No significant difference' in admissions and mortality is a safety observation from a trial powered on prescribing, not an equivalence demonstration.

shelves.title: Prewritten stop orders for urinary catheters (Loeb)
shelves.question: In hospitalised patients with urinary catheters, do prewritten stop orders (automatic removal prompts at a set interval) reduce catheter duration and inappropriate catheterisation versus usual care?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Catheters, Indwelling · Critical Pathways · Cross Infection · Device Removal · Female · Humans · Inpatients · Male · Middle Aged · Time Factors · Unnecessary Procedures · Urinary Catheterization · Urinary Tract Infections
shelves.balance: In the single randomised trial (692 hospitalised patients in three Ontario tertiary-care hospitals), prewritten stop orders reduced inappropriate catheter days by 1.69 days and total catheter days by 1.34 days versus usual care (both P<0.001), without increasing catheter reinsertion (8.6% versus 7.0%; P=0.45) — but urinary tract infections were essentially unchanged (19.0% versus 20.2%; relative risk 0.94, 95% CI 0.66–1.33; P=0.71). A citation correction is printed on the card: the topic file gives this trial as BMJ 2008; the record's journal is the Journal of General Internal Medicine. The intervention reliably shortens catheterisation; an infection benefit is unproven on this record. PROPOSED stamp: POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: Loeb 2008: stop orders cut inappropriate catheter days (−1.69) but not urinary tract infections (19.0% vs 20.2%)
cards.summary: Loeb 2008: stop orders cut inappropriate catheter days (−1.69) but not urinary tract infections (19.0% vs 20.2%)
cards.people: 692 hospitalised patients with indwelling urinary catheters inserted within 48 hours, in three tertiary-care hospitals in Ontario, Canada, randomised to prewritten orders for catheter removal if specified criteria were not met, or to usual care. The abstract does not print a mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Days of inappropriate catheter use were lower with stop orders (difference −1.69 days; 95% CI printed as −1.23 to −2.15; P<0.001), as were total catheter days (difference −1.34 days; 95% CI printed as −0.64 to −2.05; P<0.001). Urinary tract infection occurred in 19.0% of the stop-order group versus 20.2% of controls (relative risk 0.94 relative, 95% CI 0.66–1.33; P=0.71). Catheter reinsertion was 8.6% versus 7.0% (relative risk 1.23, 0.72–2.11; P=0.45).
cards.watchOut: Journal correction: the topic file cites this trial as BMJ 2008; the record's journal is the Journal of General Internal Medicine (2008) and the card follows the record. The printed confidence intervals for the day differences run in descending order in the abstract (−1.23 to −2.15; −0.64 to −2.05) — carded as printed and flagged here, not re-ordered. The trial shows faster catheter removal, not fewer infections.

shelves.title: The Antibiotic Review Kit for hospitals (ARK-Hospital)
shelves.question: In acute medical patients started on intravenous antibiotics, does a hospital-wide antibiotic review kit (a structured review-and-decide tool) reduce total antibiotic use versus usual stewardship?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Humans · Anti-Bacterial Agents · COVID-19 · Hospitalization · Hospitals · Pandemics
shelves.balance: PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C). Tier C deviation, disclosed: the topic file flags this shelf not Tier C, but 30-day all-cause mortality was a patient-level co-primary outcome (a non-inferiority safety endpoint), so it is ruled Tier C at build under the gate rule; no mortality claim — benefit or harm — is made or supported by this shelf. On the record: in the stepped-wedge cluster trial (39 UK hospital sites followed for at least 14 months; 7,160,421 acute general medical admissions), the review kit reduced total antibiotic defined daily doses per admission by 4.8% per year (95% CI −9.1 to −0.2) on adjusted analysis. The mortality co-primary was awkward: an immediate change of −2.7% (−5.7 to 0.3) and a sustained change of +3.0% (−0.1 to 6.2) in adjusted 30-day mortality, which the authors attribute to weak, inconsistent effects probably explained by the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic; the sustained estimate's interval crosses the 5% non-inferiority margin, so the safety reading is not clean. PROPOSED stamp: POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: ARK-Hospital 2023: review kit cut antibiotic use (−4.8% per year); the mortality safety co-primary was inconsistent
cards.summary: ARK-Hospital 2023: review kit cut antibiotic use (−4.8% per year); the mortality safety co-primary was inconsistent
cards.people: UK acute hospitals admitting adult non-elective general medical inpatients: 43 sites randomised to implementation dates (7 withdrew before implementation; 39 followed for at least 14 months), with outcomes assessed across 7,160,421 acute general medical admissions from routine electronic records. The intervention was a multifaceted behaviour-change kit supporting prescribers to stop antibiotics at clinical review.
cards.result: Total antibiotic defined daily doses per acute general medical admission fell by an adjusted 4.8% per year (95% CI −9.1 to −0.2) following implementation. For the co-primary 30-day all-cause mortality outcome (non-inferiority margin 5%), the intervention was associated with an immediate change of −2.7% (95% CI −5.7 to 0.3) and a sustained change of +3.0% (−0.1 to 6.2). The authors describe the mortality effects as weak and inconsistent and probably explained by the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic.
cards.watchOut: The sustained mortality estimate (+3.0%, CI −0.1 to 6.2) is compatible with an increase beyond the trial's own 5% non-inferiority margin — the abstract's reassurance rests on the pandemic explanation, not on the interval excluding harm, and the card states this plainly. Effects are hospital-level and ecological (routine data, no patient-level randomisation); seven randomised sites withdrew before implementation.

shelves.title: Faecal microbiota transplantation to eradicate multidrug-resistant organism carriage (Huttner)
shelves.question: In patients carrying multidrug-resistant Enterobacterales, does a short oral antibiotic course followed by faecal transplantation eradicate carriage versus no intervention, at the trial's 35–48-day primary assessment?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Aged · Anti-Bacterial Agents · Carbapenem-Resistant Enterobacteriaceae · Carrier State · Colistin · Drug Administration Schedule · Drug Resistance, Multiple, Bacterial · Enterobacteriaceae Infections · Fecal Microbiota Transplantation · Feces · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Tertiary Care Centers · beta-Lactamases
shelves.balance: An endpoint correction first: the topic file frames this shelf around eradication at six months, but the trial's primary outcome in the record is detectable carriage at 35–48 days after randomisation, and the abstract prints no six-month eradication figures — the shelf question follows the record and no six-month numbers are carded. On the record: in the single small randomised trial (39 patients, four European centres), decolonisation at 35–48 days was 41% (9 of 22) after 5 days of oral colistin plus neomycin followed by frozen FMT versus 29% (5 of 17) with no intervention — odds ratio 1.7 relative (95% CI 0.4–6.4), not significant — in a trial the authors note was terminated early and underpowered. Three intervention patients stopped the antibiotics for diarrhoea but received FMT. MAYBE (weak evidence) is all this record earns. This shelf is flagged as a two-trial-gate exception candidate (single small trial): it should be withdrawn or re-scoped if the developer rejects the exception.

shelves.title: Bacteriophage cocktail for Pseudomonas burn wounds (PhagoBurn)
shelves.question: In burn wounds infected with Pseudomonas aeruginosa, does a cocktail of lytic bacteriophages reduce bacterial burden as effectively as standard sulfadiazine silver cream?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Anti-Bacterial Agents · Belgium · Burns · Double-Blind Method · Drug Tolerance · Female · France · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Phage Therapy · Pseudomonas Infections · Pseudomonas Phages · Pseudomonas aeruginosa · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: In the single small phase 1/2 trial (27 patients randomised; 25 in the efficacy population), the phage cocktail reduced bacterial burden significantly more slowly than standard care: median time to sustained ≥2-quadrant burden reduction was 144 hours on phages versus 47 hours on sulfadiazine silver cream (hazard ratio 0.29 relative, 95% CI 0.10–0.79; P=0.018), and the trial was stopped for insufficient phage efficacy. The decisive caveat is printed on the record: the manufactured cocktail's titre decayed, and patients actually received about 1×10² PFU/mL per dose instead of the planned 1×10⁶ — so the trial tests a failed dose, not the phage concept at specification. Adverse events were fewer on phages (23% versus 54%); one death occurred in each group after follow-up, neither treatment-related. PROPOSED stamp: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) for the question as posed — as delivered, phages were not as effective as standard care. This shelf is flagged as a two-trial-gate exception candidate (single small trial) and should be withdrawn or re-scoped if the developer rejects the exception.

cards.headline: PhagoBurn 2019: phages cleared burden more slowly than silver cream (144 h vs 47 h; HR 0.29) — at 1/10,000 of the intended dose
cards.summary: PhagoBurn 2019: phages cleared burden more slowly than silver cream (144 h vs 47 h; HR 0.29) — at 1/10,000 of the intended dose
cards.type: Randomised, controlled phase 1/2 trial (single small trial, stopped early)
cards.people: 27 adults with burn wounds clinically infected with Pseudomonas aeruginosa at nine burn centres in France and Belgium, randomised to a cocktail of 12 lytic anti-Pseudomonas phages (PP1131; 13) or standard care with 1% sulfadiazine silver cream (14), applied daily for 7 days with 14 days of follow-up; the efficacy (modified intention-to-treat) population was 25 patients (12 phage, 13 standard). The abstract does not print a mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: The primary endpoint — median time to sustained reduction in bacterial burden by at least two quadrants — was 144 hours (95% CI 48 to not reached) in the phage group versus 47 hours (23–122) in the standard-care group (hazard ratio 0.29 relative, 95% CI 0.10–0.79; P=0.018). Maximal bacterial burden was present in 6 of 12 (50%) phage patients versus 2 of 13 (15%) on standard care. The trial was stopped because of insufficient PP1131 efficacy. Adverse events occurred in 3 of 13 (23%) phage patients versus 7 of 13 (54%) on standard care; one participant in each group died after follow-up, neither death treatment-related.
cards.watchOut: The dose failure is integral to the result, not an excuse appended to it: PP1131 titre fell after manufacturing and the delivered concentration was about 1×10² PFU/mL per daily dose against a planned 1×10⁶, and ancillary work showed isolates from phage failures were resistant to low phage doses. The record supports 'this product at this dose was slower than cream' — and no conclusion about adequately dosed phage therapy either way.

shelves.title: Audit and feedback for dental antibiotic prescribing (RAPID)
shelves.question: In general dental practice, does individualised audit and feedback reduce antibiotic prescribing rates versus no feedback?
shelves.mesh: Anti-Bacterial Agents · Feedback · Humans · Inappropriate Prescribing · Medical Audit · Practice Patterns, Dentists' · Scotland
shelves.balance: Scope boundary, stated on the shelf face: Shelf #884 covers audit and feedback to change professional practice generally, and Shelf #463 covers antibiotic prophylaxis before dental work; this shelf is the dental-prescribing setting alone, with prescribing rate as the sole target. In the single cluster trial (all 795 antibiotic-prescribing NHS general dental practices in Scotland; outcome data for 761 practices), individualised audit and feedback reduced dentists' antibiotic prescribing rate by 5.7% relative (95% CI −10.2% to −1.1%; P=0.01) versus control over 12 months — from baselines of 8.5 versus 8.3 items per 100 treatment claims, follow-up falls were 1.0 versus 0.4 items. A written behaviour-change message added benefit (−6.1% relative for recipients versus non-recipients); a health-board comparator line and a third feedback round did not significantly add. The trial could not assess appropriateness, only volume. PROPOSED stamp: POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: RAPID 2016: audit and feedback cut dental antibiotic prescribing by 5.7% relative across Scotland
cards.summary: RAPID 2016: audit and feedback cut dental antibiotic prescribing by 5.7% relative across Scotland
cards.type: Cluster-randomised controlled trial (single trial, national coverage)
cards.people: All 795 antibiotic-prescribing NHS general dental practices in Scotland, randomised to control (163 practices; 567 dentists) or individualised audit and feedback (632 practices; 1,999 dentists), with factorial variations in written behaviour-change message, health-board comparator, and feedback frequency; primary-outcome data were available for 152 control and 609 intervention practices (438 and 1,550 dentists).
cards.result: Antibiotic items per 100 NHS treatment claims fell by 0.4 in control practices and by 1.0 in intervention practices over 12 months (from baselines of 8.3 and 8.5), a significant relative reduction of −5.7% (95% CI −10.2% to −1.1%; P=0.01). Dentists who received the written behaviour-change message reduced prescribing by a further 6.1% relative to those who did not (−10.4% to −1.9%; P=0.01); neither the health-board comparator (−4.3%; P=0.06) nor a third feedback round (0.02%; P=0.99) significantly changed the effect.
cards.watchOut: The outcome is prescribing volume from routine claims data; whether the forgone prescriptions were the inappropriate ones could not be evaluated, as the record itself states. Registry ID ISRCTN49204710 appears in the abstract text; the record's databank fields are empty.
cards.source: Elouafkaoui P et al. An Audit and Feedback Intervention for Reducing Antibiotic Prescribing in General Dental Practice: The RAPiD Cluster Randomised Controlled Trial. PLoS Medicine. 2016. PMID: 27575599. Registry ID: ISRCTN49204710, printed in the abstract text (trial registration line); the record's databank fields are empty. shelves.title: Web-based prescriber training for respiratory infections (GRACE INTRO)
shelves.question: In European primary care, does internet-based training in communication skills (with or without point-of-care CRP) reduce antibiotic prescribing for lower respiratory tract infection versus usual care?
shelves.mesh: Acute Disease · Anti-Bacterial Agents · C-Reactive Protein · Clinical Competence · Cluster Analysis · Communication · Europe · Female · General Practice · Humans · Inservice Training · Internet · Male · Middle Aged · Point-of-Care Systems · Practice Patterns, Physicians' · Primary Health Care · Respiratory Tract Infections · Teaching
shelves.balance: Scope boundary, stated on the shelf face: Shelf #1003 covers point-of-care CRP testing alone and Shelf #1005 covers educational outreach visits; this shelf is internet-delivered clinician training, with CRP training as one factorial component. In the single multinational cluster trial (246 practices in six European countries; 4,264 patients recruited after randomisation), internet training in point-of-care CRP use was associated with prescribing of 33% versus 48% (adjusted risk ratio 0.54 relative, 95% CI 0.42–0.69), training in enhanced communication skills with 36% versus 45% (0.69, 0.54–0.87), and the two combined with the largest reduction (combined risk ratio 0.38 relative, 0.25–0.55). A provenance correction is printed on the card: the topic file's anchor PMID is the trial's process-analysis paper, not its results; the results report is carded instead. The outcome is prescribing for respiratory-tract infections overall (the recruited population mixed lower and upper respiratory infections). PROPOSED stamp: POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: INTRO 2013: web training in CRP use and in communication each cut prescribing; combined, most (RR 0.38 relative)
cards.summary: INTRO 2013: web training in CRP use and in communication each cut prescribing; combined, most (RR 0.38 relative)
cards.type: Multinational cluster-randomised factorial controlled trial (single trial)
cards.people: Primary-care practices in six European countries: a baseline audit in 259 practices covered 6,771 patients (55.3% lower-respiratory-tract and 20.9% upper-respiratory-tract infections; 79.1% prescribed antibiotics); after randomisation, 246 practices and 4,264 recruited patients contributed to the intervention comparison of usual care, internet training in point-of-care CRP testing, internet training in enhanced communication skills, or both.
cards.result: Antibiotic prescribing was lower with CRP training than without (33% versus 48%; adjusted risk ratio 0.54 relative, 95% CI 0.42–0.69) and with enhanced-communication training than without (36% versus 45%; 0.69, 0.54–0.87). In the combined analysis, the CRP component's risk ratio was 0.53 (0.36–0.74; P<0.0001), the communication component's 0.68 (0.50–0.89; P=0.003), and the combined intervention's 0.38 (0.25–0.55; P<0.0001) — the greatest reduction.
cards.watchOut: Anchor correction: the topic file pinned PMID 24238118, which is this trial's quantitative PROCESS analysis (Implementation Science 2013) — fenced, not carded; the carded record is the main results report (Lancet 2013, as the record prints it; the topic file gives BMJ). The question's 'lower respiratory tract infection' framing is narrower than the trial, which recruited both lower and upper respiratory infections and reports one prescribing outcome across them.

shelves.title: Oral step-down therapy for low-risk febrile neutropenia (Freifeld; Kern)
shelves.question: In low-risk febrile neutropenic patients, is oral ciprofloxacin plus amoxicillin–clavulanate as effective as intravenous therapy for empirical treatment?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Amoxicillin · Anti-Bacterial Agents · Antineoplastic Agents · Bacterial Infections · Ceftazidime · Child · Child, Preschool · Ciprofloxacin · Clavulanic Acid · Double-Blind Method · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · Fever · Fever of Unknown Origin · Humans · Infusions, Intravenous · Male · Middle Aged · Neoplasms · Neutropenia · Aged, 80 and over · Agranulocytosis · Amikacin · Bacteremia · Ceftriaxone · Prospective Studies · Survival Rate
shelves.balance: Two randomised trials published back-to-back in 1999 agree. In Freifeld (double-blind; 232 episodes), treatment succeeded without modification in 71% of oral-therapy episodes versus 67% of intravenous episodes (difference 3%, 95% CI −8 to 15; P=0.48), with no deaths in either group; oral therapy failed more often through intolerance (16% versus 1%) and intravenous therapy more often through regimen modification (32% versus 13%). In Kern (open-label, multicentre; 353 enrolled, equivalence margin 10%), success was 86% versus 84% in the per-protocol analysis and 80% versus 77% by intention to treat, meeting the trial's equivalence definition. Both trials treated patients in hospital until fever resolved — this is oral-versus-intravenous route evidence in monitored low-risk patients, not evidence for unsupervised outpatient care. Neither record carries a registry ID (1999, pre-registration era). PROPOSED stamp: LIKELY.

cards.headline: Freifeld 1999: oral therapy succeeded in 71% of episodes versus 67% intravenous; no deaths
cards.summary: Freifeld 1999: oral therapy succeeded in 71% of episodes versus 67% intravenous; no deaths
cards.people: Patients aged 5–74 years with fever and neutropenia during cancer chemotherapy, expected neutropenia of no more than 10 days and no other underlying conditions: 116 episodes in each group (84 patients oral, 79 intravenous). Oral therapy was ciprofloxacin plus amoxicillin–clavulanate; intravenous therapy was ceftazidime. Mean neutrophil counts at admission were 81 and 84 per cubic millimetre; mean neutropenia duration 3.4 and 3.8 days. All patients were hospitalised until fever and neutropenia resolved.
cards.result: Treatment was successful without modification in 71% of oral-therapy episodes versus 67% of intravenous episodes (difference 3%, 95% CI −8 to 15; P=0.48). Failure through need for regimen modification was 13% oral versus 32% intravenous (P<0.001); failure through intolerance was 16% versus 1% (P<0.001). There were no deaths. Intolerance of the oral antibiotics was 16% versus 8% for placebo (P=0.07).
cards.watchOut: Success rates count episodes, not patients (232 episodes in 163 patients). The intravenous comparator was ceftazidime monotherapy, a 1999 standard; and 'low-risk' was tightly defined — expected short neutropenia and no comorbidity — so the result does not travel to higher-risk presentations.
cards.source: Freifeld A et al. A double-blind comparison of empirical oral and intravenous antibiotic therapy for low-risk febrile patients with neutropenia during cancer chemotherapy. cards.headline: Kern 1999: equivalence demonstrated — success 86% versus 84% per protocol, 80% versus 77% intention to treat
cards.summary: Kern 1999: equivalence demonstrated — success 86% versus 84% per protocol, 80% versus 77% intention to treat
cards.type: Randomised, open-label, multicentre equivalence trial (EORTC International Antimicrobial Therapy Cooperative Group)
cards.people: 353 febrile patients with cancer and granulocytopenia expected to resolve within 10 days, randomised to oral ciprofloxacin 750 mg twice daily plus amoxicillin–clavulanate 625 mg three times daily, or intravenous ceftriaxone plus amikacin; 312 patients were evaluable per protocol. The trial stopped at its second interim analysis when equivalence was demonstrated. The abstract does not print a mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Treatment success was 86% (95% CI 80–91) on oral therapy versus 84% (78–90) on intravenous therapy in the per-protocol analysis (P=0.02 for the equivalence test), and 80% versus 77% by intention to treat (P=0.03) — within the prespecified equivalence margin of a 10-percentage-point absolute difference. Duration of fever, time to regimen change, reasons for change, duration of therapy, and survival were similar; adverse-event types differed slightly but were similar in frequency.
cards.watchOut: Open-label, and stopped early at an interim equivalence demonstration, which truncates precision. The intravenous comparator (ceftriaxone plus amikacin) differs from Freifeld's (ceftazidime) — the two trials agree on the oral regimen against different intravenous standards, which strengthens the route conclusion while leaving regimen-versus-regimen questions open.
cards.source: Kern WV et al. Oral versus intravenous empirical antimicrobial therapy for fever in patients with granulocytopenia who are receiving cancer chemotherapy. International Antimicrobial Therapy Cooperative Group of the European Organization for Research and Treatment of Cancer. The New England Journal of Medicine. 1999. PMID: 10423465. cards.headline: Synthesis: two concordant 1999 NEJM trials make oral therapy a proven route in low-risk febrile neutropenia — LIKELY
cards.summary: Synthesis: two concordant 1999 NEJM trials make oral therapy a proven route in low-risk febrile neutropenia — LIKELY
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Freifeld 1999 (232 episodes) and Kern 1999 (353 patients).
cards.result: In carefully defined low-risk patients, empirical oral ciprofloxacin plus amoxicillin–clavulanate matched intravenous therapy on success and survival in both a blinded and an open-label trial, with failure modes that differ (intolerance on oral, modification on intravenous) rather than differ in total.

shelves.title: Triple artemisinin-based combination therapies for resistant malaria (TRACII)
shelves.question: In uncomplicated falciparum malaria in the Greater Mekong Subregion and Africa, are triple ACTs (adding mefloquine to dihydroartemisinin–piperaquine, or amodiaquine to artemether–lumefantrine) as effective and safe as standard ACTs where artemisinin resistance is spreading?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Amodiaquine · Anthraquinones · Antimalarials · Artemether, Lumefantrine Drug Combination · Artemisinins · Drug Resistance · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · Humans · Malaria, Falciparum · Male · Mefloquine · Plasmodium falciparum · Polymerase Chain Reaction · Quinolines · Treatment Outcome · Young Adult · Piperazines · Artemether · Drug Combinations · Ethanolamines · Fluorenes · Malaria · Recurrence · Vomiting
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the two triple regimens answer differently in different resistance settings, and the cards do not average them. In TRACII (1,100 patients, eight countries), where dihydroartemisinin–piperaquine was failing in Cambodia, Thailand, and Vietnam, adding mefloquine restored 42-day PCR-corrected efficacy to 98% versus 48% on the dual therapy (risk difference 51%, 95% CI 42–59) — LIKELY for that rescue question. Artemether–lumefantrine plus amodiaquine performed similarly to artemether–lumefantrine alone where the dual therapy still works (98% versus 97%), and in the confirmatory Mekong trial (310 patients) the triple regimen's 42-day efficacy was 97% versus 95% (hazard ratio for recrudescence 0.6 relative, 0.2–1.9; P=0.38), including in kelch13-mutant infections (96% versus 90%; P=0.17) — supportive but not decisive: POSSIBLE. A geography correction is printed on the card: the topic file describes the confirmatory trial as African; its record places it in Cambodia and Vietnam. Both triple regimens were generally well tolerated, with more early vomiting (and, in the confirmatory trial, more bradycardia) on the amodiaquine-containing regimen.

cards.headline: TRACII 2020: adding mefloquine rescued a failing ACT (98% vs 48%); adding amodiaquine matched a working one (98% vs 97%)
cards.summary: TRACII 2020: adding mefloquine rescued a failing ACT (98% vs 48%); adding amodiaquine matched a working one (98% vs 97%)
cards.type: Randomised, open-label, multicentre trial (site-specific regimen pairs)
cards.people: 1,100 patients aged 2–65 years with uncomplicated P. falciparum malaria at 18 sites in eight countries: dihydroartemisinin–piperaquine (183), dihydroartemisinin–piperaquine plus mefloquine (269), artesunate–mefloquine (73), artemether–lumefantrine (289), or artemether–lumefantrine plus amodiaquine (286), allocated by site-specific pairs. Median age 23 years (IQR 13–34); 854 (78%) male.
cards.result: In Cambodia, Thailand, and Vietnam, 42-day PCR-corrected efficacy of dihydroartemisinin–piperaquine plus mefloquine was 98% (149 of 152) versus 48% (67 of 141) for dihydroartemisinin–piperaquine alone (risk difference 51%, 95% CI 42–59; P<0.0001); in Myanmar the same comparison was 91% (42 of 46) versus 100% (42 of 42) (difference 9%, 1–17; P=0.12). The mefloquine triple was non-inferior to artesunate–mefloquine at three Cambodian sites (96% versus 95%). Artemether–lumefantrine plus amodiaquine gave 98% (281 of 286) versus 97% (279 of 289) for artemether–lumefantrine (difference 2%, −1 to 4; P=0.30). Early vomiting was more frequent after the mefloquine triple (3.8% versus 1.5% of doses; P=0.012).
cards.watchOut: The headline 98% versus 48% is a within-region comparison against a collapsed standard — it measures rescue of a failing regimen, not superiority over working ACTs, and the Myanmar sites show the effect reversing where the dual therapy had not failed. Regimen pairs differed by site, so cross-regimen comparisons are indirect.

shelves.title: Four artemisinin-based treatments for malaria in pregnancy (PREGACT)
shelves.question: In African women in the second or third trimester with falciparum malaria, how do four artemisinin-based combinations compare with each other on cure and birth outcomes?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Africa · Amodiaquine · Antimalarials · Artemether, Lumefantrine Drug Combination · Artemisinins · Drug Combinations · Ethanolamines · Female · Fluorenes · Humans · Malaria, Falciparum · Plasmodium falciparum · Polymerase Chain Reaction · Pregnancy · Pregnancy Complications, Parasitic · Pregnancy Outcome · Quinolines · Young Adult
shelves.balance: In the single pivotal trial (3,428 pregnant women in four African countries; open-label), PCR-adjusted cure rates at day 63 (per protocol) were 94.8% on artemether–lumefantrine, 98.5% on artesunate–amodiaquine, 99.2% on dihydroartemisinin–piperaquine, and 96.8% on mefloquine–artesunate; intention-to-treat rates were 94.2%, 96.9%, 98.0%, and 95.5%. Artemether–lumefantrine's cure rate was significantly lower than the other three, although within the trial's 5-percentage-point equivalence margin, and its post-treatment prophylactic effect was clearly shortest (unadjusted cure 52.5% versus 73.8–86.9%). The record reports no significant difference among groups in serious adverse events or birth outcomes — but prints no birth-outcome figures, so none are carded. Drug-related adverse events were most frequent on mefloquine–artesunate (50.6%) and artesunate–amodiaquine (48.5%) and least on artemether–lumefantrine (11.5%). PROPOSED stamp: POSSIBLE — one large trial, comparative rather than placebo-anchored.

cards.headline: PREGACT 2016: all four ACTs cured ≥94%; artemether–lumefantrine lowest on cure and prophylaxis, gentlest on side effects
cards.summary: PREGACT 2016: all four ACTs cured ≥94%; artemether–lumefantrine lowest on cure and prophylaxis, gentlest on side effects
cards.type: Randomised, open-label, multicentre comparative trial (single pivotal trial)
cards.people: 3,428 pregnant women in the second or third trimester with falciparum malaria (any parasite density, regardless of symptoms) in four African countries, treated with artemether–lumefantrine, artesunate–amodiaquine, mefloquine–artesunate, or dihydroartemisinin–piperaquine. The abstract does not print arm sizes, mean age, or other demographic breakdown.
cards.result: PCR-adjusted cure at day 63 (per protocol) was 94.8% (artemether–lumefantrine), 98.5% (artesunate–amodiaquine), 99.2% (dihydroartemisinin–piperaquine), and 96.8% (mefloquine–artesunate); intention-to-treat rates were 94.2%, 96.9%, 98.0%, and 95.5%. The three non-lumefantrine regimens did not differ significantly from each other; artemether–lumefantrine was significantly lower than the other three but within the 5-percentage-point equivalence margin. Unadjusted cure (post-treatment prophylactic effect) was 52.5% on artemether–lumefantrine versus 82.3%, 86.9%, and 73.8% on the others. There was no significant difference in serious adverse events or birth outcomes among the groups. Drug-related adverse events (asthenia, poor appetite, dizziness, nausea, vomiting) occurred in 50.6% (mefloquine–artesunate), 48.5% (artesunate–amodiaquine), 20.6% (dihydroartemisinin–piperaquine), and 11.5% (artemether–lumefantrine) (P<0.001).
cards.watchOut: The record asserts 'no significant difference in birth outcomes' without printing any birth-outcome figures — the card repeats the assertion as an assertion and supplies no numbers. Open-label design; per-protocol cure is the headline analysis, with intention-to-treat rates printed beside it on this card. First-trimester treatment is outside the trial entirely.

shelves.title: Intermittent preventive treatment of malaria in schoolchildren (Clarke)
shelves.question: In schoolchildren in an area of high perennial transmission, does intermittent preventive treatment with sulfadoxine–pyrimethamine plus amodiaquine reduce malaria parasitaemia and anaemia and improve classroom attention?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Amodiaquine · Anemia · Animals · Antimalarials · Child · Child, Preschool · Cluster Analysis · Cognition · Cross-Sectional Studies · Double-Blind Method · Drug Administration Schedule · Drug Combinations · Feces · Female · Humans · Kenya · Malaria, Falciparum · Male · Plasmodium falciparum · Prevalence · Pyrimethamine · Sulfadoxine
shelves.balance: Two corrections from the topic file are carried on the card: the record describes an area of high PERENNIAL transmission (western Kenya), not seasonal; and the file's claim that IPT cut parasitaemia by about 88% does not appear in the trial's abstract — no parasitaemia rates are printed there, so none are carded. On the record: in the single cluster-randomised, double-blind trial (30 primary schools; 6,758 children received allocated treatment), anaemia prevalence at 12 months was 6.3% on IPT versus 12.6% on placebo (adjusted risk ratio 0.52 relative, 95% CI 0.29–0.93; P=0.028), and two of the class-based sustained-attention tests improved significantly (code transmission +6.05 points, P=0.0007; counting sounds +1.80, P=0.03), with no effect on inattentive or hyperactive-compulsive behaviours or on educational achievement. Serious adverse events within 28 days of treatment were more frequent on IPT (19 versus 4), mainly transient balance, dizziness, faintness, nausea, and vomiting shortly after dosing. Scope boundary: distinct from Shelf #968 (seasonal chemoprevention in under-fives) and from pregnancy IPT topics. PROPOSED stamp: POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: Clarke 2008: school-based IPT halved anaemia (6.3% vs 12.6%; adjusted RR 0.52) and improved two attention tests
cards.summary: Clarke 2008: school-based IPT halved anaemia (6.3% vs 12.6%; adjusted RR 0.52) and improved two attention tests
cards.people: 30 primary schools in western Kenya (an area of high perennial transmission), randomised to intermittent preventive treatment with sulfadoxine–pyrimethamine plus amodiaquine or dual placebo; children aged 5–18 years received three treatments at 4-month intervals (3,535 IPT; 3,223 placebo). The primary-outcome analysis included 2,604 IPT and 2,302 placebo children, the main exclusion being loss to follow-up. The abstract does not print a sex mix.
cards.result: Anaemia (haemoglobin below 110 g/L) at 12 months averaged 6.3% in the IPT group versus 12.6% on placebo (adjusted risk ratio 0.52 relative, 95% CI 0.29–0.93; P=0.028). Sustained attention improved on two class-based tests (code transmission score +6.05, 95% CI 2.83–9.27, P=0.0007; counting sounds +1.80, 0.19–3.41, P=0.03), with no effect on inattentive or hyperactive-compulsive behaviours or on educational achievement; per-protocol analyses were similar. Twenty-three serious adverse events were reported within 28 days of any treatment (19 IPT versus 4 placebo) — mainly problems of balance, dizziness, feeling faint, nausea, and/or vomiting shortly after treatment.
cards.watchOut: The topic file's headline parasitaemia figure (a reduction of about 88%) is not printed in this record's abstract and is not carded; the shelf's malaria claim rests on the anaemia endpoint, which was the trial's primary outcome. A third of randomised children are missing from the primary analysis, and the serious-adverse-event imbalance (19 versus 4), though transient symptoms predominated, is part of the record.

shelves.title: Single low-dose primaquine to block falciparum transmission (Eziefula; Gonçalves)
shelves.question: In children with uncomplicated falciparum malaria treated with an ACT, does adding a single low dose of primaquine clear gametocytes and reduce mosquito infectivity versus ACT alone?
shelves.mesh: Antimalarials · Artemether, Lumefantrine Drug Combination · Artemisinins · Child · Child, Preschool · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Double-Blind Method · Drug Administration Schedule · Drug Combinations · Ethanolamines · Female · Fluorenes · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Infant · Malaria, Falciparum · Male · Parasite Load · Primaquine · ROC Curve · Treatment Outcome · Uganda · Artemether · Asymptomatic Infections · Drug Therapy, Combination · Lumefantrine · Plasmodium falciparum · Prevalence
shelves.balance: Scope boundary, stated on the shelf face: Shelf #1182 covers radical cure of vivax malaria with tafenoquine and primaquine; this shelf is falciparum gametocyte clearance in children. Two randomised, double-blind trials agree. In Eziefula (468 Ugandan children with normal G6PD function, all on artemether–lumefantrine), mean gametocyte carriage was 12.4 days on placebo versus 6.6 days at the 0.75 mg/kg reference dose and 6.3 days at 0.4 mg/kg (non-inferior to reference), with 0.1 mg/kg inconclusive (8.0 days); no treatment-related haemolysis occurred and haemoglobin falls did not differ by dose. In Gonçalves (360 asymptomatic Burkinabè children), 0.25 and 0.40 mg/kg cleared gametocytes in 7.7 and 8.2 days versus 19.7 days on placebo, and after treatment only one participant — in the placebo group — infected mosquitoes. A topic-file correction is printed on the second card: the file describes that record as an individual-participant pooled analysis; it is a standalone randomised trial, and is carded as one. Both trials measure gametocyte carriage and mosquito infectivity — surrogates for community transmission, which neither measured. PROPOSED stamp: LIKELY for the gametocyte/infectivity endpoints as scoped.

cards.headline: Eziefula 2014: primaquine 0.4 mg/kg matched the reference dose for gametocyte clearance (6.3 vs 6.6 days); placebo 12.4 days
cards.summary: Eziefula 2014: primaquine 0.4 mg/kg matched the reference dose for gametocyte clearance (6.3 vs 6.6 days); placebo 12.4 days
cards.people: 468 Ugandan children aged 1–10 years with uncomplicated falciparum malaria and normal G6PD enzyme function, all treated with artemether–lumefantrine plus placebo (119) or primaquine 0.1 mg/kg (116), 0.4 mg/kg (116), or 0.75 mg/kg (117, the WHO reference dose). The abstract does not print a sex mix.
cards.result: Mean duration of gametocyte carriage was 6.6 days (95% CI 5.3–7.8) at 0.75 mg/kg, 6.3 days (5.1–7.5) at 0.4 mg/kg (P=0.74 versus reference; within the 2.5-day non-inferiority margin), 8.0 days (6.6–9.4) at 0.1 mg/kg (P=0.14; non-inferiority inconclusive), and 12.4 days (9.9–15.0) on placebo (P<0.0001 versus reference). No child showed treatment-related haemolysis; the mean maximum haemoglobin decrease did not differ significantly between any primaquine dose and placebo (10.7 g/L on placebo versus 11.4, 11.3, and 12.7 g/L by ascending dose).
cards.watchOut: Children with G6PD deficiency were excluded — the safety reading does not extend to them, which is precisely the population in which primaquine haemolysis matters. The abstract reports gametocyte carriage, not mosquito infectivity, for this trial; infectivity evidence sits on the Gonçalves card. The WHO-recommended 0.25 mg/kg dose itself was not a study arm here.
cards.source: Eziefula AC et al.
