shelves.title: Priming after a fractional dose of inactivated poliovirus vaccine (Resik)
shelves.question: In infants, does a single fractional (one-fifth) dose of inactivated poliovirus vaccine prime immunological memory as effectively as a full dose, measured by the response to a later full-dose challenge?
shelves.mesh: Antibodies, Viral · Cuba · Female · Humans · Immunization, Secondary · Infant · Injections, Intradermal · Injections, Intramuscular · Male · Poliomyelitis · Poliovirus · Poliovirus Vaccine, Inactivated · Seroepidemiologic Studies · Bangladesh · Immunization Schedule · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the two trials test different schedules and point different ways, and the cards do not average them. In Resik (320 Cuban infants, doses at 4 and 8 months), a single fractional dose primed 89.6–94.0% of infants across the three poliovirus types versus 97.6–98.3% after a full dose — close, though single-dose seroconversion was much lower with the fractional dose (for example type 1: 16.6% versus 46.6%) and cumulative two-dose seroconversion remained a few points lower (93.6–98.1% versus 99.4–100%). In Anand (975 Bangladeshi infants, doses from 6 weeks), intradermal fractional IPV FAILED its non-inferiority tests against full-dose IPV for seroconversion after one or two doses and for priming after one dose. The endpoint throughout is immunogenicity — a surrogate for protection against paralysis, which no trial here measured. The topic file's summary figures (about 95% versus 98%) match neither record exactly; the cards print the records' own type-specific rates. PROPOSED stamp: SPLIT as above.

cards.headline: Resik 2013: one fractional dose primed ~90–94% of infants (vs ~98% full dose) but seroconverted far fewer directly
cards.summary: Resik 2013: one fractional dose primed ~90–94% of infants (vs ~98% full dose) but seroconverted far fewer directly
cards.people: 320 Cuban infants randomised to a fractional (one-fifth) intradermal dose or a full intramuscular dose of IPV at 4 and 8 months of age; 310 (96.9%) completed the study requirements. Blood was sampled at 4 months, 8 months, and 7 and 30 days after the 8-month dose to assess single-dose seroconversion, priming, and two-dose seroconversion by neutralisation assay.
cards.result: After the first dose, seroconversion to poliovirus types 1, 2, and 3 was 16.6%, 47.1%, and 14.7% in the fractional-dose group versus 46.6%, 62.8%, and 32.0% in the full-dose group (P<0.008 for all comparisons). A priming response occurred in 90.8%, 94.0%, and 89.6% (fractional) versus 97.6%, 98.3%, and 98.1% (full dose). After the second dose, cumulative seroconversion was 93.6%, 98.1%, and 93.0% versus 100.0%, 100.0%, and 99.4% (P<0.006 for types 1 and 3). The intradermal group had the most adverse events, mostly minor, none serious.
cards.watchOut: The shelf question is about priming, and on priming the fractional dose is close but consistently a few points behind — not equal; on direct seroconversion it is far behind after one dose. The registry ID (ACTRN12610001046099) appears in the abstract text; the record's databank fields are empty. Immunogenicity in Cuban infants at 4–8 months is the whole of this card's world.

cards.people: 975 healthy 6-week-old infants in Bangladesh randomised across five arms (trivalent or bivalent OPV at 6, 10, and 14 weeks; intramuscular IPV or intradermal one-fifth fractional IPV at 6 and 14 weeks; or fractional IPV at 6 and 14 weeks with bOPV at 10 weeks); 922 (95%) completed follow-up; all received trivalent OPV at 18 weeks.
cards.result: Seroconversion to types 1 and 3 after two IPV doses at 6 and 14 weeks was no different from after three OPV doses. cards.summary: Synthesis: fractional IPV primes well at 4–8 months, inadequately in early infancy — SPLIT as proposed
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Resik 2013 (320 infants) and Anand 2015 (975 infants).
cards.result: Dose-sparing by fractional IPV is schedule-dependent: at 4 and 8 months a single fractional dose primed about nine in ten infants, supporting its use as a priming strategy in older infants; in the 6–14-week window it failed formal non-inferiority against the full dose. shelves.title: Prednisone for paradoxical tuberculosis-associated IRIS (Meintjes)
shelves.question: In HIV-infected patients who develop paradoxical TB-IRIS after starting antiretroviral therapy, does a tapering course of prednisone reduce a composite of hospitalisation, procedures and symptom burden versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Antiretroviral Therapy, Highly Active · CD4 Lymphocyte Count · Double-Blind Method · Glucocorticoids · HIV Infections · Humans · Immune Reconstitution Inflammatory Syndrome · Male · Middle Aged · Placebos · Prednisone · Treatment Outcome · Tuberculosis · Young Adult
shelves.balance: In the single pivotal trial (110 patients in South Africa; double-blind), prednisone (1.5 mg/kg/day for 2 weeks, then 0.75 mg/kg/day for 2 weeks) reduced the primary composite of hospital days plus outpatient therapeutic procedures: median 0 days (IQR 0–3) on prednisone versus 3 days (IQR 0–9) on placebo (P=0.04). Symptoms, Karnofsky score, and quality of life improved significantly more on prednisone at 2 and 4 weeks but not later, and chest radiographs improved more at weeks 2 and 4. Infections on study medication were more frequent on prednisone (27 versus 17 participants; P=0.05), though severe infections were not (2 versus 4). Patients with immediately life-threatening IRIS were excluded. The related NEJM 2018 trial of prednisone to PREVENT TB-IRIS in high-risk ART starters (Meintjes et al., PMID 30428290) asks a different question and is fenced in the synthesis, not carded. PROPOSED stamp: POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: Meintjes 2010: prednisone cut hospital/procedure days (median 0 vs 3; P=0.04) and sped symptom recovery
cards.summary: Meintjes 2010: prednisone cut hospital/procedure days (median 0 vs 3; P=0.04) and sped symptom recovery
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (single pivotal trial)
cards.people: 110 HIV-infected patients with paradoxical TB-IRIS after starting antiretroviral therapy (55 per arm), excluding immediately life-threatening manifestations; prednisone was 1.5 mg/kg/day for 2 weeks then 0.75 mg/kg/day for 2 weeks. The abstract does not print a mean age or sex mix. Isolates from 10 participants proved rifampicin-resistant after enrolment.
cards.result: The primary combined endpoint — days of hospitalisation plus outpatient therapeutic procedures (counted as hospital days) — was lower on prednisone: median 0 days (IQR 0–3) versus 3 days (IQR 0–9) on placebo (P=0.04). Improvements in symptoms, Karnofsky score, and quality of life (MOS-HIV) were significantly greater on prednisone at 2 and 4 weeks but not at later time points; chest radiographs improved significantly more at weeks 2 (P=0.002) and 4 (P=0.02). Infections on study medication occurred in 27 prednisone versus 17 placebo participants (P=0.05); severe infections did not differ (2 versus 4; P=0.40).
cards.watchOut: The benefit is early and symptomatic — by later time points the groups converge — and the infection imbalance (27 versus 17), though not in severe infections, is part of the trade. Ten participants turned out to have rifampicin-resistant TB, which is why the authors insist on excluding drug resistance and other causes of deterioration before giving steroids.

shelves.title: Dexamethasone in tuberculous meningitis (Thwaites)
shelves.question: In adolescents and adults with tuberculous meningitis, does adjunctive dexamethasone reduce death versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: AIDS-Related Opportunistic Infections · Adjuvants, Immunologic · Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Dexamethasone · Double-Blind Method · Female · Glucocorticoids · HIV Infections · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Multivariate Analysis · Survival Analysis · Tuberculosis, Meningeal
shelves.balance: PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C) — death is the outcome at issue. In the single pivotal trial (545 patients over 14 years of age in Vietnam; double-blind), adjunctive dexamethasone was associated with a reduced risk of death: relative risk 0.69 relative (95% CI 0.52–0.92; P=0.01), consistent across disease-severity grades (stratified RR 0.68) and in the HIV-infected subgroup (stratified RR 0.78, 0.59–1.04). The abstract prints no absolute mortality rates, so none are carded — the shelf carries the relative effect and says so. Dexamethasone did NOT significantly reduce severe disability among survivors (18.2% versus 13.8%; P=0.27), and the combined outcome of death or severe disability was not significant (odds ratio 0.81, 0.58–1.13; P=0.22): this is a survival benefit without a demonstrated disability benefit. Serious adverse events were fewer on dexamethasone (26 of 274 versus 45 of 271). Scope boundary: bacterial meningitis dexamethasone is Shelf #236; this shelf is tuberculous meningitis only. PROPOSED stamp: LIKELY.

cards.headline: Thwaites 2004: dexamethasone reduced death in tuberculous meningitis (RR 0.69 relative) — but not severe disability
cards.summary: Thwaites 2004: dexamethasone reduced death in tuberculous meningitis (RR 0.69 relative) — but not severe disability
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (single pivotal trial)
cards.people: 545 patients over 14 years of age with tuberculous meningitis, with or without HIV infection, in Vietnam, randomised to adjunctive dexamethasone (274) or placebo (271) alongside antituberculosis treatment; only 10 patients (1.8%) were lost to follow-up at 9 months. The abstract does not print a mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Treatment with dexamethasone was associated with a reduced risk of death: relative risk 0.69 relative (95% CI 0.52–0.92; P=0.01). The effect was consistent by disease-severity grade (stratified RR 0.68, 0.52–0.91; P=0.007) and by HIV status (stratified RR 0.78, 0.59–1.04; P=0.08). Severe disability among survivors was not reduced (34 of 187 [18.2%] on dexamethasone versus 22 of 159 [13.8%] on placebo; P=0.27), nor was the composite of death or severe disability (odds ratio 0.81, 0.58–1.13; P=0.22). Serious adverse events were significantly fewer on dexamethasone (26 of 274 versus 45 of 271; P=0.02).
cards.watchOut: The abstract prints the mortality effect only as a relative risk, without the per-group death rates — no absolute rates are carded, and any number-needed-to-treat quoted elsewhere is not from this record. More survivors with dexamethasone means the disability comparison is among unequal survivor pools; the honest summary is 'more patients survive; of survivors, disability is not reduced.' The record carries no registry ID (2004 trial).
cards.source: Thwaites GE et al. Dexamethasone for the treatment of tuberculous meningitis in adolescents and adults. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2004. PMID: 15496623. shelves.title: Intensified antituberculosis therapy in tuberculous meningitis (Heemskerk)
shelves.question: In adults with tuberculous meningitis, does intensified therapy — higher-dose rifampin (15 mg/kg) plus levofloxacin for the first eight weeks — reduce mortality versus the standard regimen?
shelves.mesh: AIDS-Related Opportunistic Infections · Adult · Antitubercular Agents · Double-Blind Method · Drug Resistance, Bacterial · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · HIV Infections · Humans · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Levofloxacin · Male · Middle Aged · Mycobacterium tuberculosis · Proportional Hazards Models · Rifampin · Tuberculosis, Meningeal
shelves.balance: PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C) — mortality is the primary outcome, and the result is a null. In the single pivotal trial (817 adults in Vietnam; double-blind; 349 HIV-infected), death by 9 months occurred in 113 of 408 patients on intensified therapy versus 114 of 409 on the standard regimen: hazard ratio 0.94 relative (95% CI 0.73–1.22; P=0.66), with no significant difference in any subgroup (the possible exception of isoniazid-resistant disease is hypothesis-generating only) and no significant differences in secondary outcomes. A correction is printed on the card: the topic file gives the hazard ratio as about 1.1; the record prints 0.94. Adverse events leading to treatment interruption were numerically more frequent on intensified therapy (95 versus 64 events; P=0.08). PROPOSED stamp: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference).

cards.summary: Heemskerk 2016: intensified therapy did not reduce mortality (113 vs 114 deaths; HR 0.94; P=0.66)
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (single pivotal trial)
cards.people: 817 adults with a clinical diagnosis of tuberculous meningitis at two Vietnamese hospitals (349 HIV-infected), randomised to the standard 9-month regimen with rifampin 10 mg/kg/day (409) or an intensified regimen with rifampin 15 mg/kg/day plus levofloxacin 20 mg/kg/day for the first 8 weeks (408). shelves.title: Vitamin A in children with severe measles (Hussey; Coutsoudis)
shelves.question: In children hospitalised with severe measles, does high-dose vitamin A reduce mortality and pneumonia morbidity versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Child, Preschool · Croup · Diarrhea · Diterpenes · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Infant · Male · Measles · Pneumonia · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Retinol-Binding Proteins · Retinyl Esters · Serum Albumin · Vitamin A · Morbidity · Placebos · Respiratory Tract Diseases · Respiratory Tract Infections · South Africa
shelves.balance: PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C) — mortality in children is at issue. Two South African randomised trials agree in direction. In Hussey (189 hospitalised children with measles complicated by pneumonia, diarrhoea, or croup; median age 10 months), 12 children died — 10 on placebo and 2 on vitamin A (P=0.05) — and the risk of death or a major complication was halved on vitamin A (relative risk 0.51 relative, 95% CI 0.35–0.74); recovery from pneumonia (6.3 versus 12.4 days) and diarrhoea (5.6 versus 8.5 days) was faster, croup less frequent (13 versus 27 cases), and hospital stay shorter (10.6 versus 14.8 days). A precision correction is printed on the card: the topic file's 'cut mortality by more than half' belongs to the death-or-major-complication composite (RR 0.51); the mortality counts themselves are 2 versus 10 — a large relative difference on very few events, at P=0.05. In Coutsoudis (60 hospitalised children), integrated morbidity scores were reduced by 82%, 61%, and 85% at day 8, 6 weeks, and 6 months, mainly through respiratory infection; one death occurred, on placebo. Both trials predate modern measles epidemiology and neither record carries a registry ID. PROPOSED stamp: LIKELY. Scope boundary: distinct from population vitamin A supplementation for prevention (wave-1 topic #1366).

cards.headline: Hussey 1990: deaths 2 versus 10; death-or-major-complication risk halved (RR 0.51 relative); faster recovery across outcomes
cards.summary: Hussey 1990: deaths 2 versus 10; death-or-major-complication risk halved (RR 0.51 relative); faster recovery across outcomes
cards.people: 189 children hospitalised at a regional centre in South Africa with measles complicated by pneumonia, diarrhoea, or croup (median age 10 months), assigned to vitamin A (92; total 400,000 IU of retinyl palmitate orally, begun within 5 days of rash onset) or placebo (97). Serum retinol was markedly depressed in both groups (mean 0.405 µmol/L) and 92% had hyporetinaemia, although clinically apparent vitamin A deficiency was rare.
cards.result: Of the 12 children who died, 10 were in the placebo group (P=0.05). The risk of death or a major complication during the hospital stay was half that of controls (relative risk 0.51 relative, 95% CI 0.35–0.74). Vitamin A children recovered faster from pneumonia (mean 6.3 versus 12.4 days; P<0.001) and diarrhoea (5.6 versus 8.5 days; P<0.001), had less croup (13 versus 27 cases; P=0.03), and spent fewer days in hospital (10.6 versus 14.8 days; P=0.01).
cards.watchOut: The mortality result rests on 12 deaths; the P value sits exactly at 0.05, and the trial's robust finding is the composite of death or major complication plus consistently faster recovery. The population had profoundly depressed retinol levels despite little clinical deficiency — effect size in better-nourished populations is an extrapolation, not a finding.

shelves.title: Shorter and combination benznidazole regimens for chronic Chagas disease (BENDITA)
shelves.question: In adults with chronic indeterminate Chagas disease, do shorter benznidazole courses (two weeks) or benznidazole combined with fosravuconazole achieve sustained parasitological clearance non-inferior to the standard eight-week course, with fewer adverse events?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Bolivia · Chagas Disease · Double-Blind Method · Drug Administration Schedule · Drug Therapy, Combination · Drug-Related Side Effects and Adverse Reactions · Female · Humans · Male · Nitroimidazoles · Parasite Load · Treatment Outcome · Triazoles · Young Adult
shelves.balance: In the single phase 2 trial (210 adults in Bolivia; double-blind, seven arms including placebo), sustained parasitological clearance at 6 months (the record's primary efficacy endpoint — the topic file's 12-month framing reflects the follow-up period, not the printed primary analysis) was 83–89% across all benznidazole arms versus 3% (1 of 30) on placebo: 89% for the standard 300 mg 8-week course, 89% for 4 weeks, 83% for 2 weeks, 83% for 150 mg for 4 weeks, and 83–85% for the fosravuconazole combinations (all P<0.0001 versus placebo). Adverse events leading to discontinuation (15 patients, 7%) clustered in the 8-week and combination arms; none occurred in the 2-week arm or on placebo. Six patients had serious adverse events (including leukopenia and neutropenia); there were no treatment-related deaths. The endpoint is PCR clearance — a surrogate; no cardiac or clinical outcome was measured. This shelf is flagged as a two-trial-gate exception candidate (single phase 2 trial, surrogate endpoint) and should be withdrawn or re-scoped if the developer rejects the exception. PROPOSED stamp: POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: BENDITA 2021: all benznidazole regimens cleared parasites in 83–89% versus 3% on placebo; shortest course had no discontinuations
cards.summary: BENDITA 2021: all benznidazole regimens cleared parasites in 83–89% versus 3% on placebo; shortest course had no discontinuations
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, double-dummy phase 2 trial (single trial, seven arms)
cards.people: 210 adults aged 18–50 years with chronic indeterminate Chagas disease (serology-confirmed, positive qualitative PCR) at three outpatient units in Bolivia, randomised 30 per arm to benznidazole 300 mg daily for 8, 4, or 2 weeks; benznidazole 150 mg daily for 4 weeks; 150 mg for 4 weeks plus fosravuconazole; 300 mg weekly for 8 weeks plus fosravuconazole; or placebo, with 12 months of follow-up. The intention-to-treat population was all 210; per protocol, 190.
cards.result: Sustained parasitological clearance at 6 months (intention to treat; denominators as printed reflect patients with results) was 25 of 28 (89%) on benznidazole 300 mg for 8 weeks, 25 of 28 (89%) for 4 weeks, 24 of 29 (83%) for 2 weeks, 25 of 30 (83%) on 150 mg for 4 weeks, 23 of 28 (85%) on 150 mg plus fosravuconazole, and 24 of 29 (83%) on weekly 300 mg plus fosravuconazole, versus 1 of 30 (3%) on placebo (rate differences versus placebo 79–86 percentage points; P<0.0001 for all comparisons). Fifteen patients (7%) had adverse events leading to discontinuation — most in the 8-week and combination arms, none in the 2-week or placebo arms. Ten serious adverse events occurred in six patients (including leukopenia [3] and neutropenia [2]); no treatment-related deaths.
cards.watchOut: PCR clearance is a surrogate: the trial says nothing about progression to cardiomyopathy, the outcome that matters in chronic Chagas disease. Each arm holds only about 30 patients, so between-regimen comparisons (the shelf's actual question) are imprecise — the trial shows all regimens beat placebo decisively, not that 2 weeks equals 8 weeks. Clearance denominators in the abstract run 28–30 per arm against 30 randomised.
cards.source: Torrico F et al. New regimens of benznidazole monotherapy and in combination with fosravuconazole for treatment of Chagas disease (BENDITA): a phase 2, double-blind, randomised trial. shelves.title: Dolutegravir-based first-line therapy versus efavirenz (ADVANCE; NAMSAL)
shelves.question: In treatment-naive people with HIV, is dolutegravir-based first-line therapy non-inferior to efavirenz-based therapy for viral suppression at 48 weeks — and what does it cost in weight gain?
shelves.mesh: Adenine · Adolescent · Adult · Anti-Retroviral Agents · Bone Density · CD4 Lymphocyte Count · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · HIV Infections · HIV Integrase Inhibitors · HIV-1 · Heterocyclic Compounds, 3-Ring · Humans · Intention to Treat Analysis · Male · Middle Aged · Oxazines · Phosphorous Acids · Piperazines · Pregnancy · Pregnancy Complications, Infectious · Prodrugs · Pyridones · RNA, Viral · Uracil · Viral Load · Young Adult · Dolutegravir
shelves.balance: LIKELY — two phase 3 trials in African populations agree on non-inferiority and on the weight signal. ADVANCE (South Africa, n=1,053): HIV-1 RNA below 50 copies/mL at week 48 in 84% (dolutegravir with tenofovir alafenamide) and 85% (dolutegravir with tenofovir disoproxil) versus 79% on efavirenz standard care, non-inferior against a −10-point margin. NAMSAL (Cameroon, n=613): 74.5% on dolutegravir versus 69.0% on low-dose efavirenz 400 mg (difference 5.5 points, 95% CI −1.6 to 12.7; P<0.001 for non-inferiority). Weight gain was consistently greater on dolutegravir regimens — in ADVANCE a mean of 6.4 kg on the alafenamide combination (most in women) versus 1.7 kg on efavirenz; in NAMSAL a median of 5.0 versus 3.0 kg, with obesity in 12.3% versus 5.4%. Correction printed on the ADVANCE card: the trial enrolled patients from age 12, so the topic file's 'adults' framing is wider than the record.

cards.headline: ADVANCE: suppression 84–85% on dolutegravir regimens versus 79% on efavirenz — non-inferior; weight gain greatest on TAF–dolutegravir
cards.summary: ADVANCE: suppression 84–85% on dolutegravir regimens versus 79% on efavirenz — non-inferior; weight gain greatest on TAF–dolutegravir
cards.type: Randomised, open-label, phase 3 trial (96 weeks; 48-week primary report)
cards.people: 1,053 patients in South Africa, aged 12 years or older (the record's entry criterion — adolescents were eligible), ART-naive; more than 99% Black, 59% female, mean age 32 years, mean CD4 count 337 cells/mm³. Mean weight increase was 6.4 kg (alafenamide), 3.2 kg (disoproxil), and 1.7 kg (standard care), greatest among female patients on the alafenamide combination. No resistance to integrase inhibitors was identified in patients failing dolutegravir regimens; discontinuations were more frequent in the standard-care group.
cards.watchOut: Open-label, and the comparison bundles two changes at once (integrase inhibitor and, in one arm, the tenofovir prodrug), so the weight signal cannot be apportioned between dolutegravir and alafenamide from this trial alone. shelves.question: In donor-positive/recipient-negative kidney transplant recipients, is letermovir non-inferior to valganciclovir for preventing CMV disease through week 52, with less myelosuppression?

shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — a single phase 3 non-inferiority trial (601 randomised). Committee-confirmed CMV disease through week 52 occurred in 10.4% on letermovir versus 11.8% on valganciclovir (stratum-adjusted difference −1.4%, 95% CI −6.5 to 3.8), inside the prespecified 10% non-inferiority margin; no letermovir patient developed CMV disease by week 28, versus five (1.7%) on valganciclovir. The safety separation is large: leukopenia or neutropenia through week 28 in 26% versus 64% (P<.001), and discontinuation for adverse events in 4.1% versus 13.5%. Flagged on its face as a two-trial-gate exception candidate — a single pivotal trial supports the shelf; withdraw or re-scope it if the developer rejects the exception. Distinct from Shelf #722 (letermovir prophylaxis in stem-cell transplant recipients, and maribavir rescue) by population, and from Shelf #1634 (valganciclovir duration in kidney transplant) by question — drug choice here, duration there.

cards.headline: Letermovir non-inferior for CMV disease (10.4% versus 11.8%) with leukopenia/neutropenia in 26% versus 64%
cards.summary: Letermovir non-inferior for CMV disease (10.4% versus 11.8%) with leukopenia/neutropenia in 26% versus 64%
cards.type: Randomised, double-masked, double-dummy, non-inferiority phase 3 trial
cards.people: 601 CMV-seronegative kidney transplant recipients of organs from CMV-seropositive donors at 94 sites; 589 received at least one dose (mean age 49.6 years; 71.6% men), randomised to letermovir 480 mg daily (289 analysed) or valganciclovir 900 mg daily (297 analysed) for up to 200 days after transplant.
cards.result: CMV disease through post-transplant week 52: 10.4% on letermovir versus 11.8% on valganciclovir (stratum-adjusted difference −1.4% [95% CI, −6.5% to 3.8%]) — non-inferior against the prespecified 10% margin. No letermovir participant versus five (1.7%) valganciclovir participants developed CMV disease through week 28. Quantifiable CMV DNAemia by week 28: 2.1% versus 8.8%. Leukopenia or neutropenia through week 28: 26% versus 64% (difference −37.9% [−45.1% to −30.3%]; P<.001). Discontinuation of prophylaxis for adverse events: 4.1% versus 13.5%.
cards.watchOut: Non-inferiority against a wide 10% margin in a single trial; the efficacy difference interval (−6.5 to 3.8) is compatible with letermovir being modestly better or modestly worse. The decisive practical separation is haematological, not antiviral.
cards.source: Limaye AP et al. Letermovir vs Valganciclovir for Prophylaxis of Cytomegalovirus in High-Risk Kidney Transplant Recipients: A Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA. 2023. PMID: 37279999. shelves.title: Nirmatrelvir–ritonavir as post-exposure prophylaxis for COVID-19 (EPIC-PEP)
shelves.question: In adults exposed to COVID-19 in the household, does a 5- or 10-day course of nirmatrelvir–ritonavir prevent symptomatic, confirmed infection versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Young Adult · Administration, Oral · Antiviral Agents · COVID-19 · COVID-19 Drug Treatment · Double-Blind Method · Drug Combinations · Drug Therapy, Combination · Indazoles · Indoles · Lactams · Leucine · Nitriles · Post-Exposure Prophylaxis · Proline · Ritonavir · SARS-CoV-2
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — one large placebo-controlled trial (n=2,736) found no significant reduction in symptomatic, confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection by day 14 with either a 5-day course (2.6% versus 3.9% on placebo; relative risk reduction 29.8%, 95% CI −16.7 to 57.8; P=0.17) or a 10-day course (2.4% versus 3.9%; relative reduction 35.5%, −11.5 to 62.7; P=0.12). The stamp is POSSIBLE rather than LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) because the intervals are wide: a relative benefit approaching 60% is not excluded by this record, so the honest statement is 'no benefit shown', not 'no benefit exists'. Dysgeusia was the commonest adverse event (5.9% and 6.8% versus 0.7%). Distinct from Shelf #580 (nirmatrelvir–ritonavir as treatment of early infection) — this shelf is prophylaxis after exposure, in people not yet infected.

cards.headline: EPIC-PEP: symptomatic infection in 2.6% (5-day) and 2.4% (10-day) versus 3.9% on placebo — neither significant
cards.summary: EPIC-PEP: symptomatic infection in 2.6% (5-day) and 2.4% (10-day) versus 3.9% on placebo — neither significant
cards.people: 2,736 asymptomatic, rapid-antigen-negative adults exposed to a household contact with COVID-19 within 96 hours, randomised to nirmatrelvir–ritonavir for 5 days (921), for 10 days (917), or matching placebo (898). The abstract does not print mean age or the sex split.
cards.result: Symptomatic, confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection by day 14 developed in 2.6% (5-day), 2.4% (10-day), and 3.9% (placebo). Relative risk reductions versus placebo were 29.8% (95% CI, −16.7 to 57.8; P=0.17) for 5 days and 35.5% (−11.5 to 62.7; P=0.12) for 10 days — relative measures, labelled as such; neither differed significantly from placebo. Adverse events were similar across groups except dysgeusia (5.9% and 6.8% versus 0.7%).
cards.watchOut: A null result with wide intervals: the trial rules out neither a moderate relative benefit nor a small harm. Event rates were low (under 4% overall), limiting precision for the prophylaxis question.
cards.source: Hammond J et al. Oral Nirmatrelvir-Ritonavir as Postexposure Prophylaxis for Covid-19. N Engl J Med. 2024. PMID: 39018532. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT05047601, from the record's databank fields. shelves.title: Switching suppressed patients to dolutegravir plus boosted darunavir (DUALIS)
shelves.question: In virologically suppressed adults on two NRTIs plus boosted darunavir, can the NRTI backbone be dropped — switching to dolutegravir + boosted darunavir — without losing suppression at 48 weeks?
shelves.balance: Yes for suppression, at a small tolerability cost — on one open-label trial. DUALIS randomised 263 virologically suppressed adults already taking two NRTIs plus boosted darunavir to switch to dolutegravir + boosted darunavir or to continue the three-drug regimen. At week 48, HIV RNA was below 50 copies/mL in 86.3% of switchers versus 87.9% of continuers (difference −1.6%, 95.48% CI −9.9 to +6.7), meeting the prespecified −10% noninferiority margin, and no treatment-emergent resistance developed in either arm. The trade-off: discontinuations for adverse events were 4.6% (6 patients) on the two-drug regimen versus 0.8% (1 patient) on the three-drug regimen. The interval's lower bound sits close to the margin, the trial is open-label, and everyone entered already suppressed on a darunavir-based regimen — a selected, adherent population. PROPOSED POSSIBLE — a single trial (THIN) on a virologic surrogate endpoint, adequate to support the switch in similar patients but not stronger.

cards.headline: Spinner 2020 (DUALIS): switching to dolutegravir + boosted darunavir noninferior for maintaining suppression at 48 weeks
cards.summary: Spinner 2020 (DUALIS): switching to dolutegravir + boosted darunavir noninferior for maintaining suppression at 48 weeks
cards.people: 263 virologically suppressed adults (HIV RNA <50 copies/mL for at least 24 weeks on 2 NRTIs + boosted darunavir) randomised and treated: switch to dolutegravir 50 mg + boosted darunavir (n=131) or continue 2 NRTIs + boosted darunavir (n=132). Primary endpoint: proportion with HIV RNA <50 copies/mL at week 48; noninferiority margin −10%.
cards.result: HIV RNA <50 copies/mL at week 48 in 86.3% (113/131) on the two-drug regimen versus 87.9% (116/132) on the three-drug regimen (difference −1.6%, 95.48% CI −9.9 to +6.7) — noninferior. Kaplan–Meier estimates of confirmed HIV RNA ≥50 copies/mL were 1.6% versus 3.1%. Discontinuations for adverse events: 4.6% (6) versus 0.8% (1). No treatment-emergent resistance was observed.
cards.watchOut: Open-label, and the confidence interval's lower bound (−9.9%) nearly touches the −10% margin — noninferiority is met but not roomy. Participants were already suppressed on the same boosted darunavir backbone; the result does not cover starting this combination in untreated or non-suppressed patients, or in people with darunavir or integrase resistance (excluded).
cards.source: Spinner CD et al. Efficacy and safety of switching to dolutegravir with boosted darunavir in virologically suppressed adults with HIV-1: the DUALIS study. Open Forum Infect Dis. 2020. PMID: 32965277. Registry ID: EudraCT 2015-000360-34, from the record. MeSH: none assigned on the PubMed record.

shelves.title: Long-acting cabotegravir–rilpivirine every 8 weeks versus every 4 weeks (ATLAS-2M)
shelves.question: In suppressed adults on long-acting cabotegravir + rilpivirine maintenance, is dosing every 8 weeks as effective as every 4 weeks?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Alanine Transaminase · Anti-HIV Agents · Delayed-Action Preparations · Diketopiperazines · Drug Administration Schedule · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · HIV Infections · HIV-1 · Humans · Injections, Intramuscular · Male · Middle Aged · Pyridones · RNA, Viral · Rilpivirine · Viral Load
shelves.balance: A large, definitive noninferiority trial: every-8-week injections hold suppression as well as every-4-week injections. ATLAS-2M randomised 1,045 suppressed adults on long-acting cabotegravir + rilpivirine to continue every 4 weeks or stretch to every 8 weeks. At week 48, HIV-1 RNA ≥50 copies/mL — the nonresponse endpoint — occurred in 2% on 8-weekly versus 1% on 4-weekly dosing (adjusted difference 0.8 percentage points, 95% CI −0.6 to 2.2), comfortably inside the 4% noninferiority margin. Confirmed virological failure was uncommon in both arms but numerically higher with the longer interval (8 patients, 2%, vs 2, under 1%) — the one number to keep in view, because failures on long-acting therapy can select resistance to two drug classes at once. Adverse events other than injection-site reactions were reported by 81% of participants, with no treatment-related deaths. PROPOSED LIKELY — one large trial that settles the interval question for patients already stable on this regimen. Distinct from Shelf #723, which cards the original monthly-versus-oral question (ATLAS/FLAIR).

cards.headline: Overton 2021 (ATLAS-2M): every-8-week cabotegravir–rilpivirine noninferior to every-4-week at week 48
cards.summary: Overton 2021 (ATLAS-2M): every-8-week cabotegravir–rilpivirine noninferior to every-4-week at week 48
cards.people: 1,045 virologically suppressed adults on long-acting cabotegravir + rilpivirine, randomised to injections every 8 weeks (n=522) or every 4 weeks (n=523). Primary endpoint: proportion with HIV-1 RNA ≥50 copies/mL at week 48 (FDA snapshot), noninferiority margin 4%.
cards.result: HIV-1 RNA ≥50 copies/mL at week 48 in 2% of the every-8-week group versus 1% of the every-4-week group (adjusted difference 0.8 percentage points, 95% CI −0.6 to 2.2) — noninferior. Confirmed virological failure occurred in 8 patients (2%) versus 2 (<1%). Adverse events excluding injection-site reactions were reported in 81% of participants; there were no treatment-related deaths.
cards.watchOut: Everyone entered already suppressed and stable on the monthly regimen — the trial does not address starting long-acting therapy, and the numerically higher confirmed-failure count on the 8-week schedule (8 vs 2) matters because failure on this regimen risks dual-class resistance. Missed or late injections are a different risk with a 2-month interval; the trial's visit discipline may not match every clinic's.
cards.source: Overton ET et al. Long-acting cabotegravir and rilpivirine dosed every 2 months in adults with HIV-1 infection (ATLAS-2M). Lancet. 2021. PMID: 33308425. shelves.title: Lenacapavir for multidrug-resistant HIV-1 (CAPELLA)
shelves.question: In people with multidrug-resistant HIV-1 and few remaining options, does adding the capsid inhibitor lenacapavir to an optimised background regimen suppress the virus?
shelves.mesh: Anti-HIV Agents · CD4 Lymphocyte Count · Capsid · Drug Resistance, Multiple, Viral · Drug Therapy, Combination · HIV Infections · HIV-1 · Humans · RNA, Viral · Viral Load
shelves.balance: For patients with almost no options left, lenacapavir plainly does something: in CAPELLA's randomised lead-in, 88% of patients given oral lenacapavir on top of their failing regimen achieved at least a 0.5 log₁₀ viral-load drop by day 15, versus 17% on placebo — proof the drug itself is active, not just the optimised background built around it. By week 26, with subcutaneous lenacapavir every 6 months plus that optimised background, 81–83% had viral loads below 50 copies/mL, with mean CD4 gains of 75–104 cells/mm³. The cautions are structural: only 72 patients, one cohort randomised only for the 14-day lead-in, no long-term comparator, and capsid resistance substitutions emerged in 8 patients (6 with M66I) — the drug's Achilles heel when the background regimen is weak. PROPOSED POSSIBLE — a single small trial (THIN) in a population with no alternatives; the randomised lead-in makes the activity claim solid, the durability claim less so. Distinct from Shelf #317, which covers lenacapavir as pre-exposure prophylaxis.

cards.headline: Segal-Maurer 2022 (CAPELLA): lenacapavir active against multidrug-resistant HIV-1 — 88% vs 17% early viral-load response; 81–83% suppressed at week 26
cards.summary: Segal-Maurer 2022 (CAPELLA): lenacapavir active against multidrug-resistant HIV-1 — 88% vs 17% early viral-load response; 81–83% suppressed at week 26
cards.type: Phase 3 trial with a randomised placebo-controlled lead-in cohort
cards.people: 72 people with multidrug-resistant HIV-1 infection in two cohorts of 36. Cohort 1 was randomised to oral lenacapavir or placebo for 14 days on top of their failing regimen, then all received subcutaneous lenacapavir every 6 months plus an optimised background regimen; cohort 2 received lenacapavir plus optimised background from the start. Primary endpoint: ≥0.5 log₁₀ copies/mL viral-load decline by day 15 (cohort 1).
cards.result: A ≥0.5 log₁₀ decline by day 15 occurred in 88% (21/24) on lenacapavir versus 17% (2/12) on placebo (absolute difference 71 percentage points, 95% CI 35 to 90). At week 26, viral load was <50 copies/mL in 81% of cohort 1 and 83% of cohort 2; least-squares mean CD4 increases were 75 and 104 cells/mm³. Lenacapavir-related capsid substitutions emerged in 8 patients (6 with M66I). No serious adverse events were identified as related to lenacapavir.
cards.watchOut: Only the 14-day lead-in was placebo-controlled; week-26 suppression rates are single-arm and depend heavily on how active each patient's optimised background regimen was. Emergent capsid resistance in 8 of 72 patients — mostly where the background was effectively inactive — is the central long-term risk. Small numbers throughout.
cards.source: Segal-Maurer S et al. Capsid inhibition with lenacapavir in multidrug-resistant HIV-1 infection (CAPELLA). N Engl J Med. 2022. PMID: 35544387. Registry ID: NCT04150068, from the record. shelves.title: Dolutegravir-based therapy in children and adolescents (ODYSSEY)
shelves.question: In children and adolescents (≥14 kg) starting first- or second-line ART, is dolutegravir-based therapy better than standard non-dolutegravir care?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Adolescent · Alkynes · Anti-Retroviral Agents · Benzoxazines · Child · Child, Preschool · Cholesterol · Cyclopropanes · Dolutegravir · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · HIV Infections · HIV Integrase Inhibitors · HIV Protease Inhibitors · HIV-1 · Heterocyclic Compounds, 3-Ring · Humans · Male · Oxazines · Piperazines · Pyridones · Viral Load
shelves.balance: The trial that settled paediatric first- and second-line policy, and it did more than show noninferiority — it showed superiority. ODYSSEY randomised 707 children and adolescents weighing at least 14 kg (median age 12.2 years; 44% starting first-line, 56% second-line) to dolutegravir-based therapy or standard care (mostly efavirenz-based first-line, protease-inhibitor-based second-line). By 96 weeks, treatment failure — a composite of virologic and clinical failure — had occurred in 47 children on dolutegravir versus 75 on standard care (estimated probabilities 0.14 vs 0.22; difference −0.08, 95% CI −0.14 to −0.03; P=0.004). Safety was at least as good: fewer children on dolutegravir had adverse events that forced a change of therapy (5 vs 17; P=0.01), with similar serious adverse event counts (35 vs 40). Open-label design and a composite endpoint keep this at LIKELY rather than beyond, but the effect is consistent across first- and second-line strata. PROPOSED LIKELY — one large randomised trial with a superiority result on a clinically meaningful composite.

cards.headline: Turkova 2021 (ODYSSEY): dolutegravir superior to standard care in children — treatment failure probability 0.14 vs 0.22 by 96 weeks
cards.summary: Turkova 2021 (ODYSSEY): dolutegravir superior to standard care in children — treatment failure probability 0.14 vs 0.22 by 96 weeks
cards.people: 707 children and adolescents (≥14 kg; median age 12.2 years) starting first-line (44%) or second-line (56%) antiretroviral therapy, randomised to dolutegravir-based therapy (n=350) or standard non-dolutegravir care (n=357). Primary endpoint: treatment failure (virologic or clinical) by 96 weeks.
cards.result: Treatment failure occurred in 47 participants on dolutegravir versus 75 on standard care (estimated probability 0.14 vs 0.22; difference −0.08, 95% CI −0.14 to −0.03; P=0.004) — superiority, beyond the trial's noninferiority hypothesis. At least one serious adverse event occurred in 35 versus 40 participants; grade 3 or higher adverse events in 73 versus 86; adverse events leading to a change of antiretroviral therapy in 5 versus 17 (P=0.01).
cards.watchOut: Open-label, and the composite mixes virologic failure with clinical events and regimen changes, so part of the advantage may run through tolerability-driven switching rather than antiviral potency alone. Standard care was a moving target across sites and lines of therapy (efavirenz or protease inhibitors); the trial does not compare dolutegravir against every modern alternative individually.

shelves.title: Dolutegravir when ART starts in late pregnancy (DolPHIN-2)
shelves.question: In women who start ART in the third trimester (≥28 weeks), does dolutegravir suppress viral load by delivery more reliably than efavirenz?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Alkynes · Anti-HIV Agents · Benzoxazines · Cyclopropanes · Female · HIV Infections · HIV Integrase Inhibitors · Heterocyclic Compounds, 3-Ring · Humans · Infant, Newborn · Infectious Disease Transmission, Vertical · Outcome Assessment, Health Care · Oxazines · Piperazines · Pregnancy · Pregnancy Outcome · Pregnancy Trimester, Third · Pyridones · Viral Load · Dolutegravir
shelves.balance: When treatment starts at 28 weeks or later, speed is the whole question — every unsuppressed week is transmission risk — and dolutegravir is much faster. DolPHIN-2 randomised 268 women in South Africa and Uganda starting ART in the third trimester (median time on therapy before birth: 55 days) to dolutegravir- or efavirenz-based regimens. By the post-partum visit, viral load was below 50 copies/mL in 74% on dolutegravir versus 43% on efavirenz (risk ratio 1.64, 95% CI 1.31 to 2.06 — a relative effect; the absolute gap is 31 percentage points). The safety ledger needs stating plainly: more maternal serious adverse events were reported on dolutegravir (30 vs 14 reports; P=0.013), though these clustered around pregnancy and the puerperium and were not judged drug-caused; stillbirths were 3 versus 1, judged unrelated; and all 3 infant HIV infections occurred in the dolutegravir group but were judged likely acquired in utero before suppression could be achieved — a marker of how late these women presented, not of drug failure. PROPOSED LIKELY — a single randomised trial with a large effect on the outcome that drives transmission risk, with the adverse-event imbalance disclosed on the face of the shelf.

cards.headline: Kintu 2020 (DolPHIN-2): 74% suppressed on dolutegravir vs 43% on efavirenz when ART starts in late pregnancy
cards.summary: Kintu 2020 (DolPHIN-2): 74% suppressed on dolutegravir vs 43% on efavirenz when ART starts in late pregnancy
cards.people: 268 women in South Africa and Uganda starting antiretroviral therapy at ≥28 weeks' gestation, randomised to dolutegravir-based (n=135) or efavirenz-based (n=133) therapy; median duration of therapy at birth was 55 days. Primary endpoint: viral load <50 copies/mL at the post-partum visit.
cards.result: Viral load <50 copies/mL at the post-partum visit in 74% (89/120) on dolutegravir versus 43% (50/117) on efavirenz (risk ratio 1.64, 95% CI 1.31 to 2.06 — relative; absolute rates 74% vs 43%). More maternal serious adverse events were reported in the dolutegravir group (30 vs 14 reports; P=0.013), particularly surrounding pregnancy and the puerperium. Stillbirths numbered 3 versus 1 and were judged unrelated to treatment; 3 infant HIV infections, all in the dolutegravir group, were judged likely to have occurred in utero.
cards.watchOut: Open-label, and the population is defined by very late presentation — the results answer the rescue question (start late, suppress fast), not routine first-trimester initiation. The maternal serious-adverse-event imbalance (30 vs 14) is real in the data even if the events were pregnancy-related rather than drug-attributed; it should be quoted whenever the efficacy figures are.

shelves.title: Dolutegravir with rifampicin-based tuberculosis therapy (INSPIRING)
shelves.question: In ART-naive adults being treated for drug-susceptible tuberculosis with rifampicin, can dolutegravir (dose-doubled during TB therapy) hold HIV suppression as well as efavirenz?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Anti-HIV Agents · CD4 Lymphocyte Count · Coinfection · Dolutegravir · HIV Infections · Heterocyclic Compounds, 3-Ring · Humans · Oxazines · Piperazines · Pyridones · RNA, Viral · Treatment Outcome · Tuberculosis · Viral Load
shelves.balance: Encouraging, but the study was not built to prove the comparison its question implies. INSPIRING randomised 113 ART-naive adults on rifampicin-based TB therapy to dolutegravir 50 mg twice daily (the dose doubled to offset rifampicin's enzyme induction) or efavirenz. At week 48, HIV RNA was below 50 copies/mL in 75% (52/69) on dolutegravir versus 82% (36/44) on efavirenz — numerically lower on dolutegravir, with wide, overlapping intervals. The dolutegravir shortfall was driven by non-treatment-related discontinuations (10 patients lost to follow-up), not by virologic failure or resistance, and TB-associated immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome occurred in 4 patients per arm with no IRIS discontinuations. In other words: no signal that dose-doubled dolutegravir fails during rifampicin therapy, and a clean interaction story — but a small, open-label study whose primary endpoint was noncomparative cannot establish 'as good as efavirenz'. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) — single study (THIN), underpowered for the comparison, reassuring on feasibility and safety.

cards.headline: Dooley 2020 (INSPIRING): dose-doubled dolutegravir held suppression during rifampicin TB therapy; 75% vs 82% at week 48 in a noncomparative design
cards.summary: Dooley 2020 (INSPIRING): dose-doubled dolutegravir held suppression during rifampicin TB therapy; 75% vs 82% at week 48 in a noncomparative design
cards.people: 113 ART-naive adults receiving rifampicin-based treatment for drug-susceptible tuberculosis, randomised to dolutegravir 50 mg twice daily (n=69) or efavirenz (n=44), with dolutegravir dose-doubling maintained through TB therapy. Primary endpoint: proportion with HIV-1 RNA <50 copies/mL at week 48 in the dolutegravir arm.
cards.result: HIV-1 RNA <50 copies/mL at week 48 in 75% (52/69; 95% CI 65 to 86) on dolutegravir versus 82% (36/44; 95% CI 70 to 93) on efavirenz. Dolutegravir nonresponses were driven by non-treatment-related discontinuations, including 10 patients lost to follow-up, rather than virologic failure. TB-associated IRIS occurred in 4 patients in each arm, with no discontinuations for IRIS.
cards.watchOut: The trial was designed as a noncomparative evaluation of the dolutegravir arm — the efavirenz arm is a reference, not a powered comparator — so the 75% vs 82% gap should not be read as evidence of inferiority or equivalence. Small, open-label, and the week-48 snapshot punishes the dolutegravir arm for losses to follow-up unrelated to treatment.

shelves.title: Enhanced antimicrobial prophylaxis when starting ART in advanced HIV (REALITY) ⭐ OUTSTANDING-SINGLE
shelves.question: In adults and children (CD4 <100) starting ART in Africa, does an enhanced prophylaxis package (co-trimoxazole + isoniazid, 12 weeks fluconazole, 5 days azithromycin, single-dose albendazole) reduce early death versus standard prophylaxis?
shelves.mesh: AIDS-Related Opportunistic Infections · Adolescent · Adult · Africa South of the Sahara · Aged · Anti-Infective Agents · Anti-Retroviral Agents · CD4 Lymphocyte Count · Child · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · HIV Infections · Humans · Isoniazid · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Male · Middle Aged · Pyridoxine · Trimethoprim, Sulfamethoxazole Drug Combination · Young Adult
shelves.balance: OUTSTANDING-SINGLE — flagged under the Nov 8, 2026 rule: one randomised trial, a hard mortality endpoint, a decisive result; the developer's personal verdict is required and Tier C applies (death is the primary endpoint). REALITY randomised 1,805 patients with CD4 counts under 100 starting ART in Uganda, Zimbabwe, Malawi, and Kenya to an enhanced prophylaxis package — the REALITY package: continuous trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole plus at least 12 weeks of isoniazid–pyridoxine, 12 weeks of fluconazole, 5 days of azithromycin, and a single dose of albendazole — versus standard prophylaxis (trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole alone). Death at 24 weeks was 8.9% with enhanced prophylaxis versus 12.2% with standard care (HR 0.73, 95% CI 0.55 to 0.98; P=0.03 — a relative effect; absolute difference 3.3 percentage points), and the benefit persisted at 48 weeks (11.0% vs 14.4%; HR 0.76; P=0.04). Rates of tuberculosis, cryptococcal infection, oral or oesophageal candidiasis, death of unknown cause, and new hospitalisation were all significantly lower, without compromised viral suppression. One trial is one trial — but 1,805 patients, a mortality endpoint, and concordant cause-specific effects are as strong as single-trial evidence gets. PROPOSED LIKELY, held at that level — not higher — precisely because it stands alone.

cards.headline: Hakim 2017 (REALITY): enhanced prophylaxis cut death at 24 weeks from 12.2% to 8.9% in advanced HIV starting ART
cards.summary: Hakim 2017 (REALITY): enhanced prophylaxis cut death at 24 weeks from 12.2% to 8.9% in advanced HIV starting ART
cards.people: 1,805 HIV-infected adults and children aged 5 years or older (1,733 adults, 72 children/adolescents) starting ART with CD4 counts below 100 cells/mm³ in Uganda, Zimbabwe, Malawi, and Kenya, randomised to the REALITY enhanced prophylaxis package (n=906) or standard prophylaxis with trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole alone (n=899), followed for 48 weeks. Primary endpoint: 24-week mortality.
cards.result: Death by 24 weeks occurred in 8.9% with enhanced prophylaxis versus 12.2% with standard prophylaxis (hazard ratio 0.73, 95% CI 0.55 to 0.98; P=0.03); by 48 weeks, 11.0% versus 14.4% (HR 0.76, 0.58 to 0.99; P=0.04). The hazard ratios are relative effects; the absolute mortality differences are 3.3 percentage points at both time points. The enhanced-prophylaxis group had significantly lower rates of tuberculosis (P=0.02), cryptococcal infection (P=0.01), oral or oesophageal candidiasis (P=0.02), death of unknown cause (P=0.03), and new hospitalisation (P=0.03), without compromising viral suppression or increasing toxic effects.
cards.watchOut: A factorial trial — participants were simultaneously randomised to adjunctive raltegravir and supplementary food comparisons reported elsewhere; this shelf cards only the prophylaxis comparison. Open-label, and the package is a bundle: the trial cannot say which component (fluconazole and isoniazid are the usual suspects) carries the benefit. Populations with routine cryptococcal-antigen screening already in place may gain less.

shelves.title: Cryptococcal-antigen screening plus community adherence support when starting ART (REMSTART) ⭐ OUTSTANDING-SINGLE
shelves.question: In adults with advanced HIV (CD4 <200) starting ART, does serum cryptococcal-antigen screening with pre-emptive antifungal treatment, plus four weeks of lay-worker home adherence visits, reduce mortality versus standard clinic care?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Anti-HIV Agents · Antifungal Agents · Community Health Services · Female · HIV Infections · Humans · Male · Meningitis, Cryptococcal · Middle Aged · Patient Compliance · Tanzania · Treatment Outcome · Zambia
shelves.balance: OUTSTANDING-SINGLE — flagged under the Nov 8, 2026 rule: one randomised trial, a mortality endpoint, a decisive result; the developer's personal verdict is required and Tier C applies. REMSTART randomised 1,999 adults with CD4 counts under 200 starting ART in Tanzania and Zambia to standard clinic care or the REMSTART programme: serum cryptococcal-antigen screening with pre-emptive antifungal therapy for those testing positive, plus weekly home visits by lay workers for the first 4 weeks of treatment (with TB re-screening at 6–8 weeks in Tanzania only). Mortality at 12 months was 13% (134/1,001) with the programme versus 18% (180/998) with standard care — a 28% relative reduction (95% CI 10 to 43; P=0.004) and a 5-percentage-point absolute difference. The bundle design is the honest caveat: screening and home visits were delivered together, so the trial cannot apportion credit between finding cryptococcus early and keeping people in care. It is also a service-delivery intervention, whose effect depends on the clinics and lay-worker systems delivering it. PROPOSED LIKELY, held there because a single trial of a programme — however large — is still a single trial.

cards.headline: Mfinanga 2015 (REMSTART): 12-month mortality 13% with CrAg screening + home visits vs 18% with standard care
cards.summary: Mfinanga 2015 (REMSTART): 12-month mortality 13% with CrAg screening + home visits vs 18% with standard care
cards.people: 1,999 adults with HIV and CD4 counts below 200 cells/mm³ starting ART in Tanzania and Zambia, randomised to the REMSTART programme (n=1,001) — serum cryptococcal-antigen screening with antifungal therapy if positive, plus weekly lay-worker home visits for the first 4 weeks (TB re-screening at 6–8 weeks in Tanzania only) — or standard clinic care (n=998). Primary endpoint: all-cause mortality at 12 months.
cards.result: All-cause mortality at 12 months was 13% (134/1,001) in the intervention group versus 18% (180/998) in the standard-care group — mortality was 28% relatively lower (95% CI 10 to 43; P=0.004); the absolute rates differ by 5 percentage points.
cards.watchOut: A bundled programme, not a drug: the design cannot separate the cryptococcal-screening component from the adherence-visit component, and the Tanzanian sites added a TB re-screen the Zambian sites did not have. Effects of service-delivery interventions travel poorly — the result assumes lay-worker home visiting is actually deliverable at this intensity.

shelves.title: Same-day ART initiation at the first clinic visit (RapIT)
shelves.question: In newly diagnosed, treatment-eligible adults, does offering ART dispensing at the very first clinic visit improve uptake and viral suppression versus the standard multi-visit initiation process?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Ambulatory Care · Anti-HIV Agents · CD4 Lymphocyte Count · Female · Hospitals · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Point-of-Care Testing · Primary Health Care · Public Sector · South Africa · Time Factors · Treatment Outcome · Young Adult
shelves.balance: One unblinded trial of a process, and the process won on its combined endpoint. RapIT randomised 377 newly diagnosed, treatment-eligible adults at two South African clinics (median CD4 210) to the RapIT rapid-initiation algorithm — point-of-care testing and ART dispensed at the first visit — or the standard multi-visit pathway. At 10 months, 64% of the rapid group had both started ART and achieved viral suppression, versus 51% of the standard group (relative risk 1.26, 95% CI 1.05 to 1.50 — a relative effect; absolute rates 64% vs 51%). Initiation itself within 90 days was near-universal with rapid initiation (97% vs 72%; RR 1.36). The reassuring harm check: among patients who did start, attrition was no worse (HR 1.06, 0.61 to 1.84) — rushing the start did not obviously push people out of care. The limits are those of any workflow trial: two clinics, one country's staffing and testing platforms, an unblinded design, and an endpoint that mixes starting with suppressing. PROPOSED POSSIBLE — a single trial (THIN) of a site-specific care pathway, with a clinically meaningful combined outcome.

cards.headline: Rosen 2016 (RapIT): same-day initiation raised started-and-suppressed at 10 months from 51% to 64%
cards.summary: Rosen 2016 (RapIT): same-day initiation raised started-and-suppressed at 10 months from 51% to 64%
cards.people: 377 newly diagnosed, treatment-eligible adults (median CD4 210 cells/mm³) at two South African public-sector clinics, randomised to the RapIT rapid-initiation algorithm (point-of-care tests and ART dispensed at the first visit; n=187) or standard multi-visit initiation (n=190). Primary outcome: ART initiation within 90 days plus viral suppression at 10 months.
cards.result: Initiated ART and virally suppressed at 10 months: 64% (119/187) with rapid initiation versus 51% (96/190) with standard care (relative risk 1.26, 95% CI 1.05 to 1.50 — relative; absolute rates 64% vs 51%). ART initiation within 90 days: 97% (182/187) versus 72% (136/190) (relative risk 1.36, 1.24 to 1.49). Among initiators, the attrition hazard did not differ (HR 1.06, 0.61 to 1.84).
cards.watchOut: A workflow intervention tested in two clinics: the size of the gain depends on how slow the local standard pathway is, so clinics already initiating quickly should expect less. Unblinded by necessity, and the combined endpoint cannot distinguish 'more people started' from 'starters did better' — the initiation gap (97% vs 72%) suggests the former dominates.
cards.source: Rosen S et al. Rapid initiation of ART at the first clinic visit (RapIT). PLoS Med. 2016. PMID: 27163694. Registry ID: NCT01710397, from the record. shelves.title: Bictegravir/emtricitabine/tenofovir alafenamide as initial HIV therapy (studies 1489 and 1490)
shelves.question: In treatment-naive adults, is the single-tablet bictegravir/emtricitabine/tenofovir alafenamide regimen non-inferior to dolutegravir-based initial therapy?
shelves.mesh: Abacavir · Adenine · Adult · Alanine · Amides · Anti-Retroviral Agents · Dideoxynucleosides · Dolutegravir · Double-Blind Method · Drug Combinations · Drug Therapy, Combination · Emtricitabine · Female · HIV Infections · Heterocyclic Compounds, 3-Ring · Heterocyclic Compounds, 4 or More Rings · Humans · Internationality · Lamivudine · Male · Middle Aged · Oxazines · Piperazines · Prognosis · Pyridones · Risk Assessment · Survival Rate · Tenofovir · Treatment Outcome · Young Adult
shelves.balance: Two independent double-blind phase 3 trials (DOUBLE-A) against two different dolutegravir-based comparators, same answer. In study 1489, bictegravir/emtricitabine/tenofovir alafenamide (B/F/TAF) was noninferior to dolutegravir/abacavir/lamivudine: week-48 suppression 92.4% versus 93.0% (difference −0.6%, 95.002% CI −4.8 to 3.6). In study 1490, B/F/TAF was noninferior to dolutegravir plus emtricitabine/tenofovir alafenamide: 89% versus 93% (difference −3.5%, 95.002% CI −7.9 to 1.0) — met its margin, though the point estimate and interval lean slightly toward the dolutegravir arm. No treatment-emergent resistance emerged in either trial. Tolerability favoured B/F/TAF: drug-related adverse events 26% versus 40% in 1489 (nausea 10% vs 23%) and 18% versus 26% in 1490, though adverse-event discontinuations in 1490 were 5 versus 1 the other way. Noninferiority on a virologic endpoint in two blinded trials is the strongest evidence class this library asks for on a regimen question. PROPOSED LIKELY — DOUBLE-A, both double-blind, no resistance signal; superiority over dolutegravir is not claimed by either trial.

cards.headline: Gallant 2017 (study 1489): B/F/TAF noninferior to dolutegravir/abacavir/lamivudine — 92.4% vs 93.0% suppressed at week 48
cards.summary: Gallant 2017 (study 1489): B/F/TAF noninferior to dolutegravir/abacavir/lamivudine — 92.4% vs 93.0% suppressed at week 48
cards.people: 631 treatment-naive adults randomised (314 dosed with B/F/TAF and 315 with dolutegravir/abacavir/lamivudine in the treated analysis). Primary endpoint: proportion with HIV-1 RNA <50 copies/mL at week 48.
cards.result: HIV-1 RNA <50 copies/mL at week 48 in 92.4% (290/314) on B/F/TAF versus 93.0% (293/315) on dolutegravir/abacavir/lamivudine (difference −0.6%, 95.002% CI −4.8 to 3.6; P=0.78) — noninferior. No treatment-emergent resistance was detected. Nausea occurred in 10% versus 23%, and drug-related adverse events in 26% versus 40%.
cards.watchOut: Noninferiority within a prespecified margin, not equivalence proven to the last percentage point — the interval allows up to about 5 points worse suppression on B/F/TAF. The abacavir comparator required HLA-B*5701 screening in practice, which the trial handled by design; real-world regimen choice also turns on hepatitis B status, renal function, and cost.

cards.summary: Sax 2017 (study 1490): B/F/TAF noninferior to dolutegravir + F/TAF — 89% vs 93% suppressed at week 48
cards.people: 657 treatment-naive adults assigned (327 to B/F/TAF, 330 to dolutegravir plus emtricitabine/tenofovir alafenamide; 320 and 325 dosed). Primary endpoint: proportion with HIV-1 RNA <50 copies/mL at week 48.

shelves.title: Dapivirine vaginal ring (ASPIRE + Ring Study): about a 27–31% relative reduction in HIV acquisition across two phase 3 trials
shelves.question: In women at risk in sub-Saharan Africa, does a monthly vaginal ring releasing dapivirine reduce HIV-1 acquisition versus a placebo ring?
shelves.mesh: HIV Infections / prevention & control · HIV-1 · Humans · Pyrimidines / administration & dosage · Reverse Transcriptase Inhibitors / administration & dosage
shelves.balance: Two independent phase 3 placebo-controlled trials point the same way, with a modest effect that depends on the ring actually being worn. In ASPIRE (2,629 women in Malawi, South Africa, Uganda and Zimbabwe), HIV incidence was 3.3 versus 4.5 per 100 person-years — 27% relatively lower on the dapivirine ring (95% CI 1 to 46; P=0.046), rising to 56% relative protection in women over 21 and disappearing in younger women, tracking measured adherence. In the Ring Study (1,959 women in South Africa and Uganda), incidence was 4.1 versus 6.1 per 100 person-years — 31% relatively lower (hazard ratio 0.69; 95% CI 0.49 to 0.99; P=0.04). Neither trial found a safety signal of concern. PROPOSED POSSIBLE — two concordant randomised trials, but the protection is partial, borderline in precision, and adherence-dependent. Note: the topic draft cited the Ring Study as PMID 26900911; that number resolves to an unrelated pre-eclampsia review. The Ring Study was gate-verified and is carded under its correct PubMed record, PMID 27959766.

cards.headline: ASPIRE (MTN-020) 2016: dapivirine ring cut HIV incidence by 27% relative (3.3 vs 4.5 per 100 person-years)
cards.summary: ASPIRE (MTN-020) 2016: dapivirine ring cut HIV incidence by 27% relative (3.3 vs 4.5 per 100 person-years)
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (ASPIRE / MTN-020)
cards.people: 2,629 women aged 18–45 in Malawi, South Africa, Uganda and Zimbabwe, randomised to a monthly vaginal ring containing dapivirine (a non-nucleoside HIV-1 reverse-transcriptase inhibitor) or a placebo ring. Primary outcome: HIV-1 infection.
cards.result: 168 HIV-1 infections occurred: 71 in the dapivirine group and 97 in the placebo group (incidence 3.3 and 4.5 per 100 person-years) — incidence 27% relatively lower on dapivirine (95% CI 1 to 46; P=0.046). Excluding two sites with reduced retention and adherence, protection was 37% relative (95% CI 12 to 56; P=0.007). In a post hoc analysis, protection was 56% relative (95% CI 31 to 71; P<0.001) in women over 21 but absent (−27%; 95% CI −133 to 31; P=0.45) in women 21 or younger, correlating with adherence. Adverse medical events and antiretroviral resistance among women who acquired HIV-1 were similar between groups.
cards.watchOut: The headline 27% is relative — the absolute difference was 1.2 infections per 100 person-years. The age split is post hoc and adherence-correlated: the ring cannot protect when it is not worn, and the youngest women, at highest risk, used it least.
cards.source: Baeten JM et al. Use of a Vaginal Ring Containing Dapivirine for HIV-1 Prevention in Women. N Engl J Med. 2016. PMID: 26900902. Registry ID: NCT01617096, from the record. cards.headline: Ring Study (IPM 027) 2016: dapivirine ring cut HIV incidence by 31% relative (4.1 vs 6.1 per 100 person-years)
cards.summary: Ring Study (IPM 027) 2016: dapivirine ring cut HIV incidence by 31% relative (4.1 vs 6.1 per 100 person-years)
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (Ring Study / IPM 027)
cards.people: 1,959 healthy, sexually active women aged 18–45 from seven communities in South Africa and Uganda, randomised 2:1 to vaginal rings containing 25 mg dapivirine or placebo, self-inserted every 4 weeks for up to 24 months. Primary efficacy endpoint: HIV-1 seroconversion.
cards.result: 77 participants in the dapivirine group seroconverted during 1,888 person-years (4.1 per 100 person-years) versus 56 in the placebo group during 917 person-years (6.1 per 100 person-years) — incidence 31% relatively lower on dapivirine (hazard ratio 0.69; 95% CI 0.49 to 0.99; P=0.04). Efficacy did not differ significantly by age (hazard ratio 0.63 over 21 years; 0.85 at 21 or younger; P=0.43 for interaction). NNRTI resistance mutations among those infected were similar (18.2% vs 16.1%). Serious adverse events were more frequent numerically on dapivirine (2.9% vs 0.9%) with no clear pattern identified.
cards.watchOut: Carded under PMID 27959766: the draft's cited PMID 26900911 is a different paper (a pre-eclampsia review) and was not carded. The 2:1 randomisation means the placebo group is smaller; the absolute difference was 2.0 infections per 100 person-years.
cards.source: Nel A et al. Safety and Efficacy of a Dapivirine Vaginal Ring for HIV Prevention in Women. N Engl J Med. 2016. PMID: 27959766. Registry ID: NCT01539226, from the record. shelves.title: On-demand (2-1-1) PrEP in MSM (IPERGAY): 86% relative reduction in HIV acquisition in one double-blind trial
shelves.question: In men who have sex with men at high risk, does pericoital ("2-1-1") tenofovir/emtricitabine taken around sex prevent HIV acquisition versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Emtricitabine · HIV Infections / prevention & control · HIV-1 · Homosexuality, Male · Humans · Pre-Exposure Prophylaxis · Tenofovir
shelves.balance: One double-blind trial, stopped early because the answer was already clear: in 400 high-risk men who have sex with men in France and Canada, taking tenofovir/emtricitabine only around sex (two tablets 2–24 hours before, one at 24 hours, one at 48 hours) cut HIV acquisition from 6.60 to 0.91 infections per 100 person-years — an 86% relative reduction (95% CI 40 to 98) on absolute rates of 14 infections in the placebo group versus 2 on treatment. Gastrointestinal adverse events (14% vs 5%) and renal adverse events (18% vs 10%) were more common on treatment. OUTSTANDING-SINGLE: this shelf rests on a single double-blind randomised trial, but the effect is large, the endpoint is HIV acquisition itself, and the regimen it created is now guideline-endorsed — so it is carded on that one trial and flagged here. PROPOSED LIKELY — a single trial, but a double-blind one with an outstanding hard-endpoint result.

cards.headline: IPERGAY 2015: on-demand tenofovir/emtricitabine cut HIV incidence by 86% relative (0.91 vs 6.60 per 100 person-years)
cards.summary: IPERGAY 2015: on-demand tenofovir/emtricitabine cut HIV incidence by 86% relative (0.91 vs 6.60 per 100 person-years)
cards.people: 414 men who have sex with men at high risk underwent randomisation in France and Canada; 400 without HIV infection were enrolled (199 tenofovir/emtricitabine, 201 placebo) and followed a median of 9.3 months. Regimen: two tablets 2–24 hours before sex, one tablet 24 hours after the first dose, and one tablet 48 hours after. All received risk-reduction counselling and condoms.
cards.result: 16 HIV-1 infections occurred: 2 on tenofovir/emtricitabine (incidence 0.91 per 100 person-years) versus 14 on placebo (6.60 per 100 person-years) — a relative reduction of 86% (95% CI 40 to 98; P=0.002). Participants took a median of 15 pills per month. Serious adverse events were similar between groups; gastrointestinal adverse events were higher on treatment (14% vs 5%, P=0.002) and renal adverse events higher (18% vs 10%, P=0.03). The trial was stopped early for efficacy.
cards.watchOut: Evidence is in men who have sex with men only — the trial says nothing about vaginal exposure, heterosexual men, or people who inject drugs. Participants took a median of 15 pills a month, so 'on-demand' here still meant frequent dosing; protection with truly rare sex was not what was tested. OUTSTANDING-SINGLE flag: one trial carries this shelf.
cards.source: Molina JM et al. On-Demand Preexposure Prophylaxis in Men at High Risk for HIV-1 Infection. N Engl J Med. 2015. PMID: 26624850. Registry ID: NCT01473472, from the record. shelves.title: VRC01 antibody prevention (AMP trials): no overall protection in two randomised trials — proof of concept against sensitive viruses only
shelves.question: In at-risk adults, do 8-weekly infusions of the broadly neutralising antibody VRC01 prevent HIV-1 acquisition versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Antibodies, Monoclonal · Broadly Neutralizing Antibodies · HIV Infections / prevention & control · HIV-1 · Humans
shelves.balance: Two large randomised trials, one clear overall answer and one important proof of concept. Across ~4,600 at-risk adults, 8-weekly infusions of the broadly neutralising antibody VRC01 (10 or 30 mg/kg) did NOT prevent HIV-1 acquisition overall: prevention efficacy was 26.6% (95% CI −11.7 to 51.8; P=0.15) in the Americas/Europe trial and 8.8% (−45.1 to 42.6; P=0.70) in the African women's trial, on absolute incidences of 2.35 vs 2.98 and 2.49 vs 3.10 per 100 person-years. But against viruses highly sensitive to VRC01, efficacy was 75.4% (45.5 to 88.9) — the antibody worked exactly where the virus let it, which is the proof of concept for antibody prevention, not a usable prevention method in itself. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — two independent randomised trials agree on the overall null; the sensitive-virus finding is a subgroup mechanism result, not overall protection.

cards.headline: AMP HVTN 704/HPTN 085 (2021): VRC01 prevention efficacy 26.6%, not significant (2.35 vs 2.98 per 100 person-years)
cards.summary: AMP HVTN 704/HPTN 085 (2021): VRC01 prevention efficacy 26.6%, not significant (2.35 vs 2.98 per 100 person-years)
cards.people: 2,699 at-risk cisgender men and transgender persons in the Americas and Europe, randomised to VRC01 10 mg/kg, VRC01 30 mg/kg, or placebo infusions every 8 weeks for 10 infusions, with HIV-1 testing every 4 weeks.
cards.result: HIV-1 infection occurred in 32 participants in the low-dose group, 28 in the high-dose group, and 38 in the placebo group. Incidence was 2.35 per 100 person-years in the pooled VRC01 groups versus 2.98 on placebo — estimated prevention efficacy 26.6% (95% CI −11.7 to 51.8; P=0.15), not statistically significant. Adverse events were similar in number and severity across groups.
cards.watchOut: The point estimate favours VRC01 but the confidence interval crosses zero comfortably — this is a null result, not a near-miss to be upgraded. The sensitive-isolate analysis is on the companion card and does not rescue the overall result.
cards.source: Corey L et al. Two Randomized Trials of Neutralizing Antibodies to Prevent HIV-1 Acquisition. N Engl J Med. 2021. PMID: 33730454. cards.headline: AMP HVTN 703/HPTN 081 (2021): VRC01 prevention efficacy 8.8% in African women — null; 75.4% against VRC01-sensitive viruses
cards.summary: AMP HVTN 703/HPTN 081 (2021): VRC01 prevention efficacy 8.8% in African women — null; 75.4% against VRC01-sensitive viruses
cards.people: 1,924 at-risk women in sub-Saharan Africa, randomised to VRC01 10 mg/kg, VRC01 30 mg/kg, or placebo infusions every 8 weeks for 10 infusions. The sensitive-virus analysis pooled prespecified data across both AMP trials.
cards.result: HIV-1 infection occurred in 28 participants in the low-dose group, 19 in the high-dose group, and 29 in the placebo group. Incidence was 2.49 per 100 person-years in the pooled VRC01 groups versus 3.10 on placebo — estimated prevention efficacy 8.8% (95% CI −45.1 to 42.6; P=0.70). In the pooled prespecified analysis, incidence of infection with VRC01-sensitive isolates (IC80 <1 μg/mL) was 0.20 per 100 person-years among VRC01 recipients versus 0.86 among placebo recipients — prevention efficacy 75.4% (95% CI 45.5 to 88.9); VRC01 did not prevent acquisition of other isolates.
cards.watchOut: Most circulating viruses were not highly sensitive to VRC01, which is why strong efficacy against sensitive isolates coexisted with no overall protection. The sensitive-virus result guides next-generation antibody design; it is not evidence that VRC01 itself prevents HIV in practice.

shelves.title: Daily tenofovir PrEP in people who inject drugs (Bangkok Tenofovir Study): HIV incidence roughly halved
shelves.question: In people who inject drugs, does daily oral tenofovir reduce HIV acquisition versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Anti-HIV Agents / therapeutic use · HIV Infections / prevention & control · Humans · Substance Abuse, Intravenous · Tenofovir
shelves.balance: One large double-blind trial in the population where sexual-transmission PrEP data do not reach: among 2,413 HIV-negative people who injected drugs, attending Bangkok drug-treatment clinics, daily oral tenofovir cut HIV incidence from 0.68 to 0.35 per 100 person-years — 17 infections versus 33 — a 48.9% relative reduction (95% CI 9.6 to 72.2; P=0.01). The confidence interval is wide, the absolute incidence was low, and nausea was more common on tenofovir, but serious adverse events were similar. PROPOSED POSSIBLE — a single large, clean, placebo-controlled trial with a significant hard endpoint, held at POSSIBLE because it stands alone in this population and the effect estimate is imprecise.

cards.headline: Bangkok Tenofovir Study 2013: daily tenofovir cut HIV incidence by 48.9% relative (0.35 vs 0.68 per 100 person-years)
cards.summary: Bangkok Tenofovir Study 2013: daily tenofovir cut HIV incidence by 48.9% relative (0.35 vs 0.68 per 100 person-years)
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled phase 3 trial (Bangkok Tenofovir Study)
cards.people: 2,413 HIV-negative volunteers aged 20–60 who reported injecting drugs in the previous year, enrolled at 17 drug-treatment clinics in Bangkok, Thailand; 1,204 assigned to daily tenofovir disoproxil fumarate and 1,209 to placebo, with monthly HIV testing, risk-reduction counselling, and methadone treatment offered.
cards.result: 50 participants became infected during follow-up: 17 in the tenofovir group (incidence 0.35 per 100 person-years) and 33 in the placebo group (0.68 per 100 person-years) — a 48.9% relative reduction in HIV incidence (95% CI 9.6 to 72.2; P=0.01). Serious adverse events were much the same between groups (P=0.35); nausea was more common on tenofovir (P=0.002).
cards.watchOut: A single trial in one city's clinic-based population, where participants could choose directly observed dosing — adherence support was stronger than in most real-world settings. The wide confidence interval (9.6% to 72.2% relative reduction) means the true effect could be modest. Distinct population from Shelf #317 (sexual transmission).
cards.source: Choopanya K et al. Antiretroviral prophylaxis for HIV infection in injecting drug users in Bangkok, Thailand (the Bangkok Tenofovir Study): a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial. Lancet. 2013. PMID: 23769234. Registry ID: NCT00119106, from the record. shelves.title: Tenofovir vaginal gel (CAPRISA 004): 39% relative reduction in one trial — not replicated (THIN)
shelves.question: In women at risk, does pericoital 1% tenofovir vaginal gel reduce HIV acquisition versus placebo gel?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Intravaginal · Anti-HIV Agents / administration & dosage · HIV Infections / prevention & control · Humans · Tenofovir
shelves.balance: One positive trial that the field could not repeat. In CAPRISA 004, 889 women in KwaZulu-Natal using 1% tenofovir gel before and after sex had an HIV incidence of 5.6 per 100 women-years versus 9.1 on placebo gel — incidence rate ratio 0.61, a 39% relative reduction (P=0.017), and 54% relatively lower in high adherers. But this is a single trial, and the later FACTS 001 trial of the same strategy did not replicate the result — which is why this shelf is flagged THIN. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) — a real randomised signal that failed confirmation; it should not be quoted as established protection.

cards.headline: CAPRISA 004 (2010): tenofovir gel cut HIV incidence by 39% relative (5.6 vs 9.1 per 100 women-years) — never replicated
cards.summary: CAPRISA 004 (2010): tenofovir gel cut HIV incidence by 39% relative (5.6 vs 9.1 per 100 women-years) — never replicated
cards.people: 889 sexually active, HIV-uninfected women aged 18–40 in urban and rural KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa: 445 randomised to 1% tenofovir vaginal gel and 444 to placebo gel, used pericoitally, with monthly follow-up for 30 months.
cards.result: HIV incidence was 5.6 per 100 women-years in the tenofovir gel arm (38 infections in 680.6 women-years) versus 9.1 per 100 women-years on placebo (60 in 660.7 women-years) — incidence rate ratio 0.61 (P=0.017), an estimated 39% relative reduction overall. In high adherers (gel adherence >80%) incidence was 54% relatively lower (P=0.025); reductions were 38% in intermediate adherers and 28% in low adherers. Overall adverse event rates were not increased, and there was no tenofovir resistance in seroconverters.
cards.watchOut: THIN: one trial, and the subsequent FACTS 001 confirmatory trial did not replicate the finding — the honest reading is an unconfirmed signal, not a prevention method. The adherence gradient (54% / 38% / 28%) is consistent with a real drug effect but is also exactly the pattern adherence confounding produces. No registry ID appears in the PubMed record, so none is claimed.
cards.source: Abdool Karim Q et al. Effectiveness and safety of tenofovir gel, an antiretroviral microbicide, for the prevention of HIV infection in women. Science. 2010. PMID: 20643915.
