shelves.title: RV144 prime-boost HIV vaccine (Thai trial): 31.2% efficacy in one of three analyses — a borderline, unreproduced signal (THIN)
shelves.question: In a general-population cohort at heterosexual risk, does the ALVAC prime / AIDSVAX gp120 boost regimen prevent HIV-1 infection versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: AIDS Vaccines · HIV Envelope Protein gp120 / immunology · HIV Infections / prevention & control · HIV-1 / immunology · Humans
shelves.balance: The only HIV vaccine regimen ever to show any efficacy signal — and the signal is fragile. In RV144, 16,402 Thai adults received four ALVAC-HIV primes plus two AIDSVAX B/E gp120 boosts or placebo. Vaccine efficacy was 31.2% in the modified intention-to-treat analysis (95% CI 1.1 to 52.1; P=0.04) but only 26.4% and not significant in the full intention-to-treat analysis (95% CI −4.0 to 47.9; P=0.08) and 26.2% per-protocol (P=0.16); vaccination did not affect viral load or CD4 counts in those infected. The regimen was never reproduced at scale, and its clade-C rebuild failed in HVTN 702 (Shelf #2149). THIN. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) — historically important, evidentially borderline: one of three prespecified analyses crossed significance, by a hair.

cards.headline: RV144 (2009): vaccine efficacy 31.2% in modified ITT (P=0.04) but 26.4% and non-significant in full ITT (P=0.08)
cards.summary: RV144 (2009): vaccine efficacy 31.2% in modified ITT (P=0.04) but 26.4% and non-significant in full ITT (P=0.08)
cards.people: 16,402 healthy men and women aged 18–30 in Rayong and Chon Buri provinces, Thailand, primarily at heterosexual risk, randomised to four priming injections of recombinant canarypox vector vaccine (ALVAC-HIV [vCP1521], the specific tested programme) plus two booster injections of recombinant gp120 subunit vaccine (AIDSVAX B/E, the specific tested product) or placebo; coprimary endpoints HIV-1 infection and early viraemia, followed 3 years after the 6-month series.
cards.result: Intention-to-treat (16,402 subjects): vaccine efficacy 26.4% (95% CI −4.0 to 47.9; P=0.08). Per-protocol (12,542 subjects): 26.2% (95% CI −13.3 to 51.9; P=0.16). Modified intention-to-treat (16,395 subjects, excluding 7 with HIV-1 infection at baseline): 31.2% (95% CI 1.1 to 52.1; P=0.04). Vaccination did not affect the degree of viraemia or the CD4+ T-cell count in subjects subsequently diagnosed with HIV-1 infection.
cards.watchOut: THIN: the famous 31.2% comes from the one analysis of three that reached significance, and its confidence interval nearly touches zero (1.1 to 52.1). No absolute incidence rates are given in the abstract, so none are claimed here. The concept's clade-C successor trial was null (Shelf #2149).
cards.source: Rerks-Ngarm S et al. Vaccination with ALVAC and AIDSVAX to prevent HIV-1 infection in Thailand. N Engl J Med. 2009. PMID: 19843557. Registry ID: NCT00223080, from the record. shelves.title: Male circumcision to prevent HIV acquisition: three randomised trials agree — risk roughly halved
shelves.question: In uncircumcised men in high-incidence settings, does medical male circumcision reduce HIV acquisition versus deferred circumcision?
shelves.mesh: Circumcision, Male · HIV Infections / prevention & control · Humans · Male
shelves.balance: As settled as prevention evidence gets: three independent randomised trials in South Africa, Kenya and Uganda, all stopped early for efficacy, all finding roughly the same protection. HIV incidence was 0.85 versus 2.1 per 100 person-years in South Africa (60% relative protection, 95% CI 32 to 76), 2-year incidence 2.1% versus 4.2% in Kenya (53% relative reduction, 95% CI 22 to 72), and 0.66 versus 1.33 per 100 person-years in Uganda (51% efficacy, 95% CI 16 to 72). No trial found behavioural risk compensation of consequence; surgical adverse events were uncommon and resolved. PROPOSED LIKELY — three concordant randomised trials with a hard endpoint; the stamp stops short of the top grade only because all three trials were open (circumcision cannot be blinded) and stopped early, which can inflate estimates.

cards.headline: ANRS 1265, South Africa (2005): circumcision gave 60% relative protection (0.85 vs 2.1 infections per 100 person-years)
cards.summary: ANRS 1265, South Africa (2005): circumcision gave 60% relative protection (0.85 vs 2.1 infections per 100 person-years)
cards.people: 3,274 uncircumcised men aged 18–24 in a general population in South Africa, randomised to immediate circumcision or circumcision at the end of follow-up, with visits at months 3, 12 and 21; mean follow-up 18.1 months when the trial was stopped at interim analysis.
cards.result: 20 HIV infections in the intervention group (incidence 0.85 per 100 person-years) versus 49 in the control group (2.1 per 100 person-years) — rate ratio 0.40 (95% CI 0.24 to 0.68; P<0.001), corresponding to 60% relative protection (95% CI 32 to 76). Adjusted for behavioural factors, protection was 61% (95% CI 34 to 77).
cards.watchOut: The draft named this trial 'ANRS 1215'; the PubMed record titles it ANRS 1265, which is what is carded. Stopped early at interim analysis — early stopping tends to exaggerate effects, which is why the two confirmatory trials matter.
cards.source: Auvert B et al. Randomized, controlled intervention trial of male circumcision for reduction of HIV infection risk: the ANRS 1265 Trial. PLoS Med. 2005. PMID: 16231970. cards.headline: Kisumu, Kenya (2007): 2-year HIV incidence 2.1% circumcised vs 4.2% control — 53% relative reduction
cards.summary: Kisumu, Kenya (2007): 2-year HIV incidence 2.1% circumcised vs 4.2% control — 53% relative reduction
cards.people: 2,784 men aged 18–24 in Kisumu, Kenya, randomised to circumcision (n=1,391) or delayed circumcision (n=1,393), followed up to 24 months; the trial was stopped early after a third interim analysis.
cards.result: 22 men in the intervention group and 47 in the control group tested HIV-positive. The 2-year HIV incidence was 2.1% (95% CI 1.2 to 3.0) in the circumcision group versus 4.2% (3.0 to 5.4) in the control group (P=0.0065); relative risk 0.47 (0.28 to 0.78), a 53% relative reduction (95% CI 22 to 72). Adjusting for non-adherence, the protective effect was 60% (32 to 77). Intervention-related adverse events occurred in 1.5% of those circumcised and resolved quickly; no behavioural risk compensation was observed.
cards.watchOut: Follow-up for HIV status was incomplete for 8.6% of participants. Absolute benefit depends on background incidence — 2.1 percentage points over 2 years in this high-incidence setting.
cards.source: Bailey RC et al. Male circumcision for HIV prevention in young men in Kisumu, Kenya: a randomised controlled trial. Lancet. 2007. PMID: 17321310. Registry ID: NCT00059371, from the record. cards.headline: Rakai, Uganda (2007): HIV incidence 0.66 vs 1.33 per 100 person-years — 51% efficacy
cards.summary: Rakai, Uganda (2007): HIV incidence 0.66 vs 1.33 per 100 person-years — 51% efficacy
cards.people: 4,996 uncircumcised, HIV-negative men aged 15–49 in rural Rakai district, Uganda, randomised to immediate circumcision (n=2,474) or circumcision delayed 24 months (n=2,522); primary outcome HIV incidence, modified intention-to-treat.
cards.result: HIV incidence over 24 months was 0.66 cases per 100 person-years in the intervention group versus 1.33 in the control group — estimated efficacy 51% (95% CI 16 to 72; P=0.006). As-treated efficacy was 55% (95% CI 22 to 75; P=0.002). Moderate or severe adverse events occurred in 84 circumcisions (3.6%) and all resolved with treatment. Behaviour was much the same in both groups during follow-up.
cards.watchOut: These trials measure protection for the circumcised man against acquiring HIV through vaginal sex; they do not show direct protection for female partners, and protection is partial — roughly half, not complete.
cards.source: Gray RH et al. Male circumcision for HIV prevention in men in Rakai, Uganda: a randomised trial. Lancet. 2007. PMID: 17321311. Registry ID: NCT00425984, from the record. shelves.title: Daily oral PrEP in heterosexual adults in Botswana (TDF2): 62.2% relative efficacy in one early-closed trial
shelves.question: In HIV-negative heterosexual men and women, does daily tenofovir/emtricitabine prevent acquisition versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Anti-Retroviral Agents / therapeutic use · Emtricitabine · HIV Infections / prevention & control · Humans · Tenofovir
shelves.balance: One double-blind trial in a general heterosexual population — the population Shelf #317's serodiscordant-couples trial does not cover. In TDF2, 1,219 HIV-negative men and women in Botswana (45.7% women) took daily tenofovir/emtricitabine or placebo: 9 infections on treatment versus 24 on placebo, at 1.2 versus 3.1 per 100 person-years — efficacy 62.2% relative (95% CI 21.5 to 83.4; P=0.03). The trial closed early because of low retention and logistics, only 33 infections drive the estimate, and treatment caused significantly more nausea, vomiting and dizziness plus a significant decline in bone mineral density, whose long-term meaning the authors state is unknown. PROPOSED POSSIBLE — a single, significant, double-blind trial, held at POSSIBLE by its early closure, wide interval, and the open bone-safety question.

cards.headline: TDF2 (2012): daily tenofovir/emtricitabine efficacy 62.2% relative in heterosexual adults (1.2 vs 3.1 infections per 100 person-years)
cards.summary: TDF2 (2012): daily tenofovir/emtricitabine efficacy 62.2% relative in heterosexual adults (1.2 vs 3.1 infections per 100 person-years)
cards.people: 1,219 HIV-seronegative heterosexual men and women in Botswana (45.7% women) randomised to daily tenofovir disoproxil fumarate–emtricitabine or matching placebo, with monthly visits and a comprehensive prevention package; followed for 1,563 person-years (median 1.1 years). The study was concluded early because of low retention and logistic limitations.
cards.result: In the modified intention-to-treat analysis, 33 participants became infected: 9 in the tenofovir/emtricitabine group (1.2 infections per 100 person-years) and 24 in the placebo group (3.1 per 100 person-years) — efficacy 62.2% relative (95% CI 21.5 to 83.4; P=0.03). Nausea (18.5% vs 7.1%, P<0.001), vomiting (11.3% vs 7.1%, P=0.008) and dizziness (15.1% vs 11.0%, P=0.03) were more common on treatment; serious adverse events were similar (P=0.90). Bone mineral density declined significantly on treatment. Resistance mutations (K65R, M184V, A62V) developed in one participant who had unrecognised acute HIV infection at enrolment.
cards.watchOut: Only 33 infections and early closure make the 62.2% estimate fragile — the interval runs from 21.5% to 83.4% relative efficacy. Not to be confused with the adjacent record PMID 22784037 (Partners PrEP, serodiscordant couples), which is carded on Shelf #317; TDF2 is a different trial in a general heterosexual population. The bone-density decline in young, healthy users is the unresolved safety issue.
cards.source: Thigpen MC et al. Antiretroviral preexposure prophylaxis for heterosexual HIV transmission in Botswana. N Engl J Med. 2012. PMID: 22784038. Registry ID: NCT00448669, from the record. shelves.title: Oral and vaginal PrEP in African women (VOICE): none of three strategies worked — adherence too low to deliver protection
shelves.question: In reproductive-age African women, do daily oral tenofovir, daily oral tenofovir/emtricitabine, or daily tenofovir vaginal gel prevent HIV acquisition versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Anti-Retroviral Agents / administration & dosage · HIV Infections / prevention & control · Medication Adherence · Pre-Exposure Prophylaxis · Tenofovir
shelves.balance: A large, definitive null — with the reason measured, not guessed. In VOICE, 5,029 women in South Africa, Uganda and Zimbabwe were randomised to daily oral tenofovir, daily oral tenofovir/emtricitabine, daily 1% tenofovir vaginal gel, or matching placebos. None reduced HIV acquisition: hazard ratios were 1.49 (95% CI 0.97 to 2.29) for tenofovir, 1.04 (0.73 to 1.49) for tenofovir/emtricitabine, and 0.85 (0.61 to 1.21) for the gel, against an overall incidence of 5.7 per 100 person-years. Blood testing showed why: tenofovir was detected in only 30%, 29% and 25% of samples in the three active groups — the products were largely not being used, so the trial tested a delivery strategy, and the strategy failed. Serum creatinine elevations were more frequent on oral tenofovir/emtricitabine (1.3% vs 0.2%, P=0.004). PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — as randomised and as actually delivered, in 5,029 women; the null is about use, not proof the drug cannot work when taken (see Shelves #2140, #2147).

cards.headline: VOICE (MTN-003) 2015: no PrEP strategy reduced HIV in 5,029 African women — drug detected in only ~25–30% of samples
cards.summary: VOICE (MTN-003) 2015: no PrEP strategy reduced HIV in 5,029 African women — drug detected in only ~25–30% of samples
cards.people: 5,029 reproductive-age women in South Africa, Uganda and Zimbabwe randomised to daily oral tenofovir disoproxil fumarate, daily oral tenofovir–emtricitabine, or daily 1% tenofovir vaginal gel versus matching placebos; 5,509 person-years of follow-up, 91% retention, monthly HIV-1 testing and quarterly plasma tenofovir measurement.
cards.result: 312 HIV-1 infections occurred; overall incidence 5.7 per 100 person-years. In the modified intention-to-treat analysis, effectiveness was −49.0% with tenofovir (hazard ratio 1.49; 95% CI 0.97 to 2.29), −4.4% with tenofovir–emtricitabine (hazard ratio 1.04; 95% CI 0.73 to 1.49), and 14.5% with tenofovir gel (hazard ratio 0.85; 95% CI 0.61 to 1.21) — none significant. Tenofovir was detected in 30%, 29% and 25% of available plasma samples from the three active groups. Elevations of serum creatinine were more frequent on oral tenofovir–emtricitabine than oral placebo (1.3% vs 0.2%, P=0.004); other adverse-event frequencies did not differ significantly.
cards.watchOut: Read this null correctly: with drug detectable in only a quarter to a third of samples, VOICE cannot show that tenofovir fails biologically — it shows that offering daily products to this population, this way, did not deliver protection. That distinction is the whole lesson, and it shaped the move to long-acting methods (Shelf #2140). The tenofovir-alone hazard ratio of 1.49 is a point estimate with an interval crossing 1 — not evidence of harm.
cards.source: Marrazzo JM et al. Tenofovir-based preexposure prophylaxis for HIV infection among African women. N Engl J Med. 2015. PMID: 25651245. Registry ID: NCT00705679, from the record. shelves.title: Subtype-C ALVAC/gp120 vaccine in South Africa (HVTN 702): stopped for non-efficacy — the RV144 signal did not transfer
shelves.question: In South African adults, does the subtype-C-adapted ALVAC-HIV plus bivalent gp120/MF59 regimen prevent HIV-1 acquisition versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: AIDS Vaccines / immunology · HIV Infections / prevention & control · HIV-1 / genetics · Humans · South Africa
shelves.balance: A clean, large, definitive negative. HVTN 702 rebuilt the RV144 concept for subtype C — ALVAC-HIV primes plus bivalent subtype C gp120 in MF59 (the specific tested programme) — and randomised 5,404 South African adults. Vaccinations were halted when prespecified non-efficacy criteria were met: over 24 months, HIV-1 infection was diagnosed in 138 vaccine recipients and 133 placebo recipients (hazard ratio 1.02; 95% CI 0.81 to 1.30; P=0.84), with similar adverse-event incidence. The RV144 signal did not transfer. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — one large trial, stopped by its own futility rule, with an estimate centred on zero.

cards.headline: HVTN 702 / Uhambo (2021): clade-C ALVAC/gp120 vaccine did not prevent HIV — 138 vs 133 infections, hazard ratio 1.02
cards.summary: HVTN 702 / Uhambo (2021): clade-C ALVAC/gp120 vaccine did not prevent HIV — 138 vs 133 infections, hazard ratio 1.02
cards.people: 5,404 adults without HIV-1 infection in South Africa (median age 24 years; 70% women), randomised to vaccine (2,704) or placebo (2,700). Regimen: ALVAC-HIV at months 0 and 1, then four boosters of ALVAC-HIV plus bivalent subtype C gp120–MF59 adjuvant at months 3, 6, 12 and 18. Primary outcome: HIV-1 infection from randomisation to 24 months.
cards.result: In January 2020, prespecified criteria for non-efficacy were met at an interim analysis and further vaccinations were halted. During 24 months of follow-up, HIV-1 infection was diagnosed in 138 participants in the vaccine group and 133 in the placebo group (hazard ratio 1.02; 95% CI 0.81 to 1.30; P=0.84). The incidence of adverse events was similar in the two groups.
cards.watchOut: Immunogenicity in early-phase testing did not predict protection — the regimen raised the intended responses and still failed. Together with RV144 (Shelf #2145), this closes the ALVAC/gp120 prime-boost concept as tested: a borderline signal in Thailand, a null in South Africa.

shelves.title: Four-month treatment for nonsevere childhood TB (SHINE): non-inferior to 6 months [Tier C]
shelves.question: In children with nonsevere, smear-negative, drug-susceptible tuberculosis, is 4 months of first-line therapy non-inferior to the standard 6 months?
shelves.mesh: Antitubercular Agents / administration & dosage · Child · Humans · Tuberculosis / drug therapy
shelves.balance: Tier C shelf (the primary composite includes death; presented for the developer's personal verdict). In SHINE, 1,204 children under 16 with nonsevere, smear-negative, presumably drug-susceptible tuberculosis in Uganda, Zambia, South Africa and India were randomised to 4 or 6 months of standard first-line treatment. Unfavourable status by 72 weeks occurred in 16 children (3%) on 4 months versus 18 (3%) on 6 months — adjusted difference −0.4 percentage points (95% CI −2.2 to 1.5), comfortably inside the 6-point non-inferiority margin and consistent across intention-to-treat, per-protocol and adjudicated-TB analyses. Grade 3-or-higher adverse events occurred in 8% overall, with 15 adverse drug reactions, mostly hepatic and mostly in the first 8 weeks when both groups received identical treatment. PROPOSED LIKELY — 4 months is non-inferior for this defined nonsevere population; the claim is about duration, not about a new drug.

cards.headline: SHINE (2022): 4 months non-inferior to 6 months in nonsevere childhood TB — unfavourable outcome 3% vs 3%
cards.summary: SHINE (2022): 4 months non-inferior to 6 months in nonsevere childhood TB — unfavourable outcome 3% vs 3%
cards.type: Open-label non-inferiority randomised trial (SHINE) — Tier C
cards.people: 1,204 children younger than 16 years (median age 3.5 years; 52% male; 11% with HIV infection; 14% bacteriologically confirmed) with nonsevere, symptomatic, presumably drug-susceptible, smear-negative tuberculosis in Uganda, Zambia, South Africa and India, randomised to 4 months (16 weeks) or 6 months (24 weeks) of standard first-line treatment with WHO-recommended paediatric fixed-dose combinations. Primary outcome: unfavourable status (treatment failure, loss to follow-up during treatment, or death) by 72 weeks; non-inferiority margin 6 percentage points.
cards.result: 16 participants (3%) in the 4-month group had a primary-outcome event versus 18 (3%) in the 6-month group (adjusted difference −0.4 percentage points; 95% CI −2.2 to 1.5). Non-inferiority was consistent across intention-to-treat, per-protocol and key secondary analyses, including the 958 participants (80%) independently adjudicated to have tuberculosis at baseline. Retention by 72 weeks was 95% and adherence 94%. Grade 3-or-higher adverse events occurred in 95 participants (8%), including 15 adverse drug reactions (11 hepatic events, all but 2 within the first 8 weeks, when treatment was identical in both groups).
cards.watchOut: Tier C: the unfavourable-status composite includes death, so this shelf goes to the developer personally. The result applies only to the trial's nonsevere, smear-negative definition — not to severe, smear-positive, drug-resistant, or extrapulmonary disease beyond the enrolled spectrum. Open-label design; adjudicated analyses support the main result.

shelves.title: Bedaquiline-containing short regimens for rifampicin-resistant TB (STREAM stage 2): superior to the injectable control, with less hearing loss [Tier C]
shelves.question: In rifampicin-resistant TB without fluoroquinolone or injectable resistance, do a 9-month all-oral bedaquiline regimen or a 6-month bedaquiline-plus-injectable regimen beat the 9-month injectable-containing STREAM control?
shelves.mesh: Drug Therapy, Combination · Humans · Tuberculosis, Multidrug-Resistant / drug therapy
shelves.balance: Tier C shelf (the favourable-status outcome embeds death; mortality figures are printed on the card; presented for the developer's personal verdict). In STREAM stage 2, 588 people aged 15 or older with rifampicin-resistant tuberculosis (without fluoroquinolone or aminoglycoside resistance) in seven countries were randomised to bedaquiline-containing regimens or the 9-month injectable-containing control. The 9-month all-oral bedaquiline regimen gave favourable outcomes in 83% versus 71% on control (adjusted difference 11.0 percentage points; 95% CI 2.9 to 19.0), and the 6-month bedaquiline-plus-8-weeks-injectable regimen in 91% versus 69% of concurrently randomised controls (difference 22.2 points; 95% CI 13.1 to 31.2) — both superior, not merely non-inferior. Grade 3–4 hearing loss was far less frequent without the prolonged injectable (2% oral vs 9% control; 4% on the 6-month regimen). Deaths by 76 weeks were 3% on the oral regimen and 2% on control. PROPOSED LIKELY — a phase 3 randomised trial showing superiority of the bedaquiline regimens on the composite, with a clear toxicity dividend.

cards.headline: STREAM stage 2 (2022): bedaquiline regimens beat the injectable control — favourable outcome 83% (oral) and 91% (6-month) vs 71%/69%
cards.summary: STREAM stage 2 (2022): bedaquiline regimens beat the injectable control — favourable outcome 83% (oral) and 91% (6-month) vs 71%/69%
cards.type: Randomised phase 3 non-inferiority/superiority trial (STREAM stage 2) — Tier C
cards.people: 588 participants aged 15 years or older with rifampicin-resistant tuberculosis without fluoroquinolone or aminoglycoside resistance, randomised at 13 hospital clinics in seven countries to a 9-month injectable-containing control regimen, a 9-month all-oral bedaquiline regimen, or a 6-month bedaquiline regimen with 8 weeks of second-line injectable (a 2011 WHO regimen arm was terminated early). Primary outcome: favourable status (negative cultures without a preceding unfavourable outcome) at 76 weeks; death, bacteriological failure or recurrence, and major treatment change counted as unfavourable. 517 participants were in the modified intention-to-treat population for the primary comparison.
cards.result: Favourable outcome: 162 of 196 (83%) on the 9-month oral regimen versus 133 of 187 (71%) on control — adjusted difference 11.0 percentage points (95% CI 2.9 to 19.0; P<0.0001 for non-inferiority, with superiority shown). For the 6-month regimen, 122 of 134 (91%) versus 87 of 127 (69%) concurrently randomised controls — adjusted difference 22.2 points (95% CI 13.1 to 31.2). By 76 weeks, grade 3 or 4 adverse events had occurred in 50% on the oral regimen and 53% on control; five participants (2%) on control and seven (3%) on the oral regimen had died. Grade 3 or 4 hearing loss: 2% on the oral regimen versus 9% on control (P=0.0015); 4% on the 6-month regimen.
cards.watchOut: Tier C: favourable status embeds death — deaths are printed above (2–3%) and were similar between regimens; the composite's gain comes mainly from culture outcomes and treatment completion, not mortality. Open-label (laboratory staff masked). The population excluded fluoroquinolone or aminoglycoside resistance, so the result does not cover pre-XDR disease (see ZeNix, Shelf #2152).

shelves.title: Optimising linezolid dose and duration in BPaL (ZeNix): 600 mg for 26 weeks kept efficacy with much less toxicity [Tier C]
shelves.question: In XDR, pre-XDR, or treatment-intolerant rifampicin-resistant TB, which linezolid dose/duration within bedaquiline–pretomanid–linezolid preserves efficacy with least toxicity?
shelves.mesh: Antitubercular Agents / therapeutic use · Humans · Linezolid / adverse effects · Linezolid / therapeutic use · Tuberculosis, Multidrug-Resistant / drug therapy
shelves.balance: Tier C shelf (the favourable-outcome composite includes death; presented for the developer's personal verdict). ZeNix randomised 181 people with XDR, pre-XDR, or treatment-intolerant rifampicin-resistant tuberculosis to bedaquiline–pretomanid with linezolid at 1200 mg for 26 or 9 weeks, or 600 mg for 26 or 9 weeks. Favourable outcomes were 93%, 89%, 91% and 84% respectively — efficacy held up at 600 mg — while toxicity fell steeply with dose: peripheral neuropathy in 38% (1200 mg/26 weeks) versus 24% (600 mg/26 weeks) and 13% (600 mg/9 weeks); myelosuppression in 22% versus 2% at 600 mg/26 weeks; linezolid dose modifications in 51% versus 13%. Optic neuropathy occurred in 4 participants (9%), all on 1200 mg for 26 weeks, and resolved. Six of the seven unfavourable microbiologic outcomes occurred in the 9-week linezolid groups, which is why the authors favoured 600 mg for the full 26 weeks. PROPOSED POSSIBLE — one modest-sized randomised dose-finding trial (about 45 participants per arm, no non-BPaL control); the dose ranking is clear, the absolute numbers are small.

cards.headline: ZeNix (2022): linezolid 600 mg for 26 weeks kept BPaL efficacy (91% favourable) with far less neuropathy and myelosuppression
cards.summary: ZeNix (2022): linezolid 600 mg for 26 weeks kept BPaL efficacy (91% favourable) with far less neuropathy and myelosuppression
cards.people: 181 participants with extensively drug-resistant tuberculosis (resistant to rifampin, a fluoroquinolone and an aminoglycoside), pre-XDR tuberculosis, or rifampicin-resistant tuberculosis not responding to treatment or with a discontinued second-line regimen; 88% had XDR or pre-XDR disease. All received bedaquiline for 26 weeks and pretomanid 200 mg daily for 26 weeks, randomised to linezolid 1200 mg for 26 or 9 weeks or 600 mg for 26 or 9 weeks. Primary endpoint: unfavourable outcome (treatment failure or relapse) at 26 weeks after treatment completion, modified intention-to-treat.
cards.result: Favourable outcomes: 93% (linezolid 1200 mg, 26 weeks), 89% (1200 mg, 9 weeks), 91% (600 mg, 26 weeks) and 84% (600 mg, 9 weeks). Peripheral neuropathy occurred in 38%, 24%, 24% and 13% respectively; myelosuppression in 22%, 15%, 2% and 7%; the linezolid dose was modified (interrupted, reduced or discontinued) in 51%, 30%, 13% and 13%. Optic neuropathy developed in 4 participants (9%) on 1200 mg for 26 weeks; all cases resolved. Six of the seven unfavourable microbiologic outcomes through 78 weeks occurred in the 9-week linezolid groups. The authors concluded the overall risk–benefit favoured linezolid 600 mg for 26 weeks.
cards.watchOut: Tier C: the favourable-outcome composite includes death. This is a within-regimen dose comparison — ZeNix has no non-BPaL arm, so it cannot by itself prove BPaL works (that rests on the single-arm Nix-TB parent study, PMID 32130813, named in the draft and not carded). With ~45 participants per group, a few relapses move the percentages; the 9-week groups' clustering of unfavourable microbiologic outcomes is a signal, not a precise estimate.

shelves.title: Nine-month all-oral regimens for rifampin-resistant TB (endTB): three regimens non-inferior to standard therapy [Tier C]
shelves.question: In fluoroquinolone-susceptible, rifampin-resistant TB, are experimental 9-month all-oral bedaquiline-based regimens non-inferior to standard longer therapy?
shelves.mesh: Antitubercular Agents / therapeutic use · Drug Therapy, Combination · Humans · Tuberculosis, Multidrug-Resistant / drug therapy
shelves.balance: Tier C shelf (the favourable-outcome definition embeds unfavourable outcomes including death; presented for the developer's personal verdict). In endTB, 754 participants with fluoroquinolone-susceptible, rifampin-resistant tuberculosis were randomised (Bayesian response-adaptive) to standard longer therapy or one of five experimental 9-month all-oral bedaquiline-based regimens (the specific tested programmes: BCLLfxZ, BLMZ, BDLLfxZ, DCLLfxZ and DCMZ, built from bedaquiline, delamanid, linezolid, levofloxacin or moxifloxacin, clofazimine and pyrazinamide). Favourable outcome at week 73 occurred in 80.7% on standard therapy in the modified intention-to-treat analysis; four regimens were non-inferior in that population, with risk differences favouring the experimental regimens of 9.8 points (BCLLfxZ; 95% CI 0.9 to 18.7), 8.3 (BLMZ; −0.8 to 17.4), 4.6 (BDLLfxZ; −4.9 to 14.1) and 2.5 (DCMZ; −7.5 to 12.5) against a −12-point margin — but DCMZ was not non-inferior per-protocol, and the authors' conclusion supports three regimens. Grade 3-or-higher adverse events were similar across regimens; grade 3-or-higher hepatotoxicity occurred in 11.7% overall versus 7.1% on standard therapy. PROPOSED LIKELY — a phase 3 multinational trial; non-inferiority of shortened all-oral treatment is consistent across analyses for three regimens.

cards.headline: endTB (2025): three 9-month all-oral regimens non-inferior to standard therapy for rifampin-resistant TB (standard favourable rate 80.7%)
cards.summary: endTB (2025): three 9-month all-oral regimens non-inferior to standard therapy for rifampin-resistant TB (standard favourable rate 80.7%)
cards.type: Phase 3 open-label non-inferiority randomised trial (endTB) — Tier C
cards.people: 754 participants with fluoroquinolone-susceptible, rifampin-resistant tuberculosis randomised across multiple countries to standard therapy or one of five 9-month oral regimens combining bedaquiline (B), delamanid (D), linezolid (L), levofloxacin (Lfx) or moxifloxacin (M), clofazimine (C) and pyrazinamide (Z); 699 in the modified intention-to-treat analysis and 562 per-protocol. Primary endpoint: favourable outcome at week 73 (two negative sputum cultures or favourable bacteriologic, clinical and radiologic evolution); non-inferiority margin −12 percentage points.
cards.result: Favourable outcomes in the standard-therapy group: 80.7% (modified intention-to-treat). Risk differences for the four regimens non-inferior in that population: BCLLfxZ 9.8 percentage points (95% CI 0.9 to 18.7); BLMZ 8.3 (−0.8 to 17.4); BDLLfxZ 4.6 (−4.9 to 14.1); DCMZ 2.5 (−7.5 to 12.5). Differences were similar per-protocol except DCMZ, which was not non-inferior in that population; the authors concluded that consistent results support non-inferior efficacy of three all-oral shortened regimens. Grade 3-or-higher adverse events were similar across regimens; grade 3-or-higher hepatotoxic events occurred in 11.7% of participants overall and 7.1% on standard therapy.
cards.watchOut: Tier C: favourable status is the complement of an unfavourable composite that includes death. The −12-point non-inferiority margin is wide, and one regimen (DCMZ) failed per-protocol — quote the trial as supporting three specific regimens, not 'any 9-month oral regimen'. Response-adaptive randomisation and an evolving standard-therapy comparator complicate simple comparisons. Fluoroquinolone-resistant disease is a different question (Shelf #2152).
cards.source: Guglielmetti L et al. Oral Regimens for Rifampin-Resistant, Fluoroquinolone-Susceptible Tuberculosis. N Engl J Med. 2025. PMID: 39879593. Registry ID: NCT02754765, from the record. shelves.title: Urine LAM-guided TB treatment in HIV inpatients (STAMP): 8-week mortality 21% vs 25% [Tier C · OUTSTANDING-SINGLE]
shelves.question: In hospitalised HIV-positive adults with suspected TB, does adding point-of-care urine lipoarabinomannan testing to routine diagnostics to guide treatment initiation reduce mortality?
shelves.mesh: AIDS-Related Opportunistic Infections / diagnosis · Lipopolysaccharides / urine · Point-of-Care Systems · Tuberculosis / diagnosis · Tuberculosis / mortality
shelves.balance: Tier C shelf (mortality is the primary endpoint; presented for the developer's personal verdict) and OUTSTANDING-SINGLE: one pragmatic randomised trial with a significant mortality benefit. In STAMP, 2,659 HIV-positive hospital inpatients with suspected tuberculosis in ten African hospitals were randomised to routine diagnostics plus bedside urine lipoarabinomannan testing (the specific tested product: the Alere Determine tuberculosis LAM Ag lateral-flow strip) with nurse recommendations to start treatment on a positive result, versus routine diagnostics alone. Eight-week all-cause mortality was 21% with LAM guidance versus 25% without — an absolute reduction of 4 percentage points (95% CI 1 to 7); adjusted risk ratio 0.83 (0.73 to 0.96; P=0.012), a 17% relative risk reduction, and an adjusted hazard ratio of 0.82 (0.70 to 0.96). No adverse events were associated with LAM testing. PROPOSED LIKELY — a single trial, but a large multicountry pragmatic one whose endpoint is death itself; flagged OUTSTANDING-SINGLE because it stands alone.

cards.headline: STAMP (2016): LAM-guided treatment cut 8-week mortality from 25% to 21% in HIV inpatients (adjusted RR 0.83)
cards.summary: STAMP (2016): LAM-guided treatment cut 8-week mortality from 25% to 21% in HIV inpatients (adjusted RR 0.83)
cards.type: Pragmatic open-label randomised trial (STAMP) — Tier C · OUTSTANDING-SINGLE
cards.people: 2,659 HIV-positive adults (2,528 in the modified intention-to-treat analysis: 1,257 LAM, 1,271 no LAM) admitted to ten hospitals in South Africa, Tanzania, Zambia and Zimbabwe with at least one TB symptom (fever, cough, night sweats or weight loss) and illness severity requiring admission; patients who had received anti-tuberculosis medicine in the prior 60 days were excluded. Intervention: routine diagnostics (smear microscopy, Xpert MTB/RIF, culture) plus bedside urine LAM testing with the Alere Determine tuberculosis LAM Ag lateral-flow strip, with trained nurses recommending treatment initiation on a positive result; control: routine diagnostics alone. Primary endpoint: 8-week all-cause mortality.
cards.result: Overall 8-week mortality was 578 of 2,528 (23%): 261 (21%) in the LAM group versus 317 (25%) in the no-LAM group — an absolute reduction of 4 percentage points (95% CI 1 to 7). The country-adjusted risk ratio was 0.83 (95% CI 0.73 to 0.96; P=0.012), a 17% relative risk reduction (95% CI 4 to 28). In the time-to-event analysis there were 159 versus 196 deaths per 100 person-years (adjusted hazard ratio 0.82; 95% CI 0.70 to 0.96; P=0.015). No adverse events were associated with LAM testing.
cards.watchOut: Tier C and OUTSTANDING-SINGLE: mortality benefit from a diagnostic-strategy trial rests on this one study, and the strategy only helps if a positive result actually triggers same-day treatment — the trial built nurse recommendation into the intervention, and attending physicians still decided independently. The benefit is expected to be greatest where patients are sickest, most immunosuppressed and least able to produce sputum; it does not follow that LAM testing helps outpatients or HIV-negative patients.
cards.source: Peter JG et al. Effect on mortality of point-of-care, urine-based lipoarabinomannan testing to guide tuberculosis treatment initiation in HIV-positive hospital inpatients: a pragmatic, parallel-group, multicountry, open-label, randomised controlled trial. Lancet. 2016. PMID: 26970721. Registry ID: NCT01770730, from the record. shelves.title: Empiric TB therapy versus isoniazid in advanced HIV (REMEMBER): no mortality benefit — 5% vs 5% [Tier C]
shelves.question: In outpatients with CD4 <50 starting ART in high-burden settings, does empiric four-drug TB treatment reduce early mortality versus isoniazid preventive therapy after TB screening?
shelves.mesh: Antitubercular Agents / therapeutic use · HIV Infections / drug therapy · Humans · Isoniazid / therapeutic use · Tuberculosis / prevention & control
shelves.balance: Tier C shelf (mortality was the primary endpoint, and the result is null — this shelf must not be read as implying any mortality benefit; presented for the developer's personal verdict). In REMEMBER, 850 outpatients with CD4 counts under 50 cells/μL (median 18) starting antiretroviral therapy at 18 clinics in ten countries — all screened for tuberculosis first, with confirmed or suspected TB excluded — were randomised to empiric four-drug tuberculosis therapy or to isoniazid preventive therapy. At 24 weeks, 22 participants (5%) in each group had died or were of unknown status — absolute risk difference −0.06 percentage points (95% CI −3.05 to 2.94). Grade 3 or 4 signs, symptoms and laboratory abnormalities were similar between groups. The authors' reading: systematic TB screening plus isoniazid preventive therapy is the strategy the data support; blanket empiric treatment adds nothing after screening. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — a multicountry randomised trial with an estimate centred on zero.

cards.headline: REMEMBER / ACTG A5274 (2016): empiric TB therapy did not reduce 24-week mortality vs isoniazid — 5% vs 5%
cards.summary: REMEMBER / ACTG A5274 (2016): empiric TB therapy did not reduce 24-week mortality vs isoniazid — 5% vs 5%
cards.type: Open-label randomised trial (REMEMBER / ACTG A5274) — Tier C
cards.people: 850 HIV-positive outpatients initiating antiretroviral therapy with CD4 counts under 50 cells per μL (median 18, IQR 9–32) at 18 outpatient clinics in ten countries (Malawi, South Africa, Haiti, Kenya, Zambia, India, Brazil, Zimbabwe, Peru, Uganda). All were screened for tuberculosis by symptom screen, locally available diagnostics and GeneXpert MTB/RIF where available; confirmed or suspected tuberculosis was excluded. Randomised to antiretroviral therapy plus empiric tuberculosis therapy (424) or antiretroviral therapy plus isoniazid preventive therapy (426). Primary endpoint: death or unknown status at 24 weeks, intention-to-treat.
cards.result: At week 24, 22 participants (5%) in each group had died or were of unknown status (empiric group 95% CI 3.5 to 7.8; isoniazid group 3.4 to 7.8) — absolute risk difference −0.06 percentage points (95% CI −3.05 to 2.94). Grade 3 or 4 signs or symptoms occurred in 50 participants (12%) in the empiric group and 46 (11%) in the isoniazid group; grade 3 or 4 laboratory abnormalities in 99 (23%) and 97 (23%) respectively. The authors concluded empiric tuberculosis therapy did not reduce mortality, and that the trial's low mortality supports systematic tuberculosis screening and isoniazid preventive therapy in outpatients with advanced HIV disease.
cards.watchOut: Tier C: mortality endpoint with a null result — nothing on this shelf supports empiric treatment as life-saving. Two design points matter: everyone was screened first (so this is empiric therapy after screening, not instead of it), and the endpoint counts 'death or unknown status' together — 22 events per group include unknowns. The contrast with STAMP (Shelf #2154) is instructive: a positive test triggering treatment helped inpatients; blanket empiric therapy did not help screened outpatients.
cards.source: Hosseinipour MC et al. Empirical tuberculosis therapy versus isoniazid in adult outpatients with advanced HIV initiating antiretroviral therapy (REMEMBER): a multicountry open-label randomised controlled trial. Lancet. 2016. PMID: 27025337. Registry ID: NCT01380080, from the record. shelves.title: Adjunctive prednisolone in tuberculous pericarditis (IMPI): primary composite null, less constriction, more HIV-associated cancer [Tier C · SPLIT]
shelves.question: In adults with definite or probable tuberculous pericarditis, do adjunctive prednisolone or Mycobacterium indicus pranii immunotherapy reduce death, tamponade, or constriction?
shelves.mesh: Glucocorticoids / therapeutic use · Humans · Immunotherapy · Pericarditis, Tuberculous / drug therapy · Prednisolone / therapeutic use
shelves.balance: Tier C shelf (death is a headline component of the primary composite; presented for the developer's personal verdict), with a SPLIT verdict because the outcomes genuinely diverge. In IMPI, 1,400 adults with definite or probable tuberculous pericarditis (two-thirds HIV-positive) were randomised in a 2×2 factorial design to prednisolone or placebo for 6 weeks and to Mycobacterium indicus pranii immunotherapy (the specific tested product) or placebo. Neither intervention moved the primary composite of death, tamponade requiring pericardiocentesis, or constrictive pericarditis: 23.8% versus 24.5% for prednisolone (hazard ratio 0.95; 95% CI 0.77 to 1.18; P=0.66) and 25.0% versus 24.3% for immunotherapy (hazard ratio 1.03; 0.82 to 1.29; P=0.81). The split: prednisolone did reduce constrictive pericarditis (4.4% vs 7.8%; hazard ratio 0.56; 0.36 to 0.87; P=0.009) and hospitalisation (20.7% vs 25.2%; hazard ratio 0.79; P=0.04) — but both prednisolone and immunotherapy were associated with significantly more cancer, mainly HIV-associated (1.8% vs 0.6%, hazard ratio 3.27; and 1.8% vs 0.5%, hazard ratio 3.69). PROPOSED SPLIT — LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) for the primary composite for both interventions; prednisolone carries a real secondary benefit on constriction and a real harm signal on cancer, so no single stamp is honest.

cards.headline: IMPI (2014): neither prednisolone nor M. indicus pranii reduced death/tamponade/constriction — 23.8% vs 24.5% and 25.0% vs 24.3%
cards.summary: IMPI (2014): neither prednisolone nor M. indicus pranii reduced death/tamponade/constriction — 23.8% vs 24.5% and 25.0% vs 24.3%
cards.type: 2×2 factorial randomised trial (IMPI) — Tier C · SPLIT
cards.people: 1,400 adults with definite or probable tuberculous pericarditis, two-thirds with concomitant HIV infection, randomised in a 2×2 factorial design to prednisolone or placebo for 6 weeks and to Mycobacterium indicus pranii immunotherapy (five injections over 3 months) or placebo. Primary efficacy outcome: composite of death, cardiac tamponade requiring pericardiocentesis, or constrictive pericarditis.
cards.result: Primary outcome: no significant difference for prednisolone versus placebo (23.8% vs 24.5%; hazard ratio 0.95; 95% CI 0.77 to 1.18; P=0.66) or for M. indicus pranii versus placebo (25.0% vs 24.3%; hazard ratio 1.03; 95% CI 0.82 to 1.29; P=0.81). Prednisolone significantly reduced constrictive pericarditis (4.4% vs 7.8%; hazard ratio 0.56; 95% CI 0.36 to 0.87; P=0.009) and hospitalisation (20.7% vs 25.2%; hazard ratio 0.79; 95% CI 0.63 to 0.99; P=0.04). Both prednisolone and M. indicus pranii were associated with a significant increase in cancer (1.8% vs 0.6%, hazard ratio 3.27, 95% CI 1.07 to 10.03, P=0.03; and 1.8% vs 0.5%, hazard ratio 3.69, 95% CI 1.03 to 13.24, P=0.03), owing mainly to an increase in HIV-associated cancer.
cards.watchOut: Tier C and SPLIT: do not collapse this into 'steroids don't work' or 'steroids help'. The composite is null; the constriction benefit is a secondary endpoint in a trial where two-thirds of participants had HIV; and the cancer signal — small absolute numbers (1.8% vs ~0.5–0.6%) but a threefold relative hazard, concentrated in HIV-associated cancers — is the reason routine adjunctive prednisolone did not become standard on this evidence.

shelves.title: Point-of-care Xpert MTB/RIF in primary care (TB-NEAT): faster, more accurate decisions — no reduction in TB morbidity [THIN · SPLIT]
shelves.question: In adults with suspected TB at primary-care clinics, does nurse-performed point-of-care Xpert MTB/RIF improve same-day treatment decisions and TB-related morbidity versus sputum smear microscopy?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Point-of-Care Systems / standards · Primary Health Care · Tuberculosis, Pulmonary / diagnosis
shelves.balance: A SPLIT result, and the split is the lesson. In this pragmatic randomised trial (TB-NEAT), 1,502 adults with suspected tuberculosis at five primary-care facilities in South Africa, Zimbabwe, Zambia and Tanzania were assigned to nurse-performed point-of-care Xpert MTB/RIF (the specific tested product) or sputum smear microscopy. The test itself performed: sensitivity 83% versus 50% for microscopy at similar specificity (95% vs 96%), and accuracy matched laboratory-based Xpert. Decisions sped up: same-day diagnosis in 24% versus 13% and same-day treatment initiation in 23% versus 15%, and fewer culture-positive patients never started treatment (8% vs 15% untreated). But the primary outcome did not move: tuberculosis-related morbidity (TBscore and Karnofsky score) in treated culture-positive patients was identical at 2 and 6 months — partly, the authors note, because smear-negative patients in the microscopy arm were widely treated empirically anyway. THIN: a single pragmatic trial with a morbidity-score endpoint. PROPOSED SPLIT — POSSIBLE for faster, more accurate same-day decisions; (the treatment made no difference) for patient morbidity as measured.

cards.headline: TB-NEAT (2014): point-of-care Xpert doubled same-day treatment starts (23% vs 15%) but did not reduce TB morbidity
cards.summary: TB-NEAT (2014): point-of-care Xpert doubled same-day treatment starts (23% vs 15%) but did not reduce TB morbidity
cards.type: Pragmatic randomised multicentre trial (TB-NEAT) — THIN · SPLIT
cards.people: 1,502 adults with symptoms suggestive of active tuberculosis at five primary-care facilities in South Africa, Zimbabwe, Zambia and Tanzania, randomised to nurse-performed point-of-care Xpert MTB/RIF (744; 185 culture-positive) or sputum smear microscopy (758; 182 culture-positive). Primary outcome: tuberculosis-related morbidity (TBscore and Karnofsky performance score) in culture-positive patients who began treatment, at 2 and 6 months.
cards.result: Median TBscore did not differ at 2 months (2 vs 2; P=0.85) or 6 months (1 vs 1; P=0.35), nor did median Karnofsky score at 2 months (80 vs 90; P=0.23) or 6 months (100 vs 100; P=0.85). Point-of-care Xpert sensitivity was 83% (154 of 185) versus 50% (91 of 182) for microscopy (P=0.0001), with similar specificity (95% vs 96%; P=0.25). Same-day diagnosis: 24% versus 13% (P<0.0001); same-day treatment initiation: 23% versus 15% (P=0.0002). Fewer culture-positive patients in the Xpert group never received treatment (8% vs 15%; P=0.0302), but the proportions of all patients on treatment by day 56 were similar (43% vs 42%; P=0.6408).
cards.watchOut: THIN and SPLIT: one trial, and its patient-level endpoint is a morbidity score, not mortality or cure. The null on morbidity is not evidence the test lacks value — the comparison arm's heavy empiric treatment of smear-negative patients compressed the difference. Contrast STAMP (Shelf #2154), where a test-guided strategy in much sicker inpatients did reduce mortality.

shelves.title: Digital adherence technologies for TB in China: no effect on unfavourable outcomes in a 24-cluster trial (THIN)
shelves.question: In patients with drug-sensitive pulmonary TB, does a medication-monitor package (daily reminders, monthly provider adherence review, differentiated care for poor adherence) improve treatment outcomes versus standard care?
shelves.mesh: China · Humans · Medication Adherence · Treatment Outcome · Tuberculosis, Pulmonary / drug therapy
shelves.balance: One large cluster-randomised trial in one health system, with a clear null on outcomes and a candid explanation. Across 24 counties/districts in four Chinese prefectures, 2,686 patients with drug-sensitive pulmonary tuberculosis were in clusters assigned to a medication-monitor package (the specific tested programme: a monitor giving daily dosing reminders, monthly provider review of adherence data, and differentiated care for poor adherence) or to routine care with silent-mode monitors. By 18 months, the composite unfavourable outcome (death, loss to follow-up, treatment failure, switch to multidrug-resistant treatment, or recurrence) occurred in 16% of each group — adjusted risk ratio 1.01 (95% CI 0.73 to 1.40). Loss to follow-up made up 62% of events. The authors' own diagnosis: identifying non-adherence at monthly reviews failed to change patient management. THIN: a single cluster trial in a single system, and the interval still allows meaningful benefit or harm. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — no effect was shown, but one trial in one system cannot close the question for better-implemented versions.

cards.headline: China DAT cluster trial (2023): medication-monitor package had no effect on unfavourable TB outcomes — 16% vs 16%, adjusted RR 1.01
cards.summary: China DAT cluster trial (2023): medication-monitor package had no effect on unfavourable TB outcomes — 16% vs 16%, adjusted RR 1.01
cards.people: 3,074 patients aged 18 or older with GeneXpert-positive, rifampicin-sensitive pulmonary tuberculosis on daily fixed-dose combination treatment, enrolled across 24 counties/districts (clusters) in four prefectures in China, randomised 1:1 by cluster; 2,686 (87%) in the intention-to-treat population (median age 44 years; 71% male). Intervention clusters: medication monitor with daily reminders, monthly provider review of adherence data, and differentiated care for poor adherence. Control clusters: routine care, with adherence measured by silent-mode monitors. Primary outcome: composite of death, loss to follow-up, treatment failure, switch to multidrug-resistant tuberculosis treatment, or recurrence by 18 months.
cards.result: By 18 months (multiple imputation for missing outcomes), 239 of 1,388 control patients (16%, geometric mean of cluster-level proportions) and 224 of 1,298 intervention patients (16%) had a primary composite event — adjusted risk ratio 1.01 (95% CI 0.73 to 1.40). Of 463 events, 289 (62%) were loss to follow-up during treatment and 42 (9%) were tuberculosis recurrence. The authors concluded the intervention had no effect on unfavourable outcomes and identified a failure to change patient management after non-adherence was flagged at monthly reviews.
cards.watchOut: THIN: one health system, cluster design, and a composite dominated by loss to follow-up (62% of events) rather than microbiologic failure. The draft attributed this trial to 'Wei et al.'; the PubMed record's first author is Liu X, which is what is carded. A null for this implementation — monthly review, weakly acted on — is not a null for every adherence technology.
cards.source: Liu X et al. Digital adherence technologies to improve tuberculosis treatment outcomes in China: a cluster-randomised superiority trial. Lancet Glob Health. 2023. PMID: 37061308. shelves.title: Four-drug fixed-dose combinations versus separate drugs (Study C): non-inferiority met in 2 of 3 analyses — not fully demonstrated
shelves.question: In adults with newly diagnosed smear-positive pulmonary TB, is the 4-drug fixed-dose combination non-inferior to the same drugs given separately during the intensive phase?
shelves.mesh: Antitubercular Agents / administration & dosage · Drug Therapy, Combination · Humans · Tuberculosis, Pulmonary / drug therapy
shelves.balance: The honest answer is 'almost, and the shortfall is in the analysis rules, not in a visible efficacy gap'. In Study C, 1,585 adults with newly diagnosed smear-positive pulmonary tuberculosis at 11 sites in Africa, Asia and Latin America received rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide and ethambutol as a 4-drug fixed-dose combination or as separate drugs during the 8-week intensive phase. Favourable outcome at 18 months was 93.9% versus 94.6% per-protocol (risk difference −0.7 percentage points; 90% CI −3.0 to 1.5) — inside the 4% non-inferiority margin — but the strictest modified intention-to-treat model (every treatment change counted unfavourable) gave −1.5 points (90% CI −4.7 to 1.8), crossing the margin, so prespecified non-inferiority was met in only 2 of 3 analyses. A post hoc model gave −1.2 points (−3.9 to 1.5). Adverse events related to trial drugs were similarly distributed. The authors still preferred fixed-dose combinations for their administration advantages. PROPOSED POSSIBLE — outcomes are clinically near-identical, but the trial did not demonstrate full non-inferiority by its own strict definition, and every point estimate leaned slightly toward separate drugs.

cards.headline: Study C (2011): FDC met non-inferiority in 2 of 3 analyses — favourable outcome 93.9% vs 94.6% per-protocol
cards.summary: Study C (2011): FDC met non-inferiority in 2 of 3 analyses — favourable outcome 93.9% vs 94.6% per-protocol
cards.people: 1,585 adults with newly diagnosed smear-positive pulmonary tuberculosis at 11 sites in Africa, Asia and Latin America, randomised to the 4-drug regimen (rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, ethambutol) as a fixed-dose combination (798) or as separate drugs (787) during the 8-week intensive phase. Main outcome: favourable treatment outcome (negative culture at 18 months and not previously classified unfavourable); prespecified non-inferiority margin 4%, requiring consistent results across per-protocol and two modified intention-to-treat models.
cards.result: Per-protocol: favourable outcome in 555 of 591 (93.9%) on the fixed-dose combination versus 548 of 579 (94.6%) on separate drugs — risk difference −0.7 percentage points (90% CI −3.0 to 1.5). Model 1 modified intention-to-treat (all treatment changes counted unfavourable): 83.3% versus 84.8% — difference −1.5 points (90% CI −4.7 to 1.8), crossing the 4% margin. Post hoc model 2: 89.8% versus 91.0% — difference −1.2 points (90% CI −3.9 to 1.5). Adverse events related to trial drugs were similarly distributed between groups. The authors concluded non-inferiority was satisfied in 2 of 3 analyses but not fully demonstrated under the trial's strict definition, while still preferring fixed-dose combinations for their potential administration advantages.
cards.watchOut: The inconsistency is the finding: whether the combination 'passes' depends on how treatment changes are classified, and the one failing model is the most conservative. Fixed-dose combinations were adopted for programmatic reasons (simpler supply, no selective non-adherence to single drugs) that this efficacy comparison does not capture — do not read this shelf as a verdict against their use, nor as proof of equal efficacy.
cards.source: Lienhardt C et al. shelves.title: Oral fexinidazole for rhodesiense sleeping sickness: a single-arm benchmark study met its fatality target
shelves.question: In stage 1 and stage 2 Trypanosoma brucei rhodesiense human African trypanosomiasis, is oral fexinidazole an effective alternative to suramin and melarsoprol?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Humans · Nitroimidazoles · Treatment Outcome · Trypanocidal Agents · Trypanosoma brucei rhodesiense · Trypanosomiasis, African
shelves.balance: The only modern treatment study for this rapidly lethal infection, and deliberately not a randomised one — a randomised comparison against melarsoprol, an arsenical that kills a measurable share of the people who receive it, is not a trial anyone can run. In a prospective, open-label, single-arm phase 2–3 study in Uganda and Malawi, 45 patients with parasitologically confirmed rhodesiense human African trypanosomiasis (35 stage 2, 10 stage 1) received 10 days of oral fexinidazole. The primary end point — fatality at end of hospital admission in stage 2 disease, counting only deaths possibly related to the disease or the drug — was 0 of 34 (0%; 90% CI 0 to 8.43), below the predefined 8.5% benchmark drawn from melarsoprol-era literature (p=0.0488, just under the line). One stage 2 patient relapsed at week 9; there were no stage 1 failures and no unexpected safety signals. PROPOSED POSSIBLE — the benchmark was met in a small single-arm study of a disease that is fatal untreated; the evidence is thin by design and by necessity, and the margin over the benchmark was narrow.

cards.headline: Matovu 2025: stage 2 fatality at end of hospitalisation 0 of 34 (0%) on oral fexinidazole, against a predefined 8.5% melarsoprol-era benchmark (p=0.0488)
cards.summary: Matovu 2025: stage 2 fatality at end of hospitalisation 0 of 34 (0%) on oral fexinidazole, against a predefined 8.5% melarsoprol-era benchmark (p=0.0488)
cards.type: Prospective open-label single-arm phase 2–3 benchmark study
cards.people: 45 participants aged 6 years or older, weighing 20 kg or more, with parasitologically confirmed Trypanosoma brucei rhodesiense human African trypanosomiasis at two centres (Lwala, Uganda and Rumphi, Malawi): 35 with stage 2 and 10 with stage 1 disease. All received oral fexinidazole for 10 days at the recommended bodyweight-based dosage while admitted, with 12 months of follow-up. The study was prospective, open-label, single-arm, phase 2–3, and non-randomised, using a benchmark design against predefined literature-based rates.
cards.result: One death occurred during treatment but was considered unrelated to rhodesiense human African trypanosomiasis or fexinidazole and was excluded from the efficacy analysis. No other deaths had occurred by end of hospital admission in participants with stage 2 disease, giving a fatality rate of 0 (0%) of 34 (90% CI 0 to 8.43), lower than the predefined 8.5% rate (p=0.0488). One participant with stage 2 disease had a relapse at week 9. No failures were reported in participants with stage 1 disease. No unexpected safety signals were identified on the basis of standard assessments and electrocardiograms.
cards.watchOut: Single-arm, 45 patients, and the headline p-value (0.0488) sits just inside significance against a literature-derived benchmark — historical fatality rates are an imperfect yardstick, and one differently classified death would move the result. The comparison treatments (suramin for stage 1, melarsoprol for stage 2) were not given to anyone in this study. What the study does establish is feasibility and short-term safety of an all-oral regimen in a disease with no ethical randomised alternative.

shelves.title: Paromomycin + miltefosine for East African visceral leishmaniasis: 91% cured, non-inferiority narrowly missed in mITT, met per-protocol
shelves.question: In East African visceral leishmaniasis, is 14 days of paromomycin + miltefosine non-inferior to 17 days of SSG + paromomycin?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Humans · Child · Paromomycin · Antiprotozoal Agents · Antimony Sodium Gluconate · Leishmaniasis, Visceral · Treatment Outcome · Drug Therapy, Combination · Africa, Eastern · Phosphorylcholine
shelves.balance: Statistically a near-miss, clinically a strong candidate. In this open-label phase 3 trial at seven East African sites, 439 patients were randomised to paromomycin (20 mg/kg/day) plus miltefosine (allometric dosing) for 14 days, or SSG plus paromomycin for 17 days; 424 completed the trial. Definitive cure at 6 months in the modified intention-to-treat population was 91.2% (155 of 170) on PM/MF versus 91.8% (156 of 170) on SSG/PM — a difference of 0.6% whose 97.5% confidence interval (−6.2 to 7.4) crossed the 7% non-inferiority margin, so non-inferiority narrowly failed in mITT; in the per-protocol population it was met (92% versus 91.7%; difference −0.3%, 97.5% CI −7.0 to 6.5). The challenger regimen removes SSG entirely — no antimonial cardiotoxicity risk — needs one less injection per day, and is 3 days shorter. PROPOSED POSSIBLE — one well-run phase 3 trial with cure rates above 91% in both arms and a borderline formal non-inferiority result; the evidence supports PM/MF as a comparable alternative, not yet a proven-equal replacement.

cards.headline: Musa 2023: PM/miltefosine cure 91.2% vs 91.8% for SSG/PM at 6 months — non-inferiority narrowly missed in mITT, met per-protocol
cards.summary: Musa 2023: PM/miltefosine cure 91.2% vs 91.8% for SSG/PM at 6 months — non-inferiority narrowly missed in mITT, met per-protocol
cards.people: Patients with visceral leishmaniasis randomised at seven sites in eastern Africa in an open-label, phase 3, randomised non-inferiority trial: 439 randomised, 424 completing the trial. Experimental arm: paromomycin (PM) 20 mg/kg/day plus miltefosine (MF, allometric dose) for 14 days. Control: sodium stibogluconate (SSG) 20 mg/kg/day plus PM 15 mg/kg/day for 17 days. Primary outcome: definitive cure at 6 months, in the modified intention-to-treat (mITT) population (patients with primary VL who received at least one dose); non-inferiority margin 7%.
cards.result: Definitive cure at 6 months in the mITT population was 91.2% (155 of 170) in the PM/MF arm and 91.8% (156 of 170) in the SSG/PM arm, a difference of 0.6% (97.5% CI −6.2 to 7.4): non-inferiority of PM/MF was not demonstrated in the mITT analysis because the interval crossed the 7% margin. In the per-protocol population, definitive cure was 92% (149 of 162) versus 91.7% (155 of 169), a difference of −0.3% (97.5% CI −7.0 to 6.5), and non-inferiority was demonstrated. The authors note the PM/MF combination offers one less injection per day, a 3-day shorter course, and no risk of SSG-associated cardiotoxicity.
cards.watchOut: The mITT denominators (170 per arm) are much smaller than the 439 randomised — the abstract does not reconcile the attrition here, and the non-inferiority verdict flips between analysis populations, so neither 'equivalent' nor 'inferior' is a safe one-word summary. Open-label. Miltefosine is teratogenic, which constrains use in women of childbearing potential — a practical limit the abstract's safety summary does not foreground. The SSG+PM control regimen itself rests on the 2012 LEAP trial (Shelf #2177).
cards.source: Musa AM et al. Paromomycin and Miltefosine Combination as an Alternative to Treat Patients With Visceral Leishmaniasis in Eastern Africa: A Randomized, Controlled, Multicountry Trial. shelves.title: Whipworm combinations (Pemba 2015): albendazole + oxantel pamoate cured 68.5%; albendazole + mebendazole no better than mebendazole alone
shelves.question: For Trichuris (whipworm) infection in children, which single-dose combination works — albendazole + oxantel pamoate, albendazole + ivermectin, or albendazole + mebendazole?
shelves.mesh: Albendazole · Anthelmintics · Drug Therapy, Combination · Helminthiasis · Intestinal Diseases, Parasitic · Ivermectin · Mebendazole · Pyrantel Pamoate · Trichuriasis · Trichuris
shelves.balance: One combination clearly worked against whipworm; one helped somewhat; one added nothing. In this four-arm randomised trial, 440 children aged 6–14 infected with Trichuris trichiura on Pemba Island, Tanzania (110 per arm; 431 analysed) received a single dose of albendazole plus oxantel pamoate, albendazole plus ivermectin, albendazole plus mebendazole, or mebendazole alone. Trichuris cure: 68.5% (74 of 108; 95% CI 59.6 to 77.4) with albendazole–oxantel pamoate, with a 99.2% egg-reduction rate; 27.5% (30 of 109) with albendazole–ivermectin (egg reduction 94.5%); and just 8.4% (9 of 107) for both albendazole–mebendazole and mebendazole alone — adding a second benzimidazole to mebendazole bought nothing. Adverse events were mostly mild (abdominal cramps in 9–18% across arms). PROPOSED POSSIBLE — one randomised four-arm trial with a large, internally consistent gradient; oxantel pamoate is the component that changes whipworm outcomes, and later combination work builds on exactly this result.

cards.headline: Speich 2015: albendazole+oxantel pamoate cured 68.5% of Trichuris infections versus 27.5% (albendazole+ivermectin) and 8.4% (mebendazole-based arms)
cards.summary: Speich 2015: albendazole+oxantel pamoate cured 68.5% of Trichuris infections versus 27.5% (albendazole+ivermectin) and 8.4% (mebendazole-based arms)
cards.people: 440 children aged 6–14 years in two schools on Pemba Island, Tanzania, all infected with Trichuris trichiura and concomitant intestinal nematodes, randomly assigned (110 per group) to a single oral dose of albendazole (400 mg) plus ivermectin (200 μg/kg), albendazole (400 mg) plus mebendazole (500 mg), albendazole (400 mg) plus oxantel pamoate (20 mg/kg), or mebendazole (500 mg) alone. Primary end points: the proportion of children cured of T. trichiura and the reduction in T. trichiura egg counts (geometric means), analysed by available case; 431 children were included in the primary-endpoint analysis.
cards.result: Albendazole plus oxantel pamoate (74 of 108 children cured [68.5%, 95% CI 59.6 to 77.4]; egg reduction 99.2%, 98.7 to 99.6) and albendazole plus ivermectin (30 of 109 cured [27.5%, 19.0 to 36.0]; egg reduction 94.5%, 91.7 to 96.3) were significantly more effective against T. trichiura than mebendazole alone (9 of 107 cured [8.4%, 3.1 to 13.8]; egg reduction 58.5%, 45.2 to 70.9). Albendazole plus mebendazole had similar low efficacy (9 of 107 cured [8.4%, 3.1 to 13.8]; egg reduction 51.6%, 35.0 to 65.3) to mebendazole alone. About a fifth of the children reported adverse events, mainly mild: abdominal cramps in 12.0% (albendazole+ivermectin), 9.3% (albendazole+mebendazole), 18.2% (albendazole+oxantel pamoate), and 14.5% (mebendazole) of children, and headache in 4.6%, 5.6%, 10.9%, and 6.4% respectively. The authors concluded the head-to-head comparison showed the highest efficacy for albendazole plus oxantel pamoate against T. trichiura.
cards.watchOut: Single-dose regimens in schoolchildren on one island, analysed by available case; cure was assessed against Trichuris, with concomitant Ascaris and hookworm outcomes reported separately in the full text. Note the draft for this topic paired this citation with a 2014 single-agent oxantel pamoate paper — that is a different trial (Keiser et al., N Engl J Med 2014; PMID: 24521107, named, not carded); PMID 25589326 is the four-arm combination trial carded here, and the question follows it.

shelves.question: Is the child-friendly dispersible tablet arpraziquantel (L-praziquantel) as effective as standard praziquantel for schistosomiasis in preschool children?
shelves.mesh: Anthelmintics · Child, Preschool · Praziquantel · Schistosoma mansoni · Schistosomiasis mansoni · Schistosomiasis
shelves.balance: The paediatric formulation did what it was designed to do. Arpraziquantel is the levorotatory enantiomer of praziquantel, developed as a smaller, dispersible, better-tasting tablet for children too young to swallow the standard 600 mg tablet. In this phase 3 trial in Côte d'Ivoire and Kenya, 2,663 preschool children were prescreened and 326 were diagnosed with Schistosoma mansoni or S. haematobium infection; the efficacy population was 280 children (median age 5.1 years; 47% female). In the randomised cohort of 4–6-year-olds with S. mansoni, cure rates were numerically higher on arpraziquantel than on standard praziquantel — 87.8% (95% CI 79.6 to 93.5) versus 81.3% (67.4 to 91.1) — and the formulation was well tolerated: the commonest drug-related events were abdominal pain (14% of 288 treated children), diarrhoea (9%), somnolence (7%), and vomiting (6%). PROPOSED POSSIBLE — one open-label partly randomised phase 3 trial supporting comparable efficacy with a formulation advantage in exactly the age group the standard tablet fails.

cards.headline: N'Goran 2023: arpraziquantel cured 87.8% versus 81.3% for standard praziquantel in randomised 4–6-year-olds with S. mansoni
cards.summary: N'Goran 2023: arpraziquantel cured 87.8% versus 81.3% for standard praziquantel in randomised 4–6-year-olds with S. mansoni
cards.people: Preschool children in Côte d'Ivoire and Kenya in an open-label, partly randomised phase 3 trial of arpraziquantel (the L-enantiomer of praziquantel, as an orally dispersible tablet): 2,663 children prescreened, 326 diagnosed with Schistosoma mansoni or S. haematobium infection, and 280 children in the efficacy population (median age 5.1 years; 47% female). Cohort 1 (children aged 4–6 years with S. mansoni) was randomised between arpraziquantel and standard praziquantel; other cohorts (younger children, S. haematobium) received arpraziquantel in a partly randomised design.
cards.result: Clinical cure rates in cohort 1 were high with both formulations: 87.8% (95% CI 79.6 to 93.5) for arpraziquantel versus 81.3% (67.4 to 91.1) for standard praziquantel. Across the efficacy population, arpraziquantel was efficacious against both S. mansoni and S. haematobium in children aged 3 months to 6 years. Drug-related adverse events in treated children (n=288) were mostly abdominal pain (14%, 41 of 288), diarrhoea (9%), somnolence (7%), and vomiting (6%), consistent with praziquantel's known profile. The trial supports arpraziquantel as a paediatric formulation intended to close the treatment gap for preschool-aged children, who cannot reliably swallow the standard large tablet.
cards.watchOut: Only cohort 1 was a head-to-head randomised comparison, sample sizes in the S. haematobium and infant cohorts were small, and cure was assessed parasitologically in a partly randomised design — the trial's contribution is a usable, tolerated formulation for preschool children rather than proof of superior efficacy. Dose per age band and the cure definitions follow the record; the abstract does not report egg-reduction rates here.

shelves.title: Doxycycline anti-Wolbachia therapy for lymphatic filariasis: microfilariae nearly eliminated, adult worms gone in most at 14 months
shelves.question: In lymphatic filariasis, does 8 weeks of doxycycline (anti-Wolbachia) sterilise and kill adult Wuchereria bancrofti worms?
shelves.mesh: Anti-Bacterial Agents · Double-Blind Method · Doxycycline · Elephantiasis, Filarial · Wolbachia · Wuchereria bancrofti
shelves.balance: A small trial with a striking biological result. Doxycycline does not attack the filarial worm directly; it depletes Wolbachia, the bacterial endosymbionts the worm needs to reproduce and survive. In this double-blind, placebo-controlled field trial in Tanzania, 72 people infected with Wuchereria bancrofti received doxycycline 200 mg/day for 8 weeks (n=34) or placebo (n=38), with follow-up at 5, 8, 11, and 14 months. Microfilaraemia was almost completely eliminated at 8–14 months in the doxycycline group (p<0.001 at all timepoints); at 14 months, adult worms were detectable by ultrasonography in only 22% (6 of 27) of the doxycycline group versus 88% (24 of 27) on placebo (p<0.0001) — evidence of a macrofilaricidal effect no single-dose antifilarial then offered — and circulating filarial antigen fell to about half its baseline (p=0.015). One death (HIV-related) occurred in the doxycycline group; other adverse events were few and mild. PROPOSED POSSIBLE — a single small per-protocol field trial, but with large, coherent effects across microfilariae, adult worms, and antigen; the 8-week daily course is the practical barrier to mass use.

cards.headline: Taylor 2005: 8 weeks of doxycycline nearly eliminated microfilaraemia and left adult worms undetectable in 78% versus 12% at 14 months
cards.summary: Taylor 2005: 8 weeks of doxycycline nearly eliminated microfilaraemia and left adult worms undetectable in 78% versus 12% at 14 months
cards.people: 72 individuals infected with Wuchereria bancrofti in Kimang'a village, Pangani, Tanzania, in a double-blind, placebo-controlled field trial: doxycycline 200 mg/day for 8 weeks (n=34) or placebo (n=38), with assessments before treatment and at 5, 8, 11, and 14 months after the start of treatment. Outcomes were assessed in the per-protocol analysis: microfilaraemia, circulating filarial antigenaemia, and adult-worm detection by ultrasonography, alongside Wolbachia depletion in microfilariae.
cards.result: Doxycycline treatment resulted in almost complete elimination of microfilaraemia at 8–14 months' follow-up (p<0.001 for all timepoints). At 14 months, adult worms were absent by ultrasonography in the great majority of the doxycycline group: worms were detected in 22% (6 of 27) of doxycycline-treated individuals compared with 88% (24 of 27) on placebo (p<0.0001), indicating a substantial macrofilaricidal effect. Antigenaemia fell to roughly half of pre-treatment levels (p=0.015). One death occurred in the doxycycline group, in a patient with concurrent HIV infection; other adverse events were few and mild. The authors concluded that an 8-week course of doxycycline monotherapy induces long-term decreases in Wolbachia levels, microfilaraemia, and filarial antigenaemia, with macrofilaricidal activity against W. bancrofti.
cards.watchOut: Seventy-two participants, per-protocol analysis, one village — effects this large in a trial this small earn POSSIBLE, not more. Eight weeks of daily doxycycline cannot be delivered like single-dose mass drug administration, and doxycycline is contraindicated in pregnancy and young children, which limits population strategies; later programmes combined shorter anti-Wolbachia courses with standard antifilarials (named as the field's direction, not carded here).
cards.source: Taylor MJ et al. Macrofilaricidal activity after doxycycline treatment of Wuchereria bancrofti: a double-blind, randomised placebo-controlled trial. Lancet. 2005. PMID: 15964448. No registry ID on the record (pre-registration era). shelves.title: Uniform six-month multidrug therapy for leprosy (U-MDT/CT-BR): matched 12 months on reactions and disability; relapse still the open question
shelves.question: In multibacillary leprosy, is a uniform 6-month regimen (the paucibacillary regimen given to everyone) as safe and effective as the standard 12-month multibacillary MDT?
shelves.mesh: Clofazimine · Dapsone · Drug Therapy, Combination · Leprostatic Agents · Leprosy, Multibacillary · Recurrence · Rifampin · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: Six months looked as safe as twelve on everything measured during the trial — with the decisive outcome, relapse, still thinly counted when the trial reported. In U-MDT/CT-BR, 613 newly diagnosed multibacillary patients in Brazil were randomised to the uniform regimen (dapsone, rifampicin, and clofazimine for 6 months) or regular MDT (the same three drugs for 12 months). There was no statistically significant difference between groups in the Kaplan-Meier survival functions for leprosy reactions or for disability progression, and bacilloscopic index trends were compared as a main outcome. During active follow-up, four patients in the uniform group relapsed — a rate of 2.6 per 1000 patients per year (95% CI 0.81 to 6.2) — and during passive follow-up three more relapsed in the uniform group and one in the regular group: small numbers, wide intervals, and exactly the outcome a shortened regimen must be judged on over a decade, not a trial period. PROPOSED POSSIBLE — one open-label randomised trial supporting the uniform regimen on reactions and disability, with relapse ascertainment still limited at report.

cards.headline: Penna 2017 (U-MDT/CT-BR): no significant difference in reactions or disability progression between 6-month uniform and 12-month regular MDT in 613 multibacillary patients
cards.summary: Penna 2017 (U-MDT/CT-BR): no significant difference in reactions or disability progression between 6-month uniform and 12-month regular MDT in 613 multibacillary patients
cards.people: 613 newly diagnosed, untreated multibacillary leprosy patients in Brazil, in an independent, open-label, randomised, controlled trial conducted from 2007 to 2015, comparing a uniform regimen (U-MDT: dapsone plus rifampicin plus clofazimine for six months) with WHO regular MDT (R-MDT: the same drugs for 12 months). Main outcomes: frequency of reactions, bacilloscopic index trend, disability progression, and relapse rates.
cards.result: There was no statistically significant difference in the Kaplan-Meier survival function regarding reaction or disability progression among the groups. During active follow-up, four patients in the U-MDT group relapsed, representing a relapse rate of 2.6 per 1000 patients per year of active follow-up (95% CI 0.81 to 6.2 per 1000). During passive follow-up, three patients relapsed in the U-MDT group and one in the R-MDT group. The trial registration is ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00669643.
cards.watchOut: Open-label, single-country, and — critically — powered around reactions and disability rather than relapse, the late failure mode that decides whether halving treatment is safe. Relapse counts at report were single digits in each arm. A 10-year post-trial follow-up (Penna et al., Braz J Infect Dis 2024 — named as follow-up, not carded) later reported overall relapse of 4.08% (4.95% uniform versus 3.10% regular; difference not statistically significant), which readers should weigh alongside this card.
cards.source: Penna GO et al. Uniform multidrug therapy for leprosy patients in Brazil (U-MDT/CT-BR): Results of an open label, randomized and controlled clinical trial, among multibacillary patients. PLoS Negl Trop Dis. 2017. PMID: 28704363. Registry ID: NCT00669643, from the record.
