shelves.title: Thermotherapy for cutaneous leishmaniasis (Kabul): one heat treatment matched intralesional antimony, beat intramuscular antimony
shelves.question: For a single cutaneous leishmaniasis lesion from L. tropica, does local thermotherapy cure as well as antimonial injections?
shelves.mesh: Antimony Sodium Gluconate · Antiprotozoal Agents · Hyperthermia, Induced · Leishmania tropica · Leishmaniasis, Cutaneous · Odds Ratio
shelves.balance: Heat beat the systemic drug and matched the injected-into-the-lesion drug — in one Afghan trial of single L. tropica lesions. Four hundred one patients with a single lesion were randomised to thermotherapy (localised current applied at 50°C for 30 seconds), intralesional sodium stibogluconate (SSG), or intramuscular SSG. Complete reepithelialisation at 100 days: 69.4% (75 of 108) with thermotherapy, 75.3% (70 of 93) with intralesional SSG, and 44.8% (26 of 58) with intramuscular SSG; the odds ratio for cure with thermotherapy versus intramuscular SSG was 2.80 (95% CI 1.45 to 5.41; P=.002), and median time to cure was 53 days versus 75 days (intralesional) versus more than 100 days (intramuscular) (P=.003). For programmes, the practical point is large: one heat application, no cardiotoxic systemic antimony, no weeks of painful injections. PROPOSED POSSIBLE — a single randomised trial, in a single-species, single-lesion population, with the analysed set smaller than the enrolled 401; generalisation to other species, multiple lesions, or mucosal risk is untested here.

cards.headline: Reithinger 2005: thermotherapy cured 69.4% of single L. tropica lesions at 100 days versus 75.3% intralesional SSG and 44.8% intramuscular SSG
cards.summary: Reithinger 2005: thermotherapy cured 69.4% of single L. tropica lesions at 100 days versus 75.3% intralesional SSG and 44.8% intramuscular SSG
cards.people: 401 patients with a single cutaneous leishmaniasis lesion caused by Leishmania tropica in Kabul, Afghanistan, randomised in a controlled trial to thermotherapy (localised current applied to the lesion at 50°C for 30 seconds), intralesional sodium stibogluconate (SSG; pentavalent antimony), or intramuscular SSG. The end point was clinical cure — complete reepithelialisation at 100 days after treatment initiation.
cards.result: The percentage of patients cured was 69.4% (75 of 108 patients) in the thermotherapy group, 75.3% (70 of 93) in the intralesional SSG group, and 44.8% (26 of 58) in the intramuscular SSG group. The odds ratio for cure in the thermotherapy group versus the intramuscular SSG group was 2.80 (95% CI 1.45 to 5.41; P=.002). Median time to cure was 53 days in the thermotherapy group, 75 days in the intralesional SSG group, and more than 100 days in the intramuscular SSG group (P=.003). The authors concluded that thermotherapy is a potentially valuable alternative to intralesional and intramuscular SSG, especially where antimonial drugs are unavailable or unaffordable.
cards.watchOut: The cure denominators (108, 93, and 58) sum to 259 of the 401 enrolled — the abstract reports the analysed set without reconciling the difference here. Single lesions of one species in one city: L. tropica in Kabul is typically self-limiting over longer horizons, and the trial says nothing about L. major, L. braziliensis, multiple lesions, or lesions at mucosal risk. No registry ID appears on the record (2005, pre-registration era).
cards.source: Reithinger R et al. Efficacy of Thermotherapy to Treat Cutaneous Leishmaniasis Caused by Leishmania tropica in Kabul, Afghanistan: A Randomized, Controlled Trial. Clin Infect Dis. 2005. PMID: 15791515. No registry ID on the record (pre-registration era). shelves.title: SSG + paromomycin for East African visceral leishmaniasis (LEAP 2012): 17-day combination matched 30-day SSG; paromomycin alone was worse
shelves.question: In East African visceral leishmaniasis, does 17 days of SSG + paromomycin match 30 days of SSG alone — and is paromomycin alone enough?
shelves.mesh: Antimony Sodium Gluconate · Antiprotozoal Agents · Drug Therapy, Combination · Leishmaniasis, Visceral · Paromomycin · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: The combination matched the standard; paromomycin alone did not — a clean geographic lesson. In this multicentre East African trial (the LEAP study), patients aged 4–60 with parasitologically confirmed visceral leishmaniasis were randomised in two comparisons. Paromomycin alone (20 mg/kg/day for 21 days) was significantly worse than SSG alone (20 mg/kg/day for 30 days): efficacy at 6 months 84.3% versus 94.1% (difference 9.7%, 95% CI 3.6 to 15.7; p=0.002) — the regimen registered in India underperformed in East Africa. The SSG-plus-paromomycin combination (17 days) was comparable to 30-day SSG: 91.4% versus 93.9% (difference 2.5%, 95% CI −1.3 to 6.3; p=0.198), with no apparent safety differences, nearly halving the treatment course and the antimony exposure. A WHO Expert Committee recommended SSG-plus-paromomycin as first-line for East Africa in March 2010. PROPOSED POSSIBLE — one large randomised trial supports the combination as equivalent-in-effect to standard SSG; the stamp is a single verdict on the combination question, with paromomycin-alone inferiority recorded in the card rather than split, because the shelf's question is the combination.

cards.headline: Musa 2012 (LEAP): SSG+paromomycin 17 days comparable to SSG 30 days (91.4% vs 93.9%); paromomycin alone significantly worse (84.3% vs 94.1%)
cards.summary: Musa 2012 (LEAP): SSG+paromomycin 17 days comparable to SSG 30 days (91.4% vs 93.9%); paromomycin alone significantly worse (84.3% vs 94.1%)
cards.people: Patients aged 4–60 years with parasitologically confirmed visceral leishmaniasis at six sites in Sudan, Ethiopia, Kenya, and Uganda, in a multicentre, open-label, randomised controlled trial comparing paromomycin sulphate (PM) alone (20 mg/kg/day for 21 days) and SSG plus PM (PM 15 mg/kg/day and SSG 20 mg/kg/day for 17 days) against SSG alone (20 mg/kg/day for 30 days). Primary efficacy outcome: parasite clearance at 6 months after end of treatment.
cards.result: The PM versus SSG comparison enrolled 205 patients per arm, with primary efficacy data available for 198 and 200 patients respectively; the SSG & PM versus SSG comparison enrolled 381 and 386 patients per arm, with primary efficacy data available for 359 patients per arm. In intention-to-treat complete-case analyses, the efficacy of PM was significantly lower than SSG (84.3% versus 94.1%, difference = 9.7%, 95% CI 3.6 to 15.7; p=0.002). The efficacy of SSG & PM was comparable to SSG (91.4% versus 93.9%, difference = 2.5%, 95% CI −1.3 to 6.3; p=0.198). End-of-treatment efficacy results were very similar, and there were no apparent differences in the safety profile of the three regimens. The authors concluded that the 17-day SSG & PM combination had a good safety profile and efficacy similar to the standard 30-day SSG treatment; a WHO Expert Committee recommended it as first-line treatment for VL in East Africa in March 2010.
cards.watchOut: Two comparisons share one SSG reference arm, and the paromomycin-alone arm was restarted at a higher dose mid-trial after an interim analysis showed <50% efficacy at the original 15 mg/kg dose in Sudan — the carded 20 mg/kg comparison is the restarted one. Open-label with parasitologic outcomes. The regional contrast matters: paromomycin monotherapy is registered for VL in India, where it performed better; East African results do not transfer automatically. The later all-oral combination trial (Musa 2023) is Shelf #2171.
cards.source: Musa A et al. Sodium Stibogluconate (SSG) & Paromomycin Combination Compared to SSG for Visceral Leishmaniasis in East Africa: A Randomised Controlled Trial. PLoS Negl Trop Dis. 2012. PMID: 22724029. Registry ID: NCT00255567, from the record. shelves.title: Weekly doxycycline prophylaxis against leptospirosis (Panama trial): 20 cases on placebo versus 1 on doxycycline
shelves.question: In soldiers training in a leptospirosis-endemic jungle environment, does weekly doxycycline 200 mg prevent clinical leptospirosis versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Double-Blind Method · Doxycycline · Humans · Leptospirosis · Military Medicine · Panama Canal Zone
shelves.balance: One old, large, well-run trial with a dramatic result that has never been replicated at scale. In the autumn of 1982, 940 US Army volunteers training in the Panamanian jungle were randomised, double-blind, to weekly doxycycline 200 mg or placebo for about three weeks of training plus a dose at completion. Leptospirosis struck 20 soldiers on placebo (attack rate 4.2%) versus 1 on doxycycline (attack rate 0.2%; P<0.001) — a 95.0% protective efficacy, an absolute reduction of about 4 cases per 100 soldiers over three weeks. The setting is narrow: healthy young soldiers, one jungle, one short exposure window, one season. Later evidence in civilian and flood-exposure settings is observational and mixed (named, not carded). PROPOSED POSSIBLE — a single 1982 field trial, large and blinded, with an effect too big to be noise but confined to its setting; Prevention hub cross-point: Shelf #1.

cards.headline: Takafuji 1984: leptospirosis in 20 soldiers on placebo (4.2%) versus 1 on weekly doxycycline (0.2%) — efficacy 95.0%
cards.summary: Takafuji 1984: leptospirosis in 20 soldiers on placebo (4.2%) versus 1 on weekly doxycycline (0.2%) — efficacy 95.0%
cards.people: 940 volunteers from two US Army units deployed to the Republic of Panama for approximately three weeks of jungle training in the fall of 1982, in a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled field trial. Doxycycline 200 mg or placebo was given orally once weekly and again at the completion of training. The outcome was clinical leptospirosis, an important cause of morbidity in soldiers training in Panama.
cards.result: Twenty cases of leptospirosis occurred in the placebo group (an attack rate of 4.2 per cent), as compared with only one case in the doxycycline group (attack rate, 0.2 per cent; P less than 0.001), yielding an efficacy of 95.0 per cent. In absolute terms, about 4 fewer cases per 100 soldiers over roughly three weeks of jungle training. The authors concluded the study demonstrated the value of doxycycline as a prophylactic drug against leptospirosis.
cards.watchOut: A single trial from 1982 in young male soldiers with a defined, brief, high-intensity exposure. It does not answer prophylaxis for residents of endemic areas, flood responders over longer periods, or travellers generally — and diagnostic methods and circulating serovars differ by place and era. No comparable randomised trial has repeated the experiment at this size.
cards.source: Takafuji ET et al. An efficacy trial of doxycycline chemoprophylaxis against leptospirosis. N Engl J Med. 1984. PMID: 6363930. No registry ID — pre-registration-era trial (1982). shelves.title: Two antivenoms for carpet viper envenoming (Nigeria): EchiTAb Plus-ICP slightly more effective, EchiTAb-G slightly safer
shelves.question: For Echis ocellatus envenoming, is the polyspecific antivenom EchiTAb Plus-ICP non-inferior to the monospecific EchiTAb-G for restoring blood clotting?
shelves.mesh: Antivenins · Blood Coagulation Tests · Double-Blind Method · Nigeria · Poisoning · Treatment Outcome · Viper Venoms · Viperidae
shelves.balance: Both antivenoms worked; the polyspecific one worked slightly better and reacted slightly more. In this randomised, double-blind non-inferiority trial at Kaltungo, Nigeria, patients with Echis ocellatus envenoming and incoagulable blood received either EchiTAb Plus-ICP (a polyspecific equine antivenom; initial dose 3 vials) or EchiTAb-G (a monospecific ovine antivenom; initial dose 1 vial), with additional doses as needed. Permanent restoration of blood coagulability 6 hours after the initial dose was achieved by 83.0% (161 of 194) with EchiTAb Plus-ICP versus 75.7% (156 of 206) with EchiTAb-G — a relative risk of 1.10 (one-sided 95% CI lower limit 1.01; P=0.05), meeting the non-inferiority criterion with a small superiority trend: an absolute difference of about 7 more patients per 100 restored by 6 hours. Early (anaphylactoid) reactions were more frequent with EchiTAb Plus-ICP: 25.8% (50 of 194) versus 18.9% (39 of 206) (relative risk 1.36, one-sided 95% CI upper limit 1.86; P=0.06). PROPOSED POSSIBLE — a single randomised head-to-head trial; the authors' own summary is the fair one: EchiTAb Plus-ICP slightly more effective, EchiTAb-G slightly safer, both recommended for West African Echis envenoming.

cards.headline: Abubakar 2010: EchiTAb Plus-ICP restored coagulability at 6 hours in 83.0% versus 75.7% for EchiTAb-G; early reactions 25.8% versus 18.9%
cards.summary: Abubakar 2010: EchiTAb Plus-ICP restored coagulability at 6 hours in 83.0% versus 75.7% for EchiTAb-G; early reactions 25.8% versus 18.9%
cards.people: Patients with West African savannah rat snake (Echis ocellatus) envenoming and incoagulable blood at Kaltungo, Nigeria, in a randomised, double-blind, controlled non-inferiority trial comparing two antivenoms (named tested products, given for identification because antivenoms are biological products that differ by manufacturer): EchiTAb Plus-ICP (ET-Plus), a polyspecific equine antivenom raised against Echis ocellatus, Bitis arietans, and Naja nigricollis (initial dose 3 vials), and EchiTAb-G (ET-G), a monospecific ovine antivenom (initial dose 1 vial). Primary end point: permanent restoration of blood coagulability 6 hours after the initial dose.
cards.result: Permanent restoration of coagulability at 6 hours was achieved in 83.0% (161 of 194) of patients given ET-Plus and 75.7% (156 of 206) given ET-G (relative risk 1.10, one-sided 95% CI lower limit 1.01; P=0.05), satisfying non-inferiority with a trend favouring ET-Plus. Early reactions occurred in 25.8% (50 of 194) of ET-Plus patients and 18.9% (39 of 206) of ET-G patients (relative risk 1.36, one-sided 95% CI upper limit 1.86; P=0.06). The investigators concluded that ET-Plus is at least as effective as ET-G, that ET-Plus is modestly more effective but ET-G modestly safer, and that both are recommended for treatment of West African Echis ocellatus envenoming.
cards.watchOut: Single-centre, one snake species, and a 6-hour coagulability end point — the trial does not compare mortality, tissue necrosis, or total dose required, and initial doses differed by product design (3 vials versus 1), so cost-effectiveness cannot be read off this card. Early reactions to equine versus ovine products are a class consideration for any antivenom choice, not a disqualification.

shelves.title: Micafungin vs fluconazole prophylaxis after stem cell transplant: success 80.0% vs 73.5% in 882 patients
shelves.question: In patients undergoing haematopoietic stem cell transplantation, is micafungin superior to fluconazole for preventing invasive fungal infection during neutropenia?
shelves.mesh: Echinocandins · Fluconazole · Hematopoietic Stem Cell Transplantation · Humans · Micafungin · Mycoses · Neutropenia
shelves.balance: One large, clean head-to-head answers this: in 882 adults and children undergoing haematopoietic stem cell transplantation, overall prophylaxis success during the neutropenic phase was higher with micafungin than with fluconazole — 80.0% versus 73.5%, an absolute difference of 6.5 percentage points (95% CI 0.9 to 12; P=.03). Success was a composite (no suspected, proven or probable invasive fungal infection through treatment and no proven/probable infection in the 4 weeks after). It is a single phase 3 trial, but it is large, double-blind and multicentre, and the comparator is the standard drug rather than placebo. PROPOSED LIKELY — one large double-blind randomised trial showing a modest absolute advantage for micafungin on a composite prophylaxis-success endpoint.

cards.summary: van Burik 2004: prophylaxis success 80.0% on micafungin vs 73.5% on fluconazole after HSCT (difference 6.5 points, P=.03)
cards.people: 882 adult and paediatric patients undergoing haematopoietic stem cell transplantation, randomised double-blind to micafungin 50 mg once daily (1 mg/kg if <50 kg) or fluconazole 400 mg once daily (8 mg/kg if <50 kg) during neutropenia. Success: absence of suspected, proven or probable invasive fungal infection through end of therapy and of proven/probable infection through 4 weeks after treatment.
cards.result: Overall efficacy was superior with micafungin: 80.0% versus 73.5% (difference 6.5 percentage points; 95% CI 0.9% to 12%; P=.03). No registry ID appears in the record (a pre-registration-era trial).
cards.watchOut: The endpoint is a composite dominated by 'suspected' infection and empirical-treatment decisions, not proven invasive fungal infection alone, and the absolute advantage is modest. A single trial, however large, is why the stamp is LIKELY rather than stronger.

shelves.title: Fluconazole prophylaxis in very-low-birth-weight infants
shelves.question: In preterm infants with birth weight under 1500 g, does prophylactic fluconazole prevent invasive fungal infection compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Antifungal Agents · Candida · Candidiasis · Double-Blind Method · Fluconazole · Humans · Infant, Newborn · Infant, Premature · Infant, Very Low Birth Weight
shelves.balance: Two double-blind, placebo-controlled randomised trials in preterm infants agree. In the single-centre trial of infants under 1000 g, invasive fungal infection occurred in 0% on fluconazole versus 20% on placebo over six weeks. In the larger eight-centre Italian trial of infants under 1500 g, invasive fungal infection occurred in 2.7% (6 mg/kg) and 3.8% (3 mg/kg) versus 13.2% on placebo, with colonisation roughly a third of the placebo rate, and no difference in mortality or other neonatal outcomes. A later trial in infants under 750 g confirmed fewer invasive candidiasis cases without a significant difference in the combined death-or-infection outcome. The proposed stamp is LIKELY: two independent double-blind randomised trials show a consistent, large reduction in invasive fungal infection, though neither showed a mortality benefit and routine use must be weighed against local infection rates and resistance selection.

cards.headline: Fluconazole prophylaxis prevented every invasive fungal infection in infants under 1000 g
cards.summary: Fluconazole prophylaxis prevented every invasive fungal infection in infants under 1000 g
cards.people: 100 preterm infants with birth weight under 1000 g, randomly assigned to intravenous fluconazole prophylaxis or placebo for six weeks.
cards.result: Fungal colonisation occurred in 22% of the fluconazole group versus 60% of the placebo group (risk difference 0.38; 95% CI 0.18 to 0.56; P=0.002). Invasive fungal infection occurred in 0% versus 20% (difference 0.20; 95% CI 0.04 to 0.36; P=0.008). No effect on bacterial infection, liver enzymes, or the development of resistant Candida was detected.
cards.watchOut: Small (n=100), single-centre trial in the highest-risk weight band; the zero event rate in the treatment arm makes the effect size fragile, and there was no mortality outcome benefit.
cards.source: Kaufman et al., N Engl J Med 2001. PMID: 11759644. cards.headline: Multicentre trial confirmed fewer invasive fungal infections at both fluconazole doses
cards.summary: Multicentre trial confirmed fewer invasive fungal infections at both fluconazole doses
cards.people: 322 preterm infants with birth weight under 1500 g in eight Italian neonatal intensive care units, assigned to fluconazole 6 mg/kg, fluconazole 3 mg/kg, or placebo.
cards.result: Invasive fungal infection occurred in 2.7% of the 6 mg/kg group (P=0.005) and 3.8% of the 3 mg/kg group (P=0.02) versus 13.2% on placebo. Candida colonisation occurred in 9.8% and 7.7% versus 29.2% (P<0.001 for both). Mortality and the incidence of other neonatal outcomes did not differ between groups.
cards.watchOut: Benefit is in infection prevention, not survival; units with low baseline fungal infection rates would prevent fewer infections per infant treated, and widespread prophylaxis can select for less susceptible species.

shelves.title: Micafungin prophylaxis in high-risk liver transplantation: non-inferior to standard care in one open-label trial (TENPIN)
shelves.question: In liver transplant recipients at high risk of invasive fungal infection, is micafungin non-inferior to centre standard care (fluconazole, liposomal amphotericin B, or caspofungin)?
shelves.mesh: Antifungal Agents · Chemoprevention · Echinocandins · Humans · Liver Transplantation · Micafungin · Mycoses · Transplant Recipients
shelves.balance: Micafungin met non-inferiority against a bundle of centre standard-care regimens — but that is all this single open-label trial can show. In 344 high-risk liver transplant recipients, clinical success at end of prophylaxis was 98.6% with micafungin versus 99.3% with standard care in the per-protocol set (difference 0.7 points; 95% CI −2.7 to 4.4) and 96.5% versus 93.6% in the full analysis set, within the 10% non-inferiority margin; kidney function was better with micafungin and drug-related adverse events were fewer (11.6% vs 16.3%). The comparator was three different drugs across centres, success rates were near the ceiling in both arms, and there is no placebo or single-drug comparison. PROPOSED POSSIBLE — a single open-label non-inferiority trial against heterogeneous standard care (THIN).

cards.headline: Saliba 2015 (TENPIN): micafungin non-inferior to standard care after high-risk liver transplant — success 98.6% vs 99.3% per protocol
cards.summary: Saliba 2015 (TENPIN): micafungin non-inferior to standard care after high-risk liver transplant — success 98.6% vs 99.3% per protocol
cards.people: 344 high-risk liver transplant recipients (172 per arm; mean age 51.2 years; 48.0% with MELD score ≥20), randomised open-label 1:1 to intravenous micafungin 100 mg daily or centre-specific standard care (fluconazole, liposomal amphotericin B, or caspofungin); mean prophylaxis duration 17 days. Primary endpoint: clinical success (no proven/probable invasive fungal infection and no additional antifungals) at end of prophylaxis.
cards.result: Per protocol: success 98.6% micafungin vs 99.3% standard care (Δ standard care − micafungin 0.7%; 95% CI −2.7% to 4.4%). Full analysis set: 96.5% vs 93.6% (−2.9%; −8.0% to 1.9%). Non-inferiority (10% margin) was met. Drug-related adverse events 11.6% vs 16.3%; discontinuation for adverse events 6.4% vs 11.6%; creatinine clearance was higher with micafungin at end of prophylaxis while liver tests were similar.
cards.watchOut: THIN: one open-label trial, and 'standard care' was three different antifungals chosen by centre, so this shows micafungin is in the same range as usual practice — not that it equals any one named drug. Event rates were so low that success was near 100% in both arms.

shelves.title: Caspofungin prophylaxis in high-risk ICU patients (MSG-01): fewer candida infections, but not significantly
shelves.question: In high-risk ICU patients without invasive candidiasis at baseline, does caspofungin prophylaxis (with biomarker-triggered preemptive therapy) reduce proven/probable invasive candidiasis versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Antifungal Agents · Candidiasis, Invasive · Caspofungin · Echinocandins · Humans · Intensive Care Units · Risk Factors · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: The prophylaxis question was not answered affirmatively: in MSG-01, 222 ventilated high-risk ICU patients were randomised double-blind to caspofungin or placebo, and proven/probable invasive candidiasis in patients without baseline disease occurred in 9.8% (10/102) on caspofungin versus 16.7% (14/84) on placebo — an absolute difference of about 7 points that was not statistically significant (P=.14). A secondary 'preemptive approach' analysis that included patients with baseline disease gave 18.8% versus 30.4% (P=.04), but that analysis mixes patients who already had candidiasis at entry, so it cannot rescue the prophylaxis claim. Mortality, antifungal use and length of stay did not differ, and there were no safety differences. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) — a single underpowered trial whose primary prophylaxis comparison did not reach significance (THIN).

cards.headline: MSG-01 (Ostrosky-Zeichner 2014): invasive candidiasis 9.8% on caspofungin vs 16.7% on placebo — P=.14, not significant
cards.summary: MSG-01 (Ostrosky-Zeichner 2014): invasive candidiasis 9.8% on caspofungin vs 16.7% on placebo — P=.14, not significant
cards.people: 222 adults in ICU for at least 3 days, ventilated, receiving antibiotics, with a central line and one additional risk factor (parenteral nutrition, dialysis, surgery, pancreatitis, systemic steroids or other immunosuppressants); (1,3)-β-D-glucan monitored twice weekly. Primary endpoint: proven/probable invasive candidiasis (EORTC/MSG criteria) in patients without disease at baseline.
cards.result: Prophylaxis analysis: 9.8% (10/102) caspofungin vs 16.7% (14/84) placebo (P=.14). Preemptive-approach analysis including baseline disease: 18.8% (22/117) vs 30.4% (31/102) (P=.04). No significant differences in mortality, antifungal use or length of stay; no safety differences.
cards.watchOut: THIN: the trial is small for an endpoint this uncommon, the denominators shrink in the primary analysis (186 of 222 without baseline disease), and the nominally significant preemptive analysis includes patients who already had invasive candidiasis at baseline. Note the draft cited a different journal; the PubMed record is Clin Infect Dis 2014.

shelves.title: Empirical vs preemptive antifungal therapy in febrile neutropenia: similar survival, more fungal infections when treatment waits
shelves.question: In high-risk neutropenic patients with persistent fever on broad-spectrum antibacterials, does a preemptive strategy (treat on clinical/imaging/galactomannan evidence) match empirical antifungal therapy on survival while reducing antifungal exposure?
shelves.mesh: Amphotericin B · Antifungal Agents · Fever · Humans · Mycoses · Neutropenia · Opportunistic Infections · Risk Factors
shelves.balance: The two halves of this strategy trial point different ways, so the stamp is split. In 293 high-risk neutropenic patients with persistent fever, survival 14 days after neutropenia recovery was similar with a preemptive strategy (treat only on clinical, imaging or galactomannan evidence) and with empirical treatment for everyone still febrile — 95.1% versus 97.3%, and the lower 95% confidence limit for the mortality difference (−5.9%) sat inside the −8% non-inferiority margin; antifungal drug costs fell 35% with preemptive care and nephrotoxicity was not reduced. But proven/probable invasive fungal infections were more common under the preemptive strategy — 13 of 143 versus 4 of 150 (P<.05), concentrated during induction chemotherapy (12/73 vs 3/78; P<.01) — and the authors cautioned that empirical treatment may give better survival for induction patients. PROPOSED SPLIT: POSSIBLE for preemptive care preserving survival overall with less antifungal exposure, but LIKELY (harm) on invasive fungal infection incidence, especially during induction — one open-label strategy trial, so neither half is settled.

cards.headline: Cordonnier 2009: survival 95.1% preemptive vs 97.3% empirical, but invasive fungal infection 13/143 vs 4/150
cards.summary: Cordonnier 2009: survival 95.1% preemptive vs 97.3% empirical, but invasive fungal infection 13/143 vs 4/150
cards.people: 293 high-risk neutropenic patients with haematological malignancies and persistent or recurrent fever on broad-spectrum antibacterials (median neutropenia 18 days), randomised open-label to empirical antifungal treatment for persistent fever or preemptive treatment triggered by clinical, imaging or galactomannan evidence. First-line drug was amphotericin B deoxycholate or liposomal amphotericin B by renal function. Primary outcome: alive 14 days after recovery from neutropenia.
cards.result: Survival: 97.3% empirical vs 95.1% preemptive (intention-to-treat); lower 95% confidence limit for the mortality difference −5.9%, within the −8% non-inferiority margin. Proven/probable invasive fungal infection: 13/143 preemptive vs 4/150 empirical (P<.05); during induction 12/73 vs 3/78 (P<.01). Preemptive care did not reduce nephrotoxicity but cut antifungal drug costs by 35%. No registry ID appears in the record.
cards.watchOut: SPLIT evidence: the survival non-inferiority margin was generous (−8%), the trial was open-label, and the excess invasive infections fell on induction-chemotherapy patients — the subgroup least able to wait. A strategy that is acceptable in consolidation may not be acceptable in induction.
cards.source: Cordonnier C et al. Empirical versus preemptive antifungal therapy for high-risk, febrile, neutropenic patients: a randomized, controlled trial. Clin Infect Dis. 2009. PMID: 19281327. shelves.title: Voriconazole therapeutic drug monitoring: fewer drug stoppages and better response in the only randomised trial (n=110)
shelves.question: In patients treated with voriconazole for invasive fungal infection, does routine concentration-guided dose adjustment improve treatment response and reduce drug-related adverse events versus fixed dosing?
shelves.mesh: Antifungal Agents · Aspergillosis · Cytochrome P-450 CYP2C19 · Drug Monitoring · Humans · Treatment Outcome · Triazoles · Voriconazole
shelves.balance: The only randomised trial of voriconazole therapeutic drug monitoring (TDM) found a real but narrow benefit, in a small single-centre study. In 110 adults with invasive fungal infection, dose adjustment to a trough of 1.0–5.5 mg/L did not change the overall incidence of adverse events (42% in both groups; P=.97), but far fewer TDM patients stopped voriconazole because of adverse events (4% vs 17%; P=.02), and complete or partial response at 3 months was higher with TDM (81%, 30/37, vs 57%, 20/34; P=.04) among those assessed for response. The response denominators (71 of 110) and single-centre design keep this from being stronger. PROPOSED POSSIBLE — one small single-centre randomised trial (THIN), with benefit on discontinuation and response but not on overall adverse-event rates.

cards.headline: Park 2012: voriconazole TDM cut discontinuation for adverse events (4% vs 17%) and raised response (81% vs 57%)
cards.summary: Park 2012: voriconazole TDM cut discontinuation for adverse events (4% vs 17%) and raised response (81% vs 57%)
cards.people: 110 adults with invasive fungal infection at a single Korean centre, randomised assessor-blind to TDM (dose adjusted from a day-4 trough, target 1.0–5.5 mg/L) or fixed standard dosing. Adverse events monitored throughout; treatment response assessed 3 months after starting voriconazole.
cards.result: Adverse-event incidence was identical (42% vs 42%; P=.97). Discontinuation of voriconazole due to adverse events: 4% TDM vs 17% non-TDM (P=.02) — an absolute difference of 13 percentage points. Complete or partial response: 81% (30/37) vs 57% (20/34) (P=.04). Baseline characteristics including CYP2C19 genotype were comparable.
cards.watchOut: THIN: single centre, 110 randomised, and response was assessable in only 71 patients — attrition that can move a P=.04 result. TDM did not reduce how many patients had adverse events, only how many had to stop the drug because of them.
cards.source: Park WB et al. The effect of therapeutic drug monitoring on safety and efficacy of voriconazole in invasive fungal infections: a randomized controlled trial. Clin Infect Dis. 2012. PMID: 22761409. Registry ID: NCT00890708, from the record. shelves.title: Adjunctive dexamethasone in HIV cryptococcal meningitis (CryptoDex): stopped for safety — more disability, no survival benefit
shelves.question: In HIV-associated cryptococcal meningitis treated with amphotericin B plus fluconazole, does adjunctive dexamethasone improve survival?
shelves.mesh: AIDS-Related Opportunistic Infections · Cryptococcus neoformans · Dexamethasone · Glucocorticoids · Humans · Meningitis, Cryptococcal
shelves.balance: Adjunctive dexamethasone harmed patients in the CryptoDex trial, and the trial was stopped early for safety. In 451 adults with HIV-associated cryptococcal meningitis in Asia and Africa, all receiving amphotericin B plus fluconazole, mortality at 10 weeks was 47% with dexamethasone versus 41% with placebo (hazard ratio 1.11, a relative effect; 95% CI 0.84 to 1.47; P=0.45) and 57% versus 49% by 6 months (HR 1.18; 0.91 to 1.53; P=0.20) — the mortality differences themselves were not statistically significant, but everything else pointed the same harmful way: fewer patients had a good outcome at 10 weeks (13% vs 25%; odds ratio 0.42, a relative effect; 0.25 to 0.69; P<0.001), clinical adverse events were more common (667 vs 494 events; P=0.01), grade 3/4 infections, renal and cardiac events were more frequent, and fungal clearance from cerebrospinal fluid was slower. Tier C: this is a mortality-outcome harm shelf for the developer to rule on personally. PROPOSED LIKELY (harm) — a large double-blind trial stopped for safety, with disability and adverse-event harm shown clearly and mortality numerically higher.

cards.headline: CryptoDex (Beardsley 2016): dexamethasone stopped early for safety — mortality 47% vs 41% at 10 weeks, more disability and adverse events
cards.summary: CryptoDex (Beardsley 2016): dexamethasone stopped early for safety — mortality 47% vs 41% at 10 weeks, more disability and adverse events
cards.people: 451 adults with HIV-associated cryptococcal meningitis in Vietnam, Thailand, Indonesia, Laos, Uganda and Malawi, randomised double-blind to dexamethasone or placebo for 6 weeks, all with amphotericin B plus fluconazole. Trial stopped early for safety.
cards.result: Mortality at 10 weeks 47% dexamethasone vs 41% placebo (HR 1.11, relative; 95% CI 0.84 to 1.47; P=0.45); at 6 months 57% vs 49% (HR 1.18; 0.91 to 1.53; P=0.20). Good outcome at 10 weeks 13% vs 25% (OR 0.42, relative; 0.25 to 0.69; P<0.001). Clinical adverse events 667 vs 494 (P=0.01), with more grade 3/4 infection (48 vs 25 patients; P=0.003), renal events (22 vs 7; P=0.004) and cardiac events (8 vs 0; P=0.004) on dexamethasone; fungal clearance was slower.
cards.watchOut: Tier C: survival was the decisive outcome and the mortality hazard ratios cross 1 — the harm case rests on the early safety stop, significantly worse disability, more serious adverse events and slower fungal clearance, all in the same direction. Steroids for other meningitides, or for established cryptococcal immune reconstitution syndrome, are different questions not answered here.
cards.source: Beardsley J et al. Adjunctive Dexamethasone in HIV-Associated Cryptococcal Meningitis. N Engl J Med. 2016. PMID: 26863355. Registry ID: ISRCTN59144167, from the record. shelves.title: Adjunctive sertraline in HIV cryptococcal meningitis (ASTRO-CM): no survival benefit — 52% vs 46% mortality, stopped for futility
shelves.question: In HIV-associated cryptococcal meningitis on standard amphotericin/fluconazole therapy, does adjunctive sertraline improve 18-week survival?
shelves.mesh: AIDS-Related Opportunistic Infections · Antifungal Agents · Cryptococcus · HIV Infections · Humans · Meningitis, Cryptococcal · Sertraline
shelves.balance: No: despite anticryptococcal activity in the laboratory, adjunctive sertraline did not improve survival in the ASTRO-CM phase 3 trial, which was stopped for futility. In 460 HIV-positive adults with cryptococcal meningitis in Uganda receiving amphotericin B and fluconazole, 18-week mortality was 52% (120/229) with sertraline versus 46% (106/231) with placebo (hazard ratio 1.21, a relative effect; 95% CI 0.93 to 1.57; P=0.15), fungal clearance from cerebrospinal fluid was similar (0.43 vs 0.47 −log10 CFU/mL per day; P=0.59), and grade 4/5 adverse events were similar (31% vs 32%). Tier C applies because survival was the primary endpoint — this shelf makes no mortality claim for sertraline; the result is a null on a mortality endpoint. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — a large double-blind phase 3 trial, stopped for futility, with mortality numerically higher on sertraline.

cards.headline: ASTRO-CM (Rhein 2019): sertraline did not reduce 18-week mortality — 52% vs 46%, stopped for futility
cards.summary: ASTRO-CM (Rhein 2019): sertraline did not reduce 18-week mortality — 52% vs 46%, stopped for futility
cards.people: 460 HIV-positive adults with cryptococcal meningitis at two hospitals in Uganda, randomised double-blind to adjunctive sertraline (400 mg/day for 2 weeks, then 200 mg/day for 12 weeks, then tapered) or placebo, all receiving 7–14 days of intravenous amphotericin B plus oral fluconazole 800 mg/day. Primary endpoint: 18-week survival, intention-to-treat.
cards.result: 18-week mortality 52% (120/229) sertraline vs 46% (106/231) placebo (HR 1.21, relative; 95% CI 0.93 to 1.57; P=0.15). Fungal clearance 0.43 vs 0.47 −log10 CFU/mL per day (P=0.59). Grade 4 or 5 adverse events 31% (72/229) vs 32% (75/231) (P=0.98). The trial stopped for futility after 460 of a planned 550 participants.
cards.watchOut: Tier C: survival was the primary endpoint and the result is null — the shelf must not imply any mortality effect in either direction beyond the reported hazard ratio. In-vitro anticryptococcal activity did not translate, which the authors attributed in part to insufficient duration of therapeutic sertraline concentrations.
cards.source: Rhein J et al. Adjunctive sertraline for HIV-associated cryptococcal meningitis: a randomised, placebo-controlled, double-blind phase 3 trial. Lancet Infect Dis. 2019. PMID: 31345462. shelves.title: Adjunctive interferon-γ1b in AIDS cryptococcal meningitis: faster CSF culture conversion in a 75-patient phase 2 trial
shelves.question: In AIDS-related cryptococcal meningitis on amphotericin-based therapy, does adjunctive recombinant interferon-γ1b speed CSF fungal clearance?
shelves.mesh: AIDS-Related Opportunistic Infections · Antifungal Agents · HIV Infections · Humans · Interferon-gamma · Meningitis, Cryptococcal · Recombinant Proteins · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: A promising surrogate signal, nothing more. In this phase 2 double-blind trial of 75 patients with AIDS-related acute cryptococcal meningitis, all on amphotericin B-based therapy, cerebrospinal fluid cultures had converted to negative at 2 weeks in 36% of patients receiving interferon-γ1b 100 µg and 32% receiving 200 µg, versus 13% on placebo; combined mycologic and clinical success trended the same way (26% vs 8%; P=.078). Treatment was well tolerated, with no apparent effect on CD4 counts or HIV load. But 75 patients cannot answer survival, culture conversion is a surrogate, and the combined-success comparison did not reach significance. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) — a small phase 2 trial on a surrogate endpoint (THIN); 'holds promise, warrants further study' is exactly where the evidence stops.

cards.headline: Pappas 2004: 2-week CSF culture conversion 36% (100 µg) and 32% (200 µg) with interferon-γ1b vs 13% with placebo — n=75
cards.summary: Pappas 2004: 2-week CSF culture conversion 36% (100 µg) and 32% (200 µg) with interferon-γ1b vs 13% with placebo — n=75
cards.people: 75 patients with AIDS and acute cryptococcal meningitis, randomised double-blind to recombinant interferon-γ1b 100 µg or 200 µg or placebo, three times weekly for 10 weeks, plus intravenous amphotericin B with or without flucytosine, followed by fluconazole. Endpoints included 2-week CSF culture conversion, symptom resolution and survival.
cards.result: 2-week culture conversion: 13% placebo, 36% interferon-γ1b 100 µg, 32% interferon-γ1b 200 µg. Combined mycologic and clinical success trended higher with interferon-γ1b (26% vs 8%; P=.078). Therapy was well tolerated; no apparent influence on serial CD4 counts or HIV load. No registry ID appears in the record (a pre-registration-era trial).
cards.watchOut: THIN: phase 2, 75 patients across three arms, a 2-week culture surrogate, and the headline combined-success endpoint was not significant (P=.078). Percentages on denominators this small move with a handful of patients.
cards.source: Pappas PG et al. Recombinant interferon-gamma 1b as adjunctive therapy for AIDS-related acute cryptococcal meningitis. J Infect Dis. 2004. PMID: 15181565. shelves.title: Isavuconazole for mucormycosis (VITAL study)
shelves.question: In patients with invasive mucormycosis, does isavuconazole treatment produce outcomes comparable to amphotericin B-based therapy?
shelves.mesh: Antifungal Agents · Aspergillosis · Humans · Mucormycosis · Nitriles · Pyridines · Treatment Outcome · Triazoles
shelves.balance: There is no randomised trial of isavuconazole for mucormycosis. The VITAL study was a single-arm, open-label trial: 37 patients with mucormycosis were treated with isavuconazole, and by day 42, 35% had died, 11% had a partial response and 43% had stable disease. Among patients receiving it as primary treatment, day-42 crude mortality was 33% (7/21), compared with 39% (13/33) in matched amphotericin B controls from a registry (weighted comparison 33% versus 41%, p=0.595 — not significant). The proposed stamp is MAYBE (weak evidence): the numbers are in the same range as historical amphotericin B outcomes and isavuconazole gives an oral option where amphotericin B is impossible or failing, but a single-arm study with matched controls cannot show that it works as well, and this shelf must never be read as randomised-trial evidence.

cards.headline: Single-arm VITAL study: about a third of mucormycosis patients died by day 42 on isavuconazole
cards.summary: Single-arm VITAL study: about a third of mucormycosis patients died by day 42 on isavuconazole
cards.type: Single-arm prospective study with matched external controls (not randomised)
cards.people: 37 patients with proven or probable invasive mucormycosis treated with isavuconazole in the single-arm, open-label VITAL study (median treatment duration 84 days); most had haematological malignancy, transplant, or other major immunosuppression, and many had already received other antifungals.
cards.result: By day 42: partial response 11% (4 patients), stable disease 43% (16), disease progression 3% (1), missing data 8% (3), and death 35% (13). Adverse events occurred in 95% of patients and serious adverse events in 76%, largely reflecting the underlying illnesses. In primary-treatment cases, day-42 crude mortality was 33% (7/21) on isavuconazole versus 39% (13/33) in matched amphotericin B controls (weighted 33% versus 41%; p=0.595).
cards.watchOut: No randomisation and no concurrent control group: matched registry controls cannot remove confounding, the comparison was not significant, and response assessment in a single-arm study of a disease this lethal cannot prove the drug caused the outcomes.
cards.source: Marty et al., Lancet Infect Dis 2016. PMID: 26969258. NCT00634049 (VITAL); matched controls from FungiScope, NCT01731353. shelves.title: Zoliflodacin single-dose oral treatment for uncomplicated gonorrhoea
shelves.question: In adolescents and adults with uncomplicated urogenital gonorrhoea, is a single 3 g oral dose of zoliflodacin non-inferior to ceftriaxone injection plus azithromycin for microbiological cure?
shelves.mesh: Anti-Bacterial Agents · Azithromycin · Ceftriaxone · Drug Therapy, Combination · Gonorrhea · Humans · Neisseria gonorrhoeae · Spiro Compounds · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: One large phase 3 trial (930 randomised, 17 clinics in five countries) tested a single 3 g oral dose of zoliflodacin — a first-in-class spiropyrimidinetrione antibiotic — against ceftriaxone 500 mg intramuscularly plus azithromycin 1 g orally. Urogenital microbiological cure in the microbiological intention-to-treat population was 90.9% (460/506) with zoliflodacin versus 96.2% (229/238) with the comparator; the difference of 5.3 percentage points (95% CI 1.4 to 8.6) fell within the prespecified 12% non-inferiority margin. Side effects were similar overall. The proposed stamp is POSSIBLE: a single large trial met its non-inferiority criterion, but the margin was wide, the trial was open-label, cure was numerically lower than with ceftriaxone, and zoliflodacin is a new, not yet widely available agent whose real-world performance and resistance behaviour are untested.

cards.headline: Single-dose oral zoliflodacin met non-inferiority against ceftriaxone plus azithromycin
cards.summary: Single-dose oral zoliflodacin met non-inferiority against ceftriaxone plus azithromycin
cards.people: 930 adolescents and adults (age 12 and older) with uncomplicated urogenital gonorrhoea at 17 clinics in five countries, randomised to zoliflodacin 3 g orally as a single dose (621) or ceftriaxone 500 mg intramuscularly plus azithromycin 1 g orally (309).
cards.result: Microbiological cure at the urogenital site (microbiological intention-to-treat) was 90.9% (460/506) with zoliflodacin versus 96.2% (229/238) with ceftriaxone plus azithromycin — a difference of 5.3 percentage points (95% CI 1.4 to 8.6), within the 12% non-inferiority margin. Adverse events were similar between groups (zoliflodacin: headache 10%, neutropenia 7%; comparator: injection-site pain 12%); no serious adverse events were reported.
cards.watchOut: Open-label design and a generous 12% non-inferiority margin; the primary result is urogenital cure, and a single trial of a brand-new drug class cannot yet speak to emerging resistance or performance at scale.
cards.source: Luckey et al., Lancet 2026. PMID: 41391465. NCT03959527. shelves.title: Gentamicin plus azithromycin as an alternative to ceftriaxone for gonorrhoea (G-ToG)
shelves.question: In people with uncomplicated gonorrhoea, is gentamicin 240 mg intramuscularly plus azithromycin as effective as ceftriaxone plus azithromycin at clearing infection?
shelves.mesh: Anti-Bacterial Agents · Azithromycin · Ceftriaxone · Gentamicins · Gonorrhea · Humans · Neisseria gonorrhoeae · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: The pragmatic G-ToG trial randomised 720 people in English sexual-health clinics to gentamicin 240 mg intramuscularly or ceftriaxone 500 mg intramuscularly, both with azithromycin 1 g. Clearance of infection at two weeks was 91% (267/292) with gentamicin versus 98% (299/306) with ceftriaxone — an adjusted risk difference of −6.4 percentage points (95% CI −10.4 to −2.4) — so non-inferiority was NOT established, and the gap was largest in the throat (clearance about 80% versus 96%). The proposed stamp is LIKELY (harm): on the best randomised evidence, swapping ceftriaxone for gentamicin leaves roughly 7 more infections uncured per 100 treated. Gentamicin remains a fallback when ceftriaxone truly cannot be used, but it is not an equal substitute, particularly for pharyngeal infection.

cards.headline: Gentamicin failed to prove non-inferior to ceftriaxone in the G-ToG trial
cards.summary: Gentamicin failed to prove non-inferior to ceftriaxone in the G-ToG trial
cards.people: 720 people with uncomplicated gonorrhoea at English sexual-health clinics, randomised to gentamicin 240 mg intramuscularly (358) or ceftriaxone 500 mg intramuscularly (362); all participants also received azithromycin 1 g orally.
cards.result: Clearance of Neisseria gonorrhoeae at all infected sites at two weeks was 91% (267/292) in the gentamicin group versus 98% (299/306) in the ceftriaxone group; adjusted risk difference −6.4 percentage points (95% CI −10.4 to −2.4), so the prespecified non-inferiority criterion was not met. By site, clearance was lower with gentamicin at every site — genital about 94% versus 98%, rectal about 90% versus 98%, and pharyngeal about 80% versus 96%.
cards.watchOut: Both arms received azithromycin, so the trial compares gentamicin with ceftriaxone as the partner drug, not gentamicin alone; pharyngeal infections — the hardest to clear — drove much of the difference.
cards.source: Ross et al., Lancet 2019. PMID: 31056291. ISRCTN51783227. shelves.title: Single-dose azithromycin versus benzathine penicillin for early syphilis
shelves.question: In people with early syphilis, is a single 2 g oral dose of azithromycin as effective as benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units intramuscularly for serological cure?
shelves.mesh: Anti-Bacterial Agents · Azithromycin · Humans · Penicillin G Benzathine · Syphilis · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: Two randomised equivalence trials agree that a single 2 g oral dose of azithromycin cures early syphilis about as often as a benzathine penicillin injection: in Tanzania, cure was 97.7% versus 95.0% (difference confidence interval −1.7 to 7.1, meeting equivalence criteria), and in a multinational phase 3 trial in HIV-negative patients, serological cure at six months was 77.6% (180/232) versus 78.5% (186/237). The proposed stamp is LIKELY for the narrow trial question — the equivalence finding is consistent across two independent trials. The crucial limit is outside the trials: macrolide resistance in Treponema pallidum (23S rRNA mutations) is widespread in many regions, so azithromycin should not be used where resistance is prevalent, and penicillin remains the standard — it is also the only recommended treatment in pregnancy. Nonserious side effects, mostly gastrointestinal, were more common with azithromycin (61.5% versus 46.3% in the phase 3 trial).

cards.headline: Tanzanian trial: single-dose azithromycin equivalent to penicillin for early syphilis
cards.summary: Tanzanian trial: single-dose azithromycin equivalent to penicillin for early syphilis
cards.people: 328 people in Mbeya, Tanzania — 25 with primary syphilis and 303 with high-titre latent syphilis — randomised to azithromycin 2 g orally as a single dose (163) or benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units intramuscularly (165).
cards.result: Serological cure was 97.7% (95% CI 94.0 to 99.4) with azithromycin versus 95.0% (95% CI 90.6 to 97.8) with penicillin; the 95% confidence interval for the difference (−1.7 to 7.1 percentage points) met the prespecified equivalence criteria. The authors noted reports of azithromycin-resistant Treponema pallidum in the United States and the need for continued resistance monitoring.
cards.watchOut: Conducted in a population screened in Tanzania, mostly latent syphilis; results apply where the circulating strains remain macrolide-susceptible, which is no longer true in many countries.
cards.source: Riedner et al., N Engl J Med 2005. PMID: 16177249. shelves.title: Oral cefixime plus doxycycline as a needle-free regimen for gonorrhoea
shelves.question: In people with gonorrhoea, is an all-oral regimen of cefixime 800 mg single dose plus doxycycline for seven days non-inferior to ceftriaxone injection plus azithromycin?
shelves.mesh: Anti-Bacterial Agents · Azithromycin · Cefixime · Ceftriaxone · Doxycycline · Gonorrhea · Humans · Neisseria gonorrhoeae
shelves.balance: One small open-label non-inferiority trial (161 randomised, 152 per-protocol, Prague) compared cefixime 800 mg as a single oral dose plus doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for seven days against ceftriaxone 1 g intramuscularly plus azithromycin 2 g. In the per-protocol analysis, 86% (65/76) of the oral-regimen group were both culture- and NAAT-negative at week three versus 100% of the comparator group — a risk difference of 14.5 percentage points (95% CI 6.56 to 22.38), so non-inferiority was NOT achieved overall. Crucially, every failure in the oral arm was a pharyngeal infection; efficacy was high at urogenital and rectal sites. The proposed stamp is therefore SPLIT: POSSIBLE that the all-oral regimen works well for urogenital and rectal gonorrhoea, but MAYBE (weak evidence) — effectively a warning — for pharyngeal infection, where it failed in this trial. This corrects any impression that the oral regimen was shown broadly comparable to the injection.

cards.headline: All-oral cefixime regimen missed non-inferiority, with all failures in the throat
cards.summary: All-oral cefixime regimen missed non-inferiority, with all failures in the throat
cards.people: 161 people with gonorrhoea in Prague randomised to cefixime 800 mg orally as a single dose plus doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for seven days, or ceftriaxone 1 g intramuscularly plus azithromycin 2 g orally; 152 were analysed per-protocol.
cards.result: At week three in the cefixime arm, 92% (70/76) were culture-negative, 87% (66/76) NAAT-negative, and 86% (65/76) negative on both, versus 100% on all measures in the ceftriaxone arm; the risk difference was 14.5 percentage points (95% CI 6.56 to 22.38) and non-inferiority was not achieved. All treatment failures in the cefixime group were pharyngeal infections; efficacy was high for urogenital and rectal sites.
cards.watchOut: Small, single-centre, open-label trial (THIN); the headline result depends heavily on how many participants had pharyngeal infection, and the comparator used a higher ceftriaxone dose (1 g) than many guidelines.

shelves.title: Doxycycline versus azithromycin for rectal chlamydia in men who have sex with men
shelves.question: In men who have sex with men with rectal Chlamydia trachomatis infection, is doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for seven days more effective than a single 1 g dose of azithromycin?
shelves.mesh: Anti-Bacterial Agents · Azithromycin · Chlamydia Infections · Chlamydia trachomatis · Doxycycline · Homosexuality, Male · Humans · Male · Rectal Diseases · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: A double-blind, placebo-controlled randomised trial in 177 men who have sex with men with rectal chlamydia (Seattle and Boston) compared doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for seven days with azithromycin 1 g as a single dose. Among participants who completed the study, cure was 100% (70/70) with doxycycline versus 74% (48/65) with azithromycin — a difference of 26 percentage points (95% CI 16 to 36; P<0.001); in the intention-to-treat analysis cure was 91% (80/88) versus 71% (63/89), a difference of 20 points (95% CI 9 to 31; P<0.001). The proposed stamp is LIKELY: this is a well-designed double-blind trial with a large, consistent effect in both analyses — single-dose azithromycin leaves roughly one in four rectal infections uncured, which is why doxycycline is the preferred treatment for rectal chlamydia.

cards.headline: Doxycycline cured every completer; single-dose azithromycin missed one in four rectal infections
cards.summary: Doxycycline cured every completer; single-dose azithromycin missed one in four rectal infections
cards.people: 177 men who have sex with men with rectal Chlamydia trachomatis infection in Seattle and Boston, randomised double-blind to doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for seven days or azithromycin 1 g as a single dose (with matching placebos).
cards.result: In the completer population, microbiological cure was 100% (70/70) with doxycycline versus 74% (48/65) with azithromycin — difference 26 percentage points (95% CI 16 to 36; P<0.001). In the intention-to-treat analysis, cure was 91% (80/88) versus 71% (63/89) — difference 20 percentage points (95% CI 9 to 31; P<0.001).
cards.watchOut: A single trial in MSM in two US cities; the result concerns rectal infection specifically and should not be read across to urogenital infection, where the gap between the drugs is much smaller.
cards.source: Dombrowski et al., Clin Infect Dis 2021. PMID: 33606009. NCT03608774. shelves.title: Azithromycin versus doxycycline for urogenital chlamydia
shelves.question: In adolescents and adults with uncomplicated urogenital Chlamydia trachomatis infection, is a single 1 g dose of azithromycin non-inferior to doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for seven days?
shelves.mesh: Anti-Bacterial Agents · Azithromycin · Chlamydia Infections · Chlamydia trachomatis · Doxycycline · Humans · Treatment Outcome · Urogenital System
shelves.balance: Two randomised trials give slightly different answers. The older multicentre trial (457 patients, antigen-test diagnosis) found non-response in 4% on azithromycin versus 2% on doxycycline (difference 2 points; 95% CI 0 to 6) and concluded the single dose was as effective. The modern trial — 567 adolescents in youth correctional facilities, all treatment directly observed, failure judged by nucleic acid testing with genotyping — found zero failures on doxycycline and five failures (3.2%) on azithromycin; the upper bound of the 90% confidence interval for the difference (5.9 points) exceeded the prespecified 5-point non-inferiority cutoff, so azithromycin's non-inferiority was NOT established. The proposed stamp is POSSIBLE: both drugs cure the great majority (97–100%), and any true difference is small, but on the most rigorous trial azithromycin may be a few percentage points worse, and doxycycline is now generally preferred — especially since the same drug is clearly better for rectal infection.

cards.headline: 1992 multicentre trial: single-dose azithromycin performed about the same as doxycycline
cards.summary: 1992 multicentre trial: single-dose azithromycin performed about the same as doxycycline
cards.people: 457 patients (299 women and 158 men) with uncomplicated genital chlamydial infection and a positive antigen test, randomised to azithromycin 1 g orally as a single dose or doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for seven days.
cards.result: Among evaluable patients, 5 of 141 (4%) on azithromycin did not respond versus 3 of 125 (2%) on doxycycline (difference 2 percentage points; 95% CI 0 to 6). Bacteriological cure rates on azithromycin were 97% in women and 95% in men; the authors concluded a single 1 g dose was as effective as the seven-day doxycycline course.
cards.watchOut: Diagnosis and cure were judged with antigen tests and culture, far less sensitive than modern nucleic acid testing, so failures were likely undercounted in both arms.
cards.source: Martin et al. (Azithromycin for Chlamydial Infections Study Group), N Engl J Med 1992. PMID: 1325036. cards.headline: Modern directly-observed trial: azithromycin non-inferiority not established
cards.summary: Modern directly-observed trial: azithromycin non-inferiority not established
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (non-inferiority, directly observed therapy)
cards.people: 567 adolescents with urogenital chlamydia in US youth correctional facilities, randomised to azithromycin 1 g single dose (284) or doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for seven days (283), with all doses directly observed.
cards.result: There were no treatment failures with doxycycline (efficacy 100%). Failures occurred in 5 azithromycin participants (3.2%; 95% CI 0.4 to 7.4; efficacy 97%). The observed difference was 3.2 percentage points and the upper boundary of the 90% confidence interval was 5.9 points, exceeding the prespecified 5-point cutoff — non-inferiority of azithromycin was not established.
cards.watchOut: A closed correctional-facility population with directly observed therapy removes the adherence advantage that is single-dose azithromycin's main real-world selling point; results may differ where doxycycline adherence is poor.
cards.source: Geisler et al., N Engl J Med 2015. PMID: 26699167. NCT00980148. shelves.title: Suppressive acyclovir to prevent HIV transmission in HSV-2/HIV-coinfected couples (Partners in Prevention)
shelves.question: In HIV-1/HSV-2 serodiscordant couples, does suppressive acyclovir 400 mg twice daily in the coinfected partner reduce transmission of HIV-1 to the uninfected partner?
shelves.mesh: Acyclovir · Antiviral Agents · Herpes Genitalis · Herpesvirus 2, Human · HIV Infections · HIV-1 · Humans · Sexual Partners · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: The Partners in Prevention trial randomised 3,408 HIV-1/HSV-2 serodiscordant couples at 14 African sites to acyclovir 400 mg twice daily or placebo for the coinfected partner. Despite acyclovir lowering plasma HIV-1 RNA by 0.25 log10 copies/mL (P<0.001) and reducing HSV-2-positive genital ulcers by 73% (relative risk 0.27; 95% CI 0.20 to 0.36), genetically linked HIV transmissions were 41 in the acyclovir group versus 43 on placebo (hazard ratio 0.92; 95% CI 0.60 to 1.41; P=0.69) — no reduction. The proposed stamp is LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): a large, well-conducted trial shows suppressing HSV-2 improves herpes outcomes and modestly lowers viral load but does not prevent HIV transmission to partners. (Note: this shelf is anchored on Partners in Prevention; HPTN 039 was a separate trial of HSV suppression and HIV acquisition, not transmission.)

cards.headline: Acyclovir suppressed herpes and lowered viral load but did not reduce HIV transmission
cards.summary: Acyclovir suppressed herpes and lowered viral load but did not reduce HIV transmission
cards.people: 3,408 HIV-1 and HSV-2 serodiscordant couples at 14 sites in Africa; the coinfected partner was randomised to acyclovir 400 mg twice daily or placebo.
cards.result: Of 132 HIV-1 seroconversions, 84 were genetically linked to the enrolled partner: 41 in the acyclovir group and 43 in the placebo group (hazard ratio 0.92; 95% CI 0.60 to 1.41; P=0.69). Acyclovir reduced plasma HIV-1 RNA by 0.25 log10 copies/mL (P<0.001) and HSV-2-positive genital ulcers by 73% in relative terms (relative risk 0.27; 95% CI 0.20 to 0.36).
cards.watchOut: The null result is for transmission to partners; acyclovir still treats and suppresses herpes itself. The modest viral-load reduction was simply too small to change transmission risk.
cards.source: Celum et al., N Engl J Med 2010. PMID: 20089951. NCT00194519. cards.summary: Synthesis
cards.people: HIV/HSV-2 serodiscordant couples considering HSV suppression as an HIV-prevention strategy.
cards.result: One large randomised trial (3,408 couples): linked transmissions 41 versus 43, hazard ratio 0.92 with a confidence interval excluding any large protective effect, despite clear anti-herpes and small viral-load effects.
cards.watchOut: Do not generalise this null to antiretroviral treatment as prevention, which lowers viral load far more and does prevent transmission.

shelves.title: Imiquimod cream versus podophyllotoxin solution for anogenital warts
shelves.question: In adults with anogenital warts, is self-applied imiquimod 5% cream as effective as podophyllotoxin 0.5% solution for complete clearance of warts?
shelves.mesh: Adjuvants, Immunologic · Aminoquinolines · Condylomata Acuminata · Humans · Imiquimod · Keratolytic Agents · Podophyllotoxin · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: The only head-to-head randomised trial is small and open-label: 45 evaluable patients in Graz, Austria. Complete clearance of baseline warts was 72% (95% CI 52 to 86) with podophyllotoxin 0.5% solution at the end of its four-week course, and 75% (95% CI 53 to 98) with imiquimod 5% cream at the end of its sixteen-week course (P=1, identical); side-effect frequency did not differ significantly (P=0.24). The proposed stamp is MAYBE (weak evidence): with only 45 patients and very wide confidence intervals, identical point estimates cannot establish that the two treatments are equivalent — the trial could not rule out large differences either way — and the comparison is uneven, since one treatment was assessed after four weeks and the other after sixteen. Choice in practice turns on treatment duration, tolerability, and patient preference rather than proven superiority.

cards.headline: Tiny head-to-head trial: clearance rates identical, but far too small to prove equivalence
cards.summary: Tiny head-to-head trial: clearance rates identical, but far too small to prove equivalence
cards.people: 45 evaluable adults with anogenital warts in Graz, Austria, randomised open-label to self-applied podophyllotoxin 0.5% solution (four-week course) or imiquimod 5% cream (sixteen-week course).
cards.result: Complete clearance of baseline warts was 72% (95% CI 52 to 86) with podophyllotoxin at the end of treatment versus 75% (95% CI 53 to 98) with imiquimod (P=1). The difference in side-effect frequency was not significant (P=0.24).
cards.watchOut: Very small sample (THIN) and mismatched assessment points — four weeks for podophyllotoxin versus sixteen weeks for imiquimod — so similar clearance percentages are not a like-for-like comparison, and recurrence was not addressed.
cards.source: Komericki et al., Sex Transm Dis 2011. PMID: 20938374. cards.summary: Synthesis
cards.people: Adults choosing between the two main self-applied treatments for anogenital warts.

shelves.title: Resistance-guided sequential therapy for Mycoplasma genitalium
shelves.question: In people with Mycoplasma genitalium infection, does a resistance-guided sequential programme — doxycycline first, then azithromycin if macrolide-susceptible or sitafloxacin if macrolide-resistant — achieve high cure rates?
shelves.mesh: Anti-Bacterial Agents · Drug Monitoring · Drug Resistance, Bacterial · Humans · Macrolides · Mycoplasma Infections · Mycoplasma genitalium · Prospective Studies · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: This is a prospective programme evaluation, not a randomised trial. At Melbourne Sexual Health Centre, patients with Mycoplasma genitalium first received doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for seven days (which cut organism load by a mean of 2.60 log10), then a macrolide-resistance-mutation test directed the second drug: azithromycin 2.5 g in divided doses if no resistance mutation was found, or sitafloxacin 100 mg twice daily for seven days if one was. Resistance mutations were present in 167 of 244 evaluable infections (68.4%). Cure was 94.8% (73/77) in the macrolide-susceptible group and 92.2% (154/167) in the resistant group treated with sitafloxacin, and new macrolide resistance was selected in only 2 of 76 (2.6%). The proposed stamp is POSSIBLE: a single-centre prospective evaluation (THIN, no randomised comparison) shows very high cure in both resistance strata, supporting the resistance-guided sequential programme as tested — but sitafloxacin, the fluoroquinolone used for resistant cases in this programme, is not approved in the United States, so the exact programme cannot simply be copied everywhere.

cards.headline: Resistance-guided sequential therapy cured over 92% in both resistance groups
cards.summary: Resistance-guided sequential therapy cured over 92% in both resistance groups
cards.people: Patients with Mycoplasma genitalium infection at Melbourne Sexual Health Centre; 244 evaluable infections (52 women, 68 heterosexual men, 124 men who have sex with men). All first received doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for seven days, then azithromycin 2.5 g (1 g followed by 500 mg daily for three days) if macrolide-resistance mutations were absent, or sitafloxacin 100 mg twice daily for seven days if present.
cards.result: Macrolide-resistance mutations were detected in 167 of 244 infections (68.4%; 95% CI 62.2 to 74.2). Cure was 94.8% (73/77; 95% CI 87.2 to 98.6) in macrolide-susceptible infections treated with azithromycin and 92.2% (154/167; 95% CI 87.1 to 95.8) in resistant infections treated with sitafloxacin. The initial doxycycline phase reduced organism load by a mean of 2.60 log10 (n=56; P<0.0001), and new macrolide resistance was selected in only 2 of 76 cases (2.6%).
cards.watchOut: Single-centre, non-randomised (THIN): high cure rates in an uncontrolled evaluation cannot separate the programme's effect from patient mix and follow-up completeness, and the resistant-stratum drug (sitafloxacin) is unavailable in many countries, including the United States.

cards.summary: Synthesis
cards.people: People with Mycoplasma genitalium in settings with high macrolide resistance.
cards.result: One prospective evaluation (244 infections): a doxycycline-first, resistance-test-guided sequence cured 94.8% of macrolide-susceptible and 92.2% of macrolide-resistant infections, despite 68% baseline resistance.
cards.watchOut: Promising but unrandomised; the strategy depends on access to resistance testing and to a fluoroquinolone active against resistant strains.

shelves.title: IL-6 receptor antagonists for hospitalised COVID-19: RECOVERY and REMAP-CAP agree on a survival benefit (Tier C)
shelves.question: In patients admitted to hospital with hypoxic COVID-19 and systemic inflammation, do IL-6 receptor antagonists (tocilizumab, sarilumab) reduce 28-day mortality?
shelves.mesh: COVID-19 · COVID-19 Drug Treatment · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized · Receptors, Interleukin-6 · Hospital Mortality · Hypoxia · Humans
shelves.balance: Two large platform trials point the same way: IL-6 receptor antagonists reduce mortality in hospitalised patients with hypoxic, inflamed COVID-19, most of whom were also receiving corticosteroids. In RECOVERY, 28-day mortality was 31% with tocilizumab versus 35% with usual care — an absolute reduction of 4 percentage points, a rate ratio of 0.85 (95% CI 0.76 to 0.94), i.e. a 15% relative reduction — and more patients were discharged alive (57% vs 50%). In REMAP-CAP's critically ill population, tocilizumab and sarilumab both improved organ-support-free days (median 10 and 11 vs 0 days; adjusted OR 1.64 and 1.76) with a pooled 90-day survival hazard ratio of 1.61 (95% credible interval 1.25 to 2.08). The benefit belongs to the population studied: patients sick enough to need oxygen with CRP at least 75 mg/L, on background steroids. PROPOSED LIKELY — two independent platform trials (DOUBLE-A), concordant on survival-relevant endpoints. Tier C: a mortality claim, so the developer reviews this shelf personally.

cards.headline: RECOVERY 2021: tocilizumab cut 28-day mortality from 35% to 31% (rate ratio 0.85, 95% CI 0.76 to 0.94)
cards.summary: RECOVERY 2021: tocilizumab cut 28-day mortality from 35% to 31% (rate ratio 0.85, 95% CI 0.76 to 0.94)
cards.people: 4,116 hospitalised patients with COVID-19, hypoxia (oxygen saturation <92% on air or receiving oxygen) and CRP at least 75 mg/L, randomised to tocilizumab (n=2,022) or usual care (n=2,094) in the RECOVERY platform; 82% were receiving corticosteroids. Primary outcome: 28-day mortality.
cards.result: 28-day mortality: 31% (621 deaths) on tocilizumab versus 35% (729) on usual care — rate ratio 0.85 (95% CI 0.76 to 0.94), p=0.0028; an absolute reduction of 4 percentage points, a 15% relative reduction. Discharge alive within 28 days: 57% versus 50% (rate ratio 1.22). Benefits were consistent with the concurrent corticosteroid treatment most patients received.
cards.watchOut: Tier C (mortality claim). Eligibility required hypoxia plus CRP ≥75 mg/L and the trial ran when corticosteroids were standard; the estimate is for that combination and that severity band, not for mild or non-inflamed disease. Open-label design, though mortality is a hard endpoint.

cards.headline: REMAP-CAP 2021: tocilizumab and sarilumab improved organ-support-free days (adjusted OR 1.64 and 1.76) and survival in critically ill patients
cards.summary: REMAP-CAP 2021: tocilizumab and sarilumab improved organ-support-free days (adjusted OR 1.64 and 1.76) and survival in critically ill patients
cards.people: Critically ill adults with COVID-19 in intensive care in the REMAP-CAP platform, randomised within the immune-modulation domain to tocilizumab (n=353), sarilumab (n=48), or control (n=402). Primary outcome: organ-support-free days to day 21.
cards.result: Median organ-support-free days: 10 on tocilizumab, 11 on sarilumab, 0 on control. Adjusted odds ratios for a better outcome: 1.64 (95% credible interval 1.25 to 2.14) for tocilizumab and 1.76 (1.17 to 2.91) for sarilumab, with posterior probabilities of superiority above 99.9% and 99.5% respectively. Pooled across both IL-6 antagonists, the 90-day survival hazard ratio was 1.61 (95% credible interval 1.25 to 2.08).
cards.watchOut: The sarilumab arm was small (n=48), so the class claim rests mainly on tocilizumab in both platforms. REMAP-CAP enrolled ICU patients at the point of organ support; RECOVERY enrolled a broader hypoxic ward population — concordant direction, different severity bands. shelves.title: Early outpatient remdesivir (PINETREE): hospitalisation cut from 5.3% to 0.7% in high-risk patients (Tier C)
shelves.question: In non-hospitalised patients with COVID-19 within 7 days of symptom onset and at least one risk factor, does a 3-day course of intravenous remdesivir prevent hospitalisation or death versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Not captured at build — PubMed rendering omitted MeSH term names for PMID 34937145 (see card source note)
shelves.balance: One well-run trial with a large effect. PINETREE randomised 562 non-hospitalised patients with COVID-19, symptom onset within 7 days, and at least one risk factor for progression, to 3 days of intravenous remdesivir or placebo. The composite of COVID-19-related hospitalisation or death by day 28 occurred in 0.7% (2 patients) on remdesivir versus 5.3% (15) on placebo — hazard ratio 0.13 (95% CI 0.03 to 0.59), an 87% relative reduction and a 4.6-percentage-point absolute reduction; there were no deaths in either group by day 28, so the composite is driven by hospitalisations. Medically attended visits were also fewer (1.6% vs 8.3%; HR 0.19, 95% CI 0.07 to 0.56), and adverse events were similar (42.3% vs 46.3%). The event count is small (17 events total) and the trial predates widespread vaccination and later variants, which limits how far the absolute benefit travels. PROPOSED LIKELY — a single double-blind placebo-controlled trial with a big, significant effect on hospitalisation. Tier C: death is part of the composite claim, so the developer reviews this shelf personally.

cards.headline: Gottlieb 2022 (PINETREE): hospitalisation or death 0.7% on remdesivir vs 5.3% on placebo (HR 0.13, 95% CI 0.03 to 0.59)
cards.summary: Gottlieb 2022 (PINETREE): hospitalisation or death 0.7% on remdesivir vs 5.3% on placebo (HR 0.13, 95% CI 0.03 to 0.59)
cards.people: 562 non-hospitalised patients with COVID-19 within 7 days of symptom onset and at least one risk factor for disease progression (age ≥60, obesity, or specified comorbidities), randomised to intravenous remdesivir 200 mg on day 1 then 100 mg on days 2–3 (n=279) or placebo (n=283). Primary endpoint: COVID-19-related hospitalisation or death from any cause by day 28.
cards.result: Primary composite: 0.7% (2 patients) on remdesivir versus 5.3% (15) on placebo — hazard ratio 0.13 (95% CI 0.03 to 0.59), P=0.008; an 87% relative reduction and a 4.6-percentage-point absolute reduction. COVID-19-related medically attended visits: 1.6% (4/246) versus 8.3% (21/252), HR 0.19 (95% CI 0.07 to 0.56). No participant died by day 28 in either group. Adverse events occurred in 42.3% on remdesivir versus 46.3% on placebo.
cards.watchOut: Tier C (death sits inside the composite, though no deaths occurred). Only 17 primary events in total, so the estimate is fragile despite the small p-value; participants were unvaccinated-era, high-risk outpatients treated within 7 days, and the intervention needs three days of intravenous infusion — the absolute benefit in a vaccinated, later-variant population will be smaller.
cards.source: Gottlieb RL et al. Early remdesivir to prevent progression to severe Covid-19 in outpatients. N Engl J Med. 2022. PMID: 34937145. shelves.title: Early convalescent plasma for outpatients (CSSC-004): hospitalisation 2.9% vs 6.3% when given early and high-titre
shelves.question: In symptomatic outpatients treated within 8 days of onset, does early high-titre COVID-19 convalescent plasma prevent hospitalisation versus control plasma?
shelves.mesh: Not captured at build — PubMed rendering omitted MeSH term names for PMID 35353960 (see card source note)
shelves.balance: Timing and titre were the whole story. CSSC-004 randomised 1,225 symptomatic outpatients within 8 days of symptom onset to high-titre COVID-19 convalescent plasma or control plasma, transfused within a day of randomisation. Hospitalisation within 28 days occurred in 2.9% (17/592) on convalescent plasma versus 6.3% (37/589) on control plasma — an absolute reduction of 3.4 percentage points (95% CI 1.0 to 5.8), a 54% relative reduction. Nearly everyone hospitalised was unvaccinated (53 of 54; one was partially vaccinated), so the trial speaks to an unvaccinated population treated early with potent product. This does not rehabilitate convalescent plasma given late to hospitalised patients, where the big trials were negative — a different question with its own shelf logic. PROPOSED LIKELY — one large double-blind randomised trial with a clear absolute benefit on hospitalisation, in the population and window it studied.

cards.headline: Sullivan 2022 (CSSC-004): hospitalisation 2.9% with early convalescent plasma vs 6.3% with control plasma (absolute reduction 3.4 points)
cards.summary: Sullivan 2022 (CSSC-004): hospitalisation 2.9% with early convalescent plasma vs 6.3% with control plasma (absolute reduction 3.4 points)
cards.people: 1,225 symptomatic outpatients with COVID-19 within 8 days of symptom onset, randomised to high-titre convalescent plasma or control plasma; 1,181 were transfused, within a day of randomisation. Primary outcome: hospitalisation within 28 days.
cards.result: Hospitalisation: 2.9% (17/592) on convalescent plasma versus 6.3% (37/589) on control plasma — absolute risk reduction 3.4 percentage points (95% CI 1.0 to 5.8), P=0.005, a 54% relative risk reduction. Of the 54 hospitalised participants, 53 were unvaccinated and 1 was partially vaccinated. Grade 3 or 4 adverse events among non-hospitalised participants: 7 on convalescent plasma versus 9 on control plasma.
cards.watchOut: The benefit is bound to the trial's conditions: high-titre product, transfusion within about a day of presentation and within 8 days of onset, and an almost entirely unvaccinated population. It does not generalise to vaccinated patients, to low-titre or late plasma, or to people already in hospital.
