shelves.title: Inhaled budesonide in community COVID-19: faster recovery in PRINCIPLE and STOIC; admission/death benefit not proven (Tier C)
shelves.question: In older or comorbid adults with suspected COVID-19 in the community (up to 14 days unwell), does inhaled budesonide speed recovery and reduce hospital admission or death versus usual care?
shelves.mesh: COVID-19 · COVID-19 Drug Treatment · Budesonide · Glucocorticoids · Administration, Inhalation · Hospitalization · Humans
shelves.balance: Two randomised trials agree that inhaled budesonide speeds recovery from community COVID-19; neither proves it prevents admission or death. In PRINCIPLE (older or comorbid UK adults, unwell up to 14 days), budesonide shortened time to first self-reported recovery by an estimated 2.94 days (median 11.8 vs 14.7 days; HR 1.21, 95% BCI 1.08 to 1.36; probability of superiority >0.999, meeting its threshold). The hospital admission or death outcome favoured budesonide — estimated 6.8% vs 8.8%, OR 0.75 (95% BCI 0.55 to 1.03) — but its probability of superiority, 0.963, fell short of the prespecified 0.975 threshold, so that claim is unproven. The smaller double-blind STOIC trial was concordant on early deterioration: COVID-19-related urgent care visits in 1 of 69 (1%) on budesonide versus 10 of 70 (14%) on usual care per-protocol. PROPOSED LIKELY — for faster recovery (DOUBLE-A: PRINCIPLE + STOIC); the admission/death benefit is a favourable trend only, and the balance says so plainly. Tier C: the composite includes death, so the developer reviews this shelf personally.

cards.headline: Yu 2021 (PRINCIPLE): budesonide shortened recovery by ~2.9 days; admission/death 6.8% vs 8.8% did not meet the superiority threshold
cards.summary: Yu 2021 (PRINCIPLE): budesonide shortened recovery by ~2.9 days; admission/death 6.8% vs 8.8% did not meet the superiority threshold
cards.people: UK community patients aged ≥65, or ≥50 with comorbidities, unwell for up to 14 days with suspected COVID-19 and not admitted to hospital; 4,700 were randomised across the platform (1,073 budesonide, 1,988 usual care, 1,639 other interventions) and the primary analysis included 2,530 SARS-CoV-2-positive participants (787 budesonide, 1,069 usual care, 974 other). Intervention: inhaled budesonide 800 µg twice daily for 14 days plus usual care. Coprimary endpoints: time to first self-reported recovery, and hospital admission or death within 28 days (Bayesian models).
cards.result: Recovery was faster on budesonide by an estimated 2.94 days (95% Bayesian credible interval 1.19 to 5.12): median 11.8 vs 14.7 days, HR 1.21 (95% BCI 1.08 to 1.36), probability of superiority >0.999 — meeting the prespecified 0.99 superiority threshold. Hospital admission or death (model-estimated): 6.8% on budesonide versus 8.8% on usual care, absolute difference 2.0% (95% BCI −0.2 to 4.5), OR 0.75 (95% BCI 0.55 to 1.03), probability of superiority 0.963 — below the prespecified 0.975 threshold, so superiority was not established. Serious adverse events were few (2 budesonide, 4 usual care; admissions unrelated to COVID-19).
cards.watchOut: Open-label with a self-reported recovery endpoint — expectation effects are possible, and the hard composite (admission/death) did not cross its own superiority threshold. The recovery benefit is the proven claim; the admission/death trend is not. Tier C shelf.
cards.source: Yu et al. Inhaled budesonide for COVID-19 in people at high risk of complications in the community in the UK (PRINCIPLE): a randomised, controlled, open-label, adaptive platform trial. Lancet. 2021. PMID: 34388395. Registry ID: ISRCTN86534580, from the record. cards.headline: Ramakrishnan 2021 (STOIC): COVID-19 urgent-care visits 1% on budesonide vs 14% on usual care (per-protocol)
cards.summary: Ramakrishnan 2021 (STOIC): COVID-19 urgent-care visits 1% on budesonide vs 14% on usual care (per-protocol)
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial, double-blind phase 2 (STOIC; stopped early)
cards.people: 167 adults with early COVID-19 in the community recruited; 146 were randomised (73 inhaled budesonide, 73 usual care) and 139 were in the per-protocol analysis. Primary outcome: COVID-19-related urgent care visit (including emergency department assessment or hospitalisation). The trial was stopped early after independent statistical review concluded the primary outcome difference would not change with further enrolment.
cards.result: Primary outcome per-protocol: 1 of 69 (1%) on budesonide versus 10 of 70 (14%) on usual care — difference 0.131 (95% CI 0.043 to 0.218), p=0.004; in the intention-to-treat population, 2 of 73 (3%) versus 11 of 73 (15%), p=0.009; number needed to treat 8. Self-reported recovery was faster on budesonide (median 7 vs 8 days, log-rank p=0.007). Five participants (7%) on budesonide had self-limiting adverse events.
cards.watchOut: Small trial (146 randomised) stopped early, which tends to inflate effects; its urgent-care-visit endpoint is softer than hospitalisation. Its role here is concordance with PRINCIPLE on early recovery/deterioration, not independent proof of admission prevention.
cards.source: Ramakrishnan et al. Inhaled budesonide in the treatment of early COVID-19 (STOIC). Lancet Respir Med. 2021. PMID: 33844996. Registry ID: NCT04416399, from the record. shelves.title: Vilobelimab in ventilated COVID-19 (PANAMO): mortality signal whose primary analysis missed significance — OUTSTANDING-SINGLE (Tier C)
shelves.question: In invasively ventilated patients with severe COVID-19, does the anti-C5a antibody vilobelimab improve survival versus placebo, each on standard care?
shelves.mesh: Not captured at build — PubMed rendering omitted MeSH term names for PMID 36087611 (see card source note)
shelves.balance: OUTSTANDING-SINGLE, and a borderline one: this shelf rests on a single phase 3 trial whose prespecified primary analysis did not reach significance. In PANAMO, 368 invasively ventilated patients with severe COVID-19 were randomised to the anti-C5a antibody vilobelimab or placebo, each on standard care. Deaths by day 28 were 31% (54/177) on vilobelimab versus 40% (77/191) on placebo (Kaplan–Meier estimates 32% vs 42%), but the primary site-stratified analysis gave a hazard ratio of 0.73 (95% CI 0.50 to 1.06) with p=0.094 — not significant. A predefined unstratified analysis was significant (HR 0.67, 95% CI 0.48 to 0.96; p=0.027). Serious treatment-emergent adverse events were similar (59% vs 63%). A possible ~9–10 point absolute mortality advantage that depends on which prespecified analysis you read is a genuine signal, not a settled benefit. (Desk note: the topic draft quoted mortality of 31.9% vs 41.6%; those figures do not appear in the published abstract and are not used here.) PROPOSED POSSIBLE — single trial, primary analysis formally negative, supportive secondary analysis positive. Tier C: a mortality claim, so the developer reviews this shelf personally, and the OUTSTANDING-SINGLE flag stays on it.

shelves.title: Ivermectin for early COVID-19: no benefit in TOGETHER or COVID-OUT — two large trials agree
shelves.question: In symptomatic high-risk outpatients within 7 days of onset, does ivermectin 400 µg/kg daily for 3 days reduce hospitalisation or extended emergency observation versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: COVID-19 · COVID-19 Drug Treatment · Ivermectin · Anti-Infective Agents · Hospitalization · Ambulatory Care · Humans
shelves.balance: Two large placebo-controlled platform trials, run independently on different continents, agree: ivermectin did not help. In TOGETHER (Brazil), the composite of hospitalisation or extended emergency observation occurred in 14.7% on ivermectin versus 16.3% on placebo (relative risk 0.90, 95% Bayesian credible interval 0.70 to 1.16), with the modified intention-to-treat and per-protocol analyses the same (RR 0.89 and 0.94) and no significant effects on secondary outcomes or adverse events. In COVID-OUT (USA), the ivermectin arm's adjusted odds ratio for the primary composite of hypoxemia, emergency visit, hospitalisation, or death was 1.05 (95% CI 0.76 to 1.45; P=0.78) — the point estimate on the wrong side of 1. When two adequately sized double-blind trials both land on no effect, the question is settled for this dose and population. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — DOUBLE-A concordant nulls.

shelves.title: Colchicine for community COVID-19: COLCORONA missed its primary endpoint overall; PRINCIPLE stopped for futility (Tier C)
shelves.question: In non-hospitalised patients aged 40 years or older with COVID-19 and at least one risk factor, does colchicine reduce the composite of death or hospital admission versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: COVID-19 · COVID-19 Drug Treatment · Colchicine · Anti-Inflammatory Agents · Hospitalization · Ambulatory Care · Humans
shelves.balance: Read whole, the randomised evidence does not show that colchicine helps community COVID-19. COLCORONA, the big double-blind trial, missed its primary endpoint in the full population: death or hospital admission occurred in 4.7% on colchicine versus 5.8% on placebo (OR 0.79, 95.1% CI 0.61 to 1.03; p=0.081). Only inside the prespecified PCR-confirmed subset did the difference reach significance (4.6% vs 6.0%; OR 0.75, 95% CI 0.57 to 0.99; p=0.042) — a subset of a negative trial, not a positive trial. The second randomised evaluation, PRINCIPLE's colchicine arm, was stopped for futility on recovery time (HR 0.92, 95% credible interval 0.72 to 1.16; probability of a meaningful benefit 1.8%), with hospital admission or death also null (OR 0.76, 95% CrI 0.28 to 1.89). Colchicine also caused more diarrhoea (13.7% vs 7.3% in COLCORONA), though serious adverse events were slightly fewer (4.9% vs 6.3%). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — the headline result of the only adequately sized trial is null and the platform arm was futile; the PCR-confirmed subset keeps this from a stronger null stamp, and the balance gives it its exact weight: a subset finding, nothing more. Tier C: the composite includes death, so the developer reviews this shelf personally.

cards.headline: Tardif 2021 (COLCORONA): primary endpoint missed overall — 4.7% vs 5.8% (OR 0.79, 95.1% CI 0.61 to 1.03; p=0.081); significant only in the PCR-confirmed subset
cards.summary: Tardif 2021 (COLCORONA): primary endpoint missed overall — 4.7% vs 5.8% (OR 0.79, 95.1% CI 0.61 to 1.03; p=0.081); significant only in the PCR-confirmed subset
cards.people: 4,488 non-hospitalised patients aged 40 or older with COVID-19 and at least one high-risk characteristic in six countries (2,235 colchicine, 2,253 placebo), treated within 24 hours of diagnosis in the community. Primary endpoint: the composite of death or hospital admission for COVID-19.
cards.result: Primary composite: 4.7% (104 events) on colchicine versus 5.8% (131) on placebo — OR 0.79 (95.1% CI 0.61 to 1.03), p=0.081: not significant in the full population. In the prespecified PCR-confirmed subset (4,159 patients): 4.6% (96/2,075) versus 6.0% (126/2,084), OR 0.75 (95% CI 0.57 to 0.99), p=0.042. cards.summary: Dorward 2022 (PRINCIPLE colchicine): arm stopped for futility — recovery HR 0.92 (95% CrI 0.72 to 1.16); probability of meaningful benefit 1.8%
cards.type: Randomised open-label platform trial arm (PRINCIPLE; stopped for futility)
cards.people: Community patients in the UK PRINCIPLE platform randomised to colchicine between 4 March and 26 May 2021; the primary analysis population comprised 2,755 SARS-CoV-2-positive participants (156 colchicine, 1,145 usual care, 1,454 other interventions). Endpoints: time to first self-reported recovery, and hospital admission or death within 28 days (Bayesian models). The colchicine arm was stopped for futility on the recovery endpoint.
cards.result: Time to recovery: HR 0.92 (95% credible interval 0.72 to 1.16) — no benefit, with a 1.8% probability of a meaningful benefit, prompting the futility stop. cards.watchOut: The colchicine arm was small and stopped early for futility, so it cannot exclude a modest effect on admission/death by itself; its weight is as a second, concordant non-positive randomised evaluation beside COLCORONA's overall null.

shelves.title: suPAR-guided anakinra for COVID-19 pneumonia (SAVE-MORE): better day-28 status and lower mortality in one biomarker-guided trial (Tier C)
shelves.question: In hospitalised patients with COVID-19 pneumonia selected by plasma suPAR of at least 6 ng/mL (risk of respiratory failure), does early anakinra improve day-28 clinical status versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: COVID-19 · COVID-19 Drug Treatment · Interleukin 1 Receptor Antagonist Protein · Receptors, Urokinase Plasminogen Activator · Humans
shelves.balance: A biomarker-guided strategy with a strong single-trial result. SAVE-MORE randomised 594 hospitalised patients with COVID-19 pneumonia whose plasma suPAR was at least 6 ng/mL — a marker of risk of respiratory failure — to anakinra (interleukin-1 receptor antagonist) or placebo; 85.9% were also receiving dexamethasone. By day 28, patients on anakinra had substantially better clinical status on the WHO Clinical Progression Scale (adjusted proportional odds ratio 0.36, 95% CI 0.26 to 0.50, for a worse outcome), with a greater median improvement (decrease of 4 vs 3 points; OR 0.40), less progression in organ dysfunction (day-7 SOFA odds ratio 0.63, P=0.004), shorter hospital stay, and lower 28-day mortality (HR 0.45, P=0.045). It is one trial, and the mortality result is a secondary endpoint with a p-value just under 0.05; the strategy also depends on suPAR testing being available and applied with the same threshold. PROPOSED LIKELY — a well-powered double-blind trial hitting its ordinal primary endpoint decisively, with a concordant mortality signal. Tier C: a mortality benefit will print on this shelf, so the developer reviews it personally.

cards.headline: Kyriazopoulou 2021 (SAVE-MORE): day-28 WHO scale adjusted proportional OR 0.36 (95% CI 0.26 to 0.50) for worse status; 28-day mortality HR 0.45
cards.summary: Kyriazopoulou 2021 (SAVE-MORE): day-28 WHO scale adjusted proportional OR 0.36 (95% CI 0.26 to 0.50) for worse status; 28-day mortality HR 0.45
cards.people: 594 hospitalised patients with COVID-19 pneumonia and plasma suPAR at least 6 ng/mL, randomised to anakinra or placebo in addition to standard care; 510 (85.9%) received dexamethasone. Primary endpoint: clinical status on the 11-point WHO Clinical Progression Scale at day 28.
cards.result: Adjusted proportional odds ratio for a worse day-28 WHO-CPS outcome on anakinra: 0.36 (95% CI 0.26 to 0.50). Median decrease in WHO-CPS score: 4 points on anakinra versus 3 on placebo (OR 0.40, P<0.0001). Day-7 SOFA score distribution favoured anakinra (OR 0.63, P=0.004). Twenty-eight-day mortality was lower on anakinra (HR 0.45, P=0.045), and hospital stay was shorter.
cards.watchOut: Tier C (mortality benefit). Single trial; the mortality endpoint is secondary with P=0.045, so the firm claim is the ordinal clinical-status benefit, with mortality supportive. The result applies to suPAR-selected patients (≥6 ng/mL) — it does not show anakinra helps unselected COVID-19 pneumonia, and it presumes suPAR testing is available.

shelves.title: Therapeutic-dose heparin in noncritically ill COVID-19: more organ-support-free days in the multiplatform trial and HEP-COVID (Tier C)
shelves.question: In hospitalised patients with COVID-19 who are not critically ill, does therapeutic-dose heparin increase organ-support-free days versus usual-care thromboprophylaxis?
shelves.mesh: COVID-19 · COVID-19 Drug Treatment · Heparin · Heparin, Low-Molecular-Weight · Anticoagulants · Thrombosis · Venous Thromboembolism · Hemorrhage · Humans
shelves.balance: For patients on the ward — explicitly not the critically ill — therapeutic-dose heparin improved outcomes in two randomised evaluations. The combined ATTACC / ACTIV-4a / REMAP-CAP multiplatform trial (2,219 noncritically ill patients) found a 98.6% probability that therapeutic-dose heparin increased organ-support-free days versus usual-care thromboprophylaxis (adjusted OR 1.27, 95% credible interval 1.03 to 1.58), with an adjusted absolute increase of 4.0 percentage points (95% CrI 0.5 to 7.2) in survival to discharge without organ support; results held across d-dimer subgroups. HEP-COVID, which enrolled patients with very high d-dimer or sepsis-induced coagulopathy, found the primary composite of thromboembolism or death in 28.7% on therapeutic versus 41.9% on standard dosing (RR 0.68, 95% CI 0.49 to 0.96) — with the benefit concentrated in non-ICU patients (RR 0.46) and absent in ICU patients (RR 0.92). The cost is bleeding: major bleeding 1.9% versus 0.9% in the multiplatform trial and 4.7% versus 1.6% in HEP-COVID (not significant there). PROPOSED LIKELY — DOUBLE-A concordance in noncritically ill patients, with the bleeding trade-off printed, not buried. Tier C: death is embedded in the primary ordinal outcome, so the developer reviews this shelf personally. The companion critically-ill multiplatform report is a separate question and is not this shelf.

cards.headline: Lawler 2021 (multiplatform): therapeutic heparin increased organ-support-free days (adjusted OR 1.27, 95% CrI 1.03 to 1.58); major bleeding 1.9% vs 0.9%
cards.summary: Lawler 2021 (multiplatform): therapeutic heparin increased organ-support-free days (adjusted OR 1.27, 95% CrI 1.03 to 1.58); major bleeding 1.9% vs 0.9%
cards.type: Randomised open-label adaptive multiplatform trial (ATTACC / ACTIV-4a / REMAP-CAP)
cards.people: 2,219 hospitalised patients with COVID-19 who were not critically ill, randomised across the ATTACC, ACTIV-4a, and REMAP-CAP platforms to therapeutic-dose heparin versus usual-care thromboprophylaxis. Primary outcome: organ-support-free days (an ordinal outcome incorporating in-hospital death) to day 21.
cards.result: The probability that therapeutic-dose heparin increased organ-support-free days was 98.6%; adjusted odds ratio 1.27 (95% credible interval 1.03 to 1.58). The adjusted absolute difference in survival to hospital discharge without organ support was 4.0 percentage points (95% CrI 0.5 to 7.2). Probabilities of superiority by d-dimer group: 97.3% (high), 92.9% (low), 97.3% (unknown). Major bleeding occurred in 1.9% on therapeutic-dose versus 0.9% on thromboprophylaxis dosing.
cards.watchOut: Tier C (death is embedded in the ordinal primary outcome). Noncritically ill patients only — the same platforms' critically-ill comparison did not show this benefit and is a separate record. Open-label design; the bleeding excess (about 1 extra major bleed per 100 patients) is part of the claim, not a footnote.

cards.headline: Spyropoulos 2021 (HEP-COVID): thromboembolism or death 28.7% on therapeutic vs 41.9% on standard dosing (RR 0.68, 95% CI 0.49 to 0.96) — benefit in non-ICU patients only
cards.summary: Spyropoulos 2021 (HEP-COVID): thromboembolism or death 28.7% on therapeutic vs 41.9% on standard dosing (RR 0.68, 95% CI 0.49 to 0.96) — benefit in non-ICU patients only
cards.people: 257 hospitalised patients with COVID-19 at 12 US centres with d-dimer more than 4 times the upper limit of normal or a sepsis-induced coagulopathy score of at least 4; 253 were analysed (129 therapeutic-dose, 124 standard-dose heparin/low-molecular-weight heparin). Primary outcome: the composite of venous or arterial thromboembolism or death.
cards.result: Primary composite: 28.7% (37/129) on therapeutic dosing versus 41.9% (52/124) on standard dosing — RR 0.68 (95% CI 0.49 to 0.96), P=0.03; a 32% relative reduction and a 13.2-percentage-point absolute reduction. Thromboembolism alone: 10.9% vs 29.0% (RR 0.37, 95% CI 0.21 to 0.66; P<0.001). The benefit was confined to non-ICU patients (16.7% vs 36.1%; RR 0.46, 95% CI 0.27 to 0.81; P=0.004) and absent in ICU patients (51.1% vs 55.3%; RR 0.92; P=0.71). Major bleeding: 4.7% versus 1.6% (RR 2.88, 95% CI 0.59 to 14.02; P=0.17).
cards.watchOut: HEP-COVID enrolled a selected high-d-dimer / coagulopathy population, so its larger absolute effect does not transfer to all ward patients; the multiplatform trial is the broader base. Both trials agree on the direction in noncritically ill patients and on more bleeding with therapeutic dosing.

shelves.title: After source control for intra-abdominal infection, about 4 days of antibiotics is enough (STOP-IT)
shelves.question: In complicated intra-abdominal infection with adequate source control, is a fixed course of about 4 days of antibiotics as safe as continuing until 2 days after fever, leukocytosis and ileus resolve (up to 10 days)?
shelves.mesh: Intraabdominal Infections · Anti-Bacterial Agents · Drug Administration Schedule · Peritonitis · Sepsis · Humans
shelves.balance: One large randomised trial answers this cleanly. In STOP-IT, 518 patients with complicated intra-abdominal infection and adequate source control were randomised to a fixed course of 4±1 days or to antibiotics continued until 2 days after fever, leukocytosis and ileus resolved (median 8 days). The composite of surgical-site infection, recurrent intra-abdominal infection or death within 30 days was 21.8% on the short course versus 22.3% on the longer course (absolute difference −0.5 percentage points; 95% CI −7.0 to 8.0; P=0.92), with no significant difference in any component. The lesson is conditional: the clock starts at adequate source control, and the trial says nothing about patients whose source was not controlled. PROPOSED LIKELY — the fixed short course is as safe as the longer course once source control is adequate (Tier C: death is a component of the primary composite).

cards.headline: STOP-IT 2015: fixed ~4-day course matched symptom-guided longer therapy — composite 21.8% vs 22.3%
cards.summary: STOP-IT 2015: fixed ~4-day course matched symptom-guided longer therapy — composite 21.8% vs 22.3%
cards.people: 518 patients with complicated intraabdominal infection and adequate source control, randomised to a fixed course of antibiotics for 4±1 calendar days (experimental) or antibiotics until 2 days after resolution of fever, leukocytosis and ileus, maximum 10 days (control). Primary outcome: composite of surgical-site infection, recurrent intraabdominal infection, or death within 30 days after the index source-control procedure.
cards.result: The composite occurred in 56 of 257 patients (21.8%) in the experimental group versus 58 of 260 (22.3%) in the control group (absolute difference −0.5 percentage points; 95% CI −7.0 to 8.0; P=0.92). Median antibiotic duration was 4.0 days (IQR 4.0–5.0) versus 8.0 days (IQR 5.0–10.0) (absolute difference −4.0 days; 95% CI −4.7 to −3.3; P<0.001). No significant between-group differences in the individual components or other secondary outcomes.
cards.watchOut: Every patient had adequate source control — the result does not license a 4-day stop when drainage or surgery was incomplete. Event rates were high in both arms (>20%), reflecting how sick this population is; the trial shows the extra days added nothing, not that the infection is benign.
cards.source: Sawyer RG et al. Trial of short-course antimicrobial therapy for intraabdominal infection. N Engl J Med. 2015. PMID: 25992746. Registry ID: NCT00657566, from the record. shelves.title: Prosthetic joint infection: 6 weeks of antibiotics is not enough — 12 weeks won (DATIPO)
shelves.question: In microbiologically confirmed prosthetic joint infection managed with appropriate surgery, is 6 weeks of antibiotic therapy non-inferior to 12 weeks?
shelves.mesh: Prosthesis-Related Infections · Anti-Bacterial Agents · Drug Administration Schedule · Humans
shelves.balance: This duration trial's answer is 'longer'. In DATIPO, 410 patients with microbiologically confirmed prosthetic joint infection managed with an appropriate surgical procedure were randomised to 6 or 12 weeks of antibiotics. Persistent infection within 2 years occurred in 18.1% on 6 weeks versus 9.4% on 12 weeks — an absolute risk difference of 8.7 percentage points (95% CI 1.8 to 15.6) — and non-inferiority of the shorter course was not shown. Halving therapy roughly doubled the failure rate in absolute terms. PROPOSED LIKELY (harm) — the harm belongs to the 6-week course; 12 weeks remains the course this trial supports.

cards.headline: DATIPO 2021: persistent infection 18.1% after 6 weeks vs 9.4% after 12 weeks — non-inferiority not shown
cards.summary: DATIPO 2021: persistent infection 18.1% after 6 weeks vs 9.4% after 12 weeks — non-inferiority not shown
cards.people: 410 patients from 28 French centres with microbiologically confirmed prosthetic joint infection managed with an appropriate surgical procedure, randomly assigned to antibiotic therapy for 6 weeks (205) or 12 weeks (205). Primary outcome: persistent infection (persistence or recurrence with the initial causative bacteria) within 2 years after completing antibiotic therapy.
cards.result: Persistent infection occurred in 35 of 193 patients (18.1%) in the 6-week group and 18 of 191 patients (9.4%) in the 12-week group (absolute risk difference 8.7 percentage points; 95% CI 1.8 to 15.6); non-inferiority was not shown.
cards.watchOut: Open-label, and the result is an average across surgical strategies (implant retention and exchange procedures were both included); the trial does not prove every subgroup needs 12 weeks, but it removes any presumption that 6 weeks is generally safe after surgery for prosthetic joint infection.
cards.source: Bernard L et al. Antibiotic Therapy for 6 or 12 Weeks for Prosthetic Joint Infection. N Engl J Med. 2021. PMID: 34042388. Registry ID: NCT01816009, from the record. shelves.title: De-escalating antibiotics in severe sepsis: the one randomised trial found no ICU-stay benefit and more superinfections
shelves.question: In ICU patients with severe sepsis on appropriate empiric therapy, does protocolised de-escalation to the narrowest effective regimen match continuation of the empiric regimen on ICU stay and outcomes?
shelves.mesh: Sepsis · Anti-Bacterial Agents · Intensive Care Units · Humans
shelves.balance: THIN — a single small trial, and its abstract does not say what stewardship advocates might expect. Leone and colleagues randomised 116 patients with severe sepsis in nine French ICUs to de-escalation or continuation of empiric therapy, with ICU length of stay as the primary outcome and a 2-day non-inferiority margin. Median ICU stay was 9 days with de-escalation versus 8 days with continuation (mean difference 3.4 days; 95% CI −1.7 to 8.5; P=0.71) — the authors' own conclusion was that de-escalation resulted in a prolonged ICU stay, and non-inferiority was not demonstrated. Superinfection occurred in 27% versus 11% (P=0.03) and antibiotic days were higher, not lower, with de-escalation; mortality was similar in a trial far too small to judge it. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) — the randomised evidence neither confirms de-escalation's safety on patient outcomes nor proves harm; it is one small open-label trial powered on ICU stay.

cards.headline: Leone 2014: ICU stay 9 vs 8 days (mean difference +3.4 days), superinfection 27% vs 11% with de-escalation
cards.summary: Leone 2014: ICU stay 9 vs 8 days (mean difference +3.4 days), superinfection 27% vs 11% with de-escalation
cards.people: 116 patients with severe sepsis in nine French ICUs, randomly assigned to de-escalation (n=59) or continuation of empirical antimicrobial treatment (n=57), recruited February 2012 to April 2013. Primary outcome: duration of ICU stay, with a predefined non-inferiority margin of 2 days.
cards.result: Median ICU stay was 9 days (IQR 5–22) in the de-escalation group and 8 days (IQR 4–15) in the continuation group (P=0.71); the mean difference was 3.4 days (95% CI −1.7 to 8.5). A superinfection occurred in 16 patients (27%) in the de-escalation group and 6 (11%) in the continuation group (P=0.03). Antibiotic days were 9 (IQR 7–15) versus 7.5 (IQR 6–13) (P=0.03). Mortality was similar in both groups. The authors concluded de-escalation resulted in prolonged ICU stay without affecting mortality.
cards.watchOut: Non-inferiority was not demonstrated on the trial's own primary outcome, and the trial was not powered for mortality. The superinfection excess is a secondary outcome in 116 patients — a signal to weigh, not a settled harm. This card reports the abstract as published; it corrects any summary claiming the trial 'met non-inferiority'.

shelves.title: After discharge, repeated MRSA decolonisation cut infections by about a third (CLEAR)
shelves.question: In hospitalised MRSA carriers after discharge, does repeated decolonisation (chlorhexidine body wash and mouthwash plus nasal mupirocin, 5 days twice monthly for 6 months) reduce MRSA infection and infection-related hospitalisation versus hygiene education alone?
shelves.mesh: Methicillin-Resistant Staphylococcus aureus · Staphylococcal Infections · Chlorhexidine · Mupirocin · Humans
shelves.balance: A large, clean randomised trial. In CLEAR, 2,121 MRSA carriers were randomised after discharge to hygiene education alone or education plus decolonisation (chlorhexidine mouthwash, chlorhexidine baths or showers, and nasal mupirocin, 5 days twice monthly for 6 months) and followed for 1 year. MRSA infection occurred in 9.2% with education alone versus 6.3% with decolonisation — a hazard ratio of 0.70 (95% CI 0.52 to 0.96; P=0.03), i.e. a 30% relative reduction, with a number needed to treat of 30 to prevent one infection; infection-related hospitalisation was also lower (HR 0.76; 95% CI 0.62 to 0.93). Side effects were all mild and occurred in 4.2%. PROPOSED LIKELY — one large trial with a patient-important outcome and absolute rates that make the benefit's size plain.

cards.headline: CLEAR 2019: MRSA infection 9.2% (education) vs 6.3% (decolonisation); HR 0.70 relative; NNT 30
cards.summary: CLEAR 2019: MRSA infection 9.2% (education) vs 6.3% (decolonisation); HR 0.70 relative; NNT 30
cards.people: 2,121 hospitalised MRSA carriers in the per-protocol population (1,063 education, 1,058 decolonisation), followed for 1 year after discharge. Decolonisation: chlorhexidine mouthwash, baths or showers with chlorhexidine, and nasal mupirocin for 5 days twice per month for 6 months. Primary outcome: MRSA infection by CDC criteria.
cards.result: MRSA infection occurred in 98 of 1,063 participants (9.2%) in the education group and 67 of 1,058 (6.3%) in the decolonisation group (hazard ratio 0.70 — a 30% relative reduction; 95% CI 0.52 to 0.96; P=0.03; number needed to treat 30, 95% CI 18 to 230); 84.8% of MRSA infections led to hospitalisation. Infection from any cause occurred in 23.7% versus 19.6%; the hazard of infection-related hospitalisation was lower with decolonisation (HR 0.76; 95% CI 0.62 to 0.93). Participants who adhered fully had 44% fewer MRSA infections in relative terms (HR 0.56; 95% CI 0.36 to 0.86, as-treated). Side effects (all mild) occurred in 4.2%.
cards.watchOut: Unblinded, and the regimen is burdensome — 5 days twice a month for 6 months; the per-protocol/adherent effects are larger than the effect of merely being assigned. Secondary outcomes had no prespecified adjustment for multiple comparisons, as the authors state. The population is known MRSA carriers after a hospital stay, not the general community.
cards.source: Huang SS et al. Decolonization to Reduce Postdischarge Infection Risk among MRSA Carriers. N Engl J Med. 2019. PMID: 30763195. Registry ID: NCT01209234, from the record. shelves.title: Gloves and gowns for every ICU contact: no effect on combined MRSA/VRE acquisition (BUGG)
shelves.question: In medical and surgical ICUs, does requiring gloves and gowns for all patient contact reduce acquisition of MRSA or VRE versus usual care?
shelves.mesh: Gloves, Protective · Surgical Attire · Cross Infection · Methicillin-Resistant Staphylococcus aureus · Vancomycin Resistance · Intensive Care Units · Humans
shelves.balance: A 20-ICU cluster-randomised trial with a split answer. In BUGG, universal glove-and-gown use for all patient contact did not change the primary outcome — combined MRSA or VRE acquisition (difference in change −1.71 acquisitions per 1,000 patient-days; 95% CI −6.15 to 2.73; P=.57) — and did not change VRE acquisition. MRSA acquisition alone, a secondary outcome, fell more in intervention ICUs (difference −2.98 per 1,000 patient-days; 95% CI −5.58 to −0.38; P=.046), alongside fewer room entries and better room-exit hand hygiene; the authors themselves say the secondary findings require replication. There was no significant difference in adverse events. PROPOSED SPLIT — LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) for the combined primary outcome; POSSIBLE for MRSA acquisition alone.

cards.headline: BUGG 2013: combined MRSA/VRE acquisition unchanged (P=.57); MRSA alone fell (P=.046, secondary)
cards.summary: BUGG 2013: combined MRSA/VRE acquisition unchanged (P=.57); MRSA alone fell (P=.046, secondary)
cards.people: Cluster-randomised trial in 20 medical and surgical ICUs in 20 US hospitals (26,180 patients; 92,241 swabs), January to October 2012. Intervention ICUs: all health care workers wore gloves and gowns for all patient contact and on entering any patient room. Primary outcome: acquisition of MRSA or VRE on surveillance cultures at admission and discharge.
cards.result: Intervention ICUs' primary-outcome rate fell from 21.35 to 16.91 acquisitions per 1,000 patient-days; control ICUs fell from 19.02 to 16.29 — a difference in changes that was not significant (−1.71 per 1,000 patient-days; 95% CI −6.15 to 2.73; P=.57). VRE acquisition did not differ (difference 0.89; 95% CI −4.27 to 6.04; P=.70); MRSA acquisition was lower with the intervention (difference −2.98; 95% CI −5.58 to −0.38; P=.046). Room entries fell (4.28 vs 5.24 per hour; P=.02), room-exit hand hygiene rose (78.3% vs 62.9%; P=.02), and adverse events did not differ significantly (58.7 vs 74.4 per 1,000 patient-days; P=.24).
cards.watchOut: The MRSA finding is one secondary outcome among several, with a P value of .046 — exactly the kind of result the authors flag as needing replication. Universal precautions also changed behaviour (fewer room entries), so any effect is a bundle effect, not a pure barrier effect. Acquisition is colonisation, not clinical infection.
cards.source: Harris AD et al. Universal glove and gown use and acquisition of antibiotic-resistant bacteria in the ICU: a randomized trial. JAMA. 2013. PMID: 24097234. cluster-randomised trial (bugg) cluster-randomised trial in 20 medical and surgical icus in 20 us hospitals (26,180 patients; 92,241 swabs), january to october 2012. intervention icus: all health care workers wore gloves and gowns for all patient contact and on entering any patient room. primary outcome: acquisition of mrsa or vre on surveillance cultures at admission and discharge. intervention icus' primary-outcome rate fell from 21.35 to 16.91 acquisitions per 1,000 patient-days; control icus fell from 19.02 to 16.29 — a difference in changes that was not significant (−1.71 per 1,000 patient-days; 95% ci −6.15 to 2.73; p=.57). vre acquisition did not differ (difference 0.89; 95% ci −4.27 to 6.04; p=.70); mrsa acquisition was lower with the intervention (difference −2.98; 95% ci −5.58 to −0.38; p=.046). room entries fell (4.28 vs 5.24 per hour; p=.02), room-exit hand hygiene rose (78.3% vs 62.9%; p=.02), and adverse events did not differ significantly (58.7 vs 74.4 per 1,000 patient-days; p=.24). the mrsa finding is one secondary outcome among several, with a p value of .046 — exactly the kind of result the authors flag as needing replication. universal precautions also changed behaviour (fewer room entries), so any effect is a bundle effect, not a pure barrier effect. acquisition is colonisation, not clinical infection. harris ad et al. universal glove and gown use and acquisition of antibiotic-resistant bacteria in the icu: a randomized trial. jama. 2013. pmid: 24097234. registry id: nct01318213, from the record. mesh: gloves, protective · surgical attire · aged · cross infection / prevention & control · enterococcus · female · gram-positive bacterial infections / prevention & control · guideline adherence · hand disinfection · humans · infection control / methods · intensive care units / standards · male · methicillin-resistant staphylococcus aureus · middle aged · personnel, hospital · staphylococcal infections / prevention & control · vancomycin resistance

shelves.title: Enhanced terminal room disinfection: adding UV-C helped; bleach strategies did not clearly (BETR Disinfection)
shelves.question: In hospital rooms vacated by patients infected or colonised with target organisms, do enhanced terminal disinfection strategies (ultraviolet light, bleach, or both) reduce acquisition and infection in the next occupant versus standard quaternary-ammonium disinfection?
shelves.mesh: Disinfection · Ultraviolet Rays · Clostridioides difficile · Methicillin-Resistant Staphylococcus aureus · Humans
shelves.balance: One large pragmatic cluster-randomised crossover trial, nine hospitals, with different answers by strategy. Adding UV-C to standard disinfection reduced the incidence of target-organism infection or colonisation in the next room occupant (33.9 vs 51.3 cases per 10,000 exposure days; relative risk 0.70; 95% CI 0.50 to 0.98; p=0.036). Bleach alone (RR 0.85; 95% CI 0.69 to 1.04; p=0.116) and bleach plus UV-C (RR 0.91; 95% CI 0.76 to 1.09; p=0.303) were not significantly lower, and adding UV to bleach did not change C. difficile infection (RR 1.0; 95% CI 0.57 to 1.75). The UV result is a single significant comparison among several, on a composite dominated by colonisation. PROPOSED SPLIT — POSSIBLE for adding UV-C to standard cleaning; MAYBE (weak evidence) for bleach-based strategies.

cards.headline: BETR 2017: UV added to standard cleaning cut target-organism incidence (RR 0.70 relative); bleach arms not significant
cards.summary: BETR 2017: UV added to standard cleaning cut target-organism incidence (RR 0.70 relative); bleach arms not significant
cards.people: Pragmatic cluster-randomised crossover trial at nine hospitals in the southeastern USA. Rooms vacated by patients with infection or colonisation with a target organism (MRSA, VRE, C. difficile, multidrug-resistant Acinetobacter) were terminally disinfected by one of four strategies in consecutive 7-month periods: reference quaternary-ammonium disinfectant (bleach for C. difficile rooms), UV-C added, bleach, or bleach plus UV-C. 31,226 patients were exposed; 21,395 (69%) met all inclusion criteria. Primary outcome: infection or colonisation with target organisms in the next occupant.
cards.result: Reference incidence was 51.3 cases per 10,000 exposure days (115 events in 22,426 exposure days). Adding UV-C: 33.9 per 10,000 (relative risk 0.70; 95% CI 0.50–0.98; p=0.036). Bleach: 41.6 per 10,000 (RR 0.85; 95% CI 0.69–1.04; p=0.116). Bleach plus UV-C: 45.6 per 10,000 (RR 0.91; 95% CI 0.76–1.09; p=0.303). C. difficile infection with UV added to bleach: RR 1.0 (95% CI 0.57–1.75; p=0.997). All relative risks are relative effects, printed with the absolute rates above.
cards.watchOut: One significant result (UV added) among four strategy comparisons, and the paradoxical bleach-plus-UV arm was null — a pattern that invites caution about chance and about how strategies interacted with room type (bleach was already the reference for C. difficile rooms). Outcomes combine colonisation with infection.
cards.source: Anderson DJ et al. Enhanced terminal room disinfection and acquisition and infection caused by multidrug-resistant organisms and Clostridium difficile (the Benefits of Enhanced Terminal Room Disinfection study): a cluster-randomised, multicentre, crossover study. Lancet. 2017. PMID: 28104287. Registry ID: NCT01579370, from the record. shelves.title: Surveillance plus expanded barrier precautions in the ICU did not reduce MRSA/VRE (STAR*ICU)
shelves.question: In adult ICUs, does active surveillance for MRSA/VRE with expanded barrier precautions reduce colonisation or infection versus existing practice?
shelves.mesh: Methicillin-Resistant Staphylococcus aureus · Vancomycin Resistance · Infection Control · Intensive Care Units · Humans
shelves.balance: A landmark negative cluster-randomised trial. In STAR*ICU, 18 adult ICUs were randomised to surveillance for MRSA/VRE colonisation with results reported and expanded barrier precautions for carriers, or to existing practice (surveillance cultures taken but results not reported). The intervention was delivered — carriers spent a median of 92% of ICU days under barrier precautions versus 38% in control ICUs (P<0.001) — yet the adjusted incidence of MRSA or VRE colonisation or infection was 40.4 versus 35.6 events per 1,000 patient-days at risk (P=0.35), numerically higher in the intervention group. The authors note actual use of precautions by providers was less than required, which is the standing caveat; but as a strategy as implemented, it did not work. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference).

cards.headline: STAR*ICU 2011: precautions delivered (92% vs 38% of carrier days) but incidence 40.4 vs 35.6 per 1,000 patient-days (P=0.35)
cards.summary: STAR*ICU 2011: precautions delivered (92% vs 38% of carrier days) but incidence 40.4 vs 35.6 per 1,000 patient-days (P=0.35)
cards.people: Cluster-randomised trial in 18 adult ICUs; during the 6-month intervention period there were 5,434 admissions to 10 intervention ICUs and 3,705 admissions to 8 control ICUs. Surveillance cultures were obtained in all ICUs; results were reported only to intervention ICUs, where colonised or infected patients were cared for with contact precautions. Primary outcome: incidence of MRSA or VRE colonisation or infection.
cards.result: Patients colonised or infected with MRSA or VRE were assigned barrier precautions for a median of 92% of ICU days in intervention ICUs (51% contact precautions, 43% universal gloving) versus a median of 38% of ICU days in control ICUs (P<0.001). The mean ICU-level incidence of colonisation or infection with MRSA or VRE, adjusted for baseline incidence, was 40.4 (±3.3) per 1,000 patient-days at risk in intervention ICUs versus 35.6 (±3.7) in control ICUs (P=0.35). The authors concluded the intervention was not effective in reducing transmission.
cards.watchOut: The authors' own caveat: observed use of barrier precautions by providers was less than the protocol required, so the trial tests the strategy as implemented, not a perfectly delivered intervention. Colonisation and infection are combined; the trial was not designed to separate clinical infection alone.
cards.source: Huskins WC et al. Intervention to reduce transmission of resistant bacteria in intensive care. N Engl J Med. 2011. PMID: 21488763. Registry ID: NCT00100386, from the record. shelves.title: Copper alloy surfaces in ICU rooms: fewer infections and colonisation in one small trial
shelves.question: In ICU patients, does placement in rooms fitted with copper alloy surfaces on high-touch objects reduce healthcare-acquired infection and MRSA/VRE colonisation versus standard rooms?
shelves.mesh: Copper · Cross Infection · Methicillin-Resistant Staphylococcus aureus · Vancomycin Resistance · Intensive Care Units · Humans
shelves.balance: THIN — one small randomised trial in the ICUs of three hospitals. Patients placed in rooms with copper alloy surfaces on high-touch objects had a lower rate of the composite of healthcare-acquired infection and/or MRSA or VRE colonisation than patients in standard rooms (7.1% vs 12.3% in absolute proportions; P=.020), and a lower rate of healthcare-acquired infection alone (3.4% vs 8.1%; P=.013). The direction is consistent and the mechanism (continuous antimicrobial activity of copper) is plausible, but this is a single trial, in 16 rooms, unblinded by the nature of the intervention, with a composite that includes colonisation. PROPOSED POSSIBLE — promising, not proven; replication in more settings is exactly what the authors called for.

cards.headline: Salgado 2013: HAI and/or MRSA/VRE colonisation 7.1% in copper rooms vs 12.3% in standard rooms (P=.020)
cards.summary: Salgado 2013: HAI and/or MRSA/VRE colonisation 7.1% in copper rooms vs 12.3% in standard rooms (P=.020)
cards.people: Intention-to-treat randomised trial, July 2010 to June 2011, in the ICUs of three hospitals; patients were randomly placed in available rooms with or without copper alloy surfaces on high-touch objects. Outcomes: incident healthcare-acquired infection (HAI) and/or colonisation with MRSA or VRE.
cards.result: The rate of HAI and/or MRSA or VRE colonisation was significantly lower in copper-surfaced rooms than standard rooms (0.071 vs 0.123; P=.020) — absolute proportions 7.1% versus 12.3%. For HAI only, the rate fell from 0.081 to 0.034 (8.1% vs 3.4%; P=.013).
cards.watchOut: THIN: a single trial in three hospitals and few rooms; copper's distinctive appearance means the intervention could not be blinded, so differences in cleaning or hand-hygiene behaviour between room types cannot be excluded. The composite mixes colonisation with clinical infection, and the trial was not powered to show which specific infections copper prevents.
cards.source: Salgado CD et al. Copper surfaces reduce the rate of healthcare-acquired infections in the intensive care unit. Infect Control Hosp Epidemiol. 2013. PMID: 23571364. shelves.title: Hydroxyethyl starch for resuscitation: more kidney failure and dialysis in every large test, and more deaths in sepsis — LIKELY (harm)
shelves.question: In critically ill patients needing fluid resuscitation, does hydroxyethyl starch (HES) increase death or kidney failure versus crystalloid?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Double-Blind Method · Female · Fluid Therapy*/adverse effects, methods · Hemorrhage/chemically induced · Humans · Hydroxyethyl Starch Derivatives/adverse effects, therapeutic use* · Intention to Treat Analysis · Isotonic Solutions/adverse effects, therapeutic use* · Kidney Failure, Chronic/etiology, therapy · Male · Middle Aged · Renal Replacement Therapy · Sepsis/complications, mortality, therapy*
shelves.balance: LIKELY (harm) — two large trials and a 38-trial synthesis converge, and no outcome favours the starch. In severe sepsis, 6% HES 130/0.42 raised 90-day mortality to 51% versus 43% on Ringer's acetate (RR 1.17, 95% CI 1.01 to 1.36) and renal-replacement therapy to 22% versus 16% (Perner 2012, PMID: 22738085). In 7,000 general ICU patients, HES 130/0.4 did not significantly change mortality (18.0% vs 17.0%, RR 1.06, 0.96 to 1.18) but increased renal-replacement therapy (7.0% vs 5.8%, RR 1.21) and adverse events (5.3% vs 2.8%) (Myburgh 2012, PMID: 23075127). Pooling 38 trials, and excluding seven retracted trials whose fraud had flattered HES, mortality RR was 1.09 (1.02 to 1.17), renal failure RR 1.27 (1.09 to 1.47) and renal replacement RR 1.32 (1.15 to 1.50) (Zarychanski 2013, PMID: 23423413). Tier C: a harm shelf turning on mortality and kidney outcomes, flagged for the developer's personal verdict.

cards.headline: Perner 2012 (6S): HES in severe sepsis — 90-day death 51% vs 43% (RR 1.17), renal replacement 22% vs 16%
cards.summary: Perner 2012 (6S): HES in severe sepsis — 90-day death 51% vs 43% (RR 1.17), renal replacement 22% vs 16%
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (Perner 2012, New England Journal of Medicine)
cards.people: Multicentre, parallel-group, blinded randomised trial (6S) in intensive care patients with severe sepsis: 798 patients in the modified intention-to-treat population received fluid resuscitation with 6% hydroxyethyl starch 130/0.42 or Ringer's acetate, up to 33 mL per kilogram of ideal body weight per day. The primary outcome was death or end-stage kidney failure at 90 days.
cards.result: At 90 days, 201 of 398 patients (51%) assigned to HES had died versus 172 of 400 (43%) on Ringer's acetate (relative risk 1.17, 95% CI 1.01 to 1.36; P = 0.03); one patient in each group had end-stage kidney failure. Renal-replacement therapy was given to 22% on HES versus 16% on crystalloid (RR 1.35, 95% CI 1.01 to 1.80), and severe bleeding occurred in 10% versus 6% (RR 1.52, not significant).
cards.watchOut: A sepsis population and one HES formulation (130/0.42): the mortality result is a single trial's, significant but with an interval reaching 1.01. Its weight comes from agreeing with the 7,000-patient trial and the pooled analysis carded alongside it — three designs, one direction.
cards.source: Perner A et al. Hydroxyethyl starch 130/0.42 versus Ringer's acetate in severe sepsis. New England Journal of Medicine. 2012. PMID: 22738085. cards.headline: Myburgh 2012 (CHEST): 7,000 ICU patients — death 18.0% vs 17.0% (RR 1.06, NS), but renal replacement 7.0% vs 5.8% and more adverse events on HES
cards.summary: Myburgh 2012 (CHEST): 7,000 ICU patients — death 18.0% vs 17.0% (RR 1.06, NS), but renal replacement 7.0% vs 5.8% and more adverse events on HES
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (Myburgh 2012, New England Journal of Medicine)
cards.people: Randomised trial (CHEST) of 7,000 patients admitted to intensive care units, assigned to 6% hydroxyethyl starch 130/0.4 in 0.9% sodium chloride or to 0.9% sodium chloride alone for all fluid resuscitation until ICU discharge, death, or 90 days. The primary outcome was death within 90 days.
cards.result: Death occurred in 597 of 3,315 patients (18.0%) on HES versus 566 of 3,336 (17.0%) on saline (relative risk 1.06, 95% CI 0.96 to 1.18; P = 0.26) — no significant mortality difference. Renal-replacement therapy was used in 7.0% versus 5.8% (RR 1.21, 95% CI 1.00 to 1.45; P = 0.04), and adverse events were more frequent with HES (5.3% vs 2.8%, P < 0.001).
cards.watchOut: CHEST's mortality interval (0.96–1.18) does not exclude the harm 6S found — the trials are compatible, and CHEST independently confirms the renal harm. A general ICU population, less sick than 6S's severe-sepsis cohort, is exactly where a smaller absolute harm would be expected.
cards.source: Myburgh JA et al. Hydroxyethyl starch or saline for fluid resuscitation in intensive care. New England Journal of Medicine. 2012. PMID: 23075127. cards.headline: Zarychanski 2013: across 38 trials, excluding the retracted Boldt trials, HES raised mortality (RR 1.09), renal failure (RR 1.27) and renal replacement (RR 1.32)
cards.summary: Zarychanski 2013: across 38 trials, excluding the retracted Boldt trials, HES raised mortality (RR 1.09), renal failure (RR 1.27) and renal replacement (RR 1.32)
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis, 38 RCTs (Zarychanski 2013, JAMA)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 38 randomised trials comparing hydroxyethyl starch with crystalloids, albumin or gelatin in critically ill patients requiring acute volume resuscitation; 10,880 patients contributed mortality data. Seven included trials were by an investigator whose work was later retracted for scientific misconduct, and results are reported with and without them.
cards.result: Including all trials, mortality RR was 1.07 (95% CI 1.00 to 1.14). Excluding the 7 retracted trials (10,290 patients), HES was associated with increased mortality (RR 1.09, 95% CI 1.02 to 1.17; absolute risk increase 1.51%), increased renal failure (RR 1.27, 95% CI 1.09 to 1.47; absolute increase 5.45%) and increased renal-replacement therapy (RR 1.32, 95% CI 1.15 to 1.50; absolute increase 3.12%).
cards.watchOut: Most included trials were at unclear or high risk of bias, and the pooled estimate mixes HES formulations and comparators. Note the direction of the retraction problem: removing the fraudulent trials made HES look worse, not better — the fraud had been flattering the drug.
cards.source: Zarychanski R et al. Association of hydroxyethyl starch administration with mortality and acute kidney injury in critically ill patients requiring volume resuscitation: a systematic review and meta-analysis. JAMA. 2013. PMID: 23423413. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: two large trials and a 38-trial synthesis converge — HES increases kidney failure and renal replacement, and in sepsis increases death — LIKELY (harm)
cards.summary: Synthesis: two large trials and a 38-trial synthesis converge — HES increases kidney failure and renal replacement, and in sepsis increases death — LIKELY (harm)
cards.people: 6S (798 patients with severe sepsis), CHEST (7,000 general ICU patients), and a 38-trial meta-analysis (10,880 patients with mortality data).
cards.result: Death: 51% vs 43% in severe sepsis (RR 1.17, 1.01–1.36); 18.0% vs 17.0% in general ICU patients (RR 1.06, 0.96–1.18); pooled RR 1.09 (1.02–1.17) after excluding retracted trials. Renal replacement: 22% vs 16% (6S), 7.0% vs 5.8% (CHEST), pooled RR 1.32 (1.15–1.50). Renal failure pooled RR 1.27 (1.09–1.47). No carded outcome favours HES.
cards.watchOut: These trials tested tetrastarches (130/0.4 and 130/0.42) for ICU resuscitation; older high-molecular-weight starches and elective-surgery use are outside the carded record, though nothing in it suggests a safer niche. Regulatory restrictions that followed these trials are context, not evidence, and are not carded.

shelves.title: MERINO: the carbapenem-sparing shortcut cost lives — piperacillin-tazobactam mortality 12.3% versus 3.7% on meropenem in resistant bloodstream infection
shelves.question: In patients with ceftriaxone-resistant Escherichia coli or Klebsiella pneumoniae bloodstream infection, is piperacillin-tazobactam non-inferior to meropenem for 30-day mortality?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Anti-Bacterial Agents/adverse effects/pharmacology/therapeutic use* · Bacteremia/drug therapy/mortality* · Cause of Death · Ceftriaxone/pharmacology · Drug Resistance, Bacterial · Escherichia coli/drug effects · Escherichia coli Infections/drug therapy*/mortality · Female · Humans · Klebsiella Infections/drug therapy*/mortality · Klebsiella pneumoniae*/drug effects · Male · Meropenem · Middle Aged · Penicillanic Acid/adverse effects/analogs & derivatives*/therapeutic use · Piperacillin/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Piperacillin, Tazobactam Drug Combination · Thienamycins/adverse effects/therapeutic use*
shelves.balance: LIKELY (harm) — the carbapenem-sparing idea failed its fairest test. MERINO (Harris PNA et al., PMID: 30208454) randomised 379 patients with ceftriaxone-resistant Escherichia coli or Klebsiella pneumoniae bloodstream infection — organisms susceptible to both study drugs — and piperacillin-tazobactam did not come close to non-inferiority: 30-day mortality was 12.3% (23/187) versus 3.7% (7/191) on meropenem, a risk difference of 8.6 percentage points against a 5-point margin (P=.90 for non-inferiority). The later meta-analysis (Gatti M et al., PMID: 39173739), pooling MERINO with nine retrospective studies (1,962 patients), found a smaller, non-significant mortality difference overall (OR 1.41, 95% CI 0.96 to 2.07) but a significantly higher mortality with piperacillin-tazobactam where fewer than half the infections came from urinary or biliary sources (OR 2.02, 95% CI 1.00 to 4.07) — observational softening of a randomised signal, not a refutation of it. PROPOSED LIKELY (harm): for ceftriaxone-resistant E. coli or K. pneumoniae bloodstream infection, definitive piperacillin-tazobactam carries a mortality price the randomised trial measured and the pooled literature does not erase.

cards.headline: MERINO 2018: piperacillin-tazobactam failed non-inferiority — 30-day mortality 12.3% vs 3.7% on meropenem (risk difference 8.6 points)
cards.summary: MERINO 2018: piperacillin-tazobactam failed non-inferiority — 30-day mortality 12.3% vs 3.7% on meropenem (risk difference 8.6 points)
cards.type: Randomised non-inferiority trial, 26 sites, 9 countries (MERINO, Harris 2018)
cards.people: 379 hospitalised adults (mean age 66.5 years, 47.8% women) at 26 sites in 9 countries (February 2014 to July 2017) with at least one blood culture growing Escherichia coli or Klebsiella species non-susceptible to ceftriaxone but susceptible to piperacillin-tazobactam, randomised to intravenous piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g every 6 hours (188 assigned, 187 in the primary analysis) or meropenem 1 g every 8 hours (191), for 4 to 14 days as the treating clinician decided; 1,646 patients were screened to enrol 391.
cards.result: All-cause mortality at 30 days was 12.3% (23/187) with piperacillin-tazobactam versus 3.7% (7/191) with meropenem — risk difference 8.6% (1-sided 97.5% CI, −∞ to 14.5%); P=.90 for non-inferiority against the 5% margin, so non-inferiority was not shown. Results were consistent in the per-protocol population. Nonfatal serious adverse events occurred in 2.7% (5/188) versus 1.6% (3/191). The authors conclude the findings do not support piperacillin-tazobactam in this setting.
cards.watchOut: The trial tested definitive therapy for bloodstream infection with organisms proven susceptible to piperacillin-tazobactam in the laboratory — the result should not be stretched to urinary infections without bacteraemia, to empirical therapy before susceptibilities return, or to higher-dose/continuous-infusion strategies the trial did not use. But within its ground — bacteraemia, ceftriaxone resistance — the mortality gap is the finding, and 'susceptible on the report' did not protect patients.
cards.source: Harris PNA et al. Effect of Piperacillin-Tazobactam vs Meropenem on 30-Day Mortality for Patients With E coli or Klebsiella pneumoniae Bloodstream Infection and Ceftriaxone Resistance: A Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA. 2018. PMID: 30208454. Registry ID: NCT02176122. cards.headline: Gatti 2024 meta-analysis: pooled mortality difference was not significant overall (OR 1.41) — but was significant where the source was not urinary or biliary (OR 2.02)
cards.summary: Gatti 2024 meta-analysis: pooled mortality difference was not significant overall (OR 1.41) — but was significant where the source was not urinary or biliary (OR 2.02)
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis, 1 RCT + 9 observational studies (Gatti 2024)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 10 studies (1 randomised trial — MERINO — and 9 retrospective observational studies; 1,962 hospitalised patients in total) comparing piperacillin-tazobactam with carbapenems for bloodstream infection due to extended-spectrum beta-lactamase-producing Enterobacterales, searched to 17 January 2024, pooling adjusted odds ratios for mortality.
cards.result: Mortality did not differ significantly overall (6 studies; OR 1.41, 95% CI 0.96 to 2.07; I²=23.6%), nor in the empirical-therapy subgroup (OR 1.36, 95% CI 0.99 to 1.85) or where at least 50% of infections had a urinary or biliary source (OR 1.26, 95% CI 0.84 to 1.89). Where fewer than 50% had a urinary/biliary source, mortality was significantly higher with piperacillin-tazobactam (OR 2.02, 95% CI 1.00 to 4.07). The authors conclude adjusted mortality and clinical outcomes did not significantly differ overall.
cards.watchOut: Nine of the ten pooled studies are retrospective, and clinicians choosing piperacillin-tazobactam outside a trial tend to choose it for lower-risk patients — confounding by indication that adjustment can only partly remove, and exactly the bias randomisation exists to defeat. Read this card as 'the observational literature is softer than MERINO', not as 'MERINO was wrong': the one randomised study inside the pool is the one with the clear mortality gap.
cards.source: Gatti M et al. Piperacillin-tazobactam vs. carbapenems for treating hospitalized patients with ESBL-producing Enterobacterales bloodstream infections: A systematic review and meta-analysis. cards.headline: Synthesis: the randomised trial says meropenem saves lives here; the observational pool blurs but does not reverse that — source of infection may be the moderator
cards.summary: Synthesis: the randomised trial says meropenem saves lives here; the observational pool blurs but does not reverse that — source of infection may be the moderator
cards.people: One multinational randomised trial (379 patients) of definitive therapy for ceftriaxone-resistant E. coli or K. pneumoniae bacteraemia, plus a 10-study meta-analysis (1,962 patients, 9 of them observational) of piperacillin-tazobactam versus carbapenems for ESBL bloodstream infection.
cards.result: Randomised: 30-day mortality 12.3% vs 3.7% (risk difference 8.6 points; non-inferiority not shown). Pooled adjusted: OR 1.41 (95% CI 0.96 to 2.07) overall; OR 2.02 (1.00 to 4.07) where urinary/biliary sources were under half; OR 1.26 (0.84 to 1.89) where they predominated. PROPOSED LIKELY (harm) for piperacillin-tazobactam as definitive bacteraemia therapy in this resistance pattern.
cards.watchOut: The urinary/biliary-source subgroup pattern is hypothesis-generating — it comes from study-level proportions in observational data, not from randomised strata. It should not be used to license piperacillin-tazobactam for urinary-source bacteraemia as if proven safe; MERINO's own population included such patients and still lost. Tier C is set because the randomised base is a single trial.
cards.source: Synthesis of Harris PNA et al. JAMA. 2018 (PMID: 30208454); Gatti M et al. Journal of Global Antimicrobial Resistance. 2024 (PMID: 39173739).

shelves.question: In patients with carbapenem-resistant Gram-negative infections, is meropenem-vaborbactam superior to best available therapy for clinical cure and mortality?
shelves.mesh: none in the record
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — TANGO II (Wunderink RG et al., PMID: 30270406) randomised just 77 patients with confirmed or suspected carbapenem-resistant Enterobacteriaceae infection, and only 47 with confirmed CRE formed the primary population — yet the direction was consistent across endpoints: clinical cure at end of treatment 65.6% (21/32) versus 33.3% (5/15) on best available therapy, day-28 mortality 15.6% versus 33.3%, and fewer renal adverse events (4.0% vs 24.0%). A 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis of novel beta-lactam/beta-lactamase inhibitors versus best available therapy (Al Shammari et al., PMID: 42792078; 9 studies, 2,892 patients) found a 27% relative reduction in mortality (pooled RR 0.73, 95% CI 0.59 to 0.90), with meropenem-vaborbactam the most effective agent against KPC-producing strains (RR 0.65, 95% CI 0.49 to 0.94) and no combination effective against metallo-beta-lactamase producers. Small numbers, an open-label design, a heterogeneous comparator and a trial that stopped short of its ambitions keep this at possible, not likely. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): meropenem-vaborbactam probably improves cure and spares kidneys in CRE infection, with the mortality advantage plausible but not proven by the trial alone.

cards.headline: TANGO II 2018: clinical cure doubled versus best available therapy (65.6% vs 33.3%) and day-28 mortality halved (15.6% vs 33.3%) — in only 47 confirmed-CRE patients
cards.summary: TANGO II 2018: clinical cure doubled versus best available therapy (65.6% vs 33.3%) and day-28 mortality halved (15.6% vs 33.3%) — in only 47 confirmed-CRE patients
cards.type: Phase 3, multinational, open-label randomised trial (TANGO II, Wunderink 2018)
cards.people: 77 patients with confirmed or suspected carbapenem-resistant Enterobacteriaceae infection (bacteraemia, hospital-acquired/ventilator-associated pneumonia, complicated intra-abdominal infection, or complicated urinary tract infection/acute pyelonephritis) randomised 2:1 from 2014 to 2017 to meropenem-vaborbactam 2 g/2 g over 3 hours every 8 hours for 7–14 days (50 treated) or best available therapy (25 treated) — mono- or combination therapy with polymyxins, carbapenems, aminoglycosides, tigecycline, or ceftazidime-avibactam alone. The primary analysis population (microbiologic-CRE-modified intention-to-treat) held 47 patients: 32 versus 15.
cards.result: Clinical cure was 65.6% (21/32) versus 33.3% (5/15) at end of treatment (difference 95% CI 3.3% to 61.3%; P=0.03) and 59.4% (19/32) versus 26.7% (4/15) at test of cure (95% CI 4.6% to 60.8%; P=0.02). Day-28 all-cause mortality was 15.6% (5/32) versus 33.3% (5/15) (95% CI of difference −44.7% to 9.3%). Treatment-related adverse events were 24.0% (12/50) versus 44.0% (11/25), and renal-related adverse events 4.0% (2/50) versus 24.0% (6/25). A composite of clinical failure or nephrotoxicity favoured meropenem-vaborbactam: 31.3% (10/32) versus 80.0% (12/15) (P<0.001).
cards.watchOut: Forty-seven patients in the primary population, wide confidence intervals (the mortality difference's interval runs from −44.7% to +9.3%), an open-label design, and a comparator that is a mixture of older, more toxic regimens chosen case by case — the trial can show the new drug beat a difficult grab-bag, not that it beats any specific modern alternative such as ceftazidime-avibactam, which appears inside the comparator arm. Enrolment stopped at 77 randomised patients, far short of a mortality-powered trial.
cards.source: Wunderink RG et al. Effect and Safety of Meropenem-Vaborbactam versus Best-Available Therapy in Patients with Carbapenem-Resistant Enterobacteriaceae Infections: The TANGO II Randomized Clinical Trial. Infectious Diseases and Therapy. 2018. PMID: 30270406. Registry ID: NCT02168946. MeSH: none in the record

cards.headline: Al Shammari 2026 meta-analysis: novel beta-lactam combinations cut mortality by 27% relative versus best available therapy (RR 0.73) — driven by KPC producers, absent in metallo-beta-lactamase producers
cards.summary: Al Shammari 2026 meta-analysis: novel beta-lactam combinations cut mortality by 27% relative versus best available therapy (RR 0.73) — driven by KPC producers, absent in metallo-beta-lactamase producers
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis, 6 RCTs + 3 cohorts (Al Shammari 2026)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 9 primary studies (6 randomised trials and 3 observational cohorts; 2,892 hospitalised adults with carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales infection) comparing the novel combinations ceftazidime-avibactam, meropenem-vaborbactam and imipenem-cilastatin-relebactam with best available therapy, with all-cause mortality as the outcome, searched to December 2025.
cards.result: Novel combinations reduced mortality by 27% relative (pooled RR 0.73, 95% CI 0.59 to 0.90; P=0.003; I²=38%) — a relative measure; the review does not print a single pooled absolute mortality pair. By carbapenemase type, meropenem-vaborbactam was most effective against Klebsiella pneumoniae carbapenemase (KPC) producers (RR 0.65, 95% CI 0.49 to 0.94) and ceftazidime-avibactam superior for OXA-48-like producers (RR 0.55, 95% CI 0.41 to 0.82); no combination showed efficacy against metallo-beta-lactamase producers. The proportion of KPC-producing isolates predicted effect size on meta-regression (coefficient −0.42, 95% CI −0.68 to −0.16; P=0.002), and funnel-plot asymmetry suggested possible publication bias (Egger's test P=0.09).
cards.watchOut: This pools three different drugs, randomised and observational evidence, and comparators that vary by study — the class-level RR 0.73 must not be quoted as meropenem-vaborbactam's own mortality effect, and the drug-by-enzyme pattern (KPC yes, metallo-beta-lactamase no) is the clinically usable part. Possible publication bias was flagged by the reviewers themselves. An earlier meta-analysis on this exact comparison was retracted and is deliberately not carded here.
cards.source: Al Shammari et al. Novel β-Lactam/β-Lactamase Inhibitors Versus Best Available Therapy on the Mortality-Related Carbapenem-Resistant Enterobacterales Infection: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Antibiotics (Basel, Switzerland). 2026. PMID: 42792078. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: none in the record

cards.headline: Synthesis: a very small trial and a class-level meta-analysis point the same way — benefit concentrated in KPC-type resistance, with a kidney-sparing edge over older regimens
cards.summary: Synthesis: a very small trial and a class-level meta-analysis point the same way — benefit concentrated in KPC-type resistance, with a kidney-sparing edge over older regimens
cards.people: One open-label randomised trial (77 randomised, 47 with confirmed CRE in the primary population) of meropenem-vaborbactam versus best available therapy, plus a 9-study meta-analysis (2,892 patients) of novel beta-lactam/beta-lactamase inhibitor combinations versus best available therapy.
cards.result: Trial: cure 65.6% vs 33.3% at end of treatment; day-28 mortality 15.6% vs 33.3%; renal adverse events 4.0% vs 24.0%. Pooled class effect: mortality RR 0.73 (95% CI 0.59 to 0.90), a 27% relative reduction; meropenem-vaborbactam against KPC producers RR 0.65 (0.49 to 0.94); no efficacy against metallo-beta-lactamase producers. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: Everything on this shelf is mechanism-conditional: the benefit story holds for KPC-type carbapenem resistance and collapses for metallo-beta-lactamase producers, so the organism's enzyme — not the drug's novelty — is the deciding fact, and rapid carbapenemase typing matters more than the brand of combination. Tier C is set because the anchor trial is single, small and stopped short.
cards.source: Synthesis of Wunderink RG et al. Infectious Diseases and Therapy. 2018 (PMID: 30270406); Al Shammari et al. Antibiotics (Basel, Switzerland). 2026 (PMID: 42792078).

shelves.title: Treating sick young infants when hospital referral is impossible: all three simplified regimens matched the standard injections on treatment failure (5–8% across arms) in a 3,564-infant equivalence trial
shelves.question: In young infants with possible serious bacterial infection whose families cannot accept hospital referral, do simplified oral/injectable antibiotic regimens match the standard injectable procaine benzylpenicillin plus gentamicin regimen?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Amoxicillin/therapeutic use · Anorexia/etiology · Anti-Bacterial Agents/therapeutic use · Bacterial Infections/complications · Democratic Republic of the Congo · Female · Fever/etiology · Gentamicins/therapeutic use · Humans · Infant · Infant, Newborn · Injections, Intramuscular · Kenya · Lethargy/etiology · Male · Nigeria · Penicillin G Procaine/therapeutic use · Referral and Consultation* · Single-Blind Method · Therapeutic Equivalency · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) — AFRINEST (Tshefu A et al., PMID: 25842221) randomised 3,564 young infants aged 0 to 59 days with clinical signs of severe infection, whose families did not accept hospital referral, across sites in DR Congo, Kenya and Nigeria, to the standard regimen (injectable procaine benzylpenicillin plus gentamicin for 7 days) or one of three simplified regimens: gentamicin injections plus oral amoxicillin for 7 days; 2 days of the standard injections then oral amoxicillin for 5 days; or 2 days of gentamicin injections plus oral amoxicillin for 7 days. In the per-protocol analysis, treatment failure by day 8 was 8 percent on the standard regimen versus 6 percent (risk difference −1.9 percent, 95% CI −4.4 to 0.1), 8 percent (−0.6 percent, −3.1 to 2.0), and 5 percent (−2.7 percent, −5.1 to 0.3) on the three simplified regimens — all within the prespecified 5 percent similarity margin. Deaths within 15 days were 1 to 2 percent across arms. The pooled analysis of the three African and Asian trials (Longombe AL et al., PMID: 36403158; 7,617 infants) went further: the oral amoxicillin plus gentamicin regimen had a lower risk of poor clinical outcome than the standard regimen (per-protocol risk difference −2.1 percent, 95% CI −3.8 to −0.4; P=0.016), and the switch regimen did not increase poor outcomes (−1.1 percent, −2.8 to 0.6). These results apply only where referral is genuinely not possible — hospital care remains the standard when it can be had. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): simplified regimens, including one built on oral amoxicillin, are a proven fallback that should not be withheld when the alternative is no treatment. Tier C is not set — a large equivalence trial plus a consistent pooled analysis is above the weak tier.

cards.headline: AFRINEST 2015: treatment failure 8% on standard injections versus 6%, 8% and 5% on the three simplified regimens — all within the 5% equivalence margin; deaths 1–2% in every arm
cards.summary: AFRINEST 2015: treatment failure 8% on standard injections versus 6%, 8% and 5% on the three simplified regimens — all within the 5% equivalence margin; deaths 1–2% in every arm
cards.people: 3,564 young infants aged 0 to 59 days with clinical signs of severe infection (possible serious bacterial infection) in DR Congo, Kenya and Nigeria, whose parents did not accept referral to hospital; community health workers identified unwell infants at home visits and a study nurse enrolled them, stratified by age (0–6 days and 7–59 days). Arms: A, injectable procaine benzylpenicillin plus gentamicin for 7 days (894); B, injectable gentamicin plus oral amoxicillin for 7 days (884); C, procaine benzylpenicillin plus gentamicin for 2 days then oral amoxicillin for 5 days (896); D, gentamicin for 2 days plus oral amoxicillin for 7 days (890). The per-protocol analysis included 828, 826, 862 and 848 infants respectively.
cards.result: Treatment failure by day 8 (clinical deterioration, a serious adverse event including death, no improvement by day 4, or not cured by day 8) occurred in 67 infants (8 percent) in group A, versus 51 (6 percent) in group B (risk difference −1.9 percent, 95% CI −4.4 to 0.1), 65 (8 percent) in group C (−0.6 percent, −3.1 to 2.0), and 46 (5 percent) in group D (−2.7 percent, −5.1 to 0.3) — all within the prespecified 5 percent similarity margin. During the 15 days after allocation, deaths were 12 (1 percent) in group A, 10 (1 percent) in group B, 20 (2 percent) in group C, and 11 (1 percent) in group D. One infant in group A had a serious adverse event other than death (injection abscess).
cards.watchOut: Equivalence within a 5 percent margin on an 8 percent failure rate is a generous bound, the primary analysis is per-protocol (200 randomised infants were excluded for adherence or follow-up criteria), and the trial was open-label with masked outcome assessors. The population is defined by refused referral — these results license simplified treatment when hospital care cannot be obtained, not as a substitute where it can. Group C's numerically higher deaths (20 versus 12) sit within chance but are worth noticing.
cards.source: Tshefu A et al. Simplified antibiotic regimens compared with injectable procaine benzylpenicillin plus gentamicin for treatment of neonates and young infants with clinical signs of possible serious bacterial infection when referral is not possible: a randomised, open-label, equivalence trial. The Lancet. 2015. PMID: 25842221. Registry ID: ACTRN12610000286044. cards.headline: Longombe 2022 (pooled analysis, 3 trials, 7,617 infants): oral amoxicillin plus gentamicin had FEWER poor outcomes than the standard regimen (risk difference −2.1 percent, 95% CI −3.8 to −0.4; P=0.016)
cards.summary: Longombe 2022 (pooled analysis, 3 trials, 7,617 infants): oral amoxicillin plus gentamicin had FEWER poor outcomes than the standard regimen (risk difference −2.1 percent, 95% CI −3.8 to −0.4; P=0.016)
cards.type: Pooled analysis of three randomised trials (Longombe 2022)
cards.people: 7,617 young infants aged 0 to 59 days with any sign of possible serious bacterial infection (fever, hypothermia, stopped feeding well, movement only when stimulated, or severe chest indrawing) enrolled across three individually randomised trials in Africa and Asia whose caretakers refused hospital admission; 71 percent were 7 to 59 days old and 56 percent were male; severe chest indrawing (45 percent), fever (43 percent) and feeding problems (25 percent) were the commonest signs.
cards.result: Poor clinical outcome by day 15 (death to day 15, treatment failure by day 8, or relapse between days 9 and 15) was lower with the oral amoxicillin plus gentamicin regimen (arm B) than with the standard procaine benzylpenicillin plus gentamicin regimen (arm A): per-protocol risk difference −2.1 percent (95% CI −3.8 to −0.4; P=0.016) and intention-to-treat −1.8 percent (−3.5 to −0.2; P=0.031). The switch regimen (arm C: standard injections then oral amoxicillin) did not increase poor outcomes (per-protocol risk difference −1.1 percent, 95% CI −2.8 to 0.6).
cards.watchOut: A pooled analysis of trials with differing sign-based eligibility and local care systems; the 'superiority' signal for arm B (−2.1 percent) is small in absolute terms and emerges from pooling rather than from any single trial's primary result. It strengthens confidence in equivalence — its proper use — more than it proves the oral regimen is genuinely better.
cards.source: Longombe AL et al. Oral amoxicillin plus gentamicin regimens may be superior to the procaine-penicillin plus gentamicin regimens for treatment of young infants with possible serious bacterial infection when referral is not feasible: Pooled analysis from three trials in Africa and Asia. Journal of Global Health. 2022. PMID: 36403158. Registry ID: NCT00844337, NCT01027429. cards.headline: Synthesis: simplified regimens are equivalent where referral fails, across 3,564 randomised infants and 7,617 pooled — the evidence supports treating, not withholding
cards.summary: Synthesis: simplified regimens are equivalent where referral fails, across 3,564 randomised infants and 7,617 pooled — the evidence supports treating, not withholding
cards.people: One multisite equivalence trial of 3,564 young infants in three African countries (AFRINEST 2015) plus a pooled analysis of three African and Asian trials totalling 7,617 infants (Longombe 2022).
cards.result: Treatment failure by day 8: 8 percent (standard) versus 6 percent, 8 percent and 5 percent (simplified regimens), all within the 5 percent similarity margin; deaths 1–2 percent across arms. Pooled poor outcome: oral amoxicillin plus gentamicin −2.1 percent (95% CI −3.8 to −0.4) versus standard; switch regimen −1.1 percent (−2.8 to 0.6). PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit).
cards.watchOut: The entire shelf is conditional on its setting: families who could not accept referral, community health worker case-finding, and daily professional visits for injections and first oral doses. Signs-based diagnosis without microbiology also means some treated infants had viral or self-limiting illness, which flatters all arms equally.
