shelves.title: Prophylactic platelet transfusion in dengue: bleeding in 21% transfused versus 26% on supportive care alone (not significant) — with 13 adverse events versus 2, including anaphylaxis and transfusion-related lung injury
shelves.question: In adults with dengue and thrombocytopenia without bleeding, does prophylactic platelet transfusion prevent bleeding versus supportive care alone?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Dengue/complications · Equivalence Trials as Topic · Female · Hemorrhage/etiology · Humans · Malaysia · Male · Middle Aged · Platelet Transfusion* · Singapore · Thrombocytopenia/complications · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (harm) — the randomised trial (Lye DC et al., PMID: 28283286) assigned 372 adults with laboratory-confirmed dengue and platelet counts of 20,000 per microliter or lower, without severe bleeding, at five hospitals in Singapore and Malaysia to prophylactic platelet transfusion (4 units of pooled platelets each day the count was 20,000 or lower) plus supportive care, or supportive care alone. Clinical bleeding by day 7 or discharge occurred in 40 of 187 patients (21 percent) in the transfusion group and 48 of 182 (26 percent) in the control group (risk difference −4.98 percent, 95% CI −15.08 to 5.34; relative risk 0.81, 95% CI 0.56 to 1.17; p=0.16) — no significant benefit, with an interval that still allows a moderate benefit or a small harm on bleeding itself. The harm side is clearer: 13 adverse events occurred in the transfusion group versus 2 in the control group (p=0.0064), including urticaria, rash, pruritus and chest pain, and one case each of anaphylaxis, transfusion-related acute lung injury and fluid overload as serious events; no deaths occurred in either group. The systematic review of interventions for dengue bleeding (Rajapakse S et al., PMID: 29385613; 11 studies, 1,904 patients) found no evidence that platelet transfusion or any other assessed intervention prevents or treats clinically significant bleeding in dengue. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm): routine prophylactic transfusion at a platelet threshold spends a scarce blood product and exposes patients to real transfusion risks without demonstrated protection — reserve platelets for clinically significant bleeding. Tier C is set because the randomised base is a single open-label trial.

cards.headline: Lye 2017: clinical bleeding in 40/187 (21%) with prophylactic transfusion versus 48/182 (26%) with supportive care alone (relative risk 0.81, 95% CI 0.56 to 1.17; p=0.16); adverse events 13 versus 2 (p=0.0064)
cards.summary: Lye 2017: clinical bleeding in 40/187 (21%) with prophylactic transfusion versus 48/182 (26%) with supportive care alone (relative risk 0.81, 95% CI 0.56 to 1.17; p=0.16); adverse events 13 versus 2 (p=0.0064)
cards.people: 372 adults aged at least 21 years with laboratory-confirmed dengue (confirmed or probable) and thrombocytopenia (platelet count 20,000 per microliter or lower), without persistent mild bleeding or any severe bleeding, at five hospitals in Singapore and Malaysia; 188 were assigned to transfusion and 184 to control, with the intention-to-treat analysis including 187 and 182 respectively. The transfusion group received 4 units of pooled platelets each day the platelet count was 20,000 per microliter or lower; supportive care in both groups was bed rest, fluid therapy, and fever and pain medications.
cards.result: Clinical bleeding (excluding petechiae) by study day 7 or hospital discharge occurred in 40 patients (21 percent) in the transfusion group and 48 (26 percent) in the control group (risk difference −4.98 percent, 95% CI −15.08 to 5.34; relative risk 0.81, 95% CI 0.56 to 1.17; p=0.16). Thirteen adverse events occurred in the transfusion group and two in the control group (risk difference 5.81 percent, −4.42 to 16.01; relative risk 6.26, 1.43 to 27.34; p=0.0064). Transfusion-related events included three cases of urticaria, one maculopapular rash, one pruritus and one chest pain, plus one case each of anaphylaxis, transfusion-related acute lung injury, and fluid overload resulting in serious adverse events. No death was reported in either group.
cards.watchOut: Open-label, and the bleeding interval (−15.08 to +5.34 percentage points) cannot exclude a clinically meaningful reduction in bleeding — 'not superior' is not 'proven useless'. Patients with existing severe bleeding were excluded, so this shelf governs prophylaxis only; therapeutic transfusion for significant bleeding is a separate, untested-here question. Event rates reflect Singaporean and Malaysian hospital care and dengue serotypes of 2010–2014.

cards.headline: Rajapakse 2017 (systematic review, 11 studies, 1,904 patients): no evidence that platelet transfusion — or plasma, factor VIIa, anti-D, immunoglobulin or interleukin-11 — prevents or treats clinically significant dengue bleeding
cards.summary: Rajapakse 2017 (systematic review, 11 studies, 1,904 patients): no evidence that platelet transfusion — or plasma, factor VIIa, anti-D, immunoglobulin or interleukin-11 — prevents or treats clinically significant dengue bleeding
cards.people: Eleven studies including 1,904 patients in 12 study arms, covering platelet transfusion (two randomised trials and three non-randomised studies), plasma transfusion (one RCT), recombinant activated factor VII (one RCT), anti-D globulin (two RCTs), immunoglobulin (one RCT) and interleukin-11 (one RCT) as prevention or treatment for bleeding in dengue infection.
cards.result: Due to significant heterogeneity in study design and outcome reporting, no meta-analysis was performed. The reviewers conclude that currently there is no evidence that any of the above interventions would have a beneficial effect in preventing or treating clinically significant bleeding in dengue. The review's context: global dengue incidence rose sevenfold between 1990 and 2013, case fatality is under 1 percent, and the risk of clinically significant bleeding is unpredictable.
cards.watchOut: 'No evidence of benefit' across small heterogeneous studies is a statement about the literature, not proof of no effect for every intervention in every subgroup — but for platelet transfusion it aligns with the largest trial's own null result and adverse-event excess, which is the combination this shelf's stamp rests on.

shelves.title: Vasopressin first after heart surgery: one double-blind trial cut death-or-major-complications from 49% to 32% — but the pooled mortality record is still silent
shelves.question: In adults with vasoplegic shock after cardiac surgery, does vasopressin reduce mortality and vasopressor duration compared with norepinephrine as the first-line vasopressor?
shelves.mesh: Brazil · Cardiac Surgical Procedures* · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Norepinephrine/pharmacology · Postoperative Complications/drug therapy · Prospective Studies · Shock/complications · Shock/drug therapy · Treatment Outcome · Vasoconstrictor Agents/pharmacology · Vasoplegia/complications · Vasoplegia/drug therapy · Vasopressins/pharmacology
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one well-conducted double-blind trial drives this shelf. In VANCS (Hajjar LA et al., PMID: 27841822), 300 patients with post-cardiotomy vasoplegic shock randomised to vasopressin or norepinephrine had a primary composite of death or severe complications in 32% versus 49% (hazard ratio 0.55, 95% CI 0.38 to 0.80), with much less atrial fibrillation on vasopressin (63.8% vs 82.1%) and no excess digital or mesenteric ischaemia, hyponatraemia, or myocardial infarction. The wider literature is less decisive: a 2023 systematic review and meta-analysis of ten studies (Szeles TF et al., PMID: 38055405) found no significant mortality difference between vasopressin and norepinephrine (odds ratio 1.60, 95% CI 0.47 to 5.50) and no significant difference in hospital stay, while judging vasopressin safe in postoperative vasoplegic shock. The question as asked — mortality and vasopressor duration head-to-head — is only partly answered: VANCS reports the composite and complications, not a mortality-only or duration-only win. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): vasopressin is a reasonable first-line choice in post-cardiotomy vasoplegia on one positive trial, but the pooled record does not confirm a mortality advantage, and a second large trial is still owed.

cards.headline: VANCS 2017: vasopressin first-line after cardiac surgery — death-or-severe-complication composite 32% vs 49% on norepinephrine (HR 0.55), and atrial fibrillation 63.8% vs 82.1%
cards.summary: VANCS 2017: vasopressin first-line after cardiac surgery — death-or-severe-complication composite 32% vs 49% on norepinephrine (HR 0.55), and atrial fibrillation 63.8% vs 82.1%
cards.people: 300 adults with vasoplegic shock after cardiac surgery (mean arterial pressure below 65 mmHg despite fluids, cardiac index above 2.2 l·min·m) at a single Brazilian heart institute, randomised double-blind to vasopressin 0.01–0.06 U/min (n=149) or norepinephrine 10–60 µg/min (n=151), January 2012 to March 2014; 330 were randomised and 300 received a study drug.
cards.result: The primary endpoint — a composite of mortality or severe complications (stroke, ventilation longer than 48 hours, deep sternal wound infection, reoperation, or acute renal failure) within 30 days — occurred in 32% of the vasopressin group and 49% of the norepinephrine group (unadjusted hazard ratio 0.55, 95% CI 0.38 to 0.80; P=0.0014). Atrial fibrillation was less common with vasopressin (63.8% vs 82.1%; P=0.0004). There was no difference in digital ischaemia, mesenteric ischaemia, hyponatraemia, or myocardial infarction.
cards.watchOut: A single-centre trial, and the headline is a composite: the abstract does not separate mortality from the complication components, so this shelf cannot claim a mortality-only benefit. The very high atrial fibrillation rates in both arms reflect the post-cardiotomy population, not a general ICU one.
cards.source: Hajjar LA et al. Vasopressin versus Norepinephrine in Patients with Vasoplegic Shock after Cardiac Surgery: The VANCS Randomized Controlled Trial. Anesthesiology. 2017. PMID: 27841822. cards.headline: Szeles 2023 (systematic review and meta-analysis, 10 studies): no significant mortality difference for vasopressin vs norepinephrine (OR 1.60, 95% CI 0.47 to 5.50) — vasopressin judged safe, not proven superior
cards.summary: Szeles 2023 (systematic review and meta-analysis, 10 studies): no significant mortality difference for vasopressin vs norepinephrine (OR 1.60, 95% CI 0.47 to 5.50) — vasopressin judged safe, not proven superior
cards.people: Ten studies of vasopressin in postoperative vasoplegic shock in surgical patients, selected from 2,090 retrieved articles (searches to December 2022), comparing vasopressin with norepinephrine and with placebo.
cards.result: There was no significant difference in mortality comparing vasopressin versus norepinephrine (odds ratio 1.60, 95% CI 0.47 to 5.50), nor comparing vasopressin versus placebo. Hospital length of stay was shorter in cases that used vasopressin, but the meta-analysis did not demonstrate statistical significance for that outcome either. The reviewers conclude that most studies showed vasopressin was safe and can be considered in managing postoperative vasoplegic shock.
cards.watchOut: The pooled mortality estimate is extremely imprecise (confidence interval 0.47 to 5.50) and mixes smaller, heterogeneous studies with VANCS — it tempers the single trial's composite win without refuting it. Most included studies were not powered for mortality at all.
cards.source: Szeles TF et al. Vasopressin in vasoplegic shock in surgical patients: systematic review and meta-analysis. Acta Cirurgica Brasileira. 2023. PMID: 38055405. cards.summary: Synthesis: one positive double-blind trial on a composite endpoint; the pooled mortality record is null and very imprecise
cards.people: One 300-patient double-blind RCT (VANCS) plus a ten-study systematic review and meta-analysis of vasopressin in surgical vasoplegic shock.
cards.result: Composite of death or severe complications at 30 days: 32% vs 49% favouring vasopressin (HR 0.55, 95% CI 0.38 to 0.80). Atrial fibrillation: 63.8% vs 82.1% favouring vasopressin. Pooled mortality across ten studies: odds ratio 1.60 (95% CI 0.47 to 5.50), not significant. Ischaemic and metabolic harms: no excess shown in VANCS. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: Do not quote VANCS as a mortality trial — its separation is on a composite driven in part by complications, in one centre, in post-cardiotomy patients only. Nothing here answers vasoplegia after non-cardiac surgery or vasopressin as an add-on rather than first-line. Tier C is set because the confirmatory evidence is a single trial.

shelves.title: More blood thinner in ICU COVID-19: INSPIRATION found identical outcomes at 30 days (45.7% vs 44.1%) — pooled data trade fewer lung clots for more bleeding
shelves.question: In critically ill adults with COVID-19, does intermediate-dose prophylactic anticoagulation reduce thrombotic events, need for organ support, or mortality compared with standard-dose prophylaxis?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Anticoagulants/administration & dosage · Anticoagulants/adverse effects · COVID-19/complications · COVID-19/mortality · Drug Administration Schedule · Enoxaparin/administration & dosage · Enoxaparin/adverse effects · Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation* · Female · Hemorrhage/chemically induced · Hospitalization · Humans · Intensive Care Units · Iran · Length of Stay/statistics & numerical data · Male · Middle Aged · Odds Ratio · Outcome Assessment, Health Care · Oxygen Inhalation Therapy/methods · Pulmonary Embolism/epidemiology · Thrombocytopenia/chemically induced · Thrombosis/etiology · Thrombosis/mortality · Thrombosis/prevention & control · Treatment Outcome · Venous Thrombosis/epidemiology · Venous Thrombosis/mortality
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the dose question splits by outcome, and the split does not favour escalation. In the INSPIRATION trial (Sadeghipour P et al., PMID: 33734299), 562 ICU patients with COVID-19 randomised to intermediate-dose enoxaparin (1 mg/kg daily) versus standard prophylaxis (40 mg daily) had an identical primary composite of thrombosis, ECMO treatment, or 30-day death — 45.7% versus 44.1% (odds ratio 1.06, 95% CI 0.76 to 1.48) — while severe thrombocytopenia occurred only in the intermediate arm (6 vs 0 patients) and major bleeding was numerically higher (2.5% vs 1.4%, noninferiority not met). The 90-day report (Bikdeli B et al., PMID: 33865239) was the same story extended: primary outcome 47.8% versus 45.4% (hazard ratio 1.21, 95% CI 0.95 to 1.55). A systematic review and meta-analysis of six randomised trials (Bonfim LCMG et al., PMID: 37244209) found escalated dosing did not change mortality (relative risk 1.01, 95% CI 0.90 to 1.13) or deep vein thrombosis, but did reduce pulmonary embolism (relative risk 0.35, 95% CI 0.21 to 0.60) while increasing bleeding (relative risk 1.65, 95% CI 1.08 to 2.53). PROPOSED SPLIT: escalated prophylaxis buys fewer pulmonary emboli at the price of more bleeding, with no mortality or overall-composite benefit — routine intermediate dosing in unselected ICU patients is not supported by its own trial.

cards.headline: INSPIRATION 2021: intermediate-dose enoxaparin in ICU COVID-19 — primary composite 45.7% vs 44.1% on standard prophylaxis (OR 1.06), severe thrombocytopenia 6 vs 0 patients
cards.summary: INSPIRATION 2021: intermediate-dose enoxaparin in ICU COVID-19 — primary composite 45.7% vs 44.1% on standard prophylaxis (OR 1.06), severe thrombocytopenia 6 vs 0 patients
cards.people: 562 adults with COVID-19 admitted to intensive care in 10 academic centres in Iran (median age 62, 42.2% women), randomised in a 2×2 factorial trial to intermediate-dose enoxaparin 1 mg/kg daily (n=276) or standard prophylaxis 40 mg daily (n=286), adjusted for weight and creatinine clearance, for 30 days; recruited July to November 2020.
cards.result: The primary composite — adjudicated venous or arterial thrombosis, treatment with ECMO, or mortality within 30 days — occurred in 126 patients (45.7%) in the intermediate-dose group and 126 (44.1%) in the standard-dose group (absolute risk difference 1.5%, 95% CI −6.6% to 9.8%; odds ratio 1.06, 95% CI 0.76 to 1.48; P=0.70). Major bleeding occurred in 7 (2.5%) versus 4 (1.4%) patients (odds ratio 1.83), which did not meet the prespecified noninferiority criteria (P for noninferiority >0.99). Severe thrombocytopenia (platelets below 20×10³/µL) occurred only with intermediate dosing (6 vs 0 patients; risk difference 2.2%, 95% CI 0.4% to 3.8%; P=0.01). The authors conclude the results do not support routine empirical intermediate-dose prophylaxis in unselected ICU patients with COVID-19.
cards.watchOut: A 2020, pre-vaccination, single-country ICU population, and the composite is dominated by mortality, which anticoagulant dose was never likely to move on its own. The factorial design also randomised statin therapy (reported separately) — this card is the anticoagulation comparison only.

cards.headline: INSPIRATION 90-day results 2022: still no separation — primary outcome 47.8% vs 45.4% (HR 1.21, 95% CI 0.95 to 1.55), major bleeding 2.5% vs 1.4% with 3 fatal bleeds on intermediate dosing
cards.summary: INSPIRATION 90-day results 2022: still no separation — primary outcome 47.8% vs 45.4% (HR 1.21, 95% CI 0.95 to 1.55), major bleeding 2.5% vs 1.4% with 3 fatal bleeds on intermediate dosing
cards.people: The final 90-day follow-up of the same INSPIRATION cohort: 562 patients in the modified intention-to-treat analysis (median age 62, 42.2% women), of whom 336 (59.8%) survived to hospital discharge; assigned prophylaxis continued for 30 days regardless of discharge.
cards.result: The primary outcome — adjudicated venous or arterial thrombosis, ECMO treatment, or all-cause death — occurred in 132 (47.8%) of the intermediate-dose group and 130 (45.4%) of the standard-dose group (hazard ratio 1.21, 95% confidence interval 0.95 to 1.55; p=0.11). Other efficacy outcomes and the landmark analysis from days 31 to 90 (HR 1.59, 95% CI 0.45 to 5.06) were similar. Major bleeding occurred in 7 (2.5%) intermediate-dose patients (including 3 fatal events) and 4 (1.4%) standard-dose patients (none fatal) (HR 1.82, 95% CI 0.53 to 6.24).
cards.watchOut: Same trial, longer window — not independent evidence. The point estimate at 90 days leans against intermediate dosing, but the interval is wide; the fair reading is 'no benefit shown, harm not excluded', reinforced by the fatal-bleed imbalance.
cards.source: Bikdeli B et al. Intermediate-Dose versus Standard-Dose Prophylactic Anticoagulation in Patients with COVID-19 Admitted to the Intensive Care Unit: 90-Day Results from the INSPIRATION Randomized Trial. Thrombosis and Haemostasis. 2022. PMID: 33865239. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Bonfim 2023 (systematic review and meta-analysis, 6 RCTs): escalated anticoagulation — mortality unchanged (RR 1.01), pulmonary embolism reduced (RR 0.35), bleeding increased (RR 1.65)
cards.summary: Bonfim 2023 (systematic review and meta-analysis, 6 RCTs): escalated anticoagulation — mortality unchanged (RR 1.01), pulmonary embolism reduced (RR 0.35), bleeding increased (RR 1.65)
cards.people: Six randomised trials of therapeutic or intermediate-dose versus standard prophylactic-dose heparin anticoagulation in critically ill patients with severe COVID-19 (searches to May 2022); 2,130 patients (50.2%) received escalated dosing and the remainder standard thromboprophylaxis.
cards.result: Escalated dosing had no significant impact on mortality (relative risk 1.01, 95% CI 0.90 to 1.13) and no significant difference in deep vein thrombosis (relative risk 0.81, 95% CI 0.61 to 1.08). Pulmonary embolism risk was significantly reduced with escalated dosing (relative risk 0.35, 95% CI 0.21 to 0.60), while bleeding events were significantly increased (relative risk 1.65, 95% CI 1.08 to 2.53). The reviewers conclude the analysis fails to support escalated doses to reduce mortality in critically ill COVID-19 patients. These are relative risks; the review abstract does not print the pooled absolute event rates alongside them.
cards.watchOut: The pooled trials mix intermediate and fully therapeutic dosing, so the pulmonary-embolism reduction cannot be credited to the intermediate dose specifically. A relative reduction in one thrombotic outcome alongside a relative increase in bleeding, with mortality flat, is a trade — not a win.
cards.source: Bonfim LCMG et al. Optimal dosing of heparin for prophylactic anticoagulation in critically ill COVID-19 patients a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials. Journal of Critical Care. 2023. PMID: 37244209. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: no mortality or composite benefit at 30 or 90 days in the anchor trial; pooled data trade fewer pulmonary emboli for more bleeding
cards.summary: Synthesis: no mortality or composite benefit at 30 or 90 days in the anchor trial; pooled data trade fewer pulmonary emboli for more bleeding
cards.people: One 562-patient RCT programme (INSPIRATION, 30- and 90-day reports) plus a six-trial systematic review and meta-analysis of escalated versus standard prophylaxis in critically ill COVID-19 patients.
cards.result: Primary composite at 30 days: 45.7% vs 44.1% (OR 1.06, 95% CI 0.76 to 1.48); at 90 days: 47.8% vs 45.4% (HR 1.21, 95% CI 0.95 to 1.55). Pooled mortality: relative risk 1.01 (95% CI 0.90 to 1.13). Pooled pulmonary embolism: relative risk 0.35 (95% CI 0.21 to 0.60) favouring escalation; pooled bleeding: relative risk 1.65 (95% CI 1.08 to 2.53) against it. Severe thrombocytopenia in INSPIRATION: 6 vs 0 patients. PROPOSED SPLIT — benefit on one thrombotic outcome, harm on bleeding, null on survival.
cards.watchOut: This shelf is the ICU prophylaxis-dose question only — it does not cover therapeutic-dose anticoagulation, ward-level patients, or patients with a confirmed clot, all of which are different decisions. The evidence is from the pre-vaccination pandemic era; absolute clot rates in current ICU COVID-19 care may differ. Tier C is set because one trial programme anchors the question.
cards.source: Synthesis of Sadeghipour P et al. JAMA. 2021 (PMID: 33734299); Bikdeli B et al. Thrombosis and Haemostasis. 2022 (PMID: 33865239); Bonfim LCMG et al. Journal of Critical Care. 2023 (PMID: 37244209).

shelves.title: Alpha-2 sedation vs propofol: A2B's 1,404 patients got no faster extubation from dexmedetomidine or clonidine — and more agitation and slow heart rates
shelves.question: In mechanically ventilated critically ill adults, does sedation based on an alpha-2 agonist (dexmedetomidine or clonidine) improve outcomes compared with propofol-based sedation?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Adrenergic alpha-2 Receptor Agonists*/administration & dosage · Adrenergic alpha-2 Receptor Agonists*/adverse effects · Airway Extubation/statistics & numerical data · Clonidine*/administration & dosage · Clonidine*/adverse effects · Critical Illness*/therapy · Critical Illness*/mortality · Dexmedetomidine*/administration & dosage · Dexmedetomidine*/adverse effects · Hypnotics and Sedatives*/administration & dosage · Hypnotics and Sedatives*/adverse effects · Intensive Care Units · Propofol*/administration & dosage · Propofol*/adverse effects · Respiration, Artificial/statistics & numerical data · Time Factors · Analgesia/methods · Analgesia/statistics & numerical data · Young Adult · Adult · Aged, 80 and over
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — the largest direct test says no. In the A2B trial (Walsh TS et al., PMID: 40388916), 1,404 ventilated ICU patients randomised to dexmedetomidine-based, clonidine-based, or propofol-based sedation had time to successful extubation that was not significantly shorter on either alpha-2 agonist (subdistribution hazard ratio 1.09, 95% CI 0.96 to 1.25 for dexmedetomidine; 1.05, 95% CI 0.95 to 1.17 for clonidine), 180-day mortality was similar, and both alpha-2 arms had more agitation (risk ratio about 1.55) and more severe bradycardia (risk ratio about 1.6). The older Cochrane review (Chen K et al., PMID: 25879090) had leaned the other way for dexmedetomidine — duration of mechanical ventilation reduced by 22% (95% CI 10% to 33%) and ICU stay by 14% against traditional sedatives, on low to very low quality evidence, with bradycardia doubled (risk ratio 2.11) and no mortality effect (risk ratio 0.99); it found no eligible clonidine trials at all. A2B, pragmatic and ten times the typical older trial's size, is the record to weight. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): alpha-2-based sedation remains a legitimate choice for individual patients, but a general extubation or survival advantage over propofol is unproven — and A2B's agitation and bradycardia signals are part of the price.

cards.headline: A2B 2025: dexmedetomidine or clonidine vs propofol in 1,404 ventilated patients — neither shortened time to extubation (HR 1.09 and 1.05), both caused more agitation and severe bradycardia
cards.summary: A2B 2025: dexmedetomidine or clonidine vs propofol in 1,404 ventilated patients — neither shortened time to extubation (HR 1.09 and 1.05), both caused more agitation and severe bradycardia
cards.people: 1,404 adults in 41 UK intensive care units, within 48 hours of starting mechanical ventilation, receiving propofol plus an opioid and expected to need ventilation for at least 48 hours (mean age 59.2 years, 64% men, mean APACHE II 20.3); randomised to dexmedetomidine-based (n=457), clonidine-based (n=476), or propofol-based (n=471) sedation algorithms targeting a Richmond Agitation-Sedation Scale score of −2 to +1, December 2018 to October 2023.
cards.result: The subdistribution hazard ratio for time to successful extubation was 1.09 (95% CI 0.96 to 1.25; P=0.20) for dexmedetomidine versus propofol and 1.05 (95% CI 0.95 to 1.17; P=0.34) for clonidine versus propofol — neither superior. Median time to extubation was 136 hours (dexmedetomidine), 146 hours (clonidine), and 162 hours (propofol). Agitation was more frequent with dexmedetomidine (risk ratio 1.54, 95% CI 1.21 to 1.97) and clonidine (1.55, 1.22 to 1.97), as was severe bradycardia below 50/min (1.62, 1.36 to 1.93; and 1.58, 1.33 to 1.88). Mortality over 180 days was similar (hazard ratio 0.98, 95% CI 0.77 to 1.24; and 1.04, 0.82 to 1.31). No prespecified subgroup (age, sepsis, SOFA score, delirium risk) showed an interaction.
cards.watchOut: Open-label and pragmatic: supplemental propofol was permitted in the alpha-2 arms, so this tests a sedation strategy, not a pure drug. The medians lean toward the alpha-2 arms while the primary hazard ratios do not reach significance — quote the hazard ratios, not the medians, as the trial's answer.
cards.source: Walsh TS et al. Dexmedetomidine- or Clonidine-Based Sedation Compared With Propofol in Critically Ill Patients: The A2B Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA. 2025. PMID: 40388916. Registry ID: NCT03653832. cards.headline: Chen 2015 (Cochrane): dexmedetomidine vs traditional sedatives — ventilation duration 22% shorter (relative) and ICU stay 14% shorter, low/very low quality, bradycardia doubled, no mortality effect; no clonidine trials found
cards.summary: Chen 2015 (Cochrane): dexmedetomidine vs traditional sedatives — ventilation duration 22% shorter (relative) and ICU stay 14% shorter, low/very low quality, bradycardia doubled, no mortality effect; no clonidine trials found
cards.people: Seven randomised trials, 1,624 participants, of alpha-2 agonists for sedation longer than 24 hours during mechanical ventilation in critically ill adults (searches to October 2014); all seven compared dexmedetomidine with traditional sedatives (propofol, midazolam, or lorazepam). Percent changes are relative reductions in geometric mean duration, as reported by the review.
cards.result: Compared with traditional sedatives, dexmedetomidine reduced the geometric mean duration of mechanical ventilation by 22% (95% CI 10% to 33%; four studies, 1,120 participants, low quality evidence) and ICU length of stay by 14% (95% CI 1% to 24%; five studies, 1,223 participants, very low quality evidence). There was no evidence of a delirium difference (risk ratio 0.85, 95% CI 0.63 to 1.14; very low quality) and no impact on mortality (risk ratio 0.99, 95% CI 0.79 to 1.24; six studies, 1,584 participants). Bradycardia was more than doubled (risk ratio 2.11, 95% CI 1.39 to 3.20). Six of the seven studies were judged at high risk of bias, and the review found no eligible studies of clonidine.
cards.watchOut: This synthesis predates A2B by a decade and pools dexmedetomidine against a mix of propofol and benzodiazepines — part of its apparent advantage may be a benzodiazepine comparator effect that does not apply to the propofol comparison A2B actually made. Its certainty ratings were low to very low throughout.

cards.headline: Synthesis: the big pragmatic three-way trial is neutral on extubation and mortality; the older pooled dexmedetomidine advantage has not survived contact with it
cards.summary: Synthesis: the big pragmatic three-way trial is neutral on extubation and mortality; the older pooled dexmedetomidine advantage has not survived contact with it
cards.people: One 1,404-patient three-arm pragmatic RCT (A2B) plus a seven-trial Cochrane review (1,624 participants) of dexmedetomidine against traditional sedatives.
cards.result: Time to extubation: hazard ratio 1.09 (95% CI 0.96 to 1.25) for dexmedetomidine and 1.05 (0.95 to 1.17) for clonidine versus propofol — not significant. Mortality: no difference in either source (A2B 180-day HR 0.98 and 1.04; Cochrane RR 0.99). Harms in A2B: agitation risk ratio about 1.55 and severe bradycardia about 1.6 for both alpha-2 arms; Cochrane bradycardia RR 2.11 for dexmedetomidine. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence).
cards.watchOut: A neutral strategy trial does not forbid alpha-2 sedation where propofol is problematic (for example severe hypertriglyceridaemia or a need for cooperative sedation) — it removes the expectation of faster liberation as the reason to choose it. Clonidine's evidence base remains essentially this one trial. Tier C is set because A2B is a single trial.

shelves.title: Breathing the sedative in: SAVE-ICU's 780 patients died at the same rate on isoflurane as on IV sedation (42.5% vs 43.8%) — with fewer delirium-free days
shelves.question: In mechanically ventilated adults with acute hypoxaemic respiratory failure, does inhaled isoflurane sedation improve outcomes compared with intravenous propofol sedation?
shelves.mesh: none in the record
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — the first large trial of the strategy is neutral on survival and slightly adverse on brain outcomes. In SAVE-ICU (Jerath A et al., PMID: 42872958), 780 ventilated adults with acute hypoxaemic respiratory failure randomised to isoflurane-based inhaled sedation or usual intravenous sedation had hospital mortality of 42.5% versus 43.8% (risk ratio 0.98, 95% CI 0.84 to 1.14; P=0.85), no difference in ICU-, ventilator-, or hospital-free days, quality of life, or disability — and fewer delirium- and coma-free days in the inhaled group (between-group difference −0.95 days, 95% CI −1.69 to −0.22), alongside more use of adjunctive therapies for hypoxaemia (63.9% vs 55.0%). The earlier pooled literature (Kim HY et al., PMID: 29245269), thirteen small trials and 1,027 patients, had found volatile sedation shortened awakening time by 80 minutes and extubation time by 196 minutes versus intravenous sedation, with no difference in ICU or hospital stay — process gains that SAVE-ICU's free-day outcomes do not corroborate at scale. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): inhaled isoflurane sedation is feasible in this population, but no patient-important benefit over intravenous sedation has been shown, and the delirium/coma signal points the wrong way.

cards.headline: SAVE-ICU 2026: isoflurane inhaled sedation in 780 ventilated patients with hypoxaemic respiratory failure — hospital mortality 42.5% vs 43.8% on IV sedation (RR 0.98), and 0.95 fewer delirium- and coma-free days
cards.summary: SAVE-ICU 2026: isoflurane inhaled sedation in 780 ventilated patients with hypoxaemic respiratory failure — hospital mortality 42.5% vs 43.8% on IV sedation (RR 0.98), and 0.95 fewer delirium- and coma-free days
cards.people: 780 adults (mean age 61.1 years, 34.0% women; 73.7% non-COVID respiratory failure, mean PaO2:FiO2 ratio 152.6 mmHg) in 14 Canadian intensive care units, ventilated for acute hypoxaemic respiratory failure and sedated for under 72 hours, randomised to an isoflurane inhaled-sedation strategy with intravenous adjuncts as needed (n=385) or a usual intravenous-sedation strategy (n=395); hospital-discharge outcome data were available for 379 and 390 patients respectively; enrolled September 2020 to March 2025. In the inhaled group, 49.9% to 55.4% of patients also received intravenous sedation on any given day in the first 14 days.
cards.result: At hospital discharge, 161 of 379 patients (42.5%) in the inhaled group and 171 of 390 (43.8%) in the intravenous group had died (risk ratio 0.98, 95% CI 0.84 to 1.14; P=0.85). ICU-, ventilator-, and hospital-free days were similar, as were quality-of-life and disability scores at 3 months, with no effect modification by age, sex, or COVID-19 status. The inhaled group received more adjunctive therapies for hypoxaemia (239 [63.9%] vs 214 [55.0%]; difference 8.89%, 95% CI 1.95% to 15.83%) and had fewer delirium- and coma-free days (difference −0.95, 95% CI −1.69 to −0.22).
cards.watchOut: A strategy trial, not a pure-drug trial: about half the inhaled group also received intravenous sedation daily, which dilutes any drug-specific effect in both directions. The record carries no MeSH terms yet (2026 publication), so this card's source line says so plainly rather than inventing any.
cards.source: Jerath A et al. Isoflurane-Based Inhaled Sedation in Mechanically Ventilated Adults With Acute Hypoxemic Respiratory Failure: The SAVE-ICU Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA. 2026. PMID: 42872958. Registry ID: NCT04415060. MeSH: none in the record

cards.headline: Kim 2017 (systematic review and meta-analysis, 13 trials, 1,027 patients): volatile sedation woke patients 80 minutes sooner and extubated 196 minutes sooner than IV sedation — with no difference in ICU or hospital stay
cards.summary: Kim 2017 (systematic review and meta-analysis, 13 trials, 1,027 patients): volatile sedation woke patients 80 minutes sooner and extubated 196 minutes sooner than IV sedation — with no difference in ICU or hospital stay
cards.people: Thirteen randomised trials (1,027 patients) comparing volatile sedation (sevoflurane or isoflurane delivered through an anaesthetic-conserving device) with intravenous sedation (midazolam or propofol) in adult intensive care patients.
cards.result: Volatile sedation shortened awakening time (mean difference −80.0 minutes, 95% CI −134.5 to −25.6; P=0.004) and extubation time (mean difference −196.0 minutes, 95% CI −305.2 to −86.8; P<0.001) compared with intravenous sedation. There were no differences in ICU or hospital length of stay. Serum troponin levels 6 hours after ICU admission were lower with volatile sedation in the five-study cardiac analysis, with the largest effect between 12 and 24 hours (mean difference −0.27 µg/L, 95% CI −0.44 to −0.09; P=0.003). The reviewers caution that the included studies were small with high heterogeneity and call for larger, high-quality trials.
cards.watchOut: Small, heterogeneous, mostly post-cardiac-surgery trials measuring minutes-to-wakening — a process outcome in a different population from SAVE-ICU's hypoxaemic respiratory failure patients. Faster wakening in these trials did not translate into shorter stays even there.
cards.source: Kim HY et al. Volatile sedation in the intensive care unit: A systematic review and meta-analysis. Medicine. 2017. PMID: 29245269. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: process gains in small older trials; neutrality on mortality and free days, with a worse delirium/coma count, in the one large trial that asked patient-important questions
cards.summary: Synthesis: process gains in small older trials; neutrality on mortality and free days, with a worse delirium/coma count, in the one large trial that asked patient-important questions
cards.people: One 780-patient pragmatic RCT (SAVE-ICU) in acute hypoxaemic respiratory failure plus a thirteen-trial meta-analysis (1,027 patients) of volatile versus intravenous ICU sedation.
cards.result: Hospital mortality: 42.5% vs 43.8% (risk ratio 0.98, 95% CI 0.84 to 1.14). Ventilator-, ICU-, and hospital-free days: no difference in SAVE-ICU. Delirium- and coma-free days: 0.95 fewer with isoflurane (95% CI −1.69 to −0.22). Older pooled process outcomes: awakening 80 minutes and extubation 196 minutes sooner with volatile sedation, lengths of stay unchanged. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence).
cards.watchOut: Do not generalise SAVE-ICU's neutrality to short post-operative volatile sedation, where the older trials were done, or its delirium signal to a proven harm — it is one secondary outcome in one open-label trial. What is missing is any demonstration that the strategy improves an outcome patients feel. Tier C is set because a single large trial anchors the question.
cards.source: Synthesis of Jerath A et al. JAMA. 2026 (PMID: 42872958); Kim HY et al. Medicine. 2017 (PMID: 29245269).

shelves.title: Methylene blue early in septic shock: pressors stopped a day sooner in the anchor trial, and six small trials pool to a mortality relative risk of 0.66 — on low certainty
shelves.question: In adults with septic shock on high-dose vasopressors, does early adjunctive methylene blue shorten vasopressor duration or reduce mortality compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Shock, Septic* · Methylene Blue/pharmacology · Methylene Blue/therapeutic use · Vasoconstrictor Agents/therapeutic use · Sepsis*/complications
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a coherent but small evidence base. In the anchor trial (Ibarra-Estrada M et al., PMID: 36915146), 91 patients with septic shock randomised to early adjunctive methylene blue or placebo came off vasopressors sooner (median 69 vs 94 hours; p<0.001), gained one more vasopressor-free day at day 28 (p=0.008), and left the ICU 1.5 days and hospital 2.7 days sooner, with mortality similar and no serious adverse effects attributed to the drug. A systematic review and meta-analysis of six randomised trials and 302 patients (Fernando SM et al., PMID: 38904978) points the same way and further: short-term mortality relative risk 0.66 (95% CI 0.47 to 0.94), vasopressor duration 31.1 hours shorter, and hospital stay 2.1 days shorter — every one of those estimates rated low certainty, with the methemoglobin effect uncertain (very low certainty) and no difference in adverse events. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): early methylene blue probably shortens vasopressor time in septic shock; the mortality signal is real in the pooled data but rests on about 300 randomised patients in total, which is exactly why the stamp stops at possible.

cards.headline: Ibarra-Estrada 2023: early methylene blue in septic shock — vasopressors stopped at a median 69 vs 94 hours (p<0.001), ICU stay 1.5 days and hospital stay 2.7 days shorter, mortality similar
cards.summary: Ibarra-Estrada 2023: early methylene blue in septic shock — vasopressors stopped at a median 69 vs 94 hours (p<0.001), ICU stay 1.5 days and hospital stay 2.7 days shorter, mortality similar
cards.people: 91 adults with septic shock by Sepsis-3 criteria at a single centre, randomised to methylene blue (n=45) or placebo (n=46) started within 24 hours as an adjunct to standard vasopressor care; primary outcome was time to vasopressor discontinuation at 28 days.
cards.result: The methylene blue group had a shorter time to vasopressor discontinuation (69 hours [IQR 59–83] vs 94 hours [IQR 74–141]; p<0.001), one more vasopressor-free day at day 28 (p=0.008), a shorter ICU length of stay by 1.5 days (p=0.039), and a shorter hospital length of stay by 2.7 days (p=0.027). Days on mechanical ventilation and mortality were similar between groups. There were no serious adverse effects related to methylene blue administration.
cards.watchOut: Single-centre, 91 patients, and retrospectively registered (the record notes registration on June 25, 2020, retrospectively) — the process outcomes are strong, but a trial this size cannot speak to mortality, and its length-of-stay gains are the outcomes most sensitive to local discharge practice.
cards.source: Ibarra-Estrada M et al. Early adjunctive methylene blue in patients with septic shock: a randomized controlled trial. Critical Care. 2023. PMID: 36915146. Registry ID: NCT04446871. cards.headline: Fernando 2024 (systematic review and meta-analysis, 6 RCTs, 302 patients): methylene blue — short-term mortality relative risk 0.66 (95% CI 0.47 to 0.94) and vasopressor duration 31.1 hours shorter, all low certainty
cards.summary: Fernando 2024 (systematic review and meta-analysis, 6 RCTs, 302 patients): methylene blue — short-term mortality relative risk 0.66 (95% CI 0.47 to 0.94) and vasopressor duration 31.1 hours shorter, all low certainty
cards.people: Six randomised trials (302 patients) of methylene blue versus placebo or usual care in critically ill adults with septic shock (searches to January 10, 2024), pooled with a random-effects model and GRADE certainty ratings.
cards.result: Compared with placebo or no methylene blue, methylene blue may reduce short-term mortality (risk ratio 0.66, 95% CI 0.47 to 0.94; low certainty) and hospital length of stay (mean difference −2.1 days, 95% CI −1.4 to −2.8 as printed in the record; low certainty), may reduce duration of vasopressors (mean difference −31.1 hours, 95% CI −16.5 to −45.6 as printed; low certainty), and may increase mean arterial pressure at 6 hours (mean difference 10.2 mmHg, 95% CI 6.1 to 14.2; low certainty). The effect on serum methemoglobin concentration was uncertain (mean difference 0.9%, 95% CI −0.2% to 2.0%; very low certainty), and there were no differences in adverse events. The reviewers call for rigorous larger trials. These are relative and mean-difference measures from the review; pooled absolute mortality rates are not printed in the record.
cards.watchOut: Three hundred patients across six small trials is a fragile base for a mortality claim — one neutral mid-sized trial could erase it. Populations mix early adjunctive use with rescue use in refractory shock, which are different clinical moments.
cards.source: Fernando SM et al. Methylene Blue in Septic Shock: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Critical Care Explorations. 2024. PMID: 38904978. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: vasopressor time and stay shorten consistently; the pooled mortality signal (RR 0.66) rests on roughly 300 randomised patients and low-certainty grading
cards.summary: Synthesis: vasopressor time and stay shorten consistently; the pooled mortality signal (RR 0.66) rests on roughly 300 randomised patients and low-certainty grading
cards.people: One 91-patient single-centre RCT of early adjunctive methylene blue plus a six-trial systematic review and meta-analysis (302 patients) in septic shock.
cards.result: Time to vasopressor discontinuation: median 69 vs 94 hours in the anchor trial; pooled vasopressor duration 31.1 hours shorter. Hospital stay: 2.7 days shorter in the anchor trial, 2.1 days shorter pooled. Mortality: similar in the anchor trial; pooled short-term mortality relative risk 0.66 (95% CI 0.47 to 0.94), low certainty. Adverse events: no difference shown; methemoglobin effect uncertain. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: Methylene blue has well-known practical cautions (serotonergic drugs, G6PD deficiency, pulse-oximetry interference) that these small trials were not sized to evaluate — absence of harm signals here is not proof of safety in every patient. Tier C is set because the whole randomised base is about 300 patients.

shelves.title: Dexamethasone for established ARDS: 4.8 more ventilator-free days and 60-day mortality of 21% vs 36% in DEXA-ARDS, with the pooled literature pointing the same way
shelves.question: In adults with established acute respiratory distress syndrome, does dexamethasone increase ventilator-free days and reduce mortality compared with usual care?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Intravenous · Adult · Aged · Dexamethasone/administration & dosage · Female · Glucocorticoids/administration & dosage · Humans · Intensive Care Units · Male · Middle Aged · Respiration, Artificial/adverse effects · Respiration, Artificial/statistics & numerical data · Respiratory Distress Syndrome/drug therapy · Respiratory Distress Syndrome/mortality · Severity of Illness Index · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) — a large effect in a properly randomised multicentre trial, corroborated in direction by the pooled literature. In DEXA-ARDS (Villar J et al., PMID: 32043986), 277 patients with established moderate-to-severe ARDS randomised to dexamethasone (20 mg daily for 5 days, then 10 mg daily to day 10) or routine care gained 4.8 more ventilator-free days at day 28 (95% CI 2.57 to 7.03) and had 60-day mortality of 21% versus 36% (difference −15.3%, 95% CI −25.9 to −4.9; p=0.0047), with no significant difference in adverse events — hyperglycaemia was common in both arms (76% vs 70%). A systematic review and meta-analysis of four studies and 702 patients (Feng LH et al., PMID: 36181003) found dexamethasone significantly reduced all-cause mortality (odds ratio 0.62, 95% CI 0.44 to 0.88) and improved ventilator-free status at 28 days (mean difference 3.65 days, 95% CI 1.49 to 5.80), again without a significant difference in adverse events. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): in established moderate-to-severe ARDS, early dexamethasone on this schedule likely shortens ventilation and reduces mortality — held back from the strongest grade because the anchor trial stopped for low enrolment at 88% of its planned sample and the pooled base is still only four studies.

cards.headline: DEXA-ARDS 2020: dexamethasone in established moderate-to-severe ARDS — 4.8 more ventilator-free days and 60-day mortality 21% vs 36% (difference −15.3%)
cards.summary: DEXA-ARDS 2020: dexamethasone in established moderate-to-severe ARDS — 4.8 more ventilator-free days and 60-day mortality 21% vs 36% (difference −15.3%)
cards.people: 277 adults with established moderate-to-severe ARDS (PaO2:FiO2 of 200 mmHg or less on PEEP of at least 10 cm H2O and FiO2 of at least 0.5, assessed 24 hours after ARDS onset) in 17 Spanish teaching-hospital ICUs, randomised to intravenous dexamethasone 20 mg daily on days 1–5 then 10 mg daily on days 6–10 (n=139) or continued routine intensive care (n=138), both with lung-protective ventilation; enrolled March 2013 to December 2018. Patients receiving corticosteroids or immunosuppressive drugs were excluded.
cards.result: The mean number of ventilator-free days at 28 days was higher with dexamethasone (between-group difference 4.8 days, 95% CI 2.57 to 7.03; p<0.0001). At 60 days, 29 (21%) dexamethasone patients and 50 (36%) control patients had died (between-group difference −15.3%, 95% CI −25.9 to −4.9; p=0.0047). Adverse events did not differ significantly: hyperglycaemia in the ICU 105 (76%) versus 97 (70%), new ICU infections 33 (24%) versus 35 (25%), and barotrauma 14 (10%) versus 10 (7%). The trial was stopped by its data safety monitoring board for low enrolment after reaching more than 88% (277 of 314) of the planned sample size.
cards.watchOut: Open-label routine-care control and early stopping for slow enrolment (not for efficacy) — the mortality difference is large and its interval excludes small effects, but a single trial of 277 patients in one country's ICU network is still a single trial. The population is established ARDS at 24 hours, not patients at risk of ARDS.

cards.headline: Feng 2022 (systematic review and meta-analysis, 4 studies, 702 patients): dexamethasone in ARDS — all-cause mortality odds ratio 0.62 (95% CI 0.44 to 0.88), ventilator-free days 3.65 more
cards.summary: Feng 2022 (systematic review and meta-analysis, 4 studies, 702 patients): dexamethasone in ARDS — all-cause mortality odds ratio 0.62 (95% CI 0.44 to 0.88), ventilator-free days 3.65 more
cards.people: Four randomised trials (702 patients) of dexamethasone versus routine or standard care in ARDS (searches to May 1, 2022), with all-cause mortality as the primary outcome; quality assessed with the Cochrane Risk of Bias Tool.
cards.result: Dexamethasone significantly reduced all-cause mortality (odds ratio 0.62, 95% confidence interval 0.44 to 0.88; I²=30%; P<0.001 as printed) and decreased ventilator dependence — reported as ventilator-free status at 28 days, mean difference 3.65 days (95% CI 1.49 to 5.80; I²=51%; P<0.001 as printed). No significant differences in occurrence rates of adverse events were found between dexamethasone and routine or standard care. The reviewers note the small number of eligible RCTs and that conclusions warrant confirmation in future studies. The mortality figure is an odds ratio from the review; pooled absolute mortality rates are not printed in the record.
cards.watchOut: Four studies is a thin pool and DEXA-ARDS supplies much of the weight, so the meta-analysis largely restates the anchor trial with smaller studies around it. Trial populations and dexamethasone schedules were not identical across the four studies.
cards.source: Feng LH et al. Dexamethasone for the treatment of acute respiratory distress syndrome: A systematic review and meta-analysis. Medicine. 2022. PMID: 36181003. shelves.title: Thiamine alone in septic shock: two 88-patient trials missed their primary outcomes — the only positive signals sit in small thiamine-deficient subgroups
shelves.question: In adults with septic shock, does thiamine (alone, not in a combination cocktail) improve lactate clearance, kidney outcomes, or mortality compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Lactic Acid/blood · Male · Middle Aged · Pilot Projects · Severity of Illness Index · Shock, Septic/blood · Shock, Septic/drug therapy · Shock, Septic/epidemiology · Thiamine/therapeutic use · Thiamine Deficiency/drug therapy · Thiamine Deficiency/epidemiology
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — two small placebo-controlled trials of thiamine alone, and both miss their primary outcome. Donnino's pilot (Donnino MW et al., PMID: 26771781) randomised 88 septic-shock patients with lactate above 3 mmol/L to thiamine 200 mg twice daily or placebo and found no difference in 24-hour lactate (median 2.5 vs 2.6 mmol/L; p=0.40), shock reversal, severity of illness, or mortality overall — though in the predefined subgroup who were thiamine-deficient at baseline (35% of patients), lactate was lower on thiamine (2.1 vs 3.1 mmol/L; p=0.03) with a possible mortality decrease over time (p=0.047). TRPSS (Moskowitz A et al., PMID: 37364280), also 88 patients, found no significant difference in its primary outcome of creatinine change at 72 hours (mean difference −0.57 mg/dl, 95% CI −1.18 to 0.04; P=0.07), nor in kidney replacement therapy (14.3% vs 21.7%), stage-3 acute kidney injury (54.7% vs 73.9%), or mortality (35.7% vs 54.3%) — all numerically favouring thiamine, none significant — while ICU-free days were greater on thiamine (median 22.5 vs 0.0; P<0.01). No systematic review of thiamine alone (as distinct from the vitamin C–steroid combination) was found in-session, so this shelf rests on the two trials. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): thiamine alone is unproven for lactate, kidney, or survival outcomes in unselected septic shock; the deficiency-subgroup signal is a hypothesis for a targeted trial, not a result.

cards.headline: Donnino 2016 (pilot RCT, 88 patients): thiamine alone in septic shock — 24-hour lactate 2.5 vs 2.6 mmol/L on placebo (p=0.40); only the thiamine-deficient subgroup (35%) separated (2.1 vs 3.1, p=0.03)
cards.summary: Donnino 2016 (pilot RCT, 88 patients): thiamine alone in septic shock — 24-hour lactate 2.5 vs 2.6 mmol/L on placebo (p=0.40); only the thiamine-deficient subgroup (35%) separated (2.1 vs 3.1, p=0.03)
cards.people: 88 adults with septic shock and lactate above 3 mmol/L at two US hospitals (715 screened, 2010–2014), randomised double-blind to intravenous thiamine 200 mg twice daily or matching placebo for 7 days or until hospital discharge; primary outcome was lactate 24 hours after the first dose. At baseline, 35% of patients were thiamine deficient.
cards.result: There was no difference in the primary outcome: median lactate at 24 hours was 2.5 mmol/L (IQR 1.5–3.4) on thiamine versus 2.6 (1.6–5.1) on placebo (p=0.40). There was no difference in time to shock reversal, severity of illness, or mortality in the overall group. In the predefined thiamine-deficient subgroup, lactate at 24 hours was significantly lower on thiamine (median 2.1 [1.4–2.5] vs 3.1 [1.9–8.3] mmol/L; p=0.03), and mortality over time decreased significantly in that subgroup (p=0.047).
cards.watchOut: A pilot sized for a lactate signal, not for clinical outcomes — and the positive finding lives entirely in a subgroup of about 31 deficient patients. Subgroup mortality findings in pilots are hypothesis-generating at best and are exactly the results most likely to shrink or vanish in a confirmatory trial.

cards.headline: TRPSS 2023 (88 patients): thiamine for kidney protection in septic shock — creatinine difference at 72 hours −0.57 mg/dl (95% CI −1.18 to 0.04; P=0.07), mortality 35.7% vs 54.3% (P=0.14), but more ICU-free days (22.5 vs 0.0; P<0.01)
cards.summary: TRPSS 2023 (88 patients): thiamine for kidney protection in septic shock — creatinine difference at 72 hours −0.57 mg/dl (95% CI −1.18 to 0.04; P=0.07), mortality 35.7% vs 54.3% (P=0.14), but more ICU-free days (22.5 vs 0.0; P<0.01)
cards.people: 88 adults with septic shock in a multicentre randomised placebo-controlled trial of thiamine versus placebo (42 intervention, 46 placebo); primary outcome was change in serum creatinine between enrolment and 72 hours. In the thiamine-deficient cohort (27.4% of patients), outcomes were examined separately.
cards.result: There was no significant between-group difference in creatinine at 72 hours (mean difference −0.57 mg/dl, 95% confidence interval −1.18 to 0.04; P=0.07). There was no difference in receipt of kidney replacement therapy (14.3% vs 21.7%; P=0.34), stage-3 acute kidney injury (54.7% vs 73.9%; P=0.07), or mortality (35.7% vs 54.3%; P=0.14). Patients who received thiamine had more ICU-free days (median 22.5 [IQR 0.0–25.0] vs 0.0 [0.0–23.0]; P<0.01). In the thiamine-deficient cohort there was no difference in kidney failure (57.1% thiamine vs 81.5% placebo) or in-hospital mortality (28.6% vs 68.8%) between groups, as reported without significance testing in the record.
cards.watchOut: Every clinical outcome numerically favours thiamine and none reaches significance — the classic signature of an underpowered trial, which cuts both ways: it neither proves benefit nor excludes a meaningful one. The one significant result, ICU-free days, is a secondary outcome with medians heavily shaped by deaths (the placebo median of 0 reflects its higher mortality).

cards.headline: Synthesis: 176 randomised patients in total, two missed primary outcomes, and a deficiency-subgroup signal that has never been tested as a trial's main question
cards.summary: Synthesis: 176 randomised patients in total, two missed primary outcomes, and a deficiency-subgroup signal that has never been tested as a trial's main question
cards.people: Two placebo-controlled RCTs of thiamine alone in septic shock (88 patients each): Donnino 2016 (lactate primary outcome) and TRPSS 2023 (creatinine primary outcome). No systematic review of thiamine alone, separate from combination therapy, was found in-session.
cards.result: Lactate at 24 hours: 2.5 vs 2.6 mmol/L (p=0.40) overall; 2.1 vs 3.1 mmol/L (p=0.03) in the deficient subgroup. Creatinine change at 72 hours: mean difference −0.57 mg/dl (95% CI −1.18 to 0.04; P=0.07). Mortality: no significant difference in either trial (TRPSS 35.7% vs 54.3%; P=0.14). Kidney replacement therapy: 14.3% vs 21.7% (P=0.34). PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence).
cards.watchOut: Keep this shelf separate from the combination-cocktail literature (vitamin C, thiamine, and steroids together), which asks a different question and lives on its own shelves. The honest open question is narrow: does repleting documented thiamine deficiency in septic shock help? Neither trial randomised on deficiency status as its primary design.

shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — on survival, with better blood oxygen as the consolation. The 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials (Sajawal M et al., PMID: 42965657) pooled nine trials and 585 adults with or at risk for ARDS and found no mortality benefit for airway pressure release ventilation versus conventional ventilation (risk ratio 0.95, 95% CI 0.72 to 1.26), no clear difference in ventilator-free days (mean difference 3.83 days, 95% CI −1.69 to 9.34, I²=83%) or ventilation duration (mean difference −2.44 days, 95% CI −4.96 to 0.09), but a higher PaO2/FiO2 ratio (mean difference 56.21 mm Hg, 95% CI 24.63 to 87.79, I²=84%) and a shorter ICU stay (mean difference −2.53 days, 95% CI −4.43 to −0.64). The reviewers graded the certainty of evidence low to very low, with varied populations, protocols and outcome timing — so the oxygenation gain is a physiology signal, not a survival result, and the data establish neither superiority nor equivalence on mortality. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): APRV improves oxygenation numbers without demonstrated benefit on survival or ventilator-free days.

cards.headline: Sajawal 2026 (meta-analysis, 9 RCTs, 585 patients): no mortality benefit for APRV (RR 0.95) — PaO2/FiO2 higher by 56.21 mm Hg and ICU stay 2.53 days shorter
cards.summary: Sajawal 2026 (meta-analysis, 9 RCTs, 585 patients): no mortality benefit for APRV (RR 0.95) — PaO2/FiO2 higher by 56.21 mm Hg and ICU stay 2.53 days shorter
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials (Sajawal 2026)
cards.people: Nine parallel-group randomised trials involving 585 adults with established ARDS, acute lung injury, or conditions considered to confer a high risk of ARDS, comparing airway pressure release ventilation with conventional invasive ventilation; searches of PubMed, Embase and the Cochrane Library ran from inception to 15 August 2026, with risk of bias assessed by Cochrane RoB 2 and certainty by GRADE.
cards.result: No mortality benefit was demonstrated (risk ratio 0.95, 95% CI 0.72 to 1.26). Ventilator-free days showed no clear difference (mean difference 3.83 days, 95% CI −1.69 to 9.34; I²=83%). APRV was associated with a higher PaO2/FiO2 ratio (mean difference 56.21 mm Hg, 95% CI 24.63 to 87.79; I²=84%) and shorter ICU stay (mean difference −2.53 days, 95% CI −4.43 to −0.64; I²=71%). Ventilation duration showed no clear difference (five trials, 413 participants; mean difference −2.44 days, 95% CI −4.96 to 0.09; I²=78%). Peak airway pressure was lower and mean airway pressure higher with APRV. Certainty of evidence was low to very low.
cards.watchOut: The pooled trials are small, the heterogeneity is high (I² 71–84% on the headline outcomes), and the comparator is 'conventional ventilation' as each trial defined it — not uniformly modern lung-protective ventilation. An oxygenation surrogate rising while mortality and ventilator-free days stand still is the classic pattern of a ventilation mode that helps the blood gas more than the patient.
cards.source: Sajawal M et al. Airway Pressure Release Ventilation Versus Conventional Ventilation in Adults With or at Risk for Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Trials. Lung. 2026. PMID: 42965657. cards.headline: Synthesis: nine small trials, one physiology win, every patient-important outcome drawn — and certainty rated low to very low
cards.summary: Synthesis: nine small trials, one physiology win, every patient-important outcome drawn — and certainty rated low to very low
cards.people: One 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis pooling nine randomised trials and 585 adults with or at risk for ARDS, comparing APRV with conventional invasive ventilation.
cards.result: Mortality: risk ratio 0.95 (95% CI 0.72 to 1.26) — no benefit demonstrated. Ventilator-free days: mean difference 3.83 days (95% CI −1.69 to 9.34). Oxygenation: PaO2/FiO2 higher by 56.21 mm Hg (95% CI 24.63 to 87.79). ICU stay: 2.53 days shorter (95% CI −4.43 to −0.64). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) on survival, with the oxygenation gain on the face of the shelf.
cards.watchOut: A null pooled mortality result from 585 patients cannot exclude a modest benefit or harm — the confidence interval runs from a 28% relative reduction to a 26% relative increase — and APRV protocols differ enough between centres that 'APRV' is not one standardised intervention. Tier C is set: the shelf rests on a single synthesis of small trials with low-to-very-low certainty and addresses mortality.

shelves.title: Neurally adjusted ventilatory assist: pooled invasive-ventilation trials show lower ICU and hospital mortality — but the noninvasive trials show nothing, and an earlier synthesis found no mortality difference
shelves.question: In critically ill adults, does neurally adjusted ventilatory assist improve patient–ventilator synchrony, ventilation duration, and mortality compared with pressure-support ventilation?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Critical Illness/mortality/therapy · Interactive Ventilatory Support/methods/mortality · Hospital Mortality · Intensive Care Units/statistics & numerical data · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Respiration, Artificial/methods · Patient-Ventilator Asynchrony
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — in invasive ventilation only, and on one synthesis's reading. The 2026 meta-analysis (Wu RR et al., PMID: 43026034) pooled nine randomised trials and 842 patients and found that during invasive mechanical ventilation neurally adjusted ventilatory assist (NAVA) reduced ICU mortality (risk ratio 0.72, 95% CI 0.53 to 0.99) and hospital mortality (risk ratio 0.71, 95% CI 0.56 to 0.90) versus conventional modes — relative reductions of 28% and 29%, with the pooled absolute rates not printed in the abstract — and increased ventilation success (risk ratio 1.13, 95% CI 1.04 to 1.22) and 28-day ventilator-free days (mean difference 3.48 days, 95% CI 0.97 to 6.00). In noninvasive NAVA, no mortality or success benefit was shown. The earlier 2023 synthesis (Pinto CB et al., PMID: 36958129), five trials and 643 invasively ventilated patients, found more ventilator-free days (mean difference 3.42, 95% CI 1.21 to 5.62) and less weaning failure (odds ratio 0.51, 95% CI 0.29 to 0.88) but no significant ICU mortality difference (odds ratio 0.58, 95% CI 0.33 to 1.03) — so the mortality claim rests on the newer pooling and is not corroborated trial-by-trial. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): NAVA during invasive ventilation is associated with fewer deaths and more ventilator-free days in pooled small trials; the mortality signal needs a large confirmatory trial.

cards.headline: Wu 2026 (meta-analysis, 9 RCTs, 842 patients): invasive NAVA cut ICU mortality (RR 0.72) and hospital mortality (RR 0.71) and added 3.48 ventilator-free days — noninvasive NAVA showed no benefit
cards.summary: Wu 2026 (meta-analysis, 9 RCTs, 842 patients): invasive NAVA cut ICU mortality (RR 0.72) and hospital mortality (RR 0.71) and added 3.48 ventilator-free days — noninvasive NAVA showed no benefit
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials (Wu 2026)
cards.people: Nine randomised controlled trials involving 842 critically ill patients (389 receiving neurally adjusted ventilatory assist and 453 receiving conventional ventilation), comparing NAVA with other ventilation modes in invasive and noninvasive settings; databases searched to 18 July 2026, quality assessed with the Cochrane Risk of Bias tool 2.0.
cards.result: In patients receiving invasive mechanical ventilation, NAVA reduced ICU mortality (risk ratio 0.72, 95% CI 0.53 to 0.99) and hospital mortality (risk ratio 0.71, 95% CI 0.56 to 0.90) compared with conventional modes — relative reductions of 28% and 29% respectively, with pooled absolute rates not printed in the abstract — and increased the mechanical ventilation success rate (risk ratio 1.13, 95% CI 1.04 to 1.22) and 28-day ventilator-free days (mean difference 3.48 days, 95% CI 0.97 to 6.00). In noninvasive ventilation, NAVA did not significantly reduce hospital mortality (p=0.23) or increase ventilation success (p=0.66).
cards.watchOut: Nine small trials, and the mortality result is a subgroup story: the benefit appears only in the invasive stratum, the ICU-mortality confidence interval just clears 1.0 (upper bound 0.99), and the comparators were assorted conventional modes rather than pressure-support ventilation alone, which is the comparison the shelf question poses. A pooled mortality benefit of this size from trials of this size has a poor track record of surviving a large confirmatory trial.
cards.source: Wu RR et al. Effects of neurally adjusted ventilatory assist on mortality in critically ill patients: A systematic review and meta-analysis. The Journal of International Medical Research. 2026. PMID: 43026034. cards.headline: Pinto 2023 (meta-analysis, 5 RCTs, 643 patients): NAVA added 3.42 ventilator-free days and halved weaning failure (OR 0.51) — but ICU mortality did not differ significantly (OR 0.58, CI crossing 1)
cards.summary: Pinto 2023 (meta-analysis, 5 RCTs, 643 patients): NAVA added 3.42 ventilator-free days and halved weaning failure (OR 0.51) — but ICU mortality did not differ significantly (OR 0.58, CI crossing 1)
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials (Pinto 2023)
cards.people: Five randomised trials (643 patients) comparing NAVA with standard ventilation modes in critically ill adults admitted to the ICU with invasive mechanical ventilation; the main outcome was 28-day ventilator-free days.
cards.result: Patients in the NAVA group had more ventilator-free days than controls (mean difference 3.42 days, 95% CI 1.21 to 5.62; I²=0%) and a reduced incidence of weaning failure (odds ratio 0.51, 95% CI 0.29 to 0.88; I²=0%). ICU mortality did not differ significantly (odds ratio 0.58, 95% CI 0.33 to 1.03; I²=41%), nor did the number of mechanical-ventilation days (mean difference −1.9 days, 95% CI −4.2 to 0.3). The authors conclude NAVA has a modest impact on ventilator-free days and weaning success, with no association with improvements in other relevant clinical outcomes.
cards.watchOut: This earlier, smaller pooling is the honest counterweight to the 2026 mortality claim: the point estimate favoured NAVA on mortality too, but the interval includes no effect, and only five trials inform it. Both syntheses agree on ventilator-free days and weaning; they disagree on whether anyone should yet believe the survival claim.
cards.source: Pinto CB et al. Clinical outcomes in patients undergoing invasive mechanical ventilation using NAVA and other ventilation modes - A systematic review and meta-analysis. Journal of Critical Care. 2023. PMID: 36958129. MeSH: Adult · Humans · Respiration, Artificial · Interactive Ventilatory Support · Ventilator Weaning · Tracheostomy · Hospitalization

cards.headline: Synthesis: two syntheses agree on ventilator-free days and weaning success; the mortality benefit appears in one and not the other
cards.summary: Synthesis: two syntheses agree on ventilator-free days and weaning success; the mortality benefit appears in one and not the other
cards.people: Two meta-analyses of randomised NAVA trials in critically ill adults: nine trials and 842 patients (Wu 2026, invasive and noninvasive) and five trials and 643 invasively ventilated patients (Pinto 2023).
cards.result: Ventilator-free days: +3.48 days (Wu) and +3.42 days (Pinto) — concordant. Weaning/ventilation success: risk ratio 1.13 (Wu); weaning failure odds ratio 0.51 (Pinto). Mortality: ICU risk ratio 0.72 and hospital risk ratio 0.71 in Wu's invasive stratum; ICU odds ratio 0.58 (95% CI 0.33 to 1.03, not significant) in Pinto. Noninvasive NAVA: no benefit shown. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), Tier C set because the shelf carries a mortality-benefit claim resting on small pooled trials.
cards.watchOut: Neither synthesis answers the synchrony question with patient-important weight: asynchrony reduction is NAVA's mechanism and is well documented physiologically, but this shelf grades the outcomes patients feel. NAVA also requires a dedicated oesophageal catheter and a proprietary ventilator platform, so the pooled result is not portable to every ICU.
cards.source: Synthesis of Wu RR et al. The Journal of International Medical Research. 2026 (PMID: 43026034); Pinto CB et al. Journal of Critical Care. 2023 (PMID: 36958129).

shelves.title: Letting the ventilator run the weaning: automated systems shortened weaning time by 2.68 days in the 2014 Cochrane review, and the 62-trial update still finds less time on the ventilator — with no mortality difference
shelves.question: In mechanically ventilated adults, do automated weaning and spontaneous-breathing-trial systems shorten weaning time compared with clinician-led weaning?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Automation/instrumentation · Critical Illness · Humans · Intensive Care Units · Length of Stay · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Time Factors · Ventilator Weaning/instrumentation/methods · Ventilators, Mechanical/adverse effects · Work of Breathing
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for time, not for survival. The 2014 Cochrane review (Burns KEA et al., PMID: 25203308) pooled ten SmartCare trials and 654 participants and found automated weaning cut weaning time by a mean of 2.68 days (95% CI −3.99 to −1.37), shortened time to successful extubation by 0.99 days and ICU stay by 5.70 days, and reduced the proportions ventilated beyond seven days (risk ratio 0.44) and 21 days (risk ratio 0.39), with no effect on mortality or reintubation. The 2025 Cochrane update of the broader closed-loop literature (Rose L et al., PMID: 40678933) — 62 trials, 5,052 participants — found automated systems probably reduce ventilation duration (a 24% relative reduction, 95% CI 18% to 30%, with absolute durations varying by trial), ICU stay (14% relative reduction) and reintubation (risk ratio 0.73, 95% CI 0.59 to 0.89), again with little to no mortality difference (risk ratio 0.94, 95% CI 0.82 to 1.07). Two cautions ride on the face: the 2014 effect was largest against non-protocolised clinician weaning, so part of the gain may be protocolisation rather than automation; and the evidence certainty is low to moderate. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): automated weaning systems get patients off the ventilator sooner without a shown survival effect or a reintubation penalty.

cards.headline: Burns 2014 (Cochrane review, 10 SmartCare trials, 654 patients): weaning time cut by 2.68 days and ICU stay by 5.70 days — mortality and reintubation unchanged
cards.summary: Burns 2014 (Cochrane review, 10 SmartCare trials, 654 patients): weaning time cut by 2.68 days and ICU stay by 5.70 days — mortality and reintubation unchanged
cards.people: Ten randomised and quasi-randomised trials involving 654 invasively ventilated critically ill adults weaned with the SmartCare automated weaning and SBT system versus non-automated weaning strategies; eight trials were judged at low or unclear risk of bias and two at high risk.
cards.result: SmartCare decreased weaning time (mean difference −2.68 days, 95% CI −3.99 to −1.37; p<0.0001; seven trials, 495 participants; moderate-quality evidence), time to successful extubation (mean difference −0.99 days, 95% CI −1.89 to −0.09) and length of ICU stay (mean difference −5.70 days, 95% CI −10.54 to −0.85). It reduced the proportions receiving ventilation for longer than seven days (risk ratio 0.44, 95% CI 0.23 to 0.85) and 21 days (risk ratio 0.39, 95% CI 0.18 to 0.86) and total ventilation duration (mean difference −1.68 days, 95% CI −3.33 to −0.03). SmartCare had no effect on time to first successful SBT, mortality, or adverse events, specifically reintubation.
cards.watchOut: One commercial system (SmartCare) supplies all ten trials, and the review's own subgroup analysis hints the advantage shrinks when the control arm is itself protocolised — the machine may partly be a way of enforcing a weaning protocol that good clinician-led care already follows. Evidence quality ranged from low to moderate.
cards.source: Burns KEA et al. Automated weaning and SBT systems versus non-automated weaning strategies for weaning time in invasively ventilated critically ill adults. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2014. PMID: 25203308. cards.headline: Rose 2025 (Cochrane update, 62 trials, 5,052 patients): automated closed-loop systems probably cut ventilation duration by a relative 24% and reintubation risk (RR 0.73) — mortality RR 0.94, little to no difference
cards.summary: Rose 2025 (Cochrane update, 62 trials, 5,052 patients): automated closed-loop systems probably cut ventilation duration by a relative 24% and reintubation risk (RR 0.73) — mortality RR 0.94, little to no difference
cards.type: Cochrane systematic review and meta-analysis, updated (Rose 2025)
cards.people: Sixty-two randomised trials (59 in adults, 3 in children) with 5,052 participants (4,834 adults, 218 children) receiving invasive mechanical ventilation in intensive care, evaluating ten commercially available automated closed-loop systems and one non-commercial system versus non-automated weaning (non-protocolised usual care or protocolised weaning); searches ran to 2 February 2024.
cards.result: Automated closed-loop systems probably reduce the duration of mechanical ventilation (mean difference −0.28 log hours, 95% CI −0.36 to −0.20; 51 RCTs, 3,929 participants; moderate-certainty evidence), translating to a 24% relative reduction (95% CI 18% to 30%) with absolute durations varying across trials. They probably result in little to no difference in mortality (risk ratio 0.94, 95% CI 0.82 to 1.07; 38 RCTs, 3,620 participants, 618 events) and probably reduce ICU length of stay (a 14% relative reduction, 95% CI 9% to 18%) and hospital stay (10% relative reduction). They probably reduce reintubation (risk ratio 0.73, 95% CI 0.59 to 0.89), post-extubation non-invasive ventilation (risk ratio 0.74), prolonged ventilation (risk ratio 0.54) and tracheostomy (risk ratio 0.75). No studies reported health-related quality of life.
cards.watchOut: The pooled ventilation-duration result carries I²=87% heterogeneity, and the log-scale headline means the absolute days saved depend heavily on how long a unit's patients are ventilated at baseline. Children contribute 218 of 5,052 participants, so this remains essentially an adult evidence base; the shelf question is about adults and the adult trials dominate.
cards.source: Rose L et al. Automated versus non-automated weaning for reducing the duration of mechanical ventilation for critically ill adults and children. cards.search: rose 2025 (cochrane update, 62 trials, 5,052 patients): automated closed-loop systems probably cut ventilation duration by a relative 24% and reintubation risk (rr 0.73) — mortality rr 0.94, little to no difference rose 2025 (cochrane update, 62 trials, 5,052 patients): automated closed-loop systems probably cut ventilation duration by a relative 24% and reintubation risk (rr 0.73) — mortality rr 0.94, little to no difference in mechanically ventilated adults, do automated weaning and spontaneous-breathing-trial systems shorten weaning time compared with clinician-led weaning? cochrane systematic review and meta-analysis, updated (rose 2025) sixty-two randomised trials (59 in adults, 3 in children) with 5,052 participants (4,834 adults, 218 children) receiving invasive mechanical ventilation in intensive care, evaluating ten commercially available automated closed-loop systems and one non-commercial system versus non-automated weaning (non-protocolised usual care or protocolised weaning); searches ran to 2 february 2024. automated closed-loop systems probably reduce the duration of mechanical ventilation (mean difference −0.28 log hours, 95% ci −0.36 to −0.20; 51 rcts, 3,929 participants; moderate-certainty evidence), translating to a 24% relative reduction (95% ci 18% to 30%) with absolute durations varying across trials. they probably result in little to no difference in mortality (risk ratio 0.94, 95% ci 0.82 to 1.07; 38 rcts, 3,620 participants, 618 events) and probably reduce icu length of stay (a 14% relative reduction, 95% ci 9% to 18%) and hospital stay (10% relative reduction). they probably reduce reintubation (risk ratio 0.73, 95% ci 0.59 to 0.89), post-extubation non-invasive ventilation (risk ratio 0.74), prolonged ventilation (risk ratio 0.54) and tracheostomy (risk ratio 0.75). no studies reported health-related quality of life. the pooled ventilation-duration result carries i²=87% heterogeneity, and the log-scale headline means the absolute days saved depend heavily on how long a unit's patients are ventilated at baseline. children contribute 218 of 5,052 participants, so this remains essentially an adult evidence base; cards.headline: Synthesis: a decade apart, two Cochrane syntheses agree — the machine weans faster, nobody has shown it saves lives, and reintubation does not rise
cards.summary: Synthesis: a decade apart, two Cochrane syntheses agree — the machine weans faster, nobody has shown it saves lives, and reintubation does not rise
cards.people: Two Cochrane syntheses of randomised trials of automated weaning/closed-loop systems versus non-automated weaning in invasively ventilated ICU patients: 10 SmartCare trials, 654 participants (2014) and 62 closed-loop trials, 5,052 participants (2025).
cards.result: Weaning time: −2.68 days with SmartCare (2014). Ventilation duration: 24% relative reduction (2025). ICU stay: −5.70 days (2014); 14% relative reduction (2025). Mortality: no effect (2014); risk ratio 0.94 (95% CI 0.82 to 1.07) (2025). Reintubation: no increase (2014); risk ratio 0.73 (2025). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) on time-based outcomes. Tier C is not set: two concordant Cochrane syntheses over dozens of randomised trials, and no mortality-benefit claim is made.
cards.watchOut: The fair comparator matters: where clinician-led weaning is already protocolised and daily, the automation premium is likely smaller than the pooled figures suggest. These systems also shift, rather than remove, clinician work — alarms, overrides and protocol exceptions still need a clinician at the bedside.
cards.source: Synthesis of Burns KEA et al. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2014 (PMID: 25203308); Rose L et al. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2025 (PMID: 40678933).
