shelves.title: Thirty minutes is enough: in 526 patients ready for weaning, a 30-minute breathing trial identified successful extubation as reliably as a 120-minute trial (75.9% vs 73.0% still extubated at 48 hours)
shelves.question: In patients ready for a spontaneous breathing trial, does a 30-minute trial identify successful extubation as reliably as a 120-minute trial?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Hospital Mortality · Humans · Intensive Care Units · Intubation, Intratracheal · Male · Middle Aged · Prospective Studies · Recurrence · Respiration · Respiration, Artificial/mortality · Respiratory Insufficiency/physiopathology/therapy · Treatment Outcome · Ventilator Weaning/mortality
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — the shorter trial reads the patient just as well. In the multicentre randomised comparison (Esteban A et al., PMID: 9927366), 526 ventilated patients considered ready for weaning were assigned target spontaneous-breathing-trial durations of 30 or 120 minutes: 87.8% versus 84.8% completed the trial without distress and were extubated (p=0.32), reintubation within 48 hours was 13.5% versus 13.4%, and the proportions still extubated at 48 hours were 75.9% versus 73.0% (p=0.43), with similar within-unit mortality (13% vs 9%) and in-hospital mortality (19% vs 18%). The 2025 SL-SBT trial (Hadda V et al., PMID: 39504619) asked the same question in the harder population — 119 patients who had already failed a first trial — and again found successful extubation in 58.3% on 30 minutes versus 59.3% on 120 minutes (p=0.91), with no differences in ICU or hospital stay or in in-hospital and 90-day mortality. Two randomised comparisons a quarter-century apart, in easy and difficult weaning alike, land in the same place. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): a 30-minute trial identifies successful extubation as reliably as a 120-minute trial, and the extra 90 minutes buy no information.

cards.headline: Esteban 1999 (multicentre RCT, 526 patients): still extubated at 48 hours in 75.9% after a 30-minute trial vs 73.0% after 120 minutes (p=0.43); reintubation 13.5% vs 13.4%
cards.summary: Esteban 1999 (multicentre RCT, 526 patients): still extubated at 48 hours in 75.9% after a 30-minute trial vs 73.0% after 120 minutes (p=0.43); reintubation 13.5% vs 13.4%
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (Esteban 1999, Spanish Lung Failure Collaborative Group)
cards.people: 526 ventilator-supported patients in a prospective multicentre study, considered ready for weaning, assigned to a spontaneous breathing trial with a target duration of 30 minutes (n=270) or 120 minutes (n=256) before extubation.
cards.result: Of the 30- and 120-minute groups, 237 (87.8%) and 216 (84.8%) respectively completed the trial without distress and were extubated (p=0.32); 32 (13.5%) and 29 (13.4%) of those extubated required reintubation within 48 hours. The percentage remaining extubated 48 hours after the trial did not differ (75.9% vs 73.0%; p=0.43). Within-unit mortality (13% vs 9%) and in-hospital mortality (19% vs 18%) were similar. Patients who required reintubation had much higher mortality than those who tolerated extubation (32.8% vs 4.6%; p<0.001). No measurement during or before the trial discriminated patients who would need reintubation.
cards.watchOut: A 1999 trial from the era before lung-protective ventilation was universal, conducted in patients having a first trial they were expected to pass — its event rates, not just its conclusion, belong to that population. It was a prospective randomised comparison but predates trial registration, so no registry ID exists in the record.
cards.source: Esteban A et al. Effect of spontaneous breathing trial duration on outcome of attempts to discontinue mechanical ventilation. Spanish Lung Failure Collaborative Group. American Journal of Respiratory and Critical Care Medicine. 1999. PMID: 9927366. cards.headline: Hadda 2025 (SL-SBT, single-centre RCT, 119 difficult-weaning patients): extubation success 58.3% with a 30-minute trial vs 59.3% with 120 minutes (p=0.91)
cards.summary: Hadda 2025 (SL-SBT, single-centre RCT, 119 difficult-weaning patients): extubation success 58.3% with a 30-minute trial vs 59.3% with 120 minutes (p=0.91)
cards.people: 119 adults (62.2% male, mean age 53.9 years) at a single centre who had failed their first spontaneous breathing trial, randomised to a pressure-support trial of 30 minutes (n=60) or 120 minutes (n=59); 82.4% had hypercapnic respiratory failure. The primary outcome was successful extubation without reintubation within 48 hours.
cards.result: Successful extubation rates were similar with 30- and 120-minute trials (58.3% vs 59.3%; p=0.91). There were no significant differences in ICU or hospital length of stay, or in in-hospital and 90-day mortality. The authors conclude that a 30-minute trial may be acceptable in this difficult-weaning setting.
cards.watchOut: Small and single-centre, and deliberately the mirror image of Esteban's population — these patients had already failed once, which is why success rates sit near 59% rather than 75%. Concordance across such different populations strengthens the conclusion, but neither trial was powered as a formal non-inferiority study with a pre-set margin.
cards.source: Hadda V et al. Short (30 Minutes) versus long (120 Minutes) spontaneous breathing trial among patients with difficult weaning (SL-SBT Trial). Heart & Lung. 2025. PMID: 39504619. cards.headline: Synthesis: first-trial patients in 1999 and failed-first-trial patients in 2025 give the same answer — trial length does not sort successes from failures
cards.summary: Synthesis: first-trial patients in 1999 and failed-first-trial patients in 2025 give the same answer — trial length does not sort successes from failures
cards.people: Two randomised comparisons of 30- versus 120-minute spontaneous breathing trials totalling 645 patients: 526 ready-for-weaning patients in a 1999 multicentre trial and 119 difficult-weaning patients in a 2025 single-centre trial.
cards.result: Still extubated at 48 hours: 75.9% vs 73.0% (30 vs 120 minutes, 1999). Successful extubation after a failed first trial: 58.3% vs 59.3% (2025). Reintubation, lengths of stay and mortality: no significant differences in either trial. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference). Tier C is not set: two concordant randomised trials address the question directly and no mortality claim is made.
cards.watchOut: Both trials used clinician-judged readiness and mostly pressure-support or T-piece trials as practised at the time; a unit whose 120-minute trial is really a fatigue stress-test for marginal patients is extrapolating beyond either study if it shortens trials for its frailest patients without watching reintubation rates.
cards.source: Synthesis of Esteban A et al. American Journal of Respiratory and Critical Care Medicine. 1999 (PMID: 9927366); Hadda V et al. Heart & Lung. 2025 (PMID: 39504619).

shelves.title: Wake up and breathe: pairing daily sedation interruption with breathing trials added 3.1 ventilator-free days and saved one life per seven treated in the ABC trial — the early cognitive gain had faded by 12 months
shelves.question: In mechanically ventilated adults, does pairing daily sedation interruption with spontaneous breathing trials increase ventilator-free days and improve long-term cognitive outcomes compared with usual care?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Procedural Sedation · Critical Care/methods · Female · Humans · Intensive Care Units · Male · Middle Aged · Respiration · Respiration, Artificial · Safety · Ventilator Weaning
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — on time off the ventilator and on survival in one trial; the cognitive half of the question is where the answer thins. In the Awakening and Breathing Controlled trial (Girard TD et al., PMID: 18191684), 336 ventilated patients randomised to a paired daily spontaneous awakening trial followed by a spontaneous breathing trial spent 14.7 versus 11.6 days breathing without assistance over 28 days (mean difference 3.1 days, 95% CI 0.7 to 5.6; p=0.02), left ICU earlier (median 9.1 vs 12.9 days) and hospital earlier (14.9 vs 19.2 days), and were less likely to die over the following year (hazard ratio 0.68, 95% CI 0.50 to 0.92; number needed to treat 7.4) — a mortality claim, which is why this shelf is Tier C. The harm on the face: more self-extubations in the intervention group (16 vs 6 patients; p=0.03), though reintubation after self-extubation and total reintubation rates (13.8% vs 12.5%) did not differ. The pre-planned long-term substudy (Jackson JC et al., PMID: 20299535) found cognitive impairment less common at 3 months (absolute risk reduction 20.2%, 95% CI 1.5% to 36.1%; p=0.03) but not at 12 months (absolute risk reduction −1.9%; p=0.89), with composite cognitive scores, depression, PTSD symptoms and functional outcomes similar throughout — so the survival benefit was not bought with worse brains, but a durable cognitive benefit was not shown either. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): paired awakening and breathing trials free patients from the ventilator sooner and improved one-year survival in a single trial; long-term cognition was no worse, and no better by 12 months.

cards.headline: Girard 2008 (ABC trial, 336 patients): 14.7 vs 11.6 days breathing unassisted, ICU discharge 3.8 days sooner, and 1-year mortality hazard ratio 0.68 — with more self-extubations (16 vs 6)
cards.summary: Girard 2008 (ABC trial, 336 patients): 14.7 vs 11.6 days breathing unassisted, ICU discharge 3.8 days sooner, and 1-year mortality hazard ratio 0.68 — with more self-extubations (16 vs 6)
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (Girard 2008, Awakening and Breathing Controlled trial)
cards.people: 336 mechanically ventilated patients in four tertiary-care hospitals, randomised to management with a daily spontaneous awakening trial (interruption of sedatives) followed by a spontaneous breathing trial (intervention, n=168) or sedation per usual care plus a daily spontaneous breathing trial (control, n=168); the primary endpoint was time breathing without assistance, analysed by intention to treat.
cards.result: The intervention group spent more days breathing without assistance during the 28-day study period (14.7 vs 11.6 days; mean difference 3.1 days, 95% CI 0.7 to 5.6; p=0.02) and were discharged from intensive care earlier (median 9.1 vs 12.9 days; p=0.01) and from hospital earlier (median 14.9 vs 19.2 days; p=0.04). More intervention patients self-extubated (16 vs 6 patients; 6.0% difference, 95% CI 0.6% to 11.8%; p=0.03), but reintubation after self-extubation (5 vs 3 patients) and total reintubation rates (13.8% vs 12.5%; p=0.73) were similar. At any instant during the year after enrolment, intervention patients were less likely to die (hazard ratio 0.68, 95% CI 0.50 to 0.92; p=0.01); the number needed to treat to save one life was 7.4 (95% CI 4.2 to 35.5).
cards.watchOut: A single open-label trial from 2008 whose control arm — usual-care sedation with a daily breathing trial but no awakening trial — is heavier sedation than many modern units practise, so the incremental gain over today's lighter-sedation usual care is probably smaller. The mortality result, while pre-specified follow-up, comes from one trial of 336 patients; that is why the stamp is POSSIBLE and the shelf is Tier C.

cards.headline: Jackson 2010 (ABC long-term substudy, 180 patients): cognitive impairment less common at 3 months (absolute risk reduction 20.2%) but not at 12 months (−1.9%); depression, PTSD and function similar throughout
cards.summary: Jackson 2010 (ABC long-term substudy, 180 patients): cognitive impairment less common at 3 months (absolute risk reduction 20.2%) but not at 12 months (−1.9%); depression, PTSD and function similar throughout
cards.people: 180 medical ICU patients at one tertiary-care hospital within the multicentre ABC trial, randomised to paired daily spontaneous awakening and breathing trials or usual-care sedation plus daily breathing trials, assessed for cognitive, psychological and functional/quality-of-life outcomes 3 and 12 months after discharge; the substudy was planned a priori.
cards.result: Cognitive impairment was less common in the intervention group at 3-month follow-up (absolute risk reduction 20.2%; 95% CI 1.5% to 36.1%; p=0.03) but not at 12-month follow-up (absolute risk reduction −1.9%; 95% CI −21.3% to 27.1%; p=0.89). Composite cognitive scores were similar in the two groups at 3 and 12 months (p=0.80 and 0.61), as were symptoms of depression (p=0.59 and 0.82) and post-traumatic stress disorder (p=0.59 and 0.97). Activities of daily living, functional status and mental and physical quality of life were similar between groups throughout follow-up. The authors conclude the protocol's proven benefits, including improved 1-year survival, were not offset by adverse long-term outcomes.
cards.watchOut: One centre's 180 patients, with the 3-month cognitive signal resting on a dichotomised impairment definition while the composite scores — the more sensitive measure — never differed at either time point. Survivors who return for testing are a selected subset of both arms, and the wide 12-month interval (−21.3% to 27.1%) cannot exclude meaningful effects in either direction.
cards.source: Jackson JC et al. Long-term cognitive and psychological outcomes in the awakening and breathing controlled trial. American Journal of Respiratory and Critical Care Medicine. 2010. cards.headline: Synthesis: faster liberation and better survival in the parent trial; the follow-up's job was to check the brain, and it found no lasting harm — and no lasting cognitive benefit
cards.summary: Synthesis: faster liberation and better survival in the parent trial; the follow-up's job was to check the brain, and it found no lasting harm — and no lasting cognitive benefit
cards.people: One multicentre randomised trial of 336 ventilated patients (ABC, 2008) plus its pre-planned single-centre long-term substudy of 180 patients assessed at 3 and 12 months.
cards.result: Days breathing unassisted in 28 days: 14.7 vs 11.6 (difference 3.1 days). One-year mortality: hazard ratio 0.68 (95% CI 0.50 to 0.92). Self-extubation: 16 vs 6 patients, without excess reintubation. Cognitive impairment: absolute risk reduction 20.2% at 3 months, −1.9% at 12 months; composite cognition, mood, PTSD and function similar at both points. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit). Tier C is set: a single trial carries the shelf and it claims a mortality benefit.
cards.watchOut: Do not let the 3-month cognitive headline travel without its 12-month companion — the honest summary is 'no long-term cognitive harm detected', not 'protects the brain'. Later practice has also absorbed much of the intervention into usual care, narrowing the contrast this trial measured.
cards.source: Synthesis of Girard TD et al. Lancet. 2008 (PMID: 18191684); Jackson JC et al. American Journal of Respiratory and Critical Care Medicine. 2010 (PMID: 20299535).

shelves.title: Ultrasound at the bedside: diaphragm and lung ultrasound predict weaning success with an area under the curve near 0.87 — a prediction tool, with no trial yet showing ultrasound-guided extubation helps patients
shelves.question: In mechanically ventilated patients, can diaphragm and lung ultrasound predict weaning success accurately enough to guide extubation decisions?
shelves.mesh: Airway Extubation · Critical Illness/therapy · Diaphragm/diagnostic imaging · Humans · Lung/diagnostic imaging · Reproducibility of Results · Ultrasonography/methods · Ventilator Weaning/methods · Weaning
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — as a predictor, not as a treatment: this shelf grades a test, and no stamp of benefit attaches to scanning itself. The Chest meta-analysis (Llamas-Álvarez AM et al., PMID: 28864053) pooled 19 studies and 1,071 critically ill adults: for diaphragm thickening fraction the area under the summary receiver-operating characteristic curve was 0.87 with a diagnostic odds ratio of 21 (95% CI 11 to 40); for diaphragmatic excursion, pooled sensitivity and specificity were each 75% (diagnostic odds ratio 10, 95% CI 4 to 24); for lung ultrasound the area under the curve was 0.77 with a diagnostic odds ratio of 38 but a very wide interval (95% CI 7 to 198). The 2023 Critical Care meta-analysis of diaphragmatic ultrasound (Parada-Gereda HM et al., PMID: 37147688), 19 studies and 1,204 patients in the pooled analysis, found excursion sensitivity 0.80 and specificity 0.80 and thickening-fraction sensitivity 0.85 and specificity 0.75, both with an area under the curve of 0.87 — concordant numbers, alongside significant heterogeneity and cut-off values that varied between studies. Accuracy of this order can inform an extubation decision; it cannot make one, and no randomised trial has tested whether acting on these measurements improves outcomes. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: diaphragm ultrasound predicts weaning outcome with moderate, reproducible accuracy (sensitivity and specificity around 0.75–0.85); whether ultrasound-guided extubation decisions help patients is untested.

cards.headline: Llamas-Álvarez 2017 (meta-analysis, 19 studies, 1,071 patients): diaphragm thickening fraction AUC 0.87 (DOR 21); excursion sensitivity and specificity 75%; lung ultrasound AUC 0.77
cards.summary: Llamas-Álvarez 2017 (meta-analysis, 19 studies, 1,071 patients): diaphragm thickening fraction AUC 0.87 (DOR 21); excursion sensitivity and specificity 75%; lung ultrasound AUC 0.77
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of diagnostic accuracy (Llamas-Álvarez 2017)
cards.people: Nineteen studies involving 1,071 critically ill adults undergoing mechanical ventilation, assessing lung and diaphragm ultrasound for predicting weaning outcomes; study quality was assessed with the Quality Assessment of Diagnostic Accuracy Studies-2 tool and pooled with a bivariate random-effects model.
cards.result: For diaphragm thickening fraction, the area under the summary receiver-operating characteristic curve was 0.87 and the diagnostic odds ratio was 21 (95% CI 11 to 40). For diaphragmatic excursion, pooled sensitivity was 75% (95% CI 65% to 85%), pooled specificity 75% (95% CI 60% to 85%), and the diagnostic odds ratio 10 (95% CI 4 to 24). For lung ultrasound, the area under the curve was 0.77 and the diagnostic odds ratio 38 (95% CI 7 to 198). Meta-regression found higher thickening-fraction specificity and higher excursion sensitivity in studies with applicability concerns. The authors conclude lung and diaphragm ultrasound can help predict weaning outcome, but accuracy may vary depending on the patient subpopulation.
cards.watchOut: Diagnostic odds ratios flatter tests: a DOR of 21 with sensitivity and specificity near 0.75–0.80 still misclassifies roughly one patient in four to five, and the lung-ultrasound DOR interval (7 to 198) is too wide to grade that component at all. Cut-offs for thickening fraction and excursion differed across the primary studies, so there is no single validated threshold a clinician can lift from this paper.
cards.source: Llamas-Alvarez AM et al. Diaphragm and Lung Ultrasound to Predict Weaning Outcome: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Chest. 2017. PMID: 28864053. cards.headline: Parada-Gereda 2023 (meta-analysis, 19 pooled studies, 1,204 patients): diaphragm excursion sensitivity 0.80/specificity 0.80 and thickening fraction 0.85/0.75, AUC 0.87 for both — with significant heterogeneity
cards.summary: Parada-Gereda 2023 (meta-analysis, 19 pooled studies, 1,204 patients): diaphragm excursion sensitivity 0.80/specificity 0.80 and thickening fraction 0.85/0.75, AUC 0.87 for both — with significant heterogeneity
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of diagnostic accuracy (Parada-Gereda 2023)
cards.people: Twenty-six studies of diaphragmatic ultrasound for predicting weaning success from mechanical ventilation, of which 19 entered the meta-analysis (1,204 patients); studies were published between January 2016 and July 2022 and assessed with the QUADAS-2 tool and GRADE.
cards.result: For diaphragmatic excursion, sensitivity was 0.80 (95% CI 0.77 to 0.83), specificity 0.80 (95% CI 0.75 to 0.84), area under the summary receiver-operating characteristic curve 0.87, and diagnostic odds ratio 17.1 (95% CI 10.2 to 28.6). For the thickening fraction, sensitivity was 0.85 (95% CI 0.82 to 0.87), specificity 0.75 (95% CI 0.69 to 0.80), area under the curve 0.87, and diagnostic odds ratio 17.2 (95% CI 9.16 to 32.3). Heterogeneity among studies was significant; excluding studies with atypical cut-off values raised thickening-fraction sensitivity and specificity, and patient position at testing was a source of heterogeneity in meta-regression. The authors call for high-quality studies in specific ICU subgroups.
cards.watchOut: This synthesis covers the diaphragm only — the lung-ultrasound half of the shelf question rests on the 2017 paper alone. Sensitivity of 0.85 means roughly one in seven patients destined to fail weaning still tests 'ready', which is why these measurements belong inside a clinical assessment, not in place of one.

cards.headline: Synthesis: two meta-analyses, one consistent accuracy band (AUC ≈0.87, sensitivity/specificity ≈0.75–0.85) — and a missing step between predicting failure and preventing it
cards.summary: Synthesis: two meta-analyses, one consistent accuracy band (AUC ≈0.87, sensitivity/specificity ≈0.75–0.85) — and a missing step between predicting failure and preventing it
cards.people: Two diagnostic-accuracy meta-analyses in mechanically ventilated adults: 19 studies and 1,071 patients covering lung and diaphragm ultrasound (2017), and 19 pooled studies and 1,204 patients covering diaphragm ultrasound (2023).
cards.result: Diaphragm thickening fraction: AUC 0.87 in both syntheses; sensitivity 0.85, specificity 0.75 (2023). Diaphragm excursion: sensitivity 0.75–0.80, specificity 0.75–0.80. Lung ultrasound: AUC 0.77 (2017 only). No randomised trial of ultrasound-guided extubation decisions exists in either record. PROPOSED POSSIBLE as a prediction tool. Tier C is set: this is a diagnostic-accuracy shelf resting on heterogeneous observational accuracy studies, with no trial evidence that using the test improves outcomes.
cards.watchOut: Prediction is not prevention: a test can be accurate and still useless if clinicians already know what it says, or harmful if a 'good' scan rushes a marginal patient to extubation. The missing evidence is a trial randomising patients to ultrasound-informed versus standard weaning decisions.
cards.source: Synthesis of Llamas-Alvarez AM et al. Chest. 2017 (PMID: 28864053); Parada-Gereda HM et al. Critical Care. 2023 (PMID: 37147688).

shelves.title: Training the breathing muscle: in prolonged ventilation, inspiratory muscle training tripled the odds of weaning success in the pooled small trials (OR 3.05) and strengthened the in-breath by 6.1 cm H2O — with protocols all over the map
shelves.question: In patients undergoing prolonged mechanical ventilation, does inspiratory muscle training improve weaning success and breathing-muscle strength compared with sham or usual care?
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — from seven small recent trials whose protocols barely resemble each other. The 2025 systematic review and meta-analysis (Andrade-Rebolledo FA et al., PMID: 41608455) analysed seven randomised trials published since 2019, totalling 642 ICU patients across training strategies, in prolonged mechanical ventilation. In the pooled weaning-success analysis (three studies, IMT versus T-piece control), the odds ratio was 3.05 (95% CI 1.83 to 5.10; I²=0%) — an odds ratio from randomised comparisons, printed here without absolute success rates, which the review does not pool. High-intensity training improved maximal inspiratory pressure by a pooled mean difference of 6.13 cm H2O (95% CI 3.15 to 9.11; I²=59%) versus low-intensity training or usual care across six studies. The counterweight is inside the same review: several included trials (Bissett, Roceto Ratti, Sandoval, Réginault) found no significant difference in weaning success, the positive results concentrate in high-intensity protocols (loads above roughly 50–60% of maximal inspiratory pressure), and the authors themselves state that variability in protocols and populations limits generalisability and that standardisation is urgently needed. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): high-intensity inspiratory muscle training probably improves weaning success and inspiratory strength in prolonged ventilation, but the recipe — device, load, dose — is not yet standardised.

cards.headline: Andrade-Rebolledo 2025 (meta-analysis, 7 RCTs, 642 patients): weaning success odds ratio 3.05 (95% CI 1.83 to 5.10) and maximal inspiratory pressure +6.13 cm H2O with high-intensity training
cards.summary: Andrade-Rebolledo 2025 (meta-analysis, 7 RCTs, 642 patients): weaning success odds ratio 3.05 (95% CI 1.83 to 5.10) and maximal inspiratory pressure +6.13 cm H2O with high-intensity training
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials (Andrade-Rebolledo 2025)
cards.people: Seven randomised controlled trials published since 2019, totalling 642 ICU patients across the included training strategies, in patients undergoing prolonged mechanical ventilation; trials compared various inspiratory muscle training protocols (threshold or electronic resistive devices, at intensities from low to above 60% of maximal inspiratory pressure) against sham, T-piece trials or usual care. Numbers beyond the abstract are taken from the free full text of the same record (PMC12835378), as the abstract reports no pooled estimates.
cards.result: In the forest plot pooling three studies of IMT versus T-piece control, the total odds ratio for weaning success was 3.05 (95% CI 1.83 to 5.10), with low heterogeneity (I²=0%). High-intensity IMT improved maximal inspiratory pressure compared with low-intensity IMT or usual care, with a pooled mean difference of 6.13 cm H2O (95% CI 3.15 to 9.11) and moderate heterogeneity (I²=59%); four of six studies individually favoured high-intensity training significantly. Individual trials by da Silva Guimarães, Khodabandeloo and Kazemi showed significant improvements in extubation/weaning success, while trials by Bissett, Roceto Ratti, Sandoval and Réginault found no significant difference in weaning success.
cards.watchOut: The abstract of this record contains no numbers at all — every figure on this card comes from the article's full text and forest plots, and the weaning-success pool rests on only three of the seven trials. Definitions of 'prolonged' ventilation varied (from ≥48 hours to >7 days), devices and loads varied, and the review's own conclusion is that protocol variability limits generalisability. The record carries no MeSH terms (PubMed-not-MEDLINE), so the source line says so plainly.
cards.source: Andrade-Rebolledo FA et al. Inspiratory muscle training in weaning from prolonged mechanical ventilation: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Frontiers in Medicine. 2025. PMID: 41608455. MeSH: none in the record

cards.headline: Synthesis: a real-looking signal for high-intensity training, assembled from small heterogeneous trials — enough to use, not enough to standardise
cards.summary: Synthesis: a real-looking signal for high-intensity training, assembled from small heterogeneous trials — enough to use, not enough to standardise
cards.people: One 2025 systematic review and meta-analysis of seven randomised trials (642 patients) of inspiratory muscle training in prolonged mechanical ventilation.
cards.result: Weaning success: pooled odds ratio 3.05 (95% CI 1.83 to 5.10; three studies, I²=0%). Maximal inspiratory pressure: +6.13 cm H2O (95% CI 3.15 to 9.11) for high-intensity versus low-intensity or usual care (six studies). Four of seven trials were individually null on weaning success. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit). Tier C is set: a single synthesis of small trials with non-standardised interventions carries the shelf.
cards.watchOut: An odds ratio of 3.05 without pooled absolute rates cannot tell a family how much more likely weaning becomes — baseline success in prolonged ventilation varies widely, and the review does not pool the absolute numbers. Intensity looks like the active ingredient (benefit concentrates above ~50–60% of maximal inspiratory pressure), so low-intensity 'training' should not borrow this shelf's stamp.

shelves.title: A mask straight after the tube comes out: in hypercapnic patients, immediate NIV cut post-extubation respiratory failure from 48% to 15% and lowered 90-day mortality in the Ferrer trial
shelves.question: In hypercapnic patients recovering from acute respiratory failure, does starting noninvasive ventilation immediately after extubation prevent post-extubation respiratory failure compared with standard oxygen therapy?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Chronic Disease · Device Removal · Female · Hospital Mortality · Humans · Hypercapnia/complications · Intubation, Intratracheal · Length of Stay · Male · Positive-Pressure Respiration/adverse effects · Respiration, Artificial/adverse effects · Respiratory Insufficiency/blood/etiology/physiopathology/therapy · Treatment Outcome · Ventilator Weaning
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — in the hypercapnic, chronic-respiratory-disorder population the trials actually enrolled. In Ferrer 2009 (Ferrer M et al., PMID: 19682735), 106 patients with chronic respiratory disorders who were hypercapnic during a successful breathing trial were randomised to NIV for 24 hours after extubation or conventional oxygen: respiratory failure within 72 hours occurred in 15% versus 48% (odds ratio 5.32 for the control direction as printed, 95% CI 2.11 to 13.46; p<0.0001; adjusted odds ratio 0.17, 95% CI 0.06 to 0.44, for NIV), and 90-day mortality was lower with NIV (p=0.0146; the abstract prints no absolute mortality rates, so none are claimed here). In Nava 2005 (Nava S et al., PMID: 16276167), 97 patients at risk of post-extubation failure — hypercapnia was one of several qualifying risks — received NIV at least 8 hours a day for 48 hours or standard therapy: reintubation was 4 of 48 versus 12 of 49 (p=0.027), and ICU mortality risk fell by 10% (p<0.01), an effect the authors attribute to the avoided reintubations. The boundary matters: these are prevention trials in selected high-risk and hypercapnic patients, the opposite strategy from rescue NIV once failure is established, which harmed patients in the Esteban trial (shelf #3135). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): immediate post-extubation NIV prevents respiratory failure in hypercapnic patients, with a mortality signal in both trials.

cards.headline: Ferrer 2009 (RCT, 106 hypercapnic patients): post-extubation respiratory failure 15% on immediate NIV vs 48% on oxygen (p<0.0001), and 90-day mortality lower (p=0.0146)
cards.summary: Ferrer 2009 (RCT, 106 hypercapnic patients): post-extubation respiratory failure 15% on immediate NIV vs 48% on oxygen (p<0.0001), and 90-day mortality lower (p=0.0146)
cards.people: 106 mechanically ventilated patients in three Spanish intensive care units, with chronic respiratory disorders and hypercapnia after a successful spontaneous breathing trial, randomised to non-invasive ventilation for 24 hours after extubation (n=54) or conventional oxygen treatment (n=52); the primary endpoint was avoidance of respiratory failure within 72 hours after extubation, analysed by intention to treat.
cards.result: Respiratory failure after extubation was less frequent with non-invasive ventilation than with conventional oxygen (8 [15%] vs 25 [48%]; odds ratio 5.32 [95% CI 2.11 to 13.46]; p<0.0001), and NIV was independently associated with a lower risk of post-extubation respiratory failure (adjusted odds ratio 0.17 [95% CI 0.06 to 0.44]; p<0.0001). In patients who developed respiratory failure, NIV as rescue therapy avoided reintubation in 17 of 27 patients. Ninety-day mortality was lower in the NIV group (p=0.0146); the abstract does not print the absolute mortality rates.
cards.watchOut: A 106-patient trial whose mortality result is a secondary endpoint reported as a p-value without rates — believe the respiratory-failure result (the primary endpoint, with absolute rates printed) more than the survival result. The population is specific: chronic respiratory disorders with hypercapnia documented during the breathing trial, not every patient with a high CO2 on a blood gas.

randomised controlled trial (ferrer 2009) 106 mechanically ventilated patients in three spanish intensive care units, with chronic respiratory disorders and hypercapnia after a successful spontaneous breathing trial, randomised to non-invasive ventilation for 24 hours after extubation (n=54) or conventional oxygen treatment (n=52); the primary endpoint was avoidance of respiratory failure within 72 hours after extubation, analysed by intention to treat. respiratory failure after extubation was less frequent with non-invasive ventilation than with conventional oxygen (8 [15%] vs 25 [48%]; odds ratio 5.32 [95% ci 2.11 to 13.46]; p<0.0001), and niv was independently associated with a lower risk of post-extubation respiratory failure (adjusted odds ratio 0.17 [95% ci 0.06 to 0.44]; p<0.0001). in patients who developed respiratory failure, niv as rescue therapy avoided reintubation in 17 of 27 patients. ninety-day mortality was lower in the niv group (p=0.0146); the abstract does not print the absolute mortality rates. a 106-patient trial whose mortality result is a secondary endpoint reported as a p-value without rates — believe the respiratory-failure result (the primary endpoint, with absolute rates printed) more than the survival result. the population is specific: chronic respiratory disorders with hypercapnia documented during the breathing trial, not every patient with a high co2 on a blood gas. ferrer m et al. non-invasive ventilation after extubation in hypercapnic patients with chronic respiratory disorders: randomised controlled trial. lancet. 2009. pmid: 19682735. registry id: nct00539708. mesh: aged · chronic disease · device removal · female · hospital mortality · humans · hypercapnia/complications · intubation, intratracheal · length of stay · male · positive-pressure respiration/adverse effects · respiration, artificial/adverse effects · respiratory insufficiency/blood/etiology/physiopathology/therapy · treatment outcome · ventilator weaning

cards.headline: Nava 2005 (multicentre RCT, 97 at-risk patients): reintubation 4 of 48 on early NIV vs 12 of 49 on standard therapy (p=0.027), with ICU mortality risk reduced by 10%
cards.summary: Nava 2005 (multicentre RCT, 97 at-risk patients): reintubation 4 of 48 on early NIV vs 12 of 49 on standard therapy (p=0.027), with ICU mortality risk reduced by 10%
cards.people: Ninety-seven consecutive patients ventilated for more than 48 hours and considered at risk of post-extubation respiratory failure — qualifying risks included hypercapnia, congestive heart failure, ineffective cough with excessive secretions, more than one failed weaning trial, more than one comorbidity, and upper airway obstruction — randomised after a successful weaning trial to NIV for at least 8 hours a day in the first 48 hours or standard medical therapy.
cards.result: The NIV group had a lower rate of reintubation than standard therapy (4 of 48 vs 12 of 49; p=0.027). The need for reintubation was itself associated with a higher risk of mortality (p<0.01). Use of NIV resulted in a reduction of ICU mortality risk of −10% (p<0.01), which the authors describe as mediated by the reduction in the need for reintubation. The authors note that, by contrast, NIV does not reduce reintubation in unselected patients who have already developed respiratory failure after extubation.
cards.watchOut: Hypercapnia is only one of six qualifying risks here, so this trial supports early NIV in a broader at-risk group rather than in hypercapnic patients specifically — Ferrer carries the hypercapnia-specific claim. With 97 patients and 16 reintubation events, the mortality mediation story is plausible but fragile.
cards.source: Nava S et al. Noninvasive ventilation to prevent respiratory failure after extubation in high-risk patients. Critical Care Medicine. 2005. PMID: 16276167. cards.summary: Synthesis: two small randomised trials, one strategy — support the breathing before it fails, in patients selected for risk, and reintubation and respiratory failure both fall
cards.people: Two randomised trials of immediate post-extubation NIV totalling 203 patients: 106 hypercapnic patients with chronic respiratory disorders (Ferrer 2009) and 97 patients at risk of post-extubation failure on mixed criteria including hypercapnia (Nava 2005).
cards.result: Post-extubation respiratory failure: 15% vs 48% (Ferrer). Reintubation: 4/48 vs 12/49 (Nava). Mortality: 90-day mortality lower with NIV in Ferrer (p=0.0146, rates not printed); ICU mortality risk −10% in Nava (p<0.01). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit). Tier C is set: the shelf carries a mortality-benefit claim from two small trials.
cards.watchOut: Timing is the whole shelf: NIV started immediately as prevention in selected patients helped; NIV started as rescue after failure is established delayed reintubation and raised mortality in the Esteban trial (shelf #3135). Reading this shelf as 'NIV after extubation is good' without the selection and timing qualifiers inverts the evidence.

shelves.title: High-flow oxygen for the easy weans: in low-risk patients, post-extubation high-flow nasal cannula cut reintubation within 72 hours from 12.2% to 4.9%
shelves.question: In patients at low risk of extubation failure, does post-extubation high-flow nasal cannula reduce reintubation compared with conventional oxygen therapy?
shelves.mesh: APACHE · Adult · Age Factors · Airway Extubation/adverse effects · Body Mass Index · Critical Illness · Female · Humans · Intensive Care Units · Intubation, Intratracheal/adverse effects/statistics & numerical data · Length of Stay · Male · Middle Aged · Multiple Organ Failure/etiology · Oxygen Inhalation Therapy/methods · Respiration, Artificial · Respiratory Insufficiency/etiology · Respiratory Tract Infections/etiology · Retreatment · Time Factors · Ventilator Weaning
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one well-run multicentre trial in carefully defined low-risk patients. Hernández 2016 (Hernández G et al., PMID: 26975498) randomised 527 adults at low risk for reintubation — under 65, APACHE II below 12 on the extubation day, body mass index below 30, simple weaning, at most one comorbidity, and no heart failure, significant COPD, airway problems or prolonged ventilation — to high-flow nasal cannula or conventional oxygen for 24 hours after extubation. Reintubation within 72 hours occurred in 4.9% on high-flow versus 12.2% on conventional oxygen (absolute difference 7.2%, 95% CI 2.5% to 12.2%; p=0.004) — a relative reduction of about 60%, with the absolute rates printed alongside — and post-extubation respiratory failure was also less common (8.3% vs 14.4%; p=0.03). Time to reintubation did not differ (median 19 vs 15 hours), and no adverse effects were reported. The mirror-image caution: 'low risk' here is a strict checklist, and the same group's high-risk trial asked a different question (high-flow versus NIV) — this shelf's stamp belongs to the low-risk population only. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): in low-risk extubated patients, 24 hours of high-flow nasal cannula prevents roughly one reintubation for every 14 patients treated.

cards.headline: Hernández 2016 (multicentre RCT, 527 low-risk patients): reintubation within 72 hours 4.9% on high-flow vs 12.2% on conventional oxygen (absolute difference 7.2%; p=0.004)
cards.summary: Hernández 2016 (multicentre RCT, 527 low-risk patients): reintubation within 72 hours 4.9% on high-flow vs 12.2% on conventional oxygen (absolute difference 7.2%; p=0.004)
cards.people: 527 adult critically ill patients at low risk for reintubation who fulfilled criteria for planned extubation, in seven Spanish intensive care units (September 2012 to October 2014); low risk meant younger than 65 years, APACHE II score below 12 on the day of extubation, body mass index below 30, adequate secretion management, simple weaning, zero or one comorbidity, and absence of heart failure, moderate-to-severe COPD, airway patency problems and prolonged mechanical ventilation. Mean age was 51 years and 62% were men; 264 patients received high-flow therapy and 263 conventional oxygen therapy for 24 hours after extubation.
cards.result: Reintubation within 72 hours was less common in the high-flow group (13 patients [4.9%] vs 32 [12.2%]; absolute difference 7.2% [95% CI 2.5% to 12.2%]; p=0.004) — a relative reduction of about 60%, with the absolute rates printed alongside. Post-extubation respiratory failure was less common with high-flow (22/264 [8.3%] vs 38/263 [14.4%]; absolute difference 6.1% [95% CI 0.7% to 11.6%]; p=0.03). Time to reintubation was not significantly different (median 19 hours [IQR 12–28] vs 15 hours [IQR 9–31]; p=0.66). No adverse effects were reported.
cards.watchOut: A single trial carries this shelf (Tier C), and its population is the point: patients over 65, with APACHE II of 12 or more, obesity, heart failure, significant COPD or a difficult wean were excluded by design, so the 4.9% figure must not be quoted for them. The trial was open-label — reintubation decisions were made by clinicians who knew the allocation, against pre-set criteria.
cards.source: Hernandez G et al. Effect of Postextubation High-Flow Nasal Cannula vs Conventional Oxygen Therapy on Reintubation in Low-Risk Patients: A Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA. 2016. cards.summary: Synthesis: one trial, one clean result — high-flow after extubation prevents reintubation in patients who were unlikely to need it, and the unanswered question is everyone else
cards.people: One multicentre randomised trial of 527 low-risk extubated adults in seven Spanish ICUs, comparing 24 hours of high-flow nasal cannula with conventional oxygen therapy.
cards.result: Reintubation within 72 hours: 4.9% vs 12.2% (absolute difference 7.2%, 95% CI 2.5% to 12.2%). Post-extubation respiratory failure: 8.3% vs 14.4%. shelves.title: The rescue that backfired: NIV for respiratory failure after extubation did not prevent reintubation (48% in both groups), delayed it by hours, and ICU mortality rose from 14% to 25%
shelves.question: In patients who develop respiratory failure after extubation, does rescue noninvasive ventilation improve survival — or delay reintubation and increase mortality — compared with prompt reintubation?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Female · Hospital Mortality · Humans · Intensive Care Units · Intubation, Intratracheal · Male · Middle Aged · Positive-Pressure Respiration/methods · Pulmonary Disease, Chronic Obstructive/complications/therapy · Respiration, Artificial · Respiratory Insufficiency/etiology/mortality/therapy · Treatment Outcome · Ventilator Weaning
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (harm) — the mask bought time, and the time cost lives. In the multicentre Esteban trial (Esteban A et al., PMID: 15190137), 221 patients in 37 centres in eight countries who developed respiratory failure within 48 hours of elective extubation were randomised to noninvasive positive-pressure ventilation by face mask or standard medical therapy. The need for reintubation was identical (48% in both groups; relative risk 0.99, 95% CI 0.76 to 1.30), but ICU mortality was higher with NIV (25% vs 14%; relative risk 1.78, 95% CI 1.03 to 3.20; p=0.048), and the median time from respiratory failure to reintubation was far longer in the NIV group (12 hours vs 2 hours 30 minutes; p=0.02) — the trial was stopped early at an interim analysis. The authors' interpretation, and the field's since, is that rescue NIV does not avert reintubation in unselected patients and that the delay it introduces is the plausible mechanism of the excess deaths. The contrast that keeps this shelf honest sits on shelf #3133: NIV started immediately after extubation, before failure, in selected hypercapnic and high-risk patients prevented failure — prevention and rescue are opposite strategies with opposite results. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm): rescue NIV for established post-extubation respiratory failure does not reduce reintubation and is associated with higher ICU mortality, most plausibly through delayed reintubation.

cards.headline: Esteban 2004 (multicentre RCT, 221 patients, stopped early): reintubation 48% in both groups; ICU death 25% on rescue NIV vs 14% on standard therapy (RR 1.78); time to reintubation 12 hours vs 2.5 hours
cards.summary: Esteban 2004 (multicentre RCT, 221 patients, stopped early): reintubation 48% in both groups; ICU death 25% on rescue NIV vs 14% on standard therapy (RR 1.78); time to reintubation 12 hours vs 2.5 hours
cards.people: 221 patients in 37 centres in eight countries who had been electively extubated after at least 48 hours of mechanical ventilation and who developed respiratory failure within the subsequent 48 hours, randomly assigned to noninvasive positive-pressure ventilation by face mask (n=114) or standard medical therapy (n=107); the trial was stopped early, after an interim analysis.
cards.result: There was no difference in the need for reintubation (rate 48% in both groups; relative risk with noninvasive ventilation 0.99; 95% CI 0.76 to 1.30). The rate of death in the intensive care unit was higher in the noninvasive-ventilation group (25% vs 14%; relative risk 1.78; 95% CI 1.03 to 3.20; p=0.048), and the median time from respiratory failure to reintubation was longer with NIV (12 hours vs 2 hours 30 minutes; p=0.02). The authors conclude that noninvasive positive-pressure ventilation does not prevent the need for reintubation or reduce mortality in unselected patients who have respiratory failure after extubation.
cards.watchOut: One trial, stopped early, in unselected patients — the harm signal is a single secondary outcome with a p-value of 0.048, and the trial cannot prove the delay caused the deaths, only that delay and deaths travelled together. Patients with hypercapnic COPD exacerbations, the group with the strongest NIV evidence elsewhere, were not separated out; this shelf governs the unselected rescue situation it studied.
cards.source: Esteban A et al. Noninvasive positive-pressure ventilation for respiratory failure after extubation. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2004. PMID: 15190137. cards.summary: Synthesis: the same mask that prevents failure when applied early failed as a rescue — reintubation unchanged, reintubation later, and more deaths
cards.people: One multicentre randomised trial of 221 patients with respiratory failure after extubation in 37 centres in eight countries, stopped early at interim analysis.
cards.result: Reintubation: 48% vs 48% (relative risk 0.99, 95% CI 0.76 to 1.30). ICU mortality: 25% vs 14% (relative risk 1.78, 95% CI 1.03 to 3.20). Median time from failure to reintubation: 12 hours vs 2.5 hours. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm). Tier C is set: a harm shelf resting on a single trial.
cards.watchOut: The clinical rule this shelf supports is narrow and practical: once post-extubation respiratory failure is established in an unselected patient, a trial of NIV must not become a reason to postpone a needed reintubation. shelves.title: Less pressure, same result: in 980 ICU patients without ARDS, a lower-PEEP strategy was noninferior to higher PEEP for ventilator-free days (median 18 vs 17) — with a few more rescue treatments for low oxygen
shelves.question: In ICU patients ventilated without ARDS, does a lower-PEEP strategy reduce ventilator-free days or mortality compared with a higher-PEEP strategy?
shelves.mesh: APACHE · Aged · Critical Illness · Female · Humans · Intensive Care Units · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Length of Stay · Male · Middle Aged · Oxygen/blood · Pneumonia, Ventilator-Associated · Pneumothorax/etiology · Positive-Pressure Respiration/adverse effects/methods · Respiratory Insufficiency/therapy · Ventilator Weaning
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — lower PEEP did not cost ventilator-free days or lives, which was the question the trial was built to answer. RELAx (Algera AG et al., PMID: 33295981) randomised 980 patients without ARDS, expected not to be extubated within 24 hours, in eight Dutch ICUs to the lowest PEEP level between 0 and 5 cm H2O or to a PEEP of 8 cm H2O. At day 28 the lower-PEEP group had a median of 18 ventilator-free days versus 17 with higher PEEP (mean ratio 1.04; p=0.007 for noninferiority, within the pre-set −10% margin). Mortality at 28 days was 38.4% versus 42.0% (hazard ratio 0.89, 95% CI 0.73 to 1.09) — a point estimate favouring lower PEEP that the trial was not powered to confirm. The harm on the face runs the other way: severe hypoxaemia occurred in 20.6% versus 17.6% (risk ratio 1.17, 95% CI 0.90 to 1.51) and a rescue strategy for hypoxaemia was needed in 19.7% versus 14.6% (risk ratio 1.35, 95% CI 1.02 to 1.79; adjusted p=0.54), with no significant differences in other secondary outcomes including ARDS development, pneumonia or pneumothorax. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): in patients without ARDS, lower PEEP is noninferior for ventilator-free days, so the burden of proof sits on higher PEEP, not on lower.

cards.headline: Algera 2020 (RELAx, 980 patients): median ventilator-free days 18 on lower PEEP vs 17 on higher PEEP (noninferior, p=0.007); 28-day mortality 38.4% vs 42.0% (HR 0.89)
cards.summary: Algera 2020 (RELAx, 980 patients): median ventilator-free days 18 on lower PEEP vs 17 on higher PEEP (noninferior, p=0.007); 28-day mortality 38.4% vs 42.0% (HR 0.89)
cards.people: 980 patients without ARDS in eight intensive care units in the Netherlands (October 2017 to December 2019), expected not to be extubated within 24 hours of starting ventilation; 969 (99%) completed the trial (median age 66 years [IQR 56–74]; 36% women). Patients were randomised to invasive ventilation with lower PEEP — the lowest level between 0 and 5 cm H2O (n=476) — or higher PEEP of 8 cm H2O (n=493). The primary outcome was ventilator-free days at day 28, with a noninferiority margin of −10% for the difference.
cards.result: At day 28, the lower-PEEP group had a median of 18 ventilator-free days (IQR 0–27) and the higher-PEEP group 17 (IQR 0–27) (mean ratio 1.04; 95% CI 0.95 to infinity; p=0.007 for noninferiority), the lower confidence boundary falling within the noninferiority margin. Severe hypoxaemia occurred in 20.6% versus 17.6% (risk ratio 1.17; 95% CI 0.90 to 1.51) and need for a rescue strategy in 19.7% versus 14.6% (risk ratio 1.35; 95% CI 1.02 to 1.79; adjusted p=0.54), in the lower- and higher-PEEP groups respectively. Mortality at 28 days was 38.4% versus 42.0% (hazard ratio 0.89; 95% CI 0.73 to 1.09). There were no statistically significant differences in other secondary outcomes, including ICU and hospital stay and 90-day mortality.
cards.watchOut: Noninferiority is not superiority: the −10% margin means lower PEEP could be up to a tenth worse on ventilator-free days and still pass, and the mortality point estimate (HR 0.89) is hypothesis-generating only. 'Higher PEEP' here is a fixed 8 cm H2O — modest by ARDS standards — and patients who developed ARDS or severe hypoxaemia crossed into rescue care, so the trial compares starting strategies, not rigid settings.
cards.source: Algera AG et al. Effect of a Lower vs Higher Positive End-Expiratory Pressure Strategy on Ventilator-Free Days in ICU Patients Without ARDS: A Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA. 2020. PMID: 33295981. Registry ID: NCT03167580. cards.headline: Synthesis: one large noninferiority trial — outside ARDS, starting low on PEEP loses nothing measurable, and the occasional hypoxaemia rescue is the price tag printed on the label
cards.summary: Synthesis: one large noninferiority trial — outside ARDS, starting low on PEEP loses nothing measurable, and the occasional hypoxaemia rescue is the price tag printed on the label
cards.people: One multicentre randomised noninferiority trial (RELAx) of 980 ICU patients without ARDS expected to remain ventilated beyond 24 hours, comparing PEEP 0–5 cm H2O with PEEP 8 cm H2O.
cards.result: Ventilator-free days at day 28: median 18 vs 17 (mean ratio 1.04; noninferiority p=0.007). Mortality at 28 days: 38.4% vs 42.0% (hazard ratio 0.89, 95% CI 0.73 to 1.09). Severe hypoxaemia: 20.6% vs 17.6%; rescue strategy: 19.7% vs 14.6%. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference). Tier C is set because a single trial carries the shelf.
cards.watchOut: This shelf is strictly about patients without ARDS: the ARDS PEEP question has its own shelves (#1306, #1307, #1647) with different answers, and surgical-ventilation PEEP sits on shelf #1959. Exporting RELAx's reassurance into ARDS care would repeat the classic error of treating 'no ARDS' evidence as 'all ventilation' evidence.

shelves.title: Analgesia first: a 17-study meta-analysis found lower ICU mortality with analgosedation (OR 0.72) — but no difference in hospital mortality, and delirium was higher in the trial-only subgroup (OR 1.88)
shelves.question: In ventilated ICU patients, does an analgesia-first (analgosedation) strategy reduce ventilation duration, delirium, and mortality compared with conventional sedative-based regimens?
shelves.mesh: Analgesia/adverse effects/methods · Delirium/epidemiology/etiology/physiopathology · Hospital Mortality/trends · Humans · Intensive Care Units/organization & administration
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — the three outcomes in the question point in three different directions, and the review says so itself. The 2019 systematic review and meta-analysis (Wang CT et al., PMID: 31395447) pooled 17 studies and 2,298 critically ill patients (1,170 analgosedation, 1,128 control) comparing analgesia-first strategies with conventional analgesia-plus-sedation. ICU mortality was lower with analgosedation (odds ratio 0.72, 95% CI 0.53 to 0.97; p=0.03), but 28-day/hospital mortality did not differ (odds ratio 0.91, 95% CI 0.70 to 1.18; p=0.48) and neither did the overall incidence of delirium (odds ratio 1.06, 95% CI 0.78 to 1.45; p=0.70) — while the subgroup analysis restricted to trials found delirium significantly increased (odds ratio 1.88, 95% CI 1.14 to 3.10; p=0.01), the harm printed on the face of this shelf. The review does not report a pooled ventilation-duration result in its abstract, so that part of the question goes unanswered by this record. The authors themselves warn of high clinical heterogeneity — varying analgesics and sedatives across studies, randomised trials mixed with cohort studies — and conclude the results must be interpreted cautiously. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): analgosedation may reduce ICU mortality, but the signal does not survive to hospital mortality, delirium may be worse in the trial data, and the evidence base is too heterogeneous to grade higher.

cards.headline: Wang 2019 (meta-analysis, 17 studies, 2,298 patients): ICU mortality OR 0.72 with analgosedation; hospital mortality OR 0.91 and delirium OR 1.06 — null; trial-subgroup delirium OR 1.88
cards.summary: Wang 2019 (meta-analysis, 17 studies, 2,298 patients): ICU mortality OR 0.72 with analgosedation; hospital mortality OR 0.91 and delirium OR 1.06 — null; trial-subgroup delirium OR 1.88
cards.people: Seventeen eligible studies including 2,298 critically ill patients (1,170 in analgosedation groups and 1,128 in control groups), identified through PubMed, the Cochrane Library, Embase and Web of Science; randomised trials were appraised with the Cochrane Risk of Bias Tool and cohort studies with the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale. The analgesics and sedatives investigated varied across studies, producing high clinical heterogeneity.
cards.result: Analgosedation significantly decreased the ICU mortality rate compared with conventional analgesia and sedation (odds ratio 0.72, 95% CI 0.53 to 0.97; p=0.03). No significant difference was demonstrated in 28-day/hospital mortality (odds ratio 0.91, 95% CI 0.70 to 1.18; p=0.48) or in the incidence of delirium (odds ratio 1.06, 95% CI 0.78 to 1.45; p=0.70). However, subgroup analysis of trials indicated a significant increase in the delirium rate (odds ratio 1.88, 95% CI 1.14 to 3.10; p=0.01). The authors conclude that ICU mortality was decreased by implementing analgosedation but hospital mortality and delirium rates were not, and that — given the absence of higher-quality study designs, clinical heterogeneity and the small number of studies — the results must be cautiously interpreted.
cards.watchOut: The headline mortality result and the headline delirium result cannot both be taken at face value from the same pooling: the ICU-mortality benefit leans on the mixed trial-and-cohort pool, while the delirium harm appears precisely when the analysis is restricted to trials. The abstract reports no pooled ventilation-duration outcome, so this record cannot answer the duration part of the shelf question at all.

cards.headline: Synthesis: an ICU-mortality signal that evaporates by hospital discharge, a delirium signal pointing the wrong way in trials, and no pooled answer on ventilation duration
cards.summary: Synthesis: an ICU-mortality signal that evaporates by hospital discharge, a delirium signal pointing the wrong way in trials, and no pooled answer on ventilation duration
cards.people: One 2019 systematic review and meta-analysis of 17 studies (randomised trials and cohort studies) totalling 2,298 critically ill patients, comparing analgosedation with conventional analgesia-plus-sedation regimens.
cards.result: ICU mortality: odds ratio 0.72 (95% CI 0.53 to 0.97). 28-day/hospital mortality: odds ratio 0.91 (95% CI 0.70 to 1.18). Delirium: odds ratio 1.06 overall (95% CI 0.78 to 1.45); odds ratio 1.88 (95% CI 1.14 to 3.10) in the trial subgroup. Ventilation duration: no pooled estimate in the record. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence). Tier C is set: the shelf depends on a heterogeneous mixed-design synthesis and carries a mortality claim.
cards.watchOut: 'Analgosedation' is a family of strategies, not a drug: the included studies used different analgesics as the base agent, so no single regimen inherits this result. Units adopting analgesia-first care should track their own delirium rates rather than assuming the pooled null, because the trial-only data say delirium can rise.
cards.source: Synthesis of Wang CT et al. Intensive and Critical Care Nursing. 2019 (PMID: 31395447).

shelves.title: The short-acting opioid: remifentanil-based sedation shortened mechanical ventilation (pooled mean difference −1.46) and time to extubation (−1.02) across 23 trials — with no difference in mortality, hospital stay or costs
shelves.question: In mechanically ventilated adults, does remifentanil-based sedation shorten ventilation and ICU stay compared with fentanyl- or morphine-based sedation?
shelves.mesh: Analgesics, Opioid/pharmacology/therapeutic use · Humans · Hypnotics and Sedatives/pharmacology/therapeutic use · Intensive Care Units/organization & administration · Pain/drug therapy · Piperidines/pharmacology/therapeutic use · Remifentanil · Respiration, Artificial/methods
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — on the clock, not on survival, and with heterogeneity high enough to print on the face. The 2017 systematic review and meta-analysis (Zhu Y et al., PMID: 28774327) pooled 23 randomised trials and 1,905 mechanically ventilated patients comparing remifentanil with other opioids (chiefly fentanyl and morphine based regimens). Remifentanil was associated with a shorter duration of mechanical ventilation (mean difference −1.46, 95% CI −2.44 to −0.49), a shorter time to extubation after sedation was stopped (mean difference −1.02, 95% CI −1.59 to −0.46) and a shorter ICU stay (mean difference −0.10, 95% CI −0.16 to −0.03) — the ICU-stay figure is small and its scale, as pooled across trials reporting stay differently, should not be read as a tenth of a day saved. There were no significant differences in hospital stay (mean difference −0.05, 95% CI −0.25 to 0.15), costs (mean difference −709.71, 95% CI −1590.98 to 171.55; I²=88%), mortality (mean difference −0.64, 95% CI −1.33 to 0.06; I²=87%) or agitation (I²=93%). The pharmacology predicts the pattern — remifentanil is cleared by blood esterases independently of liver and kidney function, so it should wear off faster — but pooled effects with I² values of 87–93% on several outcomes are averages over very unlike trials. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): remifentanil-based sedation probably shortens ventilation and time to extubation modestly versus fentanyl- or morphine-based sedation, with no shown effect on mortality, hospital stay or cost.

cards.headline: Zhu 2017 (meta-analysis, 23 RCTs, 1,905 patients): ventilation duration mean difference −1.46 and time to extubation −1.02 with remifentanil — mortality, hospital stay and costs not significantly different
cards.summary: Zhu 2017 (meta-analysis, 23 RCTs, 1,905 patients): ventilation duration mean difference −1.46 and time to extubation −1.02 with remifentanil — mortality, hospital stay and costs not significantly different
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials (Zhu 2017)
cards.people: Twenty-three randomised controlled trials with 1,905 mechanically ventilated patients, identified in PubMed, Embase, the Cochrane Library and SinoMed to 31 December 2016, comparing remifentanil — a selective mu-opioid metabolised by nonspecific esterases and eliminated independently of liver or renal function, with rapid onset and offset — with other opioids used for sedation and analgesia in intensive care.
cards.result: Remifentanil was associated with reductions in the duration of mechanical ventilation (mean difference −1.46; 95% CI −2.44 to −0.49), time to extubation after sedation cessation (mean difference −1.02; 95% CI −1.59 to −0.46), and ICU length of stay (mean difference −0.10; 95% CI −0.16 to −0.03). No significant differences were identified in hospital length of stay (mean difference −0.05; 95% CI −0.25 to 0.15), costs (mean difference −709.71; 95% CI −1590.98 to 171.55; I²=88%), mortality (mean difference −0.64; 95% CI −1.33 to 0.06; I²=87%) or agitation (mean difference −0.71; 95% CI −1.80 to 0.37; I²=93%).
cards.watchOut: The abstract pools several outcomes as mean differences without a single consistent unit across trials — most conspicuously ICU stay, where −0.10 cannot be a tenth of a day in any clinically meaningful sense — and heterogeneity reaches I²=87–93% on costs, mortality and agitation. Read the direction (faster awakening and extubation) as the finding; treat the decimal places as approximate. The search closed at the end of 2016, so this synthesis predates a decade of lighter-sedation practice that may compress the advantage.
cards.source: Zhu Y et al. Could remifentanil reduce duration of mechanical ventilation in comparison with other opioids for mechanically ventilated patients? A systematic review and meta-analysis. Critical Care. 2017. PMID: 28774327. cards.headline: Synthesis: pharmacology delivered what it promised — faster offset, faster extubation — and nothing beyond it: no survival, stay or cost dividend was shown
cards.summary: Synthesis: pharmacology delivered what it promised — faster offset, faster extubation — and nothing beyond it: no survival, stay or cost dividend was shown
cards.people: One 2017 systematic review and meta-analysis of 23 randomised trials (1,905 patients) comparing remifentanil-based with other opioid-based sedation in mechanically ventilated adults.
cards.result: Duration of mechanical ventilation: mean difference −1.46 (95% CI −2.44 to −0.49). Time to extubation after stopping sedation: −1.02 (95% CI −1.59 to −0.46). ICU stay: −0.10 (95% CI −0.16 to −0.03), scale as pooled. Hospital stay, costs, mortality and agitation: no significant differences. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) on time-based outcomes. Tier C is not set: the base is 23 randomised trials and no mortality-benefit claim is made.
cards.watchOut: Remifentanil's acquisition cost is the usual objection, and this record answers it only with a non-significant pooled cost difference whose interval is wide (−1590.98 to 171.55) — 'no difference shown' is not 'no difference'. Rapid offset also cuts both ways: analgesia vanishes within minutes of stopping the infusion, so pain control at extubation needs a planned handover to a longer-acting agent.
cards.source: Synthesis of Zhu Y et al. Critical Care. 2017 (PMID: 28774327).

shelves.title: One small trial, one clear signal: nocturnal dexmedetomidine kept 80% of ICU patients delirium-free versus 54% on placebo — and did not improve sleep quality
shelves.question: In ICU patients at risk of delirium, does a low-dose nocturnal dexmedetomidine infusion prevent delirium compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Intravenous · Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Benzodiazepines/*therapeutic use · Critical Care/*methods · Critical Illness · Delirium/*drug therapy/*prevention & control · Dexmedetomidine/*therapeutic use · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Hypnotics and Sedatives/*therapeutic use · Male · Middle Aged · Night Care/*methods · Placebo Effect · Propofol/*therapeutic use · Time Factors
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — a real delirium signal from a single 100-patient trial, with sleep unchanged. In the two-centre double-blind Skrobik trial (Skrobik Y et al., PMID: 29498534), delirium-free survival through the ICU stay was 80% (40 of 50) on nocturnal dexmedetomidine versus 54% (27 of 50) on placebo — delirium in 20% versus 46%, a relative risk of 0.44 (95% CI 0.23 to 0.82; P=0.006), with the absolute rates printed alongside. Patient-reported sleep quality (Leeds Sleep Evaluation Questionnaire) was similar between groups, and hypotension and bradycardia did not differ significantly. That is the whole evidence base for the nocturnal strategy: one small trial, however clean its design, in patients already receiving sedatives whose other sedative doses were halved during the infusion — so the result is one trial away from changing. This is a different question from postoperative prophylaxis after surgery (live shelf #791) and from dexmedetomidine as the primary ICU sedative. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): nocturnal low-dose dexmedetomidine may prevent ICU delirium, but a single 100-patient trial cannot carry a stronger stamp, and it did not make patients sleep better by their own report.

cards.headline: Skrobik 2018: delirium-free in 80% on nocturnal dexmedetomidine versus 54% on placebo (relative risk of delirium 0.44) — sleep scores identical
cards.summary: Skrobik 2018: delirium-free in 80% on nocturnal dexmedetomidine versus 54% on placebo (relative risk of delirium 0.44) — sleep scores identical
cards.people: 100 delirium-free critically ill adults receiving sedatives in two ICUs, randomised to nocturnal (9:30 p.m. to 6:15 a.m.) intravenous dexmedetomidine 0.2 µg/kg/h, titrated by 0.1 µg/kg/h every 15 minutes to a Richmond Agitation and Sedation Scale score of −1 (maximum 0.7 µg/kg/h), or placebo, until ICU discharge; during study infusions all other sedatives were halved and opioids unchanged. Delirium was assessed with the Intensive Care Delirium Screening Checklist every 12 hours.
cards.result: A greater proportion of dexmedetomidine patients remained delirium-free during the ICU stay: 40 of 50 (80%) versus 27 of 50 (54%) on placebo — delirium in 20% versus 46% (relative risk 0.44, 95% CI 0.23 to 0.82; P=0.006), with the absolute rates printed alongside. Average Leeds Sleep Evaluation Questionnaire scores were similar between the 34 dexmedetomidine and 30 placebo patients able to provide assessments. The incidence of hypotension, bradycardia, or both did not differ significantly between groups.
cards.watchOut: One trial, 100 patients, two centres. The infusion protocol halved every other sedative during the night, so the trial tests a nocturnal strategy (dexmedetomidine plus sedative sparing), not the molecule alone; and the sleep result — the outcome the night-time rationale most directly predicts — was flat.
cards.source: Skrobik Y et al. Low-Dose Nocturnal Dexmedetomidine Prevents ICU Delirium. A Randomized, Placebo-controlled Trial. American Journal of Respiratory and Critical Care Medicine. 2018. PMID: 29498534. Registry ID: NCT01791296. cards.headline: Synthesis: a 26-percentage-point absolute delirium gap in a single small trial — promising, unreplicated, and silent on sleep
cards.summary: Synthesis: a 26-percentage-point absolute delirium gap in a single small trial — promising, unreplicated, and silent on sleep
cards.people: One two-centre double-blind randomised trial of 100 critically ill adults receiving sedatives (Skrobik 2018).
cards.result: Delirium-free through the ICU stay: 80% versus 54% (delirium 20% versus 46%; relative risk 0.44, 95% CI 0.23 to 0.82). Patient-reported sleep quality: no difference. Hypotension/bradycardia: no significant difference. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence), Tier C set: a benefit stamp needs two randomised blinded trials, and this shelf has one.
cards.watchOut: Do not merge this shelf with postoperative dexmedetomidine prophylaxis (a different population, live shelf #791) or with dexmedetomidine as a primary sedative. What is missing is any second trial of the nocturnal low-dose strategy.

shelves.title: Rivastigmine added to haloperidol did not shorten ICU delirium — the trial was stopped early with mortality 22% versus 8%
shelves.question: In ICU patients with delirium treated with haloperidol, does adding rivastigmine shorten delirium — or increase mortality — compared with haloperidol alone?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Antipsychotic Agents/*therapeutic use · Cholinesterase Inhibitors/administration & dosage/*adverse effects · Critical Care/methods · *Critical Illness/mortality/therapy · Delirium/*drug therapy/etiology/*mortality · Double-Blind Method · Drug Administration Schedule · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · Haloperidol/*therapeutic use · Humans · Intensive Care Units · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Length of Stay · Male · Middle Aged · Phenylcarbamates/administration & dosage/*adverse effects · Rivastigmine · Severity of Illness Index · Time Factors · Treatment Failure
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (harm) — the only randomised trial of the strategy was stopped early by its safety board, pointing the wrong way on both outcomes. In van Eijk's multicentre double-blind trial (van Eijk MM et al., PMID: 21056464), 104 ICU patients with delirium received rivastigmine or placebo as an adjunct to haloperidol-based usual care; the trial had planned 440 patients but was halted because mortality was 22% (12 of 54) on rivastigmine versus 8% (4 of 50) on placebo (p=0.07), and median delirium duration was longer, not shorter, on rivastigmine (5.0 days, IQR 2.7–14.2, versus 3.0 days, IQR 1.0–9.3; p=0.06). Neither difference reached conventional significance — an early-stopped trial cannot prove harm — but a treatment that trends toward longer delirium and higher death, with no favourable signal anywhere, has no case for use. This shelf is about the rivastigmine adjunct specifically, not about antipsychotics for delirium (live shelf #341). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm): adding rivastigmine to haloperidol should not be used to treat ICU delirium; the randomised evidence points toward harm and the trial's own authors recommend against it.

cards.headline: van Eijk 2010: trial halted at 104 of 440 planned patients — mortality 22% on rivastigmine versus 8% on placebo, delirium longer (5.0 vs 3.0 days)
cards.summary: van Eijk 2010: trial halted at 104 of 440 planned patients — mortality 22% on rivastigmine versus 8% on placebo, delirium longer (5.0 vs 3.0 days)
cards.people: 104 adults with delirium in six Dutch intensive care units (54 rivastigmine, 50 placebo), enrolled November 2008 to January 2010. Rivastigmine was given as an adjunct to usual care based on haloperidol, starting at 1.5 mg twice daily and increasing in increments to 6 mg twice daily from day 10 onwards. Patients, staff and investigators were masked; the data safety and monitoring board was unmasked and reviewed interim analyses every 3 months.
cards.result: The board recommended halting the trial after 104 of a planned 440 patients because mortality in the rivastigmine group (12 of 54, 22%) was higher than in the placebo group (4 of 50, 8%; p=0.07). Median duration of delirium was longer in the rivastigmine group (5.0 days, IQR 2.7–14.2) than in the placebo group (3.0 days, IQR 1.0–9.3; p=0.06). The authors conclude rivastigmine did not decrease delirium duration, might have increased mortality, and should not be used to treat delirium in critically ill patients.
cards.watchOut: An early-stopped trial overstates whatever effect made it stop, and neither p-value crossed 0.05 — so this is a harm signal, not proof of harm. But the burden of proof sits with the treatment: there is no favourable trend to weigh against the unfavourable ones.
cards.source: van Eijk MM et al. Effect of rivastigmine as an adjunct to usual care with haloperidol on duration of delirium and mortality in critically ill patients: a multicentre, double-blind, placebo-controlled randomised trial. Lancet. 2010. PMID: 21056464. Registry ID: NCT00704301. cards.headline: Synthesis: one trial, stopped for safety, worse on duration and worse on mortality — the cholinergic hypothesis for ICU delirium failed its test
cards.summary: Synthesis: one trial, stopped for safety, worse on duration and worse on mortality — the cholinergic hypothesis for ICU delirium failed its test
cards.people: One multicentre double-blind randomised trial of 104 ICU patients with delirium (van Eijk 2010), stopped early on the recommendation of its data safety and monitoring board.
cards.result: Delirium duration: median 5.0 versus 3.0 days (p=0.06), favouring placebo. Mortality: 22% versus 8% (p=0.07), favouring placebo. No outcome favoured rivastigmine. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm), Tier C set: harm shelf resting on a single early-stopped trial.
cards.watchOut: The correct reading is 'do not use', not 'proven killer': the trial is too small and too truncated to quantify a mortality effect. Equally, no later evidence in this record rehabilitates the drug for this indication.
cards.source: Synthesis of van Eijk MM et al. Lancet. 2010 (PMID: 21056464).

shelves.title: Non-drug sleep bundles in the ICU: the pooled delirium benefit belongs to the dexmedetomidine trials — light, earplugs and multicomponent care alone showed no significant delirium effect
shelves.question: In ICU patients, do non-drug sleep-promotion protocols (noise, light, and care-clustering bundles) improve sleep and reduce delirium compared with usual care?
shelves.mesh: Humans · *Delirium/epidemiology · Critical Illness/therapy · Sleep · Intensive Care Units · Multicenter Studies as Topic
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — for delirium, the non-drug components are the null part of a positive-looking pool. Teng's meta-analysis of 15 randomised trials (Teng J et al., PMID: 37302381) found sleep interventions overall associated with less ICU delirium (risk ratio 0.73, 95% CI 0.58 to 0.93 — a relative effect), but the pooled dexmedetomidine trials drove it (risk ratio 0.43, 95% CI 0.32 to 0.59), while the nonpharmacological subgroups — light therapy, earplugs, melatonin, and multicomponent nonpharmacologic treatments — showed no significant effect on delirium incidence or duration, and the authors conclude non-pharmacological sleep interventions are not effective for preventing delirium. Sleep itself may still improve: Huang's network meta-analysis of 31 trials and 2,036 patients (Huang D et al., PMID: 38206715) found eye masks, and earplugs plus eye masks, improved sleep quality versus routine care (P<.05), though its abstract reports no pooled effect sizes and it measured no delirium outcome. So the honest split is: bundles may make the night feel better; they have not been shown to prevent delirium. This shelf is broader than the earplugs-and-eye-masks question on live shelf #1328. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): non-drug sleep-promotion protocols have not been shown to reduce ICU delirium; any benefit is on subjective sleep quality, chiefly from eye masks and earplugs.

cards.headline: Teng 2023 (meta-analysis, 15 RCTs): overall delirium risk ratio 0.73 — but the dexmedetomidine trials (0.43) carried it; every non-drug subgroup was non-significant
cards.summary: Teng 2023 (meta-analysis, 15 RCTs): overall delirium risk ratio 0.73 — but the dexmedetomidine trials (0.43) carried it; every non-drug subgroup was non-significant
cards.people: Fifteen randomised controlled trials of sleep interventions in intensive care patients, identified from six databases from inception to August 2022, pooling pharmacological and nonpharmacological sleep interventions against control care for the incidence and duration of ICU delirium.
cards.result: Sleep interventions overall were associated with a reduced incidence of ICU delirium (risk ratio 0.73, 95% CI 0.58 to 0.93; p<0.001 — a relative effect; pooled absolute rates are not reported in the abstract). The pooled result from the three dexmedetomidine trials was risk ratio 0.43 (95% CI 0.32 to 0.59; p<0.001). The pooled results for the other sleep interventions — light therapy, earplugs, melatonin, and multicomponent nonpharmacologic treatments — found no significant effect on the incidence or duration of ICU delirium (p>0.05). The authors conclude that non-pharmacological sleep interventions are not effective in preventing delirium in ICU patients, while calling for larger multicentre trials.
cards.watchOut: The headline 0.73 pools drug and non-drug interventions; quoting it for a care bundle would credit the bundle with a sedative's effect. The non-drug verdict rests on subgroup analyses of small trials — absence of a shown effect, in underpowered subgroups, rather than proof of no effect.
cards.source: Teng J et al. Effectiveness of sleep interventions to reduce delirium in critically ill patients: A systematic review and meta-analysis. Journal of Critical Care. 2023. PMID: 37302381.
