cards.headline: Huang 2023 (network meta-analysis, 31 RCTs, 2,036 patients): eye masks, and earplugs plus eye masks, improved sleep quality versus routine care — no delirium outcome measured
cards.summary: Huang 2023 (network meta-analysis, 31 RCTs, 2,036 patients): eye masks, and earplugs plus eye masks, improved sleep quality versus routine care — no delirium outcome measured
cards.type: Systematic review and network meta-analysis, 31 RCTs (Huang 2023)
cards.people: Thirty-one randomised trials totalling 2,036 critically ill patients, comparing 11 non-pharmacological nursing interventions for sleep (including routine care, music, eye masks, earplugs, earplugs plus eye masks, music plus earplugs plus eye masks, aromatherapy, relaxation with imagery, and virtual-reality meditation), in studies published up to 15 July 2023.
cards.result: Eye masks, and earplugs combined with eye masks, were associated with improved sleep quality compared with routine care (P<.05). The abstract reports no pooled effect sizes for these comparisons, and delirium was not an outcome of this analysis.
cards.watchOut: Sleep quality here is a subjective, patient-reported outcome in small unblinded trials — the interventions cannot be blinded — and the winning components (eye masks, earplugs) are exactly the subject of live shelf #1328; this card supports the sleep half of the bundle question only, not delirium prevention.
cards.source: Huang D et al. Different nursing interventions on sleep quality among critically ill patients: A systematic review and network meta-analysis. Medicine. 2023. PMID: 38206715. cards.headline: Synthesis: sleep may feel better with masks and plugs; delirium prevention by non-drug bundles is unshown — the pooled win belongs to a drug
cards.summary: Synthesis: sleep may feel better with masks and plugs; delirium prevention by non-drug bundles is unshown — the pooled win belongs to a drug
cards.people: One meta-analysis of 15 RCTs of ICU sleep interventions with delirium outcomes (Teng 2023) and one network meta-analysis of 31 RCTs (2,036 patients) of non-pharmacological interventions with sleep-quality outcomes (Huang 2023).
cards.result: Delirium: overall risk ratio 0.73 (0.58 to 0.93), driven by dexmedetomidine trials (0.43, 0.32 to 0.59); light therapy, earplugs, melatonin and multicomponent nonpharmacologic subgroups all non-significant. Sleep quality: eye masks and earplugs plus eye masks better than routine care (P<.05, no effect sizes in the abstract). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) for delirium, Tier C set because the verdict rests on subgroup analyses within one meta-analysis.
cards.watchOut: A bundle trial large enough to detect a delirium effect on its own — rather than as a subgroup — does not exist in this record. Until one does, 'quiet ICU' programmes should be sold to patients as comfort, not as delirium prevention.
cards.source: Synthesis of Teng J et al. Journal of Critical Care. 2023 (PMID: 37302381); Huang D et al. Medicine. 2023 (PMID: 38206715).

shelves.title: CLONES pilot: one night of low-dose clonidine bought postoperative high-dependency patients about 100 extra minutes of sleep (497 vs 396 minutes) — 80 patients, one night, one centre
shelves.question: In postoperative ICU patients, does a low-dose clonidine infusion improve sleep quality compared with placebo or standard care?
shelves.mesh: Humans · *Clonidine/administration & dosage/therapeutic use · Middle Aged · Male · Female · Double-Blind Method · Aged · Pilot Projects · Adrenergic alpha-2 Receptor Agonists/administration & dosage/therapeutic use · Sleep/drug effects · Infusions, Intravenous · Postoperative Complications/prevention & control
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — a genuine sleep gain in a pilot trial too small and too short to settle anything. In the double-blind CLONES pilot (Liu D et al., PMID: 39311905), 80 analysed postoperative high-dependency patients slept a mean of 497.2 minutes on low-dose clonidine versus 396.4 minutes on placebo on the night of surgery — a mean difference of 100.8 minutes (95% CI 38.2 to 163.4; p=0.002) — and reported better sleep overall. The price signal was small but real: four clonidine patients had the infusion stopped for bradycardia and hypotension (none needed additional treatment), and safety outcomes otherwise did not differ. Delirium was essentially absent in this elective population, so the trial says nothing about it. Note the setting honestly: these were elective-surgery high-dependency patients, not general ICU patients, sleep was measured with a consumer actigraphy/photoplethysmography device, and the exposure was a single night. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): low-dose clonidine probably lengthens one night's postoperative sleep, on pilot evidence that needs a larger confirmatory trial.

cards.headline: Liu 2024 (CLONES pilot): total sleep time 497.2 vs 396.4 minutes (difference 100.8 minutes, p=0.002) — four clonidine infusions stopped for bradycardia and hypotension
cards.summary: Liu 2024 (CLONES pilot): total sleep time 497.2 vs 396.4 minutes (difference 100.8 minutes, p=0.002) — four clonidine infusions stopped for bradycardia and hypotension
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled pilot trial (Liu 2024, CLONES)
cards.people: 83 randomised adult elective-surgery patients in a single academic hospital's high-dependency unit; 80 (39 clonidine, 41 placebo; median ages 61 and 59 years) contributed to the modified intention-to-treat analysis. Clonidine 0.3 µg/kg/h or saline placebo was infused on the night of surgery. The primary outcome was total sleep time measured with a consumer actigraphy/photoplethysmography device.
cards.result: Clonidine patients slept longer: mean total sleep time 497.2 versus 396.4 minutes, a mean difference of 100.8 minutes (95% CI 38.2 to 163.4; p=0.002), and reported better sleep overall. Delirium was observed in only one patient, before study-drug infusion, and in none at the end of the study. Safety outcomes were not different between groups; four clonidine patients had their medication ceased because of bradycardia and hypotension that required no additional treatment.
cards.watchOut: A pilot trial in a high-dependency unit — a step below ICU acuity — in elective surgical patients, for one night, with sleep measured by a consumer wearable rather than polysomnography. It cannot speak to ICU patients, multi-night use, or delirium.

shelves.title: Esmolol in septic shock: one open-label 154-patient trial reported 28-day mortality of 49.4% versus 80.5% — a benefit too large to take at face value without a blinded confirmatory trial
shelves.question: In patients with septic shock and persistent tachycardia despite fluids and norepinephrine, does heart-rate control with esmolol improve survival compared with standard care?
shelves.mesh: Adrenergic alpha-Agonists/administration & dosage · Adrenergic beta-1 Receptor Antagonists/*administration & dosage/adverse effects · Aged · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Female · Heart/drug effects/physiopathology · Heart Rate/*drug effects · Hemodynamics/drug effects · Humans · Intensive Care Units · Male · Middle Aged · Norepinephrine/administration & dosage · Propanolamines/*administration & dosage/adverse effects · Shock, Septic/complications/*drug therapy · Stroke Volume/drug effects · Survival Analysis · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — the direction is consistent and the size is implausible; both things are true. Morelli's open-label phase 2 trial (Morelli A et al., PMID: 24108526) randomised 154 septic-shock patients with heart rates of at least 95/min on high-dose norepinephrine: 28-day mortality was 49.4% on esmolol versus 80.5% on standard care (adjusted hazard ratio 0.39, 95% CI 0.26 to 0.59; P<.001), with lower norepinephrine requirements and less fluid given. Hasegawa's meta-analysis of seven small trials (613 patients; esmolol or landiolol) (Hasegawa D et al., PMID: 33434497) pools to a 28-day mortality risk ratio of 0.68 (95% CI 0.54 to 0.85) — a relative effect, reported alongside an absolute risk reduction of 18.2% and a number needed to treat of 5.5. The counterweights are structural: Morelli's trial was open-label and single-centre, its primary outcome was heart-rate control rather than mortality, and a control-group mortality of 80.5% is far above what comparable septic-shock cohorts show, which inflates any relative benefit. No large blinded trial has tested the claim. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): heart-rate control with an ultrashort beta-blocker may improve survival in tachycardic septic shock, but the mortality claim rests on small open-label trials and must not be read as established.

cards.headline: Morelli 2013: 28-day mortality 49.4% on esmolol versus 80.5% on standard care (adjusted HR 0.39) — open-label, single-centre, heart-rate primary outcome
cards.summary: Morelli 2013: 28-day mortality 49.4% on esmolol versus 80.5% on standard care (adjusted HR 0.39) — open-label, single-centre, heart-rate primary outcome
cards.people: 154 patients (77 esmolol, 77 control) in a single university-hospital ICU between November 2010 and July 2012, in septic shock with a heart rate of 95/min or higher and requiring high-dose norepinephrine to maintain a mean arterial pressure of at least 65 mm Hg. Esmolol was infused continuously and titrated to keep the heart rate between 80 and 94/min for the ICU stay.
cards.result: Target heart rates were achieved in all esmolol patients; the median heart-rate area under the curve over 96 hours was −28/min (IQR −37 to −21) versus −6/min for control (mean reduction 18/min; P<.001). Norepinephrine requirements and fluid requirements were lower on esmolol (fluid median AUC 3,975 versus 4,425 mL/24 h; P<.001), and stroke volume index was higher (P=.02). Twenty-eight-day mortality was 49.4% in the esmolol group versus 80.5% in the control group (adjusted hazard ratio 0.39, 95% CI 0.26 to 0.59; P<.001). No clinically relevant differences in other cardiopulmonary variables, rescue therapy, or adverse events were found.
cards.watchOut: The trial was open-label, single-centre, and designed around a heart-rate primary outcome; mortality was a secondary outcome. A control mortality of 80.5% is exceptionally high for septic shock, so the relative benefit is measured against an unusually lethal baseline — exactly the setting in which small trials most overstate effects.
cards.source: Morelli A et al. Effect of heart rate control with esmolol on hemodynamic and clinical outcomes in patients with septic shock: a randomized clinical trial. JAMA. 2013. PMID: 24108526. cards.headline: Hasegawa 2021 (meta-analysis, 7 RCTs, 613 patients): ultrashort beta-blockers and 28-day mortality risk ratio 0.68 — pooled from small trials, Morelli's among them
cards.summary: Hasegawa 2021 (meta-analysis, 7 RCTs, 613 patients): ultrashort beta-blockers and 28-day mortality risk ratio 0.68 — pooled from small trials, Morelli's among them
cards.people: Seven randomised trials with a pooled sample of 613 adults with sepsis or septic shock and persistent tachycardia despite initial resuscitation, treated with the ultrashort-acting beta-blockers esmolol or landiolol versus placebo or no intervention; six trials (572 patients) reported 28-day mortality. Literature search updated 20 April 2020.
cards.result: Esmolol or landiolol use was associated with lower 28-day mortality (risk ratio 0.68, 95% CI 0.54 to 0.85; P<.001 — a relative effect), with unimportant heterogeneity (I²=31%). The reviewers report an absolute risk reduction of 18.2% and a number needed to treat of 5.5 to prevent one death, printed alongside the relative effect.
cards.watchOut: Pooling seven small trials does not manufacture one large one: the pool is dominated by small, mostly open-label studies at high risk of bias, mixes two different drugs (esmolol and landiolol), and inherits Morelli's unusually high control mortality. The pooled precision is real; the pooled credibility is the question.

cards.headline: Synthesis: consistent direction, unbelievable size — the esmolol mortality claim awaits a blinded trial large enough to test it
cards.summary: Synthesis: consistent direction, unbelievable size — the esmolol mortality claim awaits a blinded trial large enough to test it
cards.people: One open-label single-centre phase 2 trial of 154 patients (Morelli 2013) and one meta-analysis of seven small RCTs totalling 613 patients (Hasegawa 2021).
cards.result: Anchor trial 28-day mortality: 49.4% versus 80.5% (adjusted hazard ratio 0.39, 95% CI 0.26 to 0.59). Pooled 28-day mortality: risk ratio 0.68 (95% CI 0.54 to 0.85), reported absolute risk reduction 18.2%. Physiological outcomes (heart-rate control, norepinephrine sparing) consistently favour esmolol. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence), Tier C set: a mortality-benefit claim resting on small open-label trials.
cards.watchOut: Beta-blockade in shock can also harm — the trials enrolled only patients with persistent tachycardia after resuscitation, and nothing here supports beta-blockade in septic shock without tachycardia, or with a different, longer-acting agent. The landiolol question has its own live shelf (#1079).
cards.source: Synthesis of Morelli A et al. JAMA. 2013 (PMID: 24108526); Hasegawa D et al. Chest. 2021 (PMID: 33434497).

shelves.title: LeoPARDS: levosimendan in sepsis did not reduce organ dysfunction (SOFA 6.68 vs 6.06) or mortality (34.5% vs 30.9%) — and weaning was slower, with more tachyarrhythmia
shelves.question: In patients with septic shock, does levosimendan improve organ dysfunction and survival compared with placebo on top of standard care?
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — a well-run double-blind trial whose point estimates lean, if anything, against the drug. In LeoPARDS (Gordon AC et al., PMID: 27705084), 516 adults with sepsis received levosimendan or placebo on top of standard care: mean daily SOFA score was 6.68 on levosimendan versus 6.06 on placebo (mean difference 0.61, 95% CI −0.07 to 1.29; P=0.053 — higher is worse), and 28-day mortality was 34.5% versus 30.9% (absolute difference 3.6 percentage points, 95% CI −4.5 to 11.7; P=0.43). Two secondary outcomes favoured placebo: ventilated patients on levosimendan were less likely to be weaned successfully (hazard ratio 0.77, 95% CI 0.60 to 0.97), and supraventricular tachyarrhythmia was more common (3.1% versus 0.4%; P=0.04). Chang's meta-analysis of ten trials and 1,036 patients with severe sepsis or septic shock (Chang W et al., PMID: 29602841) agrees on the outcome that matters: mortality odds ratio 0.89 (95% CI 0.69 to 1.16; P=0.39), despite better lactate and cardiac-function measures. Note the population honestly: LeoPARDS enrolled adults with sepsis, not exclusively septic shock. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): levosimendan added to standard care does not reduce organ dysfunction or mortality in sepsis, and carries a tachyarrhythmia and weaning cost.

cards.headline: Gordon 2016 (LeoPARDS): SOFA 6.68 on levosimendan versus 6.06 on placebo, mortality 34.5% versus 30.9% — weaning hazard ratio 0.77, tachyarrhythmia 3.1% versus 0.4%
cards.summary: Gordon 2016 (LeoPARDS): SOFA 6.68 on levosimendan versus 6.06 on placebo, mortality 34.5% versus 30.9% — weaning hazard ratio 0.77, tachyarrhythmia 3.1% versus 0.4%
cards.people: 516 adults with sepsis (259 levosimendan, 257 placebo) randomised to a blinded 24-hour infusion of levosimendan 0.05 to 0.2 µg per kilogram per minute or placebo, in addition to standard care. The primary outcome was the mean daily Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA) score in the ICU up to day 28 (five systems, maximum 20; higher scores indicate more severe dysfunction).
cards.result: There was no significant difference in mean SOFA score (6.68±3.96 on levosimendan versus 6.06±3.89 on placebo; mean difference 0.61, 95% CI −0.07 to 1.29; P=0.053). Mortality at 28 days was 34.5% versus 30.9% (absolute difference 3.6 percentage points, 95% CI −4.5 to 11.7; P=0.43). Among patients ventilated at baseline, levosimendan patients were less likely to be successfully weaned over 28 days (hazard ratio 0.77, 95% CI 0.60 to 0.97; P=0.03), and more had supraventricular tachyarrhythmia (3.1% versus 0.4%; absolute difference 2.7 percentage points, 95% CI 0.1 to 5.3; P=0.04).
cards.watchOut: The enrolled population was sepsis, broader than the septic shock of this shelf's question, and the SOFA point estimate favoured placebo — so 'no difference' is the generous reading. The record for this article carries no MeSH terms, so the source line says so plainly rather than inventing any.

cards.headline: Chang 2018 (meta-analysis, 10 trials, 1,036 patients): mortality odds ratio 0.89 (0.69 to 1.16) — better lactate and cardiac numbers, no survival benefit
cards.summary: Chang 2018 (meta-analysis, 10 trials, 1,036 patients): mortality odds ratio 0.89 (0.69 to 1.16) — better lactate and cardiac numbers, no survival benefit
cards.people: Ten randomised trials totalling 1,036 patients with severe sepsis or septic shock, comparing levosimendan with other inotropes or as an adjunct to standard therapy, with mortality reported; literature searched to August 2017.
cards.result: Levosimendan did not significantly reduce mortality in severe sepsis and septic shock (odds ratio 0.89, 95% CI 0.69 to 1.16; P=0.39). It reduced serum lactate more effectively and increased cardiac index and left ventricular ejection fraction, but it also increased fluid infusion and did not reduce norepinephrine dose. No mortality benefit was seen against dobutamine specifically, or in patients with proven cardiac dysfunction.
cards.watchOut: Comparators are mixed (dobutamine in some trials, standard care in others) and most included trials are small; the physiological wins (lactate, ejection fraction) are exactly the surrogates LeoPARDS showed do not convert into organ-function or survival benefit.
cards.source: Chang W et al. Effect of levosimendan on mortality in severe sepsis and septic shock: a meta-analysis of randomised trials. BMJ Open. 2018. PMID: 29602841. shelves.title: SEPSIS-ACT: selepressin stopped for futility — ventilator- and vasopressor-free days 15.0 versus 14.5, 90-day mortality 40.6% versus 39.4%
shelves.question: In adults with septic shock, does selepressin increase ventilator- and vasopressor-free days compared with placebo?
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — an 868-patient adaptive trial that stopped itself for futility. In SEPSIS-ACT (Laterre PF et al., PMID: 31577035), adults with septic shock requiring more than 5 µg/min of norepinephrine were randomised to one of three selepressin dosing regimens or placebo: the primary endpoint, ventilator- and vasopressor-free days within 30 days, was 15.0 on selepressin versus 14.5 on placebo (difference 0.6 days, 95% CI −1.3 to 2.4; P=.30), and 90-day mortality was 40.6% versus 39.4% (difference 1.1%, 95% CI −6.5% to 8.8%; P=.77), with kidney-replacement-therapy-free days and ICU-free days likewise similar. Ischaemic and arrhythmic adverse events ran numerically higher on selepressin (cardiac ischaemia 6.6% versus 5.6%; mesenteric ischaemia 3.2% versus 2.6%) without reaching a proven harm. A selective V1a agonist was an elegant idea — pressor effect without catecholamines — and the trial was large and honest enough to kill it. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): selepressin does not increase ventilator- and vasopressor-free days or improve any key secondary outcome in septic shock.

cards.headline: Laterre 2019 (SEPSIS-ACT): free days 15.0 versus 14.5 (P=.30), 90-day mortality 40.6% versus 39.4% — stopped for futility at the end of part 1
cards.summary: Laterre 2019 (SEPSIS-ACT): free days 15.0 versus 14.5 (P=.30), 90-day mortality 40.6% versus 39.4% — stopped for futility at the end of part 1
cards.people: 868 randomised adults with septic shock requiring more than 5 µg/min of norepinephrine, in 63 hospitals in Belgium, Denmark, France, the Netherlands and the United States (July 2015 to August 2017); 828 received study drug (mean age 66.3 years, 41.2% women) — 562 received one of three selepressin regimens (starting infusion rates 1.7, 2.5 and 3.5 ng/kg/min) and 266 received placebo, all titrated to haemodynamic parameters. Median study-drug duration was 37.8 hours.
cards.result: The trial was stopped for futility at the end of part 1. There were no significant differences in the primary endpoint (ventilator- and vasopressor-free days within 30 days: 15.0 versus 14.5; difference 0.6, 95% CI −1.3 to 2.4; P=.30) or key secondary endpoints (90-day mortality 40.6% versus 39.4%, difference 1.1%, 95% CI −6.5% to 8.8%, P=.77; kidney replacement therapy-free days 18.5 versus 18.2, P=.85; ICU-free days 12.6 versus 12.2, P=.41). Adverse-event rates included cardiac arrhythmias (27.9% versus 25.2%), cardiac ischaemia (6.6% versus 5.6%), mesenteric ischaemia (3.2% versus 2.6%) and peripheral ischaemia (2.3% versus 2.3%).
cards.watchOut: Three dose regimens were pooled against placebo under an adaptive design, so a single best dose cannot be read out of the result — but the futility stop after 868 patients makes a large missed benefit unlikely. The record for this article carries no MeSH terms, so the source line says so plainly.

shelves.title: Drotrecogin alfa in septic shock: the 1,697-patient PROWESS-SHOCK trial found mortality 26.4% versus 24.2% — reversing the 2001 PROWESS result that launched the drug
shelves.question: In adults with septic shock, does drotrecogin alfa (activated protein C) reduce mortality compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Anti-Infective Agents/*therapeutic use · Double-Blind Method · Drug Therapy, Combination · Humans · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Odds Ratio · Protein C/*therapeutic use · Protein C Deficiency/complications/mortality · Recombinant Proteins/therapeutic use · Shock, Septic/complications/*drug therapy/mortality · Treatment Failure
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — the definitive trial in the exact population reversed the founding trial. In PROWESS-SHOCK (Ranieri VM et al., PMID: 22616830), 1,697 patients with septic shock on fluids and vasopressors received drotrecogin alfa (activated) or placebo for 96 hours: 28-day mortality was 26.4% (223 of 846) on the drug versus 24.2% (202 of 834) on placebo (relative risk 1.09, 95% CI 0.92 to 1.28; P=0.31), 90-day mortality 34.1% versus 32.7% (relative risk 1.04, 95% CI 0.90 to 1.19), and even the predefined subgroup with severe protein C deficiency — the patients the drug most plausibly suits — showed no benefit (28.7% versus 30.8%; risk ratio 0.93, 95% CI 0.74 to 1.17). Serious bleeding during treatment was similar (10 versus 8 patients; P=0.81). The earlier PROWESS trial in severe sepsis (Bernard GR et al., PMID: 11236773) had found mortality of 24.7% versus 30.8% — a 19.4% relative risk reduction with a 6.1-percentage-point absolute reduction (P=0.005) — and more serious bleeding (3.5% versus 2.0%). Two large double-blind trials, opposite answers; the later one asked the question in septic shock itself, the population of this shelf, and its answer governs. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): drotrecogin alfa does not reduce mortality in septic shock.

cards.headline: Ranieri 2012 (PROWESS-SHOCK): 28-day mortality 26.4% on drotrecogin versus 24.2% on placebo (RR 1.09) — no benefit even in severe protein C deficiency
cards.summary: Ranieri 2012 (PROWESS-SHOCK): 28-day mortality 26.4% on drotrecogin versus 24.2% on placebo (RR 1.09) — no benefit even in severe protein C deficiency
cards.people: 1,697 patients with infection, systemic inflammation and shock who had been receiving fluids and vasopressors above a threshold dose for 4 hours, randomised to drotrecogin alfa (activated) 24 µg per kilogram per hour or placebo for 96 hours. The primary outcome was death from any cause 28 days after randomisation.
cards.result: At 28 days, 223 of 846 patients (26.4%) in the drotrecogin group and 202 of 834 (24.2%) in the placebo group had died (relative risk 1.09, 95% CI 0.92 to 1.28; P=0.31). At 90 days, 287 of 842 (34.1%) versus 269 of 822 (32.7%) had died (relative risk 1.04, 95% CI 0.90 to 1.19; P=0.56). Among patients with severe protein C deficiency at baseline, 28-day mortality was 28.7% (98 of 342) versus 30.8% (102 of 331) (risk ratio 0.93, 95% CI 0.74 to 1.17; P=0.54), and no other predefined subgroup differed significantly. Serious bleeding during the treatment period occurred in 10 drotrecogin patients and 8 placebo patients (P=0.81).
cards.watchOut: This is the trial that matters for septic shock: large, double-blind, and conducted in the exact population. Its null is not a power problem — the confidence interval excludes the benefit PROWESS reported.

cards.summary: Bernard 2001 (PROWESS): mortality 24.7% versus 30.8% — a 19.4% relative risk reduction (6.1 points absolute) that the later shock trial could not reproduce
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled phase 3 trial (Bernard 2001, PROWESS)
cards.people: 1,690 treated patients with severe sepsis — systemic inflammation and organ failure due to acute infection (850 drotrecogin alfa activated, 840 placebo) — receiving an intravenous infusion of drotrecogin alfa (activated) 24 µg per kilogram per hour or placebo for 96 hours. The prospectively defined primary endpoint was death from any cause at 28 days. This pre-registration-era trial lists no registry identifier in its record.
cards.result: Mortality was 24.7% in the drotrecogin group versus 30.8% in the placebo group: a 19.4% relative risk reduction (95% CI 6.6 to 30.5) and an absolute reduction of 6.1 percentage points (P=0.005), with the relative measure labelled and the absolute rates printed alongside. Serious bleeding was more frequent on drotrecogin (3.5% versus 2.0%; P=0.06).
cards.watchOut: PROWESS enrolled severe sepsis, not specifically septic shock, and its positive result is precisely what PROWESS-SHOCK was designed to confirm in shock — and did not. Kept on this shelf as the historical first half of the reversal, not as live support for the drug.

shelves.title: RACE: levocarnitine in septic shock missed its own phase 2 bar — SOFA improvement at the best dose had a posterior probability of 0.78 against a 0.90 threshold, mortality 43.3% versus 45.9%
shelves.question: In patients with septic shock, does adjunctive levocarnitine improve organ failure and one-year survival compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Carnitine/administration & dosage/*therapeutic use · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Organ Dysfunction Scores · Placebos/administration & dosage/*therapeutic use · Shock, Septic/*drug therapy/mortality/physiopathology
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — a dose-finding phase 2 trial that did not clear the bar it set itself. In RACE (Jones AE et al., PMID: 30646314), 250 patients with septic shock and moderate organ dysfunction were adaptively randomised to levocarnitine 6 g, 12 g or 18 g, or placebo, as a 12-hour infusion: the fitted change in SOFA score at 48 hours was −1.97 at the most promising (18 g) dose versus −1.63 on placebo, and the posterior probability that the 18 g dose was superior was 0.78 — short of the trial's prespecified 0.90 threshold for proceeding. Twenty-eight-day mortality was 43.3% (45 of 104) at 18 g versus 45.9% (34 of 74) on placebo. On the one-year survival half of this shelf's question, this record is silent: RACE as published reports organ failure at 48 hours and mortality at 28 days, and no one-year outcome appears in its record — so no one-year claim is made here. A phase 2 trial designed to pick a dose cannot prove or disprove efficacy; what it establishes is that the organ-failure signal was too weak to meet the investigators' own go/no-go criterion. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): adjunctive levocarnitine has not been shown to improve organ failure in septic shock, and its one-year survival effect is untested in this record.

cards.headline: Jones 2018 (RACE): 18 g levocarnitine SOFA change −1.97 versus −1.63 on placebo — posterior probability of superiority 0.78, below the 0.90 the trial required
cards.summary: Jones 2018 (RACE): 18 g levocarnitine SOFA change −1.97 versus −1.63 on placebo — posterior probability of superiority 0.78, below the 0.90 the trial required
cards.type: Randomised blinded adaptive dose-finding phase 2 trial (Jones 2018, RACE)
cards.people: 250 adults (mean age 61.7 years, 56.8% men) with septic shock and moderate organ dysfunction at 16 urban US medical centres, enrolled March 2013 to February 2018 and treated within 24 hours of identification. Adaptive randomisation assigned 35 patients to levocarnitine 6 g, 34 to 12 g, 106 to 18 g and 75 to placebo, each as a 12-hour infusion. The primary outcome required first a greater than 90% posterior probability that the best dose decreases the SOFA score at 48 hours, and then at least a 30% predictive probability of success on 28-day mortality in a future phase 3 trial.
cards.result: Fitted mean changes in SOFA score were −1.27 (6 g), −1.66 (12 g) and −1.97 (18 g) versus −1.63 on placebo. The posterior probability that the 18 g dose is superior to placebo was 0.78, which did not meet the a priori 0.90 threshold. Mortality at 28 days was 45.9% (34 of 74) on placebo versus 43.3% (45 of 104) at the 18 g dose, with similar findings per protocol. The authors conclude the most efficacious dose did not meaningfully reduce cumulative organ failure at 48 hours.
cards.watchOut: A Bayesian dose-finding design answers 'which dose, and is it worth a phase 3?' — not 'does it work?'. The one-year survival named in this shelf's question is not reported in this record; metabolomic substudies of survivors are a different kind of evidence and are not carded here.
cards.source: Jones AE et al. Effect of Levocarnitine vs Placebo as an Adjunctive Treatment for Septic Shock: The Rapid Administration of Carnitine in Sepsis (RACE) Randomized Clinical Trial. shelves.title: Passive leg raising predicts fluid responsiveness well (AUC 0.95 when cardiac output is measured) — but prediction is not outcome: no PLR-guided resuscitation outcome trial sits in this record
shelves.question: In patients with septic shock, does resuscitation guided by passive-leg-raise fluid-responsiveness testing improve outcomes compared with usual assessment?
shelves.mesh: Cardiac Output/*physiology · Chi-Square Distribution · Critical Illness · *Fluid Therapy · Humans · Intensive Care Units · Leg/*blood supply · Monitoring, Physiologic/methods · *Patient Positioning · ROC Curve · Sensitivity and Specificity
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — for the outcome question as asked, there is no direct evidence here at all; what exists is diagnostic accuracy, and it is strong only when flow is measured directly. Monnet's meta-analysis of 21 studies and 991 adults (Monnet X et al., PMID: 26825952) found PLR-induced changes in cardiac output predicted fluid responsiveness with pooled sensitivity 0.85 and specificity 0.91 and an area under the ROC curve of 0.95, at a best threshold of a cardiac-output rise of at least 10%; read by pulse pressure instead, sensitivity fell to 0.56 (AUC 0.77). Cherpanath's meta-analysis of 23 trials and 1,013 patients (Cherpanath TGV et al., PMID: 26741579) agrees: sensitivity 86%, specificity 92%, AUC 0.95, with pulse-pressure readings clearly inferior to flow variables. Neither review reports a trial of PLR-guided resuscitation against usual assessment on mortality, organ failure, or any patient outcome — they validate a measurement, not a strategy. So this shelf separates the two claims the question conflates: as a test, PLR with a cardiac-output measurement is reliable; as a resuscitation strategy, its outcome benefit is untested in this record. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): PLR reliably predicts fluid responsiveness when cardiac output is measured, but whether guiding resuscitation by it improves outcomes in septic shock has not been shown.

cards.headline: Monnet 2016 (meta-analysis, 21 studies, 991 patients): PLR cardiac-output change — sensitivity 0.85, specificity 0.91, AUC 0.95; by pulse pressure, sensitivity only 0.56
cards.summary: Monnet 2016 (meta-analysis, 21 studies, 991 patients): PLR cardiac-output change — sensitivity 0.85, specificity 0.91, AUC 0.95; by pulse pressure, sensitivity only 0.56
cards.people: Twenty-one studies totalling 991 adult patients and 995 fluid challenges in acute circulatory failure, testing whether passive-leg-raising-induced changes in cardiac output (measured by echocardiography, pulse contour analysis, bioreactance, oesophageal Doppler, thermodilution or suprasternal Doppler) or in arterial pulse pressure predict the response to volume expansion.
cards.result: The pooled correlation between PLR-induced and fluid-induced changes in cardiac output was 0.76 (95% CI 0.73 to 0.80). For PLR-induced changes in cardiac output, pooled sensitivity was 0.85 (0.81 to 0.88), pooled specificity 0.91 (0.88 to 0.93), and the area under the ROC curve 0.95±0.01, with a best threshold of a PLR-induced cardiac-output increase of at least 10±2%. For PLR-induced changes in pulse pressure (8 studies, 432 challenges), sensitivity was 0.56, specificity 0.83, and AUC 0.77±0.05. No patient-outcome comparison of PLR-guided versus usual resuscitation is reported.
cards.watchOut: Diagnostic accuracy against a fluid-challenge reference standard is not evidence that acting on the test improves outcomes — and the accurate version of the test requires a cardiac-output monitor; the bedside pulse-pressure version misses nearly half of responders.
cards.source: Monnet X et al. Passive leg raising for predicting fluid responsiveness: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Intensive Care Medicine. 2016. PMID: 26825952. cards.headline: Cherpanath 2016 (meta-analysis, 23 trials, 1,013 patients): sensitivity 86%, specificity 92%, AUC 0.95 — performance held across ventilation modes and techniques, pulse pressure again inferior
cards.summary: Cherpanath 2016 (meta-analysis, 23 trials, 1,013 patients): sensitivity 86%, specificity 92%, AUC 0.95 — performance held across ventilation modes and techniques, pulse pressure again inferior
cards.people: Twenty-three clinical trials totalling 1,013 patients and 1,034 fluid challenges, in which passive leg raising was performed together with a fluid challenge as the gold standard defining fluid responders and non-responders, across varied clinical settings, ventilation modes and measurement techniques.
cards.result: Pooled sensitivity was 86% (95% CI 79 to 92), pooled specificity 92% (95% CI 88 to 96), and the summary area under the ROC curve was 0.95 (95% CI 0.92 to 0.98). Mode of ventilation, type of fluid, starting position and measurement technique did not affect diagnostic performance. Changes in pulse pressure performed worse than flow variables (sensitivity 58%, 95% CI 44 to 70, versus 85%, 95% CI 78 to 90; p<0.001). No mortality or other patient-outcome data for PLR-guided management are reported.
cards.watchOut: Two meta-analyses agreeing on accuracy still leave the strategy question untouched: neither contains a randomised comparison of PLR-guided resuscitation with usual care. Concordant AUCs should not be mistaken for outcome evidence.
cards.source: Cherpanath TGV et al. Predicting Fluid Responsiveness by Passive Leg Raising: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of 23 Clinical Trials. Critical Care Medicine. 2016. PMID: 26741579. cards.result: PLR-induced cardiac-output change: sensitivity 0.85–0.86, specificity 0.91–0.92, AUC 0.95 in both reviews. PLR by pulse pressure: sensitivity 0.56–0.58. shelves.title: Lactate clearance versus ScvO2: the EMShockNet trial met non-inferiority (in-hospital mortality 17% versus 23%) — a blood test can stand in for the central-line oxygen target
shelves.question: In emergency-department patients with severe sepsis, is a lactate-clearance-guided resuscitation strategy non-inferior to central venous oxygen saturation-guided therapy for survival?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Cardiotonic Agents/therapeutic use · Central Venous Pressure · Dobutamine/therapeutic use · Erythrocyte Transfusion · Female · *Fluid Therapy · Hospital Mortality · Humans · Lactic Acid/blood/*metabolism · Male · Middle Aged · Oxygen/*blood · Prospective Studies · Sepsis/blood/mortality/*therapy · Shock, Septic/blood/mortality/*therapy · Treatment Outcome · Vasoconstrictor Agents/administration & dosage
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — non-inferior in the trial that asked, and favoured in the pool; the benefit claimed is substitutability, not superiority of a drug. In the EMShockNet randomised non-inferiority trial (Jones AE et al., PMID: 20179283), 300 emergency-department patients with severe sepsis and hypoperfusion or septic shock were resuscitated for up to 6 hours to normalise central venous pressure and mean arterial pressure plus either lactate clearance of at least 10% or ScvO2 of at least 70%: in-hospital mortality was 17% (25 of 150) with lactate clearance versus 23% (34 of 150) with ScvO2, and the observed difference did not cross the predefined −10% non-inferiority threshold (95% CI for the 6% difference, −3% to 15%), with no differences in treatments given over the first 72 hours or in adverse events. Pan's meta-analysis of seven randomised trials and 1,301 patients (Pan J et al., PMID: 30813144) goes further, finding lower in-hospital mortality with lactate-clearance-guided therapy (risk ratio 0.68, 95% CI 0.56 to 0.82 — a relative effect; the abstract does not report pooled absolute mortality rates), plus shorter ICU stay and ventilation time. The anchor trial's own absolute rates are the anchor for practice: lactate guidance performed at least as well without requiring the ScvO2 catheter target. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): lactate-clearance-guided resuscitation is a non-inferior, less invasive substitute for ScvO2-guided therapy in early severe sepsis.

cards.headline: Jones 2010 (EMShockNet): in-hospital mortality 17% on lactate-clearance guidance versus 23% on ScvO2 guidance — non-inferiority threshold not crossed
cards.summary: Jones 2010 (EMShockNet): in-hospital mortality 17% on lactate-clearance guidance versus 23% on ScvO2 guidance — non-inferiority threshold not crossed
cards.people: 300 patients (150 per group) with severe sepsis and evidence of hypoperfusion or septic shock, presenting to the emergency departments of three US urban hospitals between January 2007 and January 2009. Both groups were resuscitated to normalise central venous pressure and mean arterial pressure; the ScvO2 group additionally targeted ScvO2 of at least 70%, and the lactate-clearance group targeted lactate clearance of at least 10%, for up to 6 hours or until all goals were achieved. Clinicians who subsequently took over care were blinded to treatment assignment. The non-inferiority threshold was set at Δ=−10% for absolute in-hospital mortality.
cards.result: Thirty-four patients (23%, 95% CI 17% to 30%) in the ScvO2 group died in hospital, compared with 25 (17%, 95% CI 11% to 24%) in the lactate-clearance group. The observed difference did not reach the predefined −10% non-inferiority threshold (intention-to-treat 95% CI for the 6% difference, −3% to 15%). There were no differences in treatments administered during the first 72 hours of hospitalisation and no differences in treatment-related adverse events.
cards.watchOut: A non-inferiority verdict with a wide (−10%) margin and a confidence interval running from −3% to 15% is a statement about acceptable substitution, not proof the strategies are identical — and both arms sat inside an early goal-directed protocol of its era, so the comparison is between targets, not between protocolised and usual care.
cards.source: Jones AE et al. Lactate clearance vs central venous oxygen saturation as goals of early sepsis therapy: a randomized clinical trial. JAMA. 2010. PMID: 20179283. cards.headline: Pan 2019 (meta-analysis, 7 RCTs, 1,301 patients): lactate-clearance guidance and lower in-hospital mortality (risk ratio 0.68) — pooled absolute rates not reported in the abstract
cards.summary: Pan 2019 (meta-analysis, 7 RCTs, 1,301 patients): lactate-clearance guidance and lower in-hospital mortality (risk ratio 0.68) — pooled absolute rates not reported in the abstract
cards.people: Seven randomised controlled trials encompassing 1,301 patients with sepsis, comparing early lactate-clearance-guided resuscitation with central venous oxygen saturation (ScvO2)-guided therapy; the primary outcome was mortality.
cards.result: Compared with ScvO2-guided therapy, early lactate-clearance-directed therapy was associated with decreased in-hospital mortality (risk ratio 0.68, 95% CI 0.56 to 0.82 — a relative effect; pooled absolute mortality rates are not reported in the abstract), shorter ICU stay (mean difference −1.64 days, 95% CI −3.23 to −0.05), shorter mechanical ventilation time (mean difference −10.22 hours, 95% CI −15.94 to −4.5), and lower APACHE-II scores (mean difference −4.47, 95% CI −7.25 to −1.69). Length of hospital stay and SOFA scores were similar.
cards.watchOut: The pooled superiority claim outruns the anchor trial's non-inferiority finding and rests substantially on small trials beyond EMShockNet; without pooled absolute rates in the abstract, the size of any real mortality advantage cannot be stated from this record. Treat the pool as supportive of substitution, not as proof of superiority.
cards.source: Pan J et al. Relative efficacy and safety of early lactate clearance-guided therapy resuscitation in patients with sepsis: A meta-analysis. Medicine. 2019. PMID: 30813144. shelves.title: Drawing less blood in the ICU: conservation devices cut the volume taken by 19–80% in small studies — but the one large trial of small-volume tubes did not significantly cut transfusions in its primary analysis
shelves.question: In ICU patients, do small-volume blood-collection tubes and other blood-conservation devices reduce iatrogenic blood loss and transfusion compared with standard tubes?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Female · Humans · Male · *Anemia/prevention & control · *Blood Specimen Collection/adverse effects/instrumentation · Blood Transfusion/statistics & numerical data · Blood Volume · *Critical Care/methods · Intensive Care Units · *Vascular Access Devices
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — the devices clearly take less blood; whether that saves transfusions is unproven. The systematic review behind this shelf (Siegal DM et al., PMID: 30482081) found 8 studies (1,204 patients) of arterial access devices and reduced-volume tubes, every one reporting less blood taken for laboratory testing than standard practice (range 19%–80%), but all at serious risk of bias and too heterogeneous to pool, with no pooled transfusion result. The one large randomised test, STRATUS (Siegal DM et al., PMID: 37824152), switched 25 Canadian ICUs to small-volume tubes in a stepped-wedge design: in its primary analysis of 21,201 patients, red-cell units per patient per ICU stay did not differ significantly (relative risk 0.91, 95% CI 0.79 to 1.05; P=.19; absolute reduction 7.24 units per 100 patients, 95% CI −3.28 to 19.44); only a prespecified secondary analysis including the COVID-hiatus period reached significance (relative risk 0.88, 95% CI 0.77 to 1.00; P=.04). Specimens with insufficient volume for testing stayed rare (≤0.03%) on both strategies, so the laboratory harm feared from smaller tubes did not materialise. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): blood-conservation devices reliably reduce the volume of blood drawn, but a transfusion benefit rests on a secondary analysis of a single trial and on small studies at serious risk of bias.

cards.headline: Siegal 2020 (systematic review, 8 studies, 1,204 patients): every study reported less blood taken with conservation devices (19%–80% reduction) — all at serious risk of bias, too heterogeneous to pool
cards.summary: Siegal 2020 (systematic review, 8 studies, 1,204 patients): every study reported less blood taken with conservation devices (19%–80% reduction) — all at serious risk of bias, too heterogeneous to pool
cards.people: Eight studies (1,204 adult ICU patients) comparing blood-sampling conservation devices with standard care or another intervention, searched to October 5, 2017: five studies of arterial access devices and three of reduced-volume blood collection tubes.
cards.result: All studies reported a reduction in the volume of blood taken for laboratory testing with devices compared with standard practice (range 19%–80%). The studies were judged to have serious risk of bias, and because of heterogeneity, pooling for meta-analysis was not considered appropriate — so the review gives no pooled estimate for blood volume and none for transfusion. The authors conclude the devices appear effective at reducing volume taken and that further assessment of clinical outcomes may establish clinical benefit.
cards.watchOut: A volume outcome, not a patient outcome: taking 19%–80% less blood for tests is the mechanism, not the prize. The review cannot say whether any patient avoided a transfusion, and its studies were small and at serious risk of bias — the honest summary is 'less blood drawn, benefit downstream unmeasured here'.
cards.source: Siegal DM et al. Devices to Reduce the Volume of Blood Taken for Laboratory Testing in ICU Patients: A Systematic Review. Journal of Intensive Care Medicine. 2020. PMID: 30482081. cards.headline: STRATUS 2023 (stepped-wedge cluster trial, 25 ICUs, 21,201 patients in the primary analysis): small-volume tubes did not significantly reduce red-cell transfusion (relative risk 0.91; P=.19) — a prespecified secondary analysis did (relative risk 0.88; P=.04)
cards.summary: STRATUS 2023 (stepped-wedge cluster trial, 25 ICUs, 21,201 patients in the primary analysis): small-volume tubes did not significantly reduce red-cell transfusion (relative risk 0.91; P=.19) — a prespecified secondary analysis did (relative risk 0.88; P=.04)
cards.people: 25 adult medical-surgical ICUs in Canada randomised to transition from standard-volume to small-volume vacuum tubes for laboratory testing (February 2019 to January 2021); the primary analysis covered 21,201 patients admitted for 48 hours or more (mean age 63.5 years; 39.9% female), excluding 6,210 patients admitted during a 5.5-month COVID-19-related trial hiatus; a prespecified secondary analysis included 27,411 patients.
cards.result: In the primary analysis there was no significant difference in red-cell units per patient per ICU stay (relative risk 0.91, 95% CI 0.79 to 1.05; P=.19; absolute reduction 7.24 red-cell units per 100 patients per ICU stay, 95% CI −3.28 to 19.44). In the prespecified secondary analysis, units per patient per ICU stay decreased after transition to small-volume tubes (relative risk 0.88, 95% CI 0.77 to 1.00; P=.04; absolute reduction 9.84 units per 100 patients, 95% CI 0.24 to 20.76). The transfusion-adjusted haemoglobin decrease was not significantly different in the primary population (mean difference 0.10 g/dL, 95% CI −0.04 to 0.23) and was lower in the secondary population (0.17 g/dL, 95% CI 0.05 to 0.29). Specimens with insufficient quantity for analysis were rare (≤0.03%) before and after transition.
cards.watchOut: The headline depends on which analysis you read: the primary analysis — the one the trial was designed around, excluding the pandemic hiatus — is null, and the significant result comes from the secondary population. A stepped-wedge switch also cannot be blinded, and transfusion thresholds were not controlled, so clinician behaviour around the switch is part of what was measured.

cards.headline: Synthesis: less blood in the tube rack is certain; fewer transfusions is a secondary-analysis finding in one trial, resting on small biased studies before it
cards.summary: Synthesis: less blood in the tube rack is certain; fewer transfusions is a secondary-analysis finding in one trial, resting on small biased studies before it
cards.people: One systematic review of 8 small studies (1,204 patients) of arterial access devices and reduced-volume tubes, plus one 25-ICU stepped-wedge cluster trial (21,201 patients in the primary analysis) of small-volume tubes.
cards.result: Volume of blood taken: reduced in every study in the review (19%–80%), unpooled. Red-cell transfusion: no significant difference in STRATUS's primary analysis (relative risk 0.91, 95% CI 0.79 to 1.05); a significant reduction in its prespecified secondary analysis (relative risk 0.88, 95% CI 0.77 to 1.00; absolute reduction 9.84 units per 100 patients). Laboratory safety: insufficient specimens ≤0.03% on either tube size. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence).
cards.watchOut: Do not quote the review's 19%–80% volume range as a transfusion effect — the two numbers answer different questions, and only one trial has asked the transfusion question at scale. Tier C is set: the transfusion claim depends on a single trial's secondary analysis and on small studies at serious risk of bias.
cards.source: Synthesis of Siegal DM et al. Journal of Intensive Care Medicine. 2020 (PMID: 30482081); Siegal DM et al. JAMA. 2023 (PMID: 37824152).

shelves.title: Transfusing children at 7 g/dL: TRIPICU's restrictive threshold matched 9.5 g/dL on organ dysfunction (12% in both groups) and 54% of children needed no transfusion at all
shelves.question: In critically ill children, does a restrictive red-cell transfusion threshold (7 g/dL) give equivalent outcomes to a liberal threshold (9.5 g/dL)?
shelves.mesh: Anemia/blood/diagnosis/*therapy · Child · Child, Preschool · Critical Illness/mortality/*therapy · *Erythrocyte Transfusion · Female · Hemoglobins/*analysis · Humans · Infant · Infant, Newborn · Intensive Care Units, Pediatric · Leukocyte Reduction Procedures · Male · Multiple Organ Failure/epidemiology · Severity of Illness Index
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — on outcomes, with substantially less blood used. In TRIPICU (Lacroix J et al., PMID: 17442904), 637 stable critically ill children with haemoglobin below 9.5 g/dL were randomised to transfusion thresholds of 7 or 9.5 g/dL: new or progressive multiple-organ dysfunction developed in 12% in both groups (38 vs 39 patients; absolute risk reduction with the restrictive strategy 0.4%, 95% CI −4.6 to 5.4), deaths within 28 days were 14 in each group, and the restrictive group received 44% fewer transfusions — 54% of its children were never transfused, versus 2% in the liberal group. The trial's own sepsis subgroup (Karam O et al., PMID: 21057356; 137 children) read the same way: new or progressive multiple-organ dysfunction in 18.8% vs 19.1% (P=.97), with no difference in PICU stay or mortality. This is the paediatric question, distinct from the adult threshold trials on the adult umbrella shelf: in stable critically ill children, waiting until 7 g/dL costs nothing measurable in organ outcomes and spares about half the children any transfusion. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): a 7 g/dL threshold in stable critically ill children gives equivalent organ-dysfunction outcomes to 9.5 g/dL while markedly reducing transfusion exposure.

cards.headline: TRIPICU 2007 (Lacroix): organ dysfunction in 12% on both thresholds (38 vs 39 children), 14 deaths in each group — and 44% fewer transfusions, with 54% of the restrictive group never transfused
cards.summary: TRIPICU 2007 (Lacroix): organ dysfunction in 12% on both thresholds (38 vs 39 children), 14 deaths in each group — and 44% fewer transfusions, with 54% of the restrictive group never transfused
cards.type: Multicentre noninferiority randomised controlled trial (TRIPICU, Lacroix 2007)
cards.people: 637 stable, critically ill children who had haemoglobin concentrations below 9.5 g/dL within 7 days of admission to a paediatric intensive care unit, randomised to a transfusion threshold of 7 g/dL (restrictive, 320 patients) or 9.5 g/dL (liberal, 317 patients), using leukocyte-reduced red cells.
cards.result: New or progressive multiple-organ dysfunction syndrome (the primary outcome) developed in 38 patients in the restrictive group and 39 in the liberal group (12% in both groups; absolute risk reduction with the restrictive strategy 0.4%, 95% confidence interval −4.6 to 5.4). There were 14 deaths in each group within 28 days of randomisation, and no significant differences in other outcomes including adverse events. Haemoglobin was maintained a mean of 2.1±0.2 g/dL lower in the restrictive group (lowest average levels 8.7±0.4 vs 10.8±0.5 g/dL; P<0.001). The restrictive group received 44% fewer transfusions; 174 patients (54%) in that group received no transfusion at all, versus 7 patients (2%) in the liberal group (P<0.001).
cards.watchOut: These were stable children — enrolled only once haemodynamically settled, with haemoglobin already below 9.5 g/dL. The 7 g/dL answer does not travel to the unstable, bleeding, or severely hypoxaemic child, who was not the population randomised here; and a noninferiority margin that runs to +5.4 points of organ dysfunction cannot exclude a modest harm.
cards.source: Lacroix J et al. Transfusion strategies for patients in pediatric intensive care units. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2007. PMID: 17442904. Registry ID: ISRCTN37246456. cards.headline: Karam 2011 (TRIPICU sepsis subgroup, 137 children): organ dysfunction 18.8% restrictive vs 19.1% liberal (P=.97) — the sickest subgroup read the same way as the parent trial
cards.summary: Karam 2011 (TRIPICU sepsis subgroup, 137 children): organ dysfunction 18.8% restrictive vs 19.1% liberal (P=.97) — the sickest subgroup read the same way as the parent trial
cards.type: Subgroup analysis of a multicentre randomised controlled trial (Karam 2011)
cards.people: 137 stabilised critically ill children with sepsis from the TRIPICU trial (haemoglobin ≤9.5 g/dL within 7 days of PICU admission; cardiovascular support not increased for at least 2 hours before enrolment), randomised to transfusion at haemoglobin below 7.0 g/dL (restrictive, 69 patients) or 9.5 g/dL (liberal, 68 patients).
cards.result: In the restrictive group, 30 patients received no red-cell transfusion at all, versus only one patient in the liberal group (P<.01). No clinically significant differences were found for new or progressive multiple-organ dysfunction syndrome (18.8% vs 19.1%; P=.97), for PICU length of stay (P=.74), or for PICU mortality (P=.44) between the restrictive and liberal groups. The authors conclude a haemoglobin level of 7.0 g/dL may be safe for stabilised children with sepsis, while noting further studies are required.
cards.watchOut: A subgroup of the parent trial, not an independent replication: 137 children, stabilised sepsis only (children whose cardiovascular support was still escalating were not in this analysis), and wide uncertainty around every estimate. It corroborates TRIPICU; it does not double the evidence base.
cards.source: Karam O et al. Red blood cell transfusion thresholds in pediatric patients with sepsis. Pediatric Critical Care Medicine. 2011. PMID: 21057356. cards.summary: Synthesis: one large paediatric trial and its sepsis subgroup agree — 7 g/dL costs no organ outcomes in stable critically ill children and spares about half of them transfusion entirely
cards.people: One multicentre noninferiority RCT of 637 stable critically ill children (TRIPICU) and its prespecified sepsis subgroup of 137 children (Karam 2011).
cards.result: New or progressive multiple-organ dysfunction: 12% in both arms of TRIPICU (absolute risk reduction 0.4%, 95% CI −4.6 to 5.4); 18.8% vs 19.1% in the sepsis subgroup. shelves.title: Extended daily dialysis versus continuous therapy in ICU kidney injury: mortality the same in the randomised trials (relative risk 0.90) — the apparent EDD advantage lives only in observational studies
shelves.question: In ICU patients with acute kidney injury, does extended daily dialysis (sustained low-efficiency dialysis) give equivalent clearance, haemodynamic stability, and survival to continuous renal replacement therapy?
shelves.mesh: Acute Kidney Injury/*therapy · Critical Care/*methods · Hemodiafiltration/methods · Hemofiltration/methods · Humans · Renal Dialysis/methods · Renal Replacement Therapy/*methods · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — in the randomised evidence, the hybrid and the continuous machine are interchangeable on outcomes. The meta-analysis behind this shelf (Zhang L et al., PMID: 25843704) pooled 7 randomised trials (533 patients) and 10 observational studies (675 patients) of extended daily dialysis (EDD, sessions of more than 6 and less than 24 hours on a conventional machine) versus continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT): in the randomised trials, mortality did not differ (relative risk 0.90, 95% CI 0.74 to 1.11; P=0.3), nor did kidney recovery, fluid removal, or ICU days, and biochemical efficacy (urea, creatinine, phosphate) was similar. The lower mortality with EDD (relative risk 0.86, 95% CI 0.74 to 1.00; P=0.05) appeared only in the observational studies, where allocation bias is the obvious explanation, as the reviewers themselves state. The largest single randomised comparison (Schwenger V et al., PMID: 22839577; 232 patients, 12-hour sustained low-efficiency dialysis versus 24-hour continuous haemofiltration) found 90-day mortality of 49.6% vs 55.6% (P=0.43) with similar haemodynamic stability — and fewer ventilator days (17.7 vs 20.9; P=0.047), fewer ICU days (19.6 vs 23.7; P=0.04), and lower nursing time and cost with the extended-daily approach. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): extended daily dialysis matches CRRT on survival, kidney recovery, and clearance in the randomised trials, with practical advantages in time and cost — and no proven survival advantage for either mode.

cards.headline: Zhang 2015 (meta-analysis, 7 RCTs with 533 patients and 10 observational studies with 675): mortality in the randomised trials did not differ between EDD and CRRT (relative risk 0.90, 95% CI 0.74 to 1.11)
cards.summary: Zhang 2015 (meta-analysis, 7 RCTs with 533 patients and 10 observational studies with 675): mortality in the randomised trials did not differ between EDD and CRRT (relative risk 0.90, 95% CI 0.74 to 1.11)
cards.people: 17 studies from 2000 to 2014 in patients with acute kidney injury: 7 randomised controlled trials (533 patients) and 10 observational studies (675 patients), comparing extended daily dialysis — extended haemodialysis or haemodiafiltration for more than 6 but less than 24 hours per session using a conventional haemodialysis machine — with continuous renal replacement therapy.
cards.result: Meta-analysis of the randomised trials showed no difference in mortality between EDD and CRRT (relative risk 0.90, 95% CI 0.74 to 1.11; P=0.3; I²=0%). In observational studies, EDD was associated with lower mortality (relative risk 0.86, 95% CI 0.74 to 1.00; P=0.05; I²=15%) — relative measures; the abstract reports no pooled absolute mortality rates. In both randomised and observational studies there were no significant differences in recovery of kidney function, fluid removal, or days in the intensive care unit, and EDD showed similar biochemical efficacy to CRRT during treatment (serum urea, serum creatinine, and serum phosphate).
cards.watchOut: The only mortality signal favouring EDD comes from the observational half of this review, where clinicians chose the mode — exactly the design in which a hybrid therapy offered to more stable patients will look better. The reviewers state this limitation themselves: the survival benefit of EDD depends on observational studies and may reflect allocation or selection bias.
cards.source: Zhang L et al. Extended Daily Dialysis Versus Continuous Renal Replacement Therapy for Acute Kidney Injury: A Meta-analysis. American Journal of Kidney Diseases. 2015. PMID: 25843704. cards.headline: Schwenger 2012 (randomised trial, 232 patients): 90-day mortality 49.6% on 12-hour SLED versus 55.6% on 24-hour continuous haemofiltration (P=0.43) — with fewer ventilator and ICU days and lower cost on SLED
cards.summary: Schwenger 2012 (randomised trial, 232 patients): 90-day mortality 49.6% on 12-hour SLED versus 55.6% on 24-hour continuous haemofiltration (P=0.43) — with fewer ventilator and ICU days and lower cost on SLED
cards.people: 232 patients with acute kidney injury undergoing renal replacement therapy in a surgical ICU of a university hospital (enrolled April 2006 to January 2009), randomised to 12-hour sustained low-efficiency dialysis using a single-pass batch system (115 patients, 817 treatments) or 24-hour predilutional continuous venovenous haemofiltration (117 patients, 877 treatments), both at blood flows of 100 to 120 ml/min.
cards.result: The primary outcome, 90-day mortality, was similar between groups (SLED 49.6% vs CVVH 55.6%, P=0.43). Haemodynamic stability did not differ, whereas the SLED group had significantly fewer days of mechanical ventilation (17.7±19.4 vs 20.9±19.8, P=0.047) and fewer days in the ICU (19.6±20.1 vs 23.7±21.9, P=0.04). Patients treated with SLED needed fewer blood transfusions (1,375±2,573 ml vs 1,976±3,316 ml, P=0.02) and had a substantial reduction in nursing time spent on renal replacement therapy (P<0.001), resulting in lower costs.
cards.watchOut: A single-centre surgical-ICU trial using one specific batch dialysis system, with several secondary outcomes (ventilator days, ICU days, transfusion volume) tested without the protection of a single primary endpoint — the mortality result is the sturdy one, and it is a null. The ventilator/ICU-day advantages are hypothesis-grade, not proof.

cards.headline: Synthesis: equivalent survival, recovery, and clearance in the randomised data — the choice between extended daily dialysis and CRRT is logistics and cost, not outcomes
cards.summary: Synthesis: equivalent survival, recovery, and clearance in the randomised data — the choice between extended daily dialysis and CRRT is logistics and cost, not outcomes
cards.people: A meta-analysis of 7 RCTs (533 patients) and 10 observational studies (675 patients) plus the largest single randomised comparison (232 patients) of extended daily dialysis / sustained low-efficiency dialysis versus continuous renal replacement therapy in ICU acute kidney injury.
cards.result: Mortality in randomised trials: relative risk 0.90 (95% CI 0.74 to 1.11) for EDD vs CRRT; in the largest single trial, 90-day mortality 49.6% vs 55.6% (P=0.43). Kidney recovery, fluid removal, ICU days, and biochemical clearance: no significant differences in the pooled randomised data. An EDD mortality advantage (relative risk 0.86) appears only in observational studies. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference).
cards.watchOut: This shelf compares MODES (hybrid extended-daily versus continuous); how much therapy to give is a different question, homed with the intensity trials, and when to start is another. Tier C is set because the pooled randomised base is small — 533 patients across 7 trials in the meta-analysis — even though its result is consistent.
cards.source: Synthesis of Zhang L et al. American Journal of Kidney Diseases. 2015 (PMID: 25843704); Schwenger V et al. Critical Care. 2012 (PMID: 22839577).

shelves.title: Where to put the central line: subclavian carried the lowest infection-and-thrombosis risk in 3SITES (1.5 vs 3.6 vs 4.6 events per 1,000 catheter-days) — and the highest pneumothorax risk
shelves.question: In critically ill adults needing a central venous catheter, how do subclavian, jugular, and femoral insertion sites compare for bloodstream infection and thrombosis?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Catheter-Related Infections/*etiology · Catheterization, Central Venous/adverse effects/*methods · Female · Femoral Vein · Humans · Jugular Veins · Male · Middle Aged · Risk · Sepsis/*etiology · Subclavian Vein · Venous Thrombosis/*etiology
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for the subclavian site on infection and thrombosis, with its mechanical price on the same face. In 3SITES (Parienti JJ et al., PMID: 26398070), 3,471 catheters in 3,027 ICU patients were randomised by site: the composite of catheter-related bloodstream infection and symptomatic deep-vein thrombosis occurred at 1.5 per 1,000 catheter-days with the subclavian vein, 3.6 with the jugular, and 4.6 with the femoral (P=0.02); pairwise, risk was higher for femoral than subclavian (hazard ratio 3.5, 95% CI 1.5 to 7.8; P=0.003) and for jugular than subclavian (hazard ratio 2.1, 95% CI 1.0 to 4.3; P=0.04), with femoral and jugular similar (hazard ratio 1.3, 95% CI 0.8 to 2.1). The harm runs the other way: pneumothorax requiring a chest tube followed 13 (1.5%) of subclavian insertions versus 4 (0.5%) of jugular insertions. A network meta-analysis of 13 randomised trials (6,201 patients) (Sakuraya M et al., PMID: 36106316) points the same direction for infection — subclavian lower than jugular (relative risk 0.30, 95% CI 0.11 to 0.81, moderate certainty) and femoral higher than subclavian (relative risk 2.56, 95% CI 1.02 to 6.44) — with no significant site differences for thrombosis and fewer mechanical complications at the femoral site. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): when all three sites are available, subclavian insertion minimises bloodstream infection and symptomatic thrombosis, at the cost of the highest pneumothorax risk.

cards.headline: 3SITES 2015 (Parienti): primary events 1.5 per 1,000 catheter-days subclavian vs 3.6 jugular vs 4.6 femoral (P=0.02) — pneumothorax requiring a chest tube in 1.5% of subclavian vs 0.5% of jugular insertions
cards.summary: 3SITES 2015 (Parienti): primary events 1.5 per 1,000 catheter-days subclavian vs 3.6 jugular vs 4.6 femoral (P=0.02) — pneumothorax requiring a chest tube in 1.5% of subclavian vs 0.5% of jugular insertions
cards.people: 3,027 adults in intensive care units receiving 3,471 nontunneled central venous catheters, randomly assigned to the subclavian, jugular, or femoral vein in a 1:1:1 ratio when all three sites were suitable (three-choice scheme) or 1:1 when two sites were suitable (two-choice scheme). The primary outcome was a composite of catheter-related bloodstream infection and symptomatic deep-vein thrombosis.
cards.result: In the three-choice comparison there were 8, 20, and 22 primary outcome events in the subclavian, jugular, and femoral groups respectively (1.5, 3.6, and 4.6 per 1,000 catheter-days; P=0.02). In pairwise comparisons the risk of the primary outcome was significantly higher in the femoral group than in the subclavian group (hazard ratio 3.5, 95% confidence interval 1.5 to 7.8; P=0.003) and in the jugular group than in the subclavian group (hazard ratio 2.1, 95% CI 1.0 to 4.3; P=0.04), whereas femoral and jugular risks were similar (hazard ratio 1.3, 95% CI 0.8 to 2.1; P=0.30). Pneumothorax requiring chest-tube insertion occurred in association with 13 (1.5%) of subclavian-vein insertions and 4 (0.5%) of jugular-vein insertions.
cards.watchOut: The absolute event rates are low — the subclavian advantage is about 2–3 events per 1,000 catheter-days — and the trial randomised only among sites the clinician judged suitable, so it says nothing about patients in whom the subclavian route is contraindicated (for example, severe coagulopathy, where a compressible site matters more than the ranking here).
cards.source: Parienti JJ et al. Intravascular Complications of Central Venous Catheterization by Insertion Site. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2015. PMID: 26398070. Registry ID: NCT01479153. cards.headline: Sakuraya 2022 (network meta-analysis, 13 RCTs, 6,201 patients): subclavian beat jugular on infectious complications (relative risk 0.30) and femoral was worse than subclavian (relative risk 2.56) — no site differed on thrombosis
cards.summary: Sakuraya 2022 (network meta-analysis, 13 RCTs, 6,201 patients): subclavian beat jugular on infectious complications (relative risk 0.30) and femoral was worse than subclavian (relative risk 2.56) — no site differed on thrombosis
cards.type: Systematic review and network meta-analysis of randomised trials (Sakuraya 2022)
cards.people: 13 randomised controlled trials (6,201 hospitalised adults) comparing central venous catheter insertion sites (internal jugular, subclavian, femoral, and peripheral insertion), analysed for clinically important infectious, thrombotic, and mechanical complications.
cards.result: For clinically important infectious complications, subclavian insertion decreased risk compared with internal jugular insertion (relative risk 0.30, 95% CI 0.11 to 0.81; moderate certainty), and femoral insertion carried higher risk than subclavian insertion (relative risk 2.56, 95% CI 1.02 to 6.44; moderate certainty) — relative measures; the abstract reports no pooled absolute rates. For clinically important thrombotic complications, no significant differences were found between insertion sites. For mechanical complications, femoral insertion carried lower risk than internal jugular (relative risk 0.42, 95% CI 0.21 to 0.82) and subclavian insertion (relative risk 0.33, 95% CI 0.16 to 0.66).
cards.watchOut: A network analysis leans partly on indirect comparisons, and its thrombotic result — no difference between sites — is softer than 3SITES's composite, in which thrombosis was bundled with infection. The infection ranking agrees across both cards; the mechanical-complication ranking (femoral safest) is the mirror image of the infection ranking, which is the real clinical trade-off.
cards.source: Sakuraya M et al. Insertion site of central venous catheter among hospitalized adult patients: A systematic review and network meta-analysis. Frontiers in Medicine. 2022. PMID: 36106316. MeSH: none in the record

cards.headline: Synthesis: subclavian first for infection and thrombosis when it is usable — and first also for pneumothorax; femoral is the mechanical safe site and the infectious risky one
cards.summary: Synthesis: subclavian first for infection and thrombosis when it is usable — and first also for pneumothorax; femoral is the mechanical safe site and the infectious risky one
cards.people: One multicentre RCT of 3,471 catheters in 3,027 ICU patients (3SITES) plus a network meta-analysis of 13 RCTs (6,201 patients) comparing central venous catheter insertion sites.
cards.result: Composite of bloodstream infection and symptomatic thrombosis (3SITES, per 1,000 catheter-days): subclavian 1.5, jugular 3.6, femoral 4.6. Infectious complications (network meta-analysis): subclavian vs jugular relative risk 0.30; femoral vs subclavian relative risk 2.56. Mechanical harm: pneumothorax requiring a chest tube in 1.5% of subclavian vs 0.5% of jugular insertions (3SITES); mechanical complications lowest at the femoral site in the network analysis. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) for the subclavian site on infection/thrombosis, harm on the face.
cards.watchOut: Both sources rank sites for patients in whom more than one site was an option. Site choice in a coagulopathic patient, a patient with a dialysis catheter planned, or a difficult neck is not governed by this ranking. Tier C is not set: the base is one very large RCT corroborated by a 13-trial network meta-analysis, and the claim is on infection/thrombosis, not mortality.
cards.source: Synthesis of Parienti JJ et al. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2015 (PMID: 26398070); Sakuraya M et al. Frontiers in Medicine. 2022 (PMID: 36106316).

shelves.title: Treating fever with acetaminophen in infected ICU patients: HEAT's 700 patients gained no ICU-free days (23 vs 22) and died at the same rate (15.9% vs 16.6% at 90 days)
shelves.question: In critically ill patients with suspected infection, does acetaminophen for fever increase or decrease mortality and ICU-free days compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Acetaminophen/*therapeutic use · Aged · Body Temperature/drug effects · Critical Illness · Double-Blind Method · Female · Fever/*drug therapy/etiology · Humans · Infections/complications/*drug therapy · Intensive Care Units · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Length of Stay · Male · Middle Aged · Prospective Studies
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — the best blinded test of fever treatment in infection is neutral on both of its outcomes. In HEAT (Young P et al., PMID: 26436473), 700 ICU patients with fever (temperature ≥38°C) and known or suspected infection were randomised to intravenous acetaminophen 1 g or placebo every 6 hours: ICU-free days to day 28 were 23 (interquartile range 13 to 25) on acetaminophen versus 22 (12 to 25) on placebo (absolute difference 0 days, 96.2% CI 0 to 1; P=0.07), and 90-day mortality was 15.9% (55 of 345) versus 16.6% (57 of 344) (relative risk 0.96, 95% CI 0.66 to 1.39; P=0.84) — neither benefit nor harm, in either direction the question asks about. The wider randomised literature reads identically: a meta-analysis of antipyretic therapy in critically ill septic adults (Drewry AM et al., PMID: 28221185) found no reduction in 28-day/hospital mortality across 8 randomised studies (1,507 patients; relative risk 0.93, 95% CI 0.77 to 1.13), no change in shock reversal or nosocomial infection, and a mean temperature reduction of only 0.38°C (95% CI −0.63 to −0.13). PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): acetaminophen lowers the thermometer slightly and changes neither survival nor ICU-free days in infected critically ill patients — fever treatment here is a comfort decision, not a survival decision.

cards.headline: HEAT 2015 (Young): ICU-free days 23 vs 22 (P=0.07) and 90-day mortality 15.9% vs 16.6% (relative risk 0.96) — acetaminophen neither helped nor harmed infected ICU patients
cards.summary: HEAT 2015 (Young): ICU-free days 23 vs 22 (P=0.07) and 90-day mortality 15.9% vs 16.6% (relative risk 0.96) — acetaminophen neither helped nor harmed infected ICU patients
cards.people: 700 ICU patients with fever (body temperature ≥38°C) and known or suspected infection, randomly assigned to 1 g of intravenous acetaminophen or placebo every 6 hours until ICU discharge, resolution of fever, cessation of antimicrobial therapy, or death; 90-day mortality data were available for 345 patients in the acetaminophen group and 344 in the placebo group.
cards.result: ICU-free days to day 28 did not differ significantly between groups: 23 days (interquartile range 13 to 25) with acetaminophen and 22 days (12 to 25) with placebo (Hodges-Lehmann estimate of absolute difference 0 days; 96.2% confidence interval 0 to 1; P=0.07). By day 90, 55 of 345 patients in the acetaminophen group (15.9%) and 57 of 344 in the placebo group (16.6%) had died (relative risk 0.96, 95% CI 0.66 to 1.39; P=0.84).
cards.watchOut: The mortality confidence interval (0.66 to 1.39, relative) is wide enough to hide a meaningful effect in either direction on its own — the LIKELY null on this shelf comes from HEAT and the pooled literature agreeing, not from HEAT alone. HEAT also enrolled patients with suspected infection broadly; it does not answer fever treatment in septic shock specifically, which has its own shelf.
cards.source: Young P et al. Acetaminophen for Fever in Critically Ill Patients with Suspected Infection. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2015. PMID: 26436473. Registry ID: ACTRN12612000513819. cards.headline: Drewry 2017 (meta-analysis, 8 randomised studies, 1,507 patients): antipyretic therapy did not reduce mortality in critically ill septic adults (relative risk 0.93, 95% CI 0.77 to 1.13) and lowered temperature by only 0.38°C
cards.summary: Drewry 2017 (meta-analysis, 8 randomised studies, 1,507 patients): antipyretic therapy did not reduce mortality in critically ill septic adults (relative risk 0.93, 95% CI 0.77 to 1.13) and lowered temperature by only 0.38°C
cards.people: Eight randomised studies (1,507 patients) and eight observational studies (17,432 patients) of antipyretic treatment in critically ill septic adults, searched through February 2016; randomised and observational studies were analysed separately. Studies enrolling paediatric patients, patients with neurologic injury, or healthy volunteers were excluded.
cards.result: Antipyretic therapy did not reduce 28-day/hospital mortality in the randomised studies (relative risk 0.93, 95% CI 0.77 to 1.13; I²=0.0%) or in the observational studies (odds ratio 0.90, 95% CI 0.54 to 1.51; I²=76.1%) — relative measures; the abstract reports no pooled absolute mortality rates. Shock reversal (relative risk 1.13, 95% CI 0.68 to 1.90) and acquisition of nosocomial infections (relative risk 1.13, 95% CI 0.61 to 2.09) were also unchanged. Antipyretic therapy decreased body temperature (mean difference −0.38°C, 95% CI −0.63 to −0.13) but not heart rate or minute ventilation.
cards.watchOut: The randomised pool mixes antipyretic drugs and methods across small trials, and the observational half — where sicker patients both run higher fevers and receive more treatment — is confounded by design; the shelf rests on the randomised half and on HEAT. A 0.38°C average temperature reduction also shows how modest the physiological lever being tested actually is.
cards.source: Drewry AM et al. Antipyretic Therapy in Critically Ill Septic Patients: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Critical Care Medicine. 2017. PMID: 28221185. cards.headline: Synthesis: fever falls a little, outcomes do not move — a large blinded trial and the pooled randomised literature agree on the null
cards.summary: Synthesis: fever falls a little, outcomes do not move — a large blinded trial and the pooled randomised literature agree on the null
cards.people: One 700-patient double-blind placebo-controlled trial (HEAT) in ICU patients with fever and suspected infection, plus a meta-analysis of 8 randomised studies (1,507 patients) of antipyretic therapy in critically ill septic adults.
cards.result: ICU-free days: 23 vs 22 (absolute difference 0 days; P=0.07). 90-day mortality (HEAT): 15.9% vs 16.6% (relative risk 0.96, 95% CI 0.66 to 1.39). 28-day/hospital mortality across the randomised antipyretic literature: relative risk 0.93 (95% CI 0.77 to 1.13). Temperature: lowered by a mean of 0.38°C. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference).
cards.watchOut: Neither source tests fever treatment in brain injury, where fever control has a separate rationale and separate shelves; nor in septic shock with external cooling, which is a different intervention with its own trial. Tier C is not set: the claim is the absence of benefit or harm, supported by a large blinded trial and a concordant randomised meta-analysis.
