shelves.title: Cooling the febrile septic-shock patient: Schortgen's 200 patients needed less vasopressor early and day-14 mortality was 19% vs 34% — in one open-label trial whose own primary endpoint was not met
shelves.question: In patients with septic shock and fever, does fever control with external cooling reduce vasopressor requirements and early mortality compared with no cooling?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Body Temperature · Critical Care · *Cryotherapy · Epinephrine/therapeutic use · Female · Fever/etiology/*therapy · Humans · Intention to Treat Analysis · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Logistic Models · Male · Middle Aged · Norepinephrine/therapeutic use · Poisson Distribution · Shock, Septic/*complications/drug therapy/mortality · Treatment Outcome · Vasoconstrictor Agents/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — an early-mortality signal from a single small open-label trial whose primary endpoint was missed, uncorroborated by the pooled fever-control literature. In Schortgen's trial (Schortgen F et al., PMID: 22366046), 200 febrile patients with septic shock on vasopressors, ventilation, and sedation were randomised to external cooling to normothermia (36.5–37°C) for 48 hours or no cooling: the primary endpoint — a 50% decrease in baseline vasopressor dose at 48 hours — did not differ significantly (72% vs 61%; absolute difference 11%, 95% CI −23 to 2), although the same endpoint at 12 hours did (54% vs 20%; absolute difference 34%, 95% CI −46 to −21; P<0.001), shock reversal during the ICU stay was more common with cooling (86% vs 73%; P=0.021), and day-14 mortality was lower (19% vs 34%; absolute difference −16%, 95% CI −28 to −4; P=0.013). Against that stands the individual-patient-data meta-analysis of fever-control trials (Young PJ et al., PMID: 30741326; 1,413 participants): more active fever management did not significantly change survival time overall (hazard ratio 0.91, 95% CI 0.75 to 1.10; P=0.32) or in any prespecified subgroup with limited physiological reserve. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): external cooling speeds vasopressor weaning in the first hours and may reduce early mortality in septic shock, but the claim rests on one 200-patient trial and a secondary time point — it is a reason for a larger trial, not a practice verdict.

cards.headline: Schortgen 2012: vasopressor dose halved by 12 hours in 54% cooled vs 20% not cooled (P<0.001) — but the primary endpoint at 48 hours was not met (72% vs 61%); day-14 mortality 19% vs 34% (P=0.013)
cards.summary: Schortgen 2012: vasopressor dose halved by 12 hours in 54% cooled vs 20% not cooled (P<0.001) — but the primary endpoint at 48 hours was not met (72% vs 61%); day-14 mortality 19% vs 34% (P=0.013)
cards.people: 200 febrile patients with septic shock requiring vasopressors, mechanical ventilation, and sedation, allocated to external cooling to achieve normothermia (36.5–37°C) for 48 hours (101 patients) or no external cooling (99 patients); vasopressors were tapered to maintain the same blood-pressure target in both groups. The primary endpoint was the number of patients with a 50% decrease in baseline vasopressor dose after 48 hours.
cards.result: Body temperature was significantly lower in the cooling group after 2 hours (36.8±0.7 vs 38.4±1.1°C; P<0.01). A 50% vasopressor dose decrease was significantly more common with external cooling from 12 hours of treatment (54 vs 20%; absolute difference 34%; 95% confidence interval −46 to −21; P<0.001) but not at 48 hours (72 vs 61%; absolute difference 11%; 95% CI −23 to 2) — the primary endpoint. Shock reversal during the ICU stay was significantly more common with cooling (86 vs 73%; absolute difference 13%; 95% CI 2 to 25; P=0.021). Day-14 mortality was significantly lower in the cooling group (19 vs 34%; absolute difference −16%; 95% CI −28 to −4; P=0.013).
cards.watchOut: Read the endpoints in the trial's own order: the prespecified primary endpoint (vasopressor halving at 48 hours) was not significant, and the striking numbers — the 12-hour vasopressor result and day-14 mortality — are secondary. Two hundred patients, no blinding (cooling cannot be blinded), and a mortality read at day 14 rather than day 28 or 90: this is a signal-generating trial, and its authors' conclusion of safety and benefit outruns what one trial this size can carry.
cards.source: Schortgen F et al. Fever control using external cooling in septic shock: a randomized controlled trial. American Journal of Respiratory and Critical Care Medicine. 2012. PMID: 22366046. cards.headline: Young 2019 (individual-patient-data meta-analysis, 1,413 trial participants): more active fever management did not improve survival overall (hazard ratio 0.91, 95% CI 0.75 to 1.10) or in any subgroup with limited reserves
cards.summary: Young 2019 (individual-patient-data meta-analysis, 1,413 trial participants): more active fever management did not improve survival overall (hazard ratio 0.91, 95% CI 0.75 to 1.10) or in any subgroup with limited reserves
cards.type: Individual patient data meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials (Young 2019)
cards.people: 1,413 participants in randomised trials of fever management in ICU patients, 707 assigned to more active fever management and 706 to less active fever management; prespecified subgroups were chosen to identify patients with limited physiological reserves (older patients, higher illness acuity, patients requiring organ support). The primary outcome was unadjusted time to death after randomisation.
cards.result: More active fever management did not result in a statistically significant difference in survival time compared with less active fever management (hazard ratio 0.91; 95% CI 0.75 to 1.10; P=0.32). There was no statistically significant heterogeneity of effect in any of the prespecified subgroups. The authors conclude their findings do not support the hypothesis that more active fever management increases survival, overall or in patients with limited physiological reserves.
cards.watchOut: This pool mixes fever interventions (drug and physical) and mixes populations — most participants did not have septic shock specifically, so it cannot directly refute a shock-specific cooling effect. What it does refute is any general claim that treating fever harder saves lives in the ICU; a shock-specific benefit would need a second, larger shock trial to stand.
cards.source: Young PJ et al. Fever control in critically ill adults. An individual patient data meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials. Intensive Care Medicine. 2019. PMID: 30741326. cards.headline: Synthesis: faster vasopressor weaning and a day-14 mortality gap in one 200-patient trial; no survival effect when fever-control trials are pooled — MAYBE (weak evidence)
cards.summary: Synthesis: faster vasopressor weaning and a day-14 mortality gap in one 200-patient trial; no survival effect when fever-control trials are pooled — MAYBE (weak evidence)
cards.people: One multicentre RCT of external cooling in 200 febrile septic-shock patients (Schortgen 2012), read against an individual-patient-data meta-analysis of fever-control RCTs in 1,413 ICU patients (Young 2019).
cards.result: Schortgen: primary endpoint (50% vasopressor decrease at 48 hours) 72% vs 61%, not significant; at 12 hours 54% vs 20% (P<0.001); shock reversal 86% vs 73% (P=0.021); day-14 mortality 19% vs 34% (P=0.013). Pooled fever-control trials: survival hazard ratio 0.91 (95% CI 0.75 to 1.10; P=0.32) for more vs less active fever management. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence).
cards.watchOut: The gap between the two cards is the shelf: a population-specific, method-specific signal (external cooling, septic shock, first 48 hours) versus a null pooled across methods and populations. Either could be the artefact. Tier C is set: a single trial, and a claim of benefit on mortality.

shelves.title: Running beta-lactams continuously in sepsis: BLING III's 7,031 patients died at 24.9% vs 26.8% (P=.08) with clearly better clinical cure — and the 18-trial meta-analysis puts 90-day mortality at a relative risk of 0.86
shelves.question: In critically ill patients with sepsis, does continuous (prolonged) infusion of beta-lactam antibiotics improve clinical cure and survival compared with intermittent bolus dosing?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Critical Illness · Drug Administration Schedule · Infusions, Intravenous · *Intensive Care Units · *Meropenem/administration & dosage · *Piperacillin, Tazobactam Drug Combination/administration & dosage · *Sepsis/drug therapy/mortality · *beta Lactam Antibiotics/administration & dosage · Adult · Hospital Mortality
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the largest trial leans toward benefit without proving it on mortality, and the pooled trials cross the line. In BLING III (Dulhunty JM et al., PMID: 38864155), 7,031 critically ill adults with sepsis receiving piperacillin-tazobactam or meropenem were randomised to the same 24-hour dose by continuous or intermittent infusion: 90-day mortality was 24.9% (864 of 3,474) on continuous infusion versus 26.8% (939 of 3,507) on intermittent (absolute difference −1.9%, 95% CI −4.9 to 1.1; odds ratio 0.91, 95% CI 0.81 to 1.01; P=.08), while clinical cure was clearly higher with continuous infusion (55.7% vs 50.0%; absolute difference 5.7%, 95% CI 2.4 to 9.1), with no significant difference in resistant-organism acquisition or Clostridioides difficile infection. The companion systematic review and meta-analysis of 18 randomised trials (9,108 patients) (Abdul-Aziz MH et al., PMID: 38864162) found prolonged infusion associated with lower 90-day mortality (pooled risk ratio 0.86, 95% credible interval 0.72 to 0.98 — a 14% relative reduction, graded high certainty, with a 99.1% posterior probability of benefit), lower ICU mortality (risk ratio 0.84, 95% credible interval 0.70 to 0.97), and higher clinical cure (risk ratio 1.16, 95% credible interval 1.07 to 1.31; moderate certainty). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): continuous or prolonged beta-lactam infusion in sepsis improves clinical cure and probably reduces mortality modestly in relative terms; BLING III's own absolute mortality gap was 1.9 points and not significant on its own.

cards.headline: BLING III 2024 (Dulhunty): 90-day mortality 24.9% continuous vs 26.8% intermittent (odds ratio 0.91; P=.08) — not significant — but clinical cure 55.7% vs 50.0% (absolute difference 5.7 points)
cards.summary: BLING III 2024 (Dulhunty): 90-day mortality 24.9% continuous vs 26.8% intermittent (odds ratio 0.91; P=.08) — not significant — but clinical cure 55.7% vs 50.0% (absolute difference 5.7 points)
cards.type: International open-label randomised clinical trial (BLING III, Dulhunty 2024)
cards.people: 7,202 patients randomised in 104 ICUs in seven countries (March 2018 to January 2023), of whom 7,031 (mean age 59 years [SD 16]; 2,423 women [35%]) were included in the primary analysis: critically ill adults treated with piperacillin-tazobactam or meropenem for sepsis, randomised to the equivalent 24-hour dose by continuous infusion (3,498 randomised) or intermittent infusion (3,533 randomised) for a clinician-determined duration or until ICU discharge.
cards.result: Within 90 days, 864 of 3,474 patients (24.9%) assigned to continuous infusion had died, compared with 939 of 3,507 (26.8%) assigned to intermittent infusion (absolute difference −1.9%, 95% CI −4.9 to 1.1; odds ratio 0.91, 95% CI 0.81 to 1.01; P=.08) — not statistically significant. Clinical cure was higher in the continuous group (1,930 of 3,467 [55.7%] vs 1,744 of 3,491 [50.0%]; absolute difference 5.7%, 95% CI 2.4 to 9.1%). Other secondary outcomes — new acquisition, colonisation, or infection with a multiresistant organism or Clostridioides difficile, ICU mortality, and in-hospital mortality — were not statistically different. The authors note the mortality confidence interval includes both no important effect and a clinically important benefit.
cards.watchOut: An open-label trial (infusion mode cannot be blinded) whose primary mortality endpoint missed significance: quoting BLING III alone as proof of a survival benefit overstates it. Its firm result is clinical cure; its mortality result is a 1.9-point absolute lean that needs the pooled literature — the next card — to carry weight.
cards.source: Dulhunty JM et al. Continuous vs Intermittent beta-Lactam Antibiotic Infusions in Critically Ill Patients With Sepsis: The BLING III Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA. 2024. PMID: 38864155. Registry ID: NCT03213990. cards.headline: Abdul-Aziz 2024 (systematic review and meta-analysis, 18 RCTs, 9,108 patients): prolonged infusion associated with lower 90-day mortality (risk ratio 0.86, 95% credible interval 0.72 to 0.98; high certainty) and higher clinical cure (risk ratio 1.16)
cards.summary: Abdul-Aziz 2024 (systematic review and meta-analysis, 18 RCTs, 9,108 patients): prolonged infusion associated with lower 90-day mortality (risk ratio 0.86, 95% credible interval 0.72 to 0.98; high certainty) and higher clinical cure (risk ratio 1.16)
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials (Abdul-Aziz 2024)
cards.people: 18 eligible randomised clinical trials including 9,108 critically ill adults with sepsis or septic shock (median age 54 years; 5,961 men [65%]), comparing prolonged (continuous or extended) with intermittent infusions of beta-lactam antibiotics; 17 trials (9,014 participants) contributed data to the primary outcome of all-cause 90-day mortality. Searches ran to May 2, 2024; certainty was assessed with GRADE and the primary analysis used a Bayesian framework.
cards.result: The pooled estimated risk ratio for all-cause 90-day mortality with prolonged infusions was 0.86 (95% credible interval 0.72 to 0.98; I²=21.5%; high certainty) — a 14% relative reduction; the abstract reports relative effects, with no pooled absolute mortality rates — with a 99.1% posterior probability that prolonged infusions were associated with lower 90-day mortality. Prolonged infusion was also associated with reduced ICU mortality (risk ratio 0.84, 95% credible interval 0.70 to 0.97; high certainty) and increased clinical cure (risk ratio 1.16, 95% credible interval 1.07 to 1.31; moderate certainty). The authors conclude prolonged infusions can be considered a standard of care in sepsis and septic shock.
cards.watchOut: BLING III is itself the largest trial inside this pool, so the two cards are not fully independent witnesses — the meta-analysis adds the smaller trials around BLING III rather than replicating it. 'Prolonged' also bundles continuous infusion with extended (hours-long) infusions, which are related but not identical strategies.
cards.source: Abdul-Aziz MH et al. Prolonged vs Intermittent Infusions of beta-Lactam Antibiotics in Adults With Sepsis or Septic Shock: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. JAMA. 2024. PMID: 38864162. cards.headline: Synthesis: cure clearly better, mortality probably modestly better in relative terms — the benefit claim rests on the pool, not on BLING III alone
cards.summary: Synthesis: cure clearly better, mortality probably modestly better in relative terms — the benefit claim rests on the pool, not on BLING III alone
cards.people: One 7,031-patient international RCT (BLING III) of continuous vs intermittent piperacillin-tazobactam or meropenem in sepsis, plus a systematic review and meta-analysis of 18 RCTs (9,108 patients) of prolonged vs intermittent beta-lactam infusion in sepsis or septic shock.
cards.result: 90-day mortality: BLING III 24.9% vs 26.8% (absolute difference −1.9%; odds ratio 0.91; P=.08); pooled across 18 trials, risk ratio 0.86 (95% credible interval 0.72 to 0.98; high certainty) — a 14% relative reduction. Clinical cure: 55.7% vs 50.0% in BLING III; pooled risk ratio 1.16. Resistance/Clostridioides difficile: no significant difference in BLING III. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: Tier C is set because the shelf claims a benefit on mortality: the single largest trial did not reach significance on that endpoint, and the pooled estimate includes that same trial. The honest practice reading is 'cure better, survival probably a little better' — not a proven mortality drug-class effect of BLING III's size alone.
cards.source: Synthesis of Dulhunty JM et al. JAMA. 2024 (PMID: 38864155); Abdul-Aziz MH et al. JAMA. 2024 (PMID: 38864162).

shelves.title: Sitting the ventilated patient up: the network meta-analysis gives semirecumbent positioning a relative risk of 0.38 for pneumonia — but the trial that measured the actual angle never reached 45° and found no benefit
shelves.question: In ventilated ICU patients, does nursing in a semirecumbent (head-of-bed elevated) position prevent ventilator-associated pneumonia compared with a supine position?
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — on the pooled trial evidence, with a feasibility warning built into the same shelf. The network meta-analysis behind this shelf (Pozuelo-Carrascosa DP et al., PMID: 35193688), pooling randomised trials of body position in ventilated ICU patients, found the semirecumbent position reduced ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP) incidence compared with the supine position (risk ratio 0.38, 95% CI 0.25 to 0.52 — a 62% relative reduction; the abstract reports relative effects, with no pooled absolute VAP rates), and ranked semirecumbent positioning first for reducing VAP (71.4% ranking probability), hospital stay, and duration of ventilation; prone positioning, a different intervention, ranked first for mortality (risk ratio 0.70, 95% CI 0.50 to 0.91). The cautionary card is the randomised feasibility trial (van Nieuwenhoven CA et al., PMID: 16424720): assigned to a target backrest elevation of 45°, patients actually achieved 28.1° on day 1 and 22.6° on day 7, the target was not achieved for 85% of the study time, and VAP was diagnosed in 10.7% of the semirecumbent group versus 6.5% of the supine group (not significant), with no differences in mortality or duration of ventilation or ICU stay. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): semirecumbent positioning probably prevents VAP as tested in trials, but the delivered angle in real units is far below the 45° the policy names — the benefit belongs to achieving elevation, not to writing it on the chart.

cards.headline: Pozuelo-Carrascosa 2022 (network meta-analysis of randomised trials): semirecumbent vs supine positioning — VAP risk ratio 0.38 (95% CI 0.25 to 0.52), ranked the best position for preventing VAP
cards.summary: Pozuelo-Carrascosa 2022 (network meta-analysis of randomised trials): semirecumbent vs supine positioning — VAP risk ratio 0.38 (95% CI 0.25 to 0.52), ranked the best position for preventing VAP
cards.type: Systematic review and network meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials (Pozuelo-Carrascosa 2022)
cards.people: Randomised controlled trials of intubated, mechanically ventilated patients admitted to an ICU, comparing body positions (lateral, prone, semirecumbent) or alternative degrees of positioning; outcomes were VAP incidence, ICU and hospital length of stay, duration of mechanical ventilation, and mortality. The record does not state the total number of trials or patients in its abstract.
cards.result: Semirecumbent and prone positions showed a risk reduction for VAP incidence (risk ratio 0.38, 95% CI 0.25 to 0.52) and mortality (risk ratio 0.70, 95% CI 0.50 to 0.91) respectively, compared with the supine position — relative measures; the abstract reports no pooled absolute rates. Ranking probabilities placed the semirecumbent position first for reducing VAP incidence (71.4%), hospital length of stay (68.9%), and duration of mechanical ventilation (67.6%), and the prone position first for decreasing mortality (89.3%) and ICU length of stay (59.3%); prone positioning showed no effect on VAP incidence. The authors conclude, cautiously, that semirecumbent positioning seems best for reducing VAP incidence, hospital stay, and ventilation duration.
cards.watchOut: A network meta-analysis of position trials — small studies, VAP diagnosed by varying criteria, and indirect comparisons stitched together; the abstract does not even report how many trials or patients the network contains, and no absolute VAP rates are given, so the 0.38 is a relative effect on an unstated baseline. The prone-position mortality result belongs to a different intervention (proning for oxygenation) and is not evidence about head-of-bed elevation.
cards.source: Pozuelo-Carrascosa DP et al. Body position for preventing ventilator-associated pneumonia for critically ill patients: a systematic review and network meta-analysis. Journal of Intensive Care. 2022. PMID: 35193688. MeSH: none in the record

cards.headline: van Nieuwenhoven 2006 (randomised feasibility trial, 221 patients): the 45° target was missed 85% of the time — achieved elevation 28° vs 10° — and VAP was 10.7% semirecumbent vs 6.5% supine (not significant)
cards.summary: van Nieuwenhoven 2006 (randomised feasibility trial, 221 patients): the 45° target was missed 85% of the time — achieved elevation 28° vs 10° — and VAP was 10.7% semirecumbent vs 6.5% supine (not significant)
cards.people: 221 critically ill patients undergoing mechanical ventilation, randomly assigned to the semirecumbent position with a target backrest elevation of 45° (112 patients) or standard care in the supine position with a backrest elevation of 10° (109 patients); backrest elevation was measured continuously during the first week of ventilation with a monitor-linked device, and VAP was diagnosed by quantitative cultures of bronchoscopically obtained samples.
cards.result: Average backrest elevation in the supine group was 9.8° on day 1 and 16.1° on day 7, versus 28.1° and 22.6° in the semirecumbent group (P<.001) — the targeted 45° was not achieved for 85% of the study time. VAP was diagnosed in 8 patients (6.5%) in the supine group and 13 (10.7%) in the semirecumbent group (not significant). There were no differences in enteral feeding, stress-ulcer prophylaxis, pressure sores, mortality rates, or duration of ventilation and ICU stay between the groups. The authors conclude the achieved difference in position (28° vs 10°) did not prevent the development of VAP.
cards.watchOut: This trial does not refute a 45° effect — it shows 45° was not deliverable in its units, so it tested roughly 28° versus 10° and found nothing. Read together with the network meta-analysis, the open question is dose: how much elevation, actually achieved and sustained, is needed for the pooled benefit to appear.
cards.source: van Nieuwenhoven CA et al. Feasibility and effects of the semirecumbent position to prevent ventilator-associated pneumonia: a randomized study. Critical Care Medicine. 2006. shelves.title: Immediate angiography after resuscitated cardiac arrest without ST elevation: no survival gain in COACT or TOMAHAWK — 64.5% vs 67.2% alive at 90 days in one, and a harm lean (54.0% vs 46.0% dead at 30 days) in the other
shelves.question: In comatose survivors of out-of-hospital cardiac arrest without ST elevation, does immediate coronary angiography improve survival compared with a delayed or selective strategy?
shelves.mesh: Aged · *Coronary Angiography · *Electrocardiography · Female · Heart Diseases/complications/*diagnostic imaging/therapy · Humans · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Male · Middle Aged · Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest/*diagnostic imaging/mortality/therapy · *Percutaneous Coronary Intervention · *Time-to-Treatment
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — rushing to the cath lab did not save lives in either large trial. In COACT (Lemkes JS et al., PMID: 30883057), 552 resuscitated patients without signs of STEMI had 90-day survival of 64.5% with immediate angiography versus 67.2% with angiography delayed until after neurologic recovery (odds ratio 0.89, 95% CI 0.62 to 1.27; P = 0.51). In TOMAHAWK (Desch S et al., PMID: 34459570), 554 patients had 30-day mortality of 54.0% with immediate angiography versus 46.0% with initial intensive care assessment and delayed or selective angiography (hazard ratio 1.28, 95% CI 1.00 to 1.63; P = 0.06), and the composite of death or severe neurologic deficit also leaned against the immediate strategy (64.3% vs 55.6%; relative risk 1.16, 95% CI 1.00 to 1.34), while bleeding, stroke and renal-replacement therapy were similar. The meta-analysis of all three randomised trials (Freund A et al., PMID: 35900214; 1,167 patients) found short-term mortality odds ratio 1.19 (95% CI 0.94 to 1.52; p = 0.15) for the early approach, with no difference in severe neurological deficit, renal replacement or significant bleeding. The harm is on the face of this shelf: every point estimate in TOMAHAWK favours waiting, though none quite reaches significance. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): after resuscitated out-of-hospital cardiac arrest without ST elevation, immediate coronary angiography does not improve survival over a delayed or selective strategy, and the larger trial's estimates lean toward harm.

cards.headline: COACT 2019: 90-day survival 64.5% with immediate angiography vs 67.2% with delayed angiography (OR 0.89, 95% CI 0.62–1.27; P = 0.51)
cards.summary: COACT 2019: 90-day survival 64.5% with immediate angiography vs 67.2% with delayed angiography (OR 0.89, 95% CI 0.62–1.27; P = 0.51)
cards.people: 552 patients in a Dutch multicentre trial who had been successfully resuscitated after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest and had no signs of ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction, randomised to immediate coronary angiography or coronary angiography delayed until after neurologic recovery; all patients underwent percutaneous coronary intervention if indicated.
cards.result: At 90 days, 176 of 273 patients (64.5%) in the immediate angiography group and 178 of 265 patients (67.2%) in the delayed angiography group were alive (odds ratio 0.89, 95% CI 0.62 to 1.27; P = 0.51). The median time to target temperature was 5.4 hours in the immediate group and 4.7 hours in the delayed group (ratio of geometric means 1.19, 95% CI 1.04 to 1.36). No significant differences were found in the remaining secondary end points, which included survival with good cerebral performance, myocardial injury, duration of catecholamine support, duration of mechanical ventilation, major bleeding, acute kidney injury and need for renal-replacement therapy.
cards.watchOut: This is a timing trial, not angiography versus no angiography: the delayed group still received angiography after neurologic recovery, so the result cannot be read as 'angiography is useless' — only that doing it immediately adds nothing. The immediate pathway also delayed target temperature by about 0.7 hours, a plausible mechanism if the strategy ever harms.
cards.source: Lemkes JS et al. Coronary Angiography after Cardiac Arrest without ST-Segment Elevation. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2019. PMID: 30883057. Registry ID: NTR4973. cards.headline: TOMAHAWK 2021: 30-day death 54.0% immediate vs 46.0% delayed/selective (HR 1.28, 95% CI 1.00–1.63; P = 0.06); death or severe neurologic deficit 64.3% vs 55.6%
cards.summary: TOMAHAWK 2021: 30-day death 54.0% immediate vs 46.0% delayed/selective (HR 1.28, 95% CI 1.00–1.63; P = 0.06); death or severe neurologic deficit 64.3% vs 55.6%
cards.people: 554 patients in a German multicentre trial with successfully resuscitated out-of-hospital cardiac arrest of possible coronary origin and no ST-segment elevation on the post-resuscitation electrocardiogram, randomised to immediate coronary angiography or to initial intensive care assessment with delayed or selective angiography; 530 patients (95.7%) were included in the primary analysis.
cards.result: At 30 days, 143 of 265 patients (54.0%) in the immediate-angiography group and 122 of 265 patients (46.0%) in the delayed-angiography group had died (hazard ratio 1.28, 95% CI 1.00 to 1.63; P = 0.06). The composite of death from any cause or severe neurologic deficit occurred in 164 of 255 patients (64.3%) in the immediate group versus 138 of 248 (55.6%) in the delayed group (relative risk 1.16, 95% CI 1.00 to 1.34). Peak troponin release and the incidence of moderate or severe bleeding, stroke and renal-replacement therapy were similar in the two groups.
cards.watchOut: The point estimates lean against the immediate strategy on both mortality and the death-or-deficit composite, but both confidence intervals touch 1.00 — this is a harm lean, not proven harm. The trial was open-label, as a strategy trial must be, and 'delayed or selective' meant some control patients still received early angiography on clinical grounds, which would dilute any real difference toward the null.

cards.headline: Freund 2022 (meta-analysis, 3 RCTs, 1,167 patients): short-term mortality OR 1.19 (95% CI 0.94–1.52) for early angiography — no pooled endpoint favoured going early
cards.summary: Freund 2022 (meta-analysis, 3 RCTs, 1,167 patients): short-term mortality OR 1.19 (95% CI 0.94–1.52) for early angiography — no pooled endpoint favoured going early
cards.people: Three randomised controlled trials enrolling a total of 1,167 patients with out-of-hospital cardiac arrest of possible cardiac origin without ST-segment elevation, comparing early coronary angiography with a delayed or selective approach; the primary endpoint was all-cause short-term mortality.
cards.result: An early invasive approach was not associated with improved short-term mortality (odds ratio 1.19, 95% confidence interval 0.94 to 1.52; p = 0.15). No significant differences were shown for severe neurological deficit, the composite of all-cause mortality or severe neurological deficit, need for renal replacement therapy due to acute renal failure, or significant bleeding at short-term follow-up.
cards.watchOut: Only three trials exist and COACT and TOMAHAWK dominate the pooled estimate, so the meta-analysis adds precision rather than independent evidence. Follow-up is short-term only; a late divergence in either direction is not excluded by this record.

cards.summary: Synthesis: two large trials and their meta-analysis agree — immediate angiography after arrest without ST elevation buys no survival, and the point estimates lean the other way
cards.people: Two multicentre randomised trials (COACT, 552 patients; TOMAHAWK, 554 patients) and a meta-analysis of all three randomised trials (1,167 patients) in resuscitated out-of-hospital cardiac arrest without ST-segment elevation.
cards.result: 90-day survival (COACT): 64.5% immediate vs 67.2% delayed. 30-day mortality (TOMAHAWK): 54.0% immediate vs 46.0% delayed/selective (HR 1.28, 95% CI 1.00 to 1.63). Pooled short-term mortality: OR 1.19 (95% CI 0.94 to 1.52). Bleeding, stroke and renal-replacement therapy: similar in both trials. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference).
cards.watchOut: Neither trial enrolled patients with ST elevation, cardiogenic shock presentations mandating immediate catheterisation, or a clearly identified culprit on other grounds — the null applies to the undifferentiated no-ST-elevation arrest survivor, not to every post-arrest patient. Tier C is set because the shelf's claim is about mortality and cardiovascular events, which the developer reviews personally.

shelves.title: Music the patient chooses, whenever they want it: anxiety 19.5 points lower and roughly a third less sedation by day 5 in Chlan's 373-patient trial — though headphones alone explain part of it
shelves.question: In mechanically ventilated patients, does patient-directed music listening reduce anxiety and sedative exposure compared with usual care or noise-cancelling headphones?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Anxiety/etiology/*therapy · Critical Illness · Ear Protective Devices · Female · Humans · Hypnotics and Sedatives/*therapeutic use · Intensive Care Units · Male · Middle Aged · *Music Therapy · Noise · Patient Preference · Relaxation Therapy · Respiration, Artificial/*adverse effects/psychology · Respiratory Insufficiency/therapy · *Self Care
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the patient's own music, started by the patient, measurably calmed patients and spared sedatives. In the anchor trial (Chlan LL et al., PMID: 23689789), 373 ventilated patients randomised to patient-directed music (PDM), noise-cancelling headphones (NCH) or usual care had anxiety scores 19.5 points lower on a 100-mm scale with PDM than usual care at any time point (95% CI −32.2 to −6.8; P = .003), with anxiety reduced by 36.5% by the fifth study day; sedation frequency fell by −0.21 points/day (P = .01) and sedation intensity by −0.18 points/day (P = .05) versus usual care — about 2 fewer sedative doses (a 38% reduction) and 36% lower sedation intensity by day 5. Against headphones alone, music reduced sedation frequency (−0.18 points/day; P = .04) but not anxiety or sedation intensity, so part of the effect is simply shutting the ICU out. A meta-analysis of 14 randomised trials (Xiao M et al., PMID: 38619185) points the same way (anxiety SMD −1.09, 95% CI −1.52 to −0.67) and reported no adverse events in any included study. The economic analysis of the same trial cohort (Chlan LL et al., PMID: 29727366) estimated costs $2,322 per patient lower with music. The honest limits: the median patient listened only 12 minutes a day, anxiety is self-rated by patients who knew their group, and the whole programme rests on one trial group. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): patient-directed music reduces anxiety and sedative exposure in ventilated ICU patients, at trivial cost and with no reported harm.

cards.headline: Chlan 2013 (PDM trial): anxiety 19.5 points lower than usual care (P = .003), sedation frequency and intensity both reduced — by day 5, 2 fewer sedative doses and 36% lower sedation intensity
cards.summary: Chlan 2013 (PDM trial): anxiety 19.5 points lower than usual care (P = .003), sedation frequency and intensity both reduced — by day 5, 2 fewer sedative doses and 36% lower sedation intensity
cards.people: 373 patients (mean age 59 years, 52% female, 86% white, mean APACHE III score 63) receiving acute mechanical ventilatory support for respiratory failure in 12 intensive care units at 5 hospitals in the Minneapolis–St Paul area, enrolled September 2006 to March 2011, randomised to self-initiated patient-directed music with selections tailored by a music therapist (n = 126), self-initiated noise-cancelling headphones (n = 122), or usual care (n = 125); mean 5.7 study days.
cards.result: Patients in the music group listened for a mean of 79.8 minutes/day (median 12, range 0–796); the headphones group wore them a mean of 34.0 minutes/day (median 0). At any time point, anxiety (100-mm visual analog scale) was 19.5 points lower with music than usual care (95% CI −32.2 to −6.8; P = .003), and by the fifth study day anxiety was reduced by 36.5% in music patients. Versus usual care, music reduced sedation intensity by −0.18 points/day (95% CI −0.36 to −0.004; P = .05) and sedation frequency by −0.21 points/day (95% CI −0.37 to −0.05; P = .01); versus headphones, sedation frequency fell by −0.18 points/day (P = .04) but anxiety and sedation intensity did not differ significantly. By day 5, music patients received 2 fewer sedative doses (a 38% reduction) with a 36% reduction in sedation intensity.
cards.watchOut: Music cannot be blinded, and the primary outcome is the patient's own anxiety rating — expectation effects are built in, which is exactly why the headphones arm matters: against headphones, the anxiety advantage disappeared and only sedation frequency stayed lower. The delivered dose was also small (median 12 minutes/day), so the trial tests offering music more than sustained listening.
cards.source: Chlan LL et al. cards.headline: Xiao 2024 (meta-analysis, 14 RCTs): music therapy reduced ICU anxiety (SMD −1.09, 95% CI −1.52 to −0.67), with 15- and 30-minute sessions effective and sessions over 45 minutes not
cards.summary: Xiao 2024 (meta-analysis, 14 RCTs): music therapy reduced ICU anxiety (SMD −1.09, 95% CI −1.52 to −0.67), with 15- and 30-minute sessions effective and sessions over 45 minutes not
cards.people: Fourteen randomised controlled trials of music therapy in intensive care patients with anxiety and delirium, pooled for anxiety scales (Chinese State-Trait Anxiety Inventory, Visual Analogue Scale for Anxiety, Facial Anxiety Scale), fatigue in anxious delirium, and physiological outcomes.
cards.result: Music therapy alleviated anxiety in ICU patients (SMD −1.09, 95% CI −1.52 to −0.67; P < 0.05) and reduced mental and physical fatigue in patients with anxious delirium (WMD −2.35, 95% CI −3.37 to −1.33; P < 0.05). Both 15-minute sessions (SMD −1.70, 95% CI −2.15 to −1.24) and 30-minute sessions (SMD −0.73, 95% CI −1.16 to −0.29) reduced anxiety, but sessions longer than 45 minutes did not (SMD −1.04, 95% CI −3.06 to 0.97; P = 0.31). Heart rate, respiratory rate and systolic blood pressure were stabilised; oxygen saturation, mean arterial pressure and diastolic pressure were not affected. No adverse events occurred during music therapy in any of the 14 studies.
cards.watchOut: The pooled trials are small, use three different anxiety scales, and mix patient-directed listening with therapist-delivered music therapy — the standardised effect looks large partly because the scales and settings vary. The dose finding (longer sessions stop working) comes from between-trial comparisons, not randomised dose groups.
cards.source: Xiao M et al. Efficacy and safety of music therapy for the treatment of anxiety and delirium in ICU patients: a meta-analysis and systematic review of randomized controlled trials. Minerva Anestesiologica. 2024. PMID: 38619185. cards.headline: Chlan 2018 (economic evaluation of the same trial): music dominated usual care — anxiety 19 points lower at $2,322 less cost per patient, with savings in 70% of probabilistic iterations
cards.summary: Chlan 2018 (economic evaluation of the same trial): music dominated usual care — anxiety 19 points lower at $2,322 less cost per patient, with savings in 70% of probabilistic iterations
cards.type: Cost-effectiveness analysis of the parent RCT (Chlan 2018)
cards.people: Adult ICU patients from the parent patient-directed music trial (PMID: 23689789) receiving mechanical ventilatory support in Midwestern US intensive care units; the intervention was an MP3 player, noise-cancelling headphones and music tailored to individual preferences by a music therapist, costed from the hospital perspective.
cards.result: The base-case analysis estimated patient-directed music reduced anxiety by 19 points on the Visual Analogue Scale–Anxiety with a reduction in cost of $2,322 per patient compared with usual ICU care — music dominated usual care (better outcome, lower cost). The probabilistic analysis found average music costs $2,155 less than usual care, with cost saving achieved in 70% of 1,000 iterations. Break-even analysis: cost saving is achieved if the per-patient cost of the music intervention remains below $2,651, eight times the base-case cost of $329.
cards.watchOut: This is the same patients and the same trial as the anchor card (same registry number, NCT00440700) — it is a costing of the programme, not independent confirmation of the clinical effect. The savings are modelled from that single trial's sedation and stay data and inherit all its limits.
cards.source: Chlan LL et al. Economic Evaluation of a Patient-Directed Music Intervention for ICU Patients Receiving Mechanical Ventilatory Support. Critical Care Medicine. 2018. PMID: 29727366. cards.headline: Synthesis: one well-run trial programme plus a concordant 14-trial meta-analysis — anxiety and sedative exposure fall, harm is nil, but the blinded-control comparison trims the claim
cards.summary: Synthesis: one well-run trial programme plus a concordant 14-trial meta-analysis — anxiety and sedative exposure fall, harm is nil, but the blinded-control comparison trims the claim
cards.people: One 373-patient three-arm randomised trial of patient-directed music versus noise-cancelling headphones versus usual care, its economic evaluation, and a meta-analysis of 14 randomised trials of music therapy in ICU patients.
cards.result: Anxiety: 19.5 points lower (100-mm scale) versus usual care in the anchor trial; pooled SMD −1.09 across 14 trials. Sedative exposure: frequency −0.21 points/day and intensity −0.18 points/day versus usual care; about 2 fewer doses by day 5. Versus headphones alone: only sedation frequency stayed significantly lower. Cost: $2,322 per patient lower in the trial's economic analysis. Adverse events: none reported in the meta-analysis. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: Do not upgrade this beyond POSSIBLE: the intervention is unblindable, the primary outcome is subjective, the economic card is the same cohort as the anchor, and no trial shows an effect on ventilation duration, delirium rates or survival. Tier C is set because the benefit rests on a single trial programme.

shelves.title: In-bed cycling on top of usual mobilisation: the largest trial found no function gain (PFIT-s 7.7 vs 7.5) — and the two newest meta-analyses disagree with each other
shelves.question: In ventilated ICU patients, does adding early in-bed cycling to usual mobilisation improve physical function at hospital discharge compared with usual mobilisation alone?
shelves.mesh: Humans · *Intensive Care Units · *Critical Care/methods · *Early Ambulation/methods · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Muscle Strength/physiology · Respiration, Artificial · Adult · Length of Stay · *Bicycling · *Critical Illness/rehabilitation
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — the pooled signals point toward benefit, but the largest single trial found none on function, and the two newest meta-analyses disagree with each other. The 2026 meta-analysis (Lu D et al., PMID: 41731824; 41 randomised trials, 3,781 patients) found adding in-bed cycling to routine rehabilitation improved the Barthel Index (SMD 1.06, 95% CI 0.66 to 1.46), 6-minute walking distance (SMD 0.80) and muscle strength (SMD 0.53), and lowered ICU-acquired weakness (OR 0.49, 95% CI 0.37 to 0.67) and delirium (OR 0.50) — but graded its own certainty very low to moderate, with ICU mortality unchanged (OR 0.95, 95% CI 0.76 to 1.19). The 2025 meta-analysis (Pazo-Palacios R et al., PMID: 40107080; 32 studies, 3,052 participants) found shorter ICU stay (−0.93 days), hospital stay (−1.78 days) and ventilation duration (−0.51 days) and better functional status, yet no significant difference in mortality, muscle strength, ICU-acquired weakness or quality of life — directly contradicting the other review on strength and weakness. And in the CYCLE trial (Kho ME et al., PMID: 38865147), the largest randomised test at 360 ventilated patients, adding 30 minutes of early in-bed cycling to usual physiotherapy did not improve physical function 3 days after ICU discharge (PFIT-s 7.7 vs 7.5; difference 0.23 points, 95% CI −0.19 to 0.65; P = 0.29), with no serious adverse events in either group. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): in-bed cycling is safe and may shorten stays, but an improvement in physical function — the outcome this shelf asks about — is not established.

cards.headline: Lu 2026 (systematic review and meta-analysis, 41 RCTs, 3,781 patients): function, strength and walking all improved on pooling, ICU-acquired weakness OR 0.49 — at very low to moderate certainty
cards.summary: Lu 2026 (systematic review and meta-analysis, 41 RCTs, 3,781 patients): function, strength and walking all improved on pooling, ICU-acquired weakness OR 0.49 — at very low to moderate certainty
cards.people: 41 randomised controlled trials (3,781 patients) of passive or active in-bed cycling added to routine ICU rehabilitation in adult intensive care patients, searched to 31 July 2025; quality assessed with the Cochrane Risk of Bias tool and certainty graded with GRADE.
cards.result: Adding in-bed cycling to routine rehabilitation improved Medical Research Council strength score (SMD 0.53, 95% CI 0.01 to 1.05; P = .04), 6-minute walking distance (SMD 0.80, 95% CI 0.14 to 1.45; P = .02), handgrip (SMD 0.09, 95% CI 0.02 to 0.36; P = .03) and Barthel Index (SMD 1.06, 95% CI 0.66 to 1.46; P < .001). It shortened mechanical ventilation time (SMD −0.28; P = .001), ICU stay (SMD −0.32; P = .002) and hospital stay (SMD −0.22; P = .02), and lowered ICU-acquired weakness (OR 0.49, 95% CI 0.37 to 0.67; P < .001) and delirium (OR 0.50, 95% CI 0.33 to 0.77; P = .002). ICU mortality (OR 0.95, 95% CI 0.76 to 1.19; P = .65) and exercise-related adverse events (OR 0.77, 95% CI 0.53 to 1.14; P = .20) were not increased. Certainty of evidence was very low to moderate.
cards.watchOut: Many included trials are small, cycling dose and timing vary widely, and several headline effects rest on standardised mean differences from heterogeneous scales — an SMD of 1.06 on the Barthel Index from such a pool should be read as 'direction favourable', not as a measured patient gain. The reviewers themselves cap certainty at moderate and mostly call it very low.
cards.source: Lu D et al. In-bed cycling for adult intensive care patients: A systematic review and meta-analysis. Medicine. 2026. PMID: 41731824. cards.headline: Pazo-Palacios 2025 (systematic review and meta-analysis, 32 studies, 3,052 patients): stays and ventilation shorter, functional status better — but no difference in strength, ICU-acquired weakness, mortality or quality of life
cards.summary: Pazo-Palacios 2025 (systematic review and meta-analysis, 32 studies, 3,052 patients): stays and ventilation shorter, functional status better — but no difference in strength, ICU-acquired weakness, mortality or quality of life
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of RCTs (Pazo-Palacios 2025)
cards.people: Thirty-two randomised trials (22 in the meta-analysis) totalling 3,052 critically ill adults (≥18 years) in various intensive care units, comparing in-bed cycling alone or combined with other treatment against no intervention, placebo, rehabilitation or standard care, searched to October 2024.
cards.result: In-bed cycling plus rehabilitation significantly reduced ICU length of stay (n = 1,564; MD −0.93 days, 95% CI −1.64 to −0.21; P = 0.01), hospital length of stay (n = 1,189; MD −1.78 days, 95% CI −3.16 to −0.41; P = 0.01) and mechanical ventilation duration (n = 1,024; MD −0.51 days, 95% CI −0.92 to −0.11; P = 0.01), and improved functional status (n = 400; MD 44.88, 95% CI 3.11 to 86.65; P = 0.04). No significant differences were found for mortality, muscle strength, ICU-acquired weakness or quality of life. Programme duration did not significantly affect hospital length of stay.
cards.watchOut: This review and the 2026 review (PMID: 41731824) pool substantially overlapping trials yet reach opposite conclusions on muscle strength and ICU-acquired weakness — the disagreement is in study selection and analysis choices, which is itself the finding: the pooled answer is not robust. The functional-status result rests on only 400 patients with a very wide confidence interval.

Annals of Physical and Rehabilitation Medicine. 2025. PMID: 40107080. systematic review and meta-analysis of rcts (pazo-palacios 2025) thirty-two randomised trials (22 in the meta-analysis) totalling 3,052 critically ill adults (≥18 years) in various intensive care units, comparing in-bed cycling alone or combined with other treatment against no intervention, placebo, rehabilitation or standard care, searched to october 2024. in-bed cycling plus rehabilitation significantly reduced icu length of stay (n = 1,564; md −0.93 days, 95% ci −1.64 to −0.21; p = 0.01), hospital length of stay (n = 1,189; md −1.78 days, 95% ci −3.16 to −0.41; p = 0.01) and mechanical ventilation duration (n = 1,024; md −0.51 days, 95% ci −0.92 to −0.11; p = 0.01), and improved functional status (n = 400; md 44.88, 95% ci 3.11 to 86.65; p = 0.04). no significant differences were found for mortality, muscle strength, icu-acquired weakness or quality of life. programme duration did not significantly affect hospital length of stay. this review and the 2026 review (pmid: 41731824) pool substantially overlapping trials yet reach opposite conclusions on muscle strength and icu-acquired weakness — the disagreement is in study selection and analysis choices, which is itself the finding: the pooled answer is not robust. the functional-status result rests on only 400 patients with a very wide confidence interval. pazo-palacios r et al. effects of in-bed cycling in critically ill adults: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised clinical trials. annals of physical and rehabilitation medicine. 2025. pmid: 40107080. mesh: humans · *critical illness/rehabilitation/mortality · randomized controlled trials as topic · quality of life · intensive care units · length of stay/statistics & numerical data · *bicycling/physiology · adult · physical functional performance · *exercise therapy/methods

cards.headline: CYCLE 2024 (Kho): in 360 ventilated patients, adding early in-bed cycling to usual physiotherapy did not improve physical function (PFIT-s 7.7 vs 7.5; difference 0.23, 95% CI −0.19 to 0.65; P = 0.29)
cards.summary: CYCLE 2024 (Kho): in 360 ventilated patients, adding early in-bed cycling to usual physiotherapy did not improve physical function (PFIT-s 7.7 vs 7.5; difference 0.23, 95% CI −0.19 to 0.65; P = 0.29)
cards.people: 360 adult ICU patients undergoing invasive mechanical ventilation, randomised to 30 minutes of early in-bed cycling plus usual physiotherapy (n = 178) or usual physiotherapy alone (n = 182); cycling began a median of 2 days after ventilation started, with a median of 3 sessions of about 27 minutes; the primary outcome was the Physical Function ICU Test-scored (PFIT-s, 0–10) at 3 days after ICU discharge.
cards.result: Among survivors, PFIT-s at 3 days after ICU discharge was 7.7 ± 1.7 in the cycling group and 7.5 ± 1.7 in the usual-physiotherapy group (absolute difference 0.23 points, 95% CI −0.19 to 0.65; P = 0.29). Usual physiotherapy started within a median of 2 days in both groups; its session duration was 23.7 ± 15.1 minutes in the cycling group and 29.1 ± 13.2 minutes in the control group. No serious adverse events occurred in either group.
cards.watchOut: Function was measured 3 days after ICU discharge, not at hospital discharge as this shelf's question phrases it, and only among survivors. The control group was not immobile — usual physiotherapy began at a median of 2 days in both arms — so CYCLE tests cycling added to already-early mobilisation, and a small delivered dose (median 3 sessions) may simply be too little to move function.

cards.headline: Synthesis: safe, probably stay-shortening, unproven for function — the largest trial is null and the two meta-analyses contradict each other on strength and weakness
cards.summary: Synthesis: safe, probably stay-shortening, unproven for function — the largest trial is null and the two meta-analyses contradict each other on strength and weakness
cards.people: Two recent meta-analyses (41 RCTs, 3,781 patients; 32 RCTs, 3,052 patients) and the largest single randomised trial (CYCLE, 360 patients) of in-bed cycling added to usual mobilisation in ventilated ICU patients.
cards.result: Physical function: no difference in CYCLE (PFIT-s difference 0.23 points, 95% CI −0.19 to 0.65); pooled functional measures favour cycling in both reviews but at very low to moderate certainty. Muscle strength and ICU-acquired weakness: improved in one meta-analysis (OR 0.49 for weakness), null in the other. ICU stay: about 0.9 days shorter in the 2025 pooling. Mortality: no difference anywhere (OR 0.95, 95% CI 0.76 to 1.19 in the 2026 pooling). Serious adverse events: none in CYCLE, no excess in pooling. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence).
cards.watchOut: This shelf is deliberately narrower than the live early-mobilisation shelves: it asks only about the cycling add-on, and on that specific question the evidence genuinely conflicts — quoting either meta-analysis alone would mislead. Tier C is set because the evidence base is discordant and the largest trial is null on the primary outcome.

shelves.title: Percutaneous versus open surgical tracheostomy: wound infection risk ratio 0.24 in the Cochrane review — mortality, serious events and major bleeding not significantly different, technical difficulties slightly more
shelves.question: In critically ill adults needing a tracheostomy, does percutaneous dilatational tracheostomy cause fewer complications than open surgical tracheostomy?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Cicatrix/etiology · Critical Illness/*therapy · Dilatation/instrumentation/methods · Esophagus/injuries · Humans · Intraoperative Period · Postoperative Hemorrhage/etiology · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Stomatitis/etiology · Surgical Wound Infection/etiology · Trachea/injuries/*surgery · Tracheostomy/adverse effects/*methods/mortality
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for the wound, not for survival: the percutaneous route infects far fewer wounds, and on every grave outcome the two techniques are indistinguishable. The Cochrane review (Brass P et al., PMID: 27437615; 20 trials, 1,652 participants) found percutaneous techniques reduced wound infection/stomatitis with risk ratio 0.24 (95% CI 0.15 to 0.37; moderate-quality evidence — a 76% relative reduction; the review's abstract does not print pooled absolute rates) and unfavourable scarring with risk ratio 0.25 (95% CI 0.07 to 0.91; low quality), while procedure-related mortality (Peto odds ratio 0.52, 95% CI 0.10 to 2.60), serious intraoperative events (risk ratio 0.93, 95% CI 0.57 to 1.53), serious postoperative events (risk ratio 0.72, 95% CI 0.41 to 1.25) and major bleeding (risk ratio 0.70, 95% CI 0.45 to 1.09) did not differ significantly. A 24-trial meta-analysis (Klotz R et al., PMID: 29282535; 1,795 procedures) agrees: no difference in life-threatening events (risk difference 0.01, 95% CI −0.03 to 0.05) or mortality (risk difference 0.00), fewer stomal infections with the percutaneous route (risk difference −0.05, 95% CI −0.08 to −0.02) — but more technical difficulties with it (risk difference 0.04, 95% CI 0.01 to 0.08), the harm on the face of this shelf. The candidate-named 2016 meta-analysis (Johnson-Obaseki S et al., PMID: 27075530) reads the same way qualitatively: no significant difference in mortality or haemorrhage, infection rates and operative time favouring percutaneous. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): percutaneous dilatational tracheostomy causes fewer wound infections than open surgical tracheostomy, with no demonstrated difference in mortality, serious adverse events or major bleeding, and slightly more technical difficulty.

cards.headline: Brass 2016 (Cochrane, 20 trials, 1,652 participants): wound infection/stomatitis RR 0.24 (95% CI 0.15–0.37) with percutaneous techniques — mortality, serious events and major bleeding not significantly different
cards.summary: Brass 2016 (Cochrane, 20 trials, 1,652 participants): wound infection/stomatitis RR 0.24 (95% CI 0.15–0.37) with percutaneous techniques — mortality, serious events and major bleeding not significantly different
cards.type: Cochrane systematic review and meta-analysis, 20 trials (Brass 2016)
cards.people: 20 randomised and quasi-randomised trials from 1990 to 2011 enrolling 1,652 critically ill adults and children undergoing elective tracheostomy, comparing percutaneous techniques with surgical techniques in ICU and operating-room settings, performed by operators of widely varying experience, with and without bronchoscopic guidance.
cards.result: There was no evidence of a difference in mortality directly related to the procedure (Peto odds ratio 0.52, 95% CI 0.10 to 2.60; 4 studies, 257 participants; low-quality evidence) or in serious life-threatening adverse events intraoperatively (risk ratio 0.93, 95% CI 0.57 to 1.53; 12 studies, 1,211 participants) or directly postoperatively (risk ratio 0.72, 95% CI 0.41 to 1.25; 10 studies, 984 participants). Percutaneous techniques significantly reduced wound infection/stomatitis (risk ratio 0.24, 95% CI 0.15 to 0.37; 12 studies, 936 participants; moderate-quality evidence) and unfavourable scarring (risk ratio 0.25, 95% CI 0.07 to 0.91; 6 studies, 789 participants; low quality). Major bleeding did not differ significantly (risk ratio 0.70, 95% CI 0.45 to 1.09; very low quality), nor did tube occlusion, accidental decannulation or difficult tube change (risk ratio 1.36, 95% CI 0.65 to 2.82). Evidence quality was low for five of seven outcomes.
cards.watchOut: No included trial was at overall low risk of bias, several patient groups were excluded from the underlying trials, and long-term outcomes (tracheal stenosis, voice, swallowing) were not evaluated — the reviewers state the results cannot be applied to all critically ill adults. The infection advantage is the one moderate-quality finding; everything else is low or very low quality.
cards.source: Brass P et al. Percutaneous techniques versus surgical techniques for tracheostomy. The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2016. PMID: 27437615. cards.headline: Johnson-Obaseki 2016 (meta-analysis): no significant difference in mortality, intraoperative or postoperative haemorrhage — infection rates and operative time significantly favoured percutaneous
cards.summary: Johnson-Obaseki 2016 (meta-analysis): no significant difference in mortality, intraoperative or postoperative haemorrhage — infection rates and operative time significantly favoured percutaneous
cards.people: Critically ill patients in studies published 1985 to October 2014 (searched in Ovid MEDLINE, Embase, Google Scholar and the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews) comparing open surgical tracheostomy with percutaneous dilatational tracheostomy, where the common indications were prolonged intubation, facilitating weaning from mechanical ventilation and pulmonary toileting.
cards.result: With regard to rates of mortality, intraoperative hemorrhage and postoperative hemorrhage, there was no statistically significant difference between the two techniques. Evaluation of infection rates and operative time revealed a statistically significant difference favouring percutaneous dilatational tracheostomy over surgical tracheostomy. The authors conclude that in critically ill patients, percutaneous dilatational tracheostomy appears to be a safe and efficient alternative to open surgical tracheostomy. (This review's abstract reports its findings qualitatively, without pooled effect sizes.)
cards.watchOut: Because this abstract prints no numbers, this card is carried qualitatively and every number on this shelf comes from the Cochrane and Klotz analyses instead. Its background list of claimed percutaneous advantages (smaller incision, less tissue trauma, cost-effectiveness) is the authors' framing, not pooled results.
cards.source: Johnson-Obaseki S et al. Complication rates of open surgical versus percutaneous tracheostomy in critically ill patients. The Laryngoscope. 2016. PMID: 27075530. cards.headline: Klotz 2018 (systematic review and meta-analysis, 24 RCTs, 1,795 procedures): life-threatening events RD 0.01 and mortality RD 0.00 — stomal infection favoured percutaneous (RD −0.05), technical difficulties favoured surgical (RD 0.04)
cards.summary: Klotz 2018 (systematic review and meta-analysis, 24 RCTs, 1,795 procedures): life-threatening events RD 0.01 and mortality RD 0.00 — stomal infection favoured percutaneous (RD −0.05), technical difficulties favoured surgical (RD 0.04)
cards.people: 24 randomised controlled trials comprising 1,795 tracheostomy procedures (percutaneous dilatational 926; surgical 869) in intensive care patients, pooled for perioperative and postoperative complications with Cochrane risk-of-bias assessment.
cards.result: No significant difference was found in the risk of a potentially life-threatening event (risk difference 0.01, 95% CI −0.03 to 0.05; P = 0.62) or in mortality (risk difference −0.00, 95% CI −0.01 to 0.01; P = 0.88) between percutaneous and surgical tracheostomy. An increased rate of technical difficulties was shown for the percutaneous technique (risk difference 0.04, 95% CI 0.01 to 0.08; P = 0.01). Stomal infection occurred more often with surgical tracheostomy (risk difference −0.05, 95% CI −0.08 to −0.02; P = 0.003, favouring percutaneous). The authors note both techniques can be performed safely on the ICU, but percutaneous tracheostomy is restricted by contraindications such as abnormal anatomy, previous surgery, coagulopathies or difficult airway; meta-analysis of procedure duration was not possible owing to high heterogeneity (I² = 99%).
cards.watchOut: The technical-difficulty excess is the percutaneous route's real price and concentrates exactly where the trials excluded patients — difficult anatomy and airways — so in unselected real-world practice the gap between the techniques may be narrower for infection and wider for difficulty than these pools suggest.
cards.source: Klotz R et al. Percutaneous versus surgical strategy for tracheostomy: a systematic review and meta-analysis of perioperative and postoperative complications. Langenbeck's Archives of Surgery. 2018. PMID: 29282535. cards.headline: Synthesis: three concordant meta-analyses — percutaneous wins on wound infection only; mortality, serious events and bleeding are a draw, and technical difficulty leans surgical
cards.summary: Synthesis: three concordant meta-analyses — percutaneous wins on wound infection only; mortality, serious events and bleeding are a draw, and technical difficulty leans surgical
cards.people: Three meta-analyses of randomised comparisons of percutaneous dilatational versus open surgical tracheostomy in critically ill patients: Cochrane (20 trials, 1,652 participants), Johnson-Obaseki 2016, and Klotz 2018 (24 trials, 1,795 procedures).
cards.result: Wound/stomal infection: risk ratio 0.24 (95% CI 0.15 to 0.37) in Cochrane; risk difference −0.05 favouring percutaneous in Klotz. Mortality: no significant difference in any analysis (risk difference 0.00 in Klotz). Serious adverse events: risk ratio 0.93 intraoperative and 0.72 postoperative (both non-significant) in Cochrane; life-threatening events risk difference 0.01 in Klotz. Major bleeding: risk ratio 0.70 (95% CI 0.45 to 1.09), non-significant. Technical difficulties: risk difference 0.04 more with percutaneous. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: The benefit is a wound outcome, not survival — this shelf must not be summarised as 'percutaneous is safer' without the qualifier. Tier C is set because the underlying procedural trials cannot be blinded, so the benefit stamp rests on unblinded randomised evidence.

shelves.title: Low tidal volumes without ARDS: PReVENT's 961 patients got the same 21 ventilator-free days — and no fewer cases of ARDS (3.8% vs 5.0%) — as intermediate volumes
shelves.question: In ICU patients ventilated without ARDS, does a low tidal-volume strategy prevent lung injury and reduce ventilation duration compared with intermediate tidal volumes?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Critical Illness/mortality/therapy · Female · Hospital Mortality · Humans · Intensive Care Units · Male · Middle Aged · Outcome and Process Assessment, Health Care · Respiration, Artificial/adverse effects/*methods · Respiratory Distress Syndrome · Respiratory Insufficiency/physiopathology/*therapy · *Tidal Volume · Ventilator Weaning · Ventilator-Induced Lung Injury
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — the lung-protective reflex does not transfer to patients whose lungs are not yet injured. In PReVENT (Simonis FD et al., PMID: 30357256), 961 ICU patients without ARDS randomised to low versus intermediate tidal volumes had exactly the same median ventilator-free days at day 28 — 21 days in both groups (mean difference −0.27, 95% CI −1.74 to 1.19; P = .71) — with no difference in ICU stay (median 6 vs 6 days) or hospital stay (median 14 vs 15 days), and mortality that leaned, non-significantly, against the low-volume arm: 28-day mortality 34.9% vs 32.1% (hazard ratio 1.12, 95% CI 0.90 to 1.40; P = .30) and 90-day mortality 39.1% vs 37.8% (hazard ratio 1.07, 95% CI 0.87 to 1.31; P = .54). New lung injury was not prevented either: ARDS developed in 3.8% vs 5.0% (P = .38), pneumonia in 4.2% vs 3.7% (P = .67), severe atelectasis in 11.4% vs 11.2% (P = .94) and pneumothorax in 1.8% vs 1.3% (P = .55). The earlier individual-patient meta-analysis (Serpa Neto A et al., PMID: 24811940; 7 investigations, 2,184 patients) had associated tidal volumes ≤6 ml/kg with more patients breathing unassisted by day 28 (93.1% vs 88.6% for ≥10 ml/kg; p = 0.027) — an association from largely non-randomised comparisons that the randomised trial then failed to confirm, and its sedation analysis (only 187 patients) found no difference in sedative, opioid or neuromuscular-blockade needs. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): in ICU patients without ARDS, a low tidal-volume strategy neither prevents lung injury nor shortens ventilation compared with intermediate tidal volumes.

cards.headline: PReVENT 2018: ventilator-free days identical (median 21 vs 21; P = .71), 28-day mortality 34.9% vs 32.1% (HR 1.12, NS), ARDS developed in 3.8% vs 5.0% (P = .38)
cards.summary: PReVENT 2018: ventilator-free days identical (median 21 vs 21; P = .71), 28-day mortality 34.9% vs 32.1% (HR 1.12, NS), ARDS developed in 3.8% vs 5.0% (P = .38)
cards.people: 961 patients (65% male; median age 68 years, IQR 59–76) without ARDS in 6 Dutch intensive care units, expected not to be extubated within 24 hours of starting ventilation, enrolled September 2014 to August 2017 and randomised to invasive ventilation with low tidal volumes (n = 477) or intermediate tidal volumes (n = 484); the primary outcome was ventilator-free days and alive at day 28.
cards.result: At day 28, the low tidal volume group had a median of 21 ventilator-free days (IQR 0–26) and the intermediate group a median of 21 (IQR 0–26) (mean difference −0.27, 95% CI −1.74 to 1.19; P = .71). ICU length of stay (median 6 vs 6 days; P = .58) and hospital length of stay (median 14 vs 15 days; P = .68) did not differ. Mortality was 34.9% vs 32.1% at 28 days (hazard ratio 1.12, 95% CI 0.90 to 1.40; P = .30) and 39.1% vs 37.8% at 90 days (hazard ratio 1.07, 95% CI 0.87 to 1.31; P = .54). Adverse events did not differ significantly: ARDS 3.8% vs 5.0% (P = .38), pneumonia 4.2% vs 3.7% (P = .67), severe atelectasis 11.4% vs 11.2% (P = .94), pneumothorax 1.8% vs 1.3% (P = .55).
cards.watchOut: 'Intermediate' is not the old 10–12 ml/kg practice: the comparison is between two moderate strategies in patients selected for expected ventilation beyond 24 hours, and achieved tidal volumes in such strategy trials always drift toward each other. The trial does not license large tidal volumes, and it says nothing about patients who already have ARDS, where low volumes are proven.

cards.headline: Serpa Neto 2014 (individual patient data meta-analysis, 7 investigations, 2,184 patients): breathing unassisted by day 28 in 93.1% at ≤6 ml/kg vs 88.6% at ≥10 ml/kg (p = 0.027) — the association PReVENT was designed to test
cards.summary: Serpa Neto 2014 (individual patient data meta-analysis, 7 investigations, 2,184 patients): breathing unassisted by day 28 in 93.1% at ≤6 ml/kg vs 88.6% at ≥10 ml/kg (p = 0.027) — the association PReVENT was designed to test
cards.people: 2,184 patients without ARDS at the onset of mechanical ventilation in 7 investigations comparing different tidal volume sizes, grouped by delivered tidal volume (≤6, 6–10, or ≥10 ml/kg predicted body weight); only 2 investigations (187 patients) could contribute to the sedation-needs analysis.
cards.result: The number of patients breathing without assistance by day 28 was higher in the group ventilated with tidal volume ≤6 ml/kg predicted body weight than in the group ventilated with ≥10 ml/kg (93.1% vs 88.6%; p = 0.027). There were no differences in the percentage of study days that patients received sedatives, opioids or neuromuscular blockade, nor in the total dose of benzodiazepines, propofol, opioids or neuromuscular blocking agents. The authors concluded lower tidal volumes could be associated with shorter ventilation and explicitly called for a robust, well-powered randomised trial to confirm it.
cards.watchOut: Patients were grouped by the tidal volume they happened to receive, not by randomisation — clinicians choose volumes, and sicker lungs both attract and tolerate different settings, so confounding by indication is built in. Read beside PReVENT, this card is the hypothesis; the trial is the test, and the test was negative.

shelves.title: Inhaled prostacyclin in ARDS: oxygenation rises in uncontrolled series (PaO2/FiO2 +40, very low certainty) — the one multicentre trial missed its primary endpoint and survival was unchanged
shelves.question: In adults with ARDS, does inhaled prostacyclin improve oxygenation, ventilation duration, or survival compared with standard care?
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — the oxygen numbers move in uncontrolled series; the one proper trial missed its target and survival did not move. The systematic review and meta-analysis (Torbic H et al., PMID: 37303944) pooled 23 studies (1,658 patients) and found inhaled prostacyclins raised the PaO2/FiO2 ratio from baseline (mean difference 40.35, 95% CI 26.14 to 54.56; p < 0.00001) and PaO2 (mean difference 12.68 mm Hg, 95% CI 2.89 to 22.48), and lowered mean pulmonary artery pressure in the 3 studies measuring it (mean difference −3.67 mm Hg) — all graded very low quality evidence with extreme heterogeneity (I² = 95–96%) and high risk of bias, and almost all of it before-versus-after physiology rather than controlled comparison. The single multicentre randomised trial (Haeberle HA et al., PMID: 36805707) randomised 150 patients with moderate to severe ARDS to inhaled prostacyclin or saline placebo three times daily for 5 days: the primary analysis was negative (oxygenation improved by 20 mmHg more than placebo; p = 0.17), mortality did not differ between groups (the abstract prints no rates), and secondary organ failure and adverse events were similar; a secondary analysis in COVID-19-positive patients showed a 34 mmHg oxygenation advantage (p = 0.04), a subgroup signal, not a primary result. No study in this record shows shorter ventilation or better survival. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): inhaled prostacyclin may raise oxygenation indices in ARDS, but no patient-important benefit has been demonstrated.

cards.headline: Torbic 2023 (systematic review and meta-analysis, 23 studies, 1,658 patients): PaO2/FiO2 ratio rose by 40.35 from baseline — very low quality evidence, I² = 95%, mostly uncontrolled physiology
cards.summary: Torbic 2023 (systematic review and meta-analysis, 23 studies, 1,658 patients): PaO2/FiO2 ratio rose by 40.35 from baseline — very low quality evidence, I² = 95%, mostly uncontrolled physiology
cards.people: 23 studies (1,658 patients) of inhaled prostacyclin administration in patients with ARDS, identified from 6,339 abstracts across Medline, Embase, CINAHL, Cochrane, Scopus and Web of Science; outcomes were change in PaO2/FiO2 ratio, PaO2 and mean pulmonary artery pressure, with certainty assessed by GRADE and bias by the Cochrane tool.
cards.result: Inhaled prostacyclins increased the PaO2/FiO2 ratio from baseline (mean difference 40.35, 95% CI 26.14 to 54.56; p < 0.00001; I² = 95%; very low quality evidence). In the eight studies evaluating PaO2, inhaled prostacyclins increased PaO2 from baseline (mean difference 12.68, 95% CI 2.89 to 22.48 mm Hg; p = 0.01; I² = 96%; very low quality evidence). In the three studies evaluating mean pulmonary artery pressure, it fell (mean difference −3.67, 95% CI −5.04 to −2.31 mm Hg; p < 0.00001; I² = 68%; very low quality evidence). The reviewers conclude the data are limited, with high risk of bias and heterogeneity among included studies.
cards.watchOut: 'From baseline' is the tell: most included studies measured the same patient before and after the drug, so regression to the mean, simultaneous ventilator changes and natural fluctuation are all pooled into the apparent effect. A before–after oxygenation rise is the weakest design in this library, and the reviewers grade their own evidence very low.
cards.source: Torbic H et al. Inhaled Prostacyclins for Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Critical Care Explorations. 2023. PMID: 37303944. MeSH: none in the record

cards.headline: Haeberle 2023 (multicentre RCT, 150 patients): primary oxygenation endpoint negative (20 mmHg more than placebo; p = 0.17), mortality did not differ, adverse events similar
cards.summary: Haeberle 2023 (multicentre RCT, 150 patients): primary oxygenation endpoint negative (20 mmHg more than placebo; p = 0.17), mortality did not differ, adverse events similar
cards.people: 150 patients with moderate to severe ARDS in a prospective randomised single-blind multicentre trial across Germany (March 2019 to August 2021), randomised to inhaled prostacyclin (n = 73) or sodium chloride placebo (n = 77) three times daily for 5 days; data from 144 patients were analysed; baseline PaO2/FiO2 ratio did not differ between groups; the primary outcome was the oxygenation index on day 5.
cards.result: The primary analysis of the study was negative: prostacyclin improved oxygenation by 20 mmHg more than placebo (p = 0.17). A secondary analysis showed oxygenation was significantly improved in patients with COVID-19-positive ARDS (34 mmHg; p = 0.04). Mortality did not differ between groups (rates not printed in the abstract). Secondary organ failure and adverse events were similar in the intervention and control groups.
cards.watchOut: Single-blind and small, and the positive COVID-19 finding is a secondary subgroup analysis of a negative trial — hypothesis-generating at best. The trial also enrolled through the COVID era (2019–2021), so its population mixes classical and COVID ARDS; neither subgroup result licenses a survival claim, and no ventilation-duration benefit is reported.
cards.source: Haeberle HA et al. Inhaled prostacyclin therapy in the acute respiratory distress syndrome: a randomized controlled multicenter trial. Respiratory Research. 2023. PMID: 36805707. shelves.title: Remimazolam versus propofol for ICU sedation: non-inferior in two single-blind trials (success 97.5% vs 97.5% and 98.1% vs 96.2%) — the promised fewer hypotensive episodes are not in the record
shelves.question: In mechanically ventilated ICU patients, is remimazolam non-inferior to propofol for light-to-moderate sedation, with fewer hypotensive episodes?
shelves.mesh: *Propofol/therapeutic use/administration & dosage · Humans · Single-Blind Method · Intensive Care Units/organization & administration · *Hypnotics and Sedatives/therapeutic use/administration & dosage · Female · Male · *Benzodiazepines/therapeutic use/administration & dosage · Middle Aged · Respiration, Artificial/methods · *Procedural Sedation/methods/standards · Aged
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — remimazolam sedates as well as propofol in head-to-head trials; the advertised blood-pressure advantage is not in this record. In SHOSREB (Yang X et al., PMID: 41915173), a multicentre single-blind non-inferiority trial in 164 ventilated patients needing light sedation (RASS −2 to +1), successful sedation was 97.5% in both groups (difference 0, 95% CI −6.5% to 6.4%), comfortably inside the −8% non-inferiority margin, with time in target range 88.6% versus 89.4%. In the phase 3 trial (Guan X et al., PMID: 41855428), 211 postoperative ventilated patients had sedation success of 98.1% on remimazolam tosylate versus 96.2% on propofol (difference 1.9%, 95% CI −3.3 to 7.8%), time in target range 95.1% versus 95.0%, and adverse events in 76.4% versus 73.3%, all mild to moderate except one severe event on propofol. The long-term pilot (Tang Y et al., PMID: 36114552; 60 patients ventilated over 24 hours) found time in target range 73.2% versus 82.8% (p = 0.269) with no differences in ventilator-free days, ICU stay, 28-day mortality or adverse events. The meta-analysis of 6 randomised trials (Nakahara S et al., PMID: 42981695; 705 patients) found no significant difference in time within target range (mean difference −0.45%, 95% CI −2.46 to 1.55) nor in sedation success, 28-day or ICU mortality, ICU stay, ventilation duration or safety outcomes — including hypotension — while noting several estimates were imprecise. So the second half of this shelf's question must be answered plainly: fewer hypotensive episodes with remimazolam have not been demonstrated in any abstract-level result here. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): remimazolam is non-inferior to propofol for light-to-moderate ICU sedation in single-blind trials, with no demonstrated outcome or hypotension advantage.

cards.headline: SHOSREB 2026: successful light sedation 97.5% in both groups (difference 0, 95% CI −6.5% to 6.4%) — non-inferiority to propofol met against a −8% margin
cards.summary: SHOSREB 2026: successful light sedation 97.5% in both groups (difference 0, 95% CI −6.5% to 6.4%) — non-inferiority to propofol met against a −8% margin
cards.people: 164 mechanically ventilated ICU patients needing light sedation (Richmond Agitation-Sedation Scale −2 to +1) in a multicentre randomised single-blind non-inferiority trial, allocated equally to remimazolam besylate or propofol; median infusion durations were 10.5 hours (remimazolam) and 11.0 hours (propofol); successful sedation meant no rescue sedative while maintaining target RASS for at least 70% of infusion time.
cards.result: The percentage of participants successfully sedated was 97.5% in both groups (p = 0.497), a difference of 0 (95% CI −6.5% to 6.4%), above the predefined non-inferiority margin of −8%. The mean percentage of time within target RASS scores was 88.6% (95% CI 84.2% to 92.9%) on remimazolam versus 89.4% (95% CI 85.0% to 93.8%) on propofol (p = 0.543). The median average maintenance dose was 0.20 mg/kg/h for remimazolam and 0.61 mg/kg/h for propofol. The authors conclude remimazolam besylate could be non-inferior to propofol for short-term light sedation in the ICU. (The abstract reports no hypotension rates.)
