cards.headline: Guan 2026 (phase 3, 211 postoperative patients): sedation success 98.1% remimazolam tosylate vs 96.2% propofol (difference 1.9%, 95% CI −3.3 to 7.8%); adverse events 76.4% vs 73.3%
cards.summary: Guan 2026 (phase 3, 211 postoperative patients): sedation success 98.1% remimazolam tosylate vs 96.2% propofol (difference 1.9%, 95% CI −3.3 to 7.8%); adverse events 76.4% vs 73.3%
cards.people: 211 mechanically ventilated postoperative ICU patients (mean age 61.1 years, 63.5% male, 99.1% postoperative) requiring sedation for 6 hours or longer at target RASS −2 to +1, randomised to remimazolam tosylate (n = 106; loading 0.08 mg/kg, maintenance 0 to 2.0 mg/kg/h) or propofol (n = 105; loading 0.3 to 0.5 mg/kg, maintenance 0.3 to 4.0 mg/kg/h), maximum treatment duration 24 hours, in a multicentre randomised single-blind non-inferiority trial with an −8% margin.
cards.result: Sedation success was 98.1% with remimazolam tosylate and 96.2% with propofol (difference 1.9%, 95% CI −3.3 to 7.8%); mean percentage of time in the RASS target range was 95.1% ± 13.8% versus 95.0% ± 12.9%; rescue sedation was needed by 0 of 106 versus 1 of 105 patients. Mean treatment duration was 11.5 ± 3.6 versus 11.1 ± 3.1 hours. Adverse events occurred in 81 patients (76.4%) on remimazolam and 77 (73.3%) on propofol, all mild to moderate except one severe event with propofol. The authors conclude remimazolam tosylate was non-inferior with good tolerability. (The abstract reports no hypotension rates.)
cards.watchOut: An almost entirely postoperative population sedated for about 11 hours is the easiest ICU sedation task there is; it does not speak to days-long sedation in medical ICU patients. Adverse-event totals are printed without a hypotension split, so the trial cannot be quoted either way on blood pressure.

cards.headline: Tang 2022 (pilot, 60 patients, long-term sedation): time in target range 73.2% vs 82.8% (p = 0.269) — no difference in ventilator-free days, ICU stay, 28-day mortality or adverse events
cards.summary: Tang 2022 (pilot, 60 patients, long-term sedation): time in target range 73.2% vs 82.8% (p = 0.269) — no difference in ventilator-free days, ICU stay, 28-day mortality or adverse events
cards.people: 60 adult patients (30 per group) mechanically ventilated for longer than 24 hours in a single-centre randomised pilot study, receiving remimazolam besylate or propofol to maintain mild-to-moderate sedation (RASS −3 to 0); median infusion durations were 55.0 hours (remimazolam) and 41.0 hours (propofol).
cards.result: The median percentage of time in the target RASS range without rescue sedation was 73.2% (IQR 41.5–97.3%) with remimazolam versus 82.8% (IQR 65.6–100%) with propofol (p = 0.269). No differences were identified between the groups in ventilator-free days at day 7, length of ICU stay, 28-day mortality or adverse events. The authors describe the pilot as suggesting remimazolam besylate was effective and safe for long-term sedation compared with propofol.
cards.watchOut: A 60-patient pilot cannot establish non-inferiority — the point estimate for time in range actually favoured propofol by about 10 points, with intervals far too wide to exclude a clinically important gap. It is the only card here addressing sedation beyond 24 hours, which is precisely where the evidence is thinnest.
cards.source: Tang Y et al. Remimazolam besylate versus propofol for long-term sedation during invasive mechanical ventilation: a pilot study. Critical Care. 2022. PMID: 36114552. cards.headline: Nakahara 2026 (meta-analysis, 6 RCTs, 705 patients): no significant difference in time in target range (MD −0.45%), mortality, stay, ventilation duration — or hypotension
cards.summary: Nakahara 2026 (meta-analysis, 6 RCTs, 705 patients): no significant difference in time in target range (MD −0.45%), mortality, stay, ventilation duration — or hypotension
cards.people: Six randomised controlled trials (705 patients) comparing remimazolam with propofol in mechanically ventilated ICU patients, identified from PubMed, Embase, Cochrane and ClinicalTrials.gov; the primary outcome was percentage of time within the target sedation range, with safety outcomes including adverse events leading to dose reduction, hypotension and delirium.
cards.result: No statistically significant difference was detected in the percentage of time within the target sedation range (mean difference −0.45%, 95% CI −2.46 to 1.55; p = 0.56; I² = 0%). No significant differences were detected in sedation success rate, 28-day mortality, ICU mortality, ICU length of stay, duration of mechanical ventilation, or safety outcomes, although several estimates were imprecise. The authors conclude remimazolam probably results in little to no difference in sedation efficacy compared with propofol, with uncertainty remaining regarding clinical and safety outcomes, and call for larger multinational trials.
cards.watchOut: 'No significant difference' in hypotension across 705 patients with imprecise estimates is not proof of equal blood-pressure effects in either direction — but it is the only pooled safety read available, and it gives no support to marketing claims of fewer hypotensive episodes. This record carries no MeSH terms yet (2026 publication).

cards.headline: Synthesis: non-inferiority for keeping patients in the target sedation range is consistent across trials — and so is the absence of any demonstrated outcome or blood-pressure advantage
cards.summary: Synthesis: non-inferiority for keeping patients in the target sedation range is consistent across trials — and so is the absence of any demonstrated outcome or blood-pressure advantage
cards.people: Two multicentre single-blind non-inferiority trials (164 and 211 patients), one 60-patient long-term pilot, and a meta-analysis of 6 randomised trials (705 patients) comparing remimazolam with propofol for sedation of mechanically ventilated ICU patients.
cards.result: Sedation success: 97.5% vs 97.5% (SHOSREB) and 98.1% vs 96.2% (phase 3), both meeting −8% non-inferiority margins. Time in target range: no significant difference in any study or in pooling (MD −0.45%, 95% CI −2.46 to 1.55). Mortality, ICU stay and ventilation duration: no significant differences in pooling. Hypotension: evaluated in the meta-analysis; no significant difference, estimates imprecise; not reported in either large trial's abstract. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference).
cards.watchOut: Every large trial here is single-blind with clinician-titrated endpoints, enrols short-term (roughly 11-hour) sedation, and was designed to show sameness, not superiority — sameness is all this shelf claims. Tier C is set: single-blind non-inferiority evidence, and the hypotension half of the question is unproven rather than answered.

shelves.title: Tele-ICU: the randomised studies found no mortality or stay difference — the pooled 'benefit' (OR 0.80–0.82) comes from before–after studies
shelves.question: In adult ICUs, does telemedicine coverage (tele-ICU) reduce ICU mortality and length of stay compared with usual on-site care?
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — the randomised evidence says no difference; the mortality 'benefit' lives in before–after studies at effect sizes this library does not accept from observational data. The 2025 Cochrane-standard systematic review (Pscheidl T et al., PMID: 41397018) found 26 controlled studies covering about 2,164,508 patients, but only three were randomised (one cluster RCT of 15,230 patients and two stepped-wedge trials totalling 5,915): for ICU mortality two found no evidence of a difference and one favoured standard care (very low certainty); ICU length of stay showed no evidence of a difference in the randomised data; heterogeneity prevented any meta-analysis. The positive pooled numbers come from non-randomised designs: the meta-analysis by Kalvelage C et al. (PMID: 33710032; 20 studies, 477,637 patients) found ICU mortality risk ratio 0.82 (95% CI 0.71 to 0.94) only where the remote team held decision-making authority, while consultative tele-ICU showed no advantage and slightly longer ICU stay (mean difference +0.31 days, 95% CI 0.10 to 0.53); and the earliest meta-analysis (Young LB et al., PMID: 21444842) pooled 13 studies that were all before-and-after designs (41,374 patients), finding ICU mortality odds ratio 0.80 (95% CI 0.66 to 0.97) but in-hospital mortality odds ratio 0.82 (95% CI 0.65 to 1.03; P = .08) and no hospital length-of-stay benefit. Ratios of 0.80–0.82 sit inside the 0.5–2.0 band that is not solid evidence for observational associations — and before–after ICU studies are exactly where secular improvement masquerades as intervention effect. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): tele-ICU coverage has not been shown to reduce ICU mortality or length of stay; whether granting the remote team decision-making authority changes that is untested by randomisation.

cards.headline: Pscheidl 2025 (systematic review, 26 studies, ~2.16 million patients): only 3 studies were randomised — ICU mortality heterogeneous (two no difference, one favouring standard care), ICU stay no difference, no meta-analysis possible
cards.summary: Pscheidl 2025 (systematic review, 26 studies, ~2.16 million patients): only 3 studies were randomised — ICU mortality heterogeneous (two no difference, one favouring standard care), ICU stay no difference, no meta-analysis possible
cards.people: 26 controlled studies comparing telemedicine in adult intensive care with standard care (approximately 2,164,508 analysed patients), comprising one cluster randomised trial, two stepped-wedge cluster randomised trials and 23 non-randomised studies of interventions; searches to April 2024 with an updated randomised-trial search to September 2025, conducted to Cochrane methodological standards.
cards.result: For ICU mortality, one cluster RCT (15,230 patients) and two stepped-wedge cluster RCTs (5,915 patients) showed heterogeneous results: two found no evidence for a difference, while one favoured standard care (very low certainty). One stepped-wedge trial (1,462 patients) found no evidence of a difference in overall mortality at 180 days (very low certainty). Data from one cluster RCT (15,230 patients) and one stepped-wedge trial (1,462 patients) on ICU length of stay showed no evidence for a difference (moderate and very low certainty). Quality of life from one stepped-wedge trial (786 patients) showed no evidence for a difference. Six non-randomised studies reported adjusted ICU mortality data with heterogeneous results. High risk of bias and substantial heterogeneity limited certainty; no meta-analysis was conducted.
cards.watchOut: The enormous patient count is an illusion of weight: about 99% of patients sit in non-randomised studies, while the randomised evidence totals roughly 21,000 patients and points to no benefit. This record carries no MeSH terms. This shelf is deliberately narrower than the live general-telemedicine shelf — it covers remote ICU coverage specifically.
cards.source: Pscheidl T et al. Telemedicine in adult intensive care: A systematic review of patient-relevant outcomes and methodological considerations. PLOS Digital Health. 2025. PMID: 41397018. MeSH: none in the record

cards.headline: Kalvelage 2021 (systematic review and meta-analysis, 20 studies, 477,637 patients): ICU mortality RR 0.82 only when the tele-ICU held decision-making authority; consultative models showed no advantage and longer ICU stay
cards.summary: Kalvelage 2021 (systematic review and meta-analysis, 20 studies, 477,637 patients): ICU mortality RR 0.82 only when the tele-ICU held decision-making authority; consultative models showed no advantage and longer ICU stay
cards.people: 20 randomised and observational studies (477,637 patients: 292,319 tele-ICU, 185,318 control) comparing standard care plus tele-ICU with standard care alone in critically ill patients, subgrouped by the remote team's level of authority — decision-making authority versus expert tele-consultation; searches to 30 August 2020.
cards.result: Decision-making authority during tele-ICU care was associated with a significant reduction in ICU mortality (pooled risk ratio 0.82, 95% CI 0.71 to 0.94; p = 0.006), while expert tele-consultation showed no mortality advantage. For length of stay, decision-making authority gave an ICU mean difference of −0.78 days (95% CI −1.46 to −0.10) and hospital mean difference of −1.54 days (95% CI −3.13 to 0.05), whereas expert tele-consultation was associated with longer ICU stay (mean difference +0.31 days, 95% CI 0.10 to 0.53; p = 0.005) and hospital stay mean difference +0.58 days (95% CI −0.04 to 1.21). The authors conclude decision-making authority, unlike consultation, reduces mortality and length of stay.
cards.watchOut: The included studies are overwhelmingly observational, and a risk ratio of 0.82 is inside the 0.5–2.0 band this library treats as not solid for observational associations. The authority subgroup is a between-study comparison — hospitals that grant remote teams authority differ from those that do not in many ways besides the tele-ICU itself — so 'authority causes the benefit' is an hypothesis, not a finding.

systematic review and meta-analysis (kalvelage 2021) 20 randomised and observational studies (477,637 patients: 292,319 tele-icu, 185,318 control) comparing standard care plus tele-icu with standard care alone in critically ill patients, subgrouped by the remote team's level of authority — decision-making authority versus expert tele-consultation; searches to 30 august 2020. decision-making authority during tele-icu care was associated with a significant reduction in icu mortality (pooled risk ratio 0.82, 95% ci 0.71 to 0.94; p = 0.006), while expert tele-consultation showed no mortality advantage. for length of stay, decision-making authority gave an icu mean difference of −0.78 days (95% ci −1.46 to −0.10) and hospital mean difference of −1.54 days (95% ci −3.13 to 0.05), whereas expert tele-consultation was associated with longer icu stay (mean difference +0.31 days, 95% ci 0.10 to 0.53; p = 0.005) and hospital stay mean difference +0.58 days (95% ci −0.04 to 1.21). the authors conclude decision-making authority, unlike consultation, reduces mortality and length of stay. the included studies are overwhelmingly observational, and a risk ratio of 0.82 is inside the 0.5–2.0 band this library treats as not solid for observational associations. the authority subgroup is a between-study comparison — hospitals that grant remote teams authority differ from those that do not in many ways besides the tele-icu itself — so 'authority causes the benefit' is an hypothesis, not a finding. kalvelage c et al. decision-making authority during tele-icu care reduces mortality and length of stay-a systematic review and meta-analysis. critical care medicine. 2021. pmid: 33710032. mesh: *clinical decision-making · critical care/*methods · critical illness/mortality · hospital mortality · humans · *intensive care units · length of stay · outcome assessment, health care · *telemedicine

cards.headline: Young 2011 (systematic review and meta-analysis, 13 studies, 41,374 patients — all before-and-after): ICU mortality OR 0.80 and ICU stay −1.26 days, but in-hospital mortality and hospital stay not significantly reduced
cards.summary: Young 2011 (systematic review and meta-analysis, 13 studies, 41,374 patients — all before-and-after): ICU mortality OR 0.80 and ICU stay −1.26 days, but in-hospital mortality and hospital stay not significantly reduced
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis, before-and-after studies (Young 2011)
cards.people: 13 eligible studies involving 35 intensive care units and 41,374 patients (15,667 pre-tele-ICU and 25,707 post-tele-ICU), published to September 2010; every included study used a before-and-after design comparing outcomes before and after telemedicine ICU coverage was introduced.
cards.result: Tele-ICU coverage was associated with a reduction in ICU mortality (pooled odds ratio 0.80, 95% CI 0.66 to 0.97; P = .02) but not in-hospital mortality (pooled odds ratio 0.82, 95% CI 0.65 to 1.03; P = .08). ICU length of stay fell (mean difference −1.26 days, 95% CI −2.21 to −0.30; P = .01) but hospital length of stay did not (mean difference −0.64 days, 95% CI −1.52 to 0.25; P = .16). The authors conclude tele-ICU coverage is associated with lower ICU mortality and ICU length of stay but not with lower in-hospital mortality or hospital length of stay.
cards.watchOut: Before-and-after is the weakest comparative design in routine use: ICU mortality was falling secularly throughout this era for unrelated reasons, and units adopt tele-ICU alongside other quality programmes. An odds ratio of 0.80 from such designs, which vanishes for in-hospital mortality in the same pool, cannot carry a benefit claim under this library's observational floor.
cards.source: Young LB et al. Impact of telemedicine intensive care unit coverage on patient outcomes: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Archives of Internal Medicine. 2011. PMID: 21444842. cards.headline: Synthesis: randomised studies find no mortality or stay benefit; pooled reductions of OR/RR 0.80–0.82 rest entirely on before–after and observational designs
cards.summary: Synthesis: randomised studies find no mortality or stay benefit; pooled reductions of OR/RR 0.80–0.82 rest entirely on before–after and observational designs
cards.people: One 2025 Cochrane-standard systematic review (26 studies, ~2.16 million patients, 3 randomised), one 2021 meta-analysis (20 studies, 477,637 patients) and one 2011 meta-analysis (13 before-and-after studies, 41,374 patients) of tele-ICU coverage in adult intensive care.
cards.result: Randomised evidence: ICU mortality — two studies no difference, one favouring standard care (very low certainty); ICU length of stay — no evidence of difference. Observational pooling: ICU mortality OR 0.80 (2011) and RR 0.82 for decision-making-authority models (2021); in-hospital mortality not significantly reduced (OR 0.82, 95% CI 0.65 to 1.03). ICU stay: −1.26 days in before–after pooling; +0.31 days for consultative models in 2021 pooling. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence).
cards.watchOut: Absence of randomised benefit is not proof tele-ICU is worthless — staffing, response times and night coverage may matter in ways these outcomes miss — but on the two outcomes this shelf asks about, the claim of benefit is observational and below this library's floor for such evidence. Tier C is set because the shelf depends on observational data.

shelves.title: Nurse-led ICU follow-up programmes: no gain in quality of life at 12 months in the PRaCTICaL trial (SF-36 physical 42.0 vs 40.8) — and a Cochrane review of five studies agrees
shelves.question: After ICU discharge, do nurse-led intensive-care follow-up clinics improve quality of life and reduce post-traumatic stress compared with standard follow-up?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Cost-Benefit Analysis · Critical Care/economics/organization & administration · Critical Illness/economics/nursing · Follow-Up Studies · Hospitals, District · Hospitals, Teaching · Humans · Long-Term Care/economics · Middle Aged · Quality of Life · Quality-Adjusted Life Years · Treatment Outcome · Young Adult
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — the clinics are well liked and well organised, but the outcomes they were built to move did not move. In PRaCTICaL, 286 ICU survivors randomised to nurse-led follow-up programmes or standard care had indistinguishable SF-36 physical component scores at 12 months (42.0 vs 40.8; effect size 1.1, 95% CI -1.9 to 4.2; P=0.46), with no significant difference in the mental component score or any secondary outcome, and the programmes cost significantly more. The Cochrane review of follow-up services (5 studies, 1,707 participants) found the same pattern: little or no difference in health-related quality of life at 12 months, little or no difference in all-cause mortality (RR 0.96, 95% CI 0.76 to 1.22), and little or no difference in post-traumatic stress (SMD -0.05, 95% CI -0.19 to 0.10). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): nurse-led ICU follow-up, as tested, does not improve quality of life, survival, or PTSD at one year, and costs more than standard care.

cards.headline: PRaCTICaL (Cuthbertson 2009): SF-36 physical score 42.0 vs 40.8 at 12 months (P=0.46) — no outcome differed, and follow-up cost more
cards.summary: PRaCTICaL (Cuthbertson 2009): SF-36 physical score 42.0 vs 40.8 at 12 months (P=0.46) — no outcome differed, and follow-up cost more
cards.people: 286 adults recruited after ICU discharge at three UK hospitals (two teaching, one district general) between September 2006 and October 2007, randomised to nurse-led intensive care follow-up programmes or standard care; 192 completed one-year follow-up.
cards.result: At 12 months there was no evidence of a difference in the SF-36 physical component score (mean 42.0 (SD 10.6) vs 40.8 (SD 11.9); effect size 1.1, 95% CI -1.9 to 4.2; P=0.46) or the mental component score (effect size 0.4, 95% CI -3.0 to 3.7; P=0.83). No secondary outcome or subgroup analysis differed significantly. Follow-up programmes were significantly more costly than standard care and unlikely to be cost effective.
cards.watchOut: Non-blinded by necessity, and one in three recruits did not complete follow-up, so a modest effect in either direction cannot be excluded — but the point estimate sits almost exactly on no difference, and the extra cost is not in doubt.
cards.source: Cuthbertson BH et al. The PRaCTICaL study of nurse led, intensive care follow-up programmes for improving long term outcomes from critical illness: a pragmatic randomised controlled trial. cards.headline: Cochrane review 2018: five studies, 1,707 survivors — little or no difference in quality of life, mortality (RR 0.96), or PTSD
cards.summary: Cochrane review 2018: five studies, 1,707 survivors — little or no difference in quality of life, mortality (RR 0.96), or PTSD
cards.people: Five studies (four randomised, one non-randomised) totalling 1,707 ICU survivors; follow-up services were nurse-led in four studies and multidisciplinary in one, delivered face-to-face at home or in clinic, or by telephone, with one to eight consultations.
cards.result: Follow-up services may make little or no difference to health-related quality of life at 12 months (SMD -0.0, 95% CI -0.1 to 0.1; 1 study; 286 participants; low-certainty evidence). Moderate-certainty evidence from five studies indicates little or no difference in all-cause mortality up to 12 months (RR 0.96, 95% CI 0.76 to 1.22; 4 randomised studies; 1,289 participants), and low-certainty evidence little or no difference in PTSD (SMD -0.05, 95% CI -0.19 to 0.10; 703 participants, 3 studies). Effects on depression, anxiety, physical and cognitive function were very low certainty.
cards.watchOut: Only five studies, each with a differently designed service, and none could be blinded — the review can rule out a large benefit of follow-up as practised, but not of every conceivable model; five further studies were ongoing at the search date.
cards.source: Schofield-Robinson OJ et al. Follow-up services for improving long-term outcomes in intensive care unit (ICU) survivors. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2018. PMID: 30388297. shelves.title: Exchanging a dialysis catheter over a guidewire: no more colonisation (5.6% vs 5.6%) but more than double the dysfunction (37.6% vs 15.7%, HR 3.67)
shelves.question: In ICU patients needing a temporary dialysis catheter change, is guidewire exchange as safe as new-site placement for infection and dysfunction?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Catheter-Related Infections/etiology · Catheterization, Central Venous/methods/nursing · Catheters, Indwelling/adverse effects/microbiology · Cohort Studies · Double-Blind Method · Equipment Failure · Female · Humans · Intensive Care Units/organization & administration · Male · Middle Aged · Placebos · Proportional Hazards Models · Renal Dialysis/adverse effects/instrumentation · Renal Replacement Therapy/adverse effects/methods
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (harm) — the wire preserves the vein, and on infection it delivers what it promises; the price is a catheter that stops working. In the matched-cohort analysis nested in the ELVIS randomised trial (1,496 ICU adults needing a dialysis catheter), colonisation was identical after guidewire exchange and new-site venipuncture (5.6% in both groups), but dysfunction was far commoner after exchange: 37.6% vs 15.7% (HR 3.67, 95% CI 2.07 to 6.49; p<0.01). The older systematic review of central venous catheter replacement (12 randomised trials) points the same way on infection — trends toward more colonisation (RR 1.26, 95% CI 0.87 to 1.84) and catheter-related bacteraemia (RR 1.72, 95% CI 0.89 to 3.33) with guidewire exchange, offset by fewer mechanical complications (RR 0.48, 95% CI 0.12 to 1.91). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm): guidewire exchange does not increase colonisation, but it more than doubles catheter dysfunction — a harm that costs dialysis sessions even when it costs no infections.

cards.headline: Coupez 2016 (ELVIS nested cohort): colonisation 5.6% vs 5.6%, but dysfunction 37.6% vs 15.7% (HR 3.67, p<0.01) after guidewire exchange
cards.summary: Coupez 2016 (ELVIS nested cohort): colonisation 5.6% vs 5.6%, but dysfunction 37.6% vs 15.7% (HR 3.67, p<0.01) after guidewire exchange
cards.type: Matched-cohort analysis nested in a randomised trial (Coupez 2016, ELVIS)
cards.people: Dialysis catheters from the ELVIS randomised trial of 1,496 ICU adults requiring a catheter for renal replacement therapy or plasma exchange; 178 catheters inserted by guidewire exchange were matched to new-site venipuncture catheters on centre, SAPS II (±10), insertion site (jugular or femoral), side, and ICU stay before placement.
cards.result: Catheter colonisation did not differ between guidewire-exchange and new-site catheters (10 (5.6%) in both groups), but dysfunction was more frequent with guidewire exchange (67 (37.6%) vs 28 (15.7%); hazard ratio 3.67, 95% CI 2.07 to 6.49; p<0.01). Results were similar when the analysis was restricted to catheters changed for dysfunction.
cards.watchOut: This is a matched observational comparison inside a trial that randomised something else — residual confounding by why the catheter was being changed cannot be excluded, which is why this shelf is Tier C. The dysfunction signal is nonetheless large and mechanistically plausible (a catheter threaded through a used tract inherits its fibrin sheath).
cards.source: Coupez E et al. Guidewire exchange vs new site placement for temporary dialysis catheter insertion in ICU patients: is there a greater risk of colonization or dysfunction? Critical care (London, England). 2016. PMID: 27473868. Registry ID: NCT00563342. cards.headline: Cook 1997 systematic review: guidewire exchange trends to more colonisation (RR 1.26) and bacteraemia (RR 1.72), fewer mechanical complications (RR 0.48)
cards.summary: Cook 1997 systematic review: guidewire exchange trends to more colonisation (RR 1.26) and bacteraemia (RR 1.72), fewer mechanical complications (RR 0.48)
cards.people: Twelve randomised trials of central venous catheter replacement over a guidewire versus at a new site in critically ill patients, identified from 151 catheter-management trials.
cards.result: Compared with new-site replacement, guidewire exchange was associated with a trend toward higher catheter colonisation (relative risk 1.26, 95% CI 0.87 to 1.84), exit-site infection (RR 1.52, 95% CI 0.34 to 6.73), and catheter-related bacteraemia (RR 1.72, 95% CI 0.89 to 3.33), and with fewer mechanical complications (RR 0.48, 95% CI 0.12 to 1.91). Scheduled replacement every 3 days by either technique did not reduce infection versus as-needed replacement.
cards.watchOut: A 1997 review of general central venous catheters, not dialysis catheters specifically, from an era of different antisepsis — its infection trends are hypothesis-grade today; its value here is showing the direction of the trade-off was already visible before the dialysis-specific data.

cards.headline: Synthesis: the wire spares the vein and the infection rate — and spends both savings on catheters that fail
cards.summary: Synthesis: the wire spares the vein and the infection rate — and spends both savings on catheters that fail
cards.people: A matched-cohort analysis of 178 guidewire-exchanged dialysis catheters within a 1,496-patient ICU randomised trial, plus a systematic review of 12 randomised trials of central venous catheter replacement strategies.
cards.result: Dialysis catheters: colonisation 5.6% vs 5.6%; dysfunction 37.6% vs 15.7% (HR 3.67, 95% CI 2.07 to 6.49). Central catheters (review): colonisation RR 1.26 (95% CI 0.87 to 1.84), bacteraemia RR 1.72 (95% CI 0.89 to 3.33), mechanical complications RR 0.48 (95% CI 0.12 to 1.91) with guidewire exchange. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm), Tier C: the dialysis-specific evidence is a matched cohort, not a randomised comparison.
cards.watchOut: Where venous capital is precious and the catheter is working, exchange remains a reasonable trade; the shelf's claim is narrower — expect roughly one in three exchanged catheters to dysfunction, against roughly one in six new-site catheters, and plan dialysis accordingly.

shelves.title: Ketamine as an adjunct sedative: a meta-analysis finds less opioid use, but the largest blinded trial found none — while delirium fell from 37% to 21%
shelves.question: In mechanically ventilated patients, does ketamine as an adjunctive sedative reduce opioid and propofol requirements compared with standard sedation alone?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Analgesics, Opioid/administration & dosage/therapeutic use · Anesthetics, Dissociative/administration & dosage/therapeutic use · Procedural Sedation · Critical Care/methods · Delirium/epidemiology/prevention & control · Double-Blind Method · Drug Utilization · Female · Humans · Incidence · Intensive Care Units · Ketamine/administration & dosage/therapeutic use · Male · Middle Aged · Patients · Remifentanil/administration & dosage/therapeutic use · Respiration, Artificial
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the opioid-sparing claim splits by which evidence you stand on. The meta-analysis of randomised trials found ketamine regimens reduced opioid consumption (six RCTs, 494 participants; -13.19 µg/kg/h morphine equivalents, 95% CI -22.10 to -4.28; P=0.004), with no difference in sedative consumption, ventilation duration, length of stay, or mortality. But the largest double-blind trial inside that literature found no opioid sparing at all: remifentanil use was 7.9 vs 9.3 µg/kg/h with ketamine versus placebo (P=0.548) under a nurse-driven sedation protocol — while delirium incidence fell from 37% (30/82) on placebo to 21% (17/80) on ketamine (P=0.03). The pilot ATTAINMENT trial (83 patients) found feasibility and similar sedative use, with more patients at goal sedation scores on ketamine. PROPOSED SPLIT: ketamine's opioid-sparing is real in small heterogeneous trials and absent in the best blinded one; its most reproducible signal in that trial was less delirium, an outcome the meta-analysis was not built to judge.

cards.headline: Perbet 2018: remifentanil use unchanged (7.9 vs 9.3 µg/kg/h, P=0.548), but delirium 21% vs 37% (P=0.03) with low-dose ketamine
cards.summary: Perbet 2018: remifentanil use unchanged (7.9 vs 9.3 µg/kg/h, P=0.548), but delirium 21% vs 37% (P=0.03) with low-dose ketamine
cards.people: 162 mechanically ventilated patients in a French university-hospital general ICU, all managed with a nurse-driven sedation protocol, randomised to ketamine infusion (2 mg/kg/h as recorded) or placebo added to standard sedation with remifentanil.
cards.result: Daily remifentanil consumption did not differ between ketamine and control (7.9 ± 1.0 vs 9.3 ± 1.0 µg/kg/h; P=0.548), nor did dose escalations required for equianalgesia (P=0.78). Delirium incidence was higher on placebo (30/82, 37%) than on ketamine (17/80, 21%) (P=0.03), and delirium duration was shorter with ketamine (P=0.005). Mortality, ventilator-free days, and ICU length of stay did not differ significantly.
cards.watchOut: The delirium finding is a secondary outcome in a trial powered on opioid consumption, and the abstract's printed delirium-duration means appear transposed against its own text — the direction (shorter with ketamine, P=0.005) is what the record supports. The opioid null may reflect the nurse-driven protocol already minimising opioid use in both arms.
cards.source: Perbet S et al. Low doses of ketamine reduce delirium but not opiate consumption in mechanically ventilated and sedated ICU patients: A randomised double-blind control trial. Anaesthesia, critical care & pain medicine. 2018. PMID: 30268528. cards.headline: Amer 2021 (ATTAINMENT pilot): ketamine feasible and safe; ventilation 7 vs 5 days, ventilator-free days 19 vs 19 — a pilot, not a verdict
cards.summary: Amer 2021 (ATTAINMENT pilot): ketamine feasible and safe; ventilation 7 vs 5 days, ventilator-free days 19 vs 19 — a pilot, not a verdict
cards.people: 83 critically ill mechanically ventilated adults (40 ketamine, 43 control) at a Saudi tertiary centre, randomised to adjunct ketamine infusion 1–2 µg/kg/min for 48 hours or standard care alone, both under institutional pain and sedation protocols.
cards.result: Median ventilation duration was 7 days (IQR 3–9.25) with ketamine and 5 days (IQR 2–8) with control; median ventilator-free days were 19 in both groups (p=0.70). More ketamine patients attained goal Richmond Agitation-Sedation Scale scores at 24 hours (67.5% vs 52.4%) and 48 hours (73.5% vs 66.7%). Cumulative sedative and vasopressor use and haemodynamic changes were similar; ICU stay was 12.5 vs 12 days; no serious adverse events in either group.
cards.watchOut: A pilot designed to test feasibility (consent 89%, protocol adherence 76%), open-label, and far too small to detect outcome differences — its contribution is that a definitive trial is practical, not that ketamine works or does not.
cards.source: Amer M et al. Adjunctive ketamine for sedation in critically ill mechanically ventilated patients: an active-controlled, pilot, feasibility clinical trial. Journal of intensive care. 2021. PMID: 34462007. Registry ID: NCT04075006; ISRCTN14730035. MeSH: none in the record

cards.headline: Chan 2022 meta-analysis: opioid consumption lower with ketamine across six RCTs (-13.19 µg/kg/h morphine equivalents, P=0.004); nothing else moved
cards.summary: Chan 2022 meta-analysis: opioid consumption lower with ketamine across six RCTs (-13.19 µg/kg/h morphine equivalents, P=0.004); nothing else moved
cards.people: Nineteen studies (13 RCTs, 5 retrospective, 1 prospective cohort; 2,255 participants) of continuous-infusion ketamine versus non-ketamine analgosedation in critically ill patients; the primary opioid analysis pooled six RCTs with 494 participants.
cards.result: Ketamine regimens reduced opioid consumption in the RCT-only primary analysis (mean difference -13.19 µg/kg/h morphine equivalents, 95% CI -22.10 to -4.28; P=0.004). No significant difference was observed in sedative consumption, duration of mechanical ventilation, ICU or hospital length of stay, intracranial pressure, or mortality.
cards.watchOut: The pooled opioid effect rests on small trials with heterogeneous comparators and dosing; the largest blinded trial (Perbet 2018, carded above) found no sparing, so the pooled estimate is only as strong as its smallest members. Small samples may have limited detection of true differences in the hard outcomes.
cards.source: Chan K et al. Impact of Ketamine on Analgosedative Consumption in Critically Ill Patients: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. The Annals of pharmacotherapy. 2022. PMID: 35081769. cards.headline: Synthesis: opioid-sparing that evaporates in the best trial, and a delirium signal that appears only there
cards.summary: Synthesis: opioid-sparing that evaporates in the best trial, and a delirium signal that appears only there
cards.people: Two randomised trials (162-patient double-blind trial; 83-patient pilot) and a meta-analysis of 19 studies (2,255 participants; opioid analysis on 6 RCTs, 494 participants) of adjunctive ketamine infusion in mechanically ventilated ICU patients.
cards.result: Opioid consumption: -13.19 µg/kg/h morphine equivalents (95% CI -22.10 to -4.28) in the RCT meta-analysis, but 7.9 vs 9.3 µg/kg/h (P=0.548) in the largest blinded trial. Delirium: 21% vs 37% (P=0.03) in that trial. Ventilation duration, length of stay, and mortality: no significant difference anywhere. PROPOSED SPLIT, as the two best sources answer two different halves of the question.
cards.watchOut: Ketamine dosing, comparators, and sedation protocols vary widely across the pooled trials; a large multicentre trial powered on patient-centred outcomes remains the missing piece, and this shelf should be rebuilt when it reports.
cards.source: Synthesis of Perbet S et al. Anaesthesia, critical care & pain medicine. 2018 (PMID: 30268528); Amer M et al. Journal of intensive care. 2021 (PMID: 34462007); Chan K et al. The Annals of pharmacotherapy. 2022 (PMID: 35081769).

shelves.title: Terlipressin versus norepinephrine in septic shock: 28-day mortality 40% vs 38% — no survival difference, and serious adverse events 30% vs 12%
shelves.question: In septic shock, does terlipressin infusion improve blood pressure, organ function, and survival compared with norepinephrine?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · China · Critical Care · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Infusions, Intravenous · Male · Middle Aged · Norepinephrine/therapeutic use · Shock, Septic/mortality/therapy · Survival Rate · Terlipressin/therapeutic use · Treatment Outcome · Vasoconstrictor Agents/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — terlipressin raises blood pressure and spares catecholamines, but in the only large head-to-head trial it did not save lives, and it caused more serious harm. In 617 randomised patients with septic shock across 21 Chinese ICUs (526 in the modified intention-to-treat analysis), 28-day mortality was 40% on terlipressin and 38% on norepinephrine (odds ratio 0.93, 95% CI 0.55 to 1.56; p=0.80), day-7 SOFA change and vasopressor-free days were similar, and serious adverse events were more than twice as common on terlipressin (30% vs 12%; p<0.001). The earlier TERLIVAP pilot (45 patients) showed the pharmacology clearly — open-label norepinephrine requirements at 48 hours of 0.2 µg/kg/min on terlipressin versus 1.2 µg/kg/min on norepinephrine — without any power for outcomes. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): as a first-line infusion, terlipressin matches norepinephrine for survival and organ function while adding serious adverse events.

cards.headline: Liu 2018: 28-day mortality 40% vs 38% (p=0.80); serious adverse events 30% vs 12% (p<0.001) — terlipressin vs norepinephrine
cards.summary: Liu 2018: 28-day mortality 40% vs 38% (p=0.80); serious adverse events 30% vs 12% (p<0.001) — terlipressin vs norepinephrine
cards.people: 617 patients with septic shock randomised at 21 ICUs in 11 provinces of China (312 terlipressin, 305 norepinephrine) to terlipressin infusion (20–160 µg/h, maximum 4 mg/day) or norepinephrine (4–30 µg/min) before open-label vasopressors; modified intention-to-treat population 526 (260 terlipressin, 266 norepinephrine).
cards.result: There was no significant difference in 28-day mortality: 40% in the terlipressin group and 38% in the norepinephrine group (odds ratio 0.93, 95% CI 0.55 to 1.56; p=0.80). Change in SOFA score on day 7 was similar (-7 (IQR -11 to 3) vs -6 (IQR -10 to 5)), as were days alive and free of vasopressors. Serious adverse events were more common with terlipressin (30% vs 12%; p<0.001).
cards.watchOut: A single-country trial with 15% of randomised patients outside the modified intention-to-treat analysis, and terlipressin dosing capped at 4 mg/day — the result answers first-line infusion as tested, not bolus terlipressin or its separate, established role in hepatorenal syndrome, which lives on its own shelf.
cards.source: Liu ZM et al. Terlipressin versus norepinephrine as infusion in patients with septic shock: a multicentre, randomised, double-blinded trial. Intensive care medicine. 2018. PMID: 29971593. Registry ID: NCT01697410. cards.headline: TERLIVAP (Morelli 2009): terlipressin cut open-label norepinephrine needs to 0.2 vs 1.2 µg/kg/min at 48 hours — a 45-patient physiology pilot
cards.summary: TERLIVAP (Morelli 2009): terlipressin cut open-label norepinephrine needs to 0.2 vs 1.2 µg/kg/min at 48 hours — a 45-patient physiology pilot
cards.people: 45 patients with septic shock and mean arterial pressure below 65 mmHg despite volume resuscitation, randomised to continuous terlipressin (1.3 µg/kg/h), vasopressin (0.03 U/min), or norepinephrine (15 µg/min) as first-line therapy, with open-label norepinephrine added to hold mean arterial pressure at 65–75 mmHg.
cards.result: Systemic and regional haemodynamics did not differ among groups. Terlipressin allowed a marked reduction in open-label catecholamine requirements at 48 hours (0.2 ± 0.4 µg/kg/min) versus vasopressin (0.8 ± 1.3) and norepinephrine (1.2 ± 1.4) (each P<0.05), with less rebound hypotension. Bilirubin at 48 hours was lower with terlipressin (0.9 ± 0.3 mg/dL) than vasopressin (2.3 ± 2.8) or norepinephrine (2.8 ± 2.5); a time-dependent platelet fall was seen only in the terlipressin group.
cards.watchOut: Fifteen patients per arm and a 48-hour horizon: this trial demonstrates vasopressor pharmacology, nothing about survival or organ failure — and its platelet signal foreshadows the harm pattern the large trial later quantified.
cards.source: Morelli A et al. Continuous terlipressin versus vasopressin infusion in septic shock (TERLIVAP): a randomized, controlled pilot study. Critical care (London, England). 2009. PMID: 19664253. Registry ID: NCT00481572. cards.headline: Synthesis: equal survival, equal organ scores, unequal harm — the catecholamine-sparing is real and buys nothing measurable
cards.summary: Synthesis: equal survival, equal organ scores, unequal harm — the catecholamine-sparing is real and buys nothing measurable
cards.people: One 617-patient double-blind multicentre trial and one 45-patient randomised pilot comparing terlipressin infusion with norepinephrine (and, in the pilot, vasopressin) as first-line therapy in septic shock.
cards.result: 28-day mortality 40% vs 38% (OR 0.93, 95% CI 0.55 to 1.56). Serious adverse events 30% vs 12%. Open-label norepinephrine requirement at 48 hours 0.2 vs 1.2 µg/kg/min in the pilot. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) for survival and organ function, with the harm on the face of the shelf.

shelves.title: High-volume haemofiltration in septic shock with kidney injury: 28-day mortality 37.9% vs 40.8% in IVOIRE — doubling the dose changed nothing
shelves.question: In septic shock with acute kidney injury, does high-volume haemofiltration improve survival compared with standard-volume haemofiltration?
shelves.mesh: Acute Kidney Injury/complications/mortality · Aged · Critical Illness · Female · Hemofiltration/methods · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Prospective Studies · Shock, Septic/complications/mortality/therapy · Survival Rate · Time Factors
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — an attractive idea, tested at full dose, with a flat result. IVOIRE randomised 140 patients with septic shock and acute kidney injury to high-volume haemofiltration at 70 mL/kg/h or standard-volume at 35 mL/kg/h for 96 hours; 28-day mortality was 37.9% versus 40.8% (p=0.94), with no significant difference in any secondary endpoint, and the trial stopped early for slow accrual. The meta-analysis of four trials (470 participants) found the same: 28-day mortality odds ratio 0.76 (95% CI 0.45 to 1.29), no significant difference in kidney recovery or lengths of stay, and more hypophosphataemia and hypokalaemia at high volume. The Cochrane review (four trials, 200 participants) pooled a 28-day mortality risk ratio of 0.89 (95% CI 0.60 to 1.32) on low-quality evidence. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): high-volume haemofiltration, as applied in these trials, does not reduce mortality in septic shock with AKI and cannot be recommended for that purpose.

cards.headline: IVOIRE (Joannes-Boyau 2013): 28-day mortality 37.9% (70 mL/kg/h) vs 40.8% (35 mL/kg/h), p=0.94 — stopped early at 140 patients
cards.summary: IVOIRE (Joannes-Boyau 2013): 28-day mortality 37.9% (70 mL/kg/h) vs 40.8% (35 mL/kg/h), p=0.94 — stopped early at 140 patients
cards.people: 140 critically ill patients with septic shock and acute kidney injury for less than 24 hours, enrolled at 18 ICUs in France, Belgium, and the Netherlands (2005–2010), randomised to high-volume haemofiltration at 70 mL/kg/h or standard-volume at 35 mL/kg/h for 96 hours; 137 analysed (66 high-volume, 71 standard).
cards.result: Mortality at 28 days was lower than expected but not different between groups (high-volume 37.9% vs standard-volume 40.8%; log-rank p=0.94). There were no statistically significant differences in any secondary endpoint, including haemodynamic profile and organ function. The trial was stopped prematurely because of slow accrual and exhausted resources.
cards.watchOut: Early stopping at 140 patients leaves the trial underpowered for modest effects — but the point estimate is a 3-point difference in the wrong-sized package, and every synthesis since has centred on the same null. 'High volume' here means 70 mL/kg/h; still-higher doses were not tested.
cards.source: Joannes-Boyau O et al. High-volume versus standard-volume haemofiltration for septic shock patients with acute kidney injury (IVOIRE study): a multicentre randomized controlled trial. cards.headline: Clark 2014 meta-analysis: four trials, 470 patients — mortality OR 0.76 (95% CI 0.45 to 1.29), more electrolyte losses at high volume
cards.summary: Clark 2014 meta-analysis: four trials, 470 patients — mortality OR 0.76 (95% CI 0.45 to 1.29), more electrolyte losses at high volume
cards.people: Four randomised trials (470 participants) comparing high-volume haemofiltration (effluent rate >50 mL/kg/h) with standard-volume haemofiltration in sepsis and septic shock with acute kidney injury, from publications between 1966 and 2013.
cards.result: Pooled 28-day mortality did not differ meaningfully between high-volume and standard-volume haemofiltration (OR 0.76, 95% CI 0.45 to 1.29). No included study reported a significant difference in kidney-function recovery, ICU or hospital stay, or vasopressor dose reduction. Adverse events including hypophosphataemia and hypokalaemia were more commonly observed with high-volume treatment, though reporting was inconsistent.
cards.watchOut: Four small trials with differing dose definitions and populations; the confidence interval cannot exclude a moderate benefit or harm, which is precisely why the authors concluded the evidence supports experimental use only.
cards.source: Clark E et al. High-volume hemofiltration for septic acute kidney injury: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Critical care (London, England). 2014. PMID: 24398168. cards.people: Four randomised trials involving 200 participants with severe sepsis or septic shock in intensive care, comparing high-volume haemofiltration or haemodiafiltration with standard dialysis therapy or none; searches to 31 December 2015.
cards.result: The pooled risk ratio for 28-day mortality with high-volume haemofiltration was 0.89 (95% CI 0.60 to 1.32; two trials, 146 participants; low-quality evidence). shelves.title: Severe melioidosis intensive phase: ceftazidime halved mortality against the old four-drug regimen (37% versus 74%) — and imipenem later matched ceftazidime on survival, with fewer early treatment failures
shelves.question: In acute severe melioidosis, which intravenous intensive-phase regimen saves most lives — ceftazidime against the older conventional combination, and how does imipenem compare with ceftazidime?
shelves.mesh: Actuarial Analysis · Administration, Oral · Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Ceftazidime/therapeutic use · Child · Chloramphenicol/administration & dosage/analogs & derivatives · Clinical Trials as Topic · Doxycycline/administration & dosage · Drug Evaluation · Drug Resistance, Microbial · Drug Therapy, Combination/therapeutic use · Female · Humans · Injections, Intravenous · Male · Melioidosis/complications/mortality/prevention & control · Middle Aged · Prospective Studies · Random Allocation · Sepsis/etiology/mortality/prevention & control · Sulfamethoxazole/administration & dosage · Time Factors · Trimethoprim/administration & dosage
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) — for ceftazidime over the regimen it replaced, on mortality, from the trial that changed practice. In the open randomised Thai trial (White NJ et al., PMID: 2570956), ceftazidime 120 mg/kg/day was compared with conventional therapy (chloramphenicol, doxycycline, trimethoprim and sulfamethoxazole) in severe melioidosis; the sequential trial was stopped after 22 months because ceftazidime was associated with a 50% relative lower overall mortality (95% CI 19–81) — 37% versus 74% (p=0.009) — among the 65 culture-confirmed patients (54 septicaemic) of 161 entered. A decade later (Simpson AJH et al., PMID: 10476746), 296 patients with suspected severe melioidosis (214 culture-confirmed) were randomised to high-dose imipenem or ceftazidime for at least 10 days: overall mortality in confirmed disease was 36.9%, with no difference in survival overall (p=0.96) or after 48 hours (p=0.3), but treatment failure after 48 hours was more common on ceftazidime (p=0.011), and both drugs were well tolerated. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): ceftazidime (or a carbapenem) is the intensive-phase standard because it halved mortality against what came before; between ceftazidime and imipenem, survival is a tie. Tier C is set because the mortality claim that anchors the shelf comes from the single 1989 trial, stopped early.

cards.headline: White 1989: mortality 37% on ceftazidime versus 74% on conventional therapy — a 50% relative reduction; trial stopped at 22 months
cards.summary: White 1989: mortality 37% on ceftazidime versus 74% on conventional therapy — a 50% relative reduction; trial stopped at 22 months
cards.people: 161 patients with severe melioidosis entered into an open randomised paired restricted sequential trial in Thailand, comparing ceftazidime 120 mg/kg/day with conventional therapy (chloramphenicol 100 mg/kg/day, doxycycline 4 mg/kg/day, trimethoprim 10 mg/kg/day and sulphamethoxazole 50 mg/kg/day); 65 patients had bacteriologically confirmed melioidosis, 54 of them septicaemic; the design targeted patients surviving more than 48 hours and was powered to detect a mortality fall from 80% to 40%.
cards.result: Ceftazidime treatment was associated with a 50% lower overall mortality than conventional treatment (95% CI 19–81%) — mortality 37% versus 74% (p=0.009) — and the trial was stopped after 22 months. The authors concluded ceftazidime should become the treatment of choice for severe melioidosis.
cards.watchOut: A small, open, sequentially monitored trial stopped early on a large effect — early stopping inflates point estimates, and the 74% control mortality reflects both a bacteriostatic, mutually antagonistic old regimen and the severity of confirmed septicaemic disease in that era; the direction has never been retested against placebo-equivalent care, for obvious ethical reasons.
cards.source: White NJ et al. Halving of mortality of severe melioidosis by ceftazidime. Lancet. 1989. PMID: 2570956. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Simpson 1999: imipenem versus ceftazidime — survival identical (overall confirmed-case mortality 36.9%), but treatment failure after 48 hours commoner on ceftazidime (p=0.011)
cards.summary: Simpson 1999: imipenem versus ceftazidime — survival identical (overall confirmed-case mortality 36.9%), but treatment failure after 48 hours commoner on ceftazidime (p=0.011)
cards.people: 296 adult Thai patients with suspected acute severe melioidosis randomised to intravenous imipenem 50 mg/kg/day or ceftazidime 120 mg/kg/day for a minimum of 10 days; 214 had culture-confirmed melioidosis and 132 (61.7%) of those had positive blood cultures; main outcome measures death or treatment failure.
cards.result: Mortality among patients with confirmed melioidosis was 36.9% overall. There were no differences in survival overall (p=0.96) or after 48 hours (p=0.3). Treatment failure after 48 hours was more common among patients treated with ceftazidime (p=0.011). Both treatments were well tolerated, and the authors concluded imipenem is a safe and effective alternative to ceftazidime.
cards.watchOut: The abstract reports survival only as p-values and the pooled 36.9% mortality, so no arm-specific mortality percentages are quoted here; the trial was open-label, and 'treatment failure' is a softer, clinician-judged endpoint than the survival it accompanied.

cards.people: Two open randomised trials in Thai patients with severe melioidosis, a decade apart: ceftazidime versus the conventional four-drug regimen (161 entered, 65 confirmed), and imipenem versus ceftazidime (296 suspected, 214 confirmed).
cards.result: Mortality: 37% on ceftazidime versus 74% on conventional therapy (50% relative reduction, 95% CI 19–81). cards.watchOut: These are intensive-phase results only; the eradication phase that follows (and the relapse it prevents) is a separate question with its own shelf in this library. Meropenem, now commonly used, has no randomised mortality comparison in this card set.

shelves.title: Posaconazole for invasive aspergillosis: non-inferior to voriconazole on day-42 mortality (15% versus 21% overall; 19% versus 19% in proven/probable disease), with fewer treatment-related adverse events (30% versus 40%)
shelves.question: In patients with invasive aspergillosis needing primary treatment, is posaconazole non-inferior to voriconazole for all-cause mortality — and how do the two compare on treatment-related harm?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Intravenous · Administration, Oral · Adolescent · Adult · Antifungal Agents/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Invasive Pulmonary Aspergillosis/drug therapy/mortality · Male · Middle Aged · Prospective Studies · Triazoles/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Voriconazole/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Young Adult
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — an alternative first-line azole, proven non-inferior in one large double-blind trial. In that trial (Maertens JA et al., PMID: 33549194), 575 patients aged 13 years or older with proven, probable or possible invasive aspergillosis at 91 sites in 26 countries received posaconazole or voriconazole for up to 12 weeks. All-cause mortality to day 42 in the intention-to-treat population was 15% (44 of 288) on posaconazole versus 21% (59 of 287) on voriconazole — a treatment difference of −5.3 percentage points (95% CI −11.6 to 1.0), meeting non-inferiority (p<0.0001 for the non-inferiority test); in the subpopulation with proven or probable disease the rates were identical, 19% (31 of 163) versus 19% (32 of 171), difference 0.3 points (−8.2 to 8.8). Treatment-related adverse events were fewer on posaconazole: 30% versus 40% overall (difference −10.2 points, 95% CI −17.9 to −2.4), with liver-enzyme rises, nausea, hypokalaemia and vomiting the commonest on posaconazole, and hallucinations and blurred vision featuring on voriconazole. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): posaconazole is a first-line option with a gentler treatment-related profile — Tier C, a single trial, whose ITT mortality gap is driven partly by 'possible' cases the proven/probable analysis does not reproduce.

cards.headline: Maertens 2021 (phase 3): day-42 mortality 15% posaconazole versus 21% voriconazole (difference −5.3 points) — but 19% versus 19% in proven/probable disease; treatment-related adverse events 30% versus 40%
cards.summary: Maertens 2021 (phase 3): day-42 mortality 15% posaconazole versus 21% voriconazole (difference −5.3 points) — but 19% versus 19% in proven/probable disease; treatment-related adverse events 30% versus 40%
cards.people: 575 intention-to-treat participants aged 13 years or older, weighing at least 40 kg, with proven, probable or possible invasive aspergillosis at 91 sites in 26 countries, randomised 1:1 (stratified by risk status) to posaconazole (300 mg twice on day 1, then 300 mg daily, intravenous or oral) or voriconazole (standard loading then maintenance dosing, intravenous or oral) for up to 84 days; 288 and 287 received study drug.
cards.result: All-cause mortality to day 42 was 15% (44 of 288) on posaconazole versus 21% (59 of 287) on voriconazole (treatment difference −5.3 percentage points, 95% CI −11.6 to 1.0; p<0.0001 for non-inferiority). In the full-analysis-set subpopulation with proven or probable invasive aspergillosis, mortality was 19% (31 of 163) versus 19% (32 of 171), difference 0.3 points (−8.2 to 8.8). Treatment-related adverse events occurred in 30% on posaconazole versus 40% on voriconazole (difference −10.2 points, −17.9 to −2.4); the commonest on posaconazole were raised AST/ALT, nausea, hypokalaemia and vomiting, and on voriconazole raised liver enzymes, hallucination, raised gamma-glutamyltransferase, nausea and blurred vision.
cards.watchOut: The ITT population includes 'possible' invasive aspergillosis — patients who may not have had the disease at all — and the apparent mortality advantage disappears exactly where diagnosis is firmest (19% versus 19%). The honest claim is non-inferiority plus tolerability, not superiority; the trial was funded by posaconazole's manufacturer.

cards.result: Day-42 mortality: 15% versus 21% intention-to-treat (difference −5.3 points, 95% CI −11.6 to 1.0; non-inferiority met); 19% versus 19% in proven/probable disease. shelves.title: Tetanus: giving antitetanus immunoglobulin intrathecally as well as intramuscularly — pooled mortality relative risk 0.71 across 12 small trials; the largest trial showed better progression and shorter spasms, stay and ventilation
shelves.question: In patients being treated for tetanus, does adding intrathecal antitetanus immunoglobulin (or antiserum) to the standard intramuscular dose improve survival and clinical course compared with intramuscular treatment alone?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Animals · Horses · Humans · Immunoglobulins/administration & dosage · Infant, Newborn · Injections, Intramuscular · Injections, Spinal · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Tetanus/drug therapy · Tetanus Antitoxin/administration & dosage · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — an old, small-trial literature with a consistent direction, held as Tier C. The meta-analysis (Kabura L et al., PMID: 16827708) pooled 12 randomised trials, 942 patients (484 intrathecal, 458 intramuscular): the combined relative risk of mortality for intrathecal versus intramuscular administration was 0.71 (95% CI 0.62–0.81) — a 29% relative reduction — with superiority also in the adult and neonatal subcategories and at high and low intrathecal doses. The largest single trial (Miranda-Filho DB et al., PMID: 15003976), 120 ICU patients in Brazil randomised to intrathecal plus intramuscular human immunoglobulin or intramuscular alone, found better clinical progression (difference in proportion improved 20%, 95% CI 4% to 35%; p=0.005), more patients with spasms lasting 10 days or fewer (difference 36%, 18% to 55%), shorter hospital stay and respiratory assistance (69.2% versus 30.8% needing assistance for 10 days or fewer; difference 38%, 12% to 65%); its abstract does not report the mortality split, so the survival claim rests on the pooled analysis. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): intrathecal antitoxin probably improves the course of tetanus and may reduce mortality — but the trials are small, old, and mix human immunoglobulin with equine serum, which is why this stays Tier C.

cards.headline: Kabura 2006 meta-analysis (12 trials, 942 patients): mortality RR 0.71 (0.62–0.81) for intrathecal versus intramuscular antitoxin, consistent in adults, neonates, high and low doses
cards.summary: Kabura 2006 meta-analysis (12 trials, 942 patients): mortality RR 0.71 (0.62–0.81) for intrathecal versus intramuscular antitoxin, consistent in adults, neonates, high and low doses
cards.people: 942 patients with tetanus in 12 published randomised trials (English or French) comparing intrathecal with intramuscular administration of equine antitetanus serum or human tetanus immunoglobulin — 484 intrathecal, 458 intramuscular — spanning neonatal and adult tetanus.
cards.result: The combined relative risk of mortality for intrathecal versus intramuscular administration was 0.71 (95% CI 0.62–0.81), a 29% relative reduction. The superiority of intrathecal therapy also emerged in the subcategories of adults and of neonates, and for both high-dose and low-dose intrathecal serotherapy. The authors concluded intrathecal administration of antiserum or immunoglobulin is more beneficial than intramuscular administration in the treatment of tetanus.
cards.watchOut: The component trials are small and old, used different products (equine serum and human immunoglobulin) and predated modern intensive care; a pooled relative risk of 0.71 across such trials is a signal, not a settled standard — and the abstract reports no absolute mortality rates, so none are quoted.
cards.source: Kabura L et al. Intrathecal vs. intramuscular administration of human antitetanus immunoglobulin or equine tetanus antiserum in the treatment of tetanus: a meta-analysis. Tropical Medicine & International Health. 2006. PMID: 16827708. cards.headline: Miranda-Filho 2004 (Brazil, n=120): intrathecal plus intramuscular immunoglobulin — better progression (+20 points improved), spasms and ventilation shorter; mortality split not reported in the record
cards.summary: Miranda-Filho 2004 (Brazil, n=120): intrathecal plus intramuscular immunoglobulin — better progression (+20 points improved), spasms and ventilation shorter; mortality split not reported in the record
cards.people: 120 patients with tetanus in the intensive care unit of a university hospital in Pernambuco, Brazil, allocated to human antitetanus immunoglobulin by the intrathecal and intramuscular routes (n=58) or the intramuscular route alone (n=62, control). The cost analysis of the same trial records the doses as 3,000 IU intramuscularly in both groups, plus 1,000 IU intrathecally (preservative-free) in the treatment group.
cards.result: Patients in the treatment group showed better clinical progression than controls (chi-square for trend 7.752, p=0.005; difference in proportion of patients with improvement 20%, 95% CI 4% to 35%). Spasms, hospital stay and respiratory assistance were all shorter: the difference in proportion with spasms lasting 10 days or fewer was 36% (18% to 55%), and 69.2% of the treatment group versus 30.8% of controls needed respiratory assistance for 10 days or fewer (difference 38%, 12% to 65%). The record's abstract does not give the between-group mortality figures, so no mortality claim is made from this trial.
cards.watchOut: A single-centre, unblinded-route comparison from 2004 in one Brazilian ICU; progression and duration outcomes are softer than mortality, and the trial cannot carry the survival claim alone — that is the meta-analysis's job, with its own caveats.
cards.source: Miranda-Filho DB et al. Randomised controlled trial of tetanus treatment with antitetanus immunoglobulin by the intrathecal or intramuscular route. BMJ. 2004. PMID: 15003976. cards.headline: Synthesis: direction consistent, evidence thin — intrathecal antitoxin looks better than intramuscular alone wherever it has been randomised, but no modern trial exists
cards.summary: Synthesis: direction consistent, evidence thin — intrathecal antitoxin looks better than intramuscular alone wherever it has been randomised, but no modern trial exists
cards.people: Twelve randomised trials (942 patients) pooled, plus the largest single trial (120 ICU patients, Brazil) reported in detail.
cards.result: Pooled mortality RR 0.71 (0.62–0.81) for intrathecal versus intramuscular antitoxin; in the largest trial, better progression (+20 points), shorter spasms, stay and ventilation with the intrathecal route. PROPOSED POSSIBLE, Tier C — old, small, mixed-product trials behind a mortality claim.
cards.watchOut: Tetanus care has changed since these trials (ventilation, sedation, magnesium, metronidazole); the shelf reports what was randomised, and the intrathecal route requires preservative-free product and lumbar puncture in a spasming patient — practicalities the trials handled but readers must weigh.

shelves.title: Plague treatment: gentamicin and doxycycline both worked — favourable responses 94% versus 97% in the only randomised trial (65 patients, Tanzania); 3 early deaths were from advanced disease
shelves.question: For patients with naturally occurring plague (bubonic, septicaemic or pneumonic), is gentamicin — available where streptomycin no longer is — as effective as doxycycline in a randomised comparison?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Anti-Bacterial Agents/therapeutic use · Child · Child, Preschool · Doxycycline/therapeutic use · Female · Gentamicins/therapeutic use · Humans · Infant · Male · Middle Aged · Plague/drug therapy · Tanzania
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — between the two drugs, in the only randomised trial there is. In Tanzania (Mwengee W et al., PMID: 16447105), 65 adults and children with bubonic, septicaemic or pneumonic plague of 3 days' duration or less were randomised open-label to gentamicin (2.5 mg/kg intramuscularly every 12 hours for 7 days; n=35) or doxycycline (100 mg in adults, 2.2 mg/kg in children, orally every 12 hours for 7 days; n=30). Three patients died on the first or second day — 2 on gentamicin, 1 on doxycycline — with deaths attributed to advanced disease (pneumonia, septicaemia, haemorrhage, renal failure at presentation). All other patients were cured or improved: favourable response 94% (95% CI 81.1–99.0) with gentamicin and 97% (83.4–99.8) with doxycycline. Yersinia pestis isolates (biotype antigua) were susceptible to both drugs, serum concentrations were in range, adverse events were infrequent, and gentamicin produced a modest rise in mean serum creatinine. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): with 65 patients the trial cannot prove equivalence — it shows both drugs performed well in real plague, which is the evidence base guidelines actually rest on. Tier C: a single small open-label trial for a lethal disease.

cards.headline: Mwengee 2006 (Tanzania, n=65): favourable response 94% gentamicin versus 97% doxycycline; 3 deaths (2 versus 1), all on day 1–2 from advanced disease
cards.summary: Mwengee 2006 (Tanzania, n=65): favourable response 94% gentamicin versus 97% doxycycline; 3 deaths (2 versus 1), all on day 1–2 from advanced disease
cards.people: 65 adults and children in Tanzania with symptoms of bubonic, septicaemic, or pneumonic plague of 3 days' duration or less; bubo aspirates and blood cultured for Yersinia pestis and sera tested for fraction 1 antigen antibody; 35 randomised to gentamicin 2.5 mg/kg intramuscularly every 12 hours for 7 days, 30 to doxycycline (100 mg adults, 2.2 mg/kg children) orally every 12 hours for 7 days; serum creatinine and antibiotic peak/trough concentrations measured.
cards.result: Three patients — 2 treated with gentamicin and 1 with doxycycline — died on the first or second day of treatment, attributed to advanced disease and complications including pneumonia, septicaemia, haemorrhage and renal failure present at the start of therapy. All other patients experienced cure or an improved condition: favourable response rates 94% for gentamicin (95% CI 81.1%–99.0%) and 97% for doxycycline (83.4%–99.8%). Isolates from 30 patients were biotype antigua, susceptible to gentamicin (MIC 0.13 mg/L) and doxycycline (MIC 0.25–0.5 mg/L). Adverse events were infrequent; gentamicin patients showed a modest increase in mean serum creatinine after treatment (p<0.05). The authors concluded both drugs were effective therapies for adult and paediatric plague.
cards.watchOut: Sixty-five patients, open-label, no placebo or streptomycin arm — this trial can show that both drugs work in practice but cannot exclude a clinically important difference between them, and its pneumonic cases were few; it also predates fluoroquinolone-era guidance, which rests on other evidence not carded here.
cards.source: Mwengee W et al. Treatment of plague with gentamicin or doxycycline in a randomized clinical trial in Tanzania. Clinical Infectious Diseases. 2006. PMID: 16447105. cards.headline: Synthesis: the plague shelf rests on one small trial — both modern standbys performed well, and the deaths were sealed before antibiotics could act
cards.summary: Synthesis: the plague shelf rests on one small trial — both modern standbys performed well, and the deaths were sealed before antibiotics could act
cards.people: One randomised open-label trial, 65 adults and children with plague in Tanzania, comparing 7 days of gentamicin with 7 days of doxycycline.
cards.result: Favourable response 94% versus 97%; deaths 2 versus 1, all within 48 hours and attributed to advanced disease at presentation. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference), Tier C — a single small trial, honestly labelled, is what exists for a disease where large trials will never be run.
cards.watchOut: Do not read 'no difference shown' as 'proven equal': the confidence intervals (81–99% and 83–100%) overlap almost completely because the trial is tiny. Choice between the drugs in practice turns on route, age, pregnancy and availability — none of which this trial was sized to settle.
cards.source: Synthesis of Mwengee W et al. Clinical Infectious Diseases. 2006 (PMID: 16447105).

shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — a properly blinded head-to-head that found the class behaving like a class. The international double-blind trial (Pappas PG et al., PMID: 17806055) randomised 595 adults with candidaemia and other invasive candidiasis to micafungin 100 mg daily, micafungin 150 mg daily, or caspofungin (70 mg loading, then 50 mg daily); in the modified intention-to-treat population (191, 199 and 188 patients), about 85% had candidaemia. At the end of blinded intravenous therapy, treatment success (clinical plus mycological) was 76.4% with micafungin 100 mg, 71.4% with micafungin 150 mg and 72.3% with caspofungin; median time to culture negativity was 2 days in the micafungin 100 mg and caspofungin groups and 3 days in the micafungin 150 mg group. There were no significant differences in mortality, relapsing or emergent infections, or adverse events between the arms, and both micafungin doses were non-inferior to caspofungin. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): the higher micafungin dose bought nothing measurable — the shelf's practical content is dose discipline (100 mg suffices) and free choice between the two drugs on other grounds.

cards.headline: Pappas 2007 (n=595, double-blind): success 76.4% micafungin 100 mg, 71.4% micafungin 150 mg, 72.3% caspofungin; culture negativity at 2, 3 and 2 days; no significant mortality or adverse-event differences
cards.summary: Pappas 2007 (n=595, double-blind): success 76.4% micafungin 100 mg, 71.4% micafungin 150 mg, 72.3% caspofungin; culture negativity at 2, 3 and 2 days; no significant mortality or adverse-event differences
cards.people: 595 adults with candidaemia and other forms of invasive candidiasis at international sites, randomised to micafungin 100 mg daily, micafungin 150 mg daily, or caspofungin 70 mg followed by 50 mg daily, and receiving at least one dose; modified intention-to-treat population 191, 199 and 188 patients respectively; approximately 85% had candidaemia and the remainder non-candidaemic invasive candidiasis; primary endpoint was treatment success — clinical and mycological — at the end of blinded intravenous therapy. The record names the drugs generically and no manufacturer, so none is stated.
cards.result: Treatment was successful for 76.4% of patients in the micafungin 100 mg group, 71.4% in the micafungin 150 mg group, and 72.3% in the caspofungin group. Median time to culture negativity was 2 days in the micafungin 100 mg and caspofungin groups, compared with 3 days in the micafungin 150 mg group. There were no significant differences in mortality, relapsing and emergent infections, or adverse events between the study arms. The authors concluded that micafungin 100 mg and 150 mg daily were non-inferior to standard-dosage caspofungin for candidaemia and other invasive candidiasis.
cards.watchOut: A non-inferiority comparison within one drug class, in mostly candidaemic patients — it does not address echinocandin versus azole or amphotericin choices (the library's class shelf), resistant species, or deep-seated infection without bloodstream involvement; and 'no significant difference' in mortality is not a powered mortality equivalence claim.
cards.source: Pappas PG et al. Micafungin versus caspofungin for treatment of candidemia and other forms of invasive candidiasis. Clinical Infectious Diseases. 2007. PMID: 17806055. shelves.title: Aspirin in hospitalised COVID-19: 17% died within 28 days in both groups in RECOVERY — fewer thrombotic events, more major bleeding, and discharge about a day sooner
shelves.question: In hospitalised adults with COVID-19, does aspirin reduce 28-day mortality compared with usual care?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Aspirin/therapeutic use · Female · Hospitalization/statistics & numerical data · Humans · Indonesia · Length of Stay/statistics & numerical data · Male · Middle Aged · Mortality/trends · Nepal · Time Factors · Treatment Outcome · United Kingdom · COVID-19 Drug Treatment
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — for survival, in one very large open-label trial. In RECOVERY, 17% of patients allocated aspirin 150 mg daily and 17% allocated usual care alone died within 28 days (rate ratio 0.96, 95% CI 0.89–1.04; p=0.35). Aspirin did shift secondary outcomes in opposite directions: thrombotic events fell (4.6% vs 5.3%) while major bleeding rose (1.6% vs 1.0%), hospital stay was slightly shorter (median 8 vs 9 days), and slightly more patients were discharged alive within 28 days (75% vs 74%; rate ratio 1.06, 95% CI 1.02–1.10). The composite of invasive mechanical ventilation or death among those not ventilated at baseline was 21% vs 22% (risk ratio 0.96, 95% CI 0.90–1.03). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): aspirin does not reduce 28-day mortality in hospitalised COVID-19; its small antithrombotic gain is offset by a small bleeding cost. Single-trial shelf — flagged in the summary.

cards.headline: RECOVERY aspirin: 28-day mortality 17% vs 17% (rate ratio 0.96) — thrombotic events 4.6% vs 5.3%, major bleeding 1.6% vs 1.0%
cards.summary: RECOVERY aspirin: 28-day mortality 17% vs 17% (rate ratio 0.96) — thrombotic events 4.6% vs 5.3%, major bleeding 1.6% vs 1.0%
cards.type: Randomised open-label platform trial (RECOVERY Collaborative Group 2022)
cards.people: 14,892 adults hospitalised with COVID-19 at 177 UK hospitals and four hospitals in Indonesia and Nepal, randomised 1:1 to usual care plus aspirin 150 mg once daily until discharge (7,351) or usual care alone (7,541), between November 2020 and March 2021.
cards.result: 28-day mortality was 17% in both groups (1,222 of 7,351 on aspirin vs 1,299 of 7,541 on usual care; rate ratio 0.96, 95% CI 0.89–1.04; p=0.35), with consistent results in all prespecified subgroups. Patients allocated aspirin had a slightly shorter hospitalisation (median 8 days vs 9 days) and a higher proportion discharged alive within 28 days (75% vs 74%; rate ratio 1.06, 95% CI 1.02–1.10; p=0.0062). Among patients not on invasive mechanical ventilation at baseline, the composite of ventilation or death was 21% vs 22% (risk ratio 0.96, 95% CI 0.90–1.03; p=0.23). Thrombotic events were reduced (4.6% vs 5.3%; absolute reduction 0.6%) and major bleeding increased (1.6% vs 1.0%; absolute increase 0.6%).
cards.watchOut: Single-trial shelf: this is the only large randomised comparison of aspirin in hospitalised COVID-19, and it was open-label — discharge timing, one of the two outcomes that moved, is the outcome most open to bias in an unblinded trial. The mortality confidence interval (0.89–1.04) excludes any large benefit but not a small one.
cards.source: RECOVERY Collaborative Group. Aspirin in patients admitted to hospital with COVID-19 (RECOVERY): a randomised, controlled, open-label, platform trial. Lancet. 2022. PMID: 34800427.
