shelves.title: Remdesivir in hospitalised COVID-19: recovery five days faster in the blinded ACTT-1 trial, but no significant mortality benefit in any trial — and none at all once patients were ventilated
shelves.question: In hospitalised adults with COVID-19, does remdesivir shorten time to recovery and reduce mortality compared with placebo or standard care?
shelves.mesh: Adenosine Monophosphate/administration & dosage/adverse effects/analogs & derivatives/therapeutic use · Administration, Intravenous · Adult · Aged · Alanine/administration & dosage/adverse effects/analogs & derivatives/therapeutic use · Antiviral Agents/administration & dosage/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Betacoronavirus · COVID-19 · Coronavirus Infections/drug therapy/mortality/therapy · Double-Blind Method · Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation · Female · Humans · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Male · Middle Aged · Oxygen Inhalation Therapy · Pandemics · Pneumonia, Viral/drug therapy/mortality/therapy · Respiration, Artificial · SARS-CoV-2 · Time Factors · Young Adult · COVID-19 Drug Treatment
shelves.balance: SPLIT — recovery is faster, survival is not proven. In the double-blind ACTT-1 trial, remdesivir shortened median recovery from 15 to 10 days (rate ratio for recovery 1.29, 95% CI 1.12–1.49; p<0.001), while day-29 mortality was 11.4% vs 15.2% (hazard ratio 0.73, 95% CI 0.52–1.03) — not significant. The smaller blinded Wang trial in severe disease found no significant difference in time to clinical improvement (hazard ratio 1.23, 95% CI 0.87–1.75). The open-label WHO Solidarity final analysis, the largest comparison, found in-hospital mortality of 14.5% vs 15.6% (rate ratio 0.91, 95% CI 0.82–1.02), with a small effect in patients not yet ventilated (rate ratio 0.86, 95% CI 0.76–0.98 for those not ventilated initially) and none in those already ventilated (rate ratio 1.13, 95% CI 0.89–1.42). PROPOSED SPLIT: a real recovery-time benefit in non-ventilated hospitalised patients; no demonstrated mortality benefit overall and no benefit once ventilated.

cards.headline: Beigel 2020 (ACTT-1): median recovery 10 vs 15 days (rate ratio 1.29, p<0.001); day-29 mortality 11.4% vs 15.2%, hazard ratio 0.73 with a confidence interval crossing 1
cards.summary: Beigel 2020 (ACTT-1): median recovery 10 vs 15 days (rate ratio 1.29, p<0.001); day-29 mortality 11.4% vs 15.2%, hazard ratio 0.73 with a confidence interval crossing 1
cards.people: 1,062 adults hospitalised with COVID-19 and evidence of lower respiratory tract infection, randomised to intravenous remdesivir (200 mg on day 1, then 100 mg daily for up to 9 more days; 541 patients) or placebo (521 patients) for up to 10 days.
cards.result: Median time to recovery was 10 days (95% CI 9–11) on remdesivir versus 15 days (95% CI 13–18) on placebo (rate ratio for recovery 1.29, 95% CI 1.12–1.49; p<0.001). Kaplan–Meier mortality estimates were 6.7% vs 11.9% by day 15 and 11.4% vs 15.2% by day 29 (hazard ratio 0.73, 95% CI 0.52–1.03) — a relative difference that did not reach significance. Serious adverse events were reported in 24.6% of remdesivir patients and 31.6% of placebo patients.
cards.watchOut: The trial's win is on time to recovery, a discharge-based endpoint; its mortality estimate is compatible with anything from a 48% relative reduction to a small increase. ACTT-1 was conducted early in the pandemic, before corticosteroids became standard care.
cards.source: Beigel JH et al. Remdesivir for the Treatment of Covid-19 - Final Report. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2020. PMID: 32445440. Registry ID: NCT04280705. cards.headline: Wang 2020: no significant difference in time to clinical improvement in severe COVID-19 (hazard ratio 1.23, 95% CI 0.87–1.75) in a trial stopped short of its target
cards.summary: Wang 2020: no significant difference in time to clinical improvement in severe COVID-19 (hazard ratio 1.23, 95% CI 0.87–1.75) in a trial stopped short of its target
cards.people: 237 adults (236 in the intention-to-treat population) admitted to ten hospitals in Hubei, China with severe COVID-19 — oxygen saturation ≤94% on room air or PaO2/FiO2 ≤300 mm Hg and radiologically confirmed pneumonia, within 12 days of symptom onset — randomised 2:1 to remdesivir (158) or placebo (79) for 10 days.
cards.result: Remdesivir was not associated with a difference in time to clinical improvement (hazard ratio 1.23, 95% CI 0.87–1.75). Among patients treated within 10 days of symptom onset the point estimate was larger but still not significant (hazard ratio 1.52, 95% CI 0.95–2.43). Adverse events were reported in 66% of remdesivir recipients versus 64% on placebo; remdesivir was stopped early for adverse events in 12% versus 5% on placebo.
cards.watchOut: The trial enrolled fewer patients than planned as the Hubei outbreak waned, so it is underpowered for the effect ACTT-1 later found — a null here is weak evidence against a recovery benefit, but it is the second blinded trial and it did not confirm one in severe disease.
cards.source: Wang Y et al. Remdesivir in adults with severe COVID-19: a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, multicentre trial. Lancet. 2020. PMID: 32423584. Registry ID: NCT04257656. cards.headline: WHO Solidarity final (2022): in-hospital mortality 14.5% vs 15.6% (rate ratio 0.91) — a small effect in patients not yet ventilated, none in those already ventilated (rate ratio 1.13)
cards.summary: WHO Solidarity final (2022): in-hospital mortality 14.5% vs 15.6% (rate ratio 0.91) — a small effect in patients not yet ventilated, none in those already ventilated (rate ratio 1.13)
cards.type: Randomised open-label platform trial (WHO Solidarity Trial Consortium 2022, final results)
cards.people: 8,275 hospitalised adults with COVID-19 across 454 hospitals in 35 countries randomised to remdesivir (ten daily infusions unless discharged earlier; 4,146 analysed) or open control (4,129), all receiving local standard care; no placebos were used.
cards.result: Overall, 14.5% (602 of 4,146) assigned remdesivir died versus 15.6% (643 of 4,129) assigned control (mortality rate ratio 0.91, 95% CI 0.82–1.02; p=0.12). Among patients already ventilated, mortality was 42.1% vs 38.6% (rate ratio 1.13, 95% CI 0.89–1.42); among those not ventilated initially, 11.9% vs 13.5% (rate ratio 0.86, 95% CI 0.76–0.98; p=0.02), and progression to ventilation was 14.1% vs 15.7% (rate ratio 0.88, 95% CI 0.77–1.00). Allocation to remdesivir delayed discharge by about 1 day during the 10-day treatment period.
cards.watchOut: Open-label with no placebo, and discharge was delayed by the infusion schedule itself — the opposite direction from ACTT-1's recovery endpoint, which used a blinded placebo infusion. The mortality split by ventilation status is where the two trials can be reconciled: benefit, if any, sits before ventilation.
cards.source: WHO Solidarity Trial Consortium. Remdesivir and three other drugs for hospitalised patients with COVID-19: final results of the WHO Solidarity randomised trial and updated meta-analyses. Lancet. 2022. PMID: 35512728. randomised open-label platform trial (who solidarity trial consortium 2022, final results) 8,275 hospitalised adults with covid-19 across 454 hospitals in 35 countries randomised to remdesivir (ten daily infusions unless discharged earlier; 4,146 analysed) or open control (4,129), all receiving local standard care; no placebos were used. overall, 14.5% (602 of 4,146) assigned remdesivir died versus 15.6% (643 of 4,129) assigned control (mortality rate ratio 0.91, 95% ci 0.82–1.02; p=0.12). among patients already ventilated, mortality was 42.1% vs 38.6% (rate ratio 1.13, 95% ci 0.89–1.42); among those not ventilated initially, 11.9% vs 13.5% (rate ratio 0.86, 95% ci 0.76–0.98; p=0.02), and progression to ventilation was 14.1% vs 15.7% (rate ratio 0.88, 95% ci 0.77–1.00). allocation to remdesivir delayed discharge by about 1 day during the 10-day treatment period. open-label with no placebo, and discharge was delayed by the infusion schedule itself — the opposite direction from actt-1's recovery endpoint, which used a blinded placebo infusion. the mortality split by ventilation status is where the two trials can be reconciled: benefit, if any, sits before ventilation. who solidarity trial consortium. remdesivir and three other drugs for hospitalised patients with covid-19: final results of the who solidarity randomised trial and updated meta-analyses. lancet. 2022. pmid: 35512728. registry id: nct04315948 (isrctn 83971151), from the record. mesh: adenosine monophosphate/analogs & derivatives/therapeutic use · adult · alanine/analogs & derivatives/therapeutic use · antiviral agents/therapeutic use · humans · hydroxychloroquine/therapeutic use · interferon beta-1a/therapeutic use · lopinavir/therapeutic use · oxygen/administration & dosage · randomized controlled trials as topic · treatment outcome · world health organization · covid-19 drug treatment

cards.headline: Synthesis: three randomised trials — recovery faster in the largest blinded trial, mortality unproven everywhere, and no signal once ventilated
cards.summary: Synthesis: three randomised trials — recovery faster in the largest blinded trial, mortality unproven everywhere, and no signal once ventilated
cards.people: Three randomised trials of remdesivir in hospitalised COVID-19 totalling over 9,500 randomised patients in the remdesivir comparisons: ACTT-1 (double-blind, 1,062), Wang (double-blind, 237, severe disease), and WHO Solidarity final (open-label, 8,275).
cards.result: Time to recovery: median 10 vs 15 days in ACTT-1 (rate ratio 1.29, 95% CI 1.12–1.49); no significant improvement difference in Wang (hazard ratio 1.23, 95% CI 0.87–1.75). Mortality: 11.4% vs 15.2% at day 29 in ACTT-1 (hazard ratio 0.73, 95% CI 0.52–1.03); 14.5% vs 15.6% in-hospital in Solidarity (rate ratio 0.91, 95% CI 0.82–1.02), with rate ratio 0.86 in patients not ventilated initially and 1.13 in those already ventilated. PROPOSED SPLIT: benefit for recovery time in non-ventilated hospitalised patients; no demonstrated mortality benefit.
cards.watchOut: Era matters: all three trials ran in 2020–early 2021, largely before vaccination and later variants, and background care changed underneath them. The outpatient remdesivir question (PINETREE) is a different shelf (#2211) and is not duplicated here.
cards.source: Synthesis of Beigel JH et al. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2020 (PMID: 32445440); Wang Y et al. Lancet. 2020 (PMID: 32423584); WHO Solidarity Trial Consortium. Lancet. 2022 (PMID: 35512728).

shelves.title: Convalescent plasma in hospitalised COVID-19: 28-day mortality 24% versus 24% in RECOVERY's 11,558 patients — and no benefit in the critically ill or in CONCOR-1 either
shelves.question: In hospitalised adults with COVID-19, does high-titre convalescent plasma reduce mortality compared with usual care?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Antibodies, Viral · COVID-19/mortality/therapy · Female · Hospital Mortality · Humans · Immunization, Passive/methods/mortality · Length of Stay/statistics & numerical data · Male · Middle Aged · Pandemics · Respiration, Artificial/statistics & numerical data · SARS-CoV-2 · Treatment Outcome · United Kingdom/epidemiology · COVID-19 Serotherapy
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — three randomised trials agree. In RECOVERY, 28-day mortality was 24% in both groups (rate ratio 1.00, 95% CI 0.93–1.07; p=0.95), including in patients seronegative at randomisation, and discharge within 28 days was 66% vs 66%. In critically ill patients in REMAP-CAP, plasma met the prespecified futility criterion: median organ support-free days 0 vs 3, median-adjusted odds ratio 0.97 (95% credible interval 0.83–1.15), in-hospital mortality 37.3% vs 38.4%, and serious adverse events 3.0% vs 1.3%. In CONCOR-1, intubation or death by day 30 was 32.4% on plasma vs 28.0% on standard care (relative risk 1.16, 95% CI 0.94–1.43), with more serious adverse events on plasma (33.4% vs 26.4%; relative risk 1.27, 95% CI 1.02–1.57). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): high-titre convalescent plasma given after hospital admission does not improve survival or other clinical outcomes. The early outpatient plasma question is a different shelf (#2212) and is not duplicated here.

cards.headline: RECOVERY plasma: 28-day mortality 24% vs 24% (rate ratio 1.00, p=0.95) in 11,558 hospitalised patients — no subgroup, including the seronegative, benefited
cards.summary: RECOVERY plasma: 28-day mortality 24% vs 24% (rate ratio 1.00, p=0.95) in 11,558 hospitalised patients — no subgroup, including the seronegative, benefited
cards.type: Randomised open-label platform trial (RECOVERY Collaborative Group 2021)
cards.people: 11,558 adults admitted to 177 UK hospitals with COVID-19, randomised to usual care plus high-titre convalescent plasma (5,795) or usual care alone (5,763), between May 2020 and January 2021.
cards.result: There was no significant difference in 28-day mortality: 1,399 (24%) of 5,795 patients in the plasma group and 1,408 (24%) of 5,763 in the usual care group died (rate ratio 1.00, 95% CI 0.93–1.07; p=0.95). The rate ratio was similar in all prespecified subgroups, including patients without detectable SARS-CoV-2 antibodies at randomisation. Discharge from hospital within 28 days was 66% in both groups (rate ratio 0.99, 95% CI 0.94–1.03), and among those not ventilated at randomisation, progression to invasive mechanical ventilation or death was 29% vs 29% (rate ratio 0.99, 95% CI 0.93–1.05).
cards.watchOut: Open-label, but the primary endpoint is mortality and the confidence interval (0.93–1.07) is narrow enough to exclude any clinically useful survival benefit from plasma given at this stage of illness. The trial does not address plasma given within days of symptom onset in outpatients — that is shelf #2212's question.
cards.source: RECOVERY Collaborative Group. Convalescent plasma in patients admitted to hospital with COVID-19 (RECOVERY): a randomised controlled, open-label, platform trial. Lancet. 2021. PMID: 34000257. Registry ID: NCT04381936 (ISRCTN 50189673), from the record. cards.headline: REMAP-CAP plasma (Estcourt 2021): stopped for futility in the critically ill — organ support-free days median 0 vs 3, adjusted odds ratio 0.97, posterior probability of futility 99.4%
cards.summary: REMAP-CAP plasma (Estcourt 2021): stopped for futility in the critically ill — organ support-free days median 0 vs 3, adjusted odds ratio 0.97, posterior probability of futility 99.4%
cards.type: Randomised open-label platform trial domain (Estcourt 2021, REMAP-CAP immunoglobulin domain)
cards.people: 2,011 critically ill adults with COVID-19 at 129 sites in four countries, randomised to two units of high-titre ABO-compatible convalescent plasma within 48 hours (1,084) or no plasma (916); 1,990 completed the trial.
cards.result: The intervention was stopped after the prespecified futility criterion was met. Median organ support-free days were 0 (IQR −1 to 16) in the plasma group and 3 (IQR −1 to 16) in the no-plasma group; the median-adjusted odds ratio was 0.97 (95% credible interval 0.83–1.15) and the posterior probability of futility (odds ratio <1.2) was 99.4%. In-hospital mortality was 37.3% (401 of 1,075) vs 38.4% (347 of 904). Serious adverse events were reported in 3.0% of plasma participants and 1.3% of controls.
cards.watchOut: This is the sickest population — patients already receiving ICU organ support — so it closes the 'too late' end of the question rather than the early-treatment end. Bayesian futility at 99.4% is about as definitive a negative as platform trials produce.
cards.source: Estcourt LJ et al. Effect of Convalescent Plasma on Organ Support-Free Days in Critically Ill Patients With COVID-19: A Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA. 2021. PMID: 34606578. cards.headline: CONCOR-1 (Bégin 2021): intubation or death by day 30 in 32.4% on plasma vs 28.0% on standard care (relative risk 1.16) — stopped for futility, with more serious adverse events on plasma
cards.summary: CONCOR-1 (Bégin 2021): intubation or death by day 30 in 32.4% on plasma vs 28.0% on standard care (relative risk 1.16) — stopped for futility, with more serious adverse events on plasma
cards.people: 940 hospitalised adults with COVID-19 receiving oxygen within 12 days of respiratory symptom onset in Canada, the United States and Brazil, allocated 2:1 to 500 mL of convalescent plasma (614 in the intention-to-treat analysis) or standard care (307); the trial was terminated at 78% of planned enrolment after meeting futility criteria.
cards.result: Intubation or death occurred in 199 of 614 (32.4%) patients in the plasma arm and 86 of 307 (28.0%) in the standard care arm (relative risk 1.16, 95% CI 0.94–1.43; p=0.18). Patients in the plasma arm had more serious adverse events (33.4% vs 26.4%; relative risk 1.27, 95% CI 1.02–1.57; p=0.034). Exploratory analyses suggested the antibody content of the plasma modulated the effect, with unfavourable antibody profiles associated with worse outcomes.
cards.watchOut: The point estimate favours standard care, though its interval includes no effect; the antibody-profile analyses are exploratory and hypothesis-generating only. CONCOR-1's plasma was not uniformly high-titre, which is why it sits behind RECOVERY — where the plasma was high-titre and the answer was still null.
cards.source: Bégin P et al. Convalescent plasma for hospitalized patients with COVID-19: an open-label, randomized controlled trial. Nature Medicine. 2021. PMID: 34504336. Registry ID: NCT04348656. cards.headline: Synthesis: three trials, three populations, one answer — plasma after admission does not help
cards.summary: Synthesis: three trials, three populations, one answer — plasma after admission does not help
cards.people: Three randomised trials of convalescent plasma in hospitalised COVID-19: RECOVERY (11,558, high-titre, UK), REMAP-CAP (2,011, critically ill), and CONCOR-1 (940, oxygen-requiring, North and South America).
cards.result: Mortality and composite outcomes: RECOVERY 28-day mortality 24% vs 24% (rate ratio 1.00, 95% CI 0.93–1.07); REMAP-CAP in-hospital mortality 37.3% vs 38.4% with futility declared at 99.4% posterior probability; CONCOR-1 intubation or death 32.4% vs 28.0% (relative risk 1.16, 95% CI 0.94–1.43). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) for plasma given after hospital admission.
cards.watchOut: Timing is the honest caveat the trials themselves draw: all three gave plasma to patients already admitted, most well into their illness. Early high-titre plasma in outpatients is a separate, already-homed question (#2212) with a different answer, and nothing here should be read onto it.
cards.source: Synthesis of RECOVERY Collaborative Group. Lancet. 2021 (PMID: 34000257); Estcourt LJ et al. JAMA. 2021 (PMID: 34606578); Bégin P et al. Nature Medicine. 2021 (PMID: 34504336).

shelves.title: Casirivimab–imdevimab in hospitalised COVID-19: 28-day mortality 24% versus 30% in patients with no antibodies of their own — and no benefit in those who already had them
shelves.question: In hospitalised adults with COVID-19, does casirivimab–imdevimab reduce mortality in patients without their own antibodies compared with usual care?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Antibodies, Viral/blood · Antiviral Agents/adverse effects/therapeutic use · COVID-19/virology · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · Hospitalization · Humans · Infusions, Intravenous · Male · SARS-CoV-2/immunology · Treatment Outcome · COVID-19 Drug Treatment
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — confined to seronegative patients, in a single large open-label trial. In RECOVERY's primary efficacy population of patients without detectable anti-SARS-CoV-2 antibodies at randomisation, 24% (396 of 1,633) allocated casirivimab 4 g plus imdevimab 4 g died within 28 days versus 30% (452 of 1,520) on usual care (rate ratio 0.79, 95% CI 0.69–0.91; p=0.0009) — a 21% relative reduction in mortality with the absolute rates printed alongside. In all randomised patients regardless of antibody status, mortality was 19% vs 21% (rate ratio 0.94, 95% CI 0.86–1.02; p=0.14), and the effect differed significantly by serostatus (p for heterogeneity = 0.002). No deaths were attributed to the treatment and prespecified safety outcomes did not differ meaningfully. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): the antibody combination reduces mortality only in hospitalised patients who have not mounted their own antibody response. Single-trial shelf — flagged in the summary.

cards.headline: RECOVERY casirivimab–imdevimab: seronegative mortality 24% vs 30% (rate ratio 0.79, p=0.0009); overall population 19% vs 21% (rate ratio 0.94, p=0.14)
cards.summary: RECOVERY casirivimab–imdevimab: seronegative mortality 24% vs 30% (rate ratio 0.79, p=0.0009); overall population 19% vs 21% (rate ratio 0.94, p=0.14)
cards.type: Randomised open-label platform trial (RECOVERY Collaborative Group 2022)
cards.people: 9,785 patients aged at least 12 years admitted to 127 UK hospitals with clinically suspected or laboratory-confirmed COVID-19, randomised to usual care plus a single intravenous infusion of casirivimab 4 g and imdevimab 4 g (4,839) or usual care alone (4,946); 3,153 (32%) were seronegative at randomisation, 5,272 (54%) seropositive, and 1,360 (14%) of unknown status; 8% had received at least one vaccine dose.
cards.result: In the primary efficacy population of seronegative patients, 396 (24%) of 1,633 patients allocated casirivimab–imdevimab versus 452 (30%) of 1,520 allocated usual care died within 28 days (rate ratio 0.79, 95% CI 0.69–0.91; p=0.0009). In all randomised patients, mortality was 943 (19%) of 4,839 versus 1,029 (21%) of 4,946 (rate ratio 0.94, 95% CI 0.86–1.02; p=0.14). The proportional effect differed significantly between seropositive and seronegative patients (p for heterogeneity = 0.002). There were no deaths attributed to treatment and no meaningful differences in cause-specific mortality, cardiac arrhythmia, thrombosis, or major bleeding; serious adverse reactions believed related to treatment were reported in seven participants (<1%).
cards.watchOut: Single-trial shelf, and the benefit lives entirely in a prespecified subgroup defined by a baseline antibody test — credible because the subgroup was the primary efficacy population and the heterogeneity test is strong (p=0.002), but it means the treatment only makes sense where serostatus is known. The trial ran September 2020 to May 2021, against pre-Omicron variants; the record itself cannot speak to later-variant susceptibility.
cards.source: RECOVERY Collaborative Group. Casirivimab and imdevimab in patients admitted to hospital with COVID-19 (RECOVERY): a randomised, controlled, open-label, platform trial. Lancet. 2022. PMID: 35151397. Registry ID: NCT04381936 (ISRCTN 50189673), from the record. cards.summary: Synthesis: a real mortality benefit with a strict condition attached — the patient must not already have antibodies

shelves.title: Higher-dose dexamethasone in COVID-19: mortality rose from 12% to 19% in RECOVERY's patients on simple oxygen — while 12 mg versus 6 mg in sicker patients in COVID STEROID 2 was a non-significant trend the other way
shelves.question: In adults with hospitalised COVID-19 on oxygen, does higher-dose dexamethasone improve survival compared with usual-dose corticosteroid care?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Humans · Male · Female · COVID-19 · SARS-CoV-2 · Hospitals · Oxygen · Hypoxia/etiology · Adrenal Cortex Hormones/therapeutic use · Dexamethasone/therapeutic use · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: SPLIT — by how sick the patient is. In RECOVERY's comparison in patients with hypoxia receiving no oxygen or simple oxygen only, higher-dose corticosteroids (dexamethasone 20 mg daily for 5 days, then 10 mg for 5 days) increased 28-day mortality: 19% (123 of 659) versus 12% (75 of 613) on usual care, in which 87% received low-dose corticosteroids (rate ratio 1.59, 95% CI 1.20–2.10; p=0.0012) — recruitment to this group was stopped early on safety grounds. Non-COVID pneumonia (10% vs 6%) and hyperglycaemia requiring more insulin (22% vs 14%) were also more frequent. In COVID STEROID 2, in patients with severe hypoxemia, dexamethasone 12 mg versus 6 mg daily did not significantly change days alive without life support at 28 days (median 22.0 vs 20.5 days; adjusted mean difference 1.3 days, 95% CI 0–2.6; p=0.07), with 28-day mortality of 27.1% vs 32.3% (adjusted relative risk 0.86, 99% CI 0.68–1.08). PROPOSED SPLIT: higher-dose corticosteroids harm patients on simple oxygen; in severe hypoxemia the question remains open, with a non-significant trend favouring 12 mg that the trial may have been underpowered to settle.

cards.headline: RECOVERY higher dose: 28-day mortality 19% vs 12% (rate ratio 1.59, p=0.0012) in patients on simple oxygen — stopped early for safety, with more non-COVID pneumonia and hyperglycaemia
cards.summary: RECOVERY higher dose: 28-day mortality 19% vs 12% (rate ratio 1.59, p=0.0012) in patients on simple oxygen — stopped early for safety, with more non-COVID pneumonia and hyperglycaemia
cards.type: Randomised open-label platform trial (RECOVERY Collaborative Group 2023)
cards.people: 1,272 adults hospitalised with COVID-19 and clinical hypoxia (receiving oxygen, or saturation <92% on room air) who were receiving no oxygen (1%) or simple oxygen only (99%), at sites in Asia (59%), the UK (40%) and Africa (1%), randomised to higher-dose corticosteroids (dexamethasone 20 mg once daily for 5 days, then 10 mg once daily for 5 days or until discharge; 659) or usual care (613, of whom 87% received low-dose corticosteroids during follow-up), between May 2021 and May 2022.
cards.result: Overall, 123 (19%) of 659 patients allocated higher-dose corticosteroids versus 75 (12%) of 613 allocated usual care died within 28 days (rate ratio 1.59, 95% CI 1.20–2.10; p=0.0012). There was also an excess of pneumonia reported to be due to non-COVID infection (64 cases [10%] vs 37 [6%]; absolute difference 3.7%, 95% CI 0.7–6.6) and an increase in hyperglycaemia requiring increased insulin dose (142 [22%] vs 87 [14%]; absolute difference 7.4%, 95% CI 3.2–11.5). On May 11, 2022, the independent data monitoring committee recommended stopping recruitment of patients receiving no oxygen or simple oxygen only because of these safety concerns.
cards.watchOut: The comparator was usual care rather than a fixed 6 mg dexamethasone arm — but 87% of the usual-care group received low-dose corticosteroids, so this reads in practice as higher dose versus standard dose. The reported population is only the no-oxygen/simple-oxygen stratum; RECOVERY's assessment in ventilated patients was still ongoing at publication, so this card must not be generalised to them.

cards.headline: Munch 2021 (COVID STEROID 2): 12 mg vs 6 mg dexamethasone — days alive without life support 22.0 vs 20.5 (adjusted mean difference 1.3 days, p=0.07); 28-day mortality 27.1% vs 32.3% (adjusted relative risk 0.86, not significant)
cards.summary: Munch 2021 (COVID STEROID 2): 12 mg vs 6 mg dexamethasone — days alive without life support 22.0 vs 20.5 (adjusted mean difference 1.3 days, p=0.07); 28-day mortality 27.1% vs 32.3% (adjusted relative risk 0.86, not significant)
cards.people: 1,000 randomised adults with COVID-19 and severe hypoxemia (982 included in the analysis; median age 65 years, 31% women), randomised to dexamethasone 12 mg daily or 6 mg daily; primary outcome data were available for 971 patients (491 on 12 mg, 480 on 6 mg).
cards.result: The median number of days alive without life support at 28 days was 22.0 days (IQR 6.0–28.0) in the 12 mg group and 20.5 days (IQR 4.0–28.0) in the 6 mg group (adjusted mean difference 1.3 days, 95% CI 0–2.6; p=0.07). Mortality at 28 days was 27.1% vs 32.3% (adjusted relative risk 0.86, 99% CI 0.68–1.08) and at 90 days 32.0% vs 37.7% (adjusted relative risk 0.87, 99% CI 0.70–1.07). Serious adverse reactions, including septic shock and invasive fungal infections, occurred in 11.3% vs 13.4% (adjusted relative risk 0.83, 99% CI 0.54–1.29).
cards.watchOut: Every point estimate favours 12 mg and none is significant — the authors themselves note the trial may have been underpowered. This is a genuinely different population from RECOVERY's simple-oxygen stratum (severe hypoxemia, many on life support), which is why the shelf splits rather than averaging the two trials into one verdict.

cards.headline: Synthesis: dose escalation helps no one on simple oxygen and harms them; the severe-hypoxemia question is unresolved
cards.summary: Synthesis: dose escalation helps no one on simple oxygen and harms them; the severe-hypoxemia question is unresolved
cards.people: Two randomised trials of higher- versus usual-dose corticosteroids in hospitalised COVID-19: RECOVERY higher-dose comparison (1,272 patients on no/simple oxygen) and COVID STEROID 2 (1,000 randomised patients with severe hypoxemia, 12 mg vs 6 mg dexamethasone).
cards.result: RECOVERY (simple oxygen): 28-day mortality 19% vs 12% (rate ratio 1.59, 95% CI 1.20–2.10), stopped early for safety. COVID STEROID 2 (severe hypoxemia): days alive without life support, adjusted mean difference 1.3 days (95% CI 0–2.6; p=0.07); 28-day mortality 27.1% vs 32.3% (adjusted relative risk 0.86, 99% CI 0.68–1.08). PROPOSED SPLIT by severity, as the two trials enrolled different points on the oxygen spectrum. The usual-dose dexamethasone question itself is already homed at #185 and is not duplicated here.
cards.watchOut: Do not merge these trials: the doses (20 mg tapering vs 12 mg), comparators (usual care vs fixed 6 mg), and populations (simple oxygen vs severe hypoxemia) all differ, and the harm signal comes from the largest and least sick population. Tier C is set for every shelf in this band.

shelves.title: Corticosteroids in dengue do not prevent shock or save lives: a 225-patient placebo trial found no clinical benefit, and a Cochrane review of 8 trials (948 patients) found no effect on death
shelves.question: In patients with dengue, do corticosteroids improve outcomes in early dengue or dengue shock compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Adolescent · Adrenal Cortex Hormones/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Anti-Inflammatory Agents/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Asian People · Child · Child, Preschool · Dengue/drug therapy/pathology/virology · Female · Humans · Male · Placebos/administration & dosage · Single-Blind Method · Treatment Outcome · Viral Load · Viremia · Young Adult
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — corticosteroids are biologically plausible in dengue, where complications are thought to be immunologically mediated, and the trials say they do not work. In Vietnam (Tam DT et al., PMID: 22865871), 225 patients aged 5–20 years admitted within 72 hours of fever were randomised to low-dose (0.5 mg/kg) or high-dose (2 mg/kg) oral prednisolone for 3 days or placebo: all patients recovered fully, and apart from a trend toward hyperglycaemia in steroid recipients there was no association between treatment and any predefined clinical, haematological or virological endpoint, and no reduction in shock or other complications. The Cochrane review (Zhang F et al., PMID: 24984082) pooled eight trials enrolling 948 participants: in dengue shock, four trials in 284 children detected no effect on death, transfusion, pulmonary haemorrhage, convulsions or hospital stay; in early dengue, four trials in 664 patients found no evidence of an effect on mortality or on severe complications such as shock. The review's honest caveat is that the shock trials are old and small, so a modest effect in shock is not excluded — but nothing in the record supports giving steroids. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): corticosteroids show no benefit in early dengue or dengue shock in the randomised evidence.

cards.headline: Tam 2012: early prednisolone in 225 young dengue patients — no effect on viremia, shock or any predefined endpoint; a trend to hyperglycaemia was the only signal
cards.summary: Tam 2012: early prednisolone in 225 young dengue patients — no effect on viremia, shock or any predefined endpoint; a trend to hyperglycaemia was the only signal
cards.people: 225 Vietnamese patients aged 5–20 years admitted with dengue and fever for 72 hours or less, randomised to oral prednisolone 0.5 mg/kg or 2 mg/kg daily for 3 days or placebo, enrolled August 2009 to January 2011.
cards.result: All patients recovered fully and adverse events were infrequent. Aside from a trend toward hyperglycaemia in the steroid recipients, there was no association between treatment allocation and any predefined clinical, haematological or virological endpoint, including the viremia area-under-the-curve and time to negative viremia; there was no reduction in the development of shock or other recognised complications of dengue.
cards.watchOut: The trial was designed to detect harm (prolonged viremia) and was not powered for efficacy endpoints such as shock, which is uncommon in patients enrolled this early — a null here rules out a large early benefit, not a small one. It says nothing directly about steroids given after shock has developed.
cards.source: Tam DT et al. Effects of short-course oral corticosteroid therapy in early dengue infection in Vietnamese patients: a randomized, placebo-controlled trial. Clinical Infectious Diseases. 2012. PMID: 22865871. Registry ID: ISRCTN39575233. cards.headline: Zhang 2014 (Cochrane): 8 trials, 948 participants — no detected effect on death in dengue shock (284 children) or on mortality and severe complications in early dengue (664 patients)
cards.summary: Zhang 2014 (Cochrane): 8 trials, 948 participants — no detected effect on death in dengue shock (284 children) or on mortality and severe complications in early dengue (664 patients)
cards.people: Eight randomised or quasi-randomised trials enrolling 948 participants: four trials in children under 15 years with dengue-related shock in Southeast Asian hospitals, and four trials in 664 children and adults with early dengue in Colombia, India, Sri Lanka and Vietnam.
cards.result: In dengue shock, the trials did not detect an effect of intravenous corticosteroids on death (four trials, 284 participants, very low quality evidence), need for blood transfusion (two trials, 89 participants), pulmonary haemorrhage (one trial, 63 participants), convulsions (one trial, 63 participants) or duration of hospitalisation (one trial, 63 participants). In early dengue, there was no evidence of an effect on mortality (four trials, 664 participants, low quality evidence) or on shock (two trials, 286 participants), severe bleeding (two trials, 425 participants), severe thrombocytopaenia (one trial, 225 participants), ascites (one trial, 178 participants) or ICU admission (two trials, 286 participants). The reviewers concluded the evidence is inconclusive and of low to very low quality.
cards.watchOut: The shock trials are more than 20 years old with methodological limitations, and event rates are small — 'no detected effect' in shock is weaker than the early-dengue null. The Tam 2012 trial carded separately on this shelf is one of the review's included early-dengue trials, so the two cards are not fully independent evidence.

shelves.title: Perioperative ketamine for chronic postsurgical pain: the 17-trial meta-analysis is null overall and both carded trials agree — only an intravenous-only subgroup analysis turns positive
shelves.question: In adults having surgery, does perioperative ketamine reduce the incidence of chronic postsurgical pain at 3–12 months compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Anesthetics, Dissociative/therapeutic use · Chronic Pain/prevention & control · Humans · Ketamine/therapeutic use · Postoperative Pain/prevention & control
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — overall, perioperative ketamine has not been shown to prevent chronic postsurgical pain. The meta-analysis of 17 randomised trials (McNicol ED et al., PMID: 25060512) found the overall risk of developing persistent post-surgical pain was not significantly reduced at any time point, and pain-severity scores did not reach significance either; only a sensitivity analysis restricted to intravenous ketamine showed significant reductions at 3 months (P = 0.01) and 6 months (P = 0.04). The two individually carded trials agree with the null headline: after thoracotomy (Dualé C et al., PMID: 18783971), neuropathic pain scores at 6 weeks and 4 months were similar between ketamine and placebo, and after amputation (Hayes C et al., PMID: 15264726) phantom pain at 6 months occurred in 47% on ketamine versus 71% on control (P = 0.28 — not significant, in a trial powered only for a large effect). This shelf asks the chronic-pain question only; intraoperative ketamine for delirium and acute pain in older adults is homed at live shelf #1128 (PODCAST). PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (the treatment made no difference): an intravenous-only subgroup signal survives inside an otherwise null record, which is hypothesis-generating, not a basis for routine use.

cards.headline: McNicol 2014: across 17 randomised trials, ketamine did not significantly reduce persistent post-surgical pain overall — significance appeared only in the intravenous-only sensitivity analysis at 3 and 6 months
cards.summary: McNicol 2014: across 17 randomised trials, ketamine did not significantly reduce persistent post-surgical pain overall — significance appeared only in the intravenous-only sensitivity analysis at 3 and 6 months
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials (McNicol 2014)
cards.people: 17 randomised controlled trials in adults in which ketamine was administered perioperatively by any route, identified from CENTRAL, MEDLINE and EMBASE to December 2012; most studies gave ketamine intravenously.
cards.result: The overall risk of developing persistent post-surgical pain was not significantly reduced at any time point in the ketamine group versus placebo, nor did comparisons of pain-severity scores reach statistical significance. A sensitivity analysis of exclusively intravenous ketamine studies demonstrated statistically significant reductions in the risk of developing persistent pain at 3 months (P = 0.01) and 6 months (P = 0.04). Adverse event rates were similar between ketamine and placebo groups.
cards.watchOut: The record's own abstract prints no pooled risk ratio — only significance statements — so no effect size is quoted here. Timing and dosing of ketamine varied widely between the 17 studies, and the positive finding is a subgroup sensitivity analysis inside an overall null meta-analysis: exactly the pattern that most often fails to replicate.
cards.source: McNicol ED et al. A systematic review and meta-analysis of ketamine for the prevention of persistent post-surgical pain. Acta anaesthesiologica Scandinavica. 2014. PMID: 25060512. cards.headline: Dualé 2009 (thoracotomy): ketamine improved immediate postoperative pain but neuropathic pain at 6 weeks and 4 months was the same as placebo — NPSI 1.25 versus 1 at 6 weeks
cards.summary: Dualé 2009 (thoracotomy): ketamine improved immediate postoperative pain but neuropathic pain at 6 weeks and 4 months was the same as placebo — NPSI 1.25 versus 1 at 6 weeks
cards.people: 86 patients scheduled for thoracotomy under standardised general anaesthesia, randomised to ketamine (1 mg/kg at induction, 1 mg/kg/h during surgery, then 1 mg/kg over 24 hours; n = 42) or normal saline (n = 44), with standardised postoperative analgesia; 73 patients were followed up to 4 months.
cards.result: Ketamine improved immediate postoperative pain, but the groups were similar in neuropathic pain and analgesic intake at 6 weeks (Neuropathic Pain Symptom Inventory score: ketamine 1.25 [0–4.125]; placebo 1 [0–4]) and at 4 months after surgery. The authors conclude that ketamine given as a 24-hour perioperative regimen failed to prevent chronic neuropathic pain after thoracotomy.
cards.watchOut: Thoracotomy is one of the highest-risk operations for chronic postsurgical pain, so a null here is informative — but the trial tested one specific 24-hour regimen, and 13 of 86 patients were not followed up, so a modest preventive effect of some other regimen is not excluded.
cards.source: Dualé C et al. Perioperative ketamine does not prevent chronic pain after thoracotomy. European journal of pain (London, England). 2009. PMID: 18783971. cards.headline: Hayes 2004 (amputation): phantom pain at 6 months in 47% on ketamine versus 71% on control — a 24-point gap that was not significant (P = 0.28) in a 45-patient trial
cards.summary: Hayes 2004 (amputation): phantom pain at 6 months in 47% on ketamine versus 71% on control — a 24-point gap that was not significant (P = 0.28) in a 45-patient trial
cards.people: 45 patients undergoing above- or below-knee amputation under standardised general anaesthesia, randomised to ketamine 0.5 mg/kg as a pre-induction bolus followed by an infusion of 0.5 mg/kg/h for 72 hours postoperatively, or placebo bolus and saline infusion; both groups received patient-controlled intravenous morphine.
cards.result: There was no significant difference between groups in the surface area of stump allodynia or in morphine consumption. At 6 months, the incidence of phantom pain was 47% in the ketamine group and 71% in the control group (P = 0.28); the incidence of stump pain at 6 months was 47% versus 35% (P = 0.72). There were no significant between-group differences in pain severity throughout the study, and stump pain at day 3 was significantly more frequent in the ketamine group.
cards.watchOut: The trial was powered to find a large treatment effect, so the 47% versus 71% phantom-pain gap is compatible with anything from a real moderate benefit to chance — it cannot be quoted as evidence of benefit, and the day-3 stump-pain increase in the ketamine group points the other way.
cards.source: Hayes C et al. Perioperative intravenous ketamine infusion for the prevention of persistent post-amputation pain: a randomized, controlled trial. Anaesthesia and intensive care. 2004. PMID: 15264726. cards.headline: Synthesis: two null trials and a null overall meta-analysis, with one intravenous subgroup signal — not a preventive treatment yet
cards.summary: Synthesis: two null trials and a null overall meta-analysis, with one intravenous subgroup signal — not a preventive treatment yet
cards.people: 17 randomised trials pooled (McNicol 2014), read with a 86-patient thoracotomy trial and a 45-patient amputation trial, follow-up to 4–6 months.
cards.result: Overall persistent-pain risk: not significantly reduced at any time point (McNicol 2014); intravenous-only sensitivity analysis significant at 3 months (P = 0.01) and 6 months (P = 0.04). Thoracotomy neuropathic pain scores: no difference at 6 weeks or 4 months. Amputation phantom pain at 6 months: 47% versus 71% (P = 0.28). PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (the treatment made no difference), Tier C: the honest headline is the null; the intravenous subgroup is a reason to run a large confirmatory trial, not to adopt the practice.
cards.watchOut: Acute-pain and delirium effects of intraoperative ketamine are different questions (homed at live shelf #1128 for older adults having major surgery) and are not evidence for or against the chronic-pain claim made here.

shelves.title: Bringing down a fever in adults: fever medicines lower temperature (0.38 °C on average in sepsis) but do not improve survival — mortality relative risk 0.93 (95% CI 0.77–1.13) across the randomised trials; the big ICU paracetamol trial (HEAT) lives on Shelf #3160
shelves.question: How do I bring down a fever (in adults)? In febrile adults — the trial evidence is almost entirely in critically ill patients with infection — do paracetamol (acetaminophen), ibuprofen or physical cooling improve survival and other patient-important outcomes, or only the thermometer reading?
shelves.mesh: Body Temperature/drug effects · Critical Illness/mortality · Cross Infection/epidemiology · Hospital Mortality · Humans · Intensive Care Units/statistics & numerical data · Morgue · Observational Studies as Topic · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Sepsis/drug therapy · Sepsis/epidemiology · Sepsis/mortality
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) for outcomes beyond the thermometer. Fever can certainly be lowered: across the randomised trials in Drewry 2017's meta-analysis, antipyretic therapy reduced body temperature by 0.38 °C (95% CI −0.63 to −0.13) — but 28-day/hospital mortality was not improved (relative risk 0.93, 95% CI 0.77–1.13; 8 randomised studies, 1,507 patients), nor were shock reversal (RR 1.13, 0.68–1.90) or nosocomial infection (RR 1.13, 0.61–2.09). The largest single drug trial, Bernard 1997 (455 septic patients), found intravenous ibuprofen lowered temperature, heart rate and oxygen consumption with no extra renal or bleeding harm, yet 30-day mortality was 37% versus 40% on placebo — not significant. Physical cooling has the one positive signal: Schortgen 2012 (200 patients with septic shock) found lower day-14 mortality with external cooling (19% versus 34%), but the trial's primary endpoint — vasopressor reduction at 48 hours — was not met (72% versus 61%), so the mortality finding is hypothesis-generating, not settled. The landmark ICU paracetamol trial, HEAT, is homed on Shelf #3160 ('Treating fever with acetaminophen in infected ICU patients: HEAT's 700 patients gained no ICU-free days (23 vs 22), mortality 15.9% vs 16.6% at 90 days') and is not re-carded here. Almost all of this evidence is in critically ill patients with sepsis; there are no comparable outcome trials for ordinary fever at home, where the rational target is comfort rather than a number.

cards.headline: Drewry 2017 (meta-analysis in critically ill septic adults): antipyretics cut temperature by 0.38 °C but not mortality — randomised trials RR 0.93 (95% CI 0.77–1.13); shock reversal RR 1.13; nosocomial infection RR 1.13
cards.summary: Drewry 2017 (meta-analysis in critically ill septic adults): antipyretics cut temperature by 0.38 °C but not mortality — randomised trials RR 0.93 (95% CI 0.77–1.13); shock reversal RR 1.13; nosocomial infection RR 1.13
cards.people: Critically ill adults with sepsis: 8 randomised studies (1,507 patients) and 8 observational studies (17,432 patients) of antipyretic therapy (drugs and/or cooling), excluding paediatric patients, neurologic injury and healthy volunteers.
cards.result: Antipyretic therapy did not reduce 28-day/hospital mortality in the randomised studies (relative risk 0.93, 95% CI 0.77–1.13; I²=0.0%) or in the observational studies (odds ratio 0.90, 0.54–1.51; I²=76.1%). Shock reversal (RR 1.13, 0.68–1.90) and acquisition of nosocomial infections (RR 1.13, 0.61–2.09) were also unchanged. Antipyretic therapy did decrease body temperature (mean difference −0.38 °C, −0.63 to −0.13; I²=84.0%), but did not change heart rate or minute ventilation. The authors conclude antipyretic treatment does not significantly improve mortality in sepsis.
cards.watchOut: The randomised pool is 1,507 patients across 8 studies with different drugs, doses and cooling methods mixed together (temperature I²=84% shows how heterogeneous the temperature effect is); the confidence interval for mortality (0.77–1.13) cannot exclude a modest benefit or modest harm. This is sepsis in intensive care — it does not directly answer what to do about a feverish cold at home.
cards.source: Drewry AM, Ablordeppey EA, Murray ET, Stoll CRT, Izadi SR, Dalton CM, Hardi AC, Fowler SA, Fuller BM, Colditz GA. Antipyretic Therapy in Critically Ill Septic Patients: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Critical Care Medicine. 2017. PMID: 28221185. Registry ID: none in the record (meta-analysis). cards.headline: Bernard 1997 (455 patients with sepsis, double-blind): intravenous ibuprofen lowered temperature, heart rate and oxygen consumption — 30-day mortality 37% versus 40% on placebo, not significant; no extra renal dysfunction or gastrointestinal bleeding
cards.summary: Bernard 1997 (455 patients with sepsis, double-blind): intravenous ibuprofen lowered temperature, heart rate and oxygen consumption — 30-day mortality 37% versus 40% on placebo, not significant; no extra renal dysfunction or gastrointestinal bleeding
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, multicentre trial (Bernard 1997, Ibuprofen in Sepsis Study Group)
cards.people: 455 patients with sepsis — defined as fever, tachycardia, tachypnoea and acute failure of at least one organ system — enrolled at North American centres between October 1989 and March 1995, given intravenous ibuprofen (10 mg per kilogram, maximum 800 mg, every 6 hours for 8 doses) or placebo.
cards.result: In the ibuprofen group, but not the placebo group, there were significant declines in urinary prostacyclin and thromboxane levels, temperature, heart rate, oxygen consumption and lactic acidosis. With ibuprofen there was no increased incidence of renal dysfunction, gastrointestinal bleeding or other adverse events. However, ibuprofen did not reduce the incidence or duration of shock or of the acute respiratory distress syndrome, and did not significantly improve survival at 30 days (mortality 37% with ibuprofen versus 40% with placebo).
cards.watchOut: A 1990s trial of intravenous ibuprofen given as an anti-inflammatory sepsis therapy, not as ordinary fever relief — its dose and route are not the tablets used at home, and sepsis care has changed since 1995. Its reassurance on kidney and bleeding harm applies to 8 doses over 2 days in monitored patients, not to prolonged self-medication.
cards.source: Bernard GR, Wheeler AP, Russell JA, Schein R, Summer WR, Steinberg KP, Fulkerson WJ, Wright PE, Christman BW, Dupont WD, Higgins SB, Swindell BB; The Ibuprofen in Sepsis Study Group. The effects of ibuprofen on the physiology and survival of patients with sepsis. New England Journal of Medicine. 1997. PMID: 9070471. Registry ID: none in the record (pre-registration-era trial). cards.headline: Schortgen 2012 (200 patients with septic shock): external cooling to normothermia — day-14 mortality 19% versus 34% (absolute difference −16%), but the trial's primary endpoint at 48 hours was not met (72% versus 61%)
cards.summary: Schortgen 2012 (200 patients with septic shock): external cooling to normothermia — day-14 mortality 19% versus 34% (absolute difference −16%), but the trial's primary endpoint at 48 hours was not met (72% versus 61%)
cards.type: Multicentre randomised controlled trial of physical cooling (Schortgen 2012)
cards.people: 200 febrile adults with septic shock requiring vasopressors, mechanical ventilation and sedation, in French intensive care units: external cooling to achieve normothermia (36.5–37 °C) for 48 hours (n=101) versus no external cooling (n=99), with vasopressors tapered to the same blood-pressure target in both groups.
cards.result: Body temperature after 2 hours was significantly lower with cooling (36.8 °C, SD 0.7, versus 38.4 °C, SD 1.1; P<0.01). A 50% vasopressor dose decrease was significantly more common with cooling at 12 hours (54% versus 20%; absolute difference 34%, 95% CI −46 to −21; P<0.001) but not at 48 hours (72% versus 61%; absolute difference 11%, CI −23 to 2) — the primary endpoint. Shock reversal during the ICU stay was more common with cooling (86% versus 73%; absolute difference 13%, CI 2 to 25; P=0.021). Day-14 mortality was significantly lower in the cooling group (19% versus 34%; absolute difference −16%, CI −28 to −4; P=0.013). The authors describe fever control by external cooling as safe in this setting.
cards.watchOut: The mortality result is a secondary outcome in a 200-patient trial whose pre-specified primary endpoint was not met — exactly the situation where a striking secondary finding most needs independent confirmation before it changes practice. These were sedated, ventilated patients in septic shock cooled with devices; nothing here tests tepid sponging or cold packs for an ordinary fever at home.
cards.source: Schortgen F, Clabault K, Katsahian S, Devaquet J, Mercat A, Deye N, Dellamonica J, Bouadma L, Cook F, Beji O, Brun-Buisson C, Lemaire F, Brochard L. cards.headline: Synthesis: the thermometer always moves; survival does not — treat fever for comfort, and see Shelf #3160 for the HEAT trial
cards.summary: Synthesis: the thermometer always moves; survival does not — treat fever for comfort, and see Shelf #3160 for the HEAT trial
cards.people: Febrile adults, with the direct evidence drawn from critically ill adults with sepsis or septic shock in intensive care.
cards.result: Pooled randomised evidence (Drewry 2017) shows antipyretics lower temperature by about 0.4 °C with no improvement in mortality (RR 0.93, CI 0.77–1.13), shock reversal or new infections. The largest drug trial (Bernard 1997) matches: physiology improved, survival did not (37% versus 40%). The single positive patient-important signal — external cooling and day-14 mortality (19% versus 34%, Schortgen 2012) — comes from a trial that missed its primary endpoint and awaits confirmation. The HEAT trial of intravenous paracetamol in ICU fever (700 patients; no gain in ICU-free days, 23 versus 22; 90-day mortality 15.9% versus 16.6%) is homed on Shelf #3160 and points the same way.
cards.watchOut: There are no outcome trials of antipyretics for ordinary, non-critical fever in adults — the home question is answered by extrapolation from ICU sepsis, where if anything the stakes of fever are higher. Comfort, hydration and treating the underlying cause remain the rational goals; a normal temperature is not itself a proven route to a better outcome.
cards.source: Synthesis of Drewry AM et al. Critical Care Medicine. 2017 (PMID: 28221185); Bernard GR et al. New England Journal of Medicine. 1997 (PMID: 9070471); Schortgen F et al. American Journal of Respiratory and Critical Care Medicine. 2012 (PMID: 22366046). Cross-reference: HEAT trial, Shelf #3160.

shelves.title: Can a UTI go away on its own? Often, yes — 28% symptom-free at one week on placebo, up to 42% improved by 9 days — but most women are still symptomatic without antibiotics, and one placebo patient developed pyelonephritis
shelves.question: "Can a UTI go away on its own?" In a non-pregnant woman with uncomplicated cystitis (burning, frequency, urgency, no fever or flank pain), how often do symptoms and infection clear without antibiotics, how long does that take, and what is risked by waiting?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Amdinocillin Pivoxil/administration & dosage · Amdinocillin Pivoxil/therapeutic use · Anti-Bacterial Agents/administration & dosage · Anti-Bacterial Agents/therapeutic use · Bacteria/drug effects · Bacteria/isolation & purification · Bacterial Infections/drug therapy · Bacterial Infections/microbiology · Bacterial Infections/physiopathology · Bacteriuria/microbiology · Colony Count, Microbial · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Middle Aged · Prospective Studies · Urinary Tract Infections/drug therapy · Urinary Tract Infections/microbiology · Urinary Tract Infections/physiopathology · Urine/microbiology
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) for the honest answer 'often, yes — but slower, and not always'. The largest placebo dataset (Ferry 2004, PMID: 15198188; 1,143 women randomised, 288 in the placebo arm) found spontaneous symptom cure in 28% after the first week and 37% with neither symptoms nor bacteriuria at 5–7 weeks; the adjusted spontaneous cure of both symptoms and bacteriuria at study end was 24%. The natural-history systematic review (Hoffmann 2020, PMID: 32958533; 3 trials, 346 placebo participants) found the proportion symptom-free or improved rising to 42% over the first 9 days and standing at 36% by 6 weeks — but up to 39% had failed to improve by 6 weeks, and pyelonephritis occurred in one placebo participant. The one small placebo-controlled trial with a direct comparison (Christiaens 2002, PMID: 12236276; 78 women) shows what antibiotics add: symptomatic improvement or cure by day 7 was 30/34 on nitrofurantoin versus 17/33 on placebo (about 88% versus 52%; NNT 2.7), and bacteriological cure by day 3 was 21/26 versus 5/25 (NNT 1.6) — so roughly half of placebo patients were better by a week anyway, and antibiotics roughly doubled the chance and sped it up. The delayed-antibiotic trial (Little 2010, PMID: 20139214; 309 women) found no significant difference in symptom duration or severity between immediate antibiotics and waiting at least 48 hours, while delayed prescribing cut antibiotic use (77% versus 97% still took them) at the cost of 37% longer symptoms among those who waited and then consulted. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) for the strategy of watchful waiting with a safety net in uncomplicated cystitis: the natural history is genuinely favourable for a substantial minority, but the majority are still symptomatic at a week without treatment, a small pyelonephritis risk exists, and all of this evidence is in non-pregnant women with uncomplicated lower-tract symptoms — not men, not pregnancy, not fever or flank pain. The ibuprofen-first strategy trial is homed on Shelf #2489 and is not re-carded here.

cards.headline: Ferry 2004 (placebo arm, 1,143 women randomised): on placebo, 28% were symptom-free after one week and 37% had neither symptoms nor bacteriuria at 5–7 weeks; adjusted spontaneous cure of both was 24%
cards.summary: Ferry 2004 (placebo arm, 1,143 women randomised): on placebo, 28% were symptom-free after one week and 37% had neither symptoms nor bacteriuria at 5–7 weeks; adjusted spontaneous cure of both was 24%
cards.type: Randomised placebo-controlled trial — placebo-arm natural history (Ferry 2004)
cards.people: Prospective multicentre randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial at 18 primary healthcare centres in Sweden: 1,143 women aged 18 years and over with symptoms suggestive of urinary tract infection were randomised to pivmecillinam 200 mg twice daily for 7 days, 200 mg three times daily for 7 days, 400 mg twice daily for 3 days, or placebo for 7 days. This card reports the placebo group (n=288), of whom 39% dropped out after the first follow-up visit; clinical and bacteriological outcomes were followed to 5–7 weeks, with end-of-study spontaneous cure adjusted for the dropouts.
cards.result: In the placebo group, the rate of spontaneous cure of symptoms was 28% after the first week of treatment. At the last follow-up, 37% of placebo patients had neither symptoms nor bacteriuria; the estimated proportion with spontaneous cure of both symptoms and bacteriuria at the end of the study, adjusted for dropouts, was 24%. The authors concluded that the high number of dropouts in the placebo group was the major drawback of the study, but that the rate of spontaneous cure indicated most women with symptoms of urinary tract infection mainly need pain relief — while also concluding that it is difficult to predict which patients will benefit from antibiotic treatment and which will not.
cards.watchOut: The 39% placebo-arm dropout is not a footnote: women who stayed in a placebo study for seven weeks are a selected group, and the 24% adjusted figure is the authors' attempt to correct for exactly that. 'Symptoms cured' (28% at one week) and 'symptoms and bacteria both cleared' (24–37%) are different endpoints — symptoms settle faster and more often than bacteriuria does. And the population is women with uncomplicated lower-tract symptoms in primary care; nothing here describes men, pregnancy, diabetes with complications, catheter users, or anyone with fever or flank pain.
cards.source: Ferry SA, Holm SE, Stenlund H, Lundholm R, Monsen TJ. The natural course of uncomplicated lower urinary tract infection in women illustrated by a randomized placebo controlled study. Scandinavian Journal of Infectious Diseases. 2004. PMID: 15198188. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Christiaens 2002 (nitrofurantoin vs placebo, 78 women): by day 7, symptoms had improved or cleared in 30/34 on antibiotic versus 17/33 on placebo (NNT 2.7) — so about half the placebo group got better on its own, and antibiotics roughly doubled the chance
cards.summary: Christiaens 2002 (nitrofurantoin vs placebo, 78 women): by day 7, symptoms had improved or cleared in 30/34 on antibiotic versus 17/33 on placebo (NNT 2.7) — so about half the placebo group got better on its own, and antibiotics roughly doubled the chance
cards.people: Randomised controlled trial in Belgian general practice: of 166 women consulting with dysuria, frequency or urgency, 78 with pyuria on dipstick were enrolled — nitrofurantoin 100 mg four times daily for 3 days (n=40) versus placebo (n=38), ages 15–54 years (mean 35 in the nitrofurantoin group, 33 in the placebo group). Symptomatic and bacteriological outcomes were assessed at 3 and 7 days after the start of treatment.
cards.result: Clinical outcome at 3 days: symptomatic improvement or cure in 27 of 35 women on nitrofurantoin versus 19 of 35 on placebo (difference 23%, 95% CI 6% to 39%; P=0.008; NNT 4.4, 95% CI 2.3 to 79). At 7 days: 30 of 34 versus 17 of 33 (difference 37%, 95% CI 15% to 59%; P=0.003; NNT 2.7, 95% CI 1.8 to 6.0). Bacteriological cure at 3 days: 21 of 26 versus 5 of 25 (P<0.001; NNT 1.6, 95% CI 1.0 to 3.1); at 7 days: 17 of 23 versus 9 of 22 (P=0.05; NNT 3). The authors concluded that nitrofurantoin is effective in treating community-acquired urinary tract infection in women, with clinical cure in 88% of the nitrofurantoin group by day 7 against roughly half on placebo.
cards.watchOut: Small (78 enrolled, fewer at each analysis) and in women selected for pyuria — a group more likely to have true bacterial infection than all comers with urinary symptoms, so its placebo recovery (~52% by day 7) may actually understate spontaneous resolution in unselected symptom-only patients. A 3-day course of nitrofurantoin 100 mg four times daily is also a dated regimen. Read it as the cleanest head-to-head measure of 'how much do antibiotics add, and how fast', not as a modern prescribing guide.
cards.source: Christiaens TCM, De Meyere M, Verschraegen G, Peersman W, Heytens S, De Maeseneer JM. Randomised controlled trial of nitrofurantoin versus placebo in the treatment of uncomplicated urinary tract infection in adult women. British Journal of General Practice. 2002. PMID: 12236276. cards.headline: Hoffmann 2020 (natural-history systematic review): without antibiotics, up to 42% were symptom-free or improved by 9 days and 36% by 6 weeks — but up to 39% had not improved by 6 weeks, and one placebo patient developed pyelonephritis
cards.summary: Hoffmann 2020 (natural-history systematic review): without antibiotics, up to 42% were symptom-free or improved by 9 days and 36% by 6 weeks — but up to 39% had not improved by 6 weeks, and one placebo patient developed pyelonephritis
cards.type: Systematic review of placebo-arm natural history (Hoffmann 2020)
cards.people: Systematic review of the natural history of symptoms and bacteriuria in women with uncomplicated urinary tract infection who received no antibiotics, drawing on the placebo arms of randomised trials and any observational studies: three randomised trials with 346 placebo participants, all women. Outcomes were assessed at time points from days to six weeks.
cards.result: The proportion of placebo participants symptom-free or significantly improved rose over time, reaching 42% over the first 9 days; at 6 weeks, 36% of placebo participants had recovered. However, up to 39% of placebo participants failed to improve by 6 weeks. Adverse effects were low in the placebo groups, and pyelonephritis developed in one placebo participant (an event reported in two of the trials). The authors concluded that although most women with uncomplicated urinary tract infection who do not take antibiotics will not spontaneously recover, some will, and the benefits and harms of delaying or withholding antibiotics must be weighed and discussed with patients.
cards.watchOut: Three trials and 346 placebo participants is a thin base for a natural-history estimate, and the percentages mix 'symptom-free' with the softer 'significantly improved' and come from different trials at different time points — do not read 42% and 36% as one smooth recovery curve. The single pyelonephritis case cannot support a precise risk figure; it establishes only that the risk is not zero. The review's own bottom line cuts against over-reassurance: most women did NOT spontaneously recover within the windows studied.
cards.source: Hoffmann T, Peiris R, Del Mar C, Cleo G, Glasziou P. Natural history of uncomplicated urinary tract infection without antibiotics: a systematic review. British Journal of General Practice. 2020. PMID: 32958533. Registry ID: none in the record (systematic review). cards.headline: Little 2010 (BMJ, 309 women): waiting at least 48 hours before antibiotics did not significantly change symptom duration or severity overall — but those who waited had 37% longer symptoms (relative) and delayed prescribing cut antibiotic use from 97% to 77%
cards.summary: Little 2010 (BMJ, 309 women): waiting at least 48 hours before antibiotics did not significantly change symptom duration or severity overall — but those who waited had 37% longer symptoms (relative) and delayed prescribing cut antibiotic use from 97% to 77%
cards.type: Pragmatic randomised trial of delayed versus immediate antibiotics (Little 2010)
cards.people: Pragmatic randomised controlled trial in UK general practice: 309 non-pregnant women aged 18–70 presenting with suspected urinary tract infection, randomised to one of five management strategies — immediate antibiotics; delayed antibiotics (wait at least 48 hours); or antibiotics targeted by a symptom score (≥2 of urine cloudiness, smell, nocturia, dysuria), by dipstick result (positive nitrites, or leukocytes plus blood), or by mid-stream urine result (MSU, targeted on sensitivity). Primary outcome: duration and severity of symptoms; secondary outcomes included antibiotic use and reconsultation.
cards.result: Mean duration of symptoms rated moderately bad or worse was 3.5 days in the immediate-antibiotic group, and there were no significant differences in duration of symptoms or symptom severity between the strategies (mean symptom-frequency scores on a 0–6 scale: immediate 2.15, MSU 2.08, dipstick 1.74, symptom score 1.77, delayed 2.11; P=0.177). Antibiotic use differed: 97% in the immediate group versus 77% in the delayed group (P=0.011), with the symptom-score strategy also reducing use (78%). Waiting at least 48 hours was associated with a lower likelihood of reconsultation (hazard ratio 0.57, 95% CI 0.36–0.89; P=0.014 — relative) but with symptoms lasting 37% longer (incidence rate ratio 1.37, 95% CI 1.11–1.68; P=0.003 — relative). The authors concluded there is no support for an advantage in using MSU or dipsticks to target antibiotics, and that although symptom outcomes were similar overall, delayed prescribing is likely to make some women's symptoms last longer.
cards.watchOut: 'No significant difference between strategies' is a group-level statement that hides the split the authors themselves report: waiting was fine for the women who never needed the antibiotic and worse for the women who waited and then took one (37% longer symptoms, relative). The delayed group still used antibiotics at 77% — delayed prescribing reduced use modestly, it did not replace it. This trial tests a prescribing strategy in non-pregnant women, not the safety of never treating; worsening symptoms, fever or flank pain remain reasons to treat promptly.
cards.source: Little P, Turner S, Rumsby K, Warner G, Moore M, Lowes JA, Smith H, Hawke C, Turner D, Leydon GM, Arscott A, Mullee M. Dipsticks and diagnostic algorithms in urinary tract infection: five randomised controlled trials in primary care. BMJ. 2010. PMID: 20139214. Registry ID: ISRCTN03525333. pragmatic randomised trial of delayed versus immediate antibiotics (little 2010) pragmatic randomised controlled trial in uk general practice: 309 non-pregnant women aged 18–70 presenting with suspected urinary tract infection, randomised to one of five management strategies — immediate antibiotics; delayed antibiotics (wait at least 48 hours); or antibiotics targeted by a symptom score (≥2 of urine cloudiness, smell, nocturia, dysuria), by dipstick result (positive nitrites, or leukocytes plus blood), or by mid-stream urine result (msu, targeted on sensitivity). primary outcome: duration and severity of symptoms; secondary outcomes included antibiotic use and reconsultation. mean duration of symptoms rated moderately bad or worse was 3.5 days in the immediate-antibiotic group, and there were no significant differences in duration of symptoms or symptom severity between the strategies (mean symptom-frequency scores on a 0–6 scale: immediate 2.15, msu 2.08, dipstick 1.74, symptom score 1.77, delayed 2.11; p=0.177). antibiotic use differed: 97% in the immediate group versus 77% in the delayed group (p=0.011), with the symptom-score strategy also reducing use (78%). waiting at least 48 hours was associated with a lower likelihood of reconsultation (hazard ratio 0.57, 95% ci 0.36–0.89; p=0.014 — relative) but with symptoms lasting 37% longer (incidence rate ratio 1.37, 95% ci 1.11–1.68; p=0.003 — relative). the authors concluded there is no support for an advantage in using msu or dipsticks to target antibiotics, and that although symptom outcomes were similar overall, delayed prescribing is likely to make some women's symptoms last longer. 'no significant difference between strategies' is a group-level statement that hides the split the authors themselves report: waiting was fine for the women who never needed the antibiotic and worse for the women who waited and then took one (37% longer symptoms, relative). the delayed group still used antibiotics at 77% — delayed prescribing reduced use modestly, it did not replace it. this trial tests a prescribing strategy in non-pregnant women, not the safety of never treating; worsening symptoms, fever or flank pain remain reasons to treat promptly. little p, turner s, rumsby k, warner g, moore m, lowes ja, smith h, hawke c, turner d, leydon gm, arscott a, mullee m. dipsticks and diagnostic algorithms in urinary tract infection: five randomised controlled trials in primary care. bmj. 2010. pmid: 20139214. registry id: isrctn03525333. mesh: adolescent · adult · aged · algorithms · anti-bacterial agents/therapeutic use · female · humans · middle aged · pamphlets · patient education as topic · reagent strips · treatment outcome · urinary tract infections/diagnosis · urinary tract infections/drug therapy · young adult

cards.headline: Synthesis: yes, an uncomplicated UTI can go away on its own — roughly a quarter to two-fifths of women recover without antibiotics within one to six weeks — but most do not recover quickly, antibiotics about double the one-week cure chance, and waiting carries a small real risk
cards.summary: Synthesis: yes, an uncomplicated UTI can go away on its own — roughly a quarter to two-fifths of women recover without antibiotics within one to six weeks — but most do not recover quickly, antibiotics about double the one-week cure chance, and waiting carries a small real risk
cards.people: Placebo-arm evidence from Ferry 2004 (1,143 women randomised; 288 placebo), Christiaens 2002 (78 women, nitrofurantoin versus placebo), the Hoffmann 2020 natural-history review (3 trials, 346 placebo participants), and the Little 2010 delayed-prescribing trial (309 women, ISRCTN03525333). The ibuprofen-first strategy (Gágyör 2015; Bleidorn 2010) is homed on Shelf #2489 and is not re-carded here.
cards.result: Spontaneous recovery without antibiotics: 28% symptom-free at one week and 24% adjusted cure of symptoms plus bacteriuria by study end (Ferry 2004); 42% symptom-free or improved by 9 days, 36% recovered at 6 weeks, up to 39% not improved by 6 weeks, one case of pyelonephritis (Hoffmann 2020). What antibiotics add: day-7 symptomatic improvement or cure 30/34 versus 17/33 on placebo, NNT 2.7 (Christiaens 2002). What waiting costs and saves: no overall difference in symptom duration between immediate and delayed strategies, antibiotic use 77% versus 97%, but 37% longer symptoms (relative) in those who waited ≥48 hours before treatment (Little 2010). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) for watchful waiting with a clear safety net in uncomplicated cystitis in non-pregnant women.
cards.watchOut: Tier C — GAP-E (prognosis/natural history, not a treatment trial of 'no treatment'). Scope is strict: non-pregnant adult women with uncomplicated lower urinary symptoms. The evidence does not extend to men (urinary infection in men is complicated by definition), pregnancy, children, catheterised patients, recurrent UTI, or any red-flag presentation — fever, flank pain, vomiting, rigors, or visible blood with clots need treatment and assessment, not watchful waiting. Symptomatic relief while waiting (fluids, analgesia) and a low threshold to start antibiotics if symptoms worsen or persist beyond a few days are part of the strategy the trials actually tested.
cards.source: Synthesis of Ferry SA et al. Scandinavian Journal of Infectious Diseases. 2004 (PMID: 15198188); Christiaens TCM et al. British Journal of General Practice. 2002 (PMID: 12236276); Hoffmann T et al. British Journal of General Practice. 2020 (PMID: 32958533); Little P et al. BMJ. 2010 (PMID: 20139214).

shelves.title: Alcohol on antibiotics: the blanket ban outruns the evidence for most drugs — the metronidazole reaction is unproven under blinded challenge, but MTT-side-chain cephalosporins are a real risk
shelves.question: "Can I drink alcohol while taking antibiotics?" For a person prescribed a common antibiotic, which drug–alcohol combinations are genuinely dangerous, which are merely traditional warnings, and what does the evidence actually show for metronidazole — the most famous warning of all?

shelves.balance: SPLIT — the blanket warning ('never drink on any antibiotic') outruns the evidence, but the warning is not baseless for a specific few drugs. The systematic review (Mergenhagen 2020, PMID: 31871085) found the published data support safe use with alcohol for many common agents — oral penicillins, cefdinir, cefpodoxime, fluoroquinolones, azithromycin, tetracycline, nitrofurantoin, secnidazole, tinidazole and fluconazole — with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole equivocal. For the famous one, metronidazole, the evidence is strikingly weak: the double-blind challenge study (Visapää 2002, PMID: 12022894; 12 volunteers) found metronidazole did not raise blood acetaldehyde and produced no objective or subjective disulfiram-like effects after 0.4 g/kg ethanol; and the case-literature review (Williams & Woodcock 2000, PMID: 10676835) found that reports from 1969–1982 provided no convincing evidence the reaction exists, and that of 6 case reports covering 8 patients, 4 cases were serious (including one death) but every report simply presumed the reaction was an established fact without providing justifying evidence. Mergenhagen nonetheless records the metronidazole reaction as occurring 'with uncertain frequency and with varied severity' and the label still advises avoiding alcohol during therapy and for at least 72 hours after the last dose — so the shelf's position is: unproven, not disproven, and the official advice stands until better evidence exists. Where the interaction is on firmer ground: cephalosporins carrying a methylthiotetrazole (MTT) side chain or methylthiodioxotriazine (MTDT) ring, plus ketoconazole and griseofulvin, are associated with increased disulfiram-like reaction risk. Two non-interaction reasons to abstain survive any debunking: alcohol worsens many infections' symptoms and recovery, and several antibiotics plus alcohol share side effects (nausea, dizziness, sedation). PROPOSED SPLIT.

cards.headline: Mergenhagen 2020 (systematic review): data support drinking with most common antibiotics — penicillins, several cephalosporins, fluoroquinolones, azithromycin, tetracycline, nitrofurantoin — while MTT-side-chain cephalosporins, ketoconazole and griseofulvin carry the real disulfiram-like risk
cards.summary: Mergenhagen 2020 (systematic review): data support drinking with most common antibiotics — penicillins, several cephalosporins, fluoroquinolones, azithromycin, tetracycline, nitrofurantoin — while MTT-side-chain cephalosporins, ketoconazole and griseofulvin carry the real disulfiram-like risk
cards.people: Systematic review in Antimicrobial Agents and Chemotherapy of the evidence on ethanol interactions with antimicrobials, searching the literature to 2018 across PubMed, Medline and Embase: pharmacokinetic studies, clinical outcome reports and the case literature for oral and parenteral anti-infectives, including penicillins, cephalosporins, fluoroquinolones, macrolides, tetracyclines, nitroimidazoles (metronidazole, tinidazole, secnidazole), nitrofurantoin, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, linezolid-class agents and antifungals.
cards.result: The review found that the data support the safe use of ethanol with oral penicillins, cefdinir, cefpodoxime, fluoroquinolones, azithromycin, tetracycline, nitrofurantoin, secnidazole, tinidazole and fluconazole. Data for trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole were equivocal. For metronidazole, the labelled warning stands — patients are advised to avoid alcohol and alcohol- or propylene-glycol-containing products during therapy and for at least 72 hours after the last dose — but the review characterises the disulfiram-like reaction as occurring with uncertain frequency and varied severity. Increased disulfiram-like reaction risk was associated with cephalosporins bearing a methylthiotetrazole (MTT) side chain or a methylthiodioxotriazine (MTDT) ring, and with ketoconazole and griseofulvin. Overall, the authors found that interactions between alcohol and antimicrobials are often supported by limited evidence.
cards.watchOut: 'Data support safe use' means no interaction was demonstrated in the available pharmacokinetic and outcome literature — it is not a licence to drink heavily during an infection, and the review does not weigh alcohol's effects on the illness itself, on sleep, or on adherence. The review is a narrative-systematic synthesis of a sparse literature: for most drug–alcohol pairs the underlying studies are small or old. Linezolid-type cautions (monoamine-oxidase interactions with tyramine-rich drinks) are a different mechanism from the disulfiram-like reaction and are not quantified by any card on this shelf; patients on linezolid should follow their label.
cards.source: Mergenhagen KA, Wattengel BA, Skelly MK, Clark CM, Russo TA. Fact versus Fiction: a Review of the Evidence behind Alcohol and Antibiotic Interactions. Antimicrobial Agents and Chemotherapy. 2020. PMID: 31871085. Registry ID: none in the record (systematic review).
