cards.headline: Visapää 2002 (double-blind challenge, 12 volunteers): metronidazole did not raise blood acetaldehyde and caused no objective or subjective disulfiram-like effects after a standardised alcohol dose
cards.summary: Visapää 2002 (double-blind challenge, 12 volunteers): metronidazole did not raise blood acetaldehyde and caused no objective or subjective disulfiram-like effects after a standardised alcohol dose
cards.people: Double-blind study in 12 healthy male volunteers: half received metronidazole and half placebo for 5 days, after which all received ethanol 0.4 g/kg; blood samples were drawn every 20 minutes for 4 hours to measure ethanol and acetaldehyde (the metabolite whose accumulation causes the disulfiram reaction), alongside objective signs (blood pressure, body temperature, heart rate) and subjective symptom reporting.
cards.result: Metronidazole did not increase blood acetaldehyde concentrations compared with placebo, and it produced no objective or subjective disulfiram-like effects in the volunteers. The authors concluded that the study casts doubt on the conventional mechanism of the presumed metronidazole–ethanol interaction, while noting that disulfiram-like reactions could still occur in subgroups of patients or by another mechanism.
cards.watchOut: Twelve healthy young men, one alcohol dose, five days of metronidazole: this study can show the classic acetaldehyde mechanism did not operate here, but it cannot exclude rare reactions, reactions at higher doses, reactions in older or sicker patients, or a different mechanism entirely — the authors say so themselves. A negative 12-person challenge study is evidence the textbook story is unproven; it is not proof of safety, and it does not override the product label's advice to abstain during and for 72 hours after metronidazole.
cards.source: Visapää JP, Tillonen JS, Kaihovaara PS, Salaspuro MP. Lack of disulfiram-like reaction with metronidazole and ethanol. Annals of Pharmacotherapy. 2002. PMID: 12022894. cards.headline: Williams & Woodcock 2000 (case-literature review): of 8 reported metronidazole–alcohol cases, 4 were serious and 1 fatal — yet none provided evidence justifying the reaction, and the 1969–1982 literature contained no convincing evidence it exists
cards.summary: Williams & Woodcock 2000 (case-literature review): of 8 reported metronidazole–alcohol cases, 4 were serious and 1 fatal — yet none provided evidence justifying the reaction, and the 1969–1982 literature contained no convincing evidence it exists
cards.type: Review of the case literature (Williams & Woodcock 2000)
cards.people: Review in the Annals of Pharmacotherapy of the world's case literature on the alleged metronidazole–ethanol disulfiram-like reaction, searching MEDLINE from 1964 to June 1999: the early experimental and clinical reports (1969–1982) and all published case reports of the reaction, assessed for whether they actually demonstrated the interaction.
cards.result: The review found that reports published between 1969 and 1982 produced no convincing evidence that the metronidazole–ethanol disulfiram-like reaction exists. Six case reports covering 8 patients were identified; 4 of the 8 cases were serious, including one death. However, all of the reports presumed the reaction to be an established pharmacological fact, and none of them provided evidence that would justify describing it as one. The authors' assessment leaves the reaction as an entrenched clinical belief resting on anecdote rather than demonstrated evidence.
cards.watchOut: Hold both ends of this card. The serious cases, including a death, are real reports of real harm temporally linked to metronidazole plus alcohol — 'the reports did not prove causation' is not 'nothing happened', and alternative explanations (the underlying infection, alcohol alone, other drugs) were not excluded either. Absence of proof in a 1964–1999 case literature is a weak instrument in both directions. This card documents why the shelf calls the interaction unproven; it is not a recommendation to test it.
cards.source: Williams CS, Woodcock KR. Do ethanol and metronidazole interact to produce a disulfiram-like reaction? Annals of Pharmacotherapy. 2000. PMID: 10676835. cards.headline: Synthesis: for most antibiotics the no-alcohol rule is tradition, not evidence — but for MTT/MTDT cephalosporins the risk is real, and for metronidazole the honest verdict is 'unproven, officially warned, do not test it on yourself'
cards.summary: Synthesis: for most antibiotics the no-alcohol rule is tradition, not evidence — but for MTT/MTDT cephalosporins the risk is real, and for metronidazole the honest verdict is 'unproven, officially warned, do not test it on yourself'
cards.people: One systematic review of alcohol–antimicrobial interactions (Mergenhagen 2020), one double-blind ethanol challenge study (Visapää 2002; 12 volunteers), and one review of the case literature (Williams & Woodcock 2000; 6 case reports, 8 patients).
cards.result: Supported as compatible with alcohol by the review evidence: oral penicillins, cefdinir, cefpodoxime, fluoroquinolones, azithromycin, tetracycline, nitrofurantoin, secnidazole, tinidazole, fluconazole; equivocal: trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (Mergenhagen 2020). Metronidazole: no acetaldehyde rise and no reaction under double-blind challenge (Visapää 2002), and a case literature that presumes rather than proves the reaction, including one reported death (Williams & Woodcock 2000) — yet the labelled advice remains abstinence during therapy and ≥72 hours after. Firmer risk: cephalosporins with an MTT side chain or MTDT ring, ketoconazole, griseofulvin (Mergenhagen 2020). PROPOSED SPLIT.
cards.watchOut: Tier C — GAP-E. This shelf answers the interaction question only. It does not make drinking during an infection wise: alcohol impairs sleep and immune recovery, worsens dehydration and nausea, and adds sedation to several antibiotics' own side-effect profiles — reasons enough for many patients to abstain that have nothing to do with disulfiram chemistry. Anyone whose prescriber or label says abstain should abstain; the shelf's purpose is accuracy about which warnings are evidence-based, not permission. Specific products vary by country and formulation (including alcohol-containing liquid medicines and propylene glycol vehicles, which the metronidazole label also covers).

synthesis one systematic review of alcohol–antimicrobial interactions (mergenhagen 2020), one double-blind ethanol challenge study (visapää 2002; 12 volunteers), and one review of the case literature (williams & woodcock 2000; 6 case reports, 8 patients). supported as compatible with alcohol by the review evidence: oral penicillins, cefdinir, cefpodoxime, fluoroquinolones, azithromycin, tetracycline, nitrofurantoin, secnidazole, tinidazole, fluconazole; equivocal: trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (mergenhagen 2020). metronidazole: no acetaldehyde rise and no reaction under double-blind challenge (visapää 2002), and a case literature that presumes rather than proves the reaction, including one reported death (williams & woodcock 2000) — yet the labelled advice remains abstinence during therapy and ≥72 hours after. firmer risk: cephalosporins with an mtt side chain or mtdt ring, ketoconazole, griseofulvin (mergenhagen 2020). proposed split. tier c — gap-e. this shelf answers the interaction question only. it does not make drinking during an infection wise: alcohol impairs sleep and immune recovery, worsens dehydration and nausea, and adds sedation to several antibiotics' own side-effect profiles — reasons enough for many patients to abstain that have nothing to do with disulfiram chemistry. anyone whose prescriber or label says abstain should abstain; the shelf's purpose is accuracy about which warnings are evidence-based, not permission. specific products vary by country and formulation (including alcohol-containing liquid medicines and propylene glycol vehicles, which the metronidazole label also covers). synthesis of mergenhagen ka et al. antimicrobial agents and chemotherapy. 2020 (pmid: 31871085); visapää jp et al. annals of pharmacotherapy. 2002 (pmid: 12022894); williams cs, woodcock kr. annals of pharmacotherapy. 2000 (pmid: 10676835).

shelves.title: Long-term damage from tick-borne infections: after hospitalised Rocky Mountain spotted fever, 38% of interviewed survivors reported ongoing symptoms and 23% had neurologic sequelae on examination; after treated Lyme disease, persistent symptoms ran only about 4–6 percentage points above background rates
shelves.question: 'What long-term damage can tick-borne infections do?' — After Rocky Mountain spotted fever and after treated Lyme disease, how often do symptoms, disability or organ damage persist long-term, and how do those rates compare with people who never had the infection?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Child · Female · Humans · Logistic Models · Longitudinal Studies · Lyme Disease/drug therapy · Lyme Disease/physiopathology · Male · Matched-Pair Analysis · Sickness Impact Profile · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the two infections leave very different long-term records. After Rocky Mountain spotted fever severe enough to hospitalise for weeks, lasting damage is common and concrete: in the classic series, 9 of 20 followed patients had at least one sequela persisting a year or more — paraparesis, hearing loss, peripheral neuropathy, bladder and bowel incontinence, cerebellar and motor dysfunction, language disorders (Archibald 1995, PMID: 7619986) — and in a modern Arizona series of 80 hospitalised cases, 38% of interviewed survivors reported ongoing symptoms or reduced function and 23% had neurologic sequelae on examination, with longer hospitalisation and delayed doxycycline marking the worse outcomes (Drexler 2022, PMID: 36324320). After treated Lyme disease the picture is a small excess over a high background: a Connecticut cohort found symptom frequencies similar to matched controls without Lyme disease (Seltzer 2000, PMID: 10665700); the large Dutch prospective cohort found persistent symptoms in 27.2% of Lyme patients versus 21.2% of the general population and 23.3% of tick-bitten controls — absolute excesses of 6.0 and 3.9 percentage points (Ursinus 2021, PMID: 34557833); and a rigorous prospective US study of erythema migrans found no significant difference from matched controls in any symptom at 6 or 12 months (Wormser 2020, PMID: 31996890). PROPOSED SPLIT: RMSF's long-term damage is real, organ-based, and concentrated in severe, late-treated disease; post-treatment Lyme symptoms are common in absolute terms but only modestly more common than in comparable people who never had Lyme.

cards.headline: Archibald 1995: of 20 severely ill RMSF patients followed for up to 18 years, 9 had at least one sequela persisting a year or more — paraparesis, hearing loss, neuropathy, incontinence, language disorders
cards.summary: Archibald 1995: of 20 severely ill RMSF patients followed for up to 18 years, 9 had at least one sequela persisting a year or more — paraparesis, hearing loss, neuropathy, incontinence, language disorders
cards.type: Retrospective follow-up cohort of hospitalised Rocky Mountain spotted fever patients (Archibald 1995)
cards.people: 25 patients with Rocky Mountain spotted fever who had been hospitalised for at least 2 weeks (drawn from a database of 105 RMSF patients); follow-up information was obtained for 20 of them, at 1–18 years after illness (mean 11 years).
cards.result: Nine of the 20 followed patients suffered long-term sequelae persisting 1 year or more: paraparesis, hearing loss, peripheral neuropathy, bladder and bowel incontinence, cerebellar, vestibular and motor dysfunction, and language disorders; non-neurological sequelae included disability from limb amputation and scrotal pain after cutaneous necrosis. Mean hospitalisation had been 47 days in patients with sequelae versus 20 days in those without (P<.05) — the damage tracked the severity of the acute illness.
cards.watchOut: This is the severe end of RMSF by design — only patients hospitalised at least 2 weeks were followed, from a single centre's database, and 5 of 25 could not be followed. It cannot say how often mild or promptly treated RMSF leaves damage; what it establishes is the catalogue and durability of damage when the disease is severe: neurological, and still present a decade later.
cards.source: Archibald LK, Sexton DJ. Long-term sequelae of Rocky Mountain spotted fever. Clinical Infectious Diseases. 1995. PMID: 7619986. Registry ID: none in the record (retrospective cohort). MeSH: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Child, Preschool · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Male · Rocky Mountain Spotted Fever/complications

cards.headline: Drexler 2022: after hospitalised RMSF in Arizona, 38% of interviewed survivors reported ongoing symptoms or reduced function and 23% had neurologic sequelae on examination
cards.summary: Drexler 2022: after hospitalised RMSF in Arizona, 38% of interviewed survivors reported ongoing symptoms or reduced function and 23% had neurologic sequelae on examination
cards.type: Retrospective review of hospitalised RMSF cases with survivor follow-up (Drexler 2022)
cards.people: 80 patients hospitalised with Rocky Mountain spotted fever in two Arizona tribal communities between 2002 and 2017, reviewed retrospectively; 17 cases (21%) were fatal, and surviving patients were interviewed and examined for functional outcomes.
cards.result: Of interviewed survivors, 62% reported full recovery, while 15 (38%) reported ongoing symptoms or reduced function and 9 (23%) had neurologic sequelae on examination — impaired cognition, weakness, decreased deep tendon reflexes, seizures, and cranial nerve dysfunction; 28 patients (35%) had been discharged with documented neurologic or psychiatric sequelae. Patients with worse outcomes had longer hospitalisation (25.5 versus 6.2 days; P<.001) and higher discharge disability scores (modified Rankin Scale 1 versus 0; P=.03); doxycycline was started later in those with sequelae (6.2 versus 4.1 days; P=.12), and the authors identified delayed doxycycline — after day 5 of illness — as the strongest predictor of morbidity.
cards.watchOut: Hospitalised cases in two tribal communities with historically delayed presentation — a high-severity slice of RMSF, not the average spotted-fever illness, and the 21% fatality rate shows it. Interview denominators were smaller than 80 (deaths and non-interviewed survivors excluded), so the percentages describe interviewed survivors. The doxycycline-timing difference did not reach significance in this dataset (P=.12); it is the authors' interpretation, consistent with the severity gradient, not a proven causal estimate.
cards.source: Drexler NA, Close R, Yaglom HD, Kosoy O, Pirozzolo R, Traxler R, Bjork A, Komatsu K, Villanueva J, Heppner R, Komatsu V, Collier S, Petersen JM, McQuiston J, Paddock C. cards.headline: Seltzer 2000: a median 51 months after Lyme disease, symptom frequencies were similar to matched controls who never had Lyme — and only 19% of patients with increased symptoms blamed Lyme
cards.summary: Seltzer 2000: a median 51 months after Lyme disease, symptom frequencies were similar to matched controls who never had Lyme — and only 19% of patients with increased symptoms blamed Lyme
cards.type: Population-based cohort study with matched controls (Seltzer 2000)
cards.people: 678 Connecticut patients randomly sampled from reported suspected Lyme disease cases (1984–1991) and 212 matched controls without Lyme disease, interviewed about current symptoms and difficulties a median of 51 months after diagnosis (range 15–135 months); 85.6% of patients had been treated with antimicrobials.
cards.result: Sixty-nine percent of patients reported increased symptoms or difficulties since their Lyme episode, but only 19% of those attributed the increase to Lyme disease. The frequencies of increased symptoms and of difficulties with activities were similar between patients and the age-matched controls without Lyme disease. In other words, at group level the treated-Lyme patients looked like their peers — the background rate of fatigue, aches and difficulty in mid-life is high, and most of what patients carried years later was present at the same rate in people who never had Lyme.
cards.watchOut: Cases were 'suspected' Lyme disease reported to a health department in 1984–1991, before modern two-tier testing discipline, and interviews relied on recall of change since diagnosis — attribution bias runs in both directions. A null group average also cannot exclude a small subgroup with genuine post-treatment symptoms; the later prospective cohorts carded next measure that excess directly.
cards.source: Seltzer EG, Gerber MA, Cartter ML, Freudigman K, Shapiro ED. Long-term outcomes of persons with Lyme disease. JAMA. 2000. PMID: 10665700. Registry ID: none in the record (cohort study). cards.headline: Ursinus 2021: persistent symptoms in 27.2% after Lyme borreliosis versus 21.2% of the general population and 23.3% of tick-bitten controls — an absolute excess of about 4–6 percentage points
cards.summary: Ursinus 2021: persistent symptoms in 27.2% after Lyme borreliosis versus 21.2% of the general population and 23.3% of tick-bitten controls — an absolute excess of about 4–6 percentage points
cards.type: Prospective observational cohort study with two control cohorts (Ursinus 2021)
cards.people: 1,135 patients with physician-confirmed Lyme borreliosis enrolled prospectively at the start of antibiotic treatment in the Netherlands (1,084 in the primary analysis), compared with 1,942 general-population controls and 1,887 tick-bite controls, followed for 12 months.
cards.result: Persistent symptoms — fatigue, cognitive impairment or pain present for at least 6 months — occurred in 27.2% (95% CI 24.7–29.7) of Lyme patients, versus 21.2% of population controls (difference 6.0 percentage points; p<0.0001) and 23.3% of tick-bite controls (difference 3.9 percentage points; p=0.016). At 12 months, fatigue, cognitive impairment and pain were each more severe in erythema migrans patients than in both control cohorts; in disseminated Lyme borreliosis, only pain was more severe. The excess over background is real but small: roughly 1 extra case of persistent symptoms for every 17–26 treated patients, against a background where about 1 in 5 people report such symptoms anyway.
cards.watchOut: Symptoms were self-reported on questionnaires without blinding — patients knew they had had Lyme disease, controls knew they had not — which can inflate a subjective-symptom gap of this size; the tick-bite control comparison (3.9 points) partly guards against that. The study measures symptom prevalence and severity, not organ damage: it does not show persistent infection, and it cannot identify which individual patient's symptoms were caused by the infection.
cards.source: Ursinus J, Vrijmoeth HD, Harms MG, Tulen AD, Knoop H, Gauw SA, Zomer TP, Wong A, Friesema IHM, Vermeeren YM, Joosten LAB, Hovius JW, Kullberg BJ, van den Wijngaard CC. Prevalence of persistent symptoms after treatment for lyme borreliosis: A prospective observational cohort study. The Lancet Regional Health – Europe. 2021. PMID: 34557833. Registry ID: Netherlands Trial Register NTR4998 (per the study's protocol paper). MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Wormser 2020: prospectively, erythema migrans patients and matched controls were indistinguishable at 6 and 12 months — 39.1% versus 51.6% and 55.1% versus 51.0% with at least one symptom
cards.summary: Wormser 2020: prospectively, erythema migrans patients and matched controls were indistinguishable at 6 and 12 months — 39.1% versus 51.6% and 55.1% versus 51.0% with at least one symptom
cards.type: Prospective matched-control study of treated erythema migrans (Wormser 2020)
cards.people: 52 US patients with erythema migrans (early Lyme disease) treated prospectively and 104 matched subjects without Lyme disease, each rating the severity of 12 symptoms on visual analogue scales at baseline, 6 months and 12 months.
cards.result: At baseline, 75% of patients versus 51% of controls had at least one symptom (P=.006). By 6 months the proportions had converged and crossed: 39.1% (18 of 46) of patients versus 51.6% (49 of 95) of controls (P=.21); at 12 months, 55.1% (27 of 49) versus 51.0% (50 of 98) (P=.73). There were no significant differences between patients and controls for any symptom variable at 6 or 12 months. Ten patients were nonetheless clinically assessed as having possible post-treatment Lyme disease symptoms — a clinical judgement category, not a measured excess.
cards.watchOut: Only 52 patients, all with early localised disease (erythema migrans) treated promptly — the Lyme presentation with the best prognosis; it does not address disseminated or late Lyme, where the Dutch cohort (Ursinus 2021) still found only a modest excess. With samples this size, a small true excess like the Dutch 4–6 points could be missed; read the two cohorts together: excess after treated early Lyme is somewhere between none detected and a few percentage points.
cards.source: Wormser GP et al. Prospective Evaluation of the Frequency and Severity of Symptoms in Lyme Disease Patients With Erythema Migrans Compared With Matched Controls at Baseline, 6 Months, and 12 Months. Clinical Infectious Diseases. 2020. PMID: 31996890. Registry ID: none in the record (prospective cohort). MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Synthesis: RMSF can leave permanent neurological damage after severe disease; treated Lyme leaves, at most, a small excess of persistent symptoms over a high background rate
cards.summary: Synthesis: RMSF can leave permanent neurological damage after severe disease; treated Lyme leaves, at most, a small excess of persistent symptoms over a high background rate
cards.people: Five cohorts: two hospitalised-RMSF follow-up series (Archibald 1995 — 20 patients followed up to 18 years; Drexler 2022 — 80 hospitalised cases) and three treated-Lyme comparisons with controls (Seltzer 2000 — 678 patients, 212 controls; Ursinus 2021 — 1,084 patients, 3,829 controls; Wormser 2020 — 52 patients, 104 controls).
cards.result: RMSF: among survivors of severe hospitalised disease, long-term sequelae were found in 9 of 20 followed patients in 1995 and, in 2022, 38% of interviewed survivors reported ongoing symptoms or reduced function with 23% showing neurologic sequelae on examination; sequelae tracked acute severity (47 versus 20 days hospitalised; 25.5 versus 6.2 days) and, in the authors' reading, delayed doxycycline. Lyme: persistent symptoms after treatment were reported by 27.2% of patients versus 21.2–23.3% of controls (Ursinus 2021) — an absolute excess of 3.9–6.0 percentage points — while two controlled studies found no significant patient–control difference at all (Seltzer 2000; Wormser 2020, at both 6 and 12 months). No fetched Lyme cohort documents progressive organ damage after standard treatment; the documented burden is symptom persistence, not tissue destruction. PROPOSED SPLIT: the honest answer to 'what long-term damage?' differs by organism — for RMSF, real and sometimes permanent neurological injury after severe disease; for treated Lyme disease, a modest excess of lingering symptoms over what comparable people report anyway.
cards.watchOut: Tier C — the developer's personal verdict. Scope limits: the RMSF series cover hospitalised, often late-treated disease (mild RMSF treated early has no fetched long-term series here), and the Lyme cohorts cover standard antibiotic treatment of recognised disease — not untreated Lyme, not other tick-borne infections (ehrlichiosis, babesiosis, alpha-gal syndrome), and not the separate question of prolonged antibiotic therapy for persistent symptoms, which is homed on Shelf #586 and not re-carded here.
cards.source: Synthesis of Archibald LK, Sexton DJ. Clinical Infectious Diseases. 1995 (PMID: 7619986); Drexler NA et al. Open Forum Infectious Diseases. 2022 (PMID: 36324320); Seltzer EG et al. JAMA. 2000 (PMID: 10665700); Ursinus J et al. The Lancet Regional Health – Europe. 2021 (PMID: 34557833); Wormser GP et al. Clinical Infectious Diseases. 2020 (PMID: 31996890).

shelves.title: Bird flu (avian influenza H5N1/H7N9): oseltamivir is associated with better survival in observational registry data — 60% survived with oseltamivir versus 24% with no antiviral in H5N1 — and earlier treatment looks better; no randomised trial exists
shelves.question: How is bird flu (avian influenza) treated? In people with confirmed H5N1 or H7N9 avian influenza, does oseltamivir improve survival, and does starting it earlier matter?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Antiviral Agents/therapeutic use · Child · Child, Preschool · Female · Global Health · Humans · Infant · Influenza A Virus, H5N1 Subtype · Influenza, Human/drug therapy · Influenza, Human/epidemiology · Influenza, Human/mortality · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Male · Middle Aged · Oseltamivir/therapeutic use · Registries · Risk Factors · Time Factors · Treatment Outcome · Young Adult
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only, and the shelf says so on its face: there is NO randomised trial of oseltamivir (or any antiviral) in human avian influenza, and none is likely, because cases are sporadic and often fulminant. What exists is registry and case-series evidence that points consistently one way. In the Global Patient Registry analysis of 308 confirmed H5N1 cases from 12 countries (Adisasmito 2010, PMID: 20831384), crude survival was 60% in patients who received at least one dose of oseltamivir alone versus 24% in patients with no evidence of anti-influenza antiviral treatment (P<.001), and propensity-adjusted multivariate modelling showed a 49% relative reduction in mortality with oseltamivir treatment; the survival advantage persisted when treatment began up to 6–8 days after symptom onset. Timing analyses point the same way: in 215 oseltamivir-treated registry patients, early initiation was particularly protective in patients without respiratory failure (odds ratio 0.17; Chan 2012, PMID: 22927451); in the Indonesian case series of 127 confirmed cases (103 deaths, 81%), survival by treatment timing was 36.4% (4 of 11) when oseltamivir started at 2–4 days, 37.5% (6 of 16) at 5–6 days and 18.5% (10 of 44) at 7 days or later (Kandun 2008, PMID: 18706688); and in 193 registry children, each day of delay in starting oseltamivir raised the adjusted odds of death by 75% (Oner 2012, PMID: 22423125). For H7N9, the one comparative study found adding peramivir to oseltamivir was NOT superior to oseltamivir alone (mortality 43.59% combination versus 25.58% monotherapy, p>0.05; Zhang 2016, PMID: 26864456) — a reminder that sicker patients get more drugs in observational data. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): consistent observational survival association, strongest with early treatment, unproven by any randomised test and vulnerable to confounding (patients who live long enough and reach care get treated).

cards.headline: Adisasmito 2010 (Global Patient Registry, 308 H5N1 cases): survival 60% with oseltamivir versus 24% with no antiviral; adjusted modelling showed a 49% relative reduction in mortality
cards.summary: Adisasmito 2010 (Global Patient Registry, 308 H5N1 cases): survival 60% with oseltamivir versus 24% with no antiviral; adjusted modelling showed a 49% relative reduction in mortality
cards.people: 308 confirmed human influenza A(H5N1) cases from 12 countries, assembled from clinical records, published case series and governmental agency reports (41 cases from Azerbaijan, Hong Kong SAR, Nigeria, Pakistan and Turkey; 175 from Egypt and Indonesia; 92 from Bangladesh, Cambodia, China, Thailand and Vietnam). Effect estimated by Cox proportional hazards regression with propensity-score adjustment.
cards.result: Overall crude survival was 43.5%. Sixty percent of patients who received at least one dose of oseltamivir alone survived, versus 24% of patients who had no evidence of anti-influenza antiviral treatment (P<.001) — an absolute survival difference of 36 percentage points in unadjusted data. Survival in oseltamivir-treated groups was significantly higher than in untreated groups, and benefit persisted with treatment initiation up to 6–8 days after symptom onset. Multivariate modelling showed a 49% relative reduction in mortality from oseltamivir treatment. The authors concluded oseltamivir significantly reduces mortality when started up to 6–8 days after symptom onset and appears to benefit all age groups.
cards.watchOut: Observational, not randomised: who received oseltamivir was decided by availability, timing and survival long enough to be treated, so immortal-time and access confounding can inflate the apparent benefit even after propensity adjustment. Cases were assembled from heterogeneous sources across 12 countries and different viral clades. The 60% versus 24% contrast is crude survival; the 49% figure is a modelled relative mortality reduction, not an absolute one.
cards.source: Adisasmito W, Chan PKS, Lee N, Oner AF, Gasimov V, Aghayev F, Zaman M, Bamgboye E, Dogan N, Coker R, Starzyk K, Dreyer NA, Toovey S. Effectiveness of antiviral treatment in human influenza A(H5N1) infections: analysis of a Global Patient Registry. The Journal of Infectious Diseases. 2010. PMID: 20831384. Registry ID: none in the record (observational registry analysis). cards.headline: Chan 2012 (registry timing analysis, 215 treated patients): oseltamivir started within 2 days was protective, and in patients without respiratory failure early initiation gave an odds ratio for death of 0.17
cards.summary: Chan 2012 (registry timing analysis, 215 treated patients): oseltamivir started within 2 days was protective, and in patients without respiratory failure early initiation gave an odds ratio for death of 0.17
cards.type: Observational Avian Influenza Registry analysis of treatment determinants (Chan 2012)
cards.people: 215 patients with confirmed H5N1 infection from 10 countries in the Avian Influenza Registry, all treated with oseltamivir; risk of death examined by viral clade, age, respiratory failure and adjunctive corticosteroid or antibiotic treatment. Median age 18 years; 50% male.
cards.result: In univariate analyses, age of 5 years or younger and treatment within 2 days after symptom onset were protective against fatality. When all risk factors were accounted for, early initiation of oseltamivir was particularly effective in individuals without respiratory failure (odds ratio 0.17; P=.04). Patients who already had advanced respiratory failure requiring ventilatory support when oseltamivir was started were more likely to die than patients who did not (P<.001). Adjunctive therapy (corticosteroids or antibiotics) did not improve the likelihood of surviving. Fatality also differed by viral clade (highest where clade 2.1 circulated, lowest with clade 2.2; P<.001).
cards.watchOut: Everyone in this analysis was treated — it compares early with late treatment, not treatment with none, and late treatment is partly a marker of late presentation and established respiratory failure rather than a cause of death in itself. The odds ratio of 0.17 comes from a subgroup (no respiratory failure) in an adjusted observational model; treat it as a timing signal, not a measured treatment effect.
cards.source: Chan PKS, Lee N, Zaman M, Adisasmito W, Coker R, Hanshaoworakul W, Gasimov V, Oner AF, Dogan N, Tsang O, Phommasack B, Touch S, Bamgboye E, Swenson A, Toovey S, Dreyer NA. Determinants of antiviral effectiveness in influenza virus A subtype H5N1. The Journal of Infectious Diseases. 2012. PMID: 22927451. Registry ID: none in the record (observational registry analysis). cards.headline: Kandun 2008 (Indonesia, 127 confirmed cases, 81% died): survival was 36.4% when oseltamivir started at 2–4 days and 37.5% at 5–6 days, but 18.5% when it started at 7 days or later
cards.summary: Kandun 2008 (Indonesia, 127 confirmed cases, 81% died): survival was 36.4% when oseltamivir started at 2–4 days and 37.5% at 5–6 days, but 18.5% when it started at 7 days or later
cards.type: Multicentre case series of confirmed H5N1 infections in Indonesia (Kandun 2008)
cards.people: 127 patients with confirmed H5N1 infection in Indonesia between June 2005 and February 2008, investigated by deployed case-investigation teams; 103 (81%) died. Median time to hospitalisation was 6 days (range 1–16); median time from onset to oseltamivir treatment was 7 days (range 0–21).
cards.result: Of 122 hospitalised patients with data, 121 (99%) had fever, 107 (88%) cough and 103 (84%) dyspnoea on reaching hospital. Survival by timing of oseltamivir initiation: the one patient treated within 2 days survived; 4 (36.4%) of 11 treated within 2–4 days survived; 6 (37.5%) of 16 treated within 5–6 days survived; and 10 (18.5%) of 44 treated at 7 days or later survived (p=0.03). Initiation within 2 days was associated with significantly lower mortality than initiation at 5–6 days or at 7 days or later (p<0.0001). Mortality was lower in clustered than unclustered cases (odds ratio 33.3, 95% CI 3.13–273), and treatment started earlier in secondary cluster cases (median 5 days) than primary cases (median 8 days; p=0.04).
cards.watchOut: A case series from the country with one of the world's highest H5N1 fatality rates, in an era of very late presentation (median 7 days to treatment) — the timing gradient is entangled with how sick patients were when found and how fast clusters were recognised. The within-2-days group is a single patient. The numbers describe association in the worst-affected setting, not the effect of moving any one patient's treatment earlier.
cards.source: Kandun IN, Tresnaningsih E, Purba WH, Lee V, Samaan G, Harun S, Soni E, Septiawati C, Setiawati T, Sariwati E, Wandra T. Factors associated with case fatality of human H5N1 virus infections in Indonesia: a case series. Lancet. 2008. PMID: 18706688. Registry ID: none in the record (case series). cards.headline: Oner 2012 (registry children, n=193): case fatality 48.7%; each day of delay in starting oseltamivir raised the adjusted odds of death by 75%
cards.summary: Oner 2012 (registry children, n=193): case fatality 48.7%; each day of delay in starting oseltamivir raised the adjusted odds of death by 75%
cards.type: Observational Global Patient Registry analysis in children (Oner 2012)
cards.people: 193 children under 18 years with confirmed H5N1 infection from 13 countries in the global patient registry; 35.2% of cases were from Egypt. Bivariate and multivariate analyses of presentation and prognostic factors for survival.
cards.result: The case fatality rate for children was 48.7%, with Egypt having a very low paediatric case fatality rate. Children aged 5 years or younger had the lowest case fatality rate and were brought to hospital more quickly and treated sooner than older children. Children presenting with rhinorrhoea had a 76% relative reduction in the likelihood of death compared with those presenting without it, after adjustment for age, infection in Egypt and oseltamivir treatment (P=.02). Delayed initiation of oseltamivir increased the likelihood of death, with an overall 75% increase in the adjusted odds ratio for death for each day of delay. The authors concluded that for individuals treated with oseltamivir, early initiation substantially enhances the chance of survival.
cards.watchOut: The per-day figure is an adjusted odds ratio from registry data, not a dose-response measured in a trial: delay also tracks country, age and how the case was detected (Egypt's very low paediatric fatality rate, with 35.2% of cases, heavily shapes the pooled numbers). Children are also not the whole H5N1 population — this card corroborates the timing direction in the paediatric subset of the same registry family as Adisasmito 2010 and Chan 2012, so the three registry cards are not fully independent evidence.
cards.source: Oner AF, Dogan N, Gasimov V, Adisasmito W, Coker R, Chan PKS, Lee N, Tsang O, Hanshaoworakul W, Zaman M, Bamgboye E, Swenson A, Toovey S, Dreyer NA. H5N1 avian influenza in children. Clinical Infectious Diseases. 2012. PMID: 22423125. Registry ID: none in the record (observational registry analysis). cards.headline: Zhang 2016 (H7N9, n=82): adding peramivir to oseltamivir was not superior — time to virus-negative 7.00 versus 6.50 days, mortality 43.59% versus 25.58% (both p>0.05)
cards.summary: Zhang 2016 (H7N9, n=82): adding peramivir to oseltamivir was not superior — time to virus-negative 7.00 versus 6.50 days, mortality 43.59% versus 25.58% (both p>0.05)
cards.type: Retrospective comparative study in confirmed H7N9 infection (Zhang 2016)
cards.people: 82 patients with confirmed influenza A(H7N9) infection at the First Affiliated Hospital of Zhejiang University, China, April 2013 to February 2014, comparing oseltamivir monotherapy (43 patients) with oseltamivir–peramivir combination therapy (39 patients) from medical charts.
cards.result: Median duration from neuraminidase-inhibitor administration to H7N9 virus-negative status was 6.50 days on oseltamivir monotherapy and 7.00 days on combination therapy (p>0.05). The median decline in viral load from day 0 to day 2 was 0.00 versus 0.69 log10 copies/µL (p>0.05). New acute respiratory distress syndrome during treatment occurred in 63.89% (monotherapy) and 77.78% (combination) (p>0.05), and mortality rates were 25.58% and 43.59% respectively (p>0.05). The authors concluded that oseltamivir–peramivir combination therapy was not superior to oseltamivir monotherapy in adults with H7N9 infection.
cards.watchOut: Retrospective and small, and the combination group almost certainly received the second drug because they were doing worse — the numerically higher mortality on combination therapy (43.59% versus 25.58%) is confounding by indication, not evidence that peramivir harms. The card's value is narrower: in H7N9, no added benefit of dual neuraminidase inhibition was shown, so oseltamivir alone remains the carded treatment.
cards.source: Zhang Y, Gao H, Liang W, Tang L, Yang Y, Wu X, Yu L, Chen P, Zheng S, Ou H, Li L. Efficacy of oseltamivir-peramivir combination therapy compared to oseltamivir monotherapy for Influenza A (H7N9) infection: a retrospective study. BMC Infectious Diseases. 2016. PMID: 26864456. Registry ID: none in the record (retrospective study). cards.headline: Synthesis: no trial exists — the whole case for oseltamivir in bird flu is observational, consistent on direction and timing, and capped at POSSIBLE
cards.summary: Synthesis: no trial exists — the whole case for oseltamivir in bird flu is observational, consistent on direction and timing, and capped at POSSIBLE
cards.people: Five observational sources: the Global Patient Registry H5N1 analysis (308 cases; Adisasmito 2010), the registry timing analysis (215 treated patients; Chan 2012), the Indonesian case series (127 cases; Kandun 2008), the registry paediatric analysis (193 children; Oner 2012), and the H7N9 combination-therapy comparison (82 patients; Zhang 2016). No randomised controlled trial of any antiviral in human H5N1 or H7N9 infection exists in this record.
cards.result: Treated versus untreated (H5N1): crude survival 60% versus 24%, with a 49% relative mortality reduction on propensity-adjusted modelling (Adisasmito 2010). Timing: treatment within 2 days was protective, with an odds ratio for death of 0.17 for early initiation in patients without respiratory failure (Chan 2012); survival fell from 36.4–37.5% with treatment at 2–6 days to 18.5% at 7 days or later in Indonesia (Kandun 2008); each day of delay raised adjusted odds of death by 75% in children (Oner 2012). H7N9: adding peramivir to oseltamivir showed no superiority (Zhang 2016). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational evidence only, labelled as such; seasonal-influenza oseltamivir trials are homed on Shelf #583 and are not re-carded here.
cards.watchOut: Tier C. Three of the five cards draw on overlapping registry populations, so their agreement is partly the same patients counted in different analyses. Nothing here is randomised evidence, and the shelf must not be read as trial-grade proof: it is the honest summary of the only human evidence that exists — treat early with oseltamivir, do not expect combination neuraminidase therapy to add benefit, and expect high mortality regardless (81% in the Indonesian series). Supportive and intensive care, which no card here quantifies, is the other half of real-world treatment.

shelves.title: Glandular fever (infectious mononucleosis): steroids eased sore throat for about 12 hours only, and antivirals showed no dependable benefit — both Cochrane reviews found the evidence insufficient or uncertain
shelves.question: I have glandular fever (infectious mononucleosis) — will steroids or antiviral medicines shorten it or ease the sore throat?
shelves.mesh: Acyclovir/therapeutic use · Adrenal Cortex Hormones/therapeutic use · Antiviral Agents/therapeutic use · Dexamethasone/administration & dosage · Glucocorticoids/therapeutic use · Infectious Mononucleosis/drug therapy · Pharyngitis/drug therapy · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (the treatment made no difference) — for routine symptom control in uncomplicated infectious mononucleosis, neither steroids nor antivirals have a demonstrated lasting benefit. The Cochrane review of corticosteroids (Candy & Hotopf 2006, PMID: 16856045; 7 trials of 24–94 participants each) found a sore-throat benefit at 12 hours in two studies that was not maintained, one trial suggesting longer benefit only for a steroid-plus-antiviral combination, and one trial suggesting faster fatigue resolution at about 4 weeks with the combination question unresolved; two trials reported severe complications in steroid groups, and the reviewers concluded the evidence is insufficient to recommend steroids for symptom control. The Cochrane review of antivirals (De Paor 2016, PMID: 27933614; 7 RCTs, 333 participants, testing acyclovir, valomaciclovir and valacyclovir) rated the evidence very low quality throughout: of 12 outcomes, only time to clinical recovery (−5 days, 95% CI −8.04 to −1.08; 2 studies, 87 participants) and duration of lymphadenopathy (−9 days, −11.75 to −6.14; 2 studies, 61) reached significance, viral shedding was suppressed only while treatment continued, and the reviewers concluded effectiveness is uncertain. The single-dose steroid trial behind the 12-hour signal (Roy 2004, PMID: 14993084; 40 children) found adequate pain relief at 12 hours in 12 of 20 (60%) on dexamethasone versus 5 of 19 (26%) on placebo (P=.03), and no difference at 24, 48 or 72 hours or at day 7. BOUNDARY: these trials address symptom control in uncomplicated glandular fever; steroid use for severe complications such as airway obstruction is a different clinical question that these reviews do not test. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (the treatment made no difference): a single steroid dose may buy a few hours of throat comfort; nothing fetched shows steroids or antivirals shorten the illness.

cards.headline: Cochrane steroids review (Candy & Hotopf 2006): sore-throat benefit at 12 hours in two trials, not maintained — 'insufficient evidence to recommend'; severe complications reported in steroid groups in two trials
cards.summary: Cochrane steroids review (Candy & Hotopf 2006): sore-throat benefit at 12 hours in two trials, not maintained — 'insufficient evidence to recommend'; severe complications reported in steroid groups in two trials
cards.people: 7 randomised trials of corticosteroids for symptom control in infectious mononucleosis, with individual trial sample sizes of 24–94 participants; outcomes included sore throat, fever, fatigue and complications.
cards.result: Two studies found a benefit of steroids over placebo for sore throat at 12 hours, but the benefit was not maintained beyond that point. One trial suggested a longer benefit for a steroid combined with an antiviral, and one trial suggested fatigue resolved faster (at about 4 weeks), though whether that applied to the combination or the steroid alone was unclear. Two trials reported severe complications occurring in the steroid groups. The reviewers' conclusion: there is insufficient evidence to recommend corticosteroids for symptom control in infectious mononucleosis.
cards.watchOut: Seven small trials with inconsistent regimens and outcomes — the review can say 'not demonstrated', not 'disproven for every regimen'. The severe-complication reports in steroid arms are a caution flag from two trials, not a measured harm rate. And the review's question is symptom control in ordinary glandular fever: it does not address steroids given for airway obstruction or other severe complications, where practice rests on different grounds.

cards.headline: Cochrane antivirals review (De Paor 2016): 7 trials, 333 participants, very-low-quality evidence throughout — significant on only 2 of 12 outcomes; 'effectiveness uncertain'
cards.summary: Cochrane antivirals review (De Paor 2016): 7 trials, 333 participants, very-low-quality evidence throughout — significant on only 2 of 12 outcomes; 'effectiveness uncertain'
cards.people: 7 randomised trials with 333 participants with infectious mononucleosis, testing acyclovir, valomaciclovir (valaciclovir) or valacyclovir against placebo or no treatment, across 12 clinical and laboratory outcomes.
cards.result: The evidence was rated very low quality for every outcome. Statistically significant effects appeared on only 2 of 12 outcomes: time to clinical recovery was 5 days shorter (−5 days, 95% CI −8.04 to −1.08; 2 studies, 87 participants) and duration of lymphadenopathy 9 days shorter (−9 days, −11.75 to −6.14; 2 studies, 61 participants). Suppression of viral shedding lasted only while participants were taking the antiviral. The reviewers concluded that the effectiveness of antiviral treatment for infectious mononucleosis is uncertain.
cards.watchOut: Two significant results out of 12 outcomes, each pooled from two small studies, is the pattern chance produces — the −5-day recovery figure should not be quoted as an established benefit, and the reviewers do not. Laboratory effects (viral shedding) did not translate into consistent clinical benefit, which is why suppressing Epstein-Barr virus shedding is not the same as treating glandular fever.
cards.source: De Paor M, O'Brien K, Fahey T, Smith SM. Antiviral agents for infectious mononucleosis (glandular fever). Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2016. PMID: 27933614. cards.headline: Roy 2004: one dose of dexamethasone relieved throat pain at 12 hours (60% vs 26%, P=.03) — and at no later time point in 40 children
cards.summary: Roy 2004: one dose of dexamethasone relieved throat pain at 12 hours (60% vs 26%, P=.03) — and at no later time point in 40 children
cards.people: 40 children aged 8–18 years with infectious mononucleosis and sore throat, randomised double-blind to a single oral dose of dexamethasone 0.3 mg/kg (maximum 15 mg; n=20) or placebo (n=20); pain relief was defined as a fall of at least 20 mm on a visual analogue scale.
cards.result: Adequate pain relief at 12 hours was achieved by 12 of 20 children (60%) on dexamethasone versus 5 of 19 (26%) on placebo (P=.03) — an absolute difference of about 34 percentage points at that single time point. At 24 hours the figures were 11/20 versus 6/20 (P=.10); at 48 hours 11/20 versus 11/20; at 72 hours 15/20 versus 15/19; and by day 7, 18/19 versus 19/20 — no difference at any point after 12 hours.
cards.watchOut: This is the trial behind the Cochrane review's 12-hour signal, and its own numbers show the effect's whole lifespan: present at 12 hours, gone by 24. Forty children at one centre, a single dose, and a pain-score endpoint — it supports at most a few hours of extra throat comfort, and says nothing about multi-day steroid courses, which carry the complication reports noted in the Cochrane card.
cards.source: Roy M, Bailey B, Amre DK, Girodias JB, Bussières JF, Châtillon JG. Dexamethasone for the treatment of sore throat in children with suspected infectious mononucleosis: a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled clinical trial. cards.headline: Synthesis: a few hours of throat relief is the only reproducible steroid effect; antivirals remain unproven; neither shortens the illness on this record
cards.summary: Synthesis: a few hours of throat relief is the only reproducible steroid effect; antivirals remain unproven; neither shortens the illness on this record
cards.people: Two Cochrane reviews (steroids: 7 trials; antivirals: 7 trials, 333 participants) and the largest single-dose steroid trial within them (40 children; Roy 2004), all in uncomplicated infectious mononucleosis.
cards.result: Steroids: sore-throat benefit at 12 hours in two trials (Roy 2004: 60% vs 26% adequate relief, P=.03), absent from 24 hours onward; review conclusion — insufficient evidence to recommend; severe complications reported in steroid arms of two trials. Antivirals: significant effects on 2 of 12 outcomes in very-low-quality data; conclusion — effectiveness uncertain. No fetched study shows either drug class shortening the overall illness or preventing complications. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (the treatment made no difference) for routine symptom control.
cards.watchOut: Scope is symptom control in uncomplicated glandular fever. Steroids for airway obstruction, severe thrombocytopenia or other complications, and antivirals in immunocompromised patients, are separate questions these trials do not answer and this shelf does not judge. Supportive care, activity guidance and splenic-rupture precautions are the management backbone and are outside the drug question asked here. Tier C: developer's personal verdict.

shelves.title: Infected ear piercing (auricular perichondritis): Pseudomonas is the organism to cover - 94% resolved with culture-guided antibiotics in a 50-patient series
shelves.question: How should an infected ear piercing (auricular perichondritis) be treated, and which antibiotic cover is needed?
shelves.mesh: Anti-Bacterial Agents / therapeutic use · Otitis Externa / drug therapy · Pseudomonas Infections / drug therapy · Staphylococcal Infections / drug therapy · Retrospective Studies · Humans
shelves.balance: Piercing infections of the ear cartilage (auricular perichondritis) have never been tested in a randomised trial; everything known comes from case series. In the prospective 50-patient series of Mostafa 2025 (PMID 40583650), ear piercing was the commonest cause (56.0%), Pseudomonas aeruginosa (41.9% of isolates) and Staphylococcus aureus (27.9%) dominated, and 94% resolved completely on culture-guided antibiotics over a mean 14.2 days. In 127 inpatients with refractory disease, Zhang 2024 (PMID 38312521) found Pseudomonas in 49.2% of isolates, high susceptibility to ceftazidime (90.9%) and cefepime (94.6%) but fluoroquinolone susceptibility of only 65.2-67.4%. Klug 2019 (PMID 31079204), 112 Danish patients, found Pseudomonas in 58% of abscess cases but Staphylococcus predominant (49%) without abscess, and no significant outcome difference between Staphylococcus-covering and Pseudomonas-covering regimens in non-abscess cases. The practical reading: treat early, cover Pseudomonas where there is an abscess, a cartilage (high) piercing, or a slow response, and let cultures refine therapy. Because all the evidence is observational, the stamp is capped: PROPOSED POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: Mostafa 2025: piercing was the commonest cause (56%) and 94% of 50 perichondritis cases resolved on culture-guided antibiotics
cards.summary: Mostafa 2025: piercing was the commonest cause (56%) and 94% of 50 perichondritis cases resolved on culture-guided antibiotics
cards.people: 50 consecutive patients with auricular perichondritis at a Bangladesh teaching hospital, July 2022-June 2023; mean age 28.3 years, 60% male
cards.result: Ear piercing was the predisposing factor in 56.0%. Cultures were positive in 86.0%: Pseudomonas aeruginosa 41.9% of isolates, Staphylococcus aureus 27.9%, MRSA 11.6%. Pseudomonas susceptibility to fluoroquinolones was 88.9% and to aminoglycosides 83.3-94.4%. Complete clinical resolution in 94% with mean treatment duration 14.2 +/- 3.8 days; presentation delayed more than 3 days correlated with complications (p=0.023).
cards.watchOut: Single-centre case series with no comparison group; resolution rates reflect culture-guided care in a hospital cohort, not a trial of one antibiotic against another.
cards.source: Mostafa MG, Nuruzzaman M, Khan L, et al. Status of the Microbiological Isolates and Antibiotics Susceptibilities in Patients with Auricular Perichondritis. Mymensingh Med J. 2025. PMID: 40583650. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Zhang 2024: in 127 inpatients with refractory perichondritis, Pseudomonas was 49.2% of isolates and fluoroquinolone susceptibility was only 65.2-67.4%
cards.summary: Zhang 2024: in 127 inpatients with refractory perichondritis, Pseudomonas was 49.2% of isolates and fluoroquinolone susceptibility was only 65.2-67.4%
cards.people: 127 inpatients with refractory auricular perichondritis at a university hospital in eastern China, 2013-2022; mean age 50.6 years
cards.result: Postoperative infection was the commonest identified cause (37.8%), then trauma (18.1%); the cause was undetermined in 37%. Of 61 isolates, 55.7% were gram-negative bacteria, 21.3% gram-positive and 23.0% fungal. Pseudomonas aeruginosa was the most frequent isolate (30/61, 49.2%). Susceptibility: vancomycin 100%, amikacin 100%, cefepime 94.6%, ceftazidime 90.9%, but fluoroquinolones only 65.2-67.4% and falling. 78.7% received an initial regimen covering Pseudomonas; recurrence within 30 days of discharge was 8.5% (6/71).
cards.watchOut: A refractory inpatient population - mostly postoperative, not piercing-related - so its resistance pattern may overstate what a fresh piercing infection faces; piercing-specific cases were not separated out.
cards.source: Zhang X, Zhang Y, Pu C, et al. Etiology, Microbiological Isolates, and Antibiotic Susceptibilities in Inpatients with Refractory Auricular Perichondritis: A 10-Year Retrospective Study. cards.headline: Klug 2019: in non-abscess perichondritis, Staphylococcus cover did as well as Pseudomonas cover on every outcome measured
cards.summary: Klug 2019: in non-abscess perichondritis, Staphylococcus cover did as well as Pseudomonas cover on every outcome measured
cards.people: 112 patients treated for auricular perichondritis in Central Denmark, 1990-2018: 12 with abscess, 100 without
cards.result: Potential pathogens were found in 40 of 55 cultures. Pseudomonas aeruginosa was recovered in 58% of abscess cases; Staphylococcus aureus predominated in non-abscess infections (49%). In non-abscess cases there were no significant differences between Staphylococcus-covering and Pseudomonas-covering regimens for clinical progress (p=0.65), change of therapy (p=0.31), hospital stay (p=0.65), relapse (p=1.00) or sequelae (p=0.38).
cards.watchOut: Retrospective over 28 years with treatment chosen by clinicians, not randomised; abscess cases - where Pseudomonas dominated - still warrant Pseudomonas cover and drainage assessment.

cards.headline: Synthesis: cover Pseudomonas when there is an abscess or a cartilage piercing infection that is not settling; Staphylococcus cover alone performed equally in non-abscess cases
cards.summary: Synthesis: cover Pseudomonas when there is an abscess or a cartilage piercing infection that is not settling; Staphylococcus cover alone performed equally in non-abscess cases
cards.people: Synthesis of the 3 carded observational studies: 50 + 127 + 112 patients
cards.result: No randomised trials exist. Across the series, Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Staphylococcus aureus are the dominant organisms; resolution was 94% with culture-guided therapy (Mostafa 2025), recurrence 8.5% after discharge in refractory inpatients (Zhang 2024), and no outcome difference between Staphylococcus-only and Pseudomonas-covering regimens in non-abscess disease (Klug 2019).
cards.watchOut: All evidence is observational, so the stamp is capped at POSSIBLE; fluoroquinolone resistance varies by place and era (88.9% susceptible in Bangladesh 2022-23 vs 65.2-67.4% in the Chinese inpatient series), so local culture results should steer the final choice.
cards.source: Synthesis of Mostafa 2025 (PMID 40583650), Zhang 2024 (PMID 38312521) and Klug 2019 (PMID 31079204).

shelves.title: Nirmatrelvir-ritonavir (Paxlovid) for established long COVID: three randomised trials found no significant benefit on symptoms
shelves.question: Does nirmatrelvir-ritonavir (Paxlovid) help people who already have long COVID?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Antiviral Agents / therapeutic use · COVID-19 Drug Treatment · Double-Blind Method · Humans · Post-Acute COVID-19 Syndrome · Ritonavir / therapeutic use · SARS-CoV-2 · Severity of Illness Index · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: BOUNDARY: metformin to prevent long COVID after early COVID-19 (COVID-OUT) is homed on shelf #1935 and is not re-carded here; this shelf is about treating established long COVID with an antiviral. Three randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials tested nirmatrelvir-ritonavir in established long COVID, and all three found no significant benefit. Geng 2024 (STOP-PASC; PMID 38848477; NCT05576662) randomised 155 adults (102 nirmatrelvir-ritonavir vs 53 placebo-ritonavir) to 15 days of treatment, 300/100 mg twice daily, a mean 17.5 months after infection: there was no statistically significant difference in the pooled severity of 6 core symptoms at 10 weeks, nor in patient global impression, summative symptom scores or PROMIS fatigue, dyspnea, cognitive or physical function; adverse events were similar and mostly low grade. Sawano 2025 (PAX LC; PMID 40188838; NCT05668091) enrolled 100 adults (49 vs 51) for 15 days: the adjusted change in PROMIS-29 Physical Health Summary Score to day 28 was 0.45 (-0.93 to 1.83) on nirmatrelvir-ritonavir vs 1.01 (-0.30 to 2.31) on placebo, an adjusted mean difference of -0.55 (95% CI -2.32 to 1.21; p=0.54); drug-related adverse events were 35/46 (76%) vs 27/49 (55%), mostly dysgeusia; there were no deaths or serious adverse events to week 6. Baden 2026 (RECOVER-VITAL; PMID 42673984; NCT05595369), the largest trial, randomised 964 people (959 in the modified intention-to-treat population) across 69 US sites into cognitive, autonomic and exercise phenotypes, testing 15 days and 25 days of active drug against placebo: there was no statistically significant benefit for any phenotype on its primary endpoint - adjusted differences vs placebo for the 25-day course were 3.2% (95% CI -10.4 to 16.8, p=0.65) for cognitive, -6.4% (-18.5 to 5.7, p=0.30) for autonomic and -7.8% (-19.5 to 3.8, p=0.19) for exercise phenotypes; there were no deaths, and 52 serious adverse events in 42 (4%) of 963 participants. Three null trials, including one of nearly a thousand people: the treatment made no difference. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (the treatment made no difference).

cards.headline: Geng 2024 (STOP-PASC): 15 days of nirmatrelvir-ritonavir made no significant difference to long COVID symptoms in 155 adults
cards.summary: Geng 2024 (STOP-PASC): 15 days of nirmatrelvir-ritonavir made no significant difference to long COVID symptoms in 155 adults
cards.people: 155 adults with moderate-to-severe postacute sequelae of SARS-CoV-2 for 3 months or longer (102 nirmatrelvir-ritonavir vs 53 placebo-ritonavir), mean 17.5 months since infection, 59% female, 153 of 155 vaccinated
cards.result: Nirmatrelvir-ritonavir 300/100 mg twice daily for 15 days. There was no statistically significant difference in the pooled severity of 6 core symptoms (fatigue, brain fog, shortness of breath, body aches, gastrointestinal symptoms, cardiovascular symptoms) at 10 weeks, nor in Patient Global Impression of Severity or Change, summative symptom scores, or PROMIS fatigue, dyspnea, cognitive function and physical function. Adverse event rates were similar in both groups and mostly low grade.
cards.watchOut: A mostly vaccinated cohort with protracted symptoms (mean 17.5 months) - the result speaks to established, long-standing long COVID, not to early treatment.
cards.source: Geng LN, Bonilla H, Hedlin H, et al. Nirmatrelvir-Ritonavir and Symptoms in Adults With Postacute Sequelae of SARS-CoV-2 Infection: The STOP-PASC Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA Intern Med. 2024. PMID: 38848477. Registry ID: NCT05576662. cards.summary: Sawano 2025 (PAX LC): 15 days of nirmatrelvir-ritonavir did not improve physical health scores in 100 adults with long COVID
cards.people: 100 adults with long COVID symptoms starting within 4 weeks of infection and persisting at least 12 weeks (49 nirmatrelvir-ritonavir vs 51 placebo-ritonavir), decentralised trial across the USA
cards.result: Adjusted change in PROMIS-29 Physical Health Summary Score from baseline to day 28 was 0.45 (-0.93 to 1.83) in the nirmatrelvir-ritonavir group and 1.01 (-0.30 to 2.31) in the placebo-ritonavir group - adjusted mean difference -0.55 (95% CI -2.32 to 1.21; p=0.54). cards.headline: Baden 2026 (RECOVER-VITAL): in 959 people, neither 15 nor 25 days of nirmatrelvir-ritonavir helped any long COVID phenotype
cards.summary: Baden 2026 (RECOVER-VITAL): in 959 people, neither 15 nor 25 days of nirmatrelvir-ritonavir helped any long COVID phenotype
cards.people: 964 adults randomly allocated (959 in the modified intention-to-treat population) at 69 US sites, split into cognitive (332), autonomic (334) and exercise (332) phenotypes; median age 49 years, 67% female
cards.result: Arms were 15 days active + 10 days placebo, 25 days active, or 25 days placebo-ritonavir. No statistically significant benefit for any phenotype on primary endpoints. Adjusted differences vs placebo: cognitive 3.2% (95% CI -10.4 to 16.8, p=0.65) for 25 days and -2.2% (-15.5 to 11.1, p=0.74) for 15 days; autonomic -6.4% (-18.5 to 5.7, p=0.30) for 25 days and -0.1% (-12.5 to 12.3, p=0.99) for 15 days; exercise -7.8% (-19.5 to 3.8, p=0.19) for 25 days and 0.9% (-11.4 to 13.2, p=0.88) for 15 days. No differences in secondary endpoints; no deaths; 52 serious adverse events in 42 (4%) of 963 participants.

cards.headline: Synthesis: in three randomised trials, nirmatrelvir-ritonavir made no significant difference to established long COVID
cards.summary: Synthesis: in three randomised trials, nirmatrelvir-ritonavir made no significant difference to established long COVID
cards.people: Synthesis of the 3 carded randomised trials: 155 + 100 + 959 people with established long COVID
cards.result: No significant benefit on pooled symptom severity (Geng 2024), on PROMIS-29 physical health (adjusted difference -0.55, p=0.54; Sawano 2025), or on any of three phenotype-specific primary endpoints at 15 or 25 days (Baden 2026). The drug was generally safe; dysgeusia was the main extra adverse event (76% vs 55% in PAX LC).
cards.watchOut: These trials test an antiviral for established, months-old long COVID; they say nothing about early antiviral treatment of acute COVID-19 or about prevention, which is homed on shelf #1935.
cards.source: Synthesis of Geng 2024 (PMID 38848477), Sawano 2025 (PMID 40188838) and Baden 2026 (PMID 42673984).

shelves.title: MERS: ribavirin plus interferon has never been shown to cut deaths — in the largest cohort 90-day mortality was 73.6% with it versus 61.5% without, and identical after adjustment (adjusted odds ratio 1.03)
shelves.question: In people with Middle East respiratory syndrome (MERS), does ribavirin plus interferon improve survival compared with supportive care alone?
shelves.mesh: Antiviral Agents / pharmacology · Antiviral Agents / therapeutic use · Coronavirus Infections / drug therapy · Coronavirus Infections / mortality · Coronavirus Infections / virology · Female · Humans · Interferons / pharmacology · Interferons / therapeutic use · Male · Middle East Respiratory Syndrome Coronavirus · Risk Factors · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: No randomised trial of any MERS treatment has ever reported. Omrani 2014 (PMID: 25278221; Registry ID: none in the record), a single-centre retrospective cohort of ventilated patients, found 14-day survival of 70% (14/20) with ribavirin plus pegylated interferon alfa-2a versus 29% (7/24) with supportive care alone, but by 28 days the gap had closed (30% versus 17% survived). The largest study, Arabi 2020 (PMID: 31925415; Registry ID: none in the record), covering 349 critically ill patients in 14 Saudi hospitals with adjustment for time-varying confounders, found ribavirin/interferon was not associated with 90-day mortality (adjusted odds ratio 1.03, 95% CI 0.73 to 1.44) or faster viral clearance. The Morra 2018 systematic review and meta-analysis (PMID: 29664167; Registry ID: none in the record) likewise found case fatality of 71% in both the interferon-treated and supportive-only groups. All evidence is observational, so any stamp is capped at POSSIBLE; the adjusted data show no mortality effect. Proposed stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence) (the treatment made no difference to mortality in the adjusted analyses).

cards.headline: Omrani 2014: 14-day survival 70% with ribavirin plus interferon versus 29% without — but 28-day survival no longer differed (30% versus 17%)
cards.summary: Omrani 2014: 14-day survival 70% with ribavirin plus interferon versus 29% without — but 28-day survival no longer differed (30% versus 17%)
cards.people: Adults (aged 16 years or over) with laboratory-confirmed MERS-CoV pneumonia needing ventilation at one Riyadh hospital; n=44 (20 treated, 24 comparator)
cards.result: Survival at 14 days was 70% (14/20) in the ribavirin plus pegylated interferon alfa-2a group versus 29% (7/24) with supportive care alone (p=0.004). At 28 days survival was 30% (6/20) versus 17% (4/24) (p=0.54). Haemoglobin fell more in the treated group (4.32 g/L [SD 2.47] versus 2.14 g/L [1.90] as printed in the record; p=0.002).
cards.watchOut: Not randomised: treatment was given only to patients diagnosed after 16 September 2013, so era and selection effects can explain the early survival gap; baseline neutrophil counts also differed between groups.
cards.source: Omrani AS, Saad MM, Baig K, Bahloul A, Abdul-Matin M, Alaidaroos AY, Almakhlafi GA, Albarrak MM, Memish ZA, Albarrak AM. Ribavirin and interferon alfa-2a for severe Middle East respiratory syndrome coronavirus infection: a retrospective cohort study. Lancet Infect Dis. 2014. PMID: 25278221. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Arabi 2020: after adjustment, ribavirin/interferon was not associated with 90-day mortality (adjusted odds ratio 1.03) or faster viral clearance
cards.summary: Arabi 2020: after adjustment, ribavirin/interferon was not associated with 90-day mortality (adjusted odds ratio 1.03) or faster viral clearance
cards.people: Critically ill patients with laboratory-confirmed MERS at 14 hospitals in Saudi Arabia, 2012-2018; n=349 (144 received ribavirin and/or interferon, 205 did not)
cards.result: Crude 90-day mortality was 73.6% (106/144) with ribavirin/interferon versus 61.5% (126/205) without (p=.02). After marginal-structural-model adjustment for baseline and time-varying confounders, the adjusted odds ratio for 90-day mortality was 1.03 (95% CI 0.73 to 1.44; p=.87), and the adjusted hazard ratio for MERS-CoV RNA clearance was 0.65 (95% CI 0.30 to 1.44; p=.29).
cards.watchOut: Observational: treated patients were sicker before adjustment (crude mortality was higher in the treated group), and residual confounding cannot be excluded; no patient received interferon beta-1b, the agent used in the one randomised protocol (MIRACLE).
cards.source: Arabi YM, Shalhoub S, Mandourah Y, Al-Hameed F, Al-Omari A, Al Qasim E, Jose J, Alraddadi B, Almotairi A, Al Khatib K, et al. cards.headline: Morra 2018: pooled case fatality was 71% in the interferon group and exactly 71% with supportive treatment only
cards.summary: Morra 2018: pooled case fatality was 71% in the interferon group and exactly 71% with supportive treatment only
cards.people: Patients with MERS in the published treatment studies pooled by this systematic review and meta-analysis; N not documented in the record
cards.result: Case fatality was 71% in the ribavirin-plus-interferon group and 71% in the supportive-treatment-only group. Mean survival from illness onset to death was longer in the interferon group (46.6 days, 95% CI 30.5 to 62.6) than in the supportive-only group (18.8 days, 95% CI 10.3 to 27.4; p=.001). Chronic renal disease, diabetes and hypertension each increased mortality risk (p<.05).
cards.watchOut: The pooled studies are case series and small cohorts with no randomised trials; the longer time-to-death in treated patients may reflect who lived long enough to be treated rather than a treatment effect.
cards.source: Morra ME, Van Thanh L, Kamel MG, Ghazy AA, Altibi AMA, Dat LM, Thy TNX, Vuong NL, Mostafa MR, Ahmed SI, et al. cards.headline: Synthesis: no MERS treatment has randomised evidence; ribavirin plus interferon shows no adjusted mortality benefit
cards.summary: Synthesis: no MERS treatment has randomised evidence; ribavirin plus interferon shows no adjusted mortality benefit
cards.people: All carded evidence: one single-centre cohort (n=44), one 14-hospital cohort (n=349), and one systematic review of the published treatment literature
cards.result: The only early positive signal (Omrani 2014, 14-day survival) disappeared by 28 days and in the larger adjusted analysis (Arabi 2020, adjusted odds ratio 1.03, 95% CI 0.73 to 1.44); pooled case fatality was identical at 71% with and without interferon (Morra 2018). Supportive care remains the only proven treatment.
cards.watchOut: All evidence is observational, which caps the stamp at POSSIBLE; the randomised MIRACLE trial of lopinavir-ritonavir plus interferon beta-1b has a published protocol but no results were carded this session.
cards.source: Synthesis of Omrani 2014 (PMID: 25278221), Arabi 2020 (PMID: 31925415) and Morra 2018 (PMID: 29664167).

shelves.title: Necrotising fasciitis: urgent surgery and antibiotics are the treatment — adjunctive IVIG made no difference in the blinded INSTINCT trial (physical function 36 versus 31, p=0.81) or across 4,127 US hospital cases (mortality 27.3% versus 23.6%; adjusted odds ratio 1.00)
shelves.question: In people with necrotising fasciitis (necrotising soft-tissue infection), does adjunctive intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) — on top of urgent surgical debridement and antibiotics — improve survival or recovery?
shelves.mesh: Acute Kidney Injury / chemically induced · Aged · Critical Care / methods · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Immunoglobulins, Intravenous / administration & dosage · Immunoglobulins, Intravenous / adverse effects · Immunologic Factors / administration & dosage · Infusions, Intravenous · Intensive Care Units · Intention to Treat Analysis · Male · Middle Aged · Necrosis · Quality of Life · Self Report · Soft Tissue Infections / drug therapy · Soft Tissue Infections / mortality · Soft Tissue Infections / pathology · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: The proven treatment is immediate surgical debridement plus broad-spectrum antibiotics; the contested adjunct is IVIG. Madsen 2017 (INSTINCT; PMID: 28421246; Registry ID: NCT02111161), the only blinded placebo-controlled trial in necrotising soft-tissue infection (n=100), found no effect of IVIG 25 g daily for 3 days on 6-month physical function (median scores 36 versus 31; adjusted difference 1, 95% CI -7 to 10; p=0.81). Kadri 2017 (PMID: 28034881; Registry ID: none in the record), a propensity-matched analysis of 4,127 debrided necrotising fasciitis cases with shock, found in-hospital mortality of 27.3% with IVIG versus 23.6% without (adjusted odds ratio 1.00, 95% CI 0.55 to 1.83), including in the toxic-shock/streptococcal subgroup. Darenberg 2003 (PMID: 12884156; Registry ID: none in the record), a blinded trial in streptococcal toxic shock syndrome stopped after 21 patients, found 28-day mortality 3.6-fold higher on placebo without reaching significance, with faster organ-failure improvement on IVIG. Proposed stamp: SPLIT (IVIG in unselected necrotising soft-tissue infection: (the treatment made no difference) in the blinded RCT and the large matched analysis · IVIG in streptococcal toxic shock syndrome: unproven signal from one 21-patient trial stopped early).

cards.headline: Madsen 2017 (INSTINCT): IVIG did not improve 6-month physical function (median score 36 versus 31; adjusted difference 1, p=0.81)
cards.summary: Madsen 2017 (INSTINCT): IVIG did not improve 6-month physical function (median score 36 versus 31; adjusted difference 1, p=0.81)
cards.people: ICU patients with necrotising soft-tissue infection randomised 1:1 to IVIG or saline placebo; n=100 (87 in the primary analysis)
cards.result: Median SF-36 physical component scores at 6 months were 36 (IQR 0-43) with IVIG 25 g daily for 3 days versus 31 (IQR 0-47) with placebo; mean adjusted difference 1 (95% CI -7 to 10; p=0.81). Results were the same in per-protocol, subgroup and post hoc analyses. The tested product was Privigen (CSL Behring), as named in the publication.
cards.watchOut: The IVIG dose (25 g/day) was lower than in earlier streptococcal toxic shock reports, one pre-randomisation dose was allowed, and the trial mixed organisms — a streptococcal-only benefit is not excluded.
cards.source: Madsen MB, Hjortrup PB, Hansen MB, Lange T, Norrby-Teglund A, Hyldegaard O, Perner A. cards.headline: Kadri 2017: across 4,127 US cases of necrotising fasciitis with shock, IVIG did not change mortality (27.3% versus 23.6%; adjusted odds ratio 1.00)
cards.summary: Kadri 2017: across 4,127 US cases of necrotising fasciitis with shock, IVIG did not change mortality (27.3% versus 23.6%; adjusted odds ratio 1.00)
cards.people: Adults with necrotizing fasciitis and vasopressor-dependent shock undergoing debridement at 130 US hospitals, 2010-2014; n=4,127 (164 received IVIG; 161 matched pairs analysed)
cards.result: Only 4% (164/4,127) received IVIG. In-hospital mortality in matched groups was 27.3% with IVIG versus 23.6% without (adjusted odds ratio 1.00, 95% CI 0.55 to 1.83; p=.99). Early IVIG (within 2 days) did not alter the result, nor did the subgroup coded for toxic shock syndrome, group A Streptococcus and/or Staphylococcus aureus (59/868 [6.8%] received IVIG; p=.63). Median length of stay was 26 days in both groups.
cards.watchOut: Administrative data with coding-based case definition; IVIG recipients were younger but more severely ill, and propensity matching cannot remove confounding by indication entirely.
cards.source: Kadri SS, Swihart BJ, Bonne SL, Hohmann SF, Hennessy LV, Louras P, Evans HL, Rhee C, Suffredini AF, Hooper DC, Follmann DA, Bulger EM, Danner RL. Impact of Intravenous Immunoglobulin on Survival in Necrotizing Fasciitis With Vasopressor-Dependent Shock: A Propensity Score-Matched Analysis From 130 US Hospitals. Clin Infect Dis. 2017. cards.headline: Darenberg 2003: in streptococcal toxic shock, 28-day mortality was 3.6-fold higher on placebo — in a trial stopped at 21 patients
cards.summary: Darenberg 2003: in streptococcal toxic shock, 28-day mortality was 3.6-fold higher on placebo — in a trial stopped at 21 patients
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial, terminated early (Darenberg 2003)
cards.people: Patients with streptococcal toxic shock syndrome (the toxin-mediated syndrome that accompanies streptococcal necrotising fasciitis) in a European multicentre trial; n=21 (10 IVIG, 11 placebo)
cards.result: The trial was terminated early for slow recruitment. Mortality at 28 days was 3.6-fold higher in the placebo group than the IVIG group, without reaching statistical significance. Organ-failure (SOFA) scores fell significantly more in the IVIG group at days 2 (p=.02) and 3 (p=.04), and plasma neutralising activity against streptococcal superantigens rose after IVIG (p=.03).
cards.watchOut: Only 21 patients and stopped early, so the mortality difference is compatible with chance; the population is streptococcal toxic shock syndrome rather than all necrotising fasciitis.
cards.source: Darenberg J, Ihendyane N, Sjölin J, Aufwerber E, Haidl S, Follin P, Andersson J, Norrby-Teglund A; StreptIg Study Group. Intravenous immunoglobulin G therapy in streptococcal toxic shock syndrome: a European randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial. Clin Infect Dis. 2003. PMID: 12884156. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: IVIG has no demonstrated benefit in necrotising soft-tissue infection overall; the streptococcal toxic shock signal rests on one tiny stopped trial
cards.summary: Synthesis: IVIG has no demonstrated benefit in necrotising soft-tissue infection overall; the streptococcal toxic shock signal rests on one tiny stopped trial
cards.people: All carded evidence: one blinded RCT in necrotising soft-tissue infection (n=100), one matched analysis (n=4,127), one stopped RCT in streptococcal toxic shock (n=21)
cards.result: INSTINCT found no functional benefit (adjusted difference 1 point, p=0.81) and Kadri found no mortality benefit (adjusted odds ratio 1.00). Only Darenberg's 21-patient streptococcal toxic shock trial pointed the other way, without statistical significance. Urgent debridement and antibiotics remain the proven treatment in every carded study.
cards.watchOut: Hyperbaric oxygen and clindamycin adjunct questions were not carded this session; the IVIG question in pure streptococcal toxic shock remains genuinely unsettled because a definitive trial has never been completed.
cards.source: Synthesis of Madsen 2017 (PMID: 28421246), Kadri 2017 (PMID: 28034881) and Darenberg 2003 (PMID: 12884156).
