shelves.title: Q fever: doxycycline settles acute pneumonia fever about a day faster than erythromycin (3 vs 4.3 days, 48 patients); chronic endocarditis needs 18-24 months of doxycycline plus hydroxychloroquine on observational data
shelves.question: In people with Q fever, which antibiotic treatments work for acute disease, and what regimen and duration treat chronic Q fever endocarditis?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Double-Blind Method · Doxycycline/therapeutic use · Erythromycin/therapeutic use · Female · Humans · Male · Pneumonia/drug therapy · Pneumonia/etiology · Prospective Studies · Q Fever/complications · Q Fever/drug therapy · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: SPLIT by form of disease. For acute Q fever pneumonia, the one randomised trial (Sobradillo 1992, PMID: 1585291; 48 proven cases) found fever settled faster on doxycycline than erythromycin (3 (1.6) versus 4.3 (2) days) with far fewer side effects (2 versus 11 patients, p less than 0.01), and 47 of 48 chest radiographs were normal by day 40 — the illness is largely self-limiting. For chronic Q fever endocarditis there is no randomised trial: the Marseille comparison (Raoult 1999, PMID: 9927100; 35 patients) found doxycycline plus hydroxychloroquine cured 17 of 21 with a mean treatment duration of 31 months and no relapses beyond 18 months of therapy, versus 7 relapses among 14 on doxycycline plus a quinolone needing a mean 55 months. The 104-patient long-term survey (Million 2010, PMID: 20637694) fixed the optimum at 18 months for native valves and 24 months for prosthetic valves, with treatment under 18 months a relative hazard for relapse of 9.69. PROPOSED SPLIT: doxycycline first for acute disease on one small RCT; the chronic regimen rests entirely on observational referral-centre data and caps at POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: Sobradillo 1992: fever settled in 3 (1.6) days on doxycycline versus 4.3 (2) days on erythromycin, with side effects in 2 versus 11 patients (p less than 0.01), in 48 proven Q fever pneumonias
cards.summary: Sobradillo 1992: fever settled in 3 (1.6) days on doxycycline versus 4.3 (2) days on erythromycin, with side effects in 2 versus 11 patients (p less than 0.01), in 48 proven Q fever pneumonias
cards.people: 82 patients with pneumonia and features suggestive of Q fever randomised double-blind; 48 proved to have Q fever, of whom 23 received doxycycline 100 mg twice daily and 25 erythromycin 500 mg six-hourly, both for 10 days.
cards.result: Fever showed a more rapid reduction in the doxycycline group (3 (1.6) days versus 4.3 (2) days). Side effects were observed in 2 patients receiving doxycycline compared with 11 receiving erythromycin (p less than 0.01). No differences were observed in other clinical or radiological measures; by day 40 the chest radiograph was normal in 47 of 48 patients. The authors concluded most Q fever pneumonia is self-limiting and benign, and doxycycline was more effective than erythromycin.
cards.watchOut: Only the 48 serologically proven cases count, the trial had no placebo arm, and the disease resolved in nearly everyone — the proven gain is about a day less of fever and better tolerability, not survival.
cards.source: Sobradillo V, Zalacain R, Capelastegui A, Uresandi F, Corral J. Antibiotic treatment in pneumonia due to Q fever. Thorax. 1992. PMID: 1585291. cards.headline: Raoult 1999: doxycycline plus hydroxychloroquine cured 17 of 21 endocarditis patients with no relapse beyond 18 months, versus 7 relapses in 14 on doxycycline plus a quinolone
cards.summary: Raoult 1999: doxycycline plus hydroxychloroquine cured 17 of 21 endocarditis patients with no relapse beyond 18 months, versus 7 relapses in 14 on doxycycline plus a quinolone
cards.people: 35 patients (26 men, 9 women) with Q fever endocarditis treated at the Marseille reference centre, January 1987 to December 1997: 14 by the earlier doxycycline-plus-quinolone regimen and 21 by doxycycline plus hydroxychloroquine after May 1991 (a before-and-after comparison, not randomised).
cards.result: On doxycycline plus quinolone: 1 died, 7 relapsed, 1 still treated, 5 cured on that regimen alone; mean duration of therapy for cure 55 months (median 60). On doxycycline plus hydroxychloroquine: 1 died of a surgical complication, 2 still treated, 17 cured, 1 being evaluated; mean duration 31 months (median 26). Two patients treated for 12 months relapsed, but none treated longer than 18 months relapsed. Mortality was 5% on both regimens, with no significant difference in death, valve surgery or tolerance.
cards.watchOut: Sequential eras at one centre, not randomisation: surgical practice, diagnostics and case mix changed over the same decade, so part of the improvement may be era, not regimen. Dutch outbreak cohorts have since questioned how large the hydroxychloroquine advantage is.
cards.source: Raoult D, Houpikian P, Tissot Dupont H, Riss JM, Arditi-Djiane J, Brouqui P. Treatment of Q fever endocarditis: comparison of 2 regimens containing doxycycline and ofloxacin or hydroxychloroquine. Archives of Internal Medicine. 1999. PMID: 9927100. cards.headline: Million 2010: in 104 endocarditis patients, 18 months of doxycycline plus hydroxychloroquine sterilised all but 3 patients' valves; treatment under 18 months carried a relative hazard of relapse of 9.69
cards.summary: Million 2010: in 104 endocarditis patients, 18 months of doxycycline plus hydroxychloroquine sterilised all but 3 patients' valves; treatment under 18 months carried a relative hazard of relapse of 9.69
cards.people: 104 patients diagnosed with Q fever endocarditis at the French National Referral Centre, May 1983 to June 2006, followed for a minimum of 3 years (median follow-up 100 months, range 37-310); 1 was lost to follow-up.
cards.result: 18 months of treatment was sufficient to sterilise the valves of all patients except 3, and 2 years sterilised all except 1. Factors associated with relapse were endocarditis on a prosthetic valve (hazard ratio, a relative measure, 21.3, 95% CI 2.05-221.86, p=0.01) and treatment duration less than 18 months (hazard ratio, relative, 9.69, 95% CI 1.08-86.72, p=0.042). The authors set the optimum duration at 18 months for native valves and 24 months for prosthetic valves, with serological monitoring for at least 5 years.
cards.watchOut: Single referral-centre experience spanning 23 years with no untreated or differently treated control group; the duration thresholds come from within-cohort comparisons, and hazard ratios are relative measures with very wide confidence intervals.

retrospective cohort study (million 2010) 104 patients diagnosed with q fever endocarditis at the french national referral centre, may 1983 to june 2006, followed for a minimum of 3 years (median follow-up 100 months, range 37-310); 1 was lost to follow-up. 18 months of treatment was sufficient to sterilise the valves of all patients except 3, and 2 years sterilised all except 1. factors associated with relapse were endocarditis on a prosthetic valve (hazard ratio, a relative measure, 21.3, 95% ci 2.05-221.86, p=0.01) and treatment duration less than 18 months (hazard ratio, relative, 9.69, 95% ci 1.08-86.72, p=0.042). the authors set the optimum duration at 18 months for native valves and 24 months for prosthetic valves, with serological monitoring for at least 5 years. single referral-centre experience spanning 23 years with no untreated or differently treated control group; the duration thresholds come from within-cohort comparisons, and hazard ratios are relative measures with very wide confidence intervals. million m, thuny f, richet h, raoult d. long-term outcome of q fever endocarditis: a 26-year personal survey. lancet infectious diseases. 2010. pmid: 20637694. registry id: none in the record. mesh: adolescent · adult · aged · aged, 80 and over · antibodies, bacterial/blood · doxycycline/therapeutic use · endocarditis, bacterial/diagnosis · endocarditis, bacterial/mortality · endocarditis, bacterial/therapy · female · humans · immunoglobulin g/blood · male · middle aged · polymerase chain reaction · prognosis · proportional hazards models · q fever/diagnosis · q fever/mortality · q fever/therapy · retrospective studies · treatment outcome

cards.headline: Synthesis: doxycycline for acute Q fever on one small trial; chronic endocarditis treatment is observational only
cards.summary: Synthesis: doxycycline for acute Q fever on one small trial; chronic endocarditis treatment is observational only
cards.people: 48 proven acute cases in the randomised trial; 35 and 104 patients in the two Marseille chronic endocarditis cohorts (the later cohort includes the earlier era's patients).
cards.result: Acute pneumonia: fever 3 versus 4.3 days and side effects 2 versus 11 patients favour doxycycline over erythromycin. Chronic endocarditis: cure in 17 of 21 on doxycycline plus hydroxychloroquine versus 5 of 14 cured without relapse on the older quinolone regimen, and relapse concentrated in those treated under 18 months (relative hazard 9.69).
cards.watchOut: Proposed stamp: SPLIT (acute: POSSIBLE benefit for doxycycline over erythromycin · chronic: POSSIBLE on observational evidence only). No randomised trial of chronic Q fever treatment exists; a 2024 review explicitly calls for an international RCT. Post-exposure prophylaxis and Q fever fatigue syndrome are separate questions, not covered here.
cards.source: Synthesis of Sobradillo 1992 (PMID: 1585291), Raoult 1999 (PMID: 9927100) and Million 2010 (PMID: 20637694), carded above.

shelves.title: Ceftazidime-avibactam: non-inferior to carbapenems in all three approved uses — cUTI cure/eradication 71.2% vs 64.5%, cIAI cure 81.6% vs 85.1%, pneumonia cure 68.8% vs 73.0% in the phase 3 trials
shelves.question: In adults with complicated urinary tract infection, complicated intra-abdominal infection, or hospital-acquired/ventilator-associated pneumonia, is ceftazidime-avibactam as effective as a carbapenem?
shelves.mesh: MeSH: not captured from the record this session
shelves.balance: Across its three approved uses, ceftazidime-avibactam (Avycaz in the US; the tested combination of ceftazidime with the beta-lactamase inhibitor avibactam) was non-inferior to a carbapenem in large double-blind phase 3 trials. In cUTI (RECAPTURE; Wagenlehner 2016, PMID: 27313268; NCT01595438/NCT01599806; 1,033 randomised), symptomatic resolution at day 5 was 70.2% versus 66.2% on doripenem (difference 4.0%, 95% CI -2.39 to 10.42) and combined symptomatic resolution with microbiological eradication at test of cure was 71.2% versus 64.5% (difference 6.7%, 95% CI 0.30 to 13.12), with microbiological eradication itself higher on ceftazidime-avibactam (77.4% vs 71.0%). In cIAI (RECLAIM; Mazuski 2016, PMID: 26962078; NCT01499290/NCT01500239; 1,066 patients, ceftazidime-avibactam plus metronidazole versus meropenem), clinical cure in the microbiologically modified intention-to-treat population was 81.6% versus 85.1% (difference -3.5%, 95% CI -8.64 to 1.58), non-inferior in all analysis populations, with cure of 83.0% versus 85.9% in ceftazidime-resistant infections. In nosocomial pneumonia including VAP (REPROVE; Torres 2018, PMID: 29254862; NCT01808092; 879 randomised), clinical cure was 68.8% versus 73.0% on meropenem in the clinically modified intention-to-treat population (difference -4.2%, 95% CI -10.8 to 2.5), meeting non-inferiority, though serious adverse events were numerically more frequent on ceftazidime-avibactam (19% vs 13%). A pooled analysis of the phase 3 programme in beta-lactamase-producing pathogens (PMID: 37700689; 813 patients) found identical clinical cure rates of 88.1% in both arms among non-metallo-beta-lactamase producers. The drug has no activity against metallo-beta-lactamase producers, and none of these trials enrolled the carbapenem-resistant infections for which it is now mainly reserved. PROPOSED STAMP: LIKELY (non-inferior to carbapenems for cUTI, cIAI and HAP/VAP in the trial populations).

cards.headline: Wagenlehner 2016 (RECAPTURE): ceftazidime-avibactam non-inferior to doripenem in cUTI — combined cure/eradication 71.2% versus 64.5%
cards.summary: Wagenlehner 2016 (RECAPTURE): ceftazidime-avibactam non-inferior to doripenem in cUTI — combined cure/eradication 71.2% versus 64.5%
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised double-blind non-inferiority trial programme (Wagenlehner 2016)
cards.people: Hospitalised adults with suspected or confirmed complicated urinary tract infection including acute pyelonephritis; 1,033 randomised 1:1 to ceftazidime-avibactam 2000 mg/500 mg every 8 hours or doripenem 500 mg every 8 hours (renally adjusted, with optional oral switch after 5 days); 393 and 417 patients were eligible for the primary efficacy analyses, and 19.6% had ceftazidime-non-susceptible baseline pathogens.
cards.result: Non-inferiority was shown for both FDA co-primary endpoints: patient-reported symptomatic resolution at day 5 in 276 of 393 (70.2%) on ceftazidime-avibactam versus 276 of 417 (66.2%) on doripenem (difference 4.0% [95% CI -2.39% to 10.42%]); and combined symptomatic resolution plus microbiological eradication at test of cure in 280 of 393 (71.2%) versus 269 of 417 (64.5%) (difference 6.7% [95% CI 0.30% to 13.12%]). Microbiological eradication at test of cure (the EMA primary endpoint) occurred in 304 of 393 (77.4%) versus 296 of 417 (71.0%) (difference 6.4% [95% CI 0.33% to 12.36%]). The safety profile was consistent with ceftazidime alone.
cards.watchOut: A non-inferiority design against doripenem in mostly susceptible infections: it shows ceftazidime-avibactam works in ordinary cUTI, not that it rescues carbapenem-resistant infection, which the trial population largely did not have.
cards.source: Wagenlehner FM, Sobel JD, Newell P, et al. Ceftazidime-avibactam versus doripenem for the treatment of complicated urinary tract infections, including acute pyelonephritis: RECAPTURE, a phase 3 randomized trial program. Clinical Infectious Diseases. 2016. PMID: 27313268. Registry ID: NCT01595438; NCT01599806. MeSH: not captured from the record this session.

cards.headline: Mazuski 2016 (RECLAIM): ceftazidime-avibactam plus metronidazole non-inferior to meropenem in cIAI — clinical cure 81.6% versus 85.1%
cards.summary: Mazuski 2016 (RECLAIM): ceftazidime-avibactam plus metronidazole non-inferior to meropenem in cIAI — clinical cure 81.6% versus 85.1%
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised double-blind non-inferiority trial programme (Mazuski 2016)
cards.people: 1,066 men and women with complicated intra-abdominal infection in two identical randomised double-blind phase 3 studies, comparing ceftazidime-avibactam plus metronidazole with meropenem; primary endpoint clinical cure at the test-of-cure visit 28-35 days after randomisation.
cards.result: Ceftazidime-avibactam plus metronidazole was non-inferior to meropenem in all primary analysis populations. Clinical cure rates (ceftazidime-avibactam plus metronidazole versus meropenem) were: microbiologically modified intention-to-treat 81.6% and 85.1% (difference -3.5%; 95% CI -8.64 to 1.58); modified intention-to-treat 82.5% and 84.9% (-2.4%; -6.90 to 2.10); clinically evaluable 91.7% and 92.5% (-0.8%; -4.61 to 2.89). For ceftazidime-resistant infections, cure was 83.0% versus 85.9%, similar to the regimen's 82.0% against ceftazidime-susceptible infections. No new safety concerns were observed.
cards.watchOut: Point estimates favour meropenem slightly in every population, within the non-inferiority margin; anaerobic cover came from added metronidazole, so the result is for the combination regimen, not ceftazidime-avibactam alone.
cards.source: Mazuski JE, Gasink LB, Armstrong J, et al. Efficacy and safety of ceftazidime-avibactam plus metronidazole versus meropenem in the treatment of complicated intra-abdominal infection: results from a randomized, controlled, double-blind, phase 3 program. cards.headline: Torres 2018 (REPROVE): ceftazidime-avibactam non-inferior to meropenem in nosocomial pneumonia — clinical cure 68.8% versus 73.0%, with more serious adverse events (19% vs 13%)
cards.summary: Torres 2018 (REPROVE): ceftazidime-avibactam non-inferior to meropenem in nosocomial pneumonia — clinical cure 68.8% versus 73.0%, with more serious adverse events (19% vs 13%)
cards.people: Adults with nosocomial pneumonia including ventilator-associated pneumonia at 136 centres in 23 countries; 879 randomised to ceftazidime-avibactam 2000-500 mg every 8 hours or meropenem 1000 mg every 8 hours for 7-14 days; 726 in the clinically modified intention-to-treat population and 355 in the microbiologically modified population (Klebsiella pneumoniae 37%, Pseudomonas aeruginosa 30%; 28% ceftazidime-non-susceptible).
cards.result: In the clinically modified intention-to-treat population, 245 of 356 patients (68.8%) on ceftazidime-avibactam were clinically cured versus 270 of 370 (73.0%) on meropenem (difference -4.2% [95% CI -10.8 to 2.5]); in the clinically evaluable population, cure was 199 of 257 (77.4%) versus 211 of 270 (78.1%) (difference -0.7% [95% CI -7.9 to 6.4]) — non-inferiority met. Adverse events occurred in 302 of 405 (75%) versus 299 of 403 (74%); serious adverse events in 75 (19%) versus 54 (13%).
cards.watchOut: Cure rates again sit numerically below meropenem, and the serious-adverse-event imbalance (19% vs 13%) was not explained in the abstract; non-inferiority was judged against a wide margin in a population where most pathogens were not carbapenem-resistant.
cards.source: Torres A, Zhong N, Pachl J, et al. Ceftazidime-avibactam versus meropenem in nosocomial pneumonia, including ventilator-associated pneumonia (REPROVE): a randomised, double-blind, phase 3 non-inferiority trial. The Lancet Infectious Diseases. 2018. PMID: 29254862. Registry ID: NCT01808092. MeSH: not captured from the record this session.

cards.headline: Pooled phase 3 analysis 2023: in beta-lactamase-producing pathogens without metallo-enzymes, clinical cure was identical at 88.1% in both arms
cards.summary: Pooled phase 3 analysis 2023: in beta-lactamase-producing pathogens without metallo-enzymes, clinical cure was identical at 88.1% in both arms
cards.type: Post hoc pooled analysis of five phase 3 randomised trials (2023)
cards.people: Post hoc pooled analysis of five phase 3 trials (RECLAIM/RECLAIM 3, REPRISE, RECAPTURE, REPROVE): 813 adults with cIAI, cUTI/pyelonephritis or nosocomial pneumonia and at least one beta-lactamase-producing Gram-negative baseline pathogen (389 ceftazidime-avibactam, 424 comparator, mostly carbapenems); 792 had no metallo-beta-lactamase producers. Commonest pathogens: Escherichia coli (n=381), Klebsiella pneumoniae (n=261), Pseudomonas aeruginosa (n=53).
cards.result: In the pooled non-metallo-beta-lactamase beta-lactamase-producing population, clinical cure rates were 88.1% (334/379) for ceftazidime-avibactam and 88.1% (364/413) for comparators; favourable microbiological response rates were 76.5% (290/379) and 68.8% (284/413) respectively. The safety profile was consistent with previous observations. The authors concluded the analysis supports efficacy against ESBL, AmpC and serine carbapenemase producers.
cards.watchOut: Post hoc and pooled across different infections and comparators; it excludes metallo-beta-lactamase producers — ceftazidime-avibactam has no activity against them — and cannot substitute for trials in carbapenem-resistant infection.

cards.headline: Synthesis: ceftazidime-avibactam matched carbapenems in all three approved uses in large blinded trials, with cure rates a few points lower in cIAI and pneumonia and a serious-adverse-event imbalance in pneumonia
cards.summary: Synthesis: ceftazidime-avibactam matched carbapenems in all three approved uses in large blinded trials, with cure rates a few points lower in cIAI and pneumonia and a serious-adverse-event imbalance in pneumonia
cards.people: Synthesis of the 4 carded records: three phase 3 non-inferiority programmes (1,033 cUTI; 1,066 cIAI; 879 pneumonia patients) and a pooled analysis of 813 patients with beta-lactamase-producing pathogens.
cards.result: cUTI: combined cure/eradication 71.2% vs 64.5% versus doripenem. cIAI (with metronidazole): cure 81.6% vs 85.1% versus meropenem. HAP/VAP: cure 68.8% vs 73.0% versus meropenem, serious adverse events 19% vs 13%. Pooled beta-lactamase-producer cure: 88.1% in both arms, excluding metallo-beta-lactamase producers, against which the drug is inactive. Proposed stamp: LIKELY (non-inferior to carbapenems for cUTI, cIAI and HAP/VAP in the populations trialled).
cards.watchOut: Every trial is a non-inferiority comparison in largely carbapenem-susceptible infection; effectiveness against KPC-producing carbapenem-resistant organisms rests on the pooled/microbiological data and observational experience, not on a randomised trial in resistant infection.
cards.source: Synthesis of Wagenlehner 2016 (PMID: 27313268), Mazuski 2016 (PMID: 26962078), Torres 2018 (PMID: 29254862) and the pooled phase 3 analysis 2023 (PMID: 37700689), carded above.

shelves.title: Ceftolozane-tazobactam: non-inferior to meropenem in abdominal infection (cure 83.0% vs 87.3%) and ventilated pneumonia (28-day mortality 24.0% vs 25.3%), and ahead of levofloxacin in urinary infection (composite cure 76.9% vs 68.4%) — parity with standard agents, not superiority
shelves.question: In adults with complicated intra-abdominal infection (cIAI), complicated urinary tract infection (cUTI) or ventilated Gram-negative nosocomial pneumonia, is ceftolozane-tazobactam non-inferior to standard comparator antibiotics?

shelves.balance: Three double-blind phase 3 non-inferiority trials cover the approved uses. ASPECT-cIAI (Solomkin 2015, PMID: 25670823; NCT01445665 and NCT01445678): ceftolozane-tazobactam plus metronidazole vs meropenem in cIAI — clinical cure 83.0% (323/389) vs 87.3% (364/417), weighted difference -4.2% (95% CI -8.91 to 0.54), meeting the 10% margin; cure in ESBL-producing Enterobacteriaceae 95.8% (23/24) vs 88.5% (23/26). ASPECT-cUTI (Wagenlehner 2015, PMID: 25931244; NCT01345929 and NCT01345955): composite cure 76.9% (306/398) vs 68.4% (275/402) on high-dose levofloxacin, difference 95% CI 2.3 to 14.6 — the one superiority signal, against a comparator many enrolled pathogens already resisted. ASPECT-NP (Kollef 2019, PMID: 31563344; NCT02070757): 28-day mortality 24.0% (87/362) vs 25.3% (92/364) on meropenem and clinical cure 54% vs 53% in ventilated nosocomial pneumonia. Non-inferiority to an active comparator is parity, not proof of added benefit. Proposed stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit).

cards.headline: Solomkin 2015 (ASPECT-cIAI): ceftolozane-tazobactam plus metronidazole non-inferior to meropenem — cure 83.0% vs 87.3%
cards.summary: Solomkin 2015 (ASPECT-cIAI): ceftolozane-tazobactam plus metronidazole non-inferior to meropenem — cure 83.0% vs 87.3%
cards.people: Hospitalised adults with complicated intra-abdominal infection; 806 patients in the microbiological intent-to-treat population (389 ceftolozane-tazobactam plus metronidazole, 417 meropenem), treated intravenously for 4-14 days.
cards.result: Clinical cure at test of cure: 83.0% (323/389) on ceftolozane-tazobactam plus metronidazole vs 87.3% (364/417) on meropenem (weighted difference -4.2%; 95% CI -8.91 to 0.54), meeting the prespecified 10% non-inferiority margin. Microbiologically evaluable cure: 94.2% (259/275) vs 94.7% (304/321). In ESBL-producing Enterobacteriaceae, cure was 95.8% (23/24) vs 88.5% (23/26). Adverse events 44.0% vs 42.7%.
cards.watchOut: Non-inferiority against meropenem at a 10% margin: the point estimate favoured meropenem by 4.2 points. The trial shows the combination is an acceptable alternative, not a better treatment.

cards.headline: Wagenlehner 2015 (ASPECT-cUTI): composite cure 76.9% vs 68.4% on levofloxacin — non-inferior, with superiority indicated
cards.summary: Wagenlehner 2015 (ASPECT-cUTI): composite cure 76.9% vs 68.4% on levofloxacin — non-inferior, with superiority indicated
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, double-dummy, phase 3 non-inferiority trial (Wagenlehner 2015)
cards.people: 1,083 hospital inpatients aged 18 or older with pyuria and complicated lower urinary tract infection or pyelonephritis; 800 in the microbiological modified intent-to-treat population (398 ceftolozane-tazobactam, 402 levofloxacin), of whom 656 (82.0%) had pyelonephritis; 7 days of intravenous therapy.
cards.result: Composite cure (microbiological eradication plus clinical cure) 76.9% (306/398) on ceftolozane-tazobactam vs 68.4% (275/402) on high-dose levofloxacin (750 mg daily); the 95% CI for the treatment difference was 2.3 to 14.6, so non-inferiority was met and superiority indicated. Per-protocol composite cure: 83.3% (284/341) vs 75.4% (266/353).
cards.watchOut: The comparator was handicapped by resistance: much of ceftolozane-tazobactam's edge came from infections caused by levofloxacin-resistant and ESBL-producing organisms. Against a susceptible pathogen, no advantage is shown.
cards.source: Wagenlehner FM, Umeh O, Steenbergen J, Yuan G, Darouiche RO. Ceftolozane-tazobactam compared with levofloxacin in the treatment of complicated urinary-tract infections, including pyelonephritis: a randomised, double-blind, phase 3 trial (ASPECT-cUTI). cards.headline: Kollef 2019 (ASPECT-NP): 28-day mortality 24.0% vs 25.3% on meropenem in ventilated nosocomial pneumonia — non-inferior
cards.summary: Kollef 2019 (ASPECT-NP): 28-day mortality 24.0% vs 25.3% on meropenem in ventilated nosocomial pneumonia — non-inferior
cards.people: 726 mechanically ventilated adults with Gram-negative nosocomial pneumonia (362 ceftolozane-tazobactam 3 g every 8 hours, 364 meropenem 1 g every 8 hours), treated for 8-14 days at 263 hospitals in 34 countries; 71% had ventilator-associated pneumonia.
cards.result: 28-day all-cause mortality: 24.0% (87/362) on ceftolozane-tazobactam vs 25.3% (92/364) on meropenem (weighted treatment difference 1.1%; 95% CI -5.1 to 7.4), meeting the 10% non-inferiority margin. Clinical cure at test of cure: 54% (197) vs 53% (194) (difference 1.1%; 95% CI -6.2 to 8.3). Treatment-related adverse events: 11% (38/361) vs 8% (27/359).
cards.watchOut: A 10% mortality non-inferiority margin is wide, and patients infected with pathogens resistant to both study drugs contribute noise rather than evidence; the trial supports parity with meropenem, not superiority.
cards.source: Kollef MH, Novacek M, Kivistik U, Rea-Neto A, Shime N, Martin-Loeches I, Timsit JF, Wunderink RG, Bruno CJ, Huntington JA, Lin G, Yu B, Butterton JR, Rhee EG. Ceftolozane-tazobactam versus meropenem for treatment of nosocomial pneumonia (ASPECT-NP): a randomised, controlled, double-blind, phase 3, non-inferiority trial. The Lancet Infectious Diseases. 2019. PMID: 31563344. Registry ID: NCT02070757. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Synthesis: three phase 3 trials, three non-inferiority verdicts — a standard-agent alternative whose value is its resistance spectrum
cards.summary: Synthesis: three phase 3 trials, three non-inferiority verdicts — a standard-agent alternative whose value is its resistance spectrum
cards.people: Three double-blind phase 3 trials: ASPECT-cIAI (Solomkin 2015, 806 in the primary population), ASPECT-cUTI (Wagenlehner 2015, 1,083 enrolled) and ASPECT-NP (Kollef 2019, 726 randomised).
cards.result: Cure 83.0% vs 87.3% against meropenem in cIAI; composite cure 76.9% vs 68.4% against levofloxacin in cUTI (the only superiority signal, against a resistance-handicapped comparator); 28-day mortality 24.0% vs 25.3% against meropenem in ventilated pneumonia. Every trial was designed and powered for non-inferiority, so the honest reading is equivalence-class efficacy with activity against many multidrug-resistant Gram-negative pathogens. PROPOSED STAMP: POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: No trial compared ceftolozane-tazobactam with placebo or with best available therapy in carbapenem-resistant infection, the niche where it is most often used; that use rests on spectrum and these parity trials, not on a dedicated resistant-pathogen trial.
cards.source: Synthesis of Solomkin J et al. Clinical Infectious Diseases. 2015 (PMID: 25670823); Wagenlehner FM et al. The Lancet. 2015 (PMID: 25931244); Kollef MH et al. The Lancet Infectious Diseases. 2019 (PMID: 31563344).

shelves.title: Imipenem-cilastatin-relebactam: in the small resistant-pathogen trial, overall response tied colistin plus imipenem (71% vs 70%) with far less kidney injury (nephrotoxicity 10% vs 56%); in pneumonia it was non-inferior to piperacillin-tazobactam (28-day mortality 15.9% vs 21.3%)
shelves.question: In adults with infections caused by imipenem-nonsusceptible Gram-negative pathogens, or with hospital-acquired/ventilator-associated bacterial pneumonia, is imipenem-cilastatin-relebactam an effective and safer alternative to colistin-based or piperacillin-tazobactam therapy?
shelves.mesh: Anti-Bacterial Agents/adverse effects · Azabicyclo Compounds/adverse effects · Bacterial Infections*/drug therapy · Colistin/adverse effects · Humans · Imipenem*/adverse effects · Microbial Sensitivity Tests
shelves.balance: RESTORE-IMI 1 (Motsch 2020, PMID: 31400759; NCT02452047) randomised just 47 patients with imipenem-nonsusceptible infections: favourable overall response 71% on imipenem/relebactam vs 70% on colistin plus imipenem, day-28 clinical response 71% vs 40%, 28-day mortality 10% vs 30%, and treatment-emergent nephrotoxicity 10% vs 56% (P = .002). RESTORE-IMI 2 (Titov 2021, PMID: 32785589; NCT02493764) showed non-inferiority to piperacillin-tazobactam in HABP/VABP: 28-day mortality 15.9% vs 21.3% (difference -5.3%; 95% CI -11.9 to 1.2) and favourable clinical response 61.0% vs 55.8%. A paediatric phase 2/3 trial (Bradley 2026, PMID: 42400209; NCT03969901) found comparable outcomes against standard care in 115 children. Proposed stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit).

cards.headline: Motsch 2020 (RESTORE-IMI 1): overall response 71% vs 70% against colistin plus imipenem in imipenem-nonsusceptible infection — with nephrotoxicity 10% vs 56%
cards.summary: Motsch 2020 (RESTORE-IMI 1): overall response 71% vs 70% against colistin plus imipenem in imipenem-nonsusceptible infection — with nephrotoxicity 10% vs 56%
cards.people: Hospitalised adults with hospital-acquired/ventilator-associated pneumonia, complicated intra-abdominal infection or complicated urinary tract infection caused by imipenem-nonsusceptible (but colistin- and imipenem/relebactam-susceptible) pathogens; 47 treated (31 imipenem/relebactam, 16 colistin plus imipenem), 31 in the modified microbiological intent-to-treat population; Pseudomonas aeruginosa caused 77% of infections.
cards.result: Favourable overall response: 71% on imipenem/relebactam vs 70% on colistin plus imipenem (90% CI for difference -27.5 to 21.4). Day-28 favourable clinical response: 71% vs 40% (90% CI 1.3 to 51.5). 28-day mortality: 10% vs 30% (90% CI -46.4 to 6.7). Serious adverse events 10% vs 31%; treatment-emergent nephrotoxicity 10% vs 56% (P = .002).
cards.watchOut: Only 47 patients: every efficacy interval is very wide (the overall-response difference runs from -27.5 to +21.4 points). The firm finding is the kidney-safety gap, not an efficacy advantage.

Clinical Infectious Diseases. 2020. PMID: 31400759. Registry ID: NCT02452047. cards.headline: Titov 2021 (RESTORE-IMI 2): non-inferior to piperacillin-tazobactam in HABP/VABP — 28-day mortality 15.9% vs 21.3%
cards.summary: Titov 2021 (RESTORE-IMI 2): non-inferior to piperacillin-tazobactam in HABP/VABP — 28-day mortality 15.9% vs 21.3%
cards.people: Adults with hospital-acquired or ventilator-associated bacterial pneumonia randomised 1:1 to imipenem/cilastatin/relebactam 500/500/250 mg or piperacillin/tazobactam 4 g/500 mg intravenously every 6 hours for 7-14 days (total N not documented in the fetched record).
cards.result: Day-28 all-cause mortality: 15.9% on imipenem/cilastatin/relebactam vs 21.3% on piperacillin/tazobactam (difference -5.3%; 95% CI -11.9 to 1.2), non-inferior (P < .001). Favourable clinical response at early follow-up: 61.0% vs 55.8% (difference 5.0%; 95% CI -3.2 to 13.2). Serious adverse events: 26.7% vs 32.0%.
cards.watchOut: The comparator, piperacillin-tazobactam, has no carbapenem-resistant coverage, so this trial shows the combination works as ordinary pneumonia therapy; it does not test the resistant-pathogen niche, which rests on the 47-patient RESTORE-IMI 1.
cards.source: Titov I et al. cards.headline: Bradley 2026 (paediatric phase 2/3): outcomes comparable to standard care in 115 children with Gram-negative infection, no deaths in either arm
cards.summary: Bradley 2026 (paediatric phase 2/3): outcomes comparable to standard care in 115 children with Gram-negative infection, no deaths in either arm
cards.people: 115 children from birth to under 18 years with hospital-acquired/ventilator-associated pneumonia, complicated intra-abdominal infection or complicated urinary tract infection, randomised 3:1 (86 imipenem/cilastatin/relebactam, 29 active-control standard care).
cards.result: At end of treatment, clinical response was 78.8% on imipenem/cilastatin/relebactam vs 75.0% on active control, and microbiologic response 95.6% vs 90.9%, with no mortality in either arm. Adverse events were reported in 67.1% vs 50.0% (treatment difference 17.1%; 95% CI -3.5 to 37.2), with 3 vs 0 discontinuations of intravenous therapy.
cards.watchOut: An estimation study without hypothesis testing, open-label, with a 3:1 randomisation and only 29 control children — it supports tolerability and dosing, not comparative efficacy.
cards.source: Bradley JS et al. cards.headline: Synthesis: a colistin-sparing option with parity efficacy and a large kidney-safety advantage, on a very small resistant-pathogen evidence base
cards.summary: Synthesis: a colistin-sparing option with parity efficacy and a large kidney-safety advantage, on a very small resistant-pathogen evidence base
cards.people: Three randomised trials: RESTORE-IMI 1 (Motsch 2020, 47 adults with imipenem-nonsusceptible infection), RESTORE-IMI 2 (Titov 2021, adults with HABP/VABP) and a paediatric phase 2/3 trial (Bradley 2026, 115 children).
cards.result: Against colistin plus imipenem, overall response was 71% vs 70% with nephrotoxicity 10% vs 56% (P = .002) and 28-day mortality 10% vs 30% in 47 patients (Motsch 2020). Against piperacillin-tazobactam in pneumonia, 28-day mortality was 15.9% vs 21.3%, meeting non-inferiority (Titov 2021). Paediatric outcomes were comparable to standard care with no deaths (Bradley 2026). PROPOSED STAMP: POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: The drug's defining use — carbapenem-nonsusceptible infection — is supported by one 47-patient trial. The mortality gap there (10% vs 30%) is compatible with chance; the nephrotoxicity gap is the robust result.
cards.source: Synthesis of Motsch J et al. Clinical Infectious Diseases. 2020 (PMID: 31400759); Titov I et al. Clinical Infectious Diseases. 2021 (PMID: 32785589); Bradley JS et al. The Pediatric Infectious Disease Journal. 2026 (PMID: 42400209).

shelves.title: Eravacycline for complicated intra-abdominal infection: non-inferior to ertapenem (cure 86.8% vs 87.6% in IGNITE1) and to meropenem (90.8% vs 91.2% in IGNITE4) — an approved use resting entirely on parity trials; its urinary-tract programme failed and was never approved
shelves.question: In adults with complicated intra-abdominal infection, is intravenous eravacycline non-inferior to carbapenem therapy (ertapenem or meropenem)?
shelves.mesh: Abdominal Abscess/drug therapy* · Abdominal Abscess/microbiology · Abdominal Abscess/surgery · Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Anti-Bacterial Agents/adverse effects · Anti-Bacterial Agents/therapeutic use* · Appendicitis/complications · Bacterial Infections/complications · Bacterial Infections/drug therapy* · Double-Blind Method · Ertapenem · Female · Gram-Negative Bacteria* · Humans · Intention to Treat Analysis · Male · Middle Aged · Peritonitis/drug therapy* · Peritonitis/microbiology · Tetracyclines/adverse effects · Tetracyclines/therapeutic use* · Treatment Outcome · Young Adult · beta-Lactams/adverse effects · beta-Lactams/therapeutic use*
shelves.balance: IGNITE1 (Solomkin 2017, PMID: 27851857; NCT01844856 as printed in the record): clinical cure 86.8% on eravacycline vs 87.6% on ertapenem (difference -0.80%; 95% CI -7.1 to 5.5) in 541 patients. IGNITE4 (Solomkin 2019, PMID: 30561562; NCT01844856 as printed in that record also): cure 90.8% (177/195) vs 91.2% (187/205) on meropenem (difference -0.5%; 95% CI -6.3 to 5.3). An earlier phase 2 trial (Solomkin 2014, PMID: 24342651; NCT01265784) found clinical success above 90% in each arm in 139 patients. Both phase 3 trials were non-inferiority designs against carbapenems. The complicated urinary tract infection programme (IGNITE2, IGNITE3) failed its endpoints and produced no journal-published trial, so cIAI is the only approved use. Proposed stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit).

cards.headline: Solomkin 2017 (IGNITE1): eravacycline non-inferior to ertapenem in cIAI — cure 86.8% vs 87.6%
cards.summary: Solomkin 2017 (IGNITE1): eravacycline non-inferior to ertapenem in cIAI — cure 86.8% vs 87.6%
cards.people: 541 hospitalised adults with complicated intra-abdominal infection requiring surgical or percutaneous intervention (270 eravacycline 1.0 mg/kg every 12 hours, 271 ertapenem 1.0 g every 24 hours), for a minimum of four 24-hour dosing cycles.
cards.result: Clinical cure at test of cure in the microbiological intent-to-treat population: 86.8% on eravacycline vs 87.6% on ertapenem (difference -0.80%; 95% CI -7.1 to 5.5), meeting the prespecified non-inferiority margin. Both drugs were well tolerated.
cards.watchOut: Non-inferiority to ertapenem, a carbapenem with no Pseudomonas coverage: the trial population had largely carbapenem-susceptible infections, so the result does not by itself prove value against the resistant pathogens eravacycline is marketed for.
cards.source: Solomkin J, Evans D, Slepavicius A, Lee P, Marsh A, Tsai L, Sutcliffe JA, Horn P. cards.headline: Solomkin 2019 (IGNITE4): eravacycline non-inferior to meropenem — cure 90.8% (177/195) vs 91.2% (187/205)
cards.summary: Solomkin 2019 (IGNITE4): eravacycline non-inferior to meropenem — cure 90.8% (177/195) vs 91.2% (187/205)
cards.people: Hospitalised adults with complicated intra-abdominal infection; 400 patients in the primary analysis population (195 eravacycline 1 mg/kg every 12 hours, 205 meropenem 1 g every 8 hours), treated intravenously for 4-14 days.
cards.result: Clinical cure at test of cure: 90.8% (177/195) on eravacycline vs 91.2% (187/205) on meropenem (difference -0.5%; 95% CI -6.3 to 5.3), meeting the 12.5% non-inferiority margin. In ESBL-producing Enterobacteriaceae, cure was 87.5% (14/16) vs 84.6% (11/13).
cards.watchOut: A wide 12.5% non-inferiority margin, agreed with the FDA after IGNITE1 used 10%: parity within an eighth of the cure rate is a low bar, and the ESBL subgroup is only 29 patients.
cards.source: Solomkin JS et al. IGNITE4: Results of a Phase 3, Randomized, Multicenter, Prospective Trial of Eravacycline vs Meropenem in the Treatment of Complicated Intraabdominal Infections. Clinical Infectious Diseases. 2019. PMID: 30561562. Registry ID: NCT01844856 (registry number as printed in this record; the same number is printed in the IGNITE1 record). cards.headline: Solomkin 2014 (phase 2): both eravacycline dose regimens matched ertapenem, clinical success above 90% in each arm (139 patients)
cards.summary: Solomkin 2014 (phase 2): both eravacycline dose regimens matched ertapenem, clinical success above 90% in each arm (139 patients)
cards.people: 139 adults with confirmed complicated intra-abdominal infection requiring surgical or percutaneous intervention, randomised 2:2:1 to eravacycline 1.5 mg/kg every 24 hours, eravacycline 1.0 mg/kg every 12 hours, or ertapenem 1 g every 24 hours for 4-14 days.
cards.result: Clinical success rates were greater than 90% in each arm, and both eravacycline regimens were as efficacious as ertapenem and well tolerated. Treatment-emergent adverse events occurred in 35.8% (eravacycline every 24 hours), 28.6% (eravacycline every 12 hours) and 26.7% (ertapenem) — rates as reported in the IGNITE4 paper's summary of this trial (PMID: 30561562).
cards.watchOut: A small dose-finding trial (139 patients) designed to pick a dose, not to establish efficacy; its arm-level success rates were captured this session from the IGNITE4 report's summary rather than from this record's own abstract, which reports no numbers.
cards.source: Solomkin JS, Ramesh MK, Cesnauskas G, Novikovs N, Stefanova P, Sutcliffe JA, Walpole SM, Horn PT. cards.headline: Synthesis: two phase 3 parity results against carbapenems in cIAI — and a failed urinary programme that bounds the claim
cards.summary: Synthesis: two phase 3 parity results against carbapenems in cIAI — and a failed urinary programme that bounds the claim
cards.people: Two phase 3 trials (IGNITE1, 541 patients; IGNITE4, 400 in the primary population) and one phase 2 trial (139 patients), all in complicated intra-abdominal infection.
cards.result: Cure 86.8% vs 87.6% against ertapenem (IGNITE1) and 90.8% vs 91.2% against meropenem (IGNITE4), both meeting non-inferiority; phase 2 success above 90% per arm. No trial tested superiority, and the phase 3 complicated urinary tract infection trials (IGNITE2 and IGNITE3) failed their non-inferiority endpoints and were reported only in sponsor announcements, not journal articles, so they are described here but not carded. PROPOSED STAMP: POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: Eravacycline's approval is for cIAI only. Extrapolating the cIAI parity results to urinary or other infections is contradicted by the failed cUTI programme.
cards.source: Synthesis of Solomkin J et al. JAMA Surgery. 2017 (PMID: 27851857); Solomkin JS et al. Clinical Infectious Diseases. 2019 (PMID: 30561562); Solomkin JS et al. Antimicrobial Agents and Chemotherapy. 2014 (PMID: 24342651).

shelves.question: In adults with acute bacterial skin and skin-structure infections or community-acquired bacterial pneumonia, is omadacycline non-inferior to linezolid or moxifloxacin?

cards.headline: O'Riordan 2019 (OASIS-1): omadacycline non-inferior to linezolid in skin infection — early response 84.8% vs 85.5%
cards.summary: O'Riordan 2019 (OASIS-1): omadacycline non-inferior to linezolid in skin infection — early response 84.8% vs 85.5%
cards.people: Adults with acute bacterial skin and skin-structure infections in the modified intention-to-treat population (316 omadacycline, 311 linezolid); omadacycline 100 mg intravenously every 12 hours for two doses then daily, with optional switch to oral 300 mg daily after 3 days; total treatment 7-14 days.
cards.result: Early clinical response at 48-72 hours: 84.8% on omadacycline vs 85.5% on linezolid (difference -0.7 percentage points; 95% CI -6.3 to 4.9), meeting the 10-point non-inferiority margin. Investigator-assessed response at post-treatment evaluation: 86.1% vs 83.6% (modified intention-to-treat) and 96.3% vs 93.5% (per-protocol). Adverse events 48.3% vs 45.7%; gastrointestinal events 18.0% vs 15.8%.
cards.watchOut: Early response (at least 20% lesion shrinkage at 48-72 hours) is a regulatory endpoint, not cure; the trial shows parity with linezolid on it, and the per-protocol post-treatment rates near 96% flatter both arms.
cards.source: O'Riordan W, Green S, Overcash JS, Puljiz I, Metallidis S, Gardovskis J, Garrity-Ryan L, Das AF, Tzanis E, Eckburg PB, Manley A, Villano SA, Steenbergen JN, Loh E. cards.headline: O'Riordan 2019 (OASIS-2): oral-only omadacycline non-inferior to oral linezolid — early response 88% (315/360) vs 83% (297/360)
cards.summary: O'Riordan 2019 (OASIS-2): oral-only omadacycline non-inferior to oral linezolid — early response 88% (315/360) vs 83% (297/360)
cards.people: Adults with acute bacterial skin and skin-structure infections at 33 US sites; 720 in the modified intention-to-treat population (360 per arm), treated orally for 7-14 days (omadacycline 450 mg daily for 48 hours then 300 mg daily; linezolid 600 mg twice daily).
cards.result: Early clinical response: 88% (315/360) on omadacycline vs 83% (297/360) on linezolid (difference 5.0 percentage points; 95% CI -0.2 to 10.3), meeting non-inferiority. Investigator-assessed response at post-treatment evaluation: 84% (303/360) vs 81% (291/360) in the modified intention-to-treat population and 98% (278/284) vs 96% (279/292) in the clinically evaluable population.
cards.watchOut: The point estimate favours omadacycline but the confidence interval includes zero; this is an oral-convenience result (once daily, no intravenous start), not demonstrated superior efficacy.

cards.headline: Stets 2019 (OPTIC): omadacycline non-inferior to moxifloxacin in community-acquired pneumonia — early response 81.1% vs 82.7%
cards.summary: Stets 2019 (OPTIC): omadacycline non-inferior to moxifloxacin in community-acquired pneumonia — early response 81.1% vs 82.7%
cards.people: 774 adults with community-acquired bacterial pneumonia (Pneumonia Severity Index risk class II, III or IV), randomised to omadacycline (100 mg intravenously every 12 hours for two doses, then daily, with optional oral switch) or moxifloxacin 400 mg daily for 7-14 days.
cards.result: Early clinical response: 81.1% on omadacycline vs 82.7% on moxifloxacin (difference -1.6 percentage points; 95% CI -7.1 to 3.8), meeting the 10-point non-inferiority margin. Investigator-assessed clinical response at post-treatment evaluation: 87.6% vs 85.1% (difference 2.5; 95% CI -2.4 to 7.4).
cards.watchOut: Pneumonia Severity Index class II-IV outpatients and ward patients — not severe or ventilated pneumonia; and a post-marketing confirmatory trial (OPTIC-2, PMID: 41340860) has since repeated the non-inferiority finding against moxifloxacin (early response 89.6% vs 87.7%), which is noted here but not carded.

cards.headline: Synthesis: three non-inferiority trials across two indications — omadacycline matches linezolid and moxifloxacin, and adds oral once-daily dosing
cards.summary: Synthesis: three non-inferiority trials across two indications — omadacycline matches linezolid and moxifloxacin, and adds oral once-daily dosing
cards.people: Three phase 3 double-blind trials: OASIS-1 (627 in the modified intention-to-treat population), OASIS-2 (720) and OPTIC (774 randomised).
cards.result: Early response 84.8% vs 85.5% (OASIS-1) and 88% vs 83% (OASIS-2) against linezolid in skin infection; 81.1% vs 82.7% against moxifloxacin in pneumonia (OPTIC). Every result is a non-inferiority result at a 10-point margin; none shows superiority. PROPOSED STAMP: POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: All three trials were funded by the manufacturer (Paratek Pharmaceuticals, named as funder in the records) and all used early-response regulatory endpoints; there is no placebo-controlled or mortality-powered evidence.
cards.source: Synthesis of O'Riordan W et al. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2019 (PMID: 30726689); O'Riordan W et al. The Lancet Infectious Diseases. 2019 (PMID: 31474458); Stets R et al. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2019 (PMID: 30726692).

shelves.title: Delafloxacin: non-inferior to vancomycin plus aztreonam in skin infections (objective response 83.7% vs 80.6% in the IV-to-oral trial; 81.3% vs 80.7% pooled) and to moxifloxacin in pneumonia (early response 88.9% vs 89.0%) — fluoroquinolone parity in both approved uses
shelves.question: In adults with acute bacterial skin and skin-structure infections or community-acquired bacterial pneumonia, is delafloxacin non-inferior to vancomycin plus aztreonam or to moxifloxacin?
shelves.mesh: MeSH: not captured from the record this session
shelves.balance: Two phase 3 skin-infection trials were pooled by Giordano 2019 (PMID: 30957167): objective response 81.3% on delafloxacin vs 80.7% on vancomycin plus aztreonam (difference 0.8%; 95% CI -3.2 to 4.7) in 1,510 adults. The IV-to-oral trial alone (O'Riordan 2018, PMID: 29518178; NCT01984684) gave objective response 83.7% vs 80.6% in 850 adults. In pneumonia, DEFINE-CABP (Horcajada 2020, PMID: 31988972; NCT03534622 as printed in that record) gave early clinical response 88.9% vs 89.0% on moxifloxacin (difference -0.2; 95% CI -4.4 to 4.1) in 859 adults. All non-inferiority designs. Proposed stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit).

cards.headline: O'Riordan 2018: IV-to-oral delafloxacin non-inferior to vancomycin plus aztreonam in ABSSSI — objective response 83.7% vs 80.6%
cards.summary: O'Riordan 2018: IV-to-oral delafloxacin non-inferior to vancomycin plus aztreonam in ABSSSI — objective response 83.7% vs 80.6%
cards.people: 850 adults with acute bacterial skin and skin-structure infections, randomised to delafloxacin 300 mg intravenously every 12 hours for 3 days then 450 mg orally, or vancomycin 15 mg/kg plus aztreonam, for 5-14 days.
cards.result: Objective response (at least 20% reduction in lesion erythema at 48-72 hours) in the intent-to-treat set: 83.7% on delafloxacin vs 80.6% on vancomycin plus aztreonam. Investigator-assessed success: 87.2% vs 84.4% at follow-up and 83.5% vs 82.2% at late follow-up. MRSA eradication at follow-up: 96.0% vs 97.0%.
cards.watchOut: Monotherapy was compared with a two-drug regimen whose aztreonam component is stopped once Gram-negative infection is excluded; the practical gain is simplicity, not better cure rates.
cards.source: O'Riordan W et al. cards.headline: Giordano 2019 (pooled phase 3): objective response 81.3% vs 80.7% across both ABSSSI trials (1,510 adults)
cards.summary: Giordano 2019 (pooled phase 3): objective response 81.3% vs 80.7% across both ABSSSI trials (1,510 adults)
cards.type: Pooled analysis of two phase 3 randomised trials (Giordano 2019)
cards.people: 1,510 adults with acute bacterial skin and skin-structure infections pooled from the two phase 3 trials of intravenous (with oral switch in one trial) delafloxacin vs vancomycin 15 mg/kg plus aztreonam 1-2 g every 12 hours.
cards.result: Objective response at 48-72 hours in the intent-to-treat set: 81.3% on delafloxacin vs 80.7% on vancomycin plus aztreonam (mean treatment difference 0.8%; 95% CI -3.2 to 4.7). cards.watchOut: This pooled analysis re-presents the same two trials carded separately on this shelf (including O'Riordan 2018); it adds precision, not independent evidence.

cards.headline: Horcajada 2020 (DEFINE-CABP): delafloxacin non-inferior to moxifloxacin in pneumonia — early response 88.9% vs 89.0%
cards.summary: Horcajada 2020 (DEFINE-CABP): delafloxacin non-inferior to moxifloxacin in pneumonia — early response 88.9% vs 89.0%
cards.people: 859 adults with community-acquired bacterial pneumonia (431 delafloxacin 300 mg twice daily, 428 moxifloxacin 400 mg daily, intravenous with oral switch), treated for 5-10 days.
cards.result: Early clinical response: 88.9% (383/431) on delafloxacin vs 89.0% (381/428) on moxifloxacin (difference -0.2; 95% CI -4.4 to 4.1), meeting non-inferiority. cards.watchOut: Delafloxacin was compared with another fluoroquinolone, so the trial cannot separate delafloxacin's value from the class effect — and it inherits the fluoroquinolone class warnings (tendon, nerve, QT and aortic concerns) that the comparator shares.

cards.summary: Synthesis: parity with vancomycin-based therapy in skin infection and with moxifloxacin in pneumonia — a broad-spectrum fluoroquinolone option, nothing more proven
cards.people: Two phase 3 skin-infection trials (850 in the IV-to-oral trial; 1,510 pooled) and one phase 3 pneumonia trial (859).
cards.result: Objective response 83.7% vs 80.6% (O'Riordan 2018) and 81.3% vs 80.7% pooled (Giordano 2019) against vancomycin plus aztreonam; early response 88.9% vs 89.0% against moxifloxacin in pneumonia (Horcajada 2020). All non-inferiority findings. PROPOSED STAMP: POSSIBLE (benefit).

shelves.title: Lefamulin for community-acquired pneumonia: non-inferior to moxifloxacin intravenously (early response 87.3% vs 90.2% in LEAP 1) and as a shorter 5-day oral course (90.8% vs 90.8% in LEAP 2) — parity, with the 5-day oral regimen as its practical distinction
shelves.question: In adults with community-acquired bacterial pneumonia, is lefamulin (intravenous-to-oral, or 5-day oral) non-inferior to moxifloxacin?
shelves.mesh: MeSH: not captured from the record this session
shelves.balance: LEAP 1 (File 2019, PMID: 30722059; NCT02559310): early clinical response 87.3% on intravenous-to-oral lefamulin vs 90.2% on moxifloxacin (difference -2.9%; 95% CI -8.5 to 2.8) in 551 patients with Pneumonia Outcomes Research Team risk class III or higher. LEAP 2 (Alexander 2019, PMID: 31560372; NCT02813694): 5-day oral lefamulin vs 7-day oral moxifloxacin, early response 90.8% vs 90.8% (difference 0.1%) in 738 patients. A pooled analysis of LEAP 1, LEAP 2 and LEAP China (Liang 2025, PMID: 40964629) confirms non-inferiority across 1,411 patients with success rates of at least 84.0% on both endpoints. Proposed stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit).

cards.headline: File 2019 (LEAP 1): IV-to-oral lefamulin non-inferior to moxifloxacin — early response 87.3% vs 90.2%
cards.summary: File 2019 (LEAP 1): IV-to-oral lefamulin non-inferior to moxifloxacin — early response 87.3% vs 90.2%
cards.people: 551 adults with community-acquired bacterial pneumonia of Pneumonia Outcomes Research Team risk class III or higher (276 lefamulin 150 mg intravenously every 12 hours, 275 moxifloxacin 400 mg daily), with optional intravenous-to-oral switch.
cards.result: Early clinical response: 87.3% on lefamulin vs 90.2% on moxifloxacin (difference -2.9%; 95% CI -8.5 to 2.8), meeting the 10% non-inferiority margin. Investigator-assessed clinical response: 81.7% vs 84.2% in the modified intention-to-treat population (difference -2.6%; 95% CI -8.9 to 3.9) and 86.9% vs 89.4% in the clinically evaluable population. Discontinuation for treatment-emergent adverse events: 2.9% vs 4.4%.
cards.watchOut: The point estimates favour moxifloxacin on every endpoint; non-inferiority was met because the 10% margin is generous. Gastrointestinal effects are the recognised tolerability cost of lefamulin in the trial programme.

cards.headline: Alexander 2019 (LEAP 2): 5-day oral lefamulin non-inferior to 7-day oral moxifloxacin — early response 90.8% vs 90.8%
cards.summary: Alexander 2019 (LEAP 2): 5-day oral lefamulin non-inferior to 7-day oral moxifloxacin — early response 90.8% vs 90.8%
cards.people: 738 adults with community-acquired bacterial pneumonia of Pneumonia Outcomes Research Team risk class II, III or IV at 99 sites in 19 countries (370 oral lefamulin 600 mg every 12 hours for 5 days, 368 oral moxifloxacin 400 mg daily for 7 days).
cards.result: Early clinical response at 96 hours after the first dose: 90.8% on lefamulin vs 90.8% on moxifloxacin (difference 0.1%; 1-sided 97.5% CI -4.4 to infinity), meeting the 10% non-inferiority margin.
cards.watchOut: Identical response rates at an early (96-hour) endpoint in mostly risk class II-IV patients; the trial was not powered for mortality or for severe pneumonia, and the shorter course is a convenience claim, not an outcomes claim.

cards.headline: Liang 2025 (pooled LEAP 1, LEAP 2 and LEAP China): non-inferiority holds across 1,411 patients, success rates at least 84.0% on both endpoints
cards.summary: Liang 2025 (pooled LEAP 1, LEAP 2 and LEAP China): non-inferiority holds across 1,411 patients, success rates at least 84.0% on both endpoints
cards.type: Post hoc pooled analysis of three randomised trials (Liang 2025)
cards.people: 1,411 adults with community-acquired bacterial pneumonia pooled post hoc from the two pivotal phase 3 trials and the LEAP China bridging trial (728 lefamulin, 683 moxifloxacin).
cards.result: Early clinical response and investigator-assessed clinical response success rates were similar and at least 84.0% in both treatment groups, with non-inferiority of lefamulin confirmed at the 10% margin. In patients aged 85 or older, early response was 88.5% on lefamulin vs 82.4% on moxifloxacin; at ages 65-74 it was 87.2% vs 86.5% and at 75-84, 86.8% vs 85.4%.
cards.watchOut: A post hoc pooling of the same trials carded above (plus a bridging trial reported in full only as a conference abstract); the age-subgroup differences are descriptive and were not tested for superiority.
cards.source: Liang S et al. cards.headline: Synthesis: two phase 3 trials agree — lefamulin matches moxifloxacin in community-acquired pneumonia, IV-to-oral or 5-day oral
cards.summary: Synthesis: two phase 3 trials agree — lefamulin matches moxifloxacin in community-acquired pneumonia, IV-to-oral or 5-day oral
cards.people: LEAP 1 (551 patients), LEAP 2 (738 patients) and their pooled analysis with LEAP China (1,411 patients).
cards.result: Early response 87.3% vs 90.2% (LEAP 1) and 90.8% vs 90.8% (LEAP 2); pooled success at least 84.0% on both endpoints (Liang 2025). Both pivotal trials met a 10% non-inferiority margin against moxifloxacin; neither showed superiority. PROPOSED STAMP: POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: Community-acquired pneumonia is lefamulin's only approved indication, and the evidence is two manufacturer non-inferiority trials against one comparator; there is no trial in severe pneumonia, bacteraemic pneumonia or against beta-lactam-based standard care.
cards.source: Synthesis of File TM Jr et al. Clinical Infectious Diseases. 2019 (PMID: 30722059); Alexander E et al. JAMA. 2019 (PMID: 31560372); Liang S et al. Infection and Drug Resistance. 2025 (PMID: 40964629).

shelves.question: In adults with community-acquired pneumonia or complicated skin and skin-structure infections (including MRSA), is ceftaroline fosamil non-inferior to ceftriaxone or to vancomycin plus aztreonam?

cards.headline: File 2010 (FOCUS 1 and 2 integrated): ceftaroline non-inferior to ceftriaxone in pneumonia — cure 84.3% vs 77.7%
cards.summary: File 2010 (FOCUS 1 and 2 integrated): ceftaroline non-inferior to ceftriaxone in pneumonia — cure 84.3% vs 77.7%
cards.type: Integrated analysis of two randomised, double-blind, phase 3 non-inferiority trials (File 2010)
cards.people: 1,228 hospitalised adults (not in intensive care) with community-acquired pneumonia of Pneumonia Outcomes Research Team risk class III or IV (614 ceftaroline 600 mg every 12 hours, 614 ceftriaxone 1 g daily), treated for 5-7 days; FOCUS 1 patients also received two doses of oral clarithromycin on day 1.
cards.result: Clinical cure in the clinically evaluable population: 84.3% on ceftaroline vs 77.7% on ceftriaxone (difference 6.7%; 95% CI 1.6 to 11.8). By trial: FOCUS 1, 86.6% vs 78.2% (difference 8.4%; 95% CI 1.4 to 15.4); FOCUS 2, 82.1% vs 77.2% (difference 4.9%; 95% CI -2.5 to 12.5). Modified intent-to-treat cure: 82.6% vs 76.6% (difference 6.0%; 95% CI 1.4 to 10.7). Adverse events, serious adverse events and deaths were similar in both arms.
cards.watchOut: The trials were designed for non-inferiority (10% margin), so the numerically higher cure is not a tested superiority claim; patients with suspected MRSA pneumonia were excluded, so ceftaroline's signature MRSA activity has no pneumonia trial behind it.
cards.source: File TM Jr, Low DE, Eckburg PB, Talbot GH, Friedland HD, Lee J, Llorens L, Critchley I, Thye D. Integrated analysis of FOCUS 1 and FOCUS 2: randomized, doubled-blinded, multicenter phase 3 trials of the efficacy and safety of ceftaroline fosamil versus ceftriaxone in patients with community-acquired pneumonia. Clinical Infectious Diseases. 2010. PMID: 21067350. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Corey 2010 (CANVAS 1 and 2 integrated): ceftaroline non-inferior to vancomycin plus aztreonam in skin infection — cure 91.6% vs 92.7%, MRSA 93.4% vs 94.3%
cards.summary: Corey 2010 (CANVAS 1 and 2 integrated): ceftaroline non-inferior to vancomycin plus aztreonam in skin infection — cure 91.6% vs 92.7%, MRSA 93.4% vs 94.3%
cards.type: Integrated analysis of two randomised, double-blind, phase 3 non-inferiority trials (Corey 2010)
cards.people: 1,378 adults with complicated skin and skin-structure infection requiring intravenous therapy, randomised to ceftaroline 600 mg every 12 hours or vancomycin plus aztreonam 1 g each every 12 hours for 5-14 days across the two identical phase 3 trials.
cards.result: Clinical cure in the clinically evaluable population: 91.6% on ceftaroline vs 92.7% on vancomycin plus aztreonam; in the modified intent-to-treat population, 85.9% vs 85.5%. In MRSA infection, cure was 93.4% vs 94.3%. Ceftaroline was well tolerated with a cephalosporin-class safety profile.
cards.watchOut: An integrated analysis of two identical trials rather than two independent tests; the comparator's aztreonam arm covers Gram-negatives that ceftaroline largely lacks, so parity here is about the Gram-positive-dominated skin population actually enrolled.
cards.source: Corey GR et al. Integrated analysis of CANVAS 1 and 2: phase 3, multicenter, randomized, double-blind studies to evaluate the safety and efficacy of ceftaroline versus vancomycin plus aztreonam in complicated skin and skin-structure infection. cards.headline: File 2012 (trial-programme summary): ceftaroline non-inferior at test of cure and at day 3-4 in both programmes; pneumococcal pneumonia cure 85.5% vs 68.6%
cards.summary: File 2012 (trial-programme summary): ceftaroline non-inferior at test of cure and at day 3-4 in both programmes; pneumococcal pneumonia cure 85.5% vs 68.6%
cards.type: Review and summary of the phase 3 trial programmes (File 2012)
cards.people: The two phase 3 programmes reviewed together: FOCUS 1 and 2 in community-acquired pneumonia (ceftaroline vs ceftriaxone) and CANVAS 1 and 2 in skin infection (ceftaroline vs vancomycin plus aztreonam), including 139 patients with pneumococcal pneumonia (69 ceftaroline, 70 ceftriaxone).
cards.result: In the integrated FOCUS analysis, clinically evaluable cure was 84.3% vs 77.7% (difference 6.6%; 95% CI 1.6 to 11.8 as printed in this summary). In pneumonia caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae, cure was 85.5% (59/69) on ceftaroline vs 68.6% (48/70) on ceftriaxone. In CANVAS, microbiologically evaluable success was similar between arms, with MRSA cure 93.4% (142/152) vs 94.3% (115/122). Ceftaroline was non-inferior at both the test-of-cure and the early day 3-4 assessments in both programmes.
cards.watchOut: A summary of the same four trials carded above, not independent evidence; the pneumococcal subgroup (139 patients) is a subgroup of FOCUS, and its 17-point gap was not a prespecified superiority test.
cards.source: File TM Jr, Wilcox MH, Stein GE. Summary of ceftaroline fosamil clinical trial studies and clinical safety. Clinical Infectious Diseases. 2012. PMID: 22903949. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.summary: Synthesis: four phase 3 trials, two indications, one pattern — ceftaroline matches the standard, with MRSA skin cover as its distinction
cards.people: FOCUS 1 and 2 (1,228 treated, pneumonia) and CANVAS 1 and 2 (1,378 randomised, skin infection), as integrated analyses and a programme summary.
cards.result: Pneumonia cure 84.3% vs 77.7% against ceftriaxone (File 2010); skin cure 91.6% vs 92.7% and MRSA cure 93.4% vs 94.3% against vancomycin plus aztreonam (Corey 2010). All four trials were non-inferiority designs. PROPOSED STAMP: POSSIBLE (benefit).

shelves.title: Tedizolid: 6 days matched 10 days of linezolid in skin infections — early response 79.5% vs 79.4% in ESTABLISH-1 (oral) and 85% vs 83% in ESTABLISH-2 (IV-to-oral); pooled 81.6% vs 79.4% with less nausea (8.2% vs 12.2%)
shelves.question: In adults with acute bacterial skin and skin-structure infections, is tedizolid phosphate 200 mg once daily for 6 days non-inferior to linezolid 600 mg twice daily for 10 days?
shelves.mesh: MeSH: not captured from the record this session
shelves.balance: ESTABLISH-1 (Prokocimer 2013, PMID: 23403680; NCT01170221): early clinical response 79.5% on oral tedizolid for 6 days vs 79.4% on oral linezolid for 10 days (difference 0.1%; 95% CI -6.1 to 6.2) in 667 adults. ESTABLISH-2 (Moran 2014, PMID: 24909499; NCT01421511): intravenous-to-oral tedizolid, early response 85% vs 83% on linezolid (difference 2.6%; 95% CI -3.0 to 8.2). The pooled analysis (Shorr 2015, PMID: 25421472) gives early response 81.6% vs 79.4% across 1,333 patients, with nausea in 8.2% vs 12.2% (P = 0.02). Proposed stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit).

cards.headline: Prokocimer 2013 (ESTABLISH-1): oral tedizolid for 6 days non-inferior to oral linezolid for 10 days — early response 79.5% vs 79.4%
cards.summary: Prokocimer 2013 (ESTABLISH-1): oral tedizolid for 6 days non-inferior to oral linezolid for 10 days — early response 79.5% vs 79.4%
cards.people: 667 adults with acute bacterial skin and skin-structure infections at 81 centres (332 tedizolid phosphate 200 mg once daily for 6 days, 335 linezolid 600 mg twice daily for 10 days), all oral therapy.
cards.result: Early clinical response at 48-72 hours (no increase in lesion size and normal oral temperature in this trial's definition): 79.5% on tedizolid vs 79.4% on linezolid (difference 0.1%; 95% CI -6.1 to 6.2), meeting non-inferiority. Investigator-assessed clinical success 1-2 weeks after treatment: 85.5% vs 86.0%.
cards.watchOut: The comparison confounds drug with duration: 6 days of tedizolid vs 10 days of linezolid. The trial shows the shorter tedizolid course is enough; it cannot show tedizolid is the stronger drug at equal duration.

cards.headline: Moran 2014 (ESTABLISH-2): IV-to-oral tedizolid non-inferior to linezolid — early response 85% (283/332) vs 83% (276/334)
cards.summary: Moran 2014 (ESTABLISH-2): IV-to-oral tedizolid non-inferior to linezolid — early response 85% (283/332) vs 83% (276/334)
cards.people: 666 adults with acute bacterial skin and skin-structure infections at 58 centres in nine countries (332 tedizolid 200 mg once daily for 6 days, 334 linezolid 600 mg twice daily for 10 days), starting intravenously with switch to oral therapy when improvement criteria were met.
cards.result: Early clinical response: 85% (283/332) on tedizolid vs 83% (276/334) on linezolid (difference 2.6%; 95% CI -3.0 to 8.2), meeting the non-inferiority criterion. Intravenous-to-oral once-daily tedizolid for 6 days was non-inferior to twice-daily linezolid for 10 days.
cards.watchOut: Same drug-plus-duration confound as ESTABLISH-1, and the same early-response regulatory endpoint; late cure and relapse were secondary and similar, not the basis of the non-inferiority claim.
cards.source: Moran GJ, Fang E, Corey GR, Das AF, De Anda C, Prokocimer P. cards.headline: Shorr 2015 (pooled ESTABLISH-1 and 2): early response 81.6% vs 79.4% across 1,333 patients; nausea 8.2% vs 12.2% (P = 0.02)
cards.summary: Shorr 2015 (pooled ESTABLISH-1 and 2): early response 81.6% vs 79.4% across 1,333 patients; nausea 8.2% vs 12.2% (P = 0.02)
cards.type: Pooled analysis of two phase 3 randomised trials (Shorr 2015)
cards.people: 1,333 patients randomised across the two phase 3 trials (664 tedizolid 200 mg once daily for 6 days, 669 linezolid 600 mg twice daily for 10 days) with acute bacterial skin and skin-structure infections caused by Gram-positive pathogens.
cards.result: Pooled early clinical response: 81.6% on tedizolid vs 79.4% on linezolid, confirming non-inferiority. Nausea, the most frequent adverse event, occurred in 8.2% vs 12.2% (P = 0.02). The individual trials showed non-inferior efficacy and a favourable tolerability profile for tedizolid.
cards.watchOut: A re-analysis of the same two trials carded above — it sharpens the tolerability comparison (the nausea gap) but adds no independent efficacy evidence; platelet and interaction advantages claimed for tedizolid over linezolid were not outcomes of these 6-to-10-day trials.

shelves.title: Adjunctive glycerol in bacterial meningitis: fewer severe neurological sequelae in children (relative odds 0.31) but higher mortality in adults in a high-HIV setting (63% vs 49%) - split by population
shelves.question: In bacterial meningitis, does adjunctive oral glycerol added to antibiotics improve survival or reduce neurological sequelae and deafness?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Anti-Bacterial Agents/therapeutic use · Anti-Inflammatory Agents/adverse effects · Anti-Inflammatory Agents/therapeutic use · Ceftriaxone/therapeutic use · Chemotherapy, Adjuvant/methods · Child · Child, Preschool · Deafness/prevention & control · Death · Dexamethasone/adverse effects · Dexamethasone/therapeutic use · Double-Blind Method · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · Glycerol/adverse effects · Glycerol/therapeutic use · Humans · Latin America · Male · Meningitis, Bacterial/complications · Meningitis, Bacterial/drug therapy · Meningitis, Bacterial/microbiology · Meningitis, Haemophilus/complications · Meningitis, Haemophilus/drug therapy · Meningitis, Haemophilus/microbiology · Meningitis, Meningococcal/complications · Meningitis, Meningococcal/drug therapy · Meningitis, Meningococcal/microbiology · Nervous System Diseases/prevention & control · Placebos/administration & dosage · Prospective Studies · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: Adjunctive dexamethasone in bacterial meningitis is homed on Shelf #236 and is not re-carded here; this shelf covers the other adjuvant tested in randomised trials, oral glycerol. In 654 Latin-American children on ceftriaxone (Peltola 2007, PMID: 17968821), glycerol did not change death or deafness but cut severe neurological sequelae (relative odds ratio 0.31, 95% CI 0.13-0.76) and the composite of sequelae or death (relative OR 0.44, 0.25-0.76). In 265 adults in Malawi, a high-HIV-prevalence setting (Ajdukiewicz 2011, PMID: 21334262, ISRCTN70121840), glycerol increased day-40 mortality - 86/136 (63%) versus 61/125 (49%) on placebo, adjusted relative OR 2.4 (1.3-4.2) - and the trial was stopped early. The Cochrane review of osmotic therapy (Wall 2018, PMID: 29405037; 5 trials, 1,451 participants) found glycerol made no difference to death (relative RR 1.08, 0.90-1.30) but may reduce neurological disability (relative RR 0.73, 0.53-1.00; low certainty) and deafness (relative RR 0.64, 0.44-0.93). Proposed stamp: SPLIT (child benefit vs adult harm).

cards.headline: Peltola 2007: in 654 children, glycerol cut severe neurological sequelae (relative OR 0.31) but did not change death or deafness
cards.summary: Peltola 2007: in 654 children, glycerol cut severe neurological sequelae (relative OR 0.31) but did not change death or deafness
cards.people: 654 children aged 2 months to 16 years with bacterial meningitis in Latin America, all treated with ceftriaxone and randomised to dexamethasone (n=166), dexamethasone plus glycerol (159), glycerol (166) or placebo (163); main pathogens Haemophilus influenzae type b, pneumococcus and meningococcus.
cards.result: No adjuvant significantly affected death or deafness. Severe neurological sequelae versus placebo: glycerol relative odds ratio 0.31 (95% CI 0.13-0.76, P=.010); dexamethasone plus glycerol relative OR 0.39 (0.17-0.93, P=.033). For the composite of neurological sequelae or death: relative OR 0.44 (0.25-0.76, P=.003) and 0.55 (0.32-0.93, P=.027). The abstract reports odds ratios (relative measures) without the underlying absolute event rates for these outcomes.
cards.watchOut: Relative odds ratios are printed without absolute sequelae rates in the abstract, so the absolute benefit cannot be sized from the record; the population predates widespread Hib vaccination in the region.
cards.source: Peltola H et al. Adjuvant glycerol and/or dexamethasone to improve the outcomes of childhood bacterial meningitis: a prospective, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial. Clin Infect Dis. 2007. PMID: 17968821. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Ajdukiewicz 2011: glycerol increased day-40 deaths in adults - 63% versus 49% on placebo (adjusted relative OR 2.4) - and the trial was stopped early
cards.summary: Ajdukiewicz 2011: glycerol increased day-40 deaths in adults - 63% versus 49% on placebo (adjusted relative OR 2.4) - and the trial was stopped early
cards.people: 265 adults with bacterial meningitis in Malawi, a high-HIV-seroprevalence setting, randomised to oral glycerol 75 mL four times daily (n=137) or placebo sugar solution (n=128), after a separate 45-patient dose-finding phase.
cards.result: By day 40, 86 of 136 patients (63%) on glycerol had died versus 61 of 125 (49%) on placebo (adjusted relative odds ratio 2.4, 95% CI 1.3-4.2, P=0.003). There was no benefit for death and disability combined, nor in proven bacterial or pneumococcal disease. Two serious adverse events were possibly related to the study drug. The trial was stopped early on data and safety monitoring board advice.
cards.watchOut: A single trial in one high-HIV-prevalence, resource-poor setting with very high baseline mortality (over 50%); it may not generalise to adults in low-HIV settings, but it is the only adult randomised evidence.
cards.source: Ajdukiewicz KM et al. Glycerol adjuvant therapy in adults with bacterial meningitis in a high HIV seroprevalence setting in Malawi: a double-blind, randomised controlled trial. Lancet Infect Dis. 2011. PMID: 21334262. Registry ID: ISRCTN70121840. cards.headline: Wall 2018 (Cochrane): across 5 trials glycerol made no difference to death (relative RR 1.08) but may reduce deafness (relative RR 0.64)
cards.summary: Wall 2018 (Cochrane): across 5 trials glycerol made no difference to death (relative RR 1.08) but may reduce deafness (relative RR 0.64)
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials (Wall 2018)
cards.people: Cochrane systematic review of 5 randomised trials of osmotic therapy (glycerol in all) added to antibiotics for acute bacterial meningitis in children and adults; 1,451 participants.
cards.result: Death: relative risk 1.08 (95% CI 0.90-1.30; 1,272 participants; moderate-certainty evidence) - glycerol made no difference. Neurological disability: relative RR 0.73 (0.53-1.00; 1,270 participants; low certainty). Seizures: relative RR 1.08 (0.90-1.30; 1,090). Deafness: relative RR 0.64 (0.44-0.93; 922). Gastrointestinal bleeding: relative RR 0.93 (0.39-2.19; 607). The review reports relative risks without pooled absolute event rates.
cards.watchOut: The pooled death estimate averages the child trial setting and the adult Malawi harm signal, so the pooled null hides opposite effects in different populations; the disability and deafness estimates are low certainty.
cards.source: Wall E et al. Osmotic therapies added to antibiotics for acute bacterial meningitis. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2018. PMID: 29405037. Registry ID: none in the record. shelves.title: Enterococcal endocarditis: ampicillin plus ceftriaxone matched ampicillin plus gentamicin on death and relapse, with far less kidney injury (new renal failure 0% vs 23%)
shelves.question: In Enterococcus faecalis infective endocarditis, is ampicillin plus ceftriaxone as effective as ampicillin plus gentamicin, and is it safer?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Ampicillin/administration & dosage · Anti-Bacterial Agents/administration & dosage · Ceftriaxone/administration & dosage · Cohort Studies · Drug Therapy, Combination/methods · Endocarditis/drug therapy · Endocarditis/microbiology · Enterococcus faecalis/drug effects · Enterococcus faecalis/isolation & purification · Female · Gentamicins/administration & dosage · Gram-Positive Bacterial Infections/drug therapy · Gram-Positive Bacterial Infections/microbiology · Hospitals · Humans · Italy · Male · Middle Aged · Spain · Treatment Outcome · Young Adult
shelves.balance: Early valve surgery in infective endocarditis is homed on Shelf #1627 (EASE) and oral step-down therapy on Shelf #1628 (POET); neither is re-carded here. This shelf covers the unhomed antibiotic question for Enterococcus faecalis endocarditis. In the largest direct comparison, a nonrandomised multicentre cohort of 246 patients (Fernandez-Hidalgo 2013, PMID: 23392394), ampicillin plus ceftriaxone (AC) and ampicillin plus gentamicin (AG) had the same mortality on treatment (22% vs 21%) and at 3 months (8% vs 7%), but treatment had to be stopped for adverse events in 25% of the AG group versus 1% on AC, and new renal failure occurred in 23% versus 0%. A 2024 meta-analysis restricted to 10 observational studies at high risk of bias (Prosty 2024, PMID: 39041860; 911 patients) found no mortality difference (risk difference -0.8%, 95% CI -5.0 to 3.5) and a 26.3-percentage-point higher discontinuation-for-toxicity risk with gentamicin. A 2026 meta-analysis of 6 studies (Sugimoto 2026, PMID: 42581256; 619 patients) likewise found no difference in mortality (relative OR 1.10, 0.73-1.65) or relapse (relative OR 1.08, 0.39-3.01), with fewer total adverse events (relative OR 0.20, 0.08-0.53) and renal events (relative OR 0.34, 0.19-0.58) on AC. All evidence is observational - there is no randomised trial - so the stamp is capped. Proposed stamp: POSSIBLE (equal efficacy, less toxicity; observational evidence only).

cards.headline: Fernandez-Hidalgo 2013: mortality was the same on both regimens (22% vs 21%), but new renal failure was 23% with gentamicin versus 0% with ceftriaxone
cards.summary: Fernandez-Hidalgo 2013: mortality was the same on both regimens (22% vs 21%), but new renal failure was 23% with gentamicin versus 0% with ceftriaxone
cards.people: 246 adults with Enterococcus faecalis infective endocarditis at 17 Spanish and 1 Italian hospitals: 159 treated with ampicillin plus ceftriaxone and 87 with ampicillin plus gentamicin; the ceftriaxone group was sicker at baseline (chronic renal failure 33% vs 16%, P=.004; more cancer and healthcare-acquired infection).
cards.result: Death during treatment 22% (ampicillin-ceftriaxone) vs 21% (ampicillin-gentamicin), P=.81; death at 3 months 8% vs 7%, P=.72; treatment failure 1% vs 2%; relapse 3% vs 4%. Interruption of treatment for adverse events: 25% on the gentamicin regimen vs 1% on the ceftriaxone regimen (P<.001), mainly new renal failure, 23% vs 0% (P<.001).
cards.watchOut: Treatment was chosen by clinicians, not randomised, and the ceftriaxone group had more renal failure and comorbidity at baseline - confounding by indication could hide a real efficacy difference in either direction.
cards.source: Fernandez-Hidalgo N et al. Ampicillin plus ceftriaxone is as effective as ampicillin plus gentamicin for treating Enterococcus faecalis infective endocarditis. Clin Infect Dis. 2013. cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of observational studies (Prosty 2024)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis limited to 10 observational studies, all at high risk of bias, covering 911 patients with Enterococcus faecalis infective endocarditis treated with a gentamicin- or ceftriaxone-containing combination.
cards.result: Gentamicin versus ceftriaxone combinations: mortality risk difference -0.8% (95% CI -5.0 to 3.5); relapse risk difference -0.1% (-2.4 to 2.3); treatment failure risk difference 1.1% (-1.6 to 3.7); discontinuation because of toxicity risk difference 26.3% (19.8 to 32.7) higher with gentamicin. All estimates are absolute risk differences from observational data.
cards.watchOut: Every included study was observational and at high risk of bias; the confidence interval for mortality still allows a 5-percentage-point absolute difference either way.
