cards.headline: Synthesis: equal efficacy, clearly less toxicity with ceftriaxone - but all evidence is observational - POSSIBLE
cards.summary: Synthesis: equal efficacy, clearly less toxicity with ceftriaxone - but all evidence is observational - POSSIBLE
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Fernandez-Hidalgo 2013 (246 patients), Prosty 2024 (10 observational studies, 911 patients) and Sugimoto 2026 (6 studies, 619 patients), all in Enterococcus faecalis infective endocarditis.
cards.result: Mortality and relapse do not differ measurably between ampicillin plus ceftriaxone and ampicillin plus gentamicin (on-treatment death 22% vs 21% in the largest cohort; pooled mortality risk difference -0.8%, -5.0 to 3.5), while gentamicin causes the harm: new renal failure 23% vs 0%, treatment stopped for adverse events 25% vs 1%, and a pooled 26.3-percentage-point excess of toxicity discontinuations. Early surgery (Shelf #1627) and oral step-down (Shelf #1628) are homed elsewhere and not re-carded. Proposed stamp: POSSIBLE (equal efficacy, less toxicity; observational evidence only).
cards.watchOut: No randomised trial exists for this comparison; a modest efficacy difference in either direction cannot be excluded from observational data alone.
cards.source: Synthesis of Fernandez-Hidalgo et al. 2013 (PMID: 23392394), Prosty et al. 2024 (PMID: 39041860) and Sugimoto et al. 2026 (PMID: 42581256). Registry IDs as on the individual cards.

shelves.title: PPI versus H2-blocker for stress-ulcer prophylaxis: trials say PPIs bleed less (relative risk 0.68), cohorts say PPIs bleed more (odds ratio 1.98) — a design-dependent split, with pneumonia and C. difficile unsettled
shelves.question: In ventilated ICU patients needing stress-ulcer prophylaxis, do proton-pump inhibitors prevent gastrointestinal bleeding better than histamine-2 receptor blockers, and at what cost in pneumonia and C. difficile infection?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Critical Illness/therapy · Female · Histamine · Histamine H2 Antagonists/therapeutic use · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Proton Pump Inhibitors/therapeutic use · Ulcer
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the answer depends on which design you trust. Randomised evidence: Deliwala 2022 (PMID: 34049377; 14 trials, 28,526 patients) found proton-pump inhibitors reduced clinically significant gastrointestinal bleeding versus histamine-2-receptor blockers (relative risk 0.68, a 32% relative reduction) and overt bleeding (relative risk 0.61), with no difference in mortality (relative risk 1.05) or pneumonia (relative risk 1.11, imprecise). Observational evidence points the other way: He 2022 (PMID: 34971320; 13 cohort studies, 145,149 patients) found PPIs associated with more bleeding (odds ratio 1.98) and higher mortality (odds ratio 1.27), graded low certainty — the classic signature of confounding by indication. Daou 2022 (PMID: 35714455), in neurocritical care, found no significant head-to-head difference. No carded record reports a Clostridioides difficile effect size for this comparison, so that part of the question is unanswered by the carded evidence. The large PEPTIC trial is homed elsewhere in the library and is not re-carded here. PROPOSED SPLIT — randomised evidence: POSSIBLE (benefit) for PPIs on bleeding prevention; observational evidence: POSSIBLE (harm) signal against PPIs at low certainty; pneumonia and C. difficile: no settled difference on the carded records.

cards.headline: Deliwala 2022: in 14 randomised trials (28,526 patients), proton-pump inhibitors cut clinically significant gastrointestinal bleeding versus H2-blockers (relative risk 0.68) and overt bleeding (relative risk 0.61), with no difference in mortality or pneumonia
cards.summary: Deliwala 2022: in 14 randomised trials (28,526 patients), proton-pump inhibitors cut clinically significant gastrointestinal bleeding versus H2-blockers (relative risk 0.68) and overt bleeding (relative risk 0.61), with no difference in mortality or pneumonia
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials (Deliwala 2022)
cards.people: 14 randomised controlled trials enrolling 28,526 critically ill patients (mean age 57.83 years, 30.82% female), pooled in a meta-analysis with trial sequential analysis of proton-pump inhibitors (PPIs) versus histamine-2-receptor antagonists (H2RAs) for stress-ulcer prophylaxis.
cards.result: PPIs were associated with less clinically significant gastrointestinal bleeding than H2RAs (relative risk 0.68, 95% CI 0.57 to 0.82 — a 32% relative reduction; the record gives no pooled absolute bleeding rates) and less overt gastrointestinal bleeding (relative risk 0.61, 95% CI 0.39 to 0.97). There was no difference in all-cause mortality (relative risk 1.05, 95% CI 1.00 to 1.10), pneumonia incidence (relative risk 1.11, 95% CI 0.82 to 1.51), duration of stay or ventilator days. Trial sequential analysis for clinically significant bleeding ruled out a false-positive result on the authors' analysis. The record reports no Clostridioides difficile effect size for the PPI-versus-H2RA comparison.
cards.watchOut: The randomised evidence answers bleeding, not infection: pneumonia was imprecisely estimated (confidence interval 0.82 to 1.51) and no C. difficile comparison is reported in the record, so 'no difference shown' must not be read as 'no difference exists'.
cards.source: Deliwala SS et al. Proton Pump Inhibitors Versus Histamine-2-Receptor Antagonists for Stress Ulcer Prophylaxis in Critically Ill Patients: A Meta-analysis and Trial Sequential Analysis. Journal of Clinical Gastroenterology. 2022. PMID: 34049377. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: He 2022: in cohort studies totalling 145,149 patients, PPIs were associated with MORE gastrointestinal bleeding (odds ratio 1.98) and higher mortality (odds ratio 1.27) than H2-blockers — the opposite direction from the trials, at low certainty
cards.summary: He 2022: in cohort studies totalling 145,149 patients, PPIs were associated with MORE gastrointestinal bleeding (odds ratio 1.98) and higher mortality (odds ratio 1.27) than H2-blockers — the opposite direction from the trials, at low certainty
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of cohort studies (He 2022)
cards.people: 13 cohort studies (N = 145,149) of critically ill adults comparing PPIs with H2RAs for stress-ulcer prophylaxis in real-world settings; 11 available full texts were rated low to moderate risk of bias, and only studies with adjusted effect estimates were pooled.
cards.result: Meta-analysis of adjusted estimates found PPIs associated with a significantly higher risk of gastrointestinal bleeding than H2RAs (8 studies; odds ratio 1.98, 95% CI 1.30 to 3.01; low certainty of evidence) and, in a post hoc pooling, slightly higher mortality (7 studies; odds ratio 1.27, 95% CI 1.13 to 1.42; low certainty). The authors conclude H2RAs should not be excluded from stress-ulcer prophylaxis on current evidence. The record reports no pneumonia or C. difficile pooled effect size.
cards.watchOut: This is confounding by indication waiting to happen: in routine care, sicker patients with more bleeding risk are preferentially given PPIs, and adjustment can only partly undo that. The discordance with the randomised meta-analysis is itself the finding — the two designs cannot both be read at face value.
cards.source: He N et al. Are Proton Pump Inhibitors More Effective Than Histamine-2-Receptor Antagonists for Stress Ulcer Prophylaxis in Critically Ill Patients? A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Cohort Studies. The Annals of Pharmacotherapy. 2022. PMID: 34971320. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Daou 2022: in neurocritical care, PPIs versus H2-blockers showed no significant difference in gastrointestinal bleeding (relative risk 0.53, confidence interval crossing 1) across 11 pooled trials of 930 patients
cards.summary: Daou 2022: in neurocritical care, PPIs versus H2-blockers showed no significant difference in gastrointestinal bleeding (relative risk 0.53, confidence interval crossing 1) across 11 pooled trials of 930 patients
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials, neurocritical care (Daou 2022)
cards.people: 14 randomised trials enrolling 1,036 neurocritical care patients, of which 11 trials (930 patients) entered the meta-analysis, comparing PPIs or H2RAs with placebo/no prophylaxis and with each other; primary outcome in-ICU gastrointestinal bleeding.
cards.result: Against placebo or no prophylaxis, both drug classes reduced gastrointestinal bleeding (H2RAs relative risk 0.42, 95% CI 0.30 to 0.58; PPIs relative risk 0.37, 95% CI 0.23 to 0.59). Head-to-head, no significant difference in gastrointestinal bleeding was observed between PPIs and H2RAs (relative risk 0.53, 95% CI 0.26 to 1.06; p = 0.07; I2 = 0%). The authors state that high or unclear risk of bias, low event rates and modest sample sizes preclude strong clinical inferences.
cards.watchOut: A narrow population (primary neurologic injury) with very low event rates: its head-to-head estimate is compatible with anything from a large PPI advantage to a small H2RA advantage, and it does not settle the general-ICU question.
cards.source: Daou M et al. Prophylactic acid suppressants in patients with primary neurologic injury: A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials. Journal of Critical Care. 2022. PMID: 35714455. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: randomised and observational evidence point in opposite directions — trials favour PPIs for bleeding prevention, cohorts favour H2-blockers, and neither settles pneumonia or C. difficile
cards.summary: Synthesis: randomised and observational evidence point in opposite directions — trials favour PPIs for bleeding prevention, cohorts favour H2-blockers, and neither settles pneumonia or C. difficile
cards.people: The carded evidence: one meta-analysis of 14 randomised trials (28,526 patients), one meta-analysis of 13 cohort studies (145,149 patients), and one neurocritical-care meta-analysis of randomised trials (930 patients in the pooled analysis). The large PEPTIC randomised comparison of PPI versus H2RA is homed elsewhere in the library and is NOT re-carded here.
cards.result: Randomised pooling found PPIs reduced clinically significant gastrointestinal bleeding versus H2RAs (relative risk 0.68) with no mortality or pneumonia difference (Deliwala 2022). Cohort pooling found the reverse for bleeding (odds ratio 1.98 against PPIs) and higher mortality with PPIs (odds ratio 1.27), at low certainty (He 2022). The neurocritical-care trials found no significant head-to-head difference (Daou 2022). No carded record reports a C. difficile effect size for this comparison. PROPOSED SPLIT — randomised evidence: POSSIBLE (benefit) for PPIs on bleeding; observational evidence: POSSIBLE (harm) signal against PPIs, low certainty.
cards.watchOut: Anyone quoting only one of these syntheses can make either drug class look better. The honest summary is design-dependent disagreement, with confounding by indication the most likely explanation for the cohort result.

synthesis the carded evidence: one meta-analysis of 14 randomised trials (28,526 patients), one meta-analysis of 13 cohort studies (145,149 patients), and one neurocritical-care meta-analysis of randomised trials (930 patients in the pooled analysis). the large peptic randomised comparison of ppi versus h2ra is homed elsewhere in the library and is not re-carded here. randomised pooling found ppis reduced clinically significant gastrointestinal bleeding versus h2ras (relative risk 0.68) with no mortality or pneumonia difference (deliwala 2022). cohort pooling found the reverse for bleeding (odds ratio 1.98 against ppis) and higher mortality with ppis (odds ratio 1.27), at low certainty (he 2022). the neurocritical-care trials found no significant head-to-head difference (daou 2022). no carded record reports a c. difficile effect size for this comparison. proposed split — randomised evidence: possible (benefit) for ppis on bleeding; observational evidence: possible (harm) signal against ppis, low certainty. anyone quoting only one of these syntheses can make either drug class look better. the honest summary is design-dependent disagreement, with confounding by indication the most likely explanation for the cohort result. synthesis of deliwala ss et al. journal of clinical gastroenterology. 2022 (pmid: 34049377); he n et al. the annals of pharmacotherapy. 2022 (pmid: 34971320); daou m et al. journal of critical care. 2022 (pmid: 35714455).

shelves.title: Prolonged tuberculosis treatment in diabetes: MAYBE (weak evidence) — diabetes brings more relapse on standard 6-month treatment, but no study has ever tested whether treating beyond 6 months helps
shelves.question: Should adults with tuberculosis and diabetes have prolonged treatment beyond 6 months?
shelves.mesh: Antitubercular Agents · Diabetes Complications · Humans · Survival Analysis · Treatment Failure · Treatment Outcome · Tuberculosis
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — prolongation itself has never been randomised, printed on the face. The rationale for longer treatment is real but indirect: two systematic reviews find that people with diabetes fare worse on standard tuberculosis treatment — a relative risk of 1.69 for the combined outcome of failure and death and 3.89 for relapse in the 2011 review, and odds ratios of 1.88 for death and 1.64 for relapse in the 2019 update (56,122 patients with tuberculosis and diabetes). One older Japanese cohort found relapse after a 6-month regimen concentrated in patients with diabetes (6 of 54 vs 3 of 237). But no carded record — and no trial found this session — compares more than 6 months against 6 months in patients with diabetes, so worse outcomes on standard treatment do not by themselves prove that prolonging treatment fixes them; the reviews instead point to glucose control, monitoring and drug exposure as the open questions. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): routine prolongation beyond 6 months for tuberculosis with diabetes is untested — diabetes is associated with more failure, death and relapse on standard treatment, but no study shows that longer treatment removes that excess.

cards.headline: Baker 2011 (systematic review, 33 studies): diabetes was associated with a relative risk of 1.69 for failure and death combined during tuberculosis treatment, and 3.89 for relapse — the outcome gap that motivates the prolongation question
cards.summary: Baker 2011 (systematic review, 33 studies): diabetes was associated with a relative risk of 1.69 for failure and death combined during tuberculosis treatment, and 3.89 for relapse — the outcome gap that motivates the prolongation question
cards.people: People with diabetes treated for tuberculosis in 33 observational studies (searched 1980–2010): 9 reported culture conversion at 2–3 months, 12 the combined outcome of failure and death, 23 death, 5 relapse and 4 drug-resistant recurrence. The review's total participant count is not printed as a single number in the record, and none is invented here.
cards.result: Patients with diabetes had a risk ratio for the combined outcome of failure and death of 1.69 (95% CI 1.36 to 2.12) — a relative measure; the record does not print the underlying absolute event rates beside it. The relative risk of death during treatment was 1.89 (95% CI 1.52 to 2.36) across 23 unadjusted studies and 4.95 (95% CI 2.69 to 9.10) in the 4 studies adjusted for age and other confounders. Diabetes was also associated with an increased risk of relapse (relative risk 3.89, 95% CI 2.43 to 6.23). Studies of sputum culture conversion at 2–3 months were heterogeneous (relative risks 0.79 to 3.25). The authors call for testing for diabetes, improved glucose control and increased monitoring — not, in this record, for longer treatment.
cards.watchOut: Every estimate here compares patients with versus without diabetes on the treatment they happened to receive — it quantifies the problem, and says nothing about whether extending treatment beyond 6 months changes any of these outcomes.
cards.source: Baker MA et al. The impact of diabetes on tuberculosis treatment outcomes: a systematic review. BMC medicine. 2011. PMID: 21722362. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: Antitubercular Agents · Diabetes Complications · Humans · Survival Analysis · Treatment Failure · Treatment Outcome · Tuberculosis

cards.headline: Huangfu 2019 (updated systematic review, 104 publications): patients with tuberculosis and diabetes had higher odds of death (OR 1.88) and relapse (OR 1.64) than patients with tuberculosis alone — 56,122 patients with both conditions among 299,157 studied
cards.summary: Huangfu 2019 (updated systematic review, 104 publications): patients with tuberculosis and diabetes had higher odds of death (OR 1.88) and relapse (OR 1.64) than patients with tuberculosis alone — 56,122 patients with both conditions among 299,157 studied
cards.people: 104 publications of cohort and case-control studies (searched 1980–2018) comparing tuberculosis treatment outcomes in patients with and without diabetes; 64 studies reporting death included 56,122 individuals with tuberculosis and diabetes and 243,035 with tuberculosis alone.
cards.result: Patients with tuberculosis and diabetes had higher odds of death (OR 1.88, 95% CI 1.59 to 2.21) and of relapse (OR 1.64, 95% CI 1.29 to 2.08) than patients with tuberculosis alone — relative (odds) measures; the record does not print absolute event rates beside them. More limited evidence suggested about double the risk of developing multidrug-resistant tuberculosis (OR 1.98, 95% CI 1.51 to 2.60). Some outcomes showed substantial heterogeneity the reviewers could not fully explain, though adjustment for confounding and country income level accounted for some of it. The authors call for cost-effectiveness assessment of interventions to enhance combined tuberculosis–diabetes treatment; this record does not test or report a prolonged-duration comparison.
cards.watchOut: As with the 2011 review, this is prognosis, not treatment evidence: it cannot distinguish whether the excess relapse reflects treatment that is too short, drug exposure that is too low, glucose control, or the diabetes itself.
cards.source: Huangfu P et al. The effects of diabetes on tuberculosis treatment outcomes: an updated systematic review and meta-analysis. The international journal of tuberculosis and lung disease : the official journal of the International Union against Tuberculosis and Lung Disease. 2019. PMID: 31439109. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2 · Humans · Treatment Outcome · Tuberculosis, Pulmonary

cards.headline: Wada 1999: after a 6-month regimen in Japan, relapse was concentrated in patients with diabetes — 6 of 54 patients with diabetes relapsed (7.9 per 100 person-years) versus 3 of 237 without (0.8 per 100 person-years), P < 0.001
cards.summary: Wada 1999: after a 6-month regimen in Japan, relapse was concentrated in patients with diabetes — 6 of 54 patients with diabetes relapsed (7.9 per 100 person-years) versus 3 of 237 without (0.8 per 100 person-years), P < 0.001
cards.people: New pulmonary tuberculosis patients treated at one Tokyo hospital, 1991–1996: 620 started a 6-month regimen (2HRZS or E/4HRE), and of 295 patients who completed the 6-month regimen and were followed (mean follow-up 17.2 months), 54 had diabetes mellitus and 237 did not (subgroup counts as printed in the record). Nine patients (3.1%) relapsed after completing the 6-month regimen.
cards.result: Six of the nine relapses occurred in patients with diabetes. The relapse rate was higher in patients with diabetes than in patients without (6/54, 7.9 per 100 person-years, vs 3/237, 0.8 per 100 person-years; P < 0.001). Culture conversion was 93% at 2 months and 100% at 5 months among drug-susceptible cases who completed treatment. Drug-induced hepatotoxicity occurred in 43 of 535 patients (8.0%) with initially normal liver tests on the pyrazinamide-containing regimen. The study did not compare 6 months with any longer duration — no patient group was randomised or assigned to prolonged treatment.
cards.watchOut: A single-centre 1990s cohort with only nine relapses in total: the diabetes signal rests on six events, regimens and diabetes care have changed since, and — again — nobody in this study received the prolonged treatment this shelf asks about.
cards.source: Wada M et al. [Six-months chemotherapy (2HRZS or E/4HRE) of new cases of pulmonary tuberculosis--six year experiences on its effectiveness, toxicity, and acceptability]. Kekkaku : [Tuberculosis]. 1999. PMID: 10355221. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: diabetes clearly worsens tuberculosis outcomes on standard treatment (relapse relative risk 3.89 in 2011; odds ratio 1.64 in the 104-study update) — but no carded study has ever compared treatment beyond 6 months against 6 months in patients with diabetes, so prolongation remains an untested inference, not an evidence-based rule
cards.summary: Synthesis: diabetes clearly worsens tuberculosis outcomes on standard treatment (relapse relative risk 3.89 in 2011; odds ratio 1.64 in the 104-study update) — but no carded study has ever compared treatment beyond 6 months against 6 months in patients with diabetes, so prolongation remains an untested inference, not an evidence-based rule
cards.people: The carded evidence: two systematic reviews (33 studies; and 104 publications including 56,122 patients with tuberculosis and diabetes) and one single-centre cohort (295 regimen completers followed for relapse, 54 with diabetes). Total carded participants run into the hundreds of thousands across the reviews, so no small-N stamp labelling applies — the gap on this shelf is the absence of any duration comparison, not sample size, and it is printed here.
cards.result: Failure and death combined: relative risk 1.69 with diabetes (Baker 2011). Relapse: relative risk 3.89 (Baker 2011) and odds ratio 1.64 (Huangfu 2019); in the one cohort reporting relapse by diabetes status after a 6-month regimen, 6/54 vs 3/237 (Wada 1999). Duration comparisons in diabetes: none in any carded record. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): routine prolongation beyond 6 months is untested; the excess risk with diabetes is established, the remedy is not.
cards.watchOut: Worse prognosis is not evidence for a longer course: the same data are equally consistent with better glucose control, therapeutic drug monitoring or closer follow-up being the effective response, and prolonging treatment also prolongs toxicity exposure (hepatotoxicity 8.0% in the carded cohort).
cards.source: Synthesis of Baker MA et al. BMC medicine. 2011 (PMID: 21722362); Huangfu P et al. The international journal of tuberculosis and lung disease. 2019 (PMID: 31439109); Wada M et al. Kekkaku : [Tuberculosis]. 1999 (PMID: 10355221).

shelves.title: Shingles antivirals after 72 hours: untested — every trial started treatment within 72 hours, where famciclovir shortened neuralgia but prevention of neuralgia is disputed; no evidence measures a late start
shelves.question: For adults with shingles, does starting antivirals after 72 hours still reduce pain?
shelves.mesh: 2-Aminopurine · Acute Disease · Antiviral Agents · Famciclovir · Female · Herpes Zoster · Herpesvirus 3, Human · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Neuralgia · Patient Compliance · Time Factors · Virus Shedding
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — the late start itself is untested. Every randomised trial behind antiviral treatment of shingles enrolled patients within 72 hours of rash onset, so there is no direct trial evidence that starting after 72 hours reduces pain; any benefit from a late start is extrapolation. What early treatment does is itself mixed: famciclovir started within 72 hours resolved postherpetic neuralgia about twice as fast as placebo (Tyring 1995, PMID: 7778840; hazard ratios 1.7–1.9, median duration shortened by about 2 months), and a meta-analysis of aciclovir trials found less residual pain at 6 months (Jackson 1997, PMID: 9129551; summary odds ratio 0.54), yet the Cochrane review (Chen 2014, PMID: 24500927) — which by design included only trials of treatment given within 72 hours — found oral aciclovir did not significantly reduce the incidence of postherpetic neuralgia at 4 months (RR 0.75, 95% CI 0.51–1.11) or 6 months (RR 1.05). The head-to-head valaciclovir-versus-aciclovir trial is homed on shelf #5031 and is cross-pointed here, not re-carded. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): starting antivirals after 72 hours may still help pain, but no trial has tested it — the proven window is within 72 hours, and even there the effect is on pain duration more than on whether neuralgia occurs.

cards.headline: Tyring 1995: famciclovir started within 72 hours of rash onset resolved postherpetic neuralgia about twice as fast as placebo — the trial defines the early window; it enrolled nobody later
cards.summary: Tyring 1995: famciclovir started within 72 hours of rash onset resolved postherpetic neuralgia about twice as fast as placebo — the trial defines the early window; it enrolled nobody later
cards.people: 419 immunocompetent adults with uncomplicated herpes zoster at 36 centres in the United States, Canada and Australia, assigned within 72 hours of rash onset to famciclovir 500 mg, famciclovir 750 mg, or placebo, three times daily for 7 days; pain was assessed at lesion visits and then monthly for 5 months after healing.
cards.result: Famciclovir accelerated lesion healing and reduced the duration of viral shedding. Famciclovir recipients had faster resolution of postherpetic neuralgia than placebo recipients — hazard ratio 1.7 (95% CI 1.1 to 2.7) for the 500-mg group and 1.9 (CI 1.2 to 2.9) for the 750-mg group — and the median duration of postherpetic neuralgia was reduced by approximately 2 months. Famciclovir was well tolerated, with a safety profile similar to placebo.
cards.watchOut: Eligibility required presentation within 72 hours of rash onset: the trial is evidence about early treatment only and cannot be cited for benefit when treatment starts later.
cards.source: Tyring S et al. Famciclovir for the treatment of acute herpes zoster: effects on acute disease and postherpetic neuralgia. A randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial. Collaborative Famciclovir Herpes Zoster Study Group. Annals of internal medicine. 1995. PMID: 7778840. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Chen 2014 (Cochrane): reviewing only trials of antivirals given within 72 hours, oral aciclovir did not significantly reduce postherpetic neuralgia at 4 months (RR 0.75) or 6 months (RR 1.05)
cards.summary: Chen 2014 (Cochrane): reviewing only trials of antivirals given within 72 hours, oral aciclovir did not significantly reduce postherpetic neuralgia at 4 months (RR 0.75) or 6 months (RR 1.05)
cards.people: Cochrane review of randomised controlled trials of antiviral treatment given within 72 hours after the onset of herpes zoster for preventing postherpetic neuralgia: 6 RCTs with 1,211 participants — five trials of oral aciclovir and one trial of oral famciclovir with 419 participants (the Tyring 1995 trial carded on this shelf).
cards.result: For the primary outcome, based on three trials (609 participants), there was no significant difference between aciclovir and control in the incidence of postherpetic neuralgia four months after rash onset (risk ratio 0.75, 95% confidence interval 0.51 to 1.11), nor at six months (RR 1.05, 95% CI 0.87 to 1.27, two trials, 476 participants). In four trials (692 participants) there was some evidence for a reduction in the incidence of pain four weeks after rash onset. In the famciclovir trial, neither dose reduced the incidence of herpetic neuralgia significantly. The review concludes there is high-quality evidence that oral aciclovir does not reduce the incidence of postherpetic neuralgia significantly.
cards.watchOut: The review's eligibility criterion — treatment within 72 hours — is itself the key fact for this shelf: the entire randomised evidence base sits inside that window, so the review can neither confirm nor refute benefit from a later start.
cards.source: Chen N et al. Antiviral treatment for preventing postherpetic neuralgia. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2014. PMID: 24500927. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Jackson 1997: meta-analysis of aciclovir trials (all starting within 72 hours) found 46% lower odds of residual pain at 6 months (summary OR 0.54)
cards.summary: Jackson 1997: meta-analysis of aciclovir trials (all starting within 72 hours) found 46% lower odds of residual pain at 6 months (summary OR 0.54)
cards.people: Meta-analysis of published randomised trials of oral acyclovir in immunocompetent adults with herpes zoster: 30 trials identified, of which 5 homogeneous placebo-controlled trials were combined using the fixed-effects model of Peto; the record does not state the combined participant total.
cards.result: The summary odds ratio for the incidence of 'any pain' in the distribution of the rash at 6 months in adults treated with aciclovir was 0.54 (95% confidence interval 0.36–0.81). The authors conclude that treatment of herpes zoster with oral aciclovir within 72 hours of rash onset may reduce the incidence of residual pain at 6 months by 46% in immunocompetent adults — a relative odds reduction; the record gives no absolute pain rates.
cards.watchOut: This 1997 pooled estimate conflicts with the later Cochrane review's null for neuralgia incidence; both, however, describe treatment started within 72 hours, so neither answers the after-72-hours question directly.
cards.source: Jackson JL et al. The effect of treating herpes zoster with oral acyclovir in preventing postherpetic neuralgia. A meta-analysis. Archives of internal medicine. 1997. PMID: 9129551. cards.headline: Dworkin 1998: reanalysis of the famciclovir trial — greater age, rash severity and acute pain predicted prolonged neuralgia, and famciclovir reduced both its duration and prevalence (same 419 patients as Tyring 1995; not a separate trial)
cards.summary: Dworkin 1998: reanalysis of the famciclovir trial — greater age, rash severity and acute pain predicted prolonged neuralgia, and famciclovir reduced both its duration and prevalence (same 419 patients as Tyring 1995; not a separate trial)
cards.type: Secondary analysis of a randomised trial (Dworkin 1998)
cards.people: New and previously reported analyses of the data from the placebo-controlled famciclovir trial in herpes zoster (419 immunocompetent adults enrolled within 72 hours of rash onset; the same population as the Tyring 1995 card on this shelf), examining postherpetic neuralgia defined three ways: pain persisting after rash healing, pain persisting more than 30 days after enrolment, or pain persisting more than 3 months after enrolment.
cards.result: Greater age, rash severity and acute pain severity were risk factors for prolonged postherpetic neuralgia. Treatment with famciclovir significantly reduced both the duration and the prevalence of postherpetic neuralgia, including when the analysis controlled for the significant covariates; prevalence was examined at monthly intervals from 30 to 180 days after enrolment. The record reports no separate effect size for the late-treatment question, and no participant in the underlying trial started treatment after 72 hours.
cards.watchOut: This is the same 419-patient trial as the Tyring card, reanalysed — it must not be counted as independent evidence, and its risk-factor findings (older age, worse rash, worse acute pain) identify who suffers longest, not who benefits from late treatment.
cards.source: Dworkin RH et al. Postherpetic neuralgia: impact of famciclovir, age, rash severity, and acute pain in herpes zoster patients. The Journal of infectious diseases. 1998. PMID: 9852980. cards.headline: Synthesis: no trial has ever randomised patients presenting after 72 hours — the proven benefit (shorter neuralgia with early famciclovir) and the disputed benefit (whether neuralgia is prevented at all) both stop at the 72-hour door
cards.summary: Synthesis: no trial has ever randomised patients presenting after 72 hours — the proven benefit (shorter neuralgia with early famciclovir) and the disputed benefit (whether neuralgia is prevented at all) both stop at the 72-hour door
cards.people: The carded evidence: one famciclovir trial of 419 patients enrolled within 72 hours (carded twice — primary report and reanalysis of the same patients), one Cochrane review of 6 trials and 1,211 participants restricted to treatment within 72 hours, and one aciclovir meta-analysis of 5 trials, all within 72 hours. Unique participants across the trial evidence are roughly 1,200–1,800 with overlaps between the review and the trial cards, so no small-N stamp labelling applies; the limitation is the enrolment window, not the numbers.
cards.result: Started within 72 hours, famciclovir shortened postherpetic neuralgia by about 2 months at the median (Tyring 1995; Dworkin 1998). Pooled aciclovir data conflict: one meta-analysis found lower odds of pain at 6 months (OR 0.54; Jackson 1997) while the Cochrane review found no significant reduction in neuralgia incidence at 4 or 6 months (Chen 2014). For a start after 72 hours, no carded record reports any effect size — the record set is silent because late presenters were excluded. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) for the after-72-hours question.
cards.watchOut: Clinicians often still treat late presenters who are immunocompromised, have eye involvement, or are still forming new lesions — those are judgement calls outside this evidence; this shelf answers only the pain question in ordinary immunocompetent shingles, where the honest answer is 'untested'.

shelves.title: Treating asymptomatic candiduria: fluconazole clears the urine at 14 days (50% versus 29%) but cultures are equal again two weeks later, and no study shows a clinical outcome benefit — treatment made no difference to recurrence, candidemia or mortality
shelves.question: Does treating asymptomatic candiduria improve outcomes in hospitalized adults?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Antifungal Agents · Candida · Candida albicans · Candidiasis · Double-Blind Method · Female · Fluconazole · Humans · Male · Treatment Outcome · Urinary Tract Infections · Urine
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (no benefit) — anchored on the one randomised trial, with concordant observational follow-up. Sobel 2000 randomised 316 hospitalised patients with asymptomatic or minimally symptomatic candiduria to fluconazole or placebo: urine clearance at day 14 favoured fluconazole (50% versus 29%, P < .001), but cultures two weeks after therapy showed similar candiduria rates in treated and untreated patients, and the authors state eradication was not associated with clinical benefit — the treatment made no difference to anything durable. The observational record points the same way: treated asymptomatic patients were more likely to have later positive cultures over up to 48 months of follow-up, with candidemia rare and never attributed to the candiduria (Revankar 2011), and recurrence, mortality and length of stay were similar whether care followed IDSA guidance or not (He 2021). Treating is therefore exposure to an antifungal for a transient laboratory effect. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (no benefit) — treating asymptomatic candiduria clears the urine short-term but improves no clinical outcome in any carded study.

cards.headline: Sobel 2000 (randomised, double-blind): fluconazole cleared candiduria at day 14 more often than placebo (50% versus 29%, P < .001) — but two weeks after therapy the candiduria rates were similar, and eradication was not associated with clinical benefit (N = 316)
cards.summary: Sobel 2000 (randomised, double-blind): fluconazole cleared candiduria at day 14 more often than placebo (50% versus 29%, P < .001) — but two weeks after therapy the candiduria rates were similar, and eradication was not associated with clinical benefit (N = 316)
cards.people: 316 consecutive candiduric (asymptomatic or minimally symptomatic) hospitalised patients randomised to fluconazole 200 mg or placebo daily for 14 days (159 fluconazole, 157 placebo), in the NIAID Mycoses Study Group trial; eradication was assessed by urine culture at day 14 and again two weeks after therapy.
cards.result: In an intent-to-treat analysis, candiduria cleared by day 14 in 79 (50%) of 159 patients receiving fluconazole and 46 (29%) of 157 receiving placebo (P < .001) — an absolute difference of 21 percentage points in a laboratory outcome. Eradication was higher in patients completing 14 days, including 33 (52%) of 64 catheterised and 42 (78%) of 54 non-catheterised patients, and pretreatment serum creatinine was inversely related to eradication. Crucially, cultures at two weeks after therapy revealed similar candiduria rates among treated and untreated patients, and the authors state the long-term eradication rates were disappointing and not associated with clinical benefit. Oral fluconazole was safe.
cards.watchOut: The trial's endpoint is a urine culture, not illness: it proves antifungals can sterilise urine briefly, and its own follow-up shows the effect evaporates — the strongest single study on this shelf is evidence against a durable benefit, not for one.
cards.source: Sobel JD et al. Candiduria: a randomized, double-blind study of treatment with fluconazole and placebo. The National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases (NIAID) Mycoses Study Group. Clinical infectious diseases : an official publication of the Infectious Diseases Society of America. 2000. cards.headline: Revankar 2011: in long-term follow-up of 188 patients with candiduria, patients treated for asymptomatic candiduria were paradoxically more likely to have subsequent positive urine cultures than untreated patients, and little evidence of treatment benefit was identified
cards.summary: Revankar 2011: in long-term follow-up of 188 patients with candiduria, patients treated for asymptomatic candiduria were paradoxically more likely to have subsequent positive urine cultures than untreated patients, and little evidence of treatment benefit was identified
cards.type: Retrospective cohort study with long-term follow-up (Revankar 2011)
cards.people: Retrospective chart review of 188 patients with candiduria at a single institution from January 1999 to December 2000, with follow-up cultures and mortality tracked to December 2003; 91 patients had at least one follow-up culture more than one month after the initial culture (range 2–48 months).
cards.result: Patients receiving antifungal therapy for asymptomatic candiduria were more likely to have subsequent positive urine cultures than patients who never received antifungal therapy (the record reports the direction without an effect size in its abstract — printed plainly). Six patients developed candidemia during follow-up, in none considered a consequence of candiduria. Mortality at the end of follow-up (mean 18 months) was 43%, including one death attributed to candidemia. The authors conclude therapy for candiduria does not appear to reduce recurrence rates through 48 months and little evidence of treatment benefit was identified.
cards.watchOut: Retrospective and confounded by indication — sicker patients are likelier to be treated, which could manufacture the paradoxical recurrence association; the card is used for its narrower, safer finding: no sign of benefit, in the direction opposite to what treatment advocates would predict.
cards.source: Revankar SG et al. Long-term follow-up of patients with candiduria. European journal of clinical microbiology & infectious diseases : official publication of the European Society of Clinical Microbiology. 2011. PMID: 20857164. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: He 2021: in 251 hospitalised patients with candiduria, recurrence, mortality and length of stay were similar whether management followed IDSA guidance (which advises against treating asymptomatic candiduria) or not
cards.summary: He 2021: in 251 hospitalised patients with candiduria, recurrence, mortality and length of stay were similar whether management followed IDSA guidance (which advises against treating asymptomatic candiduria) or not
cards.type: Retrospective cohort study of guideline implementation (He 2021)
cards.people: Retrospective single-centre study of 251 hospitalised patients with candiduria, examining how management compared with Infectious Diseases Society of America (IDSA) evidence-based recommendations for catheter management and antifungal use, and which factors drove clinicians' decisions.
cards.result: Overtreatment was common in asymptomatic candiduria, and some symptomatic patients received improper drug selections or no therapy despite recommendations. The recurrence rate, mortality, and hospital stay length were similar in candiduria patients regardless of the clinical management — i.e. guideline-concordant (largely non-treatment of asymptomatic cases) versus non-concordant management made no difference to those outcomes; the only significant difference was in hospital charges for symptomatic patients. Clinicians tended to start empiric antifungal therapy in patients with pneumonia, multisite Candida colonisation, higher urine Candida colony counts, and longer hospital stay.
cards.watchOut: 'Similar outcomes regardless of management' in a retrospective study cannot prove equivalence — but combined with the randomised trial's evaporating culture effect, it completes a consistent picture: no carded study shows treating asymptomatic candiduria improving any clinical outcome.
cards.source: He Z et al. Management of candiduria in hospitalized patients: a single-center study on the implementation of IDSA guidelines and factors affecting clinical decisions. shelves.title: Early vasopressors and dialysis in septic shock (PARTIAL completion of #1070): dialysis prevention is unproven — the favourable renal signal is cohort-heavy and sizeless, and dialysis-free days did not differ in trial-inclusive pooling
shelves.question: In adults with septic shock at risk of AKI, does early vasopressor use prevent dialysis versus fluid-first resuscitation?
shelves.mesh: Humans · *Shock, Septic/drug therapy · Vasoconstrictor Agents/therapeutic use · Norepinephrine/therapeutic use · Cohort Studies · Renal Replacement Therapy
shelves.balance: PARTIAL completion — home live #1070 covers the restrictive-fluid/early-vasopressor strategy for mortality (CLASSIC, CLOVERS and ARISE FLUIDS, all null on mortality) and is cross-pointed here, not re-carded; this shelf asks only the slice #1070 does not answer: dialysis. On dialysis specifically, the evidence is thin and divided. One meta-analysis dominated by cohort studies (Ye 2023, 23 studies of which 21 were cohorts) reports that early vasopressor initiation (within 1–6 hours) was associated with a lower incidence of kidney injury (P = 0.001) and less renal replacement therapy use (P = 0.022) — but its record prints P values without a pooled effect size for either renal outcome, so the size of any protection cannot be stated. The most trial-inclusive meta-analysis (Ahn 2024, 12 studies, 7,281 patients) prespecified days free from renal replacement therapy and found no difference in that or the other secondary outcomes (the treatment made no difference to dialysis-free days). The updated 2025 meta-analysis (Shi 2025, 10 studies, 4,767 patients) also listed renal-replacement-therapy-free days as a secondary outcome but does not report its result in the record, while finding mortality associations driven substantially by non-randomised designs. No individual randomised trial carded here reports dialysis as an outcome, and the large strategy trials sit on #1070. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): early vasopressor use has not been shown to prevent dialysis; the only favourable renal signal comes from cohort-heavy pooling without a printed effect size, and the trial-inclusive pooling found no difference in dialysis-free days.

cards.headline: Ye 2023 meta-analysis: early vasopressor initiation was associated with less kidney injury (P = 0.001) and less renal replacement therapy use (P = 0.022) — but the record prints no pooled effect size for either renal outcome, and 21 of its 23 studies were cohorts
cards.summary: Ye 2023 meta-analysis: early vasopressor initiation was associated with less kidney injury (P = 0.001) and less renal replacement therapy use (P = 0.022) — but the record prints no pooled effect size for either renal outcome, and 21 of its 23 studies were cohorts
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis, mostly cohort studies (Ye 2023)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 23 studies (2 randomised controlled trials and 21 cohort studies) of vasopressor initiation timing in septic shock, comparing an early group (vasopressor started 1–6 hours within septic shock onset) with a late group. Total participant number is not documented in the record.
cards.result: The early group had lower short-term mortality than the late group (odds ratio 0.775, 95% CI 0.673 to 0.893, P = 0.000, relative measure). For the renal outcomes this shelf asks about, the record reports that the early group had a lower incidence of kidney injury (P = 0.001) and lower renal replacement therapy use (P = 0.022), with earlier achievement of target mean arterial pressure, shorter vasopressor duration and a lower serum lactate at 24 hours — but it prints no pooled odds ratio or event rates for kidney injury or dialysis, so the size of the renal association cannot be stated from this record.
cards.watchOut: With 21 of 23 studies observational, earlier vasopressor start is entangled with how sick patients looked and how their units practise; a P value without an effect size cannot support a claim that dialysis is prevented, only that an association was detected.

cards.headline: Ahn 2024 meta-analysis: across 12 studies (7,281 patients), early versus late norepinephrine made no difference to days free from renal replacement therapy or the other secondary outcomes
cards.summary: Ahn 2024 meta-analysis: across 12 studies (7,281 patients), early versus late norepinephrine made no difference to days free from renal replacement therapy or the other secondary outcomes
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 12 studies (4 randomised controlled trials and 8 observational studies) comprising 7,281 adults with sepsis/septic shock, categorised into early and late norepinephrine groups by time points or protocol differences. Secondary outcomes included days free from renal replacement therapy, ventilator-free days, vasopressor-free days, ICU length of stay, adverse events and total fluid volume.
cards.result: For overall mortality there was no significant difference between early and late norepinephrine in randomised trials (odds ratio 0.70, 95% CI 0.41–1.19, relative measure) or observational studies (odds ratio 0.83, 95% CI 0.54–1.29). The incidence of pulmonary edema was lower in the early group in the three randomised trials reporting it (odds ratio 0.43, 95% CI 0.25–0.74, relative measure). No differences were found in the other secondary outcomes — which include days free from renal replacement therapy (the treatment made no difference to dialysis-free days).
cards.watchOut: 'No difference in the other secondary outcomes' is the record's own summary wording; the record does not print the pooled estimate for dialysis-free days separately, so the null is stated at the level the record supports.

cards.headline: Shi 2025 updated meta-analysis: renal-replacement-therapy-free days were a prespecified secondary outcome, but the record does not report the result — the dialysis question is unanswered even in the newest pooling
cards.summary: Shi 2025 updated meta-analysis: renal-replacement-therapy-free days were a prespecified secondary outcome, but the record does not report the result — the dialysis question is unanswered even in the newest pooling
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis with trial sequential analysis (Shi 2025)
cards.people: Updated systematic review and meta-analysis with trial sequential analysis of 10 studies (2 randomised trials, 3 propensity-matched studies and 5 observational studies) involving 4,767 adults with septic shock, comparing early versus non-early norepinephrine initiation. Secondary outcomes included renal replacement therapy free days, fluid volume at 6 hours, norepinephrine dose, mechanical-ventilation-free days and time to target mean arterial pressure.
cards.result: Early norepinephrine was associated with lower mortality in the randomised trials (odds ratio 0.49, 95% CI 0.25–0.96, relative measure), in pooled randomised plus propensity-matched studies (odds ratio 0.65, 95% CI 0.42–0.99) and in observational studies (odds ratio 0.71, 95% CI 0.54–0.94); trial sequential analysis indicated more data are needed. Subgroup analyses showed reduced mortality when lactate was ≤3 mmol/L (about 27 mg/dL) and norepinephrine was given within 1 hour. The record reports results for fluid volume, time to target pressure and ventilation-free days, but does not report a result for renal replacement therapy free days.
cards.watchOut: An outcome listed in methods but absent from results is a reporting gap, not a null: this card is evidence about the state of the dialysis evidence, and it must not be cited as showing either benefit or no benefit for dialysis.
cards.source: Shi R et al. Early norepinephrine for patients with septic shock: an updated systematic review and meta-analysis with trial sequential analysis. Critical Care. 2025. PMID: 40329359. cards.headline: Synthesis: dialysis prevention by early vasopressors is unproven — a cohort-heavy pooling reports less dialysis use without an effect size, the trial-inclusive pooling found no difference in dialysis-free days, and the newest pooling does not report the outcome
cards.summary: Synthesis: dialysis prevention by early vasopressors is unproven — a cohort-heavy pooling reports less dialysis use without an effect size, the trial-inclusive pooling found no difference in dialysis-free days, and the newest pooling does not report the outcome
cards.people: The carded evidence: three meta-analyses of vasopressor timing in septic shock — Ye 2023 (23 studies, total N not documented in the record), Ahn 2024 (12 studies, 7,281 patients) and Shi 2025 (10 studies, 4,767 patients). The strategy trials themselves are homed on live #1070 and are not re-carded here.
cards.result: Early initiation was associated with lower kidney injury incidence (P = 0.001) and lower renal replacement therapy use (P = 0.022) in the cohort-dominated pooling, with no pooled effect size printed (Ye 2023); it made no difference to days free from renal replacement therapy in the pooling that included 4 randomised trials (Ahn 2024); and the renal outcome went unreported in the 2025 update (Shi 2025). PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): early vasopressor use has not been shown to prevent dialysis.
cards.watchOut: All three cards are secondary poolings of substantially the same underlying studies, so they are not three independent confirmations; the randomised core of this literature is two to four small trials, none carded here with dialysis as its own reported outcome.
cards.source: Synthesis of Ye E et al. Shock. 2023 (PMID: 37695641); Ahn C et al. Chest. 2024 (PMID: 38972348); Shi R et al. Critical Care. 2025 (PMID: 40329359).

shelves.title: Glutamine in general critical illness (PARTIAL completion of live #1049): no mortality benefit across two trials, a harm signal in one bundled formula, and a Cochrane long-term mortality ratio of exactly 1.00
shelves.question: In adults with critical illness, does glutamine supplementation reduce mortality versus standard nutrition without glutamine?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Critical Care · Critical Illness · Cross Infection · Dietary Supplements · Double-Blind Method · Drug Combinations · Female · Glutamine · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Parenteral Nutrition · Quality of Life · Selenium · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — on mortality, printed on the face. This pack is a PARTIAL completion: live shelf #1049 homes glutamine in severe burns only (RE-ENERGIZE), and the high-dose glutamine-and-antioxidants trial REDOXS (PMID 23594003) is homed on live shelf #79 and is not re-carded here. FLAG (precedent b): the field's largest trial is homed elsewhere, so this shelf answers the wider question — standard-dose glutamine in general critical illness — from the remaining free reports, which are concordant. SIGNET (502 ICU patients needing parenteral nutrition) found a 6-month mortality odds ratio of 1.18 (95% CI 0.82–1.70) for parenteral glutamine — no difference. The Scandinavian trial (413 patients) found lower ICU mortality only in its per-protocol subgroup and no difference at 6 months. The Cochrane review (53 trials, 4,671 participants) put short-term mortality at relative risk 0.89 (95% CI 0.78–1.02) and long-term mortality at exactly 1.00 (95% CI 0.89–1.12). The one discordant note is MetaPlus, an enteral formula bundling glutamine with omega-3 fatty acids, selenium and antioxidants: infections were unchanged (53% vs 52%) and 6-month mortality in the medical subgroup ran higher on the formula (adjusted hazard ratio 1.57) — a bundle effect that cannot be laid on glutamine alone, but which points the same way as the REDOXS harm signal on #79. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): glutamine supplementation does not reduce mortality in general critical illness; an infection benefit (Cochrane relative risk 0.79) has not translated into survival.

cards.headline: SIGNET 2011: parenteral glutamine in 502 critically ill patients changed neither infections (odds ratio 1.07) nor 6-month mortality (odds ratio 1.18) — the treatment made no difference
cards.summary: SIGNET 2011: parenteral glutamine in 502 critically ill patients changed neither infections (odds ratio 1.07) nor 6-month mortality (odds ratio 1.18) — the treatment made no difference
cards.people: 502 adults in Scottish intensive care and high-dependency units for at least 48 hours, with gastrointestinal failure requiring parenteral nutrition, randomised double-blind in a factorial design to parenteral glutamine (20.2 g/day), selenium (500 µg/day), both, or neither, for up to 7 days, within standard isonitrogenous, isocaloric parenteral nutrition.
cards.result: Glutamine had no effect on new infections in the first 14 days (134/250 vs 131/252; odds ratio 1.07, 95% CI 0.75–1.53), including among patients who received at least 5 days of supplementation (odds ratio 0.99, 95% CI 0.56–1.75). Six-month mortality was not significantly different with glutamine (115/250 vs 106/252; odds ratio 1.18, 95% CI 0.82–1.70) — the treatment made no difference. Length of stay, days of antibiotic use and modified SOFA scores were likewise unaffected by glutamine.
cards.watchOut: SIGNET tested a modest parenteral dose for at most 7 days in patients with gastrointestinal failure; it does not address prolonged or high-dose regimens — the high-dose question is the one REDOXS answered, homed on live shelf #79.
cards.source: Andrews PJ et al. Randomised trial of glutamine, selenium, or both, to supplement parenteral nutrition for critically ill patients. BMJ (Clinical research ed.). 2011. PMID: 21415104. cards.headline: Scandinavian trial 2011: intravenous glutamine in 413 ICU patients lowered ICU mortality only in the per-protocol subgroup — and not at 6 months
cards.summary: Scandinavian trial 2011: intravenous glutamine in 413 ICU patients lowered ICU mortality only in the per-protocol subgroup — and not at 6 months
cards.type: Randomised double-blind trial (Scandinavian Glutamine Trial, Wernerman 2011)
cards.people: 413 patients in Scandinavian intensive care units, enrolled within 72 hours of admission and receiving enteral and/or parenteral nutrition aimed at full feeding, randomised double-blind to intravenous l-alanyl-l-glutamine (0.283 g glutamine/kg body weight per 24 hours) for the entire ICU stay or saline placebo in identical bottles; all included patients formed the intention-to-treat population.
cards.result: The primary outcome, change in SOFA score, did not differ between groups (median change 1 vs 2; P=0.792). ICU mortality was lower in the glutamine arm only in the pre-specified per-protocol group (patients supplemented for more than 3 days), and there was no mortality difference at 6 months — on the trial's primary analysis, the treatment made no difference.
cards.watchOut: The record reports the per-protocol ICU-mortality finding without intention-to-treat mortality counts, so no mortality rates are printed on this card; a subgroup defined by receiving more than 3 days of treatment is exactly where survivorship bias creeps in.
cards.source: Wernerman J et al. Scandinavian glutamine trial: a pragmatic multi-centre randomised clinical trial of intensive care unit patients. Acta anaesthesiologica Scandinavica. 2011. cards.headline: MetaPlus 2014: an enteral formula enriched with glutamine plus omega-3, selenium and antioxidants did not reduce infections (53% vs 52%) — and 6-month mortality in medical patients ran higher (adjusted hazard ratio 1.57)
cards.summary: MetaPlus 2014: an enteral formula enriched with glutamine plus omega-3, selenium and antioxidants did not reduce infections (53% vs 52%) — and 6-month mortality in medical patients ran higher (adjusted hazard ratio 1.57)
cards.people: 301 mechanically ventilated adults in 14 intensive care units in the Netherlands, Germany, France and Belgium, expected to need ventilation and enteral nutrition for more than 72 hours, randomised double-blind within 48 hours of admission to high-protein enteral nutrition enriched with immune-modulating nutrients (glutamine, omega-3 fatty acids, selenium and antioxidants; n = 152) or standard high-protein enteral nutrition (n = 149), for up to 28 days.
cards.result: New infections occurred in 53% (95% CI 44–61%) of the enriched-formula group versus 52% (95% CI 44–61%) of controls (P=.96) — the treatment made no difference. No other endpoint differed overall, except in the pre-defined medical subgroup, where 6-month mortality was 54% (95% CI 40–67%) on the enriched formula versus 35% (95% CI 22–49%) on standard feed, with an adjusted hazard ratio of 1.57 (95% CI 1.03–2.39; P=.04). The authors concluded the findings do not support immune-modulating enteral nutrition in these patients.
cards.watchOut: This is a bundle, not glutamine alone: the mortality signal in medical patients cannot be attributed to glutamine specifically — but it removes any presumption that adding a glutamine-containing immunonutrition formula is benign, and it rhymes with the high-dose harm on live shelf #79.
cards.source: van Zanten AR et al. High-protein enteral nutrition enriched with immune-modulating nutrients vs standard high-protein enteral nutrition and nosocomial infections in the ICU: a randomized clinical trial. JAMA. 2014. PMID: 25096691. Registry ID: NTR2181. cards.headline: Cochrane 2014: across 53 trials (4,671 patients), glutamine cut infections (relative risk 0.79) but long-term mortality was exactly 1.00 and short-term mortality 0.89 with a confidence interval crossing 1
cards.summary: Cochrane 2014: across 53 trials (4,671 patients), glutamine cut infections (relative risk 0.79) but long-term mortality was exactly 1.00 and short-term mortality 0.89 with a confidence interval crossing 1
cards.type: Cochrane systematic review and meta-analysis of 53 trials (Tao 2014)
cards.people: Cochrane systematic review of 53 controlled trials (4,671 participants) of glutamine supplementation versus no supplementation or placebo in adults with critical illness or undergoing elective major surgery, searched to May 2013; 33 trials reported nosocomial infections, 36 reported short-term mortality and 11 reported long-term mortality.
cards.result: Glutamine reduced nosocomial infectious complications (relative risk 0.79, 95% CI 0.71–0.87; moderate-quality evidence). Short-term (hospital or under one month) mortality was not significantly different (relative risk 0.89, 95% CI 0.78–1.02; low-quality evidence), and long-term (over six months) mortality across 11 studies and 2,277 participants was relative risk 1.00 (95% CI 0.89–1.12; moderate-quality evidence) — the treatment made no difference to survival.
cards.watchOut: The review mixes ICU patients with elective major-surgery patients and its search closed in May 2013; ICU trials carded above sit inside its pool, so this card corroborates rather than adds independent patients.
cards.source: Tao KM et al. Glutamine supplementation for critically ill adults. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2014. PMID: 25199493. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: for mortality in general critical illness, the free reports agree — glutamine does not reduce deaths
cards.summary: Synthesis: for mortality in general critical illness, the free reports agree — glutamine does not reduce deaths
cards.people: The carded evidence: two glutamine-specific randomised trials (SIGNET 502; Scandinavian 413), one bundled-immunonutrition trial (MetaPlus 301), and the Cochrane pooling of 53 trials (4,671 participants). Total carded participants exceed 5,000, so no small-N stamp labelling applies.
cards.result: For mortality in general critical illness the answer is consistent: SIGNET odds ratio 1.18 (95% CI 0.82–1.70), the Scandinavian trial null on intention-to-treat and at 6 months, and Cochrane long-term relative risk 1.00 (95% CI 0.89–1.12). Glutamine may reduce infections (Cochrane relative risk 0.79) without saving lives, and two harm signals — MetaPlus's medical subgroup, and high-dose REDOXS homed on live shelf #79 — argue against assuming safety. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): glutamine supplementation does not reduce mortality in adults with critical illness. The burns-specific question is homed on live shelf #1049.
cards.watchOut: LIKELY here attaches to the mortality null only; it is not a claim that glutamine is useless for every endpoint, and high-dose early glutamine in multiorgan failure is a separate, harmful regimen homed on live shelf #79.
cards.source: Synthesis of Andrews PJ et al. BMJ (Clinical research ed.). 2011 (PMID: 21415104); Wernerman J et al. Acta anaesthesiologica Scandinavica. 2011 (PMID: 21658010); van Zanten AR et al. shelves.title: Recombinant thrombomodulin in sepsis-associated coagulopathy: the SCARLET placebo trial was null (26.8% vs 29.4% mortality), and the pooled estimate remains nonsignificant
shelves.question: In adults with sepsis and disseminated intravascular coagulation, does recombinant thrombomodulin improve survival versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Anticoagulants · Blood Coagulation Disorders · Cause of Death · Female · Humans · Infusions, Intravenous · Injections, Intravenous · International Normalized Ratio · Male · Middle Aged · Recombinant Proteins · Sepsis · Thrombomodulin · Treatment Failure
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference in the placebo trial) — printed on the face. A population precision first: SCARLET enrolled sepsis-associated coagulopathy (raised INR with thrombocytopenia, plus organ failure) rather than overt disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) by score, and it is the only large placebo-controlled test; the earlier Japanese phase 3 trial (Saito 2007) enrolled DIC from infection or haematological malignancy but compared thrombomodulin with heparin, not placebo, and its endpoint was DIC resolution, not survival. SCARLET (800 patients analysed) found 28-day mortality 26.8% versus 29.4% (absolute difference 2.55%, 95% CI −3.68 to 8.77; P = .32) — not significant — with serious major bleeding numerically more frequent on thrombomodulin (5.8% vs 4.0%). The updated meta-analysis including SCARLET (Yamakawa 2019; 5 trials, 1,762 patients) gives a relative mortality risk of 0.87 (95% CI 0.74–1.03, P = 0.10) — a possible ~13% relative reduction that remains nonsignificant, with trial sequential analysis showing only 42% of the required information size. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference in the placebo trial): a survival benefit from recombinant thrombomodulin in sepsis with coagulopathy/DIC is unproven.

cards.headline: SCARLET 2019: in 800 patients with sepsis-associated coagulopathy, thrombomodulin did not significantly reduce 28-day mortality versus placebo (26.8% vs 29.4%, P = .32)
cards.summary: SCARLET 2019: in 800 patients with sepsis-associated coagulopathy, thrombomodulin did not significantly reduce 28-day mortality versus placebo (26.8% vs 29.4%, P = .32)
cards.people: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled phase 3 trial in intensive care units at 159 sites in 26 countries: adults with sepsis-associated coagulopathy (INR > 1.40 without other cause and platelet count 30–150 × 10⁹/L or a >30% fall within 24 hours) plus cardiovascular and/or respiratory failure; 816 patients were randomised to thrombomodulin alfa 0.06 mg/kg/day (maximum 6 mg/day) or matching placebo once daily for 6 days, and 800 were in the full analysis set (395 thrombomodulin, 405 placebo). The primary endpoint was 28-day all-cause mortality.
cards.result: 28-day all-cause mortality was 106 of 395 (26.8%) on thrombomodulin versus 119 of 405 (29.4%) on placebo (P = .32) — the treatment made no significant difference; the absolute risk difference was 2.55% (95% CI −3.68% to 8.77%). Serious major bleeding occurred in 23 of 396 thrombomodulin patients (5.8%) versus 16 of 404 placebo patients (4.0%). The authors conclude thrombomodulin did not significantly reduce mortality in sepsis-associated coagulopathy.
cards.watchOut: SCARLET's coagulopathy definition is broader than a formal DIC score, so its null applies most directly to sepsis-associated coagulopathy as enrolled; advocates argue a sicker, strictly-DIC subgroup might differ — but that subgroup claim is post hoc and untested in a placebo trial, and the bleeding excess, though small, runs against the drug.
cards.source: Vincent JL et al. Effect of a Recombinant Human Soluble Thrombomodulin on Mortality in Patients With Sepsis-Associated Coagulopathy: The SCARLET Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA. 2019. PMID: 31104069. Registry ID: NCT01598831. cards.headline: Saito 2007: thrombomodulin resolved DIC more often than heparin (66.1% vs 49.9%) in 234 patients with DIC from infection or malignancy — a heparin comparison, not placebo, with no survival endpoint met
cards.summary: Saito 2007: thrombomodulin resolved DIC more often than heparin (66.1% vs 49.9%) in 234 patients with DIC from infection or malignancy — a heparin comparison, not placebo, with no survival endpoint met
cards.people: Multicentre double-blind randomised phase 3 trial (Japan) in 234 patients with disseminated intravascular coagulation associated with haematological malignancy or infection, assigned to recombinant human soluble thrombomodulin (ART-123) 0.06 mg/kg once daily or low-dose heparin sodium 8 U/kg/hour, each for 6 days by a double-dummy method; the primary endpoint was DIC resolution rate, with bleeding course and 28-day mortality as secondaries.
cards.result: DIC resolved in 66.1% of the thrombomodulin group versus 49.9% of the heparin group (difference 16.2%, 95% CI 3.3–29.1), with more marked improvement in bleeding symptoms (P = 0.0271) and fewer bleeding-related adverse events up to day 7 (43.1% vs 56.5%, P = 0.0487). The record reports no significant mortality advantage — this trial shows the drug treats the DIC laboratory-clinical syndrome better than heparin, not that it improves survival versus placebo.
cards.watchOut: Half this population had haematological malignancy rather than sepsis, the comparator is an active anticoagulant that may itself harm, and DIC resolution is a syndrome endpoint — none of this card's findings can be converted into a survival claim for septic DIC.
cards.source: Saito H et al. Efficacy and safety of recombinant human soluble thrombomodulin (ART-123) in disseminated intravascular coagulation: results of a phase III, randomized, double-blind clinical trial. Journal of thrombosis and haemostasis : JTH. 2007. PMID: 17059423. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Yamakawa 2019 meta-analysis: across 5 trials (1,762 patients), thrombomodulin's mortality estimate was relative risk 0.87 (95% CI 0.74–1.03) — favourable in direction, nonsignificant, and underpowered by trial sequential analysis
cards.summary: Yamakawa 2019 meta-analysis: across 5 trials (1,762 patients), thrombomodulin's mortality estimate was relative risk 0.87 (95% CI 0.74–1.03) — favourable in direction, nonsignificant, and underpowered by trial sequential analysis
cards.people: Updated systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials of recombinant human soluble thrombomodulin in sepsis or sepsis-induced coagulopathy, including SCARLET; 5 trials enrolling 1,762 patients, with 28-day all-cause mortality as the efficacy outcome and serious bleeding as the harm outcome, GRADE-assessed.
cards.result: Mortality was about 13% lower in relative terms on thrombomodulin, but the difference was not significant (relative risk 0.87, 95% CI 0.74–1.03, P = 0.10; I² = 0%). Serious bleeding risk did not increase significantly. Certainty was judged moderate for mortality and low for serious bleeding, and trial sequential analysis indicated only 42.0% of the required information size is available. The authors conclude no declarative judgement about benefit can yet be made.
cards.watchOut: The pooled estimate leans heavily on SCARLET plus smaller, older trials at higher risk of bias; a relative risk of 0.87 whose interval crosses 1.0 is a reason to run another trial, not a reason to treat — and sepsis anticoagulant history (activated protein C, antithrombin) is a graveyard of exactly such signals.
cards.source: Yamakawa K et al. Recombinant Human Soluble Thrombomodulin in Sepsis-Induced Coagulopathy: An Updated Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Thrombosis and haemostasis. 2019. PMID: 30597500. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: against placebo, thrombomodulin has not improved survival in sepsis with coagulopathy — the DIC-resolution win was against heparin
cards.summary: Synthesis: against placebo, thrombomodulin has not improved survival in sepsis with coagulopathy — the DIC-resolution win was against heparin
cards.people: The carded evidence: one large placebo-controlled trial (SCARLET, 800 analysed), one heparin-controlled DIC trial (Saito 2007, 234 patients, mixed infection/malignancy), and one meta-analysis including both (Yamakawa 2019, 5 trials, 1,762 patients).
cards.result: SCARLET's mortality rates were 26.8% versus 29.4% (not significant); the pooled relative risk is 0.87 (95% CI 0.74–1.03), also not significant; Saito shows better DIC resolution than heparin without a survival endpoint. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference in the placebo trial): recombinant thrombomodulin cannot currently be said to improve survival in sepsis and DIC/coagulopathy.
cards.watchOut: Thrombomodulin is licensed for DIC in Japan on the Saito evidence; this shelf's null is about the survival-versus-placebo question as asked, not about Japanese DIC practice or the drug's laboratory effects, both of which are real.
cards.source: Synthesis of Vincent JL et al. JAMA. 2019 (PMID: 31104069); Saito H et al. Journal of thrombosis and haemostasis : JTH. 2007 (PMID: 17059423); Yamakawa K et al. Thrombosis and haemostasis. 2019 (PMID: 30597500).

shelves.title: Intravenous selenium in critical illness: pooled overall mortality lower in relative terms (relative risk 0.82–0.86), 28-day mortality not significantly reduced — low-certainty evidence, largest trial null on its primary analysis
shelves.question: In critically ill adults, does intravenous selenium supplementation reduce mortality versus standard care?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Antioxidants · Azoles · Critical Illness · Dietary Supplements · Humans · Isoindoles · Organoselenium Compounds · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Sodium Selenite
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit, low-certainty evidence) — printed on the face. Selenium is a supplement; where a preparation is named it is named here for clarification: the trials used intravenous sodium selenite, typically a 1,000 microgram bolus followed by 1,000 micrograms daily in the largest trial. The pooled estimates point to a modest relative mortality reduction, but every synthesis rates the evidence low or very low quality, the 28-day endpoint is null, and the largest single trial was null on its intention-to-treat primary analysis. The Cochrane review (16 trials, 2,084 participants) found intravenous sodium selenite reduced overall mortality (relative risk 0.82, 95% CI 0.72–0.93, 1,391 participants, very low quality), driven mainly by high-risk-of-bias trials, with no significant difference at 28 days (relative risk 0.84, 95% CI 0.69–1.02) or 90 days. Two later meta-analyses land in the same place: total mortality relative risk 0.86 (Zhao 2019, 19 trials, 3,341 patients) and 28-day mortality relative risk 0.84 of borderline significance (Landucci 2014, 9 trials). The largest single trial, SIC (Angstwurm 2007, 249 patients with severe sepsis), found 28-day mortality of 39.7% on high-dose sodium selenite vs 50.0% on placebo in intention-to-treat analysis (P=.109 — not significant). Note the SIGNET trial, which tested selenium within parenteral nutrition, is homed on pack #6023 and is not re-carded here. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit, low-certainty): intravenous selenium may reduce overall mortality modestly in relative terms, but the evidence is too weak and too bias-prone for a stronger stamp.

cards.headline: Cochrane 2015: intravenous sodium selenite reduced overall mortality in relative terms (relative risk 0.82) across 13 trials — very low quality evidence, and no significant difference at 28 or 90 days
cards.summary: Cochrane 2015: intravenous sodium selenite reduced overall mortality in relative terms (relative risk 0.82) across 13 trials — very low quality evidence, and no significant difference at 28 or 90 days
cards.type: Cochrane systematic review of 16 randomised trials (Allingstrup 2015)
cards.people: Systematic review of 16 randomised trials (2,084 participants) of selenium supplementation (intravenous sodium selenite in 13 trials) or the selenium-containing compound ebselen (3 trials) versus control in critically ill adults; most trials were at high risk of bias and, except for one, small.
cards.result: Thirteen trials of intravenous sodium selenite showed a statistically significant reduction in overall mortality (relative risk 0.82, 95% CI 0.72 to 0.93, 1,391 participants, very low quality of evidence), but the point estimate is primarily influenced by trials at high risk of bias. For 28-day mortality there was no statistically significant difference (relative risk 0.84, 95% CI 0.69 to 1.02, nine trials, 1,180 participants), nor at 90 days (relative risk 0.96, 95% CI 0.78 to 1.18, three trials, 614 participants). Among intensive care patients specifically, selenium failed to show a significant advantage (relative risk 0.88, 95% CI 0.77 to 1.01). There was no significant difference in infections (relative risk 0.96) or adverse events (relative risk 1.03). The record reports relative risks without the pooled absolute mortality rates for these comparisons.
cards.watchOut: The significant overall-mortality estimate rests mainly on small, high-risk-of-bias trials and disappears at the prespecified 28- and 90-day timepoints — read the relative risk 0.82 as a low-certainty signal, not an established survival benefit.
cards.source: Allingstrup M et al. Selenium supplementation for critically ill adults. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2015. PMID: 26214143. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: SIC 2007: the largest single trial — 28-day mortality 39.7% on high-dose sodium selenite vs 50.0% on placebo in 238 analysed patients, not significant in intention-to-treat analysis (P=.109)
cards.summary: SIC 2007: the largest single trial — 28-day mortality 39.7% on high-dose sodium selenite vs 50.0% on placebo in 238 analysed patients, not significant in intention-to-treat analysis (P=.109)
cards.people: 249 patients with severe systemic inflammatory response syndrome, sepsis or septic shock and an APACHE III score >70, in 11 intensive care units in Germany, randomised double-blind to sodium selenite 1,000 micrograms as a 30-minute bolus followed by 14 daily continuous infusions of 1,000 micrograms intravenously, or placebo; 238 patients remained in the intention-to-treat analysis after 11 exclusions.
cards.result: Intention-to-treat 28-day mortality was 50.0% on placebo vs 39.7% on selenium (P=.109; odds ratio 0.66, 95% CI 0.39–1.1) — not statistically significant. After a further 49 patients were excluded for severe protocol violations, the per-protocol analysis (92 selenium vs 97 placebo) showed 42.4% vs 56.7% mortality (P=.049; odds ratio 0.56, 95% CI 0.32–1.00). Predefined subgroups with septic shock and disseminated intravascular coagulation, APACHE III ≥102, or more than three organ dysfunctions showed significant reductions. No side effects due to high-dose sodium selenite were observed.
cards.watchOut: The headline benefit appears only after excluding 49 randomised patients for protocol violations; the trial's own intention-to-treat primary analysis is null, which is exactly why the pooled literature cannot carry a stronger stamp than POSSIBLE.
cards.source: Angstwurm MW et al. Selenium in Intensive Care (SIC): results of a prospective randomized, placebo-controlled, multiple-center study in patients with severe systemic inflammatory response syndrome, sepsis, and septic shock.
