cards.headline: Zhao 2019: across 19 trials and 3,341 critically ill patients, intravenous selenium reduced total mortality in relative terms (relative risk 0.86) but not 28-day mortality (relative risk 0.96)
cards.summary: Zhao 2019: across 19 trials and 3,341 critically ill patients, intravenous selenium reduced total mortality in relative terms (relative risk 0.86) but not 28-day mortality (relative risk 0.96)
cards.type: Meta-analysis of 19 randomised trials with trial sequential analysis (Zhao 2019)
cards.people: Meta-analysis of 19 randomised trials involving 3,341 critically ill patients (1,694 selenium supplementation, 1,647 control), with trial sequential analysis to control type I and II error and calculate the required information size.
cards.result: Compared with control, intravenous selenium as a single therapy decreased total mortality (relative risk 0.86, 95% CI 0.78–0.95, P=.002; trial-sequential-analysis-adjusted 95% CI 0.77–0.96; required information size 4,108, n=3,297 — relative measures, with pooled absolute rates not reported in the record) and may shorten hospital stay (mean difference −2.30 days, 95% CI −4.03 to −0.57), but had no significant effect on 28-day mortality (relative risk 0.96, 95% CI 0.85–1.09, P=.54) or ICU stay. Selenium did not increase drug-induced side effects (relative risk 1.04, 95% CI 0.83 to 1.30). The authors caution the results should be used carefully because of potential limitations.
cards.watchOut: 'Total mortality' pools different follow-up windows across trials; the cleaner fixed timepoint — 28-day mortality — is null in this analysis too, and the required information size (4,108) was not quite reached (3,297 analysed).
cards.source: Zhao Y et al. The clinical outcomes of selenium supplementation on critically ill patients: A meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials. Medicine. 2019. PMID: 31096444. cards.headline: Landucci 2014: across 9 trials, selenium was associated with a borderline-significant reduction in 28-day mortality (relative risk 0.84, P=.04), with no effect at 6 months or on infections
cards.summary: Landucci 2014: across 9 trials, selenium was associated with a borderline-significant reduction in 28-day mortality (relative risk 0.84, P=.04), with no effect at 6 months or on infections
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 9 randomised trials (Landucci 2014)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 9 randomised trials comparing exogenous selenium supplementation versus standard therapy without adjuvant in critically ill adults; predefined subgroups examined dose ≤500 micrograms/day, loading bolus administration and treatment duration.
cards.result: Selenium supplementation was associated with a reduction in 28-day mortality of borderline statistical significance (relative risk 0.84, 95% CI 0.71–0.99, P=.04 — a relative measure; pooled absolute rates are not reported in the record). Subgroup analyses detected no significant effects for doses ≤500 micrograms/day, loading-bolus administration, or treatment duration. Only 2 studies analysed 6-month mortality and could not show a difference. No effects were demonstrated on hospital length of stay, pulmonary infections, or renal failure.
cards.watchOut: A P value of .04 on a pooled estimate built from small trials is fragile — one moderate null trial can erase it — and this synthesis predates the Cochrane update's risk-of-bias cautions; it is concordant in direction, not independent proof.
cards.source: Landucci F et al. Selenium supplementation in critically ill patients: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Journal of critical care. 2014. PMID: 24135013. cards.headline: Synthesis: pooled estimates suggest a modest relative mortality reduction from intravenous selenium, but the largest trial's primary analysis and the fixed-timepoint analyses are null — low-certainty POSSIBLE at best
cards.summary: Synthesis: pooled estimates suggest a modest relative mortality reduction from intravenous selenium, but the largest trial's primary analysis and the fixed-timepoint analyses are null — low-certainty POSSIBLE at best
cards.people: The carded evidence: one Cochrane review of 16 trials (2,084 participants), the largest single trial (SIC, 249 patients), and two further meta-analyses (19 trials, 3,341 patients; 9 trials). Total carded participants exceed 2,000, so no small-N stamp labelling applies. The SIGNET selenium-in-parenteral-nutrition trial is homed on pack #6023 and is not re-carded here.
cards.result: Overall/total mortality pooled at relative risk 0.82 (Cochrane, very low quality) and 0.86 (Zhao 2019); 28-day mortality was not significantly reduced in Cochrane (relative risk 0.84, 95% CI 0.69–1.02) or Zhao (0.96), was borderline in Landucci (0.84, P=.04), and SIC's intention-to-treat 28-day mortality (39.7% vs 50.0%) was not significant (P=.109). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit, low-certainty): intravenous selenium (as sodium selenite in the trials) may reduce mortality modestly in relative terms in critically ill adults, but the evidence is low quality and inconsistent at fixed timepoints.
cards.watchOut: The three syntheses overlap heavily in the trials they pool, so their agreement is not three independent confirmations; and doses/preparations varied (sodium selenite in most, ebselen in some Cochrane trials), so no specific commercial supplement product is endorsed by this shelf.
cards.source: Synthesis of Allingstrup M et al. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2015 (PMID: 26214143); Angstwurm MW et al. Critical care medicine. 2007 (PMID: 17095947); Zhao Y et al. Medicine. 2019 (PMID: 31096444); Landucci F et al. Journal of critical care. 2014 (PMID: 24135013).

shelves.title: Glutamine-supplemented parenteral nutrition after major surgery (PARTIAL completion of live #1049 and pack #6023): infections reduced in relative terms in two surgical meta-analyses, no mortality benefit
shelves.question: In adults receiving parenteral nutrition after major surgery, does glutamine-supplemented parenteral nutrition reduce infections versus standard parenteral nutrition?
shelves.mesh: Abdomen · Biomarkers · Glutamine · Humans · Length of Stay · Models, Statistical · Nitrogen · Parenteral Nutrition · Parenteral Nutrition Solutions · Perioperative Care · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Surgical Wound Infection · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — printed on the face. This pack is a PARTIAL completion with two homes cross-pointed and not re-carded: live shelf #1049 homes enteral glutamine in severe burns only (RE-ENERGIZE), and pack #6023 homes glutamine in general critical illness with mortality as the outcome (including the REDOXS trial, homed on live #79). Neither answers this slice — parenteral glutamine in patients receiving parenteral nutrition after major surgery, with infections as the outcome. On that slice, two meta-analyses of surgical randomised trials agree: perioperative glutamine-supplemented parenteral nutrition in abdominal surgery reduced infectious complications (relative risk 0.48, 95% CI 0.32–0.72; 16 trials, 773 patients; Yue 2013 — a relative measure; the record does not report pooled absolute infection rates), and parenteral glutamine in critically ill surgical patients reduced infections (relative risk 0.60, 95% CI 0.45–0.80; 7 trials; Pimentel 2020), with hospital stay about 4 days shorter and no significant mortality difference in either synthesis (Yue mortality relative risk 1.52 with a very wide interval; Pimentel 0.76, not significant). The one double-blind surgical-ICU trial carded (Estívariz 2008, 59 patients) found fewer infections with glutamine dipeptide only in the non-pancreatic-surgery subgroup and no difference after pancreatic necrosis surgery. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): glutamine-supplemented parenteral nutrition probably reduces postoperative infections in relative terms in surgical patients on parenteral nutrition, with no demonstrated mortality benefit — POSSIBLE rather than LIKELY because the underlying trials are small and the one carded trial's benefit is subgroup-only.

cards.headline: Yue 2013: across 16 trials (773 patients), perioperative glutamine-supplemented parenteral nutrition halved infectious complications in relative terms after abdominal surgery (relative risk 0.48) — with no mortality difference
cards.summary: Yue 2013: across 16 trials (773 patients), perioperative glutamine-supplemented parenteral nutrition halved infectious complications in relative terms after abdominal surgery (relative risk 0.48) — with no mortality difference
cards.people: Meta-analysis of 16 randomised trials with 773 patients undergoing abdominal surgery, comparing perioperative glutamine-supplemented parenteral nutrition with standard parenteral nutrition; outcomes were postoperative mortality, length of hospital stay, infectious complications and cumulative nitrogen balance.
cards.result: Glutamine-supplemented parenteral nutrition significantly decreased infectious complication rates (relative risk 0.48, 95% CI 0.32 to 0.72, P=0.0004 — a relative measure; pooled absolute infection rates are not reported in the record). Hospital stay was shorter with alanyl-glutamine (weighted mean difference −3.17 days, 95% CI −5.51 to −0.82) and with glycyl-glutamine (−3.40 days, 95% CI −5.82 to −0.97), and cumulative nitrogen balance improved (weighted mean difference 7.40, 95% CI 3.16 to 11.63). There was no mortality difference (relative risk 1.52, 95% CI 0.21 to 11.9, P=0.68 — the treatment made no difference, on very few events).
cards.watchOut: Sixteen trials averaging under 50 patients each, largely older and single-centre: a pooled relative risk of 0.48 from trials this size is vulnerable to small-study effects, and the mortality estimate is so imprecise it excludes nothing.
cards.source: Yue C et al. The impact of perioperative glutamine-supplemented parenteral nutrition on outcomes of patients undergoing abdominal surgery: a meta-analysis of randomized clinical trials. The American surgeon. 2013. PMID: 23635587. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Pimentel 2020: across 7 trials in critically ill surgical patients, parenteral glutamine reduced infections (relative risk 0.60) and hospital stay by about 4 days, with no significant mortality reduction
cards.summary: Pimentel 2020: across 7 trials in critically ill surgical patients, parenteral glutamine reduced infections (relative risk 0.60) and hospital stay by about 4 days, with no significant mortality reduction
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 7 randomised trials (Pimentel 2020)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 7 randomised trials (published since 1985) of parenteral glutamine supplementation in critically ill surgical patients receiving parenteral nutrition, versus parenteral nutrition without glutamine.
cards.result: Parenteral glutamine supplementation was associated with significantly reduced infections (relative risk 0.60, 95% CI 0.45–0.80 — a relative measure; pooled absolute rates are not reported in the record) and a hospital stay 4.09 days shorter (95% CI −6.71 to −1.46). Mortality was lower but not significantly (relative risk 0.76, 95% CI 0.50–1.15 — the treatment made no statistically significant difference). The authors conclude parenteral glutamine seems to decrease infection and length of stay in critical surgical patients without a demonstrated mortality reduction.
cards.watchOut: This synthesis overlaps the Yue meta-analysis in its underlying small trials, so the two pooled estimates are concordant but not independent; both also predate routine modern enhanced-recovery care, which has lowered baseline infection rates since.
cards.source: Pimentel RFW et al. Effects of parenteral glutamine in critically ill surgical patients: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Nutricion hospitalaria. 2020. PMID: 32338020. cards.headline: Estívariz 2008: in a 59-patient double-blind surgical-ICU trial, glutamine dipeptide parenteral nutrition cut infections after cardiac, vascular and colonic surgery (total infections 13 vs 36) but made no difference after pancreatic necrosis surgery
cards.summary: Estívariz 2008: in a 59-patient double-blind surgical-ICU trial, glutamine dipeptide parenteral nutrition cut infections after cardiac, vascular and colonic surgery (total infections 13 vs 36) but made no difference after pancreatic necrosis surgery
cards.people: 59 critically ill surgical patients requiring parenteral nutrition and surgical-ICU care after surgery for pancreatic necrosis, or cardiac, vascular or colonic surgery, in a double-blind randomised trial of isocaloric/isonitrogenous parenteral nutrition providing 1.5 g/kg/day standard glutamine-free amino acids (STD-PN) or 1.0 g/kg/day standard amino acids plus 0.5 g/kg/day glutamine dipeptide (GLN-PN); nosocomial infections were counted until hospital discharge.
cards.result: Glutamine dipeptide did not alter infection rates after pancreatic necrosis surgery (17 STD-PN and 15 GLN-PN patients). In non-pancreatic surgery patients (12 STD-PN and 15 GLN-PN), GLN-PN was associated with significantly decreased total nosocomial infections (STD-PN 36 vs GLN-PN 13, P<.030), bloodstream infections (7 vs 0, P<.01), pneumonias (16 vs 6, P<.05), and infections attributed to Staphylococcus aureus, fungi and enteric Gram-negative bacteria (each P<.05). Plasma glutamine concentrations were low in all groups and were increased by GLN-PN.
cards.watchOut: The infection counts are events, not patients, in a 27-patient non-pancreatic subgroup of a 59-patient trial — a subgroup finding in a small trial, printed here because it is the direct double-blind test in this population, not because it can carry the shelf alone.
cards.source: Estívariz CF et al. Efficacy of parenteral nutrition supplemented with glutamine dipeptide to decrease hospital infections in critically ill surgical patients. JPEN. Journal of parenteral and enteral nutrition. 2008. PMID: 18596310. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: two surgical meta-analyses agree that glutamine-supplemented parenteral nutrition reduces postoperative infections in relative terms (relative risk 0.48 and 0.60), with no mortality benefit — on small, older trials
cards.summary: Synthesis: two surgical meta-analyses agree that glutamine-supplemented parenteral nutrition reduces postoperative infections in relative terms (relative risk 0.48 and 0.60), with no mortality benefit — on small, older trials
cards.people: The carded evidence: two meta-analyses of surgical randomised trials (Yue 2013, 16 trials, 773 patients; Pimentel 2020, 7 trials) and one double-blind surgical-ICU trial (Estívariz 2008, 59 patients). Total carded participants exceed 800, so no small-N stamp labelling applies. The burns population (live #1049), general-critical-illness mortality (pack #6023) and REDOXS (live #79) are homed elsewhere and not re-carded here.
cards.result: Infectious complications were reduced in relative terms in both syntheses (relative risk 0.48, 95% CI 0.32–0.72; and 0.60, 95% CI 0.45–0.80), hospital stay was shorter by roughly 3–4 days in both, and neither found a significant mortality difference. The one carded trial found its infection benefit only outside pancreatic-necrosis surgery. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): glutamine-supplemented parenteral nutrition probably reduces infections in patients on parenteral nutrition after major surgery, with no demonstrated effect on mortality.
cards.watchOut: High-dose glutamine harmed patients in the REDOXS trial in multiorgan failure (homed on live #79) — that population and dose are outside this shelf's post-surgical parenteral-nutrition slice, but they are the reason this shelf claims an infection benefit only, at standard dipeptide doses, and no survival benefit.

shelves.title: Empiric vancomycin in febrile neutropenia: no survival benefit in the EORTC trial or two meta-analyses — nephrotoxicity roughly doubled
shelves.question: In adults with febrile neutropenia, does adding empiric vancomycin improve outcomes in patients without resistant gram-positive infection?
shelves.mesh: Anti-Bacterial Agents/therapeutic use · Fever · Glycopeptides/therapeutic use · Gram-Positive Bacterial Infections/drug therapy/etiology/mortality · Humans · Neutropenia/complications · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — printed on the face. The EORTC/NCIC trial (747 febrile granulocytopenic patients) found adding vancomycin to ceftazidime plus amikacin improved response in gram-positive bacteraemia (72% vs 43%) but made no difference to fever course, and no gram-positive bacteraemia patient died in the first 3 days of empirical therapy; nephrotoxicity rose (6% vs 2%). Two 2005 meta-analyses of substantially the same trials agree: mortality did not differ (Paul relative risk 0.86, 95% CI 0.58–1.26; Vardakas odds ratio 0.67, 95% CI 0.42–1.05), while nephrotoxicity roughly doubled and adverse effects rose. The only consistent gain is fewer regimen modifications — a process outcome. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): routine empirical vancomycin in patients without resistant gram-positive infection does not improve survival and adds kidney harm; it can be deferred until a resistant gram-positive infection is documented.

cards.headline: EORTC 1991: adding vancomycin to ceftazidime plus amikacin in 747 febrile granulocytopenic patients improved gram-positive bacteraemia response but not fever course — and raised nephrotoxicity (6% vs 2%)
cards.summary: EORTC 1991: adding vancomycin to ceftazidime plus amikacin in 747 febrile granulocytopenic patients improved gram-positive bacteraemia response but not fever course — and raised nephrotoxicity (6% vs 2%)
cards.people: 747 febrile granulocytopenic patients with cancer randomised to initial empirical ceftazidime plus amikacin with or without vancomycin (EORTC International Antimicrobial Therapy Cooperative Group / NCIC trial).
cards.result: Single gram-positive bacteraemias responded in 48 of 67 patients (72%) on the vancomycin arm versus 29 of 68 (43%) without it (P = .001), and clinically documented infections responded more often (75% vs 55%, P = .009). But there was no difference in the proportion febrile on each trial day or in duration of fever, and no patient with gram-positive bacteraemia died during the first 3 days of empirical therapy. Antibiotic-associated nephrotoxicity was more frequent with vancomycin (6% vs 2%, P = .02). The authors concluded the results do not support the empirical addition of vancomycin.
cards.watchOut: This trial predates modern resistant gram-positive epidemiology and used ceftazidime–amikacin as the backbone; it answers routine empirical addition in unselected febrile neutropenia, not vancomycin for documented resistant infection, shock, or known MRSA colonisation.

cards.headline: Paul 2005: pooling 13 trials (2,392 participants), empirical anti-gram-positive antibiotics made no difference to mortality (relative risk 0.86) and increased nephrotoxicity (relative risk 1.88)
cards.summary: Paul 2005: pooling 13 trials (2,392 participants), empirical anti-gram-positive antibiotics made no difference to mortality (relative risk 0.86) and increased nephrotoxicity (relative risk 1.88)
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials (Paul 2005)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 13 randomised trials (2,392 participants) comparing an added antibiotic with anti-gram-positive spectrum (glycopeptides in nine trials) against the same baseline regimen without it, given initially in 11 studies and for persistent fever in two.
cards.result: All-cause mortality did not differ (relative risk 0.86, 95% CI 0.58–1.26; seven studies, 852 participants) and overall failure at end of therapy was equal (relative risk 1.00, 95% CI 0.79–1.27). Failure leading to treatment modification was less frequent with the added drug (relative risk 0.70, 95% CI 0.61–0.80), and bacterial superinfections were less frequent, but adverse events were significantly more common and nephrotoxicity was significantly more common with added glycopeptides (relative risk 1.88, 95% CI 1.10–3.22; six studies, 1,282 participants). The authors conclude glycopeptides can be safely deferred until a resistant gram-positive infection is documented. The record reports relative risks without the absolute mortality rates for this comparison.
cards.watchOut: The mortality estimate rests on only seven of the 13 trials (852 participants), so it is imprecise; the consistent signal is harm (kidney injury) without a survival gain, not proof that no subgroup could ever benefit.
cards.source: Paul M et al. Empirical antibiotics against Gram-positive infections for febrile neutropenia: systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials. The Journal of antimicrobial chemotherapy. 2005. PMID: 15722392. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Vardakas 2005: pooling 14 trials (2,413 patients), adding a glycopeptide improved 'success without modification' (odds ratio 1.63) but made no difference to mortality (odds ratio 0.67, CI crossing 1) and multiplied adverse effects (odds ratio 4.98)
cards.summary: Vardakas 2005: pooling 14 trials (2,413 patients), adding a glycopeptide improved 'success without modification' (odds ratio 1.63) but made no difference to mortality (odds ratio 0.67, CI crossing 1) and multiplied adverse effects (odds ratio 4.98)
cards.people: Meta-analysis of 14 randomised trials (2,413 febrile neutropenic patients) of a glycopeptide added to a beta-lactam, with or without an aminoglycoside, as part of initial empirical treatment.
cards.result: Treatment success without modification of the initial regimen was better with a glycopeptide (odds ratio 1.63, 95% CI 1.17–2.28), including in microbiologically documented infection, bacteraemia and severe neutropenia subgroups. Mortality was not different (odds ratio 0.67, 95% CI 0.42–1.05) — the treatment made no difference to survival — and adding a glycopeptide for fever persisting at 72 hours or more also made no difference to overall success (odds ratio 1.02, 95% CI 0.68–1.52) or to time to defervescence. Adverse effects (odds ratio 4.98, 95% CI 2.91–8.55), including nephrotoxicity (odds ratio 2.10, 95% CI 1.12–3.95), were more common with the glycopeptide. The authors conclude glycopeptides should not be routinely used in initial empirical treatment.
cards.watchOut: The 'success without modification' advantage is a process outcome — fewer regimen changes — bought with more kidney injury; it is not a patient-important outcome, and both 2005 meta-analyses pool substantially the same underlying trials, so they are two readings of one evidence base, not two independent bases.
cards.source: Vardakas KZ et al. Role of glycopeptides as part of initial empirical treatment of febrile neutropenic patients: a meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials. The Lancet. Infectious diseases. 2005. PMID: 15978529. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: routine empirical vancomycin buys fewer regimen changes at the cost of kidney injury — no trial or pooling shows a survival benefit
cards.summary: Synthesis: routine empirical vancomycin buys fewer regimen changes at the cost of kidney injury — no trial or pooling shows a survival benefit
cards.people: The carded evidence: one large EORTC/NCIC randomised trial (747 patients) and two 2005 meta-analyses of substantially overlapping randomised trials (13 trials, 2,392 participants; 14 trials, 2,413 patients).
cards.result: Every reading agrees on the patient-important outcomes: mortality did not differ with added glycopeptide (Paul relative risk 0.86, 95% CI 0.58–1.26; Vardakas odds ratio 0.67, 95% CI 0.42–1.05) — the treatment made no difference — while nephrotoxicity roughly doubled (relative risk 1.88; odds ratio 2.10) and overall adverse effects rose sharply (odds ratio 4.98). The only gains were in gram-positive bacteraemia response in the EORTC trial and in 'success without modification' in the poolings. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): in patients without documented resistant gram-positive infection, adding empirical vancomycin does not improve survival or fever course and adds kidney harm — defer it until a resistant gram-positive infection is documented.
cards.watchOut: This shelf does not cover patients with documented or strongly suspected resistant gram-positive infection, haemodynamic instability, or known MRSA colonisation, where guidelines still support early glycopeptide cover; it answers the routine-addition question as asked.
cards.source: Synthesis of EORTC Group et al. The Journal of infectious diseases. 1991 (PMID: 2019772); Paul M et al. The Journal of antimicrobial chemotherapy. 2005 (PMID: 15722392); Vardakas KZ et al. The Lancet. Infectious diseases. 2005 (PMID: 15978529).

shelves.title: Fluconazole prophylaxis vs placebo after stem cell transplant (PARTIAL of live #2180): systemic fungal infection 2.8% vs 15.8% and 7% vs 18%
shelves.question: In adults undergoing stem cell transplantation, does fluconazole prophylaxis reduce invasive fungal infection and death versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Bone Marrow Transplantation · Candidiasis/drug therapy/prevention & control · Double-Blind Method · Fluconazole/administration & dosage/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Humans · Immunosuppression Therapy/adverse effects · Mycoses/prevention & control
shelves.balance: LIKELY — printed on the face. PARTIAL completion of live #2180 (micafungin vs fluconazole after stem cell transplant); the fluconazole-vs-placebo slice is built here and the #2180 trial is not re-carded. Goodman 1992 (356 patients): systemic fungal infection 2.8% on fluconazole 400 mg vs 15.8% on placebo (P < .001), fungal deaths 1/179 vs 10/177, overall mortality not significantly different. Slavin 1995 (300 patients): systemic infection 7% vs 18% (P = .004) and better survival to day 110 (31 vs 52 deaths, P = .004). A 64-trial meta-analysis found allogeneic transplant prophylaxis reduced all-cause mortality (relative risk 0.62, 95% CI 0.45–0.85). PROPOSED LIKELY: fluconazole prophylaxis reduces invasive candida infection after stem cell transplantation, with a probable survival benefit; it has no mould cover.

cards.headline: Goodman 1992: systemic fungal infection occurred in 2.8% on fluconazole vs 15.8% on placebo (P < .001), and fungal deaths were 1 of 179 vs 10 of 177, though overall mortality did not differ significantly
cards.summary: Goodman 1992: systemic fungal infection occurred in 2.8% on fluconazole vs 15.8% on placebo (P < .001), and fungal deaths were 1 of 179 vs 10 of 177, though overall mortality did not differ significantly
cards.people: 356 patients receiving bone marrow transplants in a double-blind, randomised, multicentre trial, assigned to fluconazole 400 mg daily (n = 179) or placebo (n = 177) from the start of conditioning until neutrophil recovery to 1,000/µL, suspected toxicity, or suspected/proved systemic fungal infection.
cards.result: By the end of treatment, a positive fungal culture from any site occurred in 29.6% on fluconazole vs 67.2% on placebo, and superficial infections in 8.4% vs 33.3% (P < .001). Systemic fungal infections occurred in 5 patients on fluconazole vs 28 on placebo (2.8% vs 15.8%, P < .001); fluconazole prevented infection with all candida strains except Candida krusei. Overall mortality did not differ significantly, but deaths ascribed to acute systemic fungal infection were 1 of 179 on fluconazole vs 10 of 177 on placebo (P < .001). Fluconazole was well tolerated, with a higher mean rise in alanine aminotransferase than placebo.
cards.watchOut: A 1992 bone-marrow-transplant population and candida-dominated epidemiology: fluconazole has no mould (aspergillus) activity and did not prevent Candida krusei, so this trial does not answer prophylaxis where mould risk dominates — the comparison live #2180 (micafungin vs fluconazole) homes.
cards.source: Goodman JL et al. A controlled trial of fluconazole to prevent fungal infections in patients undergoing bone marrow transplantation. The New England journal of medicine. 1992. PMID: 1542320. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Slavin 1995: systemic fungal infection in 7% on fluconazole vs 18% on placebo (P = .004), with better survival to day 110 — 31 deaths vs 52 (P = .004)
cards.summary: Slavin 1995: systemic fungal infection in 7% on fluconazole vs 18% on placebo (P = .004), with better survival to day 110 — 31 deaths vs 52 (P = .004)
cards.people: 300 marrow transplant recipients in a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of fluconazole 400 mg/day (n = 152) vs placebo (n = 148) for preventing fungal infection during the first 75 days after transplantation.
cards.result: During prophylaxis, systemic fungal infections occurred in 10 fluconazole patients (7%) vs 26 placebo patients (18%) (P = .004). There were no Candida albicans infections on fluconazole vs 18 on placebo (P < .001), with no significant increase in non-albicans candida infections. Fluconazole also reduced superficial infections (P < .001), fungal colonisation (P = .037) and empirical amphotericin B use (P = .005). Survival was better on fluconazole: 31 deaths by day 110 vs 52 on placebo (P = .004). No clinically significant toxicity was detected.
cards.watchOut: The survival advantage is a single trial's secondary finding in a 1995 transplant population; Goodman 1992, the sister trial, found no significant overall-mortality difference — quote the infection reduction as the settled result and the survival benefit as trial-specific.
cards.source: Slavin MA et al. Efficacy and safety of fluconazole prophylaxis for fungal infections after marrow transplantation--a prospective, randomized, double-blind study. The Journal of infectious diseases. 1995. PMID: 7769290. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Robenshtok 2007: in allogeneic stem cell transplant recipients, antifungal prophylaxis reduced all-cause mortality (relative risk 0.62, 95% CI 0.45–0.85) across the randomised literature
cards.summary: Robenshtok 2007: in allogeneic stem cell transplant recipients, antifungal prophylaxis reduced all-cause mortality (relative risk 0.62, 95% CI 0.45–0.85) across the randomised literature
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials (Robenshtok 2007)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 64 randomised trials of systemic antifungal prophylaxis vs placebo, no treatment or non-systemic antifungals in cancer patients after chemotherapy or stem cell transplantation; the transplant findings below are the allogeneic haematopoietic stem cell transplantation subgroup.
cards.result: Overall, antifungal prophylaxis reduced all-cause mortality vs control (relative risk 0.84, 95% CI 0.74–0.95). In allogeneic stem cell transplant recipients specifically, prophylaxis reduced all-cause mortality (relative risk 0.62, 95% CI 0.45–0.85), fungal-related mortality and documented invasive fungal infection. The review also notes (on two studies) that posaconazole reduced mortality and invasive infection compared with fluconazole, and itraconazole suspension reduced documented infection vs fluconazole at the cost of more adverse events. The record reports relative risks without the absolute event rates for these comparisons.
cards.watchOut: The transplant subgroup pools several antifungal agents, not fluconazole alone, so its mortality relative risk supports the prophylaxis strategy in this population rather than isolating fluconazole's own survival effect; the fluconazole-specific infection numbers are on the Goodman and Slavin cards.

cards.headline: Synthesis: two large placebo-controlled trials agree — fluconazole cuts systemic fungal infection from roughly one in six to under one in twelve, with a survival signal in one trial and in transplant pooling
cards.summary: Synthesis: two large placebo-controlled trials agree — fluconazole cuts systemic fungal infection from roughly one in six to under one in twelve, with a survival signal in one trial and in transplant pooling
cards.people: The carded evidence: two randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trials (Goodman 1992, 356 patients; Slavin 1995, 300 patients) and one meta-analysis of 64 randomised prophylaxis trials with an allogeneic transplant subgroup. This shelf is a PARTIAL completion of live #2180 (micafungin vs fluconazole after stem cell transplant); the fluconazole-vs-placebo comparison is the uncovered slice built here, and the #2180 trial is not re-carded.
cards.result: Systemic fungal infection: 2.8% vs 15.8% (Goodman, P < .001) and 7% vs 18% (Slavin, P = .004). Deaths from systemic fungal infection were 1 vs 10 in Goodman, overall mortality did not differ significantly there, but Slavin found better survival to day 110 (31 vs 52 deaths, P = .004) and transplant-subgroup pooling found lower all-cause mortality with prophylaxis (relative risk 0.62, 95% CI 0.45–0.85). PROPOSED LIKELY: fluconazole prophylaxis reduces invasive (candida) fungal infection after stem cell transplantation, with a probable survival benefit — subject to its lack of mould cover, which is the separate #2180 question.
cards.watchOut: Fluconazole does not cover aspergillus or Candida krusei; in modern high-mould-risk transplantation the agent-choice question (live #2180) governs, and this shelf's placebo comparisons come from 1990s candida-era trials.

shelves.title: Candidemia step-down to fluconazole after about 5 days: safe in responders across a prospective programme and two cohorts — observational evidence only (initial echinocandin choice is live #507)
shelves.question: In adults with candidemia that responds to an echinocandin, can therapy be safely stepped down to fluconazole after 5 days?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Intravenous · Administration, Oral · Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Anidulafungin · Antifungal Agents · Candida · Candidemia · Candidiasis · Candidiasis, Invasive · Echinocandins · Female · Fluconazole · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Republic of Korea · Research Design · Risk · Treatment Outcome · United States · Voriconazole · Young Adult
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (observational evidence) — stepping down to an oral azole after about 5 days, in patients who are already responding, appears safe in the cohorts that studied it; there is no randomised trial of the step-down decision itself. Live shelf #507 answers the different, earlier question — which drug to start (an echinocandin first) — and is cross-pointed, not re-carded here. The prospective step-down programme (Vazquez 2014) treated 250 evaluable patients with intravenous anidulafungin and allowed step-down to oral fluconazole or voriconazole after 5 days when prespecified criteria were met: global response at end of treatment was 83.7%, and the early-switch subgroup did as well as the whole population. The multicentre retrospective candidemia cohort (Husni 2021) found step-down happened at an average of day 5, that stepped-down patients survived more often (78% versus 56%) — a comparison openly exposed to confounding, because clinicians step down patients who are already improving — and that stepping down at 1–4 days carried the same mortality as stepping down after more than 5 days (20% versus 24%). In Candida glabrata candidemia specifically (Droney 2025), 30-day clinical failure was 9% in the fluconazole step-down group versus 15% in patients kept on an echinocandin, not a significant difference. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (observational): in responding, non-neutropenic-leaning candidemia populations, step-down to fluconazole at about day 5 has repeatedly been used without a safety signal; the evidence cannot prove the step-down itself is what made outcomes good.

cards.headline: Vazquez 2014: after 5 days of intravenous anidulafungin, patients who met criteria could step down to an oral azole — global response 83.7% at end of treatment
cards.summary: Vazquez 2014: after 5 days of intravenous anidulafungin, patients who met criteria could step down to an oral azole — global response 83.7% at end of treatment
cards.people: 282 hospitalised patients with candidemia or other invasive candidiasis were enrolled in an open-label, non-comparative study and 250 were in the modified intention-to-treat population; all received intravenous anidulafungin and, after 5 days, could step down to oral azole therapy (fluconazole or voriconazole) if prespecified criteria were met. Patients who switched within 7 days formed the 'early switch' subpopulation.
cards.result: The global response rate (clinical plus microbiological) at end of treatment in the modified intention-to-treat population was 83.7% (95% CI 78.7–88.8). Global response rates at all time points were generally similar in the early-switch subpopulation compared with the whole population, and were similar across Candida species including C. albicans, C. glabrata and C. parapsilosis. The most common treatment-related adverse events were nausea and vomiting (four patients each).
cards.watchOut: There is no control group that stayed intravenous, so this study shows a step-down programme can be run with good outcomes — it cannot show step-down is as safe as continuing the echinocandin. Step-down was to fluconazole or voriconazole, not fluconazole alone, and only patients meeting prespecified response criteria could switch.
cards.source: Vazquez J et al. Evaluation of an early step-down strategy from intravenous anidulafungin to oral azole therapy for the treatment of candidemia and other forms of invasive candidiasis: results from an open-label trial. BMC infectious diseases. 2014. PMID: 24559321. Registry ID: NCT00496197. cards.headline: Husni 2021: in 119 non-neutropenic candidemia patients, step-down occurred at an average of day 5; stepping down at 1–4 days carried the same mortality as after more than 5 days (20% versus 24%)
cards.summary: Husni 2021: in 119 non-neutropenic candidemia patients, step-down occurred at an average of day 5; stepping down at 1–4 days carried the same mortality as after more than 5 days (20% versus 24%)
cards.people: 119 non-neutropenic patients aged 14 years or older with documented candidemia, assembled retrospectively at four institutions in Brazil, Lebanon, Spain and the United States; 57% were in intensive care and 52% had underlying malignancy. Forty-five patients were stepped down to fluconazole and/or voriconazole in association with clinical and microbiological resolution.
cards.result: The average and median day of step-down was 5 days. Patients who were stepped down had more favourable outcomes (78% survival) than those with no step-down (56% survival, P = 0.022). However, the 20 patients who received 1–4 days of intravenous treatment before step-down had a comparable outcome (20% mortality) to the 25 patients who received more than 5 days before step-down (24% mortality, P = 0.75). Total treatment duration averaged 14 days in all patients and 16 days in those who responded and survived.
cards.watchOut: The survival advantage of the stepped-down group is the expected artefact of stepping down only patients who are already resolving — confounding by indication. The timing comparison (1–4 versus more than 5 days) is the less biased read, and it is small: 20 versus 25 patients.
cards.source: Husni R et al. Timing for Step-Down Therapy of Candidemia in Non-Neutropenic Patients: An International Multi-Center Study. Mediterranean journal of hematology and infectious diseases. 2021. PMID: 34007419. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Droney 2025: in Candida glabrata candidemia, fluconazole step-down had 30-day clinical failure of 9% versus 15% on continued echinocandin — no significant difference
cards.summary: Droney 2025: in Candida glabrata candidemia, fluconazole step-down had 30-day clinical failure of 9% versus 15% on continued echinocandin — no significant difference
cards.people: 186 inpatients aged 18–89 years with Candida glabrata candidemia at a single centre (2011–2023) who received an echinocandin within 24 hours of the initial positive blood culture: 153 continued on an echinocandin only and 33 were stepped down to fluconazole. The commonest source was line-associated in both groups, with source control in 43% (echinocandin) versus 58% (step-down).
cards.result: There was no significant difference in 30-day clinical failure between the echinocandin-only and fluconazole step-down groups (15% versus 9%, P = 0.58), in persistent candidemia (22% versus 24%, P = 0.7), or in total treatment duration (16 versus 19 days, P = 0.46). The authors conclude fluconazole appears to be a safe and reasonable step-down therapy for C. glabrata candidemia.
cards.watchOut: Only 33 patients were stepped down, and they were a selected group — they had less concomitant bacteremia (24% versus 45%) and no endovascular complications (0% versus 11%) — so equivalence in a sicker continued-echinocandin group cannot be read as proof the two strategies are equal in matched patients. C. glabrata fluconazole susceptibility must be confirmed before applying this.
cards.source: Droney M et al. Fluconazole step-down therapy versus echinocandins for the treatment of Candida glabrata invasive candidiasis with candidaemia. The Journal of antimicrobial chemotherapy. 2025. PMID: 39871615. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: step-down to fluconazole at about day 5, in patients already responding, has been used repeatedly without a safety signal — observational evidence only
cards.summary: Synthesis: step-down to fluconazole at about day 5, in patients already responding, has been used repeatedly without a safety signal — observational evidence only
cards.people: The carded evidence: one prospective non-comparative step-down programme (Vazquez, 250 evaluable patients), one retrospective multicentre candidemia cohort (Husni, 119 patients, 45 stepped down), and one retrospective single-species cohort (Droney, 186 patients with C. glabrata, 33 stepped down). No randomised trial of step-down versus continued echinocandin was found.
cards.result: Response and failure rates after step-down at about day 5 were consistently acceptable — 83.7% global response in the prospective programme; 20% versus 24% mortality for step-down at 1–4 versus more than 5 days; 9% versus 15% 30-day clinical failure for fluconazole step-down versus continued echinocandin in C. glabrata — but every comparison is exposed to the same selection: clinicians step down patients who are already improving. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (observational evidence): step-down after about 5 days in a responding patient appears safe; it is not trial-proven. The initial-choice question is homed on live shelf #507 and is not re-carded here.
cards.watchOut: All three reports step down responders; none of them licenses stepping down a patient who is not responding, has an uncontrolled source, or has a fluconazole-non-susceptible isolate.
cards.source: Synthesis of Vazquez J et al. BMC infectious diseases. 2014 (PMID: 24559321); Husni R et al. Mediterranean journal of hematology and infectious diseases. 2021 (PMID: 34007419); Droney M et al. The Journal of antimicrobial chemotherapy. 2025 (PMID: 39871615).

shelves.title: Aminoglycosides in native valve staphylococcal endocarditis: no outcome benefit in pooled trials, and a consistent kidney price — gentamicin fall in creatinine clearance 22% versus 8%
shelves.question: In adults with infective endocarditis, does adding an aminoglycoside improve outcomes in native valve staphylococcal infection?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Anti-Bacterial Agents · Bacteremia · Cohort Studies · Creatinine · Daptomycin · Drug Therapy, Combination · Endocarditis, Bacterial · Female · Gentamicins · Humans · Kidney · Male · Metabolic Clearance Rate · Middle Aged · Penicillins · Prospective Studies · Staphylococcal Infections · Staphylococcus aureus · Vancomycin · Young Adult
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (harm, observational and small-trial evidence) — adding an aminoglycoside to a beta-lactam for native valve staphylococcal endocarditis has not been shown to improve any outcome, and it does damage kidneys. This is a different organism and setting from the enterococcal combination-therapy pack #5445 (ampicillin plus ceftriaxone versus ampicillin plus gentamicin in Enterococcus faecalis), which is cross-pointed, not re-carded. The meta-analysis of the comparative trials (Falagas 2006; five trials, 261 patients with native valve endocarditis due to Staphylococcus aureus or viridans streptococci) found no significant difference in mortality (odds ratio 0.59, 95% CI 0.21–1.66), treatment success, success without surgery, or relapse — and significantly less nephrotoxicity without the aminoglycoside (odds ratio 0.38, 95% CI 0.16–0.88). The largest safety analysis (Cosgrove 2009), drawn from a randomised trial's cohort of 236 patients with S. aureus bacteremia and native valve endocarditis, found a clinically significant fall in creatinine clearance in 22% of patients who received any initial low-dose gentamicin versus 8% of those who did not, with gentamicin receipt an independent predictor. The one randomised with/without trial in staphylococcal disease (Ribera 1996, right-sided MSSA endocarditis in people who inject drugs) found success in 89% on cloxacillin alone versus 86% with gentamicin added. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm): no demonstrated benefit, a consistent kidney price — the combination should not be routine in native valve staphylococcal endocarditis.

cards.headline: Falagas 2006 meta-analysis: across five comparative trials (261 patients), adding an aminoglycoside changed neither mortality nor success — but nephrotoxicity was significantly commoner with it
cards.summary: Falagas 2006 meta-analysis: across five comparative trials (261 patients), adding an aminoglycoside changed neither mortality nor success — but nephrotoxicity was significantly commoner with it
cards.people: Meta-analysis of five prospective comparative trials (four randomised, one prospective comparative) including 261 patients with bacterial endocarditis in native valves due to Staphylococcus aureus (four studies) or viridans-group streptococci (one study), comparing beta-lactam monotherapy with beta-lactam plus aminoglycoside combination therapy.
cards.result: There was no statistically significant difference between monotherapy and combination therapy for mortality (odds ratio 0.59, 95% CI 0.21–1.66), treatment success (OR 1.25, 95% CI 0.49–3.05), treatment success without surgery (OR 1.66, 95% CI 0.64–4.30), or relapse (OR 0.79, 95% CI 0.15–4.29). Nephrotoxicity was less common in the monotherapy arm (OR 0.38, 95% CI 0.16–0.88, P = 0.024). In the staphylococcal-only subanalysis, mortality (OR 0.69, 95% CI 0.26–1.86), success and relapse likewise did not differ. The authors note the small number of available trials was the major limitation.
cards.watchOut: The pooled trials are small and old, and one of the five is streptococcal rather than staphylococcal; the confidence interval for mortality (0.21–1.66) cannot exclude a benefit — what it establishes is that no benefit has been demonstrated, while the nephrotoxicity difference was significant.
cards.source: Falagas ME et al. The role of aminoglycosides in combination with a beta-lactam for the treatment of bacterial endocarditis: a meta-analysis of comparative trials. The Journal of antimicrobial chemotherapy. 2006. PMID: 16501057. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.summary: Cosgrove 2009: any initial low-dose gentamicin was followed by a clinically significant fall in creatinine clearance in 22% versus 8% without it — in S. aureus bacteremia and native valve endocarditis
cards.type: Prospective cohort safety analysis within a randomised trial population (Cosgrove 2009)
cards.people: Prospective cohort study of safety data from a randomised trial of therapy for Staphylococcus aureus bacteremia and native valve infective endocarditis: 236 patients from 44 hospitals in four countries, receiving standard therapy (antistaphylococcal penicillin or vancomycin) plus initial low-dose gentamicin (116) or daptomycin monotherapy (120); a further 21 patients had received initial low-dose gentamicin within 2 days before enrolment and were included in the any-gentamicin analysis.
cards.result: Renal adverse events occurred in 7% of daptomycin recipients, 19% of vancomycin recipients and 17% of antistaphylococcal penicillin recipients. A clinically significant decreased creatinine clearance occurred in 22% of all patients who received any initial low-dose gentamicin versus 8% of patients who did not receive it. Independent predictors of a clinically significant decrease in creatinine clearance were age 65 years or older and receipt of any initial low-dose gentamicin. The authors conclude initial low-dose gentamicin is nephrotoxic and should not be used routinely, given the minimal existing data supporting its benefit.
cards.watchOut: This is a harm analysis, not an efficacy comparison: the gentamicin contrast is partly non-randomised (pre-enrolment gentamicin included), and the population mixes S. aureus bacteremia with native valve endocarditis rather than endocarditis alone.
cards.source: Cosgrove SE et al. Initial low-dose gentamicin for Staphylococcus aureus bacteremia and endocarditis is nephrotoxic. Clinical infectious diseases : an official publication of the Infectious Diseases Society of America. 2009. PMID: 19207079. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Ribera 1996 randomised trial: for right-sided MSSA endocarditis, cloxacillin alone succeeded in 89% versus 86% with gentamicin added — no therapeutic advantage
cards.summary: Ribera 1996 randomised trial: for right-sided MSSA endocarditis, cloxacillin alone succeeded in 89% versus 86% with gentamicin added — no therapeutic advantage
cards.people: 90 consecutive intravenous drug users with isolated tricuspid valve endocarditis caused by methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus aureus and no systemic complications requiring prolonged therapy, randomised open-label to cloxacillin alone for 14 days or cloxacillin plus gentamicin for the first 7 days; the efficacy subset was 74 patients.
cards.result: In the efficacy subset, treatment was successful in 34 of 38 patients (89%, 95% CI 75%–97%) on cloxacillin alone and 31 of 36 (86%, 95% CI 71%–95%) on cloxacillin plus gentamicin. Three patients died (one on cloxacillin alone, two on the combination). Of those completing 2-week treatment, cure was 92% on cloxacillin alone and 94% on the combination, and one patient in the combination group relapsed. The authors conclude adding gentamicin did not appear to provide any therapeutic advantages.
cards.watchOut: Right-sided (tricuspid) endocarditis in people who inject drugs, treated with a 2-week course, is the most favourable corner of staphylococcal endocarditis; the trial does not directly test left-sided native valve disease, which is why it supports rather than carries this shelf.
cards.source: Ribera E et al. Effectiveness of cloxacillin with and without gentamicin in short-term therapy for right-sided Staphylococcus aureus endocarditis. A randomized, controlled trial. Annals of internal medicine. 1996. PMID: 8967707. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: no outcome improved by adding an aminoglycoside in native valve staphylococcal endocarditis, and kidney injury consistently increased
cards.summary: Synthesis: no outcome improved by adding an aminoglycoside in native valve staphylococcal endocarditis, and kidney injury consistently increased
cards.people: The carded evidence: one meta-analysis of five small comparative trials in native valve endocarditis (Falagas, 261 patients), one prospective safety cohort in S. aureus bacteremia and native valve endocarditis (Cosgrove, 236 patients), and one randomised with/without trial in right-sided MSSA endocarditis (Ribera, 90 patients).
cards.result: Mortality, treatment success and relapse did not differ with or without an aminoglycoside in the pooled trials (mortality OR 0.59, 95% CI 0.21–1.66) or in the randomised right-sided trial (success 89% alone versus 86% combined), while nephrotoxicity was significantly less common without the aminoglycoside in the meta-analysis (OR 0.38, 95% CI 0.16–0.88) and a significant fall in creatinine clearance followed gentamicin in 22% versus 8% in the safety cohort. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm, observational and small-trial evidence): adding an aminoglycoside buys kidney injury without a demonstrated outcome benefit in native valve staphylococcal endocarditis. Enterococcal combination therapy is a different question, homed on pack #5445.
cards.watchOut: Absence of demonstrated benefit in 261 pooled trial patients is not proof of zero benefit in every subgroup; the claim this shelf makes is the narrower, supported one — no benefit shown, harm shown — which is what guideline recommendations against routine aminoglycoside addition rest on.
cards.source: Synthesis of Falagas ME et al. The Journal of antimicrobial chemotherapy. 2006 (PMID: 16501057); Cosgrove SE et al. Clinical infectious diseases. 2009 (PMID: 19207079); Ribera E et al. Annals of internal medicine. 1996 (PMID: 8967707).

shelves.title: FLAG precedent (b): prosthetic joint infection oral step-down on PJI-specific cohorts only — failure 9.2% versus 15.6% in the largest — with OVIVA kept at its home on live #312
shelves.question: In adults with prosthetic joint infection, is oral step-down antibiotic therapy as effective as continued intravenous therapy?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Male · Female · Anti-Bacterial Agents · Cohort Studies · Arthritis, Infectious · Knee Joint · Prosthesis-Related Infections · Retrospective Studies
shelves.balance: FLAG — PRECEDENT (b) BUILD: the anchor trial for this question, OVIVA (2019), is already carded as an evidence card on live shelf #312 (the general adult oral-versus-intravenous bone and joint infection question), so OVIVA is NOT re-carded here and its PMID is kept out of every card's source line, exactly as precedent (b) requires. This pack is built only on prosthetic-joint-infection-specific reports that are free of the library, and its evidence is entirely observational — hence the POSSIBLE (observational) cap. In the largest PJI-specific cohort (Roger 2024; 172 patients, 13 institutions), management failure over 24 months was 9.2% (7 of 76) in patients treated with oral therapy (exclusively oral or at most 3 days parenteral) versus 15.6% (15 of 96) in patients treated with prolonged parenteral therapy. In Staphylococcus aureus prosthetic bone and joint infection (Boclé 2021; 140 patients), 85% were switched to oral therapy within 5 days of intravenous treatment, the overall failure rate was 8.5%, and intravenous duration (5 days or less versus more than 5 days) was not associated with failure. In two-stage exchange PJI (Ascione 2017; 122 patients), administration of oral therapy was associated with a favourable outcome in both univariate and multivariate analysis. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (observational evidence): in selected PJI patients after appropriate surgery, oral step-down has repeatedly achieved failure rates no worse than prolonged intravenous therapy in cohorts — consistent with, but independent of, the randomised answer homed on live #312. The PJI duration question (6 versus 12 weeks) is a different question, homed on live #2223 (DATIPO).

cards.headline: Roger 2024: in 172 prosthetic joint infections, failure was 9.2% on oral therapy versus 15.6% on prolonged parenteral therapy over 24 months
cards.summary: Roger 2024: in 172 prosthetic joint infections, failure was 9.2% on oral therapy versus 15.6% on prolonged parenteral therapy over 24 months
cards.people: Retrospective multicentre cohort of 172 patients with prosthetic joint infection managed from 2017 to 2021 at 13 institutions (60% male; mean age 73 years); sites were mainly hip (50%) and knee (35%), 41% were chronic infections, 24% had implant exchange, and Staphylococcus species caused 60% of monomicrobial infections. Oral antibiotic therapy was defined as exclusive oral treatment or at most 3 days of parenteral treatment (76 patients); the other 96 received prolonged parenteral therapy. Median total antimicrobial duration was 42 days.
cards.result: Management failure — clinical and/or microbial relapse of the prosthetic joint infection over 24 months after surgical treatment — was observed in 7 of 76 patients (9.2%) treated with oral therapy and 15 of 96 (15.6%) treated with prolonged parenteral therapy. In multivariate analysis, the risk factors for failure were a knee prosthetic joint infection (adjusted odds ratio 3.27, 95% CI 1.27–8.40) and a polymicrobial infection (adjusted OR 4.09, 95% CI 1.46–11.49); route of therapy was not identified as a risk factor. The authors conclude oral therapy for 6 weeks for prosthetic joint infection was associated with a low rate of management failure.
cards.watchOut: Retrospective and non-randomised: patients given prolonged parenteral therapy may have been those clinicians judged higher-risk, so the lower failure rate on oral therapy cannot be read as oral superiority — the supported claim is that carefully selected oral-treated patients did not do worse.
cards.source: Roger PM et al. Prosthetic joint infections: 6 weeks of oral antibiotics results in a low failure rate. The Journal of antimicrobial chemotherapy. 2024. PMID: 38113529. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: Humans · Male · Female · Anti-Bacterial Agents · Cohort Studies · Arthritis, Infectious · Knee Joint · Prosthesis-Related Infections · Retrospective Studies

cards.headline: Boclé 2021: in 140 Staphylococcus aureus prosthetic infections, 85% switched to oral therapy within 5 days and failure was 8.5% — intravenous duration was not associated with failure
cards.summary: Boclé 2021: in 140 Staphylococcus aureus prosthetic infections, 85% switched to oral therapy within 5 days and failure was 8.5% — intravenous duration was not associated with failure
cards.people: Retrospective cohort of 140 adults with Staphylococcus aureus prosthetic bone and joint or orthopedic metalware-associated infection treated at a French university hospital (2008–2015); mean age 60.4 years, 66% male, 81% methicillin-susceptible S. aureus. Mean duration of intravenous antibiotic treatment was 4.1 days, and 119 patients (85%) had 5 days or less of intravenous therapy before oral switch.
cards.result: Twelve patients (8.5%) experienced treatment failure — recurrence of S. aureus prosthetic infection within 2 years of follow-up. In the Cox model, methicillin-resistant S. aureus infection (hazard ratio 11.1, 95% CI 1.5–111.1), obesity (HR 6.9, 95% CI 1.4–34.4) and non-conventional empiric antibiotic therapy (HR 7.1, 95% CI 1.8–25.2) were significantly associated with treatment failure, whereas duration of intravenous antibiotic therapy (5 days or less versus more than 5 days) was not. The authors conclude there was a low treatment failure rate with early oral switch.
cards.watchOut: The population mixes prosthetic joint infection with orthopedic metalware infection and is single-organism (S. aureus) and single-centre; with only 12 failures, the hazard ratios are imprecise, and there is no prolonged-intravenous comparison group of any size — most patients switched early by local practice.
cards.source: Boclé H et al. Effectiveness of early switching from intravenous to oral antibiotic therapy in Staphylococcus aureus prosthetic bone and joint or orthopedic metalware-associated infections. BMC musculoskeletal disorders. 2021. PMID: 33784991. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Ascione 2017: in 122 prosthetic joint infections undergoing two-stage exchange, use of oral therapy was associated with a favourable outcome in multivariate analysis
cards.summary: Ascione 2017: in 122 prosthetic joint infections undergoing two-stage exchange, use of oral therapy was associated with a favourable outcome in multivariate analysis
cards.people: Retrospective cohort of 122 patients with prosthetic joint infection undergoing two-stage exchange over 5 years (2009–2013) at an Italian centre (median age 69 years; 48% male; 47 hip and 75 knee infections); microbiological definition was obtained in 101 patients (83%), with Staphylococcus aureus in 36% and coagulase-negative staphylococci in 34%. Cure was defined as disappearance of infection after 96 weeks of follow-up.
cards.result: A favourable outcome was obtained in 102 of 122 patients (84%). After univariate analysis, bacterial growth from operative specimens (P = .007), growth of Gram-positive bacteria (P < .001), use of oral therapy (P = .01), and absence of known comorbidities (P = .02) were associated with favourable outcome; administration of rifampin was not predictive (P = .99). After multivariate analysis, infection sustained by Gram-positive bacteria, administration of oral antibiotics, and absence of known comorbidities remained associated with favourable outcome. The record reports the association without an odds ratio for oral therapy, and none is printed here.
cards.watchOut: Oral therapy here is one variable in a prognostic-factor analysis of two-stage exchange patients, not a randomised route comparison; patients well enough to take oral therapy differ from those who are not, and the abstract gives no effect size for the oral-therapy association.
cards.source: Ascione T et al. Oral Therapy, Microbiological Findings, and Comorbidity Influence the Outcome of Prosthetic Joint Infections Undergoing 2-Stage Exchange. The Journal of arthroplasty. 2017. PMID: 28372916. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: PJI-specific cohorts consistently show oral step-down achieving failure rates no worse than prolonged intravenous therapy — observational evidence, with the randomised anchor homed on live #312
cards.summary: Synthesis: PJI-specific cohorts consistently show oral step-down achieving failure rates no worse than prolonged intravenous therapy — observational evidence, with the randomised anchor homed on live #312
cards.people: The carded evidence: three retrospective PJI-specific cohorts — Roger (172 prosthetic joint infections), Boclé (140 S. aureus prosthetic bone/joint or metalware infections), and Ascione (122 two-stage exchange prosthetic joint infections). The randomised OVIVA trial is deliberately not carded here: it is homed on live shelf #312 under the one-home rule (precedent (b) build — see the balance).
cards.result: Failure on oral or early-switch therapy was 9.2% versus 15.6% on prolonged parenteral therapy (Roger), 8.5% overall with intravenous duration not associated with failure (Boclé), and oral therapy was independently associated with favourable outcome after two-stage exchange (Ascione). No PJI-specific randomised trial of route was found. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (observational evidence): oral step-down after appropriate surgery is as effective as continued intravenous therapy in the selected PJI patients these cohorts describe.
cards.watchOut: All three cohorts are retrospective and selection runs in oral therapy's favour (stable, absorbing, susceptible-organism patients get switched); this pack supports step-down in selected patients and must not be quoted as trial-level proof for unselected prosthetic joint infection.
cards.source: Synthesis of Roger PM et al. The Journal of antimicrobial chemotherapy. 2024 (PMID: 38113529); Boclé H et al. BMC musculoskeletal disorders. 2021 (PMID: 33784991); Ascione T et al. The Journal of arthroplasty. 2017 (PMID: 28372916).

shelves.title: Doxycycline vs benzathine penicillin for early syphilis (PARTIAL completion of live #2192): no randomised trial — three retrospective series show no significant serological difference
shelves.question: In adults with early syphilis, is doxycycline as effective as benzathine penicillin for cure?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Anti-Bacterial Agents · Doxycycline · Drug Evaluation · Female · Humans · Male · Penicillin G Benzathine · Retrospective Studies · Syphilis · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: PARTIAL completion: live shelf #2192 already answers single-dose azithromycin versus benzathine penicillin for early syphilis; this shelf answers the doxycycline slice only, and no azithromycin study is re-carded here. FLAG — premise correction: the slate described the Ghanem 2006 anchor as a 'pilot randomised study'; the fetched PubMed record shows it is a retrospective comparative study (Publication Type: Comparative Study; MeSH: Retrospective Studies), and every other cardable report found is also retrospective. There is no randomised trial of doxycycline versus benzathine penicillin for early syphilis in the fetched records. What the observational evidence shows is consistent: serological failure/response rates on doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 14 days are statistically indistinguishable from single-dose benzathine penicillin G in Baltimore clinic patients (failure 0% vs 5.5%), in a 601-case Chinese clinic series (12-month response 92.4% vs 96.2%), and in HIV-infected patients treated during a penicillin shortage (response 72% vs 70%). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (observational): the retrospective evidence is compatible with doxycycline being as effective as benzathine penicillin for serological cure of early syphilis, but confounding by indication — doxycycline is usually given when penicillin cannot be — caps the stamp at POSSIBLE and the finding is labelled observational throughout.

cards.headline: Ghanem 2006 (retrospective): serological failure 0% on doxycycline vs 5.5% on benzathine penicillin in 107 Baltimore clinic patients with early syphilis
cards.summary: Ghanem 2006 (retrospective): serological failure 0% on doxycycline vs 5.5% on benzathine penicillin in 107 Baltimore clinic patients with early syphilis
cards.people: Patients with early syphilis (primary, secondary or early latent, with reactive serology and at least one follow-up titre) at two Baltimore sexually transmitted disease clinics, 1993–2000: 34 treated with doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily for 14 days and 73 age-matched controls treated with a single 2.4 million unit intramuscular dose of benzathine penicillin G, drawn from 1,558 patients treated for early syphilis in the period.
cards.result: Serological failure (lack of a 4-fold rapid plasma reagin titre drop by 270–400 days, or a 4-fold rise) occurred in 0 of 34 doxycycline patients (0%; 95% CI 0%–10.3%) and 4 of 73 penicillin patients (5.5%; 95% CI 1.6%–13.8%; P=.2). Median time to successful serological response was 106 days on doxycycline and 137 days on penicillin (P=.6) — no significant difference on either measure.
cards.watchOut: Retrospective and small on the doxycycline side: only 34 of 87 doxycycline-treated patients met the follow-up inclusion criteria, and the 0% failure rate carries a confidence interval up to 10.3% — this study cannot exclude a clinically important difference in either direction.
cards.source: Ghanem KG et al. Doxycycline compared with benzathine penicillin for the treatment of early syphilis. Clinical infectious diseases. 2006. PMID: 16477545. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Xiao 2017 (retrospective, 601 cases): serological response at 12 months 92.4% on doxycycline vs 96.2% on benzathine penicillin — no significant difference
cards.summary: Xiao 2017 (retrospective, 601 cases): serological response at 12 months 92.4% on doxycycline vs 96.2% on benzathine penicillin — no significant difference
cards.people: 601 patients with early syphilis at a Chinese sexually transmitted disease clinic, 2008–2014: 105 treated with oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 14 days and 496 with a single dose of benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units.
cards.result: Serological response did not differ significantly between doxycycline and penicillin at 6 months (69.52% vs 75.00%, P=0.245) or at 12 months (92.38% vs 96.17%, P=0.115). The authors conclude doxycycline remains an effective agent for early syphilis.
cards.watchOut: Retrospective record review with a 5:1 imbalance between the arms; patients were not randomised, so who received doxycycline (typically penicillin allergy or refusal of injection) may differ systematically from who received penicillin.
cards.source: Xiao H et al. Comparison of Doxycycline and Benzathine Penicillin G for the Treatment of Early Syphilis. Acta dermatovenerologica Croatica. 2017. PMID: 28871924. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Antonio 2019 (retrospective, HIV-infected patients): serological response 72% on doxycycline vs 70% on benzathine penicillin (P=0.753)
cards.summary: Antonio 2019 (retrospective, HIV-infected patients): serological response 72% on doxycycline vs 70% on benzathine penicillin (P=0.753)
cards.type: Retrospective comparative study (natural experiment, Antonio 2019) — observational
cards.people: 165 HIV-infected patients with early, late latent or unknown-duration syphilis: 50 treated with doxycycline during a benzathine penicillin shortage period (September 2014 to December 2016) and 115 treated with benzathine penicillin; neurosyphilis and suboptimal-dose cases excluded.
cards.result: Serological response (nonreagent VDRL or at least a 4-fold titre reduction at 6–12 months) was seen in 72% (95% CI 58–84) of doxycycline patients and 70% (95% CI 60–78) of penicillin patients (P=0.753) — no statistically significant difference, leading the authors to call doxycycline an acceptable treatment in HIV-infected patients with non-tertiary syphilis.
cards.watchOut: The cohort mixes early with late latent and unknown-duration syphilis, so it supports the early-syphilis answer only in part; it is also confined to HIV-infected patients, and allocation was by drug availability during a shortage, not by randomisation.
cards.source: Antonio MB et al. Natural experiment of syphilis treatment with doxycycline or benzathine penicillin in HIV-infected patients. AIDS (London, England). 2019. PMID: 30102654. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: three retrospective series agree — no significant serological difference between doxycycline and benzathine penicillin in early syphilis
cards.summary: Synthesis: three retrospective series agree — no significant serological difference between doxycycline and benzathine penicillin in early syphilis
cards.people: The carded evidence: three retrospective comparative studies totalling 873 analysed patients (Ghanem 2006, 107 patients; Xiao 2017, 601 cases; Antonio 2019, 165 HIV-infected patients). No randomised trial was found in the fetched records — the Ghanem anchor named in the slate as a pilot randomised study is, on its PubMed record, retrospective.
cards.result: Failure/response rates were statistically indistinguishable in all three: failure 0% vs 5.5% (Ghanem), 12-month response 92.4% vs 96.2% (Xiao), and response 72% vs 70% in HIV-infected patients (Antonio). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (observational): doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 14 days appears as effective as single-dose benzathine penicillin G for serological cure of early syphilis, on observational evidence only.
cards.watchOut: Serological response is a surrogate for cure, follow-up titres can be distorted by reinfection, and none of these studies can prove equivalence — absence of a significant difference in small retrospective series is not a non-inferiority finding. Penicillin also remains the only recommended treatment in pregnancy, a population none of these cards addresses.
cards.source: Synthesis of Ghanem KG et al. Clinical infectious diseases. 2006 (PMID: 16477545); Xiao H et al. Acta dermatovenerologica Croatica. 2017 (PMID: 28871924); Antonio MB et al. AIDS (London, England). 2019 (PMID: 30102654).

shelves.title: TAF/emtricitabine versus TDF/emtricitabine PrEP (DISCOVER): HIV incidence 0.16 versus 0.34 per 100 person-years at the primary analysis — non-inferior, with better bone and renal biomarkers; a single trial programme
shelves.question: In people at high risk of HIV, is tenofovir alafenamide/emtricitabine PrEP as effective as tenofovir disoproxil/emtricitabine PrEP?
shelves.mesh: Adenine/adverse effects,analogs & derivatives,therapeutic use · Adult · Anti-HIV Agents/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Double-Blind Method · Emtricitabine/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Emtricitabine, Tenofovir Disoproxil Fumarate Drug Combination/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Europe/epidemiology · Female · HIV Infections/drug therapy,epidemiology,prevention & control · HIV-1/drug effects · Homosexuality, Male/ethnology · Humans · Male · North America/epidemiology · Placebos/administration & dosage · Pre-Exposure Prophylaxis/methods · Prevalence · Safety · Sexual and Gender Minorities · Tenofovir/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (as effective; single programme). DISCOVER is the only head-to-head trial of the two tenofovir prodrug formulations as PrEP, and all three carded reports are reports of that one programme — the stamp cap for a single programme therefore applies despite the trial's size (5,387 participants who received study drug). At the primary analysis (Mayer 2020), HIV incidence was 0.16 per 100 person-years on tenofovir alafenamide/emtricitabine (7 infections) versus 0.34 on tenofovir disoproxil/emtricitabine (15 infections) over 8,756 person-years; the incidence rate ratio of 0.47 (95% CI 0.19 to 1.15) met the prespecified noninferiority margin of 1.62. At week 96 (Ogbuagu 2021) noninferiority was maintained (8 vs 15 infections; 0.16 vs 0.30 per 100 person-years; rate ratio 0.54, 95% CI 0.23 to 1.26), and in the week-144 open-label extension (Wohl 2024) incidence in those originally assigned to the alafenamide regimen was 0.13 per 100 person-years, with the 3 extension-phase infections all in non-adherent participants and no drug resistance. The alafenamide regimen was superior on all six prespecified bone mineral density and renal biomarker endpoints at the primary analysis, and both regimens were well tolerated (discontinuation for adverse events 1% vs 2%). Population limits are printed on the cards: DISCOVER enrolled cisgender men and transgender women who have sex with men in Europe and North America — it does not answer this question for receptive vaginal exposure. The neighbouring PrEP homes are different questions: daily tenofovir in people who inject drugs (live #2143) and on-demand tenofovir disoproxil/emtricitabine (live #2141). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (as effective; single programme): noninferiority is established within DISCOVER; independent replication does not exist.

cards.headline: Mayer 2020 (DISCOVER primary): TAF/emtricitabine non-inferior to TDF/emtricitabine — 7 versus 15 HIV infections, incidence 0.16 versus 0.34 per 100 person-years
cards.summary: Mayer 2020 (DISCOVER primary): TAF/emtricitabine non-inferior to TDF/emtricitabine — 7 versus 15 HIV infections, incidence 0.16 versus 0.34 per 100 person-years
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial, phase 3, noninferiority (DISCOVER primary; Mayer 2020)
cards.people: Randomised, double-blind, active-controlled phase 3 noninferiority trial at 94 clinics in Europe and North America: 5,387 participants received study drug — cisgender men and transgender women who have sex with men at high risk of HIV — assigned 1:1 to daily emtricitabine/tenofovir alafenamide (200/25 mg; n = 2,694) or emtricitabine/tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (200/300 mg; n = 2,693), each with matched placebo tablets. The primary analysis was done when all participants had completed 48 weeks and half had completed 96 weeks.
cards.result: After 8,756 person-years of follow-up, 22 participants were diagnosed with HIV: 7 on tenofovir alafenamide/emtricitabine (0.16 infections per 100 person-years, 95% CI 0.06 to 0.33) and 15 on tenofovir disoproxil/emtricitabine (0.34 per 100 person-years, 95% CI 0.19 to 0.56). The incidence rate ratio was 0.47 (95% CI 0.19 to 1.15); its upper bound was below the prespecified noninferiority margin of 1.62, establishing noninferiority. Tenofovir alafenamide/emtricitabine was superior on all six prespecified bone mineral density and renal biomarker safety endpoints. Both regimens were well tolerated; adverse events led to discontinuation in 36 of 2,694 (1%) versus 49 of 2,693 (2%).
cards.watchOut: Noninferiority against a 1.62 rate-ratio margin is not proof of identical efficacy, and event counts are small (22 infections) because both regimens work well and adherence was high. The population is men and transgender women who have sex with men — no receptive-vaginal-exposure data.
cards.source: Mayer KH et al. Emtricitabine and tenofovir alafenamide vs emtricitabine and tenofovir disoproxil fumarate for HIV pre-exposure prophylaxis (DISCOVER): primary results from a randomised, double-blind, multicentre, active-controlled, phase 3, non-inferiority trial. Lancet (London, England). 2020. PMID: 32711800. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02842086. cards.headline: Ogbuagu 2021 (DISCOVER week 96): noninferiority maintained — 8 versus 15 infections, incidence 0.16 versus 0.30 per 100 person-years (rate ratio 0.54)
cards.summary: Ogbuagu 2021 (DISCOVER week 96): noninferiority maintained — 8 versus 15 infections, incidence 0.16 versus 0.30 per 100 person-years (rate ratio 0.54)
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial, phase 3, week-96 report (DISCOVER; Ogbuagu 2021)
cards.people: Week-96 analysis of the same DISCOVER trial: 5,387 randomised participants (2,694 tenofovir alafenamide/emtricitabine; 2,693 tenofovir disoproxil/emtricitabine) contributing 10,081 person-years of follow-up after all participants had completed 96 weeks.
cards.result: HIV infections numbered 8 on tenofovir alafenamide/emtricitabine (0.16 per 100 person-years, 95% CI 0.07 to 0.31) versus 15 on tenofovir disoproxil/emtricitabine (0.30 per 100 person-years, 95% CI 0.17 to 0.49); incidence rate ratio 0.54 (95% CI 0.23 to 1.26) — noninferiority maintained. About 78–82% of participants reported taking study medication more than 95% of the time. Sexually transmitted infection rates remained high and similar in both groups (rectal gonorrhoea 21 and rectal chlamydia 28 cases per 100 person-years). The alafenamide regimen continued to show superiority on bone mineral density and renal safety biomarkers.
cards.watchOut: A later report of the same single trial, not an independent replication — it extends confidence in durability, not in generalisability. The record's title says 'placebo-controlled' but the design was double-dummy active-controlled; there was no placebo-only arm.
cards.source: Ogbuagu O et al. Long-term safety and efficacy of emtricitabine and tenofovir alafenamide vs emtricitabine and tenofovir disoproxil fumarate for HIV-1 pre-exposure prophylaxis: week 96 results from a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, phase 3 trial. The lancet. HIV. 2021. PMID: 34197772. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02842086.
