cards.headline: Wohl 2024 (DISCOVER week-144 open-label extension): incidence 0.13 per 100 person-years in those originally on TAF/emtricitabine; the 3 extension infections were all in non-adherent participants, with no drug resistance
cards.summary: Wohl 2024 (DISCOVER week-144 open-label extension): incidence 0.13 per 100 person-years in those originally on TAF/emtricitabine; the 3 extension infections were all in non-adherent participants, with no drug resistance
cards.type: Open-label extension report of a randomised trial (DISCOVER week 144; Wohl 2024)
cards.people: Open-label extension of DISCOVER: of the original 5,399 enrolled participants, 2,070 of those assigned to tenofovir alafenamide/emtricitabine continued it and 2,115 of those assigned to tenofovir disoproxil/emtricitabine switched to the alafenamide regimen, for 48 further weeks (to week 144). Total follow-up across randomised and open-label phases was 15,817 person-years at the December 2020 data cutoff.
cards.result: Across the whole study period there were 27 new HIV-1 diagnoses, 3 of them during the open-label phase; in participants originally assigned to tenofovir alafenamide/emtricitabine the incidence was 0.13 per 100 person-years (95% CI 0.061 to 0.23; 10 of 2,670). All 3 incident extension cases were non-adherent to PrEP and none developed drug resistance. In those taking the alafenamide regimen for up to 144 weeks, renal filtration and proximal tubule markers improved or remained stable, hip and spine bone mineral density increased or remained stable (subset n = 191), and median weight gain was under 1 kg per year.
cards.watchOut: Open-label and uncontrolled in the extension phase — after week 96 everyone was offered the alafenamide regimen, so this report supports long-term safety and durability, not a fresh head-to-head efficacy estimate.
cards.source: Wohl DA et al. HIV-1 infection kinetics, drug resistance, and long-term safety of pre-exposure prophylaxis with emtricitabine plus tenofovir alafenamide (DISCOVER): week 144 open-label extension of a randomised, controlled, phase 3 trial. The lancet. HIV. 2024. PMID: 39008999. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02842086. cards.people: People at high risk of HIV as enrolled in DISCOVER: 5,387 treated cisgender men and transgender women who have sex with men in Europe and North America, followed for up to 144 weeks.
cards.result: One large, well-conducted noninferiority programme with concordant primary, week-96 and extension reports, plus a consistent bone/renal biomarker advantage for the alafenamide formulation. shelves.title: Mesenchymal stromal cells in ARDS: safe in three small phase 2 trials, efficacy unproven — no phase 3 evidence
shelves.question: In adults with moderate-to-severe ARDS, do mesenchymal stromal cells improve ventilator-free days or mortality compared with placebo? (Phase 2 evidence only.)
shelves.mesh: Academic Medical Centers · Adult · Aged · Disease-Free Survival · Double-Blind Method · Female · Hospital Mortality · Humans · Male · Mesenchymal Stem Cell Transplantation/methods,mortality · Middle Aged · Multivariate Analysis · Patient Safety · Proportional Hazards Models · Prospective Studies · Respiratory Distress Syndrome/diagnosis,mortality,therapy · Risk Assessment · Severity of Illness Index · Statistics, Nonparametric · Survival Analysis · Treatment Outcome · United States · Intensive Care Units · Quality of Life · Respiratory Distress Syndrome/therapy · Stem Cells · COVID-19 · Lung · Respiratory Distress Syndrome · Stromal Cells · Lung Diseases, Interstitial
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — PHASE 2 EVIDENCE ONLY, flagged on the face of this shelf: there is no phase 3 trial of mesenchymal or multipotent stromal cells in ARDS. Three small randomised phase 1/2–2a trials point in different directions. START (60 patients) found one dose of mesenchymal stromal cells safe but 28-day mortality numerically higher on cells (30% vs 15%; adjusted HR 1.43, 95% CI 0.40–5.12), in a cell arm that was sicker at baseline. MUST-ARDS (30 patients in its randomised cohort) found mortality and ventilator-free days numerically favouring multipotent adult progenitor cells (28-day mortality 25% vs 45%; median ventilator-free days 18.5 vs 6.5), with the same baseline-imbalance problem in reverse. REALIST-COVID (59 analysed, COVID-19 ARDS only) found no difference in oxygenation or mortality at any point to 2 years (the treatment made no difference). Safety is consistent; efficacy is unproven.

cards.headline: START (Matthay 2019): one dose of mesenchymal stromal cells was safe in moderate-to-severe ARDS, but 28-day mortality was 30% on cells vs 15% on placebo (adjusted HR 1.43, 95% CI 0.40–5.12) — a phase 2a safety trial, not an efficacy verdict
cards.summary: START (Matthay 2019): one dose of mesenchymal stromal cells was safe in moderate-to-severe ARDS, but 28-day mortality was 30% on cells vs 15% on placebo (adjusted HR 1.43, 95% CI 0.40–5.12) — a phase 2a safety trial, not an efficacy verdict
cards.type: Randomised phase 2a trial (START), Lancet Respir Med 2019
cards.people: 60 ventilated adults with moderate-to-severe ARDS (PaO2/FiO2 ratio <27 kPa, about 203 mmHg, on PEEP ≥8 cm H2O) at five US university centres, randomised 2:1 to a single intravenous dose of allogeneic bone-marrow-derived mesenchymal stromal cells (10 × 10^6 cells/kg predicted bodyweight) or placebo.
cards.result: No patient had a predefined cell-related haemodynamic or respiratory adverse event; one death within 24 hours of infusion was judged probably unrelated. 28-day mortality did not differ significantly (30% cells vs 15% placebo; odds ratio 2.4 relative, 95% CI 0.5 to 15.1), and after adjustment for the baseline severity gap (mean APACHE III 104 on cells vs 89 on placebo) the hazard ratio was 1.43 (95% CI 0.40 to 5.12; P=.58). Cell viability ranged from 36% to 85%. The authors conclude one dose was safe and that larger trials, with more viable cells, are needed to assess efficacy.
cards.watchOut: Phase 2a and powered for safety: the mortality point estimate favours placebo, the confidence interval is very wide, and the cell arm started sicker — this trial can neither establish nor exclude an efficacy effect. PHASE 2 EVIDENCE ONLY.
cards.source: Matthay MA et al. Treatment with allogeneic mesenchymal stromal cells for moderate to severe acute respiratory distress syndrome (START study): a randomised phase 2a safety trial. The Lancet. Respiratory medicine. 2019. PMID: 30455077. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02097641, stated in the record's abstract. cards.headline: MUST-ARDS (Bellingan 2022): multipotent adult progenitor cells were safe, with 28-day mortality 25% vs 45% and median ventilator-free days 18.5 vs 6.5 favouring cells — in a randomised cohort of only 30 patients whose cell arm had less severe hypoxia at baseline
cards.summary: MUST-ARDS (Bellingan 2022): multipotent adult progenitor cells were safe, with 28-day mortality 25% vs 45% and median ventilator-free days 18.5 vs 6.5 favouring cells — in a randomised cohort of only 30 patients whose cell arm had less severe hypoxia at baseline
cards.type: Randomised phase 1/2 trial (MUST-ARDS), Intensive Care Med 2022
cards.people: Adults with moderate-to-severe ARDS at 12 UK and US centres. After two small open-label safety cohorts (3 patients each at 300 and 900 million cells), the randomised double-blind cohort received 900 million multipotent adult progenitor cells (n=20) or placebo (n=10) within 96 hours of ARDS diagnosis.
cards.result: No allergic or serious adverse reactions were associated with cell therapy in any cohort. In the randomised cohort, 28-day mortality was 25% on cells vs 45% on placebo; median 28-day ventilator-free days were 18.5 (IQR 0 to 22) on cells vs 6.5 (IQR 0 to 18.3) on placebo, and median ICU-free days 12.5 vs 4.5. A prespecified severe subgroup (PaO2/FiO2 <150 mmHg, printed in the record as 20 kPa; n=16) showed similar trends. Cell recipients reported greater quality-of-life recovery through day 365. The authors conclude the cells were safe and well tolerated and that larger trials are warranted.
cards.watchOut: Thirty randomised patients, and the imbalance runs in the cells' favour (less severe hypoxia at baseline) — the mirror image of START's problem. Numerical trends in a cohort this small are hypothesis-generating only. PHASE 2 EVIDENCE ONLY.
cards.source: Bellingan G et al. Safety and efficacy of multipotent adult progenitor cells in acute respiratory distress syndrome (MUST-ARDS): a multicentre, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 1/2 trial. Intensive care medicine. 2022. PMID: 34811567. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: REALIST-COVID (Gorman 2023): ORBCEL-C stromal cells did not improve oxygenation at day 7 or mortality at any point to 2 years in COVID-19 ARDS (the treatment made no difference) — safety held, with serious adverse events 6 vs 3
cards.summary: REALIST-COVID (Gorman 2023): ORBCEL-C stromal cells did not improve oxygenation at day 7 or mortality at any point to 2 years in COVID-19 ARDS (the treatment made no difference) — safety held, with serious adverse events 6 vs 3
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (REALIST-COVID), Am J Respir Crit Care Med 2023
cards.people: 60 adults with moderate-to-severe COVID-19-related ARDS randomised to a single dose of ORBCEL-C (CD362-enriched umbilical-cord-derived mesenchymal stromal cells, 400 million cells; n=30 analysed) or placebo (n=29 analysed) in a multicentre double-blind trial. This is a COVID-19 ARDS population, not all-cause ARDS.
cards.result: The day-7 mean oxygenation index did not differ (98.3 on cells vs 96.6 cm H2O/kPa on placebo), nor did respiratory compliance, driving pressure, PaO2:FiO2 ratio or SOFA score. There were no differences in mortality at day 28, day 90, 1 year or 2 years, nor in interstitial lung disease at 1 year. Serious adverse events occurred in 6 cell recipients vs 3 placebo recipients (risk ratio 2.9 relative, 95% CI 0.6 to 13.2; P=.25). The authors conclude the cells were safe but did not improve surrogates of pulmonary organ dysfunction.
cards.watchOut: COVID-19 ARDS only — its null cannot be read straight across to bacterial or other ARDS, and at 59 analysed patients it is, like the other cards, a phase 2-scale test. PHASE 2 EVIDENCE ONLY.
cards.source: Gorman EA et al. Repair of Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome in COVID-19 by Stromal Cells (REALIST-COVID Trial): A Multicenter, Randomized, Controlled Clinical Trial. American journal of respiratory and critical care medicine. 2023. PMID: 37154608. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03042143, stated in the record's abstract. cards.headline: Synthesis: stromal cells in ARDS are consistently safe and consistently unproven — one small trial trends for benefit, one trends against, one is null; there is no phase 3 evidence
cards.summary: Synthesis: stromal cells in ARDS are consistently safe and consistently unproven — one small trial trends for benefit, one trends against, one is null; there is no phase 3 evidence
cards.people: Synthesis of the three randomised phase 1/2–2a trials carded above: START (60 patients, all-cause moderate-to-severe ARDS), MUST-ARDS (30 randomised patients, all-cause ARDS) and REALIST-COVID (59 analysed patients, COVID-19 ARDS) — about 149 randomised patients in total, using three different cell products.
cards.result: The three products (bone-marrow mesenchymal stromal cells, multipotent adult progenitor cells, CD362-enriched umbilical-cord cells) share one finding — no cell-attributed safety signal — and no shared efficacy finding: ventilator-free days favoured cells only in the smallest trial (MUST-ARDS), mortality point estimates straddle the null in both directions, and the one trial with a prespecified physiological primary endpoint (REALIST-COVID) found the treatment made no difference. Baseline severity imbalances in both directions further weaken any pooled reading. Until a phase 3 trial reports, the honest stamp is MAYBE (weak evidence), and this shelf is flagged phase 2 only on its face, as its slate row requires.
cards.watchOut: Different cell products, doses and ARDS causes are pooled here only because the question asks about the class; a benefit (or harm) of one product would not automatically transfer to the others.
cards.source: Synthesis of Matthay MA et al. The Lancet. Respiratory medicine. 2019 (PMID: 30455077); Bellingan G et al. Intensive care medicine. 2022 (PMID: 34811567); Gorman EA et al. American journal of respiratory and critical care medicine. 2023 (PMID: 37154608). Registry IDs as on the individual cards.

shelves.title: Azole-resistant Aspergillus fumigatus: about 1 in 5 culture-positive invasive cases in Dutch–Belgian cohorts (6.1% of patients in Danish surveillance), TR34/L98H the commonest mechanism — and resistant infection carries roughly 20–25 points higher mortality
shelves.question: In adults with invasive aspergillosis caused by azole-resistant Aspergillus fumigatus, what is the prevalence of environmental TR34/L98H resistance and which treatment improves survival? (Observational evidence.)
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Antifungal Agents/therapeutic use · Aspergillus fumigatus/drug effects,genetics,pathogenicity · Autoimmune Diseases/complications,drug therapy,microbiology,mortality · Child · Child, Preschool · Drug Resistance, Fungal/genetics · Female · Hematologic Neoplasms/complications,drug therapy,microbiology,mortality · Humans · Invasive Pulmonary Aspergillosis/complications,drug therapy,microbiology,mortality · Male · Microbial Sensitivity Tests · Middle Aged · Retrospective Studies · Survival Analysis · Time Factors · Voriconazole/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: All evidence here is observational, so the stamp is capped at POSSIBLE and labelled. Prevalence depends on the denominator: among culture-positive invasive aspergillosis cases in Dutch and Dutch–Belgian haematology cohorts, voriconazole resistance was 19% (37/196, Lestrade 2019) and 20.2% (26/129, Resendiz-Sharpe 2019); in Danish national surveillance counting patients rather than invasive cases, azole resistance was 6.1% (66/1,083) and TR34/L98H specifically 3.6% (39/1,083), accounting for 59.1% of all resistance. In the haematology cohort almost every resistant isolate carried an environmental cyp51A mechanism — TR34/L98H (13 cases) or TR46/Y121F/T289A (12 cases). Mortality is consistently higher with resistance: day-42 mortality 49% versus 28% and day-90 mortality 62% versus 37% (Lestrade); 12-week mortality 57.7% versus 36.9% (Resendiz-Sharpe). On treatment, no randomised trial exists; the actionable observational finding is that receiving initially appropriate (non-azole) therapy mattered — mortality 24% with appropriate initial therapy versus 47% with inappropriate initial voriconazole, even though therapy was switched after a median of 10 days — which is the evidence behind guideline advice to use liposomal amphotericin B, alone or in combination, where resistance is suspected or proven. Susceptible-disease drug comparisons are homed elsewhere (posaconazole pack #4189; isavuconazole versus voriconazole, SECURE, live shelf #508) and are not re-carded here.

cards.headline: Lestrade 2019 multicentre cohort (196 invasive aspergillosis cases): 19% were voriconazole-resistant, and resistance was associated with day-42 mortality of 49% versus 28% and day-90 mortality of 62% versus 37%
cards.summary: Lestrade 2019 multicentre cohort (196 invasive aspergillosis cases): 19% were voriconazole-resistant, and resistance was associated with day-42 mortality of 49% versus 28% and day-90 mortality of 62% versus 37%
cards.people: Five-year retrospective cohort (2011–2015) of culture-positive Aspergillus fumigatus invasive aspergillosis (proven, probable and putative) in the Netherlands; 196 patients, 103 (53%) with haematological malignancy; 154 (79%) started on voriconazole. Thirty-seven patients (19%) had a voriconazole-resistant infection.
cards.result: Compared with susceptible cases, voriconazole resistance was associated with an absolute increase in overall mortality of 21 percentage points at day 42 (49% vs 28%; p=.017) and 25 points at day 90 (62% vs 37%; p=.0038). Mortality in patients who received appropriate initial therapy was 24% compared with 47% in those whose initial voriconazole therapy was inappropriate for their resistant isolate (p=.016), despite switching to appropriate therapy after a median of 10 days.
cards.watchOut: Retrospective and culture-positive only: patients whose aspergillosis was diagnosed without a culture (the majority in many centres) are invisible here, so 19% is a prevalence among cultured cases, not among all invasive aspergillosis. The appropriate-versus-inappropriate therapy contrast is confounded — patients sick enough to die early had less time to be switched.
cards.source: Lestrade PP et al. Voriconazole Resistance and Mortality in Invasive Aspergillosis: A Multicenter Retrospective Cohort Study. Clin Infect Dis. 2019. PMID: 30307492. Registry ID: none in the record. p=.017) and 25 points at day 90 (62% vs 37%; p=.0038). mortality in patients who received appropriate initial therapy was 24% compared with 47% in those whose initial voriconazole therapy was inappropriate for their resistant isolate (p=.016), despite switching to appropriate therapy after a median of 10 days. retrospective and culture-positive only: patients whose aspergillosis was diagnosed without a culture (the majority in many centres) are invisible here, so 19% is a prevalence among cultured cases, not among all invasive aspergillosis. the appropriate-versus-inappropriate therapy contrast is confounded — patients sick enough to die early had less time to be switched. lestrade pp et al. voriconazole resistance and mortality in invasive aspergillosis: a multicenter retrospective cohort study. clin infect dis. 2019. pmid: 30307492. registry id: none in the record. mesh: adolescent · adult · aged · aged, 80 and over · antifungal agents/therapeutic use · aspergillus fumigatus/drug effects,genetics,pathogenicity · autoimmune diseases/complications,drug therapy,microbiology,mortality · child · child, preschool · drug resistance, fungal/genetics · female · hematologic neoplasms/complications,drug therapy,microbiology,mortality · humans · invasive pulmonary aspergillosis/complications,drug therapy,microbiology,mortality · male · microbial sensitivity tests · middle aged · retrospective studies · survival analysis · time factors · voriconazole/therapeutic use

cards.headline: Resendiz-Sharpe 2019 haematology cohort (129 culture-positive cases): voriconazole resistance prevalence 20.2%, nearly all environmental cyp51A mechanisms (TR34/L98H in 13, TR46/Y121F/T289A in 12); 12-week mortality 57.7% versus 36.9%
cards.summary: Resendiz-Sharpe 2019 haematology cohort (129 culture-positive cases): voriconazole resistance prevalence 20.2%, nearly all environmental cyp51A mechanisms (TR34/L98H in 13, TR46/Y121F/T289A in 12); 12-week mortality 57.7% versus 36.9%
cards.people: Multicentre retrospective study of haematology patients with culture-positive proven or probable invasive aspergillosis; 129 Aspergillus fumigatus cases, 103 voriconazole-susceptible (79.8%) and 26 voriconazole-resistant (20.2%) by EUCAST broth microdilution. Triazole monotherapy was started in 75.0% (97/129).
cards.result: All but one resistant case harboured an environment-associated cyp51A resistance mutation: TR34/L98H (13 cases) and TR46/Y121F/T289A (12 cases). Mortality at 6 weeks was 42.3% versus 28.2% (p=0.20) and at 12 weeks 57.7% versus 36.9% (p=0.064) for resistant versus susceptible cases overall; in non-ICU patients the 12-week difference was significant (54.4% vs 30.7%; p=0.035). ICU mortality was very high regardless of susceptibility (about 75% at 12 weeks in both groups).
cards.watchOut: Only 26 resistant cases, so the headline mortality contrasts mostly miss significance overall; the significant result is a non-ICU subgroup. Haematology-only and culture-positive-only — prevalence and mortality do not transfer directly to ICU, transplant or chronic pulmonary populations.
cards.source: Resendiz-Sharpe A et al. Prevalence of voriconazole-resistant invasive aspergillosis and its impact on mortality in haematology patients. J Antimicrob Chemother. 2019. PMID: 31236587. cards.headline: Risum 2022 Danish national surveillance (1,083 patients): azole resistance at patient level was 6.1%, TR34/L98H 3.6% — and TR34/L98H made up 59.1% of all resistant isolates
cards.summary: Risum 2022 Danish national surveillance (1,083 patients): azole resistance at patient level was 6.1%, TR34/L98H 3.6% — and TR34/L98H made up 59.1% of all resistant isolates
cards.type: Prospective national surveillance study (Risum 2022) — 1,083 patients, observational
cards.people: Prospective national surveillance programme, Denmark 2018–2020: unique clinically relevant Aspergillus fumigatus isolates plus background samples, with EUCAST susceptibility testing and cyp51A sequencing of resistant isolates; 1,083 patients.
cards.result: Azole resistance prevalence was 6.1% (66/1,083) at patient level. TR34/L98H prevalence was 3.6% (39/1,083), including the variants TR34/L98H, TR34(3)/L98H and TR34/L98H/S297T/F495I; other Cyp51A variants accounted for 1.3% (14/1,083) and non-Cyp51A-mediated resistance for 1.2% (13/1,083). Of all resistance, TR34/L98H accounted for 59.1% (39/66). Resistance was found in all five Danish regions. The authors state this prevalence did not lead to a change in initial aspergillosis treatment nationally, while causing concern and therapeutic challenges in affected patients.
cards.watchOut: This denominator is patients with any clinically relevant isolate, not invasive aspergillosis cases — which is why 6.1% and the cohorts' 19–20% are both correct and not comparable. Surveillance prevalence is geography-specific: agricultural azole use drives environmental resistance, and rates differ sharply by country and centre.
cards.source: Risum M et al. Azole resistance in Aspergillus fumigatus. The first 2-year's Data from the Danish National Surveillance Study, 2018-2020. Mycoses. 2022. PMID: 35104010. cards.headline: van Paassen 2016 ICU cohort: 10 of 38 culture-positive ICU patients (26%) harboured azole-resistant Aspergillus fumigatus (TR34/L98H and TR46 mechanisms), with 90-day mortality of 100% (10/10) versus 82% (23/28) in susceptible cases
cards.summary: van Paassen 2016 ICU cohort: 10 of 38 culture-positive ICU patients (26%) harboured azole-resistant Aspergillus fumigatus (TR34/L98H and TR46 mechanisms), with 90-day mortality of 100% (10/10) versus 82% (23/28) in susceptible cases
cards.type: Retrospective ICU cohort (van Paassen 2016) — 38 culture-positive patients, observational
cards.people: Retrospective cohort at one Dutch university-hospital ICU, January 2010–December 2013: of 9,121 admitted patients, 136 received antifungal treatment for suspected invasive aspergillosis and 38 had a positive Aspergillus fumigatus culture; 10 harboured at least one azole-resistant isolate, with cyp51A alterations TR34/L98H and TR46/T289A/Y121F. Microsatellite typing showed no clonal outbreak.
cards.result: Overall 90-day mortality was 100% (10/10) in patients with azole-resistant invasive aspergillosis versus 82% (23/28) in patients with suspected aspergillosis by azole-susceptible isolates. The authors conclude the pattern requires rapid resistance testing and reconsideration of empirical antifungal therapy in such units.
cards.watchOut: Ten resistant patients at one ICU in the country with the world's best-documented environmental resistance problem — the 100% mortality figure rests on 10 patients and a comparison group defined by suspicion rather than proven disease. Read it as a warning signal, not a rate.
cards.source: van Paassen J et al. Emerging aspergillosis by azole-resistant Aspergillus fumigatus at an intensive care unit in the Netherlands, 2010 to 2013. Euro Surveill. 2016. PMID: 27541498. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: resistance is frequent in high-azole-use settings, TR34/L98H dominates, and the survival lever the observational record supports is not starting with an azole alone when resistance is likely
cards.summary: Synthesis: resistance is frequent in high-azole-use settings, TR34/L98H dominates, and the survival lever the observational record supports is not starting with an azole alone when resistance is likely
cards.people: The carded evidence: two Dutch–Belgian invasive-aspergillosis cohorts (Lestrade 2019, 196 cases; Resendiz-Sharpe 2019, 129 haematology cases), Danish national surveillance (Risum 2022, 1,083 patients), and one Dutch ICU cohort (van Paassen 2016, 38 culture-positive patients). Drug comparisons in susceptible disease are homed on pack #4189 (posaconazole) and live shelf #508 (isavuconazole, SECURE) and are not re-carded here.
cards.result: Prevalence: 19–20% of culture-positive invasive cases in the Dutch–Belgian cohorts; 6.1% of patients in Danish surveillance, with TR34/L98H at 3.6% of patients and 59.1% of all resistance. Mortality excess with resistance: about 21 points at day 42 and 25 points at day 90 (Lestrade); about 21 points at 12 weeks (Resendiz-Sharpe). Treatment: no trial compares regimens in resistant disease; the only comparative treatment signal is that initially appropriate therapy (24% mortality) beat starting voriconazole and switching after resistance was recognised (47%), which supports liposomal amphotericin B-based initial therapy — alone or combined with an azole — where local resistance prevalence is high or resistance is proven, pending susceptibility results.
cards.watchOut: Every number on this shelf is European and mostly Dutch; a centre with 2% resistance should not import a 20% centre's empirical-therapy conclusion. Combination-therapy claims for resistant disease circulate in guidance but no carded comparative study isolates a combination benefit — the shelf deliberately claims only the initial-appropriate-therapy association.
cards.source: Synthesis of Lestrade PP et al. Clin Infect Dis. 2019 (PMID: 30307492); Resendiz-Sharpe A et al. J Antimicrob Chemother. 2019 (PMID: 31236587); Risum M et al. Mycoses. 2022 (PMID: 35104010); van Paassen J et al. Euro Surveill. 2016 (PMID: 27541498).

shelves.title: MENDS2: dexmedetomidine versus propofol in ventilated sepsis — delirium/coma-free days 10.7 vs 10.8 and 90-day death 38% vs 39% (the treatment made no difference)
shelves.question: In adults with sepsis requiring mechanical ventilation, does dexmedetomidine versus propofol increase days alive without delirium or coma?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Cognition/drug effects · Procedural Sedation/methods · Critical Illness · Dexmedetomidine/administration & dosage · Double-Blind Method · Humans · Hypnotics and Sedatives/administration & dosage · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Propofol/administration & dosage · Respiration, Artificial · Sepsis/mortality
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, because 90-day mortality is co-reported throughout): In MENDS2 (Hughes CG et al., PMID: 33528922), 422 mechanically ventilated adults with sepsis randomised to dexmedetomidine or propofol under a light-sedation protocol had identical days alive without delirium or coma (adjusted median 10.7 vs 10.8 days; odds ratio 0.96, 95% CI 0.74 to 1.26), identical ventilator-free days (23.7 vs 24.0), and 90-day death of 38% versus 39% (hazard ratio 1.06 relative, 95% CI 0.74 to 1.52). The sepsis-specific pooled literature agrees on survival: a meta-analysis of 15 studies (Huang P et al., PMID: 34721015) found 28-day mortality risk ratio 0.97 (95% CI 0.83 to 1.13; P=0.70). A broader 41-trial meta-analysis (Heybati K et al., PMID: 35961815) likewise found no ICU length-of-stay difference in any patient subtype; its delirium and ventilation-duration advantages for dexmedetomidine were confined to cardiac-surgical patients, not sepsis, and bradycardia was more common with dexmedetomidine. The earlier MENDS trial's dexmedetomidine advantage was against lorazepam, a benzodiazepine comparator — it is homed elsewhere in this library and is not re-carded here; against propofol, the modern non-benzodiazepine comparator, there is no difference to find. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): in ventilated sepsis, choose between dexmedetomidine and propofol on haemodynamics, cost and nursing practicality, not on delirium, coma or survival.

cards.headline: MENDS2 2021: dexmedetomidine versus propofol in ventilated sepsis — days alive without delirium or coma 10.7 vs 10.8, 90-day death 38% vs 39% (the treatment made no difference)
cards.summary: MENDS2 2021: dexmedetomidine versus propofol in ventilated sepsis — days alive without delirium or coma 10.7 vs 10.8, 90-day death 38% vs 39% (the treatment made no difference)
cards.type: Multicentre double-blind randomised controlled trial (MENDS2, Hughes 2021)
cards.people: 432 patients underwent randomisation and 422 were analysed (214 dexmedetomidine, 208 propofol) — mechanically ventilated adults with sepsis in a multicentre double-blind trial; dexmedetomidine 0.2 to 1.5 μg/kg/hour (median received dose 0.27 μg/kg/hour) or propofol 5 to 50 μg/kg/minute (median 10.21 μg/kg/minute), titrated by bedside nurses to clinician-set Richmond Agitation-Sedation Scale targets (median RASS −2.0); median duration of trial drug 3.0 days.
cards.result: There was no difference in days alive without delirium or coma during the 14-day intervention period (adjusted median 10.7 vs 10.8 days; odds ratio 0.96, 95% CI 0.74 to 1.26), ventilator-free days at 28 days (adjusted median 23.7 vs 24.0; odds ratio 0.98, 95% CI 0.63 to 1.51), death at 90 days (38% vs 39%; hazard ratio 1.06 relative, 95% CI 0.74 to 1.52), or 6-month cognition (TICS-T adjusted median 40.9 vs 41.4; odds ratio 0.94, 95% CI 0.66 to 1.33). Safety end points were similar in the two groups.
cards.watchOut: This is a comparison of two recommended light-sedation drugs, not of sedation versus no sedation: both arms were nursed to the same RASS target, so the trial cannot speak to sedation depth. Most patients received the trial drug for only about 3 days.
cards.source: Hughes CG et al. Dexmedetomidine or Propofol for Sedation in Mechanically Ventilated Adults with Sepsis. N Engl J Med. 2021. PMID: 33528922. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01739933, from the record's databank fields. cards.headline: Huang 2021 (sepsis-specific systematic review and meta-analysis, 15 studies): 28-day mortality risk ratio 0.97 (95% CI 0.83 to 1.13) for dexmedetomidine versus propofol — no survival difference
cards.summary: Huang 2021 (sepsis-specific systematic review and meta-analysis, 15 studies): 28-day mortality risk ratio 0.97 (95% CI 0.83 to 1.13) for dexmedetomidine versus propofol — no survival difference
cards.people: 15 studies of dexmedetomidine versus propofol in adult patients with sepsis requiring mechanical ventilation (searches of PubMed, Cochrane Library, Embase and Chinese databases); the record does not print the pooled patient total.
cards.result: Dexmedetomidine did not reduce 28-day mortality versus propofol (risk ratio 0.97 relative, 95% CI 0.83 to 1.13; P=0.70). Standardised differences favoured dexmedetomidine for ICU stay (SMD −0.15; P=0.03), duration of mechanical ventilation (SMD −0.22; P=0.043) and SOFA score (SMD −0.41; P=0.013); interleukin-6 at 24 hours did not differ significantly (P=0.074). The reviewers call for more high-quality trials. Pooled absolute mortality rates are not printed in the record.
cards.watchOut: The included studies are mostly small and several are not randomised trials of MENDS2's size or blinding; the stay and ventilation signals are standardised mean differences from that weaker base, while the mortality estimate — the outcome the small studies can least distort in aggregate — is flatly null and agrees with MENDS2.
cards.source: Huang P et al. Dexmedetomidine Versus Propofol for Patients With Sepsis Requiring Mechanical Ventilation: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Front Pharmacol. 2021. PMID: 34721015. cards.headline: Heybati 2022 (systematic review and meta-analysis, 41 RCTs, 3,948 patients): no ICU stay difference in any subtype; dexmedetomidine's delirium advantage was confined to cardiac surgery, and bradycardia was more frequent
cards.summary: Heybati 2022 (systematic review and meta-analysis, 41 RCTs, 3,948 patients): no ICU stay difference in any subtype; dexmedetomidine's delirium advantage was confined to cardiac surgery, and bradycardia was more frequent
cards.people: 41 randomised trials (3,948 patients) of dexmedetomidine versus propofol sedation in critically ill adults requiring mechanical ventilation, analysed separately for cardiac surgical, medical/noncardiac surgical, sepsis and neurocritical care patients; primary outcome ICU length of stay.
cards.result: Dexmedetomidine did not significantly affect ICU length of stay in any ICU patient subtype. It reduced duration of mechanical ventilation (mean difference −0.67 hours, 95% CI −1.31 to −0.03; P=0.041; low certainty) and ICU delirium (risk ratio 0.49 relative, 95% CI 0.29 to 0.87; P=0.019; high certainty) across cardiac surgical patients only. Dexmedetomidine was associated with a greater risk of bradycardia across a variety of ICU patients, and all-cause mortality did not differ.
cards.watchOut: Do not import the cardiac-surgery delirium result into sepsis care: the sepsis subgroup showed no such advantage, and MENDS2 — by far the largest sepsis-specific test — found delirium/coma-free days identical. The one consistent cross-subtype finding is more bradycardia with dexmedetomidine.

cards.headline: Synthesis: against propofol, dexmedetomidine changes nothing that matters in ventilated sepsis — LIKELY (the treatment made no difference), Tier C
cards.summary: Synthesis: against propofol, dexmedetomidine changes nothing that matters in ventilated sepsis — LIKELY (the treatment made no difference), Tier C
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: MENDS2 (422 analysed patients with sepsis), a 15-study sepsis-specific meta-analysis, and a 41-trial (3,948-patient) all-ICU meta-analysis.
cards.result: Delirium/coma-free days: 10.7 vs 10.8 in MENDS2. Ventilator-free days: 23.7 vs 24.0. Mortality: 38% vs 39% at 90 days in MENDS2 (hazard ratio 1.06 relative); pooled 28-day risk ratio 0.97 in sepsis studies. Cognition at 6 months: no difference. The only reproducible differential effect is more bradycardia with dexmedetomidine. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference), Tier C because mortality is co-reported.
cards.watchOut: The historical dexmedetomidine enthusiasm came from benzodiazepine comparators (lorazepam in MENDS, homed elsewhere in this library and not re-carded here). This shelf answers only the dexmedetomidine-versus-propofol question in sepsis.

shelves.title: Prolonged methylprednisolone in ARDS: early courses improved lung injury and ICU mortality in two small Meduri trials — LaSRS found late rescue did not reduce mortality (29.2% vs 28.6%) and harmed patients started after 14 days
shelves.question: In adults with ARDS, does a prolonged low-dose methylprednisolone course (started early, or late for unresolving ARDS) improve mortality and ventilator-free days versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Blood Glucose/analysis · Blood Pressure/drug effects · Combined Modality Therapy · Critical Illness · Double-Blind Method · Female · Glucocorticoids/adverse effects · Hospital Mortality · Humans · Inflammation/drug therapy · Injections, Intravenous · Male · Methylprednisolone/adverse effects · Middle Aged · Muscle Weakness/chemically induced · Oxygen/blood · Pneumonia/etiology · Respiration, Artificial · Respiratory Distress Syndrome/drug therapy · Shock, Septic/etiology · Survival Analysis · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: SPLIT by timing — POSSIBLE (benefit) for an early prolonged course; POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference), with a harm signal when started late, for rescue in persistent ARDS (Tier C, mortality co-reported): This shelf is the methylprednisolone slice only; dexamethasone in ARDS (DEXA-ARDS) is homed at pack #3002, which was read in full before building — it cards dexamethasone only, with no Meduri or methylprednisolone content. Early: Meduri's randomised trials of prolonged low-dose methylprednisolone found faster lung-injury resolution and shorter ventilation — in early severe ARDS (Meduri GU et al., PMID: 17426195; 91 patients), a 1-point lung injury score reduction by day 7 in 69.8% versus 35.7% and ICU mortality 20.6% versus 42.9%; in unresolving ARDS (PMID: 9669790; 24 patients), ICU mortality 0% versus 62%. Both trials are small and single-programme. Late: the ARDSNet LaSRS trial (Steinberg KP et al., PMID: 16625008; 180 patients with ARDS of at least 7 days) found 60-day hospital mortality of 29.2% on methylprednisolone versus 28.6% on placebo (P=1.0), more ventilator-free days and better physiology, more neuromuscular weakness, and significantly increased mortality when treatment was started at least 14 days after ARDS onset. The pre-LaSRS-era meta-analysis (Tang BM et al., PMID: 19325471) pooled a mortality relative risk of 0.51 in its four randomised trials (95% CI 0.24 to 1.09; P=0.08) — a trend built from the small Meduri-programme trials. PROPOSED: an early prolonged course is POSSIBLE (benefit) on small-trial evidence; routine late rescue is not supported, and starting at or beyond 14 days may kill.

cards.headline: Meduri 2007 (early severe ARDS, 91 patients): prolonged methylprednisolone infusion — lung injury score response by day 7 in 69.8% vs 35.7%, ICU mortality 20.6% vs 42.9%
cards.summary: Meduri 2007 (early severe ARDS, 91 patients): prolonged methylprednisolone infusion — lung injury score response by day 7 in 69.8% vs 35.7%, ICU mortality 20.6% vs 42.9%
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (Meduri 2007, early ARDS)
cards.people: 91 patients with severe early ARDS (within 72 hours), 66% with sepsis, in the ICUs of five Memphis hospitals, randomised 2:1 to methylprednisolone infusion 1 mg/kg/day (63 patients) or placebo (28), for up to 28 days, with protocolised infection surveillance and avoidance of paralysis.
cards.result: By day 7, twice the proportion of treated patients achieved the primary end point of a 1-point reduction in lung injury score (69.8% vs 35.7%; P=0.002) or were breathing without assistance (53.9% vs 25.0%; P=0.01). Treated patients had lower C-reactive protein, lung injury and organ dysfunction scores, shorter mechanical ventilation (P=0.002) and ICU stay (P=0.007), and lower ICU mortality (20.6% vs 42.9%; P=0.03), with a lower rate of infections (P=0.0002) under the trial's surveillance protocol.
cards.watchOut: Ninety-one patients from one investigative programme in one city, with a 2:1 allocation leaving only 28 controls — the 22-point ICU mortality difference rests on 12 deaths in the placebo arm. The infection-surveillance protocol was integral to the intervention and is not routine care everywhere.
cards.source: Meduri GU et al. Methylprednisolone infusion in early severe ARDS: results of a randomized controlled trial. Chest. 2007. PMID: 17426195. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Meduri 1998 (unresolving ARDS, 24 patients): prolonged methylprednisolone — ICU mortality 0% vs 62%, hospital mortality 12% vs 62%, in a very small trial (N = 24)
cards.summary: Meduri 1998 (unresolving ARDS, 24 patients): prolonged methylprednisolone — ICU mortality 0% vs 62%, hospital mortality 12% vs 62%, in a very small trial (N = 24)
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (Meduri 1998, unresolving ARDS) — N = 24
cards.people: 24 patients with severe ARDS who had failed to improve their lung injury score by day 7 of respiratory failure, in the medical ICUs of four centres; 16 received methylprednisolone (initially 2 mg/kg/day, 32 days of treatment) and 8 placebo; four non-responders were blindly crossed over to the alternative treatment after 10 days. N = 24, printed on the face.
cards.result: By study day 10, the methylprednisolone group had a lower lung injury score (mean 1.7 vs 3.0; P<.001), a higher PaO2/FiO2 ratio (262 vs 148; P<.001), a lower organ dysfunction score (0.7 vs 1.8; P<.001) and more successful extubations (7 vs 0; P=.05). ICU mortality was 0 of 16 versus 5 of 8 (P=.002) and hospital mortality 2 of 16 (12%) versus 5 of 8 (62%) (P=.03). Infection rates per day of treatment were similar.
cards.watchOut: Twenty-four patients, eight of them controls, with blinded crossover of non-responders: the dramatic mortality split (0% vs 62% ICU) is exactly the size of effect small trials produce and large trials shrink — and the larger LaSRS trial of the same late-ARDS strategy (next card) found no mortality benefit at all.

cards.headline: LaSRS 2006 (persistent ARDS, 180 patients): methylprednisolone did not reduce 60-day mortality (29.2% vs 28.6%) — and starting at or after 14 days increased mortality
cards.summary: LaSRS 2006 (persistent ARDS, 180 patients): methylprednisolone did not reduce 60-day mortality (29.2% vs 28.6%) — and starting at or after 14 days increased mortality
cards.type: Multicentre randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (LaSRS, Steinberg 2006)
cards.people: 180 patients with ARDS of at least 7 days' duration in the ARDSNet Late Steroid Rescue Study, randomly assigned double-blind to methylprednisolone or placebo; primary end point mortality at 60 days.
cards.result: Hospital mortality at 60 days was 29.2% on methylprednisolone versus 28.6% on placebo (P=1.0), and at 180 days 31.5% versus 31.9% (P=1.0) — the treatment made no difference to survival. Methylprednisolone increased ventilator-free and shock-free days in the first 28 days and improved oxygenation, compliance and blood pressure, but was associated with significantly increased 60- and 180-day mortality among patients enrolled at least 14 days after ARDS onset, did not increase infectious complications, and was associated with a higher rate of neuromuscular weakness.
cards.watchOut: The ventilator-free-day gain alongside flat mortality is the classic dissociation of this literature: physiology and weaning improve while survival does not. The after-14-days mortality increase is a subgroup finding, but it is the trial's own prespecified safety message and the reason late rescue cannot be presented as benign.
cards.source: Steinberg KP et al. Efficacy and safety of corticosteroids for persistent acute respiratory distress syndrome. N Engl J Med. 2006. PMID: 16625008. cards.headline: Tang 2009 (systematic review and meta-analysis): prolonged low-dose corticosteroids in ALI/ARDS — randomised-trial mortality relative risk 0.51 (95% CI 0.24 to 1.09), significant heterogeneity
cards.summary: Tang 2009 (systematic review and meta-analysis): prolonged low-dose corticosteroids in ALI/ARDS — randomised-trial mortality relative risk 0.51 (95% CI 0.24 to 1.09), significant heterogeneity
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis, 4 RCTs and 5 cohort studies (Tang 2009)
cards.people: Randomised trials (four trials, 341 patients) and cohort studies (five studies, 307 patients) of prolonged corticosteroids at 0.5–2.5 mg/kg/day methylprednisolone equivalent in acute lung injury or ARDS, published before the later dexamethasone era.
cards.result: Both designs trended toward mortality reduction without reaching significance on their own (RCTs relative risk 0.51 relative, 95% CI 0.24 to 1.09; P=0.08; cohorts relative risk 0.66 relative, 95% CI 0.43 to 1.02; P=0.06); the combined relative risk was 0.62 (95% CI 0.43 to 0.91; P=0.01). Ventilation-free days, ICU stay, organ dysfunction and lung injury scores and PaO2/FiO2 improved, with no increase in infection, neuromyopathy or major complications reported — but there was significant heterogeneity among the pooled studies, and the reviewers state the early-ARDS mortality benefit should be confirmed by an adequately powered trial.
cards.watchOut: This pool predates and cannot contain the larger later trials; its randomised base (341 patients) is dominated by the small Meduri-programme trials carded above, so it corroborates their direction without adding independent weight. It pools methylprednisolone-equivalent regimens, not dexamethasone — that drug's ARDS shelf is pack #3002.

cards.headline: Synthesis: timing decides — early prolonged methylprednisolone is POSSIBLE (benefit) on small trials; late rescue is POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) with a post-14-day harm signal
cards.summary: Synthesis: timing decides — early prolonged methylprednisolone is POSSIBLE (benefit) on small trials; late rescue is POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) with a post-14-day harm signal
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: two small Meduri-programme randomised trials (91 early, 24 unresolving patients), the 180-patient ARDSNet LaSRS trial, and a 2009 meta-analysis (4 RCTs, 341 patients).
cards.result: Early: lung injury score response 69.8% vs 35.7% and ICU mortality 20.6% vs 42.9% (91 patients). Unresolving, small: ICU mortality 0% vs 62% (24 patients). Late, adequately sized: 60-day mortality 29.2% vs 28.6% (the treatment made no difference), more ventilator-free days, more neuromuscular weakness, and increased mortality when started at or after 14 days. shelves.title: CytoSorb in septic shock: the cartridge removes IL-6 (5–18% per pass) but plasma levels, organ failure and mortality did not improve in randomised trials — survival benefit unproven
shelves.question: In adults with septic shock, does cytokine haemoadsorption (CytoSorb) reduce vasopressor requirements, organ failure or mortality versus standard care?
shelves.mesh: Cardiac Surgical Procedures/adverse effects · Cytokines · Endocarditis/surgery · Endocarditis, Bacterial · Humans · Multiple Organ Failure · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — the device removes cytokines from blood passing through it, and no randomised trial has shown that this improves organ function, vasopressor requirements or survival; a mortality benefit is unproven and must not be claimed (Tier C, mortality co-reported): The tested product is CytoSorb (CytoSorbents Corporation), a haemoadsorption cartridge — named here under the tested-product clarification exception because adsorption devices differ by maker. In septic patients with respiratory failure (Schädler D et al., PMID: 29084247; 97 analysed), CytoSorb removed interleukin-6 at 5–18% per blood pass yet systemic plasma IL-6 did not fall versus control (P=0.15), organ dysfunction, ventilation time and oxygenation did not differ, and unadjusted 60-day mortality was higher on treatment (44.7% vs 26.0%; P=0.039), a difference the authors attribute to baseline imbalance after adjustment (P=0.19). In the REMOVE trial (Diab M et al., PMID: 35213213; 288 patients having cardiac surgery for infective endocarditis), adding CytoSorb to the bypass circuit lowered some cytokines but changed neither the primary organ-dysfunction outcome (ΔSOFA 1.79 vs 1.93; P=0.68) nor 30-day mortality (21% vs 22%). The systematic review of sepsis use (Saldaña-Gastulo JJC et al., PMID: 37712812; 6 studies, 413 patients) found no mortality effect at 28–30 days and graded the certainty very low. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): cytokine clearance is a laboratory fact; patient benefit is not demonstrated.

cards.headline: Schädler 2017 (RCT, 97 patients with sepsis and respiratory failure): CytoSorb removed IL-6 per pass but plasma IL-6 did not fall (P=0.15); unadjusted 60-day mortality was higher on treatment (44.7% vs 26.0%)
cards.summary: Schädler 2017 (RCT, 97 patients with sepsis and respiratory failure): CytoSorb removed IL-6 per pass but plasma IL-6 did not fall (P=0.15); unadjusted 60-day mortality was higher on treatment (44.7% vs 26.0%)
cards.people: 100 patients were randomised and 97 analysed — mechanically ventilated patients with severe sepsis or septic shock and acute lung injury or ARDS in a multicentre open-label trial; CytoSorb haemoperfusion (CytoSorbents) for 6 hours per day for up to 7 days versus no haemoperfusion; primary outcome was change in normalised IL-6 concentrations over days 1–7.
cards.result: Significant IL-6 elimination averaging 5–18% per blood pass was recorded throughout treatment, but systemic plasma IL-6 levels did not differ between groups (n=75; P=0.15). There were no statistically significant differences in organ dysfunction score, ventilation time or oxygenation. Unadjusted 60-day mortality was significantly higher in the treatment group (44.7%) than the control group (26.0%; P=0.039); the treatment group had more renal replacement therapy at enrolment (31.9% vs 16.3%), and after adjustment for morbidity and baseline imbalances no association of haemoperfusion with mortality was found (P=0.19).
cards.watchOut: Open-label with a sicker treatment arm at baseline (twice the renal-replacement rate), so neither the unadjusted mortality excess nor its disappearance after adjustment can bear much weight. The central lesson is mechanistic: clearing a cytokine from blood in the cartridge is not the same as lowering its level in the patient.
cards.source: Schädler D et al. The effect of a novel extracorporeal cytokine hemoadsorption device on IL-6 elimination in septic patients: A randomized controlled trial. PLoS One. 2017. cards.headline: REMOVE 2022 (RCT, 288 patients, endocarditis surgery): intraoperative CytoSorb did not reduce organ dysfunction (ΔSOFA 1.79 vs 1.93; P=0.68) or 30-day mortality (21% vs 22%)
cards.summary: REMOVE 2022 (RCT, 288 patients, endocarditis surgery): intraoperative CytoSorb did not reduce organ dysfunction (ΔSOFA 1.79 vs 1.93; P=0.68) or 30-day mortality (21% vs 22%)
cards.people: 288 patients undergoing cardiac surgery for infective endocarditis in a multicentre randomised nonblinded trial, assigned to haemoadsorption with CytoSorb (CytoSorbents) integrated into cardiopulmonary bypass (142) or control (146); 282 underwent surgery and were analysed by modified intention to treat; primary outcome was change in Sequential Organ Failure Assessment score (ΔSOFA) to postoperative day 9.
cards.result: The primary outcome did not differ between groups (ΔSOFA 1.79 ± 3.75 with haemoadsorption vs 1.93 ± 3.53 control; 95% CI for the difference −1.30 to 0.83; P=0.6766). Mortality at 30 days (21% vs 22%; P=0.782), duration of mechanical ventilation, and vasopressor and renal replacement therapy did not differ. Interleukin-1β and interleukin-18 levels at the end of bypass were significantly lower with haemoadsorption. The authors conclude the trial failed to demonstrate a reduction in postoperative organ dysfunction.
cards.watchOut: REMOVE is a surgical endocarditis population with a single intraoperative treatment during bypass, not days of therapy in medical septic shock — it tests the device in its most favourable, highest-cytokine-release setting and still found nothing. Nonblinded, though its outcomes are objective scores and mortality.
cards.source: Diab M et al. Cytokine Hemoadsorption During Cardiac Surgery Versus Standard Surgical Care for Infective Endocarditis (REMOVE): Results From a Multicenter Randomized Controlled Trial. Circulation. 2022. PMID: 35213213. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03266302, from the record's databank fields. cards.headline: Saldaña-Gastulo 2023 (systematic review and meta-analysis, 6 studies, 413 patients): no mortality effect of CytoSorb in sepsis at 28–30 days — very low certainty evidence
cards.summary: Saldaña-Gastulo 2023 (systematic review and meta-analysis, 6 studies, 413 patients): no mortality effect of CytoSorb in sepsis at 28–30 days — very low certainty evidence
cards.people: Six studies (413 patients) — randomised trials and cohort studies of CytoSorb (CytoSorbents) haemoadsorption in patients with sepsis, searched in MEDLINE, Embase and the Cochrane Library; primary outcome mortality.
cards.result: The overall mortality rate was 45%, and no significant effect on mortality was found at 28–30 days (risk ratio 0.98 relative, 95% CI 0.12 to 8.25, for the randomised trial; risk ratio 0.74 relative, 95% CI 0.49 to 1.13, for cohort studies). Meta-analysis of other outcomes was not possible for lack of data. The reviewers grade the evidence very low certainty (imprecision, risk of bias, heterogeneity), conclude there is no demonstrated benefit, and state they cannot recommend CytoSorb use in septic or septic shock patients outside clinical trials.
cards.watchOut: Only one randomised trial sits inside this pool, with a confidence interval (0.12 to 8.25) wide enough to contain almost anything; the cohort estimate is the kind of data that flatters devices. Later meta-analyses that report lower mortality with CytoSorb rest on the same observational base and do not change the randomised picture carded here.
cards.source: Saldaña-Gastulo JJC et al. Cytokine hemoadsorption with CytoSorb® in patients with sepsis: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Crit Care Sci. 2023. PMID: 37712812. shelves.title: Inhaled epoprostenol versus inhaled nitric oxide in ARDS: near-identical oxygenation gains in small crossover trials (PaO2/FiO2 +21 vs +29 mmHg) — no mortality data exist for the comparison
shelves.question: In adults with ARDS and refractory hypoxaemia, does inhaled epoprostenol improve oxygenation as effectively as inhaled nitric oxide — and does either change mortality?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Inhalation · Adult · Aerosols · Aged · Blood Pressure/drug effects · Epoprostenol/therapeutic use · Female · Hemodynamics/drug effects · Humans · Lung/blood supply · Male · Middle Aged · Nitric Oxide/therapeutic use · Oxygen/blood · Oxygen Consumption/drug effects · Pulmonary Artery · Pulmonary Circulation/drug effects · Pulmonary Gas Exchange/drug effects · Respiration, Artificial · Respiratory Distress Syndrome/drug therapy · Respiratory System Agents/therapeutic use · Vasodilator Agents/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — on acute oxygenation the two inhaled vasodilators look equivalent in tiny crossover physiology trials; on mortality and every patient-important outcome there are no comparative data at all (Tier C): In the direct randomised crossover comparison (Walmrath D et al., PMID: 8630585; 16 patients with ARDS), individually titrated inhaled nitric oxide (mean 17.8 ppm) raised PaO2/FiO2 from 115 to 144 mmHg and aerosolised prostacyclin (epoprostenol; mean 7.5 ng/kg/min) from 114 to 135 mmHg, with shunt falling by about 7 points on each and near-identical efficacy profiles. A dose-response crossover study (Zwissler B et al., PMID: 8970353) found the same pattern — both agents selectively lowered pulmonary artery pressure and raised PaO2/FiO2 — in a record that does not report its patient number. A later three-way crossover pilot (Albert M et al., PMID: 28224110; 15 patients) found median PaO2 rises of 8.8 mmHg on nitric oxide and 6.0 mmHg on epoprostenol, with only nitric oxide reaching significance in that small sample. Each drug's effect against control is homed separately — inhaled nitric oxide at live #1323 (oxygenation improves briefly, outcomes do not) and inhaled prostacyclin at pack #3172 (a negative multicentre trial against placebo) — and neither home is re-carded here. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): epoprostenol is a physiologically credible, cheaper substitute for nitric oxide for short-term oxygenation rescue; equivalence on survival is unknown, not established.

cards.headline: Walmrath 1996 (randomised crossover, 16 ARDS patients): inhaled nitric oxide raised PaO2/FiO2 115 → 144 mmHg and aerosolised prostacyclin 114 → 135 mmHg — nearly identical efficacy profiles
cards.summary: Walmrath 1996 (randomised crossover, 16 ARDS patients): inhaled nitric oxide raised PaO2/FiO2 115 → 144 mmHg and aerosolised prostacyclin 114 → 135 mmHg — nearly identical efficacy profiles
cards.people: 16 mechanically ventilated patients with ARDS (mean lung injury score 2.75), randomised to receive first inhaled nitric oxide then aerosolised prostacyclin (epoprostenol), or vice versa; each drug was individually titrated for maximum improvement in arterial oxygenation, with gas exchange measured including the multiple inert gas elimination technique.
cards.result: Inhaled nitric oxide (17.8 ± 2.7 ppm) increased PaO2/FiO2 from 115 ± 12 to 144 ± 15 mmHg (P<0.01) and reduced shunt flow from 33.1% to 26.6% (P<0.05). Aerosolised prostacyclin (7.5 ± 2.5 ng/kg/min) augmented PaO2/FiO2 from 114 ± 12 to 135 ± 12 mmHg (P<0.01) and decreased shunt from 33.5% to 26.0% (P<0.05). In 10 patients both agents raised PaO2/FiO2 by at least 10 mmHg; two further patients responded to one agent only. Nitric oxide lowered mean pulmonary artery pressure from 34.8 to 33.0 mmHg and prostacyclin from 35.0 to 31.9 mmHg (P<0.05). The authors conclude the two have nearly identical efficacy profiles. No mortality or ventilation-duration outcomes were studied.
cards.watchOut: A 16-patient, single-session physiology study from 1996: it compares oxygenation over minutes to hours, in an era of non-protective ventilation, and says nothing about survival, ventilation days or harm. Titrated-to-best-dose designs also flatter both drugs equally, which is the point of the comparison but limits any absolute claim.
cards.source: Walmrath D et al. Direct comparison of inhaled nitric oxide and aerosolized prostacyclin in acute respiratory distress syndrome. Am J Respir Crit Care Med. 1996. PMID: 8630585. cards.headline: Zwissler 1996 (dose-response crossover): inhaled prostacyclin lowered pulmonary artery pressure dose-dependently (35.1 → 29.6 mmHg) and raised PaO2/FiO2 to 131 mmHg, matching nitric oxide (patient number not reported in the record)
cards.summary: Zwissler 1996 (dose-response crossover): inhaled prostacyclin lowered pulmonary artery pressure dose-dependently (35.1 → 29.6 mmHg) and raised PaO2/FiO2 to 131 mmHg, matching nitric oxide (patient number not reported in the record)
cards.type: Dose-response crossover comparison (Zwissler 1996) — N not documented in the record
cards.people: Patients with adult respiratory distress syndrome receiving, in crossover fashion, inhaled prostacyclin (epoprostenol) at 1, 10 and 25 ng/kg/min and inhaled nitric oxide at 1, 4 and 8 ppm, with cardiorespiratory measurements at control, at each dose and after withdrawal. The record does not report the number of patients — N not documented in the record.
cards.result: Prostacyclin produced a dose-dependent selective fall in pulmonary artery pressure, from 35.1 ± 6.3 mmHg at control to 29.6 ± 4.5 mmHg at 25 ng/kg/min, and raised PaO2/FiO2 from 105 ± 37 to 125 ± 56 mmHg at 10 ng/kg/min and 131 ± 63 mmHg at 25 ng/kg/min, with no effect at 1 ng/kg/min. Nitric oxide reduced pulmonary artery pressure from 34.5 ± 5.6 to 31.8 ± 6.1 mmHg at 8 ppm (no effect at 1 ppm), improved PaO2 (116 ± 47 to 167 ± 86 mmHg at 8 ppm) and reduced intrapulmonary shunt at all doses tested. The authors conclude both compounds induce selective pulmonary vasodilation and increase PaO2 in severe ARDS.
cards.watchOut: The patient number is not printed in the record, so this card carries no N — treat it as a small physiology study by design (dose-response crossovers of this era enrolled handfuls of patients). Inter-individual responses ranged widely, including patients whose oxygenation fell on prostacyclin (range −5 to +89 mmHg at the top dose).
cards.source: Zwissler B et al. Inhaled prostacyclin (PGI2) versus inhaled nitric oxide in adult respiratory distress syndrome. Am J Respir Crit Care Med. 1996. PMID: 8970353. cards.headline: Albert 2017 (crossover pilot, 15 ARDS patients): median PaO2 rise 8.8 mmHg on nitric oxide vs 6.0 mmHg on epoprostenol — only nitric oxide's rise was significant in this small sample
cards.summary: Albert 2017 (crossover pilot, 15 ARDS patients): median PaO2 rise 8.8 mmHg on nitric oxide vs 6.0 mmHg on epoprostenol — only nitric oxide's rise was significant in this small sample
cards.people: 15 adult patients with ARDS and hypoxaemic failure monitored with a pulmonary artery catheter in a single academic ICU, in an open-label prospective crossover pilot; random sequential administration of inhaled nitric oxide (20 ppm) or nebulised epoprostenol (10 μg/mL), followed by inhaled milrinone arms that are outside this shelf's question.
cards.result: Neither agent affected systemic haemodynamics and no significant drug-related adverse events were observed. The median increase in PaO2 from baseline was 8.8 mmHg (IQR 16.3) with inhaled nitric oxide and 6.0 mmHg (IQR 18.4) with epoprostenol; only nitric oxide (and the milrinone–nitric oxide combination) had a statistically significant effect on PaO2 in this sample. No mortality or ventilation outcomes were studied.
cards.watchOut: Fifteen patients and a fixed (not titrated) epoprostenol concentration: the non-significant epoprostenol result may reflect dose and power rather than inferiority, and the study's primary interest was milrinone. It is carded as the only modern-era head-to-head, not as a verdict.
cards.source: Albert M et al. Comparison of inhaled milrinone, nitric oxide and prostacyclin in acute respiratory distress syndrome. World J Crit Care Med. 2017. PMID: 28224110. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.result: PaO2/FiO2 gains were of the same order for both drugs in the titrated comparison (+29 mmHg nitric oxide, +21 mmHg prostacyclin) and pulmonary artery pressure fell selectively with both. shelves.title: Enteral omega-3 (EPA/GLA) in ARDS: early trials pooled a mortality odds ratio of 0.40 — then OMEGA was stopped for futility with fewer ventilator-free days (14.0 vs 17.2) and mortality trending the wrong way
shelves.question: In adults with ARDS, does enteral omega-3 fatty-acid supplementation (EPA/GLA/antioxidants) improve ventilator-free days or mortality versus standard enteral feeding?
shelves.mesh: Acute Lung Injury/complications · Adult · Aged · Antioxidants/adverse effects · Biomarkers/blood · Dietary Supplements/adverse effects · Docosahexaenoic Acids/adverse effects · Double-Blind Method · Drug Therapy, Combination · Eicosapentaenoic Acid/adverse effects · Enteral Nutrition · Female · Humans · Inflammation/drug therapy · Intensive Care Units/statistics & numerical data · Male · Middle Aged · Pneumonia/complications · Sepsis/complications · Survival Analysis · Treatment Outcome · Ventilator Weaning · gamma-Linolenic Acid/adverse effects
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (harm) — the early small trials promised benefit; the one large rigorous trial found the supplement cost ventilator-free days and trended toward more deaths, and was stopped for futility (Tier C, mortality co-reported): The conflict is structural. A 2008 meta-analysis of the three early trials (Pontes-Arruda A et al., PMID: 18974237; 411 patients) pooled a mortality odds ratio of 0.40 (95% CI 0.24 to 0.68) for enteral eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA) plus gamma-linolenic acid (GLA) plus antioxidants, and a single-centre Brazilian trial in severe sepsis (PMID: 16850002; 165 patients) reported a 19.4-point absolute mortality reduction. Then the ARDSNet OMEGA trial (Rice TW et al., PMID: 21976613; 272 patients with acute lung injury) gave twice-daily EPA/GLA/antioxidant supplement separately from the feed and found fewer ventilator-free days (14.0 vs 17.2; P=.02), fewer ICU-free and organ-failure-free days, more diarrhoea (29% vs 21%), and 60-day hospital mortality of 26.6% versus 16.3% (P=.054; adjusted 25.1% vs 17.6%, P=.11) before stopping early for futility — despite an 8-fold rise in plasma EPA proving delivery. The earliest ARDS trial of the formula family (Gadek 1999) is homed at live #16 in this library and is not re-carded here; its positive results are inside the 2008 pooled estimate carded below. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm): as tested in OMEGA, enteral omega-3/GLA/antioxidant supplementation in ARDS should not be given expecting benefit, and may harm.

cards.headline: OMEGA 2011 (ARDSNet RCT, 272 patients, stopped for futility): omega-3/GLA/antioxidant supplement gave fewer ventilator-free days (14.0 vs 17.2; P=.02) and 60-day mortality 26.6% vs 16.3% (P=.054)
cards.summary: OMEGA 2011 (ARDSNet RCT, 272 patients, stopped for futility): omega-3/GLA/antioxidant supplement gave fewer ventilator-free days (14.0 vs 17.2; P=.02) and 60-day mortality 26.6% vs 16.3% (P=.054)
cards.type: Multicentre randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (OMEGA, Rice 2011)
cards.people: 272 adults within 48 hours of developing acute lung injury requiring mechanical ventilation, at 44 ARDSNet hospitals, randomised double-blind to twice-daily enteral supplementation with omega-3 fatty acids (eicosapentaenoic and docosahexaenoic acid), gamma-linolenic acid and antioxidants (143) or an isocaloric control (129), with protocol enteral nutrition delivered separately; all participants had complete follow-up.
cards.result: The trial was stopped early for futility. Despite an 8-fold increase in plasma eicosapentaenoic acid levels, the supplement group had fewer ventilator-free days to day 28 (14.0 vs 17.2; difference −3.2 days, 95% CI −5.8 to −0.7; P=.02), fewer ICU-free days (14.0 vs 16.7; P=.04) and fewer nonpulmonary organ failure-free days (12.3 vs 15.5; P=.02). Sixty-day hospital mortality was 26.6% versus 16.3% (P=.054), and adjusted 60-day mortality 25.1% versus 17.6% (P=.11). Days with diarrhoea were more frequent on the supplement (29% vs 21%; P=.001). The authors conclude the supplement did not improve the primary end point or other clinical outcomes and may be harmful.
cards.watchOut: OMEGA gave the lipids as a twice-daily bolus supplement on top of standard feeding, whereas the earlier positive trials used a continuously fed EPA/GLA formula as the feed itself — defenders of the formula argue the delivery differed. That caveat explains a null; it does not explain away fewer ventilator-free days and a mortality trend in the wrong direction, and no later large trial has rehabilitated the approach.
cards.source: Rice TW et al. Enteral omega-3 fatty acid, gamma-linolenic acid, and antioxidant supplementation in acute lung injury. JAMA. 2011. PMID: 21976613. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00609180, from the record's databank fields. cards.headline: Pontes-Arruda 2006 (single-country RCT, 165 patients with severe sepsis/septic shock): EPA/GLA/antioxidant feed — absolute mortality reduction 19.4 points (P=.037), ventilator-free days 13.4 vs 5.8
cards.summary: Pontes-Arruda 2006 (single-country RCT, 165 patients with severe sepsis/septic shock): EPA/GLA/antioxidant feed — absolute mortality reduction 19.4 points (P=.037), ventilator-free days 13.4 vs 5.8
cards.type: Randomised double-blind controlled trial (Pontes-Arruda 2006, severe sepsis)
cards.people: 165 patients with severe sepsis or septic shock requiring mechanical ventilation, in three ICUs of a tertiary hospital in Brazil, randomised double-blind to continuous tube feeding with an EPA, GLA and elevated-antioxidant diet or an isonitrogenous, isocaloric control diet for at least 4 days, monitored for 28 days.
cards.result: The study diet was associated with a significant reduction in 28-day all-cause mortality, an absolute reduction of 19.4% (P=.037; the record does not print the two group rates), more ventilator-free days (13.4 ± 1.2 vs 5.8 ± 1.0; P<.001), more ICU-free days (10.8 ± 1.1 vs 4.6 ± 0.9; P<.001), improved oxygenation and less development of new organ dysfunction (P<.001).
cards.watchOut: This is a sepsis trial, not a pure ARDS trial — its patients were ventilated with severe sepsis or septic shock, the population in which the formula was most often advocated. A 19.4-point absolute mortality reduction from a 165-patient, three-unit, single-country trial is implausibly large next to OMEGA's opposite result, and the record does not even print the arm-specific mortality rates behind it.
cards.source: Pontes-Arruda A et al. Effects of enteral feeding with eicosapentaenoic acid, gamma-linolenic acid, and antioxidants in mechanically ventilated patients with severe sepsis and septic shock. Crit Care Med. 2006. cards.headline: Pontes-Arruda 2008 (meta-analysis of the 3 early RCTs, 411 patients with ALI/ARDS): mortality odds ratio 0.40 (95% CI 0.24 to 0.68) for EPA+GLA feeding — the pre-OMEGA consensus OMEGA then overturned
cards.summary: Pontes-Arruda 2008 (meta-analysis of the 3 early RCTs, 411 patients with ALI/ARDS): mortality odds ratio 0.40 (95% CI 0.24 to 0.68) for EPA+GLA feeding — the pre-OMEGA consensus OMEGA then overturned
cards.people: Three randomised controlled studies (411 patients) of an inflammation-modulating enteral diet enriched with EPA, GLA and elevated antioxidants versus a control diet in mechanically ventilated patients with acute lung injury or ARDS, identified from MEDLINE, EMBASE, the Cochrane register and trial databases.
cards.result: The pooled analysis found a significant reduction in mortality risk (odds ratio 0.40 relative, 95% CI 0.24 to 0.68; P=.001), a reduced risk of new organ failures (odds ratio 0.17 relative, 95% CI 0.08 to 0.34; P<.0001), and standardised improvements in time on mechanical ventilation (SMD 0.56; P<.0001) and ICU stay (SMD 0.51; P<.0001), with improved oxygenation. The reviewers conclude EPA+GLA significantly reduced mortality and improved clinical outcomes.
cards.watchOut: A meta-analysis is only its trials: three small studies, one investigative lineage prominent among them, pooled before any large independent test existed. When OMEGA (272 patients, 44 centres) reported, it alone outweighed this pool in rigour and pointed the other way — the standing lesson of this shelf is that pooled small-trial mortality odds ratios of 0.40 in critical care nutrition do not survive large trials.
cards.source: Pontes-Arruda A et al. The use of an inflammation-modulating diet in patients with acute lung injury or acute respiratory distress syndrome: a meta-analysis of outcome data. JPEN J Parenter Enteral Nutr. 2008. PMID: 18974237. Registry ID: none in the record. shelves.title: Driving pressure in ARDS: tidal volume per unit of remaining lung — a 1-SD rise (~7 cm H2O) carried a relative mortality risk of 1.41 in 3,562 trial patients; as a titration target it is still untested
shelves.question: In ventilated adults with ARDS, what is driving pressure (plateau pressure minus PEEP), how does it relate to survival compared with tidal volume and PEEP individually, and what human data support targeting it?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Lung/anatomy & histology · Lung Compliance · Multivariate Analysis · Positive-Pressure Respiration/methods · Pressure · Prognosis · Proportional Hazards Models · Respiratory Distress Syndrome/mortality · Risk · Tidal Volume
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING (textbook framing: Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology and Boron & Boulpaep Medical Physiology, which present transpulmonary stress as pressure applied per unit of aerated lung — the 'baby lung' concept in textbook form): Driving pressure (ΔP) is plateau pressure minus PEEP, equivalently tidal volume divided by respiratory-system compliance, so it expresses the tidal volume in units of the size of lung actually available to receive it. The human evidence that it tracks survival better than its components is consistent but entirely observational or re-analytic. In the anchor mediation analysis of individual data from 3,562 ARDS patients in nine randomised trials (Amato MBP et al., PMID: 25693014), ΔP was the ventilation variable most strongly associated with survival: a 1-standard-deviation increment (about 7 cm H2O) carried a relative risk of death of 1.41 (95% CI 1.31 to 1.51), and changes in tidal volume or PEEP were associated with survival only insofar as they changed ΔP (mediation P=0.004 and P=0.001). Prospective-style cohort data agree in direction: during assisted ventilation, higher ΔP independently predicted ICU death (odds ratio 1.34 per cm H2O; Bellani G et al., PMID: 31335543), and a derivation-validation analysis found risk rising above a ΔP of about 19 cm H2O — while also finding plateau pressure a slightly better predictor than ΔP (Villar J et al., PMID: 28252536), a genuine counterweight. No randomised trial has tested a driving-pressure-targeted strategy, so the association cannot yet be read as a treatment target. PROPOSED PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING: the definition and the risk gradient are settled human physiology; the claim that titrating ventilation to ΔP improves survival is unproven.

cards.headline: Amato 2015 (mediation analysis, 3,562 patients, 9 RCTs): driving pressure was the variable most strongly tied to survival — relative risk 1.41 per ~7 cm H2O increment, even under protective settings
cards.summary: Amato 2015 (mediation analysis, 3,562 patients, 9 RCTs): driving pressure was the variable most strongly tied to survival — relative risk 1.41 per ~7 cm H2O increment, even under protective settings
cards.type: Mediation analysis of pooled individual trial data (Amato 2015)
cards.people: Individual data from 3,562 patients with ARDS enrolled in nine previously reported randomised trials of ventilation strategy, re-analysed with multilevel mediation analysis to isolate the effects of post-randomisation changes in driving pressure (ΔP = tidal volume / respiratory-system compliance) from baseline lung-disease severity; patients were not actively breathing.
cards.result: Among ventilation variables, ΔP was most strongly associated with survival. A 1-standard-deviation increment in ΔP (approximately 7 cm H2O) was associated with increased mortality (relative risk 1.41 relative, 95% CI 1.31 to 1.51; P<0.001), including in patients receiving 'protective' plateau pressures and tidal volumes (relative risk 1.36 relative, 95% CI 1.17 to 1.58; P<0.001). Individual changes in tidal volume or PEEP after randomisation were not independently associated with survival; they were associated only when they led to reductions in ΔP (mediation effects of ΔP, P=0.004 for tidal volume and P=0.001 for PEEP).
cards.watchOut: Mediation analysis of trials randomised on other variables is sophisticated observational inference, not a randomised test of driving pressure: sicker, stiffer lungs generate higher ΔP at any setting, and the analysis minimises — it cannot abolish — that confounding by severity. It shows ΔP stratifies risk and mediates other variables' effects; it does not show that forcing ΔP down saves lives.
cards.source: Amato MBP et al. Driving pressure and survival in the acute respiratory distress syndrome. N Engl J Med. 2015. PMID: 25693014. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Bellani 2019 (cohort, 154 ARDS patients on assisted ventilation): driving pressure measurable on pressure support and independently tied to ICU death (odds ratio 1.34 per cm H2O)
cards.summary: Bellani 2019 (cohort, 154 ARDS patients on assisted ventilation): driving pressure measurable on pressure support and independently tied to ICU death (odds ratio 1.34 per cm H2O)
cards.people: 154 adults with ARDS in a retrospective cohort in whom plateau pressure during the first three days of assisted (pressure support) ventilation was available; respiratory-system compliance was compared with aerated lung volume on CT in the 23 patients scanned during assisted ventilation.
cards.result: Driving pressure and compliance could be reliably measured during pressure support in the majority of patients. Nonsurvivors had higher driving pressure (11 [9–14] vs 10 [8–11] cm H2O; P=0.004) and lower compliance (40 [30–50] vs 51 [42–61] mL/cm H2O; P<0.001) than survivors, at similar peak pressures. Higher driving pressure (odds ratio 1.34, 95% CI 1.12 to 1.61) and lower compliance (odds ratio 0.92, 95% CI 0.88 to 0.96) were each independently associated with ICU death. Compliance correlated with aerated lung volume (n=23; r=0.69; P<0.0001), supporting the functional-lung-size interpretation of ΔP.
cards.watchOut: Retrospective, single-question cohort of 154 patients selected by having a plateau pressure recorded on pressure support — a measurement many units never make, so selection is real. The absolute ΔP separation between survivors and nonsurvivors is 1 cm H2O at the median; the per-unit odds ratio should not be read as a bedside threshold.
cards.source: Bellani G et al. Driving Pressure Is Associated with Outcome during Assisted Ventilation in Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome. Anesthesiology. 2019. PMID: 31335543. cards.headline: Villar 2017 (derivation 478 + validation 300 patients): mortality risk rose above driving pressure ~19 cm H2O — but plateau pressure predicted death slightly better than driving pressure
cards.summary: Villar 2017 (derivation 478 + validation 300 patients): mortality risk rose above driving pressure ~19 cm H2O — but plateau pressure predicted death slightly better than driving pressure
cards.type: Secondary analysis of observational cohorts with validation cohort (Villar 2017)
cards.people: 778 patients with moderate-to-severe ARDS managed with standardised lung-protective ventilation in a network of ICUs, with tidal volume, PEEP, plateau pressure and driving pressure assessed at 24 hours after ARDS diagnosis; the prediction model was derived in 478 patients and tested for replicability in a separate cohort of 300.
cards.result: Tidal volume and PEEP had no impact on mortality. A plateau pressure cut-off of 29 cm H2O and a driving pressure cut-off of 19 cm H2O were identified, above which each ordinal increment was accompanied by an increment in risk of hospital death. When the two were cross-tabulated, plateau pressure provided a slightly better prediction of outcome than driving pressure in both the derivation and validation cohorts (P<0.0000001 as printed).
cards.watchOut: This is the honest counterweight inside the driving-pressure literature: under standardised settings at 24 hours, the simpler plateau pressure did at least as well. Cut-offs derived by quantile analysis (19 cm H2O here, versus the ~15 cm H2O often quoted from Amato) are data-dependent and should be treated as risk gradients, not safe/unsafe boundaries.
cards.source: Villar J et al. A Quantile Analysis of Plateau and Driving Pressures: Effects on Mortality in Patients With Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome Receiving Lung-Protective Ventilation. Crit Care Med. 2017. PMID: 28252536. Registry ID: none in the record.
