cards.headline: Synthesis: driving pressure stratifies ARDS mortality risk across every human dataset — as a target for titration it remains untested (PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING)
cards.summary: Synthesis: driving pressure stratifies ARDS mortality risk across every human dataset — as a target for titration it remains untested (PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING)
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: a 3,562-patient mediation analysis of nine trials, a 154-patient assisted-ventilation cohort, and a 778-patient derivation-validation analysis.
cards.result: Direction is uniform: higher ΔP, higher mortality (relative risk 1.41 per ~7 cm H2O in the mediation analysis; odds ratio 1.34 per cm H2O on assisted ventilation; risk rising above ~19 cm H2O in the cohort analysis). The mechanism is textbook-coherent — ΔP is tidal volume normalised to the aerated lung that remains. What no carded study provides is a randomised comparison of ΔP-targeted versus conventional titration. PROPOSED PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING, not ESTABLISHED, for exactly that reason.
cards.watchOut: Textbook framing (Guyton & Hall; Boron & Boulpaep) supplies the stress-per-unit-lung rationale only; every quantitative claim on this shelf comes from the carded human analyses, and all of them are observational in design even when their data began inside randomised trials.

shelves.title: Mechanical power: the ventilator's energy per minute — associated with death in 8,207 ICU patients (odds ratio ~1.06–1.10 per 5 J/min), yet no better a predictor than driving pressure plus rate in ARDS
shelves.question: In ventilated patients, what is mechanical power (the energy per minute delivered by the ventilator), and how does it relate to ventilator-induced lung injury and mortality in human data?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Airway Resistance/physiology · Case-Control Studies · Female · Humans · Logistic Models · Lung/physiopathology · Male · Middle Aged · Positive-Pressure Respiration/methods · Respiratory Distress Syndrome/therapy · Respiratory Mechanics/physiology · Tidal Volume/physiology · Ventilator-Induced Lung Injury/etiology · Ventilators, Mechanical/adverse effects
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING (textbook framing: Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology and Boron & Boulpaep Medical Physiology, which ground lung injury in the stress and strain energy applied to lung tissue each breath): Mechanical power is the energy the ventilator delivers to the respiratory system per minute — the per-breath energy (a function of tidal volume, driving pressure, flow and PEEP) multiplied by respiratory rate — proposed by Gattinoni's group as the single variable unifying the ventilator settings that cause ventilator-induced lung injury (VILI). The formulation paper (Gattinoni L et al., PMID: 27620287) showed the power computed from the equation of motion matched power measured from pressure-volume loops in 30 patients with normal lungs and 50 with ARDS (slopes 0.96–1.12, R²>0.96), and that power rises exponentially with tidal volume, driving pressure and flow and linearly with PEEP. The mortality association is human and consistent but observational: in 8,207 patients ventilated for at least 48 hours across two large databases (Serpa Neto A et al., PMID: 30291378), each 5 J/min increment in mechanical power carried an odds ratio for hospital death of 1.06–1.10, with risk rising consistently above about 17 J/min. The strongest counterweight is also carded: in 4,549 ARDS patients pooled from six trials and a cohort (Costa ELV et al., PMID: 33784486), mechanical power predicted mortality, but a simpler model using only driving pressure and respiratory rate was equivalent — power added no predictive information beyond its two dominant components. The animal threshold experiments behind the concept (piglets developing VILI above roughly 12 J/min) are animal data and are described here as labelled background only, not carded. PROPOSED PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING: the quantity is real, measurable and associated with death in humans; that reducing power, as such, prevents VILI or death is unproven, and its information may be carried almost entirely by driving pressure and rate.

cards.headline: Gattinoni 2016 (formulation, validated in 80 patients): mechanical power computed from the equation of motion matched measured power (R²>0.96) in normal and ARDS lungs
cards.summary: Gattinoni 2016 (formulation, validated in 80 patients): mechanical power computed from the equation of motion matched measured power (R²>0.96) in normal and ARDS lungs
cards.type: Human physiology formulation and validation study (Gattinoni 2016)
cards.people: 30 patients with normal lungs and 50 patients with ARDS, in whom mechanical power was computed from the power equation (built from tidal volume, driving pressure, flow, PEEP, respiratory rate, elastance and airway resistance) and measured directly from dynamic pressure-volume curves, at PEEP of 5 and 15 cm H2O and tidal volumes of 6, 8, 10 and 12 mL/kg.
cards.result: Computed and measured mechanical powers were similar at both PEEP levels in both groups (slopes 0.96, 1.06, 1.01 and 1.12; R²>0.96; P<0.0001 for all). Mechanical power increased exponentially with tidal volume, driving pressure and flow (exponent 2) and with respiratory rate (exponent 1.4), and linearly with PEEP. The authors propose the equation lets clinicians estimate each ventilator variable's contribution to the total power — and therefore to ventilator-related lung injury — at the bedside.
cards.watchOut: This card establishes that the number can be computed and what it contains — not that it injures human lungs at any threshold. The threshold story comes from piglet experiments by the same group (labelled background in the balance, not carded), and animal power thresholds do not transfer numerically to adult humans.
cards.source: Gattinoni L et al. Ventilator-related causes of lung injury: the mechanical power. Intensive Care Med. 2016. PMID: 27620287. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Serpa Neto 2018 (two observational cohorts, 8,207 patients): each 5 J/min of mechanical power carried an odds ratio of 1.06–1.10 for hospital death; risk rose consistently above ~17 J/min
cards.summary: Serpa Neto 2018 (two observational cohorts, 8,207 patients): each 5 J/min of mechanical power carried an odds ratio of 1.06–1.10 for hospital death; risk rose consistently above ~17 J/min
cards.type: Pooled analysis of two observational cohorts (Serpa Neto 2018)
cards.people: 8,207 critically ill patients receiving invasive ventilation for at least 48 hours, analysed from the MIMIC-III and eICU databases; the exposure was mechanical power during the second 24 hours of ventilation (median 21.4 J/min [IQR 16.2–28.1] in MIMIC-III and 16.0 J/min [11.7–22.1] in eICU); primary outcome in-hospital mortality.
cards.result: Mechanical power was independently associated with in-hospital mortality (odds ratio per 5 J/min increase 1.06 relative, 95% CI 1.01 to 1.11; P=0.021 in MIMIC-III, and 1.10 relative, 95% CI 1.02 to 1.18; P=0.010 in eICU), and also with ICU mortality, 30-day mortality, ventilator-free days and length of stay. Even at low tidal volume, high mechanical power was associated with in-hospital mortality (odds ratio 1.70 relative, 95% CI 1.32 to 2.18; P<0.001). There was a consistent increase in the risk of death with mechanical power higher than 17.0 J/min.
cards.watchOut: Retrospective database physiology: mechanical power is computed from recorded settings in patients whose settings were chosen because they were sick, so confounding by severity is intrinsic and adjustment is statistical only. The ~17 J/min 'threshold' is where the fitted risk curve steepens in these data, not a validated safe limit.
cards.source: Serpa Neto A et al. Mechanical power of ventilation is associated with mortality in critically ill patients: an analysis of patients in two observational cohorts. Intensive Care Med. 2018. PMID: 30291378. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Costa 2021 (pooled trials and cohort, 4,549 ARDS patients): mechanical power predicted mortality — but driving pressure plus respiratory rate alone predicted it equally well
cards.summary: Costa 2021 (pooled trials and cohort, 4,549 ARDS patients): mechanical power predicted mortality — but driving pressure plus respiratory rate alone predicted it equally well
cards.type: Pooled individual-data analysis of trials and a cohort (Costa 2021)
cards.people: 4,549 patients with ARDS (38% women; mean age 55 ± 23 years) pooled from six randomised trials of protective mechanical ventilation and one large observational cohort; average mechanical power 0.32 ± 0.14 J/min/kg predicted body weight, driving pressure 15.0 ± 5.8 cm H2O, respiratory rate 25.7 ± 7.4 breaths/min; primary outcome mortality at 28 or 60 days.
cards.result: Driving pressure, respiratory rate and mechanical power were each significant predictors of mortality in adjusted analyses. The impact of driving pressure on mortality was four times as large as that of respiratory rate. Mechanical power was associated with mortality during controlled ventilation, but a simpler model using only driving pressure and respiratory rate was equivalent — the composite power variable added no predictive advantage over its two main components in this dataset.
cards.watchOut: Equivalence of prediction is not equivalence of mechanism: power may still be the causal quantity while driving pressure and rate are its best-measured proxies. But for a clinician deciding what to watch at the bedside, this analysis says the composite number currently buys no extra prognostic information in ARDS.
cards.source: Costa ELV et al. Ventilatory Variables and Mechanical Power in Patients with Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome. Am J Respir Crit Care Med. 2021. PMID: 33784486. cards.headline: Synthesis: a real, computable energy rate, consistently tied to death in human observational data, whose added value over driving pressure and rate is unproven (PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING)
cards.summary: Synthesis: a real, computable energy rate, consistently tied to death in human observational data, whose added value over driving pressure and rate is unproven (PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING)
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: an 80-patient formulation/validation study, an 8,207-patient two-cohort analysis, and a 4,549-patient pooled ARDS analysis.
cards.result: Formulation: computed power matches measured power (R²>0.96) and scales exponentially with volume, pressure and flow. Association: odds of hospital death rise ~6–10% per 5 J/min, steepening above ~17 J/min in general ICU cohorts. Increment: none demonstrated over driving pressure plus rate in ARDS. No study — human or otherwise carded here — shows that titrating power itself changes outcomes. PROPOSED PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING.
cards.watchOut: The piglet threshold experiments (VILI appearing above roughly 12 J/min in Cressoni 2016 and related work) are the concept's mechanistic root but are animal data: they appear in this shelf's balance as labelled background only and are not evidence cards, and their numbers must not be quoted as human thresholds.

shelves.title: Pendelluft and patient self-inflicted lung injury: gas shifts to dependent lung when effort is strong — shown on tomography in human ARDS and scaled to effort in 20 patients, but human injury evidence rests on a single-patient observation and animal mechanics
shelves.question: In spontaneously breathing patients with injured lungs, what is pendelluft, how strong is the human evidence that vigorous inspiratory effort worsens lung injury (patient self-inflicted lung injury), and how is effort measured at the bedside?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Positive-Pressure Respiration/methods · Retrospective Studies · Respiratory Distress Syndrome/therapy · Lung/physiology · Respiration, Artificial/methods
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING (textbook framing: Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology and Boron & Boulpaep Medical Physiology, on pleural-pressure transmission and regional lung stress): Pendelluft is gas moving inside the lung from non-dependent to dependent regions at the start of inspiration — without any change in tidal volume at the airway — when a strong diaphragmatic contraction drops pleural pressure locally, in dependent lung, instead of uniformly. The concept entered human medicine through a single-patient electrical impedance tomography observation during mechanical ventilation, after which the same group demonstrated the mechanism experimentally in injured pig lungs (Yoshida T et al., PMID: 24199628): the human component of that paper is one patient (N = 1, printed on the face), and its quantitative mechanics are animal data, labelled as such on the card and not treated as human evidence. Human cohort data now confirm the phenomenon is real and effort-dependent: in 20 ventilated ARDS patients, pendelluft during patient-triggered breaths grew with oesophageal pressure swing, with distinct high- and low-pendelluft response patterns (Lin WC et al., PMID: 38092775). What remains unproven in humans is the injury claim itself — patient self-inflicted lung injury (P-SILI): no human study carded here shows pendelluft or effort causing worse lung injury or death. Effort, at least, can be measured at the bedside: a brief airway occlusion swing (ΔPocc) detected muscle pressure above 10 cm H2O with AUROC 0.92 and transpulmonary driving pressure above 15 cm H2O with AUROC 0.93 in 16 patients, validated in 12 more (Bertoni M et al., PMID: 31694692), and ventilator-displayed occlusion pressure (P0.1) tracks drive and flags potentially injurious effort (Telias I et al., PMID: 32097569). PROPOSED PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING: pendelluft exists in human ARDS and scales with effort; effort is measurable non-invasively; that vigorous effort worsens human lung injury is a coherent, experimentally grounded hypothesis without direct human outcome evidence.

cards.headline: Yoshida 2013: pendelluft seen on impedance tomography in one ventilated patient with injured lungs (human N = 1) — the mechanism then demonstrated in injured pig lungs (animal data, labelled)
cards.summary: Yoshida 2013: pendelluft seen on impedance tomography in one ventilated patient with injured lungs (human N = 1) — the mechanism then demonstrated in injured pig lungs (animal data, labelled)
cards.type: Human case observation (N = 1) with animal mechanistic experiments (Yoshida 2013)
cards.people: Human component: a single patient with injured lungs undergoing mechanical ventilation, in whom electrical impedance tomography showed air moving from non-dependent to dependent lung regions during spontaneous breathing effort without change in tidal volume — N = 1, printed on the face as the physiology labelling rule requires. Experimental component (animal, not human evidence): anaesthetised pigs with lung injury studied with impedance tomography, dynamic CT and intrabronchial pleural-pressure catheters.
cards.result: In the patient, spontaneous breathing during mechanical ventilation produced pendelluft visible on impedance tomography. In the animal experiments, spontaneous effort made dependent pleural pressure far more negative than non-dependent (−13.0 ± 4.0 vs −6.4 ± 3.8 cm H2O; P<0.05), pendelluft occurred during early inflation despite tidal volume limited below 6 mL/kg, and matching the dependent inflation under paralysis required almost threefold greater driving pressure (28.0 ± 0.5 vs 10.3 ± 0.6 cm H2O; P<0.01) — that is, effort overstretched dependent lung at unchanged tidal volume. The authors conclude strong spontaneous effort may enhance lung damage even when it does not increase tidal volume.
cards.watchOut: Read the denominators: the human evidence in this founding paper is one patient's tomogram; every number on this card except the existence of the phenomenon in that patient comes from pigs. It is carded because it is the origin of the concept and its human observation is genuine — not because its mechanics are human data.
cards.source: Yoshida T et al. Spontaneous effort causes occult pendelluft during mechanical ventilation. Am J Respir Crit Care Med. 2013. PMID: 24199628. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Lin 2023 (20 ARDS patients): pendelluft during triggered breaths scaled with breathing effort (oesophageal pressure swing), with distinct high- and low-response patterns
cards.summary: Lin 2023 (20 ARDS patients): pendelluft during triggered breaths scaled with breathing effort (oesophageal pressure swing), with distinct high- and low-response patterns
cards.people: 20 mechanically ventilated patients with ARDS during transition from controlled to active breaths under volume-cycled ventilation, studied prospectively with electrical impedance tomography plus respiratory mechanics; breaths were grouped by oesophageal pressure swing (ΔPes): low (<5 cm H2O; 471 breaths), moderate (5 to <10 cm H2O; 906 breaths) and high effort (≥10 cm H2O; 565 breaths).
cards.result: The pendelluft response to breathing effort was significantly greater in patient-triggered breaths than in reverse-triggered breaths (P<0.0001). By pendelluft-ΔPes slope, patients split into a high-pendelluft group (n=9; slope 0.7–2.4 mL/cm H2O) and a low-pendelluft group (n=11; slope −0.1 to 0.3 mL/cm H2O); for triggered breaths the high group had lower peak/plateau pressures and lower respiratory-system and lung elastance. Using ΔPes to predict pendelluft had a low positive predictive value. No clinical outcomes were measured.
cards.watchOut: Twenty patients, breath-level analysis (thousands of breaths are not thousands of patients), and a retrospectively analysed dataset. It establishes that pendelluft occurs and is effort-related in human ARDS — and, usefully, that effort alone predicts it poorly, so the phenomenon cannot be inferred from the ventilator screen alone.
cards.source: Lin WC et al. Pendelluft in patients with acute respiratory distress syndrome during trigger and reverse triggering breaths. Sci Rep. 2023. PMID: 38092775. cards.headline: Bertoni 2019 (16 patients + 12-patient validation): a brief occlusion swing (ΔPocc) detected excessive effort — muscle pressure >10 cm H2O with AUROC 0.92, transpulmonary driving pressure >15 cm H2O with AUROC 0.93
cards.summary: Bertoni 2019 (16 patients + 12-patient validation): a brief occlusion swing (ΔPocc) detected excessive effort — muscle pressure >10 cm H2O with AUROC 0.92, transpulmonary driving pressure >15 cm H2O with AUROC 0.93
cards.people: Mechanically ventilated patients in two Toronto ICUs, with daily measurements of respiratory muscle pressure (Pmus), dynamic transpulmonary driving pressure (ΔPL,dyn) and the airway-pressure swing during a brief end-expiratory occlusion (ΔPocc): 52 recordings in 16 patients for derivation, and an independent external validation cohort of 12 patients in Nanjing, China.
cards.result: Excessive effort was frequent: Pmus exceeded 10 cm H2O on 84% of study days and ΔPL,dyn exceeded 15 cm H2O on 53%. ΔPocc accurately detected Pmus >10 cm H2O (AUROC 0.92, 95% CI 0.83 to 0.97) and ΔPL,dyn >15 cm H2O (AUROC 0.93, 95% CI 0.86 to 0.99), and in the external cohort estimated values detected both conditions with AUROC ≥0.94. The authors conclude measuring ΔPocc enables accurate non-invasive screening for elevated respiratory muscle pressure and transpulmonary driving pressure.
cards.watchOut: The thresholds (Pmus 10, ΔPL 15 cm H2O) are the investigators' definitions of 'excessive', chosen from the P-SILI framework itself — the study validates a measurement against those definitions, not the definitions against patient outcomes. Twenty-eight patients in total is a small validation base.
cards.source: Bertoni M et al. A novel non-invasive method to detect excessively high respiratory effort and dynamic transpulmonary driving pressure during mechanical ventilation. Crit Care. 2019. PMID: 31694692. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Telias 2020: airway occlusion pressure (P0.1) is a reliable bedside estimate of drive and effort — P0.1 above 3.5 cm H2O was 80% sensitive for high effort (patient number not reported in the record)
cards.summary: Telias 2020: airway occlusion pressure (P0.1) is a reliable bedside estimate of drive and effort — P0.1 above 3.5 cm H2O was 80% sensitive for high effort (patient number not reported in the record)
cards.type: Physiological validation studies (Telias 2020) — N not documented in the record
cards.people: Patients under assisted ventilation (three patient studies) and healthy subjects (one study), plus a bench study of six ventilators; ventilator-displayed P0.1 was validated against diaphragmatic electrical activity, muscular pressure-time measures and a reference occlusion P0.1, with oesophageal pressure-time product as the reference standard for effort. The record does not print the total patient number — N not documented in the record.
cards.result: Ventilator P0.1 correlated well with measures of drive and with the oesophageal pressure-time product (within-subjects R²=0.8). A reference P0.1 above 3.5 cm H2O was 80% sensitive and 77% specific for detecting high effort (≥200 cm H2O·s·min⁻¹), and P0.1 at or below 1.0 cm H2O was 100% sensitive and 92% specific for low effort (≤50 cm H2O·s·min⁻¹); areas under the curve for ventilator P0.1 were 0.81 (high effort) and 0.92 (low effort). Bench testing showed low mean bias for most ventilators but variable precision, worse in patients.
cards.watchOut: P0.1 measures drive in the first 100 milliseconds of an occluded breath — a proxy for effort, not effort itself, and ventilators that estimate it without a true occlusion can underestimate it. Like the ΔPocc card, it validates detection of a physiological state whose harmfulness in humans is the unproven part of P-SILI.
cards.source: Telias I et al. Airway Occlusion Pressure As an Estimate of Respiratory Drive and Inspiratory Effort during Assisted Ventilation. Am J Respir Crit Care Med. 2020. PMID: 32097569. cards.headline: Synthesis: pendelluft is real and effort-scaled in human ARDS, effort is measurable at the bedside — and direct human evidence that effort injures the lung does not yet exist (PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING)
cards.summary: Synthesis: pendelluft is real and effort-scaled in human ARDS, effort is measurable at the bedside — and direct human evidence that effort injures the lung does not yet exist (PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING)
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: a one-patient founding observation with animal mechanics, a 20-patient ARDS cohort, and two effort-measurement validation studies (16 + 12 patients; one with N not documented).
cards.result: Existence: pendelluft demonstrated on tomography in ventilated human ARDS, scaling with oesophageal pressure swing. Mechanism: dependent overstretch at unchanged tidal volume — demonstrated in animals, inferred in humans. Measurement: ΔPocc (AUROC 0.92–0.93) and P0.1 (AUROC 0.81–0.92) detect high effort non-invasively. Outcomes: no carded human study links pendelluft or effort to worsened injury or mortality. PROPOSED PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING, with the human-data limit stated plainly.
cards.watchOut: P-SILI is routinely invoked to justify deep sedation or paralysis decisions; this shelf's evidence supports monitoring effort, not any particular response to it. The Brochard/Goligher review literature frames the hypothesis — reviews are discussed in the balance, not carded, because they are not primary human data.

shelves.title: Alveolar fluid clearance in human ALI/ARDS: mean 6%/hour and impaired in 56% of patients (Ware & Matthay) — maximal clearance predicts survival, and the human epithelium answers beta-adrenergic stimulation
shelves.question: In human acute lung injury, how fast is alveolar fluid clearance, how often is it impaired, and does its rate predict mortality and response to beta-adrenergic stimulation?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Epinephrine/blood · Female · Hemodynamics · Humans · Logistic Models · Male · Middle Aged · Mucociliary Clearance · Prognosis · Pulmonary Alveoli/physiopathology · Pulmonary Edema/etiology · Respiration, Artificial/adverse effects · Respiratory Distress Syndrome/blood · Sepsis/complications · Severity of Illness Index · Sex Distribution · Time Factors · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED (textbook framing: Boron & Boulpaep Medical Physiology and Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, which present alveolar oedema resolution as active epithelial sodium transport driving water reabsorption, upregulated by beta-adrenergic/cAMP signalling): In human acute lung injury the alveolar epithelium's ability to clear its own oedema fluid is measurable at the bedside from serial oedema-fluid protein concentrations, and the carded human studies agree quantitatively across two decades. In 79 patients with ALI/ARDS (Ware LB & Matthay MA, PMID: 11371404), mean net alveolar fluid clearance was 6%/hour; 56% had impaired clearance (<3%/hour), 32% submaximal and only 13% maximal (≥14%/hour) — and patients with maximal clearance had significantly lower mortality and shorter ventilation. The uninjured-lung comparator shows what intact epithelium does: in 65 patients with hydrostatic oedema (Verghese GM et al., PMID: 10517756), 75% had intact clearance and 38% maximal clearance at a mean of 25%/hour, and intact clearance tracked with better oxygenation and an 18% lower hospital mortality. Clearance fails further exactly where the textbook mechanism predicts — with epithelial/endothelial injury from shock and bacteraemia (Zeyed YF et al., PMID: 22821995; 116 patients). Beta-adrenergic stimulation increases clearance in the ex vivo human lung (salmeterol effective at 10⁻⁶ M; human basal clearance 11 ± 2% over 4 hours — Sakuma T et al., PMID: 9032186, ex vivo human lungs, with the paper's parallel rat experiments not carded), and the in-vivo proof of principle exists: intravenous salbutamol lowered extravascular lung water by day 7 in a 40-patient randomised trial (Perkins GD et al., PMID: 16254268) — a physiological effect that later large outcome trials of beta-agonists in ARDS, homed elsewhere, did not convert into survival benefit. PROPOSED PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED for the clearance rates, their impairment in ALI/ARDS and their prognostic meaning in humans; the beta-adrenergic responsiveness is established ex vivo and as an in-vivo physiological effect, not as a treatment.

cards.headline: Ware & Matthay 2001 (79 patients with ALI/ARDS): mean alveolar fluid clearance 6%/hour — impaired (<3%/hour) in 56%, maximal (≥14%/hour) in only 13%, and maximal clearance meant lower mortality
cards.summary: Ware & Matthay 2001 (79 patients with ALI/ARDS): mean alveolar fluid clearance 6%/hour — impaired (<3%/hour) in 56%, maximal (≥14%/hour) in only 13%, and maximal clearance meant lower mortality
cards.people: 79 patients with acute lung injury or ARDS, in whom pulmonary oedema fluid and plasma were sampled serially in the first 4 hours after intubation and net alveolar fluid clearance was calculated from sequential oedema-fluid protein measurements; results were contrasted with the group's hydrostatic-oedema cohort (carded separately below).
cards.result: Mean alveolar fluid clearance was 6%/hour. Of the patients, 56% had impaired clearance (<3%/hour), 32% submaximal clearance (≥3%/hour, <14%/hour) and 13% maximal clearance (≥14%/hour). Patients with maximal clearance were more likely to be female (P=0.03) and less likely to have sepsis (P=0.01). Endogenous and exogenous catecholamines did not correlate with clearance. Patients with maximal alveolar fluid clearance had significantly lower mortality and a shorter duration of mechanical ventilation (the record does not print the group mortality rates).
cards.watchOut: Clearance is measured only in patients with an endotracheal tube and accessible oedema fluid in the first hours — a selected, sicker subset of ALI/ARDS — and the mortality association is observational: fast clearance may mark a less injured epithelium rather than cause the better outcome. The record reports the mortality difference as significant without printing the rates, so none are quoted here.
cards.source: Ware LB, Matthay MA et al. Alveolar fluid clearance is impaired in the majority of patients with acute lung injury and the acute respiratory distress syndrome. cards.headline: Verghese 1999 (65 patients with hydrostatic pulmonary oedema): the uninjured lung clears fast — 75% intact clearance, 38% maximal at a mean 25%/hour
cards.summary: Verghese 1999 (65 patients with hydrostatic pulmonary oedema): the uninjured lung clears fast — 75% intact clearance, 38% maximal at a mean 25%/hour
cards.people: 65 mechanically ventilated patients with severe hydrostatic pulmonary oedema, with oedema fluid and plasma sampled within the first 4 hours after intubation; alveolar fluid clearance was calculated from the change in oedema-fluid protein concentration over time. This is the comparator cohort that defines intact human clearance.
cards.result: Overall, 75% of patients had intact alveolar fluid clearance (≥3%/hour). Maximal clearance (≥14%/hour) was present in 38%, at a mean rate of 25 ± 12%/hour. Haemodynamic factors (including wedge pressure and ejection fraction) and plasma epinephrine levels did not correlate with clearance. Impaired clearance was associated with lower arterial pH and higher severity score. Intact clearance was associated with greater improvement in oxygenation at 24 hours, a trend toward shorter mechanical ventilation, and an 18% lower hospital mortality (reported as a percentage difference in the record, without arm rates).
cards.watchOut: Hydrostatic oedema is the control condition, not the disease: the epithelium here is stretched but not inflamed, which is precisely why the contrast with ALI/ARDS (previous card) is informative. The catecholamine-independence the authors report is for endogenous plasma levels in this population — it does not contradict the pharmacological beta-stimulation findings carded below.

cards.headline: Zeyed 2012 (116 patients with ALI): circulatory shock and bacteraemia slow alveolar fluid clearance further — clearance fell as vasopressor count rose
cards.summary: Zeyed 2012 (116 patients with ALI): circulatory shock and bacteraemia slow alveolar fluid clearance further — clearance fell as vasopressor count rose
cards.people: 116 patients with acute lung injury in a multicentre study, with net alveolar fluid clearance measured by serial sampling of pulmonary oedema fluid; 86 patients had circulatory shock and 30 did not, and 21 had positive blood cultures.
cards.result: Patients with ALI and shock had significantly slower rates of net alveolar fluid clearance than those without shock (P=0.03), and clearance decreased significantly as the number of vasopressors increased. Patients with positive blood cultures had slower clearance than those with negative cultures (P=0.023). The oedema fluid-to-plasma protein ratio — an index of alveolar-capillary barrier permeability — was highest in patients requiring the most vasopressors (P<0.05). The authors conclude impaired reabsorption may contribute to the high mortality of sepsis-induced ALI.
cards.watchOut: Association, with vasopressor count standing in for shock severity: the study cannot separate shock itself, the vasopressors used to treat it, and the barrier injury that causes both the leak and the failed clearance. The record reports significance levels without printing the group clearance rates, so none are quoted.
cards.source: Zeyed YF et al. The severity of shock is associated with impaired rates of net alveolar fluid clearance in clinical acute lung injury. Am J Physiol Lung Cell Mol Physiol. 2012. cards.headline: Sakuma 1997 (ex vivo human lungs): basal alveolar fluid clearance 11 ± 2% over 4 hours — and beta-adrenergic stimulation with salmeterol increased it at 10⁻⁶ M (human lung number not reported in the record)
cards.summary: Sakuma 1997 (ex vivo human lungs): basal alveolar fluid clearance 11 ± 2% over 4 hours — and beta-adrenergic stimulation with salmeterol increased it at 10⁻⁶ M (human lung number not reported in the record)
cards.type: Ex vivo human lung physiology study (Sakuma 1997) — N not documented in the record
cards.people: Ex vivo human lungs (donor lungs not used for transplantation; the record does not report how many — N not documented in the record), inflated with 100% oxygen and incubated at 37°C after instillation of an isosmolar 5% albumin solution into the distal air spaces; clearance was measured from the rise in protein concentration over 1 or 4 hours, with dose-response testing of terbutaline and salmeterol. The paper's parallel ex vivo rat-lung experiments are not carded here.
cards.result: Basal, unstimulated alveolar fluid clearance in human lungs was 11 ± 2% over 4 hours — significantly slower than in rat lungs (24 ± 4% over 4 hours; P<0.05). Salmeterol, a long-acting beta-adrenergic agonist, was more potent than terbutaline in stimulating clearance from the ex vivo human lung, and relatively low doses were effective in human lungs (10⁻⁶ M). Stimulated clearance rates were also faster in rat than in human lungs at equivalent doses. The authors note ex vivo rates may underestimate maximal clearance in the intact human lung.
cards.watchOut: Ex vivo lungs have no circulation, no lymphatics and no systemic inflammation: they prove the human epithelium can respond to beta stimulation, at concentrations achieved by instillation, not that giving beta-agonists to patients clears oedema faster — the in-vivo test is the next card. Only the human-lung results are carded; the rat data are mentioned solely as the paper's own comparison.
cards.source: Sakuma T et al. Beta-adrenergic agonist stimulated alveolar fluid clearance in ex vivo human and rat lungs. Am J Respir Crit Care Med. 1997. PMID: 9032186. cards.headline: BALTI 2006 (RCT, 40 patients with ALI/ARDS): intravenous salbutamol lowered extravascular lung water by day 7 (9.2 vs 13.2 mL/kg; P=0.038) — the in-vivo proof of principle
cards.summary: BALTI 2006 (RCT, 40 patients with ALI/ARDS): intravenous salbutamol lowered extravascular lung water by day 7 (9.2 vs 13.2 mL/kg; P=0.038) — the in-vivo proof of principle
cards.people: 40 adults with acute lung injury or ARDS at a single centre, randomised double-blind to a sustained intravenous infusion of salbutamol (albuterol) 15 μg/kg/hour or placebo for 7 days; the primary end point was extravascular lung water by thermodilution at day 7.
cards.result: Patients in the salbutamol group had significantly lower lung water at day 7 than the placebo group (9.2 ± 6 vs 13.2 ± 3 mL/kg; 95% CI for the difference 0.2 to 8.3 mL/kg; P=0.038). Plateau airway pressure was lower at day 7 on salbutamol (23.9 ± 3.8 vs 29.5 ± 7.2 cm H2O; P=0.049), the lung injury score trended lower (1.7 vs 2.0; P=0.2), and supraventricular arrhythmias were more frequent on salbutamol (26% vs 10%; P=0.2). The authors call this the first proof of principle that sustained beta-agonist treatment reduces extravascular lung water in humans with ALI/ARDS; mortality was not an outcome of this small trial.
cards.watchOut: A 40-patient, single-centre, surrogate-endpoint trial: lung water fell, but this study says nothing about survival, and the subsequent large beta-agonist outcome trial in ARDS (BALTI-2) was stopped for harm — homed with the beta-agonist intervention literature, not here. This card's role on a physiology shelf is narrow: the clearance mechanism is druggable in vivo.

cards.headline: Synthesis: human alveolar fluid clearance is fast when the epithelium is intact (up to ~25%/hour), impaired in most ALI/ARDS (mean 6%/hour), predicts outcome, and is beta-responsive ex vivo and in vivo (PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED)
cards.summary: Synthesis: human alveolar fluid clearance is fast when the epithelium is intact (up to ~25%/hour), impaired in most ALI/ARDS (mean 6%/hour), predicts outcome, and is beta-responsive ex vivo and in vivo (PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED)
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: human cohorts of 79 ALI/ARDS, 65 hydrostatic-oedema and 116 ALI patients; an ex vivo human lung study (N not documented); and a 40-patient randomised physiological trial.
cards.result: Rates: mean 6%/hour in ALI/ARDS with 56% impaired, versus 75% intact and maximal rates averaging 25%/hour in hydrostatic oedema. Prognosis: maximal clearance tracks with lower mortality and shorter ventilation in both disease and comparator cohorts; shock and bacteraemia slow clearance further. Regulation: beta-adrenergic stimulation raises clearance in ex vivo human lung (salmeterol at 10⁻⁶ M) and lowers lung water in vivo. PROPOSED PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED for the human clearance physiology and its prognostic meaning, on concordant primary human data framed by Boron & Boulpaep and Guyton & Hall.
cards.watchOut: Established physiology is not a treatment recommendation: the beta-agonist outcome literature in ARDS is negative-to-harmful at trial scale, and nothing on this shelf licenses salbutamol as ARDS therapy. Clearance measurement itself remains a research technique requiring oedema-fluid sampling.

shelves.title: Aztreonam–avibactam (Emblaveo) for carbapenem-resistant Gram-negative infection: descriptive phase 3 support, MBL trial of only 15 patients
shelves.question: In adults with complicated urinary tract infection, intra-abdominal infection or hospital-acquired pneumonia caused by metallo-beta-lactamase-producing or otherwise carbapenem-resistant Gram-negative bacteria, is aztreonam–avibactam effective versus best available therapy?
shelves.mesh: Aztreonam · Azabicyclo Compounds · Gram-Negative Bacterial Infections · Drug Combinations · Humans
shelves.balance: EVIDENCE-STRUCTURE CAVEAT, stated plainly: aztreonam–avibactam (Emblaveo — product named under the clarification exception) was approved (FDA, February 2025) substantially on a pooled descriptive programme plus prior aztreonam data, not on a large superiority trial in metallo-β-lactamase producers. REVISIT (n = 422, cIAI and HAP-VAP) was descriptive with no formal hypothesis testing: cure 68.4% vs 65.7% on meropenem, 28-day mortality 4% vs 7% — but only 19 of 80 tested isolates were carbapenemase-positive. ASSEMBLE, the one trial in confirmed MBL producers, randomised just 15 patients (cure 5/12 vs 0/3 on best available therapy; mortality 1/12 vs 1/3). REJUVENATE (n = 34) set the dose and showed aztreonam-like tolerability (hepatic enzyme rises 26.5%). The pharmacological logic — aztreonam survives MBLs, avibactam covers co-produced serine enzymes — is sound and the small data point the right way, but the MBL-specific randomised evidence is 15 patients, and the stamp is capped at POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: REVISIT 2025: aztreonam–avibactam (Emblaveo) matched meropenem descriptively on cure (68.4% vs 65.7%) — a descriptive trial with no formal hypothesis testing, n = 422
cards.summary: REVISIT 2025: aztreonam–avibactam (Emblaveo) matched meropenem descriptively on cure (68.4% vs 65.7%) — a descriptive trial with no formal hypothesis testing, n = 422
cards.type: Phase 3 descriptive randomised open-label trial (REVISIT), Lancet Infect Dis 2025
cards.people: 422 hospitalised adults with complicated intra-abdominal infection or hospital-acquired/ventilator-associated pneumonia caused or suspected to be caused by Gram-negative bacteria, randomised 2:1 to aztreonam–avibactam (plus metronidazole for cIAI) or meropenem ± colistin for 5–14 days. 271 (64%) had a baseline Gram-negative pathogen; of 80 isolates tested for carbapenemases, only 19 (24%) were carbapenemase-positive (serine, metallo-β-lactamase, or both).
cards.result: Clinical cure at test-of-cure (day 28 ± 3) was 193/282 (68.4%) on aztreonam–avibactam vs 92/140 (65.7%) on meropenem (treatment difference 2.7%, 95% CI −6.6 to 12.4). Cure in cIAI was 76.4% vs 74.0%; in HAP-VAP 45.9% vs 41.7%. 28-day mortality was 4% (12/282) vs 7% (10/140). No treatment-related serious adverse events occurred in the aztreonam–avibactam group. The trial was descriptive by design — no formal hypothesis testing was planned, so these are point estimates, not a noninferiority verdict.
cards.watchOut: Most REVISIT infections were NOT carbapenemase-producers — this trial mainly shows the combination performs like meropenem in largely susceptible Gram-negative infection. It is not the MBL evidence; that is ASSEMBLE, with 15 patients.
cards.source: Carmeli Y, Cisneros JM, Paul M, Daikos GL, Wang M, Torre-Cisneros J, et al. Aztreonam-avibactam versus meropenem for the treatment of serious infections caused by Gram-negative bacteria (REVISIT): a descriptive, multinational, open-label, phase 3, randomised trial. The Lancet Infectious Diseases. 2025. PMID: 39389071. Registry ID: NCT03329092 (EudraCT 2017-002742-68). cards.summary: ASSEMBLE 2025: in confirmed MBL-producing infections, cure was 5/12 on aztreonam–avibactam vs 0/3 on best available therapy — the entire randomised MBL evidence base is 15 patients (printed on the face)
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised open-label trial (ASSEMBLE) — only 15 patients, descriptive, JAC-Antimicrob Resist 2025
cards.people: 15 hospitalised adults (single-arm-sized randomised cohort, 2:1) with cIAI, cUTI, HAP/VAP or bloodstream infection caused by confirmed metallo-β-lactamase-producing multidrug-resistant pathogens: 12 assigned aztreonam–avibactam, 3 best available therapy. Pathogens were mainly Klebsiella pneumoniae; MBL types included NDM-1, NDM-5, VIM-2 and L1. SINGLE-DIGIT COMPARATOR ARM — printed on the face.
cards.result: Clinical cure at test-of-cure was 5/12 (42%) with aztreonam–avibactam vs 0/3 (0%) with best available therapy; per-patient microbiological responses were generally consistent with clinical responses. 28-day mortality was 1/12 (8%) vs 1/3 (33%). No treatment-related serious adverse events. No formal hypothesis testing was planned — with 15 patients, no statistical comparison is meaningful; these numbers are a feasibility signal, not an effect estimate.
cards.watchOut: The question this shelf answers — does the drug work against MBL producers? — rests on 12 treated patients. Anyone citing ASSEMBLE as proof of efficacy is overstating a 15-patient descriptive study; its real contribution is showing enrolment is possible and outcomes were not futile.
cards.source: Daikos GL, Cisneros JM, Carmeli Y, Wang M, Leong CL, Pontikis K, et al. Aztreonam-avibactam for the treatment of serious infections caused by metallo-β-lactamase-producing Gram-negative pathogens: a Phase 3 randomized trial (ASSEMBLE). JAC-Antimicrobial Resistance. 2025. cards.headline: REJUVENATE 2020: the phase 2a dose-finding study (n = 34) set the phase 3 dose; hepatic enzyme rises in 26.5%, diarrhoea in 14.7%
cards.summary: REJUVENATE 2020: the phase 2a dose-finding study (n = 34) set the phase 3 dose; hepatic enzyme rises in 26.5%, diarrhoea in 14.7%
cards.type: Phase 2a open-label pharmacokinetic/safety study (REJUVENATE), J Antimicrob Chemother 2020
cards.people: 34 hospitalised adults with complicated intra-abdominal infection in sequential dose cohorts (all also received IV metronidazole); the higher-dose cohorts received a 500/167 mg loading dose then 1500/500 mg maintenance every 6 hours, adjusted for renal impairment. Primary objectives were pharmacokinetics and safety.
cards.result: Exposures in the higher-dose cohorts matched those predicted for >90% joint PK/pharmacodynamic target attainment, and that regimen was carried into phase 3. Adverse events were similar between cohorts; the commonest were hepatic enzyme increases (9/34, 26.5%) and diarrhoea (5/34, 14.7%), consistent with aztreonam monotherapy's known profile. Clinical cure at test-of-cure was 20/34 (58.8%) in the modified ITT population — a secondary, uncontrolled figure.
cards.watchOut: A dose-selection study, not efficacy evidence: 34 patients, no comparator, and its cure rate should never be quoted as the drug's effectiveness.
cards.source: Cornely OA, Cisneros JM, Torre-Cisneros J, Rodríguez-Hernández MJ, Tallón-Aguilar L, Calbo E, et al. Pharmacokinetics and safety of aztreonam/avibactam for the treatment of complicated intra-abdominal infections in hospitalized adults: results from the REJUVENATE study. The Journal of Antimicrobial Chemotherapy. 2020. PMID: 31828337. Registry ID: NCT02655419 (EudraCT 2015-002726-39). cards.headline: Synthesis: a biologically sound combination with descriptive phase 3 support — and an MBL evidence base of 15 randomised patients
cards.summary: Synthesis: a biologically sound combination with descriptive phase 3 support — and an MBL evidence base of 15 randomised patients
cards.people: Hospitalised adults with serious Gram-negative infection, including metallo-β-lactamase producers, across the REVISIT (n = 422), ASSEMBLE (n = 15) and REJUVENATE (n = 34) programme carded above. The product is marketed as Emblaveo (named under the tested-product clarification exception).
cards.result: The logic is strong — aztreonam is stable to metallo-β-lactamases and avibactam shields it from the serine enzymes MBL producers usually co-carry — and the descriptive data are consistent with it: REVISIT cure rates matched meropenem in mostly non-resistant infection, and ASSEMBLE's 12 MBL-infected patients had a 42% cure rate against 0/3 on best available therapy. EVIDENCE-STRUCTURE CAVEAT, on the face: approval rests substantially on this pooled programme plus prior aztreonam data, not on a large superiority or noninferiority trial in MBL producers; no carded study performed formal hypothesis testing. POSSIBLE (benefit) is the ceiling this structure allows.
cards.watchOut: Do not upgrade on mechanism alone: elegant β-lactamase logic has failed at trial before in this library. Until a powered MBL trial exists, use is a reasoned extrapolation supported by small descriptive data.
cards.source: Synthesis of the carded records above (PMIDs 39389071, 40727714, 31828337). Registry ID: NCT03329092 / NCT02655419 (programme). MeSH: not captured from the record this session

shelves.title: ADAPT-Sepsis: procalcitonin guidance saved about a day of antibiotics in ICU sepsis; CRP guidance saved none
shelves.question: In critically ill adults with sepsis, does daily procalcitonin-guided (or CRP-guided) antibiotic discontinuation shorten treatment duration without increasing mortality versus usual care?
shelves.mesh: Procalcitonin · C-Reactive Protein · Sepsis · Anti-Bacterial Agents · Duration of Therapy · Humans
shelves.balance: A single very large trial answers this, and its two biomarker arms split. ADAPT-Sepsis (2,760 ICU patients with suspected sepsis, 41 UK units) found daily procalcitonin-guided discontinuation shortened antibiotic duration by a mean of 0.88 days (9.8 vs 10.7 days; P = .01), with 28-day mortality noninferior only against a wide 5.4-percentage-point margin (20.9% vs 19.4%). Daily CRP-guided discontinuation made no difference to duration (difference 0.09 days; P = .79) and its mortality comparison was inconclusive — CRP guidance is not supported. The trial's own economic evaluation found PCT guidance cost €427 more per patient with a tiny QALY loss within the trial (dominated), becoming cost-effective only when pooled with older trials; the process evaluation shows clinicians often overruled early PCT stop advice, blunting the effect. The broader procalcitonin-guidance question is homed on live Shelf 314; this pack covers the ADAPT-Sepsis ICU sepsis-discontinuation slice. One trial, however large, caps the stamp at POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: ADAPT-Sepsis 2025: daily procalcitonin guidance cut antibiotic duration by 0.88 days with mortality noninferior — CRP guidance made no difference to duration (the CRP protocol did not shorten treatment)
cards.summary: ADAPT-Sepsis 2025: daily procalcitonin guidance cut antibiotic duration by 0.88 days with mortality noninferior — CRP guidance made no difference to duration (the CRP protocol did not shorten treatment)
cards.people: 2,760 critically ill adults (mean age 60.2 years; 60.3% men) in 41 UK NHS intensive care units, randomised within 24 hours of starting IV antibiotics for suspected sepsis: 918 to a daily procalcitonin-guided protocol, 924 to a daily CRP-guided protocol, 918 to standard care. Primary outcomes: total antibiotic duration and 28-day all-cause mortality.
cards.result: PCT guidance shortened antibiotics: mean duration 9.8 (SD 7.2) days vs 10.7 (7.6) on standard care — mean difference 0.88 days (95% CI 0.19–1.58; P = .01). 28-day mortality was 20.9% (184/879) on PCT vs 19.4% (170/878) on standard care (absolute difference 1.57, 95% CI −2.18 to 5.32; P = .02 for noninferiority against a wide 5.4% margin). CRP guidance did not shorten duration (10.6 days; mean difference 0.09, −0.60 to 0.79; P = .79 — the treatment made no difference) and its mortality comparison was inconclusive (21.1% [184/874]; absolute difference 1.69, −2.07 to 5.45).
cards.watchOut: The duration gain is under one day, and mortality 'noninferiority' was declared against a generous 5.4-percentage-point margin with a point estimate 1.57 points in the wrong direction — safe within that margin is not the same as proven equally safe. The broader procalcitonin question is homed on live Shelf 314; this pack is the ADAPT-Sepsis ICU-discontinuation slice only.
cards.source: Dark P, Hossain A, McAuley DF, Brealey D, Carlson G, Clayton JC, et al. Biomarker-Guided Antibiotic Duration for Hospitalized Patients With Suspected Sepsis: The ADAPT-Sepsis Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA. 2025. PMID: 39652885. Registry ID: ISRCTN47473244. cards.headline: ADAPT-Sepsis cost-effectiveness 2025: within the trial, PCT guidance cost €427 more per patient with a small QALY loss — cost-effectiveness appears only when meta-analysed with older trials
cards.summary: ADAPT-Sepsis cost-effectiveness 2025: within the trial, PCT guidance cost €427 more per patient with a small QALY loss — cost-effectiveness appears only when meta-analysed with older trials
cards.type: Economic evaluation of a randomised trial (ADAPT-Sepsis), Crit Care 2025
cards.people: Economic evaluation built on the ADAPT-Sepsis trial (2,760 patients, carded above), plus a second analysis meta-analysing ADAPT-Sepsis with other PCT-guidance studies over a lifetime horizon. Costs as printed in the record are in euros.
cards.result: Within ADAPT-Sepsis itself, daily PCT guidance cost €427 more per patient and was associated with a small QALY loss (0.001) — i.e. it was dominated by standard care on the trial's own numbers. Using the meta-analysed data it cost €330 more with 0.139 more QALYs (€2,384 per QALY gained). If only antibiotic use and PCT test costs are counted, the extra cost is at most €110 per patient with equal QALYs. Results were driven by the assumed mortality effect, whose intervals included no effect in both analyses.
cards.watchOut: Not independent clinical evidence — an economic model of the same trial, whose favourable version depends on pooling older trials' mortality signal that ADAPT-Sepsis itself did not show.
cards.source: Stevenson M, Forsyth JE, Hossain A, Lall R, Dark P, et al. Cost-effectiveness of procalcitonin-guided antibiotic duration for hospitalized patients with sepsis. Critical Care. 2025. PMID: 41316366. Registry ID: ISRCTN47473244 (parent trial). MeSH: Humans · Procalcitonin · Sepsis · Cost-Benefit Analysis · Anti-Bacterial Agents · Quality-Adjusted Life Years · Biomarkers · Male · Middle Aged · Hospitalization · Female · Aged · Intensive Care Units

cards.headline: ADAPT-Sepsis process evaluation 2026: PCT advice said 'stop' 1.7 days earlier than CRP advice — but clinicians followed CRP advice more often
cards.summary: ADAPT-Sepsis process evaluation 2026: PCT advice said 'stop' 1.7 days earlier than CRP advice — but clinicians followed CRP advice more often
cards.people: Pre-planned in-trial descriptive process evaluation within ADAPT-Sepsis (2,760 patients, 41 UK critical care units, carded above): timing and frequency of algorithm-generated stop advice, clinician adherence, and reasons for non-adherence, with treating teams blinded to allocation.
cards.result: Strong stop advice came earlier in the PCT group than the CRP group (mean difference −1.7 days, 95% CI −2.5 to −0.9; P < 0.001), and CRP guidance generated a higher proportion of 'standard care' (continue) advice. Overall adherence was nevertheless greater in the CRP group (mean difference −6.8%, 95% CI −9.0 to −4.5), driven by its later, more conservative stop advice being followed more. Non-adherence reasons — fixed-duration microbiology guidance, illness severity, continuing fever, raised routine inflammatory markers — did not differ between groups.
cards.watchOut: A delivery study, not an efficacy study: it explains why the PCT effect was small (clinicians often overruled early stop advice) but adds no new outcome evidence, and it shares the parent trial's patients.
cards.source: Lall R, Hossain A, Poole R, Lloydwin C, Anderson H, White J, et al. Delivery and adherence of biomarker-guided antibiotic treatment protocols in the ADAPT-Sepsis clinical trial: an in-trial descriptive process evaluation of daily procalcitonin- and C-reactive protein-guided protocols. Anaesthesia. 2026. PMID: 42901145. Registry ID: ISRCTN47473244 (parent trial). MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Synthesis: one large trial — PCT guidance buys about a day of antibiotics, CRP guidance buys nothing
cards.summary: Synthesis: one large trial — PCT guidance buys about a day of antibiotics, CRP guidance buys nothing
cards.people: Critically ill adults with suspected sepsis, from the single ADAPT-Sepsis programme carded above (main trial, its economic evaluation and its process evaluation — one patient population, three reports).
cards.result: ADAPT-Sepsis is the definitive-sized test of biomarker-guided stopping in ICU sepsis, and its answer is split by biomarker: daily procalcitonin guidance shortened antibiotic courses by a mean of 0.88 days with 28-day mortality noninferior within a wide 5.4-point margin; daily CRP guidance made no difference to duration (the treatment made no difference) and its mortality read was inconclusive. The process evaluation shows the PCT effect was blunted by clinician non-adherence to early stop advice. A single (large) trial caps the stamp at POSSIBLE: PCT-guided discontinuation is a modest stewardship tool, not a mortality intervention, and CRP-guided discontinuation is not supported.
cards.watchOut: Do not merge this with the older procalcitonin literature on live Shelf 314 without noting ADAPT-Sepsis is the ICU-sepsis discontinuation question specifically — and that its own economic analysis found PCT guidance dominated within the trial.

shelves.title: Olorofim in invasive mould disease: 28.7% strict response in a single-arm phase 2b study — no comparator, and no Mucorales activity
shelves.question: In patients with invasive mould disease (including azole-resistant Aspergillus and Mucorales) with limited options, what response and survival does olorofim achieve?
shelves.mesh: Antifungal Agents · Invasive Fungal Infections · Aspergillosis · Pyrimidines · Humans
shelves.balance: SINGLE-ARM EVIDENCE ONLY — printed on the face of every card; no randomised comparator exists. In the phase 2b study of 202 patients with invasive fungal disease and few or no options, olorofim's strict global response rate was 28.7% at day 42 (75.2% if stable disease is counted as success — both definitions are carded, and must travel together), with all-cause mortality of 11.9% at day 42 and 16.3% at day 84. A French compassionate-use cohort (n = 17) found success in 5 of 15 evaluable patients. PREMISE CORRECTION: the question as posed included Mucorales, but olorofim has no Mucorales activity and no Mucorales patients were studied — its spectrum covers Aspergillus (including azole-resistant strains), Lomentospora, Scedosporium and Coccidioides. Liver enzyme elevations occurred in about 10%. With no comparator, benefit magnitude is unknowable from these data; the stamp is POSSIBLE, never LIKELY.

cards.headline: Maertens 2025 (phase 2b, SINGLE-ARM, no comparator — printed on the face): olorofim global response 28.7% at day 42 by the strict definition, 75.2% counting stable disease; mortality 11.9% at day 42
cards.summary: Maertens 2025 (phase 2b, SINGLE-ARM, no comparator — printed on the face): olorofim global response 28.7% at day 42 by the strict definition, 75.2% counting stable disease; mortality 11.9% at day 42
cards.type: Single-arm open-label phase 2b study (NO comparator), Lancet Infect Dis 2025
cards.people: 202 patients (203 treated) aged ≥16 years with proven invasive fungal disease or probable invasive pulmonary aspergillosis and few or no treatment options, at 22 centres in 11 countries; open-label oral olorofim for up to 84 days plus extended therapy as needed. Pathogens: Aspergillus spp 101 (including 22 azole-resistant), Lomentospora prolificans 26, Scedosporium spp 22, Coccidioides spp 41, other fungi 12. NO MUCORALES — olorofim has no Mucorales activity and none were treated. SINGLE-ARM: there is no randomised or concurrent comparator.
cards.result: Successful global response (complete/partial improvement in clinical, radiological and mycological components, data-review-committee adjudicated) was 58/202 (28.7%, 95% CI 22.6–35.5) at day 42 and 27.2% at day 84. Counting stable disease as success, the figures were 75.2% at day 42 and 63.4% at day 84; clinical-component response alone was 59.9% at day 42. All-cause mortality was 11.9% (24 patients) at day 42 and 16.3% at day 84. Medically significant liver enzyme elevations at least possibly due to olorofim occurred in 20/203 (10%) and gastrointestinal intolerance in 20 (10%); there were no treatment-related deaths.
cards.watchOut: Every number here is uncontrolled: in patients with no options, a 28.7% strict response rate cannot be separated from what supportive care or natural history would have produced, and the flattering 75.2% figure depends on counting stable disease as success. Both definitions are printed — quote them together or not at all.

cards.headline: Maertens 2026: within the SAME single-arm phase 2b study, adding an azole did not visibly worsen olorofim outcomes (aspergillosis: 77 without azole vs 24 with)
cards.summary: Maertens 2026: within the SAME single-arm phase 2b study, adding an azole did not visibly worsen olorofim outcomes (aspergillosis: 77 without azole vs 24 with)
cards.type: Within-study subgroup analysis of a single-arm phase 2 study (no comparator), J Antimicrob Chemother 2026
cards.people: Subgroup analysis of the same phase 2b salvage study population (NCT03583164, carded above — not an independent cohort): patients with aspergillosis (77 not receiving an azole, 24 receiving one), coccidioidomycosis (11 vs 30) and other fungal infections (50 vs 10), comparing outcomes with and without concomitant azole therapy.
cards.result: Outcomes at days 42 and 84 — MSG-EORTC responses and all-cause mortality — were similar for olorofim with and without a concomitant azole (mould-active or fluconazole), and the rate of drug-induced liver injury was not increased with combination therapy, despite preclinical unidirectional antagonism in which azoles reduced olorofim's effect against Aspergillus fumigatus. The authors state the analyses are limited by study size.
cards.watchOut: Same patients as the card above — this is not corroboration. Subgroups as small as 10–24 patients cannot exclude the preclinical antagonism; 'no pattern seen' is not 'no interaction'.

cards.headline: French compassionate-use cohort 2026: 17 patients with refractory non-Mucorales mould infection — 5/15 evaluable achieved clinical and mycological success; 3-month mortality 29.4%
cards.summary: French compassionate-use cohort 2026: 17 patients with refractory non-Mucorales mould infection — 5/15 evaluable achieved clinical and mycological success; 3-month mortality 29.4%
cards.type: Retrospective observational compassionate-use cohort (n = 17), Open Forum Infect Dis 2026
cards.people: 17 patients (median age 39 years) treated with olorofim under compassionate use in France, 2020–2023, for proven or probable non-Mucorales invasive mould infections refractory to, or with intolerance/no options on, standard antifungals; median prior antifungal therapy 9.1 months. Retrospective multicentre cohort. Small N — printed on the face.
cards.result: Among 15 evaluable patients, 5 (33.3%) achieved clinical and mycological success, 7 (46.7%) had partial responses and 3 (20%) failed treatment. Three-month mortality was 29.4% (5/17). Olorofim was combined with other antifungals in 82.4% of cases, and no severe adverse events were reported.
cards.watchOut: Seventeen highly selected patients, most on combination therapy — outcomes cannot be attributed to olorofim alone, and compassionate-use cohorts systematically differ from trial populations.

cards.headline: Synthesis: single-arm evidence only — a real response signal in no-option mould disease, with no comparator to measure it against
cards.summary: Synthesis: single-arm evidence only — a real response signal in no-option mould disease, with no comparator to measure it against
cards.people: Patients with invasive mould disease and few or no options, from the single-arm phase 2b study (n = 202), its azole-combination subgroup analysis (same patients) and a French compassionate-use cohort (n = 17) carded above. PREMISE CORRECTION: the question as posed included Mucorales — olorofim is not active against Mucorales and no Mucorales patients appear in any carded study; its spectrum is Aspergillus (including azole-resistant), Lomentospora, Scedosporium and dimorphic fungi such as Coccidioides.
cards.result: Strict global response was 28.7% at day 42 in the phase 2b study, with day-42 mortality of 11.9% in a population whose expected mortality is high but unmeasured here; the small French cohort is directionally consistent (33.3% success in evaluable patients). There is no randomised comparator anywhere in this evidence base, so no relative benefit can be stated and the stamp can be no higher than POSSIBLE. Liver enzyme elevations in about 10% are the main tolerability signal. A phase 3 comparison is what this question still needs.
cards.watchOut: Never present the 75.2% 'response including stable disease' figure without the 28.7% strict figure beside it, and never imply Mucorales coverage — the drug has none.
cards.source: Synthesis of the carded records above (PMIDs 40541222, 41914555, 41531505). Registry ID: NCT03583164. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

shelves.title: Oral sulopenem (Orlynvah) for uncomplicated UTI: superior in ciprofloxacin-resistant infection, noninferior overall — not for complicated UTI
shelves.question: In women with uncomplicated urinary tract infection, is oral sulopenem etzadroxil plus probenecid non-inferior to nitrofurantoin (or ciprofloxacin in susceptible infection) for composite clinical/microbiological response?
shelves.mesh: Urinary Tract Infections · Anti-Bacterial Agents · Lactams · Female · Humans
shelves.balance: Oral sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid (Orlynvah — product named under the clarification exception; FDA approval October 2024, for uncomplicated UTI in adult women with limited or no alternative oral options) rests on two phase 3 trials with a split pattern. SURE-1 (n = 1,671, vs ciprofloxacin): superior where the pathogen was ciprofloxacin-resistant (overall success 62.6% vs 36.0%), but it FAILED noninferiority where the pathogen was susceptible (66.8% vs 78.6%), driven by asymptomatic bacteriuria. REASSURE (n = 2,222, vs amoxicillin–clavulanate): noninferior overall (60.9% vs 55.6%). The programme's complicated-UTI trial failed noninferiority (67.8% vs 73.9% vs ertapenem step-down) — the licence is uncomplicated UTI only. PREMISE NOTE: no published nitrofurantoin-comparator trial exists in PubMed; the tested comparators are ciprofloxacin and amoxicillin–clavulanate. Diarrhoea 8–12% is the main cost. Single programme, mixed subgroup verdicts: POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: SURE-1 (Dunne 2023): sulopenem beat ciprofloxacin where the pathogen was ciprofloxacin-resistant (62.6% vs 36.0%) but FAILED noninferiority where it was susceptible (66.8% vs 78.6%)
cards.summary: SURE-1 (Dunne 2023): sulopenem beat ciprofloxacin where the pathogen was ciprofloxacin-resistant (62.6% vs 36.0%) but FAILED noninferiority where it was susceptible (66.8% vs 78.6%)
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised double-blind trial (SURE-1), Clin Infect Dis 2023
cards.people: 1,671 adult women with uncomplicated UTI randomised (total from the trial's full text; the abstract record does not print it) to 5 days of oral sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid or 3 days of ciprofloxacin. Primary endpoint: overall success (clinical + microbiological response) at day 12, tested hierarchically — superiority in the ciprofloxacin-nonsusceptible population, noninferiority in the susceptible population.
cards.result: In the ciprofloxacin-nonsusceptible population, sulopenem was superior: overall success 62.6% vs 36.0% (difference 26.6 percentage points; P < .001). In the ciprofloxacin-susceptible population, sulopenem was NOT noninferior: 66.8% vs 78.6% (difference −11.8 points), driven by more post-treatment asymptomatic bacteriuria on sulopenem. In the combined population it was noninferior: 65.6% vs 67.9% (difference −2.3; 95% CI −7.9 to 3.3). Diarrhoea was commoner on sulopenem (12.4% vs 2.5%).
cards.watchOut: The two subgroup verdicts point opposite ways and both are real: this drug's value is precisely in resistant infection, and in susceptible infection it lost on a composite driven by asymptomatic bacteriuria — a laboratory endpoint whose clinical meaning is contested. (The abstract record prints internally inconsistent confidence limits for the subgroup differences; the percentages, differences and P value above are as printed.)
cards.source: Dunne MW, Aronin SI, Das AF, Akinapelli K, Zelasky MT, Puttagunta S, et al. cards.headline: REASSURE 2025: sulopenem was noninferior to amoxicillin–clavulanate overall (60.9% vs 55.6%) — the trial that carried the approval
cards.summary: REASSURE 2025: sulopenem was noninferior to amoxicillin–clavulanate overall (60.9% vs 55.6%) — the trial that carried the approval
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised double-blind noninferiority trial (REASSURE), NEJM Evid 2025
cards.people: 2,222 women with uncomplicated UTI randomised (median age 51 years) to 5 days of sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid or 5 days of amoxicillin–clavulanate, double-blind. Primary endpoint: overall success (clinical cure + microbiological eradication) by day 12 in the microbiologic-modified ITT population (positive baseline culture ≥10⁵ CFU/mL of an Enterobacterales uropathogen).
cards.result: Overall success was 318/522 (60.9%) on sulopenem vs 260/468 (55.6%) on amoxicillin–clavulanate (difference 5.4 percentage points, 95% CI −0.8 to 11.5), meeting noninferiority. In the amoxicillin–clavulanate-susceptible population: 61.7% vs 55.0% (difference 6.7; 0.3 to 13.0). In the small non-susceptible population (42 vs 25 patients): 52.4% vs 68.0% (difference −15.6; −37.5 to 9.1). Adverse events were commoner on sulopenem, including diarrhoea (8.1% vs 4.1%), nausea (4.3% vs 2.9%) and headache (2.2% vs 1.5%).
cards.watchOut: Noninferiority on a composite whose success rates are only ~55–61% in both arms — much of the 'failure' is microbiological, not symptomatic. The non-susceptible subgroup was tiny (67 patients) and numerically favoured the comparator; do not cite REASSURE as evidence for resistant infection — that is SURE-1's resistant-population result.
cards.source: Puttagunta S, Aronin SI, Gupta J, Das AF, Gupta K, Dunne MW, et al. Sulopenem versus Amoxicillin/Clavulanate for the Treatment of Uncomplicated Urinary Tract Infection. cards.headline: SURE cUTI trial (Dunne 2023): in complicated UTI, sulopenem step-down FAILED noninferiority vs ertapenem step-down (67.8% vs 73.9%) — why the approval is for uncomplicated UTI only
cards.summary: SURE cUTI trial (Dunne 2023): in complicated UTI, sulopenem step-down FAILED noninferiority vs ertapenem step-down (67.8% vs 73.9%) — why the approval is for uncomplicated UTI only
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised trial in complicated UTI (SURE programme), Clin Infect Dis 2023
cards.people: 1,392 hospitalised adults with complicated UTI including pyelonephritis randomised to 5 days of IV sulopenem then oral sulopenem etzadroxil/probenecid, or 5 days of IV ertapenem then oral ciprofloxacin or amoxicillin–clavulanate by susceptibility; 444 (sulopenem) and 440 (ertapenem) patients formed the primary efficacy population. ESBL producers in 26.6%, fluoroquinolone-nonsusceptible pathogens in 38.6%. Programme context card — a different (complicated) syndrome from this shelf's question.
cards.result: For the primary endpoint (overall clinical + microbiological response at day 21 test-of-cure), noninferiority was NOT demonstrated: 67.8% vs 73.9% (difference −6.1 percentage points, 95% CI −12.0 to −0.1), again driven by asymptomatic bacteriuria rates in the ertapenem patients who stepped down to ciprofloxacin. No substantial difference was seen at other time points, and both IV and oral sulopenem were well tolerated.
cards.watchOut: Carded deliberately as the programme's negative result: anyone generalising sulopenem from uncomplicated to complicated UTI is going beyond both the trial evidence and the licence (Orlynvah is approved for uncomplicated UTI in adult women with limited or no alternative oral options).
cards.source: Dunne MW, Aronin SI, Das AF, Akinapelli K, Breen J, Zelasky MT, et al. cards.headline: Synthesis: an oral penem whose proven niche is resistant uncomplicated UTI — with two failed noninferiority tests on the record
cards.summary: Synthesis: an oral penem whose proven niche is resistant uncomplicated UTI — with two failed noninferiority tests on the record
cards.people: Adult women with uncomplicated UTI in SURE-1 (n = 1,671, vs ciprofloxacin) and REASSURE (n = 2,222, vs amoxicillin–clavulanate), plus the programme's complicated-UTI trial (n = 1,392) carded for context. The product is marketed as Orlynvah (named under the tested-product clarification exception). PREMISE NOTE: the question as posed named nitrofurantoin as a comparator — no published sulopenem-vs-nitrofurantoin trial was found in PubMed this session; the published comparators are ciprofloxacin and amoxicillin–clavulanate.
cards.result: The pattern is consistent: sulopenem is noninferior overall in uncomplicated UTI and clearly superior when the pathogen is ciprofloxacin-resistant (62.6% vs 36.0%), but it failed noninferiority in ciprofloxacin-susceptible infection and in complicated UTI — both times on asymptomatic-bacteriuria components of composite endpoints. Diarrhoea is its price (8–12%). A single sponsor programme with mixed subgroup verdicts caps the stamp at POSSIBLE: a genuinely useful oral option where resistance closes the standard options, not a first-line replacement where they remain open.
cards.watchOut: Composite endpoints dominated by post-treatment bacteriuria cut both ways: they made sulopenem look worse in susceptible infection and may understate its clinical (symptom) performance — judge it on the resistant niche, where the difference was large and clinical.
cards.source: Synthesis of the carded records above (PMIDs 36069202, 40552968, 36068705). Registry ID: NCT03354598 / NCT05584657 / NCT03357614 (programme). MeSH: not captured from the record this session

shelves.title: Cefepime–enmetazobactam (Exblifep) in complicated UTI: 79.1% vs 58.9% composite success vs piperacillin–tazobactam in one phase 3 trial
shelves.question: In adults with complicated urinary tract infection (including acute pyelonephritis), is cefepime–enmetazobactam non-inferior to piperacillin–tazobactam for composite cure?
shelves.mesh: Cefepime · beta-Lactamase Inhibitors · Urinary Tract Infections · Pyelonephritis · Humans
shelves.balance: One phase 3 trial carries this question, and it is a strong one: ALCHEMIST (1,041 adults with complicated UTI or acute pyelonephritis, double-blind) found overall treatment success — clinical cure combined with microbiological eradication — in 79.1% on cefepime–enmetazobactam (Exblifep; product named under the clarification exception) vs 58.9% on piperacillin–tazobactam (difference 21.2 percentage points, 95% CI 14.3–27.9), meeting both its −10% noninferiority margin and its prespecified superiority test on that composite. Adverse events were somewhat commoner on the new drug (50.0% vs 44.0%). Support beyond the trial is indirect: a 28-trial network meta-analysis ranks it ahead of carbapenems on composite/eradication endpoints, and a 20-volunteer study shows lung penetration (pharmacology, not efficacy). The record does not split the composite, so the 21-point gap must not be read as a clinical-cure gap. Single trial: POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: ALCHEMIST (Kaye/Belley 2022): cefepime–enmetazobactam beat piperacillin–tazobactam on the composite cure endpoint, 79.1% vs 58.9% — noninferiority AND superiority met, n = 1,041
cards.summary: ALCHEMIST (Kaye/Belley 2022): cefepime–enmetazobactam beat piperacillin–tazobactam on the composite cure endpoint, 79.1% vs 58.9% — noninferiority AND superiority met, n = 1,041
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised double-blind noninferiority trial (ALCHEMIST), JAMA 2022
cards.people: 1,041 adults (mean age 54.7 years; 55.0% women) with complicated UTI or acute pyelonephritis from gram-negative pathogens, at 90 sites, randomised double-blind to cefepime 2 g/enmetazobactam 0.5 g or piperacillin 4 g/tazobactam 0.5 g, 2-hour infusions every 8 hours for 7 days (up to 14 with bacteraemia). Primary outcome: overall treatment success (clinical cure + microbiological eradication <10³ CFU/mL) in the primary analysis set (345 vs 333 patients).
cards.result: Overall success was 79.1% (273/345) on cefepime–enmetazobactam vs 58.9% (196/333) on piperacillin–tazobactam — between-group difference 21.2 percentage points (95% CI 14.3 to 27.9), meeting the −10% noninferiority margin and the prespecified superiority test on this composite endpoint. Treatment-emergent adverse events occurred in 50.0% (258/516) vs 44.0% (228/518), mostly mild to moderate; discontinuation for adverse events was 1.7% vs 0.8%.
cards.watchOut: Superiority was on the composite of clinical cure PLUS microbiological eradication; the abstract record does not split the components, and eradication endpoints typically drive such gaps — do not read this as a 21-point advantage in how patients feel or fare. One trial, however clean, caps the stamp.
cards.source: Kaye KS, Belley A, Barth P, Lahlou O, Knechtle P, Motta P, et al. Effect of Cefepime/Enmetazobactam vs Piperacillin/Tazobactam on Clinical Cure and Microbiological Eradication in Patients With Complicated Urinary Tract Infection or Acute Pyelonephritis: A Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA. 2022. PMID: 36194218. Registry ID: NCT03687255. cards.headline: Wagenlehner 2025 network meta-analysis: across 28 cUTI trials, cefepime–enmetazobactam ranked ahead of carbapenems on composite and eradication endpoints (indirect evidence)
cards.summary: Wagenlehner 2025 network meta-analysis: across 28 cUTI trials, cefepime–enmetazobactam ranked ahead of carbapenems on composite and eradication endpoints (indirect evidence)
cards.type: Systematic review and Bayesian network meta-analysis (indirect comparisons), J Comp Eff Res 2025
cards.people: Systematic literature review of randomised trials in complicated UTI/acute pyelonephritis (40 trials assessed; 28 in the master Bayesian network meta-analysis, fixed-effects model), comparing established and novel agents including cefepime–enmetazobactam, with carbapenems as a reference node. Outcomes: composite response, microbiological eradication and clinical cure at test-of-cure.
cards.result: For the composite outcome at test-of-cure, cefepime + enmetazobactam (with ceftolozane + tazobactam, cefiderocol, levofloxacin and plazomicin) showed significantly higher relative risks versus carbapenems; for microbiological eradication it was among the agents significantly ahead of carbapenems, and its relative risks were also significantly higher than several established and novel comparators across composite, eradication and clinical-cure endpoints. The authors frame it as a potentially effective carbapenem-sparing option. (The abstract record prints directions and significance, not the numerical relative risks.)
cards.watchOut: Network estimates are indirect and inherit every included trial's biases; rankings among modern agents in such networks are fragile and are not a substitute for a head-to-head trial. This card supports, and cannot extend, the ALCHEMIST result.
cards.source: Wagenlehner F, Caballero VR, Maheshwari V, Biswas A, Saini P, Quevedo J, et al. cards.headline: Das 2020: in 20 healthy volunteers, cefepime and enmetazobactam reached lung epithelial lining fluid at ~61% and ~53% of plasma concentrations (pharmacokinetic card — not efficacy)
cards.summary: Das 2020: in 20 healthy volunteers, cefepime and enmetazobactam reached lung epithelial lining fluid at ~61% and ~53% of plasma concentrations (pharmacokinetic card — not efficacy)
cards.type: Human pharmacokinetic study in healthy volunteers (n = 20), Antimicrob Agents Chemother 2020
cards.people: 20 healthy volunteers given cefepime–enmetazobactam 2 g/1 g every 8 hours intravenously, with serial plasma sampling and one bronchoalveolar lavage per volunteer for epithelial lining fluid (ELF) concentrations; population PK modelling with Monte Carlo simulation against preclinical pharmacodynamic targets.
cards.result: Mean ELF partitioning was 60.59% ± 28.62% for cefepime and 53.03% ± 21.05% for enmetazobactam relative to plasma. Simulation of the licensed-style regimen (2 g/0.5 g every 8 hours over 2 hours) gave ≥90% probability of target attainment for Enterobacterales with MICs ≤8 mg/L — the authors' rationale for studying the combination in nosocomial pneumonia.
cards.watchOut: Healthy-volunteer lung penetration is pharmacology, not patient evidence: it says nothing about curing pneumonia or UTI, and the simulated dose differed from the regimen tested in ALCHEMIST. Carded as programme support only.
cards.source: Das S, Fitzgerald R, Ullah A, Bula M, Collins AM, Mitsi E, et al. Intrapulmonary Pharmacokinetics of Cefepime and Enmetazobactam in Healthy Volunteers: Towards New Treatments for Nosocomial Pneumonia. Antimicrobial Agents and Chemotherapy. 2020. PMID: 33077666. Registry ID: none printed in the record.
