cards.headline: Synthesis: one strong trial in cUTI — noninferior and composite-superior to piperacillin–tazobactam, with indirect and PK support only
cards.summary: Synthesis: one strong trial in cUTI — noninferior and composite-superior to piperacillin–tazobactam, with indirect and PK support only
cards.people: Adults with complicated UTI or acute pyelonephritis, from the ALCHEMIST phase 3 trial (n = 1,041), a 28-trial network meta-analysis and a 20-volunteer PK study carded above. The product is marketed as Exblifep (named under the tested-product clarification exception).
cards.result: ALCHEMIST is a well-executed double-blind trial whose composite result (79.1% vs 58.9%; difference 21.2 points, 95% CI 14.3–27.9) cleared both noninferiority and prespecified superiority against a standard agent — the strongest single-trial result in this wave's antibiotic packs. But it remains ONE trial, the superiority sits on a composite with a microbiological component the record does not split out, and everything else carded is indirect (network meta-analysis) or pharmacological (healthy-volunteer PK). Single-trial discipline caps the stamp at POSSIBLE, with the carbapenem-sparing role in ESBL-type infection its clearest use.
cards.watchOut: Do not quote the 21.2-point difference as a clinical-cure advantage: it is a composite with microbiological eradication, and no mortality or length-of-stay benefit is shown anywhere in this evidence base.
cards.source: Synthesis of the carded records above (PMIDs 36194218, 39817442, 33077666). Registry ID: NCT03687255. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

shelves.title: Intravenous peramivir: futility-stopped and unproven in hospitalised influenza — licensed on outpatient data
shelves.question: In patients with influenza who cannot take oral/oseltamivir therapy, does intravenous peramivir improve time to clinical stability versus placebo or oseltamivir?
shelves.mesh: Influenza, Human · Antiviral Agents · Guanidines · Hospitalization · Humans
shelves.balance: The honest answer is split by setting, and this pack keeps the halves separate. In HOSPITALISED influenza — the setting IV therapy exists for — peramivir is unproven: the pivotal placebo-controlled phase 3 trial (de Jong 2014) was terminated for futility after its interim analysis (median time to clinical resolution 42.5 vs 49.5 hours, P = .97 — the treatment made no difference), and the other hospitalised study (234 patients, 2009 pandemic) compared two doses with no control arm. In OUTPATIENT uncomplicated influenza, a single IV dose beat placebo on time to symptom alleviation (Kohno 2010, n = 300) and was noninferior to 5 days of oral oseltamivir (Kohno 2011, n = 1,091) — that outpatient evidence is what the licence rests on. For a hospitalised patient who cannot take oral/oseltamivir therapy, peramivir is a route choice extrapolated from outpatients, not a proven hospital treatment: MAYBE (weak evidence).

cards.headline: de Jong 2014: the pivotal hospitalised-influenza trial was STOPPED FOR FUTILITY — peramivir 42.5 h vs placebo 49.5 h to clinical resolution, P = .97 (the treatment made no difference)
cards.summary: de Jong 2014: the pivotal hospitalised-influenza trial was STOPPED FOR FUTILITY — peramivir 42.5 h vs placebo 49.5 h to clinical resolution, P = .97 (the treatment made no difference)
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised placebo-controlled trial in hospitalised influenza — terminated for futility, Clin Infect Dis 2014
cards.people: Patients hospitalised with suspected influenza randomised to 5 days of IV peramivir 600 mg once daily or placebo, all receiving institutional standard of care; influenza confirmed in 338 of 405 enrolled. The primary efficacy population at the preplanned interim analysis was 121 patients who had not received a concurrent neuraminidase inhibitor as part of standard care.
cards.result: Median time to clinical resolution was 42.5 hours (95% CI 34.0–57.9) on peramivir vs 49.5 hours (40.0–61.9) on placebo (P = .97 — the treatment made no difference on the primary endpoint). Viral shedding fell somewhat more on peramivir, not significantly. A larger effect was described in patients treated within 48 hours of symptoms or in ICU, but the trial was terminated for futility at the interim analysis, so those subgroups are hypothesis-generating only. Adverse events were similar between groups.
cards.watchOut: This is the honest centre of the peramivir story: the one placebo-controlled test in the population IV therapy is for failed its primary endpoint and was stopped. Most hospitalised patients in real practice also receive standard-of-care neuraminidase inhibitors, shrinking any measurable added effect further.
cards.source: de Jong MD, Ison MG, Monto AS, Metev H, Clark C, O'Neil B, et al. Evaluation of intravenous peramivir for treatment of influenza in hospitalized patients. cards.headline: Ison 2013 (2009 pandemic): 234 hospitalised patients randomised between two peramivir doses — viral titres fell, with no placebo arm and no difference between doses
cards.summary: Ison 2013 (2009 pandemic): 234 hospitalised patients randomised between two peramivir doses — viral titres fell, with no placebo arm and no difference between doses
cards.type: Randomised dose-comparison trial in hospitalised influenza (no placebo), Antivir Ther 2014
cards.people: 234 hospitalised patients (≥6 years) during the 2009 H1N1 pandemic, randomised open-label to peramivir 300 mg twice daily or 600 mg once daily for 5–10 days; 127 had laboratory-confirmed influenza. Primary endpoint was virological (change in tissue culture infective dose); clinical endpoints included time to clinical resolution.
cards.result: In patients with detectable virus at baseline, viral titres declined on both regimens with no differences between them, and there were no significant differences in clinical or virological endpoints between arms; apparent differences were explained by baseline severity imbalance. Peramivir was generally safe and well tolerated. With no placebo or standard-care-only arm, the study cannot show peramivir changed any outcome — only that patients improved while receiving it.
cards.watchOut: A dose-comparison with no untreated arm is a safety/virology study. Citing it as evidence peramivir 'works' in hospitalised patients is the classic uncontrolled-improvement error.
cards.source: Ison MG, Fraiz J, Heller B, Jauregui L, Mills G, O'Riordan W, et al. Intravenous peramivir for treatment of influenza in hospitalized patients. Antiviral Therapy. 2014. PMID: 23985625. cards.headline: Kohno 2010: in OUTPATIENTS, a single IV peramivir dose shortened symptom duration vs placebo (hazard ratios 0.681 and 0.666 as printed in the record) — the data the licence rests on
cards.summary: Kohno 2010: in OUTPATIENTS, a single IV peramivir dose shortened symptom duration vs placebo (hazard ratios 0.681 and 0.666 as printed in the record) — the data the licence rests on
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised placebo-controlled trial in outpatients, Antimicrob Agents Chemother 2010
cards.people: 300 previously healthy adults aged 20–64 years with rapid-antigen-positive uncomplicated seasonal influenza, recruited within 48 hours of symptom onset and randomised to a single IV infusion of peramivir 300 mg, peramivir 600 mg or placebo; 296 formed the intent-to-treat infected population.
cards.result: Peramivir significantly reduced the time to alleviation of symptoms at both doses versus placebo (hazard ratio 0.681 for 300 mg and 0.666 for 600 mg, as printed in the record; adjusted P = 0.0092 for both comparisons). No serious adverse events were reported, and the adverse-event profile resembled placebo. This is an outpatient, uncomplicated-influenza result in healthy adults — a different population from the hospitalised patients of the cards above.
cards.watchOut: Effective in healthy outpatients treated within 48 hours says little about patients sick enough to be hospitalised, who are typically older, comorbid and later in their illness — precisely the extrapolation the hospitalised trial then failed to confirm.
cards.source: Kohno S, Kida H, Mizuguchi M, Shimada J, et al. Efficacy and safety of intravenous peramivir for treatment of seasonal influenza virus infection. Antimicrobial Agents and Chemotherapy. 2010. PMID: 20713668. Registry ID: none printed in the record. cards.headline: Kohno 2011: single-dose IV peramivir was noninferior to 5 days of oral oseltamivir in outpatients (symptoms 78.0 / 81.0 vs 81.8 hours), n = 1,091
cards.summary: Kohno 2011: single-dose IV peramivir was noninferior to 5 days of oral oseltamivir in outpatients (symptoms 78.0 / 81.0 vs 81.8 hours), n = 1,091
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised double-blind noninferiority trial in outpatients, Antimicrob Agents Chemother 2011
cards.people: 1,091 patients aged ≥20 years with influenza A or B in South Korea, Japan and Taiwan, randomised double-blind double-dummy to a single IV peramivir infusion (300 mg, n = 364; or 600 mg, n = 362) or oral oseltamivir 75 mg twice daily for 5 days (n = 365); intent-to-treat infected population.
cards.result: Median symptom durations were 78.0 hours (300 mg peramivir), 81.0 hours (600 mg) and 81.8 hours (oseltamivir). Hazard ratios vs oseltamivir were 0.946 (97.5% CI 0.793–1.129) and 0.970 (0.814–1.157); both peramivir doses met the noninferiority criterion (upper confidence limit < 1.170). Adverse drug reactions were less frequent in the 300 mg group, with no difference in severe reactions.
cards.watchOut: Again outpatients. Noninferiority to oseltamivir in uncomplicated influenza supports the IV route as an alternative when oral therapy is impossible — it does not rescue the failed hospitalised-patient question.

cards.headline: Synthesis: unproven in hospitalised patients, licensed on outpatient data — the two halves must not be merged
cards.summary: Synthesis: unproven in hospitalised patients, licensed on outpatient data — the two halves must not be merged
cards.people: Patients with influenza across four randomised trials carded above: two in hospitalised patients (n = 405 enrolled and n = 234, neither showing benefit over control) and two in outpatients (n = 300 vs placebo; n = 1,091 vs oseltamivir, both positive).
cards.result: The honest framing, as the evidence forces it: intravenous peramivir shortens symptoms in uncomplicated outpatient influenza (vs placebo) and matches oseltamivir there — that is what it is licensed on. In hospitalised patients, the pivotal placebo-controlled trial was stopped for futility with P = .97 on its primary endpoint (the treatment made no difference), and the other hospitalised study had no control arm. For a hospitalised patient who cannot take oral therapy, peramivir is a route-of-administration choice resting on outpatient evidence, not a treatment of proven benefit in that setting. MAYBE (weak evidence) for the hospitalised question as posed.
cards.watchOut: Subgroup whispers from the futility-stopped trial (earlier treatment, ICU patients) are not evidence; they are the standard residue of a negative trial and should be labelled as such wherever they are quoted.
cards.source: Synthesis of the carded records above (PMIDs 25115871, 23985625, 20713668, 21825298). Registry ID: NCT00958776 / NCT00957996 (hospitalised trials). MeSH: not captured from the record this session

shelves.title: Cell-based influenza vaccine (Flucelvax) vs egg-based: a possible small relative edge in observational data — hospitalisation benefit unproven
shelves.question: In adults, does cell-culture-based quadrivalent influenza vaccine (Flucelvax) prevent more laboratory-confirmed influenza and influenza hospitalisations than egg-based vaccines?
shelves.mesh: Influenza Vaccines · Influenza, Human · Cell Culture Techniques · Vaccine Efficacy · Humans
shelves.balance: OBSERVATIONAL ONLY — test-negative designs throughout, no randomised head-to-head trial exists; capped at POSSIBLE and labelled. The cell-culture quadrivalent vaccine (Flucelvax — product named because the question is product-specific) avoids egg-adaptation of the seed virus, and one large 3-season EHR/claims analysis (Stein 2024) found a consistent RELATIVE advantage over egg-based quadrivalent vaccine against test-confirmed outpatient influenza: rVE 14.8%, 12.5% and 10.0% across 2017–2020 (relative measures — not percentage-point gains). But the CDC US Flu VE Network's product-specific analysis (2014–2019) found relative VE not statistically significant, with absolute VE of 30% for each product, and the single hospitalisation study (Kaiser, 2017–2018) found non-significant relative estimates (43% under 65; 6% at 65+, CI −46 to 39). A modest relative edge in some datasets is possible; a hospitalisation advantage is unproven.

cards.headline: Stein 2024: over 3 seasons, cell-based vaccine beat egg-based on test-confirmed influenza by a RELATIVE 14.8%, 12.5% and 10.0% (test-negative, ages 4–64)
cards.summary: Stein 2024: over 3 seasons, cell-based vaccine beat egg-based on test-confirmed influenza by a RELATIVE 14.8%, 12.5% and 10.0% (test-negative, ages 4–64)
cards.type: Retrospective test-negative observational study (3 seasons), Open Forum Infect Dis 2024
cards.people: Retrospective test-negative study of people aged 4–64 years tested for influenza during routine outpatient care for acute respiratory/febrile illness in the US, using linked electronic health records and claims: 31,824 patients in 2017–2018, 33,388 in 2018–2019 and 34,398 in 2019–2020; about 10% had received cell-based quadrivalent vaccine (Flucelvax) and 90% egg-based quadrivalent vaccine. Doubly robust adjustment (inverse probability weighting plus regression).
cards.result: Relative vaccine effectiveness (rVE) of cell-based vs egg-based vaccine against test-confirmed influenza was 14.8% (95% CI 7.0–22.0) in 2017–2018, 12.5% (4.7–19.6) in 2018–2019 and 10.0% (2.7–16.7) in 2019–2020 — consistent, modest RELATIVE advantages (relative reductions in the odds of test-positive influenza among vaccinees, not absolute percentage-point gains in protection).
cards.watchOut: Observational and industry-linked by design (EHR/claims, ~10% cell-vaccine share): residual confounding by who receives which product is the standing threat, and a 10–15% relative edge is small enough for such confounding to manufacture. Read against the CDC-network card below, which found no significant difference.
cards.source: Stein AN, Mills CW, McGovern I, McDermott KW, Dean A, Bogdanov AN, et al. Relative Vaccine Effectiveness of Cell- vs Egg-Based Quadrivalent Influenza Vaccine Against Test-Confirmed Influenza Over 3 Seasons Between 2017 and 2020 in the United States. cards.headline: Bruxvoort 2019: against influenza HOSPITALISATION in 2017–2018, cell-based vaccine's relative advantage was 43% under 65 and 6% at 65+ — neither statistically significant (the difference made no proven difference)
cards.summary: Bruxvoort 2019: against influenza HOSPITALISATION in 2017–2018, cell-based vaccine's relative advantage was 43% under 65 and 6% at 65+ — neither statistically significant (the difference made no proven difference)
cards.people: Test-negative case-control study at Kaiser Permanente Southern California in the severe 2017–2018 season: 1,186 hospitalised cases with laboratory-confirmed influenza and 6,946 controls; 74% of cases and 59% of controls were aged ≥65 years.
cards.result: Adjusted relative VE of cell-based vs egg-based vaccine against influenza hospitalisation was 43% (95% CI −45 to 77) for patients under 65 and 6% (−46 to 39) for those 65 and older; for influenza A(H3N2) hospitalisation it was 61% (−63 to 91) under 65 and −4% (−70 to 37) at 65+. No comparison was statistically significant — on the outcome that matters most (hospitalisation), in the age group that fills hospitals, the point estimate was 6% with an interval spanning harm to substantial benefit.
cards.watchOut: One season, one health system, and very wide intervals — this study cannot exclude a real hospitalisation benefit either. Its role on this shelf is to show the hospitalisation claim is unproven, not disproven.
cards.source: Bruxvoort KJ, Luo Y, Ackerson B, Tanenbaum HC, Sy LS, Gandhi A, et al. Comparison of vaccine effectiveness against influenza hospitalization of cell-based and egg-based influenza vaccines, 2017-2018. Vaccine. 2019. PMID: 31445771. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: US Flu VE Network 2026: across 2014–2019, cell-based and egg-based quadrivalent vaccines protected similarly — relative VE not statistically significant; absolute VE 30% for each in the head-to-head seasons
cards.summary: US Flu VE Network 2026: across 2014–2019, cell-based and egg-based quadrivalent vaccines protected similarly — relative VE not statistically significant; absolute VE 30% for each in the head-to-head seasons
cards.type: Observational test-negative study (CDC US Flu VE Network), Clin Infect Dis 2026
cards.people: Outpatients enrolled in the US Influenza Vaccine Effectiveness (Flu VE) Network over five seasons (2014–2015 to 2018–2019), test-negative design with multivariable logistic regression; product-specific absolute VE estimated across seasons, and relative VE of cell-culture quadrivalent vaccine (Flucelvax Quadrivalent) vs egg-based quadrivalent products estimated over 2017–2019 in participants aged ≥4 years.
cards.result: Absolute VE against symptomatic laboratory-confirmed outpatient influenza was 30% for the cell-based product and 30% for the egg-based comparator product in the pooled head-to-head seasons (across the wider seasons, egg-based Fluarix VE was 32% and Fluzone 37%). The relative VE estimates were not statistically significant, indicating similar protection across products; VE was lowest against A(H3N2) and in patients aged ≥50 years for all products.
cards.watchOut: The most independent dataset on this shelf found no significant relative advantage — the tension with the positive EHR/claims analyses is the story of this shelf, and it is unresolved. Product-specific VE also pools different egg-based brands, which can dilute or invent contrasts.
cards.source: Gaglani M, Raiyani C, Murthy K, Smith M, da Graca B, Dubrocq G, et al. cards.headline: Synthesis: a small relative edge in some observational datasets, none in the CDC network, and hospitalisation unproven — observational evidence caps this at POSSIBLE
cards.summary: Synthesis: a small relative edge in some observational datasets, none in the CDC network, and hospitalisation unproven — observational evidence caps this at POSSIBLE
cards.people: Adults and children aged ≥4 years in three test-negative observational studies carded above (a 3-season EHR/claims analysis, a single-season hospitalisation case-control study, and the 5-season CDC Flu VE Network analysis). The cell-culture product is Flucelvax (named — the question is product-specific). All percentages labelled rVE are RELATIVE measures comparing vaccinees with vaccinees.
cards.result: The mechanism is plausible — egg adaptation can distort the H3N2 antigen, and cell-grown seed virus avoids it — and one large 3-season analysis found a consistent relative advantage of 10.0–14.8% against test-confirmed outpatient influenza. Against that: the CDC network's product-specific analysis found relative VE not statistically significant with identical 30% absolute VE, and the only hospitalisation study's estimates were non-significant (6% relative at age ≥65). There are no randomised head-to-head trials. Observational-only evidence with an independent null caps the stamp at POSSIBLE: a modest relative edge in some seasons and datasets is possible, not established, and a hospitalisation advantage is unproven.
cards.watchOut: Never convert rVE into absolute terms: '14.8% relative effectiveness' means vaccinees' odds of influenza were about 15% lower relative to other vaccinees — a small absolute difference when baseline VE is ~30–40%.
cards.source: Synthesis of the carded records above (PMIDs 38698895, 31445771, 41102880). Registry ID: none (observational studies). MeSH: not captured from the record this session

shelves.title: SESAR: sevoflurane sedation in ARDS backfired — fewer ventilator-free days and 90-day survival 47.1% vs 55.7% on propofol
shelves.question: In adults with ARDS, does inhaled sevoflurane sedation, compared with intravenous propofol sedation, improve oxygenation and survival?
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (harm) — one large trial found harm, against a small earlier pilot's oxygenation signal. In SESAR (PMID 40098564), 687 adults with early moderate-to-severe ARDS in 37 French ICUs randomised to inhaled sevoflurane versus intravenous propofol for up to 7 days had fewer ventilator-free days at day 28 (median difference −2.1 days, 95% CI −3.6 to −0.7) and lower 90-day survival (47.1% vs 55.7%; hazard ratio 1.31, 95% CI 1.05 to 1.62, a relative measure), with higher 7-day mortality (19.4% vs 13.5%; relative risk 1.44, 95% CI 1.02 to 2.03). The earlier 50-patient pilot (PMID 27611637) had found better day-2 oxygenation with sevoflurane versus midazolam — a surrogate, in a different comparator, that the large trial's patient-important outcomes reversed. A retrospective COVID-19 ARDS study (PMID 36614813, n=196, observational) found no ventilator-free-day difference. This shelf is cross-pointed to pack #2999, which homes the separate SAVE-ICU question of inhaled isoflurane in hypoxaemic respiratory failure; SESAR's sevoflurane harm signal in ARDS is a different agent and a different lesson and is not folded into that shelf. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm): in moderate-to-severe ARDS, sevoflurane sedation should not be assumed equivalent to propofol — the one large trial found fewer ventilator-free days and lower survival with sevoflurane.

cards.headline: SESAR 2025: sevoflurane sedation in 687 patients with moderate-to-severe ARDS — fewer ventilator-free days (median difference −2.1) and lower 90-day survival than propofol (47.1% vs 55.7%)
cards.summary: SESAR 2025: sevoflurane sedation in 687 patients with moderate-to-severe ARDS — fewer ventilator-free days (median difference −2.1) and lower 90-day survival than propofol (47.1% vs 55.7%)
cards.people: 687 adults (mean age 65 years, 30% women) with early moderate-to-severe ARDS (PaO2:FiO2 <150 mmHg on PEEP ≥8 cm H2O) in 37 French intensive care units, randomised to inhaled sevoflurane (n=346) or intravenous propofol (n=341) sedation for up to 7 days; median sedation duration 7 days in both groups; enrolled May 2020 to October 2023 with 90-day follow-up.
cards.result: Ventilator-free days at day 28: median 0.0 in both groups, median difference −2.1 days (95% CI −3.6 to −0.7) favouring propofol. 90-day survival was 47.1% with sevoflurane vs 55.7% with propofol (hazard ratio 1.31, 95% CI 1.05 to 1.62, a relative measure). Sevoflurane was also associated with higher 7-day mortality (19.4% vs 13.5%; relative risk 1.44, 95% CI 1.02 to 2.03) and fewer ICU-free days (median difference −2.5, 95% CI −3.7 to −1.4). The trial's own conclusion: inhaled sevoflurane resulted in fewer ventilator-free days and lower 90-day survival than propofol.
cards.watchOut: Open-label (assessor-blinded) strategy trial of a sedation approach, not a blinded drug comparison. 90-day survival was the key secondary endpoint; the harm direction is consistent across ventilator-free days, ICU-free days and 7-day mortality, but this remains a single trial — hence POSSIBLE (harm), not a stronger stamp.
cards.source: SESAR (Jabaudon M et al.) Inhaled Sedation in Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome: The SESAR Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA. 2025. PMID: 40098564. Registry ID: NCT04235608. cards.headline: Jabaudon 2017 pilot (50 patients): sevoflurane improved day-2 oxygenation versus midazolam in ARDS (PaO2:FiO2 205 vs 166) — the surrogate signal SESAR did not confirm
cards.summary: Jabaudon 2017 pilot (50 patients): sevoflurane improved day-2 oxygenation versus midazolam in ARDS (PaO2:FiO2 205 vs 166) — the surrogate signal SESAR did not confirm
cards.people: 50 adults with moderate-to-severe ARDS at a French university hospital (three ICUs), randomised within 24 hours of ARDS onset to inhaled sevoflurane (n=25) or intravenous midazolam (n=25) for 48 hours, April 2014 to February 2016.
cards.result: Day-2 PaO2:FiO2 ratio was higher with sevoflurane than midazolam (mean 205 ± 56 vs 166 ± 59; P=0.04). Levels of some inflammatory markers and a marker of epithelial injury fell more over time in the sevoflurane group, and no serious adverse event was observed with sevoflurane in this small sample.
cards.watchOut: A 50-patient, 48-hour pilot against midazolam (not propofol) measuring oxygenation — a physiological surrogate. A pilot of this size cannot detect the mortality difference SESAR later found, and its oxygenation gain did not translate into ventilator-free days.
cards.source: Jabaudon M et al. Sevoflurane for Sedation in Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome. A Randomized Controlled Pilot Study. Am J Respir Crit Care Med. 2017. PMID: 27611637. cards.headline: Coupet 2022 (retrospective, 196 COVID-19 ARDS patients, observational): inhaled sedation for at least 24 hours was not associated with more ventilator-free days
cards.summary: Coupet 2022 (retrospective, 196 COVID-19 ARDS patients, observational): inhaled sedation for at least 24 hours was not associated with more ventilator-free days
cards.people: 196 mechanically ventilated adults with COVID-19-related ARDS requiring sedation in 10 European and US intensive care units; 111 received inhaled sedation for at least 24 hours and 85 received intravenous sedation only; 78 patients died within 28 days.
cards.result: Ventilator-free days through day 28 did not differ significantly between inhaled and intravenous sedation (median 0 [IQR 0–8] vs 0 [IQR 0–17]; odds ratio for having zero ventilator-free days 1.63, 95% CI 0.91 to 2.92; P=0.10), with similar results after multivariable adjustment and propensity matching.
cards.watchOut: Observational and retrospective, in COVID-19 ARDS only, with mixed inhaled agents — it can neither confirm nor refute SESAR's randomised harm signal; it is carded as context that no observational benefit signal exists either.
cards.source: Coupet R et al. Inhaled Sedation in Patients with COVID-19-Related Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome: An International Retrospective Study. J Clin Med. 2022. PMID: 36614813. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Synthesis: a small pilot's oxygenation gain, no observational benefit, and one large trial showing fewer ventilator-free days and lower survival with sevoflurane in ARDS
cards.summary: Synthesis: a small pilot's oxygenation gain, no observational benefit, and one large trial showing fewer ventilator-free days and lower survival with sevoflurane in ARDS
cards.people: One 687-patient phase 3 RCT (SESAR), one 50-patient pilot RCT, and one 196-patient retrospective observational study of inhaled sedation in ARDS.
cards.result: SESAR: ventilator-free days median difference −2.1 (95% CI −3.6 to −0.7); 90-day survival 47.1% vs 55.7% (hazard ratio 1.31, relative); 7-day mortality 19.4% vs 13.5% (relative risk 1.44). Pilot: day-2 oxygenation better with sevoflurane vs midazolam. Observational COVID-19 study: no ventilator-free-day difference. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm). Cross-point: pack #2999 homes the different SAVE-ICU isoflurane question.
cards.watchOut: Do not generalise SESAR beyond early moderate-to-severe ARDS or to isoflurane (pack #2999's separate question). What is missing is any second large trial; until one exists the stamp stays at POSSIBLE (harm) on a single programme.

shelves.title: VExUS ultrasound: severe congestion grades tracked kidney injury in cohorts of 145, 30 and 75 patients — observational only, no management trial
shelves.question: In critically ill adults with suspected venous congestion, does VExUS (venous excess ultrasound) grading identify clinically important congestion and predict kidney injury or guide decongestion, compared with conventional assessment?
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (observational) — VExUS grading identifies venous congestion associated with subsequent acute kidney injury, but every carded study is observational and no randomised trial of VExUS-guided management exists, so this shelf answers a diagnostic/prognostic question, not a treatment claim. In the derivation cohort of 145 post-cardiac-surgery patients, severe congestion (dilated IVC ≥2 cm plus severe flow abnormalities in multiple Doppler patterns) carried a hazard ratio of 3.69 (95% CI 1.65 to 8.24) for subsequent AKI and a positive likelihood ratio of 6.37 at ICU admission, outperforming central venous pressure (PMID 32270297). A 30-patient cardiorenal cohort found AKI resolution tracked improvement in VExUS grade (PMID 33132560), and a 75-patient septic-shock pilot found severe congestion in 19% on day 1 with a non-significant association with renal replacement therapy (hazard ratio 3.35, 95% CI 0.94 to 11.88; P=0.06) (PMID 38548949). Cohort sizes are printed on every card: the total carded base is 395 patients, dominated by one 145-patient surgical cohort reported twice. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (observational): VExUS can flag clinically important congestion linked to AKI; whether acting on it improves outcomes is untested.

cards.headline: Beaubien-Souligny 2020 (145 cardiac-surgery patients): severe VExUS grade predicted subsequent AKI (hazard ratio 3.69) and beat central venous pressure at ICU admission (+LR 6.37)
cards.summary: Beaubien-Souligny 2020 (145 cardiac-surgery patients): severe VExUS grade predicted subsequent AKI (hazard ratio 3.69) and beat central venous pressure at ICU admission (+LR 6.37)
cards.people: 145 adults undergoing cardiac surgery at a single centre, with 706 repeated daily ultrasound assessments (hepatic, portal and intrarenal vein Doppler plus IVC) over the first 72 hours after surgery; this is the derivation cohort for the VExUS grading system.
cards.result: Defining severe venous congestion as severe flow abnormalities in multiple Doppler patterns with a dilated IVC (≥2 cm) gave the strongest association with subsequent AKI of five prototype scores (hazard ratio 3.69, 95% CI 1.65 to 8.24; P=0.001), remaining significant after adjustment for baseline AKI risk and vasopressor/inotropic support (hazard ratio 2.82, 95% CI 1.21 to 6.55; P=0.02). At ICU admission the severe grade's positive likelihood ratio was 6.37 (95% CI 2.19 to 18.50), outperforming central venous pressure.
cards.watchOut: Post-hoc derivation in one centre's cardiac-surgery patients — the score was built and tested in the same data, which inflates apparent performance. Observational: congestion predicting AKI does not prove that decongesting by VExUS prevents AKI.
cards.source: Beaubien-Souligny W et al. Quantifying systemic congestion with Point-Of-Care ultrasound: development of the venous excess ultrasound grading system. Ultrasound J. 2020. PMID: 32270297. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Beaubien-Souligny 2018 (same 145-patient cohort, earlier report): portal flow pulsatility (HR 2.09) and severe intrarenal venous flow alteration (HR 2.81) each predicted AKI after cardiac surgery
cards.summary: Beaubien-Souligny 2018 (same 145-patient cohort, earlier report): portal flow pulsatility (HR 2.09) and severe intrarenal venous flow alteration (HR 2.81) each predicted AKI after cardiac surgery
cards.type: Prospective observational cohort — earlier report of the same cohort as the card above (Beaubien-Souligny 2018)
cards.people: 145 adults undergoing cardiac surgery with cardiopulmonary bypass at a single centre — the same prospective cohort as the VExUS derivation report above, analysed here by individual Doppler components; 49 patients (33.8%) developed AKI after surgery.
cards.result: Portal flow pulsatility was associated with AKI (hazard ratio 2.09, 95% CI 1.11 to 3.94; P=0.02), as were severe alterations of intrarenal venous flow (hazard ratio 2.81, 95% CI 1.42 to 5.56; P=0.003); both remained significant in multivariable models and improved prediction over preoperative risk factors and central venous pressure (continuous net reclassification improvement 0.364 for portal Doppler and 0.343 for intrarenal Doppler).
cards.watchOut: This is NOT an independent validation: it is the same 145 patients as the derivation card, reported by components before the combined grade existed. Counting it as a second cohort would double-count the evidence base.
cards.source: Beaubien-Souligny W et al. Alterations in Portal Vein Flow and Intrarenal Venous Flow Are Associated With Acute Kidney Injury After Cardiac Surgery: A Prospective Observational Cohort Study. J Am Heart Assoc. 2018. cards.headline: Bhardwaj 2020 (30 cardiorenal-syndrome ICU patients): two-thirds had VExUS grade III, and AKI resolution tracked improvement in VExUS grade (P=0.003)
cards.summary: Bhardwaj 2020 (30 cardiorenal-syndrome ICU patients): two-thirds had VExUS grade III, and AKI resolution tracked improvement in VExUS grade (P=0.003)
cards.people: 30 adults (mean age 59.5 years, 70% men, mean SOFA 5.03) admitted to an ICU with cardiorenal syndrome, with serial VExUS examinations (IVC, hepatic vein waveform, portal vein pulsatility) until AKI resolved or dialysis began; 46.7% were AKI stage 1 and 26.7% each stages 2 and 3.
cards.result: Twenty patients (66.7%) had VExUS grade III. Resolution of AKI correlated significantly with improvement in VExUS grade (P=0.003), and changes in VExUS grade were associated with fluid balance (P=0.006). There was no correlation between central venous pressure, left or right ventricular function and change in VExUS grade.
cards.watchOut: Only 30 patients, single centre, no comparator assessment strategy, and correlation of grade change with AKI resolution cannot show that VExUS-guided fluid removal caused the resolution.
cards.source: Bhardwaj V et al. Combination of Inferior Vena Cava Diameter, Hepatic Venous Flow, and Portal Vein Pulsatility Index: Venous Excess Ultrasound Score (VEXUS Score) in Predicting Acute Kidney Injury in Patients with Cardiorenal Syndrome: A Prospective Cohort Study. cards.headline: Prager 2024 (75 septic-shock patients, pilot): VExUS scanning was feasible (94.5% completion); severe congestion in 19% on day 1, with a non-significant RRT signal (HR 3.35, P=0.06)
cards.summary: Prager 2024 (75 septic-shock patients, pilot): VExUS scanning was feasible (94.5% completion); severe congestion in 19% on day 1, with a non-significant RRT signal (HR 3.35, P=0.06)
cards.people: 75 adults with septic shock recruited within 12 hours of ICU admission at two ICUs (January 2022 to January 2023), with VExUS scoring on days 1 and 3; severe venous congestion was present in 14 of 75 (19%) on day 1 and 10 of 61 (16%) on day 3.
cards.result: Completion of the two VExUS scores succeeded in 94.5% (95% CI 89.5 to 97.6) — the pilot's primary feasibility outcome. Venous congestion on admission may be associated with a higher hazard of renal replacement therapy (unadjusted hazard ratio 3.35, 95% CI 0.94 to 11.88; P=0.06), which did not reach significance.
cards.watchOut: A feasibility pilot, not powered for outcomes: the renal-replacement hazard ratio's confidence interval runs from 0.94 to 11.88. It shows the score can be measured in septic shock, not that it predicts or guides anything there yet.
cards.source: Prager R et al. Venous congestion in septic shock quantified with point-of-care ultrasound: a pilot prospective multicentre cohort study. Can J Anaesth. 2024. PMID: 38548949. cards.headline: Synthesis: VExUS grades congestion that tracks AKI in small observational cohorts — 395 patients total, no management trial
cards.summary: Synthesis: VExUS grades congestion that tracks AKI in small observational cohorts — 395 patients total, no management trial
cards.people: Four observational reports totalling 395 patients (145 cardiac-surgery patients reported twice, 30 cardiorenal patients, 75 septic-shock patients, plus the derivation analysis of the same 145).
cards.result: Severe VExUS grade: hazard ratio 3.69 for subsequent AKI and +LR 6.37 in the derivation cohort; AKI resolution correlated with grade improvement in 30 cardiorenal patients; feasibility shown in septic shock with a non-significant RRT signal. No randomised trial of VExUS-guided decongestion exists in the carded record. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (observational).
cards.watchOut: The evidence base is thinner than four cards suggest: two cards are one cohort. Populations (cardiac surgery, cardiorenal syndrome, septic shock) differ, and operator skill and IVC/Doppler windows limit general use. The open question is interventional, and it is unanswered.

shelves.title: Ventilator-induced diaphragm dysfunction: human fibres shrank by over half within 18–69 hours of inactivity, and the diaphragm is weak in most patients by the first breathing trial
shelves.question: In mechanically ventilated patients, what is ventilator-induced diaphragm dysfunction — its mechanism, time course and contribution to weaning failure?
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. The human physiology, as framed in standard texts (Boron & Boulpaep's Medical Physiology and Guyton and Hall's Textbook of Medical Physiology describe the diaphragm as a continuously active skeletal muscle exquisitely dependent on its own activity, and skeletal-muscle disuse proteolysis via the ubiquitin–proteasome system generally), is that complete diaphragmatic inactivity under controlled ventilation triggers rapid proteolysis and fibre atrophy — measurable within 18 to 69 hours in humans (Levine et al., PMID 18367735: slow- and fast-twitch fibre cross-sectional areas 57% and 53% smaller than controls, with atrogin-1 and MuRF-1 expression up 200% and 590%). By the time of the first spontaneous breathing trial, diaphragm dysfunction is commoner than limb weakness (63% vs 34% in 76 patients, PMID 27310484) and independently tracks weaning failure and mortality, and it is present in 80% of patients with ICU-acquired weakness (PMID 26572511). Cross-point: pack #3131 asks whether diaphragm ultrasound predicts weaning success — a test question; this shelf is the underlying physiology it rests on. Textbook framing is context, not an evidence card; every quantitative claim here is tied to a carded human study.

cards.headline: Levine 2008 (14 brain-dead donors vs 8 surgical controls — small human biopsy study, Ns printed): 18–69 hours of complete diaphragm inactivity shrank slow-twitch fibres 57% and fast-twitch fibres 53%
cards.summary: Levine 2008 (14 brain-dead donors vs 8 surgical controls — small human biopsy study, Ns printed): 18–69 hours of complete diaphragm inactivity shrank slow-twitch fibres 57% and fast-twitch fibres 53%
cards.people: Diaphragm biopsy specimens from 14 brain-dead organ donors (case subjects) who had complete diaphragmatic inactivity and mechanical ventilation for 18 to 69 hours before organ harvest, compared with intraoperative diaphragm biopsies from 8 patients undergoing surgery for benign lesions or localised lung cancer (controls, ventilation/inactivity 2 to 3 hours). N = 14 vs 8 — a small study, labelled plainly.
cards.result: Compared with controls, case-subject diaphragms showed decreased cross-sectional areas of slow-twitch fibres by 57% (P=0.001) and fast-twitch fibres by 53% (P=0.01), decreased glutathione concentration by 23% (P=0.01), increased active caspase-3 expression by 100% (P=0.05), and higher ratios of atrogin-1 mRNA (200% higher, P=0.002) and MuRF-1 mRNA (590% higher, P=0.001) to a housekeeping gene — a proteolysis signature consistent with disuse atrophy within under three days of inactivity.
cards.watchOut: Very small (14 vs 8) and in brain-dead donors, whose physiology differs from ordinary ICU patients; it establishes that human diaphragm atrophy can begin within 18–69 hours of complete inactivity, not the exact rate in a typical ventilated patient, in whom the diaphragm is rarely completely inactive.
cards.source: Levine S et al. Rapid disuse atrophy of diaphragm fibers in mechanically ventilated humans. N Engl J Med. 2008. PMID: 18367735. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Dres 2017 (76 medical ICU patients at first breathing trial): diaphragm dysfunction in 63% — twice as frequent as limb weakness (34%) — and independently associated with weaning failure
cards.summary: Dres 2017 (76 medical ICU patients at first breathing trial): diaphragm dysfunction in 63% — twice as frequent as limb weakness (34%) — and independently associated with weaning failure
cards.people: 76 medical ICU patients assessed at their first spontaneous breathing trial after at least 24 hours of mechanical ventilation; diaphragm dysfunction was measured by twitch tracheal pressure after magnetic phrenic-nerve stimulation (pressure <11 cm H2O defined dysfunction) and by ultrasound thickening fraction and excursion; limb weakness was an MRC score <48.
cards.result: Diaphragm dysfunction was present in 63%, limb muscle weakness in 34%, and both in 21%, with only weak correlation between the two (ρ = 0.26–0.28). Low twitch pressure (odds ratio 0.60, 95% CI 0.45 to 0.79; P<0.001) and low thickening fraction (odds ratio 0.84, 95% CI 0.76 to 0.92; P<0.001) were independently associated with weaning failure, while the limb MRC score was not. Diaphragm dysfunction was also associated with higher ICU and hospital mortality.
cards.watchOut: A single-centre cohort measured at one time point (first breathing trial); it quantifies how common and how prognostic diaphragm dysfunction is, but cannot separate how much was caused by the ventilator versus the underlying illness and immobility.
cards.source: Dres M et al. Coexistence and Impact of Limb Muscle and Diaphragm Weakness at Time of Liberation from Mechanical Ventilation in Medical Intensive Care Unit Patients. Am J Respir Crit Care Med. 2017. PMID: 27310484. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Jung 2016 (40 patients with ICU-acquired weakness): diaphragm dysfunction in 80%, poorly correlated with the limb MRC score — half still extubated successfully
cards.summary: Jung 2016 (40 patients with ICU-acquired weakness): diaphragm dysfunction in 80%, poorly correlated with the limb MRC score — half still extubated successfully
cards.people: 40 patients (of 185 consecutive patients ventilated more than 48 hours) diagnosed with ICU-acquired weakness (MRC score <48; median score 31) and undergoing a spontaneous breathing trial; diaphragm function was assessed by magnetic phrenic-nerve stimulation (change in endotracheal-tube pressure <11 cmH2O defined dysfunction), maximal inspiratory pressure and ultrasound thickening fraction.
cards.result: Diaphragm dysfunction accompanied ICU-acquired weakness in 32 of 40 patients (80%), and thickening fraction was <20% in 70%; yet change in endotracheal-tube pressure did not correlate with the MRC score, so limb weakness does not stand in for diaphragm weakness. Half the patients were extubated without reintubation within 72 hours; half of those who failed weaning died during the ICU stay.
cards.watchOut: Selected population — only patients who already had ICU-acquired weakness — so the 80% figure is not the prevalence in all ventilated patients. Dysfunction was frequent yet half still extubated successfully: it shifts the odds of weaning failure rather than deciding them.
cards.source: Jung B et al. Diaphragmatic dysfunction in patients with ICU-acquired weakness and its impact on extubation failure. Intensive Care Med. 2016. PMID: 26572511. cards.headline: Synthesis: an activity-dependent muscle that proteolyses within days of silence, is weak in most patients by the first breathing trial, and independently tracks weaning failure
cards.summary: Synthesis: an activity-dependent muscle that proteolyses within days of silence, is weak in most patients by the first breathing trial, and independently tracks weaning failure
cards.people: Three primary human studies: a 14-vs-8 biopsy comparison, a 76-patient cohort at first breathing trial, and a 40-patient ICU-acquired-weakness cohort (138 patients in total).
cards.result: Mechanism and time course: fibre atrophy of 53–57% with a ubiquitin–proteasome proteolysis signature after 18–69 hours of complete inactivity (Levine 2008). Contribution to weaning: dysfunction in 63% at first breathing trial, independently associated with weaning failure and mortality (Dres 2017), and in 80% of ICU-acquired weakness (Jung 2016). Stamp: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. Cross-point: pack #3131 (diaphragm ultrasound for weaning prediction).
cards.watchOut: The textbook account (Boron & Boulpaep; Guyton and Hall) frames the diaphragm as activity-dependent skeletal muscle — framing, not a card. What the human studies do not settle is how much assisted (rather than controlled) ventilation prevents the atrophy, or whether any diaphragm-protective strategy improves outcomes; those are intervention questions, not physiology.
cards.source: Synthesis of Levine S et al. N Engl J Med. 2008 (PMID: 18367735); Dres M et al. Am J Respir Crit Care Med. 2017 (PMID: 27310484); Jung B et al. Intensive Care Med. 2016 (PMID: 26572511).

shelves.title: What lactate actually is: in stable sepsis a raised level mainly means failed clearance, not overproduction — and some production is adrenergic, not hypoxic
shelves.question: In sepsis and critical illness, what does the blood lactate concentration actually represent — production, clearance, adrenergic aerobic glycolysis vs tissue hypoxia?
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED (core), with one EMERGING element flagged as such. A blood lactate concentration is a balance — production minus clearance — not a direct readout of tissue hypoxia; that core is established human physiology, framed in standard texts (Guyton and Hall's Textbook of Medical Physiology; Ganong's Review of Medical Physiology) and demonstrated directly in septic patients: in Levraut 1998 (PMID 9563714), mildly hyperlactataemic stable septic patients produced lactate at the same rate as normolactataemic patients but cleared it at less than half the rate (473 vs 1,002 mL/kg/h), and across patients lactate tracked the reciprocal of clearance (r²=0.73), not production (r²=0.03). Clearance also carries prognosis even when the level is near-normal (PMID 12626973). The EMERGING element — worded here as the current best interpretation, not settled fact — is how much of septic lactate production is adrenergic aerobic glycolysis (catecholamine-driven Na+/K+-ATPase activity in well-oxygenated muscle) rather than anaerobic production from hypoperfusion; the human endotoxin experiment carded here (PMID 12446281, N = 8, labelled plainly) supports that mechanism but is very small. Cross-point: pack #3152 asks the different, strategic question of lactate-clearance-guided resuscitation; this shelf explains what lactate is. Values no carded record confirms are not asserted.

cards.headline: Levraut 1998 (34 stable septic patients): mild hyperlactataemia was a clearance defect, not overproduction — clearance 473 vs 1,002 mL/kg/h, production identical
cards.summary: Levraut 1998 (34 stable septic patients): mild hyperlactataemia was a clearance defect, not overproduction — clearance 473 vs 1,002 mL/kg/h, production identical
cards.people: 34 stable septic patients studied prospectively with a 1 mmol/kg L-lactate infusion over 15 minutes to model lactate kinetics: 20 with blood lactate ≤1.5 mmol/L (13.5 mg/dL) (mean 1.2 mmol/L, 10.8 mg/dL) and 10 with lactate ≥2 mmol/L (18 mg/dL) (mean 2.6 mmol/L, 23.4 mg/dL) in the grouped analysis as reported.
cards.result: Hyperlactataemic patients had lower lactate clearance (473 ± 102 mL/kg/h) than normolactataemic patients (1,002 ± 284 mL/kg/h; P<0.001), while lactate production was essentially the same (1,194 ± 230 vs 1,181 ± 325 µmol/kg/h; P=0.90). Across all patients, blood lactate was closely linked to the reciprocal of clearance (r²=0.73; P<0.001) but not to production (r²=0.03; P=0.29). The authors conclude mild hyperlactataemia in stable sepsis mainly reflects defective lactate utilisation (clearance), not overproduction.
cards.watchOut: Stable septic patients with only mild hyperlactataemia — the clearance-dominant picture may differ in florid shock with severe hypoperfusion, where production can also rise. The grouped analysis as reported covers 30 of the 34 patients.
cards.source: Levraut J et al. Mild hyperlactatemia in stable septic patients is due to impaired lactate clearance rather than overproduction. Am J Respir Crit Care Med. 1998. PMID: 9563714. cards.headline: Levraut 2003 (56 severely septic patients, lactate <3 mmol/L [27 mg/dL]): low clearance predicted 28-day death even when the lactate level itself did not
cards.summary: Levraut 2003 (56 severely septic patients, lactate <3 mmol/L [27 mg/dL]): low clearance predicted 28-day death even when the lactate level itself did not
cards.people: 56 patients with severe sepsis and blood lactate <3 mmol/L (27 mg/dL) in a 19-bed mixed ICU; lactate clearance and production were measured by modelling the response to a 1 mmol/kg sodium-lactate infusion over 15 minutes; 17 patients (30.3%) died by day 28.
cards.result: Basal lactate concentration did not differ between survivors and non-survivors, but clearance was higher in survivors (0.86 ± 0.32 vs 0.58 ± 0.18 L/h/kg; P<0.005). A rise in blood lactate of ≥0.6 mmol/L (5.4 mg/dL) 45 minutes after the infusion predicted 28-day mortality with 53% sensitivity and 90% specificity, and in multivariable analysis it was independently associated with death (odds ratio 14.2; P=0.042) alongside more than two organ failures and age over 70. The level alone misleads; the clearance behind it carries the signal.
cards.watchOut: The clearance here is clearance of an exogenous lactate load — a probe of utilisation capacity — in patients pre-selected for near-normal lactate. It does not by itself prove that improving clearance improves outcome.
cards.source: Levraut J et al. Low exogenous lactate clearance as an early predictor of mortality in normolactatemic critically ill septic patients. Crit Care Med. 2003. PMID: 12626973. cards.headline: Bundgaard 2003 (N = 8 healthy volunteers — very small, labelled plainly): human endotoxaemia raised lactate to 2.5 mmol/L (22.5 mg/dL) under aerobic conditions, alongside epinephrine and muscle Na+/K+-ATPase signatures
cards.summary: Bundgaard 2003 (N = 8 healthy volunteers — very small, labelled plainly): human endotoxaemia raised lactate to 2.5 mmol/L (22.5 mg/dL) under aerobic conditions, alongside epinephrine and muscle Na+/K+-ATPase signatures
cards.people: 8 healthy volunteers (leg-balance measurements in 6–7) who received an intravenous endotoxin bolus or placebo on two separate days in randomised order — an experimental human endotoxaemia model, not sepsis patients. N = 8: a classic small physiology experiment, carded with its size on the face.
cards.result: Endotoxaemia raised plasma epinephrine (peak 0.7 ± 0.1 vs 0.3 ± 0.1 nmol/L at 2 hours; P<0.05) and plasma lactate (peak 2.5 ± 0.5 vs 0.9 ± 0.1 mmol/L — 22.5 vs 8.1 mg/dL — at 1 hour; P<0.05), with increased lactate release from the legs, a fall in plasma potassium consistent with Na+/K+-ATPase stimulation, and no evidence of hypoperfusion or hypoxia. The authors interpret this as catecholamine-driven aerobic glycolysis: lactate produced by well-oxygenated muscle, not by oxygen starvation.
cards.watchOut: N = 8 healthy volunteers given endotoxin — a model of the early adrenergic state, not established sepsis, and the Na+/K+-ATPase link is inferred from potassium and lactate patterns rather than measured directly in muscle. This is why the adrenergic aerobic-glycolysis contribution is presented in this shelf as EMERGING interpretation, not settled fact.
cards.source: Bundgaard H et al. Endotoxemia stimulates skeletal muscle Na+-K+-ATPase and raises blood lactate under aerobic conditions in humans. Am J Physiol Heart Circ Physiol. 2003. human physiology / experimental endotoxaemia study (bundgaard 2003) 8 healthy volunteers (leg-balance measurements in 6–7) who received an intravenous endotoxin bolus or placebo on two separate days in randomised order — an experimental human endotoxaemia model, not sepsis patients. n = 8: a classic small physiology experiment, carded with its size on the face. endotoxaemia raised plasma epinephrine (peak 0.7 ± 0.1 vs 0.3 ± 0.1 nmol/l at 2 hours; p<0.05) and plasma lactate (peak 2.5 ± 0.5 vs 0.9 ± 0.1 mmol/l — 22.5 vs 8.1 mg/dl — at 1 hour; p<0.05), with increased lactate release from the legs, a fall in plasma potassium consistent with na+/k+-atpase stimulation, and no evidence of hypoperfusion or hypoxia. the authors interpret this as catecholamine-driven aerobic glycolysis: lactate produced by well-oxygenated muscle, not by oxygen starvation. n = 8 healthy volunteers given endotoxin — a model of the early adrenergic state, not established sepsis, and the na+/k+-atpase link is inferred from potassium and lactate patterns rather than measured directly in muscle. this is why the adrenergic aerobic-glycolysis contribution is presented in this shelf as emerging interpretation, not settled fact. bundgaard h et al. endotoxemia stimulates skeletal muscle na+-k+-atpase and raises blood lactate under aerobic conditions in humans. am j physiol heart circ physiol. 2003. pmid: 12446281. registry id: none in the record. mesh: adult · aerobiosis · arm · arteries · endotoxemia · endotoxins · epinephrine · fever · humans · hypokalemia · kidney · lactic acid · leg · lipopolysaccharides · muscle, skeletal · potassium · reference values · sodium-potassium-exchanging atpase · tumor necrosis factor-alpha · veins

cards.headline: Synthesis: lactate is a balance of production and clearance; in stable sepsis the level mainly reports failed clearance, and part of production may be adrenergic and aerobic — that part is still interpretation
cards.summary: Synthesis: lactate is a balance of production and clearance; in stable sepsis the level mainly reports failed clearance, and part of production may be adrenergic and aerobic — that part is still interpretation
cards.people: Three primary human studies: 34 and 56 septic patients in lactate-kinetic studies, and 8 healthy volunteers in an endotoxin experiment (98 people in total).
cards.result: Established core: blood lactate tracks clearance (r²=0.73) far more than production in stable sepsis, and impaired clearance predicts death at near-normal levels. Emerging element: catecholamine-stimulated aerobic glycolysis in oxygenated muscle can raise lactate without hypoxia, shown experimentally in 8 volunteers. Stamp chosen: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED for the production/clearance core, with the adrenergic contribution explicitly labelled emerging in the balance. Cross-point: pack #3152 (lactate-clearance-guided resuscitation strategy).
cards.watchOut: Textbook framing (Guyton and Hall; Ganong) supplies the production/clearance framework, not the numbers. A high lactate in a shocked, hypoperfused patient can still mean tissue hypoxia — this physiology refines, and does not abolish, the perfusion interpretation; the proportions in real septic shock are not settled.
cards.source: Synthesis of Levraut J et al. Am J Respir Crit Care Med. 1998 (PMID: 9563714); Levraut J et al. Crit Care Med. 2003 (PMID: 12626973); Bundgaard H et al. Am J Physiol Heart Circ Physiol. 2003 (PMID: 12446281).

shelves.title: Pivmecillinam (Pivya): a 40-year-old Scandinavian UTI drug whose re-scored historical trials beat placebo and ibuprofen and matched cephalexin
shelves.question: In adult women with uncomplicated urinary tract infection, does pivmecillinam, compared with placebo, cephalexin or ibuprofen-based symptomatic treatment, achieve clinical and microbiological cure?
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the efficacy base is largely reanalysed historical (predominantly Scandinavian) trials plus modern supportive analyses, and that vintage is stated plainly here rather than hidden. The US product is Pivya (pivmecillinam, Utility Therapeutics), approved by the FDA in April 2024 for uncomplicated UTI in women ≥18 years. The 2025 reanalysis (PMID 40567143) applied current FDA criteria to the three historical randomised trials with usable subject-level data (185 mg three times daily for 3–7 days) and found overall (composite clinical + microbiological) success of 62.0%–71.7%, clearly above placebo (95% CI for the difference 41.2 to 62.0) and ibuprofen (31.2 to 56.5) and similar to cephalexin (−15.6 to 7.4). A 24-trial meta-analysis (PMID 28341436) could not identify an optimal dose/duration and rated the underlying trials at high risk of bias. A susceptibility caveat runs through the whole base: mecillinam testing is method-sensitive — S. saprophyticus is conventionally reported non-susceptible yet responded clinically in 72% of 74 women (PMID 31067667), and a 2025 laboratory study found no commercial susceptibility test met ISO standards on carbapenemase-producing isolates (disc-diffusion categorical agreement 77.0%–84.5%) — so a 'resistant' report and a clinical failure are not the same thing, and breakpoints deserve the correspondence they have attracted. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): pivmecillinam cures uncomplicated UTI more often than placebo or ibuprofen and about as often as cephalexin, on a historical-trial base re-scored by modern criteria.

cards.headline: Lodise 2025 reanalysis (3 historical RCTs re-scored by current FDA criteria): pivmecillinam overall success 62.0%–71.7% — above placebo and ibuprofen, similar to cephalexin
cards.summary: Lodise 2025 reanalysis (3 historical RCTs re-scored by current FDA criteria): pivmecillinam overall success 62.0%–71.7% — above placebo and ibuprofen, similar to cephalexin
cards.people: Women ≥18 years with uncomplicated UTI in the microbiological intention-to-treat population (urine culture ≥10⁵ CFU/mL, ≤2 species, no baseline pathogen non-susceptible to the comparator) from 3 of 14 reviewed historical randomised trials that had suitable subject-level data; treatment was pivmecillinam 185 mg three times daily for 3–7 days; test of cure at days 7–15. Pathogens included E. coli, Proteus mirabilis, Klebsiella pneumoniae and Staphylococcus saprophyticus.
cards.result: Overall (composite clinical and microbiological) success with pivmecillinam was 62.0%–71.7% across the three trials (clinical success 63.5%–82.7%; microbiological success 74.3%–86.9%). Overall success was higher than with placebo (95% CI for the difference 41.2 to 62.0 percentage points) and ibuprofen (31.2 to 56.5) and similar to cephalexin (−15.6 to 7.4). This reanalysis formed the basis of the April 2024 FDA approval of pivmecillinam (US product Pivya, Utility Therapeutics) — over 40 years after its first European approval.
cards.watchOut: These are historical (predominantly Scandinavian) trials re-scored decades later against modern FDA endpoints, and only 3 of 14 reviewed studies had data suitable for reanalysis — the base's vintage and selectivity are the central caveats, stated on the face of this shelf. The modern ibuprofen-comparator RCT by Vik et al. is part of this literature but is not carded separately here.
cards.source: Lodise TP et al. Pivmecillinam for Treatment of Uncomplicated Urinary Tract Infection: New Efficacy Analysis. Clin Infect Dis. 2025. PMID: 40567143. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Pinart 2017 (systematic review and meta-analysis, 24 RCTs): no pivmecillinam dose or duration was shown optimal, and the trial base was at high risk of bias
cards.summary: Pinart 2017 (systematic review and meta-analysis, 24 RCTs): no pivmecillinam dose or duration was shown optimal, and the trial base was at high risk of bias
cards.people: 24 randomised trials of pivmecillinam regimens (high, moderate and low total dosage) versus each other or other antibiotics in adults or children with symptoms of uncomplicated lower UTI.
cards.result: No difference in clinical cure was found between high and moderate dosage (short-term risk ratio 1.01; long-term 1.09) or high and low dosage; bacteriological cure showed only a non-significant trend favouring higher dosage (short-term risk ratio 1.05 and 1.02 respectively). Relapse, re-infection and failure results were inconclusive, and patients on high dosages reported more mild-to-moderate adverse events (40%–44% relatively more likely, non-significant). The reviewers concluded the evidence is insufficient to define an optimal regimen, limited by high risk of bias, poor reporting and heterogeneity.
cards.watchOut: A dose-finding review, not a placebo comparison: it tempers confidence in any specific regimen (including the marketed 3–7 day course) rather than in the drug's efficacy itself. Its risk-of-bias verdict applies to the same historical base the approval rests on.

cards.headline: Jansåker 2019 (74 women, cumulative data from four RCTs): pivmecillinam cured 72% of S. saprophyticus UTIs clinically and 86% bacteriologically — despite the organism testing 'non-susceptible'
cards.summary: Jansåker 2019 (74 women, cumulative data from four RCTs): pivmecillinam cured 72% of S. saprophyticus UTIs clinically and 86% bacteriologically — despite the organism testing 'non-susceptible'
cards.type: Cumulative observational analysis of four RCT cohorts (Jansåker 2019)
cards.people: 74 women aged 18–55 years (mean 25) empirically treated with pivmecillinam in four randomised trials, whose confirmed UTI was caused by Staphylococcus saprophyticus — an organism conventionally characterised as non-susceptible to mecillinam on disc-diffusion testing (EUCAST methodology).
cards.result: Cumulative clinical effect (symptom resolution within 8 days without recurrence at ~4 weeks) was 53 of 74 (72%), and bacteriological effect (elimination of the causative agent at first control urine) was 51 of 59 (86%). The authors conclude the non-susceptibility characterisation of S. saprophyticus for mecillinam may need revision — a worked example of the susceptibility-testing/breakpoint caveat that surrounds this drug.
cards.watchOut: Observational pooling of a pathogen subgroup across trials not designed for it, with bacteriological follow-up in only 59 of 74 women. It illustrates the breakpoint problem; it is not independent proof of efficacy. Laboratory corroboration of testing unreliability: in a 2025 study of 161 carbapenemase-producing Enterobacterales isolates (PMID 40227038, laboratory study, not carded as clinical evidence), no commercial mecillinam susceptibility test met ISO standards against agar dilution.
cards.source: Jansåker F et al. Pivmecillinam for Uncomplicated Lower Urinary Tract Infections Caused by Staphylococcus saprophyticus — Cumulative Observational Data from Four Recent Clinical Studies. Antibiotics (Basel). 2019. cards.headline: Synthesis: an old Scandinavian drug re-scored by modern FDA criteria — better than placebo and ibuprofen, similar to cephalexin, with dose and breakpoint questions still open
cards.summary: Synthesis: an old Scandinavian drug re-scored by modern FDA criteria — better than placebo and ibuprofen, similar to cephalexin, with dose and breakpoint questions still open
cards.people: A 3-trial regulatory reanalysis, a 24-trial dose/duration meta-analysis, and a 74-woman pathogen-subgroup analysis.
cards.result: Overall success 62.0%–71.7% on pivmecillinam vs placebo and ibuprofen differences whose confidence intervals exclude no-effect by wide margins, and a cephalexin difference spanning zero (−15.6 to 7.4). No optimal dose/duration is established, and susceptibility reporting is method-sensitive. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) for Pivya (pivmecillinam, Utility Therapeutics) in uncomplicated UTI in women.
cards.watchOut: No large modern placebo-controlled trial in a contemporary US population exists; the approval rests on reanalysis. Resistance patterns and breakpoints in current local isolates may differ from the historical Scandinavian base — check local guidance rather than assuming the trial rates transfer.

shelves.title: Cefepime–taniborbactam (CERTAIN-1): beat meropenem 70.6% vs 58.0% in complicated UTI — but Venatorx's drug is not yet FDA-approved
shelves.question: In adults with complicated urinary tract infection including acute pyelonephritis, does cefepime–taniborbactam, compared with meropenem, achieve composite clinical/microbiological success, including against resistant Gram-negative pathogens?
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a single phase 3 programme. In CERTAIN-1 (PMID 38354140), 661 hospitalised adults with complicated UTI or acute pyelonephritis were randomised 2:1 to cefepime–taniborbactam 2.5 g or meropenem 1 g every 8 hours; in the microbiological intention-to-treat population (436 patients), composite clinical + microbiological success at days 19–23 was 70.6% vs 58.0% (treatment difference 12.6 percentage points, 95% CI 3.1 to 22.2; P=0.009) — superiority after non-inferiority was confirmed, with adverse events in 35.5% vs 29.0%. A prespecified resistance-subset report of the same trial (PMID 38780262) found success preserved against cefepime-, multidrug- and carbapenem-resistant pathogens, in very small subsets. Regulatory status, stated honestly: the sponsor is Venatorx Pharmaceuticals, and the FDA issued a complete response letter on manufacturing grounds — cefepime–taniborbactam was NOT yet FDA-approved at the time this evidence was mined, so this shelf describes an investigational therapy with a positive trial, not an available treatment. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), capped by the single-programme rule.

cards.headline: CERTAIN-1 2024: cefepime–taniborbactam beat meropenem in complicated UTI — composite success 70.6% vs 58.0% (difference 12.6 points, P=0.009)
cards.summary: CERTAIN-1 2024: cefepime–taniborbactam beat meropenem in complicated UTI — composite success 70.6% vs 58.0% (difference 12.6 points, P=0.009)
cards.people: 661 hospitalised adults with complicated UTI including acute pyelonephritis, randomised 2:1 to intravenous cefepime–taniborbactam 2.5 g or meropenem 1 g every 8 hours for 7 days (up to 14 days with bacteraemia); mean age 56.2 years, 38.1% aged ≥65. The primary microbiological intention-to-treat population was 436 patients (66.0%), of whom 57.8% had complicated UTI, 42.2% acute pyelonephritis and 13.1% bacteraemia.
cards.result: Composite success (microbiological + clinical, days 19–23) occurred in 207 of 293 (70.6%) on cefepime–taniborbactam vs 83 of 143 (58.0%) on meropenem — treatment difference 12.6 percentage points (95% CI 3.1 to 22.2; P=0.009), meeting non-inferiority and then superiority. Differences were sustained at late follow-up (days 28–35). Adverse events occurred in 35.5% vs 29.0% (headache, diarrhoea, constipation, hypertension, nausea most frequent); serious adverse-event frequency was similar.
cards.watchOut: Funded by Venatorx Pharmaceuticals and others. The microITT population required a qualifying Gram-negative pathogen susceptible to BOTH study drugs, which excludes the fully resistant infections where the drug is most hoped for; and the combination was NOT yet FDA-approved at mining (FDA complete response letter on manufacturing grounds) — do not present it as an available therapy.
cards.source: CERTAIN-1 (Wagenlehner FM et al.) Cefepime-Taniborbactam in Complicated Urinary Tract Infection. N Engl J Med. 2024. PMID: 38354140. Registry ID: NCT03840148. cards.headline: CERTAIN-1 resistance-subset report 2024 (second report of the same trial): success held in resistant subsets — 7 of 8 with carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales — but the subsets are tiny
cards.summary: CERTAIN-1 resistance-subset report 2024 (second report of the same trial): success held in resistant subsets — 7 of 8 with carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales — but the subsets are tiny
cards.type: Prespecified subset analysis — second report of the CERTAIN-1 trial (Moeck 2024)
cards.people: Patients within CERTAIN-1's microbiological population whose baseline pathogens were cefepime-, multidrug- or carbapenem-resistant, or carried β-lactamase genes: among Enterobacterales, 26.8% carried ESBL genes, 4.1% AmpC and 3.0% carbapenemase genes.
cards.result: Cefepime–taniborbactam achieved composite success in 7 of 8 patients (87.5%) with carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales and 8 of 9 (88.9%) with a carbapenemase gene (5 OXA-48-group, 2 KPC-3, 2 NDM-1); against P. aeruginosa, composite success was 8 of 16 (50.0%) vs 4 of 7 (57.1%) on meropenem, with clinical success 13 of 16 (81.3%) vs 6 of 7 (85.7%). On meropenem, success was numerically lower in cefepime-resistant E. coli (9 of 19, 47.4%) and ESBL E. coli (13 of 25, 52.0%) than in E. coli overall (62.0%).
cards.watchOut: Explicitly a second report of the same trial, not independent evidence. The headline resistant-pathogen numbers rest on 8, 9, 16 and 7 patients — hypothesis-supporting, not proof of efficacy in carbapenem-resistant infection, and the trial's microITT design had already excluded pathogens non-susceptible to either drug.
cards.source: Moeck G et al. cards.summary: Dowell 2021 (first-in-human taniborbactam study, healthy volunteers; N not documented in the record): no serious adverse events, ~90% recovered unchanged in urine
cards.people: Healthy adult volunteers receiving single intravenous taniborbactam doses of 62.5 to 1,500 mg or multiple doses of 250 to 750 mg every 8 hours for 10 days (2-hour infusions), in a randomised first-in-human safety/pharmacokinetic study. N not documented in the fetched record — printed as such rather than estimated.
cards.result: No subject had a serious adverse event or discontinued for an adverse event; headache was the commonest event in both taniborbactam and placebo subjects. Pharmacokinetics were dose-proportional with low variability and minimal accumulation; about 90% of the dose was recovered in urine as intact drug, with no appreciable metabolism — supporting the urinary-tract exposure the combination relies on.
cards.watchOut: Healthy volunteers and pharmacokinetics only — this card supports feasibility and urinary exposure, not efficacy. It is carded so the shelf rests on more than one human study, and it should not be read as a second efficacy trial.

cards.people: One 661-patient phase 3 RCT (436 in the primary population) with a prespecified subset report, plus one healthy-volunteer phase 1 study (N not documented).

shelves.title: Simnotrelvir: symptoms resolved ~36 hours sooner in a 1,208-patient Chinese trial — a symptom endpoint only, single-country evidence
shelves.question: In adults with mild-to-moderate COVID-19 at risk of progression, does oral simnotrelvir (with ritonavir), compared with placebo, shorten time to symptom resolution?
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one randomised programme, single-country, on a symptom endpoint. In the phase 2/3 trial (PMID 38231624), 1,208 adults with mild-to-moderate COVID-19 at 35 sites in China — flagged on the face: all sites were in China — randomised within 3 days of symptom onset to simnotrelvir 750 mg plus ritonavir 100 mg or placebo twice daily for 5 days had a shorter time to sustained resolution of 11 COVID-19 symptoms (180.1 vs 216.0 hours; median difference −35.8 hours, 95% CI −60.1 to −12.4; P=0.006) and a greater day-5 viral-load fall (mean difference −1.51 log10 copies/mL). The endpoint is symptom resolution, not hospitalisation or mortality — no such benefit is shown. Adverse events were commoner on simnotrelvir (29.0% vs 21.6%), mostly mild or moderate. A Chinese retrospective cohort (PMID 40597719, observational) found no difference from nirmatrelvir–ritonavir in disease progression, death or respiratory support. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): simnotrelvir–ritonavir shortens symptoms by about a day and a half when started within 3 days, in the population and variant era studied.

cards.headline: Cao 2024 (phase 2/3, 1,208 patients, China only): simnotrelvir–ritonavir shortened sustained symptom resolution by 35.8 hours vs placebo
cards.summary: Cao 2024 (phase 2/3, 1,208 patients, China only): simnotrelvir–ritonavir shortened sustained symptom resolution by 35.8 hours vs placebo
cards.people: 1,208 adults with mild-to-moderate COVID-19 and symptom onset within the past 3 days, enrolled at 35 sites in China and randomised 1:1 to simnotrelvir 750 mg plus ritonavir 100 mg (n=603) or placebo (n=605) twice daily for 5 days; the primary analysis population received the first dose within 72 hours of symptom onset. SINGLE-COUNTRY flag: every site was in China.
cards.result: Time to sustained resolution of 11 COVID-19 symptoms (absent for 2 consecutive days) was 180.1 hours (95% CI 162.1 to 201.6) on simnotrelvir vs 216.0 hours (95% CI 203.4 to 228.1) on placebo — median difference −35.8 hours (95% CI −60.1 to −12.4; P=0.006). Day-5 viral-load decrease was greater on simnotrelvir (mean difference −1.51 ± 0.14 log10 copies/mL, 95% CI −1.79 to −1.24). Adverse events during treatment: 29.0% vs 21.6%, mostly mild or moderate. No hospitalisation or mortality benefit was assessed as the primary question — the endpoint is symptom resolution.
cards.watchOut: Single-country (China), in the variant and immunity landscape of that time and place; funded by Jiangsu Simcere Pharmaceutical. A ~36-hour symptom gain in mild-to-moderate illness must not be read as protection against severe disease — that outcome was not the trial's endpoint.
cards.source: Cao B et al. Oral Simnotrelvir for Adult Patients with Mild-to-Moderate Covid-19. N Engl J Med. 2024. PMID: 38231624. Registry ID: NCT05506176. cards.headline: Yang 2023 (phase 1, 88 healthy subjects): simnotrelvir–ritonavir at the trial dose was tolerated and held trough levels above the in-vitro inhibitory target
cards.summary: Yang 2023 (phase 1, 88 healthy subjects): simnotrelvir–ritonavir at the trial dose was tolerated and held trough levels above the in-vitro inhibitory target
cards.type: Phase 1 randomised study in healthy volunteers (Yang 2023)
cards.people: Healthy adult subjects in a first-in-human dose-escalation study: 72 received simnotrelvir alone or with ritonavir across dose cohorts and 16 received placebo, including a food-effect assessment (registry NCT05339646 as printed in the record).
cards.result: Adverse-event incidence was 22.2% in intervention groups vs 6.3% on placebo, with no safety signal stopping development. Ritonavir cut simnotrelvir's apparent clearance from 135–369 L/h to 19.5–29.8 L/h; exposure rose roughly dose-proportionally between 250 and 750 mg with ritonavir, accumulation was low (index 1.39–1.51), and food raised exposure by 44.0%–47.3%. Trough concentrations at 750 mg/100 mg twice daily exceeded the level required for 90% inhibition of SARS-CoV-2 in vitro, supporting the dose the phase 2/3 trial used.
cards.watchOut: Healthy volunteers, pharmacokinetics and tolerability only — carded as programme support, not efficacy. The in-vitro inhibition target is a laboratory benchmark, not a clinical outcome.
cards.source: Yang XM et al. A first-in-human phase 1 study of simnotrelvir, a 3CL-like protease inhibitor for treatment of COVID-19, in healthy adult subjects. Eur J Pharm Sci. 2023. PMID: 37783378. cards.headline: Li 2025 (retrospective cohort, 585 hospitalised patients, China, observational): simnotrelvir vs nirmatrelvir — no difference in progression, death or respiratory support at 28 days
cards.summary: Li 2025 (retrospective cohort, 585 hospitalised patients, China, observational): simnotrelvir vs nirmatrelvir — no difference in progression, death or respiratory support at 28 days
cards.people: 585 hospitalised adults with COVID-19 during the Omicron wave in China treated with simnotrelvir–ritonavir (n=264) or nirmatrelvir–ritonavir (n=321); after propensity matching, 186 patients per group. Observational — treatment was chosen clinically, not randomised.
cards.result: There was no statistically significant difference between the groups in cumulative risk of the composite of disease progression, all-cause death and respiratory support at 28 days (P>0.05). Clinical improvement occurred more often with simnotrelvir (33.602 vs 30.913 events per 1,000 person-days; adjusted hazard ratio for clinical improvement 1.395, 95% CI 1.118 to 1.741; P=0.003, a relative measure from an observational model).
cards.watchOut: Retrospective and confounded by treatment choice despite propensity matching; hospitalised patients are also a different population from the trial's mild-to-moderate outpatients. The clinical-improvement hazard ratio is a model-adjusted relative measure from non-randomised data.
cards.source: Li C et al.
