shelves.title: Sipavibart (SUPERNOVA): 34.9% relative protection for immunocompromised people — and none shown against the Phe456Leu variants that came to dominate
shelves.question: In immunocompromised people, does monoclonal-antibody pre-exposure prophylaxis with sipavibart, compared with placebo or comparator antibody, prevent symptomatic COVID-19?
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit, variant-dependent and time-limited) — the variant caveat is the headline, not a footnote. In SUPERNOVA (PMID 40015292), 3,349 immunocompromised participants aged ≥12 years in 18 countries received intramuscular sipavibart 300 mg or a comparator (tixagevimab–cilgavimab or placebo): symptomatic COVID-19 from any variant within 181 days occurred in 7.4% vs 10.9% (relative risk reduction 34.9%, 97.5% CI 15.0 to 50.1 — a relative measure; absolute difference 3.5 percentage points). Against non-Phe456Leu variants the relative reduction was 42.9%, but against Phe456Leu-containing variants (e.g. KP.2/KP.3 lineages, dominant by November 2024) the trial showed NO efficacy (2.9% vs 3.9%; relative reduction 30.4%, 95% CI −1.8 to 52.5, spanning no effect; the authors' own conclusion states no efficacy was shown against resistant variants). Protection is therefore only as good as the match to currently circulating variants, and wanes with the 181-day dosing interval studied. The second programme, pemivibart (CANOPY, PMID 40410927), showed a large relative reduction in a randomised cohort without immunocompromise (composite COVID-19 1.9% vs 11.9% through month 6; standardised relative risk reduction 84.1%) with an anaphylaxis risk (4 of 623 recipients, 0.6%). Products are named exactly as the publications name them: sipavibart and pemivibart. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) with the variant caveat carried in the stamp itself.

cards.headline: SUPERNOVA 2025 (3,349 immunocompromised participants): sipavibart cut symptomatic COVID-19 by 34.9% relative overall — but showed no efficacy against Phe456Leu variants
cards.summary: SUPERNOVA 2025 (3,349 immunocompromised participants): sipavibart cut symptomatic COVID-19 by 34.9% relative overall — but showed no efficacy against Phe456Leu variants
cards.people: 3,349 immunocompromised participants aged ≥12 years at 197 centres in 18 countries, randomised 1:1 to intramuscular sipavibart 300 mg on days 1 and 181 (n=1,674 assigned; 1,669 dosed) or comparator (n=1,675 assigned; 1,105 tixagevimab–cilgavimab on day 1 and 561 placebo); 56.8% women; screened March to October 2023. Primary efficacy set: participants RT-PCR-negative at baseline who received at least one dose.
cards.result: Within 181 days, symptomatic COVID-19 from any variant: 122 of 1,649 (7.4%) on sipavibart vs 178 of 1,631 (10.9%) on comparator (relative risk reduction 34.9%, 97.5% CI 15.0 to 50.1; P=0.0006 — a relative measure; absolute rates 7.4% vs 10.9%). From non-Phe456Leu variants: 3.3% vs 5.5% (relative reduction 42.9%, 95% CI 19.9 to 59.3). From Phe456Leu-containing variants: 2.9% vs 3.9% (relative reduction 30.4%, 95% CI −1.8 to 52.5) — the trial's conclusion states no efficacy was shown against these resistant variants, which dominated by November 2024. Adverse events within 3 months: 49.9% vs 51.5%; intervention-related serious adverse events 0.1% vs 0.4%; one COVID-19 death, in the comparator group.
cards.watchOut: Funded by AstraZeneca, the manufacturer. The comparator mixed an active antibody (tixagevimab–cilgavimab) with placebo, and efficacy is variant-dependent and time-limited to the 181-day window: a result earned against 2023 variants does not transfer to seasons when Phe456Leu lineages dominate. The variant caveat is on the face of this card deliberately.

cards.headline: CANOPY 2025 (pemivibart): composite COVID-19 through month 6 was 1.9% vs 11.9% on placebo in the randomised non-immunocompromised cohort (84.1% relative reduction) — with anaphylaxis in 0.6%
cards.summary: CANOPY 2025 (pemivibart): composite COVID-19 through month 6 was 1.9% vs 11.9% on placebo in the randomised non-immunocompromised cohort (84.1% relative reduction) — with anaphylaxis in 0.6%
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial, phase 3 interim analysis (CANOPY, Wolfe 2025)
cards.people: Adults ≥18 years, SARS-CoV-2-negative at entry, enrolled September–November 2023: cohort A, 306 participants with significant immunocompromise, all received open pemivibart 4,500 mg intravenously twice, 90 days apart; cohort B, participants without significant immunocompromise randomised 2:1 to pemivibart (n=317) or placebo (n=162). Interim analysis; the immunocompromised cohort's primary endpoint was immunobridging, reported elsewhere.
cards.result: Cohort B composite (RT-PCR-confirmed symptomatic COVID-19, COVID-19 hospitalisation, or all-cause mortality) through month 6: 6 of 317 (1.9%) on pemivibart vs 19 of 160 (11.9%) on placebo (standardised relative risk reduction 84.1%, 95% CI 60.9 to 93.5; nominal P<0.001 — a relative measure); through month 12, 4.7% vs 18.1% (relative reduction 73.9%). Cohort A composite incidence through month 6 was 11 of 298 (3.7%, including 2 deaths), with no internal comparator. Infusion reactions were the commonest drug-related events (3.6% cohort A; 2.2% cohort B pemivibart); 4 of 623 pemivibart recipients (0.6%) had anaphylactic reactions, serious in 2.
cards.watchOut: A different antibody (pemivibart) from SUPERNOVA's sipavibart, carded alongside as the second prophylaxis programme — not pooled with it. The randomised efficacy cohort (B) was NOT immunocompromised; the immunocompromised cohort (A) had no placebo arm, so its 3.7% is a rate, not an effect. Interim analysis, and the same variant-dependence applies.
cards.source: CANOPY (Wolfe CR et al.) Safety and Efficacy of Pemivibart, a Long-Acting Monoclonal Antibody, for Prevention of Symptomatic COVID-19: Interim Results From a Phase 3 Randomized Clinical Trial (CANOPY). Clin Infect Dis. 2025. cards.headline: Okada 2026 (phase 1, 24 healthy Japanese adults — small, N printed): single sipavibart doses were tolerated, with a linear concentration–neutralisation relationship
cards.summary: Okada 2026 (phase 1, 24 healthy Japanese adults — small, N printed): single sipavibart doses were tolerated, with a linear concentration–neutralisation relationship
cards.type: Phase 1 randomised study in healthy volunteers (Okada 2026)
cards.people: 24 healthy Japanese adults aged 18–55 years randomised in three cohorts of 8 (6 sipavibart, 2 placebo each) to sipavibart 300 mg intramuscular, 600 mg intramuscular, or 1,200 mg intravenous, followed for about a year. N = 24 — a small phase 1 study, labelled plainly.
cards.result: Through day 91, adverse events were reported in 5 of 18 (27.8%) sipavibart recipients and 1 of 6 (16.7%) on placebo; there were no deaths, serious or treatment-related adverse events, or discontinuations. Exposure was consistent across routes and doses, neutralising titres against all tested variants rose, and the concentration–neutralisation relationship was linear; no participant developed treatment-emergent anti-drug antibodies.
cards.watchOut: 24 healthy volunteers — tolerability and pharmacokinetics only, in a population unlike the immunocompromised target group. Carded as programme support; the neutralisation rises are laboratory measures against the variants tested at the time.
cards.source: Okada H et al. cards.headline: Synthesis: real but variant-conditional protection — 34.9% relative overall, none shown against Phe456Leu variants; a second antibody shows the same class pattern plus anaphylaxis risk
cards.summary: Synthesis: real but variant-conditional protection — 34.9% relative overall, none shown against Phe456Leu variants; a second antibody shows the same class pattern plus anaphylaxis risk
cards.people: One 3,349-participant phase 3 RCT in immunocompromised people (SUPERNOVA), one phase 3 programme with 306 open-label immunocompromised and 479 randomised non-immunocompromised participants (CANOPY), and one 24-volunteer phase 1 study.
cards.result: Sipavibart: symptomatic COVID-19 7.4% vs 10.9% (relative reduction 34.9%); non-Phe456Leu 42.9% relative; Phe456Leu — no efficacy shown. Pemivibart randomised cohort: 1.9% vs 11.9% composite through month 6 (84.1% relative), anaphylaxis 0.6%. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit, variant-dependent and time-limited).
cards.watchOut: Both programmes were run against earlier variant mixes; circulating-variant match at the time of any real-world use decides whether these numbers mean anything, and neither trial shows protection against severe disease or death as a powered endpoint. Stamps must be revisited as variants move.

shelves.title: Oral vancomycin prophylaxis during systemic antibiotics: observational data favour secondary prevention after a prior C. difficile episode, primary prevention was not significant, and the two small randomised trials (N=81 and N=21) did not reach significance
shelves.question: In hospitalised adults receiving high-risk systemic antibiotics, does oral vancomycin prophylaxis, compared with no prophylaxis, prevent Clostridioides difficile infection?
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — and the primary/secondary split is the whole story. This is an OBSERVATIONAL-ONLY evidence base for the main signal, with confounding by indication as the dominant bias: clinicians give prophylaxis to the patients they judge highest-risk, so cohort comparisons can flatter or sink the drug for reasons unrelated to it. For SECONDARY prevention (prophylaxis during new systemic antibiotics in patients with a prior CDI episode), the Tariq 2021 meta-analysis of observational studies found future CDI in 13.3% on prophylaxis vs 21.9% without (OR 0.34, 95% CI 0.20-0.59; 10 studies, 9,258 patients). For PRIMARY prevention the same meta-analysis found NO significant effect (7.4% vs 10.4%; OR 0.18, 95% CI 0.03-1.03; p=0.06; 4 studies, 1,352 patients; heterogeneity I2=76%). A 2025 Bayesian meta-analysis of primary prophylaxis in stem-cell transplant (6 studies, 1,236 patients) found OR 0.31 before adjustment but OR 0.88 and non-significant after accounting for strong publication bias. The two randomised trials are small and both non-significant: Keating 2025 (N=81) recurrence 43.6% vs 57.1% on placebo (absolute difference -13.5 percentage points, 95% CI -35.1 to 8.0), with vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus carriage doubled (50.0% vs 24.0%, P=.048); PREVAN 2026 (N=21) recurrence 14.3% vs 42.9% (P=0.30), explicitly underpowered. Stamp wording must not imply proven prevention: no adequately powered randomised trial exists.

cards.headline: Tariq 2021 meta-analysis (all observational): secondary prevention worked on paper (future CDI 13.3% vs 21.9%; OR 0.34) — primary prevention did not (7.4% vs 10.4%; OR 0.18, CI crossing 1; p=0.06)
cards.summary: Tariq 2021 meta-analysis (all observational): secondary prevention worked on paper (future CDI 13.3% vs 21.9%; OR 0.34) — primary prevention did not (7.4% vs 10.4%; OR 0.18, CI crossing 1; p=0.06)
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of observational studies (Tariq 2021)
cards.people: Patients on systemic antimicrobial therapy in case-control and cohort studies (searched 2000 to January 2020). Primary prevention: 4 studies, 1,352 patients (402 on oral vancomycin prophylaxis, 950 not). Secondary prevention (prior CDI, new systemic antibiotics): 10 studies, 9,258 patients (713 on prophylaxis, 8,545 not).
cards.result: Primary prevention: CDI occurred in 29/402 (7.4%) on prophylaxis vs 99/950 (10.4%) without; pooled OR 0.18 (95% CI 0.03-1.03; p=0.06) — not significant, with substantial heterogeneity (I2=76%). Secondary prevention: future CDI in 91/713 (13.3%) on prophylaxis vs 1,875/8,545 (21.9%) without; pooled OR 0.34 (95% CI 0.20-0.59; p<0.00001), heterogeneity I2=59%. The authors conclude prophylaxis appears to decrease future CDI after a prior episode but was not effective for primary prevention.
cards.watchOut: Every included study is observational — confounding by indication is the dominant bias (prophylaxis is prescribed to patients judged highest-risk), and the primary-prevention confidence interval (0.03-1.03) is so wide it is compatible with anything from near-elimination to no effect. The secondary-prevention OR is a relative measure from non-randomised data; the absolute rates (13.3% vs 21.9%) are printed beside it on this card deliberately.
cards.source: Tariq R et al. Efficacy of oral vancomycin prophylaxis for prevention of Clostridioides difficile infection: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Therapeutic advances in gastroenterology. 2021. PMID: 33747124. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Viana-Cardenas 2025 Bayesian meta-analysis (primary prophylaxis in stem-cell transplant, 6 studies, 1,236 patients): OR 0.31 unadjusted — but OR 0.88 and non-significant after correcting for strong publication bias
cards.summary: Viana-Cardenas 2025 Bayesian meta-analysis (primary prophylaxis in stem-cell transplant, 6 studies, 1,236 patients): OR 0.31 unadjusted — but OR 0.88 and non-significant after correcting for strong publication bias
cards.type: Systematic review and Bayesian meta-analysis of observational studies (Viana-Cardenas 2025)
cards.people: 1,236 patients undergoing haematopoietic stem-cell transplantation in 6 studies (searched to 21 March 2025) comparing CDI incidence with vs without oral vancomycin primary prophylaxis; four of the six studies were rated fair to good quality.
cards.result: Oral vancomycin primary prophylaxis was associated with lower CDI incidence during hospitalisation (OR 0.31; 95% credible interval 0.16-0.59). However, the analysis detected strong publication bias, and after accounting for it the estimated reduction shrank to OR 0.88 (95% CrI 0.32-1.16) — no longer statistically significant. Secondary outcomes (VRE cultures, bloodstream infections, graft-versus-host disease, length of stay) were similar between groups. The authors conclude further studies are needed to provide stronger evidence for or against the intervention.
cards.watchOut: A textbook publication-bias lesson: the headline OR of 0.31 rests on small positive cohorts being published while null ones were not; the bias-adjusted estimate is the honest one and it is null-compatible. All six studies are observational.
cards.source: Viana-Cardenas E et al. A systematic literature review and bayesian meta-analysis of oral vancomycin primary prophylaxis for Clostridioides difficile infection in stem cell transplant patients. Antimicrobial stewardship & healthcare epidemiology : ASHE. 2025. PMID: 41127168. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Ganetsky 2019 retrospective cohort (allogeneic transplant, n=145): CDI in 0 of 90 patients on oral vancomycin prophylaxis vs 11 of 55 (20%) without (P<.001)
cards.summary: Ganetsky 2019 retrospective cohort (allogeneic transplant, n=145): CDI in 0 of 90 patients on oral vancomycin prophylaxis vs 11 of 55 (20%) without (P<.001)
cards.people: 145 consecutive adult allogeneic haematopoietic cell transplant recipients at the University of Pennsylvania (April 2015 to November 2016). The prophylaxis group (n=90) received oral vancomycin 125 mg twice daily from admission to discharge; 55 patients received no prophylaxis.
cards.result: No cases of CDI occurred in patients who received prophylaxis (0/90, 0%), whereas 11/55 (20%) patients without prophylaxis developed CDI (P<.001). Prophylaxis was not associated with higher risk of grade 2-4 acute graft-versus-host disease (subhazard ratio 1.59; 95% CI 0.88-2.89), grade 3-4 GVHD, or gastrointestinal GVHD at day 180, and no associations with relapse or survival were observed. The authors call for prospective evaluation.
cards.watchOut: A single-centre retrospective before/after-style comparison with a zero-event arm: 0/90 is striking but fragile — era effects, infection-control changes and confounding by indication cannot be separated from the drug effect in this design, and a zero numerator makes the effect size unquantifiable rather than infinite.
cards.source: Ganetsky A et al. Oral Vancomycin Prophylaxis Is Highly Effective in Preventing Clostridium difficile Infection in Allogeneic Hematopoietic Cell Transplant Recipients. Clinical infectious diseases. 2019. PMID: 30256954. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Keating 2025 randomised trial (secondary prophylaxis, N=81 — small, printed): recurrence 43.6% on oral vancomycin vs 57.1% on placebo (difference -13.5 points, CI -35.1 to 8.0) — not significant; VRE carriage 50.0% vs 24.0% (P=.048)
cards.summary: Keating 2025 randomised trial (secondary prophylaxis, N=81 — small, printed): recurrence 43.6% on oral vancomycin vs 57.1% on placebo (difference -13.5 points, CI -35.1 to 8.0) — not significant; VRE carriage 50.0% vs 24.0% (P=.048)
cards.people: 81 adults in 4 large US health systems who had completed treatment for CDI within the past 180 days and were taking a systemic antibiotic for a non-CDI indication (enrolled May 2018 to March 2023); randomised 1:1 to oral vancomycin 125 mg once daily (n=39) or placebo (n=42) during the antibiotic course plus 5 days after it ended, with 8 weeks of follow-up after treatment. N=81 printed plainly — a small trial.
cards.result: Recurrent CDI occurred in 17/39 (43.6%) on oral vancomycin vs 24/42 (57.1%) on placebo — an absolute difference of -13.5 percentage points (95% CI -35.1 to 8.0), which includes no effect. Adverse events occurred in 69.2% vs 64.3%. Vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus carriage in stool 8 weeks after treatment was found in 15/30 (50.0%) on vancomycin vs 6/25 (24.0%) on placebo (P=.048).
cards.watchOut: The only double-blind randomised test of secondary prophylaxis at this size, and it does not confirm the observational signal — its confidence interval spans a 35-point benefit and an 8-point harm. The doubled VRE carriage is the clearest randomised harm signal in this literature and belongs beside any efficacy claim.
cards.source: Keating JA et al. Oral Vancomycin for Prevention of Recurrent Clostridioides difficile Infection: A Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA network open. 2025. PMID: 40601321. randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 2 trial (keating 2025) 81 adults in 4 large us health systems who had completed treatment for cdi within the past 180 days and were taking a systemic antibiotic for a non-cdi indication (enrolled may 2018 to march 2023); randomised 1:1 to oral vancomycin 125 mg once daily (n=39) or placebo (n=42) during the antibiotic course plus 5 days after it ended, with 8 weeks of follow-up after treatment. n=81 printed plainly — a small trial. recurrent cdi occurred in 17/39 (43.6%) on oral vancomycin vs 24/42 (57.1%) on placebo — an absolute difference of -13.5 percentage points (95% ci -35.1 to 8.0), which includes no effect. adverse events occurred in 69.2% vs 64.3%. vancomycin-resistant enterococcus carriage in stool 8 weeks after treatment was found in 15/30 (50.0%) on vancomycin vs 6/25 (24.0%) on placebo (p=.048). the only double-blind randomised test of secondary prophylaxis at this size, and it does not confirm the observational signal — its confidence interval spans a 35-point benefit and an 8-point harm. the doubled vre carriage is the clearest randomised harm signal in this literature and belongs beside any efficacy claim. keating ja et al. oral vancomycin for prevention of recurrent clostridioides difficile infection: a randomized clinical trial. jama network open. 2025. pmid: 40601321. registry id: nct03462459. mesh: humans · *vancomycin/administration & dosage,therapeutic use · male · female · *clostridium infections/prevention & control,drug therapy,epidemiology · middle aged · double-blind method · *anti-bacterial agents/administration & dosage,therapeutic use · administration, oral · aged · clostridioides difficile/drug effects · secondary prevention/methods · recurrence · adult

cards.headline: PREVAN 2026 randomised trial (secondary prophylaxis, N=21 — very small, printed): recurrence 14.3% on oral vancomycin vs 42.9% on placebo (P=0.30) — explicitly underpowered
cards.summary: PREVAN 2026 randomised trial (secondary prophylaxis, N=21 — very small, printed): recurrence 14.3% on oral vancomycin vs 42.9% on placebo (P=0.30) — explicitly underpowered
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial (PREVAN, San-Juan 2026)
cards.people: 21 adults at a tertiary hospital in Spain with documented CDI within the previous 180 days who required hospitalisation and systemic antibiotics, randomised 2:1 to oral vancomycin 125 mg every 6 hours (n=14) or placebo (n=7) for 10 days. Mean age 73.5 years; 76.7% had malignancy and/or immunosuppression. N=21 printed plainly — far below any adequate sample size.
cards.result: CDI recurrence within 60 days occurred in 2/14 (14.3%) on vancomycin vs 3/7 (42.9%) on placebo (P=0.30). Recurrence-free survival at 60 days was 83% (95% CI 48-95) vs 42% (95% CI 6-77) (log-rank P=0.09). No treatment-related serious adverse events were observed. The authors describe the reduction as clinically relevant but the trial as underpowered, and call for adequately powered randomised studies.
cards.watchOut: Twenty-one patients: five total events decide this trial, and neither endpoint reaches significance. It is carded because the slate requires the small trial Ns on the face — read it as 'randomised evidence is still essentially absent', not as support.

cards.headline: Synthesis: an observational secondary-prevention signal that randomised evidence has not confirmed — and no support for primary prevention
cards.summary: Synthesis: an observational secondary-prevention signal that randomised evidence has not confirmed — and no support for primary prevention
cards.people: Two meta-analyses of observational studies (Tariq 2021: 1,352 primary-prevention and 9,258 secondary-prevention patients; Viana-Cardenas 2025: 1,236 transplant patients), one retrospective transplant cohort (Ganetsky 2019, n=145), and the only two randomised trials (Keating 2025, N=81; PREVAN 2026, N=21).
cards.result: Secondary prevention after a prior CDI episode: observational pooled OR 0.34 (absolute rates 13.3% vs 21.9%), but the two small RCTs were both non-significant (43.6% vs 57.1%; 14.3% vs 42.9%). Primary prevention: meta-analysis non-significant (OR 0.18, CI 0.03-1.03), and the transplant-specific estimate collapses to OR 0.88 after publication-bias correction. Randomised harm signal: VRE carriage 50.0% vs 24.0%. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence).
cards.watchOut: Confounding by indication pervades every non-randomised number on this shelf, and stamp wording must not imply proven prevention. An adequately powered RCT of secondary prophylaxis would change this stamp; until then the honest answer differs by indication — possible help after a prior episode, unproven for primary prevention.

shelves.title: Rapid multiplex PCR for hospital-acquired and ventilator-associated pneumonia (INHALE WP3): stewardship clearly improved (76.5% vs 55.9% on appropriate therapy at 24 h) — but clinical cure was numerically worse and non-inferiority was not demonstrated (56.7% vs 64.5%)
shelves.question: In critically ill adults with suspected hospital-acquired or ventilator-associated pneumonia, does rapid syndromic multiplex PCR testing of respiratory samples, compared with standard culture-based microbiology, improve antimicrobial stewardship and clinical cure?
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the stewardship half and the clinical half of this question point in different directions, and both halves are on the face of this shelf. The panel carried into the INHALE WP3 randomised trial was the FilmArray Pneumonia Panel (BioFire/bioMérieux), named here per the clarification exception because the evidence is panel-specific. In INHALE WP3 (n=554, 14 UK ICUs), the stewardship co-primary endpoint was met clearly: 76.5% vs 55.9% of patients were on antibacterially appropriate and proportionate antibiotics at 24 hours (estimated difference 21 percentage points, 95% CI 13-28). But the clinical-cure co-primary endpoint FAILED its non-inferiority test: cure at 14 days was 56.7% on PCR-guided care vs 64.5% on standard care (estimated difference -6 points, 95% CI -15 to 2; the pre-set non-inferiority margin was -13%), and secondary mortality and SOFA outcomes narrowly favoured the control arm without clear statistical significance. Two smaller randomised trials rhyme: a French HAP trial (n=109 analysed, stopped early) improved day-0 appropriateness (47% vs 24%) but did not reduce broad-spectrum exposure; a VAP/vHAP trial (n=146 analysed) found targeted therapy at 24 hours in 35.1% vs 23.6% (p=0.13, not significant overall). The INHALE economic analysis found PCR-guided care cheaper overall (-£7,802 per patient, CI crossing zero) and dominant on the stewardship outcome, but could not show cost-effectiveness on clinical cure. Faster, better-targeted antibiotics: shown. Patients doing better: not shown, and the largest trial's cure point estimate favours standard care.

cards.headline: INHALE WP3 RCT (n=554, 14 UK ICUs): stewardship co-primary met — 76.5% vs 55.9% on appropriate, proportionate antibiotics at 24 h — but clinical-cure non-inferiority NOT demonstrated (56.7% vs 64.5%; margin -13%)
cards.summary: INHALE WP3 RCT (n=554, 14 UK ICUs): stewardship co-primary met — 76.5% vs 55.9% on appropriate, proportionate antibiotics at 24 h — but clinical-cure non-inferiority NOT demonstrated (56.7% vs 64.5%; margin -13%)
cards.type: Multicentre, open-label, pragmatic randomised controlled trial (INHALE WP3, Enne 2025)
cards.people: 554 eligible adults and children with suspected hospital-acquired or ventilator-associated pneumonia recruited at 14 UK ICUs (July 2019 to August 2021, with a COVID-enforced pause); data analysed for 453 adults and 92 children (68.4% male). Intervention: rapid in-ICU syndromic PCR (the FilmArray Pneumonia Panel, BioFire/bioMérieux — named as the publications name it) coupled with optional prescribing guidance, vs standard of care.
cards.result: Stewardship co-primary endpoint (superiority): 205/268 (76.5%) reviewable intervention patients were receiving antibacterially appropriate and proportionate antibiotics at 24 h, vs 147/263 (55.9%) on standard care (estimated difference 21 percentage points; 95% CI 13-28). Clinical-cure co-primary endpoint (non-inferiority): 152/268 (56.7%) intervention patients were deemed cured of pneumonia at 14 days vs 171/265 (64.5%) on standard care (estimated difference -6 points; 95% CI -15 to 2) — the confidence interval crossed the predefined -13% non-inferiority margin, so non-inferiority was NOT demonstrated. Secondary mortality and change-in-SOFA outcomes narrowly favoured the control arm, without clear statistical significance.
cards.watchOut: Both halves of this result must travel together: quoting the 21-point stewardship win without the failed cure endpoint misrepresents the trial. The cure analysis set is smaller than the randomised total (reviewable patients), the trial was open-label, and recruitment spanned the COVID period. The authors' own conclusion: stewardship improved; whether those gains can be safely and advantageously implemented needs further clinical-effectiveness research.
cards.source: Enne VI et al. INHALE WP3, a multicentre, open-label, pragmatic randomised controlled trial assessing the impact of rapid, ICU-based, syndromic PCR, versus standard-of-care on antibiotic stewardship and clinical outcomes in hospital-acquired and ventilator-associated pneumonia. Intensive care medicine. 2025. PMID: 39961847. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: INHALE WP3 economic evaluation (second report of the same trial): PCR-guided care cost £7,802 less per patient overall (CI crossing zero) and dominated on stewardship — but not on clinical cure
cards.summary: INHALE WP3 economic evaluation (second report of the same trial): PCR-guided care cost £7,802 less per patient overall (CI crossing zero) and dominated on stewardship — but not on clinical cure
cards.type: Cost-effectiveness analysis of the INHALE WP3 RCT — second, explicitly labelled report of the same trial (Enne programme, 2025)
cards.people: The INHALE WP3 randomised population (ICU patients with hospital-acquired pneumonia, including ventilator-associated pneumonia), with resource use and costs collected inside the trial; the test evaluated is named in the report as the bioMérieux BioFire FilmArray Pneumonia Panel used in-ICU.
cards.result: Average total ICU costs (including PCR costs) were £33,149 in the intervention group vs £40,951 for standard care — a difference of -£7,802 (95% CI -£15,696 to £92). For the antibiotic-stewardship outcome, PCR-guided therapy was both less costly and more effective than routine management (dominant). For clinical cure, the analysis did not find PCR-guided therapy cost-effective in the same way — the report's cure-based analysis reflects the trial's failure to demonstrate cure non-inferiority.
cards.watchOut: This is a second report of the same single trial, not independent evidence — it is labelled as such and must not be double-counted. The cost difference's confidence interval just crosses zero (£92), and a cost saving built partly on shorter ICU stay sits uneasily beside a numerically worse cure rate: cheaper and better-targeted is not the same as better for patients.
cards.source: Wagner AP et al. Cost-effectiveness of rapid, ICU-based, syndromic PCR in hospital-acquired pneumonia: analysis of the INHALE WP3 multi-centre RCT. cards.headline: French multicentre RCT in non-ventilated HAP (n=109 analysed; stopped at half its planned size): multiplex PCR with expert advice improved day-0 appropriate therapy (47% vs 24%, P=0.01) but did not reduce broad-spectrum antibiotic exposure (P=0.41)
cards.summary: French multicentre RCT in non-ventilated HAP (n=109 analysed; stopped at half its planned size): multiplex PCR with expert advice improved day-0 appropriate therapy (47% vs 24%, P=0.01) but did not reduce broad-spectrum antibiotic exposure (P=0.41)
cards.people: Adults with non-ventilator-associated hospital-acquired pneumonia in ICU or non-ICU wards at seven French tertiary hospitals (February 2020 to August 2023); 116 randomised, 109 included in follow-up (multiplex PCR n=55; conventional microbiology n=54). Median age 66 years; 66% were in ICU. Recruitment was disrupted by the COVID-19 pandemic and the trial terminated early at half the planned sample size.
cards.result: Mean duration of broad-spectrum antibiotics (primary endpoint) was 37.6 days of therapy/100 patient-days (SD 44.1) with multiplex PCR vs 48.7 (SD 54.5) with conventional microbiology (P=0.41) — not significantly different. Appropriate antibiotic therapy at day 0 was significantly more frequent with PCR (47% vs 24%, P=0.01). No differences were found in adverse outcomes, length of stay or costs.
cards.watchOut: An early-terminated, underpowered trial: its primary endpoint is null, and the positive day-0 appropriateness result is a secondary process measure. The pattern matches INHALE (better targeting, no demonstrated patient-outcome gain) at a fraction of the size.

cards.headline: VAP/vHAP FilmArray RCT (n=146 analysed): targeted antimicrobial therapy at 24 h in 35.1% with the panel vs 23.6% without (absolute difference 11.5 points, CI -0.03 to 26.2; p=0.13) — significant only in culture-confirmed pneumonia
cards.summary: VAP/vHAP FilmArray RCT (n=146 analysed): targeted antimicrobial therapy at 24 h in 35.1% with the panel vs 23.6% without (absolute difference 11.5 points, CI -0.03 to 26.2; p=0.13) — significant only in culture-confirmed pneumonia
cards.people: Immunocompetent adults with suspected ventilator-associated pneumonia or hospital-acquired pneumonia requiring ventilation (June 2020 to September 2023); 156 randomised, 146 analysed (74 FilmArray Pneumonia Panel plus conventional microbiology; 72 conventional microbiology alone). Median age 58 years; 84.9% had VAP; mean SOFA 8.0. The panel is named in the report as the FilmArray Pneumonia Panel (FAPP).
cards.result: Targeted antimicrobial therapy at 24 h (primary outcome): 35.1% in the panel group vs 23.6% in controls (absolute difference 11.5 percentage points; 95% CI -0.03 to 26.2; p=0.13) — not statistically significant. Secondary outcomes did not differ significantly. In the subgroup with culture-documented pneumonia (45.9% of patients), targeted therapy at 24 h was 55.3% vs 31.0% (absolute difference 24.2 points; 95% CI 1.1 to 47.4; p=0.048).
cards.watchOut: The headline comparison misses significance, and the positive finding lives in a subgroup defined by post-randomisation culture results — hypothesis-generating, not confirmatory. Even the stewardship endpoint most favourable to the panel is therefore unproven in suspected (as opposed to confirmed) pneumonia.

cards.headline: Synthesis: three randomised trials agree on process, none shows patients doing better — stewardship yes, clinical benefit unproven
cards.summary: Synthesis: three randomised trials agree on process, none shows patients doing better — stewardship yes, clinical benefit unproven
cards.people: INHALE WP3 (n=554, plus its economic second report), a French non-ventilated-HAP RCT (n=109 analysed, terminated early), and a VAP/vHAP FilmArray RCT (n=146 analysed) — all testing rapid syndromic multiplex PCR of respiratory samples against culture-based microbiology.
cards.result: Appropriate/proportionate therapy at 24 h: 76.5% vs 55.9% (INHALE, significant); day-0 appropriateness 47% vs 24% (French trial, significant) with broad-spectrum exposure unchanged; targeted therapy at 24 h 35.1% vs 23.6% (VAP trial, not significant). Clinical cure in the one trial powered to test it: 56.7% vs 64.5%, non-inferiority not demonstrated. PROPOSED SPLIT.
cards.watchOut: Do not let the stewardship numbers carry a clinical claim: the largest trial's cure point estimate favours standard care, and no trial shows a mortality or cure benefit. Panel-specific evidence (FilmArray Pneumonia Panel) should not be read across to other platforms without their own trials.
cards.source: Synthesis of Enne VI et al. Intensive care medicine. 2025 (PMID: 39961847); Wagner AP et al. Critical care (London, England). 2025 (PMID: 40781331); Kernéis S et al. JAC-antimicrobial resistance. 2026 (PMID: 42534393); Millot G et al. Intensive care medicine. 2026 (PMID: 42622675).

shelves.title: PCV20 and PCV21 in adults: licensed on antibody bridging, not disease endpoints — immunogenicity was non-inferior to older vaccines, and ACIP now recommends a single conjugate dose for all adults aged 50 and over
shelves.question: In adults, do the higher-valency pneumococcal conjugate vaccines PCV20 and PCV21, compared with earlier PCV15/PCV13 and PPSV23 strategies, provide immunogenic and clinically meaningful protection against pneumococcal disease?
shelves.balance: IMMUNOGENICITY-ONLY evidence — this shelf is a recommendations-and-evidence-quality answer, and it says so plainly. No clinical-endpoint efficacy randomised trial exists for PCV20 or PCV21 in adults: licensure rests on opsonophagocytic antibody (OPA) bridging against vaccines whose disease protection was established in earlier eras. PCV20's pivotal phase 3 trial met its primary immunogenicity objectives — responses non-inferior to PCV13 for the 13 matched serotypes and to PPSV23 for 6 of 7 additional serotypes (serotype 8 missed the statistical criterion). PCV21 (V116, an adult-specific 21-valent vaccine) was non-inferior to PCV20 for the 10 shared serotypes in STRIDE-3 (2,663 randomised) and superior for 10 of its 11 unique serotypes (15C excepted), and it was immunogenic in 717 vaccine-experienced adults regardless of which vaccine they had received before. Serotype-coverage percentages must never be quoted as effectiveness: a vaccine covering serotypes that cause a given share of disease has not been shown to prevent that share of disease. What clinicians actually use is the recommendation layer: since October 2024, ACIP recommends a single dose of a conjugate vaccine (PCV20, PCV21, or PCV15 followed by PPSV23) for all PCV-naive adults aged 50 years and over, extending the previous age-65 threshold, with risk-based recommendations unchanged at 19-49 years. Products are named exactly as the ACIP report names them: PCV20 is Prevnar 20 (Wyeth Pharmaceuticals); PCV21 is CAPVAXIVE (Merck Sharp & Dohme); PCV15 is VAXNEUVANCE (Merck Sharp & Dohme).

cards.headline: PCV20 pivotal phase 3 (Essink 2022): OPA responses non-inferior to PCV13 for all 13 matched serotypes and to PPSV23 for 6 of 7 additional serotypes — serotype 8 missed the criterion; no disease endpoints
cards.summary: PCV20 pivotal phase 3 (Essink 2022): OPA responses non-inferior to PCV13 for all 13 matched serotypes and to PPSV23 for 6 of 7 additional serotypes — serotype 8 missed the criterion; no disease endpoints
cards.type: Pivotal phase 3 randomised, double-blind immunogenicity trial (Essink 2022)
cards.people: Adults in three age groups (60 years and over, 50-59 years, and 18-49 years) at US and Swedish sites, randomised to a single dose of PCV20 or PCV13; participants aged 60 and over then also received saline or PPSV23 one month later so the 7 additional PCV20 serotypes could be compared against PPSV23. The record does not state the total enrolled N, so this card prints N not documented.
cards.result: Primary immunogenicity objectives were met: one month after vaccination, OPA geometric mean titres after PCV20 were non-inferior to PCV13 for the 13 matched serotypes and to PPSV23 for 6 of the 7 additional serotypes in participants aged 60 and over, using a non-inferiority criterion of the lower 95% CI bound for the titre ratio exceeding 0.5; serotype 8 missed the statistical non-inferiority criterion. Responses in younger participants were bridged to those in 60-64-year-olds. Local reactions and systemic events were similar in severity and frequency after PCV20 or PCV13, and no safety concerns were identified.
cards.watchOut: Every endpoint is an antibody titre at one month. Non-inferiority of a laboratory correlate against PCV13/PPSV23 is the licensing logic — it is not a measurement of pneumonia or invasive disease prevented, and the one serotype that missed (serotype 8) shows the bridging is not uniformly clean.
cards.source: Essink B et al. Pivotal Phase 3 Randomized Clinical Trial of the Safety, Tolerability, and Immunogenicity of 20-Valent Pneumococcal Conjugate Vaccine in Adults Aged ≥18 Years. Clinical infectious diseases. 2022. PMID: 34940806. Registry ID: NCT03760146. cards.headline: STRIDE-3 (PCV21/V116 vs PCV20; 2,663 randomised): non-inferior for the 10 shared serotypes and superior for 10 of 11 unique serotypes — 15C the exception — again on antibody titres only
cards.summary: STRIDE-3 (PCV21/V116 vs PCV20; 2,663 randomised): non-inferior for the 10 shared serotypes and superior for 10 of 11 unique serotypes — 15C the exception — again on antibody titres only
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised, double-blind, active-comparator immunogenicity trial (STRIDE-3, Platt 2024)
cards.people: 2,663 adults randomised at 112 sites in 11 countries or territories (2,656 vaccinated): cohort 1, aged 50 years and over (1,179 V116; 1,177 PCV20), stratified 50-64, 65-74, 75-84 and 85-plus; cohort 2, aged 18-49 years (200 V116; 100 PCV20). V116 is the 21-valent adult-specific conjugate vaccine (PCV21). Adults with or without stable chronic medical conditions were eligible.
cards.result: At day 30, V116 met non-inferiority criteria vs PCV20 for the ten serotypes common to both vaccines in cohort 1 (p<0.0001 for each). It met superiority criteria for ten of the eleven serotypes unique to V116 (OPA GMT ratio p<0.0001 for all except 15C, p=0.41; four-fold-rise criterion likewise excepting 15C, p=0.67). Responses in 18-49-year-olds were non-inferior to those in 50-64-year-olds for all 21 serotypes (immunobridging). Adverse events in cohort 1 were reported by 58.2% on V116 and 66.2% on PCV20; six deaths occurred, all in cohort 1 and none vaccine-related; there were no vaccine-related serious adverse events. Funded by Merck Sharp & Dohme.
cards.watchOut: A head-to-head of two vaccines neither of which has adult disease-endpoint efficacy data: 'superior' here means higher antibody titres against serotypes PCV20 does not contain — a formulation property, not demonstrated extra disease prevented. The 15C miss is printed because superiority claims for this vaccine are serotype-by-serotype, not blanket.
cards.source: Platt HL et al. Safety, tolerability, and immunogenicity of an adult pneumococcal conjugate vaccine, V116 (STRIDE-3): a randomised, double-blind, active comparator controlled, phase 3 study. The Lancet. Infectious diseases. 2024. PMID: 38964361. Registry ID: NCT05425732. cards.headline: STRIDE-6 (V116 in vaccine-experienced adults 50 and over; n=717): immunogenic for all 21 serotypes whatever the prior vaccine — PPSV23, PCV13, or combinations
cards.summary: STRIDE-6 (V116 in vaccine-experienced adults 50 and over; n=717): immunogenic for all 21 serotypes whatever the prior vaccine — PPSV23, PCV13, or combinations
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised immunogenicity study in pneumococcal vaccine-experienced adults (Scott 2024)
cards.people: 717 adults aged 50 years and over who had previously received pneumococcal vaccination: cohort 1 (n=350) had received PPSV23 and were randomised 2:1 to V116 or PCV15; cohort 2 (n=261) had received PCV13 and were randomised 2:1 to V116 or PPSV23; cohort 3 (n=106) had received various two-vaccine sequences and all received open-label V116.
cards.result: V116 was immunogenic in all three cohorts, as assessed by serotype-specific OPA geometric mean titres and IgG geometric mean concentrations 30 days after vaccination for all 21 serotypes. It elicited responses comparable to PCV15 (cohort 1) or PPSV23 (cohort 2) for shared serotypes and higher responses to serotypes unique to V116. Solicited adverse-event proportions were generally comparable across cohorts, and the authors describe a safety profile comparable to currently licensed pneumococcal vaccines.
cards.watchOut: This answers the practical 'which vaccine next for someone already vaccinated' question only at the antibody level, in a trial funded by the manufacturer; prior-vaccination histories were self-selected clinical populations, and no disease outcomes were measured.
cards.source: Scott P et al. A Phase 3 Clinical Study to Evaluate the Safety, Tolerability, and Immunogenicity of V116 in Pneumococcal Vaccine-Experienced Adults 50 Years of Age or Older (STRIDE-6). Clinical infectious diseases. 2024. PMID: 39082735. Registry ID: NCT05420961; EudraCT 2021-006679-41. cards.headline: ACIP 2025 (MMWR): a single conjugate dose now recommended for all PCV-naive adults aged 50 and over — PCV20 (Prevnar 20) or PCV21 (CAPVAXIVE) alone, or PCV15 (VAXNEUVANCE) plus PPSV23
cards.summary: ACIP 2025 (MMWR): a single conjugate dose now recommended for all PCV-naive adults aged 50 and over — PCV20 (Prevnar 20) or PCV21 (CAPVAXIVE) alone, or PCV15 (VAXNEUVANCE) plus PPSV23
cards.type: Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices recommendations (Kobayashi 2025, MMWR)
cards.people: US adults: the age-based recommendation was expanded on 23 October 2024 from 65 years and over to all PCV-naive adults aged 50 years and over; recommendations for adults aged 19-49 years with risk conditions, and for adults who began their series with PCV13, were unchanged. Product names are given exactly as the MMWR report gives them: PCV20 (Prevnar 20; Wyeth Pharmaceuticals), PCV21 (CAPVAXIVE; Merck Sharp & Dohme), PCV15 (VAXNEUVANCE; Merck Sharp & Dohme), PPSV23 (Pneumovax 23; Merck Sharp & Dohme), PCV13 (Prevnar 13; Wyeth Pharmaceuticals).
cards.result: ACIP recommended a single dose of a pneumococcal conjugate vaccine for all PCV-naive adults aged 50 years and over, using its Evidence to Recommendations framework; options are PCV20 or PCV21 alone, or PCV15 in series with PPSV23. Before October 2024 the age-based threshold was 65 years, with risk-based recommendations at 19-64 years. The report summarises the evidence considered — which for the newer valencies is the immunogenicity programme carded on this shelf, not disease-endpoint trials.
cards.watchOut: A recommendation is a policy judgement weighing immunobridging, serotype epidemiology, feasibility and cost — it is not itself evidence of clinical efficacy, and this card must not be cited as though ACIP's vote measured disease prevented. Recommendations also change; this is the January 2025 MMWR statement of the October 2024 vote.

cards.headline: Synthesis: strong antibody bridging, no disease-endpoint trials — the honest shelf is recommendations plus evidence quality
cards.summary: Synthesis: strong antibody bridging, no disease-endpoint trials — the honest shelf is recommendations plus evidence quality
cards.people: PCV20 pivotal phase 3 (Essink 2022; total N not documented in the record), PCV21 STRIDE-3 (2,663 randomised) and STRIDE-6 (717 vaccine-experienced adults), read against the ACIP recommendations for adults (MMWR 2025).
cards.result: PCV20: OPA non-inferiority met for 13/13 PCV13-matched and 6/7 PPSV23-additional serotypes (serotype 8 missed). PCV21: non-inferior to PCV20 on shared serotypes, superior on 10/11 unique serotypes (15C missed), immunogenic after any prior vaccine. Neither vaccine has an adult efficacy trial with pneumonia or invasive-disease endpoints; ACIP nonetheless recommends one conjugate dose from age 50. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit, immunogenicity only).
cards.watchOut: Never quote serotype-coverage percentages as effectiveness on this shelf, and do not upgrade the stamp on the strength of recommendations: the gap between antibody bridging and measured disease prevention is exactly what this shelf exists to make visible. Post-licensure effectiveness studies, when published, are the evidence that could change it.

shelves.title: Single-dose moxidectin vs ivermectin for uncomplicated strongyloidiasis: cure 93.6% vs 95.7% in a 726-person trial — non-inferior only against a wide -10-point margin, in endemic community settings
shelves.question: In adults with uncomplicated strongyloidiasis, does single-dose moxidectin, compared with ivermectin, achieve parasitological cure?
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a genuine non-inferiority result, read at the width of its margin. In the phase 2b/3 trial (Sprecher 2024; 726 adults in communities in Laos and Cambodia), single-dose moxidectin 8 mg cured 93.6% vs 95.7% on single-dose ivermectin 200 micrograms/kg — a difference of -2.1 percentage points (95% CI -5.5 to 1.3). Non-inferiority was declared because the CI's lower limit stayed above the pre-set margin of -10 PERCENTAGE POINTS, printed here on the face as required: that margin would have accepted a cure rate up to 10 points worse than ivermectin, so 'non-inferior' means 'not shown to be more than 10 points worse', not 'equal'. The earlier exploratory trial (Barda 2017; n=127) could NOT demonstrate non-inferiority against its tighter 7-point margin (difference -1.5 points, 95% CI -9.6 to 6.5), and the phase 2a dose-ranging trial (Hofmann 2021; n=223 randomised) is what fixed the 8 mg dose (predicted cure 87%, plateauing across 4-12 mg). Safety was similar throughout (abdominal pain about 9% in both arms of the large trial; no serious adverse events in the dose-ranging trial). APPLICABILITY CAVEAT: all three trials enrolled adults in endemic community settings in Laos/Cambodia; the patients in whom strongyloidiasis is most dangerous — immunocompromised people at risk of hyperinfection — were not the tested population, and nothing on this shelf speaks to hyperinfection or disseminated disease.

cards.headline: Sprecher 2024 phase 2b/3 (Laos and Cambodia, n=726): moxidectin cure 93.6% (324/346) vs ivermectin 95.7% (335/350); difference -2.1 points (CI -5.5 to 1.3) — non-inferior against the -10-point margin
cards.summary: Sprecher 2024 phase 2b/3 (Laos and Cambodia, n=726): moxidectin cure 93.6% (324/346) vs ivermectin 95.7% (335/350); difference -2.1 points (CI -5.5 to 1.3) — non-inferior against the -10-point margin
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, parallel-group non-inferiority trial, phase 2b/3 (Sprecher 2024)
cards.people: 726 adults aged 18-65 years in communities in Laos and Cambodia with parasitologically confirmed Strongyloides stercoralis infection (two or more positive quantitative Baermann assays), randomised 1:1 to single oral moxidectin 8 mg (n=363) or ivermectin 200 micrograms/kg (n=363), each with matched placebo; 4,291 people were screened. Primary endpoint: cure at 14-21 days in participants with outcome data (346 moxidectin; 350 ivermectin).
cards.result: Cure rate was 93.6% (95% CI 90.5-96.0; 324/346) on moxidectin vs 95.7% (93.0-97.6; 335/350) on ivermectin — a between-group difference of -2.1 percentage points (95% CI -5.5 to 1.3). Because the CI's lower limit (-5.5) was greater than the pre-specified non-inferiority margin of -10 percentage points, moxidectin was declared non-inferior. The most common adverse events were abdominal pain (9% vs 9%) and headache (7% vs 8%), predominantly mild and transient. The authors note moxidectin's fixed dose and lower cost as practical advantages. Funded by the Swiss National Science Foundation.
cards.watchOut: The -10-point margin is wide: this trial rules out moxidectin being more than about 5.5 points worse (the observed CI bound), but the design would have passed a drug up to 10 points worse. Participants were community-dwelling adults in an endemic setting — not immunocompromised patients, in whom cure assessment and stakes (hyperinfection) are entirely different.

cards.headline: Hofmann 2021 phase 2a dose-ranging (northern Laos, 223 randomised): predicted cure rose from 75% at 2 mg to about 87-88% at 8-12 mg, fixing the 8 mg dose taken into phase 3
cards.summary: Hofmann 2021 phase 2a dose-ranging (northern Laos, 223 randomised): predicted cure rose from 75% at 2 mg to about 87-88% at 8-12 mg, fixing the 8 mg dose taken into phase 3
cards.type: Randomised, single-blind, placebo-controlled dose-ranging trial, phase 2a (Hofmann 2021)
cards.people: 223 adults aged 18-65 years in four villages in northern Laos with S. stercoralis infection (at least 0.4 larvae per gram of stool in at least two samples), randomised across seven groups: moxidectin 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 or 12 mg single dose, or placebo; 209 completed and were analysed for the primary outcome (cure at 28 days).
cards.result: Predicted cure rates (Emax model): 75% (95% CI 59-87) at 2 mg vs 14% (5-31) on placebo, rising to 83% at 4 mg, 86% at 6 mg and 87% (80-92) at 8 mg, then levelling at 88% at both 10 mg and 12 mg. Observed cure at 8 mg was 24/29 (83%). Moxidectin was well tolerated at all doses, with no serious adverse events and all reported symptoms mild. The authors recommended the 8 mg dose (the dose used for onchocerciasis) for phase 2b/3 trials.
cards.watchOut: A dose-finding study with about 30 participants per arm and model-predicted cure rates — it justifies the dose, not the drug's comparative efficacy; the placebo arm (14% cure) reflects spontaneous/assay clearance in this design and should not be compared with the phase 3 cure rates, which used a different follow-up window (14-21 days) and population.
cards.source: Hofmann D et al. Efficacy and safety of ascending doses of moxidectin against Strongyloides stercoralis infections in adults: a randomised, parallel-group, single-blind, placebo-controlled, dose-ranging, phase 2a trial. The Lancet. Infectious diseases. 2021. PMID: 33798487. Registry ID: NCT04056325. cards.headline: Barda 2017 exploratory trial (n=127): cure 93.7% (59/63) on moxidectin vs 95.2% (59/62) on ivermectin — but non-inferiority was NOT demonstrated against its 7-point margin (difference -1.5 points, CI -9.6 to 6.5)
cards.summary: Barda 2017 exploratory trial (n=127): cure 93.7% (59/63) on moxidectin vs 95.2% (59/62) on ivermectin — but non-inferiority was NOT demonstrated against its 7-point margin (difference -1.5 points, CI -9.6 to 6.5)
cards.people: 127 participants with S. stercoralis infection randomised to single-dose moxidectin 8 mg or ivermectin 200 micrograms/kg; one participant per arm was lost to follow-up, leaving 63 and 62 analysed for cure. Cure rate against S. stercoralis was the primary outcome; efficacy against co-infections (hookworm, Opisthorchis viverrini) was secondary.
cards.result: Cure was 93.7% (59/63) on moxidectin vs 95.2% (59/62) on ivermectin — an estimated difference of -1.5 percentage points (95% CI -9.6 to 6.5). Because the CI's lower limit (-9.6) exceeded (crossed) the 7-percentage-point non-inferiority margin, non-inferiority could not be demonstrated despite the near-identical point estimates. No side effects were observed. Cure against hookworm was 57% vs 56%; both drugs had low efficacy against O. viverrini. The authors concluded moxidectin might be a safe and efficacious alternative but that larger trials were needed.
cards.watchOut: The contrast with Sprecher 2024 is a lesson in margins: almost the same point difference (-1.5 vs -2.1 points) failed a 7-point margin in a small trial and passed a 10-point margin in a large one. 'Non-inferior' is a property of the margin and the sample size, not of the drug alone — both margins are printed on this shelf for that reason.

cards.headline: Synthesis: cure rates within about 2 points of ivermectin in 1,076 randomised adults — non-inferiority rests on a wide margin, and the highest-risk group is untested
cards.summary: Synthesis: cure rates within about 2 points of ivermectin in 1,076 randomised adults — non-inferiority rests on a wide margin, and the highest-risk group is untested
cards.people: Three randomised trials in endemic community settings in Laos and Cambodia: Sprecher 2024 (n=726, phase 2b/3), Hofmann 2021 (n=223 randomised, phase 2a dose-ranging) and Barda 2017 (n=127). No trial enrolled immunocompromised patients or patients with hyperinfection.
cards.result: Head-to-head cure: 93.6% vs 95.7% (difference -2.1 points, CI -5.5 to 1.3; -10-point margin met) and 93.7% vs 95.2% (difference -1.5 points, CI -9.6 to 6.5; 7-point margin not met). Dose-ranging supports the fixed 8 mg dose (predicted cure about 87%). Adverse events were mild and similar between drugs. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: Endemic-setting applicability caveat: these are parasitological cure rates in otherwise well adults with uncomplicated infection. They say nothing about disseminated strongyloidiasis or hyperinfection in immunosuppressed patients — the setting where treatment failure is fatal — and single-dose moxidectin should not be extrapolated there from this shelf.
cards.source: Synthesis of Sprecher VP et al. The Lancet. Infectious diseases. 2024 (PMID: 37949090); Hofmann D et al. The Lancet. Infectious diseases. 2021 (PMID: 33798487); Barda B et al. Clinical infectious diseases. 2017 (PMID: 28369530).

shelves.title: The cuff-leak test predicts post-extubation stridor with high specificity but only moderate sensitivity: pooled specificity 0.87–0.88 and sensitivity 0.62–0.66 across 28 studies (4,493 extubations) — a low leak flags risk, but a normal leak does not clear a patient, and early single-centre cut-offs (110–130 mL) performed better than the pooled test
shelves.question: In mechanically ventilated adults being considered for extubation, does the cuff-leak test (cuff-leak volume/percentage) predict post-extubation stridor and reintubation accurately enough to guide extubation decisions?
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE, framed as diagnostic accuracy (GAP-E), not as a treatment effect. The three classic prospective cohorts agree that patients who develop post-extubation stridor have much smaller cuff leaks: Miller & Cole 1996 (100 intubations; stridor in 6%; mean leak 180 vs 360 mL; a leak <110 mL had positive predictive value 0.80 and specificity 0.99), Jaber 2003 (112 extubations; stridor incidence 12%; at thresholds of 130 mL and 12% of tidal volume, sensitivity 85% and specificity 95%), and Sandhu 2000 (110 trauma patients; stridor/reintubation groups had leaks of about 8–9% of tidal volume; a leak <10% had 96% specificity). The 2020 meta-analysis (28 studies, 4,493 extubations) tempers the early numbers: pooled sensitivity 0.62 and specificity 0.87 for post-extubation airway obstruction, and sensitivity 0.66 / specificity 0.88 for reintubation, with substantial heterogeneity. The clinical reading the source literature supports: use a low leak to trigger preparation (steroids, anaesthesia presence, delayed extubation in selected patients) — but do not treat a reassuring leak as clearance, and do not let a single low leak postpone extubation indefinitely, since most low-leak patients still extubate without stridor. Extubation-strategy shelves (packs #1309/#3133–#3135) and the SBT shelf (live #1321) ask different questions and are not duplicated.

cards.headline: Miller & Cole 1996: pre-extubation cuff leak was 180 vs 360 mL in patients who did vs did not develop stridor; a leak <110 mL had PPV 0.80 and specificity 0.99 (100 intubations)
cards.summary: Miller & Cole 1996: pre-extubation cuff leak was 180 vs 360 mL in patients who did vs did not develop stridor; a leak <110 mL had PPV 0.80 and specificity 0.99 (100 intubations)
cards.people: 100 consecutive intubations in a general medical ICU population; cuff-leak volume (inspiratory minus averaged expiratory tidal volume with the cuff deflated) was recorded within 24 h of starting and of ending mechanical ventilation. Post-extubation stridor accompanied 6% of extubations.
cards.result: Mean pre-extubation cuff-leak volume was significantly lower in patients who developed stridor than in those who did not (180 ± 157 mL vs 360 ± 157 mL; p=0.012). For a cuff leak <110 mL, the positive predictive value for post-extubation stridor was 0.80, the predictive value for absence of stridor with a leak >110 mL was 0.98, and specificity was 0.99. No other demographic or ventilation variables differed significantly between the groups.
cards.watchOut: Only about six stridor events underpin the cut-off: a PPV of 0.80 built on a handful of cases is fragile, and stridor prevalence (6%) was low — predictive values will fall further where stridor is rarer and rise where it is commoner. Single-centre, 1996 ventilator practice.
cards.source: Miller RL, Cole RP. Association between reduced cuff leak volume and postextubation stridor. Chest. 1996. PMID: 8874265. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Jaber 2003: stridor incidence 12%; at cut-offs of 130 mL and 12%, cuff-leak sensitivity was 85% and specificity 95% (112 extubations)
cards.summary: Jaber 2003: stridor incidence 12%; at cut-offs of 130 mL and 12%, cuff-leak sensitivity was 85% and specificity 95% (112 extubations)
cards.people: 112 extubations in 112 patients in a university-hospital ICU over 14 months, each preceded by a cuff-leak test; the study also evaluated risk factors for post-extubation stridor.
cards.result: Stridor incidence was 12%. Patients who developed stridor had a much lower cuff leak than the others, in absolute values (59 ± 92 mL vs 372 ± 170 mL; p<0.001) and relative values (9 ± 13% vs 56 ± 20%; p<0.001). At thresholds of 130 mL and 12% of tidal volume, sensitivity was 85% and specificity 95%. Stridor was also associated with higher SAPS II score, medical admission, traumatic or difficult intubation, self-extubation history, an over-inflated cuff at ICU admission and prolonged intubation.
cards.watchOut: The best-performing cut-offs in the literature come from this single centre; the same paper shows stridor is multifactorial (intubation trauma, duration, cuff over-inflation), so the leak is one risk marker among several, not a standalone gate.
cards.source: Jaber S et al. Post-extubation stridor in intensive care unit patients. Risk factors evaluation and importance of the cuff-leak test. Intensive care medicine. 2003. PMID: 12528025. cards.headline: Sandhu 2000: patients with stridor or stridor requiring reintubation had cuff leaks of only ~8–9% of tidal volume; a leak <10% had 96% specificity (110 trauma patients)
cards.summary: Sandhu 2000: patients with stridor or stridor requiring reintubation had cuff leaks of only ~8–9% of tidal volume; a leak <10% had 96% specificity (110 trauma patients)
cards.people: 110 consecutive trauma patients at a level I trauma centre who met standard weaning-protocol criteria and were studied prospectively at extubation; the commonest reason for intubation was closed-head injury. Percent cuff leak was the exhaled tidal-volume change on cuff deflation divided by the pre-deflation exhaled tidal volume; patients were followed for 24 h after extubation.
cards.result: Seven patients (6.4%) developed stridor alone, with a mean cuff leak of 58 mL (8.4% of tidal volume); six patients (5.5%) developed stridor requiring reintubation, with a mean leak of 68 mL (9.2%). Patients who developed stridor or needed reintubation had been intubated significantly longer. A cuff leak of less than 10% of tidal volume identified patients at risk for stridor or reintubation with 96% specificity. The authors note the leak decreases after more than 3 days of intubation.
cards.watchOut: A young trauma population with head injury predominating is not a general medical ICU population; event counts are small (7 and 6 patients), and the record's own numbers show intubation duration confounds the leak–stridor relationship.
cards.source: Sandhu RS et al. Measurement of endotracheal tube cuff leak to predict postextubation stridor and need for reintubation. Journal of the American College of Surgeons. 2000. PMID: 10873003. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Meta-analysis 2020: across 28 studies and 4,493 extubations, pooled sensitivity was only 0.62 for airway obstruction (specificity 0.87) and 0.66 for reintubation (specificity 0.88)
cards.summary: Meta-analysis 2020: across 28 studies and 4,493 extubations, pooled sensitivity was only 0.62 for airway obstruction (specificity 0.87) and 0.66 for reintubation (specificity 0.88)
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of diagnostic-accuracy studies
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of diagnostic-accuracy studies of the cuff-leak test in intubated adults in critical care, searching to March 2020: 28 studies involving 4,493 extubations; only three studies were at low risk of bias across all QUADAS-2 domains. Sensitivities and specificities were pooled with a bivariate random-effects model.
cards.result: For post-extubation airway obstruction, pooled sensitivity was 0.62 (95% CI 0.49–0.73; I²=81.6%) and pooled specificity 0.87 (95% CI 0.82–0.90; I²=97.8%). For reintubation, pooled sensitivity was 0.66 (95% CI 0.46–0.81) and specificity 0.88 (95% CI 0.83–0.92). Subgroup analyses suggested the type of cuff-leak test influenced sensitivity heterogeneity and intubation length influenced specificity heterogeneity. The authors conclude the test has excellent specificity but moderate sensitivity: clinicians should consider intervening when the test is positive, but patients still need close monitoring after extubation when it is negative.
cards.watchOut: Heterogeneity is very high (I² up to 97.8%) and test methods (qualitative vs quantitative, absolute vs percent thresholds) varied across studies — the pooled pair is an average over different tests, which is why the early single-centre cut-offs should not be quoted as the test's settled performance.
cards.source: Kuriyama A et al. Performance of the cuff leak test in adults in predicting post-extubation airway complications: a systematic review and meta-analysis. cards.headline: Synthesis: a rule-in aid, not a rule-out — POSSIBLE as a GAP-E accuracy shelf; prepare for stridor when the leak is low, monitor regardless when it is not
cards.summary: Synthesis: a rule-in aid, not a rule-out — POSSIBLE as a GAP-E accuracy shelf; prepare for stridor when the leak is low, monitor regardless when it is not
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: three prospective cohorts (100, 112 and 110 patients/extubations) and a 28-study meta-analysis (4,493 extubations).
cards.result: The direction is unanimous — smaller leak, more stridor — and the pooled specificity (0.87–0.88) makes a low leak a useful rule-in signal. The pooled sensitivity (0.62–0.66) is the discipline on enthusiasm: roughly a third of patients who will develop obstruction or need reintubation pass the test, so a normal leak changes monitoring intensity, not vigilance. The classic cut-offs (110 mL, 130 mL, 10–12% of tidal volume) come from small single-centre cohorts and performed better there than the test performs on average. Nothing carded here shows that acting on the test (steroids, delayed extubation) improves outcomes — that is a treatment question this accuracy shelf does not answer, and a low leak by itself should not postpone extubation indefinitely.
cards.watchOut: Predictive values (unlike sensitivity/specificity) move with local stridor prevalence: Miller & Cole's PPV of 0.80 was earned at 6% prevalence in one ICU and will not travel unchanged.
cards.source: Synthesis of Miller RL, Cole RP. Chest. 1996 (PMID: 8874265), Jaber S et al. Intensive Care Med. 2003 (PMID: 12528025), Sandhu RS et al. J Am Coll Surg. 2000 (PMID: 10873003) and Kuriyama A et al. Crit Care. 2020 (PMID: 33160405).

shelves.title: Xuebijing injection in sepsis: EXIT-SEP (n=1,817, 45 Chinese ICUs) cut 28-day mortality to 18.8% vs 26.1% with placebo, and a severe-pneumonia trial found the same direction — large, double-blind and concordant, but the entire randomised base is single-country, and the product is a specific non-FDA-approved herbal preparation
shelves.question: In adults with sepsis, does Xuebijing injection added to standard care versus standard care alone reduce 28-day mortality?
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit). Product naming under the clarification exception: Xuebijing injection is a specific herbal-based intravenous preparation, not a generic class; it is not FDA-approved, and preparations of this kind may differ by maker. The fetched PubMed records for the trials carded here do not name the manufacturer, so no manufacturer is printed on this shelf. EXIT-SEP (JAMA Intern Med 2023; 1,817 randomised patients with sepsis at 45 ICUs in China; Xuebijing 100 mL every 12 h for 5 days vs volume-matched saline placebo) found 28-day mortality of 18.8% vs 26.1% — an absolute difference of 7.3 percentage points (95% CI 3.4–11.2); adverse events were similar (22.9% vs 25.3%). The earlier severe community-acquired pneumonia trial (Song 2019; 710 critically ill patients, 33 Chinese hospitals) found the same direction on its secondary mortality outcome (28-day mortality 15.87% vs 24.63%; absolute difference 8.8 percentage points) alongside its positive primary pneumonia-severity endpoint. A 2022 network meta-analysis of integrative medicines in sepsis rated the Xuebijing mortality estimate (OR 0.71 — a relative measure) as very-low-level evidence, which is the honest counterweight: the two big trials are modern and well-conducted, but every randomised patient was enrolled in China, by overlapping investigator networks, for one manufacturer's preparation — independent replication outside that system does not exist, and that is why the stamp caps at POSSIBLE despite the trial sizes.

cards.headline: EXIT-SEP 2023: Xuebijing cut 28-day mortality to 18.8% vs 26.1% with placebo (absolute difference 7.3 percentage points) in 1,817 patients with sepsis at 45 Chinese ICUs
cards.summary: EXIT-SEP 2023: Xuebijing cut 28-day mortality to 18.8% vs 26.1% with placebo (absolute difference 7.3 percentage points) in 1,817 patients with sepsis at 45 Chinese ICUs
cards.people: 1,817 randomised patients with sepsis (Sepsis-3) present for less than 48 hours, aged 18–75 years with SOFA scores of 2–13, in intensive care units at 45 sites in China (mean age 56.5 years; 66.0% men); 1,760 (96.9%) completed the trial. Intervention: intravenous Xuebijing injection 100 mL (911 patients) or volume-matched saline placebo (906 patients) every 12 hours for 5 days, in a multicentre double-blind placebo-controlled trial.
cards.result: Twenty-eight-day mortality was 165 of 878 patients (18.8%) with Xuebijing vs 230 of 882 (26.1%) with placebo (P<.001); the absolute risk difference was 7.3 percentage points (95% CI 3.4 to 11.2). Adverse events occurred in 200 of 872 patients (22.9%) in the Xuebijing group and 222 of 878 (25.3%) in the placebo group.
cards.watchOut: A single trial for the sepsis question, conducted entirely in China with a sepsis population aged 18–75 and SOFA 2–13 — the result does not automatically transfer to other health systems, older or more severely ill populations, or to other herbal preparations. The fetched record does not name the product's manufacturer, so none is printed (clarification-exception rule).
cards.source: Liu S et al. Effect of an Herbal-Based Injection on 28-Day Mortality in Patients With Sepsis: The EXIT-SEP Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA internal medicine. 2023. PMID: 37126332. cards.headline: Severe pneumonia trial 2019: Xuebijing improved the primary pneumonia-severity endpoint and 28-day mortality was 15.87% vs 24.63% with placebo (n=710, 33 Chinese hospitals)
cards.summary: Severe pneumonia trial 2019: Xuebijing improved the primary pneumonia-severity endpoint and 28-day mortality was 15.87% vs 24.63% with placebo (n=710, 33 Chinese hospitals)
cards.type: Multicentre randomised placebo-controlled trial (severe community-acquired pneumonia)
cards.people: 710 adults aged 18–75 years with severe community-acquired pneumonia, critically ill, at 33 hospitals in China, randomised to Xuebijing injection 100 mL every 12 hours or a visually indistinguishable placebo, in a prospective randomised controlled study. The primary outcome was 8-day improvement in pneumonia severity index risk rating; 28-day mortality was a secondary outcome.
cards.result: Improvement in pneumonia severity index risk rating occurred in 203 Xuebijing participants (60.78%) vs 158 placebo participants (46.33%) (between-group difference 14.4%, 95% CI 6.9 to 21.8; p<0.001). Twenty-eight-day mortality was 53 (15.87%) with Xuebijing vs 84 (24.63%) with placebo (difference 8.8%, 95% CI 2.4 to 15.2; p=0.006). Median mechanical ventilation time was 11.0 vs 16.5 days (p=0.012) and total ICU stay 12 vs 16 days (p=0.004). Adverse events occurred in 119 (35.63%) Xuebijing vs 137 (40.18%) placebo patients (p=0.235).
cards.watchOut: This is a pneumonia trial, not a general-sepsis trial: its mortality result is a secondary outcome in a single-organ-source population, supportive of EXIT-SEP rather than an independent answer to this shelf's question. Same country and overlapping investigator network as EXIT-SEP.

cards.headline: Network meta-analysis 2022: Xuebijing plus Western treatment ranked below Shenfu and Shenmai injections, with its 28-day mortality odds ratio 0.71 rated very-low-level evidence (29 studies, 3,201 patients)
cards.summary: Network meta-analysis 2022: Xuebijing plus Western treatment ranked below Shenfu and Shenmai injections, with its 28-day mortality odds ratio 0.71 rated very-low-level evidence (29 studies, 3,201 patients)
cards.people: Systematic review and network meta-analysis of randomised trials of Chinese integrative medicines combined with Western medicine treatment for sepsis, searching Chinese and international databases to September 2020: 29 studies with 3,201 patients, covering Shenfu, Shenmai, Shengmai, Dahuang Fuzi and Xuebijing preparations.
cards.result: Combined with Western treatment, Xuebijing injection was associated with significantly reduced 28-day mortality (odds ratio 0.71, 95% CI 0.52 to 0.96 — a relative measure), as was Shenfu injection (OR 0.63, 0.47 to 0.83); Shenmai injection (OR 0.40, 0.16 to 1.03) and Dahuang Fuzi decoction (OR 1.00) were not significant. The efficacy ranking placed Shenmai first, Shenfu second and Xuebijing third, but the evidence level for the Xuebijing estimate was rated very low (and low for Shenfu and Shenmai).
cards.watchOut: The pooled Xuebijing estimate rests mostly on small, older Chinese trials of uncertain quality (hence the very-low rating) and predates EXIT-SEP — carded as the sceptical counterweight to the two large trials, not as independent support. Indirect network comparisons between different herbal products should not be read as head-to-head evidence.
cards.source: Xiaoxia Q et al. Effect of integrative medicines on 28-day mortality from sepsis: a systematic review and network meta-analysis. European review for medical and pharmacological sciences. 2022. PMID: 35113442. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: a 7.3-point absolute mortality reduction in one large trial, echoed in pneumonia — POSSIBLE, held there by single-country, single-product evidence
cards.summary: Synthesis: a 7.3-point absolute mortality reduction in one large trial, echoed in pneumonia — POSSIBLE, held there by single-country, single-product evidence
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: EXIT-SEP (1,817 patients with sepsis), the severe community-acquired pneumonia trial (710 patients) and a 29-study network meta-analysis (3,201 patients).
cards.result: The randomised signal is unusually consistent for an herbal adjunct: 28-day mortality 18.8% vs 26.1% in EXIT-SEP (absolute difference 7.3 percentage points) and 15.87% vs 24.63% in severe pneumonia, with no excess adverse events in either trial. What prevents a higher stamp is provenance, not internal validity: all patients were enrolled in China, the investigator networks overlap, the synthesis literature rates the older evidence very low, and the intervention is one specific non-FDA-approved preparation (Xuebijing injection; the fetched records do not name its manufacturer, so none is printed) whose composition other makers' products cannot be assumed to match. Replication in another health system would be the event that moves this stamp.
cards.watchOut: Do not generalise from Xuebijing to 'herbal injections' as a class — the network meta-analysis itself shows sibling preparations with null or unproven mortality effects — and do not generalise beyond the studied sepsis population (age 18–75, SOFA 2–13).
cards.source: Synthesis of Liu S et al. JAMA Intern Med. 2023 (PMID: 37126332), Song Y et al. Crit Care Med. 2019 (PMID: 31162191) and Xiaoxia Q et al. Eur Rev Med Pharmacol Sci. 2022 (PMID: 35113442).

shelves.title: Infectious-diseases consultation in Staphylococcus aureus bacteraemia: every strand of evidence is observational — consultation is associated with roughly halved mortality in meta-analysis (30-day RR 0.53; absolute mortality 12.39% vs 26.07%) and with better adherence to quality measures, but no randomised trial exists and confounding by indication is the central caveat
shelves.question: In adults with Staphylococcus aureus bacteraemia, is infectious-diseases consultation (versus no consultation) associated with lower mortality and better adherence to quality-of-care measures?
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational evidence only, capped and labelled per the standing rule; this is a GAP-E (evidence/strategy) shelf, not a proven intervention effect. Lahey 2009 (retrospective cohort, 240 patients) found hospital mortality of 13.9% with infectious-diseases consultation vs 23.7% without (adjusted hazard ratio 0.46 — a relative measure), alongside closer blood-culture follow-up, better antibiotic selection and more frequent removal of pus or prosthetic material; notably, consulted patients were sicker (more endocarditis, CNS involvement and osteomyelitis), which biases against consultation, yet they still fared better. The Vogel 2016 meta-analysis (18 studies, 5,337 patients) pooled 30-day mortality of 12.39% vs 26.07% (relative risk 0.53, a relative measure), with better appropriateness of antistaphylococcal agent and duration and more follow-up cultures and echocardiography. The largest recent cohort (Papadimitriou-Olivgeris 2023; 839 episodes) found consultation within 48 h independently associated with better survival in a multivariable model, as was early source control. The central caveat stays on the face: none of this is randomised — consultation may be a marker for better-resourced care or for surviving long enough to be consulted, and the meta-analysis authors themselves call for cluster-randomised trials. SAB treatment questions (oral switch, live #502; dalbavancin, live #1636) are separate homes and are not duplicated.

cards.headline: Lahey 2009 (retrospective cohort, labelled): hospital mortality 13.9% with ID consultation vs 23.7% without (adjusted HR 0.46) — despite consulted patients having more endocarditis and metastatic infection (n=240)
cards.summary: Lahey 2009 (retrospective cohort, labelled): hospital mortality 13.9% with ID consultation vs 23.7% without (adjusted HR 0.46) — despite consulted patients having more endocarditis and metastatic infection (n=240)
cards.people: 240 hospitalised patients with Staphylococcus aureus bacteraemia in a retrospective cohort study comparing patients who did vs did not receive infectious-diseases consultation. Consulted patients were older (57.9 vs 51.7 years) and more likely to have healthcare-associated infection (63% vs 45%), CNS involvement (5% vs 0%), endocarditis (20% vs 2%) or osteomyelitis (15.6% vs 3.4%). Observational evidence, labelled as such.
cards.result: Hospital mortality was 13.9% in patients who received consultation vs 23.7% in those who did not (p=0.05). In multivariate survival analysis, consultation was associated with a substantially lower hazard of hospital mortality (hazard ratio 0.46; p=0.03 — a relative measure), with the benefit accruing predominantly in methicillin-resistant SAB (hazard ratio 0.3) and in patients not requiring ICU admission (hazard ratio 0.15). Consulted patients had closer blood-culture follow-up, better antibiotic selection, and were more likely to have pus or prosthetic material removed.
cards.watchOut: Retrospective and single-centre: adjustment cannot remove confounding by indication or immortal-time effects (a patient must survive and remain hospitalised to be consulted). The subgroup hazard ratios (0.3, 0.15) rest on small strata and should not be quoted as precise effects.
