cards.headline: Vogel 2016 meta-analysis (observational studies): 30-day mortality 12.39% with consultation vs 26.07% without (RR 0.53), with better antibiotic choice/duration and more echocardiography (18 studies, 5,337 patients)
cards.summary: Vogel 2016 meta-analysis (observational studies): 30-day mortality 12.39% with consultation vs 26.07% without (RR 0.53), with better antibiotic choice/duration and more echocardiography (18 studies, 5,337 patients)
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of observational studies
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of studies of infectious-disease consultation in Staphylococcus aureus bacteraemia, searching three databases to May 2015: 18 studies fulfilling inclusion criteria, accounting for 5,337 patients. All underlying studies were observational.
cards.result: Overall 30-day mortality was 19.95% (95% CI 14.37–27.02), significantly lower with consultation: 12.39% vs 26.07%, relative risk 0.53 (95% CI 0.43–0.65 — a relative measure). Ninety-day mortality (RR 0.77, 0.64–0.92) and relapse risk (RR 0.62, 0.39–0.99) were also reduced. Appropriateness of antistaphylococcal agent (RR 1.14, 1.08–1.20) and treatment duration (RR 1.85, 1.39–2.46) were improved by consultation, and follow-up blood cultures (RR 1.35, 1.25–1.46) and echocardiography (RR 1.98, 1.66–2.37) were performed more frequently.
cards.watchOut: Pooling observational studies pools their biases as well as their data: if consultation is a marker for better overall care or for patients who survive to be seen, the pooled RR 0.53 overstates any causal effect. The authors themselves conclude that well-designed cluster-randomised trials are needed to confirm the finding.

cards.headline: Lausanne cohort 2023 (retrospective, labelled): ID consultation within 48 h was independently associated with better survival across 839 bacteraemia episodes, as was early source control
cards.summary: Lausanne cohort 2023 (retrospective, labelled): ID consultation within 48 h was independently associated with better survival across 839 bacteraemia episodes, as was early source control
cards.people: Retrospective cohort of 839 episodes of Staphylococcus aureus bacteraemia in adults at Lausanne University Hospital, Switzerland, 2015–2021 (7.9% methicillin-resistant). Sources included bone or joint infection (31.9%), unknown origin (18.8%), proven endocarditis (14.1%) and lower respiratory tract infection (9.4%). Overall 28-day mortality was 14.5%. Observational evidence, labelled as such.
cards.result: In a Cox multivariable model, infectious-diseases consultation within 48 h of infection onset was associated with better survival (P<0.001), while a Charlson comorbidity index >5, nosocomial bacteraemia, time to blood-culture positivity ≤13 h, persistent bacteraemia ≥48 h, sepsis, bacteraemia of unknown origin and lower-respiratory source were associated with higher 28-day mortality. Source control was warranted in 575 episodes and performed within 48 h in 345 (60.0%); a second multivariable analysis confirmed early source control was also associated with better survival (P<0.001). The fetched record reports the consultation association qualitatively (P value) without an effect-size estimate, so none is printed.
cards.watchOut: Retrospective, single-centre, and the consultation variable is entangled with early source control — consultation may work precisely by getting source control done, or both may mark a better-organised service. No effect size for consultation is given in the record, and none should be inferred from the P value.

cards.headline: Synthesis: a consistent, large observational association with a plausible mechanism (better process adherence) — POSSIBLE, capped, because randomisation has never been done
cards.summary: Synthesis: a consistent, large observational association with a plausible mechanism (better process adherence) — POSSIBLE, capped, because randomisation has never been done
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Lahey 2009 (240 patients), the Vogel 2016 meta-analysis (18 observational studies, 5,337 patients) and the Lausanne 2023 cohort (839 episodes).
cards.result: Every strand points the same way: mortality with consultation is roughly half that without (13.9% vs 23.7% in Lahey; pooled 30-day 12.39% vs 26.07%, RR 0.53, in Vogel — a relative measure), early (≤48 h) consultation is independently associated with survival in the largest recent cohort, and the process measures that plausibly mediate benefit (follow-up cultures, echocardiography, correct agent and duration, source control) are all more frequent with consultation. The stamp is nevertheless POSSIBLE and the observational label is part of the claim: there is no randomised trial, confounding by indication and immortal-time bias both operate, and the true causal effect is very likely smaller than RR 0.53. The practical reading — build systems that make early ID consultation and source control the default in S. aureus bacteraemia — is a service-design inference from observational data, and this shelf presents it as exactly that.
cards.watchOut: Do not quote RR 0.53 to a clinician as the expected effect of adding consultation in a new hospital: it is the pooled association from studies where consultation already existed and was selectively delivered.
cards.source: Synthesis of Lahey T et al. Medicine. 2009 (PMID: 19745684), Vogel M et al. J Infect. 2016 (PMID: 26453841) and Papadimitriou-Olivgeris M et al. Eur J Clin Microbiol Infect Dis. 2023 (PMID: 36729318).

shelves.title: PHYSIOLOGY — Dynamic heart–lung indices of fluid responsiveness: pulse pressure variation above ~13% identifies fluid responders (sensitivity 94%, specificity 96% in the founding study), stroke volume variation behaves similarly, and a 15-second end-expiratory occlusion that raises cardiac index ≥5% predicts responsiveness — all of it valid only under controlled ventilation, adequate tidal volume, sinus rhythm and no spontaneous effort
shelves.question: In mechanically ventilated adults, how do respiratory variations in pulse pressure and stroke volume, and the end-expiratory occlusion test, predict fluid responsiveness — what are the thresholds, and under what conditions (tidal volume, rhythm, spontaneous effort, lung compliance) do they fail?
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. The textbook framing (Guyton & Hall's account of heart–lung interaction: positive-pressure inspiration cyclically raises intrathoracic pressure, impedes venous return and left-ventricular preload, and so makes arterial pulse pressure swing with the breath — the swing is large only when the ventricles sit on the steep part of the Frank–Starling curve, which is precisely the fluid-responsive state) is borne out by concordant primary human data. Michard 2000 (40 septic, ventilated patients): a pre-infusion pulse pressure variation of 13% separated responders from non-responders with sensitivity 94% and specificity 96%, and the variation correlated tightly with the cardiac-index response (r²=0.85). Berkenstadt 2001 (15 neurosurgical patients, 140 graded volume loads): stroke volume variation ≥9.5% predicted a stroke-volume rise with sensitivity 79% and specificity 93%, far outperforming central venous pressure (AUC 0.870 vs 0.493). Monnet 2009 (34 ventilated patients with shock): a 15-second end-expiratory occlusion — which removes the cyclic inspiratory impediment and acts as a reversible internal fluid challenge — predicted responsiveness when cardiac index rose ≥5% (sensitivity 91%, specificity 100%). The meta-analytic average (Yang 2014: 22 studies, 807 patients, pooled AUC 0.94) was earned only in patients ventilated with tidal volume >8 mL/kg, without spontaneous breathing and without arrhythmia — those validity conditions are part of the physiology, printed on the cards, not fine print: with low tidal volumes, spontaneous efforts, irregular rhythm or poor lung compliance the indices lose discrimination. Passive leg raising is a separate, already-homed test (pack #3151), cross-pointed and not duplicated.

cards.headline: Michard 2000: pre-infusion pulse pressure variation was 24% in fluid responders vs 7% in non-responders; a 13% threshold gave sensitivity 94% and specificity 96% (40 septic ventilated patients)
cards.summary: Michard 2000: pre-infusion pulse pressure variation was 24% in fluid responders vs 7% in non-responders; a 13% threshold gave sensitivity 94% and specificity 96% (40 septic ventilated patients)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (prospective, ventilated septic patients)
cards.people: 40 mechanically ventilated patients with acute circulatory failure related to sepsis, instrumented with systemic and pulmonary artery catheters, studied before and after volume expansion. Responders (16) were patients whose cardiac index rose ≥15% with volume expansion; 24 were non-responders. Respiratory pulse pressure variation (ΔPp) was calculated over one respiratory cycle as (Ppmax − Ppmin) divided by their mean.
cards.result: Before volume expansion, ΔPp was 24 ± 9% in responders vs 7 ± 3% in non-responders (p<0.001), and respiratory systolic pressure variation was 15 ± 5% vs 6 ± 3%. ROC analysis showed ΔPp was a more accurate indicator of fluid responsiveness than systolic pressure variation; a ΔPp of 13% discriminated responders from non-responders with sensitivity 94% and specificity 96%. Pre-infusion ΔPp correlated closely with the volume-induced cardiac-index increase (r²=0.85, p<0.001), and volume expansion itself reduced ΔPp from 14 ± 10% to 7 ± 5%.
cards.watchOut: Forty patients with sepsis on controlled ventilation in one centre, against a pulmonary-artery-catheter reference standard. The 13% threshold's performance degrades outside its validity conditions (spontaneous breathing, arrhythmia, low tidal volume) — see the meta-analysis card.
cards.source: Michard F et al. Relation between respiratory changes in arterial pulse pressure and fluid responsiveness in septic patients with acute circulatory failure. American journal of respiratory and critical care medicine. 2000. PMID: 10903232. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Berkenstadt 2001: stroke volume variation ≥9.5% predicted a stroke-volume response (sensitivity 79%, specificity 93%; AUC 0.870), while central venous pressure performed at chance (AUC 0.493) — 15 patients, 140 graded volume loads
cards.summary: Berkenstadt 2001: stroke volume variation ≥9.5% predicted a stroke-volume response (sensitivity 79%, specificity 93%; AUC 0.870), while central venous pressure performed at chance (AUC 0.493) — 15 patients, 140 graded volume loads
cards.people: 15 patients undergoing brain surgery, monitored with a PiCCO continuous cardiac output monitor displaying stroke volume variation (SVV: the percentage change between maximal and minimal stroke volumes over a floating 30-second period). Graded volume loading was performed in 100 mL steps of 6% hydroxyethyl starch, repeated while each step raised stroke volume >5% (responsive) until a step changed it <5% (non-responsive): 140 volume-loading steps in total.
cards.result: Responsive and non-responsive loading steps differed in pre-load systolic blood pressure, stroke volume and SVV, but not in heart rate or central venous pressure. By ROC analysis, the area under the curve for SVV was 0.870 (95% CI 0.809–0.903), statistically greater than for central venous pressure (0.493, 0.397–0.590), heart rate (0.593) and systolic blood pressure (0.729). An SVV of 9.5% or more predicted an increase in stroke volume of at least 5% after a 100 mL load with sensitivity 79% and specificity 93%.
cards.watchOut: Only 15 patients (the 140 observations are repeated loads within them, not 140 patients), in neurosurgical patients receiving a colloid, with a lenient response definition (stroke volume +5% after only 100 mL). The durable lesson is the contrast with static pressures, not the exact 9.5% cut-off.
cards.source: Berkenstadt H et al. Stroke volume variation as a predictor of fluid responsiveness in patients undergoing brain surgery. Anesthesia and analgesia. 2001. PMID: 11273937. cards.headline: Monnet 2009: a 15-second end-expiratory occlusion raised cardiac index ≥5% only in fluid responders — sensitivity 91%, specificity 100% (34 ventilated patients with shock)
cards.summary: Monnet 2009: a 15-second end-expiratory occlusion raised cardiac index ≥5% only in fluid responders — sensitivity 91%, specificity 100% (34 ventilated patients with shock)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (prospective, ventilated ICU patients)
cards.people: 34 mechanically ventilated patients with shock in a medical ICU in whom volume expansion was planned. Each patient underwent a 15-second end-expiratory occlusion followed by a 500 mL saline infusion, with arterial pressure and pulse-contour cardiac index (PiCCOplus) measured at baseline, during passive leg raising, in the last 5 seconds of the occlusion, and after volume expansion. Twenty-three patients were responders (cardiac index rise >15% after volume expansion).
cards.result: Before volume expansion, the end-expiratory occlusion increased arterial pulse pressure by 15 ± 15% and cardiac index by 12 ± 11% in responders, with no significant change in non-responders. A pulse-pressure rise ≥5% during occlusion predicted fluid responsiveness with sensitivity 87% and specificity 100%; a cardiac-index rise ≥5% predicted it with sensitivity 91% and specificity 100% (ROC area 0.972). Accuracy was similar to the cardiac-index response to passive leg raising and significantly better than the pulse-pressure response to leg raising (ROC area 0.675).
cards.watchOut: The occlusion test needs a ventilator that can hold an end-expiratory pause and a patient making no inspiratory effort during it — a spontaneous breath inside the 15 seconds invalidates the manoeuvre. Thirty-four patients, one centre, one monitoring platform (PiCCO pulse contour).
cards.source: Monnet X et al. Predicting volume responsiveness by using the end-expiratory occlusion in mechanically ventilated intensive care unit patients. Critical care medicine. 2009. cards.headline: Yang 2014 meta-analysis: pooled PPV performance (sensitivity 0.88, specificity 0.89, AUC 0.94) was demonstrated only at tidal volume >8 mL/kg, without spontaneous breathing or arrhythmia (22 studies, 807 patients)
cards.summary: Yang 2014 meta-analysis: pooled PPV performance (sensitivity 0.88, specificity 0.89, AUC 0.94) was demonstrated only at tidal volume >8 mL/kg, without spontaneous breathing or arrhythmia (22 studies, 807 patients)
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of diagnostic-accuracy studies
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of clinical trials of pulse pressure variation (PPV) for predicting fluid responsiveness after fluid challenge in mechanically ventilated ICU patients: 22 studies with 807 patients, of whom 465 (58%) were responders. Included studies enrolled patients with tidal volume more than 8 mL/kg and without spontaneous breathing and cardiac arrhythmia.
cards.result: Pooled sensitivity was 0.88 (95% CI 0.81 to 0.92) and pooled specificity 0.89 (95% CI 0.84 to 0.92); the summary ROC area under the curve was 0.94 (95% CI 0.91 to 0.95). A significant threshold effect was identified across studies.
cards.watchOut: The eligibility conditions are the finding: this pooled accuracy does not describe modern lung-protective ventilation at 6 mL/kg, patients triggering the ventilator, or patients in atrial fibrillation — in those settings the founding thresholds should not be applied as if validated.
cards.source: Yang X, Du B. Does pulse pressure variation predict fluid responsiveness in critically ill patients? A systematic review and meta-analysis. Critical care (London, England). 2014. PMID: 25427970. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: textbook heart–lung interaction, quantified — ESTABLISHED physiology whose thresholds carry their validity conditions with them
cards.summary: Synthesis: textbook heart–lung interaction, quantified — ESTABLISHED physiology whose thresholds carry their validity conditions with them
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Michard 2000 (40 patients), Berkenstadt 2001 (15 patients, 140 volume loads), Monnet 2009 (34 patients) and the Yang 2014 meta-analysis (22 studies, 807 patients). Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall (heart–lung interaction, venous return and the Frank–Starling mechanism) and Ganong.
cards.result: The mechanism the textbooks describe — cyclic inspiratory impedance of venous return translating into arterial pressure swings whose size reports position on the Frank–Starling curve — is directly quantified in humans: pulse pressure variation threshold ~13% (sensitivity 94%, specificity 96%), stroke volume variation threshold ~9.5% (AUC 0.870 vs 0.493 for central venous pressure), and the end-expiratory occlusion test (cardiac-index rise ≥5% during a 15-second hold; sensitivity 91%, specificity 100%), which works by transiently removing the inspiratory impediment rather than by giving fluid. The stamp is PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED because the primary studies and their synthesis are concordant; the conditions are part of the establishment — controlled ventilation, tidal volume ≥8 mL/kg for classic PPV, sinus rhythm, no spontaneous effort, and adequate lung compliance — and outside them the same numbers are not established at all. Passive leg raising, the non-ventilator-dependent alternative, is homed on pack #3151 and is cross-pointed, not duplicated.
cards.watchOut: Fluid responsiveness is a physiological state, not an instruction to give fluid: these indices say the circulation can respond, and say nothing about whether it should — that judgement needs the clinical picture (perfusion, congestion, lung water) the indices do not measure.

shelves.title: Sublingual microcirculation in sepsis: perfused-vessel density and flow fall, dissociate from systemic pressures, and persistent loss predicts organ failure and death
shelves.question: In humans with sepsis and septic shock, what happens to sublingual microvascular flow and perfused-vessel density, how do these changes relate to systemic haemodynamics, and do persistent alterations predict organ failure and death?
shelves.mesh: Acetylcholine/administration & dosage/pharmacology · Administration, Sublingual · Adult · Aged · Case-Control Studies · Humans · Image Interpretation, Computer-Assisted · Microcirculation/drug effects · Microscopy, Polarization · Middle Aged · Mouth Floor/blood supply · Severity of Illness Index · Shock, Septic/physiopathology · Statistics, Nonparametric · Vasodilator Agents/administration & dosage/pharmacology
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED (descriptive physiology). Framed by the textbook account of capillary exchange and distributive shock (Guyton & Hall; Ganong; Boron & Boulpaep — framing, not evidence), the primary human OPS/SDF imaging studies agree: in severe sepsis the proportion of perfused small sublingual vessels falls from about 90% (healthy volunteers) to 48% (De Backer 2002, PMID: 12091178) and vessel density falls from 5.4 to 4.5/mm, while mean arterial pressure and cardiac index may be near-normal — a dissociation between the systemic circulation and the microcirculation. In septic shock (Sakr 2004, PMID: 15343008), perfusion recovered in survivors and stayed low (57.4% versus 79.3%) in patients dying with multiple organ failure. In the pooled 252-patient analysis (De Backer 2013, PMID: 23318492), perfused small-vessel proportion was the strongest outcome predictor (AUC 0.818), independent of systemic variables. This is prognostic physiology: no trial shows that treating the microcirculation improves outcome.

cards.headline: De Backer 2002 (first OPS description): perfused small vessels 48% in severe sepsis versus 90% in volunteers; vessel density 4.5 versus 5.4/mm; worse in non-survivors
cards.summary: De Backer 2002 (first OPS description): perfused small vessels 48% in severe sepsis versus 90% in volunteers; vessel density 4.5 versus 5.4/mm; worse in non-survivors
cards.people: 86 humans imaged with orthogonal polarisation spectral (OPS) imaging of the sublingual microcirculation: 10 healthy volunteers, 16 patients before cardiac surgery, 10 acutely ill ICU patients without sepsis, and 50 patients with severe sepsis; topical acetylcholine tested in 11 patients with sepsis.
cards.result: Density of all vessels was reduced in severe sepsis (4.5 [4.2-5.2] versus 5.4 [5.4-6.3]/mm in volunteers, p<0.01) and the proportion of perfused small (<20 microm) vessels was 48 [33-61]% versus 90 [89-92]% in volunteers (p<0.001). Alterations were more severe in non-survivors. Topical acetylcholine totally reversed the alterations, showing the vessels could still respond.
cards.watchOut: Small control groups (10 volunteers, 10 ICU controls) — printed on the face per the physiology labelling rule. Semiquantitative scoring, single centre; an observational description, not a treatment test.
cards.source: De Backer D et al. Microvascular blood flow is altered in patients with sepsis. American journal of respiratory and critical care medicine. 2002. PMID: 12091178. cards.headline: Sakr 2004: in 49 patients with septic shock, small-vessel perfusion improved over time in survivors but not in patients dying with multiple organ failure (57.4% versus 79.3% perfused at end of shock)
cards.summary: Sakr 2004: in 49 patients with septic shock, small-vessel perfusion improved over time in survivors but not in patients dying with multiple organ failure (57.4% versus 79.3% perfused at end of shock)
cards.people: 49 patients with septic shock in a 31-bed university ICU; sublingual OPS imaging on the day of shock onset and daily until shock resolved; 46 analysed (26 survivors, 20 deaths) after 3 unrelated deaths were excluded.
cards.result: At shock onset survivors and non-survivors had similar vascular density and perfused small vessels (65.0% versus 58.4%, NS). Small-vessel perfusion then improved over time in survivors but not in non-survivors (p<0.05 between groups). Patients dying of multiple organ failure after shock had resolved still had fewer perfused small vessels than survivors (57.4 [46.6-64.9]% versus 79.3 [67.2-83.2]%, p=0.02), despite similar systemic haemodynamics — persistence, not the first measurement, tracked outcome.
cards.watchOut: Observational and prognostic only: persistence may mark severity rather than cause organ failure, and no trial has shown that targeting the microcirculation improves outcome.
cards.source: Sakr Y et al. Persistent microcirculatory alterations are associated with organ failure and death in patients with septic shock. Critical care medicine. 2004. PMID: 15343008. cards.headline: De Backer 2013 (252 patients with severe sepsis): proportion of perfused small vessels was the strongest outcome predictor (AUC 0.818); survival 70-75% in the best two quartiles versus 3% and 44% in the worst two
cards.summary: De Backer 2013 (252 patients with severe sepsis): proportion of perfused small vessels was the strongest outcome predictor (AUC 0.818); survival 70-75% in the best two quartiles versus 3% and 44% in the worst two
cards.people: 252 patients with severe sepsis pooled from the group's previously published prospective studies; sublingual microcirculation visualised by OPS or sidestream dark-field (SDF) imaging, early (within 24 h, n=204) or later (after 48 h, n=48).
cards.result: Systemic variables were relatively preserved (mean arterial pressure 70 [65-77] mmHg, cardiac index 3.3 [2.7-4.0] L/min/m2) while microvascular variables were markedly altered (perfused small vessels 65 [50-74]%). Perfused small-vessel proportion was the strongest predictor of outcome (ROC area 0.818, p<0.001) and, with SOFA score, an independent predictor in multivariable analysis; microcirculatory alterations were stronger outcome predictors than global haemodynamic variables.
cards.watchOut: A pooled re-analysis of one research group's own earlier cohorts (including the 2002 and 2004 studies above), so it is not independent confirmation; observational throughout.
cards.source: De Backer D et al. Microcirculatory alterations in patients with severe sepsis: impact of time of assessment and relationship with outcome. Critical care medicine. 2013. PMID: 23318492. cards.headline: Synthesis: sublingual perfused-vessel density and flow fall in sepsis, dissociate from systemic pressures, and persistent loss tracks organ failure and death — physiology, not a treatment target
cards.summary: Synthesis: sublingual perfused-vessel density and flow fall in sepsis, dissociate from systemic pressures, and persistent loss tracks organ failure and death — physiology, not a treatment target
cards.people: Three primary human observational studies (2002-2013) using OPS or SDF sublingual imaging in severe sepsis and septic shock, framed by the standard textbook account of microvascular exchange and its failure in sepsis (Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology; Ganong's Review of Medical Physiology; Boron & Boulpaep Medical Physiology) — the textbooks are framing, not evidence cards.
cards.result: Across the studies: perfused small-vessel proportion falls from about 90% in healthy volunteers to about 48-65% in sepsis, vessel density falls, systemic pressures and cardiac index can look near-normal while the microcirculation is markedly abnormal, and failure of perfusion to recover — not the admission value — is what accompanies multiple organ failure and death. PROPOSED PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED for the descriptive physiology (the alterations and their prognostic association are consistently shown); no intervention claim is made.
cards.watchOut: Observational prognostic evidence only. Imaging techniques (OPS, then SDF) and semiquantitative scores changed across the era, most data come from one Brussels group, and no randomised trial has shown benefit from microcirculation-guided therapy — the shelf must not be read as endorsing a target.
cards.source: Synthesis of the three cards above; textbook framing: Guyton & Hall, Ganong, and Boron & Boulpaep accounts of microcirculatory exchange (framing only, not an evidence card).

shelves.title: Ridinilazole for C. difficile infection: sustained response not superior to vancomycin at phase 3 (73.0% versus 70.7%), but recurrence lower (8.1% versus 17.3%)
shelves.question: In adults with C. difficile infection, does ridinilazole versus vancomycin achieve sustained clinical response and reduce recurrence?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Vancomycin/therapeutic use/adverse effects · Clostridium Infections/drug therapy/microbiology · Male · Female · Middle Aged · Double-Blind Method · Anti-Bacterial Agents/therapeutic use/adverse effects · Aged · Clostridioides difficile/drug effects · Gastrointestinal Microbiome/drug effects · Adult · Treatment Outcome · Metabolome/drug effects · Oxadiazoles/therapeutic use/adverse effects · Dysbiosis/chemically induced · Benzimidazoles · Pyridines
shelves.balance: SPLIT. Ridinilazole is a narrow-spectrum antibiotic designed to treat C. difficile infection while sparing the gut microbiota. The phase 2 CoDIFy trial (PMID: 28461207) found sustained clinical response in 66.7% versus 42.4% on vancomycin, but the efficacy population was only 69 patients. The phase 3 Ri-CoDIFy 1 and 2 programme (PMID: 38305378) did NOT meet superiority on that same primary endpoint: 73.0% versus 70.7% (difference 2.2%, 95% CI -4.2% to 8.6%). Recurrence, a secondary endpoint, was lower: 8.1% versus 17.3% — a 53% relative reduction, 9.2 percentage points absolute (p=0.0002) — and a nested microbiota cohort (PMID: 30071046) showed far less disruption of gut flora with ridinilazole, the plausible mechanism. Ridinilazole is not FDA-approved.

cards.headline: Vickers 2017 (CoDIFy, phase 2): sustained clinical response 66.7% on ridinilazole versus 42.4% on vancomycin (difference 21.1%); non-inferiority met, superiority shown at the 10% level
cards.summary: Vickers 2017 (CoDIFy, phase 2): sustained clinical response 66.7% on ridinilazole versus 42.4% on vancomycin (difference 21.1%); non-inferiority met, superiority shown at the 10% level
cards.people: 100 patients with C. difficile infection at 33 centres in the USA and Canada, randomised to oral ridinilazole 200 mg every 12 h or oral vancomycin 125 mg every 6 h for 10 days; primary efficacy (modified intention-to-treat, toxin-confirmed) population 69 patients (36 ridinilazole, 33 vancomycin).
cards.result: Sustained clinical response (cure at end of treatment with no recurrence within 30 days) occurred in 24 of 36 (66.7%) on ridinilazole versus 14 of 33 (42.4%) on vancomycin (treatment difference 21.1%, 90% CI 3.1 to 39.1; p=0.0004), establishing non-inferiority (15% margin) and statistical superiority at the 10% level. Adverse events were reported by 82% versus 80%, with no ridinilazole-related discontinuations.
cards.watchOut: Small phase 2 trial: the efficacy population was only 69 of 100 randomised patients, so the superiority signal rested on few events and needed the phase 3 test below — which did not confirm it on the same endpoint.
cards.source: Vickers RJ et al. Efficacy and safety of ridinilazole compared with vancomycin for the treatment of Clostridium difficile infection: a phase 2, randomised, double-blind, active-controlled, non-inferiority study. The Lancet. Infectious diseases. 2017. PMID: 28461207. Registry ID: NCT02092935. cards.headline: Okhuysen 2024 (Ri-CoDIFy 1 and 2, phase 3): sustained clinical response 73.0% versus 70.7% — superiority NOT met; recurrence 8.1% versus 17.3%, a 53% relative reduction
cards.summary: Okhuysen 2024 (Ri-CoDIFy 1 and 2, phase 3): sustained clinical response 73.0% versus 70.7% — superiority NOT met; recurrence 8.1% versus 17.3%, a 53% relative reduction
cards.people: Adults with toxin-confirmed C. difficile infection randomised to 10 days of ridinilazole 200 mg twice daily or vancomycin 125 mg four times daily in the combined Ri-CoDIFy 1 and 2 superiority programme.
cards.result: Sustained clinical response was 73% on ridinilazole versus 70.7% on vancomycin (treatment difference 2.2%, 95% CI -4.2% to 8.6%) — the primary superiority endpoint was not met. Recurrence was 8.1% versus 17.3% (95% CI for the difference -14.1% to -4.5%; p=0.0002), a 53% relative reduction in recurrence. Ridinilazole preserved microbiota diversity and secondary bile acids; vancomycin worsened dysbiosis and increased the resistome.
cards.watchOut: The headline benefit is on recurrence, a secondary endpoint, after the primary endpoint missed — read the shelf as split, not as a win. Absolute recurrence difference was 9.2 percentage points. Ridinilazole is not FDA-approved.

cards.headline: Thorpe 2018 (nested phase 2 microbiota cohort): ridinilazole disrupted the gut microbiota far less than vancomycin, with composition returning to baseline sooner
cards.summary: Thorpe 2018 (nested phase 2 microbiota cohort): ridinilazole disrupted the gut microbiota far less than vancomycin, with composition returning to baseline sooner
cards.type: Nested human cohort study within the phase 2 trial (Thorpe 2018)
cards.people: Participants in the phase 2 CoDIFy trial with stool collected at baseline, day 5, end of treatment (day 10), day 25, end of study (day 40) and at recurrence; microbiota assessed by qPCR and high-throughput sequencing.
cards.result: At end of treatment, vancomycin caused profound losses of Bacteroides, C. coccoides, C. leptum and Prevotella groups and a persistent rise in Enterobacteriaceae, while ridinilazole caused only a modest C. leptum decrease recovering by day 25. Alpha diversity fell with both drugs but significantly less with ridinilazole (p<0.0001), and microbiota composition returned to baseline sooner with ridinilazole.
cards.watchOut: A mechanistic, surrogate-outcome cohort nested in a 100-patient trial — it explains the recurrence finding biologically but is not itself clinical-outcome evidence, and the phase 3 primary endpoint still missed.
cards.source: Thorpe CM et al. Enhanced preservation of the human intestinal microbiota by ridinilazole, a novel Clostridium difficile-targeting antibacterial, compared to vancomycin. PloS one. 2018. PMID: 30071046. cards.headline: Synthesis: sustained response not superior at phase 3 (73.0% versus 70.7%); recurrence roughly halved in relative terms (8.1% versus 17.3%) with far less microbiota disruption — a split result
cards.summary: Synthesis: sustained response not superior at phase 3 (73.0% versus 70.7%); recurrence roughly halved in relative terms (8.1% versus 17.3%) with far less microbiota disruption — a split result
cards.people: One phase 2 trial (n=100 randomised, 69 in the efficacy population), the combined phase 3 Ri-CoDIFy 1 and 2 programme, and a nested microbiota cohort from the phase 2 trial — all ridinilazole versus vancomycin for C. difficile infection.
cards.result: Phase 2 suggested superiority on sustained clinical response (66.7% versus 42.4%); phase 3 did not confirm superiority on that endpoint (73.0% versus 70.7%, difference 2.2%, 95% CI -4.2% to 8.6%) but recurrence was lower (8.1% versus 17.3%; 53% relative reduction, 9.2 percentage points absolute), consistent with the much smaller microbiota disruption seen with ridinilazole. PROPOSED SPLIT: no advantage on the primary sustained-response endpoint; a real recurrence advantage on a secondary endpoint.
cards.watchOut: Ridinilazole is not FDA-approved, so availability is the practical limit regardless of the recurrence data. The recurrence claim rests on a secondary endpoint of one phase 3 programme reported in a single paper combining two trials.
cards.source: Synthesis of the three cards above (PMIDs: 28461207, 38305378, 30071046).

shelves.title: The low-dose endotoxin challenge model in humans: a brief TNF pulse at 90–180 minutes drives fever, cytokine release, leukocyte trafficking and cortisol — dose-, preparation- and sex-dependent
shelves.question: In healthy humans, what happens in the standardised low-dose endotoxin challenge model — the dose–response and time course of fever, cytokine release (TNF, IL-6), leukocyte trafficking, heart-rate/blood-pressure change and cortisol activation after intravenous reference endotoxin?
shelves.mesh: Endotoxins · Escherichia coli · Tumor Necrosis Factor-alpha · Fever · Humans
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED — for the human experimental endotoxemia model as a standardised, reproducible inflammatory stimulus (physiology under a controlled stimulus, not resting physiology), framed by Guyton & Hall / Ganong (fever and innate immunity). The classic characterisation (Michie, 4 ng/kg E. coli endotoxin, 13 healthy men) fixes the clock: a brief TNF pulse peaking at 90–180 minutes (240 ± 70 vs 35 ± 5 pg/mL after saline), IL-1β unchanged, symptoms, white-cell change and ACTH tracking the TNF peak, and ibuprofen attenuating the responses without blocking TNF; infusing TNF to similar peaks reproduced the package. Later programmes fill in the dials: at 2 ng/kg the response is sex-modulated (TNF-α 965 ± 193 in women vs 411 ± 35 pg/mL in men; 15 + 15); in a placebo-controlled 4 ng/kg trial the LPS-alone limb moved vital signs, white cells, cytokines, cortisol and echocardiographic haemodynamics together; and dose–response has a floor (systemic activation at 0.4 ng/kg, a downstream pain-sensitivity effect only at 0.8 ng/kg, at 3 hours). Every value is carded with its dose and preparation — they are never pooled. The repeat-challenge tolerance limb is explicitly not carded: no systemic human tolerance primary met the carding standard this session (stated on the Synthesis card).

cards.headline: Michie 1988 (NEJM): after 4 ng/kg intravenous E. coli endotoxin, circulating TNF appeared as a brief pulse — peak 240 ± 70 pg/mL at 90–180 minutes versus 35 ± 5 after saline — while IL-1β and interferon-γ did not change (13 healthy men, 8 more with ibuprofen)
cards.summary: Michie 1988 (NEJM): after 4 ng/kg intravenous E. coli endotoxin, circulating TNF appeared as a brief pulse — peak 240 ± 70 pg/mL at 90–180 minutes versus 35 ± 5 after saline — while IL-1β and interferon-γ did not change (13 healthy men, 8 more with ibuprofen)
cards.type: Human experimental endotoxemia study (cytokine time course after reference endotoxin), N Engl J Med 1988
cards.people: 13 healthy men given intravenous Escherichia coli endotoxin (4 ng per kilogram of body weight) and, in a control period, saline, with plasma tumour necrosis factor alpha (cachectin), interleukin-1 beta and gamma interferon measured alongside physiologic and hormonal responses; 8 additional subjects received ibuprofen before endotoxin or saline.
cards.result: TNF was generally below 35 pg/mL through the control period, then rose 90–180 minutes after endotoxin to a mean peak of 240 ± 70 pg/mL, versus 35 ± 5 pg/mL after saline. Host responses were temporally associated with the TNF rise at 90 minutes, and symptoms, white-cell-count change and ACTH production tracked the peak TNF concentration. Ibuprofen pretreatment did not prevent the TNF rise (mean peak 170 ± 70 pg/mL) but greatly attenuated the symptoms and other responses — placing the symptomatic response downstream of TNF, through the cyclooxygenase pathway. Circulating IL-1β and gamma interferon did not change. This is the model's signature: a single early cytokine pulse, then the physiology.
cards.watchOut: The 4 ng/kg dose is the high end of the modern low-dose range; later cards use 2 ng/kg and below — cytokine peaks scale with dose and preparation, and are carded per dose, never pooled.
cards.source: Michie HR, Manogue KR, Spriggs DR, Revhaug A, O'Dwyer S, Dinarello CA, et al. Detection of circulating tumor necrosis factor after endotoxin administration. The New England Journal of Medicine. 1988. PMID: 2835680. Registry ID: none in the record (pre-registration era). cards.headline: Michie 1988 (Surgery): the endotoxin response is reproducible by TNF itself — infusions producing similar peak TNF gave similar fever, ACTH/cortisol and acute-phase responses, defining TNF as the model's afferent signal
cards.summary: Michie 1988 (Surgery): the endotoxin response is reproducible by TNF itself — infusions producing similar peak TNF gave similar fever, ACTH/cortisol and acute-phase responses, defining TNF as the model's afferent signal
cards.type: Human experimental study (recombinant TNF infusion versus endotoxin challenge), Surgery 1988
cards.people: 16 tumour-bearing humans with normal renal and hepatic function given 24-hour continuous intravenous infusions of escalating recombinant TNF doses (4 to 636 micrograms/m²/24 h), with serial vital signs and plasma TNF, interleukin-1, ACTH, cortisol, iron, glucose and C-reactive protein — compared with the healthy-human (n = 13) intravenous bolus E. coli endotoxin (4 ng/kg) responses from the companion programme.
cards.result: Low TNF doses had minimal metabolic effects, but infusions of ≥545 micrograms/m²/24 h (n = 8) produced fever, pituitary and stress-hormone release and acute-phase changes, with peak plasma TNF concentrations and metabolic responses similar to those after the endotoxin injection. Interleukin-1 concentrations remained basal after either TNF or endotoxin. The comparison is the model's internal validation: the standardised endotoxin challenge works, in large part, by generating one measurable mediator pulse, whose magnitude predicts the fever, hormonal and acute-phase limbs.
cards.watchOut: The TNF-infusion limb was in tumour-bearing patients, not healthy volunteers — carded as the model's mechanistic comparison, with its population printed on the face; the endotoxin limb (n = 13) is the healthy-volunteer limb.
cards.source: Michie HR, Spriggs DR, Manogue KR, Sherman ML, Revhaug A, O'Dwyer ST, et al. Tumor necrosis factor and endotoxin induce similar metabolic responses in human beings. Surgery. 1988. PMID: 2456628. Registry ID: none in the record (pre-registration era). cards.headline: van Eijk 2007: at 2 ng/kg, the response is sex-modulated — women's TNF-α rose to 965 ± 193 versus 411 ± 35 pg/mL in men, CRP rose higher, leukopenia ran deeper, and blood pressure fell more (15 women, 15 men)
cards.summary: van Eijk 2007: at 2 ng/kg, the response is sex-modulated — women's TNF-α rose to 965 ± 193 versus 411 ± 35 pg/mL in men, CRP rose higher, leukopenia ran deeper, and blood pressure fell more (15 women, 15 men)
cards.type: Human experimental endotoxemia study (sex differences at 2 ng/kg LPS), Crit Care Med 2007
cards.people: 15 female and 15 male healthy volunteers given an intravenous injection of 2 ng/kg Escherichia coli lipopolysaccharide, with C-reactive protein, leukocytes and cytokines at regular intervals, continuous heart rate and blood pressure, and forearm blood flow with norepinephrine responsiveness measured before and 4 hours after endotoxin.
cards.result: Females showed a more pro-inflammatory response: CRP rose to 42 ± 3 versus 29 ± 3 mg/L (P = 0.002), leukocyte sequestration was deeper (leukopenia nadir 1.8 ± 0.1 versus 2.4 ± 0.1 in the record's printed units, P = 0.003), and the TNF-α increase was higher (965 ± 193 versus 411 ± 35 pg/mL, P < 0.0001), while the anti-inflammatory IL-10 increase did not differ significantly (95 ± 15 versus 129 ± 15 pg/mL, P = 0.288). The heart-rate change did not differ by sex, but blood pressure decreased more in females (P < 0.0001), and endotoxin attenuated norepinephrine sensitivity in males only. At the now-standard 2 ng/kg dose, then, the model's cytokine and vascular readouts carry a sex difference large enough to matter for any pooled analysis.
cards.watchOut: One dose, one preparation, 15 per sex — the sex difference is shown for this protocol; it should not be assumed identical at 4 ng/kg or with other endotoxin preparations.
cards.source: van Eijk LT, Dorresteijn MJ, Smits P, van der Hoeven JG, Netea MG, Pickkers P. Gender differences in the innate immune response and vascular reactivity following the administration of endotoxin to human volunteers. Critical Care Medicine. 2007. PMID: 17452928. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Kumar 2005: in the placebo-controlled 4 ng/kg model, lipopolysaccharide alone produced the full time-dependent package — vital signs, white-cell count, cytokines, cortisol and echocardiographic haemodynamics all moved (24 healthy men)
cards.summary: Kumar 2005: in the placebo-controlled 4 ng/kg model, lipopolysaccharide alone produced the full time-dependent package — vital signs, white-cell count, cytokines, cortisol and echocardiographic haemodynamics all moved (24 healthy men)
cards.type: Randomised placebo-controlled human endotoxemia trial (model characterisation in the LPS-alone limb), Crit Care Med 2005
cards.people: 24 healthy male volunteers in a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of recombinant human IL-10 given at 1, 10 or 25 µg/kg either 2 minutes or 2 hours before Escherichia coli lipopolysaccharide (4 ng/kg) or placebo; the lipopolysaccharide-alone (placebo-pretreatment) group is this card's model limb.
cards.result: The group receiving lipopolysaccharide alone showed significant, time-dependent changes in vital signs, white blood cell counts, inflammatory cytokine and cortisol levels, and haemodynamic/cardiovascular parameters including echocardiographic measures, over the study's duration — the complete standard response against which the intervention was judged. IL-10 given concurrently blunted temperature, heart rate, TNF-α, IL-6, IL-1 receptor antagonist, cortisol and leukocyte/neutrophil responses (with no dose-dependence across 1–25 µg/kg), but did not modulate the major cardiovascular responses (cardiac output, stroke volume index, ejection fraction); IL-10 given 2 hours beforehand instead augmented parts of the cytokine response. For this shelf the card's weight is the control limb: at 4 ng/kg the model reproducibly moves fever, leukocyte trafficking, cytokines, cortisol and haemodynamics together in a placebo-controlled design.
cards.watchOut: An intervention trial carded for its placebo-controlled model limb; the record reports the LPS-alone changes as significant and time-dependent without printing each value, so no invented magnitudes are attached to them here.
cards.source: Kumar A, Zanotti S, Bunnell G, Habet K, Añel R, Neumann A, et al. Interleukin-10 blunts the human inflammatory response to lipopolysaccharide without affecting the cardiovascular response. Critical Care Medicine. 2005. PMID: 15699836. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.summary: Wegner 2014: the dose–response has a floor — 0.8 ng/kg lowered pressure-pain thresholds at 3 hours, 0.4 ng/kg did not, and cytokine, temperature and mood effects were dose-graded (healthy men, placebo-controlled)
cards.type: Randomised placebo-controlled human endotoxemia study (dose–response, 0.4 versus 0.8 ng/kg), Brain Behav Immun 2014
cards.people: Healthy male subjects randomised double-blind to intravenous moderate-dose lipopolysaccharide (0.8 ng/kg E. coli), low-dose lipopolysaccharide (0.4 ng/kg) or saline placebo; pressure pain thresholds, mechanical and cold pain sensitivity assessed before and 1, 3 and 6 hours after injection, with plasma cytokines (TNF-α, IL-6, IL-8, IL-10) and state anxiety measured before and 1–6 hours after. The record does not print the total subject N in its abstract — N not documented in the record.
cards.result: Lipopolysaccharide induced systemic immune activation — significant increases in cytokine levels, body temperature and negative mood — with pronounced effects at the higher dose. Pressure pain thresholds fell significantly only 3 hours after the moderate (0.8 ng/kg) dose; mechanical and cold pain sensitivity were unaffected, and the threshold fall correlated with peak IL-6 increases and negative mood. The low-dose limb is the model's sensitivity boundary: at 0.4 ng/kg the systemic activation occurs without the downstream pain-sensitivity effect — dose, preparation and readout timing jointly define what a given challenge study can claim.
cards.watchOut: N not documented in the record, printed on the face. A pain-readout study carded for its dose–response characterisation of the model, not as pain physiology in itself.
cards.source: Wegner A, Elsenbruch S, Maluck J, Grigoleit JS, Engler H, Jäger M, et al. Inflammation-induced hyperalgesia: effects of timing, dosage, and negative affect on somatic pain sensitivity in human experimental endotoxemia. Brain, Behavior, and Immunity. 2014. PMID: 24814500. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: a standardised inflammatory stimulus with a known clock — TNF pulses at 90–180 minutes, fever, leukocyte trafficking and cortisol follow, and the size of everything depends on dose, preparation and sex
cards.summary: Synthesis: a standardised inflammatory stimulus with a known clock — TNF pulses at 90–180 minutes, fever, leukocyte trafficking and cortisol follow, and the size of everything depends on dose, preparation and sex
cards.people: Synthesis of the five carded human records above (the two 1988 NIH-programme characterisations, the Nijmegen sex-difference study, the placebo-controlled IL-10 trial's model limb, and the Essen dose–response study), framed by Guyton & Hall / Ganong on fever and the innate immune response. This is physiology measured under a controlled inflammatory stimulus, not resting physiology — graded as such, as this row's slate directs.
cards.result: The model's reproducible sequence: intravenous reference E. coli endotoxin produces a brief circulating TNF pulse peaking at 90–180 minutes (240 ± 70 pg/mL at 4 ng/kg; ~400–1,000 pg/mL at 2 ng/kg, higher in women), with IL-1β not detectably rising in the classic record; symptoms, white-cell trafficking, ACTH/cortisol activation, fever and haemodynamic change follow the pulse in time and track its height; and infusing TNF itself to similar peak levels reproduces the package, identifying the afferent signal. Dose is a dial with a floor: systemic activation at 0.4 ng/kg, downstream functional effects (pain sensitivity) appearing at 0.8 ng/kg, the full classic package at 2–4 ng/kg — and preparations differ between programmes, so every value on this shelf is printed with its dose and preparation and none is pooled across them. The repeat-challenge (endotoxin-tolerance) limb named in this row's question is not carded: the tolerance records retrieved this session were reviews or non-systemic (nasal) challenges, so no systemic human tolerance primary met this shelf's carding standard, and the shelf says so rather than borrowing one. Nothing here is sepsis: the model is a transient, self-limited, dose-controlled stimulus in screened volunteers, and its values must not be read onto infected patients.
cards.watchOut: Endotoxin preparations (reference E. coli endotoxin versus purified LPS lots) and doses (0.4–4 ng/kg across this shelf) are not interchangeable; cross-study comparisons must carry both.

shelves.title: High-dose antithrombin III in severe sepsis: KyberSept was null overall (28-day mortality 38.9% vs 38.7%) — signals only in non-randomised no-heparin subgroups
shelves.question: In adults with severe sepsis, does high-dose antithrombin III versus placebo reduce 28-day mortality — and does concomitant heparin change the answer?
shelves.mesh: Antithrombin III · Sepsis · Shock, Septic · Heparin · Disseminated Intravascular Coagulation · Hemorrhage
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence): KyberSept (n=2,314) — the only large trial — found high-dose antithrombin III made no difference to 28-day mortality in severe sepsis (38.9% versus 38.7%, P=.94). Favourable signals appear only in the non-randomised subgroup that received no concomitant heparin (90-day mortality 44.9% versus 52.5%) and, within it, in patients with DIC (absolute 28-day mortality reduction 14.6%) — subgroup findings inside a null trial, graded as such and never as the headline. Antithrombin plus heparin increased bleeding (23.8% versus 13.5%). A historical programme: the drug was never adopted for sepsis.

cards.headline: KyberSept 2001: high-dose antithrombin III made no difference to 28-day mortality in 2,314 patients with severe sepsis — 38.9% versus 38.7% (the treatment made no difference)
cards.summary: KyberSept 2001: high-dose antithrombin III made no difference to 28-day mortality in 2,314 patients with severe sepsis — 38.9% versus 38.7% (the treatment made no difference)
cards.people: 2,314 adults with severe sepsis and septic shock randomised in the double-blind, placebo-controlled, multicentre phase 3 KyberSept trial (March 1997–January 2000) to intravenous antithrombin III (30,000 IU total over 4 days, started within 6 hours of onset; n=1,157) or placebo (1% human albumin; n=1,157).
cards.result: Overall 28-day all-cause mortality was 38.9% with antithrombin III versus 38.7% with placebo (P=.94) — the treatment made no difference. Mortality at 56 and 90 days and ICU survival time also did not differ. In the subgroup not receiving concomitant heparin during the 4-day treatment phase (n=698), 28-day mortality was 37.8% versus 43.6% (P=.08, not significant), becoming significant only at 90 days (44.9% versus 52.5%, P=.03). Bleeding was significantly more frequent when antithrombin was combined with heparin (23.8% versus 13.5%, P<.001).
cards.watchOut: The headline result is null. The no-heparin finding is a subgroup result — non-significant at the primary 28-day endpoint — and must not be read as the trial's answer.
cards.source: Warren BL, Eid A, Singer P, et al. High-dose antithrombin III in severe sepsis: a randomized controlled trial. JAMA. 2001. PMID: 11597289. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: KyberSept no-heparin DIC analysis 2006: in patients with disseminated intravascular coagulation and no heparin, antithrombin was associated with a 14.6% absolute lower 28-day mortality; no effect without DIC
cards.summary: KyberSept no-heparin DIC analysis 2006: in patients with disseminated intravascular coagulation and no heparin, antithrombin was associated with a 14.6% absolute lower 28-day mortality; no effect without DIC
cards.type: Subgroup analysis of a phase 3 RCT (KyberSept no-heparin, DIC-stratified), J Thromb Haemost 2006
cards.people: 563 KyberSept patients who received no concomitant heparin and had sufficient data for DIC scoring by the adapted ISTH algorithm (placebo n=277, antithrombin n=286); 229 (40.7%) had DIC at baseline.
cards.result: DIC itself carried excess mortality on placebo (28-day mortality 40.0% with DIC versus 22.2% without, P<0.01). Among patients with DIC, antithrombin was associated with an absolute 14.6% lower 28-day mortality versus placebo (P=0.02); among patients without DIC the difference was 0.1% (P=1.0). Major bleeding on antithrombin versus placebo was 7.0% versus 5.2% with DIC (P=0.6) and 9.8% versus 3.1% without DIC (P=0.02).
cards.watchOut: A subgroup of a subgroup (no heparin, then DIC-positive) inside a null trial — hypothesis-generating only; the DIC score used was an adapted algorithm applied retrospectively.
cards.source: Kienast J, Juers M, Wiedermann CJ, et al. cards.headline: KyberSept heparin-interaction analysis 2006: any mortality signal was confined to the 698 patients without heparin; with heparin there was none, and bleeding rose
cards.summary: KyberSept heparin-interaction analysis 2006: any mortality signal was confined to the 698 patients without heparin; with heparin there was none, and bleeding rose
cards.type: Secondary benefit/risk analysis of a phase 3 RCT (KyberSept), Thromb Haemost 2006
cards.people: All 2,314 KyberSept patients, split by concomitant heparin during the 4-day treatment phase: 1,616 received heparin (placebo 811, antithrombin 805) and 698 did not (placebo 346, antithrombin 352).
cards.result: Without heparin, 28-day mortality was 37.8% on antithrombin versus 43.6% on placebo (absolute reduction 5.8%; risk ratio 0.860, 95% CI 0.725–1.019), widening by day 90 (44.9% versus 52.5%; absolute reduction 7.6%; risk ratio 0.851, 0.735–0.987). With heparin, 28-day mortality was 39.4% versus 36.6% (absolute increase 2.8%; risk ratio 1.08, 0.96–1.22) — no effect. Bleeding was more frequent with antithrombin plus heparin than with antithrombin alone; thromboembolic event rates were similar with or without heparin.
cards.watchOut: Heparin use was not randomised — it rose during the trial as routine prophylaxis — so the heparin/no-heparin contrast is observational within the trial and confounded by era and practice.
cards.source: Hoffmann JN, Wiedermann CJ, Juers M, et al. Benefit/risk profile of high-dose antithrombin in patients with severe sepsis treated with and without concomitant heparin. Thrombosis and Haemostasis. 2006. PMID: 16676077. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: KyberSept quality-of-life report 2002: among survivors, some quality-of-life attributes favoured antithrombin, again only in the no-heparin subgroup
cards.summary: KyberSept quality-of-life report 2002: among survivors, some quality-of-life attributes favoured antithrombin, again only in the no-heparin subgroup
cards.type: Quality-of-life follow-up report of a phase 3 RCT (KyberSept), Crit Care 2002
cards.people: Survivors of the KyberSept trial followed for up to 90 days with a visual analogue scale and the Karnofsky scale for physical, psychological and social quality of life; the record's abstract does not state the number of survivors assessed — N not documented in the record's abstract.
cards.result: Among all sepsis survivors there was a significant advantage on some quality-of-life attributes in the antithrombin subgroup that did not receive heparin, compared with the corresponding placebo group; the authors describe improvements particularly in social and psychological functioning over 90 days. No mortality claim is made by this report, and none is carried here.
cards.watchOut: Survivors only, multiple quality-of-life attributes, and the same non-randomised no-heparin split — supportive colour for the subgroup hypothesis, not independent evidence of benefit.

cards.headline: Synthesis: KyberSept was null overall; the only favourable signals sit inside non-randomised subgroups defined by heparin co-treatment — a closed, historical programme
cards.summary: Synthesis: KyberSept was null overall; the only favourable signals sit inside non-randomised subgroups defined by heparin co-treatment — a closed, historical programme
cards.people: Synthesis of the four carded KyberSept reports above (Warren 2001; Kienast 2006; Hoffmann 2006; Rublee 2002) — one trial of 2,314 patients reported four ways, not four trials.
cards.result: The trial's own primary answer is that high-dose antithrombin III made no difference to 28-day mortality in severe sepsis (38.9% versus 38.7%). Every favourable number on this shelf — the 90-day no-heparin difference, the DIC-positive absolute reduction, the quality-of-life advantage — comes from subgroups defined by whether clinicians happened to give heparin, which was never randomised, and the DIC analysis narrows that further. Combined antithrombin plus heparin increased bleeding (23.8% versus 13.5%). Cross-points, not duplicated: the library's thrombomodulin (SCARLET) shelf and its drotrecogin shelf ask the same sepsis-anticoagulation question for different agents; this shelf is the antithrombin answer, and the programme was never adopted for sepsis.
cards.watchOut: One trial, four reports. Subgroup signals in a null trial are graded MAYBE (weak evidence) on this shelf and are never promoted to the headline claim.
cards.source: Synthesis of the carded records above (PMIDs 11597289, 16409457, 16676077, 12225612). Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

shelves.title: Interleukin-1 receptor antagonist in sepsis: SPLIT — phase 3 trials null overall; a post-hoc macrophage-activation subgroup (n=43) is the only signal
shelves.question: In adults with sepsis/severe sepsis, does recombinant human interleukin-1 receptor antagonist versus placebo reduce mortality?
shelves.mesh: Interleukin 1 Receptor Antagonist Protein · Sepsis · Shock, Septic · Macrophage Activation Syndrome · Disseminated Intravascular Coagulation
shelves.balance: SPLIT: for unselected sepsis, interleukin-1 receptor antagonist (anakinra) failed — the phase 2 dose gradient (n=99) was not confirmed: the first phase 3 trial's pre-specified analyses were null (n=893) and the confirmatory phase 3 was stopped for futility (28-day mortality 33.1% versus 36.4%, P=.36; n=696). The split is a post-hoc 2016 reanalysis: in the 43 patients (5.6%) with macrophage-activation-syndrome features (hepatobiliary dysfunction plus DIC), 28-day survival was 65.4% versus 35.3% (hazard ratio for death 0.28) — hypothesis-generating only, awaiting the prospective trial its authors call for.

cards.headline: Phase 2 trial 1994: a dose-related survival gradient in 99 patients (mortality 44% placebo, then 32%, 25% and 16% across rising IL-1ra doses) — the signal the phase 3 trials then failed to confirm
cards.summary: Phase 2 trial 1994: a dose-related survival gradient in 99 patients (mortality 44% placebo, then 32%, 25% and 16% across rising IL-1ra doses) — the signal the phase 3 trials then failed to confirm
cards.type: Phase 2 randomised placebo-controlled trial, Crit Care Med 1994
cards.people: 99 patients with sepsis syndrome or septic shock at 12 US academic ICUs, given a 100 mg intravenous loading dose of recombinant human interleukin-1 receptor antagonist or placebo, then a 72-hour infusion at one of three IL-1ra doses (17, 67 or 133 mg/hr) or placebo, on standard supportive and antimicrobial care.
cards.result: 28-day mortality fell with dose: 11 of 25 (44%) on placebo, 8 of 25 (32%) at 17 mg/hr, 6 of 24 (25%) at 67 mg/hr and 4 of 25 (16%) at 133 mg/hr (dose-dependent benefit, P=.015); the gradient was also seen in septic shock at entry (n=65, P=.002) and Gram-negative infection (n=45, P=.04). APACHE II score fell in a dose-related way by the end of infusion (P=.038). The drug was well tolerated.
cards.watchOut: 99 patients split four ways — about 25 per arm — so each step of the gradient rests on a handful of deaths; exactly the kind of early signal large confirmatory trials exist to test.
cards.source: Fisher CJ Jr, Slotman GJ, Opal SM, et al. Initial evaluation of human recombinant interleukin-1 receptor antagonist in the treatment of sepsis syndrome: a phase II study. Critical Care Medicine. 1994. PMID: 8124953. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Phase 3 trial 1994: in 893 patients the primary analyses were null — no significant survival benefit overall or in shock; favourable findings were secondary and retrospective
cards.summary: Phase 3 trial 1994: in 893 patients the primary analyses were null — no significant survival benefit overall or in shock; favourable findings were secondary and retrospective
cards.people: 893 patients with sepsis syndrome in a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, multicentre, multinational trial: a 100 mg loading dose of recombinant human IL-1 receptor antagonist or placebo, then a 72-hour infusion of IL-1ra at 1.0 or 2.0 mg/kg/hr or placebo; 713 had shock at entry.
cards.result: There was no significant increase in survival time with IL-1ra versus placebo among all patients treated (n=893, P=.22) or among patients with shock at entry (n=713, P=.23) — the two pre-specified primary analyses. Secondary and retrospective analyses suggested a dose-related survival increase in patients with organ dysfunction (n=563, P=.009), predicted mortality risk of 24% or more (n=580, P=.005), or both (n=411, P=.002).
cards.watchOut: The favourable numbers are explicitly secondary and retrospective in the record; the pre-specified primary analyses are the trial's answer, and they were null.
cards.source: Fisher CJ Jr, Dhainaut JF, Opal SM, et al. Recombinant human interleukin 1 receptor antagonist in the treatment of patients with sepsis syndrome: results from a phase III clinical trial. JAMA. 1994. PMID: 8196140. cards.headline: Confirmatory phase 3 trial 1997: stopped at interim analysis — 28-day mortality 33.1% on IL-1ra versus 36.4% on placebo (P=.36), no subgroup rescued it
cards.summary: Confirmatory phase 3 trial 1997: stopped at interim analysis — 28-day mortality 33.1% on IL-1ra versus 36.4% on placebo (P=.36), no subgroup rescued it
cards.type: Confirmatory phase 3 randomised placebo-controlled trial, Crit Care Med 1997
cards.people: 696 patients with severe sepsis or septic shock at 91 academic ICUs in North America and Europe, randomised to a 100 mg intravenous bolus of recombinant human IL-1 receptor antagonist then a 72-hour infusion at 2.0 mg/kg/hr, or placebo, on standard care (350 IL-1ra, 346 placebo); about half were in shock at entry.
cards.result: The trial was terminated after a planned interim analysis found the primary endpoints unlikely to be met. 28-day all-cause mortality was 33.1% (116/350) on IL-1ra versus 36.4% (126/346) on placebo — a relative 9% lower mortality rate that was not significant (P=.36). No difference emerged by infection site, organism, bacteraemia, shock, organ dysfunction or predicted risk. No excess adverse reactions or superinfections were attributable to IL-1ra. The authors conclude any true benefit in this population would be small and hard to demonstrate.
cards.watchOut: A stopped-for-futility confirmatory trial is the strongest evidence on this shelf: the phase 2 gradient and the first phase 3's retrospective signals did not replicate.
cards.source: Opal SM, Fisher CJ Jr, Dhainaut JF, et al. Confirmatory interleukin-1 receptor antagonist trial in severe sepsis: a phase III, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, multicenter study. Critical Care Medicine. 1997. PMID: 9233735. cards.headline: Reanalysis 2016: in the 43 patients (5.6%) with macrophage-activation-syndrome features — hepatobiliary dysfunction plus DIC — 28-day survival was 65.4% on anakinra versus 35.3% on placebo (hazard ratio for death 0.28)
cards.summary: Reanalysis 2016: in the 43 patients (5.6%) with macrophage-activation-syndrome features — hepatobiliary dysfunction plus DIC — 28-day survival was 65.4% on anakinra versus 35.3% on placebo (hazard ratio for death 0.28)
cards.type: Post-hoc reanalysis of a phase 3 RCT, Crit Care Med 2016
cards.people: Reanalysis of deidentified data from 763 adults in the 1997 phase 3 trial (91 centres, 11 countries), regrouped by concurrent hepatobiliary dysfunction and disseminated intravascular coagulation as features of macrophage activation syndrome; 43 patients (5.6%) had both features.
cards.result: In patients without both features, 28-day survival was essentially identical (71.4% anakinra versus 70.8% placebo, P=0.88). In the 43 patients with both hepatobiliary dysfunction and DIC, 28-day survival was 65.4% on anakinra versus 35.3% on placebo, with a hazard ratio for death of 0.28 (95% CI 0.11–0.71, P=0.0071). The authors themselves call for a prospective randomised trial using macrophage-activation features for risk stratification to confirm the finding.
cards.watchOut: 43 patients, a post-hoc regrouping of a stopped trial, and a very wide confidence interval — hypothesis-generating only; no prospective trial of this subgroup strategy is carded on this shelf.
cards.source: Shakoory B, Carcillo JA, Chatham WW, et al. Interleukin-1 receptor blockade is associated with reduced mortality in sepsis patients with features of macrophage activation syndrome. Critical Care Medicine. 2016. PMID: 26584195. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: SPLIT — two phase 3 primaries null and the programme negative overall; the only live signal is a post-hoc hyperinflammatory subgroup of 43 patients
cards.summary: Synthesis: SPLIT — two phase 3 primaries null and the programme negative overall; the only live signal is a post-hoc hyperinflammatory subgroup of 43 patients
cards.people: Synthesis of the four carded reports above (Fisher phase 2, 1994; Fisher phase 3, 1994; Opal confirmatory phase 3, 1997; Shakoory reanalysis, 2016).
cards.result: The split, named: as a treatment for sepsis in general, interleukin-1 receptor blockade failed — a promising phase 2 dose gradient (n=99) was followed by two phase 3 trials whose pre-specified mortality analyses were null, the second stopped for futility at interim analysis. Against that, a 2016 reanalysis found a large survival difference confined to the 5.6% of patients with macrophage-activation-syndrome features (hepatobiliary dysfunction plus DIC) — a post-hoc subgroup of 43 patients that its own authors say needs a prospective trial. Cross-point, not merged: the library's suPAR-guided anakinra shelf in COVID-19 asks a different, biomarker-guided question in a different disease and is not evidence for this one.
cards.watchOut: Do not let the reanalysis outvote the trials: the shelf's verdict for unselected sepsis is negative; the subgroup is a research hypothesis, not a treatment claim.
cards.source: Synthesis of the carded records above (PMIDs 8124953, 8196140, 9233735, 26584195). Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

shelves.title: Filgrastim in pneumonia and severe sepsis: neutrophils rose, outcomes did not — three trials, no survival benefit (the treatment made no difference)
shelves.question: In non-neutropenic adults hospitalised with pneumonia (including multilobar pneumonia and pneumonia with severe sepsis), does adjunctive filgrastim versus placebo improve survival and shorten illness?
shelves.mesh: Filgrastim · Granulocyte Colony-Stimulating Factor · Pneumonia, Bacterial · Sepsis · Community-Acquired Infections
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence): three randomised trials (1998–2003) in non-neutropenic hospitalised pneumonia — community-acquired, multilobar (n=480) and pneumonia with severe sepsis — agree: filgrastim raised neutrophil counts as designed and the treatment made no difference to mortality, resolution of morbidity, organ dysfunction, ICU or ventilator days. It was safe and well tolerated throughout. A closed question, settled against routine adjunctive use; the only favourable notes are unvalidated secondary/subgroup observations.

cards.headline: Community-acquired pneumonia trial 1998: filgrastim tripled neutrophils but time to resolution of morbidity, mortality and length of stay were unaffected (the treatment made no difference)
cards.summary: Community-acquired pneumonia trial 1998: filgrastim tripled neutrophils but time to resolution of morbidity, mortality and length of stay were unaffected (the treatment made no difference)
cards.type: Randomised placebo-controlled trial, J Infect Dis 1998
cards.people: Hospitalised adults with community-acquired pneumonia in a randomised, placebo-controlled, multicentre trial of filgrastim 300 micrograms/day for up to 10 days as an adjunct to antibiotics; the record's abstract does not state the total enrolled — N not documented in the record's abstract.
cards.result: Filgrastim increased blood neutrophils 3-fold, but time to resolution of morbidity (a composite of temperature, respiratory rate, oxygenation and chest radiograph), 28-day mortality and length of hospitalisation were not affected — the treatment made no difference to the clinical endpoints. Radiological improvement appeared faster and serious complications (empyema, adult respiratory distress syndrome, disseminated intravascular coagulation) appeared fewer, as secondary observations. Filgrastim was safe and well tolerated.
cards.watchOut: The complication and radiology findings are secondary observations in a trial null on its named clinical endpoints; the authors themselves say additional trials are needed.
cards.source: Nelson S, Belknap SM, Carlson RW, et al. A randomized controlled trial of filgrastim as an adjunct to antibiotics for the treatment of hospitalized patients with community-acquired pneumonia. Journal of Infectious Diseases. 1998. PMID: 9806037. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Multilobar pneumonia trial 2000: in 480 patients, no endpoint differed significantly; a trend in pneumococcal bacteraemia was left explicitly unvalidated
cards.summary: Multilobar pneumonia trial 2000: in 480 patients, no endpoint differed significantly; a trend in pneumococcal bacteraemia was left explicitly unvalidated
cards.type: Randomised placebo-controlled trial (phase 3), J Infect Dis 2000
cards.people: 480 hospitalised adults with multilobar community-acquired pneumonia randomised to filgrastim 300 micrograms/day (n=237) or placebo (n=243) alongside standard therapy, for 10 days or until peak white cell count reached 75×10⁹/L, discharge, death or intravenous antibiotics stopped; observations to day 29.
cards.result: Filgrastim raised white cell counts (baseline median 13.3×10⁹/L; median peak 43.8×10⁹/L). The two groups were not statistically different on any study endpoint. There was a trend toward lower mortality in patients with pneumococcal bacteraemia, which the authors state requires further study to validate. Filgrastim was safe and well tolerated.
cards.watchOut: The largest of the three trials and still null; the pneumococcal-bacteraemia trend is a subgroup trend, printed as such and never upgraded on this shelf.

cards.headline: Pneumonia with severe sepsis trial 2003: filgrastim raised the white count as designed and changed nothing else — mortality, organ dysfunction, ICU days and ventilator days all similar
cards.summary: Pneumonia with severe sepsis trial 2003: filgrastim raised the white count as designed and changed nothing else — mortality, organ dysfunction, ICU days and ventilator days all similar
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial, Crit Care Med 2003
cards.people: Adults in intensive care units with bacterial pneumonia (community-acquired or nosocomial, radiograph- and culture/Gram-stain-confirmed) and severe sepsis (sepsis-induced hypotension or organ dysfunction), randomised double-blind to standard antibiotics plus filgrastim 300 micrograms/day intravenously for 5 days or placebo, started within 24 hours of enrolment; the record's abstract does not state the total enrolled — N not documented in the record's abstract.
cards.result: Filgrastim raised the white cell count to a median peak of 31.7×10⁹/L from a baseline of 12.3×10⁹/L. The groups did not differ significantly in severe adverse events, time to death, subsequent organ dysfunction, ICU days or ventilator days; mortality was low in both groups, and mortality in the subgroup with adult respiratory distress syndrome was similar. The authors conclude filgrastim appeared safe but not efficacious in reducing mortality or complications.
cards.watchOut: This is the sickest population of the three trials (pneumonia plus severe sepsis) and the answer is the same; low overall mortality also limited the trial's power to show a mortality difference.
cards.source: Root RK, Lodato RF, Patrick W, et al. Multicenter, double-blind, placebo-controlled study of the use of filgrastim in patients hospitalized with pneumonia and sepsis. cards.headline: Synthesis: three randomised trials, one consistent answer — filgrastim does its pharmacology (neutrophils rise 3-fold or more) and makes no difference to survival or illness course in non-neutropenic pneumonia
cards.summary: Synthesis: three randomised trials, one consistent answer — filgrastim does its pharmacology (neutrophils rise 3-fold or more) and makes no difference to survival or illness course in non-neutropenic pneumonia
cards.people: Synthesis of the three carded trials above (Nelson 1998; Nelson 2000, n=480; Root 2003).
cards.result: Across community-acquired pneumonia, multilobar pneumonia and pneumonia with severe sepsis, adjunctive filgrastim reliably raised neutrophil and white cell counts and reliably failed to improve mortality, time to resolution of morbidity, organ dysfunction, ICU stay or ventilation. The residual signals — fewer serious complications in 1998, a pneumococcal-bacteraemia trend in 2000 — are secondary or subgroup observations their own authors left unvalidated, and no later trial on this shelf validates them. This is a closed, Surviving-Sepsis-era question that guidelines settled against routine use, presented as such — not a live option. Cross-points, not duplicated: the library's G-CSF shelves in liver failure, granulocyte transfusion and chemotherapy prophylaxis ask different questions in different populations.
cards.watchOut: All three populations were non-neutropenic; nothing on this shelf speaks to filgrastim's established uses in neutropenia, which are different questions homed elsewhere.

shelves.title: Intravenous immunoglobulin in sepsis: SPLIT — small old trials positive, the large SBITS trial (n=653) null
shelves.question: In adults with sepsis or septic shock, does adjunctive polyclonal intravenous immunoglobulin versus placebo or albumin reduce mortality?
shelves.mesh: Immunoglobulins, Intravenous · Sepsis · Shock, Septic · Immunoglobulin G · Immunoglobulin M
shelves.balance: SPLIT: the evidence divides by rigour. Three small randomised trials from 1991–2005 (n=62, 55 and 56) report large mortality benefits for polyclonal IVIG in sepsis, while SBITS — the one large, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (n=653) — found 28-day mortality of 39.3% versus 37.3% (the treatment made no difference), and the Cochrane review's low-risk-of-bias sensitivity analysis likewise shows no benefit (relative risk 0.97). ⚠ Several older trials are small and at high risk of bias. Preparations differ (IgG versus IgM-enriched), so the positive limb is not a single consistent intervention.

cards.headline: Dominioni 1991: in 62 surgical patients with sepsis scores of 20 or more, high-dose IgG mortality was 38% versus 67% on albumin — the small positive trial the field was built on
cards.summary: Dominioni 1991: in 62 surgical patients with sepsis scores of 20 or more, high-dose IgG mortality was 38% versus 67% on albumin — the small positive trial the field was built on
cards.type: Randomised double-blind controlled trial, Arch Surg 1991
cards.people: 62 consecutive septic surgical ICU patients who reached a sepsis score of 20 or greater, randomised double-blind to intravenous IgG 0.4 g/kg (n=29) or human albumin (n=33), repeated on days +1 and +5, on standard multimodal intensive care; groups were similar in age, sepsis score and APACHE II.
cards.result: Mortality was 38% in the IgG group versus 67% in controls — a significantly lower mortality as reported in the record. Death from septic shock occurred in 7% of IgG-treated patients versus 33% of controls.
cards.watchOut: 62 patients: a difference of this size rests on roughly 18 deaths; small, single-era surgical-ICU trial at high risk of bias by modern standards — the abstract-era caveat this shelf carries throughout.
cards.source: Dominioni L, Dionigi R, Zanello M, et al. Effects of high-dose IgG on survival of surgical patients with sepsis scores of 20 or greater. Archives of Surgery. 1991. PMID: 1992998. cards.headline: Schedel 1991: in 55 patients with Gram-negative septic shock, sepsis-related death was 1 of 27 (4%) with an IgG/IgM/IgA preparation versus 9 of 28 (32%) in controls
cards.summary: Schedel 1991: in 55 patients with Gram-negative septic shock, sepsis-related death was 1 of 27 (4%) with an IgG/IgM/IgA preparation versus 9 of 28 (32%) in controls
cards.type: Prospective randomised clinical trial, Crit Care Med 1991
cards.people: 55 patients with septic shock at a university hospital clinical immunology ward, randomised to a commercially available polyclonal immunoglobulin preparation containing IgG, IgM and IgA with high titres against bacterial endotoxin determinants, given over the first 3 days (n=27), or no immunoglobulin (n=28).
cards.result: Death related to the septic process within 6 weeks occurred in 1 of 27 (4%) immunoglobulin patients versus 9 of 28 (32%) controls (P<.01). Non-survivors had shown higher circulating endotoxin activity and lower specific IgG titres to lipid A in the first 48 hours.
cards.watchOut: The control group received no infusion rather than a placebo, and 10 deaths in total drive the result; a different (IgM/IgA-containing) preparation from SBITS's IgG — preparations are not interchangeable on this shelf.
