cards.headline: Rodríguez 2005: IgM-enriched IVIG in 56 surgical patients with abdominal sepsis — mortality 27.5% versus 48.1% on albumin (P=0.06); inappropriate initial antibiotics, not IVIG, independently predicted death
cards.summary: Rodríguez 2005: IgM-enriched IVIG in 56 surgical patients with abdominal sepsis — mortality 27.5% versus 48.1% on albumin (P=0.06); inappropriate initial antibiotics, not IVIG, independently predicted death
cards.people: 56 ICU patients with severe sepsis or septic shock of intra-abdominal origin after surgery, admitted within 24 hours of symptom onset at seven teaching hospitals, randomised double-blind to IgM-enriched polyclonal immunoglobulin (Pentaglobin — the tested product as named in the record; a named preparation, given here under the clarification exception) at 7 mL/kg/day for 5 days, or 5% human albumin, each with antibiotics.
cards.result: Overall mortality was 37.5% (55.0% in shock, 25.0% in severe sepsis). In the intention-to-treat analysis, mortality was 27.5% with IVIG versus 48.1% with albumin (P=0.06 — not significant). Organ failure and dysfunction scores and reoperation rates did not differ. Eight patients (14.3%) received initially inappropriate antibiotics and seven of them died; inappropriate initial therapy was the only independent predictor of death (odds ratio 19.4).
cards.watchOut: 56 patients and a P value of 0.06: a trend, not a demonstration — and the trial's own regression says antibiotic appropriateness, not immunoglobulin, drove survival.
cards.source: Rodríguez A, Rello J, Neira J, et al. Effects of high-dose intravenous immunoglobulin and antibiotics on survival for severe sepsis undergoing surgery. Shock. 2005. PMID: 15803051. cards.headline: SBITS 2007: the large rigorous test — in 653 patients with score-defined severe sepsis, IVIG 28-day mortality was 39.3% versus 37.3% on placebo (P=.67) (the treatment made no difference)
cards.summary: SBITS 2007: the large rigorous test — in 653 patients with score-defined severe sepsis, IVIG 28-day mortality was 39.3% versus 37.3% on placebo (P=.67) (the treatment made no difference)
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (SBITS), Crit Care Med 2007
cards.people: 653 patients with score-defined sepsis (sepsis score 12–27) and APACHE II 20–35 at 23 medical and surgical ICUs, randomised double-blind to intravenous immunoglobulin G (0.6 g/kg on day 0, 0.3 g/kg on day 1; total 0.9 g/kg) or placebo; 624 formed the per-protocol group.
cards.result: 28-day mortality was 39.3% on IVIG versus 37.3% on placebo (P=.6695) — the treatment made no difference. Seven-day mortality was not reduced and day-4 pulmonary function was not improved; drug-related adverse events were rare in both groups. An exploratory finding of 3 days' shorter mechanical ventilation among survivors is the only favourable note, and the trial's conclusion is plain: IVIG at this dose does not reduce mortality in score-defined severe sepsis.
cards.watchOut: SBITS tested IgG only, at a defined score window; it does not directly test IgM-enriched preparations — but it is an order of magnitude larger than every positive trial on this shelf combined and methodologically the strongest.
cards.source: Werdan K, Pilz G, Bujdoso O, et al. Score-based immunoglobulin G therapy of patients with sepsis: the SBITS study. Critical Care Medicine. 2007. PMID: 18074471. cards.headline: Cochrane review 2013: pooled adult trials favoured polyclonal IVIG (relative risk 0.81), but in the low-risk-of-bias sensitivity analysis the benefit vanished (relative risk 0.97)
cards.summary: Cochrane review 2013: pooled adult trials favoured polyclonal IVIG (relative risk 0.81), but in the low-risk-of-bias sensitivity analysis the benefit vanished (relative risk 0.97)
cards.type: Cochrane systematic review and meta-analysis, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2013
cards.people: Cochrane systematic review of 43 randomised trials of intravenous immunoglobulin (monoclonal or polyclonal) versus placebo or no intervention in bacterial sepsis or septic shock, searching CENTRAL, MEDLINE and EMBASE to 2012; the adult polyclonal subgroup pooled 10 trials (n=1,430) and the IgM-enriched subgroup 7 trials (n=528); the low-bias sensitivity analysis pooled 5 adult trials (n=945).
cards.result: In adults, polyclonal IVIG was associated with lower mortality (relative risk 0.81, 95% CI 0.70–0.93 — a relative measure, printed as such) and IgM-enriched IVIG likewise (relative risk 0.66, 0.51–0.85). But restricted to trials at low risk of bias, polyclonal IVIG showed no mortality reduction (relative risk 0.97, 0.81–1.15). In neonates, standard IVIG showed no benefit (relative risk 1.00). The review's conclusion: the apparent adult benefit is not seen in the trustworthy trials, and the IgM-enriched evidence is too small for a robust conclusion.
cards.watchOut: A synthesis card, not a trial: its pooled relative risks inherit the small-trial bias its own sensitivity analysis exposes — which is precisely the point the card exists to make.
cards.source: Alejandria MM, Lansang MA, Dans LF, Mantaring JB 3rd. Intravenous immunoglobulin for treating sepsis, severe sepsis and septic shock. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2013. PMID: 24043371. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: SPLIT — small, old, high-bias-risk trials say IVIG saves lives; the one large rigorous trial (SBITS, n=653) and the low-bias synthesis say it makes no difference
cards.summary: Synthesis: SPLIT — small, old, high-bias-risk trials say IVIG saves lives; the one large rigorous trial (SBITS, n=653) and the low-bias synthesis say it makes no difference
cards.people: Synthesis of the five carded reports above (Dominioni 1991, n=62; Schedel 1991, n=55; Rodríguez 2005, n=56; SBITS 2007, n=653; Cochrane 2013).
cards.result: The split is by trial quality and size, and it is named as such: three randomised trials of 55–62 patients each, from 1991–2005, with striking mortality differences (38% versus 67%; 4% versus 32%; 27.5% versus 48.1% at P=0.06), against SBITS — 653 patients, double-blind, placebo-controlled — finding 39.3% versus 37.3% (the treatment made no difference), and a Cochrane sensitivity analysis in which the pooled benefit disappears once high-bias-risk trials are removed (relative risk 0.97). ⚠ Abstract-era caveat: several of the older trials are small and at high risk of bias, exactly as flagged when this shelf was commissioned. Preparations also differ (IgG versus IgM-enriched), so even the positive limb is not one consistent intervention. Cross-point: the library's IVIG shelf for streptococcal toxic shock asks a different, syndrome-specific question and is not duplicated here.
cards.watchOut: Weight the limbs by rigour, not by count: one 653-patient blinded trial outweighs three trials totalling 173 patients from an earlier era of sepsis care.

shelves.title: Obeldesivir in COVID-19: viral load fell in both phase 3 trials, but hospitalisation (0 vs 1 event) and symptom time (5.9 vs 6.0 days) did not significantly improve
shelves.question: In non-hospitalised adults with COVID-19 (high-risk and low-risk populations), does oral obeldesivir versus placebo reduce hospitalisation or death and speed symptom resolution?
shelves.mesh: COVID-19 · SARS-CoV-2 · Antiviral Agents · Drug Resistance, Viral · COVID-19 Drug Treatment
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence): a two-trial programme (BIRCH, high-risk, n=465; OAKTREE, low-risk, n=1,955) reported four ways. Obeldesivir reduced viral RNA and infectious titre and showed a high barrier to resistance, but neither clinical endpoint was met: BIRCH had one hospitalisation/death event in total (0 versus 1; the authors state the trial was underpowered), and OAKTREE's time to symptom alleviation was 5.9 versus 6.0 days (P=0.068, not significant). No mortality claim is made. Safety was comparable to placebo in both trials.

cards.headline: BIRCH 2026 (high-risk): hospitalisation or death by day 29 was 0 of 211 on obeldesivir versus 1 of 207 on placebo — an event count too small to answer the question; viral load fell faster
cards.summary: BIRCH 2026 (high-risk): hospitalisation or death by day 29 was 0 of 211 on obeldesivir versus 1 of 207 on placebo — an event count too small to answer the question; viral load fell faster
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (BIRCH), Clin Infect Dis 2026
cards.people: 465 non-hospitalised adults with risk factors for severe COVID-19, enrolled within 5 days of symptom onset and randomised 1:1 to obeldesivir 350 mg or placebo twice daily for 5 days; 58% had received at least one COVID-19 vaccination and 92% were seropositive for SARS-CoV-2 antibodies. The primary-endpoint population printed in the record is 211 obeldesivir and 207 placebo participants.
cards.result: COVID-19-related hospitalisation or all-cause death by day 29 occurred in 0 of 211 (0%) on obeldesivir versus 1 of 207 (0.5%) on placebo (log-rank P=.32) — the treatment made no demonstrable difference to the primary endpoint, in a trial the authors state was underpowered as event rates collapsed. Time to symptom alleviation was numerically shorter on obeldesivir; viral RNA copy number at day 5 and infectious titre at days 3 and 5 fell more on obeldesivir. Safety was generally comparable between arms.
cards.watchOut: One primary-endpoint event in 418 assessed participants: no mortality or hospitalisation claim can rest on this, in either direction. The registry ID in the record is NCT05603143 (with EudraCT 2022-002741-18).

cards.headline: OAKTREE 2025 (low-risk): symptom alleviation was not significantly faster (median 5.9 versus 6.0 days, P=0.068); viral RNA fell modestly more on obeldesivir
cards.summary: OAKTREE 2025 (low-risk): symptom alleviation was not significantly faster (median 5.9 versus 6.0 days, P=0.068); viral RNA fell modestly more on obeldesivir
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (OAKTREE), Lancet Infect Dis 2025
cards.people: 1,955 low-risk, non-hospitalised adults and adolescents with mild-to-moderate COVID-19 at 107 centres in Japan and the USA, enrolled within 3 days of symptom onset and randomised 1:1 to obeldesivir 350 mg (n=979) or placebo (n=976) twice daily for 5 days; 70.0% had completed a primary vaccination series and 99.6% were seropositive. The symptom analysis set comprised 879 obeldesivir and 882 placebo participants.
cards.result: Median time to symptom alleviation was 5.9 days (95% CI 5.4–6.1) on obeldesivir versus 6.0 days (5.8–6.3) on placebo (hazard ratio 1.099, 0.997–1.211; P=0.068) — not significant. Viral RNA at day 5 fell more on obeldesivir (least-squares mean difference −0.18 log10 copies/mL, −0.30 to −0.06; P=0.0037). Treatment-emergent adverse events were 5.4% versus 5.7%; graded laboratory abnormalities were common in both arms (77.5% versus 78.5%), mostly grade 1–2.
cards.watchOut: A 0.1-day median symptom difference in an almost universally seropositive, low-risk population is the realistic ceiling this trial could show; hospitalisation events were not the endpoint here and no mortality claim arises.

cards.headline: BIRCH resistance analysis 2026: emergent Nsp12 substitutions were common in both arms; only one (V792I, in one participant) showed even low-level reduced susceptibility (EC50 fold change 4.01)
cards.summary: BIRCH resistance analysis 2026: emergent Nsp12 substitutions were common in both arms; only one (V792I, in one participant) showed even low-level reduced susceptibility (EC50 fold change 4.01)
cards.type: Resistance analysis of a phase 3 RCT (BIRCH), Antiviral Res 2026
cards.people: Participants from BIRCH with nasal-swab sequencing: 252 of the 465 randomised (190 obeldesivir, 62 placebo) had baseline sequencing data; emergent-substitution analysis covered 73 obeldesivir and 54 placebo participants with paired samples, phenotyped in a replicon system.
cards.result: Baseline Nsp12 substitutions changed susceptibility by at most 1.8-fold — no change. Emergent Nsp12 substitutions appeared in 12 of 73 (16.4%) obeldesivir and 5 of 54 (9.3%) placebo participants; of nine emergent substitutions seen only on obeldesivir, just one — V792I, in a single participant, first detected at day 15 in someone never hospitalised — showed reduced susceptibility, at a low level (EC50 fold change 4.01). The authors conclude a high barrier to resistance in this population.
cards.watchOut: A report of the BIRCH trial, not a new trial — this shelf is a two-trial programme reported four ways, and the resistance denominators are the sequenced subsets, not the randomised populations.

cards.headline: OAKTREE resistance analysis 2026: emergent substitution rates were similar on drug and placebo (16.8% versus 19.2%); one substitution (C799F, one participant) showed reduced susceptibility (3.35-fold)
cards.summary: OAKTREE resistance analysis 2026: emergent substitution rates were similar on drug and placebo (16.8% versus 19.2%); one substitution (C799F, one participant) showed reduced susceptibility (3.35-fold)
cards.type: Resistance analysis of a phase 3 RCT (OAKTREE), Antiviral Res 2026
cards.people: Participants from OAKTREE meeting sequencing criteria: 1,425 (725 obeldesivir, 700 placebo) with baseline sequencing data; the paired emergent-substitution analysis covered 208 obeldesivir and 120 placebo participants, with replicon phenotyping.
cards.result: Thirty-five baseline Nsp12 substitutions were seen in at least 3 participants; all phenotyped within assay variability (≤2.15-fold EC50 change). Emergent Nsp12 substitutions occurred in 35 of 208 (16.8%) on obeldesivir versus 23 of 120 (19.2%) on placebo; 25 emergent substitutions were seen only on obeldesivir, of which one — C799F, in one participant — was associated with reduced susceptibility (3.35-fold EC50 change). The authors conclude a high barrier to resistance in low-risk patients.
cards.watchOut: Emergent substitutions arising at similar rates on placebo mark background viral evolution under sampling, not drug-selected resistance; the single reduced-susceptibility findings in each trial are one participant each.

cards.headline: Synthesis: a two-trial programme with real antiviral activity and no demonstrated clinical benefit — viral load falls, symptoms and hospitalisation do not significantly change
cards.summary: Synthesis: a two-trial programme with real antiviral activity and no demonstrated clinical benefit — viral load falls, symptoms and hospitalisation do not significantly change
cards.people: Synthesis of the four carded reports above — two trials (BIRCH, n=465, high-risk; OAKTREE, n=1,955, low-risk) and their two resistance analyses.
cards.result: Obeldesivir, an oral nucleoside prodrug of the remdesivir parent nucleoside, consistently reduced viral RNA and infectious titre, and resistance analyses in both trials found a high barrier to resistance (one low-level reduced-susceptibility substitution per trial, one participant each). But neither clinical endpoint was met: BIRCH recorded a single hospitalisation/death event across both arms (0 versus 1; underpowered by the authors' own statement), and OAKTREE's symptom-alleviation difference was 0.1 days and not significant (P=0.068). In highly immune populations, event rates and symptom durations leave little room for any antiviral to show clinical benefit, and this programme did not show it. Cross-points, not duplicated: the library's nirmatrelvir, remdesivir, ensitrelvir and simnotrelvir shelves cover the other COVID antivirals, each on its own trial base.
cards.watchOut: Antiviral activity on a laboratory endpoint is not clinical efficacy: this shelf grades the programme MAYBE (weak evidence) for clinical benefit, and prints no mortality claim.
cards.source: Synthesis of the carded records above (PMIDs 40694627, 40675167, 41565160, 41475511). Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

shelves.title: Cefazolin for MSSA bacteraemia: non-inferior to flucloxacillin/cloxacillin in SNAP (90-day mortality 15.0% vs 17.0%) with less kidney injury
shelves.question: In adults with MSSA bacteraemia, is cefazolin non-inferior to flucloxacillin/cloxacillin (antistaphylococcal penicillins) for 90-day mortality, with fewer adverse events?
shelves.mesh: Cefazolin · Bacteremia · Staphylococcus aureus · Cloxacillin · Floxacillin · Acute Kidney Injury
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: the randomised evidence is one platform domain (SNAP, 1,287 evaluable patients): cefazolin was non-inferior to flucloxacillin/cloxacillin for 90-day mortality (15.0% versus 17.0%; probability of non-inferiority 99.2%) with less acute kidney injury (13.9% versus 19.6%). The pre-2026 observational literature (30 studies, 15,513 patients) pointed the same way but is confounded by indication and graded separately. A single randomised programme caps this shelf at POSSIBLE; superiority for survival is not claimed.

cards.headline: SNAP MSSA domain 2026: cefazolin was non-inferior to flucloxacillin/cloxacillin for 90-day mortality (15.0% versus 17.0%; probability of non-inferiority 99.2%) and caused less acute kidney injury (13.9% versus 19.6%)
cards.summary: SNAP MSSA domain 2026: cefazolin was non-inferior to flucloxacillin/cloxacillin for 90-day mortality (15.0% versus 17.0%; probability of non-inferiority 99.2%) and caused less acute kidney injury (13.9% versus 19.6%)
cards.type: Randomised open-label platform trial domain (SNAP), N Engl J Med 2026
cards.people: Adults with penicillin-resistant, methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus aureus bacteraemia in the SNAP international Bayesian adaptive platform trial, randomised open-label to cefazolin or an antistaphylococcal penicillin (flucloxacillin or cloxacillin) between February 2022 and August 2024; 645 cefazolin and 642 penicillin patients were evaluable for the primary outcome (kidney-injury denominators 660 and 648).
cards.result: 90-day mortality was 15.0% (97/645) on cefazolin versus 17.0% (109/642) on antistaphylococcal penicillin (adjusted odds ratio 0.81, 95% credible interval 0.59–1.12; probability of non-inferiority 99.2% against the pre-specified criterion of an adjusted odds ratio below 1.2, approximating an absolute mortality difference under 2.5 percentage points at a 15% baseline; probability of superiority 89.8%). Acute kidney injury within 14 days occurred in 13.9% (92/660) versus 19.6% (127/648) (adjusted odds ratio 0.67, 0.50–0.89; probability of superiority 99.7%).
cards.watchOut: Open-label, and a Bayesian platform domain stopped when the non-inferiority criterion was met — the superiority probability (89.8%) does not cross the trial's own threshold, so this shelf claims non-inferiority plus a kidney-safety advantage, not superior survival.
cards.source: SNAP trial investigators. Cefazolin for methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus aureus bacteremia. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2026. PMID: 42308484. cards.headline: SNAP review 2026: the platform's randomised results, read with CloCeBa, argue cefazolin is equally efficacious and safer — flucloxacillin kidney injury has been under-recognised
cards.summary: SNAP review 2026: the platform's randomised results, read with CloCeBa, argue cefazolin is equally efficacious and safer — flucloxacillin kidney injury has been under-recognised
cards.type: Narrative review of randomised platform results (SNAP), J Antimicrob Chemother 2026
cards.people: A review of the randomised results from the Staphylococcus aureus Network Adaptive Platform (SNAP) trial, including its MSSA/PSSA domains, read alongside the CloCeBa trial, written for clinicians managing S. aureus bloodstream infection; no new patients are reported — N not documented as a new study population in the record, as this is a review of the carded platform trial.
cards.result: The review's reading: guidelines have recommended intravenous (flu)cloxacillin first-line for MSSA bacteraemia on decades of practice rather than randomised evidence; the SNAP trial — described as the largest randomised trial ever in S. aureus bacteraemia — exposed high acute kidney injury rates with high-dose (flu)cloxacillin, whose contribution to kidney injury has likely been under-recognised. Its conclusion: cefazolin provides a safer and equally efficacious treatment for S. aureus bacteraemia.
cards.watchOut: An interpretive review of the same trial carded above — it adds framing (and the CloCeBa cross-reference), not independent patients; it is never counted as a second trial on this shelf.

cards.summary: Observational meta-analysis 2025: across 30 observational studies (15,513 patients), cefazolin met non-inferiority for 30-day mortality (odds ratio 0.73) with point estimates favouring it on safety — at moderate-to-high risk of bias
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of observational studies, Clin Microbiol Infect 2025
cards.people: 30 comparative observational studies of MSSA bacteraemia comprising 3,869 patients treated with cefazolin and 11,644 with antistaphylococcal penicillins (flucloxacillin 6,721; unspecified 2,440; nafcillin 1,305; cloxacillin 1,258; oxacillin 120), assessed with a non-randomised-studies risk-of-bias tool and rated moderate or high risk of bias; no randomised data existed when it was done.
cards.result: Cefazolin was associated with lower odds of 30-day all-cause mortality (odds ratio 0.73, 95% CI 0.62–0.85), meeting the pre-specified non-inferiority margin (pooled odds ratio below 1.2); against flucloxacillin alone the estimate was 0.92 (0.73–1.16). Point estimates favoured cefazolin for 90-day mortality, treatment-related adverse events, nephrotoxicity and discontinuation for toxicity in almost every individual-penicillin comparison. The authors grade the data moderate-to-low quality.
cards.watchOut: Observational and confounded by indication — cefazolin was preferentially given to lower-risk patients for decades — so its apparent mortality advantage is exactly what the randomised SNAP domain was needed to test; this shelf keeps the two limbs visibly separate and grades the observational limb as such.
cards.source: Prosty C, Noutsios D, Lee TC, et al. Cefazolin vs. antistaphylococcal penicillins for the treatment of methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus aureus bacteraemia: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Clinical Microbiology and Infection. 2025. PMID: 40349971. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: one large randomised platform domain settles what 30 observational studies could only suggest — cefazolin is non-inferior for survival and kinder to kidneys
cards.summary: Synthesis: one large randomised platform domain settles what 30 observational studies could only suggest — cefazolin is non-inferior for survival and kinder to kidneys
cards.people: Synthesis of the three carded reports above (SNAP MSSA domain, N Engl J Med 2026; SNAP review, 2026; observational meta-analysis, 2025).
cards.result: The randomised and observational limbs point the same way on safety and are kept separate on efficacy: the observational literature (15,513 patients, moderate-to-high bias risk) suggested cefazolin was at least as good and possibly better, but confounding by indication made that unreadable until SNAP randomised 1,287 evaluable patients and found non-inferior 90-day mortality (15.0% versus 17.0%) with significantly less acute kidney injury (13.9% versus 19.6%). The cefazolin inoculum effect remains a laboratory caveat, not a clinical outcome, and is not upgraded here. As a single randomised programme, this shelf caps at POSSIBLE. Cross-points, not duplicated: the library's S. aureus bacteraemia shelves on infectious-diseases consultation, oral switch (SABATO) and daptomycin ask different questions.
cards.watchOut: Non-inferiority is the claim — not superiority: SNAP's probability of superiority for mortality (89.8%) did not meet a decisive threshold, and the shelf does not present it as one.
cards.source: Synthesis of the carded records above (PMIDs 42308484, 42396858, 40349971). Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

shelves.title: Tigecycline in complicated intra-abdominal infection: non-inferior for clinical cure in three randomised comparisons — under an FDA boxed warning on all-cause mortality
shelves.question: In hospitalised adults with complicated intra-abdominal infection, is tigecycline non-inferior to imipenem/cilastatin (or ceftriaxone plus metronidazole) for clinical cure?
shelves.mesh: Tigecycline · Bacterial Infections · Imipenem · Cilastatin · Ceftriaxone · Metronidazole · Intraabdominal Infections
shelves.balance: LIKELY: across three randomised comparisons (2005–2010), tigecycline was non-inferior to imipenem/cilastatin and to ceftriaxone plus metronidazole for clinical cure of complicated intra-abdominal infection (evaluable-population cure ~81–86% versus ~82–86% against imipenem/cilastatin), with consistently more nausea and vomiting. On the face of the shelf: tigecycline carries an FDA boxed warning of increased all-cause mortality pooled across indications, which these cure-endpoint trials do not settle, and the trial era predates current resistance epidemiology.

cards.headline: Phase 3 trial 2005: tigecycline clinical cure 80.6% versus 82.4% for imipenem/cilastatin in the microbiologically evaluable population — non-inferior, with more nausea and vomiting
cards.summary: Phase 3 trial 2005: tigecycline clinical cure 80.6% versus 82.4% for imipenem/cilastatin in the microbiologically evaluable population — non-inferior, with more nausea and vomiting
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised double-blind trial, BMC Infect Dis 2005
cards.people: 825 hospitalised adults with complicated intra-abdominal infection received at least one dose in a prospective, double-blind, multinational trial of intravenous tigecycline (100 mg loading dose, then 50 mg every 12 hours) versus imipenem/cilastatin (500/500 mg every 6 hours) for 5–14 days; in the microbiologically evaluable group the primary diagnoses were complicated appendicitis (59%), intestinal perforation (8.8%) and gastric/duodenal perforation (4.6%).
cards.result: Clinical cure at test-of-cure (14–35 days after therapy) in the microbiologically evaluable population was 80.6% (199/247) on tigecycline versus 82.4% (210/255) on imipenem/cilastatin (95% CI for the difference −8.4 to 5.1, within the non-inferiority margin); in the microbiological modified intention-to-treat population, 73.5% (227/309) versus 78.2% (244/312) (95% CI −11.0 to 2.5). Nausea (31.0% versus 24.8%), vomiting (25.7% versus 19.4%, P=0.037) and diarrhoea (21.3% versus 18.9%) were the commonest adverse events.
cards.watchOut: Non-inferiority on clinical cure in evaluable populations is a weaker currency than mortality; cure rates fall by roughly 7–9 points in the modified intention-to-treat population in both arms, printed here rather than hidden.
cards.source: Oliva ME, Rekha A, Yellin A, et al. A multicenter trial of the efficacy and safety of tigecycline versus imipenem/cilastatin in patients with complicated intra-abdominal infections. BMC Infectious Diseases. 2005. PMID: 16236177. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00081744. cards.headline: Pooled phase 3 analysis 2005: across 1,642 patients, cure rates were 86.1% versus 86.2% (microbiologically evaluable) — non-inferiority confirmed at programme level
cards.summary: Pooled phase 3 analysis 2005: across 1,642 patients, cure rates were 86.1% versus 86.2% (microbiologically evaluable) — non-inferiority confirmed at programme level
cards.type: Pooled analysis of two phase 3 randomised trials, Clin Infect Dis 2005
cards.people: Pooled analysis of two phase 3, double-blind trials randomising 1,642 adults with complicated intra-abdominal infection to tigecycline (100 mg, then 50 mg intravenously every 12 hours) or imipenem-cilastatin (500/500 mg every 6 hours) for 5–14 days; the trial carded above is one of the two pooled trials, so patients overlap and are not additive.
cards.result: Clinical cure at test-of-cure (12–42 days) in the microbiologically evaluable population was 86.1% (441/512) on tigecycline versus 86.2% (442/513) on imipenem-cilastatin (95% CI for the difference −4.5% to 4.4%; P<.0001 for non-inferiority); in the microbiological modified intention-to-treat population, 80.2% (506/631) versus 81.5% (514/631) (95% CI −5.8 to 3.2%). Nausea (24.4% versus 19.0%, P=.01) and vomiting (19.2% versus 14.3%, P=.008) were significantly commoner on tigecycline; diarrhoea was similar (13.8% versus 13.2%).
cards.watchOut: A pooled re-presentation of the programme, not a third trial: this shelf counts two imipenem-controlled trials plus the ceftriaxone/metronidazole trial below as its randomised base.
cards.source: Babinchak T, Ellis-Grosse E, Dartois N, et al. The efficacy and safety of tigecycline for the treatment of complicated intra-abdominal infections: analysis of two phase 3 studies. Clinical Infectious Diseases. 2005. PMID: 16080073. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: European phase 3 analysis 2008: at European sites, cure was 92.4% on tigecycline versus 88.8% on imipenem/cilastatin (microbiologically evaluable)
cards.summary: European phase 3 analysis 2008: at European sites, cure was 92.4% on tigecycline versus 88.8% on imipenem/cilastatin (microbiologically evaluable)
cards.type: Combined regional analysis of two phase 3 randomised trials, J Chemother 2008
cards.people: Combined analysis of European-site patients from the same two phase 3, double-blind trials of tigecycline versus imipenem/cilastatin (5–14 days) in adults with complicated intra-abdominal infection; 237 tigecycline and 223 imipenem/cilastatin patients formed the microbiologically evaluable group.
cards.result: Clinical cure at test-of-cure (12–44 days) was 92.4% (219/237) on tigecycline versus 88.8% (198/223) on imipenem/cilastatin (95% CI −2.2 to 9.4) in the microbiologically evaluable population, and 87.3% (247/283) versus 83.5% (228/273) (95% CI −2.5 to 10.0) in the modified intention-to-treat population. No pre-therapy isolate showed tigecycline resistance by the breakpoints used, and the tigecycline MIC90 against common aerobes and anaerobes was at most 2.0 micrograms/mL. Nausea (14.7% versus 11.8%) and vomiting (10.7% versus 7.3%) were the commonest events.
cards.watchOut: A regional subset of the same two trials — supportive consistency, not independent evidence; isolate susceptibility from 2005–2008 predates current resistance epidemiology.
cards.source: Fomin P, Koalov S, Cooper A, et al. The efficacy and safety of tigecycline for the treatment of complicated intra-abdominal infections — the European experience. Journal of Chemotherapy. 2008. PMID: 19036670. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00081744; ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00136201. cards.headline: Tigecycline versus ceftriaxone plus metronidazole 2010: cure 70.4% versus 74.3% in the clinically evaluable population — non-inferior (P=0.009), with more nausea, vomiting and discontinuations
cards.summary: Tigecycline versus ceftriaxone plus metronidazole 2010: cure 70.4% versus 74.3% in the clinically evaluable population — non-inferior (P=0.009), with more nausea, vomiting and discontinuations
cards.type: Open-label randomised comparative trial, Clin Microbiol Infect 2010
cards.people: 473 hospitalised adults with complicated intra-abdominal infection randomised 1:1, open-label, to tigecycline (100 mg, then 50 mg every 12 hours) or ceftriaxone 2 g daily plus metronidazole 1–2 g daily for 4–14 days; 376 were clinically evaluable (189 tigecycline, 187 comparator).
cards.result: Clinical cure at test-of-cure was 70.4% (133/189) on tigecycline versus 74.3% (139/187) on ceftriaxone/metronidazole (95% CI −13.1 to 5.1; P=0.009 for non-inferiority); in patients with APACHE II scores of 10 or more, 56.8% (21/37) versus 58.3% (21/36). Microbiological eradication was 68.1% (94/138) versus 71.5% (98/137). Nausea (38.6% versus 27.7%) and vomiting (23.3% versus 17.7%) were commoner on tigecycline, and discontinuation for an adverse event was 8.9% versus 4.8%.
cards.watchOut: Open-label with a wide non-inferiority interval (−13.1 to 5.1): 'non-inferior' here tolerates a substantially lower cure rate, and the sicker subgroup (APACHE II ≥10) cured at only ~57% in both arms.
cards.source: Towfigh S, Pasternak J, Poirier A, et al. A multicentre, open-label, randomized comparative study of tigecycline versus ceftriaxone sodium plus metronidazole for the treatment of patients with complicated intra-abdominal infections. Clinical Microbiology and Infection. 2010. PMID: 20670293. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00195351. cards.headline: Synthesis: tigecycline is non-inferior for clinical cure across three randomised comparisons — a cure-endpoint answer that sits under the FDA boxed warning on all-cause mortality
cards.summary: Synthesis: tigecycline is non-inferior for clinical cure across three randomised comparisons — a cure-endpoint answer that sits under the FDA boxed warning on all-cause mortality
cards.people: Synthesis of the four carded reports above — three distinct randomised comparisons (two imipenem/cilastatin trials, one of them carded singly and both pooled and regionally re-analysed; one ceftriaxone/metronidazole trial), 2005–2010.
cards.result: On the question asked — clinical cure of complicated intra-abdominal infection — the trials agree: tigecycline matched imipenem/cilastatin (cure ~81–86% versus ~82–86% in evaluable populations) and ceftriaxone plus metronidazole (70.4% versus 74.3%), at the price of more nausea and vomiting throughout. Two cautions ride on the face of this shelf. First, the FDA boxed warning: tigecycline carries a boxed warning of increased all-cause mortality pooled across indications — a mortality signal from the wider programme that these cure-endpoint cIAI trials were not designed to settle, and which no card here contradicts. Second, the comparators and resistance patterns are those of 2005–2010. Cross-points, not duplicated: the library's ceftazidime–avibactam, eravacycline and imipenem–relebactam shelves cover the newer cIAI agents on their own trial bases.
cards.watchOut: Non-inferiority for cure is not a mortality verdict: any use decision must weigh the boxed warning, which this shelf prints rather than buries.

shelves.title: Rebyota (fecal microbiota, live-jslm) for recurrent C. difficile: randomised subgroups favour it over placebo; the large open-label cohort succeeded in 73.8% at 8 weeks
shelves.question: In adults with recurrent Clostridioides difficile infection after standard antibiotic therapy, does a single rectally administered live microbiota suspension (RBX2660) versus placebo reduce recurrence at 8 weeks?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Anti-Bacterial Agents/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Bayes Theorem · Clostridioides difficile/isolation & purification · Clostridium Infections/prevention & control,microbiology · Double-Blind Method · Fecal Microbiota Transplantation · Feces/microbiology · Gastrointestinal Microbiome · Recurrence · Risk Factors · Secondary Prevention/methods · Treatment Outcome · Vancomycin/administration & dosage,therapeutic use · Clostridium Infections/therapy,prevention & control · Prospective Studies · Fecal Microbiota Transplantation/methods,adverse effects · Clostridioides difficile · Anti-Bacterial Agents/therapeutic use · Canada · United States · Young Adult · Inflammatory Bowel Diseases/microbiology,complications
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — a single programme (one randomised phase 3 trial, reported through subgroup and post-hoc analyses, plus a large single-arm phase 3 cohort) for one named product. Clarification exception applied: the tested product is fecal microbiota, live-jslm (Rebyota, Ferring Pharmaceuticals) — a single rectally administered dose given after standard-of-care antibiotics — and it is named, with its manufacturer, because the product is the intervention. The randomised limb: subgroup and post-hoc analyses of the PUNCH CD3 placebo-controlled trial (with its phase 2 predecessor) show treatment differences favouring the product over placebo at 8 weeks that were consistent across risk-factor subgroups, with the largest relative reductions in patients with a 3-day antibiotic washout and with four or more previous episodes; older adults with comorbidities likewise stayed recurrence-free more often than on placebo in all but two subgroups. The open-label limb: in PUNCH CD3-OLS, 697 treated participants had a 73.8% treatment success rate at 8 weeks and, among successes, a 91.0% sustained response at 6 months — single-arm, so those percentages have no comparator and are graded weaker. Safety across five prospective trials (1,192 recipients): treatment-emergent adverse events in 70.9%, mostly mild-to-moderate and gastrointestinal; serious events mostly reflected pre-existing conditions or the infection itself. This shelf's home neighbour, live shelf #983, asks the microbiome question for donor-faeces infusion and the defined oral spore product SER-109; the rectal live suspension is the unasked slice carded here, and the PUNCH CD3 primary report itself is not re-carded (one home per study). Single programme, so POSSIBLE caps the stamp.

cards.headline: PUNCH CD3 subgroup analysis (2024): the product's advantage over placebo at 8 weeks held across risk-factor subgroups, largest with a 3-day antibiotic washout and with four or more previous episodes
cards.summary: PUNCH CD3 subgroup analysis (2024): the product's advantage over placebo at 8 weeks held across risk-factor subgroups, largest with a 3-day antibiotic washout and with four or more previous episodes
cards.type: Subgroup analysis of two randomised trials (phase 2 and phase 3), Bayesian hierarchical model
cards.people: Participants in the randomised, placebo-controlled PUNCH CD3 trial of fecal microbiota, live-jslm (with data borrowed from the phase 2 PUNCH CD2 trial in a Bayesian hierarchical model), grouped by recurrent C. difficile risk factors and treatment variables; one rectal dose after standard-of-care antibiotics.
cards.result: Treatment differences between the product and placebo at 8 weeks were similar to the total population for most subgroups; effect sizes were similar by diagnostic test, larger after oral vancomycin courses longer than 14 days than after shorter courses, and larger with a 3-day antibiotic washout than with 2 days or less. The largest relative reductions in recurrence were in the 3-day washout subgroup and in participants with at least four previous episodes. Most treatment-emergent adverse events in treated participants were mild or moderate and related to pre-existing conditions.
cards.watchOut: A subgroup analysis, not the primary report: it shows consistency of the randomised effect, and its abstract does not restate the overall primary percentages, which are not re-printed here.

cards.summary: PUNCH CD3-OLS (2025): single-arm phase 3 cohort of 697 treated patients — 73.8% treatment success at 8 weeks, 91.0% of successes sustained at 6 months (no comparator)
cards.people: 793 adults with documented recurrent C. difficile infection after standard-of-care antibiotics enrolled across the US and Canada; 697 received a single rectal dose of fecal microbiota, live-jslm within 24-72 hours of completing antibiotics. Patients with inflammatory bowel disease and mild-to-moderate immunocompromising conditions could enrol.
cards.result: Treatment-emergent adverse events through 8 weeks were reported by 47.3% of participants, mostly mild or moderate gastrointestinal disorders; serious events occurred in 3.9%. Treatment success at 8 weeks was 73.8%; among those who succeeded, the sustained clinical response rate at 6 months was 91.0%. Rates were similar across demographic and baseline subgroups.
cards.watchOut: Single-arm: 73.8% success has no placebo beside it, and the randomised trial's placebo success was substantial — read this card for reach (who can be treated) and durability, not for the size of the drug effect.

cards.people: Adults with recurrent C. difficile infection who completed standard-of-care therapy and received one or two rectal doses of fecal microbiota, live-jslm or placebo across three phase 2 and two phase 3 trials; events recorded for up to 6 months.
cards.result: Treatment-emergent adverse events were reported in 70.9% (845 of 1,192) of product recipients; most were mild to moderate and gastrointestinal. shelves.title: Pulmonary artery catheter-guided management in general intensive care, shock and ARDS: two randomised trials found no survival benefit (PAC-Man hospital mortality 68% versus 66%; Richard 28-day mortality 59.4% versus 61.0%)
shelves.question: In critically ill adults with shock, ARDS or general ICU admission (not acute heart failure specifically), does management guided by a pulmonary artery catheter versus clinical assessment without a catheter improve survival?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Catheterization, Swan-Ganz/adverse effects · Critical Care · Critical Illness · Female · Hospital Mortality · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Monitoring, Physiologic · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — this shelf asks the general intensive care, shock and ARDS question only. The heart-failure slice of this question is homed separately at pack #3306, where the ESCAPE trial of catheter-guided therapy in severe heart failure sits; ESCAPE stays in that home under the one-home rule and is cross-pointed here in prose only, not re-carded. On the general-ICU question, two randomised trials agree: PAC-Man (1041 patients in 65 UK intensive care units) found hospital mortality of 68% with a pulmonary artery catheter versus 66% without (adjusted hazard ratio 1.09, 95% CI 0.94 to 1.27), and the French trial of early catheter use in shock and ARDS (676 patients) found 28-day mortality of 59.4% versus 61.0% (relative risk 0.97, 95% CI 0.86 to 1.10), with no difference at 14 or 90 days or in organ-support-free days. The older observational SUPPORT analysis (5735 patients) had associated catheterisation with higher 30-day mortality (odds ratio 1.24, 95% CI 1.03 to 1.49) and higher cost — it is carded as the hypothesis-generating limb that prompted the trials, graded below them: it is confounded by indication, and the randomised trials that followed found neither the harm it suggested nor any benefit. Insertion complications occurred in 46 of 486 PAC-Man patients in whom a catheter was placed, none fatal. This is a closed historical question: routine catheter-guided management was abandoned on this evidence, and the shelf presents it as such, not as a live option.

cards.headline: PAC-Man (Harvey 2005): hospital mortality 68% with a pulmonary artery catheter versus 66% without (adjusted HR 1.09, 95% CI 0.94 to 1.27; P=0.39) — no benefit and no clear harm
cards.summary: PAC-Man (Harvey 2005): hospital mortality 68% with a pulmonary artery catheter versus 66% without (adjusted HR 1.09, 95% CI 0.94 to 1.27; P=0.39) — no benefit and no clear harm
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial, multicentre (65 UK intensive care units)
cards.people: 1041 critically ill patients were enrolled and randomised to management with (n=519) or without (n=522) a pulmonary artery catheter; 1014 were eligible for analysis. Timing of insertion and subsequent management were at the treating clinician's discretion, and units could pre-specify an alternative cardiac-output monitor for control patients.
cards.result: There was no difference in hospital mortality between patients managed with or without a catheter: 68% (346 of 506) versus 66% (333 of 507), P=0.39; adjusted hazard ratio 1.09 (95% CI 0.94 to 1.27). Complications of insertion occurred in 46 of 486 patients in whom the device was placed, none of them fatal. The authors conclude there is no clear evidence of benefit or harm from managing critically ill patients with a catheter.
cards.watchOut: Management after insertion was discretionary, not protocolised — the trial tests the catheter as actually used, not a specific catheter-driven treatment algorithm, and control-arm use of alternative cardiac-output monitors may dilute any contrast.
cards.source: Harvey S et al. Assessment of the clinical effectiveness of pulmonary artery catheters in management of patients in intensive care (PAC-Man): a randomised controlled trial. Lancet. 2005. PMID: 16084255. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.summary: Richard 2003: early catheter use in shock and ARDS — 28-day mortality 59.4% versus 61.0% (relative risk 0.97, 95% CI 0.86 to 1.10); no difference at 14 or 90 days or in support-free days
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial, multicentre (36 French intensive care units)
cards.people: 676 adults meeting standard criteria for shock (mainly septic), acute respiratory distress syndrome, or both, enrolled 1999–2001, were randomised to receive a pulmonary artery catheter early (n=335) or not (n=341); treatment thereafter was at each physician's discretion. Primary endpoint: 28-day mortality.
cards.result: Mortality did not differ with or without the catheter at day 14 (49.9% versus 51.3%; relative risk 0.97, 95% CI 0.84 to 1.13; P=.70), day 28 (59.4% versus 61.0%; relative risk 0.97, 95% CI 0.86 to 1.10; P=.67) or day 90 (70.7% versus 72.0%; relative risk 0.98, 95% CI 0.89 to 1.08; P=.71). Days free of organ failure, renal support and vasoactive agents at day 14, and hospital, ICU and ventilator-free days at day 28, also did not differ.
cards.watchOut: A relative risk of 0.97 is a relative measure; the absolute mortality difference at day 28 was 1.6 percentage points (59.4% versus 61.0%), and the confidence interval spans meaningful effects in both directions — the trial excludes a large benefit, not every small one. As in PAC-Man, post-insertion management was unprotocolised.
cards.source: Richard C et al. Early use of the pulmonary artery catheter and outcomes in patients with shock and acute respiratory distress syndrome: a randomized controlled trial. JAMA. 2003. PMID: 14645314. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: SUPPORT (Connors 1996, observational): right heart catheterisation in the first 24 hours was associated with higher 30-day mortality (odds ratio 1.24, 95% CI 1.03 to 1.49) and higher cost — the hypothesis the trials then tested
cards.summary: SUPPORT (Connors 1996, observational): right heart catheterisation in the first 24 hours was associated with higher 30-day mortality (odds ratio 1.24, 95% CI 1.03 to 1.49) and higher cost — the hypothesis the trials then tested
cards.type: Prospective cohort study with propensity-score case-matching (SUPPORT) — observational limb, graded below the randomised cards
cards.people: 5735 critically ill adults cared for in intensive care units at five US teaching hospitals (1989–1994) for one of nine prespecified disease categories; the analysis compared patients who did and did not receive right heart catheterisation in the first 24 hours, adjusting for treatment selection with a propensity score by case-matching and multivariable modelling.
cards.result: By case-matching, patients with catheterisation had increased 30-day mortality (odds ratio 1.24, 95% CI 1.03 to 1.49). Mean cost per hospital stay was $49,300 with catheterisation versus $35,700 without, and mean ICU stay was 14.8 versus 13.0 days; multivariable modelling confirmed all three findings, and no subgroup or site showed an association with improved outcomes. Sensitivity analysis estimated an unmeasured confounder would need to raise both death risk and catheterisation risk about 6-fold to hide a true benefit.
cards.watchOut: Observational and confounded by indication — sicker patients receive catheters, and propensity adjustment cannot remove unmeasured confounding. This card is the reason the randomised trials were done; it must never outvote them, and the trials found neither its suggested harm nor any benefit.
cards.source: Connors AF Jr et al. The effectiveness of right heart catheterization in the initial care of critically ill patients. SUPPORT Investigators. JAMA. 1996. PMID: 8782638. cards.headline: Synthesis: the trials settled what the cohort raised — catheter-guided management made no difference to survival — LIKELY (the treatment made no difference)
cards.summary: Synthesis: the trials settled what the cohort raised — catheter-guided management made no difference to survival — LIKELY (the treatment made no difference)
cards.people: Synthesis of the three cards above: PAC-Man (1041 randomised, general ICU), Richard 2003 (676 randomised, shock and ARDS) and the SUPPORT cohort (5735 observed). The heart-failure trial of the same question is homed at pack #3306 and is not re-carded here.
cards.result: Two randomised trials in different populations and health systems found mortality within 2 percentage points between catheter and no-catheter care, with confidence intervals excluding a large benefit; the observational association with harm (odds ratio 1.24) was not reproduced as either harm or benefit under randomisation. Insertion complications were common enough to count (46 of 486 placements) but not fatal in PAC-Man.
cards.watchOut: The verdict covers catheter-guided management as practised in these trials — discretionary, unprotocolised use. It does not address catheter use for diagnosis in selected patients, which none of these studies tested.
cards.source: Synthesis of Harvey S et al. Lancet. 2005 (PMID: 16084255), Richard C et al. JAMA. 2003 (PMID: 14645314), Connors AF Jr et al. JAMA. 1996 (PMID: 8782638). Registry IDs: none in the records.

shelves.title: Sivelestat in ALI/ARDS: SPLIT — STRIVE negative (no mortality or ventilator-free-day benefit, 180-day mortality signal) versus Japanese physiological benefit; meta-analysis null
shelves.question: In adults with acute lung injury or ARDS associated with systemic inflammatory response syndrome, does intravenous sivelestat versus placebo improve mortality, ventilator-free days or oxygenation?
shelves.mesh: Australia · Belgium · Canada · Double-Blind Method · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Glycine · Guideline Adherence · Humans · Infusions, Intravenous · Leukocyte Elastase · Male · Middle Aged · New Zealand · Outcome and Process Assessment, Health Care · Prospective Studies · Respiration, Artificial · Respiratory Distress Syndrome · Serine Proteinase Inhibitors · Spain · Sulfonamides · Survival Analysis · Tidal Volume · Time · Treatment Outcome · United States
shelves.balance: SPLIT — by region and era, and the split is the answer. The international STRIVE trial (492 mechanically ventilated patients with acute lung injury) was negative: no effect on ventilator-free days (11.4 vs 11.9, P=0.536) or 28-day mortality (64 deaths in each group), the trial was stopped early on a negative long-term mortality trend, and 180-day all-cause mortality was significantly higher on sivelestat (P=0.006 in the curve comparison reported). The earlier Japanese phase 3 programme (230 patients, ALI with systemic inflammatory response syndrome) reported the opposite direction on physiological endpoints: improved pulmonary-function rating, reduced duration of mechanical ventilation and shortened ICU stay, with no significant effect on survival. A 2017 meta-analysis of 6 randomised trials (804 patients) sits with STRIVE on clinical endpoints: no significant difference in 28–30-day mortality (relative risk 0.94, 95% CI 0.71 to 1.23), ventilation days or ICU stay, with a possible oxygenation signal only in sensitivity analysis. Sivelestat is licensed only in Japan (and a small number of other Asian markets) — that regulatory status is part of the face of this shelf.

cards.headline: STRIVE (Zeiher 2004): sivelestat had NO effect on ventilator-free days (11.4 vs 11.9) or 28-day mortality (64 deaths in each group) in 492 ventilated ALI patients — and 180-day mortality was higher on sivelestat (P=0.006)
cards.summary: STRIVE (Zeiher 2004): sivelestat had NO effect on ventilator-free days (11.4 vs 11.9) or 28-day mortality (64 deaths in each group) in 492 ventilated ALI patients — and 180-day mortality was higher on sivelestat (P=0.006)
cards.type: International multicentre double-blind placebo-controlled trial (STRIVE), intravenous sivelestat vs placebo in ALI
cards.people: 492 mechanically ventilated patients with acute lung injury at 105 institutions in the United States, Canada, Belgium, Spain, Australia and New Zealand, randomised 1:1 to continuous intravenous sivelestat 0.16 mg/kg/hour or placebo for the duration of mechanical ventilation plus 24 hours (maximum 14 days); all patients were managed with low tidal volume ventilation. Primary objectives: 28-day all-cause mortality and ventilator-free days (days alive and free of mechanical ventilation, days 1–28).
cards.result: The study was stopped prematurely on the recommendation of an external Data and Safety Monitoring Board, which noted a negative trend in long-term mortality. Final analysis: no effect on ventilator-free days (mean 11.4 sivelestat vs 11.9 placebo; P=0.536) or 28-day all-cause mortality (64 deaths in each treatment group). There was no evidence of effect on pulmonary function measures including PaO2/FiO2, static lung compliance, or time to meeting weaning criteria, and no difference in adverse or serious adverse events. Kaplan-Meier 180-day survival curves did not differ overall (P=0.102), but 180-day all-cause mortality was increased in the sivelestat group compared with placebo (P=0.006) in the comparison reported in the record (absolute 180-day rates are not printed in the record).
cards.watchOut: Stopped early for a negative long-term mortality trend — the 180-day mortality signal (P=0.006, absolute rates not in the record) is a harm signal from a stopped trial, to be reported as such, neither hidden nor overstated. Heterogeneous ALI population, 2004-era care alongside low-tidal-volume ventilation.
cards.source: Zeiher BG et al. Neutrophil elastase inhibition in acute lung injury: results of the STRIVE study. Critical care medicine. 2004. PMID: 15286546. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Tamakuma 2004 (Japanese phase 3 programme): sivelestat improved the pulmonary-function rating, reduced ventilation duration and shortened ICU stay in 230 ALI-with-SIRS patients — with NO significant effect on survival
cards.summary: Tamakuma 2004 (Japanese phase 3 programme): sivelestat improved the pulmonary-function rating, reduced ventilation duration and shortened ICU stay in 230 ALI-with-SIRS patients — with NO significant effect on survival
cards.type: Japanese phase 3 double-blind trial report (Study 1, n=230) with an unblinded follow-on study (Study 2, n=20) in the same publication
cards.people: Japanese programme in acute lung injury associated with systemic inflammatory response syndrome: Study 1, a phase 3 double-blind study in 230 patients, with pulmonary function improvement (PFI) rating as the primary endpoint and ventilator weaning rate, ICU discharge rate and survival rate as secondary endpoints; Study 2, a subsequent unblinded study in 20 patients re-evaluating efficacy with ventilator-free days as the primary endpoint, compared with the Study 1 subgroup meeting Study 2's selection criteria.
cards.result: In Study 1, sivelestat increased the PFI rating, reduced the duration of mechanical ventilation and shortened ICU stay, although there was no significant efficacy on the survival rate (the fetched record reports these directions without printing the effect sizes). In Study 2 (unblinded, 20 patients), the ventilator-free-days value was comparable to that of the optimal-dose subgroup of Study 1, and increases in ventilator-free days correlated with PFI rating and ICU-free days. The authors conclude neutrophil elastase may be involved in the pathogenesis of human ALI.
cards.watchOut: The primary endpoint is a pulmonary-function rating, not mortality or ventilator-free days, and the record prints no effect sizes — the claim carded is direction only. Study 2 is unblinded with only 20 patients and is a programme limb, never load-bearing. This is the Japanese limb of a split evidence base; do not pool it with STRIVE.
cards.source: Tamakuma S et al. Relationship between neutrophil elastase and acute lung injury in humans. Pulmonary pharmacology & therapeutics. 2004. PMID: 15477122. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Pu 2017 (meta-analysis): 6 RCTs, 804 patients — no significant effect of sivelestat on 28–30-day mortality (relative risk 0.94, 95% CI 0.71 to 1.23), ventilation days or ICU stay
cards.summary: Pu 2017 (meta-analysis): 6 RCTs, 804 patients — no significant effect of sivelestat on 28–30-day mortality (relative risk 0.94, 95% CI 0.71 to 1.23), ventilation days or ICU stay
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials in ALI/ARDS
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials comparing sivelestat versus control in acute lung injury / ARDS (PubMed, Embase and Cochrane Library to April 2017); 6 RCTs reporting data on 804 patients were included, analysed with a random-effects model.
cards.result: No significant difference between sivelestat and control for 28–30-day mortality (relative risk 0.94, 95% CI 0.71 to 1.23; P=0.718 — a relative measure; the record does not print the pooled absolute mortality rates), ventilation days (standardised mean difference 0.05, 95% CI −0.27 to 0.38; P=0.748), PaO2/FiO2 level (SMD 0.48, 95% CI −0.45 to 1.41; P=0.315) or ICU stay (SMD −9.87, 95% CI −24.30 to 4.56; P=0.180). A sensitivity analysis suggested sivelestat might increase PaO2/FiO2 (SMD 0.87, 95% CI 0.39 to 1.35; P<0.001). The authors conclude sivelestat might increase PaO2/FiO2 while having little or no effect on mortality, ventilation days and ICU stay, and that large-scale trials are needed.
cards.watchOut: Only 6 trials and 804 patients, mixing the Japanese and international programmes whose results conflict — a pooled null over a split base. The oxygenation signal appears only in sensitivity analysis.
cards.source: Pu S et al. Effect of sivelestat sodium in patients with acute lung injury or acute respiratory distress syndrome: a meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials. BMC pulmonary medicine. 2017. PMID: 29162066. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: SPLIT by region and era — the large international trial was negative with a long-term mortality harm signal, the Japanese programme reported physiological benefit without survival benefit, and the meta-analysis is null on clinical endpoints
cards.summary: Synthesis: SPLIT by region and era — the large international trial was negative with a long-term mortality harm signal, the Japanese programme reported physiological benefit without survival benefit, and the meta-analysis is null on clinical endpoints
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf (STRIVE 492 patients; Japanese phase 3 programme 230 + 20 patients; meta-analysis 6 RCTs, 804 patients).
cards.result: No randomised evidence shows sivelestat improves mortality or ventilator-free days in ALI/ARDS. STRIVE, the largest and only international trial, found no benefit on either primary endpoint and a significantly higher 180-day mortality on sivelestat in the reported comparison. The Japanese phase 3 programme found improved pulmonary-function ratings and shorter ventilation and ICU stay without a survival effect. The 2017 meta-analysis found no significant effect on 28–30-day mortality, ventilation days or ICU stay. Sivelestat remains licensed only in Japan and a small number of other Asian markets.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards for each trial's limits; this synthesis adds no new data.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.balance: SPLIT — and era-bound. This shelf is a single research programme (the Studies of Ocular Complications of AIDS, SOCA, in collaboration with the AIDS Clinical Trials Group): TWO trials and FOUR reports — the Foscarnet-Ganciclovir CMV Retinitis Trial (FGCRT) contributes three of the four reports (mortality, visual outcomes, morbidity/toxicity) and must not be read as three trials. In the FGCRT (234 patients), foscarnet was associated with longer survival (deaths 34% vs 51%; relative risk 1.79 for ganciclovir vs foscarnet; median survival 12.6 vs 8.5 months; the treatment protocol was suspended early on this signal), while retinitis control and vision were equivalent (relative risk of progression 0.97; progression in 85% of each group by 120 days). Tolerability pointed the other way: neutropenia was more common on ganciclovir (34% vs 14%), infusion-related symptoms on foscarnet (58% vs 24%), and 46% of foscarnet patients switched treatment, mostly for toxicity. In the second trial (Cytomegalovirus Retreatment Trial, 279 patients with relapsed retinitis), combination reinduction/maintenance controlled retinitis longest (median time to progression 4.3 vs 2.0 and 1.3 months) with no mortality difference and the greatest quality-of-life cost. ERA FLAG (load-bearing): this is pre-HAART AIDS care, against zidovudine-era antiretroviral therapy — foscarnet's anti-HIV activity and the ganciclovir–zidovudine neutropenia interaction are part of the record, and the foscarnet survival advantage must not be carried into modern practice. Both trials were unblinded.

cards.headline: FGCRT mortality report (NEJM 1992; report 1 of 3 from this ONE trial): deaths 34% on foscarnet vs 51% on ganciclovir (RR 1.79); median survival 12.6 vs 8.5 months — protocol suspended early on this signal
cards.summary: FGCRT mortality report (NEJM 1992; report 1 of 3 from this ONE trial): deaths 34% on foscarnet vs 51% on ganciclovir (RR 1.79); median survival 12.6 vs 8.5 months — protocol suspended early on this signal
cards.type: Multicentre randomised unblinded trial — Foscarnet-Ganciclovir CMV Retinitis Trial (FGCRT), mortality report (1 of 3 reports of this single trial)
cards.people: 234 patients with AIDS and previously untreated cytomegalovirus retinitis at 11 centres, randomised unblinded to ganciclovir (127) or foscarnet (107); antiretroviral therapy (zidovudine, didanosine or dideoxycytidine) was given as dictated by best medical judgment.
cards.result: Excess mortality on ganciclovir led the Policy and Data Monitoring Board to recommend suspension of the treatment protocol 19 months after the trial started. By then 65 of 127 ganciclovir patients and 36 of 107 foscarnet patients had died (51% vs 34%; P=0.007; relative risk 1.79, 95% CI 1.17 to 2.73 — a relative measure, absolute rates beside it). Median survival was 8.5 months on ganciclovir versus 12.6 months on foscarnet. The excess mortality could not be explained entirely by differences in antiretroviral exposure, although ganciclovir patients received less antiretroviral therapy on average; the only foscarnet subgroup with excess mortality was patients whose renal function was compromised at entry. There was no difference in retinitis progression (relative risk 0.95; P=0.751).
cards.watchOut: Pre-HAART, zidovudine-era trial, stopped early on the mortality signal: early stopping can exaggerate an effect, the trial was unblinded, and the survival difference is entangled with era antiretroviral therapy (including foscarnet's own anti-HIV activity) — it must not be carried into modern practice.
cards.source: Studies of Ocular Complications of AIDS Research Group et al.. Mortality in patients with the acquired immunodeficiency syndrome treated with either foscarnet or ganciclovir for cytomegalovirus retinitis. The New England Journal of Medicine. 1992. PMID: 1345799. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: FGCRT visual-outcomes report (1994; report 2 of 3 from the SAME trial): retinitis progression equivalent — RR 0.97, median time to first progression 53 vs 47 days, progression in 85% of each group by 120 days
cards.summary: FGCRT visual-outcomes report (1994; report 2 of 3 from the SAME trial): retinitis progression equivalent — RR 0.97, median time to first progression 53 vs 47 days, progression in 85% of each group by 120 days
cards.type: Report of the SAME FGCRT trial as the mortality card (2 of 3 reports of this single trial) — visual outcomes
cards.people: The same Foscarnet-Ganciclovir CMV Retinitis Trial population as the mortality card above (234 patients with previously untreated CMV retinitis in AIDS), followed for progression of retinitis, visual acuity and visual fields, with progression assessed by a masked central fundus photograph reading centre.
cards.result: The efficacy of the two drugs in controlling CMV retinitis was similar: the relative risk for progression was 0.97 (ganciclovir versus foscarnet; P=0.833), and median time to first progression was 53 days on foscarnet versus 47 days on ganciclovir (P=0.997). By 120 days, progression was observed in 85% of patients in each group. Visual acuity outcomes were similar (at 6 months, best-corrected acuity of 20/40 or better in the better eye in 88% on foscarnet vs 93% on ganciclovir; P=0.325), as were visual field scores (mean loss 29 vs 31 degrees/month; P=0.674). The report restates that foscarnet was associated with longer survival while the drugs appeared equivalent for the eye.
cards.watchOut: Not a second trial: this is the FGCRT's visual-outcomes report. The eye equivalence it shows is equivalence in delaying progression by weeks in a pre-HAART population — 85% of both groups had progressed by 120 days.
cards.source: Studies of Ocular Complications of AIDS Research Group et al.. Foscarnet-Ganciclovir Cytomegalovirus Retinitis Trial. 4. Visual outcomes. Studies of Ocular Complications of AIDS Research Group in collaboration with the AIDS Clinical Trials Group. Ophthalmology. 1994. PMID: 8035989. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: FGCRT morbidity/toxicity report (1995; report 3 of 3 from the SAME trial): neutropenia 34% on ganciclovir vs 14% on foscarnet; infusion symptoms 58% vs 24%; 46% of foscarnet patients switched, mostly for toxicity
cards.summary: FGCRT morbidity/toxicity report (1995; report 3 of 3 from the SAME trial): neutropenia 34% on ganciclovir vs 14% on foscarnet; infusion symptoms 58% vs 24%; 46% of foscarnet patients switched, mostly for toxicity
cards.type: Report of the SAME FGCRT trial as the two cards above (3 of 3 reports of this single trial) — morbidity and toxicity
cards.people: The same 234 FGCRT patients (107 foscarnet, 127 ganciclovir) at 11 university centres; medical histories, laboratory tests and drug treatment histories during the first 6 months of treatment were analysed.
cards.result: Neutropenia was more common on ganciclovir than foscarnet (34% vs 14%; P=.001). Patients on foscarnet reported more infusion-related symptoms (58% vs 24%; P<.001) and, in men, more genitourinary symptoms (36% vs 16%), with a trend to more nephrotoxic effects (13% vs 6%; P=.082) and electrolyte abnormalities; seizures were similar (12% vs 9%). Patients on foscarnet were far more likely to switch to the alternative treatment (46% vs 11%; P<.001), most of the excess attributable to toxic reactions; in 88% of toxicity switches with follow-up data the reaction resolved after switching, and no permanent disability or death resulted from toxic reactions. The authors concluded foscarnet was more often limited by toxicity, but that the previously reported survival benefit supported its use for initial treatment in that era.
cards.watchOut: Not a third trial. The toxicity comparison is the mirror image of the mortality report: foscarnet's survival association came with substantially worse tolerability and a 46% switch rate.
cards.source: Studies of Ocular Complications of AIDS Research Group et al.. Morbidity and toxic effects associated with ganciclovir or foscarnet therapy in a randomized cytomegalovirus retinitis trial. Studies of ocular complications of AIDS Research Group, in collaboration with the AIDS Clinical Trials Group. Archives of Internal Medicine. 1995. PMID: 7802522. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Cytomegalovirus Retreatment Trial (1996; the programme's SECOND trial): for relapsed retinitis, combination therapy controlled retinitis longest (median 4.3 vs 2.0 vs 1.3 months) with NO mortality difference and the worst quality-of-life impact
cards.summary: Cytomegalovirus Retreatment Trial (1996; the programme's SECOND trial): for relapsed retinitis, combination therapy controlled retinitis longest (median 4.3 vs 2.0 vs 1.3 months) with NO mortality difference and the worst quality-of-life impact
cards.type: Multicentre randomised controlled trial — Cytomegalovirus Retreatment Trial (the SOCA programme's second trial), combination vs monotherapy for relapsed retinitis
cards.people: 279 patients with AIDS and persistently active or relapsed CMV retinitis at tertiary centres, randomised to foscarnet reinduction/maintenance (90 mg/kg every 12 hours for 2 weeks, then 120 mg/kg/day), ganciclovir reinduction/maintenance (5 mg/kg every 12 hours for 2 weeks, then 10 mg/kg/day), or continuation of previous maintenance plus induction with the other drug followed by maintenance with both drugs.
cards.result: Mortality was similar among the three groups (median survival 8.4 months foscarnet, 9.0 ganciclovir, 8.6 combination; P=.89). Combination therapy was the most effective regimen for controlling retinitis on masked central reading: median times to retinitis progression were 1.3 months (foscarnet), 2.0 months (ganciclovir) and 4.3 months (combination) (P<.001). Visual field loss and increase in retinal area involved paralleled the progression results (visual field loss 28, 18 and 16 degrees/month respectively; P=.009), with no detectable difference in visual acuity outcomes. Side effects were similar among groups, but combination therapy had the greatest negative impact on quality-of-life measures. The authors concluded combination therapy appears most effective for relapsed retinitis in patients who can tolerate both drugs.
cards.watchOut: A relapsed-retinitis population in the same pre-HAART era: the combination's advantage is months of retinitis control bought with two intravenous drugs and the worst quality-of-life scores — a historical record of pre-HAART salvage therapy.
cards.source: Studies of Ocular Complications of AIDS Research Group et al.. Combination foscarnet and ganciclovir therapy vs monotherapy for the treatment of relapsed cytomegalovirus retinitis in patients with AIDS. The Cytomegalovirus Retreatment Trial. The Studies of Ocular Complications of AIDS Research Group in Collaboration with the AIDS Clinical Trials Group. Archives of Ophthalmology (Chicago, Ill. : 1960). 1996. PMID: 8540847. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: one programme, two trials, four reports — foscarnet's pre-HAART survival association, equivalent eye control, worse tolerability; combination therapy best for relapsed retinitis, at a quality-of-life cost

cards.result: The SOCA programme's structure must stay visible: the FGCRT (234 patients) generated the mortality, visual-outcomes and toxicity reports carded here, and the Cytomegalovirus Retreatment Trial (279 patients) is the programme's second, separate trial. Within the FGCRT, foscarnet was associated with fewer deaths (34% vs 51%; median survival 12.6 vs 8.5 months) in a trial suspended early on that signal, with equivalent retinitis control (progression in 85% of each group by 120 days) and worse tolerability (46% switched, mostly for toxicity). For relapsed retinitis, combination therapy delayed progression longest (4.3 months median) without a mortality difference. All of this is pre-HAART AIDS care and is carded as that era's record.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards for each report's limits; this synthesis adds no new data.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Nitazoxanide in childhood cryptosporidiosis: the HIV split is the answer — benefit in HIV-negative children (56% vs 23% resolution), none in HIV-positive children
shelves.question: In children with cryptosporidial diarrhoea — stratified by HIV status — does nitazoxanide versus placebo (or standard care) improve clinical and parasitological response and reduce mortality?
shelves.mesh: Antiprotozoal Agents · Child, Preschool · Cryptosporidiosis · Diarrhea · Female · HIV Seronegativity · HIV Seropositivity · Humans · Infant · Male · Nitro Compounds · Nutritional Status · Thiazoles · Treatment Outcome · Zambia
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the split is HIV status, and it is the answer. In HIV-seronegative Zambian children, a 3-day course resolved diarrhoea in 56% vs 23% on placebo and eradicated C. parvum in 52% vs 14%, with 0 vs 4 deaths by day 8 (100 recruited, 96 analysed). HIV-seropositive children did not benefit in that trial's stratum, and a dedicated high-dose prolonged-course trial in HIV-positive children was negative (clinical response 42% vs 35%; eradication 27% vs 35%; mortality 31% overall; 60 randomised). A 2025 Bangladeshi pilot in undernourished children (64 randomised; standard-care arm n=10) found no difference in infection duration or growth in any arm. Paediatric, low-income-setting programme throughout.

cards.headline: Zambian trial, HIV-SERONEGATIVE stratum (Amadi 2002): diarrhoea resolved in 56% on nitazoxanide vs 23% on placebo, C. parvum eradicated in 52% vs 14%, and no deaths vs 4 deaths by day 8
cards.summary: Zambian trial, HIV-SERONEGATIVE stratum (Amadi 2002): diarrhoea resolved in 56% on nitazoxanide vs 23% on placebo, C. parvum eradicated in 52% vs 14%, and no deaths vs 4 deaths by day 8
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial, nitazoxanide 100 mg twice daily for 3 days vs placebo — HIV-SERONEGATIVE stratum (the benefit stratum)
cards.people: 100 children with cryptosporidial diarrhoea admitted to the University Teaching Hospital, Lusaka, Zambia (50 HIV-seropositive, 50 HIV-seronegative), randomised to nitazoxanide 100 mg twice daily orally for 3 days or placebo, stratified by HIV serology; 96 were analysed after exclusion of children subsequently found C. parvum-negative or co-infected at baseline. This card reports the HIV-seronegative stratum (25 nitazoxanide, 22 placebo).
cards.result: In HIV-seronegative children, diarrhoea resolved in 14 of 25 (56%) on nitazoxanide versus 5 of 22 (23%) on placebo (difference 33 percentage points, 95% CI 7 to 59; P=0.037), and C. parvum was eradicated from stool in 13 of 25 (52%) versus 3 of 22 (14%) (difference 38 points, 95% CI 14 to 63; P=0.007). By day 8, four children (18%) in the placebo group had died versus none of 25 in the nitazoxanide group (difference −18 points, 95% CI −34 to 2; P=0.041). Nitazoxanide was not significantly associated with adverse events.
cards.watchOut: One trial, one stratum: the mortality contrast is 0 versus 4 deaths in 47 children, so it is fragile; the same trial's HIV-seropositive stratum (next card's programme) did not benefit.
cards.source: Amadi B et al. Effect of nitazoxanide on morbidity and mortality in Zambian children with cryptosporidiosis: a randomised controlled trial. Lancet (London, England). 2002. PMID: 12423984. Registry ID: none in the record. randomised controlled trial, nitazoxanide 100 mg twice daily for 3 days vs placebo — hiv-seronegative stratum (the benefit stratum) 100 children with cryptosporidial diarrhoea admitted to the university teaching hospital, lusaka, zambia (50 hiv-seropositive, 50 hiv-seronegative), randomised to nitazoxanide 100 mg twice daily orally for 3 days or placebo, stratified by hiv serology; 96 were analysed after exclusion of children subsequently found c. parvum-negative or co-infected at baseline. this card reports the hiv-seronegative stratum (25 nitazoxanide, 22 placebo). in hiv-seronegative children, diarrhoea resolved in 14 of 25 (56%) on nitazoxanide versus 5 of 22 (23%) on placebo (difference 33 percentage points, 95% ci 7 to 59; p=0.037), and c. parvum was eradicated from stool in 13 of 25 (52%) versus 3 of 22 (14%) (difference 38 points, 95% ci 14 to 63; p=0.007). by day 8, four children (18%) in the placebo group had died versus none of 25 in the nitazoxanide group (difference −18 points, 95% ci −34 to 2; p=0.041). nitazoxanide was not significantly associated with adverse events. one trial, one stratum: the mortality contrast is 0 versus 4 deaths in 47 children, so it is fragile; the same trial's hiv-seropositive stratum (next card's programme) did not benefit. amadi b et al. effect of nitazoxanide on morbidity and mortality in zambian children with cryptosporidiosis: a randomised controlled trial. lancet (london, england). 2002. pmid: 12423984. registry id: none in the record. mesh: antiprotozoal agents · child, preschool · cryptosporidiosis · diarrhea · female · hiv seronegativity · hiv seropositivity · humans · infant · male · nitro compounds · nutritional status · thiazoles · treatment outcome · zambia

cards.headline: Zambian trial, HIV-SEROPOSITIVE stratum, and the high-dose prolonged trial (Amadi 2002; Amadi 2009): HIV-positive children did NOT benefit — in the dedicated trial, clinical response 42% vs 35% and eradication 27% vs 35%, with 31% mortality overall
cards.summary: Zambian trial, HIV-SEROPOSITIVE stratum, and the high-dose prolonged trial (Amadi 2002; Amadi 2009): HIV-positive children did NOT benefit — in the dedicated trial, clinical response 42% vs 35% and eradication 27% vs 35%, with 31% mortality overall
cards.type: Double-blind randomised placebo-controlled trial of high-dose prolonged nitazoxanide in HIV-POSITIVE children (the negative stratum/programme), read with the HIV-seropositive stratum of PMID 12423984
cards.people: Amadi 2002 randomised 50 HIV-seropositive children within the trial carded above. Amadi 2009 separately randomised 60 HIV-positive Zambian children aged 1–11 years (52 fully evaluated) to high-dose nitazoxanide suspension (200 mg twice daily for 28 days at ages 1–3; 400 mg twice daily at ages 4–11; only five children were 4 or older) or matching placebo.
cards.result: In the 2002 trial, HIV-seropositive children did not benefit from nitazoxanide (the record reports no significant benefit in that stratum). In the 2009 high-dose prolonged trial, a 'well' clinical response occurred in 11 of 26 (42%) on nitazoxanide versus 8 of 26 (35%) on placebo, and parasitological eradication in 27% versus 35% — no benefit, with eradication numerically favouring placebo. Mortality was 16 of 52 (31%) and did not differ by treatment allocation. The authors conclude this is the second randomised trial suggesting nitazoxanide does not eradicate the infection or reduce symptoms in Zambian children with HIV-related immunosuppression.
cards.watchOut: A higher dose and a 28-day course still failed in HIV-positive children — dose and duration do not rescue the HIV-positive result. Background severity is part of the face: 31% of evaluated children died.
cards.source: Amadi B et al. High dose prolonged treatment with nitazoxanide is not effective for cryptosporidiosis in HIV positive Zambian children: a randomised controlled trial. BMC infectious diseases. 2009. PMID: 19954529. Registry ID: ISRCTN41089957.
