cards.headline: Bangladeshi pilot trial (Noor 2025): no difference in infection duration or growth in any arm — nitazoxanide plus Lactobacillus reuteri, nitazoxanide plus placebo, or standard care (standard-care arm n=10, on the face)
cards.summary: Bangladeshi pilot trial (Noor 2025): no difference in infection duration or growth in any arm — nitazoxanide plus Lactobacillus reuteri, nitazoxanide plus placebo, or standard care (standard-care arm n=10, on the face)
cards.type: Pilot randomised clinical trial, nitazoxanide ± probiotic vs standard care (combination/pilot-structured limb)
cards.people: 64 undernourished Bangladeshi children positive for Cryptosporidium spp., with weight-for-length Z score between −1 and −3, randomised to nitazoxanide plus Lactobacillus reuteri DSM 17938 (n=26), nitazoxanide plus placebo (n=28), or standard care (n=10).
cards.result: There was no difference in the duration of infection or in improvement in child anthropometric measurements in any treatment group compared with control. The authors conclude the pilot does not support nitazoxanide, Lactobacillus, or the combination as an effective means of reducing Cryptosporidium infection duration or improving growth in growth-stunted children.
cards.watchOut: A pilot with a 10-child standard-care arm and combination-structured nitazoxanide arms — it cannot overturn the Zambian strata, and its null result is in undernourished children without the HIV stratification of the Zambian trials.
cards.source: Noor Z et al. Effect of Nitazoxanide and Probiotic Treatment on Bangladeshi Children with Cryptosporidiosis. The American journal of tropical medicine and hygiene. 2025. PMID: 39933176. cards.headline: Synthesis: the HIV split is the answer — benefit was confined to the HIV-seronegative stratum of one Zambian trial (resolution 56% vs 23%); HIV-positive children did not benefit in that trial or in a dedicated high-dose prolonged trial, and a 2025 Bangladeshi pilot was negative

cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf: three randomised reports in children — the stratified Zambian trial (100 recruited, 96 analysed), the HIV-positive high-dose prolonged trial (60 randomised, 52 evaluated), and the Bangladeshi pilot (64 randomised). The Cochrane cryptosporidiosis review retrieved in mining (immunocompromised populations, searches to 2005) is a cross-point, not a card, for this paediatric shelf.
cards.result: HIV-seronegative (Amadi 2002): diarrhoea resolution 56% versus 23%, eradication 52% versus 14%, deaths 0 versus 4 by day 8. HIV-seropositive: no benefit in the 2002 stratum, and no benefit from high-dose prolonged treatment in 2009 (clinical response 42% versus 35%; eradication 27% versus 35%; mortality 31% overall). Bangladeshi undernourished children (Noor 2025): no difference in infection duration or growth in any arm. Any shelf verdict that averages these strata into a single number would misstate the evidence.
cards.watchOut: Paediatric, low-income-setting programme throughout (Zambia, Bangladesh) — generalisability limits are stated, not implied away. See the individual cards; this synthesis adds no new data.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: IV cidofovir for CMV retinitis in AIDS (pre-HAART): progression delayed 120 vs 22 days in two trials of one programme — nephrotoxicity priced in probenecid and monitoring
shelves.question: In patients with AIDS and previously untreated peripheral cytomegalovirus retinitis, does immediate intravenous cidofovir versus deferred treatment delay retinitis progression, and what are its long-term outcomes and toxicities?
shelves.mesh: AIDS-Related Opportunistic Infections · Adolescent · Adult · Antiviral Agents · Cidofovir · Cytomegalovirus Retinitis · Cytosine · Disease Progression · Female · Humans · Infusions, Intravenous · Male · Middle Aged · Organophosphonates · Organophosphorus Compounds · Prospective Studies · Visual Acuity
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit, in its pre-HAART setting) — two distinct randomised immediate-versus-deferred trials in one programme family: median time to progression 120 vs 22 days (P<0.001; n=48) and, in the HPMPC trial (n=64), 64 days on low-dose maintenance (P=0.052) and not reached on high-dose maintenance (P=0.009) vs about 21 days deferred. The HPMPC long-term follow-up (58 patients) is a report OF the second trial, not a third trial: median progression 2.5 months, discontinuation for intolerance at a median 6.6 months. Toxicity leads the safety face: nephrotoxicity managed with probenecid and hydration in every report (treatment-limiting in 24% in the first trial; proteinuria at least 2+ at 1.22 per person-year in follow-up; probenecid intolerance 0.35 and uveitis 0.20 per person-year). ERA FLAG: pre-HAART care; deferred comparators must not be carried into modern practice.

cards.headline: Immediate vs deferred trial (Lalezari 1997): median time to retinitis progression 120 days on immediate cidofovir vs 22 days deferred (P<0.001)
cards.summary: Immediate vs deferred trial (Lalezari 1997): median time to retinitis progression 120 days on immediate cidofovir vs 22 days deferred (P<0.001)
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial, immediate vs deferred intravenous cidofovir (trial 1 of 2)
cards.people: 48 patients with AIDS and previously untreated peripheral cytomegalovirus retinitis at eight academic medical centres, randomised to immediate cidofovir (n=25) or deferred treatment (n=23); deferred patients could receive cidofovir after documented progression. Cidofovir was 5 mg/kg intravenously once weekly for 2 weeks, then once every other week, with oral probenecid and intravenous saline hydration to minimise nephrotoxicity; progression was read from retinal photographs by a masked ophthalmologist.
cards.result: Median time to progression was 22 days (95% CI 10 to 27) in the deferred group versus 120 days (95% CI 40 to 134) in the immediate group (P<0.001). Neutropenia (15%) and proteinuria (12%), both asymptomatic, were the most common serious adverse events possibly related to cidofovir. Treatment was discontinued in 10 of 41 treated patients (24%) for protocol-defined treatment-limiting nephrotoxicity. Transient probenecid reactions occurred in 23 of 41 (56%) and were dose-limiting in 3 (7%).
cards.watchOut: Pre-HAART era: a deferred-treatment comparator was ethical only in that era's context and must not be carried into modern practice. N=48 — small, and a quarter of treated patients stopped for nephrotoxicity.
cards.source: Lalezari JP et al. Intravenous cidofovir for peripheral cytomegalovirus retinitis in patients with AIDS. A randomized, controlled trial. Annals of internal medicine. 1997. PMID: 9036797. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: HPMPC trial (Studies of Ocular Complications of AIDS 1997): median time to progression 21 days deferred vs 64 days on low-dose maintenance (P=0.052) and not reached on high-dose maintenance (P=0.009)
cards.summary: HPMPC trial (Studies of Ocular Complications of AIDS 1997): median time to progression 21 days deferred vs 64 days on low-dose maintenance (P=0.052) and not reached on high-dose maintenance (P=0.009)
cards.type: Two-stage multicentre phase II/III randomised controlled trial (HPMPC; trial 2 of 2), deferral vs low-dose vs high-dose maintenance cidofovir
cards.people: 64 patients with AIDS and previously untreated, small, peripheral CMV retinitis lesions (low risk for loss of visual acuity), randomised to deferral, low-dose cidofovir (5 mg/kg weekly for 2 weeks, then 3 mg/kg every 2 weeks) or high-dose cidofovir (5 mg/kg weekly for 2 weeks, then 5 mg/kg every 2 weeks), with hydration and probenecid; progression was assessed masked by a fundus photograph reading centre.
cards.result: Median time to progression was 21 days on deferral versus 64 days on low-dose maintenance (P=0.052) and was not reached on high-dose maintenance (deferral median 20 days in that comparison; P=0.009); rates of increase in retinal area affected confirmed the time-to-progression data, and visual loss rates were similar across groups. Proteinuria of 2+ or more occurred at 2.6 per person-year (deferral), 2.8 per person-year (low-dose; P>0.02 as printed) and 6.8 per person-year (high-dose; P=0.135). No patient developed 4+ proteinuria, but two cidofovir recipients developed persistent serum creatinine elevations above 177 micromol/L (2.0 mg/dL). Probenecid reactions occurred at 0.70 per person-year.
cards.watchOut: The low-dose comparison missed conventional significance (P=0.052) — printed as such, not rounded into a win. Pre-HAART era and small, peripheral lesions only (patients at low risk of visual loss).
cards.source: Studies of Ocular Complications of AIDS Research Group in Collaboration with the AIDS Clinical Trials Group et al. cards.headline: HPMPC long-term follow-up (Studies of Ocular Complications of AIDS 2000): median time to progression 2.5 months; median time to discontinuation for intolerance 6.6 months; proteinuria at least 2+ at 1.22 per person-year — a follow-up report OF the HPMPC trial, not a third trial
cards.summary: HPMPC long-term follow-up (Studies of Ocular Complications of AIDS 2000): median time to progression 2.5 months; median time to discontinuation for intolerance 6.6 months; proteinuria at least 2+ at 1.22 per person-year — a follow-up report OF the HPMPC trial, not a third trial
cards.type: Long-term follow-up report of the HPMPC randomised trial (same trial as the previous card — not independent evidence)
cards.people: 58 patients with AIDS and small peripheral CMV retinitis lesions followed for long-term outcomes, including 21 patients initially in the deferral group who received cidofovir after progression; maintenance was low-dose (3 mg/kg, 35 patients) or high-dose (5 mg/kg, 23 patients) every 2 weeks after induction.
cards.result: Median time to progression of retinitis was 2.5 months. Median time to discontinuation of cidofovir because of intolerance was 6.6 months, and for intolerance other than probenecid reaction was 16.3 months on low-dose versus 5.0 months on high-dose maintenance (P=0.021). Proteinuria of 2+ or more occurred at 1.22 per person-year; in patients with sufficient follow-up, 89.9% of episodes resolved, with a median time to resolution of 20 days. Rates of probenecid intolerance and cidofovir-associated uveitis were 0.35 and 0.20 per person-year respectively.
cards.watchOut: Labelled as a follow-up report: it adds duration and toxicity information for the HPMPC trial, not a third trial. Toxicity typically resolved on discontinuation, but monitoring and probenecid/hydration co-therapy were integral to the programme.
cards.source: Studies of Ocular Complications of AIDS Research Group in collaboration with the AIDS Clinical Trials Group et al. cards.headline: Synthesis: two distinct randomised trials in one pre-HAART programme family — immediate cidofovir delayed progression (120 vs 22 days) and HPMPC high-dose maintenance delayed it significantly — priced in nephrotoxicity managed with probenecid and hydration; the third report is the HPMPC follow-up, not a third trial

cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf: two distinct 1997 randomised immediate-versus-deferred trials (n=48; n=64, the HPMPC trial) plus the HPMPC long-term follow-up (58 patients). One programme family (the Studies of Ocular Complications of AIDS / HPMPC programme) — that structure is stated, not disguised. Cross-point the foscarnet-versus-ganciclovir SOCA question (slate-13 row S13-2-15): same era and overlapping programme family, different drug and question — do not merge.
cards.result: Lalezari 1997: median progression 120 versus 22 days (P<0.001), with 24% of treated patients discontinuing for treatment-limiting nephrotoxicity. HPMPC 1997: 64 days on low-dose maintenance (P=0.052) and not reached on high-dose maintenance (P=0.009) versus about 21 days deferred. HPMPC follow-up 2000: median progression 2.5 months on treatment, median discontinuation for intolerance at 6.6 months, proteinuria at least 2+ at 1.22 per person-year, probenecid intolerance 0.35 and cidofovir-associated uveitis 0.20 per person-year. ERA FLAG (load-bearing): pre-HAART AIDS care — deferred-treatment comparators and this toxicity-management programme belong to that era and must not be carried into modern practice.

shelves.title: Aerosolised ribavirin in infant RSV (SPLIT, small old programme): positive in 1983/1991, negative in ventilated infants in 1994/1999; 2004 Cochrane non-significant — 2010 version withdrawn and fenced
shelves.question: In infants and young children hospitalised with RSV lower respiratory tract infection — spontaneously breathing and mechanically ventilated — does aerosolised ribavirin versus placebo improve illness severity, oxygenation, duration of ventilation, hospital stay and survival?
shelves.mesh: Aerosols · Antiviral Agents · Child, Preschool · Clinical Trials as Topic · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Infant · Infant, Newborn · Male · Random Allocation · Respiratory Syncytial Viruses · Respiratory Tract Infections · Respirovirus Infections · Ribavirin · Ribonucleosides
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the split leads, and this shelf must not be averaged into a benefit claim. The programme is small and old: every primary trial enrolled 28–41 infants. The two earliest trials were positive — spontaneously breathing infants improved faster on ribavirin (1983, n=33), and ventilated infants spent fewer days on ventilation (4.9 versus 9.9), oxygen and in hospital (1991, n=28). The two later ventilated-infant trials were NEGATIVE: no significant difference in ventilator, oxygen, ICU or hospital days in 1994 (n=41) or in 1999 (n=41 analysed). The cardable synthesis — the 2004 Cochrane version — found mortality of 5.8% on ribavirin versus 9.7% on placebo across 4 trials and 158 patients (odds ratio 0.58, 95% CI 0.18 to 1.85 — non-significant, wide intervals) and concluded the trials lack sufficient power. FENCE: the 2010 Cochrane update of this review (PMID 20464715) is typed WITHDRAWN and is fenced — it is named here only as fenced and is never carded. This is a pre-palivizumab/nirsevimab-era treatment question; aerosol administration carried occupational-exposure concerns and high cost in its era. It does not bear on the RSV prevention shelves.

cards.headline: First trial (Hall 1983, NEJM): aerosolised ribavirin improved severity scores, lower-respiratory signs and oxygen saturation in 33 hospitalised infants — a small early positive trial
cards.summary: First trial (Hall 1983, NEJM): aerosolised ribavirin improved severity scores, lower-respiratory signs and oxygen saturation in 33 hospitalised infants — a small early positive trial
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial, aerosolised ribavirin vs placebo in spontaneously breathing hospitalised infants
cards.people: 33 infants hospitalised with lower-respiratory-tract disease from respiratory syncytial virus, treated double-blind with ribavirin (16 infants) or placebo (17 infants) by continuous aerosol for three to six days.
cards.result: By the end of treatment, infants receiving ribavirin had significantly greater improvement in their overall score for severity of illness, in lower-respiratory-tract signs, and in arterial oxygen saturation. Viral shedding was diminished in the treated group compared with placebo. No side effects or toxicity were associated with the aerosol therapy, and RSV isolates obtained over the course of therapy showed no change in sensitivity to ribavirin.
cards.watchOut: 33 infants — small, and the earliest trial in a split programme: its positive result was not reproduced by the two later ventilated-infant trials carded below. Outcomes are severity scores and oxygen saturation, not ventilation or survival.

cards.headline: Ventilated-infant trial (Smith 1991, NEJM): ventilation 4.9 versus 9.9 days, oxygen 8.7 versus 13.5 days, hospital stay 13.3 versus 15.0 days — a small positive trial (n=28)
cards.summary: Ventilated-infant trial (Smith 1991, NEJM): ventilation 4.9 versus 9.9 days, oxygen 8.7 versus 13.5 days, hospital stay 13.3 versus 15.0 days — a small positive trial (n=28)
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial, aerosolised ribavirin vs placebo in mechanically ventilated infants
cards.people: 28 infants (mean age 1.4 months) receiving mechanical ventilation for respiratory failure caused by documented RSV infection, randomised double-blind to aerosolised ribavirin 20 mg/mL (14 infants) or placebo (14 infants); 7 infants had underlying diseases predisposing them to severe infection and 21 were previously normal.
cards.result: Mean duration of mechanical ventilation was 4.9 days on ribavirin versus 9.9 days on placebo (P=0.01); mean supplemental oxygen use was 8.7 versus 13.5 days (P=0.01); mean hospital stay was 13.3 versus 15.0 days (P=0.04). Among the 21 previously normal infants, hospital stay was 9.0 versus 15.3 days (P=0.005). The authors concluded aerosolised ribavirin decreases the duration of ventilation, oxygen treatment and hospital stay in ventilated infants with severe RSV infection.
cards.watchOut: 28 infants — the smallest trial on this shelf, and the most positive. Its result is directly contradicted by the two later ventilated-infant trials below (n=41 each); read all four primaries together, never this one alone.

cards.headline: Ventilated-children trial (Meert 1994): NO significant difference in ventilator days (6.4 vs 8.2), oxygen, ICU or hospital days — a negative trial (n=41)
cards.summary: Ventilated-children trial (Meert 1994): NO significant difference in ventilator days (6.4 vs 8.2), oxygen, ICU or hospital days — a negative trial (n=41)
cards.type: Prospective randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial, aerosolised ribavirin vs saline in mechanically ventilated children
cards.people: 41 children requiring mechanical ventilation for RSV lower-respiratory-tract disease in a paediatric intensive care unit, stratified by underlying disease and randomised double-blind to aerosolised ribavirin 20 mg/mL or saline for 18 hours a day for 5 days or until extubation.
cards.result: Ribavirin and placebo groups did not differ significantly in ventilator days (6.4 versus 8.2; P=0.5), oxygen days (10.8 versus 12.2; P=0.9), ICU days (7.9 versus 10.3; P=0.7) or hospital days (12.9 versus 16.2; P=0.6) after starting aerosol therapy, and the change in FiO2, ventilatory rate, PaO2/FiO2 ratio and ventilatory-efficiency index did not differ. Six deaths from intractable hypoxaemia occurred in children with underlying cardiopulmonary disease — four on placebo and two on ribavirin (P=0.5). No ventilator malfunction was observed. The authors concluded ribavirin could be given safely but did not appear to affect immediate clinical outcome.
cards.watchOut: Negative trial, and larger than the positive 1991 ventilated trial it contradicts. Standard deviations on the day counts are wide (for example ventilator days 6.4 ± 6.9 versus 8.2 ± 10.1), so the trial is also imprecise — but its point estimates do not reproduce the 1991 result.

cards.headline: Ventilated previously-well infants (Guerguerian 1999): NO significant difference in ventilation duration (102 vs 126 hours; P=0.29) or course of illness — a negative trial (41 analysed)
cards.summary: Ventilated previously-well infants (Guerguerian 1999): NO significant difference in ventilation duration (102 vs 126 hours; P=0.29) or course of illness — a negative trial (41 analysed)
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial, aerosol ribavirin vs saline in ventilated previously well infants
cards.people: Previously well infants ventilated for respiratory distress secondary to RSV bronchiolitis, randomised double-blind to aerosol ribavirin or 0.9% saline within 24 hours of starting ventilation, 18 hours a day for up to 7 days or until extubation (March 1994 to March 1997); 42 children were randomised and 41 were retained for analysis (20 ribavirin, 21 placebo).
cards.result: Intention-to-treat analysis found no significant differences in length of ventilation (102.16 versus 126.28 hours; P=0.29), aerosol therapy, ICU stay, total oxygen therapy or hospitalisation. The aerosols were well tolerated and no deaths occurred. The authors concluded the trial 'demonstrates the lack of effectiveness of aerosolized ribavirin in reducing the length of ventilation and course of illness' in previously well ventilated infants with RSV bronchiolitis.
cards.watchOut: Negative trial in the cleanest population (previously well infants, no underlying illness) — the subgroup in which the 1991 trial's subgroup analysis looked most favourable. Together with the 1994 trial, it is why this shelf is stamped SPLIT.

cards.headline: Cochrane synthesis 2004 (Ventre & Randolph): 12 trials, all in infants under 6 months — mortality 5.8% vs 9.7% (odds ratio 0.58, 95% CI 0.18 to 1.85, non-significant); the reviewers concluded the trials lack sufficient power

cards.type: Systematic review / meta-analysis (Cochrane 2004 version — the cardable synthesis; the 2010 update is withdrawn and fenced)
cards.people: The 2004 Cochrane review included 12 randomised trials of ribavirin versus placebo in infants and children with RSV lower-respiratory-tract infection; all trials enrolled infants below the age of six months. The mortality analysis covers 4 trials with 158 patients.
cards.result: Mortality was 5.8% on ribavirin versus 9.7% on placebo across 4 trials / 158 patients (odds ratio 0.58, 95% CI 0.18 to 1.85 — a relative measure, non-significant). Respiratory deterioration occurred in 7.1% versus 18.3% across 3 trials / 116 patients (odds ratio 0.37, 95% CI 0.12 to 1.18). In 3 studies with 104 ventilated patients, the weighted mean difference was 1.9 fewer hospital days (95% CI −4.6 to +0.9) and 1.8 fewer ventilation days (95% CI −3.4 to −0.2) with ribavirin. No significant differences in long-term pulmonary function or recurrent wheezing were found. The reviewers' conclusion: 'Trials of ribavirin for RSV lack sufficient power to provide reliable estimates of the effects.'
cards.watchOut: This is the 2004 version of the Cochrane review. The 2010 update of the same review (PMID 20464715) is typed WITHDRAWN and is FENCED — named on this shelf's Synthesis card only, and never carded. The pooled estimates rest on the same small trials carded above and inherit their split.

cards.result: Named as fenced, per the commissioning row: the 2010 Cochrane version of this review (PMID 20464715) is a WITHDRAWN record and is not carded anywhere on this shelf; the cardable synthesis is the 2004 version. On the primaries: ribavirin improved severity scores in spontaneously breathing infants (1983, n=33) and shortened ventilation in one small ventilated trial (1991, n=28), but the two later ventilated trials (1994, n=41; 1999, n=41 analysed) found no significant difference in ventilation, oxygen, ICU or hospital days. This is a pre-palivizumab/nirsevimab-era treatment question with occupational-exposure and cost concerns from its era; the RSV vaccine and nirsevimab prevention shelves are different questions and nothing here bears on them (one-home rule).

shelves.title: PCP primary prophylaxis in HIV (pre-HAART): regimens close on PCP, split on toxoplasmosis and toxicity — pentamidine protects the lung only, dapsone-pyrimethamine stopped for toxicity 42 vs 3
shelves.question: In HIV-infected patients with CD4 counts below 200–250/mm3 and no prior Pneumocystis pneumonia, do dapsone (± pyrimethamine) or aerosolised pentamidine, versus co-trimoxazole (trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole) or each other, prevent first episodes of Pneumocystis pneumonia and toxoplasmosis, and at what cost in toxicity and discontinuation?

shelves.balance: SPLIT — a trade-off, not a ranking, in pre-HAART HIV care (1993–1995; era flag load-bearing). For PCP the regimens were close: per-year rates 3% on co-trimoxazole, 5.6% on aerosolised pentamidine and 8.3% on dapsone + pyrimethamine (not significant); PRIO found 10 PCP cases per group (adjusted relative risk 1.13); intermittent co-trimoxazole beat dapsone-pyrimethamine head-to-head (0 of 104 evaluable vs 6.3%). The deciding split is toxoplasmosis versus toxicity: aerosolised pentamidine protects the lung only (toxoplasmosis adjusted relative risk 1.81 vs dapsone-pyrimethamine), while dapsone-pyrimethamine had by far the most toxicity discontinuations (42 vs 3 in PRIO). Open-label designs throughout.

cards.headline: Mallolas 1993 (three arms): 1-year PCP probability 5.3% overall — per-year rates 3% co-trimoxazole, 5.6% aerosolised pentamidine, 8.3% dapsone + pyrimethamine (P>0.05); moderate/severe side-effects 10, 1 and 9 patients
cards.summary: Mallolas 1993 (three arms): 1-year PCP probability 5.3% overall — per-year rates 3% co-trimoxazole, 5.6% aerosolised pentamidine, 8.3% dapsone + pyrimethamine (P>0.05); moderate/severe side-effects 10, 1 and 9 patients
cards.type: Open randomised three-arm trial — primary PCP prophylaxis (co-trimoxazole vs aerosolised pentamidine vs dapsone + pyrimethamine), pre-HAART era
cards.people: 331 HIV-infected patients with CD4 counts below 200 x 10(6)/l or AIDS, without prior PCP or cerebral toxoplasmosis, randomised to aerosolised pentamidine 300 mg every 4 weeks, co-trimoxazole 160/800 mg 3 days a week, or dapsone 100 mg plus pyrimethamine 25 mg weekly; mean follow-up 313 days.
cards.result: PCP developed in 16 patients; the estimated 1-year cumulative probability was 5.3%. Intention-to-treat PCP rates per year were 5.6% on pentamidine, 3% on co-trimoxazole and 8.3% on dapsone plus pyrimethamine (P>0.05). Moderate or severe side-effects occurred in 1 patient on pentamidine, 10 on co-trimoxazole and 9 on dapsone plus pyrimethamine (P<0.05), and the study drug was discontinued in 0, 10 and 6 patients respectively. Neither co-trimoxazole alone nor pyrimethamine combinations prevented first toxoplasmosis episodes among Toxoplasma-IgG-positive patients in this trial.
cards.watchOut: Open-label, 1993, pre-HAART: CD4-guided prophylaxis as then practised. The trial could detect differences larger than 15% with 90% certainty — 'not significantly worse' within that margin is the honest reading, not proven equivalence.

cards.headline: PRIO Study Group 1993: dapsone-pyrimethamine vs aerosolised pentamidine — PCP 10 patients per group (adjusted relative risk 1.13), but toxoplasmosis risk higher on pentamidine (adjusted RR 1.81) and discontinuations for toxicity 42 vs 3
cards.summary: PRIO Study Group 1993: dapsone-pyrimethamine vs aerosolised pentamidine — PCP 10 patients per group (adjusted relative risk 1.13), but toxoplasmosis risk higher on pentamidine (adjusted RR 1.81) and discontinuations for toxicity 42 vs 3
cards.type: Randomised trial (PRIO) — primary prophylaxis, dapsone-pyrimethamine vs aerosolised pentamidine, pre-HAART era
cards.people: 349 patients with symptomatic HIV infection, no history of PCP or symptomatic toxoplasmosis and CD4 counts below 200 per cubic millimetre, randomised to dapsone 50 mg/day plus pyrimethamine 50 mg/week (173) or aerosolised pentamidine 300 mg/month (176); median follow-up 539 days.
cards.result: PCP developed in 10 patients in each group (adjusted relative risk with pentamidine 1.13, 95% CI 0.44 to 2.92, P=0.79 — a relative measure). Toxoplasmosis developed in 32 of 176 on pentamidine versus 19 of 173 on dapsone-pyrimethamine (adjusted relative risk 1.81, 95% CI 1.12 to 2.94, P=0.02, relative); among the 262 Toxoplasma-seropositive patients the relative risk was 2.37 (95% CI 1.3 to 4.4). Discontinuation for toxicity: 42 on dapsone-pyrimethamine versus 3 on pentamidine (P<0.001). Survival was similar.
cards.watchOut: The toxoplasmosis limb is half the answer: aerosolised pentamidine protects the lung only and left patients exposed to toxoplasmic encephalitis, while the systemic regimen that prevented toxoplasmosis was also the regimen 42 patients had to stop for toxicity. Efficacy and tolerability point in opposite directions.
cards.source: Girard PM et al. Dapsone-pyrimethamine compared with aerosolized pentamidine as primary prophylaxis against Pneumocystis carinii pneumonia and toxoplasmosis in HIV infection. The PRIO Study Group. The New England journal of medicine. 1993. PMID: 8479488. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Torres 1993: intermittent dapsone vs aerosolised pentamidine — PCP failures 18% vs 14% (P=0.4); dapsone superior for primary toxoplasmosis prophylaxis (0 vs 6 events, P=0.01)
cards.summary: Torres 1993: intermittent dapsone vs aerosolised pentamidine — PCP failures 18% vs 14% (P=0.4); dapsone superior for primary toxoplasmosis prophylaxis (0 vs 6 events, P=0.01)
cards.type: Randomised trial — dapsone vs aerosolised pentamidine for PCP and toxoplasmic-encephalitis prophylaxis, pre-HAART era
cards.people: 278 HIV-seropositive patients with AIDS or advanced AIDS-related complex and CD4 counts below 250/mm3, randomly assigned to intermittent dapsone 100 mg twice weekly or aerosolised pentamidine 100 mg every 2 weeks; mean follow-up 42–44 weeks. The trial mixed primary and secondary PCP prophylaxis.
cards.result: PCP failures were 15 (18%) on dapsone versus 15 (14%) on aerosolised pentamidine (P=0.4) across primary and secondary prophylaxis combined. For primary prophylaxis of toxoplasmic encephalitis, dapsone was more effective: 0 events on dapsone versus 6 on pentamidine (P=0.01). Primary prophylaxis was more effective than secondary with either agent; survival did not differ between regimens, and zidovudine use was independently associated with improved survival.
cards.watchOut: Primary and secondary prophylaxis are pooled in the headline PCP failure rates — only the toxoplasmosis result is a primary-prophylaxis-specific reading. Pentamidine dose here (100 mg every 2 weeks) also differs from the 300 mg monthly schedule in the other cards.
cards.source: Torres RA et al. Randomized trial of dapsone and aerosolized pentamidine for the prophylaxis of Pneumocystis carinii pneumonia and toxoplasmic encephalitis. The American journal of medicine. 1993. PMID: 8018144. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Podzamczer 1995: intermittent co-trimoxazole vs dapsone-pyrimethamine — PCP in 0 of 104 evaluable patients on co-trimoxazole vs 6.3% on dapsone-pyrimethamine (P<0.0001)
cards.summary: Podzamczer 1995: intermittent co-trimoxazole vs dapsone-pyrimethamine — PCP in 0 of 104 evaluable patients on co-trimoxazole vs 6.3% on dapsone-pyrimethamine (P<0.0001)
cards.type: Nonblinded randomised trial — simultaneous primary prophylaxis of PCP and toxoplasmosis (intermittent co-trimoxazole vs dapsone-pyrimethamine), pre-HAART era
cards.people: 230 HIV-infected patients with CD4 counts below 200 x 10(6)/L and no prior PCP or toxoplasmosis, randomised to trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole 160/800 mg twice daily three times weekly or dapsone 100 mg plus pyrimethamine 50 mg twice weekly; median follow-up 430 days; 200 patients were evaluable for the PCP endpoint (104 and 96).
cards.result: PCP developed in 0 of 104 evaluable patients on co-trimoxazole versus 6 (6.3%) of 96 on dapsone-pyrimethamine (P<0.0001); cumulative PCP rates at 12 and 24 months were 0% and 0% versus 4% and 11% (P=0.014) — although only one episode developed while a patient was actually taking the assigned drug. Toxoplasmosis did not differ (1 vs 2 episodes). Mortality was similar, and discontinuations for adverse effects were similar (10 vs 9 patients).
cards.watchOut: Nonblinded, and the evaluable denominator (200 of 230 randomised) plus the fact that only one PCP episode occurred on-treatment mean the 0% figure should be read as 'no on-treatment failures observed', not as proof of absolute protection. Pre-HAART era throughout this shelf.

cards.result: Pre-HAART era (1993–1995) throughout — CD4-guided prophylaxis as then practised, before modern antiretroviral therapy. On PCP itself the regimens were close: three-arm rates per year 3% (co-trimoxazole), 5.6% (aerosolised pentamidine) and 8.3% (dapsone + pyrimethamine), not significant; PRIO found 10 PCP cases per group (adjusted relative risk 1.13); and the head-to-head intermittent trial found PCP in 0 of 104 evaluable patients on co-trimoxazole versus 6.3% on dapsone-pyrimethamine. The split that decides the shelf is toxoplasmosis and toxicity: aerosolised pentamidine protects the lung only (toxoplasmosis adjusted relative risk 1.81 versus dapsone-pyrimethamine; 0 vs 6 primary-prophylaxis events in Torres), while dapsone-pyrimethamine carried the most toxicity discontinuations (42 vs 3 in PRIO). The balance is a trade-off, not a ranking. Cross-point: pack #2966 homes when prophylaxis can stop after CD4 recovery — a different question, not re-carded here; shelf #7526 homes atovaquone prophylaxis in patients who cannot tolerate co-trimoxazole.

shelves.title: Atovaquone for PCP in AIDS: treatment — less effective than co-trimoxazole (non-response 20% vs 7%; deaths 11 vs 1) but gentler; prophylaxis in sulfa-intolerant patients — similar to dapsone and pentamidine
shelves.question: In patients with AIDS and mild-to-moderate Pneumocystis pneumonia, does oral atovaquone versus co-trimoxazole or intravenous pentamidine achieve treatment success — and in HIV-infected patients intolerant of trimethoprim/sulfonamides, does atovaquone versus dapsone or aerosolised pentamidine prevent Pneumocystis pneumonia?

shelves.balance: SPLIT — two limbs, never pooled, pre-/early-HAART era. Treatment (mild-to-moderate PCP only; no severe-PCP evidence): atovaquone was less effective than co-trimoxazole — non-response 20% vs 7% (P=0.002) and 11 vs 1 deaths within four weeks of treatment (P=0.003), the death split printed on the face — but had fewer treatment-limiting adverse effects (7% vs 20%); versus intravenous pentamidine the small trial split (success 57% vs 40%, non-response 29% vs 17%, discontinuations 4% vs 36%). Prophylaxis in sulfa-intolerant patients: atovaquone similar to dapsone (15.7 vs 18.4 per 100 person-years; relative risk 0.85) and to aerosolised pentamidine, at the 1500-mg suspension dose.

cards.headline: TREATMENT LIMB — Hughes 1993 vs co-trimoxazole: non-response 20% vs 7% (P=0.002) and deaths within 4 weeks of treatment 11 on atovaquone (4 due to PCP) vs 1 on co-trimoxazole (P=0.003) — printed on the face

cards.type: Double-blind multicentre randomised trial — TREATMENT limb (atovaquone vs co-trimoxazole, mild-to-moderate PCP in AIDS), pre-HAART era
cards.people: 322 patients with AIDS and histologically confirmed mild or moderately severe Pneumocystis carinii pneumonia, randomised double-blind to 21 days of oral atovaquone 750 mg three times daily (160; the trial's title gives atovaquone's development code, 566C80) or trimethoprim 320 mg plus sulfamethoxazole 1600 mg three times daily (162); 138 and 146 respectively were evaluable for therapeutic efficacy.
cards.result: Non-response: 28 of 138 (20%) on atovaquone versus 10 of 146 (7%) on co-trimoxazole (P=0.002). Treatment-limiting adverse effects forced a change of therapy in 7% versus 20% (P=0.001), and therapy with only the initial drug was successful and free of adverse effects in 62% versus 64%. Within four weeks of completing treatment there were 11 deaths on atovaquone (4 due to PCP) versus 1 on co-trimoxazole (P=0.003). In the atovaquone group, diarrhoea at entry was associated with lower plasma drug concentrations, therapeutic failure and death. The authors concluded atovaquone is less effective than co-trimoxazole but has fewer treatment-limiting adverse effects.
cards.watchOut: The 11-vs-1 death split belongs on the face of this shelf — it is the treatment limb's decisive fact. Mild-to-moderate disease only: there is no severe-PCP evidence for atovaquone. The authors' own caveat — diarrhoea at entry lowering atovaquone absorption, concentrations, response and survival — is part of the result, not an excuse that removes it.
cards.source: Hughes W et al. Comparison of atovaquone (566C80) with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole to treat Pneumocystis carinii pneumonia in patients with AIDS. The New England journal of medicine. 1993. PMID: 8479489. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: TREATMENT LIMB — Dohn 1994 vs intravenous pentamidine: success 57% vs 40% (difference 17%, 95% CI −3% to 38%), non-response 29% vs 17%, discontinuation for adverse events 4% vs 36% (P<0.001)
cards.summary: TREATMENT LIMB — Dohn 1994 vs intravenous pentamidine: success 57% vs 40% (difference 17%, 95% CI −3% to 38%), non-response 29% vs 17%, discontinuation for adverse events 4% vs 36% (P<0.001)
cards.type: Open-label multicentre randomised trial — TREATMENT limb (oral atovaquone vs intravenous pentamidine, mild/moderate PCP in AIDS), pre-HAART era
cards.people: 109 patients with AIDS and histologically confirmed mild or moderate Pneumocystis carinii pneumonia (56 atovaquone, 53 pentamidine), randomised to 21 days of open-label oral atovaquone 750 mg three times daily with meals or intravenous pentamidine 3–4 mg/kg once daily, with 8 weeks of post-treatment follow-up.
cards.result: Successful treatment: 57% on atovaquone versus 40% on pentamidine (difference 17%, 95% CI −3% to 38%; P=0.085 — the interval crosses zero). Non-response was nonetheless more frequent on atovaquone (29% vs 17%; difference 12%, 95% CI −6% to 29%). Discontinuation of the original therapy for treatment-limiting adverse events: 4% on atovaquone versus 36% on pentamidine (difference −32%, 95% CI −48% to −17%; P<0.001). Nine patients in each group died during the study.
cards.watchOut: Success and non-response point in opposite directions in the same small trial (109 patients) because discontinuations count differently in each — read both numbers, not either alone. Open-label, and again mild-to-moderate disease only.
cards.source: Dohn MN et al. Oral atovaquone compared with intravenous pentamidine for Pneumocystis carinii pneumonia in patients with AIDS. Atovaquone Study Group. Annals of internal medicine. 1994. PMID: 7880228. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: PROPHYLAXIS-IN-INTOLERANCE LIMB — El-Sadr 1998 vs dapsone in sulfa-intolerant patients: PCP 15.7 vs 18.4 cases per 100 person-years (relative risk 0.85, 95% CI 0.67 to 1.09)
cards.summary: PROPHYLAXIS-IN-INTOLERANCE LIMB — El-Sadr 1998 vs dapsone in sulfa-intolerant patients: PCP 15.7 vs 18.4 cases per 100 person-years (relative risk 0.85, 95% CI 0.67 to 1.09)
cards.type: Multicentre open-label randomised trial — PROPHYLAXIS limb in trimethoprim/sulfonamide-intolerant patients (atovaquone vs dapsone), pre-/early-HAART era
cards.people: 1,057 HIV-infected patients who could not tolerate trimethoprim, sulfonamides or both, randomised open-label to daily atovaquone 1500 mg suspension (536) or daily dapsone 100 mg (521); 298 had a prior history of PCP; median follow-up 27 months.
cards.result: PCP developed in 122 of 536 on atovaquone (15.7 cases per 100 person-years) versus 135 of 521 on dapsone (18.4 per 100 person-years): relative risk 0.85 (95% CI 0.67 to 1.09; P=0.20 — a relative measure, not significant). Relative risk of death was 1.07 (95% CI 0.89 to 1.30) and of discontinuation for adverse events 0.94 (95% CI 0.74 to 1.19) overall — but among patients already taking dapsone at baseline, switching to atovaquone raised discontinuation risk (relative risk 3.78), while among those not on dapsone atovaquone was better tolerated (relative risk 0.42).
cards.watchOut: This limb's population is defined by co-trimoxazole intolerance — it says nothing about patients who can take co-trimoxazole (that question is shelf #7525, and no trial is shared between the shelves). The baseline-dapsone subgroup split means 'similarly tolerated' is true only on average.
cards.source: El-Sadr WM et al. Atovaquone compared with dapsone for the prevention of Pneumocystis carinii pneumonia in patients with HIV infection who cannot tolerate trimethoprim, sulfonamides, or both. Community Program for Clinical Research on AIDS and the AIDS Clinical Trials Group. The New England journal of medicine. 1998. PMID: 9862944. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: PROPHYLAXIS-IN-INTOLERANCE LIMB — Chan 1999 vs aerosolised pentamidine: no significant difference in PCP incidence (26%, 22% and 17% across atovaquone 750 mg, atovaquone 1500 mg and pentamidine) or mortality; more treatment-limiting adverse events on atovaquone
cards.summary: PROPHYLAXIS-IN-INTOLERANCE LIMB — Chan 1999 vs aerosolised pentamidine: no significant difference in PCP incidence (26%, 22% and 17% across atovaquone 750 mg, atovaquone 1500 mg and pentamidine) or mortality; more treatment-limiting adverse events on atovaquone
cards.type: Randomised trial — PROPHYLAXIS limb in trimethoprim/sulfonamide-intolerant patients (atovaquone suspension, two doses, vs aerosolised pentamidine), pre-/early-HAART era
cards.people: 549 HIV-infected subjects intolerant of trimethoprim or sulfonamides (or both), in an intention-to-treat analysis of atovaquone suspension 750 mg once daily, atovaquone 1500 mg once daily, or aerosolised pentamidine 300 mg once monthly; median time on assigned therapy 6.6 months, median follow-up 11.3 months.
cards.result: No statistically significant differences in PCP incidence (26%, 22% and 17% respectively) or mortality (20%, 13% and 18%). Treatment-limiting adverse events were significantly more frequent with atovaquone (P<.01), though time on therapy did not differ significantly. PCP and death incidences were higher on atovaquone 750 mg than on 1500 mg; the authors concluded atovaquone suspension 1500 mg once daily has efficacy similar to aerosolised pentamidine in this intolerant population.
cards.watchOut: The 750-mg atovaquone arm ran numerically worst on both PCP and death — dose matters, and the shelf's prophylaxis reading rests on the 1500-mg suspension. Intolerance-defined population only, as with the El-Sadr card.
cards.source: Chan C et al. Atovaquone suspension compared with aerosolized pentamidine for prevention of Pneumocystis carinii pneumonia in human immunodeficiency virus-infected subjects intolerant of trimethoprim or sulfonamides. The Journal of infectious diseases. 1999. PMID: 10395851. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis
cards.summary: Synthesis
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: Two limbs, labelled, never pooled — and an era flag (pre-/early-HAART AIDS care) over both. Treatment of mild-to-moderate PCP: atovaquone was LESS effective than co-trimoxazole (non-response 20% vs 7%; deaths 11 vs 1 within four weeks of treatment, 4 of the 11 due to PCP) though with fewer treatment-limiting adverse effects (7% vs 20%); against intravenous pentamidine, success and tolerability favoured atovaquone while non-response favoured pentamidine, in a 109-patient trial. There is no severe-PCP evidence. Prophylaxis in patients intolerant of trimethoprim/sulfonamides: atovaquone was similar to dapsone (relative risk 0.85, 95% CI 0.67 to 1.09, relative) and to aerosolised pentamidine (no significant difference), with the 1500-mg suspension the supported dose. Formulations as published: the 1993 treatment trial used the 750 mg tablet three times daily (development code 566C80, as its title gives it); the prophylaxis trials used the suspension. Cross-point: shelf #7525 homes primary prophylaxis in patients who CAN take co-trimoxazole — the shared comparator trials are not re-carded there or here.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards for each report's limits; this synthesis adds no new data.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Intravitreal fomivirsen for CMV retinitis in AIDS (one programme, three reports): immediate treatment delayed progression 71 vs 13 days in a 28-patient trial; schedules did not differ; drug since withdrawn
shelves.question: In patients with AIDS and cytomegalovirus retinitis, does intravitreal fomivirsen versus deferred treatment delay retinitis progression in newly diagnosed peripheral disease, do dosing schedules differ in reactivated or persistently active disease, and what are its ocular toxicities?
shelves.mesh: AIDS-Related Opportunistic Infections/drug therapy,pathology · Adult · Antiviral Agents/administration & dosage,therapeutic use · Cytomegalovirus Retinitis/drug therapy,pathology · Disease Progression · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Injections · Male · Ophthalmic Solutions · Prospective Studies · Thionucleotides/administration & dosage,therapeutic use · Treatment Outcome · Vitreous Body
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one programme, labelled: three reports of a single development programme (Vitravene), not independent trials. Immediate fomivirsen delayed progression versus deferred treatment in newly diagnosed peripheral CMV retinitis (median 71 vs 13 days, P=.0001) but in only 28 patients; in reactivated/persistently active disease a more-intense schedule did not beat a less-intense one (106 vs 267 days, P=.2179). Pooled safety (150 patients): ocular adverse events dose- and schedule-dependent (4.06–8.35 events/patient-year), chiefly anterior-chamber inflammation and raised intraocular pressure. Era flag load-bearing: pre-/early-HAART AIDS care; fomivirsen has since been withdrawn from the market.

cards.headline: Vitravene programme, newly diagnosed limb: immediate vs DEFERRED fomivirsen — median time to first progression 71 days vs 13 days (P=.0001); n=28, printed on the face
cards.summary: Vitravene programme, newly diagnosed limb: immediate vs DEFERRED fomivirsen — median time to first progression 71 days vs 13 days (P=.0001); n=28, printed on the face
cards.type: Randomised immediate-vs-deferred treatment trial (Vitravene Study Group) — newly diagnosed peripheral CMV retinitis limb, pre-/early-HAART era
cards.people: 28 patients with AIDS and newly diagnosed peripheral cytomegalovirus retinitis (lesions at least 750 micrometres outside zone 1): 18 randomised to immediate intravitreous fomivirsen sodium 165 µg (weekly for three induction doses, then every other week as maintenance) and 10 to deferral of treatment until lesions progressed; deferred patients were offered fomivirsen at progression. N=28 — a small trial, printed on the face.
cards.result: Median time to first progression was 71 days (95% CI 28 days to not determinable) on immediate fomivirsen versus 13 days (95% CI 9 to 15 days) on deferral (P=.0001). Progression occurred in 44% of the immediate group versus 70% of the deferred group during the study. There were no retinal detachments among fomivirsen-treated eyes. Time to progression was assessed by two independent masked fundus-photography reading centres and by clinician investigators.
cards.watchOut: The comparator is deferred treatment, not another antiviral — this shows fomivirsen delays progression versus waiting, in 28 patients, in pre-/early-HAART AIDS care. Fomivirsen has since been withdrawn from the market; the withdrawal and the era belong on the face of this shelf.
cards.source: Vitravene Study Group A randomized controlled clinical trial of intravitreous fomivirsen for treatment of newly diagnosed peripheral cytomegalovirus retinitis in patients with AIDS. American journal of ophthalmology. 2002. PMID: 11931780. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Programme report (pooled, labelled): two randomised dose-comparison trials in reactivated / persistently active retinitis — more-intense vs less-intense 330 µg schedules; median time to progression 106 vs 267 days in the USA/Brazilian trial (P=.2179, not significant)
cards.summary: Programme report (pooled, labelled): two randomised dose-comparison trials in reactivated / persistently active retinitis — more-intense vs less-intense 330 µg schedules; median time to progression 106 vs 267 days in the USA/Brazilian trial (P=.2179, not significant)
cards.type: Programme report: pooled report of TWO randomised dose-comparison trials (Vitravene Study Group) — reactivated / persistently active CMV retinitis limb, same programme as the card above, not independent evidence
cards.people: 93 patients with AIDS whose CMV retinitis had reactivated or remained persistently active despite other therapies, across two multicentre randomised trials (USA/Brazilian and EuroCanadian): 61 patients (67 eyes) on the more-intense schedule (three weekly 330 µg induction injections, then every 2 weeks) and 32 (39 eyes) on the less-intense schedule (injections on days 1 and 15, then every 4 weeks). This report POOLS the programme's two dose-comparison trials — it is one report of the same programme, not two independent confirmations.
cards.result: In the USA/Brazilian trial, median time to progression was 106 days on the more-intense schedule versus 267 days on the less-intense schedule (P=.2179 — not significant, and numerically favouring the less-intense schedule). In the EuroCanadian trial, median time to progression was not determinable for the more-intense schedule (25th percentile 91 days) and was 403 days for the less-intense schedule. In the USA/Brazilian trial, lesion activity decreased in 80% of patients and became inactive in 55% during therapy. The authors concluded both regimens can be effective and the less-intense regimen may be preferable for convenience and safety.
cards.watchOut: No untreated or standard-therapy comparator — this is a schedule comparison inside one programme, and the more-intense schedule did not win. Labelled as a programme report so the shelf is not read as three independent trials.

cards.type: Programme report: pooled safety report of the programme's three randomised trials plus expanded access (Vitravene Study Group) — not independent evidence
cards.people: 150 patients in the pooled safety population: 30 patients (35 eyes) at 165 µg per injection and 120 patients (153 eyes) at 330 µg per injection, drawn from the programme's three randomised trials plus an expanded-access programme. A pooled report of the same programme — not independent evidence.
cards.result: Ocular adverse-event incidence was dose- and schedule-dependent: 4.06 events/patient-year at 165 µg, and at 330 µg 6.58 events/patient-year on the less-intense regimen versus 8.35 on the more-intense regimen. The most frequently reported events were anterior-chamber inflammation and increased intraocular pressure; there was no evidence that the proportion of patients with events rose with the number of injections, and the authors concluded the events could be managed successfully with medical therapy.
cards.watchOut: A safety pool of the same trials carded above, plus expanded access — it prices the programme's ocular toxicity; it adds no efficacy evidence and must never be counted as a third trial.

cards.headline: Synthesis
cards.summary: Synthesis
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: One programme, labelled as one programme: three reports of the Vitravene (fomivirsen) development programme, not three independent trials. The only placebo-style contrast is immediate versus deferred treatment in newly diagnosed peripheral CMV retinitis — median time to progression 71 versus 13 days (P=.0001) in just 28 patients. In reactivated or persistently active disease, a more-intense 330 µg schedule did not beat a less-intense one (106 vs 267 days, P=.2179, in the USA/Brazilian trial). Pooled safety: ocular adverse events were dose- and schedule-dependent (4.06–8.35 events/patient-year), led by anterior-chamber inflammation and raised intraocular pressure. Era flag, load-bearing: pre-/early-HAART AIDS care, a deferred-treatment comparator, and an intravitreal antisense therapy — fomivirsen sodium, the first antisense oligonucleotide, as the publications give it — that has since been withdrawn from the market.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards for each report's limits; this synthesis adds no new data.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: NEWS/NEWS2 discrimination for 24-hour death, arrest or ICU admission: AUROCs 0.72–0.89, best or joint-best in 120 of 123 diagnostic groups, confirmed in an independent Finnish cohort
shelves.question: On general wards and in acute medical admissions, how well does the National Early Warning Score (NEWS, and its NEWS2 revision) discriminate patients who will die, suffer cardiac arrest or need unanticipated intensive-care admission within 24 hours, how does it compare with other early warning scores, and does its performance hold across diagnostic groups and in COVID-19?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Early Diagnosis · Female · Heart Arrest · Hospital Mortality · Humans · Intensive Care Units · Male · Patient Admission · ROC Curve · Risk Assessment · Severity of Illness Index · United Kingdom · Vital Signs
shelves.balance: LIKELY (predictive) — a predictive-performance balance, not a treatment effect. NEWS discriminated patients who would die, arrest or need unanticipated ICU admission within 24 hours with AUROCs of 0.894 (death), 0.857 (ICU admission), 0.722 (cardiac arrest) and 0.873 (combined) in the original database study, above all 33 comparator scores; NEWS2 was best or joint-best in 120 of 123 diagnostic groups against 36 other scores; and the independent Finnish prospective ward cohort (18,889 patients) found AUROC 0.91 for 1-day mortality but only 0.75 for 30-day mortality, with respiratory rate the strongest single component. Performance held in COVID-19 (AUROC 0.882, within the 0.842–0.894 range of the control cohorts). Three of the four reports share the Smith group's Portsmouth database lineage and are labelled as one data programme; the Finnish cohort is the independent limb. No report here shows that using the score changes outcomes.

cards.headline: Smith-group database report (Smith 2013): in 35,585 consecutive acute medical admissions (198,755 observation sets), NEWS discriminated 24-hour outcomes with AUROCs of 0.722 for cardiac arrest, 0.857 for unanticipated ICU admission and 0.894 for death — above all 33 comparator early warning scores
cards.summary: Smith-group database report (Smith 2013): in 35,585 consecutive acute medical admissions (198,755 observation sets), NEWS discriminated 24-hour outcomes with AUROCs of 0.722 for cardiac arrest, 0.857 for unanticipated ICU admission and 0.894 for death — above all 33 comparator early warning scores
cards.type: Retrospective database discrimination study (Smith group, Portsmouth vital-signs database), NEWS vs 33 other early warning scores for 24-hour cardiac arrest / ICU admission / death — Smith-group database limb
cards.people: 35,585 consecutive, completed acute medical admissions contributing 198,755 vital-signs observation sets to a large vital-signs database. The ability of the National Early Warning Score to discriminate patients at risk of cardiac arrest, unanticipated intensive care unit admission or death within 24 hours of a NEWS value was tested with the area under the receiver-operating characteristic curve (AUROC) and compared with 33 other early warning scores in use. This report is from the Smith group's Portsmouth vital-signs database programme — the same database lineage as two other cards on this shelf, labelled there.
cards.result: The AUROCs (95% CI) for NEWS were 0.722 (0.685 to 0.759) for cardiac arrest, 0.857 (0.847 to 0.868) for unanticipated ICU admission, 0.894 (0.887 to 0.902) for death, and 0.873 (0.866 to 0.879) for any of the outcomes, all within 24 hours. The corresponding ranges for the other 33 scores were 0.611 to 0.710 (cardiac arrest), 0.570 to 0.827 (unanticipated ICU admission), 0.813 to 0.858 (death) and 0.736 to 0.834 (any outcome) — NEWS had a greater ability to discriminate the combined outcome than all 33 comparators.
cards.watchOut: Discrimination is not outcome improvement: this study shows the score ranks patients by risk, not that computing it changes what happens to them. Observation sets, not patients, are the unit of analysis (198,755 sets from 35,585 admissions), and performance in a single database lineage may not transfer. No registry ID is in the PubMed record.

cards.headline: Smith-group database report (Price 2023): across 123 diagnostic groups, NEWS2 performed best or joint-best in 120 groups against 36 other early warning scores, and where it was outperformed the difference was marginal
cards.summary: Smith-group database report (Price 2023): across 123 diagnostic groups, NEWS2 performed best or joint-best in 120 groups against 36 other early warning scores, and where it was outperformed the difference was marginal
cards.type: Retrospective database evaluation across 123 diagnostic groups (Smith group), NEWS/NEWS2 vs 36 other early warning scores — Smith-group database limb
cards.people: 123 patient groups defined by diagnosis, evaluated through AUROC analysis comparing the National Early Warning Score / NEWS2 against 36 other early warning scores for their ability to discriminate death, ICU admission, or the combined outcome within 24 hours of an observation set. From the same Smith-group database programme as the 2013 card above — labelled as a related report of one data programme, not an independent cohort.
cards.result: NEWS2 performed either best or joint best within 120 of the 123 patient groups evaluated, and was only outperformed in prediction of unanticipated ICU admission. In the remaining 3 patient groups where other scores outperformed it, the performance difference was marginal. The authors concluded that consistently high performance indicates NEWS is a suitable early warning score for all diagnostic groups considered, and that patients are not disadvantaged by its use compared with any of the other evaluated scores.
cards.watchOut: This report shares the Smith group's vital-signs database lineage with the 2013 and 2021 cards on this shelf — three reports, substantially one data programme, and they must not be counted as three independent validations. The abstract does not print group-level AUROC values, so none are claimed here. No registry ID is in the PubMed record.

cards.headline: INDEPENDENT limb — Finnish prospective validation (Loisa 2022): in 18,889 general-ward patients at three centres, NEWS discriminated 1-day mortality with AUROC 0.91 and 30-day mortality with AUROC 0.75; the respiratory-rate component (0.78) was the strongest single subcomponent
cards.summary: INDEPENDENT limb — Finnish prospective validation (Loisa 2022): in 18,889 general-ward patients at three centres, NEWS discriminated 1-day mortality with AUROC 0.91 and 30-day mortality with AUROC 0.75; the respiratory-rate component (0.78) was the strongest single subcomponent
cards.type: Prospective three-centre observational validation (Finland), NEWS and its subcomponents for short-term mortality on general wards — independent limb
cards.people: All 19,001 adult patients admitted to 45 general wards at one university hospital and two regional hospitals in Finland over one year, in a prospective three-centre observational study using first measured vital-sign datasets collected during routine care; after excluding 102 patients (0.53%) with some vital signs missing, the final cohort was 18,889 patients. Median age 70 years, 51% men, 31% admitted for a surgical reason. One-day mortality was 0.36% and 30-day mortality 3.9%. This cohort is independent of the Smith-group database.
cards.result: NEWS discriminated 1-day non-survivors with excellent accuracy (AUROC 0.91, 95% CI 0.87 to 0.95) and 30-day mortality with acceptable accuracy (AUROC 0.75, 95% CI 0.73 to 0.77). The respiratory-rate component discriminated 1-day non-survivors better (AUROC 0.78, 0.72 to 0.84) than the oxygen saturation (0.66), systolic blood pressure (0.65) and heart rate (0.67) subcomponents (P<0.01 in all comparisons). As with the total score, the individual components' performance decreased substantially for 30-day mortality.
cards.watchOut: The headline AUROC of 0.91 is for 1-day mortality, an outcome with a prevalence of only 0.36% — discrimination this high alongside so few events still leaves most high scores as false alarms in absolute terms, and performance for 30-day mortality (0.75) is materially weaker. Only the first vital-sign set per patient was used.

cards.headline: Smith-group database report (Kostakis 2021): NEWS/NEWS2 discrimination for death or ICU admission within 24 hours was similar across five cohorts — AUROC 0.882 in COVID-19-positive patients (n=405) and 0.842–0.894 in the non-COVID and 2018/2019 control cohorts — supporting no COVID-specific amendment
cards.summary: Smith-group database report (Kostakis 2021): NEWS/NEWS2 discrimination for death or ICU admission within 24 hours was similar across five cohorts — AUROC 0.882 in COVID-19-positive patients (n=405) and 0.842–0.894 in the non-COVID and 2018/2019 control cohorts — supporting no COVID-specific amendment
cards.type: Retrospective database evaluation in COVID-19 and control cohorts (Smith group), NEWS/NEWS2 for 24-hour death or ICU admission — Smith-group database limb
cards.people: Five cohorts drawn from the Smith group's database programme (labelled, same lineage as the 2013 and 2023 cards): COVID-19 POSITIVE (n=405), COVID-19 NOT DETECTED (n=1,716), COVID-19 NOT TESTED (n=2,686), CONTROL 2018 (n=6,273) and CONTROL 2019 (n=6,523). The outcome was the combination of death or intensive care unit admission within 24 hours of a vital-sign set, assessed by AUROC for NEWS or NEWS2.
cards.result: AUROC values for NEWS or NEWS2 for the combined outcome were: COVID-19 POSITIVE 0.882 (95% CI 0.868 to 0.895); COVID-19 NOT DETECTED 0.875 (0.861 to 0.89); COVID-19 NOT TESTED 0.876 (0.85 to 0.902); CONTROL 2018 0.894 (0.884 to 0.904); CONTROL 2019 0.842 (0.829 to 0.855). Performance was good and similar in all five cohorts (range 0.842 to 0.894), leading the authors to conclude that amendments to NEWS or NEWS2 — new covariates or changed weightings — are unnecessary when evaluating patients with COVID-19.
cards.watchOut: The COVID-19-positive cohort is small (405 patients) beside the control cohorts, and NEWS and NEWS2 are reported together rather than separately in the abstract, so this card cannot separate the two versions' performance. Same database lineage as the other two Smith-group cards — labelled, not independent. No registry ID is in the PubMed record.

cards.headline: Synthesis: NEWS and NEWS2 discriminate 24-hour deterioration well — AUROCs 0.722 (cardiac arrest), 0.857 (unanticipated ICU admission) and 0.894 (death) in the original Smith-group database study, best or joint-best in 120 of 123 diagnostic groups against 36 comparators, and AUROC 0.91 for 1-day mortality in the one independent prospective cohort (Finland, 18,889 patients), with similar performance in COVID-19 (0.882) — three of the four reports share one database lineage, labelled on their cards, and none of this shows that using the score improves outcomes

shelves.title: ROX index for HFNC failure: AUROC 0.68→0.76 over 12 h in pneumonia (≥4.88 = success), but only 0.57–0.61 at 2 h in COVID-19 validations
shelves.question: In adults with acute hypoxaemic respiratory failure treated with high-flow nasal cannula (HFNC), how well does the ROX index (oxygen saturation / inspired oxygen fraction divided by respiratory rate), measured at 2, 6 and 12 hours, predict HFNC failure (intubation) — what cut-offs separate success from failure at each time point, and does the index hold up in external validation, including in COVID-19 pneumonia and emergency-department cohorts?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Blood Gas Analysis · Catheterization · Cohort Studies · Data Accuracy · Diagnostic Techniques and Procedures · Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Noninvasive Ventilation · Oxygen Inhalation Therapy · Pneumonia · Practice Guidelines as Topic · Prospective Studies · Respiratory Rate · Adult · Oxygen · Cannula · Oxygen Saturation · Retrospective Studies · COVID-19 · Respiratory Insufficiency
shelves.balance: PREDICTIVE PERFORMANCE — time-point- and population-dependent. In the pre-COVID pneumonia derivation/validation cohort, the ROX index (SpO2/FiO2 divided by respiratory rate) discriminated modestly and better with time: AUROC 0.679 at 2 hours, 0.703 at 6 hours and 0.759 at 12 hours, with ROX ≥4.88 at any of those points associated with a lower risk of intubation and failure cut-offs of <2.85, <3.47 and <3.85 respectively. The two COVID-19 validations are materially weaker early: in 300 Japanese patients ROX AUROC was 0.57 at 2 hours, rising to 0.75 only at 48 hours; and in 173 Thai emergency-department patients the plain SpO2/FiO2 ratio (AUROC 0.651) discriminated better than ROX (0.612) at 2 hours. Cut-offs are time-point-specific and are never a single number. This is a prognostic-accuracy shelf: no randomised ROX-guided strategy trial is carded, and no card claims that acting on a ROX threshold improves outcomes. Two of the three reports are COVID-19 cohorts; the pre-COVID pneumonia cohort is the generalisable limb.

cards.headline: Derivation/validation (Roca 2019): ROX discrimination rose with time — AUROC 0.679 at 2 h, 0.703 at 6 h, 0.759 at 12 h; ROX ≥4.88 at any point marked lower intubation risk, with failure cut-offs <2.85, <3.47 and <3.85
cards.summary: Derivation/validation (Roca 2019): ROX discrimination rose with time — AUROC 0.679 at 2 h, 0.703 at 6 h, 0.759 at 12 h; ROX ≥4.88 at any point marked lower intubation risk, with failure cut-offs <2.85, <3.47 and <3.85
cards.type: Multicentre prospective cohort — derivation and validation of the ROX index (pneumonia, pre-COVID)
cards.people: Multicentre prospective observational cohort of patients with pneumonia and acute hypoxaemic respiratory failure treated with high-flow nasal cannula (HFNC) over 2 years; in the 191-patient validation cohort, 68 patients (35.6%) required intubation.
cards.result: The prediction accuracy of the ROX index (oxygen saturation by pulse oximetry / FiO2, divided by respiratory rate) increased over time: AUROC 0.679 at 2 hours, 0.703 at 6 hours and 0.759 at 12 hours after HFNC initiation. ROX ≥4.88 measured at 2, 6 or 12 hours was consistently associated with a lower risk of intubation (hazard ratios 0.434, 95% CI 0.264 to 0.715; 0.304, 95% CI 0.182 to 0.509; and 0.291, 95% CI 0.161 to 0.524 respectively — relative measures, printed beside the cohort's 35.6% intubation rate). ROX below 2.85 at 2 hours, below 3.47 at 6 hours and below 3.85 at 12 hours predicted HFNC failure. Of the index's components, the SpO2/FiO2 ratio carried greater weight than respiratory rate.
cards.watchOut: A pneumonia cohort from before COVID-19: its early (2-hour) discrimination was already modest (AUROC 0.679), and the COVID-19 validations below are weaker still at 2 hours — the ≥4.88 threshold is a 2/6/12-hour rule, not a single early reading.
cards.source: Roca O et al. An Index Combining Respiratory Rate and Oxygenation to Predict Outcome of Nasal High-Flow Therapy. American journal of respiratory and critical care medicine. 2019. PMID: 30576221. Registry ID: NCT02845128. cards.headline: COVID-19 external validation, Japan (Okano 2024): ROX AUROC only 0.57 at 2 hours in 300 patients, rising to 0.75 at 48 hours; at the published <2.85 cut-off, 2-hour sensitivity was 3% with 100% specificity
cards.summary: COVID-19 external validation, Japan (Okano 2024): ROX AUROC only 0.57 at 2 hours in 300 patients, rising to 0.75 at 48 hours; at the published <2.85 cut-off, 2-hour sensitivity was 3% with 100% specificity
cards.type: Multicentre retrospective external validation (COVID-19 pneumonia, Japan) — ROX index and HACOR score
cards.people: 300 adults (median age 60 years) with COVID-19 pneumonia treated with HFNC at nine Japanese institutions, January 2020 to March 2022 (retrospective multicentre study); treatment failure — intubation or death within 7 days — occurred in 127 patients (42%). The comparator HACOR score was validated alongside ROX. This record carries no MeSH terms (see source line).
cards.result: At the primary 2-hour time point, ROX AUROC was 0.57 and HACOR 0.63 (P = 0.24) — the authors judged 2-hour predictive performance potentially inadequate. ROX AUROC rose with time: 0.62 at 6 hours, 0.68 at 12 hours, 0.69 at 24 hours and 0.75 at 48 hours (HACOR 0.58, 0.70, 0.68 and 0.75 at the same points). At the previously reported 2-hour cut-offs, sensitivity and specificity were 3% and 100% for ROX <2.85, and 18% and 91% for HACOR >5. Visual calibration assessment found the HACOR score well calibrated but not the ROX index.
cards.watchOut: Retrospective, COVID-19-only, and its failure outcome includes death within 7 days as well as intubation — a broader outcome than the derivation cohort's intubation endpoint; the 2-hour ROX performance here (0.57) is close to chance.
cards.source: Okano H et al. cards.headline: COVID-19 emergency-department validation, Thailand (Ruangsomboon 2023): at 2 hours the plain SpO2/FiO2 ratio (AUROC 0.651) discriminated better than ROX (0.612) and modified ROX (0.606) in 173 patients
cards.summary: COVID-19 emergency-department validation, Thailand (Ruangsomboon 2023): at 2 hours the plain SpO2/FiO2 ratio (AUROC 0.651) discriminated better than ROX (0.612) and modified ROX (0.606) in 173 patients
cards.type: Multicentre retrospective validation (COVID-19, emergency department) — SF ratio vs ROX vs modified ROX
cards.people: 173 adults with COVID-19 treated with HFNC in five Thai emergency departments, January to December 2021 (multicentre retrospective study); HFNC success — no mechanical ventilation required at HFNC termination — occurred in 55 patients (31.8%). The SpO2/FiO2 (SF) ratio, the ROX index and the modified ROX index (ROX divided by heart rate) were recorded at 0 and 2 hours.
cards.result: The 2-hour SF ratio had the highest discrimination (AUROC 0.651, 95% CI 0.558 to 0.744), ahead of the 2-hour ROX index (0.612) and modified ROX index (0.606), and also had the best calibration and overall model performance. At its optimal cut-point of 128.19, the SF ratio gave a sensitivity of 65.3% and specificity of 61.8%; an SF ratio ≥128.19 at 2 hours was independently associated with HFNC success (adjusted odds ratio 0.29 for failure, 95% CI 0.13 to 0.65; P = 0.003 — a relative measure).
cards.watchOut: Retrospective ED cohort in COVID-19 only, with success defined at HFNC termination rather than a fixed horizon: it questions ROX's added value over its own SpO2/FiO2 component in this setting, not ROX's performance in the derivation population.
cards.source: Ruangsomboon O et al. Ratio of Oxygen Saturation to Inspired Oxygen, ROX Index, Modified ROX Index to Predict High Flow Cannula Success in COVID-19 Patients: Multicenter Validation Study. The western journal of emergency medicine. 2023. PMID: 37278775. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: ROX predicts HFNC failure modestly and increasingly with time in pneumonia (AUROC 0.759 by 12 h), but its early discrimination in COVID-19 validations was weak (0.57–0.61 at 2 h) — and at 2 hours in the ED its own SpO2/FiO2 component did better
cards.summary: Synthesis: ROX predicts HFNC failure modestly and increasingly with time in pneumonia (AUROC 0.759 by 12 h), but its early discrimination in COVID-19 validations was weak (0.57–0.61 at 2 h) — and at 2 hours in the ED its own SpO2/FiO2 component did better
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: The derivation cohort (Roca 2019, pneumonia, pre-COVID) set time-point-specific cut-offs — success at ROX ≥4.88, failure below 2.85 / 3.47 / 3.85 at 2 / 6 / 12 hours — with discrimination rising from 0.679 to 0.759 over 12 hours. Both COVID-19 external validations found materially weaker early performance: AUROC 0.57 at 2 hours rising to 0.75 at 48 hours in Japan (Okano 2024), and 0.612 at 2 hours in Thai emergency departments, where the simpler SpO2/FiO2 ratio reached 0.651 (Ruangsomboon 2023). The honest reading: ROX is a serial, time-point-specific index whose later readings carry the information; a single 2-hour value — especially in COVID-19 — discriminates weakly. No carded report tests a ROX-guided management strategy.

shelves.title: CURB-65 in community-acquired pneumonia: mortality 0.7% to 57% by score at derivation — but the gradient flattens in lower-mortality settings and discrimination is modest (0.67)
shelves.question: In adults presenting to hospital with community-acquired pneumonia, how well does the CURB-65 score (confusion, urea above 7 mmol/L — about 20 mg/dL as blood urea nitrogen, respiratory rate at least 30/min, low blood pressure, age at least 65) stratify 30-day mortality at the bedside, how does its discrimination compare with the Pneumonia Severity Index, and where does it misclassify — at low scores in low-mortality settings and at high scores?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Community-Acquired Infections/diagnosis,mortality · England/epidemiology · Female · Home Care Services · Hospitalization · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · New Zealand/epidemiology · Patient Selection · Pneumonia/diagnosis,mortality · Prognosis · Prospective Studies · Regression Analysis · Severity of Illness Index
shelves.balance: PREDICTIVE PERFORMANCE — real stratification, setting-dependent calibration, modest discrimination. In its international derivation and validation (1,068 hospitalised patients), CURB-65 ordered 30-day mortality from 0.7% at score 0 to 57% at score 5. In a prospective 14-hospital Korean cohort (883 patients, overall mortality 4.5%) the gradient flattened at low scores — 2.3%, 4.0%, 6.0%, 5.7% and 23.5% at scores 0 to 4, with the score-5 cell resting on n=2 — and the authors judged CURB-65 more valid at low scores and the Pneumonia Severity Index at high scores. A UK cohort measured a ROC area of only 0.67, no better than two comparator indices. No card implies scoring changes outcomes or settles admission by itself.

cards.headline: Derivation and validation (Lim 2003): 30-day mortality by CURB-65 score was 0.7%, 3.2%, 3%, 17%, 41.5% and 57% for scores 0 to 5, confirmed in the validation cohort
cards.summary: Derivation and validation (Lim 2003): 30-day mortality by CURB-65 score was 0.7%, 3.2%, 3%, 17%, 41.5% and 57% for scores 0 to 5, confirmed in the validation cohort
cards.type: International derivation and validation study of the CURB-65 score
cards.people: 1,068 adults hospitalised with community-acquired pneumonia, combining three prospective studies from the UK, New Zealand and the Netherlands (mean age 64 years, 51.5% male, 30-day mortality 9%); 80% of the data formed the derivation cohort and the remainder the validation cohort.
cards.result: One point each for Confusion, Urea above 7 mmol/L (about 20 mg/dL as blood urea nitrogen), Respiratory rate at least 30/min, low blood pressure (systolic below 90 mm Hg or diastolic at most 60 mm Hg) and age at least 65 years stratified patients by 30-day mortality: score 0, 0.7%; 1, 3.2%; 2, 3%; 3, 17%; 4, 41.5%; 5, 57% — absolute rates as published, with a similar pattern in the validation cohort.
cards.watchOut: These are derivation-era gradients from hospitalised cohorts with 9% overall mortality; the next cards show the gradient flattening in a lower-mortality setting — the score's mortality figures are setting-dependent and must be quoted with their setting.
cards.source: Lim WS et al. Defining community acquired pneumonia severity on presentation to hospital: an international derivation and validation study. Thorax. 2003. PMID: 12728155. cards.type: Prospective multicentre external validation cohort (Korea) of CURB-65 and the Pneumonia Severity Index
cards.people: 883 patients aged over 18 years with community-acquired pneumonia in a prospective cohort across 14 Korean hospitals (2009–2011); 40 patients (4.5%) died within 30 days. Mortality was calculated by both CURB-65 score and Pneumonia Severity Index (PSI) class.
cards.result: Thirty-day mortality by CURB-65 score was: 0, 2.3% (6/260); 1, 4.0% (12/300); 2, 6.0% (13/216); 3, 5.7% (5/88); 4, 23.5% (4/17); and 5, 0% (0/2 — only two patients, printed here with its N). By PSI class, mortality was 2.3%, 2.7%, 2.3%, 4.5% and 21.7% for classes I to V. The authors conclude CURB-65 is more valid at the lower scores and PSI at the higher scores in Korean patients, and that these variations must be considered when using either score.
cards.watchOut: At low scores this cohort's mortality (2.3% at score 0) is three times the derivation figure (0.7%) — a score of 0 does not carry the same reassurance in every setting, and the score-5 cell rests on two patients.

cards.headline: UK prospective cohort (Musonda 2011): CURB-65's ROC area for death was 0.67 — no better than two comparator indices derived against it (0.64 and 0.64), with no evidence of a difference between the tools
cards.summary: UK prospective cohort (Musonda 2011): CURB-65's ROC area for death was 0.67 — no better than two comparator indices derived against it (0.64 and 0.64), with no evidence of a difference between the tools
cards.type: Prospective UK cohort — head-to-head discrimination comparison of CURB-65 against two derived comparator indices
cards.people: 190 patients hospitalised with community-acquired pneumonia in Norfolk and Suffolk, UK (53% men, median age 76 years, range 18 to 101), in a prospective study; 54 patients died, all within 30 days of admission (follow-up to 6 weeks). Sixty-five patients (34%) had severe pneumonia by CURB-65.
cards.result: The receiver operating characteristic curve values for predicting death were 0.67 (95% CI 0.60 to 0.75) for CURB-65, 0.64 (0.60 to 0.71) for the CARSI index and 0.64 (0.57 to 0.71) for CARASI, with no evidence of a difference between CURB-65 and either comparator (P=0.35 and P=0.33). Sensitivity was slightly lower but specificity higher with the new indices, predictive values were comparable, and agreement was good (kappa 0.56 and 0.54).
cards.watchOut: A small single-region cohort (190 patients) in which the comparators were derived from the authors' own prior observations — this card bounds CURB-65's discrimination (0.67, modest) rather than establishing a rival score.
cards.source: Musonda P et al. Prediction of mortality in community-acquired pneumonia in hospitalized patients. The American journal of the medical sciences. 2011. PMID: 21876427.
