cards.headline: Synthesis: CURB-65 stratifies pneumonia mortality at the bedside, but its gradient is setting-dependent — derivation mortality rose from 0.7% to 57% across scores 0 to 5, while a Korean cohort with half the overall mortality showed a flattened low-score gradient (2.3% at score 0) and a UK cohort measured only modest discrimination (ROC area 0.67)
cards.summary: Synthesis: CURB-65 stratifies pneumonia mortality at the bedside, but its gradient is setting-dependent — derivation mortality rose from 0.7% to 57% across scores 0 to 5, while a Korean cohort with half the overall mortality showed a flattened low-score gradient (2.3% at score 0) and a UK cohort measured only modest discrimination (ROC area 0.67)
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf: the international derivation/validation study (n=1,068), the Korean prospective cohort (n=883) and the UK prospective cohort (n=190).
cards.result: The score does what it was built to do — order hospitalised pneumonia patients by 30-day mortality using five bedside items, with urea above 7 mmol/L (about 20 mg/dL as blood urea nitrogen) as its laboratory item. But the absolute mortality attached to each score travels with the setting: 0.7% at score 0 in derivation versus 2.3% in Korea, and 57% at score 5 in derivation versus a Korean score-5 cell of two patients with no deaths. Against the Pneumonia Severity Index, the Korean authors judge CURB-65 more valid at low scores and PSI at high scores. This is a prognostic-accuracy shelf: no card implies that scoring changes outcomes, or that a score alone settles admission. Pneumonia treatment shelves presuppose this stratification without asking it, and NEWS/NEWS2 (shelf #7542) is a general ward early-warning score — a different instrument in a different population.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards; this synthesis adds no new data.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: HSV suppression to slow HIV progression in ART-naive dually infected people: acyclovir cut progression hazards by 16% and 25% in relative terms (HR 0.84 and 0.75, absolutes beside) — a pre-treat-all-era record
shelves.question: In people dually infected with HIV-1 and HSV-2 who are not taking antiretroviral therapy, does daily suppressive acyclovir (or valacyclovir) versus placebo delay HIV-1 disease progression (CD4 decline, ART initiation, death) and lower plasma HIV-1 RNA?
shelves.mesh: Acyclovir/therapeutic use · Adult · Antiviral Agents/therapeutic use · CD4 Lymphocyte Count · Disease Progression · Double-Blind Method · Female · HIV Infections/complications/drug therapy/immunology/virology · HIV-1/isolation & purification · Herpes Genitalis/complications/drug therapy/virology · Herpesvirus 2, Human/isolation & purification · Humans · Male · Viral Load
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a real but modest and now-superseded effect. Two randomised progression trials in ART-naive people dually infected with HIV-1 and HSV-2 found daily acyclovir slowed a composite progression endpoint: hazard ratio 0.84 (284 vs 324 events, n=3,381) and adjusted hazard ratio 0.75 (95 vs 110 events, n=440) — both relative measures, labelled relative, with absolute event counts beside them. A postpartum valacyclovir trial (n=148) moved CD4 and viral-load markers only and is a labelled supportive limb, never load-bearing. The composites were driven mainly by CD4 thresholds and ART initiation, not mortality, and every participant was ART-naive by pre-treat-all standards — in the treat-all era this intervention has no place in routine care. The transmission question is homed at shelf #2196 and is not re-carded here.

cards.headline: Multicentre African RCT (Lingappa 2010): acyclovir slowed HIV-1 progression — 284 vs 324 composite events, hazard ratio 0.84 (a 16% relative reduction)
cards.summary: Multicentre African RCT (Lingappa 2010): acyclovir slowed HIV-1 progression — 284 vs 324 composite events, hazard ratio 0.84 (a 16% relative reduction)
cards.type: Randomised placebo-controlled trial (multicentre, Africa), acyclovir vs placebo — HIV-1 progression
cards.people: 3,381 heterosexual people dually infected with HIV-1 and HSV-2 at 14 sites in southern and east Africa, CD4 count 250 cells/µL or higher, not taking antiretroviral therapy; acyclovir 400 mg orally twice daily or placebo, followed up to 24 months. Median CD4 at enrolment 462 cells/µL, median plasma HIV-1 RNA 4.1 log10 copies/mL.
cards.result: The primary composite endpoint (CD4 falling below 200 cells/µL, ART initiation, or non-trauma death) occurred in 284 participants on acyclovir versus 324 on placebo — hazard ratio 0.84 (95% CI 0.71–0.98), p=0.03, a 16% relative reduction in the hazard, printed beside its absolute event counts (284 vs 324). In participants with CD4 counts of 350 cells/µL or more, acyclovir delayed CD4 falling below 350 cells/µL by 19% in relative terms (hazard ratio 0.81, 95% CI 0.71–0.93, p=0.002).
cards.watchOut: ERA FLAG, load-bearing: every participant was ART-naive with a CD4 count above the ART-initiation thresholds of the time. In the treat-all era this strategy has no place in routine care; this shelf is a record of a real but now-superseded approach. The composite was driven mainly by CD4 thresholds and ART initiation, not by mortality. HIV TRANSMISSION to a partner is a different question, homed at shelf #2196 — cross-point only, never re-carded here.
cards.source: Lingappa JR et al. Daily acyclovir for HIV-1 disease progression in people dually infected with HIV-1 and herpes simplex virus type 2: a randomised placebo-controlled trial. Lancet. 2010. PMID: 20153888. Registry ID: NCT00194519. cards.headline: Rakai RCT (Reynolds 2012): aciclovir slowed progression — 95 vs 110 events, adjusted hazard ratio 0.75 (a 25% relative reduction)
cards.summary: Rakai RCT (Reynolds 2012): aciclovir slowed progression — 95 vs 110 events, adjusted hazard ratio 0.75 (a 25% relative reduction)
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (Rakai, Uganda), aciclovir vs placebo — HIV-1 progression
cards.people: 440 adults in Rakai, Uganda, dually infected with HIV-1 and HSV-2, CD4 cell counts 300–400 cells/µL, no AIDS-defining illness or active genital ulcer disease, not on antiretroviral therapy; aciclovir 400 mg orally twice daily (220) or placebo (220) for 24 months, double-blind.
cards.result: The primary outcome (CD4 below 250 cells/µL or ART initiation for WHO stage 4 disease) occurred in 95 participants on aciclovir versus 110 on placebo — adjusted hazard ratio 0.75 (95% CI 0.58–0.99), p=0.040, a relative measure printed beside its absolute event counts. The effect was concentrated in participants with baseline viral load of 50,000 copies/mL or more (hazard ratio 0.62, 95% CI 0.43–0.96, p=0.03) and was absent below that viral load (0.90, 95% CI 0.54–1.5, p=0.688). No safety issues related to aciclovir were identified.
cards.watchOut: A single-site trial in a narrow CD4 band (300–400 cells/µL), ART-naive by the standards of its era — the same treat-all era flag as the Lingappa card applies. The subgroup split by baseline viral load is a stratified analysis of one trial, not a second trial.

cards.headline: Supportive limb, markers only, never load-bearing (Roxby 2012): valacyclovir in pregnancy/postpartum — CD4 rise 73 cells/µL greater, HIV-1 RNA rise 0.40 log10 copies/mL smaller
cards.summary: Supportive limb, markers only, never load-bearing (Roxby 2012): valacyclovir in pregnancy/postpartum — CD4 rise 73 cells/µL greater, HIV-1 RNA rise 0.40 log10 copies/mL smaller
cards.type: Randomised trial, valacyclovir vs placebo in pregnancy/postpartum — progression markers only (supportive limb)
cards.people: 148 pregnant Kenyan women co-infected with HIV-1 and HSV-2, not eligible for antiretroviral therapy (WHO stage 1–2, CD4 above 250 cells/µL), randomised to valacyclovir 500 mg twice daily or placebo from 34 weeks of gestation through 12 months postpartum; all received zidovudine and single-dose nevirapine to prevent mother-to-child transmission. 136 (92%) completed 12 months of postpartum follow-up.
cards.result: At 12 months the adjusted mean CD4 count was 638 cells/µL on valacyclovir versus 565 cells/µL on placebo — a mean increase 73 cells/µL greater on valacyclovir (p=0.03; increase 154 vs 78 cells/µL). Plasma HIV-1 RNA rose by 0.21 log10 copies/mL on valacyclovir versus 0.66 log10 copies/mL on placebo, a 0.40 log10 copies/mL smaller rise (p=0.001). These are progression MARKERS, not clinical progression endpoints.
cards.watchOut: LABELLED SUPPORTIVE LIMB, never load-bearing and never pooled with the acyclovir trials: a different drug (valacyclovir), a peripartum population on zidovudine/nevirapine prophylaxis, and marker outcomes only — no CD4-threshold, ART-initiation or death endpoint was tested here.
cards.source: Roxby AC et al. Effects of valacyclovir on markers of disease progression in postpartum women co-infected with HIV-1 and herpes simplex virus-2. PLoS One. 2012. PMID: 22701683. cards.headline: Synthesis: two progression RCTs show modest relative slowing of HIV-1 progression with daily acyclovir in ART-naive, dually infected people; a third, marker-only valacyclovir limb supports the direction and is never load-bearing
cards.summary: Synthesis: two progression RCTs show modest relative slowing of HIV-1 progression with daily acyclovir in ART-naive, dually infected people; a third, marker-only valacyclovir limb supports the direction and is never load-bearing
cards.people: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.
cards.result: Synthesis: the clinical-endpoint base is exactly the two acyclovir progression trials carded above — Lingappa 2010 (n=3,381; 284 vs 324 composite events; hazard ratio 0.84, a 16% relative reduction) and Rakai 2012 (n=440; 95 vs 110 events; adjusted hazard ratio 0.75, a 25% relative reduction) — both labelled relative with their absolute event counts beside them. The Kenyan postpartum valacyclovir trial (n=148) moved markers only (CD4 +73 cells/µL; HIV-1 RNA rise 0.40 log10 copies/mL smaller) and is a labelled supportive limb. The effects are modest, the composites were driven mainly by CD4 thresholds and ART initiation rather than mortality, and the whole question belongs to the pre-treat-all era: HSV suppression as a progression-delaying measure where ART was unavailable. HIV transmission to partners is homed at shelf #2196 and is not carded here.

shelves.title: Thymosin alpha-1 in sepsis (FLOOR-RISK — exactly 2 trials): ETASS borderline positive (26.0% vs 35.0% mortality), TESTS phase 3 null (23.4% vs 24.1%)
shelves.question: In adults with severe sepsis / sepsis (Sepsis-3), does thymosin alpha-1 added to standard care versus placebo or standard care reduce 28-day all-cause mortality?
shelves.mesh: Adjuvants, Immunologic/administration & dosage · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Female · Humans · Injections, Subcutaneous · Male · Middle Aged · Prospective Studies · Sepsis/diagnosis/drug therapy/mortality · Single-Blind Method · Survival Rate/trends · Thymalfasin · Thymosin/administration & dosage/analogs & derivatives · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: SPLIT — FLOOR-RISK, exactly 2 trials. ETASS (n=361, single-blind, China) reported lower 28-day mortality on thymosin alpha-1 (26.0% vs 35.0%; relative risk 0.74, 95% CI 0.54–1.02 — a relative measure beside its absolute rates), but the result was borderline: P=0.062 unstratified and P=0.049 by log-rank, printed exactly as reported. TESTS (n=1,106, double-blind placebo-controlled phase 3, China) then found nothing: 23.4% vs 24.1% (hazard ratio 0.99, 95% CI 0.77–1.27; P=0.93) and no secondary-outcome benefit. That arc — not an averaged estimate — is the shelf's answer. Ulinastatin + thymosin combination trials are never counted here; the hepatitis B question is homed at pack #7524.

cards.headline: ETASS (Wu 2013): thymosin alpha-1 in severe sepsis — 28-day mortality 26.0% vs 35.0%, relative risk 0.74 (0.54–1.02); unstratified P=0.062, log-rank P=0.049 — borderline, printed exactly as reported
cards.summary: ETASS (Wu 2013): thymosin alpha-1 in severe sepsis — 28-day mortality 26.0% vs 35.0%, relative risk 0.74 (0.54–1.02); unstratified P=0.062, log-rank P=0.049 — borderline, printed exactly as reported
cards.type: Multicentre single-blind randomised controlled trial (ETASS, severe sepsis), thymosin alpha-1 vs control
cards.people: 361 patients with severe sepsis admitted to intensive care in six tertiary teaching hospitals in China (2008–2010), randomised 1:1 to thymosin alpha-1 (Tα1; 181) plus conventional therapy or control (180), single-blind. The primary outcome was death from any cause at 28 days.
cards.result: 28-day all-cause mortality was 26.0% on thymosin alpha-1 versus 35.0% on control — an absolute difference of 9.0 percentage points, with relative risk 0.74 (95% CI 0.54–1.02), a relative measure whose confidence interval crosses 1. The unstratified comparison gave P=0.062 and the log-rank test P=0.049 — a borderline pair, printed exactly as the abstract reports it and never rounded into 'significant'. Monocyte HLA-DR improved more on thymosin alpha-1 at day 3 (mean difference 3.9%, 95% CI 0.2–7.6%, P=0.037) and day 7 (5.8%, 95% CI 1.0–10.5%, P=0.017). No serious drug-related adverse event was recorded.
cards.watchOut: FLOOR-RISK base — this is one of exactly two reports on this shelf. Single-blind (not double-blind), single-country (China), and borderline: the headline P value depends on which of the two reported tests is read. Product naming: thymosin alpha-1 (thymalfasin), as the publication gives it.
cards.source: Wu J et al. The efficacy of thymosin alpha 1 for severe sepsis (ETASS): a multicenter, single-blind, randomized and controlled trial. Critical Care. 2013. PMID: 23327199. cards.headline: TESTS phase 3 (Wu 2025): thymosin alpha-1 in sepsis — 28-day mortality 23.4% vs 24.1% on placebo, hazard ratio 0.99 (0.77–1.27), P=0.93 — no benefit on the primary or any secondary outcome
cards.summary: TESTS phase 3 (Wu 2025): thymosin alpha-1 in sepsis — 28-day mortality 23.4% vs 24.1% on placebo, hazard ratio 0.99 (0.77–1.27), P=0.93 — no benefit on the primary or any secondary outcome
cards.type: Multicentre double-blind placebo-controlled phase 3 trial (TESTS, sepsis), thymosin alpha-1 vs placebo
cards.people: 1,106 adults aged 18–85 years with sepsis by Sepsis-3 criteria in 22 centres in China (2016–2020), randomised 1:1 to subcutaneous thymosin alpha-1 (552) or placebo (554) every 12 hours for 7 days, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3. Modified intention-to-treat set: 1,089 (542 thymosin alpha-1, 547 placebo).
cards.result: 28-day all-cause mortality occurred in 127 participants (23.4%) on thymosin alpha-1 versus 132 (24.1%) on placebo — hazard ratio 0.99 (95% CI 0.77–1.27), P=0.93, a relative measure beside its absolute rates (23.4% vs 24.1%). No secondary or safety outcome differed significantly between the groups. Prespecified subgroup interactions by age (under 60: hazard ratio 1.67, 95% CI 1.04–2.67; 60 or over: 0.81, 95% CI 0.61–1.09; P for interaction=0.01) and diabetes (with diabetes: 0.58, 95% CI 0.35–0.99; without: 1.16, 95% CI 0.87–1.53; P for interaction=0.04) were reported.
cards.watchOut: FLOOR-RISK base — the second of exactly two reports, and the decisive one: double-blind, phase 3, three times ETASS's size, and null. The age and diabetes subgroup interactions are prespecified but hypothesis-generating only; the age interaction, if anything, points toward harm under 60. Single-country (China) programme, as with ETASS.

cards.result: Synthesis: FLOOR-RISK — exactly 2 randomised reports exist for thymosin alpha-1 alone in sepsis, and they are split. ETASS (n=361, single-blind) reported 28-day mortality 26.0% versus 35.0% (relative risk 0.74, 95% CI 0.54–1.02; P=0.062 unstratified, P=0.049 log-rank — borderline, printed as reported). TESTS (n=1,106, double-blind phase 3) reported 23.4% versus 24.1% (hazard ratio 0.99, 95% CI 0.77–1.27; P=0.93) with no benefit on any secondary outcome. Both trials are Chinese single-country programmes. The ulinastatin-combination trials were never counted, and the hepatitis B question is homed at pack #7524. On this two-trial base, the larger and better-blinded trial governs: no mortality benefit has been shown.

shelves.title: Rapid shallow breathing index: founding sensitivity 0.97 settles to pooled sensitivity 0.83 and specificity 0.58 at <105 — a permissive test, not an extubation rule
shelves.question: In mechanically ventilated adults being assessed for liberation from the ventilator, how accurately does the rapid shallow breathing index (RSBI — respiratory frequency divided by tidal volume, f/VT) predict successful weaning and extubation, what does the classic threshold of 105 breaths/min/L actually deliver in sensitivity and specificity on modern pooled evidence, and how far does the threshold (105 vs 80 vs 65, and the measurement conditions) move the answer?
shelves.mesh: Arteries · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Oxygen · Partial Pressure · Prognosis · Prospective Studies · Respiration · Sensitivity and Specificity · Thorax · Tidal Volume · Ventilator Weaning · APACHE · Coronary Care Units · Postoperative Care · Predictive Value of Tests · Pulmonary Disease, Chronic Obstructive · Respiration, Artificial · Treatment Outcome · Airway Extubation · Clinical Decision Rules · Clinical Decision-Making · Respiratory Rate
shelves.balance: PREDICTIVE PERFORMANCE — a founding near-perfect result settling to moderate sensitivity and poor specificity. The rapid shallow breathing index (f/VT) began with sensitivity 0.97 and the largest ROC area (0.89) among weaning indexes in Yang & Tobin's 100-patient founding study. On modern pooled evidence — 48 studies, 10,946 patients — RSBI <105 breaths/min/L has sensitivity 0.83 (95% CI 0.78 to 0.87) and specificity only 0.58 (95% CI 0.49 to 0.66) for extubation success, with thresholds <80 and 80–105 performing similarly; the 2001 evidence review already showed the asymmetry (positive likelihood ratios ≤2.23; negative 0.09 to 0.23). The index is permissive / rule-out-flavoured, not a pass–fail extubation rule, and no card implies acting on it improves outcomes.

cards.headline: Founding study (Yang & Tobin 1991): f/VT derived in 36 patients and tested prospectively in 64 — largest ROC area of the indexes tested (0.89), sensitivity 0.97 and specificity 0.64 at its best threshold
cards.summary: Founding study (Yang & Tobin 1991): f/VT derived in 36 patients and tested prospectively in 64 — largest ROC area of the indexes tested (0.89), sensitivity 0.97 and specificity 0.64 at its best threshold
cards.type: Prospective derivation and validation cohort (founding RSBI study, 36 + 64 patients)
cards.people: Mechanically ventilated patients being assessed for weaning: index thresholds were derived in 36 patients and then tested prospectively in an additional 64 patients; the rapid shallow breathing index (f/VT, respiratory frequency divided by tidal volume) was compared with minute ventilation, maximal inspiratory pressure and the CROP index.
cards.result: Sensitivity was highest for maximal inspiratory pressure (1.00), followed closely by f/VT (0.97); specificity was highest for f/VT (0.64) and lowest for maximal inspiratory pressure (0.11). The area under the ROC curve for f/VT (0.89) was larger than for CROP (0.78; P < 0.05), maximal inspiratory pressure (0.61; P < 0.001) and minute ventilation (0.40; P < 0.001). The authors concluded rapid shallow breathing was the most accurate predictor of weaning failure, and its absence the most accurate predictor of success.
cards.watchOut: A founding result from 100 patients in total at one centre in 1991: the near-perfect sensitivity of 0.97 is the derivation-era figure, and the pooled modern estimate on the next cards is materially lower — both ends of that arc are the content of this shelf.
cards.source: Yang KL et al. A prospective study of indexes predicting the outcome of trials of weaning from mechanical ventilation. The New England journal of medicine. 1991. PMID: 2023603. cards.headline: Evidence-based weaning review (65 observational studies, 70 publications): pooled positive likelihood ratios for RSBI were limited (highest 2.23) while negative results carried substantial weight (likelihood ratios 0.09 to 0.23)
cards.summary: Evidence-based weaning review (65 observational studies, 70 publications): pooled positive likelihood ratios for RSBI were limited (highest 2.23) while negative results carried substantial weight (likelihood ratios 0.09 to 0.23)
cards.type: Systematic evidence review of weaning predictors (65 observational studies)
cards.people: 65 observational studies of weaning predictors reported in 70 publications, grouped across heterogeneous populations, COPD patients and cardiovascular ICU patients; predictors for stepwise reduction of support, trials of unassisted breathing, and successful extubation were assessed separately.
cards.result: For trials of unassisted breathing, pooled results for the power of a positive RSBI result were limited (highest likelihood ratio 2.23), while the power of a negative result was substantial (likelihood ratios 0.09 to 0.23). For prediction of successful extubation, an RSBI <100 or 105 breaths/min/L had sensitivity ranging 65 to 96% and specificity 0 to 73% across studies. Judged by ROC areas, no variable showed more than modest accuracy for weaning outcome; the authors note clinicians had already considered these results when choosing patients for weaning trials, which may itself depress measured accuracy.
cards.watchOut: A 2001 review of small, heterogeneous observational studies with widely varying thresholds and measurement conditions; its likelihood-ratio framing — a negative (low) RSBI helps, a positive one barely moves probability — is not interchangeable with a single sensitivity / specificity pair.
cards.source: Meade M et al. Predicting success in weaning from mechanical ventilation. Chest. 2001. PMID: 11742961. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Modern pooled estimate (48 studies, 10,946 patients): RSBI <105 gives sensitivity 0.83 and specificity 0.58 for extubation success; thresholds <80 and 80–105 perform similarly
cards.summary: Modern pooled estimate (48 studies, 10,946 patients): RSBI <105 gives sensitivity 0.83 and specificity 0.58 for extubation success; thresholds <80 and 80–105 perform similarly
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of RSBI diagnostic accuracy (48 studies, 10,946 patients)
cards.people: 48 studies involving RSBI measurements in 10,946 mechanically ventilated patients, searched to September 2019, with study data extracted and quality assessed independently and in duplicate; subgroup analyses covered differing patient characteristics and operational differences in RSBI measurement.
cards.result: Pooled sensitivity for RSBI <105 breaths/min/L predicting extubation success was moderate at 0.83 (95% CI 0.78 to 0.87; moderate certainty) whereas specificity was poor at 0.58 (95% CI 0.49 to 0.66; moderate certainty), with a diagnostic odds ratio of 5.91 (95% CI 4.09 to 8.52). RSBI thresholds of <80 or 80 to 105 yielded similar sensitivity, specificity and diagnostic odds ratios, consistently across subgroup analyses. The authors conclude the RSBI as a stand-alone test has moderate sensitivity and poor specificity, and propose studying it as a permissive criterion for a spontaneous breathing trial in patients at intermediate pretest probability.
cards.watchOut: The classic threshold of 105 is not a pass–fail extubation rule on this evidence: specificity of 0.58 means many patients below the threshold still fail, and similar performance at <80 shows the exact cut-off matters less than the founding literature implied. Measurement conditions (ventilator vs disconnected, timing relative to the breathing trial) vary across the pooled studies.
cards.source: Trivedi V et al. The Usefulness of the Rapid Shallow Breathing Index in Predicting Successful Extubation: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis. Chest. 2022. PMID: 34181953. cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: The arc is the finding. Yang & Tobin's founding prospective study gave f/VT the largest ROC area (0.89) with sensitivity 0.97 and specificity 0.64; the 2001 evidence review found positive results weak (likelihood ratios up to 2.23) and negative results substantial (0.09 to 0.23); and the 2022 meta-analysis of 48 studies and 10,946 patients gives RSBI <105 a pooled sensitivity of 0.83 (95% CI 0.78 to 0.87) and specificity of 0.58 (95% CI 0.49 to 0.66), with thresholds <80 and 80–105 performing similarly. No card on this shelf shows that acting on the RSBI improves outcomes — this is a prognostic-accuracy shelf. Cross-point only: diaphragm-ultrasound weaning prediction (including diaphragmatic RSBI variants) and spontaneous-breathing-trial method shelves ask different questions and share no PMID with this shelf.

shelves.title: CAM-ICU for ICU delirium: specificity stays ~0.95 on pooling while sensitivity falls to 0.80–0.84 — better than ICDSC chiefly at ruling delirium out
shelves.question: In critically ill adults, including mechanically ventilated patients who cannot speak, how accurately does the Confusion Assessment Method for the Intensive Care Unit (CAM-ICU) detect delirium against a DSM reference standard — what are its pooled sensitivity and specificity, how do they compare with the Intensive Care Delirium Screening Checklist (ICDSC), and what moderates accuracy (hypoactive delirium, ventilation, ICU type)?
shelves.mesh: APACHE · Aged · Critical Illness · Delirium · Female · Humans · Intensive Care Units · Male · Middle Aged · Prospective Studies · Reference Standards · Reproducibility of Results · Respiration, Artificial · Sensitivity and Specificity · Severity of Illness Index · Checklist · Confusion · Critical Care · Adult
shelves.balance: PREDICTIVE PERFORMANCE — very high specificity, moderate pooled sensitivity. CAM-ICU's founding validation was near-perfect (sensitivities 100% and 93%, specificities 98% and 100%, kappa 0.96 in 96 evaluable ventilated patients), but pooling costs sensitivity: 80.0% sensitivity with 95.9% specificity (9 studies, 969 patients; AUC 0.97) in 2012, and 0.84 / 0.95 across 29 studies in the 2021 bivariate meta-analysis. Against ICDSC (74% / 81.9%, then 0.83 / 0.87), CAM-ICU's advantage is chiefly specificity. Accuracy is moderated by hypoactive-delirium proportion, ICU type, ventilation and case mix — no single pooled pair is the test's performance in all ICUs, and no card implies screening improves outcomes.

cards.headline: Founding validation (Ely 2001): in 96 evaluable ventilated patients (471 paired evaluations), two nurses using CAM-ICU had sensitivities of 100% and 93%, specificities of 98% and 100%, kappa 0.96 vs DSM-IV expert assessment
cards.summary: Founding validation (Ely 2001): in 96 evaluable ventilated patients (471 paired evaluations), two nurses using CAM-ICU had sensitivities of 100% and 93%, specificities of 98% and 100%, kappa 0.96 vs DSM-IV expert assessment
cards.type: Prospective validation cohort (founding CAM-ICU study, 96 evaluable patients, 471 paired evaluations)
cards.people: 111 consecutive mechanically ventilated patients enrolled in adult medical and coronary ICUs at a US university centre, of whom 96 (86.5%) were evaluable (15 remained comatose throughout); 471 daily paired evaluations by 2 critical care study nurses using CAM-ICU against delirium-expert assessment using DSM-IV criteria; mean CAM-ICU administration time 2 (SD 1) minutes.
cards.result: Against the reference standard, the two nurses' CAM-ICU sensitivities were 100% and 93% and specificities 98% and 100%, with interrater reliability kappa 0.96 (95% CI 0.92 to 0.99); subgroup kappas were 0.92 (age ≥65), 0.99 (suspected dementia) and 0.94 (APACHE II at or above the median of 23), with no significant sensitivity / specificity differences by age, suspected dementia or severity of illness. Delirium occurred in 80 of 96 patients (83.3%) during their ICU stay for a mean of 2.4 days.
cards.watchOut: Near-perfect founding figures from two trained study nurses at one centre against expert assessment: routine-staff performance in unselected ICUs is the pooled question on the next cards, where sensitivity — not specificity — is what falls.
cards.source: Ely EW et al. Delirium in mechanically ventilated patients: validity and reliability of the confusion assessment method for the intensive care unit (CAM-ICU). JAMA. 2001. cards.headline: First meta-analysis (9 CAM-ICU studies, 969 patients; 4 ICDSC studies, 361 patients): pooled CAM-ICU sensitivity 80.0% and specificity 95.9% (AUC 0.97) vs ICDSC sensitivity 74% and specificity 81.9%
cards.summary: First meta-analysis (9 CAM-ICU studies, 969 patients; 4 ICDSC studies, 361 patients): pooled CAM-ICU sensitivity 80.0% and specificity 95.9% (AUC 0.97) vs ICDSC sensitivity 74% and specificity 81.9%
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of CAM-ICU and ICDSC diagnostic accuracy (2012)
cards.people: Systematic review of studies evaluating CAM-ICU or the Intensive Care Delirium Screening Checklist (ICDSC) against DSM-IV criteria in adult ICU patients: 9 CAM-ICU studies (969 patients) and 4 ICDSC studies (361 patients), quality assessed with the QUADAS scale.
cards.result: Pooled CAM-ICU sensitivity was 80.0% (95% CI 77.1 to 82.6%) and specificity 95.9% (95% CI 94.8 to 96.8%), diagnostic odds ratio 103.2 (95% CI 39.6 to 268.8), with pooled area under the summary ROC curve 0.97. For ICDSC, pooled sensitivity was 74% (95% CI 65.3 to 81.5%) and specificity 81.9% (95% CI 76.7 to 86.4%), diagnostic odds ratio 21.5 and AUC 0.89. The authors describe CAM-ICU as an excellent diagnostic tool and ICDSC as having moderate sensitivity and good specificity.
cards.watchOut: The ICDSC limb rests on only 4 studies and 361 patients against CAM-ICU's 9 and 969: the comparison favours CAM-ICU, but the two pooled estimates are not equally firm, and both predate the larger 2021 bivariate analysis.
cards.source: Gusmao-Flores D et al. cards.headline: Bivariate meta-analysis (29 CAM-ICU and 12 ICDSC studies): pooled sensitivity 0.84 and specificity 0.95 for CAM-ICU vs 0.83 and 0.87 for ICDSC; hypoactive-delirium proportion, ICU type, ventilation and case mix moderate accuracy
cards.summary: Bivariate meta-analysis (29 CAM-ICU and 12 ICDSC studies): pooled sensitivity 0.84 and specificity 0.95 for CAM-ICU vs 0.83 and 0.87 for ICDSC; hypoactive-delirium proportion, ICU type, ventilation and case mix moderate accuracy
cards.type: Bivariate systematic review and meta-analysis of CAM-ICU vs ICDSC diagnostic accuracy (2021)
cards.people: 29 CAM-ICU studies and 12 ICDSC studies identified from PubMed, Embase, CINAHL and ProQuest to 26 April 2019, with data abstracted and accuracy summarised by two researchers independently using a bivariate random-effects model against standard references.
cards.result: Pooled sensitivity was 0.84 and pooled specificity 0.95 for CAM-ICU, versus 0.83 and 0.87 for ICDSC; CAM-ICU had higher summary specificity than ICDSC (P = 0.04). The percentage of hypoactive delirium, ICU type, use of mechanical ventilation, number of participants and female percentage moderated the accuracy of the tools. The authors conclude CAM-ICU is superior in ruling out patients without ICU delirium and in detecting delirium in medical ICU patients and those receiving mechanical ventilation; most bias domains were rated low or unclear risk.
cards.watchOut: Accuracy is moderator-dependent — hypoactive delirium is the hard case — so no single pooled pair describes the test's performance in every ICU; the near-equal sensitivities (0.84 vs 0.83) mean the CAM-ICU advantage over ICDSC is chiefly a specificity advantage.
cards.source: Chen TJ et al. Diagnostic accuracy of the CAM-ICU and ICDSC in detecting intensive care unit delirium: A bivariate meta-analysis. International journal of nursing studies. 2021. shelves.title: Ulinastatin in sepsis: FLOOR-RISK, exactly 2 multicentre trials, split — Karnad's signal only in a modified-ITT subset; ADJUST (n=347) null with more adverse events on treatment
shelves.question: In adults with severe sepsis / sepsis (Sepsis-3), does intravenous ulinastatin (urinary trypsin inhibitor) added to standard care versus placebo or standard care reduce 28-day all-cause mortality?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Double-Blind Method · Female · Glycoproteins · Humans · Infusions, Intravenous · Male · Pilot Projects · Prospective Studies · Sepsis · Trypsin Inhibitors
shelves.balance: SPLIT — FLOOR-RISK, exactly 2 multicentre randomised reports, stated on the face, and they split the way small-positive / large-negative programmes split. Karnad 2014 (122 randomised, seven Indian hospitals): 28-day mortality 7.3% on ulinastatin versus 20.3% on placebo in the modified intention-to-treat analysis (p=0.045), but the intention-to-treat comparison did NOT reach significance (10.2% versus 20.6%, p=0.11) — both analyses are printed exactly as reported. ADJUST 2026 (347 randomised, multicentre, Sepsis-3): 28-day mortality 23.6% on ulinastatin versus 22.9% on placebo — an absolute difference of 0.7 percentage points in the wrong direction (p=0.98; hazard ratio 1.03, relative) — with adverse events MORE frequent on ulinastatin (56.8% versus 42.7%, p=0.009). Two small single-centre reports (post-traumatic sepsis, n=60, no mortality difference; a mechanistic lymphocyte-apoptosis study, n=40) are carded labelled and are never load-bearing. Both multicentre trials are single-country (India; China). The ulinastatin-plus-thymosin combination trials ask a different, combination question and are not counted.

cards.headline: Karnad 2014 multicentre pilot (122 randomised): 28-day mortality 7.3% vs 20.3% in the MODIFIED intention-to-treat analysis (p=0.045) — but the intention-to-treat analysis did NOT reach significance (10.2% vs 20.6%, p=0.11)
cards.summary: Karnad 2014 multicentre pilot (122 randomised): 28-day mortality 7.3% vs 20.3% in the MODIFIED intention-to-treat analysis (p=0.045) — but the intention-to-treat analysis did NOT reach significance (10.2% vs 20.6%, p=0.11)
cards.type: Multicentre randomised double-blind placebo-controlled pilot trial (7 Indian hospitals), intravenous ulinastatin vs placebo, severe sepsis
cards.people: 122 patients with severe sepsis randomised within 48 hours of onset of one or more organ failures in seven Indian hospitals, double-blind, to intravenous ulinastatin 200,000 IU or placebo 12-hourly for 5 days; 114 completed the study (55 ulinastatin, 59 placebo). Mean APACHE II score was 13.4; 42% were mechanically ventilated and 51% were on vasopressors at baseline.
cards.result: In the modified intention-to-treat analysis (patients receiving six or more doses), 28-day all-cause mortality was 7.3% with ulinastatin (4 deaths) versus 20.3% with placebo (12 deaths), p=0.045; on multivariate analysis ulinastatin was independently associated with lower mortality (odds ratio 0.26, 95% CI 0.07-0.95; p=0.042 — a relative measure). However, the mortality difference did not reach statistical significance in the intention-to-treat analysis: 10.2% (6 of 59) versus 20.6% (13 of 63), p=0.11. The ulinastatin group had fewer patients with new-onset organ failure (10 versus 26, p=0.003), more ventilator-free days (19.4 versus 10.2 days, p=0.019) and shorter hospital stay (11.8 versus 24.2 days, p<0.001). Both mortality analyses are printed exactly as the abstract reports them — the p=0.045 / p=0.11 pair is never rounded into 'significant'.
cards.watchOut: A pilot trial whose positive mortality reading exists only in its modified intention-to-treat subset; its own intention-to-treat analysis is null. One of exactly 2 multicentre reports on this shelf.
cards.source: Karnad DR et al. Intravenous administration of ulinastatin (human urinary trypsin inhibitor) in severe sepsis: a multicenter randomized controlled study. Intensive care medicine. 2014. PMID: 24737258. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: ADJUST 2026 multicentre trial (347 randomised): 28-day mortality 23.6% on ulinastatin vs 22.9% on placebo (absolute difference 0.7 points the wrong way, p=0.98) — with adverse events MORE frequent on ulinastatin (56.8% vs 42.7%, p=0.009)
cards.summary: ADJUST 2026 multicentre trial (347 randomised): 28-day mortality 23.6% on ulinastatin vs 22.9% on placebo (absolute difference 0.7 points the wrong way, p=0.98) — with adverse events MORE frequent on ulinastatin (56.8% vs 42.7%, p=0.009)
cards.type: Multicentre randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (ADJUST), intravenous ulinastatin vs placebo, Sepsis-3 sepsis
cards.people: 347 adult ICU patients with sepsis meeting Sepsis-3 criteria within 48 hours of admission, randomised (1:1) in a multicentre double-blind placebo-controlled trial to intravenous ulinastatin 400,000 IU every 8 hours or placebo for up to 10 days plus standard care; 340 received the intervention (169 ulinastatin, 171 placebo) and 335 were included in the intention-to-treat analysis.
cards.result: At 28 days, death had occurred in 39 of 165 patients (23.6%) on ulinastatin and 39 of 170 (22.9%) on placebo (absolute difference 0.7%, 95% CI -8.4% to 9.7%; p=0.98; hazard ratio 1.03, 95% CI 0.66 to 1.61 — a relative measure centred on no effect). Secondary outcomes (ICU, hospital and 90-day mortality; lengths of stay) were similar. Adverse events occurred in 56.8% (96 of 169) on ulinastatin versus 42.7% (73 of 171) on placebo (absolute difference 14.1%, 95% CI 3.6%-24.6%; p=0.009). The authors conclude adjunctive ulinastatin did not reduce mortality and routine use is not supported.
cards.watchOut: The larger, definitive limb of a two-report base: a null mortality result with a statistically significant excess of adverse events on treatment. One of exactly 2 multicentre reports on this shelf.
cards.source: Chen Y et al. Efficacy and Safety of Ulinastatin in the Treatment of Patients with Sepsis: The ADJUST Trial. Chest. 2026. PMID: 42994751. Registry ID: NCT02647554. MeSH: none in the record

cards.summary: Labelled support, never load-bearing — post-traumatic sepsis trial (Yang 2025, n=60, single-blind, single centre): NO difference in 28-day mortality
cards.type: Labelled support (never load-bearing): single-blind single-centre randomised trial, ulinastatin in post-traumatic sepsis, n=60
cards.people: 60 adult patients with post-traumatic sepsis at a single hospital (Eastern Theater General Hospital, 2022-2024), in a single-blind randomised controlled trial of ulinastatin versus control; primary endpoint was 28-day all-cause mortality.
cards.result: No statistically significant difference was observed in 28-day mortality between the ulinastatin and control groups (p>0.05). The ulinastatin group had significantly shorter ICU and hospital stays and improvements in C-reactive protein, interleukin-6, procalcitonin, SOFA and APACHE II scores (p<0.05), with no significant difference in duration of mechanical ventilation and no serious adverse events reported.
cards.watchOut: Labelled support only: a 60-patient single-centre, single-blind trial in the post-traumatic subgroup, with a null mortality result. It is not a third multicentre report and carries no part of this shelf's balance.

cards.headline: Labelled support, never load-bearing — mechanistic trial (Zhang 2024, n=40): ulinastatin inhibited lymphocyte apoptosis and promoted autophagy, with lower inflammatory markers — biomarker outcomes only, no mortality claim
cards.summary: Labelled support, never load-bearing — mechanistic trial (Zhang 2024, n=40): ulinastatin inhibited lymphocyte apoptosis and promoted autophagy, with lower inflammatory markers — biomarker outcomes only, no mortality claim
cards.type: Labelled support (never load-bearing): mechanistic randomised study, ulinastatin vs standard treatment, n=40, biomarker primary outcomes
cards.people: 40 patients with sepsis randomly assigned to standard treatment plus intravenous ulinastatin or standard treatment alone, in a mechanistic randomised study measuring lymphocyte apoptosis, autophagy, inflammatory markers and organ function at multiple time points.
cards.result: Ulinastatin treatment significantly inhibited lymphocyte apoptosis and promoted autophagy (autophagy-related proteins LC3-II and Beclin-1 substantially elevated; the Bcl-2 to Bax ratio increased), and interleukin-6, procalcitonin and C-reactive protein were markedly reduced versus control, with improved liver, kidney and cardiac function measures. The primary readouts are biomarkers and organ-function measures — the report makes and supports no mortality claim.
cards.watchOut: Labelled support only: a 40-patient mechanistic study. Mechanistic plausibility is not efficacy evidence, and this card carries no part of this shelf's balance.
cards.source: Zhang D et al. The impact of ulinastatin on lymphocyte apoptosis and autophagy in sepsis patients. Scientific reports. 2024. PMID: 39567616. Registry ID: none in the record. shelves.title: qSOFA vs SIRS predicting death in suspected infection outside the ICU: pooled non-ICU sensitivity only 51.2% (specificity 79.6%) — the prompt misses about half who die (GAP-E)
shelves.question: In adults with suspected infection outside the intensive care unit — on wards, in the emergency department and before admission — how accurately does the quick Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (qSOFA: systolic blood pressure ≤100 mm Hg, respiratory rate ≥22/min, altered mentation; score ≥2) predict death, how do its sensitivity and specificity trade off against the systemic inflammatory response syndrome (SIRS) criteria, and how far does its accuracy move between ICU and non-ICU populations?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Female · Hospital Mortality · Humans · Hypotension/diagnosis · Infections/blood/diagnosis/epidemiology · Intensive Care Units/statistics & numerical data · Lactic Acid/blood · Length of Stay · Male · Organ Dysfunction Scores · Pennsylvania/epidemiology · Regression Analysis · Reproducibility of Results · Retrospective Studies · Sepsis/blood/diagnosis/mortality · Systemic Inflammatory Response Syndrome/diagnosis · Tachypnea/diagnosis · Decision Support Techniques · Emergency Service, Hospital · Intensive Care Units · Predictive Value of Tests · Prognosis · Sepsis/mortality · Systemic Inflammatory Response Syndrome/mortality · Observational Studies as Topic · Systemic Inflammatory Response Syndrome/diagnosis/pathology
shelves.balance: PREDICTIVE PERFORMANCE — a specific but insensitive prompt outside the ICU (GAP-E). qSOFA (systolic BP ≤100 mm Hg, respiratory rate ≥22/min, altered mentation; ≥2 positive) was derived in the Sepsis-3 analysis of 1.3 million encounters, where outside the ICU it discriminated in-hospital mortality better than SOFA and SIRS (AUROC 0.81 vs 0.79 and 0.76) — but discrimination is not bedside sensitivity. Two independent meta-analyses put pooled non-ICU sensitivity at only 51.2% (38 studies, 385,333 patients; specificity 79.6%) and 0.48 (45 studies, 406,802 patients; specificity 0.83): the prompt misses roughly half of non-ICU patients who die. SIRS is the mirror image (sensitivity 88.1%, specificity 25.8%). In the ICU the pattern partly reverses (qSOFA sensitivity 87.2%, specificity 33.3%; SOFA AUROC 0.74 vs qSOFA 0.66). No carded evidence shows scoring itself improves outcomes.

cards.headline: Sepsis-3 derivation and validation (Seymour 2016): qSOFA was derived in 1.3 million encounters; outside the ICU it discriminated in-hospital mortality better than SOFA and SIRS (AUROC 0.81 vs 0.79 and 0.76), but inside the ICU it was worse than SOFA (AUROC 0.66 vs 0.74)
cards.summary: Sepsis-3 derivation and validation (Seymour 2016): qSOFA was derived in 1.3 million encounters; outside the ICU it discriminated in-hospital mortality better than SOFA and SIRS (AUROC 0.81 vs 0.79 and 0.76), but inside the ICU it was worse than SOFA (AUROC 0.66 vs 0.74)
cards.type: Retrospective derivation and validation study (Sepsis-3 clinical criteria) — the qSOFA derivation report
cards.people: 1.3 million electronic-health-record encounters (2010–2012) at 12 hospitals in southwestern Pennsylvania, of which 148,907 encounters had suspected infection (74,453 derivation, 74,454 validation; 6,347 deaths, 4%); confirmatory analyses in 4 further datasets totalling 706,399 encounters at 165 US and non-US hospitals. qSOFA (range 0–3) gives 1 point each for systolic blood pressure ≤100 mm Hg, respiratory rate ≥22/min, or altered mentation.
cards.result: Among non-ICU encounters in the validation cohort (66,522 with suspected infection, 1,886 deaths, 3%), qSOFA's predictive validity for in-hospital mortality (AUROC 0.81, 95% CI 0.80 to 0.82) was greater than SOFA (0.79) and SIRS (0.76). Relative to qSOFA scores below 2, encounters scoring 2 or higher had a 3- to 14-fold increase in hospital mortality across baseline-risk deciles. Among ICU encounters (7,932 with suspected infection, 1,289 deaths, 16%), the order reversed: SOFA (AUROC 0.74) and LODS (0.75) discriminated better than qSOFA (0.66) and SIRS (0.64). Findings were similar in the external datasets and for the secondary outcome (death or ICU stay ≥3 days).
cards.watchOut: Discrimination (AUROC) is not sensitivity at the bedside cut-off: this derivation report does not show how many dying patients a qSOFA ≥2 prompt would miss — that is the next two cards, and it is the clinically decisive number. Retrospective electronic-record data throughout.
cards.source: Seymour CW et al. Assessment of Clinical Criteria for Sepsis: For the Third International Consensus Definitions for Sepsis and Septic Shock (Sepsis-3). JAMA. 2016. PMID: 26903335. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Meta-analysis of 38 studies, 385,333 patients (Fernando 2018): pooled qSOFA sensitivity for mortality was only 51.2% outside the ICU (specificity 79.6%), versus 87.2% sensitivity in the ICU (specificity 33.3%); SIRS was far more sensitive overall (88.1%) and far less specific (25.8%)
cards.summary: Meta-analysis of 38 studies, 385,333 patients (Fernando 2018): pooled qSOFA sensitivity for mortality was only 51.2% outside the ICU (specificity 79.6%), versus 87.2% sensitivity in the ICU (specificity 33.3%); SIRS was far more sensitive overall (88.1%) and far less specific (25.8%)
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of prognostic accuracy (qSOFA vs SIRS) — the pooled sensitivity / specificity card
cards.people: 38 studies of adults with suspected infection in the intensive care unit, emergency department or hospital wards, using qSOFA to predict in-hospital, 28-day or 30-day mortality (total 385,333 patients); two investigators independently extracted data and assessed quality. This shelf's headline card, as commissioned.
cards.result: qSOFA was associated with a pooled sensitivity of 60.8% (95% CI 51.4% to 69.4%) and a pooled specificity of 72.0% (63.4% to 79.2%) for mortality. The SIRS criteria had a pooled sensitivity of 88.1% (82.3% to 92.1%) and a pooled specificity of 25.8% (17.1% to 36.9%). Split by setting, qSOFA's pooled sensitivity was higher in the ICU population (87.2%, 95% CI 75.8% to 93.7%) than in the non-ICU population (51.2%, 43.6% to 58.7%), while its pooled specificity was higher outside the ICU (79.6%, 73.3% to 84.7%) than inside it (33.3%, 23.8% to 44.4%). The authors concluded qSOFA had poor sensitivity and moderate specificity for short-term mortality, and that SIRS's superior sensitivity supports its use for screening and as a prompt for treatment initiation.
cards.watchOut: ICU and non-ICU accuracy are different claims and are never pooled on this shelf: outside the ICU — the setting this shelf's question asks about — a qSOFA ≥2 prompt misses roughly half of the patients who die (sensitivity 51.2%). The review notes potential risk of bias from qSOFA interpretation and patient selection in the included studies.

cards.headline: Second meta-analysis (Maitra 2018): 45 observational studies, 406,802 patients — pooled non-ICU sensitivity of qSOFA ≥2 for in-hospital mortality 0.48 (specificity 0.83), confirming qSOFA as a poorly sensitive predictive marker outside the ICU
cards.summary: Second meta-analysis (Maitra 2018): 45 observational studies, 406,802 patients — pooled non-ICU sensitivity of qSOFA ≥2 for in-hospital mortality 0.48 (specificity 0.83), confirming qSOFA as a poorly sensitive predictive marker outside the ICU
cards.type: Meta-analysis of observational studies (qSOFA and SIRS accuracy for in-hospital mortality) — an independent second synthesis, concordant with the card above
cards.people: 45 observational studies of hospitalised patients with suspected or proven infection reporting the predictive utility of qSOFA for in-hospital mortality (406,802 patients), conducted under the MOOSE consensus statement for meta-analyses of observational studies.
cards.result: For patients who were not in an intensive care unit, the pooled sensitivity of qSOFA ≥2 for predicting mortality was 0.48 (95% CI 0.41 to 0.55) and pooled specificity 0.83 (0.78 to 0.87). Across both ICU and non-ICU settings, pooled sensitivity was 0.56 (0.47 to 0.65) and pooled specificity 0.78 (0.71 to 0.83). The authors concluded qSOFA is a poorly sensitive predictive marker for in-hospital mortality in hospitalised patients with suspected infection and recommended developing another scoring system with higher sensitivity.
cards.watchOut: Observational-study meta-analysis: its pooled estimates inherit the designs and case mixes of the primary studies, and its all-settings pooled figures (0.56 / 0.78) must not be substituted for the non-ICU figures (0.48 / 0.83) that answer this shelf's question.

cards.headline: Synthesis: qSOFA ≥2 is a specific but insensitive bedside prompt outside the ICU — pooled non-ICU sensitivity 51.2% (Fernando) and 0.48 (Maitra), specificity about 0.80–0.83 — so it misses roughly half of non-ICU patients with suspected infection who die, while SIRS misses far fewer (sensitivity 88.1%) at the cost of specificity (25.8%); in the ICU the pattern partly reverses and SOFA discriminates better than either
cards.summary: Synthesis: qSOFA ≥2 is a specific but insensitive bedside prompt outside the ICU — pooled non-ICU sensitivity 51.2% (Fernando) and 0.48 (Maitra), specificity about 0.80–0.83 — so it misses roughly half of non-ICU patients with suspected infection who die, while SIRS misses far fewer (sensitivity 88.1%) at the cost of specificity (25.8%); in the ICU the pattern partly reverses and SOFA discriminates better than either
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf: the Sepsis-3 derivation/validation study (1.3 million encounters; 148,907 with suspected infection) and two independent meta-analyses (38 studies, 385,333 patients; 45 studies, 406,802 patients).
cards.result: Derivation: outside the ICU qSOFA discriminated mortality better than SOFA and SIRS (AUROC 0.81 vs 0.79 and 0.76); inside the ICU it did not (0.66 vs SOFA 0.74). Pooled accuracy at the ≥2 cut-off: non-ICU sensitivity 51.2% and specificity 79.6% (Fernando 2018); non-ICU sensitivity 0.48 and specificity 0.83 (Maitra 2018); ICU sensitivity 87.2% and specificity 33.3% (Fernando). SIRS overall: sensitivity 88.1%, specificity 25.8%. This is a prognostic-accuracy shelf only: no carded report shows that scoring patients, or any escalation a score triggers, improves outcomes, and no card may imply it. Distinct from the NEWS/NEWS2 deterioration shelf and the CURB-65 pneumonia shelf — different instruments, populations and literatures, no shared reports.
cards.watchOut: Setting is decisive: never quote an all-settings or ICU figure for a ward or emergency-department patient, and never quote the derivation AUROC as if it were bedside sensitivity.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Albendazole–ivermectin vs albendazole alone for Trichuris/STH (PARTIAL vs pack #2172): large cure gains in Laos, Pemba, Uganda and the FDC trial — but a NULL in Côte d'Ivoire (limbs never pooled)
shelves.question: In children, adolescents and adults infected with soil-transmitted helminths — principally Trichuris trichiura (whipworm), also hookworm and Strongyloides stercoralis — does a single dose of albendazole 400 mg combined with ivermectin (co-administered, or as a fixed-dose combination tablet) versus albendazole 400 mg alone achieve parasitological cure 14–21 days after treatment? PARTIAL beside pack #2172, which homes the Pemba 2015 four-arm combination trial (no albendazole-alone arm) — that trial is not re-carded here.
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Albendazole · Animals · Anthelmintics · Child · Cote d'Ivoire · Double-Blind Method · Drug Therapy, Combination · Feces · Female · Humans · Islands · Ivermectin · Laos · Male · Middle Aged · Parasite Egg Count · Tanzania · Trichuriasis · Trichuris · Young Adult
shelves.balance: SPLIT by setting — the setting limbs are never pooled on this shelf. PARTIAL beside pack #2172, which homes the Pemba 2015 four-arm whipworm-combination trial (no albendazole-alone arm); only the combination-versus-albendazole-alone trials are carded here. In the three-country phase 3 trial (1,673 randomised), Trichuris cure on the combination versus albendazole alone was 66% vs 8% in Laos (difference 58 percentage points) and 49% vs 6% on Pemba Island (43 points) — but 14% vs 10% in Côte d'Ivoire (4 points, 95% CI −2 to 10, P = 0.24): the Côte d'Ivoire null is load-bearing and forbids any pooled headline. The fixed-dose coformulation trial (1,001 recruited, ages 5–18) found Trichuris cure of 82.9% (single-dose FDC) and 97.2% (3-day FDC) versus 35.9% on albendazole, with its Strongyloides efficacy sample size NOT met (unproven, printed as such); the Ugandan co-administration trial found 31.3% vs 12.3% cure (difference 18.9 points). Absolute cure rates vary widely by setting and product (12–36% on albendazole alone across trials), so no cross-trial pooled rate is printed. The endpoint throughout is parasitological cure / egg reduction at 14–21 days — no trial measures anaemia, growth, transmission or clinical outcomes. Product naming (clarification exception): the fixed-dose albendazole–ivermectin coformulation is the tested product as the publication names it — an investigational coformulation, not a marketed product at publication; co-administered separate tablets are the programme's other tested form, and current products may differ.

cards.headline: Three-country phase 3 RCT (Hürlimann 2022): combination cure far higher in Laos (66% vs 8%) and on Pemba Island (49% vs 6%) — but NOT in Côte d'Ivoire (14% vs 10%, P = 0.24); the setting limbs are printed separately and never pooled
cards.summary: Three-country phase 3 RCT (Hürlimann 2022): combination cure far higher in Laos (66% vs 8%) and on Pemba Island (49% vs 6%) — but NOT in Côte d'Ivoire (14% vs 10%, P = 0.24); the setting limbs are printed separately and never pooled
cards.type: Phase 3 double-blind parallel-group randomised trial (three countries, limbs reported separately), co-administered ivermectin + albendazole vs albendazole alone
cards.people: 1,673 community members aged 6–60 years infected with Trichuris trichiura (at least 100 eggs per gram of stool) in Côte d'Ivoire, Laos and Pemba Island, Tanzania, randomised double-blind (835 albendazole alone, 838 ivermectin–albendazole) to a single dose of ivermectin 200 µg/kg plus albendazole 400 mg or albendazole 400 mg plus placebo; primary-outcome data were available for 722 albendazole and 733 combination participants.
cards.result: Cure (no eggs in faeces 14–21 days after treatment) on the combination versus albendazole alone: Laos 66% (140 of 213) vs 8% (16 of 194) — difference 58 percentage points (95% CI 50 to 65, P < 0.0001); Pemba Island 49% (140 of 288) vs 6% (18 of 293) — 43 points (36 to 49, P < 0.0001); Côte d'Ivoire 14% (32 of 232) vs 10% (24 of 235) — 4 points (−2 to 10, P = 0.24), i.e. no demonstrated advantage in that setting. No serious adverse events were reported; observed events were mostly mild (95% in the albendazole group, 91% in the combination group) and all transient.
cards.watchOut: The Côte d'Ivoire null is part of the result, not an exception to it: efficacy differed by epidemiological setting for reasons the trial does not resolve, and any single pooled cure-rate headline for this programme misstates the evidence.

cards.headline: Fixed-dose coformulation phase 2/3 RCT (Krolewiecki 2025): Trichuris cure 82.9% (single-dose FDC) and 97.2% (3-day FDC) versus 35.9% on albendazole alone in 1,001 children and adolescents; the Strongyloides efficacy sample size was NOT met
cards.summary: Fixed-dose coformulation phase 2/3 RCT (Krolewiecki 2025): Trichuris cure 82.9% (single-dose FDC) and 97.2% (3-day FDC) versus 35.9% on albendazole alone in 1,001 children and adolescents; the Strongyloides efficacy sample size was NOT met
cards.type: Adaptive phase 2/3 randomised active-controlled superiority trial, fixed-dose albendazole–ivermectin coformulation (×1 or ×3 days) vs albendazole alone
cards.people: 1,001 participants aged 5–18 years in 15 schools in Ethiopia, Kenya and Mozambique infected with Trichuris trichiura (636), hookworm (360) or Strongyloides stercoralis (104; 9% had co-infections), randomised to single-dose fixed-dose combination (FDC×1: albendazole 400 mg plus ivermectin 9 or 18 mg; n = 381), three daily FDC doses (FDC×3; n = 377), or single-dose albendazole 400 mg alone (n = 243); outcome assessors were masked, participants and administrators were not.
cards.result: For Trichuris, cure at day 21 was 97.2% (95% CI 95.2 to 99.3) on FDC×3 and 82.9% (78.2 to 87.5) on FDC×1 versus 35.9% (27.7 to 44.1) on albendazole — absolute differences of 61.3 percentage points (98% CI 50.2 to 71.2) and 47.0 points (34.7 to 58.1). For hookworm, FDC×3 cured 95.0% versus 65.1% on albendazole (difference 29.9 points), while FDC×1 (79.8%) was similar to albendazole. The sample size for efficacy evaluation of Strongyloides was not met, so no Strongyloides efficacy finding is printed. At least one treatment-related adverse event occurred in 14% (albendazole), 20% (FDC×1) and 23% (FDC×3); gastrointestinal symptoms were most common, resolved within 48 hours, and no serious adverse events occurred. The registry record is marked 'terminated', printed as the abstract gives it.
cards.watchOut: The tested product is an investigational fixed-dose coformulation, not a marketed product at publication (clarification naming, not promotion); the Strongyloides limb is unproven (sample size not met) and the registry status 'terminated' is printed as reported.

cards.headline: Ugandan co-administration RCT (Palmeirim 2024): combination cure 31.3% versus 12.3% on albendazole alone (difference 18.9 points, P < 0.004) in schoolchildren aged 6–12 — enrolment N is not stated in the fetched abstract and no N is printed for this trial
cards.summary: Ugandan co-administration RCT (Palmeirim 2024): combination cure 31.3% versus 12.3% on albendazole alone (difference 18.9 points, P < 0.004) in schoolchildren aged 6–12 — enrolment N is not stated in the fetched abstract and no N is printed for this trial
cards.type: Open-label randomised superiority trial, co-administered albendazole + ivermectin vs albendazole alone (enrolment N not documented in the fetched abstract)
cards.people: Children aged 6–12 years positive for Trichuris trichiura in two primary schools in south-western Uganda, randomised 1:1 open-label to a single dose of albendazole alone or co-administered albendazole plus ivermectin, with follow-up samples at 14–21 days. The fetched abstract does not state the total enrolment number, and none is printed here.
cards.result: Cure against Trichuris was 31.3% on the combination versus 12.3% on albendazole alone (difference 18.9 percentage points, 95% CI 6.2 to 31.2, P < 0.004), and egg reduction rates were 91.4% versus 52.7%. Cure of co-infecting Ascaris lumbricoides was 100% on the combination versus 83.9% on albendazole alone. Both treatments showed few, mild and transient treatment-emergent adverse events (22 events in the albendazole arm, 19 in the combination arm).
cards.watchOut: Open-label, two schools, one country — and its absolute cure rates (31.3% vs 12.3%) are far below the coformulation trial's, underlining that absolute rates travel with setting, infection intensity and diagnostics and must not be pooled across this shelf's trials.

cards.headline: Programme report — long-term follow-up (Keller 2021): a follow-up report of the phase 3 programme's trials, labelled as such — the combination's cure and egg-reduction advantages persisted at 6 and 12 months in Laos and on Pemba Island
cards.summary: Programme report — long-term follow-up (Keller 2021): a follow-up report of the phase 3 programme's trials, labelled as such — the combination's cure and egg-reduction advantages persisted at 6 and 12 months in Laos and on Pemba Island
cards.type: Programme report: 6- and 12-month follow-up of the phase 3 programme's randomised trials (same programme as the first card above — not a fourth trial)
cards.people: Participants of the phase 3 programme's double-blind trials in Lao PDR and Pemba Island followed at 6 and 12 months after treatment (Lao PDR: 466 and 413 participants; Pemba Island: 558 and 515), with re-treatment at 6 months for those found helminth-positive, according to their allocated treatment.
cards.result: Against Trichuris, cure rates on ivermectin–albendazole versus albendazole were 65.8% vs 13.4% at 6 months and 74.0% vs 23.4% at 12 months in Lao PDR (differences 52.4 and 50.6 percentage points), and 17.8% vs 1.4% at 6 months and 19.5% vs 3.4% at 12 months on Pemba Island (differences 16.4 and 16.1 points); egg reduction rates were likewise higher on the combination at both timepoints in both settings. Apparent Trichuris reinfection rates at 12 months were considerably higher on Pemba Island than in Lao PDR in the albendazole-alone group.
cards.watchOut: This report follows the Laos and Pemba Island limbs of the phase 3 programme only — the two settings where the combination had already won; it includes no Côte d'Ivoire follow-up and does not soften that setting's null.

cards.headline: Synthesis: PARTIAL slice beside pack #2172 — against albendazole alone, the combination's Trichuris cure advantage is large in Laos, on Pemba Island, in Uganda and in the coformulation trial, and absent in Côte d'Ivoire; the limbs are the answer and are never pooled

cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: Three randomised comparisons against albendazole alone (1,673 randomised in the phase 3 programme; 1,001 recruited in the coformulation trial; the Ugandan trial, whose enrolment N is not stated in its abstract) plus one labelled follow-up report of the phase 3 programme. Cure advantages for the combination ranged from 58 percentage points (Laos) and 43 points (Pemba Island) through 47–61 points for the coformulation in East African schoolchildren and 18.9 points in Uganda — to 4 points and non-significance in Côte d'Ivoire. No serious adverse events occurred in any trial. All endpoints are parasitological (cure / egg reduction at 14–21 days, 6–12 months in the follow-up report); no trial measures anaemia, growth, transmission or clinical outcomes. The Pemba 2015 four-arm trial and its reinfection report stay homed at pack #2172 under the one-home rule and are not re-carded here; a 2025 systematic review of this programme is a cross-point only.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards for each trial's limits; this synthesis adds no new data.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Posaconazole for chronic Chagas disease (FLOOR-RISK — exactly 2 RCTs): durable clearance failed in both — at placebo level in STOP-CHAGAS (13.3% vs 10%), far below benznidazole in CHAGASAZOL
shelves.question: In adults with chronic Trypanosoma cruzi infection, does oral posaconazole — alone or combined with benznidazole — versus benznidazole (or placebo) achieve sustained parasite clearance on real-time PCR after treatment? FLOOR-RISK — exactly 2 randomised trials.
shelves.mesh: Adult · Chagas Disease · Chronic Disease · DNA, Protozoan · Female · Humans · Intention to Treat Analysis · Male · Middle Aged · Nitroimidazoles · Prospective Studies · Transaminases · Treatment Outcome · Triazoles · Trypanocidal Agents · Trypanosoma cruzi
shelves.balance: LIKELY (no difference) from placebo for durable parasite clearance — FLOOR-RISK: exactly 2 randomised trials, printed on the face. Both trials tell the same arc: posaconazole suppressed Trypanosoma cruzi on treatment and failed after it. In CHAGASAZOL (78 patients, intention-to-treat), during follow-up 92% on low-dose and 81% on high-dose posaconazole tested PCR-positive, versus 38% on benznidazole (P < 0.01). In STOP-CHAGAS (120 asymptomatic carriers), persistent negative PCR by day 180 was achieved by 13.3% on posaconazole and 10% on placebo, versus 80% on benznidazole plus posaconazole and 86.7% on benznidazole alone (P < 0.0001); at 360 days both benznidazole arms stood at 96% versus 16–17% on posaconazole/placebo, and adding posaconazole to benznidazole gave no advantage over benznidazole alone. The outcome in both trials is PCR parasite detection — a surrogate, not clinical cure, cardiomyopathy progression or mortality; neither trial measures a clinical endpoint. Populations were chronic carriers without advanced cardiomyopathy, so the results do not speak to established Chagas cardiomyopathy (benznidazole's clinical-outcome question is homed at pack #3309 and is not imported here).

cards.headline: CHAGASAZOL RCT (Molina 2014): posaconazole cleared PCR on treatment but failed durably — during follow-up 92% (low-dose) and 81% (high-dose) tested PCR-positive versus 38% on benznidazole (P < 0.01)
cards.summary: CHAGASAZOL RCT (Molina 2014): posaconazole cleared PCR on treatment but failed durably — during follow-up 92% (low-dose) and 81% (high-dose) tested PCR-positive versus 38% on benznidazole (P < 0.01)
cards.type: Randomised trial (CHAGASAZOL), posaconazole (two doses) vs benznidazole in chronic Chagas disease
cards.people: 78 patients in the intention-to-treat population with chronic Trypanosoma cruzi infection, randomised to posaconazole 400 mg twice daily (high-dose), posaconazole 100 mg twice daily (low-dose), or benznidazole 150 mg twice daily, all for 60 days, with real-time PCR testing during treatment and for 10 months after the end of treatment.
cards.result: During treatment, all patients tested negative for T. cruzi DNA beyond day 14 except 2 low-dose posaconazole patients who tested positive on day 60. During follow-up, in the intention-to-treat analysis, 92% of the low-dose and 81% of the high-dose posaconazole groups tested PCR-positive, versus 38% on benznidazole (P < 0.01 for benznidazole against either posaconazole group); in the per-protocol analysis the figures were 90% and 80% versus 6% (P < 0.001). In the benznidazole group, 5 patients discontinued for severe cutaneous reactions; in the posaconazole groups, 4 patients had aminotransferase levels over 3 times the upper limit of normal, with no discontinuations.
cards.watchOut: The endpoint is PCR parasite detection, not clinical cure: on-treatment negativity in every arm shows how completely this surrogate can mislead when read before follow-up — the trial's answer is its follow-up failure rates.
cards.source: Molina I et al. Randomized trial of posaconazole and benznidazole for chronic Chagas' disease. The New England journal of medicine. 2014. PMID: 24827034. Registry ID: NCT01162967. cards.headline: STOP-CHAGAS RCT (Morillo 2017): posaconazole performed at placebo level for durable clearance — persistent negative PCR by day 180 in 13.3% on posaconazole and 10% on placebo versus 80% (combination) and 86.7% (benznidazole alone)
cards.summary: STOP-CHAGAS RCT (Morillo 2017): posaconazole performed at placebo level for durable clearance — persistent negative PCR by day 180 in 13.3% on posaconazole and 10% on placebo versus 80% (combination) and 86.7% (benznidazole alone)
cards.type: Prospective multicentre randomised placebo-controlled trial (STOP-CHAGAS), posaconazole vs benznidazole vs combination vs placebo in asymptomatic carriers
cards.people: 120 asymptomatic Trypanosoma cruzi carriers from Latin America and Spain, randomised to four groups: posaconazole 400 mg twice daily; benznidazole 200 mg plus placebo; benznidazole 200 mg plus posaconazole 400 mg twice daily; or placebo — with PCR testing at 30, 60, 90, 120, 150, 180 and 360 days.
cards.result: The primary outcome (persistent negative PCR by day 180) was achieved by 13.3% on posaconazole and 10% on placebo, versus 80% on the combination and 86.7% on benznidazole monotherapy (P < 0.0001 vs posaconazole/placebo). On-treatment PCR conversion at 30–60 days was high and similar for posaconazole, the combination and benznidazole (about 89–93%), all superior to placebo — but at 360 days the benznidazole arms (both 96%) stood far above placebo (17%) and posaconazole (16%, P < 0.0001), and no advantage was observed for combined therapy over benznidazole monotherapy. Serious adverse events were rare (6 patients, all in benznidazole-treated patients); permanent discontinuation was reported in 19 patients (31.7%) receiving benznidazole alone or combined.
cards.watchOut: Asymptomatic carriers without advanced cardiomyopathy, and a PCR surrogate endpoint: the trial settles posaconazole's durable-clearance failure in this population and says nothing about clinical outcomes in established Chagas cardiomyopathy.
cards.source: Morillo CA et al. Benznidazole and Posaconazole in Eliminating Parasites in Asymptomatic T. Cruzi Carriers: The STOP-CHAGAS Trial. Journal of the American College of Cardiology. 2017. PMID: 28231946. Registry ID: NCT01377480. cards.type: Fence-position / programme-lineage card — not a trial report and not comparative evidence
cards.people: No patients are carded on this card; it records where the neighbouring Chagas evidence lives in the library.
cards.result: Pack #1709 homes shorter and combination benznidazole regimens (BENDITA) and pack #3309 homes benznidazole in established cardiomyopathy (BENEFIT); neither asks about azole therapy, and neither is re-carded here. Posaconazole prophylaxis and aspergillosis shelves elsewhere in the library are different questions in different populations. This shelf asks only whether posaconazole — alone or combined with benznidazole — achieves sustained PCR parasite clearance in chronic Chagas disease. Exactly 2 randomised trials answer that question (n = 78 and n = 120); there is no third trial to card.

cards.headline: Synthesis: FLOOR-RISK — exactly 2 trials, both durable-clearance failures: posaconazole suppressed parasites on treatment in both and then failed in both, performing at placebo level by day 180–360 in STOP-CHAGAS while benznidazole's clearance persisted
cards.summary: Synthesis: FLOOR-RISK — exactly 2 trials, both durable-clearance failures: posaconazole suppressed parasites on treatment in both and then failed in both, performing at placebo level by day 180–360 in STOP-CHAGAS while benznidazole's clearance persisted
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: CHAGASAZOL (78 patients): follow-up PCR positivity 81–92% on posaconazole versus 38% on benznidazole. STOP-CHAGAS (120 carriers): persistent negative PCR by day 180 in 13.3% on posaconazole versus 10% on placebo and 80–86.7% on the benznidazole arms; at 360 days, 16% versus 96%. Adding posaconazole to benznidazole conferred no advantage over benznidazole alone. Both trials measured PCR parasite detection only — not clinical cure, cardiomyopathy progression or mortality. The shelf's answer is the arc itself: a mechanistically promising azole that is trypanostatic on treatment and ineffective for durable clearance in chronic Chagas disease.

shelves.title: Behavioural pain scales in patients who cannot self-report: BPS separates nociceptive from non-nociceptive procedures (4.9 vs 3.5), CPOT is 'a fair but not excellent tool' (diagnostic odds ratio 11.52 during procedures), and a BPAT score >3.5 classifies severe pain with sensitivity and specificity of only 61.8–75.1%
shelves.question: In critically ill adults who cannot self-report pain — sedated, mechanically ventilated, or brain-injured — how accurately and reliably do the behavioural pain scales (the Behavioral Pain Scale, BPS; the Critical-Care Pain Observation Tool, CPOT; and the 8-item Behavior Pain Assessment Tool, BPAT) detect pain, what scores separate nociceptive from non-nociceptive procedures and rest, and how far does accuracy fall outside the derivation settings?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Facial Expression · Factor Analysis, Statistical · Female · Hemodynamics · Humans · Hypnotics and Sedatives/pharmacology · Intensive Care Units · Male · Middle Aged · Movement · Nonverbal Communication · Observer Variation · Pain Measurement/drug effects,methods · Prospective Studies · Reproducibility of Results · Respiration, Artificial · Critical Illness · Midazolam/pharmacology · Pain Measurement · Critical Care · Pain · Critical Illness/epidemiology,psychology · International Cooperation · Pain/diagnosis,psychology · Psychometrics · Self Report
shelves.balance: MEASUREMENT ACCURACY — reliable observation, fair classification. The BPS derivation (Payen 2001; the scale originators' own report, labelled as such) separated nociceptive from non-nociceptive procedures (4.9 vs 3.5) in 30 patients; an independent validation (Aïssaoui 2005) found inter-rater ICC 0.95 and rest-versus-procedure means of 3.9 vs 6.8, again in 30 patients — the patient N, not the 269–360 observation counts, is the evidence size. The CPOT synthesis (Zhai 2020; 25 articles, 1,920 subjects) gives diagnostic odds ratios of 11.52 during nociceptive procedures and 9.14 at rest or during non-nociceptive procedures (odds ratios, as published), with heterogeneity I² 57.2% and the authors' own verdict: 'a fair but not excellent tool.' The BPAT's international validation (Gélinas 2017; 3,851 patients) is the largest and the most sobering: a cut-point >3.5 classified severe pain (≥8/10) with sensitivity and specificity ranging from 61.8% to 75.1%, and scores correlated only moderately with self-reported intensity (r = 0.54). Three different item sets — never pooled into one accuracy figure. This shelf measures detection, not treatment: whether acting on these scores improves outcomes is a different, unrowed question.

cards.headline: BPS derivation (Payen 2001 — the scale originators' own report): 30 ventilated patients, 269 assessments — BPS 4.9 during nociceptive vs 3.5 during non-nociceptive procedures (P < .01), with comparable pre-procedure values (3.1 vs 3.0)
cards.summary: BPS derivation (Payen 2001 — the scale originators' own report): 30 ventilated patients, 269 assessments — BPS 4.9 during nociceptive vs 3.5 during non-nociceptive procedures (P < .01), with comparable pre-procedure values (3.1 vs 3.0)
cards.type: Behavioural Pain Scale derivation / validation study (originators' report; 30 patients, 269 assessments)
cards.people: 30 mechanically ventilated patients receiving analgesia and sedation in a 10-bed trauma and surgical ICU; 269 paired assessments by nurse / nurse's-aide pairs across non-nociceptive procedures (compression stockings, catheter dressing change; 104 measurements), nociceptive procedures (endotracheal suctioning, mobilisation; 134) and retested nociceptive procedures (31). The BPS sums three 1–4 items: facial expression, upper-limb movements and compliance with mechanical ventilation. Programme-labelled: this is the instrument originators' own derivation / validation report.
cards.result: Nociceptive stimulation produced significantly higher BPS values than non-nociceptive care (4.9 vs 3.5, P < .01), while pre-stimulation values were comparable (3.1 vs 3.0) and Ramsay sedation scores did not differ between groups (Ramsay 4–6). Higher sedation/analgesia dosage trended with lower BPS values and smaller responses. Retested nociceptive procedures gave values similar to the first test at rest (3.2 vs 3.2) and during the procedure (4.4 vs 4.5), with interrater correlations r² = .71 and .50 respectively.
cards.watchOut: Thirty patients is the evidence size — 269 is an observation count from repeated measures in the same 30 people, and prints as such. Derivation by the scale's own authors; the independent check is the next card.
cards.source: Payen JF et al. Assessing pain in critically ill sedated patients by using a behavioral pain scale. Critical care medicine. 2001. PMID: 11801819. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Independent BPS validation (Aïssaoui 2005): 360 observations in 30 patients — inter-rater ICC 0.95, Cronbach alpha 0.72, mean BPS 3.9 ± 1.1 at rest vs 6.8 ± 1.9 during painful procedures
cards.summary: Independent BPS validation (Aïssaoui 2005): 360 observations in 30 patients — inter-rater ICC 0.95, Cronbach alpha 0.72, mean BPS 3.9 ± 1.1 at rest vs 6.8 ± 1.9 during painful procedures
cards.type: Independent validation of the Behavioral Pain Scale (30 patients, 360 observations)
cards.people: 30 critically ill, sedated, mechanically ventilated patients; two assessors scored pain simultaneously with the BPS at rest and during painful procedures, yielding 360 observations; reliability, validity and responsiveness were assessed.
cards.result: The BPS was internally reliable (Cronbach alpha = 0.72) and inter-rater reliability was high (intraclass correlation coefficient 0.95). Scores were significantly higher during painful procedures than at rest (3.9 ± 1.1 vs 6.8 ± 1.9, P < 0.001); principal-components analysis found a large first factor accounting for 65% of the variance in pain expression, and responsiveness effect sizes ranged from 2.2 to 3.4. The authors conclude the BPS can be valid and reliable for measuring pain in noncommunicative ICU patients.
cards.watchOut: Again 30 patients: reliability between two simultaneous observers (ICC 0.95) is not accuracy against the patient's own pain report, which these patients could not give. Rest-versus-procedure separation is responsiveness, not a diagnostic cut-off.
cards.source: Aïssaoui Y et al. Validation of a behavioral pain scale in critically ill, sedated, and mechanically ventilated patients. Anesthesia and analgesia. 2005. PMID: 16244013.
