cards.headline: CPOT synthesis (Zhai 2020): 25 articles, 1,920 subjects — diagnostic odds ratio 11.52 (95% CI 7.42 to 17.87) during nociceptive procedures vs 9.14 at rest / non-nociceptive procedures; the authors call CPOT 'a fair but not excellent tool'
cards.summary: CPOT synthesis (Zhai 2020): 25 articles, 1,920 subjects — diagnostic odds ratio 11.52 (95% CI 7.42 to 17.87) during nociceptive procedures vs 9.14 at rest / non-nociceptive procedures; the authors call CPOT 'a fair but not excellent tool'
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of CPOT diagnostic accuracy (25 articles, 1,920 subjects)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of CPOT diagnostic-accuracy studies (2006 to February 2020): 25 articles involving 1,920 subjects with 3,493 experimental results; study quality appraised with QUADAS-2; most studies were of fair quality.
cards.result: Heterogeneity was high (I² = 57.2%, P < 0.001). Youden index values were 1.56 at a CPOT threshold of two and 1.55 at three, as published. Diagnostic performance depended on the reference standard. The diagnostic odds ratio — an odds ratio, printed as published — was 11.52 (95% CI: 7.42 to 17.87) during nociceptive procedures compared with 9.14 (95% CI: 5.38 to 15.53) at rest or during non-nociceptive procedures. The authors conclude CPOT has moderate diagnostic parameters at a threshold of two or three, 'suggesting that it is a fair but not excellent tool', and call for subgroup research.
cards.watchOut: A diagnostic odds ratio is not a sensitivity/specificity pair and must not be converted into one. The pooled figure carries I² 57.2% heterogeneity and reference-standard dependence — both print beside it.
cards.source: Zhai Y et al. The Diagnostic Accuracy of Critical Care Pain Observation Tool (CPOT) in ICU Patients: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Journal of pain and symptom management. 2020. cards.headline: BPAT international validation (Gélinas 2017): 3,851 patients in 192 ICUs — a cut-point >3.5 classified severe pain (≥8/10) with sensitivity and specificity ranging 61.8% to 75.1%; scores correlated r = 0.54 with self-reported intensity
cards.summary: BPAT international validation (Gélinas 2017): 3,851 patients in 192 ICUs — a cut-point >3.5 classified severe pain (≥8/10) with sensitivity and specificity ranging 61.8% to 75.1%; scores correlated r = 0.54 with self-reported intensity
cards.type: International multicentre validation of the Behavior Pain Assessment Tool (3,851 patients, 4,812 procedures)
cards.people: Validation of the 8-item Behavior Pain Assessment Tool in 192 intensive care units in 28 countries: 4,812 procedures in 3,851 patients, each assessed before and during procedures by 2 raters; patients able to self-report rated pain intensity and distress on 0–10 scales.
cards.result: Interrater reliability of behavioural observations was supported by kappa coefficients from moderate (0.43–0.60) to excellent (>0.60). Most behaviours were more likely during procedures than before and in less sedated patients (discriminant validation). During procedures, mean BPAT scores correlated moderately with mean pain intensity (r = 0.54) and pain distress (r = 0.49) (P < 0.001); all behaviours significantly predicted intensity and distress, accounting for 35% and 29% of their variance. A BPAT cut-point >3.5 classified patients with or without severe pain (≥8/10) with sensitivity and specificity findings ranging from 61.8% to 75.1%. The authors call for research on feasibility and on whether implementation affects outcomes.
cards.watchOut: The largest dataset gives the weakest classification: at >3.5, roughly a quarter to two-fifths of severe-pain classifications are wrong in one direction or the other. Criterion validation rests on the subgroup able to self-report — not the noncommunicative patients the tool is for.
cards.source: Gélinas C et al. The Behavior Pain Assessment Tool for critically ill adults: a validation study in 28 countries. Pain. 2017. PMID: 28362678. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: three different scales, one pattern — behavioural observation is reproducible (BPS ICC 0.95) and rises with nociceptive procedures, but classification of an individual patient's pain is only fair (CPOT 'fair but not excellent'; BPAT severe-pain sensitivity / specificity 61.8–75.1%); the BPS base is two cohorts of 30 patients each
cards.summary: Synthesis: three different scales, one pattern — behavioural observation is reproducible (BPS ICC 0.95) and rises with nociceptive procedures, but classification of an individual patient's pain is only fair (CPOT 'fair but not excellent'; BPAT severe-pain sensitivity / specificity 61.8–75.1%); the BPS base is two cohorts of 30 patients each
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf: the BPS derivation (30 patients, 269 assessments; originators' report, labelled), an independent BPS validation (30 patients, 360 observations), a CPOT meta-analysis (25 articles, 1,920 subjects, 3,493 results) and the BPAT international validation (3,851 patients, 4,812 procedures).
cards.result: The scales are different item sets and their figures are never pooled. What the evidence supports: trained observers agree with each other, and scores separate rest / non-nociceptive care from nociceptive procedures. What it does not support: a precise individual pain diagnosis — the field's own synthesis calls its best-studied tool 'fair but not excellent', and the largest validation classifies severe pain with sensitivity and specificity no better than 61.8–75.1%. Whether scale-guided analgesia improves patient outcomes is not tested by any card here.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards for each report's limits; this synthesis adds no new data.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Pulse oximetry across skin pigmentation: occult hypoxaemia is more common in Black patients (pooled prevalence ratio 1.67, a relative measure) and Hispanic patients (adjusted odds ratio 1.44 and 1.31 in one 151,070-reading cohort); with objectively measured skin tone, readings ran 0.6–1.5 points higher at the darkest tone — but one controlled laboratory study of a signal-extraction device found bias of only −0.20% vs −0.05%
shelves.question: At the bedside and in hospital, how accurate is pulse oximetry across skin pigmentation — how much more common is occult hypoxaemia (arterial saturation <88% while the oximeter reads >92%) in Black, Hispanic and other darker-skinned patients than in White patients, how large is the device bias when skin tone is measured objectively rather than by self-reported race, and what does the one controlled laboratory study of a modern signal-extraction device find against the clinical cohorts?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Ethnicity · Healthcare Disparities/ethnology · Hospitalization/statistics & numerical data · Hypoxia/ethnology,epidemiology,diagnosis,etiology · Oximetry · Prevalence · Racial Groups · Hypoxia/diagnosis,epidemiology · Oxygen · Retrospective Studies · Self Report · Adult · Aged · Female · Male · Middle Aged · COVID-19/diagnosis,therapy,blood · Critical Illness · England/epidemiology · Intensive Care Units · Oximetry/instrumentation,methods,standards · Oxygen Saturation · Skin Pigmentation · State Medicine · Reproducibility of Results · Oximetry/methods · Hypoxia
shelves.balance: MEASUREMENT ACCURACY — a consistent clinical-cohort signal and one discordant laboratory result, kept apart. The synthesis (Parr 2024; 15 studies, 732,505 paired measurements in 207,464 hospitalised patients) finds occult hypoxaemia more common in Black patients than White patients (pooled prevalence ratio 1.67 — a relative measure) and in patients identifying as Asian, Latinx, Indigenous, multiracial or other (1.39). The largest single cohort (Burnett 2022; 151,070 intraoperative paired readings) found occult hypoxaemia in 2.1% of Black, 1.8% of Hispanic and 1.1% of White paired readings, with adjusted odds ratios of 1.44 and 1.31 (odds ratios, as published) — small absolute rates, consistently ordered. The objective-measurement study (Martin 2026, BMJ; 903 ICU patients, skin tone by spectrophotometer) found SpO2 read 0.6–1.5 percentage points higher at the darkest than the lightest tone, with false-negative proportions 5.3–35.3 percentage points higher in darker tones (rate ratio 2.3–7.1, a relative measure). Against all of this, the laboratory study (Barker 2023; 75 healthy volunteers, controlled desaturation, one manufacturer's signal-extraction sensor) found bias of −0.20% in Black and −0.05% in White subjects and no occult hypoxaemia in Black subjects — under conditions its authors state do not reflect clinical care. Race/ethnicity in the clinical cohorts is self-reported; the BMJ study measured skin tone objectively; the two operationalisations are never merged. The field's founding report (Sjoding 2020) is NOT carded: its PubMed record carries an empty abstract and it is excluded under the standing fetch discipline, as recorded on the Synthesis card. No card implies any corrective action improves outcomes — that intervention question is unrowed.

cards.headline: Meta-analysis (Parr 2024): 15 studies, 732,505 paired measurements in 207,464 hospitalised patients — occult hypoxaemia pooled prevalence ratio 1.67 (95% CI 1.47 to 1.90) for Black vs White patients and 1.39 for Asian, Latinx, Indigenous, multiracial or other patients (relative measures)
cards.summary: Meta-analysis (Parr 2024): 15 studies, 732,505 paired measurements in 207,464 hospitalised patients — occult hypoxaemia pooled prevalence ratio 1.67 (95% CI 1.47 to 1.90) for Black vs White patients and 1.39 for Asian, Latinx, Indigenous, multiracial or other patients (relative measures)
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of occult hypoxaemia prevalence by race / ethnicity (15 studies, 207,464 hospitalised patients)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of studies in hospitalised adults reporting occult hypoxaemia prevalence stratified by self-identified race or ethnicity (searches to January 2024): 15 primary studies, 732,505 paired oximetry measurements from 207,464 hospitalised patients; no evidence was found from outpatient settings.
cards.result: Compared with White patients, occult hypoxaemia is likely more common among Black patients (pooled prevalence ratio = 1.67, 95% CI 1.47 to 1.90 — a relative measure) and among patients identifying as Asian, Latinx, Indigenous, multiracial, or other race or ethnicity (pooled prevalence ratio = 1.39, 95% CI 1.19 to 1.64 — a relative measure). Studies reporting clinical outcomes suggest Black patients with undetected hypoxaemia may experience poorer treatment-delivery outcomes than White patients with undetected hypoxaemia. The review notes its included studies rely on self-identified race or ethnicity, which may obscure variability in risk, and that oximeter accuracy could vary substantially between and within patients.
cards.watchOut: Prevalence ratios are relative measures: a ratio of 1.67 on a low absolute base is a small absolute excess — the largest cohort's absolute rates (2.1% vs 1.1%) are on the next card and print beside any use of the ratio. Self-identified race is a proxy for skin pigmentation, not a measurement of it.
cards.source: Parr NJ et al. Racial and Ethnic Disparities in Occult Hypoxemia Prevalence and Clinical Outcomes Among Hospitalized Patients: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis. cards.headline: Intraoperative cohort (Burnett 2022): 151,070 paired readings in 46,253 patients — occult hypoxaemia in 2.1% of Black, 1.8% of Hispanic and 1.1% of White readings; adjusted odds ratios 1.44 (Black) and 1.31 (Hispanic), odds ratios as published
cards.summary: Intraoperative cohort (Burnett 2022): 151,070 paired readings in 46,253 patients — occult hypoxaemia in 2.1% of Black, 1.8% of Hispanic and 1.1% of White readings; adjusted odds ratios 1.44 (Black) and 1.31 (Hispanic), odds ratios as published
cards.type: Retrospective intraoperative cohort, occult hypoxaemia by self-reported race / ethnicity (151,070 paired readings, 46,253 patients)
cards.people: Retrospective cohort from a departmental data warehouse: patients receiving an anaesthetic with at least one arterial blood gas, January 2008 to December 2019; 151,070 paired SaO2–SpO2 readings (70,722 White; 16,011 Black; 21,223 Hispanic; 8,121 Asian; 34,993 Other) from 46,253 unique patients; occult hypoxaemia defined as SaO2 <88% despite SpO2 >92%, analysed within the SpO2 range 92–100%; race/ethnicity self-reported.
cards.result: Occult hypoxaemia prevalence was significantly higher in Black (339 of 16,011 [2.1%]) and Hispanic (383 of 21,223 [1.8%]) versus White (791 of 70,722 [1.1%]) paired readings (P < 0.001 for both). In multivariable analysis, Black (odds ratio, 1.44 [95% CI, 1.11 to 1.87]; P = 0.006) and Hispanic (odds ratio, 1.31 [95% CI, 1.03 to 1.68]; P = 0.031) race/ethnicity were associated with occult hypoxaemia — odds ratios, printed as published. Asian and Other race/ethnicity were not associated with occult hypoxaemia.
cards.watchOut: Percentages are per paired reading, not per patient — patients contribute multiple readings. The absolute excess is about 1 percentage point (2.1% vs 1.1%); the adjusted odds ratios must never be quoted without it.

cards.headline: Objective skin-tone study (Martin 2026, BMJ; EXAKT): 903 critically ill adults, 11,018 paired measurements, skin tone by spectrophotometer — SpO2 read 0.6–1.5 percentage points higher at the darkest tone, and readings >94% despite SaO2 ≤92% were 5.3–35.3 points more frequent in darker tones (rate ratio 2.3–7.1, a relative measure)
cards.summary: Objective skin-tone study (Martin 2026, BMJ; EXAKT): 903 critically ill adults, 11,018 paired measurements, skin tone by spectrophotometer — SpO2 read 0.6–1.5 percentage points higher at the darkest tone, and readings >94% despite SaO2 ≤92% were 5.3–35.3 points more frequent in darker tones (rate ratio 2.3–7.1, a relative measure)
cards.type: Measurement and diagnostic accuracy study of five fingertip oximeters with objectively measured skin tone (903 ICU patients, 11,018 paired measurements; EXAKT)
cards.people: Measurement and diagnostic accuracy study of five fingertip pulse oximeters used in the NHS England COVID Oximetry @home scheme, in 24 English intensive care units (June 2022 to August 2024): 903 critically ill adults with 11,018 paired SpO2–SaO2 measurements against co-oximetry; skin tone (individual typology angle) measured objectively by handheld spectrophotometer.
cards.result: All tested oximeters overestimated at lower SaO2 values and underestimated at higher values. On average, SpO2 readings were 0.6–1.5 percentage points higher for patients with darker skin tone (individual typology angle −44°) than for those with lighter skin tone (46°). At both SpO2 thresholds assessed, false negative rates increased with darker skin tones; the proportion of SpO2 measurements >94% despite a paired SaO2 ≤92% ranged from 5.3 to 35.3 percentage points higher for darker than lighter skin tones (7.6–62.2% vs 1.2–26.9%; rate ratio 2.3–7.1 — a relative measure). False positive rates decreased with darker skin tones.
cards.watchOut: The 5.3–35.3-point range spans five different devices — device performance varies widely, so no single 'oximeter bias' number exists. These are fingertip devices from one national scheme, tested in ICU patients; ward and home performance is inferred, not measured here.
cards.source: Martin DS et al. The impact of skin tone on performance of pulse oximeters used by NHS England COVID Oximetry @home scheme: measurement and diagnostic accuracy study. BMJ (Clinical research ed.). 2026. PMID: 41534914. Registry ID: NCT05481515. cards.headline: Laboratory counterpoint (Barker 2023): controlled desaturation in 75 healthy Black and White volunteers with a Masimo RD SET sensor — bias −0.20 ± 1.40% in Black vs −0.05 ± 1.35% in White subjects, and occult hypoxaemia in 0.2% of White pairs and no Black pairs
cards.summary: Laboratory counterpoint (Barker 2023): controlled desaturation in 75 healthy Black and White volunteers with a Masimo RD SET sensor — bias −0.20 ± 1.40% in Black vs −0.05 ± 1.35% in White subjects, and occult hypoxaemia in 0.2% of White pairs and no Black pairs
cards.type: Controlled laboratory desaturation study of one signal-extraction device in healthy volunteers (75 subjects) — discordant counterpoint
cards.people: Retrospective analysis of healthy volunteers who self-identified as Black or White (75 subjects) undergoing a controlled desaturation protocol (SaO2 decreased from 100% to 70%) with simultaneous SpO2 recorded using Masimo RD SET sensors — one manufacturer's signal-extraction technology, designed and calibrated with nearly equal numbers of dark- and light-skinned subjects. Product named under the clarification exception: the finding is specific to this tested device and sensor.
cards.result: Statistical bias (mean difference) and precision were −0.20 ± 1.40% for Black and −0.05 ± 1.35% for White subjects, with no significant visible differences between races across saturations 70–100%. Occult hypoxaemia (SaO2 <88% when SpO2 = 92–96%) occurred in only 0.2% of White subject data pairs and in no Black subject pairs. The authors conclude there were no clinically significant differences in bias between healthy Black and White subjects — and state in the record itself that these laboratory results were obtained in well-controlled experimental conditions in healthy volunteers, not reflecting actual clinical conditions or patients.
cards.watchOut: Device-specific, healthy-volunteer, controlled-desaturation evidence: it answers whether THIS sensor shows bias under laboratory conditions, not whether clinical oximetry is unbiased in sick patients. It is carded as the counterpoint and is never pooled with the clinical cohorts.
cards.source: Barker SJ et al. Racial effects on Masimo pulse oximetry: a laboratory study. Journal of clinical monitoring and computing. 2023. PMID: 36370242. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: Humans · Retrospective Studies · Reproducibility of Results · Oximetry/methods · Oxygen · Hypoxia

cards.headline: Synthesis: clinical cohorts consistently find more occult hypoxaemia in darker-skinned patients (pooled prevalence ratio 1.67; absolute rates 2.1% vs 1.1% in the largest cohort; objectively measured bias 0.6–1.5 points) — the single laboratory study of one device in healthy volunteers does not, and the founding 2020 report is excluded for an empty abstract, recorded here

cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf: a meta-analysis (15 studies, 207,464 hospitalised patients), a retrospective intraoperative cohort (46,253 patients, 151,070 paired readings), an objective-skin-tone accuracy study (903 ICU patients, 11,018 paired measurements) and a controlled laboratory study (75 healthy volunteers). Excluded anchor, recorded per the standing fetch discipline: the field's founding report (Sjoding 2020, NEJM letter) was fetched this session and its PubMed record carries an empty abstract, so it is refused as an anchor and appears in no source line.
cards.result: Two measurement traditions must not be merged: self-reported race/ethnicity (the synthesis and the intraoperative cohort) and spectrophotometer-measured skin tone (the BMJ study) point the same way by different operationalisations. Absolute excesses are small (about 1 percentage point of paired readings in the largest cohort) while relative measures (prevalence ratio 1.67; rate ratio 2.3–7.1) are larger — both print together. The laboratory result is not a refutation of the clinical cohorts: different device, different subjects, different conditions, by its authors' own caveat.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards for each report's limits; this synthesis adds no new data.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Sitamaquine for visceral leishmaniasis (3 randomised phase II reports): day-180 cure 87% in India and 83% in Kenya in uncontrolled dose-ranging trials, 85% vs 95% on amphotericin B in the one comparative trial — and recurrent renal harm; programme abandoned
shelves.question: In patients with visceral leishmaniasis in India and Kenya, does oral sitamaquine (dose-ranging 1.5–3.0 mg/kg/day for 21–28 days) versus another dose, or versus intravenous amphotericin B, achieve clinical cure at 6 months, and what renal toxicity appears?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Adolescent · Adult · Aminoquinolines/administration & dosage,adverse effects,therapeutic use · Antiprotozoal Agents/administration & dosage,adverse effects,therapeutic use · Child · Drug Administration Schedule · Female · Humans · India · Leishmaniasis, Visceral/drug therapy,pathology · Male · Middle Aged · Treatment Outcome · Aged · Animals · Child, Preschool · Cohort Studies · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Kenya · Leishmania donovani/drug effects · Leishmaniasis, Visceral/drug therapy,parasitology · Aminoquinolines/pharmacokinetics · Amphotericin B/pharmacokinetics · Antiprotozoal Agents/pharmacokinetics · Area Under Curve · Cross-Over Studies · Fasting · Food · Food-Drug Interactions · Half-Life · Prospective Studies · Young Adult
shelves.balance: Three randomised phase II reports, and the design limits lead: two of the three trials compare sitamaquine doses with each other, not with a standard treatment, so their day-180 cure rates (87% overall in India, 92 of 106 intention-to-treat; 83% overall in Kenya, 79 of 95) are uncontrolled absolutes with no dose-response in either trial. The only comparative readout is the 61-patient Bihar trial: final clinical cure at day 180 was 85% on sitamaquine vs 95% on intravenous amphotericin B (no p-value for the comparison printed in the abstract). The harm limb is load-bearing: nephrotic syndrome in 3% (3 of 120) and glomerulonephritis in 2% (2 of 120) in the Indian trial, and a severe renal adverse event at each of the two highest doses in the Kenyan trial — renal injury recurred across the programme and is a named reason it was abandoned. Sitamaquine is an investigational oral 8-aminoquinoline that was never marketed — stated plainly. Populations were Indian and Kenyan Leishmania donovani patients (mean ages 21 and 16 years in the two dose-ranging trials); no HIV-co-infected or relapsed-patient data.

cards.headline: Indian dose-ranging trial (Jha 2005): day-180 final cure 87% overall (92 of 106 intention-to-treat) across four sitamaquine doses with NO dose-response (81% / 89% / 100% / 80%); nephrotic syndrome 3% and glomerulonephritis 2%
cards.summary: Indian dose-ranging trial (Jha 2005): day-180 final cure 87% overall (92 of 106 intention-to-treat) across four sitamaquine doses with NO dose-response (81% / 89% / 100% / 80%); nephrotic syndrome 3% and glomerulonephritis 2%
cards.type: Randomised open-label phase II dose-ranging trial, sitamaquine in Indian visceral leishmaniasis — no comparator arm
cards.people: 120 Indian patients with visceral leishmaniasis, aged 5–64 years (mean 21.2 years), randomised in an open-label multicentre study to sitamaquine 1.5, 1.75, 2.0 or 2.5 mg/kg/day for 28 days. There was no comparator arm.
cards.result: At day 180, final cure (the primary efficacy outcome) was achieved in 92 of 106 (87%) patients overall in the intention-to-treat population, and in 25 of 31 (81%), 24 of 27 (89%), 23 of 23 (100%) and 20 of 25 (80%) at the ascending doses — no dose-response. The most common adverse events were vomiting (8%), dyspepsia (8%) and cyanosis (3%). Nephrotic syndrome occurred in 3 of 120 (3%) and glomerulonephritis in 2 of 120 (2%).
cards.watchOut: The cure rates are uncontrolled absolutes: with no standard-treatment or placebo arm, this trial cannot show how sitamaquine compares with anything. The 100% cell is 23 of 23 patients at one dose, printed with its denominator.
cards.source: Jha TK et al. A phase II dose-ranging study of sitamaquine for the treatment of visceral leishmaniasis in India. The American journal of tropical medicine and hygiene. 2005. cards.headline: Kenyan dose-increasing trial (Wasunna 2005): day-180 cure 83% overall (79 of 95) across four doses, again with no dose-response (92% / 80% / 82% / 91%); a severe renal adverse event at each of the two highest doses
cards.summary: Kenyan dose-increasing trial (Wasunna 2005): day-180 cure 83% overall (79 of 95) across four doses, again with no dose-response (92% / 80% / 82% / 91%); a severe renal adverse event at each of the two highest doses
cards.type: Open-label phase II dose-increasing study, sitamaquine in Kenyan visceral leishmaniasis — no comparator arm
cards.people: 97 Kenyan patients with visceral leishmaniasis caused by Leishmania donovani (mean age 15.9 years, range 5–47) treated in an open-label dose-increasing study with sitamaquine daily for 28 days at 1.75 (n = 12), 2.0 (n = 61), 2.5 (n = 12) or 3.0 (n = 12) mg/kg/day. There was no comparator arm.
cards.result: Cure (absence of parasites on splenic aspirate) at day 180 in the intention-to-treat population was achieved in 79 of 95 (83%) patients overall, and in 11 of 12 (92%), 49 of 61 (80%), 9 of 11 (82%) and 10 of 11 (91%) at the ascending doses — no dose-response. The most frequent adverse events were abdominal pain (12 of 97) and headache (11 of 97); one patient in each of the 2.5 and 3.0 mg/kg/day groups had a severe renal adverse event. The authors state the effects of sitamaquine on the kidney need further investigation.
cards.watchOut: Uncontrolled absolutes again, in a young population (mean age 15.9 years). The renal events at the two highest doses are the programme's recurring harm signal, not an incidental finding.
cards.source: Wasunna MK et al. A phase II dose-increasing study of sitamaquine for the treatment of visceral leishmaniasis in Kenya. The American journal of tropical medicine and hygiene. 2005. PMID: 16282296. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Bihar food-effect trial (Sundar 2011): the programme's only comparative readout — final clinical cure at day 180 was 85% on sitamaquine vs 95% on intravenous amphotericin B; on-therapy adverse events in 10% on sitamaquine vs 85% on amphotericin B
cards.summary: Bihar food-effect trial (Sundar 2011): the programme's only comparative readout — final clinical cure at day 180 was 85% on sitamaquine vs 95% on intravenous amphotericin B; on-therapy adverse events in 10% on sitamaquine vs 85% on amphotericin B
cards.type: Randomised open-label pharmacokinetic (food-effect) study with an amphotericin B comparator arm, sitamaquine in Bihar visceral leishmaniasis
cards.people: 61 patients in Bihar, India, with visceral leishmaniasis, randomised to oral sitamaquine 2 mg/kg/day for 21 days across four fed/fasted schedules (n = 41) or intravenous amphotericin B 1 mg/kg every other day for 30 days (n = 20). The study's primary purpose was the effect of food on sitamaquine pharmacokinetics; no significant food effect was found.
cards.result: Final clinical cure at day 180 was 85% (95% CI 70.8–94.4%) for sitamaquine and 95% (95% CI 75.1–99.9) for amphotericin B — no p-value for the comparison is printed in the abstract. On-therapy adverse events were observed in 4 of 41 (10%) patients on sitamaquine and 17 of 20 (85%) on amphotericin B.
cards.watchOut: A 61-patient pharmacokinetic study is a thin comparative base: its confidence intervals are wide and overlap, and it was not designed as an efficacy non-inferiority trial. The adverse-event contrast (10% vs 85%) compares on-therapy events only and does not capture sitamaquine's renal signal, which appeared in the larger dose-ranging trials.
cards.source: Sundar S et al. Pharmacokinetics of oral sitamaquine taken with or without food and safety and efficacy for treatment of visceral leishmaniais: a randomized study in Bihar, India. The American journal of tropical medicine and hygiene. 2011. PMID: 21633025. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: 3 randomised phase II reports — sitamaquine cured 87% (India) and 83% (Kenya) of patients at day 180 in dose-ranging trials with no comparator arm and no dose-response, and 85% vs 95% on amphotericin B in the one 61-patient comparative trial; renal harm (nephrotic syndrome, glomerulonephritis, severe renal events at higher doses) recurred across the programme, which was abandoned
cards.summary: Synthesis: 3 randomised phase II reports — sitamaquine cured 87% (India) and 83% (Kenya) of patients at day 180 in dose-ranging trials with no comparator arm and no dose-response, and 85% vs 95% on amphotericin B in the one 61-patient comparative trial; renal harm (nephrotic syndrome, glomerulonephritis, severe renal events at higher doses) recurred across the programme, which was abandoned
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: The honest summary is an orally active drug with high uncontrolled cure rates whose comparative evidence is one small pharmacokinetic trial reading numerically below amphotericin B, and whose kidney toxicity ended the programme. Sitamaquine was never marketed.
cards.watchOut: Never print the 83–87% cure rates without the uncontrolled-design flag beside them, and never average the renal harm away: it is in the balance, not a footnote.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Ganaplacide (KAF156) plus lumefantrine solid dispersion formulation for uncomplicated falciparum malaria (one programme: 2 patient trials plus a labelled challenge study): day-29 PCR-corrected response 92–100% in dose-finding, and non-inferior to artemether–lumefantrine in children in KALUMI (99% vs 99%)
shelves.question: In patients with uncomplicated Plasmodium falciparum malaria, does the novel combination ganaplacide plus lumefantrine solid dispersion formulation versus artemether–lumefantrine achieve PCR-corrected adequate clinical and parasitological response at day 29, and is it non-inferior?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Adolescent · Child · Humans · Lumefantrine/pharmacology,therapeutic use · Artemisinins · Fluorenes/therapeutic use,pharmacology · Ethanolamines/therapeutic use,pharmacology · Antimalarials · Malaria, Falciparum/drug therapy,parasitology · Artemether/pharmacology,therapeutic use · Malaria/drug therapy · Drug Combinations · Plasmodium falciparum · Treatment Outcome · Imidazoles · Piperazines · Animals · Antimalarials/therapeutic use · Imidazoles/therapeutic use · Malaria, Falciparum/drug therapy,prevention & control
shelves.balance: One programme only — 2 patient trials plus a labelled controlled-human-infection (challenge) study — stated in exactly those terms. The phase 2 dose-finding trial (337 patients in part A, 175 in part B) found day-29 PCR-corrected response of 92–100% across the ganaplacide–lumefantrine regimens vs 100% on artemether–lumefantrine in the per-protocol set, with only the 3-day regimen meeting the prespecified endpoint in children in part B. KALUMI, the phase 2 non-inferiority trial in children, met non-inferiority in its main part (220 children enrolled, 110 per arm): day-29 PCR-corrected response 99% (97 of 98) on ganaplacide–lumefantrine vs 99% (98 of 99) on artemether–lumefantrine, treatment difference −0.0% (95% CI −2.9 to 2.8), the lower limit above the −10% margin. Design flags on the face: both patient trials are open-label; KALUMI is phase 2, not phase 3, and its main-part population is children under 12 in five African countries — efficacy in adults beyond the dose-finding trial and in Southeast Asian artemisinin-resistant settings is not established by this base. Ganaplacide (development code KAF156) plus lumefantrine solid dispersion formulation is an investigational combination that is not a marketed product — named as the publications give it under the clarification exception. Vomiting (29% vs 11%) and hypokalaemia (25% vs 15%) were more common on ganaplacide–lumefantrine in KALUMI.

cards.headline: Phase 2 dose-finding trial (Ogutu 2023): day-29 PCR-corrected response 92–100% across seven ganaplacide–lumefantrine regimens vs 100% on artemether–lumefantrine (per-protocol, part A); in children (part B) only the 3-day regimen met the prespecified primary endpoint (95% vs 96% on control)
cards.summary: Phase 2 dose-finding trial (Ogutu 2023): day-29 PCR-corrected response 92–100% across seven ganaplacide–lumefantrine regimens vs 100% on artemether–lumefantrine (per-protocol, part A); in children (part B) only the 3-day regimen met the prespecified primary endpoint (95% vs 96% on control)
cards.type: Open-label randomised controlled phase 2 dose-finding trial, ganaplacide + lumefantrine-SDF in uncomplicated falciparum malaria
cards.people: Open-label randomised phase 2 trial at 13 centres in 10 African and Asian countries in uncomplicated Plasmodium falciparum malaria: part A, 337 adults and adolescents (≥12 years) across seven ganaplacide–lumefantrine regimens vs artemether–lumefantrine; part B, 175 children (≥2 to <12 years) across four groups. A 12-patient run-in cohort preceded part A.
cards.result: In part A, the lower limit of the 95% CI for day-29 PCR-corrected adequate clinical and parasitological response was above the 80% null threshold for all regimens: 92% (46 of 50), 98% (47 of 48) and 98% (42 of 43) for ganaplacide 400 mg plus lumefantrine-SDF 960 mg for 1, 2 or 3 days; 94% (45 of 48) for single-dose ganaplacide 800 mg; 100% (47 of 47) and 100% (44 of 44) for the 480 mg lumefantrine-SDF regimens; and 100% (25 of 25) on artemether–lumefantrine. In part B, only the 3-day regimen met the prespecified primary endpoint (38 of 40 [95%] vs 21 of 22 [96%] on control). No patients died. Ganaplacide 400 mg plus lumefantrine-SDF 960 mg once daily for 3 days was identified as the optimal regimen.
cards.watchOut: Open-label, per-protocol primary analysis, and a small control arm (25 of 25 responders in part A) — the response percentages are dose-finding readings against an 80% null threshold, not a powered comparison with artemether–lumefantrine. That comparison is KALUMI's job, below.
cards.source: Ogutu B et al. Ganaplacide (KAF156) plus lumefantrine solid dispersion formulation combination for uncomplicated Plasmodium falciparum malaria: an open-label, multicentre, parallel-group, randomised, controlled, phase 2 trial. The Lancet. Infectious diseases. 2023. PMID: 37327809. Registry ID: NCT03167242. cards.headline: KALUMI (Fofana 2026): non-inferiority MET in children — day-29 PCR-corrected response 99% (97 of 98) on ganaplacide–lumefantrine vs 99% (98 of 99) on artemether–lumefantrine, treatment difference −0.0% (95% CI −2.9 to 2.8), lower limit above the −10% margin; vomiting 29% vs 11%
cards.summary: KALUMI (Fofana 2026): non-inferiority MET in children — day-29 PCR-corrected response 99% (97 of 98) on ganaplacide–lumefantrine vs 99% (98 of 99) on artemether–lumefantrine, treatment difference −0.0% (95% CI −2.9 to 2.8), lower limit above the −10% margin; vomiting 29% vs 11%
cards.type: Open-label randomised adaptive phase 2 non-inferiority trial (KALUMI), ganaplacide + lumefantrine-SDF in children with uncomplicated falciparum malaria
cards.people: Open-label randomised adaptive phase 2 non-inferiority trial at ten clinics and hospitals in Burkina Faso, Mali, Côte d'Ivoire, Gabon and DR Congo. Main part: 220 children enrolled (110 per arm; ages 6 months to <12 years) receiving ganaplacide 400 mg plus lumefantrine-SDF 480 mg once daily for 3 days with a light meal, or artemether–lumefantrine for 3 days. Run-in cohorts (75 adolescents) assessed food effects and dose selection and are not part of the main-part efficacy count.
cards.result: For day-29 PCR-corrected adequate clinical and parasitological response in the per-protocol population, response was 97 of 98 (99% [95% CI 94 to 100]) on ganaplacide plus lumefantrine-SDF and 98 of 99 (99% [95% CI 95 to 100]) on artemether–lumefantrine (treatment difference −0.0% [95% CI −2.9 to 2.8]), with the lower limit of the 95% CI above −10% — non-inferiority met. The most common adverse events were vomiting (32 of 110 [29%] vs 12 of 110 [11%]) and hypokalaemia (27 [25%] vs 16 [15%]).
cards.watchOut: A phase 2 non-inferiority result in African children under 12, analysed per-protocol — not a phase 3 result, and not evidence in adults or in Southeast Asian artemisinin-resistant settings. This record carries no MeSH terms, and its source line says so.
cards.source: Fofana B et al. The Lancet. Infectious diseases. 2026. PMID: 42994442. Registry ID: NCT04546633. MeSH: none in the record

cards.headline: Challenge study (Kublin 2021) — LABELLED SUPPORT, never a patient trial: KAF156 (ganaplacide) given before or after controlled human malaria infection protected all participants at doses of 100–800 mg, and none on placebo in part 1
cards.summary: Challenge study (Kublin 2021) — LABELLED SUPPORT, never a patient trial: KAF156 (ganaplacide) given before or after controlled human malaria infection protected all participants at doses of 100–800 mg, and none on placebo in part 1
cards.type: Controlled human malaria infection (challenge) study, KAF156 causal prophylaxis in healthy volunteers — labelled support only
cards.people: Healthy malaria-naive volunteers in a controlled human malaria infection model: part 1, a single 800 mg dose of KAF156 or placebo 3 hours before infection by mosquito bite; part 2, single KAF156 doses of 800, 300, 100, 50 or 20 mg given 21 hours after infection. Each cohort enrolled 7–14 participants to KAF156 and up to 4 to placebo.
cards.result: In part 1, all KAF156-treated participants and none of those randomised to placebo were protected against malaria infection. In part 2, all participants on placebo or 20 mg KAF156 developed infection; 50 mg protected 3 of 14, and 800, 300 and 100 mg protected all subjects. KAF156 was safe and well tolerated at all dose levels; two serious adverse events resolved without sequelae and neither was considered related.
cards.watchOut: A prophylaxis challenge study in healthy volunteers asks a different question from treating patients with malaria — it is carded as programme support only and is never counted as a third patient trial.

shelves.balance: One programme only — 3 trials — stated in exactly those terms. The arc is the answer: ferroquine plus artesunate cleared parasites rapidly with no recurrence to day 28 in the small safety-focused phase 2a trial (72 adult men), and in the phase 2 dose-ranging trial the three artesunate combination doses met non-inferiority against a 90% reference cure rate (day-28 PCR-corrected cure 97%, 99% and 99%, vs 79% on ferroquine monotherapy). The programme's decisive test then failed: in the single-dose phase 2b trial of artefenomel 800 mg plus ferroquine, no treatment arm met the target efficacy criterion (lower 95% confidence limit >90% for PCR-adjusted response at day 28); response ranged from 78.4% to 91.7% across doses in African children ≤5 years and only 20–40% in Vietnamese patients. Safety flags from the early trials: grade-1 alanine-aminotransferase rises with a dose trend, and one QTcF prolongation >60 ms on the lowest ferroquine dose in phase 2a. Ferroquine (development code SSR97193) is an investigational drug that was never marketed — stated plainly under the clarification exception. Populations differ by trial and are labelled per card: adult men only in phase 2a; the phase 2b primary population is African children ≤5 years.

cards.headline: Phase 2a dose-ranging trial (Supan 2017): safety-focused — parasitaemia cleared quickly in all arms with no recurrence through day 28 in 72 adult men; grade-1 ALT rises with a dose trend from 400 mg, two grade-2 ALT events, and one QTcF prolongation >60 ms on the lowest ferroquine dose
cards.summary: Phase 2a dose-ranging trial (Supan 2017): safety-focused — parasitaemia cleared quickly in all arms with no recurrence through day 28 in 72 adult men; grade-1 ALT rises with a dose trend from 400 mg, two grade-2 ALT events, and one QTcF prolongation >60 ms on the lowest ferroquine dose
cards.type: Phase 2a open-label randomised safety-focused dose-ranging study, ferroquine (SSR97193) + artesunate in African adult men
cards.people: 72 adult men with symptomatic uncomplicated Plasmodium falciparum monoinfection at three African hospitals (two in Gabon, one in Kenya), randomised to ferroquine 100, 200, 400 or 600 mg plus artesunate 200 mg/day, or amodiaquine 612 mg/day plus artesunate, daily for 3 days (12 patients per ferroquine dose; 6 per amodiaquine comparator group).
cards.result: Ferroquine plus artesunate showed generally mild (grade 1) increases in alanine aminotransferase with a dose trend starting at 400 mg; two grade-2 ALT events occurred (200 mg: 3.8× the upper limit of normal at day 7; 600 mg: 3.3× at day 14), neither with increased bilirubin. One patient on ferroquine 100 mg plus artesunate was withdrawn after one dose for QTcF prolongation >60 ms over baseline. Parasitaemias in all patients cleared quickly, with no recurrence through day 28.
cards.watchOut: A safety-first report in adult men only, with 12 patients per ferroquine dose — its clearance finding is a signal, not an efficacy estimate, and its liver and cardiac flags are why the authors say hepatic and cardiac profiles should be monitored closely in future trials.

cards.headline: Phase 2 dose-ranging trial (Held 2015): all three ferroquine + artesunate doses met non-inferiority against a 90% reference cure rate — day-28 PCR-corrected cure 97% (2 mg/kg), 99% (4 mg/kg) and 99% (6 mg/kg), vs 79% on ferroquine monotherapy
cards.summary: Phase 2 dose-ranging trial (Held 2015): all three ferroquine + artesunate doses met non-inferiority against a 90% reference cure rate — day-28 PCR-corrected cure 97% (2 mg/kg), 99% (4 mg/kg) and 99% (6 mg/kg), vs 79% on ferroquine monotherapy
cards.type: Phase 2 multicentre randomised double-blind dose-ranging non-inferiority trial, ferroquine + artesunate in African adults and children
cards.people: 326 patients randomised at eight African hospitals in two sequential cohorts (adults and adolescents; children aged 2–13 years) with acute Plasmodium falciparum monoinfection, to artesunate 4 mg/kg/day plus ferroquine 2, 4 or 6 mg/kg, or ferroquine monotherapy 4 mg/kg, once daily for 3 days; follow-up to day 63. 284 patients (87%) were available for per-protocol analyses.
cards.result: At day 28, PCR-confirmed cure was 68 of 70 (97% [95% CI 90–100]) on ferroquine 2 mg/kg plus artesunate, 73 of 74 (99% [93–100]) on 4 mg/kg, 71 of 72 (99% [93–100]) on 6 mg/kg, and 54 of 68 (79% [68–88]) on ferroquine 4 mg/kg monotherapy. The three combination dose groups met the non-inferiority hypothesis (against a 90% reference cure rate, 10% margin). The most common adverse events were headache in cohort 1 (30 of 162) and worsening malaria in cohort 2 (23 of 164), similar between groups.
cards.watchOut: Non-inferiority here is against a fixed 90% reference cure rate, not against a concurrent standard combination arm — and the monotherapy arm's 79% shows the artesunate partner is doing necessary work. Per-protocol analysis of 284 of 326 randomised.
cards.source: Held J et al. cards.headline: Single-dose phase 2b trial (Adoke 2021): NO treatment arm met the target efficacy criterion — PCR-adjusted response at day 28 ranged 78.4–91.7% across ferroquine doses in African children ≤5 years and only 20–40% in Vietnamese patients; vomiting within 6 h in 24.6%
cards.summary: Single-dose phase 2b trial (Adoke 2021): NO treatment arm met the target efficacy criterion — PCR-adjusted response at day 28 ranged 78.4–91.7% across ferroquine doses in African children ≤5 years and only 20–40% in Vietnamese patients; vomiting within 6 h in 24.6%
cards.type: Randomised double-blind phase 2b trial, single-dose artefenomel + ferroquine in uncomplicated falciparum malaria
cards.people: 373 patients treated (289 African children ≤5 years [77.5%], 64 African patients >5 years, 20 Asian patients) from six African countries and Vietnam, randomised to a single dose of artefenomel 800 mg plus ferroquine 400, 600, 900 or 1,200 mg; follow-up 63 days. The primary efficacy endpoint was PCR-adjusted adequate clinical and parasitological response at day 28 in the per-protocol set of African patients ≤5 years.
cards.result: None of the treatment arms met the target efficacy criterion (lower limit of the 95% CI >90%). PCR-adjusted response at day 28 in the per-protocol set ranged from 78.4% (95% CI 64.7–88.7%) to 91.7% (81.6–97.2%) across the 400 mg to 1,200 mg ferroquine doses. Efficacy rates were low in Vietnamese patients, ranging from 20 to 40%. A clear exposure–response relationship was found, with higher day-7 concentrations of both drugs giving higher efficacy; vomiting within 6 hours of artefenomel administration was common (24.6%) and associated with lower drug exposures. Kelch-13 mutations were detected in 10 of 272 African patients and in 18 of 20 Asian patients (all C580Y). The authors conclude efficacy was suboptimal in African children ≤5 years, the population of interest.
cards.watchOut: This is the programme's headline, not a footnote: the single-dose concept failed its own prespecified target in its primary population, and the Vietnamese results (20–40%, in patients whose isolates almost all carried the C580Y kelch-13 mutation) must never be averaged into the African figures.

shelves.title: Richmond Agitation-Sedation Scale (RASS): inter-rater reliability was high at derivation (r = 0.956), in independent JAMA validation (weighted kappa 0.91, vs Glasgow Coma Scale 0.64) and in Swedish translation (kappa 0.86, N = 15)
shelves.question: In critically ill adults, how reliable and valid is the Richmond Agitation-Sedation Scale (RASS) as the bedside measure of sedation and agitation — what inter-rater reliability did its derivation study and the independent JAMA validation deliver, how does it compare with the Glasgow Coma Scale and the Ramsay scale head-to-head, and does reliability survive translation?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Procedural Sedation · Female · Humans · Intensive Care Units · Male · Middle Aged · Point-of-Care Systems · Psychomotor Agitation · Reproducibility of Results · Respiration, Artificial · Statistics as Topic · Urban Health · Virginia · Weights and Measures
shelves.balance: MEASUREMENT PERFORMANCE — high inter-rater reliability in every setting tested, and that is all this shelf claims. The derivation study (the scale originators' own report, Richmond) found inter-rater r = 0.956 (kappa 0.73) across 192 encounters and, after implementation, r = 0.964 (kappa 0.80) between a nurse educator and 27 trained bedside nurses. The independent Vanderbilt validation in JAMA found RASS weighted kappa 0.91 — equal to the Ramsay scale's 0.94 and superior to the Glasgow Coma Scale's 0.64 — with criterion and construct validity in 411 paired observations. A Swedish translation kept weighted kappa 0.86, but in only 15 patients (40 paired assessments). This is a measurement shelf: no card claims that RASS-guided sedation protocols improve outcomes.

cards.summary: RASS derivation (Sessler 2002 — the scale originators' own report, Richmond): inter-rater reliability r = 0.956 (kappa 0.73) across 192 ICU encounters rated by five investigators, robust across ICU types and by ventilation and sedation status, and r = 0.93 against a visual-analogue reference; after implementation, nurse educator vs 27 trained bedside nurses r = 0.964 (kappa 0.80) in 101 encounters
cards.type: Derivation and validation study — the RASS originators' own report (programme-labelled), adult ICU patients
cards.people: Adult ICU patients in two phases at the scale's home centre (Richmond): phase 1, 192 patient encounters rated by five investigators (two physicians, two nurses, one pharmacist) across medical, surgical, cardiac-surgery, coronary and neuroscience ICUs; phase 2, 101 encounters rated by a nurse educator and 27 RASS-trained bedside nurses after implementation in the medical ICU.
cards.result: Phase 1 inter-rater reliability was r = 0.956 (lower 90% confidence limit 0.948; kappa 0.73, 95% CI 0.71 to 0.75), with subgroup r = 0.922–0.983 (kappa 0.64–0.82) by ICU type, ventilation and sedation status. RASS correlated r = 0.93 with a visual-analogue scale anchored by 'combative' and 'unresponsive'. Phase 2 reliability was r = 0.964 (kappa 0.80, 95% CI 0.69 to 0.90); correlations with the Ramsay scale (r = −0.78) and the Sedation Agitation Scale (r = 0.78) supported validity.
cards.watchOut: This is the instrument's own derivation report from its home centre — labelled as such, and never merged with the independent-centre figures on the next card. Reliability and validity of a score are not evidence that sedation protocols built on it improve outcomes.
cards.source: Sessler et al. The Richmond Agitation-Sedation Scale: validity and reliability in adult intensive care unit patients. American journal of respiratory and critical care medicine. 2002. PMID: 12421743. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Independent JAMA validation (Ely 2003, Vanderbilt): RASS inter-rater weighted kappa 0.91 and Ramsay 0.94, both superior to the Glasgow Coma Scale's 0.64 (P<.001 for both comparisons) in 290 paired observations; criterion validity tested in 411 paired observations in ventilated patients
cards.summary: Independent JAMA validation (Ely 2003, Vanderbilt): RASS inter-rater weighted kappa 0.91 and Ramsay 0.94, both superior to the Glasgow Coma Scale's 0.64 (P<.001 for both comparisons) in 290 paired observations; criterion validity tested in 411 paired observations in ventilated patients
cards.type: Prospective independent-centre validation cohort, RASS vs Ramsay scale and Glasgow Coma Scale in ICU patients
cards.people: Adult medical and coronary ICU patients at a university medical centre independent of the derivation centre: 38 medical ICU patients for reliability testing (46% mechanically ventilated) and an independent cohort of 275 mechanically ventilated patients for validity testing.
cards.result: In 290 paired observations by nurses, inter-rater reliability was weighted kappa 0.91 for RASS and 0.94 for the Ramsay Scale, both superior to the Glasgow Coma Scale's 0.64 (P<.001 for both comparisons). In 411 paired observations in the first 96 validation patients, RASS distinguished levels of consciousness (P<.001) and tracked within-patient change over time (P<.001); construct validity included correlation with an attention screening examination (r = 0.78), GCS scores (r = 0.91) and bispectral electroencephalography (r = 0.63), and 92% of 26 surveyed critical care nurses agreed or strongly agreed with the RASS scoring scheme.
cards.watchOut: The validity cohort was mechanically ventilated patients only — the derivation study, not this one, carries the non-ventilated limb. Kappa 0.91 (RASS) and 0.94 (Ramsay) are close; the head-to-head win is over the Glasgow Coma Scale, not over Ramsay.
cards.source: Ely et al. Monitoring sedation status over time in ICU patients: reliability and validity of the Richmond Agitation-Sedation Scale (RASS). JAMA. 2003. PMID: 12799407. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Swedish translation (Almgren 2010): the translated RASS kept good inter-rater reliability — weighted kappa 0.86 — but in only 15 mechanically ventilated sedated patients (40 paired assessments), an N that prints on the face
cards.summary: Swedish translation (Almgren 2010): the translated RASS kept good inter-rater reliability — weighted kappa 0.86 — but in only 15 mechanically ventilated sedated patients (40 paired assessments), an N that prints on the face
cards.type: Translation and reliability study, Swedish RASS in a general ICU (small N = 15 patients)
cards.people: 15 mechanically ventilated, sedated patients in a general ICU at a university hospital in southern Sweden; 40 in-pair assessments with the Swedish RASS, translated with back-translation, critical review and pilot testing.
cards.result: The Swedish version was judged satisfactory and applicable in the ICU, and inter-rater reliability was weighted kappa 0.86 (linear weighting). The authors concluded the Swedish RASS can be useful for sedation assessment of mechanically ventilated patients in Swedish general ICUs.
cards.watchOut: Small at patient level — N = 15 patients, 40 paired assessments — so this card shows reliability survives translation in one small sample; it does not re-establish the derivation or validation figures, and its kappa is never pooled with theirs.
cards.source: Almgren et al. The Richmond Agitation-Sedation Scale: translation and reliability testing in a Swedish intensive care unit. Acta anaesthesiologica Scandinavica. 2010. PMID: 20002362. cards.headline: Synthesis: across three reports from three centres, RASS inter-rater reliability was r = 0.956 / kappa 0.73 at derivation (originators' report, Richmond), weighted kappa 0.91 in the independent Vanderbilt validation — superior to the Glasgow Coma Scale (0.64) and level with Ramsay (0.94) — and weighted kappa 0.86 for the Swedish translation in 15 patients
cards.summary: Synthesis: across three reports from three centres, RASS inter-rater reliability was r = 0.956 / kappa 0.73 at derivation (originators' report, Richmond), weighted kappa 0.91 in the independent Vanderbilt validation — superior to the Glasgow Coma Scale (0.64) and level with Ramsay (0.94) — and weighted kappa 0.86 for the Swedish translation in 15 patients
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf: derivation (192 + 101 encounters, Richmond), independent validation (38 patients for reliability; 275 ventilated patients for validity, Vanderbilt) and Swedish translation (15 patients, 40 paired assessments) — three centres, figures kept separate and never merged into one reliability number.
cards.result: Reliability and validity of the score itself are consistently high; the evidence says nothing about whether RASS-guided sedation management improves patient outcomes, which is a different, uncarded question.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards for each report's limits; this synthesis adds no new data.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Capillary refill time in adults: pooled prognostic accuracy is poor (AUC 0.66, sensitivity 54%), unaided visual assessment shows no agreement with image-derived CRT (κ = 0.00), and quantitative CRT crosses the 3-s threshold in both directions during one inflammatory episode
shelves.question: At the bedside, what is capillary refill time (CRT) worth as a perfusion measure in adults — how well does a prolonged CRT predict death or adverse events in acute circulatory failure (and how does it compare with lactate), how much of its unreliability is removed by a standardised timed technique, and what does a controlled human endotoxemia study show about the behaviour of quantitative CRT and its 3-second threshold during acute inflammation?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Adult · Prognosis · Hemodynamics · Shock · Odds Ratio
shelves.balance: MEASUREMENT / PROGNOSTIC PERFORMANCE — poor pooled accuracy is the headline, not a caveat. One synthesis is carded beside three primary reports, labelled as such: across 23 studies and 60,656 patients, prolonged CRT predicted death in acute circulatory failure with pooled AUC 0.66, sensitivity 54% and specificity 72% (pooled AUC 0.69 across all at-risk / confirmed-failure analyses), not significantly different from lactate, with accuracy greater when CRT measurement was high-quality. A single-centre septic-shock cohort found much higher AUCs (0.84 index finger, 0.90 knee at 6 hours) — never printed without the pooled figure beside them. Technique moves the value materially: unaided visual CRT showed no agreement with image-derived CRT (κ = 0.00), while a chronograph-standardised method correlated strongly (r = 0.64). And in a controlled human endotoxemia study, quantitative CRT crossed the 3-second threshold in both directions within one inflammatory episode. No card implies CRT-targeted resuscitation improves outcomes — the ANDROMEDA-SHOCK programme asks that different question and is deliberately not carded here.

cards.headline: Synthesis carded beside primaries, labelled (Jacquet-Lagrèze 2023 — systematic review and meta-analysis, 23 studies, 60,656 patients): for death in acute circulatory failure, pooled AUC 0.66 (95% CI 0.59 to 0.76), sensitivity 54%, specificity 72% and diagnostic odds ratio 3.4 (95% CI 1.4 to 8.3); pooled AUC 0.69 across all at-risk / confirmed-failure analyses; prognostic value not significantly different from lactate
cards.summary: Synthesis carded beside primaries, labelled (Jacquet-Lagrèze 2023 — systematic review and meta-analysis, 23 studies, 60,656 patients): for death in acute circulatory failure, pooled AUC 0.66 (95% CI 0.59 to 0.76), sensitivity 54%, specificity 72% and diagnostic odds ratio 3.4 (95% CI 1.4 to 8.3); pooled AUC 0.69 across all at-risk / confirmed-failure analyses; prognostic value not significantly different from lactate
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of CRT prognostic value in adults (labelled synthesis, carded beside primary reports)
cards.people: Adults at risk of or with confirmed acute circulatory failure in 23 studies totalling 60,656 patients (13 studies in the primary analysis of death in acute circulatory failure), drawn from MEDLINE, EMBASE and Google Scholar.
cards.result: Primary analysis: pooled AUC 0.66 (95% CI 0.59 to 0.76), pooled sensitivity 54% (95% CI 43 to 64), pooled specificity 72% (95% CI 55 to 84) and pooled diagnostic odds ratio 3.4 (95% CI 1.4 to 8.3) — a relative odds measure, labelled as such. Secondary analysis across all 23 studies: pooled AUC 0.69 (95% CI 0.65 to 0.74). CRT's prognostic value compared with lactate was not significantly different, and high-quality CRT measurement was associated with greater accuracy. The authors concluded CRT poorly predicted death and adverse events.
cards.watchOut: This is the shelf's one synthesis, not a fourth primary cohort — it is labelled as such and its pooled figures govern the balance. A sensitivity of 54% means a normal CRT misses nearly half of deaths; the single-centre AUCs on the next card may not be read without this pooled figure beside them.
cards.source: Jacquet-Lagrèze et al. Prognostic value of capillary refill time in adult patients: a systematic review with meta-analysis. Critical care (London, England). 2023. PMID: 38042855. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: Humans · Adult · Prognosis · Hemodynamics · Shock · Odds Ratio

cards.headline: Septic-shock cohort (Ait-Oufella 2014, N = 59 after initial resuscitation): 6-hour CRT predicted 14-day mortality with AUC 84% (index finger) and 90% (knee); index threshold 2.4 s gave sensitivity 82% and specificity 73%, knee threshold 4.9 s sensitivity 82% and specificity 84%; inter-rater concordance 80% (index) and 95% (knee)
cards.summary: Septic-shock cohort (Ait-Oufella 2014, N = 59 after initial resuscitation): 6-hour CRT predicted 14-day mortality with AUC 84% (index finger) and 90% (knee); index threshold 2.4 s gave sensitivity 82% and specificity 73%, knee threshold 4.9 s sensitivity 82% and specificity 84%; inter-rater concordance 80% (index) and 95% (knee)
cards.type: Prospective observational cohort in septic shock (single centre, N = 59)
cards.people: 59 consecutive patients with septic shock in a tertiary teaching hospital, assessed after initial resuscitation at 6 hours (H6); median SOFA 10, SAPS II 61, and 14-day mortality 36%. CRT was measured on the index fingertip and the knee.
cards.result: CRT was higher in non-survivors than survivors at both sites (index 5.6 ± 3.5 vs 2.3 ± 1.8 s; knee 7.6 ± 4.6 vs 2.9 ± 1.7 s; P<0.0001 for both). AUC for 14-day mortality was 84% (index) and 90% (knee); an index threshold of 2.4 s gave sensitivity 82% (95% CI 60 to 95) and specificity 73% (95% CI 56 to 86), and a knee threshold of 4.9 s gave sensitivity 82% and specificity 84% (95% CI 68 to 94). CRT related to arterial lactate and SOFA score, and CRT changes during resuscitation were associated with prognosis.
cards.watchOut: Single-centre, N = 59, one time point (6 hours after resuscitation) and two measurement sites with different thresholds (2.4 s index, 4.9 s knee) — its AUCs of 0.84–0.90 sit far above the pooled 0.66 and are printed only beside it. Site and timing are part of the measurement, not details.
cards.source: Ait-Oufella et al. Capillary refill time exploration during septic shock. Intensive care medicine. 2014. PMID: 24811942. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Standardisation study (Shinozaki 2021, 30 ED patients): unaided visual CRT showed NO agreement with image-derived CRT (κ = 0.00), while a chronograph-standardised visual method correlated strongly with it (r = 0.64, P<0.01), and reliability rose with clinician experience
cards.summary: Standardisation study (Shinozaki 2021, 30 ED patients): unaided visual CRT showed NO agreement with image-derived CRT (κ = 0.00), while a chronograph-standardised visual method correlated strongly with it (r = 0.64, P<0.01), and reliability rose with clinician experience
cards.type: Cross-sectional standardisation / reliability study in emergency-department patients (N = 30)
cards.people: 30 patients in an emergency department, assessed by health care providers using unaided visual CRT (method 1), a chronograph-standardised visual CRT by an ED attending (method 2), image-software CRT from video as the criterion standard (method 3), and video-review visual CRT by 9 providers (method 4).
cards.result: Standardised visual CRT identified 10 abnormal patients (CRT >2 s) where unaided CRT identified 2. There was no correlation (κ = 0.00) between unaided CRT and image CRT, while standardised visual CRT correlated strongly with image CRT (r = 0.64, P<0.01). Intra-observer reliability and correlation with image CRT were higher for more experienced clinicians reviewing video CRT. The authors concluded a standardised method such as a chronograph, and/or clinical experience, may improve the reliability of visually assessed CRT.
cards.watchOut: κ = 0.00 for the unaided bedside method is the shelf's reliability floor: any CRT figure from an unstandardised visual assessment — including those pooled in the synthesis — carries this caveat. Small study (30 patients); it measures agreement between methods, not prognosis.
cards.source: Shinozaki et al. The standardized method and clinical experience may improve the reliability of visually assessed capillary refill time. The American journal of emergency medicine. 2021. PMID: 32507474. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Human endotoxemia study (Gustavsson 2026, 25 healthy volunteers, double-blind randomised crossover, E. coli lipopolysaccharide 0.8 ng/kg vs saline): quantitative finger CRT was biphasic — prolonging to 8.31 s at 1.5 h (14 of 25 hitting the 10-s ceiling) then shortening to 1.27 s at 5 h despite persisting inflammation — crossing the 3-s threshold in both directions within one episode; skin temperature was the strongest covariate
cards.summary: Human endotoxemia study (Gustavsson 2026, 25 healthy volunteers, double-blind randomised crossover, E. coli lipopolysaccharide 0.8 ng/kg vs saline): quantitative finger CRT was biphasic — prolonging to 8.31 s at 1.5 h (14 of 25 hitting the 10-s ceiling) then shortening to 1.27 s at 5 h despite persisting inflammation — crossing the 3-s threshold in both directions within one episode; skin temperature was the strongest covariate
cards.type: Double-blind randomised crossover human endotoxemia challenge study (healthy volunteers, N = 25) — physiological-limits evidence
cards.people: 25 healthy volunteers in a double-blind randomised crossover study receiving an intravenous bolus of Escherichia coli lipopolysaccharide (0.8 ng/kg) or saline placebo, with finger quantitative CRT measured by polarised reflectance imaging at baseline and 1.5, 3.5 and 5 hours. Registry ID: NCT06618716.
cards.result: From a baseline near 3.5 s, quantitative CRT prolonged to 8.31 s at 1.5 h (14 of 25 reaching the 10-s ceiling) then shortened to 1.27 s at 5 h during persisting systemic inflammation; estimated marginal contrasts against placebo were +4.13 s and −3.10 s at those time points (both P<0.0001). Each standard-deviation increase in skin temperature was associated with a 1.62 s decrease in CRT, and between-subject differences explained only a minority of total variance (intraclass correlation 0.30). The authors concluded a single value against a fixed threshold is unreliable, whereas change over time within a participant is informative, and that findings in healthy participants are not directly generalisable to septic shock.
cards.watchOut: A healthy-volunteer challenge model (N = 25), carded as physiological-limits evidence and never pooled with patient cohorts. It tests what a fixed 3-second threshold can mean during inflammation — it does not test CRT's prognostic use in patients, and its authors say so.

cards.headline: Synthesis: pooled prognostic accuracy of CRT is poor (AUC 0.66 for death in acute circulatory failure, sensitivity 54%, in one labelled synthesis of 23 studies / 60,656 patients), the best single-centre figures (AUC 0.84–0.90) come from 59 resuscitated septic-shock patients at one time point and two body sites, unaided visual assessment agrees not at all with image-derived CRT (κ = 0.00) while standardisation restores correlation (r = 0.64), and quantitative CRT crosses the 3-s threshold in both directions during one inflammatory episode in healthy volunteers
cards.summary: Synthesis: pooled prognostic accuracy of CRT is poor (AUC 0.66 for death in acute circulatory failure, sensitivity 54%, in one labelled synthesis of 23 studies / 60,656 patients), the best single-centre figures (AUC 0.84–0.90) come from 59 resuscitated septic-shock patients at one time point and two body sites, unaided visual assessment agrees not at all with image-derived CRT (κ = 0.00) while standardisation restores correlation (r = 0.64), and quantitative CRT crosses the 3-s threshold in both directions during one inflammatory episode in healthy volunteers
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf: one labelled synthesis (23 studies, 60,656 patients), one septic-shock cohort (N = 59), one ED standardisation study (N = 30 patients) and one healthy-volunteer endotoxemia study (N = 25) — syntheses, patient cohorts and the challenge model kept in their own lanes and never pooled together.
cards.result: CRT's worth at the bedside is technique-, site-, temperature- and time-dependent, and weak as a stand-alone prognostic test on the pooled evidence. No card on this shelf addresses CRT-targeted resuscitation; that intervention question (the ANDROMEDA-SHOCK programme) is deliberately not carded here.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards for each report's limits; this synthesis adds no new data.

shelves.title: Cadazolid for C. difficile infection: non-inferiority to vancomycin met in one identical phase 3 twin and missed in the other — development stopped
shelves.question: In adults with C. difficile infection, does oral cadazolid 250 mg twice daily versus oral vancomycin 125 mg four times daily for 10 days achieve clinical cure, and is it non-inferior within a −10% margin? (GAP-T: one programme — 2 publications covering 3 trials, labelled on the face; phase 3 twins split on non-inferiority.)

shelves.balance: GAP-T — one programme, labelled: this shelf rests on one programme's reports — 2 publications covering 3 trials (the phase 2 dose-ranging trial, and IMPACT 1 and IMPACT 2 reported together in one phase 3 publication, which is never counted as two publications) — and the face states the count in exactly those terms. The split verdict is the answer: two identical phase 3 twins disagreed on the programme's own primary question (non-inferiority met in IMPACT 1, missed in IMPACT 2), and the publication itself concludes further commercial development is unlikely — a discontinued antibiotic whose phase 2 recurrence signal never became a phase 3 endpoint win, not an available alternative. Design flags: the comparator is vancomycin 125 mg four times daily (not fidaxomicin), in the 2015–2019 CDI landscape before fidaxomicin-first and microbiome-therapy sequencing; the phase 2 recurrence contrast rests on 84 patients with 80% confidence intervals printed in that report, as reported. Product naming under the clarification exception: cadazolid is an investigational quinoxolidinone antibiotic that was never marketed — stated plainly. The surotomycin shelf (#7775) asks the same vancomycin-comparator question for a different molecule and shares no anchor; the two must not be merged into a class shelf.

cards.headline: Trial 1 of 3, in the phase 3 publication (one publication covering two trials) — IMPACT 1 (2019): modified intention-to-treat clinical cure was 84% (253/302) on cadazolid vs 85% (271/318) on vancomycin, treatment difference −1.4 (95% CI −7.2 to 4.3) — non-inferiority within the −10% margin was shown in this twin
cards.summary: Trial 1 of 3, in the phase 3 publication (one publication covering two trials) — IMPACT 1 (2019): modified intention-to-treat clinical cure was 84% (253/302) on cadazolid vs 85% (271/318) on vancomycin, treatment difference −1.4 (95% CI −7.2 to 4.3) — non-inferiority within the −10% margin was shown in this twin
cards.type: Primary report — IMPACT 1 phase 3 trial, reported with IMPACT 2 in one publication (one programme; the publication is one report covering two trials)
cards.people: Adults aged ≥18 years with mild-to-moderate or severe C. difficile infection in IMPACT 1 (run across 12 countries), randomised 1:1 to oral cadazolid 250 mg twice daily or oral vancomycin 125 mg four times daily for 10 days with 30 days of follow-up; 632 participants were randomised in IMPACT 1 (306 cadazolid, 326 vancomycin) of 1,263 across both twins. Clinical cure was resolution of diarrhoea with no additional CDI treatment, assessed in modified intention-to-treat and per-protocol populations against a −10% non-inferiority margin.
cards.result: In the modified intention-to-treat population, 253 (84%) of 302 on cadazolid versus 271 (85%) of 318 on vancomycin achieved clinical cure (treatment difference −1.4 [95% CI −7.2 to 4.3]); in the per-protocol population, 247 (88%) of 282 versus 264 (92%) of 288 (difference −4.1 [−9.2 to 1.0]). Non-inferiority for clinical cure to vancomycin was shown in IMPACT 1. Safety and tolerability profiles of the two antibiotics were similar.
cards.watchOut: IMPACT 1 met non-inferiority and its identical twin did not (card 2) — neither twin may be printed without the other. The comparator is vancomycin, not fidaxomicin.

cards.headline: Trial 2 of 3, in the same phase 3 publication — IMPACT 2 (2019): modified intention-to-treat clinical cure was 81% (235/290) on cadazolid vs 86% (258/301) on vancomycin, treatment difference −4.7 (95% CI −10.7 to 1.3), crossing the −10% margin — non-inferiority was NOT shown in this twin, and the publication concludes further commercial development is unlikely
cards.summary: Trial 2 of 3, in the same phase 3 publication — IMPACT 2 (2019): modified intention-to-treat clinical cure was 81% (235/290) on cadazolid vs 86% (258/301) on vancomycin, treatment difference −4.7 (95% CI −10.7 to 1.3), crossing the −10% margin — non-inferiority was NOT shown in this twin, and the publication concludes further commercial development is unlikely
cards.type: Primary report — IMPACT 2 phase 3 trial, reported with IMPACT 1 in one publication (one programme; the publication is one report covering two trials)
cards.people: Adults aged ≥18 years with mild-to-moderate or severe C. difficile infection in IMPACT 2 (run across 15 countries), identically designed to IMPACT 1: oral cadazolid 250 mg twice daily versus oral vancomycin 125 mg four times daily for 10 days; 631 participants were randomised in IMPACT 2 (298 cadazolid, 311 vancomycin).
cards.result: In the modified intention-to-treat population, 235 (81%) of 290 on cadazolid versus 258 (86%) of 301 on vancomycin achieved clinical cure (treatment difference −4.7 [95% CI −10.7 to 1.3]); in the per-protocol population, 214 (87%) of 247 versus 237 (92%) of 259 (difference −4.9 [−10.4 to 0.6]). Non-inferiority was not shown in IMPACT 2 in either population. The authors' interpretation: cadazolid was safe and well tolerated but did not achieve its primary endpoint in one of two phase 3 trials, so further commercial development for C. difficile infection is unlikely.
cards.watchOut: The missed margin is the programme's verdict: the lower confidence bound (−10.7) crossed the −10% non-inferiority margin. This card and card 1 are two trials in one publication — never two publications.

cards.headline: Trial 3 of 3 — phase 2 dose-ranging trial (2015, N = 84 enrolled): clinical cure was 76.5% / 80.0% / 68.4% across cadazolid 250/500/1,000 mg twice daily vs 68.2% on vancomycin, with no dose-response; recurrence was lower on every cadazolid dose (18.2–25.0%) than on vancomycin (50%) in this small trial — a small-sample recurrence signal the phase 3 trials were not designed around, labelled as such
cards.summary: Trial 3 of 3 — phase 2 dose-ranging trial (2015, N = 84 enrolled): clinical cure was 76.5% / 80.0% / 68.4% across cadazolid 250/500/1,000 mg twice daily vs 68.2% on vancomycin, with no dose-response; recurrence was lower on every cadazolid dose (18.2–25.0%) than on vancomycin (50%) in this small trial — a small-sample recurrence signal the phase 3 trials were not designed around, labelled as such
cards.type: Primary report — multicentre randomised double-blind phase 2 dose-ranging trial (one programme)
cards.people: 84 adult patients with first occurrence or first recurrence of CDI randomised 1:1:1:1 to cadazolid 250, 500 or 1,000 mg twice daily (20, 22 and 20 patients) or oral vancomycin 125 mg four times daily (22 patients) for 10 days; the primary endpoint was clinical cure at test of cure (48 ± 24 hours after end of treatment) in the modified intent-to-treat population.
cards.result: Clinical cure was 76.5% (80% CI 58.4 to 89.3), 80.0% (63.9 to 91.0) and 68.4% (51.1 to 82.5) across the cadazolid doses versus 68.2% (52.3 to 81.3) on vancomycin, with no evidence of a dose-dependent response. Each cadazolid dose had a lower recurrence rate than vancomycin (18.2–25.0% versus 50%), and sustained clinical response was higher on cadazolid (46.7–60.0%) than vancomycin (33.3%). Times to diarrhoea resolution were similar, and cadazolid was well tolerated with no safety signal.
cards.watchOut: 84 patients with 80% confidence intervals, as the report prints them: the recurrence contrast (down to 18.2% vs 50%) is a small-sample signal that the phase 3 programme — designed around cure non-inferiority — never converted into an endpoint win.

(GAP-T: one programme — 3 randomised reports, labelled on the face; the phase 2 abstract does not document N, labelled 'N not documented'.)

shelves.balance: GAP-T — one programme, labelled: this shelf rests on one programme's reports — 3 randomised reports covering 3 trials (phase 2 plus two phase 3 trials) — and the face states the count in exactly those terms. The arc is the answer: a phase 2 recurrence advantage (17.2% vs 35.6%) shrank to nothing in phase 3 — the first phase 3 trial failed even non-inferiority on cure, and the second met non-inferiority while missing superiority on every sustained-response endpoint; the programme was discontinued. The phase 2 recurrence p-value must never be printed without the two phase 3 verdicts beside it. Count flag (binding): the phase 2 report's fetched abstract does not state its total randomised N — the face prints 'N not documented' for that report rather than importing a number from outside the fetched abstract. The 26-patient enteric-microbiome substudy of the phase 2 trial is a cross-point only, never a fourth report; it records in its own conclusions that surotomycin is no longer in development due to failed phase 3 efficacy results. Era flag: programme 2015–2019, vancomycin-comparator CDI landscape before fidaxomicin-first and microbiome-therapy sequencing. Product naming under the clarification exception: surotomycin (development codes CB-183,315 / MK-4261, as the substudy publication gives them) is an investigational cyclic lipopeptide that was never marketed — stated plainly. Cadazolid (#7774) shares the comparator and era but is a different molecule with a different phase 3 verdict; the two are never merged into a class shelf.

cards.summary: Report 1 of 3 — phase 2 trial (2016; total randomised N not documented in the fetched abstract — labelled 'N not documented' for this report): clinical cure was 92.4% on surotomycin 125 mg twice daily, 86.6% on surotomycin 250 mg twice daily and 89.4% on vancomycin; recurrence was 27.9% / 17.2% / 35.6%, the 250 mg vs vancomycin contrast significant (p = 0.035); sustained clinical response was 66.7% / 70.1% / 56.1%
cards.type: Primary report — phase 2 randomised double-blind non-inferiority trial (one programme; N not documented in its abstract)
cards.people: Patients with CDI in a phase 2 randomised controlled double-blind non-inferiority multicentre trial, receiving surotomycin 125 mg twice daily, surotomycin 250 mg twice daily or vancomycin 125 mg four times daily for 10 days; the primary efficacy outcome was clinical response at end of treatment. The fetched abstract does not state the total number randomised — N not documented in the abstract, per the standing labelling rule.
cards.result: Clinical cure rates were similar among treatment groups (92.4%, 86.6% and 89.4%). Recurrence was 27.9% on surotomycin 125 mg, 17.2% on surotomycin 250 mg and 35.6% on vancomycin; the lower recurrence rate with surotomycin 250 mg versus vancomycin was statistically significant (P = 0.035), and recurrence rates were similar between the two surotomycin doses (P = 0.193). Sustained clinical response at end of study was 66.7%, 70.1% and 56.1% respectively. Adverse-event incidence was similar among arms.
cards.watchOut: 'N not documented' applies to this report exactly as printed: no total N is imported from outside the fetched abstract. Its recurrence p-value (0.035) must never be printed without the two phase 3 verdicts beside it (cards 2 and 3).
