cards.headline: Report 2 of 3 — first phase 3 trial (2017, N = 570 randomised): clinical cure at end of treatment was 79.0% on surotomycin vs 83.6% on vancomycin (difference −4.6% [95% CI −11.0 to 1.9]) and sustained response was 60.6% vs 61.4% — the trial did not meet non-inferiority or superiority criteria on the primary or key secondary endpoints
cards.summary: Report 2 of 3 — first phase 3 trial (2017, N = 570 randomised): clinical cure at end of treatment was 79.0% on surotomycin vs 83.6% on vancomycin (difference −4.6% [95% CI −11.0 to 1.9]) and sustained response was 60.6% vs 61.4% — the trial did not meet non-inferiority or superiority criteria on the primary or key secondary endpoints
cards.type: Primary report — first phase 3 randomised double-blind active-controlled trial (one programme)
cards.people: 570 subjects with CDI confirmed by a positive toxin result, randomised to surotomycin 250 mg twice daily (290) or vancomycin 125 mg four times daily (280) orally for 10 days, in a randomised double-blind active-controlled multicentre international trial; primary endpoints were clinical response at end of treatment and safety, with sustained clinical response through a 30- to 40-day follow-up a key secondary endpoint, in the microbiological modified intention-to-treat population.
cards.result: Clinical cure at end of treatment was 79.0% versus 83.6% (difference −4.6%; 95% CI −11.0 to 1.9); clinical response over time did not differ (stratified log-rank P = .832); sustained clinical response at end of trial (day 40–50) was 60.6% versus 61.4% (difference −0.8%; 95% CI −8.8 to 7.1). The trial did not meet noninferiority or superiority criteria versus vancomycin for the primary or key secondary endpoints. Both treatments were generally well tolerated.
cards.watchOut: A failed phase 3: it missed even non-inferiority, so the phase 2 recurrence advantage did not survive contact with an adequately sized trial. This record carries no MeSH terms and no registry ID in its PubMed record, and its source line says so.

cards.result: Surotomycin clinical response at end of treatment was non-inferior to vancomycin (83.4% versus 82.1%; difference 1.4%, 95% CI −4.9 to 7.6). Both treatments were generally well tolerated.
cards.watchOut: Non-inferiority on cure with no superiority on any sustained-response endpoint is the programme's best phase 3 result — it does not revive the phase 2 recurrence claim, and the programme was discontinued.

shelves.title: Sedation-Agitation Scale (SAS) reliability and validity in critically ill adults: weighted kappa 0.92 at validation, 0.85–0.87 in inexperienced nurses' hands, psychometric score 19/20 — agitation limb under-validated
shelves.question: In critically ill adults, how reliable and valid is the Sedation-Agitation Scale (SAS / Riker scale — seven levels from 1, unarousable, through 4, calm and cooperative, to 7, dangerous agitation) as the bedside measure of sedation and agitation — what inter-rater reliability did its prospective validation show against the Ramsay and Harris scales, how reliably do ICU nurses with no prior experience of the scale score it against investigators, and where does the scale rank in the systematic psychometric analysis of eleven subjective sedation scales?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Female · Humans · Hypnotics and Sedatives/administration & dosage · Intensive Care Units · Intubation · Male · Middle Aged · Nursing Assessment/methods · Observer Variation · Prospective Studies · Psychometrics/methods · Psychomotor Agitation/diagnosis · Reproducibility of Results · Hypnotics and Sedatives/pharmacology · Nursing Care · Pain Measurement · Psychometrics · Psychomotor Agitation/classification/diagnosis · Procedural Sedation/nursing · Critical Illness/nursing · Deep Sedation/nursing · Hypnotics and Sedatives/therapeutic use · Nursing Assessment/methods/standards
shelves.balance: A measurement shelf, not a sedation-strategy shelf: no card implies SAS-guided sedation improves outcomes. The Sedation-Agitation Scale (SAS / Riker scale — 1 unarousable, 4 calm and cooperative, 7 dangerous agitation) was prospectively validated by its originators (programme-labelled) in 45 ICU patients examined 69 times: inter-rater weighted kappa 0.92, correlations with the Ramsay (r² = 0.83) and Harris (r² = 0.86) scales, and three agitation categories where Ramsay used one. ICU nurses with no prior experience of the scale scored it against investigators at weighted kappa 0.85–0.87 (investigators 0.93 between themselves) in 60 medical-cardiac ICU patients, and SAS tracked the sedation visual-analogue scale (ρ = −0.77) — but agitation validity could not be determined in that study because few agitated patients were observed, and that under-validation prints on the face. The 2013 SCCM-guideline psychometric analysis of 11 subjective sedation scales scored SAS 19/20 ('very good'), second only to RASS (19.5), with Ramsay moderate at 13.2. All validity evidence here is construct validity against other subjective scales, not against a physiological standard.

cards.headline: SAS prospective validation (Riker 1999, Critical Care Medicine — 45 ICU patients examined 69 times by trained evaluator pairs in a 34-bed multidisciplinary ICU; programme-labelled: the scale originator's own report): inter-rater weighted kappa for SAS was 0.92, SAS correlated strongly with the Ramsay (r² = 0.83) and Harris (r² = 0.86) scales, and SAS stratified agitation into three categories where Ramsay used one
cards.summary: SAS prospective validation (Riker 1999, Critical Care Medicine — 45 ICU patients examined 69 times by trained evaluator pairs in a 34-bed multidisciplinary ICU; programme-labelled: the scale originator's own report): inter-rater weighted kappa for SAS was 0.92, SAS correlated strongly with the Ramsay (r² = 0.83) and Harris (r² = 0.86) scales, and SAS stratified agitation into three categories where Ramsay used one
cards.type: Prospective validation study — originator's own report (programme-labelled)
cards.people: 45 adult ICU patients (surgical and medical; mean age 63.2 years, 36% female, 71% intubated) examined a total of 69 times simultaneously and independently by pairs of trained evaluators using the revised Sedation-Agitation Scale (SAS, 1 unarousable to 7 dangerous agitation), the Ramsay scale and the Harris scale. By SAS, 45% were anxious or agitated (SAS 5–7), 26% calm (SAS 4) and 29% sedated (SAS 1–3). Originator's own report — programme-labelled.
cards.result: Inter-rater correlation was high for SAS (r² = 0.83, P < 0.001) and the weighted kappa for inter-rater agreement was 0.92 (P < 0.001). SAS was highly correlated with the Ramsay (r² = 0.83, P < 0.001) and Harris (r² = 0.86, P < 0.001) scales. Of 41 assessments scored Ramsay 1, 49% scored SAS 6, 41% SAS 5, 5% SAS 4 and 2% each SAS 3 or 7 — SAS provides additional information by stratifying agitation into three categories (compared with one for Ramsay) without sacrificing validity or reliability, as published.
cards.watchOut: Programme-labelled: the scale originator's own validation, in 45 patients (69 paired examinations). The Ramsay/Harris correlations are construct-validity evidence against other subjective scales, not against a physiological standard, and print as such.
cards.source: Riker RR et al. Prospective evaluation of the Sedation-Agitation Scale for adult critically ill patients. Critical care medicine. 1999. PMID: 10446827. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: SAS nurse psychometric evaluation (Brandl 2001, Pharmacotherapy — 60 medical-cardiac ICU patients rated simultaneously by staff nurses and two investigators): inter-rater weighted kappa was 0.93 between investigators and 0.85–0.87 between investigators and nurses with NO prior experience of the scale; SAS correlated with the nurse-specialist sedation visual-analogue scale (Spearman ρ = −0.77), but validity for agitation could NOT be determined because few agitated patients were observed
cards.summary: SAS nurse psychometric evaluation (Brandl 2001, Pharmacotherapy — 60 medical-cardiac ICU patients rated simultaneously by staff nurses and two investigators): inter-rater weighted kappa was 0.93 between investigators and 0.85–0.87 between investigators and nurses with NO prior experience of the scale; SAS correlated with the nurse-specialist sedation visual-analogue scale (Spearman ρ = −0.77), but validity for agitation could NOT be determined because few agitated patients were observed
cards.type: Psychometric evaluation by inexperienced nurse raters
cards.people: 60 adult medical-cardiac ICU patients observed simultaneously but independently by ICU staff nurses with no experience in the scale's use and by two trained investigators, with an experienced clinical nurse specialist's visual-analogue scales for sedation (VAS-S) and agitation (VAS-A) as the comparison.
cards.result: SAS correlated well with VAS-S (Spearman ρ = −0.77, P < 0.001). Neither SAS nor VAS-A correlated for agitation (Spearman ρ = 0.05, P > 0.5), but there were few observations of agitated patients. SAS inter-rater agreement was excellent between the two trained investigators (weighted kappa 0.93, P < 0.001) and between investigators and staff nurses (weighted kappa 0.85 and 0.87, P < 0.001 for both). The authors conclude SAS is reliable when administered by staff nurses with no experience of it; due to the paucity of agitated-patient observations, its validity for assessing agitation could not be determined.
cards.watchOut: The agitation limb is under-validated here, exactly as in the derivation report's framing: reliability is established, agitation validity is not — few agitated patients were observed, and no card may present the kappa values as agitation-validity evidence.
cards.source: Brandl KM et al. Confirming the reliability of the sedation-agitation scale administered by ICU nurses without experience in its use. Pharmacotherapy. 2001. PMID: 11310516. cards.headline: Systematic psychometric analysis (Robinson 2013, Critical Care Medicine — 36 articles covering 11 subjective sedation scales, scored 0–20 for the 2013 SCCM guidelines): only two scales reached 'very good' published psychometric properties — RASS (19.5) and SAS (19) — with the Ramsay scale moderate at 13.2
cards.summary: Systematic psychometric analysis (Robinson 2013, Critical Care Medicine — 36 articles covering 11 subjective sedation scales, scored 0–20 for the 2013 SCCM guidelines): only two scales reached 'very good' published psychometric properties — RASS (19.5) and SAS (19) — with the Ramsay scale moderate at 13.2
cards.type: Systematic psychometric analysis of 11 subjective sedation scales (synthesis; its primary-article set overlaps the primary reports' literature)
cards.people: Subjective sedation scales developed for critically ill adults, identified from the 19,000+ citations screened for the 2013 Society of Critical Care Medicine pain/agitation/delirium guidelines and scored by two independent reviewers on a standardised 0–20 psychometric scoring system; 36 articles encompassing 11 scales.
cards.result: Two scales demonstrated scores indicating 'very good' published psychometric properties: the Richmond Agitation-Sedation Scale (19.5) and the Sedation-Agitation Scale (19). 'Moderate' scores included the Vancouver Interaction and Calmness Scale (14.3), Adaptation to the Intensive Care Environment (13.7), the Ramsay Sedation Scale (13.2), the Minnesota Sedation Assessment Tool (13) and the Nursing Instrument for the Communication of Sedation (12.8); the lowest were the Observer's Assessment of Alertness/Sedation Scale (3.7) and the New Sheffield Sedation Scale (8.5). The authors conclude RASS and SAS are the most valid and reliable subjective sedation scales for critically ill adults on the current literature.
cards.watchOut: A psychometric-properties score (0–20) ranks published scale development/validation quality — it is not a patient-outcome comparison, and this shelf makes no claim that SAS-guided sedation improves outcomes. Cross-point: RASS is a different, later instrument with its own built shelf (S21-4-01 territory); the two rows share this synthesis's comparison, stated here.
cards.source: Robinson BR et al. Psychometric analysis of subjective sedation scales in critically ill adults. Critical care medicine. 2013. PMID: 23989092. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: SAS inter-rater reliability is established in both primary reports (weighted kappa 0.92 in the originators' validation, N = 45 patients / 69 examinations; 0.85–0.87 for nurses with no prior experience of the scale, N = 60), its construct validity rests on correlations with other subjective scales (Ramsay r² = 0.83, Harris r² = 0.86, sedation VAS ρ = −0.77), and the guideline psychometric analysis ranks it second of 11 scales (19/20, behind RASS 19.5) — while its agitation limb remains under-validated, because few agitated patients were observed in the nurse study

shelves.title: Modified Early Warning Score (MEWS) prognostic accuracy: derivation odds ratios at ≥5, AUC 0.83 in a Chinese ED (cut-off 3.5), AUROC 0.76 vs NEWS 0.805 in a Zambian surgical cohort — cut-offs not portable
shelves.question: In acutely admitted hospital patients, how well does the Modified Early Warning Score (MEWS — systolic blood pressure, heart rate, respiratory rate, temperature and AVPU consciousness, each scored 0–3) identify patients who will die or need higher-level care — what odds of death and intensive-care admission did its derivation cohort show at a score of 5 or more, what discrimination and cut-off did a prospective Chinese emergency-department validation find, and how did MEWS compare with NEWS for 30-day mortality in a Zambian surgical cohort?

shelves.balance: A prognostic-accuracy shelf, not an intervention shelf: no card implies MEWS-triggered escalation pathways improve outcomes. The Modified Early Warning Score (systolic blood pressure, heart rate, respiratory rate, temperature and AVPU consciousness, each scored 0–3) was derived by its own development group (programme-labelled) in 709 medical emergency admissions: a score of 5 or more carried odds ratios (relative measures, unadjusted, from a single 2000 admissions unit) of 5.4 for death (95% CI 2.8–10.7), 10.9 for ICU admission (2.2–55.6) and 3.3 for HDU admission (1.2–9.2). A prospective Chinese emergency-department validation (383 patients, triage categories 1–3) found AUC 0.83 (0.786–0.881) for in-hospital mortality at a locally derived cut-off of 3.5 (sensitivity 87%, specificity 66%) — a different cut-off from derivation, printed with its cohort: cut-offs are not portable. In a Zambian surgical cohort (254 patients), MEWS AUROC for 30-day mortality was 0.76 (0.63–0.88) against NEWS 0.805 (0.688–0.92) in the same patients — a single small cohort whose difference is not a settled hierarchy. MEWS remains in use in many low-resource settings, which the Zambian cohort documents.

cards.headline: MEWS derivation/validation (Subbe 2001, QJM — prospective cohort of 709 medical emergency admissions to a district general hospital admissions unit; programme-labelled: the score's own development group): a MEWS of 5 or more was associated with increased risk of death (odds ratio 5.4, 95% CI 2.8 to 10.7), ICU admission (odds ratio 10.9, 2.2 to 55.6) and HDU admission (odds ratio 3.3, 1.2 to 9.2) — all labelled as odds ratios, as published
cards.summary: MEWS derivation/validation (Subbe 2001, QJM — prospective cohort of 709 medical emergency admissions to a district general hospital admissions unit; programme-labelled: the score's own development group): a MEWS of 5 or more was associated with increased risk of death (odds ratio 5.4, 95% CI 2.8 to 10.7), ICU admission (odds ratio 10.9, 2.2 to 55.6) and HDU admission (odds ratio 3.3, 1.2 to 9.2) — all labelled as odds ratios, as published
cards.type: Derivation/validation prospective cohort — development group's own report (programme-labelled)
cards.people: 709 medical emergency admissions to the 56-bed acute Medical Admissions Unit of a UK District General Hospital during March 2000, scored prospectively with the Modified Early Warning Score (systolic blood pressure, heart rate, respiratory rate, temperature and AVPU consciousness, each 0–3), with death, ICU/HDU admission, cardiac arrest, survival and discharge at 60 days as outcomes. The score's own development group — programme-labelled.
cards.result: Scores of 5 or more were associated with increased risk of death (OR 5.4, 95% CI 2.8–10.7), ICU admission (OR 10.9, 95% CI 2.2–55.6) and HDU admission (OR 3.3, 95% CI 1.2–9.2) — odds ratios (relative measures), printed labelled as such. The authors conclude MEWS can be applied easily in a district general hospital medical admissions unit and identifies patients at risk of deterioration who require increased levels of care.
cards.watchOut: Programme-labelled derivation from a single March-2000 admissions unit: the odds ratios are unadjusted associations with wide intervals (the ICU interval spans 2.2–55.6) and print with them. The ≥5 threshold is this cohort's, not a portable constant — the Chinese validation below derived 3.5.

cards.headline: MEWS prospective Chinese ED validation (Xie 2018, BMJ Open — 383 emergency-department patients triaged categories 1–3 in South China): AUC for in-hospital mortality was 0.83 (95% CI 0.786 to 0.881); at the locally derived cut-off of 3.5, sensitivity was 87% and specificity 66% (negative predictive value 97%, positive predictive value 28%)
cards.summary: MEWS prospective Chinese ED validation (Xie 2018, BMJ Open — 383 emergency-department patients triaged categories 1–3 in South China): AUC for in-hospital mortality was 0.83 (95% CI 0.786 to 0.881); at the locally derived cut-off of 3.5, sensitivity was 87% and specificity 66% (negative predictive value 97%, positive predictive value 28%)
cards.people: 383 patients aged 18 or older presenting to a tertiary-hospital emergency department in South China (17 May to 27 September 2017), triaged categories 1–3; in-hospital mortality was 13.6% (52/383) and ICU transfer 21.7% (83/383).
cards.result: The area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of MEWS for in-hospital mortality prediction was 0.83 (95% CI 0.786 to 0.881). At the cut-off point of 3.5, 158 patients had MEWS >3.5, with sensitivity 87%, specificity 66%, accuracy 69%, positive predictive value 28% and negative predictive value 97%. The authors note the cut-off defined in this study differed from that in many other studies — cut-offs are not portable, and print with their cohorts.
cards.watchOut: Single-centre, single-season cohort; the 3.5 cut-off is locally derived and its positive predictive value at this mortality prevalence was only 28% — most patients above the cut-off did not die in hospital.
cards.source: Xie X et al. Prognostic value of Modified Early Warning Score generated in a Chinese emergency department: a prospective cohort study. BMJ open. 2018. PMID: 30552276. prospective single-centre validation cohort 383 patients aged 18 or older presenting to a tertiary-hospital emergency department in south china (17 may to 27 september 2017), triaged categories 1–3; in-hospital mortality was 13.6% (52/383) and icu transfer 21.7% (83/383). the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of mews for in-hospital mortality prediction was 0.83 (95% ci 0.786 to 0.881). at the cut-off point of 3.5, 158 patients had mews >3.5, with sensitivity 87%, specificity 66%, accuracy 69%, positive predictive value 28% and negative predictive value 97%. the authors note the cut-off defined in this study differed from that in many other studies — cut-offs are not portable, and print with their cohorts. single-centre, single-season cohort; the 3.5 cut-off is locally derived and its positive predictive value at this mortality prevalence was only 28% — most patients above the cut-off did not die in hospital. xie x et al. prognostic value of modified early warning score generated in a chinese emergency department: a prospective cohort study. bmj open. 2018. pmid: 30552276. registry id: none in the record. mesh: adult · aged · area under curve · china · critical care · emergency service, hospital/organization & administration · female · hospital mortality · hospitalization · humans · male · middle aged · patient discharge · prognosis · prospective studies · sensitivity and specificity · triage/methods

cards.headline: MEWS vs NEWS in a Zambian surgical cohort (Foy 2020, Canadian Journal of Anesthesia — prospective cohort of 254 adult surgical patients, excluding obstetrics, at a Zambian tertiary centre): all four scores tested predicted 30-day mortality — MEWS AUROC 0.76 (95% CI 0.63 to 0.88) against NEWS at 0.805 (0.688 to 0.92) in the same patients
cards.summary: MEWS vs NEWS in a Zambian surgical cohort (Foy 2020, Canadian Journal of Anesthesia — prospective cohort of 254 adult surgical patients, excluding obstetrics, at a Zambian tertiary centre): all four scores tested predicted 30-day mortality — MEWS AUROC 0.76 (95% CI 0.63 to 0.88) against NEWS at 0.805 (0.688 to 0.92) in the same patients
cards.people: 254 adult surgical patients (excluding obstetrics) admitted for more than 24 hours at University Teaching Hospital, Lusaka, Zambia (March to July 2017), with physiology collected on days 1–3 of admission; 18 patients (7.5% of those with outcome data, as published) died at 30 days. Four scores were compared head-to-head in the same patients.
cards.result: All four early warning scores predicted 30-day mortality: MEWS (AUROC 0.76, 95% CI 0.63 to 0.88, P < 0.001), NEWS (AUROC 0.805, 95% CI 0.688 to 0.92, P < 0.001), mHOTEL (0.759, 0.63 to 0.89) and TOTAL (0.782, 0.66 to 0.90). The authors conclude the four systems were validated in a Zambian surgical population and that further work is required to assess whether implementing them improves outcomes.
cards.watchOut: A single 254-patient cohort with 18 deaths: the MEWS-vs-NEWS difference (0.76 vs 0.805, intervals widely overlapping) is not a settled hierarchy, and prints as such. Cross-point: NEWS/NEWS2 discrimination has its own built shelf (S15-4-01 territory) — a different, later score; no anchor is shared.

cards.headline: Synthesis: MEWS identifies higher-risk acutely admitted patients in three unlike cohorts — derivation odds ratios at ≥5 (death OR 5.4, ICU OR 10.9, HDU OR 3.3, all relative odds measures with wide intervals, N = 709), AUC 0.83 for in-hospital mortality in a Chinese ED at a locally derived 3.5 cut-off (sensitivity 87%, specificity 66%, N = 383), and AUROC 0.76 for 30-day mortality in a Zambian surgical cohort, beside NEWS at 0.805 in the same patients (N = 254) — with cut-offs that do not transport between cohorts (≥5 vs 3.5)
cards.summary: Synthesis: MEWS identifies higher-risk acutely admitted patients in three unlike cohorts — derivation odds ratios at ≥5 (death OR 5.4, ICU OR 10.9, HDU OR 3.3, all relative odds measures with wide intervals, N = 709), AUC 0.83 for in-hospital mortality in a Chinese ED at a locally derived 3.5 cut-off (sensitivity 87%, specificity 66%, N = 383), and AUROC 0.76 for 30-day mortality in a Zambian surgical cohort, beside NEWS at 0.805 in the same patients (N = 254) — with cut-offs that do not transport between cohorts (≥5 vs 3.5)
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf: Subbe 2001 (derivation, programme-labelled), Xie 2018 (Chinese ED validation) and Foy 2020 (Zambian surgical comparison). Cross-points: the NEWS shelf (different, later score) and the respiratory-rate measurement shelf #7822 (the rate is a MEWS input whose measurement error propagates into the score).
cards.result: A prognostic-accuracy shelf, not an intervention shelf: no card implies MEWS-triggered escalation pathways improve outcomes — the Zambian authors themselves state that implementation benefit is untested.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards for each report's limits; this synthesis adds no new data.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.
